description: A few stunted specimens of ssp. viridifolia are very villose and therefore habitually approaching ssp. natalensis, but the roots are not swollen. Ssp. natalensis is typically recognized by the swollen roots and the extremely long villose indumentum of the crown, leaves and scapes; the scapes appear before the leaves, or the plant flowers when the leaves are immature. Ssp. natalensis is typically smaller than ssp. viridifolia and much less variable.
bibliographicCitation: Hansen, HV. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the genus Gerbera (Compositae, Mutisieae) sections Gerbera, Parva, Piloselloides (in Africa), and Lasiopus. Opera Bot. 78: 5-36. [All rights reserved]

description: O. spinosum is a much and intricately branched, somewhat viscid, aromatic shrub. As indicated by the specific name it develops spines, which are transformed sterile branchlets or peduncles, for after the falling off of the heads the peduncles are frequently modified into spines. O. spinosum varies considerably both with respect to the shape of the leaves and to that of the achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: E. ursinoides is in habit somewhat intermediate between E. pinnatipartitus and E. munitus. It has usually been confused with the latter species, from which it is readily distinguished by its much larger leaves, bigger flowerheads, and larger and more distinctly ribbed achenes. The achenes are very unlike those of E. pinnatipartitus, which have a much sculptured surface, but they are rather similar to those of E. brachypodus. Also the involucre has a certain resemblance to that of E. brachypodus, which is in other respects very different, however, e.g. in leaf-shape and peduncle-length.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from H. miconiifolium by its flowering stem only remotely bracteate above, soft, 5-nerved leaves and blunt involucral bracts, and from H. nudifolium by its soft leaves crowded at the base of the stem and more golden and brown involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: In habit it may be quite similar to the narrow-leaved forms of D. acutifolia. It differs mainly from this species by its small achenes, only c. 3 mm long, whose angles are crenatetuberculate and not swollen at the base. In contradistinction to this, the achenes of D. acutifolia are twice as long, with entire and smooth angles swollen at the base. D. dregei seems besides to be smaller, and it has even narrower leaves than D. acutifolia usually has. On one and the same specimen there are often entire, sparsely dentate as well as pinnatifid leaves. D. acutifolia, on the other hand, seems never to have any pinnatifid leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The indumentum of this taxon varies immensely from plants with a more or less equal number of spreading and glandular hairs to plants with dense spreading hairs and sparsely glandular to almost no glandular hairs. In the Northern Cape plants are found that are densely glandular and with no or only a few, short, spreading hairs. In one specimen from Namibia (E. Jensen 185, WIND) the hairs are appressed. The leaves are usually small and mostly narrowly obovate, even the longer leaves are distinctly obovate. In a few cases the leaves are narrowly elliptic, but still usually quite small. Only rarely are the leaves linear-obovate.
bibliographicCitation: Herman, PPJ. 2013. Cypsela morphology in the genus Nolletia (Asteraceae, Astereae) and a revision of the genus. Phytotaxa 122(1): 1-44. [All rights reserved]

description: Much confused with H. sessile, which is readily distinguished by its narrowly oblong leaves enveloped in thick white silky wool.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Bears a superficial resemblance to S. reptans Turcz. and it has been misidentified as that species. S. reptans has a flat rosette of glabrous, sometimes gland-dotted, leaves from which radiate leafy stolons rooting at the nodes, and peduncles and involucre with short, harsh glandular pubescence. It is a plant of the western and northern Cape.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: The specimens are in very poor condition, but seem to belong to a well marked species. The foliage is very glaucous, and the rays seem to have been dull, purple-red. Leaves 1-1 1/2 in. long, 4-5 lines wide.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1865. Compositae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 44-530. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/1/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Inflorescence in a terminal globule, floret lobes spreading, cypsela with unique horizontal ridges.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2019. Taxonomy and reclassification of South African Asteraceae genus Elytropappus (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae), the description of two new genera and two new species. Phytotaxa 403(4): 248-284. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.403.4.1] [All rights reserved]

description: A distinctive species, rarely collected.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Usually specimens from South Africa and Namibia have larger flower heads on longer peduncles (up to 2 cm) and the involucrum is often conspicuously enclosed by one or two green and densely pilose bracts, which are larger than the other outer involucral bracts. The leaves are mainly entire and lanceolate. However, the observed variation is more or less continuous and exceptions do occur. Pluchea integrifolia described as endemic to South Africa is identical with this variant of P. bojeri.
bibliographicCitation: King-Jones, S. 2001. Revision of Pluchea Cass. (Compositae, Plucheeae) in the Old World. Englera 23: 1-136. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/3776750] [All rights reserved]

description: This species is an annual and one of the less showy spring-flowering Namaqualand daisies. It has always pedunculate capitula and is thus distinguished from the related R. sessiliflora. Dwarf specimens with crowded leaves of R. pumila look similar to R. sessiliflora, but can still be recognized on the peduncles, which in R. sessiliflora only develop occasionally in luxuriant, laxly leafy and bigger specimens. Normally R. pumila also has wider, many-flowered capitula with long ray-florets, although the variation is great as stated below. Variation. Size and number of florets in the capitula are subject to considerable variation. There were formerly two species distinguished, R. pedunculata (DC.) Harv. and R. pumila (L.f.)Thunb., differing in these characters, viz. length of ray-floret lamina and number of disc-florets. However, this variation is continuous and not distinctly geographical, although the plants with smaller, few-flowered capitula are more abundant in the southern parts whereas those with larger, many-flowered capitula mainly occur in Namaqualand. Apparently the species is polymorphic, consisting of several populations of slightly different genetic constitution. I do not find this variation distinct enough to merit taxonomic recognition.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: Frequently confused with C. obscura, but differs in its stoloniferous habit, less copious pubescence and generally toothed leaf lobes. It favours damper situations than C. obscura, which often becomes a roadside weed. C. podocephala can also be confused with either species. It has the stoloniferous habit of C. pinnata, but is distinguished by its differently shaped and less deeply cut leaves and larger heads, solitary on long nude peduncles, which may be aggregated into a few-headed corymb. The larger heads, longer peduncles and stoloniferous habit serve to distinguish C. podocephala from C. obscura.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Ifloga verticillata and I.polycnemoides have been much confused; however, not only do they differ in the shape and colour of the involucral bracts and the number of female flowers in a head, but they are also allopatric: while I. verticillata has not been recorded above c. 250 m, I. polycnemoides occurs at altitudes ranging from c. 600 to 900 m.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1981. A revision of Ifloga in southern Africa, with comments on the northern hemisphere species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 82: 293-312. [All rights reserved]

description: This annual is the smallest species in the genus, in habit as well as in floral parts. R. sessiliflora and the related R. pumila are usually easily distinguished on the sessile versus pedunculate capitula, respectively. Luxuriant, laxly leafy and big specimens of R. sessiliflora can have peduncles, but the capitula are still urceolate and few-flowered, never many-flowered as in R. pumila.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: This species was previously known as Cineraria humifusa, but the Lamarck name C. angulosa predates it and should be applied, as indicated. The short eglandular trichomes (6-8 cells long) on the involucral bracts distinguish Cineraria angulosa from C. geifolia, which has much longer, spreading hairs (10-12 cells long). The hairs on the calyculus bracts and on young buds are clearly glandular, and glandular hairs are also present on the petiole and in the angles between the lobes of the leaves, also on the veins on the ventral surface of leaves of some specimens, and there are also cobwebby hairs around the young buds and in the axils of the leaves. The dried leaves have a thin, membranous or papery texture and the petioles are very slender. Cineraria angulosa is also characterised by solitary or few capitula on fairly long peduncles. The specimen [Drège 556 (G-DC) from Graaff-Reinet] seen and cited by de Candolle and Harvey is not Cineraria angulosa. It is ecalcyculate with tomentose leaves and is most likely a specimen of Bolandia pedunculosa (previously C. pedunculosa). Willdenow listed C. pumila Thunb. [Type: Thunberg 19935 (UPS-THUNB)] as a synonym for C. angulosa, but this was matched to Senecio repandus Thunb. by Harvey.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Flowering material has been collected during all months except January, March, and April, but mainly in August-October. A. arborescens is closely allied to.A. laeve, the chief differences being the almost entirely glabrous outer involucral bracts, and the shorter pappus bristles in both types of florets. The two species also are vicarious A. arborescens is not very variable.
bibliographicCitation: Lundgren, J. 1972. Revision of the genus Anaxeton Gaertn. (Compositae). Opera Bot. 31: 5-59. [All rights reserved]

description: E. bolusii is more closely related to E. pinnatipartitus, however, by leaf and fruit characters. It differs from the latter, i.a., by the less regularly pinnatisect (not pectinate) leaves and the longer peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: This widespread species in the eastern regions of southern Africa is characterised by its grey-green, semi-succulent leaves and discoid capitula with pale pink or lilac florets. Its most southerly distribution is noted to be Mkuzi in KwaZulu-Natal. Bolus 12304 was selected as the lectotype because it has the most duplicates of the three syntypes, and the BOL specimen still has capitula attached whereas the PRE one does not.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV. 2014. A synopsis of Emilia (Senecioneae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa. Phytotaxa 159(3): 195-210. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.159.3.3] [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from S. decurrens by its different involucre and more rays.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Although described in Senecio, S. transvaalensis is better placed in the tropical genus Emilia, and Mkuze is about as far south as this genus occurs in eastern Africa. Emilia is distinguished from Senecio by its shortly tailed style branches. This plant may prove to be S. lambomboensis Muschler, but there are several discrepancies with his description and the type specimen (Wilms 826, Olifantsriver, in den Lambombobergen) has not been traced.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: O. leptolobum is very closely allied to O. spinescens, and these species hardly differ from each other in anything but the shape of the leaves. The heterophylly is considerably more pronounced in O. leptolobum than in O. spinescens. In O. leptolobum the inferior leaves of the branches are usually pinnately 5-7-partite, the superior 3-5-dentate or 3-5-lobed at the point, and the uppermost sometimes entire or inconspicuously dentate at the point. The rachis and the lobes are exactly linear and semiterete. In contradistinction to this, O. spinescens has flat, or nearly flat, and as a rule broader leaves, which are only 3-dentate or 3-lobed at the point, or entire. In all its parts, leaves, achenes, etc., O. leptolobum seems to be smaller than O. spinescens. It is also more sparingly furnished with spinescent twigs than O. spinescens.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The specific epithet chosen alludes to the moss-like appearance of the plant. E. hypnoides is closely allied to E. polytrichoides but at once distinguished by its finely pinnatipartite leaves. Furthermore, the involucral bracts are more connate, and the rays are normally fewer. Like in E. polytrichoides there is a tendency towards monopodial branching. The peduncles, which in E. hypnoides usually occur two together, thus often appear in a seemingly lateral position.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: M. capitata is recognized by its proliference of subtending leaves appressed underneath very dense synflorescenses; different foliage on the flowering shoots; comparatively thin and membraneous involucral bracts; and pappus bristles which are comparatively broad apically. It might be confused with M. cephalotes and its close relatives but they differ in the foliage on flowering shoots; the presence of glands; the capitula being much more conspicuously arranged in clusters; distinctly petaloid outermost involucral bracts; and the pappus bristles being less conspicuously broad apically. Further, in M. capitata the capitula are fused mainly by hairs from the many subtending leaves, not by hairs from the involucral bracts, which is generally the case for similar species.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: A specimen collected by Nordenstam in the Richtersveld differs from typical H. oxybelium in its lack of stalked glands, persistently woolly leaves with scarcely revolute margins and obtuse rather than very acute involucral bracts (Richtersveld, Granite Boss, S. of Kuboos, W. slope, granite rocks and coarse sand, 5 xi 1962, Nordenstam 1778, E; S!). However, H. oxybelium is known from so few collections that I hesitate to give formal recognition to this variant.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: M. calcicola has leaves that are non-twisted or only slightly twisted, strongly incurvate and which subtend large axillary brachyblasts; and truncate, emarginate to irregularly dentate innermost involucral bracts. These characters distinguish it from M. densa, M. muricata and species similar to them. It is also similar in habit to M. luteola, but that species has yellowish-white synflorescenses and leaves that are twisted and not incurvate.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Dittrichia is monophyletic, diagnosed by proximally concrescent pappus bristles forming a cupule. The two species of this genus are sometimes placed in Inula, but differ for example in having polarized endothecial tissue.
bibliographicCitation: Anderberg, AA. 1991. Taxonomy and phylogeny of the tribe Inuleae (Asteraceae). Pl. Syst. Evol. 176(3/4): 75-123. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is recognized easily by its large solitary capitula with herbaceous involucral bracts. P. lanceolata seems to be a very rare species; I have examined only 20 collections, 19 of which were collected before 1920. The most recent gathering is from 1960. This species should be sought as it may be extinct.
bibliographicCitation: Anderberg, AA. 1986. The genus Pegolettia (Compositae, Inuleae). Cladistics 2(2): 158-186. [All rights reserved]

description: Twiggy shrubs with solitary heads and short more or less appressed leaves look very different from loosely branched specimens with long lax leaves and heads in small glomerules, but many intermediate states occur, making the recognition of infraspecific categories impossible. Just such an intermediate plant with heads solitary or few in small glomerules and short but lax leaves, was described as var. laxior, now relegated to synonymy.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This species, as well as S. cristimontanus newly described here, were dealt with by Hilliard in Compositae in Natal (1977) as Senecio sp. no. 70 and 71 respectively. Now that more material has come to hand, it is clear that these two species are indeed distinct: although alike in facies, S. telmateius, with glabrous ovaries and thinly hairy leaves, is consistently found in marshy places (whence the epithet), while S. cristimontanus, with villous ovaries and very nearly glabrous leaves, is always found in dry stony places.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1982. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: IX. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 40(2): 247-298. [CC BY-SA]

description: In Roessler's revision of Berkheya, the plant runs down to B. caffra MacOwan because the leaves are glandular below, not tomentose. B. caffra has narrowly obovate leaves cut into broad rounded lobes margined with short (up to 2 mm) spines, very different from the triangular lobes of B. griquana armed with spines up to 7 mm long. The relationship of B. griquana seems to lie more with B. bergiana, which is not dissimilar in leaf cutting and spines, but the leaves are white tomentose below, a not altogether reliable character in Berkheya. However, the pappus scales of B. bergiana are shorter than those of B. griquana, and we suspect that B. bergiana lacks underground runners.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XI. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 227-260. [CC BY-SA]

description: Varying considerably in leaf size, texture, and the degree to which the stem leaves are decurrent, in toothing of the leaf margins, and to a lesser extent in headsize, reflected in the length of the involucral bracts, but there seems to be no pattern to this variation; for example, in Natal, a large-headed plant with big membranous leaves decurrent on the stem in broad wings is common in damp gullies in the high mountains between Mont aux Sources and Giant's Castle and was given the name S. macroalatus but it is indistinguishable from some coastal specimens (S. caulopterus) and some specimens from tropical Africa. Despite its variability, S. inornatus is easily recognized by its small 5-rayed heads with only c. 12 involucral bracts much shorter than the disc, and long radical leaves. Too many entities may be included under the name, but I cannot find satisfactory characters to separate them.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: The generally 8-rayed heads and long-attenuated leaves with finely reticulate venation, as well as its habitat preferences, serve to distinguish it from, S. inornatus (5 rays) and, S. albanopsis (8 rays, but involucre 7.5-11 mm long, equalling the disc), both of which are plants of open grassland. Often in herbaria as 'S. hydrorhizus Moss, ined.'
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Without examination of the capitula it is often impossible to distinguish E. multifidus from E. subcarnosus ssp. subcarnosus. The very striking resemblance explains the prevailing confusion in literature and herbaria. The best distinguishing character is provided by the involucral bracts, which in E. multifidus are connate to the middle but in E. subcarnosus almost free from the base. The hair-covering of the achenes is different, too, in E. multifidus consisting of very long and thin hairs, which do not become mucilaginous in water. The disc-florets normally do not produce mature achenes, although the styles are provided with stigmatic areas. Often the styles do not grow out through the anther tube, and the stigmatic surfaces are thus not exposed to foreign pollen.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Large trees. Leaves narrowly elliptic, acute and ± acuminate at apex but more constant in male than female plants. Synflorescence very dense; male and female capitula small, mostly sessile or subsessile with involucral bracts extending to the base of the stalk; involucres globose to cyathiform, (3.5-)4.0-6.5(-7.0) x (1.5-)2.5-3.5(-4.0) mm in male capitula and (4.0-)5.5-7.0(-8.5) x (2.0-)3.0-4.5(-8.5) mm in female capitula.
bibliographicCitation: Phillips, EP; Schweickerdt, HGWJ. 1937. A revision of the South African species of Brachylaena R.Brown. Bothalia 3(2): 205-221. [CC BY]

description: A very distinctive species, known from only four collections.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: A relatively distinctive species recognized by the pinnatifid leaves with suborbicular to quadrate lobes, often flexed upwards along the lower edges, and the glabrous involucral bracts. In all other species at least the outer bracts are partly tomentose. The dark-tipped pappus bristles are another distinctive feature of most collections not encountered elsewhere in the genus. G. linnaei hybridizes with both G. crocea and G. wrightii where they co-occur.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Simka, B; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2016. A revised taxonomy of Gerbera sect. Gerbera (Asteraceae: Mutisieae). S. African J. Bot. 104: 142-157. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2015.10.002] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: This species, based on specimens collected by Rand from the Klipriviersberg, south of Johannesburg, was uncollected for 45 years, until it was rediscovered after a determined search over a number of years in the hills in the southern suburbs of Johannesburg. It has since been rediscovered in both the Klipriviersberg Nature Reserve and the Suikerbosrand Nature Reserve, near Heidelberg. Cineraria longipes is a fairly weak (possibly short-lived) perennial herb, recognisable by its solitary or few capitula on relatively long glabrous peduncles, shallowly-lobed reniform (to deltoid-reniform) leaves with long petioles. The leaves are entirely glabrous and their base is characteristically cuneate to truncate. It could possibly be confused with C. lobata, but has glabrous cypselae, as opposed to the ciliate and hairy cypselae in that species, and generally larger capitula.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Much confused with P. undulatum, but distinguished by the leaves, not or only shortly decurrent on the stems, the heads with generally more flowers, and the stereomes of the inner bracts undivided (not fenestrated as in P. undulatum).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: M. galpinii is recognized by its narrow leaves which are non-twisted, slightly curved inwards and lack axillary brachyblasts; by the involucre, which is greyish (tomentose) below, brownish around the middle and then white above (with petaloid involucral bracts); and by most involucral bracts being apically revolute to erect-spreading. It sometimes resembles M. pulcherrima f. pallescens, but that species generally has broader leaves; an involucre that is tomentose higher up; and petaloid involucral bracts generally conspicuously carinate apically. M. galpinii is similar to M. pallida in foliage, but M. pallida is distinguished by the many, individually arranged and usually 6- to 15-flowered capitula, with generally obtuse, finely serrate petaloid involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Very variable in leaf size and to some degree in indumentum; distinctive by virtue of its extraordinarily long fimbrils and reduced pappus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by its winged stems, discolorous rugose leaves and large panicles of small creamy heads.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: MacOwan's species S. prionites is conspecific with S. hypochoerideus DC. (see Hilliard, Compositae in Natal 448, 1977), which has thick-textured, oblong-lanceolate radical leaves that are not clammy to the touch. In contrast the radical leaves of S. macowanii are relatively thin, elliptic-oblanceolate in outline, and very viscid. MacOwan himself noted that in his variety of S. prionites 'the leaves are almost as glandular as in S. concolor DC [i.e. S. speciosus Willd.]. Senecio macowanii has been recorded from a few mountains in the eastern Cape and we have recently found it above Bushman's Nek in Natal, near the Lesotho border at Sehlabathebe. Its ally S. hypochoerideus has a much wider range and is relatively common in the mountains from Bruintjeshoogte, near Somerset East, to Lesotho and Natal.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XI. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 227-260. [CC BY-SA]

description: S. cissampelinus is the southernmost representative of a tropical group of climbers described in the genus Mikaniopsis in Africa (West Africa, Ethiopia, East Africa, Zambia, Angola), Cissampelopsis in Asia (India, Ceylon, Indonesia), but generally reduced to Senecio, and perhaps in Senecio (S. penicellatus) in Madagascar. Easily recognized by its leathery leaves with their very distinctive twisting petioles, and short axillary inflorescences with pale flowers. In Natal, recorded only from Hlokozi and Hlutankungu forests in Umzinto district, and the Zuurberg, north of the Ngeli slopes on the Cape-Natal border. Further search should be made for this interesting plant, which is seldom collected, possibly because it flowers in midwinter.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: The specific name refers to the leaves, which are more or less densely covered with hard, raised points or very short bristles. It is a small shrub characterized by its dense, linear-subulate, rigid, subacicular leaves and its small, incurvate, reniform achenes (2-3 mm long), which have quite a large, closed ventral cavity.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is an annual, more or less densely glandular-pubescent herb, with several stems arising from the crown of the root. The stems are slender, at first ascendent but finally prostrate. The size of the leaves and above all the breadth of the leaves varies greatly owing to the habitat conditions. The small, short ray flowers, which are about as long as the involucral scales or but little longer, constitute an important character for separating it from the majority of the species in the genus Osteospermum.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Phymaspermum athanasioides was previously considered to be a part of a complex with P. holusii and P. montanum, distinguished by apparent differences in their involucral bracts. However, upon further study, these characters were found to be highly variable and no clearly recognisable characters could be found to distinguish between them. As a result only a single variable species, P. athanasioides, is recognised here. It is readily distinguished from all other species in the genus by the marginal filiform florets and from the other species with corymbosely arranged capitula by the absence of fascicles in the leaf axils and by the mostly entire leaves, which rarely become 2- or 3-fid.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: E. galpinii is readily recognized on the sessile capitula, the rigidly ciliolated leaf-margins, and the very short and sparse pappus. The leaves vary from entire to three-lobed, often on the same specimen.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: De Candolle's type of P. turbinata is an exact match of Thunberg's specimen of P. ciliata; both have the long leaves which were given as the difference between the two species; the shorter-leaved form represented by Harvey's var. EcMonis does not seem worthy of varietal distinction.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, J; Phillips, EP. 1917. A revision of the genus Pteronia (Compositae). Ann. S. African Mus. 9(1): 277-329. [All rights reserved]

description: Robust plants in water and dwarfed plants from seasonally dry habitats can look startlingly different, but the floral morphology including the pappus bristles is unmistakable.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Apparently not nearly so common in South Africa as H. radicata, which it closely resembles superficially, but is distinguished by its annual, not perennial, habit, in having the leaves usually glabrous, rarely somewhat hairy, the corollas about equalling the involucre, not exceeding it, and the outer achenes truncate, not beaked, all 3-4 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Cineraria deltoidea is the most widespread and variable of all the species in Cineraria, ranging from near sea level in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa to over 3000 m in the mountains of East Africa and Ethiopia. It varies in terms of growth form (erect herb or suffrutex to lax creeper) and leaf size and shape of leaves (lyratiform to deltoid), the type of trichome and extent of indumentum, the number and size of capitula and the length of the peduncles. Much of this variation is regional, but there is also altitudinal variation in East Africa. A detailed multivariate analysis of C. deltoidea was undertaken, but no recognition of infraspecific taxa was justified. Further field work in Malawi and Zimbabwe was recommended to further investigate the status of the previously recognised C. buchanani. In South Africa, Cineraria deltoidea is distinguished from the two other deltoid-leaved species occurring in KwaZulu-Natal, C. decipiens and C. atriplicifolia, by growth form; these two species are short-lived perennial herbs to lax subshrubs, not perennial creepers. Cineraria decipiens has ciliate and hairy cypselae, whereas C. deltoidea from KwaZulu-Natal has glabrous cypselae. Cineraria decipiens is also usually not as hairy as C. deltoidea, having only glandular hairs in the angles of its leaf lobes. It also flowers mainly in the summer months vs. winter months for C. deltoidea. The lobing in the leaves of C. atriplicifolia is more pronounced, with a distinct apical lobe, about two thirds of the total leaf length. The shape of the auricles differs, being more lanceolate than auriform in C. decipiens and C. atriplicifolia. Trichomes present in C. deltoidea vary from the long cobwebby type with a narrow base to a tapering granular or agranular base to short eglandular and glandular hairs, the last two occurring in the angles of the leaf lobes. Most common in southern Africa is the trichome with a six-celled tapering granular base and a long multi-celled apical appendage.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Closely resembles H. hebelepis in foliage but easily recognized by its different involucre, fimbrilliferous receptacle and glabrous ovaries.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: E. brevipapposus resembles much E. tenuissimus, floribundus, arabicus, and other narrow-leaved species of the section. Some important characteristics are the campanulate involucre, the glabrous flat leaves, the short pappus, and the silky achenes. In contrast to, e.g., E. tenuissimus and floribundus, the hair covering of the achenes is not becoming mucilaginous when moistened. In the southern part of the range the species has usually rather thin involucral bracts, which are connate at base only and basally somewhat gibbous. In the northern range the involucre is firm and more connate, and the pappus is very short and sparse. Generally speaking the northern forms tend to be more variable. This holds true also for the width and length of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Osteospermum spathulatum is very nearly related to the polymorphous species O. scariosum, but differs from it by its glabrous leaves, which are usually entire or more rarely distantly dentate, and by the narrow wings on its achenes. The inferior and medial leaves are, as indicated by the specific name, spathulate with a rounded apex that often has a small mucro. Older stems are strongly lignified except in the upper part. The achenes are smooth with pellucid wings only c. 1 mm broad.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: M. muraltiifolia is a distinct and easily recognized species which is rigid and sparsely branched; with often long and carinate leaves; dense and comparatively broad synflorescenses; and 5-flowered capitula often with spathulate involucral bracts, of which the innermost ones are rounded to truncate and apically plicate. The anthers have a peculiar toothed margin, a feature not seen in any other species. With its dense synflorescenses with fused capitula clusters, it resembles for example, M. cephalotes. However, that species has a less robust habit, with mostly smaller and non-carinate leaves; usually smaller synflorescenses; and glands on young branches, leaves and involucral bracts. M. cephalotes also has anthers with entire margins apically. M. muraltiifolia is the sister group to the M. cephalotes group.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with S. praeteritus with differently shaped radical leaves and shorter involucral bracts. There appear to be two forms of the species. The plant originally described had leaves glabrous except for the ciliate margins, and these spread flat on the ground. Plants with nearly erect, hairy leaves may be found mixed with the typical plant. Until more is known, it seems best to leave them under the same name. The typical plant has been recorded only from the Natal Drakensberg between Bushman's Nek and Ngeli Mt. in the south and Cathedral Peak in the north.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is closely allied to R. genistifolia. Specimens of R. squarrosa are usually distinguished from the former in the typically squar-rose-recurved, elliptic, larger leaves and the campanulate, wider involucres, which often have a distinctly spotted appearance. Furthermore, young vegetative shoots often have a decussate leaf-arrangement, not expressed in R. genistifolia. Specimens without the last character and spreading, more irregularly bent leaves and uniformly coloured involucres might look very similar to R. genistifolia. They can be distinguished by the more slender achenes with shorter pappus, less than 1/5 of the length of the achene. Lastly, achenes of ray-florets are almost always glabrous, only occasionally pilose and then much more sparsely than in R. genistifolia. Another closely related species is R. conferta, which however is smaller and easily distinguished. As evident from the description this species varies considerably in foliage. Only in one case is this correlated with distribution. Specimens from Piketberg and even more noticeably just north thereof, have wider, almost orbicular leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: Very closely allied to H. krebsianum but distinguished by its flowering stems only distantly bracteate upwards and by its crisped involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to H. asperum but distinguished by its different habit, minutely radiating involucral bracts, and often more flowers in the head. Distinguished from H. lineare by its caespitose habit, narrower leaves, larger heads with usually more flowers but fewer heads clustered together, and minutely radiating bracts. Sometimes confused with H. paronychioides.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Cineraria geraniifolia is a widespread and quite variable species, characterised mainly by its slender stems, reniform leaves on relatively long petioles, long peduncles with solitary or few capitula and glabrous, narrow-winged cypselae. The upper leaves tend to become pinnatisect and frequently have lateral pinnae below the lamina, which is then deeply lobed. The leaves are glabrous or sparsely hairy, with short eglandular hairs mainly on the veins below and glandular or eglandular hairs in the angles of the lobes. De Candolle described three varieties: stipulosa, oligocephala and paniculata based on the branching of the peduncle and the number of capitula, as well as the indumentum of the leaves (either glabrous or hairy below). Hilliard designated Drège 5902 (G-DC) as the lectotype, (var. ?, C. geraniifolia var. oligocephala), because the type for var. ? (stipulosa), Burchell 5063 (G-DC) was found to have sparsely hairy cypselae and therefore not match the original description for the species. Both Burchell 5063 (G-DC) and Krebs 170 (G-DC, var. paniculata) are better placed in C. lobata. DrPge 5902 (G-DC, K, P) comes from Klein Bruintjieshoogte in the Albany district of the Eastern Cape, at an altitude of c. 1000 m, collected flowering in October. It is characterised by shallowly-lobed reniform leaves (rarely with pinnae below the lamina), long unbranched peduncles with solitary capitula or branching into two only, glabrous cypselae with a narrow wing, and a stoloniferous, slightly woody base off which the stems branch. These specimens are well matched by collections from the nearby Boschberg, as well as specimens from Winterhoek, Goshen and Happy Valley near the Hogsback Mts. There is, however, tremendous variation in the leaves of C. geraniifolia, so much so that extreme forms look like a subspecies or even a different species. However, there are sufficient intermediate specimens showing the full range of variation to preclude distinguishing of any unique taxa from Honeydale Farm near Fort Hare and Flanagan 692 (BOL, MO, Z) from Prospect Farm near Komgha in the Eastern Cape). In the most extreme forms, the leaf becomes very pinnatisect with narrow lobes/pinnae. These specimens occur in the Amatole Mountains in the Eastern Cape, including the Hogsback , Mount Thomas and Cata Forest Reserve. Most of these specimens are reportedly from fields that have been heavily grazed or frequently burnt. Some of the low-altitude specimens from Gonubie in the Eastern Cape are also very unusual, with very elongate narrow lobes to their leaves, were growing in marshy conditions. Cineraria geraniifolia in the mountains near Maclear in the Eastern Cape have smaller capitula with 5 rays and 8 involucral bracts, but otherwise match well. They do not have the very large, acutely lobed auricles of C. dryogeton from the Umtamvuna Nature Reserve, nor are their leaves as acutely lobed/toothed or hairy. Plants resembling Cineraria geraniifolia in leaf shape and habit, with long peduncles, but with ciliate and sparsely hairy cypselae, have been placed uncertainly/temporarily in C. erodioides, as their auricles, though not conspicuous, are procurrent, their trichomes are long and wispy and their ray cypselae often have a broader wing as is common in C. erodioides in the Eastern Cape. These include Phillipson 291 (K, PRE) from the mountains south of Cradock; Hilliard & Burtt 10573 (NU) and Muller 543 (PRE) from the Mountain Zebra National Park; and Compton 10740 (NBG) from near Oudtshoorn. This area is drier than usual for C. geraniifolia, and these plants may well prove to be a distinct variety of either C. erodioides or C. geraniifolia or perhaps a distinct species.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Rarely collected. The compact habit of the plant, the characteristic toothing of the leaves, arid its large heads with copious silky pappus well exserted from the involucre make it easy to recognize. There is, however, another grassland plant with foliage like that of S. sandersonii, but the heads are smaller (involucral bracts (8-)9-11 mm long), with fewer, smaller calyculus bracts, and are borne on long sparsely bracteate peduncles arranged in spreading corymbs. It is the lax arrangement of the heads that gives it an aspect different from that of S. sandersonii but in the present state of our knowledge of this group, it is best designated S. sandersonii sens. lat. It occupies the area between that of S. Glanduloso-lanosus in the south and S. sandersonii in the north (that is, Natal from near sea level to c. 1675 m), and overlaps with S. sandersonii at Ngome. It grades into S. erubescens var. crepidifolius: see under that species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Across its range, Cineraria lobata varies in size and number of capitula, presence and type of indumentum, robustness of the stems, size and shape of the auricles, as well as shape, colour and degree of indumentum of its cypselae. It is characterised by its distinctly lobed leaves, generally small capitula with 5 or 6 (rarely 8 rays), and ciliate and/or hairy cypselae. Its stem and leaves are usually glabrous or sparsely hairy, although a few populations in the Western Cape are densely hairy, and some of the more northerly populations in the Karoo and Limpopo Province are cobwebby. There appears to be a trend from west to east in terms of increasing size of the capitula in C. lobata, and also increased width of the cypsela margin or wing. Two varieties previously recognised for Cineraria lobata: C. lobata var. gracillima DC. and C. lobata var. pappei Harv. are not retained in this revision. Cineraria lobata var. gracillima, from the Uitenhage District in the Eastern Cape, described as being simple, erect and slender with a weak fibrous root system, is most likely simply flowering in its first year of growth, as noted by de Candolle. Cineraria lobata var. pappei, with very many small heads and based on a specimen collected by Dr Pappe from the Winterhoek mountains, Tulbagh, has been included in form 1 of C. lobata subsp. lobata. Cineraria lobata has been distinguished from C. geifolia by being glabrous in all parts, with many more, but smaller capitula, with 6 or 7 involucral bracts (not 12 or 13) and a more branching inflorescence. Many of these features are however quite variable in C. lobata, especially the presence and type of indumentum on the leaves and stem. Nevertheless, C. lobata usually has more distinctly lobed leaves, either glabrous or sparsely hairy in the Western Cape, and its trichomes differ from C. geifolia, being narrower and longer, commonly with an apical appendage in the hairy form. Cineraria lobata generally has more slender stems than C. geifolia, although the form of C. lobata subsp. lobata from the Cape Peninsula and near Saldanha Bay is more robust than usual and may have slightly larger capitula with 7 or 8 rays (instead of 5), and occasionally more than 8 involucral bracts (9-12). In this region, it is sometimes difficult to distinguish from C. geifolia, and it is possible that the two species are hybridising on the Cape Peninsula, where C. lobata grows close to sea level. Cineraria lobata also resembles C. saxifraga from the Eastern Cape, but the leaves of C. saxifraga are slightly succulent, smaller, more shallowly lobed with distinctly cuneate to truncate bases and are exauriculate. In the Eastern Cape, C. lobata subsp. platyptera may be confused with C. erodioides, but the trichomes and auricles of that species differ from C. lobata.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: O. rotundifolium is characterized by its obovoid-ellipsoid achenes with three slightly prominent longitudinal ridges. The sides of the achenes are smooth, except at the base, where they are slightly furrowed, and towards the apex, where they are furnished with some small pits. This species is habitally very like both O. polygaloides var. latifolium and the extremely broad-leafed forms of O. imbricatum, but it is easily distinguished from these species by the shape of the achenes. It differs from O. imbricatum besides by its dense, glandularmuriculate involucral scales. If the fruits are missing, it is practically impossible accurately to separate O. rotundifolium from O. polygaloides var. latifolium. The leaves are broadly ovate or suborbicular, and more or less conspicuously mucronate. This description applies only to the leaves of the branches and of the upper and medial parts of the stem. In the herbarium material there are no specimens with basal leaves, but they are probably linear or linear-lingulate just like the corresponding leaves in the other species in sect. Polygalina.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: A. asperum, as defined here, is the most widely distributed and also the most variable species within the genus. Two sub species can be distinguished. Without examination of the capitula it is often impossible to separate ssp. asperum from ssp pauciflorum. The best distinguishing characters are the number of male florets and of involucral bracts in a capitulum (but in very young specimens it is often difficult to get an exact number). The variation partly overlaps. These morphological distinctions are correlated with a vicarious distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Lundgren, J. 1972. Revision of the genus Anaxeton Gaertn. (Compositae). Opera Bot. 31: 5-59. [All rights reserved]

description: G. jamesonii is easily recognized by the large, elegant capitula, the extremely large rays, and the large, pinnatifid, very longed stalked leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Hansen, HV. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the genus Gerbera (Compositae, Mutisieae) sections Gerbera, Parva, Piloselloides (in Africa), and Lasiopus. Opera Bot. 78: 5-36. [All rights reserved]

description: Much confused with S. rhyncholaenus We have twice collected specimens with deep yellow flowers, but could find no character other than this to distinguish them from typical S. subrubriflorus. See also note under S. consanguineous.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Usually readily distinguished from other southern African species by its opposite or subopposite (rarely alternate) leaves with deltoid-ovate and sinuate-dentate or hastiform blade. The leaves and young stems are roughly pubescent with ± appressed eglandular hairs and sessile glands. The 5-ribbed cypselas with slender, white pappus bristles are also characteristic. Occasional specimens with alternate, entire leaves may be confused with the slightly later-flowering D. anisochaetoides where the two co-occur around Durban but that species has the young leaves and stems whitish felted with shaggy, eglandular hairs that persist on the older stems as a tissue-paper like indumentum between the ribs, exposing the prominent, sessile glands; stiffly divaricate and ± flexuous or zigzag inflorescence branches; capitula with shorter inner bracts ±3 mm long, and more numerous, ±15 florets; and 8- to 10-ribbed cypselas with a buff pappus with the inner bristles ± clavate.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC. 2014. The genus Distephanus (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 94: 238-248. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2014.07.007] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2014); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The achenes do not prove to coincide with those of O. junceum for they lack the three blunt, ridge-like processes at the apex, which are characteristic of the achenes in O. junceum, and moreover they are only about half as large as in O. junceum. With regard to the shape of the leaves the two species are easy to keep separate. In O. asperulum all the leaves are linear or narrowly oblanceolate-linear and sessile, while in O. junceum at least the lower and medial leaves of the stem are elliptic or broadly lanceolate, and conspicuously petioled. The leaves, younger branches and parts of the stem are as a rule asperous owing to very small raised points, as indicated by the specific name asperulum, but forms are also found which may be described as almost smooth. In contrast to O. junceum, the stem in O. asperulum is also branched in its lower and medial parts. The heads are usually disposed singly at the apices of the branches, but sometimes they form a few-headed, racemose inflorescence. In O. junceum, on the other hand, the heads are arranged in a corymbose or paniculate inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The closest relative of O.burttii is undoubtedly O. natalensis Sch. Bip., the chromosome number of which is unknown. Harvey placed O. natalensis in the section Scapigerae Harv., but this is an unnatural as semblage of taxa. O. burttii does not fit into the section as defined by Harvey, and the sectional limits will be thoroughly revised in a forthcoming monograph of the whole genus. O. natalensis is a species of lowland to mon­tane grasslands and with a different habit from that of O. burttii. It has a short and thick subterranean caudex with distinct tufts of wool at the leaf-bases. The peduncles are usually, but not always, branched, and the leaves are larger, up to 30 cm long and 6 cm wide and provided with a very distinct midrib. In floral details the two species are fairly similar with differences of a mainly quantitative nature. For example, the achenes of O. natalensis are about twice as large as those of O. burttii, and the grown-out pappus is distinctly longer.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1980. Othonna burttii sp. nov. (Compositae) from the Drakensberg, South Africa. Bot. Not. 133: 555-557. [All rights reserved]

description: Osteospermum rosulatum occupies an intermediate position between O. monocephalum and O. scariosum. As regards the shape and size of the achenes it comes very close to the former species. It differs, however, from it by having rosette leaves and never having any distinctly opposite leaves. Apart from the characters of the achenes it is morphologically nearest allied to the polymorphous species O. scariosum.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: It resembles T. ekmanii in leaf shape, but the apical lobe is more rounded than in that species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: There is considerable confusion between Pentzia globosa and P. lanata. The main differences are the densely white-tomentose branches, the bigger capitula and longer leaves in P. lanata. However there are a lot of intermediate forms and these two taxa might prove to be conspecific.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Sometimes confused with H. odoratissimum, but that species has leaves generally broadest in the upper half and decurrent on the stem in broad or narrow wings.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: It is a perennial herb with one or several erect stems up to 4 cm high, arising from a strongly lignified subterranean caudex. The plant at least in its younger parts is clothed with short glandular hairs, which feel rough when the plant is dried. As a rule all the leaves on the stem are entire, but forms are also found with a few slightly dentate leaves.

description: Osteospermum sinuatum is a dwarf shrub, characterized by its opposite, sinuate-dentate to sparsely denticulate leaves. It comes very near to O. oppositifolium, differing mainly from this species by not having entire leaves. The leaves are very variable in shape and amount of toothing in this species. The leaves are slightly succulent and glaucous, the younger ones, like the younger branches, having a glandular, pulverulent (hardly puberulous) covering.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: As is common in pyrophytic plants, a high degree of variation in leaf characters was observed in S. africanus. The following specimen showed atypical leaf characters: Bally 7356! from Kenya, Subukia, has leaves that are up to 9 cm long with irregularly spaced, long-protruding lobes that give the plant a superficial resemblance to S. zambiensis R.M.King & H.Rob. However, Bally's collection differs from this taxon in that the leaves are not in whorls of 3, phyllaries are wider and more obtuse, achenes are not glabrous, and the inflorescence is a dense corymb as opposed to laxly cymose.

description: Uncertain status, might be confused with e.g. P. ciliata Thunb.

description: Several characters make M. fastigiata easily recognizable, for example, its dense whitish to white tomentum on the young branches; generally brownish outermost involucral bracts forming a distinct pattern between the hairy base of the capitula and the petaloid upper part; obtuse, slightly serrate pappus bristles; often slightly notched anthers; and ribbed cypselas. It resembles M. erubescens, but that species usually has curved leaves, 3-flowered capitula and cypselas without ribs. See Taxonomic note under M. agathosmoides and M. albescens for comparison with those species.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Very variable in leaf shape, width and indumentum, which shows no clear geographical partitioning. In the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg for instance, specimens with narrow glabrous leaves and wide-spreading inflorescences are common in grassland and stabilized boulder beds, while on moist rocky grass slopes, plants may have leaves white-tomentose below and the radical ones more disticntly petiolate than those of the glabrous-leaved plants and the inflorescence may be more contracted. These are possibly local ecological races: a thorough field study of the whole complex is needed, a formidable task. Narrow-leaved specimens with only 3 main veins in the radical leaves are easily confused with H. miconiifolium, but can usually be distinguished by the stems being only distantly bracteate above. However, some specimes may be difficult to place, and it is not improbable that crossing takes place.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The broad, cordate-clasping loosely woolly grey cauline leaves and the very open and leafy inflorescence are characteristic.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The species is recognized by the large flowerheads with the crowded, usually deep blood-red, long ray florets and the commonly black disc. Furthermore the entire leaves and the short, winged petiole separate it from G. jamesonii. It is less easily distinguished from the taxon described by S. Moore as G. speciosa. This taxon has rather large heads, sometimes as large as in G. aurantiaca, and the tomentum of the upper leaf surface (as well as rarely also the lower one) typically resembles that of G. aurantiaca; besides, the pappus is often more or less violet-purple. However, the ray florets are smaller and more narrow than in G. aurantiaca, and they are not typically blood-red. Furthermore G. speciosa is restricted to Transvaal, and it is best explained as one of several forms of G. viridifolia (see under that species). According to Hilliard G. aurantiaca hybridizes with G. kraussii Schultz-Bip. (i.e. G. ambigua (Cass.) Schultz-Bip. according to the present work). The hybrid shows every gradation in leaf shape and indumentum between the two parents and has larger heads than either of them. The rays are very variable in colour: Pink, yellow, orange, red, white tinged pink or creamy white; the disc also varies in colour and often seems to be whitish, while the pappus varies from violet-prurple over whitish to more or less whitish-tawny. Two varieties of G. aurantiaca established by Dümmer, var. wyliei (type specimen: Medley-Wood 10150 (K, lectotype, NH, isolectotype)) and var. alba (type specimen: Medley-Wood 10151 (K, lectotype, BOL, L, NH, isolectotypes)), are considered by Hilliard as representatives of this hybrid. It is not always easy to separate the hybrid form from the true G. aurantiaca on the herbarium sheets. The hybrid shows much affinity to that species, having prominent rays and large heads, the heads generally being slightly larger than in the true G. aurantiaca, but by no means always. The lower leaf surface varies from woolly or cobwebby to dense, persistently whitish to lemon tomentose (as in G. ambigua). The rays may reach 40 mm in length, the achenes 10 mm on the few specimens studied.

description: E. serra is easily distinguished from its consectioners on the leaf-shape. The leaves are serratilobed or shallowly pinnatilobate with many pairs of lobes. The involucres are extremely large and wide.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: A. epaleata has larger leaves than any of its congeners, usually around 1 cm long and distinctly spatulate with a narrow revolute margin.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1996. Anderbergia B.Nord., a new genus of everlastings (Compositae-Gnaphalieae) from the Cape Province  . Ann. Naturhist. Mus. Wien 98(Suppl.B): 403-418. [All rights reserved]

description: The flowers of E. floribundus are said to have a sweet scent. The hair covering of the achenes swells in water and becomes mucilaginous, a phenomenon also observed in several other species of Euryops. The achenes are generally small but variable in size. During this century it has spread as a weed and become a real pest in some areas, e.g., around Queenstown. It invades many types of vegetation, especially damaged grassveld (e.g. Themeda veld), and easily becomes dominant, since it is fire-resistant (when green) and not touched by stock (except perhaps for the flowerheads).
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Only the radiate plant has been recorded from Natal. Much confused with S. macroglossus: see under that species. It also closely resembles S. quinquelobus but that species always has discoid heads with smaller flowers (corolla 9.5-11 mm long, not (0.5-)11-12 mm). Furthermore, the calyculus bracts of S. quinquelobus lack ciliate margins, and the margins of the leaf lobes are slightly convex, not mostly concave or straight as in S. macroglossoides.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: H. molestum can easily be confused with H. difficile, but is usually more robust, with broader leaves; it is distinguished from H. cooperi by its perennial habit and usually larger heads. The leaves of H. molestum are usually green below. However, Hilliard & Burtt 14207 (E; NU; PRE) is probably no more than a variant with leaves thinly white-woolly below; it grew in the vicinity of normal green-leaved plants. Hilliard & Burtt 14162 (E; K; NU; PRE; S) from Elandshoogte near Machadodorp has leaves thinly woolly on both surfaces. Hybrids are also known.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: R. multipunctata is a usually tall species with slender capitula. It is related to R. sedifolia and R. resinifera. It differs from the former in having the capitula arranged in cymes and from the latter in the characters of the achenes (see key) and leaves, which are distinctly glandular-punctate, narrowly obovate and not very glutinous as in R. resinifera.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: E. namibensis is closely allied to E. subcarnosus, differing by the more flattened and fleshy leaves with broader lobes, and the presence of at least some pinnately lobed leaves. Furthermore, the leaf tips are more obtuse and less distinctly apiculate, and the cortex of the stout main branches is ash-grey and sulcate. Further details, like differences in epidermis cells, are discussed in Nordenstam 1966, but it should be pointed out, that the characters listed for subcarnosus hold true mainly for the S. W. African material of ssp. vulgaris. When in full flower E. namibensis is a quite conspicuous plant with a multitude of bright yellow flowerheads. In some localities it grows together with E. subcarnosus ssp. vulgaris but without intermediates.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Although S. submontanus belongs to a difficult and confusing group of species, it is not easily confounded with any of them, radiate or discoid. Its small, narrow heads (reflected in the few involucral bracts and small number of flowers) immediately set it apart from all allied species except S. adnatus, S. hygrophilus, S. isatidioides and S. isatideus, which stand apart in details of leaf morphology and head structure. It appears to hybridize with S. parentalis, see under that species. S. bupleuroides, S. latifolius and their close allies are a close-knit and taxonomically very difficult group. It has been mooted that hybridization is the underlying cause of this difficulty, but this needs confirmation by experimental means. However, it is possible to place most specimens, and names are available for nearly all the entities that can be recognised. The whole group (together with S. isatideus and its immediate allies) is poisonous to stock.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: O. pterigoideum is nearest allied to O. ciliatum. It is easily distinguished from that species, however, by its entire leaves and by the involucral scales being shortly hispidulous on the dorsal side. The younger leaves and branches of the plant are floccosely cobwebbed, but never hispid as in O. hispidum. It also differs from these species by having its rays as long as, or somewhat longer than, the inner involucral scales.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Cineraria saxifraga is mainly recognised by its slightly succulent glabrous leaves with a more cuneate to truncate base than is common in C. lobata, to which it is otherwise similar in leaf shape and lobing, although the lobes are not as deeply cut. The leaves are exauriculate, unusual in Cineraria.

description: Easily overlooked, despite its size, because it somewhat resembles the common H. nudifolium; readily distinguished, however, by its soft-textured leaves and small heads with brownish involucral bracts.

description: Specimens in the southern part of the range have distinctly glandular as well as woolly leaves and heads mostly ±15 mm long; in the Transvaal and Swaziland, leaves are generally smaller and less markedly glandular and heads are ±13 mm long.

description: Very closely allied to G. pectidea Harv., but differs in having broader, usually oblong, very obtuse leaves, always solitary much larger heads which terminate the branches and short branchlets.

description: Naturalized in W. Europe, Madeira and Hawaii. Records from tropical Africa are either introductions or misdeterminations: H. foetidum var. microcephalum A. Rich is a distinct species (probably H. glutinosum A. Braun fide Wild, pers. comm.). H. foetidum is closely allied to H. cooperi, which gradually replaces it from the Amatola Mountains and Transkei northeastwards to the summer rainfall area. H. cooperi can be distinguished by its leaves, often decurrent on the stem and lacking white wool below.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to S. tanacetopsis but distinguished by its more compact, well-branched habit, peculiar white-woolly leaf buds contrasting with the glabrous mature foliage, and generally larger heads (involucral bracts (6-)7-8 mm long, not 4-5 (-7) mm). S. prostratus Klatt, based on a specimen from Insizwa Mt. near Tabankulu in the Transkei, is probably synonymous with S. seminiveus, but does not have such markedly woolly leaf buds and the peduncles and involucral bracts are only gland-dotted, without stalked glands. A similar plant has been collected on the summit of Giant's Castle.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: The tree-like form, large leaves and capitula and glabrous achenes distinguish O. grandis from all other members of the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Bond, P. 1987. A revision of Oldenburgia (Asteraceae - Mutisieae). S. African J. Bot. 53: 493-500. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1987); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: M. dregeana is characterized by very densely whitish-tomentose young branches; generally squarrose involucral bracts, of which the petaloid ones are usually creamy white; and by often very acute pappus bristles. Specimens in herbaria may have almost yellowish synflorescenses. It is sympatric, for example, with M. densa, a species sometimes similar to M. dregeana, but with a differently coloured involucre, viz. brownish to brown below, with white petaloid involucral bracts. M. densa also usually has less acute to obtuse pappus bristles.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: At Katberg and Hogsback, the rosette leaves are much narrower than in specimens from further north, and the heads are often solitary. However, these rosettes of very sticky leaves are diagnostic. But even detached flowering stems are easily recognized by the loose white wool on the stem and enveloping the base of each head, and the crisped-undulate leaf margins.

description: Plants with small heads have been recorded from many of the high Drakensberg passes from Organ Pipes to Bushman's River Pass; elsewhere, plants tend to have large heads. Small-headed specimens may be difficult to distinguish from compact specimens of H. sutherlandii.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Specimens from Namaqualand have very long hairs on the ovaries (often c. 10 times as long as broad); the only other specimens I have seen (Giess & van Vuuren 776 from Aus in S.W. Africa-Namibia, and Acocks 18961 from Wolwe Graafwater in Calvinia district, Cape) have shorter hairs, c. 3-4 times as long as broad, but I can find no other difference. Ifloga paronychioides can be confused with I. Candida; in addition to the characters given in the diagnosis below, I. Candida differs from I. paronychioides in the much shorter hairs on the ovaries; these are not much longer than broad.
