description: Tarchonanthus minor is distinguished from the other species by the small, narrowly elliptic, entire leaves, dense, spicate synflorescences and flowering time in spring and summer. The leaves in some of the Lesotho specimens reach the upper limit of the range in leaf size.
bibliographicCitation: Herman, PPJ. 2002. Revision of the Tarchonanthus camphoratus complex (Asteraceae-Tarchonantheae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 32(1): 21-28. [CC BY]

description: This species shows an incredible range of variation in response to edaphic factors which has led to the description of many infraspecific taxa and the proliferation of superfluous names. However, in East Africa, the key distinguishing features of A. conyzoides are sufficiently reliable to allow the species to be treated as one widespread taxon.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, SAL. 2005. Eupatorieae. In: HJ Beentje SA Ghazanfar (eds), Compositae, Fl. Trop. E. Africa (3): 819-839. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognizable by its apically curved to hooked leaves and by semiglobose, dense synflorescenses with individually arranged capitula only. In addition M. umbelliformis has scarious involucral bracts which are comparatively thick, appressed and slightly carinate, as well as apically erect-spreading petaloid involucral bracts. It sometimes resembles M. muricata, its sister species with similar foliage and involucres, but that species has leaves which are obtuse at the very apex, often obtuse, erect scarious involucral bracts, and larger sessile capitula arranged in clusters.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Cineraria albicans is typically a well-branched, fairly straggly herb or shrublet, usually with deltoid-reniform, distinctly lobed leaves and a grey indumentum on stem, leaves, peduncles and involucral bracts. Certain characters in C. albicans are very variable: the size and persistence of its auricles, glabrescence of involucral bracts and the degree of hairiness of the cypselae. A detailed study of the variation in C. albicans and a potentially distinct species described as ‘species A’ of Hilliard revealed a lack of any consistent correlation of the variable features and the latter is considered to be within C. albicans. The isolation of the Msikaba Formation sandstone gorges and associated valley bushveld in the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands and Pondoland region, a common habitat for C. albicans, may be promoting fixation of combinations of characters in disjunct populations. Cineraria albicans is distinguished from C. grandibracteata by having smaller and more capitula, as opposed to the solitary capitula of C. grandibracteata (rarely in twos) which are subtended by very large bracts (up to 20 mm long) at the base of the peduncles, and by its cypselae having some degree of hairiness (never glabrous). Specimens from higher altitude in the Eastern Cape have larger capitula and tend to be very tomentose. Cineraria albicans may also be confused with C. erodioides, but that species has very characteristic procurrent auricles and a different type of trichome on the leaves of most specimens: with c. six sharply tapering basal cells and a long apical appendage that often rubs off, leaving the leaves with a slightly scabrid appearance (similar to C. erosa). Cineraria albicans has trichomes of the fine kind only, with 2-4 narrow basal cells and a long apical appendage, attached either obliquely or perpendicularly. Some specimens from the Graaff-Reinet District are very similar to C. albicans in tomentum and have thickly cobwebby involucral bracts, but have auricles like C. erodioides.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Easily confused with H. adenocarpum, but readily distinguished by its linear radical leaves and small heads.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The most morphologically distinct member of the genus, due to its small size, dark green, glabrous and slender leaves, small, sessile capitula partly enveloped by the upper leaves, and habit of growing in the crevices of sandstone rocks. The leaves, stems and involucral bracts are markedly less glandular-scabrid than all other species in the genus, although small, somewhat sunken glands are present. Probably the most distinctive feature of Heterolepis mitis is its glabrous foliage, giving the plant a dark-green appearance in contrast to the grey-green or whitish appearance of the other species. Heterolepis mitis also has the easternmost distribution. Several collections note the fact that the plants are ‘aromatic’, and rehydrated material is exceptionally pungent-smelling. The stems and leaves frequently become viscid on drying, as if covered with a clear varnish layer, a feature which has not been observed on other species of Heterolepis.

description: The native L. dregeana DC. is very like L. serriola but is distinguished by at least the upper stem leaves being lanceolate, not pinnately divided. It seems to be confined to the drier parts of the northern Cape and O.F.S.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: It is at once distinguished by its stoloniferous, succulent branches forming a subterranean network and short aerial branches bearing succulent, linear-lanceolate to elliptic to oblong-oblanceolate leaves with distinct revolute margins, becoming deciduous in winter. The plants flower in early spring, the flowers borne at the tips of the leafless stems of the previous season. The only other stoloniferous South African species is Kleinia stapeliiformis (E.Phillips) Stapf, which is immediately distinguished by its aerial, cylindrical, grooved, succulent stems and rudimentary scale-like leaves 3-7 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2005. Kleinia venteri, a new succulent species from Limpopo Province. Aloe 42(1&2): 12-13. [All rights reserved]

description: Close to H. grandiflorum but distinguished by its larger heads (involucre ±11 mm long, not 7 mm, with involucral bracts much exceeding the flowers) arranged in a spreading corymb, not in a tight cluster.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A striking feature of some specimens of M. quinqueflora is their habit of branching from ground level. Another peculiar feature of M. quinqueflora is the occurrence of crystals in certain floral parts, viz. in the pappus bristles, corolla, anthers and styles. Specimens with wholly pink petaloid involucral bracts are rare. M. quinqueflora varies considerably in some characters, for example the stance of the leaves and the size of the involucral bracts. It is recognizable by the revolute to erect-spreading outer and inner involucral bracts in combination with its rather small habit. M. quinqueflora may resemble M. humilis, a species that has fewer capitula per synflorescense, and innermost involucral bracts apically revolute to erect-spreading rather than erect. Small, sparsely leafed specimens of M. quinqueflora resemble M. tenuifolia, but the former species is distinguished by its different involucre, by generally white, not creamy white, petaloid involucral bracts, and by 5-, not 3-flowered capitula.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Also recorded as a common coastal plant in Mozambique. Can be confused with B. montana, but in that species the leaves are not, or scarcely, decurrent on the stem, and are cobwebby, but not white-felted, below, with denticulate or repand-denticulate, not deeply toothed, margins.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to H. capense but distinguished by its differently shaped leaves, often much smaller than those of H. capense.

description: C. mollis closely resembles C. albicans and C. erodioides.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Cineraria mollis is a perennial herb with a tufted appearance due to the closely clustered leaves along its woody rhizome. It is fairly easily identified by its growth form, leaf shape and the solitary (to few) capitula on long peduncles. The dorsal surface of the leaves varies from dark green with a thin cobwebby indumentum to grey with a thicker tomentum of fine, narrow-based long trichomes. The ventral surface is usually thickly white woolly or grey. Drége 666c (G-DC, K) was chosen as the lectotype as both G-DC and K specimens are in good condition, whereas there is only one mature capitulum remaining on the Ecklon 433c(G-DC) specimen, although both specimens match the original description. Specimens from the Victoria West District and Williston District are unusual in that the peduncles branch and bear three capitula and their leaves are larger and more dentate or crenate than usual, as in plants previously known as C. arctotidea. They occur at a lower altitude than usual for C. mollis (1200 m), but otherwise match it well. Cineraria mollis may be confused with Bolandia pedunculosa (DC.) Cron, especially when the leaves are mostly lyrate-pinnatifid, but Bolandia has ecalyculate capitula and fusiform heteromorphic cypselae. Species now comprising Bolandia were previously included in Cineraria, but have pinnately-veined exauriculate leaves and truncate style apices, in addition to the ecalyculate capitula and fusiform cypselae.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: E. abrotanifolius can always be recognized on the achenes, which are glabrous, 10-nerved, and provided with a distinct apical appendage formed by the persistent stylophore. The well-developed stylophore is easily observed also in young florets. Similar (although smaller) achenes are found only in E. lasiocladus, which has lateral peduncles and is referred to a different section. Several other species have a superficial and sometimes very striking resemblance to E. abrotanifolius, e.g., E. pinnatipartitus, trilobus, inops, and rupestris, but they are readily distinguishable on examination of the floral parts, especially achenes and pappus. In vegetative characters E. abrotanifolius is highly variable, notably in shape and size of leaves and length of peduncles. This has led to the recognition by earlier authors of too many taxa, which have to be put into synonymy. The number of involucral bracts is usually about 13 but sometimes higher. The rays are sometimes red or coppery beneath. This character occurs in different parts of the distribution area, and since it is not constant within the populations or combined with other characters, I regard it as taxonomically unimportant.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Stems and leaves are densely glandular; all glands stalked, never sessile; innermost involucral bracts are mucronate; capitula are generally 2-flowered.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2019. Taxonomy and reclassification of South African Asteraceae genus Elytropappus (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae), the description of two new genera and two new species. Phytotaxa 403(4): 248-284. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.403.4.1] [All rights reserved]

description: The salient features of I. repens are its prostrate main branches giving rise to numerous short erect flowering branchlets terminating in glomerules or short racemes (up to c. 30 mm long) of tightly clustered heads. Occasionally the heads are more laxly set, so that the racemes are much longer; it is then clear that each head is surrounded by only a few leaves, some of which are lightly webbed to the outer involucral bracts. This is in contrast to I. ambigua, in which the heads terminate dwarf branchlets, the many leaves of which are webbed to each other and to the outer involucral bracts. Ifloga repens may be confused with I. pilulifera.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1981. A revision of Ifloga in southern Africa, with comments on the northern hemisphere species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 82: 293-312. [All rights reserved]

description: Poisonous to stock.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Leaves oblanceolate to obovate, rounded or sometimes briefly acuminate at apex but more constant in male than female plants; capitula large, mostly with distinct stalks with only a few scattered bracts; involucres of female capitula widely infundibuliform to cyathiform at base, (7-)10-18(-23) x (3.5-)5.0-10.0 (-12.0) mm, bracts narrowly ovate with apex acute and somewhat spreading; involucres of male capitula globose to cyathiform, (5.5-)6.0-13.0(-15.0) x (2.5-)4.0-6.0(-8.5) mm, bracts narrowly ovate with apex acute, somewhat spreading; synflorescences less dense than in B. transvaalensis.
bibliographicCitation: Pope, GV. 1992. 97. Compositae (part 1), Fl. Zambes. 6(1): 1-264. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, London. [CC BY]

description: Can be confused with H. sessilioide but is easily distinguished by its different habit, leaves silky below, not woolly, and different pappus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the ± parallel-sided, retrorsely serrate leaves with cuneate or cordate bases and densely yellowish-brownish felted under surface. The species typically has ± oblong leaves but populations from Riviersondered and Swellendam are distinctive in their narrow, almost linear leaves 2-5 mm wide. Such plants formed the basis for G. asplenifolia var. linearis described by Harvey (1865) and examples with closely notched leaves can be confused with G. linnaei. The leaves are, however, retrorsely notched to toothed and not pinnatisect as in true G. linnaei. Typical G. serrata can also be confused with G. tomentosa from west of Swellendam but that species has elliptic to oblanceolate leaves without parallel sides and distinctive, imbricate involucral bracts not ± arranged in series.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Simka, B; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2016. A revised taxonomy of Gerbera sect. Gerbera (Asteraceae: Mutisieae). S. African J. Bot. 104: 142-157. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2015.10.002] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: H. interjacens may be of hybrid origin between H. melanacme and H. polycladum: it is known from only a small geographical area where the ranges of these two species overlap, and may grow in close proximity to one or both of its putative parents. It closely resembles H. melanacme in general facies, but is readily distinguished by female flowers in a head far outnumbering homogamous; also, where these two species have been recorded together, H. interjacens has decidedly paler involucral bracts than H. melanacme. H. polycladum is easily distinguished from both by its much narrower leaves and white involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: E. gilfillanii is a well defined species by its acaulescent habit and its-narrow leaves and long, slender peduncles from a woolly crown.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: The commonest form of H. sutherlandii is a lax rounded shrublet with the flowering stems standing well away from the body of the plant. A compact, small-leaved form with very short flowering twigs occurs in parts of the Drakensberg, mainly above ±2600 m, and may be difficult to distinguish from small-headed plants of H. confertum, which may grow with H. sutherlandii, but generally flowers earlier, in spring and late winter. It is possible that there is some crossing between the species, but field and laboratory studies are needed to confirm this.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: O. grandidentatum is a plant of coarse grassland often mixed with scrub, at the margins of forest patches and amongst rocks. It has a woody caudex (unlike the thin creeping rhizomes of O. attenuatum), from which arise long sprawling or subscandent branches in contrast to the tufted, mat-forming shoots of O. attenuatum. The specific epithet attenuatum draws attention to another significant character, the tapering leaf bases, in contrast to the auriculate or subcordate clasping leaves of O. grandidentatum.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XI. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 227-260. [CC BY-SA]

description: E. ciliatus resembles in foliage E. sulcatus and E. lateriflorus, but the involucre comes closest to that of E. spathaceus. From all these three species it differs by the glabrous achenes. The often four- or even three-lobed disc-florets are unusual but probably only occasional aberrations, evidently caused by a connation of adjacent corolla lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: H. umbraculigerum displays remarkable variation in leaf shape, and there is some geographical partitioning of this variation. For instance, plants with ovate or rhomboid-ovate leaves much narrowed to a distinctly petiolar part are very nearly confined to KwaZulu-Natal, where they have a wide altitudinal range from near sea level to ±2 000 m. But in the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg between ±1 500 and 2 300 m, leaves may range from linear-lanceolate through all intermediates to ovate or rhomboid-ovate; narrow-leaved plants may occur in the same area as broad-leaved ones, but the former are generally found in wetter situations than the latter. In the Transvaal and Zimbabwe, leaves are mostly more or less elliptic, tapering at the base, but I have seen one very narrow-leaved specimen from near Lake Chrissie. In the Cape, within an area roughly circumscribed by a line encircling Grahamstown, Cathcart, Barkly Pass, Qumbu, Port St Johns (Transkei) and East London, leaves tend to be oblong-spathulate, slightly narrowed towards the base then expanded and ear-clasping, and the flowers frequently lack a pappus. Elsewhere in the Cape, as well as in the area just mentioned, leaves may taper to a more markedly petiolar base but are never ovate nor rhomboid as in KwaZulu-Natal; the flowers generally have a pappus. We have not been able to trace the type specimen, but Lessing described the leaves as spathulate-oblong-obovate, slightly acute, much narrowed below, and the flowers as having a pappus. Krebs lived in Grahamstown for a while, and his specimen was possibly collected thereabouts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: D. montana is a very distinct species. It is a dwarf, perennial herb with golden yellow ray flowers, and is especially characterized by its conspicuously 3-winged ray achenes and its entire leaves. In its habit of growth it resembles D. zeyheri most, but is easy to distinguish from that species in respect of the shape of the achenes and the colour of the flowers. It seems to be most closely allied to D. chrysanthemifolia, the triangular ray achenes in the last-mentioned plant also being winged, although only very slightly so in relation to those in D. montana. The colour of the flowers corresponds quite well in these two species. The principal differences consist in D. montana not having toothed or lobate leaves and in it not being fruticose.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is distinguished by its often compact habit; leaves which are non-twisted, often narrowly triangular and flat on the upper surface at the base and more narrow and rounded on the under surface towards the apex; dense to very dense and obscurely branched synflorescenses; outer and inner involucral bracts with concave to deeply concave lamina; and distinctly ribbed cypselas. M. fastigiata, the sister species, resembles M. agathosmoides in its generally pink synflorescenses with 5-flowered capitula, but the synflorescenses are more branched and contain conspicuously peduncled capitula clusters. The foliage is also entirely different. Other species that superficially resemble M. agathosmoides are M. brevifolia, M. erubescens and M. seriphiifolia but they all have 3-flowered capitula as well as different foliage.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Often found growing with C. bonariensis and C. sumatrensis var. sumatrensis [as 'C. floribunda']. It is readily distinguished by its small heads with white rays, sometimes tinged mauve below.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Diagnostic features: Leaves glabrous; blades narrowly linear to sub-falcate, sometimes canaliculate, margins involute. Corymbophore glabrous, dichotomously branched. Heads solitary, distinctly pedunculate. Involucral bracts glabrous. Flowers mauve, pedicel present. Ovary hirsute. Populations from the Cedarberg are characterized by a more lax conflorescence while the lateral branching of the corymbophore occurs more than half way down the length of the corymbophore. In populations from the Villiersdorp area the conflorescence is more congested with the arrangement of the heads approaching a condition towards a corymbose arrangement with lateral branching not more than half way down the length of the corymbophore.
bibliographicCitation: Weitz, FM. 1989. A revision of the genus Corymbium L. (Asteraceae). S. African J. Bot. 55: 598-629. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1989); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Plants from higher altitudes have a more condensed growth habit, with fewer capitula and smaller, densely pubescent leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Can be confused with S. gerrardii.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily recognized by its shrubby habit, grey leaves and lemon-yellow heads, more like the tropical species H. petersii Oliv. & Hiern than any S. African species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Very variable in leaf form. It is closely allied to S. rhomboideus but is easily distinguished by its differently shaped leaves on long terete petioles. Although both species are discoid, it seems possible that radiate forms may occur (a radiate specimen is cited under S. rhomboideus). Then S. tropaeoli-folius MacOwan (Grahamstown, MacOwan 905, K, PRE, type) appears to be little more than a radiate form of S. oxyriifolius and is known only from Grahamstown and the Zuurberg.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: At higher altitudes, the radical leaves of H. pallidum tend to be lanceolate-elliptic; at lower altitudes they tend to be ovate-elliptic, more like those of H. oxyphyllum, and some specimens are difficult to place. It may be significant that difficulty arises when the two species are sympatric.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: 1-2 feet high, with purplish stems and pale pedunc. and foliage. Leaves 1-1 1/2 inch long, their lobes 6-8 lines long, 1-3/4 line diameter. Pedunc. straw-colour, 2-3 times forked; pedicels 1 1/2-2 1/2 inches long.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1865. Compositae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 44-530. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/1/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: A very distinctive species, easily recognized by its subglobose heads with golden-brown, concave bracts, the innermost bracts often tipped opaque white and minutely radiating.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Phymaspermum scoparium is unlikely to be confused with any of the other discoid species. It is easily recognised by the subsessile, axillary heads, apically spinescent stems, and florets with a pilose corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: Cineraria atriplicifolia is distinguished from C. decipiens by its glabrous cypselae, and from C. deltoidea by the deeper lobing of its leaves, which are also more pinnatifid, and by its lanceolate (not auriform) auricles. Its growth form also differs from C. deltoidea in that it does not form scrambling shrubs or creepers. The entire plant is essentially glabrous, except for a few trichomes in the angles of the lobes of the leaves. These trichomes are of two types: (i) glandular and capitate, c. 6 cells forming uniseriate stalk; and (ii) short, eglandular, slightly tapering, 8-9 cells.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: This species appears to be very similar to or the same as E. integrifolia Baker which occurs in the DRC, Congo, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Malawi, and Madagascar. Emilia integrifolia has more capitula than E. limosa, as many as 14 in lax or congested terminal corymbs and the capitula are smaller. However, intermediate specimens exist, e.g. Fanshawe F7937 (SRGH) from Broken Hill, Zambia and Robinson 2645 (SRGH) from Mkushi, Zambia are like E. integrifolia with many capitula, but of the larger size seen in E. limosa. Similarly, Gilbert & Mesfin Tadesse 6455 (PRE) from Kenya has the larger capitula typical of E. limosa but more than 3 or 4 per corymb, whereas Robinson 3597 (SRGH) from Kalenda Plain in the Mwinilungu District of Zambia has slightly smaller capitula but few (2 or 3) per stem branch.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV. 2014. A synopsis of Emilia (Senecioneae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa. Phytotaxa 159(3): 195-210. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.159.3.3] [All rights reserved]

description: E. speciosissimus is variable in leaf size, peduncle length, and involucre size, but nevertheless it is an always easily recognized species. Forms from Calvinia Division often have comparatively small involucres. Occasionally many leaves are entire, and in the Bidouw Mountains I have found entire-leaved forms, connected with normal pinnatipartite-leaved forms by all kinds of transitions.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. othonnoides is a characteristic and easily recognized species, although the leaves are fairly variable. Apart from in thickness the leaves vary in lobation from pinnatipartite to few-lobed or entire. Rarely (e.g., in my collection from Laingsburg Div.) most leaves are entire.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: This new species is related to R. sedifolia. It differs in a number of characters, notably by the campanulate involucres, smaller and much more pilose achenes and distinctly foveolate leaves, a condition caused by the impressed glands. The wide involucres with apically spreading bracts is probably a derived condition in this species.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with H. trilineatum but has differently shaped leaves, broadest at the base.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The smallest species in the genus, Steirodiscus gamolepis is distinctive in its short, few-lobed leaves and diminutive, markedly pedunculate capitula with the peduncle grading into the narrowly campanulate or obconic involucre. The rays are relatively few, up to half as many as the involucral lobes, and the ovaries and cypselas are pubescent in the basal two thirds but glabrous above. The corollas of the disc florets are glabrous and unique in the genus in the short upper expanded portion of the perianth tube, much shorter than both the cylindrical lower portion and the lobes. Other members of sect. Psilothonna are larger in all respects, with less conspicuous peduncles that are sharply differentiated from the involucre, ± as many rays as involucral lobes, disc florets that are sparsely puberulous on the corolla, with the upper expanded portion ± as long as the lobes and the lower portion, and glabrous ovaries and cypselas. The peduncles in S. gamolepis are, unusually tough and wiry. The seasonally inundated habitat is unique in the genus, other species preferring drier, mostly sandy flats.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Joubert, L. 2013. A taxonomic revision of the small Cape genus Steirodiscus (Asteraceae: Senecioneae). Bothalia 43(1): 109-119. [CC BY]

description: E. ericoides is fairly variable, e.g. in height, leaf-shape, and length of the rays. Forms from Bredasdorp Division have particularly short and rather appressed leaves, and their stems are often several dm tall. Plants from Riversdale Division are normally more dwarf with stems often less than 10 cm high, and their leaves are longer and basally spreading. The ligule length varies with no distinct geographical pattern. The species has been much confused with E. ericifolius ever since Harvey in `Flora capensis' (1865, p. 159) included De Candolle's two species of Psilothamnus in Gamolepis ericoides. Admittedly, E. ericoides is very similar in habit to E. ericifolius, especially to the forms with erecto-patent leaves [= Psilothamnus ericifolius (Belang.) DC.]. Some differences in leaf-shape, like the curvation, the lateral grooves and the broad leaf-base of E. ericoides, may serve to distinguish the two. The absence of long papillae on the achenes of E. ericoides is another reliable distinguishing character.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Sterile specimens can be confused with St. rugulosa, but St. nervigera specimens are generally more robust and have larger leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2016. A monograph of Stoebe and Seriphium (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa and neighbouring islands. Phytotaxa 242(1): 1-84. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.242.1.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Closely resembles S. natalicola, a coastal species that flowers in spring, but distinguished by its fewer, longer involucral bracts. The type specimen is nearly glabrous; the specimen quoted below is thinly glandular-hairy.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: A. virgatum is a distinct and easily recognized species especially by its minute and densely crowded capitula with few involucral bracts and only 2-3 florets. The male florets are broadly campanulate above, more distinctly campanulate than in any other species within Anaxeton.
bibliographicCitation: Lundgren, J. 1972. Revision of the genus Anaxeton Gaertn. (Compositae). Opera Bot. 31: 5-59. [All rights reserved]

description: Two distinct leaf shapes can be distinguished, viz. filiform leaves up to 1.5 mm broad and linear to falcate leaves more than 1.5 mm broad. Populations with the above-mentioned leaf shapes occur sympatrically. Isolated populations studied from the Swartberg and Lang Kloof areas revealed that the linear leaves are rigid with cartilaginous, thickened margins. Anatomical studies of the leaf indicated that these populations have lignified epidermal cell walls. From the above it is clear that the leaves may either be terete, involute or flat and that the flat leaves may possess thickened margins and lignified epidermal cell walls.
bibliographicCitation: Weitz, FM. 1989. A revision of the genus Corymbium L. (Asteraceae). S. African J. Bot. 55: 598-629. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1989); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: It overlaps with S. brachypodus in the southernmost part of its area. In the Umgeni valley, Natal, for instance, they grow together and flower at the same time. Although maintained here as a separate species, it is possible that subspecific rank might be more appropriate. The Rhodesian S. callimocephalus S. Moore is closely allied.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its relatively broad leaves, mostly oblong-elliptic to broadly obovate with sub-cordate or cordate base, the upper surface sparsely pilose and the lower surface densely woolly-tomentose and prominently reticulately veined. The inner two series of involucral bracts are oblong-elliptic, 3-4 mm long and abruptly apiculate or shortly mucronate. Hilliardiella flanaganii, with similar vestiture, is sympatric with H. hirsuta in the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg but favours moister situation and is distinguished by the leaves cuneate or attenuate at the base and the larger capitula with longer, lanceolate inner involucral bracts, 5-7 mm long, narrowing gradually to a long-acuminate, almost pungent apex.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Hilliardiella (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 106: 41-59. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: M. bodkinii is a small shrublet immediately recognizable by its densely greyish tomentose leaves, mostly without axillary brachyblasts. The midveins are easily seen if the tomentum is removed from the leaves. Further, M. bodkinii has comparatively few capitula per synflorescense, scarious involucral bracts usually covered by hairs towards the apex, petaloid involucral bracts spreading to erect-spreading, and clavate-tipped pappus bristles with clavate cells. M. quinqueflora is similar with 5-flowered capitula and spreading to erect-spreading petaloid involucral bracts. However, it has different foliage, often foliaceous outermost involucral bracts, the other involucral bracts being scarious and glabrous towards the apex, often obtuse and erect innermost involucral bracts, and pappus bristles with flattened to subterete rather than clavate tips. M. bodkinii may resemble M. humilis, which is endemic to the Houw Hoek Mountains, but the latter species has different foliage, though the leaves are sometimes densely greyish, but less persistently, tomentose. Furthermore, M. humilis has scarious involucral bracts that are often reddish with hairs at the base, white to creamy white petaloid involucral bracts, and pappus bristles with less conspicuous clavate cells. For comparison with M. oligocephala, which is similar.

description: E. scariosus is probably the most aromatic species of Eriocephalus. The leaves are semisucculent and, like those of the related E. africanus, have a very variable indumentum. description: E. sulcatus is closely related to E. lateriflorus, from which it differs in the more fleshy, sulcate, and more spreading leaves of a brighter green colour, and in the ciliolate leaf-margins. The involucre is somewhat different, too, with oblong and obtuse phyllaries, which are free almost from the base. The florets are similar to those of E. lateriflorus, although the pappus is normally longer in the latter species.

description: It is a very distinct species, easily distinguished from the other Dimorphotheca species. It differs from D. sinuata, which it most resembles, int. al. by being lignified and perennial, and by the shape of its leaves.

description: This species is similar to St. microphylla but can be distinguished by the white or pink florets with spreading corolla lobes, absence of pappus, and relatively few and short involucral bracts.

description: O. subulatum is a shrub with decumbent or prostrate branches. It is characterized by its densely crowded, linear, entire, and subulatemucronate leaves with more or less strongly revolute margins. The heads are disposed singly at the apices of the branches on short peduncles, the involucral scales being biseriate or subuniseriate. Unfortunately, I have only seen young, incompletely developed achenes of this species. However, it is clear from their appearance that the species belongs to the genus Osteospermum. They are 3-angled with slightly winged angles. O. subulatum's affinity to other species is not easily determined.

description: Cineraria dryogeton shows an affinity with C. geraniifolia in its growth form and leaf shape, but differs markedly in the dense covering of hairs on its stems and leaves. Cineraria geraniifolia is typically a multi-stemmed (though slender) perennial herb with reniform, lobed leaves and two or three fairly large capitula on long peduncles, with 8-13 rays and 12 or 13 involucral bracts. In contrast, C. dryogeton appears to be a single-stemmed trailing annual or biennial herb, with smaller capitula with 5 (rarely 7 or 8) rays and 8 involucral bracts. The auricles also differ, being much more sharply toothed and deeply dissected and conspicuous in C. dryogeton than in C. geraniifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: S. variabilis has been much confused with S. erubescens but is quite distinct from that species in even the broadest sense. It can be recognized by its upright habit and long-petioled radical leaves with a rather harsh indumentum. The short, very broad-based white hairs on the backs of the involucral bracts and on the peduncles are not found in S. erubescens and its close allies. These hairs are often mixed with the more delicate gland-tipped hairs common to many purple-flowered species. The whole plant has a strong sweetish odour that often persists in dried specimens. S. rhyncholaenus and S. subrubriflorus have a similar odour, but S. erubescens sens, lat.does not. Certain plants recorded mainly from Zululand (e.g. Nkandla, Gerstner 3612, NH; Nongoma, Gerstner 3824, NH; Hluhluwe Game Reserve, Ward 3684, NU, NH) but also from southernmost Natal (e.g. Ngeli slopes, Hilliard 1802) approach S. variabilis in general aspect but differ mainly in their more copious and softer glandular pubescence and lack of broad-based hairs on the involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: In the NE. part of the range (roughly Katberg, Hogsback and King William's Town to the Transkei), leaves tend to be rhomboid-elliptic and only cobwebby above, not ovate to subrotund and grey-woolly-felted as they often are in the western part of the range. Specimens from Suurberg Pass, Storms River and Komadagga are more or less intermediate in shape and cobwebby above. H. petiolare is distinguished from its close allies, H. patulum and H. pandurifolium, by its flat, not crisped-undulate, leaf margins, and from the latter also by its more obtuse, concave involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Diagnostic features: Basal leaves villous, glandular hairs on both surfaces, viscid; blades linear to sub-falcate. Corymbophore hispid. Heads in corymbose clusters arranged in a corymb. Involucral bracts scabrid, viscid. Flowers white. Ovary hirsute. The specific epithet villosum refers to the villous leaves described by Linneaus filius as 'villoso-lanatum'. C. villosum is closely related to C. africanum subsp. scabridum, but differs from the latter in habit, especially the leaves which are villous and viscid, the longer corolla tube and the longer pedicel. It differs from C. enerve by its villous leaves, longer corolla tube and bracts which are scabrid. Populations from the Elim, Bredasdorp localities have a coarser leaf surface, a more ramified conflorescence, but still typically corymbose.

description: A magnificent sight, curtaining the trees with brilliant yellow. The stems root easily and it is often cultivated. The heads are subject to insect attacks, the larvae producing hard top-shaped galls.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Specimens can be much dwarfed with densely tufted branches and small leaves, or laxer with relatively large leaves. Variation, which is probably induced by growing conditions, is continuous and there is no geographical patterning to it; it is not possible to uphold the two varieties described, purportedly distinguishable in characters of leaf size, shape and degree of reflexion of the tips. Sometimes confused with H. litorale, but the crisped-undulate leaf margins of H. obtusum are a good distinguishing feature, and so is the uniseriate pappus.

description: Much confused with G. declinatum and G. capense, G. austroafricanum is characterized by its lax habit, spreading and generally obtuse leaves, clusters of heads on conspicuous peduncles that carry the heads well above the foliage, erect involucral bracts, and pappus wanting in the ('female') flowers. In both G. declinatum and G. capense the compound head is closely surrounded by leaves and the ('female') flowers are pappose. There are differences too in the shapes and set of the leaves and in the involucral bracts.

description: Phymaspermum appressum is easily recognised by the prominently appressed leaves, entirely scarious involucral bracts and purplish ray florets. It can only be confused with the closely related P. oppositifolium, from which it differs in the alternate leaves, the hemispherical to cyathiform involucres, and the ovate to obovate involucral bracts.

description: A distinctive species with several unusual or unique features, viz. coarse haired and hence greyish-green leaves, which gradually diminish in size towards the synflorescenses and which gives an impression of a corymbophore; generally rosy flowering shoots, peduncles and synflorescenses; dense and campanulate often flattened synflorescenses; and comparatively small capitula. M. riparia sometimes has similar foliage, but the leaves are green rather than greyish-green; the capitula clusters have long peduncles and are free from one another; and the cypselas are blackish-brown and whitish-papillose. M. confusa, like M. rhoderoides generally has rosy synflorescenses: however, it has green, not greyish-green, leaves; free capitula clusters; and only three pappus bristles per flower.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to H. herniarioides but differing in its smaller heads and involucral bracts with tips pellucid or subopaque, whitish suffused with brown, not opaque snow-white nor with a red or brown patch.

description: H. odoratissimum shows great variation in leaf size and indumentum; particularly robust plants with large leaves are found in the Transvaal and Swaziland, but these can be matched elsewhere in the geographical range of the species. The distinguishing features of H. odoratissimum are its leaves, generally broadest in the upper part, and decurrent on the stems in long wings, and the heterogamous heads with hairy achenes and pappus bristles cohering strongly by patent cilia. H. gymnocomum is very closely allied.

description: Although closely related to E. microphyllus, E. microcephalus can be distinguished by the thin, small leaves 0.8-1.6 x 0.3-0.5 mm, slender, delicate branches and mostly red-purple young shoots with a diameter of less than 1 mm. The leaves of E. microphyllus are (1.2-)1.5-4.0(-7.0) x 0.6-0.8 mm on rigid branches. Internodes of young shoots of E. microcephalus are 4.0-8.5 mm long as opposed to the 3-5 mm of those of E. microphyllus. Side branches are mostly opposite, forming an angle of 70-90° with the main axis in E. microcephalus, but less than 70° in E. microphyllus. E. microcephalus is fairly rare and restricted to a few high mountains, whereas E. microphyllus is common in Namaqualand.

description: Typically, S. latifolius has simple leafy stems, the leaves mostly more or less oblong, thick-textured, the side nerves rather obscure, margins distantly callose-denticulate. It is the unbranched stem more or less uniformly leafy right up to the inflorescence branches that gives the plant its characteristic facies, and serves to distinguish it from S. retrorsus DC, which often has the main stem branching from near ground level and leaves crowded on the lower part of the stem then more distant and decreasing rapidly in size upwards, the upper leaves mostly markedly lanceolate-acuminate. I cannot distinguish them on any characters other than this difference in leaf shape and arrangement, though there is also a slight tendency for the involucral bracts to be longer in S. latifolius. Not all specimens can be placed, but S. retrorsus grows mainly at higher altitudes in Natal than S. latifolius and their areas barely overlap.

description: Ifloga pilulifera can be confused with I. repens, but I. pilulifera is an erect shrub, and although both species have the heads clustered in dense glomerules or short oblong racemes, these are differently arranged because of this difference in habit. In I. pilulifera, the compound heads terminate very short lateral branchlets set round the main branches; in I. repens, the flowering branchlets arise from only one side of the prostrate main branches. This arrangement is not apparent in every specimen, but a further distinguishing character is the size of the heads: c. 4-5 mm long in I. pilulifera, up to 3.25 mm long in I. repens. The type specimen of I. pilulifera has hirsute involucral bracts, which make recognition easy: specimens with glabrous or nearly glabrous bracts may present difficulty. As in I. repens, the individual heads in I. pilulifera are surrounded by very few leaves, a character that precludes confusion with I. ambigua, which in addition has smaller heads.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1981. A revision of Ifloga in southern Africa, with comments on the northern hemisphere species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 82: 293-312. [All rights reserved]

description: A very variable species as far as growth form and involucral bracts are concerned. I could not find any reason to keep the northern African and southern African specimens separate, although there is some degree of variation in the growth form (the North African specimens tend to be more dwarf shrubs), the degree of hairiness (often more densely hairy in North African specimens), the slightly longer lobe of the female florets in the North African specimens and the short penicillate, apical appendages more often present on the apices of the style branches of the female florets in the North African specimens. Abnormal inflorescences were observed in some specimens from Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia (North Africa) (Mairé s.n. (P), Cosson s.n. (P), Cosson et al. (P) and Chevallier s.n. (P)). The individual florets are borne on elongated pedicels or ovaries, crowned with abnormal pappus hairs, so that the individual florets rise above the involucral bracts. Some inflorescences appear spicately arranged: the capitula arranged one above the other.
bibliographicCitation: Herman, PPJ. 2013. Cypsela morphology in the genus Nolletia (Asteraceae, Astereae) and a revision of the genus. Phytotaxa 122(1): 1-44. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with H. acutatum but that species has nearly smooth receptacles and hairy achenes, and with H. pannosum, which has similar receptacle and ovaries, but smooth, lemon-yellow, acute involucral bracts.

description: M. burchellii is recognised by the rigid, erect, often dark red or brownish, linear or narrowly elliptic or very narrowly obovate leaves. During flowering time, (January) February to May (June), no or at most two leaves are present, as the leaves from the previous growing season are burnt down and only the spiky petiole-like bases are persistent. In M. burchellii, as in M. coriacea, flowering is induced by fire. Plants collected before or long after flowering, usually have many leaves (up to 30), leaves are only present from June onwards. Plants of M. burchellii without leaves resemble M. coriacea plants without leaves and it is almost impossible to separate the two taxa in this condition. M. burchellii can be distinguished from M. coriacea by the linear or narrowly elliptic or very narrowly obovate leaves with a single main vein and entire margins; in M. coriacea, the leaves are mostly obovate, sometimes elliptic to broadly elliptic with 3 to 5 main veins and entire or apically few, broad dentate margins. Although M. coriacea mostly has solitary or 2-headed synflorescences while M. burchellii usually has corymbosely arranged capitula, solitary capitula are also sometimes found in M. burchellii.

[Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: E. subcarnosus in the present circumscription is the most widely spread and also the most variable of the South African species. It belongs to a critical group, which has suffered much confusion in literature and herbaria. The complex pattern in this group is partly due to the wide distribution in ecologically very diverse environments and partly to the occurrence of polyploidy. A full understanding of the group can be accomplished only by detailed cytological and experimental investigations, and the present taxonomic treatment should be regarded as preliminary. The considerable variation in, e.g., size of pollen grains indicates the urgency of further cytological studies. My attempts at a more natural classification have resulted in 1) the separation of several taxa as species distinct from E. subcarnosus (E. multifidus, cuneatus, pleiodontus, namaquensis, namibensis), and 2) the distinction of four subspecies within E. subcarnosus. The four subspecies are quite characteristic in their extreme forms, but they are apparently closely related and in some cases connected by transitional forms. There is considerable variation in length of style branches of the disc-florets between and within the subspecies, but the pistils are always functionally fertile. Size and shape of the florets are less variable.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: M. crenata can be distinguished by the usually succulent, shortly petioled leaves with dark red, shiny, crenate margins. The leaves of M. crenata and M. hirsuta are very similar and these two species could be confused with each other. M. hirsuta is larger in all aspects. M. crenata is distinguished by the shorter (up to 18.5 mm long) ray florets (up to 29 mm long in M. hirsuta), the presence of staminodes in the ray florets (staminodes absent in M. hirsuta), and the `2-ribbed' cypselae (4- or 5-ribbed in M. hirsuta) with colourless ribs [mature fruits not seen] (ribs dark brown in M. hirsuta).
bibliographicCitation: Herman, PPJ; Zinnecker, U. 2016. A taxonomic revision of the genus Mairia (Asteraceae, Astereae) in South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 105: 45-60. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The first collection of this plant was made by Maurice Evans on the upper Polela in July 1895. Evans was a pioneer collector in the Drakensberg, and the specific epithet honours him. S. mauricei is allied to S. caudatus, which has larger heads (involucral bracts c. 11-14 mm long), glabrous or only sparsely hispidulous achenes, and grows in marshy places, flowering between September and November.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: M. oligocephala is a small densely tomentose shrublet possessing a few unique characters that make the species easily recognizable: only one or two capitula at the tips of the flowering branches, innermost involucral bracts with dorsal hairs, zygomorphic corollas, as well as spheroid, dark brown cypselas. Another small densely tomentose plant with 5-flowered capitula is M. bodkinii, but it has a larger number of capitula arranged in clusters, glabrous innermost involucral bracts, actinomorphic corollas and glabrous cypselas. These features also distinguish M. humilis from M. oligocephala. Yet another sometimes densely tomentose Metalasia with a similar habit is M. tenuifolia, but it has 3-flowered capitula in clusters, glabrous innermost involucral bracts, actinomorphic corollas and smaller, glabrous, cypselas.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Phymaspermum leptophyllum is unique in that the epidermal cells of the cypselas are anticlinally elongated so that they obscure the ribs and hide much of the stalk on the trichomes, making them appear sessile. It can be confused with the sympatric and closely related P. aphyllum both of which have linear leaves and lanceolate to oblong involucral bracts (outer bracts of P. leptophyllum are sometimes triangular). However, in addition to the anticlinally elongated epidermal cells of the cypselas P. leptophyllum differs from P. aphyllum in that it is more densely leafy, with persistent leaves, ± 1.0-2.0 mm wide, the branches are not longitudinally white striped and the peduncles do not become spinescent.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: Differs from D. montana only in that the colour of the ray florets is not yellow or orange-yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1957. Contributions to the knowledge of Dimorphotheca montana T.Norl. Bot. Not. 110(2): 141-292. [All rights reserved]

description: The Madagascan B. merana (Baker) Humbert is very similar, differing mainly in its narrower involucres and phyllaries and longer corolla-lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Beentje, HJ. 2000. The genus Brachylaena (Compositae: Mutisieae). Kew Bull. 55(1): 1-41. [All rights reserved]

description: The margins of the ray achenes wings are irregularly crenale or sinuate and in extreme cases the primary wings are partly divided into a few small secondary wings.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1957. Contributions to the knowledge of Dimorphotheca montana T.Norl. Bot. Not. 110(2): 141-292. [All rights reserved]

description: E. erectus is an easily recognized species on account of the short curved leaves and the free involucral bracts. The latter character led Compton to propose the new genus Lysichlamys, comprising two species with L. erecta as the type. This species is certainly closely related to E. rehmannii, and I have interpreted a few specimens from the Witteberg as hybrids between these two species. It should be mentioned that two collections of E. erectus were found to have rather poor pollen without showing signs of hybridity (Esterhuysen 24907 and Wall s.n., with 32-67% perfect pollen grains). In spite of this they have formed well-developed achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: H. aureofolium is allied to H. cylindriflorum but can be distinguished by its broadly campanulate, not cylindric campanulate, heads containing ±60-75 flowers, not 15-35, and involucral bracts with tips ±2 mm long, not 1 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The distinguishing marks of S. bupleuroides are its few long narrow leaves, mostly at least 10 times as long as broad (ignore the lowermost and the uppermost leaves, which are often somewhat reduced), turbinate heads with 8 involucral bracts mostly 4-5 mm long, and 5, very rarely 6, rays. In Natal it seems to be common up to c. 1000 m above sea level, and has been more rarely collected up to c. 1500 m. Above c. 1300 m, it overlaps in distribution with S. scitus, which has the same facies as S. bupleuroides but is distinguished by its larger, more campanulate heads (involucral bracts mostly 12-14), rarely only 8-10, mostly 4.5-6.5 mm long, rays generally 8, rarely only 5). It is possible intermediates occur where the two species are sympatric: this needs investigation in the field. See also S. urophyllus and S. glaberrimus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Similar to B. setifera, but easily distinguished by its leaves, harshly pubescent, not bristly, above and white-felted, not harshly pubescent, below. Also, it has very different achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: This species vegetatively is almost identical to Se. incana but may be clearly separated from that species by floral and involucral characters.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2016. A monograph of Stoebe and Seriphium (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa and neighbouring islands. Phytotaxa 242(1): 1-84. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.242.1.1] [All rights reserved]

description: M. embescens is a variable species that is not easily characterized. The leaves are often slightly curved outwards. M. embescens is further recognized by its usually pink synflorescenses with generally distinctly branched capitula clusters, containing 3-flowered free capitula. It belongs to a small group of similar and closely related species that are characterized by a transverse ridge beneath the tip on the innermost involucral bracts. It is also similar to a few other more distantly related species, e. g. M. fastigiata, which however differs in that its leaves are usually more acute and straight, and it has 5-flowered capitula and ribbed cypselas. Populations from the western part of the distribution have different foliage, viz. straight leaves with more conspicuous axillary brachyblasts. However, such specimens are typical in other features, e. g. the involucre. Such is the type of M. embescens. M. cymbifolia also has slightly or distinctly curved but concave leaves. Similar leaves occur very rarely in M. embescens, but the former species has involucral bracts that are concave to deeply concave apically, and capitula that are fused to one another by many hairs into obscurely branched clusters. Anomalous specimens are found, for example, on the Caledon Swartberg, where plants with sparse foliage, and dense pink or white synflorescenses have been collected. I saw depauperate specimens with comparatively small and few capitula in a recently burnt area on the northwestern slopes of the Caledon Swartberg. The disjunct populations in Bredasdorp Div., i. e. in the east to southeastern part of the distribution range, have the longest leaves, the most robust appearance, and, comparatively, the shortest outermost involucral bracts. Specimens from the Klein River and the Babylon's Tower Mountain ranges, and from towards the northwestern part of the distribution area, have outermost involucral bracts about half as long as, or slightly longer than, the innermost ones, and conspicuously reddish outer involucral bracts. For comparison with M. seriphiifolia and M. serrata, which may be similar to M. erubescens, see taxonomic note under those species.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: E. euryopoides is well characterized by its glabrous, normally three-forked leaves with linear lobes, in combination with the comparatively short peduncles. E. brachypodus, too, has short peduncles and often three-forked leaves but differs, i.a., in the much more pointed leaf-lobes and distinctly woolly leaf-axils. The most closely related species appears to be E. chrysanthemoides. In spite of the very different foliage there are several important characters in common between E. euryopoides and chrysanthemoides, like the subbiseriate and rather unequal involucral bracts, and the shape and surface of the achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: G. griquense is characterized by its linear or linear-lanceolate acute to acuminate leaves, heads borne well above the foliage leaves, outer involucral bracts white-woolly on the backs and inner bracts with long snow-white tips overtopping the flowers. The ('bisexual') flowers are generally epappose. G. griquense is sometimes sympatric with G. austroafricanum, which is easily distinguished by its spreading, narrowly spathulate and generally obtuse leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This collection was misidentified as Petalacte epaleata (now Anderbergia epaleata) by Hilliard. The leaves are distinctly smaller and more closely set, often crowded on brachyblasts. The leaves are oblong rather than spatulate, and their margins are more distinctly revolute than in A. epaleata. Furthermore, the capitulescence is more lax and broad with a different type of indumentum. Thus, the outer involucral bracts of A. rooibergensis are glossy and whitish sericeous, as compared to the greyish-brownish, thin and araneose tomentum in A. epaleata. Other distinctive features of A. rooibergensis are the larger petaloid tips of the inner involucral bracts, the pubescent cypselas, and the very different pappus with short and obtuse apical teeth.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1996. Anderbergia B.Nord., a new genus of everlastings (Compositae-Gnaphalieae) from the Cape Province  . Ann. Naturhist. Mus. Wien 98(Suppl.B): 403-418. [All rights reserved]

description: P. camphorata seems to be a polymorphic species as regards the arrangement and the surface-covering of the leaves, varying from opposite to alternate in var. laevigata, alternate in the other forms, and from entirely glabrous in var. laevigata to densely setose all over the surface in var. armata. These differences, however, are not associated with any others, the flower-heads being identical in all.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, J; Phillips, EP. 1917. A revision of the genus Pteronia (Compositae). Ann. S. African Mus. 9(1): 277-329. [All rights reserved]

description: M. divergens may be recognized by the often declinate leaves, and by the outermost involucral bracts having a petaloid and generally brown to dark brown lamina. It shows some variation in habit, colour and shape of the synflorescenses, as well as in shape and size of the outermost involucral bracts. Other species that might have similar synflorescenses are M. pulchella, M. cephalotes and M. inversa, but they all have white, pink or reddish outermost involucral bracts, not brown to dark brown. M. pulchella also has a more erect habit, spreading to erect-spreading, longer leaves, white synflorescenses with outermost involucral bracts that are often light brownish above the stereome. Specimens of ssp. divergens from the southern part of the Cape Peninsula are comparatively slender, with an often creeping, sometimes erect, sometimes mat-forming habit and often have acicular leaves. Similar specimens are sometimes also found in other parts of the distribution. The slender habit is possibly a modification due to environmental factors. Harvey described M. divergens á gracilis from such material. Specimens on the summit of Table Mountain are often low and compact, and such is the type of M. depressa Harv. The species comprises two subspecies based on morphological features of the synflorescense and involucre. In localities where the two taxa are more or less sympatric, individuals are not easily placed in either subspecies as the character patterns merge into one another. Such specimens that have been investigated possess normal and obviously fully fertile pollen.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely related to E. ericoides and E. awmaticus from which it can be distinguished by its much-branched, spinescent habit, shiny, light green leaves, often with a red-purple tinge, and marginal female florets with lamina about as long as style branches.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: E. transvaalensis is a highly variable species, which has been described under six different valid specific names. Some of the characters used for distinction of these `species', e.g., length of the annual stems, length of the rays, and striation of the peduncles, vary independently and without any distinct geographical pattern. The most striking variation is found in shape, venation and colour of the leaves. Correlated variation of some leaf characters and more or less distinct discontinuities combined with distributional data form the basis for a subdivision of the species into two subspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to H. chionosphaerum but distinguished by its broader and differently shaped leaves with nerves scarcely visible.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Much confused with H. stoloniferum and may be found in herbaria under that name, but easily distinguished by its different foliage, smaller heads, and different pappus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Unique in the genus in its rosulate habit and dimorphic foliage, with a basal rosette of obovate to oblanceolate leaves that are glabrescent at flowering, and cauline leaves that are scattered or distant and linear-ericoid with revolute margins. The rather lax inflorescences are also characteristic although the individual capitula are not especially distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Hilliardiella (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 106: 41-59. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: H. longifolium is distinguished by its long and often relatively narrow leaves, glabrous above at maturity, woolly below, heads in an open panicle (though this is often congested initially), and glossy yellow acute involucral bracts. It is very closely allied to H. mixtum.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A rather variable species, recognized by non-twisted, erect-spreading to erect, distinctly mid-veined, generally acuminate leaves; 3-flowered, narrow capitula; very acute to acuminate outermost and outer involucral bracts that are less hairy than is otherwise usual; and also by cypselas with obtuse papillae. M. pungens is rarely short, compact and rigid, and most often has a habit like many other Metalasia species. Short-leaved specimens may in rare cases resemble short-leaved specimens of M. densa, since the dividing line between twisted and non-twisted for short leaves is not always clear. The involucres may also be similar, but the papillae on the cypselas always differ between species. Some aberrant specimens have been collected. The foliage and sometimes the involucres vary a lot. Specimens from the westernmost localities have narrowly obconical, often almost glabrous involucres with truncate and apically irregularly and coarsely dentate innermost involucral bracts, but these specimens do not represent discrete units, since these features merge with the more usual ones.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: D. zeyheri is a perennial herb with stems only up to 2.5 dm high: these are closely leafy at the base, but above it sparsely leafy and terminating in a naked, one-headed peduncle. The leaves are lanceolate-linear or linear and vary very much as regards the shape of the margin, for in one and the same individual one may find entire, dentate, pinnatifid, and occasionally pinnatipartite leaves. The ray flowers are white above, but beneath their colour varies a little just as in D. cuneata, and may be bluish, purplish brown or brown goldish.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The chief distinguishing mark of H. lepidissimum is its leaves with crisped margins and upper surface eventually free of wool to reveal long shaggy hairs, green when fresh, brown when dried; in contrast, the leaves of both H. mimetes and H. rudolfii, its close allies, are persistently tomentose above and grey, with smooth margins. Colour of the involucral bracts varies from white to cream to pale or deep straw-colour. Plants with white or straw-coloured bracts may grow together, though plants with white bracts are commoner on the Transvaal Highveld and in the Soutpansberg than plants with straw-coloured bracts, and the opposite is true in KwaZulu-Natal. There is also some variation in size of heads, big-headed plants being commonest in the Soutpansberg and in the mountains of the NE. Transvaal.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This little known new species is a rather tall shrub with slender capitula. It is very glutinous with leaves as sticky as those of R. viscosa. However, R. resinifera is more closely allied to R. multipunctata, from which it differs in its elliptic, very glutinous leaves and characters of the achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: Its narrow heads with short appressed outer involucral bracts, and relatively large achenes with short beak and buff-coloured pappus make recognition simple among species recorded in South Africa.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: E. decumbens is allied to E. montanus, with which it sometimes grows together. The two species are quite distinct, although both are often found under the name E. montanus. Some of the most obvious differences are the decumbent growth, the bluish leaf colour, the less connate involucral bracts, and the pubescent achenes of E. decumbens. Specimens cultivated in greenhouses keep their decumbent growth and characteristic leaf colour.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: M. montana is a compact shrublet with generally only slightly involute leaves; dense and com-paratively small synflorescenses with often less than 30 capitula; and petaloid involucral bracts often erect-spreading. It resembles the common and very variable M. densa, but that species often has larger synflorescenses containing more and often narrower capitula; and 6-8 series of involucral bracts, of which the outermost are less than half as long as the innermost ones. M. montana is also similar to M. alfredii, another montane species with the same habit, but M. alfredii has densely greyish tomentose young leaves and larger capitula with larger involucral bracts. M. trivialis has an involucre similar to that of M. montana, but differs in its wholly different foliage and generally obtuse pappus bristles.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with H. argentissimum but that species has linear or linear-lanceolate leaves with silky indumentum.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by the lyrate-pinnatisect leaves and hirsute tips to the corolla lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Much confused with H. ecklonis whose tufted rosettes contrast in the field with the tight mats of H. vernum, but in the herbarium this difference disappears. However, the leathery leaves of H. vernum, glabrous above and with side veins scarcely discernible, will generally serve to distinguish it from glabrous-leaved specimens of H. ecklonis, where the side veins are clearly visible in the membranous blade.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Osteospermum ilicifolium is characterized, as the specific name indicates, by its more or less Ilex-like, subcoriaceous leaves. The breadth of the leaves varies enormously in one and the same individual as well as in separate individuals. On Table Mt. in the Cape district there are extremely broad-leafed forms with broadly ovate leaves up to 4 cm broad, and in Bains Kloof in the Paarl district extremely narrow-leafed forms with narrowly lanceolate leaves hardly 0.5 cm broad are found. These differences in the shape of the leaves are in this case probably due to the habitat alone. The plant has a strong scent, and at least when dried feels rough from hard, raised points or short, rigid hairs, which are glanduliferous.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]
