description: Cineraria decipiens is distinguished from C. deltoidea by its growth form, i.e. a short-lived perennial herb, not rambling as the more long-lived C. deltoidea does, and by its ciliate and hairy cypselae, vs. glabrous in C. deltoidea in KwaZulu-Natal, where it co-occurs. It also has lanceolate auricles, which may be conspicuous or very small, whereas those of C. deltoidea are distinctly auriform. Cineraria decipiens is distinguished from C. atriplicifolia by having ciliate and hairy cypselae and the apical lobe tends to be shorter than in that species. Two types of trichomes are present on C. decipiens: (i) glandular capitate trichomes, 6-8 cells long; (ii) short eglandular tapering trichomes, 8-10 cells long, both mostly in the angles of the lobes of the leaves. Ward 8858 (K) from near Matubatuba is an unusual specimen with very few disc florets per capitulum and ray florets with very short limbs (1.5-2.0 mm long). Specimens from Swaziland also have small capitula with short rays and unusually narrow involucral bracts. Compton 31515 (K, NBG, PRE) from Komati Pass in the Mbabane District has ciliate and hairy cypselae and its auricles match C. decipiens, although it appears to be a climber like C. deltoidea and has cobwebby axils like C. lobata subsp. soutpansbergensis. Burtt & Hilliard 3287 (NU) from the Swaziland-KwaZulu-Natal border, Nsubane Pass from Ingwavuma to Gollell (508 m) is fairly typical of C. decipiens, but has quite hairy leaves with short eglandular trichomes.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: A very fine species closely allied to P. adenocarpa, Harv., but distinguished by its conspicuously puberulous branchlets, frequently trinerved leaves with very finely and densely scabrid-ciliolate margins. Unfortunately there is no record of the locality in which Masson collected the specimen. Named in compliment to Mr. Spencer Moore, of the Natural History Museum, South Kensington.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, J; Phillips, EP. 1917. A revision of the genus Pteronia (Compositae). Ann. S. African Mus. 9(1): 277-329. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its suberect, rod-like, densely leafy stems with ascending, subsessile, overlapping leaves that are coarsely toothed in the upper half, with a pale greenish, crisped-felted pubescence on the undersurface. Gymnanthemum crataegifolium is often confused with G. corymbosum, with which it co-occurs in some places and which is very similar in habit and foliage but with densely silvery, appressed indumentum on the leaf underside.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Gymnanthemum Cass. (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 102: 81-101. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2015.07.015] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: At first glance this plant recalls an Athrixia in the spreading almost pungent points of the outer involucral bracts, the colour of the ray florets and the slender leaves (cf. Athrixia angustissima DC). From Athrixia, however, it differs markedly in the presence of numerous long palae on the receptacle, in the short hairy achene, and in the pappus. Its short achene and receptacle characters recall Geigeria, but there are marked differences in general habit, flower colour, and involucre. The pappus characters, moreover, distinguish Alatoseta from all other genera. The winged pappus bristles are curiously like the awned bilobed membranous glumes of some grasses, e.g. Pentaschistis. They are clearly related to the awned pappus scales in some Geigeria spp., but the wings in Alatoseta are attached near the base of the bristle, whereas in Geigeria the bristle is apparently excurrent from the entire scale.
bibliographicCitation: Compton, RH. 1931. The Flora of the Whitehill District. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 19: 269-326. [All rights reserved]

description: Although S. polelensis is known from only two localities, it will certainly be found elsewhere in these ill-botanized mountains.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1982. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: IX. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 40(2): 247-298. [CC BY-SA]

description: This species is distinguished from C. erosa by its indumentum, which comprises mainly fine narrow-based trichomes giving it a very grey (or white-woolly on younger parts) appearance. It does not have trichomes with tapering basal cells with the long apical appendage as evident in C. erosa, although a few trichomes with broad cells are evident on some leaves of some specimens of C. canescens var. flabellifolia from Namaqualand, but then these have glabrous involucral bracts, whereas those of C. erosa are thickly cobwebby, although glabrescent to some degree. The degree of dissection and depth of lobing in the leaves is generally less in C. canescens than in C. erosa, and there are fewer lateral pinnae below the lamina; however the leaves on the type specimen of C. canescens resemble C. erosa quite closely. Certain specimens of C. canescens have very short internodes and a compact growth form, probably a response to the very arid conditions in which they grow. Schlechter 8278 (E, K, WAG) is a good match of the type of C. canescens, with both some larger leaves with longer internodes on a branch and some smaller ones on a very compact branch on the WAG specimen. The Masson type of Cineraria parviflora was probably collected in Namaqualand, as Masson did journey as far north as the Khamiesberg during the period 1786 to 1795 (his third visit to South Africa), despite instructions from Banks for him to remain centred around Cape Town. The name ‘C. parviflora’ was illegitimate as it had been previously applied by Marschall von Bieberstein to plants now considered to be Caucasalia parviflora (M.Bieb.) B. Nord. Cineraria canescens var. flabellifolia has more rounded leaves, with shallower lobing, and slightly larger capitula with the glabrous involucral bracts subtended by glabrous peduncles, as opposed to cobwebby or tomentose, glabrescent involucral bracts and peduncles in var. canescens. Harvey distinguished C. canescens var. flabellifolia Harv. from var. canescens by its ‘having no lateral leaf-lobes, a broader lamina and a denser and more glabrous inflorescence.’ However, Salter 797 (K, sheet 1) has very small lateral pinnae on a few (about two) leaves. The trichomes on the type of var. flabellifolia are of the fine type; however, some of the other specimens from Namaqualand have trichomes with larger basal cells, gradually tapering to join with the fine apical appendage. An extremely tomentose form of C. canescens var. flabellifolia from Lord’s Hill, Karasburg in Namibia, known from two collections [Örtendahl 500 (K, UPS) and Pearson 7922 (K)], also has glabrous involucral bracts and fine trichomes. However, these specimens have larger leaves with shallow lobing and lack auricles. These plants could be an extension of the taxon northwards, but molecular evidence is needed to definitely conclude this. In contrast, Pearson 6239 (BOL, K) is extremely glabrescent to almost glabrous, but matches C. canescens var. canescens in terms of leaf shape, branching, size and density of capitula. It is possible that C. canescens is a more northerly form of C. erosa with a transition region in between. However without substantial evidence in the form of molecular studies at the population level, we have maintained the two species as separate.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Leaf glands wart-like, widely spaced; innermost involucre bract tips acuminate, capitula 1-flowered.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2019. Taxonomy and reclassification of South African Asteraceae genus Elytropappus (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae), the description of two new genera and two new species. Phytotaxa 403(4): 248-284. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.403.4.1] [All rights reserved]

description: A slender shrublet distinguished by its small leaves; dense and pink synflorescenses; rounded, spathulate outermost and outer involucral bracts; the petaloid bracts, which are strikingly reddish above the stereome; and by generally acute and apically not widened pappus bristles. M. serrulata is similar but differs in its foliage and pappus. The head-like synflorescenses make M. rogersii resemble M. cephalotes and its close relatives, but the latter species have an entirely different foliage, outermost involucral bracts with a conspicuous petaloid lamina and 5-flowered capitula. M. rogersii sometimes resembles M. tenuis, which, however, is often even more slender, without conspicuously head-like synflorescenses, has generally acute outermost involucral bracts without a distinct lamina and often obtuse pappus bristles. M. brevifolia has foliage similar to that of M. rogersii, but it differs in its erect habit; white, less dense and often distinctly branched synflorescenses; and apically thickened to subterete pappus bristles.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: O. triquetrum is characterized by its long, very crowded, linear-subulate and subcarnous leaves, which have a canaliculate superior surface and a keeled inferior surface due to the elevated midrib. The apices of the leaves are not at all, or only very slightly, pungent in contrast to those in O. aciphyllum. The basal leaves in O. triquetrum differ from the other leaves in not being exactly linear, but somewhat broader above the middle: in some cases they may be described as narrowly oblanceolate-linear.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: H. micropoides is very variable in the degree to which the tips of the involucral bracts are produced; there is a tendency for plants in the E. half of the range to have bracts more markedly acuminate than in plants from the W. part, but there is neither discontinuity in bract length nor absolute geographical separation. Similarly, plants with homogamous heads are commoner in the W. than in the E. The species can usually be recognized by the peculiar arrangement of the heads in racemose compound inflorescences, but this is not always clearly visible in young specimens. However, it is a character that serves to distinguish H. micropoides immediately from its close ally, H. lentonyx, which has heads crowded in terminal glomerules. Also, in H. leontonyx the heads are always heterogamous with generally more flowers and more female flowers than in H. micropoides. H. micropoides is also much confused with H. tinctum, which it resembles in the involucre. However, the pappus is clearly uniseriate, a character requiring careful observation; also, the heads are much smaller.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This species can be confused with St. fusca, which has yellow involucral bracts, or alternatively with St. phyllostachya, which has flatter leaves and long, rigid hairs towards the base of the abaxial leaf surface. Although the variation in St. capitata is extremely wide, there is no justified reason to subdivide the species.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2016. A monograph of Stoebe and Seriphium (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa and neighbouring islands. Phytotaxa 242(1): 1-84. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.242.1.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Only 1 record in PRE for EC.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Diagnostic features: Radical leaves glabrous; blades narrowly linear to falcate, sometimes chanelled, margins involute. Corymbophore scabrid. Heads distinctly pedunculate or with a short peduncle or sessile, arranged in a panicle. Involucral bracts scabrid, trifid. Flowers mauve. Ovary hirsute. C. elsiae is closely allied to C. laxum differing in scabridity of the corymbophore, cauline leaves and bracts, and with cellulosic leaf epidemal cell walls. There is a considerable variation in the arrangement of heads in the conflorescence of C. elsiae. It is either distinctly pedunculate or with a very short peduncle or sessile. The conflorescence of certain populations may vary from a simple to a much-branched panicle with pedunculated or sessile heads. Therefore, pedunculated heads is not a constant character for this species as in C. laxum. Although local races may appear distinct, continuous variation of the corymbophore morphology within a race does not warrant the subdivision of this species into infraspecific taxa.
bibliographicCitation: Weitz, FM. 1989. A revision of the genus Corymbium L. (Asteraceae). S. African J. Bot. 55: 598-629. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1989); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: There is no doubt that H. litorale is very close to H. tinctum and some specimens are difficult to place; but the fact that plants with more or less obtuse bracts are very nearly confined to low altitudes, plants with acuminate bracts to higher altitudes, seems sufficient reason to keep them apart. Also, although both species appear to be at the peak of their flowering in November, H. tinctum begins flowering in September and is fading in December, while early flowering records are few in H. litorale, which may flower as late as February.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Allied to H. tongense from which it is distinguished by its habit, at least some leaves generally greyish-white woolly on one or both surfaces, and brown outer involucral bracts. The leaf indumentum is very variable: frequently the lower leaves are woolly on one or both surfaces but the upper leaves, on the flowering twigs, are merely green and glandular; sometimes all the leaves are woolly below, glandular above; sometimes all the leaves lack wool; occasionally all the leaves are persistently woolly on both surfaces. At Witklip near Nelspruit, plants with woolly leaves, others with green leaves, still others with lower leaves woolly, upper green, grow together; elsewhere, all the plants in a colony may be wholly green, or wholly woolly, or woolly below, green above.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Resembles solitary-headed specimens of H. adenocarpum, but is readily distinguished by its glabrous ovaries.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by its 3-4-lobed, not radiate, outer flowers, with sparse pappus shorter than the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Plants in moist shady places, such as forest margins, have larger and less woolly leaves and are of laxer habit than plants out in the open.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: See notes under S. telmateius. Kamberg means 'crested mountain', its shape being not unlike that of a cock's comb, and the specific epithet is derived from this.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1982. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: IX. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 40(2): 247-298. [CC BY-SA]

description: A low, often decumbent shrublet, characterized by small synflorescenses containing comparatively few capitula, which are clearly overshot by a few bractlike leaves. Young shoots, leaves and outermost and outer involucral bracts have glands. The innermost involucral bracts are conspicuously transparent above the stereome, and hence petaloid only at the very apex.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Dense, globular synflorescences, glandular leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2019. Taxonomy and reclassification of South African Asteraceae genus Elytropappus (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae), the description of two new genera and two new species. Phytotaxa 403(4): 248-284. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.403.4.1] [All rights reserved]

description: The stems root easily, and the plant is often cultivated. It has long been a favourite house or greenhouse plant in Europe where a form with variegated leaves is commonly seen. Much confused with S. macroglossoides but that species has deltoid-ovate leaves with 3-5 sharply acute to subacute shallow lobes on either side, and calyculus bracts approximately half the length of the involucral bracts and spreading or reflexed. S. macroglossoides is found at higher altitudes in Natal than S. macroglossus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: E. discoideus is an insufficiently known species, closely allied to E. gilfillanii. It differs from the latter by the flat, not canaliculate leaves, the hispid adaxial surface and margins of the leaves, the glabrous leaf-bases, the acute leaf-tips, and the discoid heads. The constancy of these characters has to be checked when more material becomes available.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. namaquensis grows in association with E. microphyllus var. pubescens, which it superficially resembles. Especially in the western part of its distribution range where E. namaquensis is less spinescent, it is difficult to distinguish between the two species in their natural habitat. E. namaquensis has a permanently silver-sericeous indumentum in contrast to E. microphyllus var. pubescens which is basically felty, clearly seen at the growing point. As the leaves age, the indumentum becomes more sericeous, slightly wavy, and this can lead to confusion with E. namaquensis. If there is doubt, the growing points and peduncles of the specimen should be examined. In E. microphyllus var. pubescens, the young leaves at the growing points stick together because of the intertwined felty indumentum of the overlapping leaves. The leaves of E. namaquensis are always free.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Variable in leaf cutting: for example, the plant in Natal between c. 900 and 1300 m above sea level has rather distant leaf lobes that are mostly simple, while at higher altitudes the lobes may be more closely set and are often forked or with one or two lobes. The involucral bracts are nearly always minutely gland-dotted; var. glanduloso-scaber describes a plant from Leribe in Lesotho with stalked glands; similar plants have been found on the summit plateau of Lesotho near Organ Pipes Pass and Langalibalele Pass, but other high altitude material has sessile glands. Despite this variation, the stiff, rod-like branches and sharply ascending inflorescence branches producing a congested compound inflorescence give the species a distinctive facies.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: E. leiocarpus is in habit more similar to species like E. pedunculatus, dyeri and rupestris than to any of its consectioners. The absence of a pappus immediately distinguishes it from these species, however, and the true affinities are in sect. Psilosteum. No species can be singled out as very closely related to E. leiocarpus. Possibly E. hypnoides comes closest (in spite of the striking differences in size and habit), having rather similar involucres and achenes. The often sterile disc-florets with undivided or very shallowly lobed styles are remarkably similar to those typical of the genus Othonna. This must be regarded as a case of parallel evolution rather than as evidence of relationship.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: M. cymbifolia is recognized by its densely leafed, tomentose branches; by its very distinctly incurvate leaves, generally non-twisted, and concave; by its capitula being fused by hairs in the clusters; by its apically concave involucral bracts and by its apically comparatively broad pappus bristles. Specimens from the upper slopes of the Babylon's Tower have comparatively short peduncles and sometimes less concave involucral bracts. However, the capitula are fused by hairs in the clusters and the leaves are similar to those of specimens from other localities.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: The only species, and a most distinctive plant in both general aspect and peculiar pappus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Cineraria erosa is characterised by very deeply lobed leaves with a reniform outline and a ‘frilly’ appearance due to lobing and dentition with the lobes often divided into three or pinnatilobed and dentate. The capitula are small (3-5 rays) and involucral bracts are cobwebby, glabrescent but not glabrous. This helps to distinguish C. erosa from C. aspera. The trichomes have a tapering multi-celled base of 4-6(-8) cells and a long multi-celled apical appendage. The appendage often breaks off creating a papillose appearance to the leaves, what Thunberg referred to as ‘Folia..tota scabra, papillis minutis simis eminentibus, subtus pubescentia’. This species is also very similar to Cineraria canescens, distinguished mainly by the degree of the dissection of the leaves and the types of trichomes, where C. canescens mainly has fine trichomes, or ones with broader bases (in some specimens of C. canescens var. flabellifolia), but not sharply tapering as in C. erosa. Some anomalous specimens include: Pole Evans H-15841 (K) from Taungs, which has leaves like C. erosa and the trichomes match, but it has glabrous involucral bracts and a very disjunct distribution pattern; Pillans 14159 (BOL) from the Cederberg has the very dissected leaf of C. erosa, but lacks the typical trichomes, having only the fine trichomes (like C. canescens). Some specimens from the Clanwilliam/Cederberg/Piketberg area have much more shallowly lobed leaves and some have very glabrescent involucral bracts (similar to Cineraria canescens). However their trichomes match those of C. erosa. Isozyme studies at the population level are required to fully investigate the relationship between C. erosa and C. canescens.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: O. rigidum is an erect, rigid, more or less strongly lignified suffrutex or, when older, a real shrub. The leaves are sparsely dentate or dentate-pinnatifid. The upper leaves are most frequently furnished with auricles, but the lower leaves have no, or only slightly developed, auricles. The plant is clothed in all parts except the oldest ones with short glandular hairs. In a dried state it is asperous, but when living it will probably feel viscidulous owing to the glands and not at all or only very slightly asperous. O. rigidum is morphologically closely allied both to O. grandiflorum and O. spinosum. Normally at least it has one or several 3-winged achenes in each head and its branches are unarmed. It is easily distinguished from O. grandiflorum by its narrow, sessile leaves and its small, heteromorphous achenes, only c. 5 mm long. O. rigidum differs from O. spinosum by its branches never being transformed into spines. O. rigidum is besides less densely branched than O. spinosum and has, as a rule, a larger involucre than O. spinosum; in the former species it is usually more and in the latter less than 5 mm high. As regards the. shape of the achenes, O. rigidum is one of the most polymorphous species in the genus Osteospermum. Most frequently both bluntly and sharply 3-angled and 3-winged achenes occur in the same head, In several collections the winged achenes seem, however, to be entirely absent, the plants having, for instance, bluntly 3-angled and almost globular achenes. In other collections most of the achenes are sharply 3-angled, only occasional achenes being slightly 3-winged or bluntly 3-angled.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Much confused with S. quinquelobus but easily distinguished by its foliaceous calyculus bracts and hispid achenes. Also the leaf sinuses are often denticulate, not smooth.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is a small shrub and not difficult to recognize with its characteristic foliage and congested capitula. It is distantly related to the group of species around R. genistifolia and R. squarrosa.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: E. namaquensis is a low shrublet, not exceeding 5 dm in height The species comes very close to E. subcarnosus but differs by the depressed and divaricate growth, the long peduncles, and the large capitula. The pollen grains are larger than in most other taxa of the group, comparable in size only to the hexaploid E. cuneatus.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Bidens kirkii, as presently delimited, is variable in the degree of dissection of the leaf lamina. The leaves are usually pinnatisect with the linear segments often 3-5 mm wide. Some specimens from Transvaal, S. Africa, e.g. Vahrmeijr 2361 (EA, MO, SRGH) have once to twice pinnatisect leaves with narrow (c. 1-2 mm wide) segments; others (e.g. Wild 4320, type of B. schlechteri var. wildii) from Belingwe Distr., Zimbabwe have tripinnatisect leaves with the segments being only c. 1 mm wide. Specimens from Angola (B. rufovenosa ) have ovate segments.
bibliographicCitation: Mesfin Tadesse. 1993. An account of Bidens (Compositae: Heliantheae) for Africa. Kew Bull. 48(3): 437-516. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/4118718.pdf] [All rights reserved]

description: A variant with narrowly elliptic leaves, acute at the apex and gently tapering to petioles up to c. 8 mm. long, occurs in central Mozambique from Dombe to Gorongosa Mt., eg. Mendonça 2387 (LISC), Pedro 4404 (K) and Tinley 2698 (K; SRGH). Similar leaf shapes are found in specimens from the Nyoni Hills area of SE. Zimbabwe, eg. Müller 682 (K; SRGH) and Harvie 1/53 (K; SRGH), these intergrading here with the more typical B. rotundata leaf.This narrow-leaved, long-petioled variant approaches Brachylaena transvaalensis in leaf shape but has the capitula characteristic for B. rotundata with larger obconic not cyathiform involucres, and with narrow inner phyllaries blunt at the apex, not broadly acute.
bibliographicCitation: Pope, GV. 1992. 97. Compositae (part 1), Fl. Zambes. 6(1): 1-264. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, London. [CC BY]

description: Similar in aspect to H. subfalcatum, with which it may be found growing, but easily distinguished by its different indumentum, homogamous heads, and different pappus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: S. oxyondontus is part of a more or less sympatric group similar in habit, inflorescence branching and floral structure, but highly polymorphic in leaf shape and cutting. However, all show development of the peculiar leaf-like basal lobes that resemble the leaf at whose base they arise, and may therefore range from linear and entire to ovate or deltoid and deeply toothed or laciniate. Names to be considered here are S. longifolius L.f., a southern Cape species reaching as far as King Williams Town, with linear, entire leaves, S. lancifolius Turcz. based on part of Zeyher 2959, type of S. zeyheri (above in syn.) and S. surculosus MacOwan, based on MacOwan 594 from Grahamstown with narrowly lanceolate leaves. S. blattarioides, here reduced to synonymy, seems to be no more than a pubescent form of S. oxyodontus. All degrees of pubescence occur, and both glabrous and pubescent plants may grow in the same area. S. oxyodontus is sometimes confused with S. angulatus Linn. f. but that is a scandent plant with more or less rhomboid leaves with usually two (one each side) upward-pointing lobes or large teeth, and larger heads (involucral bracts (5.5-)6.5 mm long); it does not occur further east than about Grahamstown.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Roodebergia kitamurana has a characteristic habit, being a perennial herb rooting at the nodes, with opposite leaves and solitary discoid capitula with reddish hermaphroditic florets. The style is typical of the tribe Astereae with a large, apical, sterile narrowly triangular-ovate appendage and with narrow ventromarginal stigmatic lines along the lower half of the style branch. The cypselas look glabrous to the naked eye, but carry microscopic scattered twin hairs especially proximally. They are of the normal three-celled type with two parallel cells and a smaller basal cell.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 2002. A new monotypic genus of the Compositae-Astereae from the Cape Province, South Africa. Acta Phytotax. Geobot. 53(2): 101-105. [All rights reserved]

description: This handsome species is easily recognized on the flat and wide, sparsely denticulate leaves, the terminal and stout peduncles, and the large flowerheads with much-connate involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: D. sinuata is very closely allied to D. pluvialis, these species differing from each other almost exclusively by the ray flowers in the former being yellow or orange on both sides, while in the latter they are always white above and blue-violet-purple or partly also somewhat coppery, brown or white beneath. As a rule D. sinuata is less hairy than D. pluvialis, and one can sometimes meet with nearly glabrous forms of the former species. These species have different distribution centres with different climatic conditions, but they overlap in a zone between the Cape region and the Namaqua region. D. pluvialis, however, is also known from a few localities in Little Namaqualand.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Often confused with H. pandurifolium, from which it is easily distinguished by its concave obtuse involucral bracts; distinguished from H. petiolare by its crisped-undulate leaf margins.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The ray flowers are white like alabaster above and violet-blue, striate and often bordered with white beneath. The disc is azure-blue, and the inner disc flowers have slightly gibbous corolla lobes. D. ecklonis is nearly related to D. fruticosa and D. acutifolia. It differs from the former species int. al. by its acutely triangular, usually reticulate-rugose achenes, by its narrower, never broadly obovate leaves, and by its habit of growth. It is distinguished from the latter species int. al. by its achenes, which are not bluntly triangular, and by its broader leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily recognized by its small grey spathulate leaves and small heads with bright yellow squarrose bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by its congested inflorescences, leafy stems and shaggy indumentum; not unlike S. macrocephalus, but lacking rays.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: M. erectifolia is characteristic with erect to appressed and non-twisted leaves; small and dense synflorescenses with comparatively small capitula; and small cypselas. Similar to M. pungens, which however has different foliage and larger synflorescenses with wider capitula. M. erectifolia has obtuse, and darker inner involucral bracts. M. pungens and M. erectifolia are sister species.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: According to Dr. Atherstone, who collected in Little Namaqualand in 1856, this species grows in the sandy flats near the coast at Port Nolloth. The leaves are succulent and very aromatic, and, mixed with fat, used by the Namaquaa and Bastards as a perfume under the name of 'Buchu.' It is called 'Sab' in the Namaqua language, and is dried and collected for sale.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, J; Phillips, EP. 1917. A revision of the genus Pteronia (Compositae). Ann. S. African Mus. 9(1): 277-329. [All rights reserved]

description: M. alfredii is a compact much-branched shrublet with dense foliage and often tomentose young leaves, comparatively few capitula per synflorescense, acuminate outermost and outer involucral bracts, apically spreading to erect-spreading and plicate petaloid involucral bracts, and also very narrow pappus bristles. It is sometimes confused with M. montana, but that species has mainly glabrous leaves, petaloid involucral bracts that are apically erect-spreading to erect and usually not plicate. Another similar species is M. strictifolia, but this has entirely different foliage, obtuse and truncate innermost involucral bracts, and obtuse pappus bristles with clavate tips and clavate cells. M. alfredii is distinguishable from M. densa by its fewer and broader capitula per synflorescense, and by inner and innermost involucral bracts that are spreading to erect-spreading and plicate.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Much confused with H. adenocarpum, but most easily distinguished by its flowering stems, terminal in H. monticola, lateral in H. adenocarpum.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: E. integrifolius, represented by a single collection, is allied to E. munitus but sufficiently distinct to deserve recognition as a species. It differs from the latter i.a. by the entire, obtuse leaves and the papillate achenes. Possibly it can be regarded as a high montane derivative of the latter species. It also resembles E. ericoides, which likewise has entire and short curved leaves but differs by other leaf as well as fruit characters.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Diagnostic features: Basal leaves glabrous; blades narrowly to broadly linear, sometimes falcate, rigid, venation prominent. Corymbophore glabrous. Heads in corymbose clusters arranged in a corymb or lax panicle. Involucral bracts glabrous. Flowers mauve. Ovary hirsute. C. glabrum is a remarkably variable species. The differences between population groups are mainly due to the great diversity in shape and size of the radical leaves and the conflorescences. Intermediates between forms with differently shaped leaves and conflorescence structure are not uncommon and there seems to be no sharp genetic barriers between some of them. However, there are certain populations with distinct leaf shapes which differ quite radically from others. Populations occurring from the Olifants River Mountains southwards as far as the Houwhoek Mountains have filiform leaves with corymbose clusters arranged in a corymb. Within the same distribution range are also found populations with linear, rigid, cartilaginous leaves with prominent veins growing in close proximity. Populations occurring from Hottentots Holland to the Van Stadens Mountains have broad, coriaceous leaves which become rugulose when dry. They appear in the same distribution range with populations having linear, rigid, cartilaginous leaves with prominent venation. A form with broad, coriaceous leaves is found in the vicinity of Swellendam where the leaves have a slightly wavy, muricated margin, sometimes with marginal cilia. Much variation in the size and shape of the leaves can be observed under varying ecological conditions.
bibliographicCitation: Weitz, FM. 1989. A revision of the genus Corymbium L. (Asteraceae). S. African J. Bot. 55: 598-629. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1989); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Pteronia quadrifaria was treated by Merxmüller as a synonym of Pteronia lucilioides DC., based mainly on the papillate leaves of the Dinter 6190 specimen. He argued that the growth form of P. lucilioides is very variable in Namibia and that Dinter 6190 represents a densely branched, small, shrubby form. Around Aus, however, P. lucilioides is a tall, virgate shrub and the stunted dwarf shrub forms are found mostly nearer to the coast. Based on recent flowering and fruiting collections the differences between the two species were confirmed, such as the apex of the budding capitula that is constricted to truncate in P. quadrifaria and sharply acute in P. lucilioides. Furthermore the densely imbricate, decussate leaf arrangement of P. quadrifaria clearly differs from the opposite leaves of P. lucilioides, and the undulate, reflexed phyllaries of the former differ from the smooth, straight phyllaries of the latter. P. quadrifaria can also be clearly distinguished from P. lucilioides by the maroon-purple pappus (straw-coloured in the latter). Reviewing all presented evidence we conclude that this merits the resurrection of P. quadrifaria as a distinct entity. Pteronia quadrifaria is similar to P. mucronata in its leaves with ciliate margins and truncate phyllaries, but differs in its decussate-imbricate leaf arrangement, its phyllary apex not being mucronate but undulate-reflexed, and the conspicuous maroon-purple pappus.
bibliographicCitation: Kolberg, HH; Van Slageren, MWSJM. 2014. A synopsis of the genus Pteronia in Namibia including the resurrection of Pteronia quadrifaria. Kew Bull. 69(1): 9488. [DOI 10.1007/S12225-014-9488-Y] [All rights reserved]

description: Very variable in leaf size and indumentum and has the curious habit, shared with related and other species, of sometimes producing broad grey-woolly leaves at the base of the branches, narrow glabrous bright yellow-green ones at the tips. But more usually plants are either grey-woolly or green, growing in mixed communities or in pure stands of grey-leaved or green-leaved plants. Green-leaved plants are sometimes confused with H. tenuifolium and H. witbergense, but H. tenuifolium has minute appressed-trichomes, not gland dots, on the upper leaf surface, while H. witbergense has differently shaped leaves.Not eaten by stock, but used as fuel, the branches burning readily when green.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: M. plicata is distinguished by its large capitula; whitish or often yellowish-white petaloid involucral bracts which are apically regularly plicate; and by dark to blackish-brown cypselas with long, acute papillae. It is similar to both M. muricata and M. densa, of which the first species has conspicuously curved leaves and scarious, apically faintly carinate involucral bracts; whereas the latter has white petaloid involucral bracts without conspicuously plicate tips. Both these species have much shorter papillae on paler brown cypselas. Other species with yellowish to yellow synflorescenses are discussed under M. aurea.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: M. pallida is distinguished by its foliage; its individually arranged and many-flowered capitula; and by generally obtuse and apically dentate to serrate petaloid involucral bracts. M. pungens, M. galpinii and M. pulcherrima have similar foliage, but their capitula are generally arranged in clusters. Other species with individually arranged capitula only are M. octoflora, M. umbelliformis and M. strictifolia. The two former species have twisted leaves with axillary brachyblasts and different capitula, whereas the latter species has persistently tomentose branches, coarse haired leaves, pappus bristles with clavate tips and glabrous cypselas. M. strictifolia and M. pallida are sister species. A few specimens of M. pallida are aberrant, e.g. they may have 5-flowered capitula, or inner and innermost involucral bracts with apically entire margins, or with plicate tips. However, these seem to be only minor variants. It is the only Metalasia species that has been found near Graaff Reinet.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: This species has been much overlooked. Authors and collectors have often regarded it as an aberrant form of R. genistifolia. However, although closely related to that species, it is a distinct, fairly constant species distinguished by its slightly bigger capitula and characteristic foliage. The leaves are much thicker and very glutinous, if pressed together in a fresh state they will stick firmly together.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: Osteospermum polycephalum is characterized by its small, triangular-pear-shaped achenes, only 3-4 mm long, with wings c. 1 mm broad, and by its entire, glabrous, somewhat succulent leaves. The stem terminates in a corymb, and this is greatly overtopped by lateral branches, which also terminate in a corymb, and these in their turn may branch in the same way. The plant has numerous heads, as indicated by the specific epithet polycephalum. The leaves are faintly glaucous and often somewhat pulverulent, the inferior ones being elliptic or oblanceolate, tapering towards the base in a petiole, and the others oblanceolate or linear-lanceolate.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: O. corymbosum is a stately plant with its rigidly erect stem 1-2 metres in height, which bears at the summit corymbose inflorescences. The stem is strongly lignified, and of a finger's thickness at the base. The lowest leaves are lingulate, up to 10 cm long and 3 cm broad; the cauline leaves are lanceolate or narrowly oblong, erect and imbricating, decreasing in size upwards. This species resembles most the tall, mountain form of O. imbricatum, but differs from it, int. al., as regards the shape of the achenes and of the cauline leaves. O. corymbosum is characterized by its ellipsoid-cylindrical achenes, which are smooth, or nearly smooth, except at the base, where they are more or less conspicuously furrowed. In contrast to this, O. imbricatum has achenes furnished with three sharp or very narrow-winged primary ridges and six more or less pronounced secondary ridges.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: I flora decumbens is very easily recognized by its dwarf bushy habit and snow-white pappus, which is more conspicuous than the flowers. The inner involucral bracts frequently, but not always, have snow-white tips contrasting with the rich brown outer bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1981. A revision of Ifloga in southern Africa, with comments on the northern hemisphere species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 82: 293-312. [All rights reserved]

description: Although E. tenuifolius is closely related to E. punctulatus, the two species can be separated by their leaf size, peduncle length, the length of the subtending leaves of the peduncles and their distribution. A further distinguishing character is the fact that E. punctulatus is hardly browsed in contrast to E. tenuifolius, which is heavily browsed.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: O. grandidentatum is a perennial herb, whose stem is slightly lignified in its inferior part. In older specimens the stem and branches are usually decumbent if they lack support; otherwise they are upheld by bushes and rocks. In O. grandidentatum the ripe achenes are smooth and cylindrical or slightly narrowed towards both ends, so that they ought rather to be described as fusiform-cylindrical. As regards the appearance of the achenes, it is closely allied to O. ciliatum and the other species in sect. Homocarpa, but it is easily distinguished from them by the involucral scales being of the same relative length one to the other, and by their not being imbricate.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: M. densa is the most common species in the genus, showing a great deal of variation in habit and foliage, but very little in the features of the involucre. Many different names have been applied to various aberrant specimens of this species. Even though there is considerable vegetative variation within the species, it is well delimited in relation to its relatives. M. densa has straight leaves with axillary brachyblasts; 3- to 5-flowered capitula; generally narrow involucres that are brownish below with white innermost involucral bracts; and outer to inner involucral bracts with apiculate tips. It may resemble the following species: M. dregeana, M. pungens, M. massonii, M. montana, M. muricata, M. plicata, M. trivialis and M. umbelliformis. M. dregeana always has very densely tomentose young branches, mostly squarrose and creamy white to whitish involucral bracts and more acute pappus bristles. M. pungens has non-twisted leaves with or without axillary brachyblasts, more acute outermost and outer involucral bracts and short, obtuse papillae on the cypselas. M. massonii has 5-flowered broader capitula with generally squarrose involucral bracts, and a corolla with a conspicuous, rigid base and long lobes. M. montana generally has wider capitula with longer outermost involucral bracts that are lacerate apically. M. muricata has apically curved to hooked leaves that are obtuse at the very apex; an involucre which is brownish-white to creamy white below, and creamy white to pure white above; and apically comparatively thick and faintly carinate scarious involucral bracts. M. plicata has larger capitula with whitish-yellow to yellowish petaloid involucral bracts, apically characteristically plicate innermost involucral bracts, and dark to blackish brown cypselas with longer papillae. M. trivialis has involute to highly involute and carinate leaves with longer axillary brachyblasts, whitish involucres with longer outermost involucral bracts, and more obtuse pappus bristles. M. umbelliformis is distinguished by its usually curved to hooked leaves, individually arranged capitula, and apically comparatively thick and faintly keeled scarious involucral bracts. Some populations of M. densa from Malmesbury and Paarl have usually shorter leaves, denser and smaller synflorescenses and dark brown to dark reddish inner involucral bracts. These features are part of the normal range of variation within the species. This population has been called 'M. ericoides Sieber'.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: This handsome species is closely related to E. speciosissimus, differing by the smaller and more greyish leaves with narrower and more closely set segments, the more flat-based and straightly widening involucre, the wide and many-veined and more orange-coloured rays, and the much shorter pappus.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. annae is characterized, i.a., by its spreading, linear, obtuse leaves, which like the branches are often covered with resin, and its glabrous achenes. E. oligoglossus and E. nodosus are similar in habit but differ, i.a., by the villous achenes and different leaf-shapes. E. petraeus (see below) conies very close to E. annae but is distinguished by the distinctly ciliolate short leaves. The leaf-margins of E. annae are quite smooth or in a few specimens seen very sparsely and minutely denticulate. E. annae is said to be used in Lesotho as a medicine and for preparation of charms.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. brevilobus was collected already by Burchell but confused with E. serra until it was finally described by Compton. The species is, however, more related to E. speciosissimus and wageneri by the pinnatipartite leaves. It is best distinguished on the short and rigid, spreading leaf-lobes, which are longest in the middle part of the leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to T. tenellum but distinguished by its subacute, not very obtuse, involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Much confused with N. agria. In both species the central flowers have aborted or empty ovaries, which sets them apart from other species of Nidorella. N. undulata is usually glandular pubescent on the inflorescence branches and bracts, but is otherwise glabrous or very nearly so, whereas N. agria is harshly pubescent on both stems and leaves. Also, N. undulata favours damp or wet situations, while N. agria is found in dry places.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: On account of the free involucral bracts E. muirii was transferred by Compton to his genus Lysichlamys, which however must be sunk in Euryops. The small and imbricated, somewhat curved leaves together with the small capitula give this species a quite characteristic appearance. From the other small-leaved species, e.g. E. candollei, it is distinguished by the free involucral bracts and the pubescent achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to H. rutilan, Can also be confused with H. callicomum but distinguished by its different indumentum and different involucre.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Flower head composed of individual capitula in secondary arrangement, up to 37 mm diam. Midrib of leaves and bracts prominent Margins of leafy involucral bracts with regularly spaced stiff hairs, usually also on the leaves Bracts mostly lanceolate (narrow or broad) with a distinct 'petiole' Can be mistaken for O. capensis, which has longer, spreading leaves with minutely toothed margins and sprouts after fire. Often growing on the same slopes as O. capensis, but usually associated with rocky outcrops, has broader more rounded leaves but an identical flower structure. Ray florets of O. imbricata are more yellow than those of O. capensis in fresh specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2017. Key to the southern African species of the Relhania and Macowania groups in the Gnaphalieae (Asteraceae). https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/04040f0a-0603-4405-880c-010703060006/media/Html/default.html [All rights reserved]

description: Sometimes mistaken for Helichrysum but easily recognized by its narrow decurrent leaves and heads with paleae resembling the involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Osteospermum auriculatum is a shrub with opposite branches, growing up to 2.4 m high. The leaves of the branches are opposite with the exception of the uppermost ones, which form a transition to the linear-subulate bracts of the peduncles. It is, however, only the youngest parts of the branches that are herbaceous. Otherwise the plant has strongly lignified branches. It differs from O. sinuatum by its size, growing up to 2-3 m high, by the longer internodes of the branches (up to 1 0 cm long), by the larger laminae, which reach as much as 9 cm in length and 5 cm in breadth, and by at least some of the leaves (the lowermost ones) having auricles.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: KwaZulu-Natal specimens have slightly greyer foliage, more closely leafy flowering stems, and fewer flowers in the head than Cape specimens, but these are scarcely specific differences.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species recognised by the stiffly divaricate, more or less flexuous or zig-zag, inflorescence branches, more or less obovate leaves with large sessile glands on both surfaces, small capitula with inner bracts ±3 mm long, and unusual, clavate inner pappus bristles.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC. 2014. The genus Distephanus (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 94: 238-248. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2014.07.007] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2014); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from H. griseolanatum by its differently shaped leaves, and from H. cymosum subsp. calvum, by its woolly obtuse leaves with strongly revolute margins and homogamous heads.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: M. humilis is a small highly branched and often compact shrublet. Some specimens have densely greyish-tomentose leaves. The tomentum is not persistent, however. M. humilis has comparatively few capitula per synflorescense, though these are sometimes aggregated into secondary synflorescenses. The outermost involucral bracts are often reddish, and the petaloid involucral bracts are white to creamy white and apically revolute to erect-spreading. Some specimens may resemble M. tenuifolia, especially those with densely greyish-tomentose leaves, but this species has 3-flowered capitula with apically erect petaloid involucral bracts. Other Metalasia species which are small shrublets and have 5-flowered capitula are discussed under M. oligocephala.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: The distinguishing characters of I. ambigua are its generally erect habit and its generally solitary heads terminating dwarf lateral shoots, the leaves of which are webbed together and to the outer involucral bracts; these shoots then arranged in long loose or sometimes congested terminal and lateral racemes. Each dwarf shoot is sometimes terminated by two to several heads webbed together and forming small glomerules.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1981. A revision of Ifloga in southern Africa, with comments on the northern hemisphere species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 82: 293-312. [All rights reserved]

description: There are no characters to distinguish the genus Thodaya from Euryops, and the former has to be put into synonymy. E. microphyllus is easily recognized on its small, entire and fleshy leaves. The collection from Sutherland has comparatively short and stout peduncles but is no doubt conspecific with the Whitehill population.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: P. camphorata seems to be a polymorphic species as regards the arrangement and the surface-covering of the leaves, varying from opposite to alternate in var. laevigata, alternate in the other forms, and from entirely glabrous in var. laevigata to densely setose all over the surface in var. armata. These differences, however, are not associated with any others, the flower-heads being identical in all.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, J; Phillips, EP. 1917. A revision of the genus Pteronia (Compositae). Ann. S. African Mus. 9(1): 277-329. [All rights reserved]

description: This species has in the past been confused with M. cymbifolia, its sister species, but differs in a number of characters, viz. its generally less tomentose young branches; spreading and only slightly curved to straight leaves; innermost involucral bracts which have a comparatively short lamina; and apically coarsely serrate pappus bristles: hence, the specific epithet. Only a few ripe cypselas have been seen, none of which have an annular ridge and are quite different in shape from those of M. cymbifolia. In M. cymbifolia material available for study, the cypselas all had a distinct annular ridge, and were broader. M. serrata might also resemble M. erubescens, but in the latter species, the capitula are mostly free from one another, the inner and innermost involucral bracts have a transverse subapical ridge, and the pappus bristles often have entire margins, apically.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: P. camphorata seems to be a polymorphic species as regards the arrangement and the surface-covering of the leaves, varying from opposite to alternate in var. laevigata, alternate in the other forms, and from entirely glabrous in var. laevigata to densely setose all over the surface in var. armata. These differences, however, are not associated with any others, the flower-heads being identical in all.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, J; Phillips, EP. 1917. A revision of the genus Pteronia (Compositae). Ann. S. African Mus. 9(1): 277-329. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily confused with H. mimetes, but distinguished by its smooth white involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A characteristic species obviously with no close allies, except perhaps E. marlothii, easily recognized on the small and finely pinnatipartite leaves and the cupshaped, basally truncate involucres. The disc-florets are sterile with simple or shallowly lobed styles. The corolla tube of the rays becomes firm and persists on the achene as an apical appendage.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: It can be confused with S. purpureus (see under that species, above), and with S. panduriformis (no. 14), but the leaves of that species have a very close cottony-cobwebby indumentum below and closely callose-denticulate margins. The flowers are yellow; they are generally purple in gerrardii, though Gerrard recorded them as yellow. It is possible they change colour as they do sometimes in S. polyodon.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: O. scariosum is a perennial herb with a lignified rootstock and one to several erect or ascendent stems. The steins and branches are often somewhat lignified in the lower part. The basal leaves are more or less rosulate, distantly denticulate to sinuate-dentate (or occasionally lyre-shaped), but there are sometimes a few entire leaves among them too. The achenes are slightly curved and normally 9-12 mm long excluding the wings. Like most of the species that are distributed over extensive areas with different climatic conditions and soils, it shows strong variation especially in respect of the shape of the leaves, pubescence and size.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with Doellia cafra but that species has purple florets and outer female florets are filiform and arranged in many rows.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A. nycthemerum is easily recognized by its dark outer involucral bracts, and elliptic-obovate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Lundgren, J. 1972. Revision of the genus Anaxeton Gaertn. (Compositae). Opera Bot. 31: 5-59. [All rights reserved]

description: Erect plants with the heads in long racemes are frequently confused with I. verticillata; prostrate plants with the heads in discrete glomerules with I. paronychioides, but I. glomerata is easily distinguished from both by the numerous female flowers and fully fertile hermaphrodite flowers. The pappus setae differ too: there are minute patent cilia at the base in I. glomerata and the tips are neat, while the base is naked in I. verticillata and I. paronychioides and the tips are irregular.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1981. A revision of Ifloga in southern Africa, with comments on the northern hemisphere species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 82: 293-312. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is very closely allied to P. inflexa, Thunb., with which it has been associated in Herbaria. The glabrous leaf-surfaces, the more strikingly saccate involucral bracts, and its more easterly distribution seem sufficient to distinguish it.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, J; Phillips, EP. 1917. A revision of the genus Pteronia (Compositae). Ann. S. African Mus. 9(1): 277-329. [All rights reserved]

description: Medley Wood first collected this species on Mawahqua Mountain nearly one hundred years ago, and Mrs Rennie kindly sought it there for us in 1974. It is enumerated as Senecio sp. 39 in Hilliard, Compositae in, Natal 436, 1977, but we hesitated to name it until more was known of its distribution. We have now found it on Mulangane ridge, which lies above Carter's Nek between the Nzinga and Loteni rivers, and in the gorge of the Tugela river, about 145km to the north west of Mawahqua. Senecio marginalis is found in scrubby growth on the margins of forest patches (which suggested the trivial name). It may be biennial; initially there is a tuft of radical leaves and presumably only in the second season of growth are the flowering stems produced. These are subsimple, thin and weak, and may be supported by other vegetation. In contrast, its ally, S. poseideonis is erect, well-branched from the base, and without radical leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XI. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 227-260. [CC BY-SA]

description: Characterized by its glabrous leaves, stems glabrous or nearly so in the lower part, and glabrous, rarely minutely hispid, achenes. Can be confused with S. ngoyanus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Steirodiscus linearilobus is distinguished from S. capillaceus by its glabrous ovaries and cypselas, and by its glabrous disc florets. The ray florets are slightly fewer than the involucral bracts, which number 13-16 vs. 8-12 in S. linearilobus, and the uppermost leaves are either simple or pinnatisect, but invariably simple in S. capillaceus.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Joubert, L. 2013. A taxonomic revision of the small Cape genus Steirodiscus (Asteraceae: Senecioneae). Bothalia 43(1): 109-119. [CC BY]

description: Resembling G. latifolium in its alternate, sessile, membranous leaves, coarsely toothed or more deeply cut halfway to midrib but distinguished by the sub-biseriate vs. 3-seriate involucre.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N. 2013. FSA Contribution 22: Asteraceae: Calenduleae: Garuleum. Bothalia 43(2): 167-178. [CC BY]

description: Easily confused with B. zeyheri but that species has long flexible bristles only in the lower half of the leaf, and with B. subulata in which the leaf margins are beset with short rigid spines, not flexible bristles.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Resembling G. sonchifolium in the alternate, membranous, coarsely toothed or more deeply cut leaves, but distinguished by the involucral bracts in 3 series, ovate-linear, with the outer bracts much shorter than the inner.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N. 2013. FSA Contribution 22: Asteraceae: Calenduleae: Garuleum. Bothalia 43(2): 167-178. [CC BY]

description: Frequently confused with S. burchellii DC, S. inaequidens and S. pellucidus DC S. burchellii and S. pellucidus both have turbinate heads with c. 12 involucral bracts and 5-8 rays and are plants of the southern and western Cape. S. inaequidens is a more woody plant than S. madagascariensis, branching vigorously at ground level and having mostly linear leaves and often slightly larger heads (involucral bracts generally 5-6 mm long; plants of S. madagascariensis with 6 mm long involucral bracts are often near the sea). In Natal, S. inaequidens does not occur below c. 1400 m altitude, and therefore scarcely overlaps with the area of S. madagascariensis. Some specimens are difficult to place.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: M. seriphiifolia is easily recognized by its slender habit, acicular leaves, apically tridentate innermost involucral bracts, and by comparatively small cypselas almost lacking an annular ridge. It is a rare species, collected only a few times. It is similar to M. erubescens, which also occurs in the same area, but differs in the characters given above.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: H. asperum var. asperum can be confused with H. oxybelium, which much resembles it in habit, in disposition of the heads, and in colour of the involucral bracts, but var. asperum is easily recognized by its homogamous heads containing 7-13 flowers, not heterogamous and containing 19-29 flowers. In the type specimen, which is unlocalized, only the young leaves are loosely woolly; the older leaves are merely glandular-hispid. Modern collections from the Cedarberg and from the mountains near Groot Kloof, De Doorns and Worcester tend to be glandular-hispid; elsewhere prominent glands are lacking but both glandular and eglandular plants may grow together.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: L. poterioides can easily be confused with L. pedunculare. The presence of the felty indumentum at the tip of the peduncle and involucral bracts, the conspicuous, broad, transparent, membranous margin of the bracts, the leaf lobes that are almost obtuse and the distribution with one exception above 1 500 m altitude, distinguish L. poterioides from L. pedunculare.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Harvey did not see any authentic material and regarded the species as a synonym partly to E. punctatus, with which it has not much in common, and partly to Gamolepis trifurcata Less. E. tenuilobus could easily be mistaken for E. anthemoides (syn. Gamolepis trifurcata), which has also been done in several herbaria. The leaf-lobes are very slender with acuminate tips, however, and they are not curved like in the latter species. The tuberculate achenes also serve to distinguish the species from E. anthemoides.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: A shrub or small tree with subentire leaves and corymbs of characteristically large, subglobose to broadly cup-shaped involucres with acute to acuminate or sometimes caudate (east tropical African populations only) involucral bracts, capitula with 10 to 25 florets, and diagnostic cypselas lacking any hairs and so only gland-dotted between the ribs. Gymnanthemum coloratum resembles G. amygdalinum in habit and foliage, including the foliar indumentum of short-spurred hairs, but the latter typically has narrower leaves, elliptic to lanceolate, and smaller, 5-flowered capitula with obtuse bracts, and setulose cypselas.

description: The name H. cooperi is frequently misapplied to plants in the Transvaal and tropical Africa. It is not clear, however, if H. cooperi occurs further north than the low Drakensberg on the Transvaal-KwaZulu-Natal border. It is characterized by its biennial habit, green leaves shortly to strongly decurrent on the stem, heads in a spreading corymbose panicle, and involucral bracts usually bright yellow inside and out.

description: Readily confused with H. dasycephalum which, however, has mainly silvery, not lemon-yellow, involucral bracts, and these are webbed together with delicate 'tissue-paper-like' indumentum composed of woolly hairs. The area of H. dasycephalum lies east of that of H. rutilans, overlapping only in the Queenstown area (±27°E).

description: Capitula 10-12-flowered; involucre with conspicuous white tomentose patches abaxially; innermost bracts with tips hooded; restricted to Witsand.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 1999. The genus Amphiglossa (Gnaphalieae, Relhaniinae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 21(1): 65-75. [CC BY]

description: This very distinct species was first described by De Candolle as a variety of E. longipes. Harvey merely transferred the variety to his E. diversifolius and altered the name to var. á. integrifolius, which is thus illegitimate. Some of the characteristic features of E. lasiocladus are the indumentum of the young branches, the long and slender peduncles, the narrow involucral bracts, and the glabrous achenes, which are provided with an apical appendage formed by the persistent stylophore.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: M. octoflora is easily recognized by its individually arranged capitula and involucres that are hairy almost throughout. The involucral bracts contrast clearly with the greyish colour of the interlocking hairs. Other notable features are the yellowish petaloid bracts, the basally clavate styles, the apicaily coarsely serrate pappus bristles and the dark to blackish-brown cypselas with comparatively long, acute papillae. It may be similar to M. aurea, but that species has capitula arranged in clusters, as have M. luteola and M. plicata, two other species with yellowish synflorescenses.

bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: M. brevifolia is a species which varies in habit and in the shape and size of the involucre. It can be recognized by the comparatively short leaves and by its generally petaloid, white, and apically concave involucral bracts. Material from Clanwilliam and Calvinia may look aberrant, with comparatively large involucres and robust habit, whereas material from the Hex River Valley may have comparatively tiny involucres with deeply concave involucral bracts and a very slender habit. The distantly related species M. tenuis also has short leaves and deeply concave involucral bracts, but this species is often decumbent and usually has pink petaloid involucral bracts as well as wider pappus bristles. M. quinqueflora, also a distantly related species, is sometimes similar in habit but has 5-flowered capitula with apically spreading petaloid involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: A handsome, large-flowered species, whose flower heads when fully out may measure 5 cm in diam. The ray flowers are white above, and beneath violet and often slightly purple. It comes nearest to D. acutifolia and D. ecklonis, but differs from these above all in the shape of the achenes. D. wallianum has subterete, very broadly ellipsoid or globose achenes. D. acutifolia on the other hand, has bluntly 3-angled achenes, which are about twice as long as they are broad, and D. ecklonis acutely 3-angled achenes, which are also about twice as long as broad. The main form of D. acutifolia has leaves only c. 1-3 mm broad, and is thus easily distinguished from D. wallianum, whose leaves are up to 10-12 mm in breadth. There are, however, broad-leafed forms of D. acutifolia, especially from the Drakenstein Mts., which may be quite similar to D. wallianum, and for an accurate determination it is therefore important to have specimens with ripe achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]
