description: O. polygaloides is characterized by its linear-oblanceolate or narrowly oblong to linear leaves, and by its dense, glanduloso-muriculate pedicels and involucral scales. The achenes, which have three primary ridges and six geminate secondary ridges with pitted furrows between the ridges, differ from those in O. imbricatum by having obtuse primary ridges.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: (i) Small-headed form from the Western Cape (including var. pappei). Stems glabrous, slender (2-3.5 mm in diameter), rigid, lined. Leaves distinctly lobed. Few to many small capitula, fairly laxly arranged on glabrous peduncles 5-30 mm long. Involucral bracts 5-8, 3.0-4.0 mm long, glabrous, rays 3-5, 4.5-6.5 mm long, disc florets 8-18. Cypselae ciliate and hairy, margined. (ii) Hairy form mainly from the Worcester and Montagu regions in the Western Cape, also from the Cederberg. Stems and leaves very hairy, otherwise habit similar to form described above. Trichomes comprise a tapering multi-celled base with long apical appendage. Few capitula, peduncles hairy. Involucral bracts 7 or 8, hairy; rays 4 or 5 (rarely 6). Ray cypselae margined or distinctly winged, ciliate, sparsely hairy or hairy on outer faces, almost glabrous on inner faces; disc cypselae margined or narrow-winged, ciliate, hairy, mature cypselae 3-4 mm long. (iii) Robust form from Saldanha Bay to the Cape Peninsula in the Western Cape. A more robust growth form, stems 4-5 mm in diameter, glabrous. Leaves reniform, auricles usually conspicuous. Capitula many, larger than in other forms. Involucral bracts 8-13, rays 5-8, disc florets 26-36. Cypselae with paler narrow wing (rarely margined), ciliate, hairy or sparsely hairy on faces, 2.0-3.8 mm long. (iv) Small-leaved, jointed stem form from the vicinity of Uniondale and Humansdorp in the Western Cape, extending slightly into the Eastern Cape. Characteristically small shrublets with branching woody stems, short internodes creating a jointed appearance. Leaves small, some with lateral pinnae, glabrous. Capitula few, laxly arranged. Involucral bracts 8(-10), (3.5-)4-6 mm long; rays 5 (rarely 8). Cypselae distinctly winged (ray cypselae occasionally fairly broad-winged). (v) Compactly many-headed form from the southern region of the Western Cape. Spreading suffrutex. Stems robust. Leaves reniform to deltoid-reniform or rounded-reniform, mostly shallowly lobed, (13-)18-46 × (18-)26-56 mm, glabrous to sparsely hairy or hairy above, sparsely to densely hairy below, trichomes eglandular, multi-celled, usually with an apical appendage; petioles relatively long (11-87 mm long); auricles small or large. Capitula small, very many 38-90(-120), compactly arranged on short peduncles 2-8(-12) mm long. Involucral bracts 8, 3-4 mm long, rays commonly 4 or 5 (rarely 3 or 6), disc florets 12-14(-17); corolla 3-3.5 mm long. Cypselae narrow-winged or margined, brown or black with a paler margin, ciliate with hairy to sparsely hairy outer faces, inner faces sparsely hairy to glabrous, 1.8-2.5 mm long. NOTES. The first and last forms described above both have many small capitula, but differ markedly in their habit and compactness of capitula (i.e. peduncle length). The compact, many-headed form grows as a spreading bush covering rocks along the seashore or scrambling on south facing slopes near the sea, with fairly robust stems. It is a coastal form growing near Mossel Bay, George, Knysna and at Eersterivier. In contrast, the many-headed form from more inland mountains in the Western Cape is a herb or small suffrutex, with more laxly arranged capitula, generally on longer peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Steirodiscus tagetes is distinguished by the characteristic compound trichomes on the ray florets. These palmate structures form a fleshy, collar-like fringe around the top of the corolla tube at the base of the limb, and are readily visible with a hand lens. The capitula are typically larger than in S. gamolepis and S. speciosus, with a campanulate involucre 4-5 mm diam. It is superficially very similar to S. speciosus, but in this species the trichomes on the ray florets are not coalescent into compound structures and the involucre is generally smaller, 2-3 mm diam. The flowers in both species are typically bright yellow but may also be tinged orange. The species is variable in flower size with the largest and most attractive forms occurring west of Atlantis.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Joubert, L. 2013. A taxonomic revision of the small Cape genus Steirodiscus (Asteraceae: Senecioneae). Bothalia 43(1): 109-119. [CC BY]

description: E. acraeus is a very characteristic species, easily recognized, i.a., on the apically toothed leaves and the involute leaf-margins. The possibly closest relative is E. brownei from East Tropical Africa, which differs in having entire leaves with serrulate margins and pubescent peduncles. Even before it was described the species was successfully grown in England (under the name of E. evansii) and proved perfectly hardy in the open.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Very closely allied to S. pentactinus Klatt, found along the Witwatersrand and Magaliesberg and in the eastern Transvaal and Zoutpansberg, but that species has differently shaped leaves, lanceolate, tapering at both ends, and with 12 or more side veins, not raised like those of S. colensoensis and not so well defined. S. pentactinus in turn is closely allied to S. triactinus S. Moore and S. homoplastious S. Moore, found in the eastern highlands of Rhodesia and neighbouring Mozambique.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Much resembles S. ingeliensis.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: T. lerouxiae resembles T. verticillata in general facies, but differs in having 3 [not (0)-1-2] female flowers in a head, the rounded to obtuse (not acuminate) bracts which surround the hermaphrodite flowers and the scanty or absent (not present) pappus. Its affinities also lie with T. polycnemoides but it can be readily distinguished by the differently coloured involucral bracts (translucent straw-coloured versus reddish central patch with whitish tip) and the number of female flowers (3 versus 5-10) in a head.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 1995. Notes on African Plants: Asteraceae. A new species of Trichogyne fropm Namaqualand. Bothalia 25(1&2): 107-109. [CC BY]

description: E. linearis resembles in habit the narrow-leaved species of sect. Angustifoliae (e.g., E. tenuissimus, rehmannii, linifolius, brevipapposus, etc.). The terminal and umbellately disposed peduncles immediately distinguish the species from that section, however. Further characteristics are the flat leaves and the much connate involucres. None of the other members of sect. Chrysops can be said to be very closely allied to E. linearis, but E. inops perhaps comes closest.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. asparagoides is a very characteristic species. The stems are repeatedly branched in a zig-zag way, giving the shrub a compact and very twiggy appearance. The most striking features are the spinescent branches, the usually fascicled short leaves with a woolly basal tuft, the turbinate involucres on very short and slender peduncles, and the discoid or disciform capitula.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Osteospermum tomentosum is a very distinct species, differing considerably from the other species in the subgenus Tripteris. It is characterized by the scape-like stem, by the more or less densely lanate-tomentose and rosulate leaves and above all by the shape of the achenes. The latter are quite large (c. 9 mm long) with a broad, truncate apex, enclosing a large air-chamber, which may be nearly as large as the seed-cavity. The walls of the apical cavity are not provided with a fenestra with a pellucid membrane. The upper wall is often thin, but the others are as thick as the walls round the seed-cavity. O. tomentosum has only winged achenes, the wings being c. 3 mm broad, subrigid and almost impellucid. The leaves, as shown by my diagnosis, are remarkably variable, and even in one and the same rosette one may find leaves of several different shapes.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with H. roseo-niveum, H. marlothianum and H. hemiarioides (below); see under those species to distinguish. An occasional specimen is difficult to place e.g. Giess, Volk & Bleissner 5317 (M; WIND) with heads only ±5 mm long containing ±35-40 flowers, 2 of them female, thus approaching H. marlothianum; H. marlothianum appears to differ in its homogamous heads. However, H. marlothianum is a poorly known species, requiring field study.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: H. incarnatum is allied to H. cylindriflorum but is distinguished by subtle differences in the involucre. The bracts are decidedly lanceolate, not mostly oblong as they are in H. cylindriflorum, and although there is some wool on the backs of the shafts, it is not so conspicuous as it is in H. cylindriflorum and does not web the bracts together. Many of the bracts have a rosy cast (rare in H. cylindriflorum) though the tips of the inner bracts may be creamy white: these tips are more acute than they generally are in H. cylindriflorum, longer (the longest ±2-2.5 mm), flatter, and always opaque, and the outer bracts are not squarrose. There appear to be generally more flowers in the head too, though counts are too few to be certain. Bolus 9020 (BOL; K; PRE) may be a variant of H. incarnatum: the leaves are slightly larger (up to 35 x 7 mm), the heads slightly larger (±7 x 7 mm), containing ±60 flowers, and the tips of the inner involucral bracts are bright yellow, not pink. The specimen was collected between Pakhuis and Biedouw at an altitude of 360 m, in October 1897 (when the flowers were only in bud); this is well north of the known area of H. incarnatum. Specific rank may be appropriate.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Osteospermum pinnatilobatum is a very distinct species. In respect of the type of ramification, the shape and size of the achenes and the appearance of the flower heads it agrees most closely with 0. microcarpum, but it differs by the shape of its leaves, the leaves being bipinnatipartite or the upper ones pinnatipartite. In addition it is more strongly lignified and may be described as a suffrutex.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: G. cordata is a distinct species, easily recognized by the rufous tomentum and the broadly cordate leaf base. The leaves are persistently densely tomentose below and often broader in outline than in G. piloselloides. Rather surprisingly, G. elliptica on Madagascar is the species most difficult to distinguish from G. cordata, but G. elliptica is more slender, never rufous tomentose, the leaves are more narrow and less distinctly cordate (sometimes cuneate at the base), and the achenes are almost or totally glabrous. The similiarities between the two species must be explained as convergence, but several traits connect sect. Pseudoseris and sect. Piloselloides.
bibliographicCitation: Hansen, HV. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the genus Gerbera (Compositae, Mutisieae) sections Gerbera, Parva, Piloselloides (in Africa), and Lasiopus. Opera Bot. 78: 5-36. [All rights reserved]

description: E. cuneatus is the only hexaploid known in the genus. The type of leaf division is essentially the same as in the related species E. multifidus, subcarnosus and namaquensis, i.e., the leaves are normally three-lobed with forked lateral lobes. The leaves are broader and more distinctly cuneate than in any of the allied species, however, and they are further greyish glaucous. The achenes are similar to those of E. multifidus, viz., copiously woolly with long and thin hairs, not becoming mucilaginous in water. There is a correlation between size of pollen grains and degree of ploidy in this group of species, the hexaploid (E. cuneatus) having the largest pollen grains. In cultivation in greenhouses the leaves become considerably enlarged, but they keep their characteristic cuneate shape and glaucous bloom.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Osteospermum breviradiatum has achenes of the same type and size as O. amplectens. It also agrees quite well with certain forms of the variable O. amplectens in respect of the shape of the leaves as well as of the ramification and pubescence. The essential difference between O. breviradiatum and O. amplectens consists in the relation between the length of the ray flowers and the involucre. In O. breviradiatum the ray flowers are as long as the involucre or but little (I-2 mm) longer, but in O. amplectens on the other hand they are about three times as long as the involucre.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: It has the same habit of growth as O. calendulaceum, and resembles this species, but is easily distinguished from it by its characteristic, prickly achenes, and its serrate-dentate or pinnatifid-dentate leaves. The specific name acanthosperma refers to the achenes. which are furnished with quite thick, rigid aculei, up to 5 mm long. The achenes are almost obpyramidal, with three rows of longer aculei and one or two rows of shorter aculei between them. Each row usually consists of only 3-5 prickles, and they are largest towards the apex of the achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The ripe achenes in O. grandiflorum are straight, thick-walled, large (c. 12 mm long), and furnished with three broad, rigid wings, but they lack an apical cavity. In view of the shape of the achenes this species can thus neither belong to the genus Calendula, in which it was originally placed, nor to Tripteris, to which it was subsequently transferred. It belongs instead to the subgenus Euosteospermum. In addition to the large, rigidly winged achenes, the species is characterized by the long ray flowers, which are usually 3-4 times longer than the involucre, and often more than 2 cm in length. The stem and branches are strongly lignified, and are glandular just like the leaves; in a dried state at least, they are scabrous due to hard, raised points. When living, the plant will, however, probably feel viscid owing to the glands and only slightly, or not at all, asperous.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Although related to E. africanus var. paniculatus, it can be distinguished from that taxon by the dense, felty, sericeous indumentum of the leaves resulting in a grey-green appearance, as opposed to the silvery white appearance of E. africanus var. paniculatus. The capitula have a light brown, long-pilose indumentum in contrast to the white, long-pilose indumentum of E. africanus var. paniculatus. E. africanus var. paniculatus is hardly or not browsed, while E. brevifolius is readily browsed where it occurs.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The younger parts of the plant are densely gland-dotted and viscid. The older branches are robust and naked with dark grey bark, the younger ones short and closely leafy, usually terminating in a peduncle. The leaves, which throughout have a more or less pronouncedly cuneate base, vary in shape from broadly obovate to sublinear, and their margins from sparsely grosse-dentate or subpinnatifid to denticulate. D. cuneata comes nearest to D. zeyheri, but differs from it int. al. by its disc achenes being twice as large (c. 10 mm long) and by being a real shrub. Younger specimens of D. cuneata, which have not yet developed into shrubs, may be difficult to distinguish from D. zeyheri, if ripe achenes are lacking, for the shape of the leaves is so variable in the two species that it is not completely reliable as a specific character.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: M. tenuis is distinguished by its slender appearance, often decumbent habit, small leaves, small synflorescenses with mostly less than 25 capitula, pink and apically deeply concave outer and inner involucral bracts and broad pappus bristles. Apparently the pink colour of the involucral bracts fades quite quickly. In living plants the synflorescenses on the annual flowering shoots are bright pink, whereas the ones remaining from previous flowering seasons are whitish or white. M. tenuis may resemble M. brevifolia. However, this species has white generally larger synflorescenses with numerous capitula, an erect habit, often apically more flattened involucral bracts and apically narrower pappus bristles, which are often subterete rather than flattened to flat towards the very apex. Other species which also have comparatively small synflorescenses are M. tenuifolia, M. humilis and M. bodkinii. All these species differ in foliage, none have pink synflorescenses and the latter two have apically revolute to spreading petaloid involucral bracts, as well as 5-flowered capitula.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: H. tinctum is characterized by its acuminate, hooked involucral bracts and hairy ovaries; only very rarely are the bracts emarginate. The type of Leontonyx bicolor seems to be no more than an extreme variant with solitary or 2-3 heads at the branch tips.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Very variable particularly in stature and leaf shape and Harvey (1. c.) recognized three varieties based primarily on leaf shape and the degree of undulation of the leaf margins, but these are scarcely tenable now a wide range of material is available. Not easily confused with any species in our area other than its close ally H. tomentosulum, but that species has generally much larger leaves (mostly 20-80 x 6-15 mm), differently shaped and with generally flat, not undulate nor crisped, margins, and all but the uppermost reduced leaves distinctly though often minutely petiolate, not sessile. Also, the involucral bracts in H. zeyheri are generally blunter than in H. tornentosulum.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This characteristic species has remained undescribed and confused with E. longipes. This confusion seems unnecessary, since E. zeyheri differs from E. longipes, subcarnosus, etc., in having terminal peduncles and is here referred to a different section. The peduncles are remarkably long in comparison to the leaves. The markedly asymmetrical disc-florets are unique in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: This is a distinct species with cushion-like habit and small, slender capitula, solitary or paired in cymes. It is related to R. squarrosa, but is not likely to be confused with that species. It might be more difficult to distinguish R. conferta from small specimens of R. sedifolia, but a closer examination of the involucres will reveal obvious differences. Furthermore the leaves are different being ± flat and elliptic-obovate in the former species and somewhat semiterete and narrowly oblong in the latter.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from S. digitalifolius by its different involucre and fewer rays.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: A. angustifolium is obviously closely related to A. asperum and in habit especially similar to some northern forms of A. asperum ssp. pauciflorum. The species is distinct, especially by its smooth and narrow leaves, premorse inner involucral bracts, and densely white-villous achene. From A. asperum ssp. pauciflorusm it seems to differ also in the number of male florets in a capitulum. A. aserum ssp. pauciflorum usually has 4-5 male florets in each capitulum, while capitula with up to 7 male florets are found in A. angustifolium.
bibliographicCitation: Lundgren, J. 1972. Revision of the genus Anaxeton Gaertn. (Compositae). Opera Bot. 31: 5-59. [All rights reserved]

description: Although closely related to E. ericoides, it can easily be distinguished from that species by the alternate leaves and sessile capitula in terminal spikes.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A very handsome plant, worth cultivating.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: This subspecies consists of a number of morphologically more or less different form series. Some of these are often fairly characteristic.
bibliographicCitation: Lundgren, J. 1972. Revision of the genus Anaxeton Gaertn. (Compositae). Opera Bot. 31: 5-59. [All rights reserved]

description: Phymaspermum peglerae shares the discoid non-corymbose heads and large fruit with P. erubescens and P. aciculare but can be distinguished by the densely bronze villous indumentum (sparse to dense silvery villous or hispid indumentum in P. erubescens and glabrous in P. aciculare), the usually larger leaves 9.0-18.0 mm long and the largest fruit in the genus >4 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: E. nodosus is very similar to E. oligoglossus and E. annae but distinguished from both by the stouter peduncles, larger flowerheads, and more numerous involucral bracts. From the former it further differs by the constriction at the leaf-base and from the latter by the more erect and acute leaves and the villous achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Specimens of this species with distinctly lobed leaves were described as S. delagoeensis by Thellung (the leaf lobes being strap-shaped, spreading and apically obtuse). Intermediate leaf forms occur and Thellung's plant cannot be maintained as a separate species. However, the specimens with lobed leaves appear to be recorded only from coastal localities and may therefore represent an infra-specific taxon.
bibliographicCitation: Pope, GV. 1992. 97. Compositae (part 1), Fl. Zambes. 6(1): 1-264. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, London. [CC BY]

description: Some specimens of this species are very similar to St. fusca, although St. fusca has yellow involucral bracts and does not have long, flexible hairs on the abaxial leaf surface.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2016. A monograph of Stoebe and Seriphium (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa and neighbouring islands. Phytotaxa 242(1): 1-84. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.242.1.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Cineraria lyratiformis is characterised by its lyratiform, often dissected leaves and glabrous, broad-winged cypselae. Only two other species of Cineraria have such broad-winged cypselae: C. vallis-pacis from the Northern Cape and Namibia, and a form of C. platycarpa from the Karoo region of the Western and Eastern Cape. In both these species, the cypsela wings are thickly fringed with hairs, whereas in C. lyratiformis, they are glabrous or occasionally bear a few short hairs on the shoulders. Cineraria lyratiformis may be confused with C. parvifolia in the more northerly provinces of South Africa due to some similarity in habit and leaf form, but that species has narrowly margined, hairy and ciliate cypselae as opposed to the broad-winged, glabrous (rarely sparsely ciliate) cypselae of C. lyratiformis. Trichomes are sparsely present in C. lyratiformis and have an agranular tapering base and long apical appendage, and/or glandular hairs may occur in the angles between the lobes of the leaves. Cineraria lyratiformis is a weedy species and may often be found growing in disturbed soil at the sides of roads or in ploughed fields. It tends to require fairly moist soil, and often grows near dams and pans and along rivers. It was reported to have tainted the flavour of milk and cheese by dairy cows that eat the herb when little else is available, and has been suspected of poisoning pigs in the Free State. It is also problematic in that it may contaminate crop seed collections and may competitively replace grass.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: E. evansii is a very characteristic species with its apically three-toothed, flat and broad leaves. Within the species three races are easily distinguishable, for which the subspecific rank was found appropriate.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. anthemoides is characterized by its lobed leaves with apically curved and somewhat tongue-shaped lobes. Normally the species grows as a rather compact, divaricate shrublet with numerous, long and slender peduncles. The rare and perhaps extinct species E. tenuilobus is somewhat similar in habit, but it differs in leaf-shape (rather straight and acuminate lobes) and has very different achenes. E. anthemoides is here divided into two subspecies, differing in some morphological features and in geographical distribution. The main difference is in type of pubescence, but there is also a slight difference in length of ligules. Ssp. astrotrichus normally has somewhat longer rays than ssp. anthemoides, but the variation is overlapping.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: An erect shrub, 1 foot or more in height. The peduncles, involucral scales, and the younger branches and leaves are densely clothed with soft, appressed, subferruginous hair, up to 3 mm long. The older branches and leaves are on the contrary glabrate. The achenes are cylindric and nearly smooth, resembling those of O. hispidum and closely allied species. O. hirsutum undoubtedly comes nearest to O. hispidum, but it has much larger flower heads (about twice as large). It further differs from O. hispidum by not having short, stiff, erect hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Senecio dissimulans is common on moist grassy mountain slopes on the Drakensberg from Platberg at Harrismith in the north-eastern Orange Free State through Lesotho and Natal to Naude's Nek across the Cape Drakensberg between Maclear and Rhodes. It bears a striking resemblance to the radiate form of S. hypochoerideus, which is also common at high altitudes in Natal, Lesotho and the north-eastern Cape, and this resemblance suggested the specific epithet. The leaves of 5. hypochoerideus are mostly 15-30 mm broad, broader than those of S. dissimulans; but they are not viscid. A dissecting microscope shows that the hairs in S. dissimulans have a relatively large turbinate tip composed of 4 secretory cells, but the tips of the hairs in S. hypochoerideus are ellipsoid and are composed of 4 cells that presumably do not secrete viscous matter. The relationship of S. dissimulans probably lies, not with S. hypochoerideus, but with S. hastatus. Senecio hastatus was described by Linnaeus from a specimen collected at the Cape of Good Hope, and the species ranges north and east across the mountains to Lesotho, the Natal Drakensberg and the north-eastern Orange Free State. The hairs on S. hastatus are similar to those of S. dissimulans, but the leaves are thinner and at least the radical ones are pinnatifid or lobulate, with rounded sinuses and lobes oblong or rounded in outline, further lobed and toothed. In the Cape, the heads of S. hastatus have 8 rays, and about 12 involucral bracts 9-10 mm long; in Natal there are 12-13 rays and 14-20 involucral bracts 10-13 mm long. Thus, in Natal, the heads of S. hastatus are much the same size as those of S. dissimulans.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XI. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 227-260. [CC BY-SA]

description: Has notably large heads.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: E. purpureus has distinct, large, pale to dark purple, strap-shaped ray florets, which easily distinguish it from related species. However, sterile and fruiting material presents problems in identification as it closely resembles E. ericoides. If no remains of the ray florets are present, the two species can be distinguished by the connate, marginal paleae forming a hard, cylindrical, coriaceous sheath in E. purpureus as opposed to the short, yellow, marginal female florets and free, marginal paleae in E. ericiodes.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Can be confused with V. niveum, which is a coarser plant with longer, narrower leaves and translucent, not opaque white, cilia at the tips of the pappus bristles.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Poisonous to stock.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This plant is a perennial herb or suffrutex, with stem and branches at first ascendent but finally prostrate. It has either only obovate leaves or both obovate and oblanceolate leaves. The ray flowers are white above, and violet, pale pink or mauve beneath. The disc flowers are reddish purple with narrowly triangular to lanceolate, acute lobes. A more or less large number of the inner disc flowers have lobes with a usually small, sometimes hardly visible, hooded apical swelling on the outer surface. The achenes are narrowly triangular-obovoid, with two acute outer angles and a sometimes blunt inner angle. The angles form three small tubercles on the top of the achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinctive and easily recognized.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Phymaspermum aciculare is the only species in the genus which can have either discoid or radiate heads. It can be distinguished from the other radiate species by the sparsely radiate heads with no more than four rays, with limbs less than 5 mm long. Amongst the discoid species it shares the non-corymbose capitula and large cypselas (>0.8 mm wide) with P. erubescens and P. peglerae. It can however be readily distinguished by the glabrous stem and leaves and the smaller (3.0-6.0 mm wide), obconical, sometimes few radiate capitula with 3-5 additional capitula from leaf axils below.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: This new species is characterized, i.a., by the decumbent habit, the very slender peduncles, the small capitula, the short rays, and the sparse and short pappus. It has some resemblance to E. longipes, which is a species of south-western Cape with a more erect growth and different involucres with broader phyllaries, etc. E. gracilipes is only known from a single, recent collection. The inconspicuous habit together with the unusual flowering time (early autumn) may explain why the species has not been collected earlier.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. linifolius is allied to E. rehmannii and E. thunbergii, with which it is often confused in herbaria. From the former it may be distinguished on the quite glabrous and usually narrower leaves, the pubescent branches, the partly overlapping involucral bracts, and the glabrous achenes. The differences from E. thunbergii are discussed under the latter species.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Initially, when we saw a single specimen of this plant just coming into flower in February 1982, we mistook it for a white form of Berkheya purpurea, but two years later, seeing it in full flower with the panicle expanded, we realized our mistake. The most striking difference between the two species lies in the inflorescence, a wide-spreading corymbose-panicle in B. leucaugeta, a raceme in B. purpurea. Also, the leaves arc differently cut: shallowly rounded lobes in B. leucaugeta, the principal spines 2.5-4(-5) mm long, sharply pointed triangular lobes in B. purpurea with spines (5-)7-10 mm long. The heads of B. leucaugeta have white rays and yellow disc flowers, whereas the heads of B. purpurea are concolorous, usually mauve, occasionally white, and there are only five main veins in the rays of B. leucaugeta whereas there are 9-10 in B. purpurea (counted at the base of the limb; the veins may branch in the upper part). Berkheya leucaugeta most resembles B. cirsiifolia and B. onopordifolia. (DC.) Burtt Davy in habit and in its broad involucral bracts; both these species may have white rays and yellow disc. But their deeply and sharply cut leaves will at once distinguish them, as well as other morphological detail in both leaves and involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM; Burtt, BL. 1988. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XV. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 45(2): 179-210. [CC BY-SA]

description: A slender low shrublet, distinguished by its small synflorescenses with comparatively few capitula, which become campanulate at anthesis and have whitish to creamy white petaloid involucral bracts. The petaloid involucral bracts on dried specimens sometimes become yellowish. Populations at higher altitude at Houw Hoek have densely tomentose leaves and involucres, but sparsely tomentose young branches. This phenomenon also occurs in M. densa and M. humilis. M. humilis, which occurs at Houw Hoek, also resembles M. tenuifolia in stature, but is easily distinguished by its 5-flowered capitula with apically revolute to spreading petaloid involucral bracts. M. erubescens occasionally resembles M. tenuifolia, but has comparatively larger capitula with involucral bracts often arranged in a greater number of series, and often pink petaloid involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: E. hebecarpus has the longest peduncles and largest flowerheads in sect. Psilosteum. In many characters it is reminiscent of members of sect. Euryops (general habit, elongate stout peduncles, large capitula, numerous much-connate involucral bracts, and conspicuous rays). Sometimes a minute pappus is present, consisting of a few very short bristles. Also this character links the species (and the sect. Psilosteum) with other groups of Euryops. The leaves are more or less distinctly pilose with long multicellular hairs, especially when young. The hair-covering on the achenes consists of short tri-cellular obtuse hairs, giving the surface a hoary appearance.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is diagnosed by the densely yellowish-brownish felted leaf under surface and the imbricate involucral bracts, not subseriately arranged as in other species in the genus, and often with conspicuous dark tips. The difference in the involucre is sometimes difficult to assess in the absence of comparative material. The leaves vary in shape from ovate to elliptic and are variously sinuate to serrate or doubly serrate. Gerbera tomentosa is most easily confused with G. serrata, which has ± parallel-sided leaves and a distinctly subseriate involucre, and the two species overlap shortly in their distribution from the Riviersonderend Mountains to the Langeberg near Swellendam.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Simka, B; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2016. A revised taxonomy of Gerbera sect. Gerbera (Asteraceae: Mutisieae). S. African J. Bot. 104: 142-157. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2015.10.002] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Often in small dense stands, probably clonal.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: E. trifidus was collected by Thunberg and Masson and not found again until 1940. The species has been much misunderstood, partly due to its rarity. The confusion started already with Thunberg, who gave a wrong locality ('Picketberg', Thunberg 1823, p. 721) for the true trifidus, i.e., the sheet marked 'a' in Thunberg's herbarium. The sheet marked 'á' belongs to E. oligoglossns and is said to originate from the Hantam Mountains (on the sheet and in Thunberg 1823, p. 722). The latter species is not known from Hantams, and it is likely that instead litt. 'a' was collected there. E. trifidus in the sense of De Candolle and of Harvey included also E. namibensis and E. cuneatus. The leaves of E. trifidus vary from entire to three-lobed on the same specimen. The copious indumentum of the achenes is of the same type as in E. multifidus and E. cuneatus (but different from, e.g., E. subcarnosus and E. namibensis), i.e., it consists of long and thin hairs which do not become slimy in water.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: This variety forms a dense, compact shrub, which is densely leafy at branch tips. The synflorescence is a dense, drooping, spicate raceme. Capitula are mostly sessile. Doubtful cases with shortly pedunculate capitula can therefore be positively identified by the number of disc florets. E. racemosus var. racemosus which forms part of the Coastal Fynbos, can survive veld fires and has become an invader in certain areas.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: O. bolusii is a very distinct species, which holds a fairly isolated position in the genus, and it is only with a certain hesitation I include it in sect. Trialata. It is a perennial herb, with a thick, lignified, subterranean caudex and numerous, narrow, strict, furrowed stems, striate in the upper part. The plant seems somewhat xeromorphic on account of its narrow, sparse, often linear-subulate leaves. The achenes, which are always 3-winged and lack an apical cavity, are among the smallest ones in the genus Osteospermum, being only c. 3 mm long. They have a very characteristic appearance, for when magnified the three wings of the achenes are seen to be composed not of one single membrane, but of a row of processes with membranous, hyaline margins, which are concrescent at least in the lower part. The processes, which form the wings, are dark-coloured, and from them arise some equally dark, fine strengthening ribs supporting the hyaline membranes. The sides between the wings have two longitudinal, cristate ridges with low, blunt processes.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: In a large colony beside the main Natal-Cape road where it cuts through the forest on the Ngeli slopes near Weza there is considerable variation in ray colour, purples and pinks predominating, white rare, and occasionally rays are wanting. The discoid plants can be distinguished from S. purpureus by the more open inflorescence (the terminal groups of heads not congested as in S. purpureus') and the hispid, not glabrous, achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: H. rosum var. rosum is characterized by its bushy growth, `fascicled' leaves, and white-tipped involucral bracts that are usually smooth and concave; when the bract tips are crisped, as they occasionally are, confusion can arise with H. athrixiifolium which is indeed very closely allied to H. rosum and is distinguished morphologically by this bract character, and perhaps by a difference in habit that cannot be detected in the herbarium.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Cineraria glandulosa resembles C. erodioides in its reniform leaf shape and procurrent auricles, but differs in the dense coverage of glandular hairs on the leaves and stem, and sometimes on the involucral bracts (always on the calyculus bracts) and the generally smaller capitula (five ray florets and 18-24 disc florets).
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Despite the fact that it has been collected only once, M. tricolor is a distinct species. The leaves are non-twisted, the capitula are 6- to 8-flowered and comparatively long with many series of involucral bracts without hyaline margins. The inner involucral bracts are generally pink, whereas the innermost ones are usually white. This colouring pattern may show greater variation, if further material is collected. Specimens of M. massonii may resemble M. tricolor but M. massonii has declinate twisted leaves, 5-flowered capitula, squarrose involucral bracts, and corolla bases conspicuously rigid. Other species that may look like M. tricolor are M. densa and M. muricata, both of which have different foliage, fewer series of involucral bracts and only 3-(4-) or 5-flowered capitula.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Cineraria erodioides is a highly variable species, characterised mainly by deltoid-reniform to reniform leaves with very conspicuous auricles clasping the stem and running up the petiole on some of the leaves, notably the uppermost ones. The complement of leaf trichomes is also a useful aid to identifying this species: fine, cobwebby trichomes above and trichomes with c. 6 tapering basal cells and a long, multi-celled apical appendage on the ventral surface (and sometimes also dorsally). A few specimens from the Eastern Cape, Free State and North-West provinces have fine cobwebby trichomes above and below. The cypselae have a distinct wing (often paler than the body of the cypsela), which tends to become broad in plants growing at low altitude in the Eastern Cape. The cypselae commonly have a ciliate wing, with faces glabrous or sparsely hairy, or are rarely entirely glabrous. There is also considerable variation in the degree of lobing, bushiness, and the presence of the characteristic auricles running up the stem (although all are auriculate to some degree). The type specimens of C. erodioides are themselves quite variable in terms of leaf shape, with the Paris isotype lacking the very characteristic auricles and being more lobed than the other two types, but matching in other respects. Good matches of the type specimen from Uitenhage (Eastern Cape) at low altitude are: Long 16 (GRA, K) from Bethalsdorp, Britten 2838 (GRA) and Acocks 18322 (PRE) both from the Bathurst District and Olivier 1216 (NBG) from the Baakens River, Fern Glen. Although the type is thickly cobwebby on the lower surface of the leaves, it appears that there is a tendency for the plants growing at low altitude to be more glabrescent and have finer trichomes limited to the young leaves, remaining at the base of the lamina of older leaves and in the axils of the petioles. Cineraria erodioides was originally collected from near the mouth of the Boschmans River in the Uitenhage District of the Eastern Cape, at low altitude by Ecklon and Zeyher. However, it occurs much more commonly at higher altitude, with the type well matched by specimens from the southern Drakensberg (near Rhodes) in the Eastern Cape, viz. Hilliard & Burtt 16603 (K, NU, PRE, S), Hilliard & Burtt 16434 (MO, NU, S), Hilliard & Burtt 6727 (MO, NU, S), as well as Bayliss BS.1303 (GRA, MO, PRE, S, WAG, Z) from Sehlabathebe, Lesotho. These high altitude plants tend to have larger capitula with 8-12 rays as opposed to the 5 rays in the type specimens (G-DC, P and S). However, this trend is not without exception, as seen in the study of populations from the Witteberg and Naudé’s Nek, e.g. Cron & Goodman 559(J) from the summit of Naudé’s Nek has 5-8 rays. The currently known distribution of Cineraria erodioides now extends from the lower altitudes of the Western Cape and Eastern Cape into the high southern Drakensberg as well as into KwaZulu-Natal, the eastern Free State, North West Province, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces in South Africa. It also occurs at very high altitude in Lesotho, reportedly reaching 3600 m on the Sentinel. These high altitude plants were previously thought to be a distinct form of C. geifolia. Many of them have the distinctive auricles of C. erodioides, although their leaves tend to be more shallowly lobed than usual and they generally have larger capitula. A study of the variation amongst these specimens in terms of depth of leaf lobing, size of capitula and cypsela indumentum revealed no justification for recognising it as a distinct taxon at any level. The range of variation seen in Cineraria erodioides also includes plants previously known as C. dieterlenii, mainly from KwaZulu-Natal, but extending along the ‘Transvaal Drakensberg’ into Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces. Although the type specimens of C. dieterlenii [Dieterlen 567 (P, PRE, NBG, NH, Z)] from Hlotse (Leribe), Lesotho all have glabrous cypselae, other similar specimens (e.g. Dieterlen 576b (PRE) from Maboloka Mountain, Lesotho) have cypselae with ciliate margins and hairy faces. Specimens from Mariepskop (at the northern end of the Transvaal Drakensberg escarpment) with deeply lobed, reniform (to deltoid-reniform) leaves, usually with rounded sinuses between lobes, 5-8 rays, 8(-10) involucral bracts, and ciliate and hairy cypselae were originally thought to be a distinct taxon, but they match plants previously known as C. dieterlenii well and therefore are considered to be part of C. erodioides.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by its long, branched, glabrescent scape, and tufted, but not cushion-forming habit. It is found at lower altitudes (250-450 m) than the other three species.
bibliographicCitation: Bond, P. 1987. A revision of Oldenburgia (Asteraceae - Mutisieae). S. African J. Bot. 53: 493-500. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1987); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Allied to S. digitalifolius and S. conrathii, but the heavily calycled discoid heads on long scaly peduncles give S. exuberans a distinctive and easily recognized facies.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with T. capillaceum but easily distinguished by its heterogamous heads sub-corymbosely rather than racemosely arranged.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: M. pulcherrima f. pallescens sometimes resembles M. pungens, e. g. in foliage, but the former species only rarely has axillary brachyblasts; has larger, 5-flowered capitula; often whitish to greyish involucres; involucral bracts with almost no hyaline margins; innermost involucral bracts that are often carinate towards the apex; and three-ribbed cypselas. M. pungens has leaves with or without axillary brachyblasts; 3-flowered and mostly brownish involucres; involucral bracts with hyaline margins; and cypselas without ribs. The two species are sometimes sympatric. Other species exhibiting similar foliage and habit are M. galpinii and M. pallida. M. pallida is easily distinguished on account of its individually arranged capitula, and less acute and apically finely serrate involucral bracts. For comparison with M. galpinii, see Taxonomic note under M. galpinii. M. pulcherrima f. pulcherrima is not likely to be confused with any other yellow-headed Metalasia species, as it is the only one with non-twisted leaves. The rank form has been chosen to distinguish between yellow and white variants of M. pulcherrima. These taxa are identical in all other respects. It is not known whether they actually grow side by side, but they are sympatric in terms of locality, as given on the herbarium sheets. The reasons behind the colour variation in M. pulcherrima are unknown. The two forms may represent genetically isolated populations, or it may be a case of spontaneous mutation and subsequent vicinism, enabling the new mutant to disperse (f. pulcherrima). Another possibility is a (Mendelian) genetic system within the species that enables two different pigments to be alternatively expressed.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: O. spinescens is a much branched shrub up to 1 metre high, with ascending or suberect rigid woody branches. It has glandular viscid and usually glaucous leaves. With regard to the achenes and the shape of the leaves O. spinescens is easily distinguished from O. spinosum, for the latter species has unwinged or only narrowly winged achenes with a wing breadth of 1 mm at most. The leaves are short glandular-pubescent and never glaucous. The margins of the dentate or pinnatifid leaves in 0. spinosum are furnished with teeth or lobes even below the middle or at all events from the middle. O. spinescens, on the other hand, has only winged achenes, whose wings are much broader than those in the other species, the breadth being c. (2-)3-5 mm. The leaves are glabrous, glandular, and usually glaucous. The entire leaves are often similar in shape to those in O. spinosum, but the others are unlike them, being in contradistinction to O. spinosum only dentate or cleft at the apex.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: It is largely replaced in Natal by the related S. gerrardii with ovate-elliptic, coarsely toothed or lyrate-pinnatifid leaves narrowed to a petiole-like, auriculate base, and numerous ascending lateral veins, raised on the lower surface. S. gerrardii also flowers later, generally in March and April.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Senecio austromontanus is an undistinguished plant, easily passed by. The only two known records, both from c.2350 m in damp montane grassland, suggest that the species should be sought further north along the Cape Drakensberg and in the southern Natal Drakensberg.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1982. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: IX. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 40(2): 247-298. [CC BY-SA]

description: Much confused with S. albanensis and S. albanopsis, but a very distinctive plant with a characteristic facies imparted by its long narrow crowded erect and rather stiff stem leaves, campanulate heads with the involucre much shorter than the disc, and short reflexed rays. See also S. lydenburgensis, below.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: There is some variation in the size of the heads and the degree of crisping of the involucral bracts, the larger heads often having the bracts less crisped than the smaller. Nevertheless, the species is not easily confused with any other.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by its woolly crown and basal rosette of rather fleshy leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: This is the plant commonly called 'S. burchellii', but that name belongs to a virgate shrub with linear leaves and turbinate heads with c. 12 involucral bracts and 5-8 rays, common in the S.W. and W. Cape. See also S. madagascariensis and S. harveianus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: M. albescens is recognized by its densely and persistently whitish-tomentose branches; short leaves; pink 3-flowered capitula; and acute to very acute pappus bristles. M. albescens is strikingly similar to M. fastigiata, but the latter species mostly has longer leaves that are more twisted; 5-flowered capitula; involucral bracts in series of 5-7 rather than 4-5; and less acute, often obtuse pappus bristles. Another species with 3-flowered, pink capitula is M. erubescens. It is distinguished by its less tomentose branches; often erect-spreading leaves, which are usually curved outwards; inner and innermost involucral bracts, which have a transverse ridge subapically; and also by less acute pappus bristles. M. seriphiifolia also has 3-flowered, pink and generally free capitula, but it is more slender, and has longer, more twisted leaves. M. phillipsii is also more slender, has less tomentose branches, smaller synflorescenses, and less acute and narrower pappus bristles.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its suberect, rod-like, densely leafy stems with subsessile, ascending and imbricating leaves that are strongly discolorous and coarsely toothed in the upper half with a densely silvery, appressed pubescence on the undersurface. Gymnanthemum corymbosum may be confused with G. crataegifolium, with which it co-occurs in some places and which is very similar in habit and foliage but with scarcely discolorous leaves with a pale greenish, crisped-felted indumentum on the leaf undersurface.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Gymnanthemum Cass. (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 102: 81-101. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2015.07.015] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: This rare and little-known species comes near to E. cuneatus and E. namaquensis but differs from both by the peculiar, many-lobed leaves. These are short and wide with much shorter and more numerous lobes than in E. namaquensis. The new species differs from E. cuneatus, apart from in number of leaf-lobes, by the more numerous, biseriate involucral bracts, the shorter (and in water mucilaginous) indumentum of the achenes, and the smaller pollen grains. The white-tipped leaf-lobes probably afford effective protection against insolation. The lobes stand close together, apparently forming a white, reflecting surface directed towards the sun rays and sheltering the green parts of the leaf. E. pleiodontus has only been collected twice by the Schlechter brothers. The locality 'I'us' has not been located but both localities are probably situated in the same area to the east of Steinkopf.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Close ally, H. cephaloideum is found nearby in drier grassland. H. ingomense is easily recognized even in the vegetative state by its linear-lanceolate, very acute leaves that soon lose the wool from the upper surface. It should be looked for elsewhere in northern KwaZulu-Natal and in the SE. Transvaal.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Can be confused with Pulicaria scabra, but that species has yellow florets and outer female florets are shortly radiate, arranged in only 1 or 2 rows.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: M. acuta is distinctive and can be recognized by the following characters: sharply pungent leaves, sparsely tomentose involucres, petaloid involucral bracts that are mostly conspicuously transparent above the stereome and apically irregularly and coarsely serrate, dark cypselas with short round papillae. Some specimens resemble sharply pungent variants of M. trivialis, but the latter species is in general coarser and has less acuminate leaves, has an entirely different involucre and less acute pappus bristles. The two species are sympatric in some localities. M. densa has also been found growing together with M. acuta.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Much confused with S. helminthioides, which is easily distinguished by its foliaceous calyculus bracts and hispid achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: S. umgeniensis is characterized among related species by its erect, relatively short flowering stems, usually branching from the base to bear the relatively large turbinate heads in a very open inflorescence, and leaves on long, thin petioles.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Gorteria diffusa The area from where the type was collected (see under Notes) corresponds to the area we refer to as “middle“ and Gorteria diffusa from this area can actually be recognized by always having 13 orange coloured ray florets, always 1-4 dark raised spots per capitulum and the spots always display only one white dot. Gorteria diffusa from further north in Namaqualand has 13 dark orange, orange, yellow or sulphur yellow ray florets always with some kind of spot pattern but in Richtersveld, close to the Namibian border, Gorteria diffusa has only 8 ray florets yellow or yellowish white with or without spots.
bibliographicCitation: Stangberg, F; Anderberg, AA. 2014. Morphology and taxonomic reclassification of Gorteria (Asteraceae). Willdenowia 44: 97-120. [http://dx.doi.org/10.3372/wi.44.44112] [All rights reserved]

description: Pillans applied the name M. cephalotes in a very wide sense, with the result that it included four closely related species now recognized. M. cephalotes shows variation in habit, foliage, colour of petaloid involucral bracts, and the shape and size of the cypselas. It is recognized by its declinate leaves, generally pink synflorescenses, and subspathulate outermost involucral bracts, which are usually clearly overtopped by the inner and innermost ones. In M. pulchella, which has a similar appearance, all the involucral bracts usually reach a similar height. M. muraltiifolia is similar to M. cephalotes in features of the synflorescense, but is often much taller and more robust; with rigid branches with broader, spreading and carinate leaves; involucral bracts without glands. The synflorescenses are usually larger. Pink specimens of M. cephalotes sometimes resemble M. divergens ssp. fusca, but M. cephalotes has reddish to white outermost involucral bracts, not brown to dark brown. Specimens with white synflorescenses could in turn be mistaken for M. divergens ssp. divergens, but the latter taxon is distinguished by its decumbent habit, and being smaller in all parts. M. inversa and M. pulchella also have white synflorescenses, but the first has generally brownish-yellow comparatively large, coarse hairs on the branches and on the synflorescenses as well as involucral bracts that gradually become shorter inwards; whilst the latter species has spreading to erect-spreading leaves and capitula clusters that are usually distinguishable.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to T. elsiae, but a coarser plant with larger, homogamous, heads.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Often growing with C. sumatrensis var. sumatrensis (= C. floribunda) and C. canadensis and easily distinguished by its larger heads and lateral branches overtopping the main axis.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: E. imbricatus differs from E. lateriflorus by being smaller in all parts, and especially in leaf-shape. The leaves are short and broad, usually spathulate, very obtuse or even truncate, bright green, fleshy and rugulose.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: A very distinctive species with comparatively broad, flat and carinate leaves; very dense and often rosy pubescent capitula clusters; involucral bracts with a comparatively thin stereome, with only three large pappus bristles per flower; and distinctly scabrid and whitish-brown cypselas. Other 5-flowered species with dense synfloresenses or clusters are not likely to be confused with M. confusa. They never have reddish hairs on capitula clusters, always have 10-20 much narrower pappus bristles per flower, and glabrous cypselas. M. confusa may resemble M. riparia, but that species has more than four capitula clusters on often longer peduncles; usually 3-flowered capitula; many pappus bristles per flower; and also blackish-brown, whitish-papillose cypselas.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: E. spathaceus is readily known by its characteristic involucre, which is completely closed when young and later splits up into a few, broad and thin segments. Only E. ciliatus has a similar involucre, but a very different foliage. There is a considerable but continuous variation in leaf width within E. spathaceus (from c. 0.5 to 5 mm). The centre of this variation lies in the Humansdorp, Uitenhage, and Port Elizabeth Divisions. Outside this area only narrow-leaved forms occur. The species has a connecting position in the section between the narrow-leaved species (e.g., E. Tenuissimus, brevipapposus) and the broad-leaved species (e.g., E. ciliatus, lateriflorns).
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Diagnostic features: Basal leaves glabrous; blades linear to falcate, flat slightly involute or filiform, sometimes chanelled Corymbophore scabrid. Heads in corymbose clusters arranged in a corymb or panicle. Involucral bracts scabrid. Flowers mauve, pink or white. Ovary hirsute. C. africanum together with C. glabrum is the most widely ranging and variable species of the genus. A close study of the populations in the field and of the herbarium material revealed that the most significant variable characters in the complex are leaf shape and size, and the arrangement of the heads. Populations occurring in the mountains around Ceres have flat to involute leaves with heads arranged in a panicle. These populations differ from the rest of the distribution area, where the populations have either involute or terete leaves with heads arranged in a corymb.
bibliographicCitation: Weitz, FM. 1989. A revision of the genus Corymbium L. (Asteraceae). S. African J. Bot. 55: 598-629. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1989); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: E. decussatus and E. microphyllus occur together, they resemble each other in habit, but can be distinguished by the silvery sericeous indumentum in E. decussatus, giving the plants a silvery grey appearance, as opposed to the blue-green to grey-green to bright green colour of E. microphyllus.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: O. glabrum is an erect, corymbosely branched shrub, with crowded leaves. It is a very distinct species, characterized inter alia by its linear, acicular, triquetrous leaves, its sessile heads and its, for the genus, unusually long (12-15 mm), narrowly lanceolate involucral scales. The achenes are ellipsoid-trigonous with blunt angles, and each side has two quite deep, longitudinal furrows with a blunt ridge between them.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to T. hamatiforme but distinguished by the longer, narrower, more recurved and more strongly toothed leaf lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily confused with B. onopordifolia, but in that species the spines tipping the involucral bracts are c. 3-4 mm long, about one eighth the overall length of the bract, in B. cirsiifolia they are c. 5-10 mm long, about one third to one half the total length of the bract.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: The disc-florets are sterile and the styles not produced above the tips of the anthers. The style branches vary in length but are usually quite short, and they lack stigmatic surfaces.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with H. nanum, which is readily distinguished by its leaves with strongly revolute margins and very acute outer involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Cineraria austrotransvaalensis is distinguished from C. albicans by a more shrubby, robust growth form, extremely dentate leaves, and shorter peduncles with more capitula, frequently in compound corymbs. Its trichome complement also differs, having trichomes with c. 6 tapering basal cells and a long multi-celled apical appendage on the dorsal surface of the leaves, vs. the narrow-based fine trichomes found in C. albicans. It is more tomentose grey than C. erodioides and its auricles are not procurrent, as seen in that species.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: Variation in leaf shape seems to have some slight geographic basis, broader, more obtuse leaves being commoner at the coast, narrow, tapering leaves more common at higher altitudes, but the distinction is not absolute, and in addition lower leaves can be broad, upper narrow, and there is a wealth of intermediates.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Displays considerable variation in leaf length and degree of woolliness. Some variation may be induced by growing conditions: plants on rock sheets for instance often have much shorter leaves than nearby plants in grassland.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Cultivated as a window plant in Europe, it has escaped in parts of the Low Countries and on the south coast of England; it does not flower there in the open, but does so in the warmer Scilly Isles. Also on St. Helena, where it is probably introduced. It is also established around Buenos Aires, Argentine, and in South Australia and Victoria.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: E. petraeus is closely allied to E. annae, chiefly differing by the ciliolate leaf-margins. Further, the leaves are shorter and more distinctly semiterete and the peduncles are shorter than is normal in E. annae. I have seen the two species growing together on the Compassberg, where they appeared quite distinct and with no intermediate forms.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: De Candolle erected four varieties to accommodate variation in leaf toothing and indumentum.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: M. lichtensteinii has comparatively large and wide capitula containing about 10 flowers. The involucres are whitish below, pinkish around the middle, broader and white above, with apically revolute to erect-spreading petaloid involucral bracts. All parts in the capitulum of M. lichtensteinii are larger than usual for Metalasia. The involucres may resemble those of M. galpinii, but in that species they are smaller and 5-flowered. The foliage is entirely different, too.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with H. pilosellum but easily distinguished by its very acute squarrose bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species by recurved-spreading, bipinnati-partite leaves with sharply incised, pectinate lobes, and heads borne on a short, inconspicuous peduncle.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N. 2013. FSA Contribution 22: Asteraceae: Calenduleae: Garuleum. Bothalia 43(2): 167-178. [CC BY]

description: Though commonly discoid, and seemingly always so in the Cape, rayed plants occur sporadically throughout Natal and further north, often growing with discoid plants.
