bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: It differs strikingly from S. dregeanus in its lack of descending calyculus bracts. Their general aspect and wispy, cobwebby indumentum sets these two species, as well as S. anomalochrous, apart from all the other purple-flowered senecios; their affinity seems to be with S. macrospermus, as Harvey thought.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Gorteria corymbosa is recognized by eight yellow ray florets without spots in combination with bristle-like phyllaries.
bibliographicCitation: Stangberg, F; Anderberg, AA. 2014. Morphology and taxonomic reclassification of Gorteria (Asteraceae). Willdenowia 44: 97-120. [http://dx.doi.org/10.3372/wi.44.44112] [All rights reserved]

description: The name 'S. fibrosus' became attached to this plant, but belongs to a spring-flowering species (no. 86). The types of S. flanaganii are discoid; colonies of discoid plants occur sporadically (e.g. Ngotshe distr., Ngome forest reserve, Hilliard & Burtt 5932).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: In the vegetative parts this species is very similar to E. trifidus, with which it often grows together. In the floral parts, however, E. marlothii is clearly distinct by its smaller and somewhat cupshaped involucres, its glabrous and papillate achenes, and its sterile disc-florets. E. marlothii is probably nearest related to E. virgatus, which has somewhat similar achenes and disc-florets, but pinnatipartite leaves with finer segments, and more distinctly cupshaped involucres with more connate phyllaries.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Although it seems to be allied to S. paucicalyoulatus, the species which it most resembles is S. ruwenzoriensis, particularly the less robust specimens of that species, but it is easily distinguished by the woolly hairs at the lower nodes and by its penninerved, not triplinerved, leaves; also, it is not tuberous at the base. S. parentalis always grows in marshes. We have seen three marshes in Garden Castle Nature Reserve, each many acres in extent, yellow with this plant. The interesting point is that while the heads mostly have rays 7-10 mm long, the number varies from 2-5, and even in the 5-rayed heads, the rays are often not symmetrically set; also, in some the rays are very narrow, in others they are very short and broad, or the outer flowers may be somewhat bilabiate or malformed, while yet others may be discoid with normal tubular flowers. It seems likely that these are hybrid swarms resulting from crosses between S. parentalis and S. submontanus with discoid heads. S. submontanus grows on dry ground bordering the marsh, very rarely in the marsh itself. S. parentalis and the hybrid progeny are confined to the marsh. Discoid plants in the marsh are noticeably shorter than plants of S. submontanus on nearby dry ground and are further easily distinguished by their foliage and heads with shorter and broader involucres containing more flowers, all characters of S. parentalis. Critical studies of these colonies are obviously necessary.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Extreme forms of De Candolle's two species of Psilothamnus at first sight look rather distinct. The forms named ericifolius have long erecto-patent leaves, whereas adpressifolius was originally applied to forms with very small and closely appressed leaves. These extremes are connected by transitional forms, however, and they are not geographically or ecologically differentiated.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: A distinctive and easily recognized species with non-twisted leaves, curved outwards and apically hooked, and without axillary brachyblasts; apically concave innermost involucral bracts; and a subclavate corolla. M. adunca also has comparatively few capitula in its synflorescenses. The hooks on the leaves are easily felt with the fingertips (even on herbarium-specimens). The distinctive shape of the corolla can also be seen on dried material. The synflorescenses may resemble those of the aberrant northern populations of M. brevifolia with similar petaloid involucral bracts, but M. brevifolia has more conspicuous peduncles and entirely different foliage.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Phymaspermum argenteum shares the fleshy, usually silvery sericeous leaves with the closely related P. comptonii, but can be readily distinguished by the narrowly campanulate involucres with closely appressed, deltoid to ovate involucral bracts with prominent dark margins.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: Leaves glossy, smooth, erect, overlapping, tip acuminate. Very rare and poorly known species.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2017. Key to the southern African species of the Relhania and Macowania groups in the Gnaphalieae (Asteraceae). https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/04040f0a-0603-4405-880c-010703060006/media/Html/default.html [All rights reserved]

description: M. trivialis is well represented in most herbaria, and is always identified as M. muricata (i. e. M. densa). It is distinguished by carinate leaves with rather long axillary brachyblasts; whitish to greyish synflorescenses and involucres; and by usually obtuse pappus bristles. M. densa may be similar to M. trivialis, but differs in the characters outlined above. Apart from these characters U. densa also differs in that its brownish involucre has a greater number of series of involucral bracts and comparatively shorter outermost involucral bracts. The involucres of M. trivialis sometimes have the same shape as those of M. galpinii or M. lichtensteinii, but these two species are distinguishable by foliage and number of flowers per capitulum respectively. Some populations on the Groot Swartberg differ in their sharply pungent leaves and rigid habit, but otherwise resemble the normal form. Pillans' 'form B' of Metalasia muricata was characterized by often long-pointed sharply pungent leaves. Some of the material cited under 'form B' is M. trivialis. M. trivialis is often sympatric with M. densa and M. acuta. At least on the Swartberg, the flowering times seem to differ greatly between M. densa and M. trivialis.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Diagnostic features: Basal leaves scabrid, glandularly hispid on both surfaces viscid; blades broadly elliptic-lanceolate. Corymbophore hispid. Heads in corymbose clusters arranged in a panicle. Involucral bracts scabrid, viscid, trifid. Flowers mauve. Ovary hirsute. The specific epithet congestum is probably derived from the closely arranged capitula which resulted in a 'congested corymb', described by De Candolle as 'corymbo congesto'. C. congestum is not very variable. It is easily recognized in the veld. However, the leaves of specimens from the Cold Bokkeveld area tend to be narrower than those from the Du Toits Kloof - Hottentots Holland area - possibly moisture related.
bibliographicCitation: Weitz, FM. 1989. A revision of the genus Corymbium L. (Asteraceae). S. African J. Bot. 55: 598-629. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1989); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Osteospermum microcarpum is nearly allied to O. polycephalum and agrees well with it in respect of the shape and size of the achenes as well as of the appearance of the heads and the type of ramification. The essential difference consists in O. microcarpum not having entire leaves, but sinuate-dentate or inciso-pinnatifid or, as regards the uppermost, only distantly denticulate to subentire ones. In contrast to O. polycephalum the younger leaves at least are besides distinctly and densely glandular-pubescent, and feel rough when dried. In older leaves the pubescence often disappears entirely or partially. The inferior leaves of the stem are as a rule broad, rhomboid to ovate or elliptic, and taper cuneately to a petiole. The superior ones are much narrower, oblanceolate-lanceolate-sublinear, sessile or inconspicuously petioled, with or without distinct auricles.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: This subspecies is closely allied to C. elsiae, but differs in the clustered heads, shorter corolla tube and anthers.

description: Can be confused with S. latifolius (see under that species), and the very narrow-leaved forms approach S. bupleuroides. The plant given the illegitimate name graminicolus appears to be no more than a very local, more or less recognizable form with linear-lanceolate or linear-oblong leaves growing in disturbed ground around Pietermaritzburg and along the road to Richmond and to Greytown. Typical S. latifolius has not been recorded in these areas, where it is replaced by S. retrorsus, and indeed, this plant, with leaves tending to crowd at the base, closely approaches S. retrorsus. Artificial crosses between S. retrorsus and S. glaberrimus or S. bupleuroides might prove illuminating.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to H. cephaloideum from which it is distinguished by its larger heads, (6-)7-8 mm long with, typically, all the involucral bracts acute, and longer, narrower and more acute radical leaves, a character difficult to define precisely. It is possible that some crossing takes place.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Heterolepis peduncularis is most easily confused with the discoid-headed H. anomala. However, H. anomala has thicker leaves that do not noticeably decrease in length upwards on the stem, and also has a very narrow distribution range only on the northern slopes of the Langeberg in the Garcia's Pass area. Heterolepis peduncularis is distinguished from the remaining members of the genus by its long peduncles, usually 100 mm or longer, and by its lax, slender leaves that decrease in length moving acropetally up the stem. It is a plant with a very ‘straggly’ appearance, which is probably exacerbated by grazing. Several collectors noted an aromatic or sharp odour associated with this species, with one collector classifying the odour as lanolin, and another as apples. One specimen of (le Roux 1452, collected between Worcester and Robertson) has discoid heads. However, in all other characteristics, this is clearly H. peduncularis.

description: H. cymosum subsp. cymosum shows considerable variation in head size. Heads are commonly ±3 x 1 mm but larger-headed plants occur erratically from the Cape Peninsula to the Umzimkulu River on KwaZulu-Natal's southern border, and, from the herbarium records, appear often to grow with the typical small-headed plant. This increase in head size is due, not to an increase in flower number, but to an increase in flower size: corolla length ranges from 2-3.5 mm, and there is a corresponding increase in corolla width.

description: Sometimes confused with forms of H. nudifolium but distinguished by its brown silky-woolly crown and larger heads.

description: Closely allied to T. tenellum but distinguished by its subacute, not very obtuse, involucral bracts.

description: Distinguished by its broad, obtuse involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Gerbera tomentosa displays a wide range of variation in leaf morphology and indumentum. Some specimens from the Hottentots Holland Mountains are more densely felted than usual on the scapes and involucral bracts, and this is also especially evident in specimens from Bredasdorp, which have the leaves very densely yellowish-brownish felted. The lower leaf lobes do not usually decrease in size but we have seen one collection with broadly elliptic-obovate leaves with serrulate-lobed margins with the lobes decreasing in size basipetally. Some collections from Worcester have unusually small leaves, with blades 28-35 x 15-20 mm, which is not typical for the species.

description: Basal leaves glabrous; blades linear to falcate, coriaceous, margins thickened, slightly muricate. Corymbophore scabrid. Heads in corymbose clusters arranged in a corymb. description: There appear to be two distinct forms of Cineraria platycarpa based on the extensions of the cypselae, (i) a form with black, margined cypselae, fringed with white hairs, and (ii) a form with brown, broadly or distinctly winged cypselae, also fringed with hairs. The first form matches the type, but the name has been applied equally to the second form, which is very similar in growth form, leaf shape and texture. A transitional specimen is seen in Page 47 (PRE) from Montagu Baths, in which most of the cypselae in a capitulum are not broad-winged, except for one. The weak root system of this annual herb is evident on a number of specimens. This species could be (and has on occasion been) mistaken for Stilpnogyne bellidioides DC., which also occurs in the Karoo and has a similar growth form and leaf texture. However Stilpnogyne is disciform and ecalyculate with the involucral bracts connate at the base. It is also sometimes very difficult to distinguish young plants of C. lobata subsp. platyptera from C. platycarpa in the Eastern Cape, as both have the broad-winged ray cypselae and are small and softly herbaceous.

description: This species is in herbaria and literature usually named E. sulcatus or E. sulcatus var. densifolius, sometimes even 'E. densifolius', although the latter name has never been combined in accordance with the rules. E. sulcatus is a different species, however, and the correct name, E. empetrifolius, has been neglected until now. description: O. hafstroemii is a low shrub with fairly crowded, narrowly oblanceolate or sublinear, coriaceous leaves with a short, pungent mucro. The involucral scales, peduncles, younger branches and leaves are clothed with a more or less dense, whitish, arachnoid-woolly indument. O. hafstroemii most resembles O. subulatum, but differs from it by the margins of its leaves not being distinctly revolute, and by the leaves not being exactly linear and 1-2 mm broad, but oblanceolate (or a few sublinear) and (2-)3-5 mm broad. In contrast to O. subulatum, the younger parts of the plant have besides quite a dense hairy covering.

description: This new species of Pteronia is unique in its vegetative characters, possessing closely set, opposite and decussate leaves, which resemble some members of the tribe Diosmeae, in the Rutaceae. In inflorescence characters it resembles P. divaricate (Berg.) Less. most, where this species will key out in the last revision of Pteronia (Hutchinson & Phillips, 1917). However, besides the vegetative differences, these two species are very different in floret characters, and are not related. P. divaricate has much longer style-branches and filament collars than P. diosmifolia, the latter being 1.5-1.6 mm long in P. divaricate and only 0.47-0.57 mm long in P. diosmifolia. The corolla lobes are also longer (about 3.5 mm long) and spreading in P. divaricate, whereas they only reach 2 mm long in P. diosmifolia, and show no tendency to spread. Another conspicuous difference is the achene, being only sparsely pubescent and very glandular-papillate in P. divaricate, and very pubescent and sparsely glandular-papillate in P. diosmifolia. The shape of the achene also differs in these two species. The achene of P. divaricate is urn-shaped, being broadest very near the apex, whereas that of P. diosmifolia is vase-shaped, being broadest about two-thirds up from the base. No other species is similar to P. diosmifolia.

description: A very handsome species, of which I only know about a score of bushes in the one locality. The long brown and white involucres are characteristic. description: E. thunbergii has been confused with E. linifolius, which it much resembles. It differs in the more slender, filiform, almost terete leaves, which are provided with a narrow woolly strip on the adaxial side and have truncate tips. Furthermore, the involucres are hemispherical and mostly herbaceous and rather thin, and the achenes are puberulous. The colour of the young branches, and sometimes also of the leaves, is normally reddish brown. E. linifolius has more flattened, acute or acuminate leaves of a pure green colour, campanulate involucres with firm and usually distinctly nerved involucral bracts, and always glabrous achenes. A few intermediate collections are interpreted as hybrids. Some plants have the involucral bracts free from the base. In this respect they differ from one of the generally accepted generic and even subtribal characters. Previously two species with free involucral bracts have been separated as a genus of its own, viz. Lysichlamys Compt. In my opinion the discrete involucre is a derived condition within the genus. As shown elsewhere, the genus Lysichlamys must be sunk in Euryops. In the case of E. thunbergii I have found no other significant differences between plants with free involucral bracts and those with a connate involucre. The collections with free phyllaries are from Clanwilliam Div. (Lewis 2032, Barker 6579 in BOL, the same number in NBG has mostly connate involucral bracts), Worcester Div. (Barker 5928), and Malmesbury Div. (Maguire 89 p.p.; part of this collection is normal with connate phyllaries). The collection from the Giftberg (Vanrhynsdorp Div., Phillips 7424) is somewhat intermediate with some phyllaries free and others connate to various degree.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is recognized on its glandular-punctate leaves and slender involucres. It is related to R. multipunctata, but it has not the capitula arranged in cymes and the leaves are much smaller. Another related species is R. foveolata, from which it differs e.g. in characters of the achenes (see key and discussion under R. foveolata). Variation. The size of the capitula varies considerably in this species. Generally the involucres are narrowly cyathiform and slender with few florets, but they may be widely campanulate with increased space for more florets. The greatest variation is in Cedarbergen and it decreases further north and south respectively. In one collection (Compton 4293) the pappus of the disc-florets consists both of scales and bristles, a condition earlier discussed under Morphological aspects.

description: Recognized by the dentate or irregularly sinuate, usually scarcely discolorous leaves with the under surface glabrous or only thinly tomentose, rarely more densely whitish-felted, and the dark brown to blackish anther appendages. Plants with the leaf under surface more densely felted can be confused with G. tomentosa but that species has a yellowish-tawny indumentum and pale yellow anther appendages. The pappus in most collections of G. crocea is snow white and this is a useful diagnostic character in these instances as most other species have a tawny pappus. A similar white pappus and dark anther appendages are also characteristic of G. sinuata but that species has leaves with more deeply crenate margins and a densely white-felted under surface. G. crocea hybridizes with G. linnaei where they co-occur on the Cape Peninsula.

description: E. mirus in my original description was said to possess a subterranean caudex. When studying the species in nature I found this to be only partly true, however. The plant can be characterized as a low shrub with a vigorous long taproot and a compactly branching stem, which is subterranean in the lower parts and aerial in the upper portions. The leaves appear almost rosulate at the tips of the short aerial branches. The peculiar leaves are pinnatipartite with the lateral lobes often lobed and furnished with an abaxial lobe at the base. The leaves are further sparsely pubescent with long and thin hairs as well as short and stiff ones, and the leaf-lobes are bristle-pointed. The disc-florets are sterile, and the achenes have a characteristic velvety coat of short hairs. In this species there is thus an assemblage of characters, which are unique or rare in the genus. The only closely related species is E. rosulatus, which has the same growth-form, pinnatipartite leaves and similar achenes.

description: A. brevipes, only represented by a few collections, is obviously closely allied to A. nycthemerum, but sufficiently distinct to receive recognition as a species. A. brevipes can possibly be regarded as a high montane derivative of A. nycthemerum. A. brevipes shows very little variation.

description: The distinguishing features of var. aureum are the large heads and green, woolly-margined cauline leaves. Much of the E. Cape coastal material in herbaria lacks radical leaves, but these, when present, may be green with woolly margins or thickly to thinly grey-woolly. The original material of H. aureum probably came from the Humansdorp-Port Elizabeth area, the furthest east that Thunberg collected, and radical leaves are wanting on his specimens. Plants from coastal KwaZulu-KwaZulu-Natal, whence came Drège's specimen of H. fulgidum var. heterotrichum, have grey-woolly radical leaves and green cauline leaves. It seems that variation in the indumentum of the radical leaves must be accepted as characteristic of var. aureum.

description: Phymaspermum acerosum shares the narrowly lobed pinnatifid leaves, the absence of myxogenic trichomes on the cypselas and the presence of prominent resin canals in the cypsela ribs with P. pinnatifidum. It can be distinguished by its narrowly campanulate to oblong involucres and the absence of a prominent apical crown on the cypselas (only at most a thickened apical rim which can be entire to shortly dentate). Phymaspermum acerosum is also a much larger more robust shrub growing to more than 0.5 m tall with much thicker and woodier stems than the smaller P. pinnatifidum which tends to have much more slender and herbaceous stems. The previously recognised species P. villosum was at first distinguished from P. acerosum by having much broader oblong and hairy involucres. Phymaspermum acerosum was considered to only have narrowly campanulate involucres however, after many specimens were examined, P. acerosum is now considered to have involucres which vary from narrowly campanulate to broad and oblong and P. villosum is now a synonym of P. acerosum.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: This species and P. gariepina are easily recognized as a pair by their dentate, shining leaves, broad involucral bracts, much branched anther tails, and the deeply incised external pappus scales with almost bristle-like extensions.
bibliographicCitation: Anderberg, AA. 1986. The genus Pegolettia (Compositae, Inuleae). Cladistics 2(2): 158-186. [All rights reserved]

description: Osteospermum spinigerum is a strongly xeromorphous, much branched dwarf shrublet with spreading branches. It differs from all the other species in the subgenus Tripteris by very many of its branchlets being transformed into hard spines. It has typical Tripteris achenes with an apical cavity with three fenestrae and wings c. 2 mm broad. In habit O. spinigerum may be confusingly like Osteospermum spinosum, but its leaves are much more crowded at the base of the branches and most of them are distinctly oblanceolate. O. spinigerum will probably be nearest related to the extremely polymorphous and widely distributed species O. scuriosum, which, however, never has any branches ending in spines.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: S. petitianus A. Rich. (Ethiopia, Somaliland, Uganda, Kenya and Congo) seems to be allied. See also S. pleistocephalus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Plants are commonly thickly tomentose, but all degrees of development of woolly hairs occur, and sometimes wool is either completely wanting or confined to the leaf margins.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Rays which are white above and reddish below (with various shades) are confined to E. Cape, Natal, Orange Free State, Swaziland, Transvaal, and (fide Wild, 1972) Southern Mozambique. The yellow ray colour is universal in all other parts of the distribution area, but can also be found in the areas mentioned. The violet-purple pappus colour is similarly confined to the E. Cape-Transvaal area, while the whitish-tawny pappus is universal in all other areas, but also common in E. Cape-Transvaal.
bibliographicCitation: Hansen, HV. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the genus Gerbera (Compositae, Mutisieae) sections Gerbera, Parva, Piloselloides (in Africa), and Lasiopus. Opera Bot. 78: 5-36. [All rights reserved]

description: As pointed out by Compton E. rehmannii is closely allied to E. tenuissimus and E. linifolius, and it has often been confused with these two species. Even one of the collections cited by Compton (I.c.) belongs to E. tenuissimus (Pillans in herb. Bolus 14175). The species is quite variable, and some of the characters mentioned by Compton are not always reliable. The statement that the capitula are 'borne high above the leaves' holds true in most cases, but there is no sharp discontinuity in this respect against E. tenuissimus. This is illustrated in the scatter diagram, showing the combined variation of peduncle length and leaf length in E. rehmannii and E. tenuissimus ssp. tenuissimus. The number of involucral bracts is useless as a separating character, but the shape of the involucre is more distinct. In E. rehmannii the involucre is cupshaped with much-connate phyllaries, whereas it is more hemispherical and expanded in E. tenuissimus. The hair-covering of the achenes affords one of the best distinguishing characters. In E. rehmannii the hairs are short and papilliform and only slightly mucilaginous when soaked. E. tenuissimus has densely villous achenes with longer hairs, which in water swell and become strongly mucilaginous. E. linifolius and E. thunbergii could also be confused with E. rehmannii but differ in the narrower leaves, pubescent branches, and different achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Could be confused with S. cathcartensis, but is distinguished by its smaller heads (involucral bracts 4.5-5 mm, not (5.5-)6-7 mm) and the minute 'pinhead' glands, not uniseriate glandular hairs, on the involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: An easily recognized slender species with very sparse foliage; linear and often long leaves without distinct axillary brachyblasts; comparatively narrow outer and inner involucral bracts, which give a reddish impression; apically clavate pappus bristles; and dark to blackish-brown cypselas with long, acute papillae. Old specimens may resemble M. densa, but that species is only very rarely similar in habit, has different foliage, broader outer and inner involucral bracts and brown cypselas with short, though acute, papillae. The involucres may look like those of M. muricata which however always has completely different foliage. Both M. plicata and M. octoflora have similar cypselas, but are much different in habit, foliage, and features of the involucre.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Hilliard cited Hilliard & Burtt 8971 (in Compositae in Natal All, 1977) as S. oxyodontus, but it proves to be distinct from S. oxyodontus, not only by its larger heads as described in the diagnosis, but by its lack of stipule-like lobes at the base of each leaf: the leaf base is only minutely auriculate. Also, in S. oxyodontus there is generally only one median resinous strand in each involucral bract, whereas in S. thamathuensis there are mostly two or three. 5. thamathuensis is not fleshy as S. oxyodontus. It was possible to grow a form of S. oxyodontus with dissected leaves not unlike those of S. thamathuensis side by side with plants of S. thamathuensis: the differences in stem and leaf texture and in head size were then strikingly apparent. The species differ too in habit, S. oxyodontus having many long whip-like branches from the base, while S. thamathuensis is bushy. Both species favour much the same type of habitat, among rocks with some shade, but S. thamathuensis probably requires damper situations than does S. oxyodontus, and grows at considerably higher altitudes. In addition to the three collections cited, S. thamathuensis has also been seen below cliffs on the upper reaches of the Umzimouti river in Underberg district, north of Thamathu, but the plants were not in flower in November 1977.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1982. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: IX. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 40(2): 247-298. [CC BY-SA]

description: A very handsome, rounded shrub, the leaves almost rosetted at the tips of the new shoots, the dark green mass starred with big yellow heads on long leafy peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is recognized by the oblanceolate, obtuse-mucronate leaves mostly with denticulate margins towards the apex. The synflorescences tend to be more open and the capitula are smaller than in the other species.
bibliographicCitation: Herman, PPJ. 2002. Revision of the Tarchonanthus camphoratus complex (Asteraceae-Tarchonantheae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 32(1): 21-28. [CC BY]

description: O. connatum is closely allied to O. dentatum. Its lowermost and often also its medial leaves are opposite, and the flower heads have as a rule not only winged achenes but also 1-3 wingless, terete achenes with a more or less distinct, solid beak just as in O. dentatum. It differs from O. dentatum above all by its sessile, broad, triangular-ovate lowermost leaves, the base of which is more or less cordate-hastate, and by the winged achenes being considerably smaller, only c. 5-6 mm long. In O. dentatum on the other hand, the leaves are oblonglanceolate to narrowly obovate, tapering towards the base in a petiole, and the winged achenes are 9-12 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: See also B. robusta and B. debilis.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: A. ellipticum is not very variable. It is readily recognized by the patent-reflexed, elliptic or broadly elliptic leaves, and the quite glabrous involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Lundgren, J. 1972. Revision of the genus Anaxeton Gaertn. (Compositae). Opera Bot. 31: 5-59. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily recognized by its stiff, somewhat falcate leaves and flowers subtended by paleae.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Osteospermum hyoseroides is very nearly related to O. clandestinum, differing from it mainly by the length of the ray flowers in relation to the involucre. In O. hyoseroides the ray flowers are large, 2-3 times longer than the involucre, whereas the ray flowers in O. clandestinum are small, as long as the involucre or but little longer.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: One collection (Pietermaritzburg distr., 1.5 miles from Foxhill Station on road to Thornville Junction, G. Gordon-Gray s.n.) has the foliage of S. rhomboideus but the heads are rayed (see under S. oxyriifolius).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its broad, relatively soft-textured leaves that are equally thinly to more densely hispid-pilose on both surfaces, often with coarsely toothed margins, the vestiture of prominently stalked hairs with relatively short arms mostly shorter than the stalks. The stems are typically closely leafy only in the lower part and nearly nude in the upper part but this is not invariable. The capitula are relatively large, 10-15 mm across when pressed, with inner involucral bracts 5-10 mm long. The 1-armed or spurred hairs on the perianth lobes are also characteristic for the species. The often leafless upper parts of the stem, fewer and larger capitula, and scarcely discolorous foliage with characteristic, harsh vestiture of long-stalked trichomes with short, stiff arms distinguish Hilliardiella sutherlandii from H. flanaganii and H. hirsuta, both with stems leafy to the top and with more numerous, smaller capitula, the inner involucral bracts 3-7 mm long, and more or less discolorous leaves, thinly tomentose above and densely woolly-tomentose beneath, with short-stalked eglandular hairs with long, slender arms.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Hilliardiella (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 106: 41-59. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Gorteria personata is characterised by eight ray-florets with a basal dark spot and the phyllaries are hard and pungent already at anthesis and reach further than the ray-florets.
bibliographicCitation: Stangberg, F; Anderberg, AA. 2014. Morphology and taxonomic reclassification of Gorteria (Asteraceae). Willdenowia 44: 97-120. [http://dx.doi.org/10.3372/wi.44.44112] [All rights reserved]

description: O. junceum is characterized by its large, obovoid- to broadly ellipsoid-trigonous achenes, which are furnished towards the apex with three quite short, more or less ridge-like, blunt processes. Between these apical processes there are one or more furrows. The base of the achenes is as a rule conspicuously furrowed. The involucre is very characteristic and unusually large as compared with that in other Osteospermum species, and the inner involucral scales may be up to 15 mm long and 6 mm broad. The involucral scales are imbricate, floccosely white-woolly or, in course of time, partly glabrous. The younger parts of the plant are covered with a more or less dense, light grey indument, which soon falls off.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Plants rooting at nodes and forming mat-like clones; ligulae of ray florets non-yellow. Achenes 3-angular, angles crenate or cristate or irregularly incised.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1980. Dimorphotheca venusta (T. Norl.) T. Norl. stat. nov. and additional notes on D. montana T. Norl. (Compositae). Bot. Not. 133: 559-563. [All rights reserved]

description: E. longipes is closely allied to E. rupestris, differing in the more slender growth, the more erect and often entire leaves, the usually longer and more slender peduncles, and the smaller achenes. Like in E. rupestris the disc-florets are sterile with simple or shallowly lobed styles, which lack stigmatic areas. Two varieties with remarkably different achenes may be distinguished. The southern populations have glabrous and distinctly tuberculate achenes, whereas the collections from Ceres Division have densely villous achenes. The isolated population in Paarl Division is somewhat deviating, but it has here been included in the southern form series. The occurrence of different achene types with distinct distribution ranges is an interesting parallel to the condition within E. rupestris. In the latter species, however, the two varieties have largely overlapping areas.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: A. strigosus (Thunb.) Less. subsp. pseudoscabridus Rommel is endemic to EC.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is closely allied to R. squarrosa and they are liable to be mixed up. R. genistifolia has typically spreading, linear, smaller leaves and urceolate-cyathiform, smaller, uniformly light yellowish brown involucres than R. squarrosa. Specimens with wider and somewhat irregularly bent leaves may be very similar to specimens of R. squarrosa with spreading leaves. They can be distinguished in the less slender achenes with longer pappus, more than 1/5 of the length of the achene, usually 1/3-1/2. Lastly, achenes of ray-florets are always ± densely pilose, never glabrous as they often, but not always are in R. squarrosa. R. viscosa is another closely related species. R. genistifolia, however, never has the thick, very glutinous leaves of R. viscosa and the capitula are usually smaller than in the latter species. This species varies considerably in leaf size and shape. The variation does not seem to be correlated with variation in other vegetative and floral characters. It is only possible to point out some general tendencies in leaf variation and geographical distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: As regards the habit of growth and the shape of the achenes, etc., O. hispidum coincides well with O. ciliatum. It differs from O. ciliatum by being densely hispid in all its parts, and by the inferior surface of the leaves and the involucre being greyish cobweb-cottony. The leaves in O. hispidum are entire or irregularly 1-3-dentate on each margin, the margins not being cartilaginous crenate as in O. ciliatum, but thin-edged. The branches are terete or only slightly angled. The breadth of the leaves varies very much just as in O. ciliatum.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Erect shrub with whip-like branches; leaves and branches with a yellowish sheen; leaves linear, at least 5 times longer than wide; involucre tips acute.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2019. Taxonomy and reclassification of South African Asteraceae genus Elytropappus (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae), the description of two new genera and two new species. Phytotaxa 403(4): 248-284. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.403.4.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to the widespread H. pilosellum, but in that species the crown is conspicuously brown silky-woolly, the leaves are usually scarcely petiolate, harshly pubescent above with long coarse multicellular hairs, and mostly lack wool on the upper surface. Sometimes confused with H. coriaceum, which is immediately distinguished by its different leaves and straw-coloured involucral bracts. The type of H. gerberifolium has leaves initially silky grey-woolly on both surfaces, later with only traces of wool; the type of H. davyi also has leaves persistently grey silky-woolly above, but plants with leaves scarcely woolly above seem just as common. The type of H. brunneum has only traces of wool clinging to the upper leaf surface.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: In the past, E. aromaticus was often confused with E. punctulatus, a closely related species. It can be easily distinguished from that species by the consistently opposite leaves, even on flowering shoots. On brachyblasts the leaves are distinctly decussate. The otherwise glabrous leaves have a felty floccose indumentum in the axil. Although they (paleae) look free superficially, a thorough study showed that they are connate from the base for about one third of their length.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to H. cooperi and not easy to distinguish in the herbarium. The persistent white wool on the inflorescence branches to well below the first forking is a useful character to distinguish H. ruderale; white wool is usually wanting in H. cooperi except sometimes immediately below the heads. H. ruderale flowers in spring, H. cooperi in summer. In the field, the obliquely-ascending inflorescence branches of H. ruderale immediately distinguish it from H. cooperi with inflorescence branches wide-spreading to nearly horizontal.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Although G. galpinii seems closely allied to G. viridifolia, it is easily recognized by the rather rigid, entire, lancelote, glabrous leaves with hardly visible nerves and long, winged petiole. G. galpinii has a limited ecological range, being confined to moist habitats, places not occupied by any other species of the genus. It seems to be specialized to the moist habitats; the glabrous leaves may be an adaptation to this.
bibliographicCitation: Hansen, HV. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the genus Gerbera (Compositae, Mutisieae) sections Gerbera, Parva, Piloselloides (in Africa), and Lasiopus. Opera Bot. 78: 5-36. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is closely allied to O. ciliatum and O. pterigoideum, and has achenes of nearly the same shape. O. pyrifolium differs from the two last-mentioned species chiefly by its long-petioled leaves and its larger involucre (about twice as large). The woolly covering on the leaves and branches usually loosens and falls off at an early stage, and is therefore of no great diagnostic value for this species. The branches are not angled or narrowly winged as in O. ciliatum and O. pterigoideum. The leaves are thickly coriaceous, entire or very slightly repando-denticulate, but never rigidly ciliate or aculeolate as in O. ciliatum.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: O. herbaceum and also O. volkensii are easily distinguished from the other species of the genus, being the only ones with opposite leaves. Only the very uppermost part of the stem, the floriferous part, sometimes has alternate leaves. These species differ from each other above all in the habit of growth and the shape of the leaves. O. herbaceum is an erect, perennial herb with broad, ovate or rhomboid leaves. O. volkensii, on the oilier hand, is a much branched shrub with narrowly oblong or lanceolate leaves. The stem and the leaves in O. herbaceum are hispidulous or, when older, subglabrous. The stem, which is about 1 metre high, is only very slightly lignified in its inferior part. The leaves are cobwebbed beneath, at all events in their earlier stage. The lower and medial leaves are usually subcordate-auriculate at the base, and their margins are coarsely paucidentate from the middle. The achenes are obovoid or ellipsoid with, as a rule, three slightly prominent, longitudinal angles.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily confused with B. cirsiifolia but distinguished by the spines at the tips of the involucral bracts being c. 3-4 mm long, about one eighth the overall length of the bract, not c. 5-10 mm long, one half to one third the overall length of the bracts as in B. cirsiifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: D. jucunda differs from D. caulescens mainly by the ray flowers being deep pink on the upper surface instead of white. The achenes are narrowly triangular-obovoid-ellipsoid, with conspicuously elevated, acute angles (or the inner angle sometimes bluntish) in contrast to D. caulescens, which usually has blunt and as a rule slightly prominent angles. The sides are smooth or slightly rugose and foveolate, the two radial sides sometimes having an indistinct, longitudinal ridge. D. jucunda has beautiful pink flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: H. athrixiifolium is frequently confused with H. rugulosum, but that species produces simple or subsimple stems from a creeping stock, rarely has dwarf axillary shoots, and the fimbrils on the receptacle much exceed the ovaries. However, H. athrixiifolium is closely allied to H. rosum, from which it is scarcely distinguishable in habit, foliage and size and shape of the heads. But the tips of the involucral bracts are always much crisped in H. athrixiifolium, while they are nearly always smooth, rarely slightly crisped, in H. rosum.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Although the nectary is absent and pollen spines are short in this species, like those in Seriphium, the floret colour and structure, as well as the synflorescence structure are better accommodated in Stoebe.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2016. A monograph of Stoebe and Seriphium (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa and neighbouring islands. Phytotaxa 242(1): 1-84. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.242.1.1] [All rights reserved]

description: O. imbricatum has narrowly obovoid or ellipsoid achenes, furnished with three acute or very narrow-winged primary ridges and six more or less prominent (sometimes inconspicuous), obtuse secondary ridges with pitted interspaces between the ridges. The involucral scales are usually sparsely glanduloso-muriculate. The closely allied species O. polygaloides has, in contradistinction to O. imbricatum, achenes with obtuse primary ridges and dense glanduloso-muriculate involucral scales. In younger, well-developed specimens of O. imbricatum the stem is erect, c. 1-2 m high, and strongly lignified, usually simple except at the summit, where it ends in more or less corymbose flowering-branches. In older specimens, particularly such as have been damaged by fire or by animals and have lost the primary stem, a varying number of prostrate or ascendent lateral branches, furnished with divaricate twigs, arise from the crown of the root. Thus, older and younger specimens of this species may have quite a different habit of growth.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: H. stoloniferum and H. lancifolium are closely allied, but they are nearly allopatric; their areas appear to overlap only in the Baviaansberg NE. of Ceres. H. lancifolium is distinguished by its leaves, generally narrower and more pointed than those of H. stoloniferum, and by its heads, generally larger with more pointed inner involucral bracts. Peduncle-like flowering twigs seem to be a constant feature of H. lancifolium.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Replaced in eastern South Africa by subsp. kraussii.
bibliographicCitation: Gilbert, MG; Jeffrey, C. 1988. A revision of Ethulia (Compositae: Vernonieae). Kew Bull. 43(2): 165-193. [https://doi.org/10.2307/4113733] [All rights reserved]

description: Ssp. transvaalensis is a quite characteristic taxon in its typical forms from Central Transvaal. It is easily recognized on its greyish green or glaucous leaves with a broad and many-nerved rachis (Fig. 481). The limits against ssp. setilobus are more vague in the area where the two subspecies meet (SE. Transvaal, W. Swaziland). Most specimens can be referred without difficulty to either of the subspecies, however. The single collection from Swaziland (Compton 28007) and also Codd 3690 from Witbank Div. are somewhat atypical, with many leaves few-lobed and unusually narrow (rachis c. 1 mm wide). These collections clearly belong to ssp. transvaalensis, however, by the leaf colour and the nervation of the broader leaves. Rogers 5142 and Acocks 11539, both from the sympatric range of the two subspecies, show some tendencies towards ssp. setilobus (leaf lobes up to 4-6 mm long) but in most respects agree best with ssp. transvaalensis. Generally speaking, ssp. transvaalensis is less variable than ssp. setilobus, which is not surprising in view of the more restricted distribution of the former.

description: Var. doroniciflorus is doubtfully distinct from the species, but this needs further investigation on Cape material. The name albanensis is sometimes misapplied to S. albanopsis, which has 12(-16) involucral bracts, short calyculus bracts, only 8 rays, and very scaly peduncles. The name fibrosus (see synonymy above) is misapplied to the plant listed here as S. conrathii. It is possibly a mistake to equate S. fibrosus with S. albanensis var. doroniciflorus but the plant needs to be better known before its status can be determined.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: The considerable variation within ssp. tenuissimus follows a geographical pattern, which may be of interest to elucidate further. Four regional form series may be distinguished. They are often fairly characteristic, and it could perhaps be tempting to give them sub-specific rank. I have refrained from doing so, however, on account of the considerable number of transitional forms or collections which cannot with certainty be referred to any of the form series.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: This is the most complex variety found in C. glabrum and sometimes local forms can be recognized, but these on the other hand merge with other forms at other places. The following noteworthy trends are evident within C. glabrum var. glabrum. The most typical form of this variety is found on the mountains of the Cape Peninsula. It has linear leaves with prominent veins and the corymbose clusters are arranged in corymbs The forms present in the Bain's Kloof-Ceres area also have the typical corymbose arrangement, but with the conflorescence more ramified (open). In the Cold Bokkeveld and Cedarberg areas, the conflorescence is extremely ramified while the leaves have prominent veins. From the Hottentots Holland Mountains eastwards as far as Van Stadens Mountains populations with broad leaves, up to 20 mm occur. Considerable thought has been given to the possibility of making this another variety of C. glabrum, but because of the many local races that are recognizable another variety is unwarranted. Population studies done in the Tradouw's Pass revealed that there are specimens with narrow leaves ca. 5 mm broad and those with broad leaves up to 15 mm broad, which occur less than 2 m apart. The conflorescence varies from a typical corymbose to a lax panicle, but with individual heads grouped in corymbose clusters. A noteworthy population occurs in the southern Cape Peninsula near Silvermine. The plants are up to 250 mm tall, with leaves 100-225 mm long and 2-6.2 mm broad. In close proximity (2-3 m) are populations with plants up to 500 mm high with leaves up to 300 mm long, and up to 115 mm broad. Intermediates between these populations are also present.

description: In its southern area (Little Karroo) this taxon is very characteristic and gives the impression of a quite distinct species. The peduncles are very long, most leaves are entire, the capitula are large and many-flowered, and the involucral bracts are numerous and somewhat gibbous towards the base. These forms are usually named E. punctatus or E. longipes. In the northern localities, however, the peduncles are gradually shorter and more slender, and the capitula are often small. It appears that no distinct boundary line towards ssp. vulgaris exists. The type of á. indivisus is extremely small-leaved and short-peduncled. Another collection from the same Division (Braun s.n. in GRA) shows some characteristics of ssp. vulgaris and is only with hesitation referred to ssp. subcarnosus. The Witteberg population, described as Thodaya elongata, and the sub-specific type specimen are transitional between the extreme 'indivisus' forms and the Little Karroo forms. The pollen grains of ssp. subcarnosus are generally larger than in ssp. vulgaris. Also the stomata are comparatively large, and the epidermis cells sometimes have a striate surface.

description: M. aurea is easily recognized by its yellowish synflorescenses in combination with comparatively small capitula and petaloid involucral bracts with a thin, and slightly concave, lamina. M. aurea is distinguished from the other species of Metalasia with yellow or yellowish synflorescenses. Of these, M. octoflora has individually arranged and often fewer capitula with 5-7 flowers, whilst M. pulcherrima f. pulcherrima has non-twisted leaves and brighter yellow petaloid involucral bracts. M. luteola is a shrublet of lower stature, and has carinate leaves with long axillary brachyblasts, and also lighter yellow, emarginate to truncate, petaloid involucral bracts. Yet another species which often has yellowish synflorescenses is M. plicata, but this species has fewer and generally larger capitula in the synflorescenses, and conspicuously plicate innermost involucral bracts.

description: Plants in grassland are generally shorter and less lush than those in really wet places, the latter often showing considerable variation in leaf cutting. Nevertheless, S. polyodon is a well-marked species, easily recognized by its long narrow leaves clothing most of the flowering stem and its small campanulate corymbosely arranged heads, yet none of the available names have ever been taken up and specimens are usually found labelled 'aff. erubescens' or 'discoid S. concolor', the latter name reflecting not only the long standing confusion over the correct application of the name S. concolor, but drawing attention to the existence of rayed and discoid forms of the species. The two forms may be found growing together, for example at Nottingham Road and Mooi River in the Natal Midlands, but frequently only one or the other occurs and the radiate plant has a more restricted distribution than the discoid.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: A species with declinate leaves; involucral bracts with mostly revolute to erect-spreading tips; and a corolla with a conspicuous, rigid and resiniferous base, and comparatively long lobes. It is sometimes confused with M. densa, but differs in the characters outlined above. Some specimens from the Kouga Mountains and eastwards have shorter leaves, fewer capitula per synflorescense and fewer involucral bracts. Other aberrant collections are from Groot Swartberg. However, these deviant specimens, or populations, do possess the features of the corolla, which are unique to this species.

description: Var. rupestris is usually a shrublet less than 0.5 m high, growing in rock crevices at altitudes between c. 360 and 1800 m s.m. The distribution ranges from the mountains of Somerset West and northern Caledon Divisions to Tulbagh in the north.

description: Few herbarium specimens could be traced under the name E. pedicellaris. Most material was found under E. punctulatus or misidentified as E. africanus. Although closely related to E. punctulatus, E. pedicellaris can be distinguished from that species by the long, blue-green, succulent leaves which turn noticeably darker upon drying, the relatively large capitula, 4-5 x 5-8 mm, on long peduncles, 10-30(-40) mm, and by the brittle stems. E. pedicellaris grows mostly at 300-600 m altitude, but often below 300 m, in contrast to E. punctulatus which grows at and above 600 m.

description: O. thodei is a shrubby plant, c. 0.5 m high, with densely and shortly glandular-pilose leaves, peduncles, involucral scales, and younger branches. In dried specimens the hairiness must be described as asper or hispidulous, but in living ones it is probably pubescent. In habit O. thodei may be very similar to O. grandidentatum, but it differs from it int. al. by its narrowly ellipsoid achenes, which are provided with numerous pits, and its broader, lanceolate to oblong involucral scales. O. grandidentatum, on the other hand, has cylindrical-fusiform achenes without any pits, and linear-lanceolate involucral scales. The shape of the leaves in O. grandidentatum is very variable, forms of that species being sometimes met with whose leaves much resemble those of O. thodei.

description: Cineraria parvifolia is a very slender herb, with small leaves and capitula. Its uppermost leaves are usually lyrate-pinnatifid, but its lower leaves are often reniform with a few lateral pinnae below the lamina. Cineraria parvifolia could be confused with C. pinnata, but that species grows at much lower altitude in marshy conditions in the Maputaland region and adjacent coastal regions of southern Mozambique. Its uppermost leaves tend to be more dissected than in C. pinnata with smaller lobes, and its middle to lower leaves (if entire) are reniform, not deltoid or deltoid-reniform as in C. pinnata. Cineraria parvifolia could also possibly be confused with C. geraniifolia, especially when its leaves are not very dissected, but that species has longer peduncles, larger capitula and glabrous cypselae. Its habit and leaves may also resemble C. lyratiformis, but that has glabrous, broad-winged cypselae. The degree of hairiness on the cypselae varies, especially on the faces, occasionally being entirely glabrous. A collection from 2000 m on the Steenkampsberg mountain pass, the highest in the region previously known as the ‘Transvaal’, matches Cineraria parvifolia but has much larger capitula than usual, probably a function of the high altitude.

description: E. montanus is a usually erect, compact and rounded, dwarf shrub. The leaves have a characteristic constriction above the dilated base, and they are more or less pure green, not glaucous or dull greyish green as in the closely allied species E. decumbens.

description: Differs from D. caulescens by the upper surface of the ray flowers not being white but bright purple, and by the lobes of the outer disc flowers being bearded on the outside and the lobes of the inner disc flowers being inflated or cap-like. description: Phymaspermum pinnatifidum is a small, spring flowering multistemmed shrublet with discoid corymbosely arranged capitula and cypselas with a prominent membranous apical crown. Together with P. acerosum it does not have myxogenic trichomes on the cypselas (the generic synapomorphy) but rather prominent resin canals in the cypsela ribs. It can be readily distinguished from P. acerosum by its earlier flowering time, smaller stature (less than 0.5 m tall) with thin herbaceous stems, the broader funnel or cupshaped involucres and the prominent membranous apical crown on the cypselas. Its small size means that it could also be confused with P. woodii but can be readily distinguished by the broader, not apically constricted involucres with loosely appressed involucral bracts, the prominent membranous apical crown on the cyselas and the absence of myxogenic trichomes.

description: E. rosulatus is closely allied to E. mirus, from which it differs by the glabrous, regularly pinnatipartite leaves with narrower segments, and the larger, fertile disc-florets with longer style branches. The leaves are so densely crowded on the reduced branches as to appear rosulate. The achenes are similar to those of E. mirus but smaller.

description: H. mimetes is easily confused with H. lepidissimum, but can be recognized by its decidedly grey leaves, persistently woolly on both surfaces and with flat margins; in H. lepidissimum the leaves tend to be green above (drying brown) because the wool is soon shed from the upper surface to reveal the underlying coarse shaggy hairs, and the leaf margins are crisped. H. mimetes can be distinguished from H. rudolfii by its graded, crisped, straw-coloured involucral bracts (not subequal, smooth, white). There is a difference in leaf shape too, but this is difficult to express in words. All three species are sympatric and may grow in close proximity. It seems likely that the original material of H. mimetes was of hybrid origin: the leaves are more coarsely hairy above than is usual and the wool tends to be evanescent, so that the leaves are not distinctly grey; also, the leaf margins are very slightly crisped, Codd 1618 (NU; PRE) and Acocks 12865 (PRE), from the same site in the Barberton Mountains, somewhat resemble the type.

description: E. spinescens is a robust shrub, up to 1 m high and in diameter, with rigid, strong spines. E. namaquensis, another closely related species, is a delicately branched shrub barely 400 mm tall and in diameter. The capitula of E. spinescens are relatively large, 4.5-5.2 mm long, and fairly shortly pedunculate, 0-3.5 (-5.0) mm long, to almost sessile, borne only terminally on brachyblasts. It is therefore easy to distinguish E. spinescens from the closely related E. karooicus and E. namaquensis, which are also spinescent, since E. karooicus has a small, but distinct ray lamina and sessile capitula and E. namaquensis has long-pedunculate capitula, solitary on brachyblasts, as well as in racemes borne terminally on dolichoblasts.

description: Often behaves as a weed. Over the eastern part of the range, specimens resemble the type of H. obvallatum and have large heads (both in overall size and in the number of flowers in a head) and large leaves with margins scarcely revolute. North-westwards, from the N. central Cape to Zimbabwe, Botswana and Namibia, both heads and leaves tend to become smaller, and the leaves are more spreading with margins more strongly revolute. The types of both H. cerastioides and var. gracile match this form. In Namibia, H. cerastioides is sometimes confused with pale-headed specimens of H. pumilio subsp. fleckii, but the narrow, more or less linear, patent leaves of H. cerastioides in this region tend to give it a characteristic facies. Also H. cerastioides grows on the flats, while H. pumilio subsp. fleckii is on the mountains. However, var. aurosicum is problematical.

Taken as they are, these specimens may look like taxonomically distinct, but when the whole of the wide range of the variation displayed by St. cyathuloides is observed, their narrow leaves appear to represent one end of the extreme, whereas specimens like Bolus 8552, with wide robust leaves, represent the opposite extreme.

description: The commonest and most widespread member of the genus, and also the most variable. It is generally distinguishable from all other species by its much larger and showier heads, with a greater number of florets. The usual H. aliena head bears roughly double the number of both rays and discs of H. mitis and H. peduncularis; however, some plants have smaller heads with fewer rays. The leaves are generally stouter than those of the other species, and the peduncles of H. aliena are almost always much shorter than those of either H. peduncularis or H. anomala. The presence of milky-white sap has been noted in H. aliena, but this feature, observable only in fresh specimens, has not been investigated in the other species.

description: This taxon has hitherto been treated as a separate species. Apart from the leaf-shape there are no essential characters to distinguish it from E. tenuissimus. I have given it subspecific rank, since it is nearly always readily distinguishable from ssp. tenuissimus and has a distinct distribution area west of the range of the latter. Some specimens from the meeting zone of the two subspecies show a somewhat intermediary character, viz. have many or several divided leaves. They appear to be fully fertile and have been classified with the subspecies to which they were judged to come closest.

description: Much confused with H. rosum, but distinguished by its few heads in subumbellate clusters, involucral bracts ranging from almost colourless to tawny, tips all crisped, inner ones pellucid or subopaque, ranging from pale to deep tawny through pink or red tints to dingy white, and receptacles only very shortly toothed. In H. rosum, the heads are few to many, often in corymbose panicles, but sometimes clustered, especially in dwarfed specimens, bract tips smooth, all but the outermost opaque milk-white (but see var. arcuatum) and the receptacle has teeth shorter than the ovaries or about equalling them. See also notes under H. ammitophilum.

The inner involucral bracts perform hydrochastic movements. After flowering the bracts are bent inwards, over the receptacle, thus enclosing the cypselas. When exposed to water they straighten and the cypselas are released. A. minuta ssp. minuta is distinguished from A. minuta ssp. inermis by the presence of spines.

description: Typical H. cephaloideum from the E. Cape is characterized by its congested compound heads, the individual heads 4-5.5 mm long with subequal involucral bracts, the outer acute, the inner very obtuse and apiculate, and containing ±30-60 flowers. Similar plants occur over the rest of the range, but in KwaZulu-Natal and the Transvaal heads are often larger (5-6 mm long) and may contain up to 100 flowers. In both provinces, the area of H. cephaloideum overlaps with that of its close ally H. mixtum, and in KwaZulu-Natal with H. auriceps as well, and it is possible that some crossing takes place. However, the species seems also to be inherently variable, particularly in leaf size and woolliness and in the colour and imbrication of the involucral bracts. The bracts are often bright yellow overlaid or tipped golden-brown. Plants from the Transvaal with tawny or straw-coloured, closely imbricate, bracts were described as H. polyphyllum and H. campaneum; apart from the colour of the bracts, they closely resemble H. cephaloideum var. polycephalum, described from Grahamstown. The type of H. infuscum is very young, but it is perhaps no more than a specimen of H. cephaloideum in which the bracts are heavily overlaid with chestnut or purplish brown; plants with similarly coloured bracts occur sporadically in both KwaZulu-Natal and the Transvaal, often together with ordinary yellow-headed plants. Two other Transvaal specimens need special mention: Venter 1163 (PRE), from the top of Mt Lebojane near The Downs, whence came the type of H. infuscum, and Van der Merwe 1315 (PRE) from Kliprivier north of Dullstroom, have straw-coloured involucral bracts tipped with purplish brown; the heads resemble those of H. infuscum, but are larger, 8 mm long, not 5 mm. Specimens with remarkably large radical leaves (up to 200 x 40 mm) have been collected in the grassland adjoining Ngome and Nkandla forests in KwaZulu-Natal (Hilliard & Burtt 5945, E; K; NH; NU; and Hilliard 2652, NU) and are possibly a local race. H. cephaloideum is part of a very closely allied group that includes H. subluteum and H. ingomense, both of which may have been derived from H. cephaloideum, as well as H. auriceps (below), H. longifolium and H. mixtum. Further study, including experimental work, is desirable.

description: Thus S. erubescens sens. strict, is characterized by its basal rosette of sinuately lobed or toothed or pinnately lobed leaves, lax flowering stems, distantly leafy in the lower part, pedunculoid above, small heads (bracts 6.5-7 mm) corymbose-paniculately arranged, and its range of characters can be stretched to include specimens with toothed rather than lobed leaves and slightly larger heads. 'S. erubescens' has become a dumping ground for a great many of the grassland senecios of south east Africa with discoid purple-flowered heads. These plants range from the Cape Peninsula through the eastern half of South Africa to the Flora Zambesiaca area and to the mountainous parts of East Africa. It is far beyond the scope of the present work to attempt to sort out this highly polymorphic group. But there are a number of more or less clearly defined entities and names are often available for these. They will be used here as rallying points in the jungle, but by no means all specimens can be placed. The situation is further complicated by the fact that some species may be either radiate or discoid (S. polyodon, the plants from Stillerust Vlei described in the discussion under S. polyodon following S. polyodon), while S. erubescen sens. strict. and S. speciosus sens. strict. (that is, plants from the Cape Peninsula and nearby) and S. barbatus and S. macrocephalus sens. strict. are extra ordinarily alike except that in each pair the last mentioned species is radiate, not discoid. The term 'purple-flowered' is a very loose one: it is common to find white or dull yellow corollas, while all shades of pink, mauve, magenta and blue, as well as true purple and red-purple or brown-purple, may be found; sometimes the corolla is pale dull yellow or whitish with 'purple' tips. Colour may well change with age: this has been recorded for instance in S. versicolor (in syn. under S. polyodon), where the young corollas are pale violet, soon becoming dull yellow. The anthers are often 'purple' when the corollas are white or yellow. However, corollas are never the bright canary yellow so common in the genus.

The typical form is found in the Grabouw-Villiersdorp area. Further eastwards towards the Langeberg the conflorescence tends to become more ramified but with the corymbose clusters still in a corymb.

description: Widespread in Natal, from near the sea to c. 2100 m and one of the commonest spring-flowering grassland herbs. Like so many grassland plants, it is highly variable in stature and leaf size. The smallest plants, some not more than 10 cm high, have been recorded at c. 2000 m in the crevices of rock platforms; although there is a tendency for the shorter and narrower-leaved plants to occur above c. 1500 m, similar plants have been collected near the sea, and broad-leaved plants occur up to c. 1700 m. The extremes look very different. Nevertheless, S. coronatus is easily recognized among grassland species in Natal by its silky-woolly crown and loosely woolly vegetative parts. Even the roots are woolly.

description: This is a large shrub, which may be as much as three metres high. It is the largest plant within the tribe Calenduleae. The youngest parts of the plant are cobwebbed or woolly, but soon lose their hairy indument. The adult leaves are glabrous, glossy and subcoriaceous. If the fruits when ripe are not eaten by animals the succulent pulp dries up and forms a tough layer round the putamen. The inner involucral scales are usually more or less broadly ovate, seldom broadly lanceolate, 3-4(-5) mm in length. Within the widely distributed and extremely polymorphous speciesit is possible to distinguish five quite characteristic geographical races predominating in their respective areas. As the drupes are eaten by birds these different races are continually being spread by birds to each other's distribution areas. That is why a coastal form may occasionally occur far from the coast and a mountain form far from mountain areas. If, for instance, the coastal form from Natal is transferred by birds to the lower parts of the Drakensberg it will of course develop to flowering and fructification, even though the conditions of existence are less favourable for it there than down at the coast. It will probably easily hybridize with the Drakensberg form so that transitional forms arise. If the coastal form is spread to higher levels of the Drakensberg, it will, however, probably not survive the climate there, but will quickly disappear. The vaguely delimited distribution areas of the races and the large number of transitional forms occurring in areas where these races overlap, make a satisfactory division into taxonomical units very difficult or almost impossible.

description: E. latifolius is a very characteristic species. Its flat and wide leaves, which are distinctly many-nerved and serrate, are unique in the genus. The leaves of seedlings and young plants, however, are much narrower and more dissected, giving an indication of the possible origin from some narrow-leaved ancestor. The closest relative among existing species appears to be E. algoensis, a flat-leaved species with similar involucres.

description: The plant that De Candolle described as S. hypochoerideus was discoid. The radiate plants here included in a broader concept of the species occur in the northern half of the range, from about Naude's Nek (between Maclear and Rhodes) northwards to the limits of Lesotho and may grow together with the discoid plant, as, for instance, below the summit cliffs on Sani Pass. The plants differ only in the presence or absence of rays. Discoid specimens closely resemble broad-leaved specimens of S. asperulus, but that species has more acute radical leaves with differently toothed margins. Discoid S. hypochoerideus is also remarkably similar to S. schweinfurthii O. Hoffm., endemic on the high mountains of East Africa. A comparison of the two might prove of phyto-geographical interest. S. hypochoerideus is also closely allied to S. mooreanus: see under that species.
