description: Leaves 3 in. long, 1/2 in. wide, the petiole broad and channelled. Peduncles 8-12 in. long, whole plant thinly canescent. Stem herbaceous, branched, silvery, the flowering branches ending in long, nude, one-headed peduncles; leaves simple and tapering at base, petioled, linear-oblong, repand-crenate, with sometimes a pair of small lateral lobes, 3-5-nerved, cobwebby or glabrous above, silvery tomentose beneath; involucre cobwebby, the outer scales with linear, tomentose points.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1865. Compositae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 44-530. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/1/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: A sprawling shrub or undershrub with a biseriate involucre and with rays about twice as long as the involucre. O. elsieae is most closely allied to O. ciliatum and O. hispidum. It differs from O. ciliatum by the leaves being more or less distinctly petiolate and completely entire, and by the inferior surface of the leaves and the involucre being greyish cobweb-cottony. From O. hispidum it differs, among other things, by the leaves not being hispid and membranaceous.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1960. Additions to the monograph on Osteospermum. Bot. Not. 113(4): 385-399. [All rights reserved]

description: Shrubs or trees. Leaves oblanceolate to obovate, rounded or sometimes briefly acuminate at apex. Synflorescences very dense; male and female capitula small; involucres of both male and female capitula narrowly infundibuliform, slender, 2.5-4.0(-5.5) x 1-3 mm in male capitula and (3-)4-7(-10) x 1-5 mm in female capitula; inner bracts narrowly triangular to almost linear, acuminate, stiffly erect.
bibliographicCitation: Phillips, EP; Schweickerdt, HGWJ. 1937. A revision of the South African species of Brachylaena R.Brown. Bothalia 3(2): 205-221. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species recognized by its dense to very dense foliage with large axillary brachyblasts; whitish-yellow, dense synflorescenses; and by obtuse and emarginate to truncate innermost involucral bracts. It differs from other species with yellow to yellowish synflorescenses in its foliage. The synflorescenses of M. luteola are also quite different in colour, viz. yellowish-white, from the other yellow to yellowish species. In habit it resembles M. calcicola, a species with either non-twisted or only slightly twisted, conspicuously carinate, strongly incurvate leaves, and whitish, though otherwise similar synflorescenses. A poorly collected and rare species.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: M. pulchella is similar to M. cephalotes, M. divergens, and M. inversa. It differs from these species in its erect habit; spreading to erect-spreading and comparatively narrow leaves; discrete and often urceolate capitula clusters; and innermost involucral bracts conspicuously folded at the apex and emarginate to irregularly dentate. M. compacta has similar synflorescenses, but is generally taller and more robust; has entirely different foliage; pure white tomentum on young branches and capitula clusters; no glands on any parts; 6-flowered capitula; and different pappus bristles and cypselas. Old specimens of M. cephalotes and M. pulchella are not always easily distinguished from one another.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: This striking new species is very distinct, and I am unable to suggest any immediate allies. In the classification of Hutchinson and Phillips (1917) the species would belong to sect. Ciliatae Hutch. & Phill. The key designed by these authors leads to P. adenocarpa Harv., a species of the Upper Karroo, distributed from Worcester to Victoria West and eastwards to Albany. This is a very different species, however, with much larger capitula and glandular, glabrous achenes. The new species may have closer affinities to P. gymnocline DC. and P. lucilioides DC, both of which are known from the Richtersveld. These two species differ from P. elata by their narrower, linear to oblanceolate leaves, which are not obligately opposite, and by the pointed tips of the young involucres. By characters of leaf pubescence these three species belong to three different sections in the essentially artificial scheme proposed by Hutchinson and Phillips. The leaves are glabrous in P. gymnocline (sect. Glabratae), papillate in P. lucilioides (sect. Papillatae), and glabrous with ciliate margins in P. elata (sect. Ciliatae). In the modest vegetation of the desolate mountains near Stinkfontein (now: Ecksteinfontein), the tall and lanky shrubs of P. elata are a quite conspicuous feature.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1971. New South African Compositae. Bot. Not. 124: 9-15. [All rights reserved]

description: Cineraria grandibracteata was initially (but not formally) described as ‘species B’ by Hilliard. Cineraria grandibracteata is a slightly straggling herb, supported by other vegetation, often among rock outcrops in grassland. It is fairly easily distinguished from C. albicans by its relatively large solitary heads, long peduncles with large bracts and glabrous cypselae. It is usually exauriculate, but some specimens have small persistent auricles from the summit of Mount Ngeli; Coleman s.n. (NU) from Weza, Alfred District], which also have capitula in twos and threes, not solitary. Other specimens from the Eastern Cape from Mount Ngeli and from the Maclear District, have glabrous cypselae and long bracts as in C. grandibracteata, but also have fairly large capitula in twos and threes and are auriculate like C. albicans. It is possible that they are hybrids. Trichomes in C. grandibracteata are of two main kinds: (i) c. 4 basal agranular tapering cells and a long multi-celled apical appendage; (ii) two narrow basal cells and long apical appendage joined at right angles to the basal cells.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: A comparatively small and highly branched shrublet, with dense foliage, short leaves, very dense synflorescenses, whitish to bright pink petaloid involucral bracts, and very narrow and comparatively small pappus bristles. The foliage sometimes resembles that of M. brevifolia, but the latter species has declinate leaves, and white, less dense synflorescenses with petaloid involucral bracts that are often concave apically. M. erubescens is also similar, but differs in foliage, and has less dense synflorescenses. The tips of the petaloid involucral bracts are also different. M. seriphiifolia also resembles M. phillipsii, but has more twisted, acicular leaves, and petaloid involucral bracts with conspicuously tridentate tips. M. cymbifolia and M. serrata have 3-flowered capitula in dense, pink synflorescenses. However, in these species the capitula are fused by hairs in the clusters and the foliage and pappus bristles are entirely different. Circumscribed as above, M. phillipsii comprises two largely allopatric subspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Garuleum bipinnatum is the only species where both ray and outer disc florets develop fertile cypselae; the leaves are twice-pinnate, decreasing in size and degree of lobing towards the inflorescence; inner bracts have whitish-scarious margins and often violet tips, and the plant is glabrous. It can be easily confused with Garuleum schinzii, but in G. schinzii the fruits develop from ray florets only, and the plant is glandular-hispid.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N. 2013. FSA Contribution 22: Asteraceae: Calenduleae: Garuleum. Bothalia 43(2): 167-178. [CC BY]

description: M. strictifolia is recognized by its compact, much-branched habit; non-twisted and erect to appressed leaves; comparatively few, individually arranged capitula with erect-spreading petaloid involucral bracts; and by clavate-tipped pappus bristles. For comparison with the sometimes similar M. alfredii.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: This little-known species differs from its consectioners by its entire, obtuse leaves in combination with the comparatively long postfloral peduncles and the distinctly three-nerved involucral bracts, which are connate only for half their length. In foliage the species has some resemblance to E. annae, which in other respects is very different, however, and belongs to a different section (peduncles numerous and lateral, involucral bracts c. 5, achenes 5-ribbed, etc.). The closest ally may be E. montanus, which has likewise entire leaves and similar achenes. In the latter species, however, the leaves are distinctly narrowed towards the base, and the peduncles are much more reduced. The styles of the disc-florets appear to have poorly developed stig-matic surfaces, and probably they are at least sometimes sterile. The scanty material available did not permit investigation of a large number of florets. E. brevipes is only known from a single collection. Only a few flowering capitula are present in the material, and it is likely that the species has its main flowering period in summer.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: The highly distinctive C. hantamensis is readily separated from all other species of Chrysocoma by its 3-5-fid leaves and large capitula, 12-15 mm diam. with lanceolate, 3-veined involucral bracts, the largest 9-10 x 2 mm. In its distinctly lobed leaves it approaches C. tridentata DC. (including C. pinnatifida DC.) but this species from the Little Karoo is a divaricately branched shrublet with rather fleshy, mostly subterete leaves, and with short peduncles at most 30 mm long, bearing capitula 10-12 mm diam. In addition, the involucral bracts, like those of all other species of Chrysocoma, are smaller, ± 5 x 1.0-1.5 mm, linear-lanceolate and 1-veined. C. hantamensis is probably most closely allied to C. oblongifolia DC., which extends from Namaqualand through the Hantam and into the Tanqua Karoo. Both species are subshrubs with decumbent annual stems bearing relatively broad leaves with strigose margins and large capitula carried on long peduncles. The decussate lower leaves of C. hantamensis and C. oblongifolia are also evident in the few other species of Chrysocoma that are subshrubs rather than true shrubs, although their opposite arrangement is easily overlooked. C. oblongifolia differs from C. hantamensis in its entire, oblanceolate leaves, glandular-hairy rather than villous stems and peduncles, slightly smaller capitula, 10-12 mm diam., and smaller, 1-veined involucral bracts.C. hantamensis bears a remarkable superficial resemblance to another distinctive, narrow endemic of this region, Euryops mirus B.Nord. The two species, which grow together at the type locality east of Nieuwoudtville, are extraordinarily similar in vegetative form, sharing short, partially subterranean stems and branches bearing pinnatifid leaves, and producing annual flowering shoots with long, naked peduncles bearing solitary flowerheads. It would appear to be a marked instance of ecological convergence.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2005. Two new species of Asteraceae from Northern and Western Cape, South Africa, and a new synonym. Bothalia 35(1&2): 55-61. [CC BY]

description: This is the most common taxon of the genus in the northen parts of southern Africa. It can be distinguished by the narrowly elliptic to slightly oblanceolate, entire leaves with a grey-green or khaki-green colour and the cypselas enveloped by yellowish cottony hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Herman, PPJ. 2002. Revision of the Tarchonanthus camphoratus complex (Asteraceae-Tarchonantheae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 32(1): 21-28. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to E. africanus and E. eximius. Differs from E. africanus by its larger leaves, larger capitula with large conspicuous ray florets and its much-branched rigid habit. It differs from E. eximius by its pedunculate capitula.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: H. lineare has been much confused with H. asperum. However, the two species are nearly allopatric, their areas overlapping only in the eastern part of the country; it is only there that difficulty may arise in placing specimens, but H. lineare is always prostrate, H. asperum is always erect, and H. lineare generally flowers earlier than H. asperum.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: O. microphyllum is a low, much branched shrub, with linear or linear-lanceolate, somewhat pungent leaves, only about 0.5-1 cm in length. Particularly older shrubs have numerous brachyblasts. The involucral scales are more or less obtuse, possibly with the exception of 1-3 of the outer ones, which form a transition to the bracts on the peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily confused with B. multijuga but that species has several heads together on the flowering stem, very rarely only one, leaves generally cobwebby below, very rarely only glandular, and shortly pubescent or nearly glabrous achenes with short (up to c. 1.2 mm), blunt pappus scales. B. macrocephala flowers in spring, B. multijuga in summer and autumn.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: In the S.W. Cape, leaves are thinner and may be more deeply pinnately dissected than in specimens from the eastern Cape and beyond. Here, distribution overlaps with that of S. macrocephalus, which is absent from the S.W. Cape. S. speciosus is characterized by its leaves, mostly with long broad flat petioles and deeply toothed or lobed margins, and smaller heads (involucral bracts mostly 10 mm long) corymbosely arranged. S. macrocephalus has leaves narrowed to the base but scarcely petioled, margins entire, repand or shallowly toothed, involucral bracts mostly 12 mm long, the heads tending to be racemosely arranged. The involucral bracts and inflorescence branches are often more or less invested with long jointed hairs. Although some specimens are difficult to place, both names are upheld here as the taxonomy of these concolorous purple senecios is far from understood. In Natal and the Transkei, typical S. speciosus is coastal in its distribution, not being found above c. 750 m. See also under S. macrocephalus.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: H. albo-brunneum displays considerable variation in size of the heads; the larger heads tend to be solitary or few together, while the smaller ones are clustered in groups of about 5-15.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: E. decipiens is a fairly slender shrublet with more or less erect, mostly entire leaves, and rather long and slender peduncles. In habit it has considerable resemblance to some species of sect. Chrysops (e.g., E. dyeri), but it belongs to sect. Euryops by the characters of involucre, disc-florets, and achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. dregeanus is a distinct and easily recognized species, although the leaf-shape is variable to a certain extent. The leaves are normally more or less spathulate or flabelliform, distinctly narrowed to the base, and with a dilated, apically toothed or shortly lobed lamina. More deeply cleft leaves with thickened linear lobes are rare, occurring only in the north-eastern inland localities (Kenhardt and Gordonia Divisions). The most characteristic feature is the dense canescent tomentuni of the leaves and young branches. In this character the species differs from the allied E. mucosus.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: M. inversa is a variable species, particularly in habit. It is recognized by its mainly yellowish-tomentose shoots and synflorescenses, involucral bracts diminishing in length inwards, and apically obtuse and usually subterete pappus bristles. Specimens from the Palmiet River area are mostly slender, have comparatively small synflorescenses and branches and synflorescenses which are not always brownish-yellow tomentose. Such slender specimens were recognized as 'form F' of M. cephalotes by Pillans. His 'form B' of M. cephalotes from outside the Cape Peninsula is M. inversa. Other species with dense and sometimes white synflorescenses are M. cephalotes and M. pulchella. However, white variants of the first species have whitish tomentum on the branches and synflorescenses, and smaller lamina on the outermost involucral bracts. M. pulchella may resemble M. inversa in its discrete and similarly shaped capitula clusters, but differs in the whitish tomentum on branches and synflorescenses, and involucral bracts of more or less equal length.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Hilliardiella aristata is the only species in the genus with a densely silvery-silky indumentum on both surfaces of the leaves, rarely slightly thinner on the upper surface, the blades mostly linear-oblanceolate to narrowly elliptic but rarely ovate or almost sub-orbicular in some specimens from Swaziland. The involucral bracts are distinctive, mostly narrowly lanceolate and long-attenuate-conduplicate or smoothly acute, with a conspicuously bristle-like apex. Both H. elaeagnoides and H. capensis have more or less discolorous leaves with the upper surface thinly silky and the lower surface densely silvery-silky, and the inner involucral bracts more or less abruptly contracted to an apiculate tip. Intermediates among all three species are known, however, and introgression seems likely where they co-occur.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Hilliardiella (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 106: 41-59. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: In habit the species resembles P. flexicaulis L.f. and P. adhaerens Compton, but the plant is not viscid and the capitula are smaller with very different phyllaries. The specific epithet chosen alludes to the aromatic smell, which is to my nose reminiscent of aniseed. The resin contents are noticeable in many parts of the plant, e.g. the papillate appearance of the leaves, the bead-like veins of the involucral scales, and the gland-like structures of corolla lobes and style branches.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1971. New South African Compositae. Bot. Not. 124: 9-15. [All rights reserved]

description: Well defined and easily recognized among related species by its short broad leaves with ascending-spreading nerves.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: D. tragus is a perennial herb. The stems, which are simple or sparingly branched and lignified at the base, arise from a quite thick, subterranean, lignified caudex. On one and the same individual may be found both entire and sparsely sinuate-dentate leaves. The colour of the ray flowers varies from orange to brighter yellow. The corolla lobes of the inner disc flowers seem throughout to be cuculliform at the top. It has been pointed out above that the ray flowers lack styles. It happens in exceptional cases, however, that the sterile ray flowers are furnished with a style, and in that case this is either entire, or very slightly cleft at the apex. The achenes are suborbicular with a slight incurvation at the apex, or if they have a more emarginate apex they may be described as obcordate.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The chief distinguishing mark of H. decorum is its oblong or elliptic-oblong leaves, generally broadest in the upper half, cobwebby above, tomentose below, most shortly decurrent on the stem. It lacks the persistent foetid odour of H. foetidum with which it is often confused, and the heads are larger.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Closely resembles H. lingulatum, but is distinguished by its linear, not lingulate, leaves and silky-woolly, not merely woolly, indumentum. Possibly hybridizes with other species; see under H. ecklonis.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The leaves of E. glutinosus are sticky with rich surface resin. The species is one of the few tetraploids known in the genus and quite characteristic.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Much confused with H. setosum but distinguished by its differently shaped leaves, persistently white-woolly ultimate branches and leaves much reduced near the heads.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Closely resembles E. sesamoides in foliage, fimbrils and achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The typical form has grey-woolly leaves, but green-leaved plants are not uncommon, and the two may grow together.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Resembles B. macrocephala: see under that species. See also B. cirsiifolia, which is, however, readily distinguished by its winged stems.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Diagnostic features: Basal leaves glabrous; blades linear to falcate, margins smooth, thickened, venation prominent. Corymbophore scabrid, villous at base. Heads in corymbose clusters arranged in a panicle. Involucral bracts scabrid, trifid. Flowers mauve. Ovary hirsute. C. theileri is closely allied to C. glabrum var. glabrum but differs from the latter in the scabrid corymbophore, with a villous base, the scabrid involucral bracts which are sometimes trifid and the coroniform pappus with bristles almost completely fused. It differs from C. africanum subsp. scabridum in leaf texture, lax conflorescence, villous base of corymbophore, slightly longer corolla tube and longer style branches.
bibliographicCitation: Weitz, FM. 1989. A revision of the genus Corymbium L. (Asteraceae). S. African J. Bot. 55: 598-629. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1989); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the crenately incised or lobed leaves with finely toothed incisions, the upper surface glabrous and the under surface densely whitish-felted, the mostly pink to reddish-purple or magenta rays, and the snow white pappus. Populations on the Piketberg are uniformly pink to magenta-flowered but elsewhere both white-flowered and pink-flowered forms occur. Gerbera crocea, which may also have dark pink to purple rays, has leaves with crenate to sinuate margins and thinly tomentose or subglabrous under surface. Gerbera linnaei, the only other species with markedly incised leaves, has deeply and often quadrately pinnatisect leaves and glabrous involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Simka, B; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2016. A revised taxonomy of Gerbera sect. Gerbera (Asteraceae: Mutisieae). S. African J. Bot. 104: 142-157. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2015.10.002] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Two very distinct leaf forms are known, which superficially appear very different. One form has flat cymbiform leaves, which are widest in the middle and generally adpressed or ascending. The other form has ericoid leaves, which are widest at the base and often geniculate and tightly inrolled. Levyns discussed the two forms and concluded that they were conspecific. Presently, there are many more specimens now available for examination and the variation can be studied more easily. The cypsela morphology of both forms is identical, and several specimens with both leaf forms on the same plant were examined: the flat, cymbiform leaves were inserted just below the synflorescence and the more ericoid leaves lower down the stem. Both forms are distributed in the same geographic areas and, although, the plants can look very different, there is no justification to subdivide the species. A similar type of leaf variation was observed in Seriphium passerinoides on Réunion where linear ericoid leaves and small scale-like leaves can be found on the same plants.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2016. A monograph of Stoebe and Seriphium (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa and neighbouring islands. Phytotaxa 242(1): 1-84. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.242.1.1] [All rights reserved]

description: The bright purple pappus is a striking feature of this species.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, J; Phillips, EP. 1917. A revision of the genus Pteronia (Compositae). Ann. S. African Mus. 9(1): 277-329. [All rights reserved]

description: H. uninervium, in common with a great many other species, has triplinerved leaves, but frequently only the midvein is visible, which clearly suggested the specific epithet. A very distinctive species, but clearly allied to H. excisum.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: R. biennis is an annual species. During favourable years it can survive for another season, hence the specific epithet. It grows rather stiffly upright and has slender involucres and inconspicuous florets. The linear achenes with a white cup-like pappus, easily discernible in the old persistent capitula, are also a characteristic feature. It is probably related to, but easily distinguished from the two other annuals of the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: O. glabratum is easily distinguished from all the other species in the subgenus by its entire, opposite leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Fenzl suggested that his new species, I. polycnemoides, might equal I. paronychioides, which he had not seen, but the two species are amply distinct in the arrangement of the heads, in the shape and colour of the involucral bracts, and in the hairs on the achenes. Harvey placed Lpolycnemoides under I. verticillata on the authority of Drège, but Drège was mistaken and much confusion has arisen from this. The two species are easily distinguished by their differently shaped and differently coloured involucral bracts, and by the number of female Mowers in a head.

description: E. laxus has the same fire-resistant life-form as E. transvaalensis, producing short or elongated annual stems from a thick subterranean caudex. From the latter species E. laxus is distinguished by the longer and less coriaceous leaves with linear or filiform rachis and lobes, which are not rigid and subulate. Like many other fire-resistant species it is highly variable, especially in vegetative features. The leaves vary much in length, width, and degree of lobation. The name Gamolepis debilis has been applied to forms with small and pinnati-partite leaves with more or less filiform segments. Other forms have longer and broader, three-lobed leaves with linear, flat segments, and in some collections the leaves are quite entire. Between the extremes all kinds of transitions occur. There is also considerable variation in the floral parts, e.g., in size of capitula and florets. The pappus of E. laxus consists of very few short bristles, which sometimes may lack altogether. This feature explains the original treatment under Gamolepis, but the species takes a more natural position in sect. Chrysops.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. calvescens resembles E. galpinii in involucre, achenes, and pappus, and the two species are no doubt closely related. The species is remarkably similar to some forms of E. brachypodus, as already noted by Harvey (1865, p. 412), but the latter species is more distinctly woolly on the young branches and is easily distinguished by the wanting pappus and the less connate involucral bracts.

description: Cineraria geifolia is generally distinguished from C. lobata by having more rounded reniform leaves with very shallow lobing and larger capitula. The mature capitula of C. geifolia have very abundant pappus setae, a useful diagnostic characteristic for the species. The leaves of C. lobata are usually more distinctly and acutely lobed than those of C. geifolia.

description: Cineraria alchemilloides is very closely allied to C. lobata subsp. lobata which occurs in the same area, but differs in its indumentum (cobwebby to tomentose vs. glabrous or sparsely hairy in C. lobata subsp. lobata). It also shows some affinity with C. canecens due to having similar trichomes, but is a much more slender plant with capitula not as compactly arranged. Only a few specimens from the Western and Northern Cape have been matched to Cineraria alchemilloides and they are not as thickly cobwebby as the types from the Worcester/Tulbagh area. Nevertheless, they are cobwebby to varying degrees and have the same type of trichome and small capitula. Van der Schijff 8088(PRE) from the Kouberg is possibly an outlier of C. alchemilloides ssp. namibiensis in the Northern Cape in that it has glabrous peduncles and involucral bracts, but has very thinly cobwebby leaves. Ecklon 1360 (G-DC) has been chosen as the lectotype as there is a duplicate at S. Both Ecklon 1360 and Ecklon 845 (G-DC) have old capitula that are not in good condition, but otherwise are good matches of the original description.

description: In spite of a considerable variability E. brachypodus is always easily recognized, i.a. by its large and shortly peduncled, sometimes almost sessile capitula, and its distinctly woolly leaf-axils. In inland localities it prefers rocky places, being found e.g. on rocks of Witteberg Quartzite. In the more luxuriant vegetation of the coastal districts the species is often fairly tall with long leaves and large capitula. In inland localities, e.g. on the hills around Grahamstown, it is usually much more slender and dwarfish with short and often few-lobed leaves.

description: This distinctive, highly floriferous species is readily distinguished from all other species of Felicia by its broad, white or cream-coloured rays and deep purple disc. The rounded plants become covered with dainty white flower heads that in their broad rays and small, convex, purple discs are quite unlike any other species of Felicia. The central disc florets, which are functionally male, have somewhat longer ovaries than the surrounding florets, with the result that the disc is conspicuously convex and projects prominently above the rays. F. josephinae is one of a handful of annual species in section Neodetris Grau that have a strictly biseriate involucre and that lack pappus bristles on the ray florets. Among these species it appears to be most closely allied to F. heterophylla, the only other species in the genus known to have blue or purple disc florets. The two species also resemble one another in their involucral bracts, which bear both glandular and setose hairs, in their cypselas, which are rather scantily clad with long hairs, and in their subplumose pappus bristles. F. josephinae is distinguished from F. heterophylla by its relatively broader (10-12 x 4-6 mm vs 15 x 4 mm) rays that are white to cream-coloured rather than deep blue, by the shorter peduncles (30-50 mm long vs 50-150 mm long), resulting in a more compact appearance to the plants, and by the narrower involucres (4 mm vs 6-8 mm diam.) that contain relatively few disc florets in which the petal lobes are conspicuously recurved rather than suberect or slightly recurving. Herbarium material of the two species in which the colour of the rays has faded or is not noted, can always be separated by the characteristically short peduncles and compact habit of F. josephinae.

It can be distinguished from green-leaved plants of H. mutabile most readily by its generally longer and broader leaves; it is an altogether more robust plant than H. mutabile.

description: The name has been much misused. The species is characterized by its bushy habit, glandular-setose leaves mostly ovate or oblong-ovate, obtuse or acute, and heads solitary at the tips of long leafy branches arranged in a corymbose panicle; these branches are glandular-setose like the leaves; any white woolly hairs are confined to the area immediately below the heads and to the leaf margins and main vein. Although the leaves under the heads are a little smaller than those further back down the branches, they are nevertheless relatively large and crowded, often equalling or exceeding the involucre, and contribute to the very leafy appearance of the compound inflorescence. The arrangement of the heads alone will immediately distinguish H. setosum from H. cooperi, with which it is frequently confused: H. cooperi has a well-branched compound inflorescence, and furthermore the main stem leaves are usually at least shortly decurrent. H. tongense and specimens of H. mutabile lacking wool on the leaves have also been confused with H. setosum, but the leaves on the inflorescence branches are reduced and distant near the heads, not close-set and relatively large as in H. setosum.

description: O. aciphyllum greatly resembles the extremely narrow-leafed form of O. ciliatum. The margins of the leaves in O. aciphyllum are sparsely spinulose-ciliate, but not cartilaginous dentate-crenate as in O. ciliatum. The midrib of the leaves forms on the inferior surface a carina, which is decurrent as a ridge or narrow wing on the branches.

Sympatric with, for example, M. divergens and M. pulchella both of which have dense, white synflorescenses. They differ in that the tomentum on young branches and synflorescenses is not as white; 5-flowered capitula; entirely different foliage, pappus bristles and cypselas.

description: As only very immature flowers and fruits were studied, we have not included measurements of flower and fruit parts. Although Dicoma kurumanii is easily distinguishable from other species of the genus, the most morphologically similar species, particularly as regards indumentum and leaf morphology, are probably D. cuneneënsis Wild and D. nachtigalii. It can be distinguished from the former very easily by its isomorphous pappus comprising several series of slender barbellate bristles of equal morphology, though the innermost are somewhat wider; in D. cuneneënsis, by contrast, the pappus is markedly heteromorphic, with several series of slender barbellate bristles and one internal series of scale-like bristles, broadly membraneous towards the base. In addition, D. cuneneënsis often shows a characteristic leaf dimorphism that is never present in D. kurumanii: leaves are either small (3-8 x 2-4 mm) with a dense indumentum similar to that of the leaves of D. kurumanii, or larger (12-30 x 4-12 mm) with a markedly more lax indumentum than that of D. kurumanii. Finally, the leaves are also much more narrowly elliptical, never suborbicular, the involucre shorter (10-13 mm) and the barbellae usually shorter than bristle width. As regards D. cuneneënsis, it should be noted that we have detected certain morphological differences between the typical populations of the Cunene River valley and other populations located further south, in the Damaraland area; these Damaraland populations may constitute a different subspecies or variety, because they show much less marked leaf dimorphism and generally shorter involucres, with glabrous or glabrescent phyllaries, contrasting with the tomentose phyllaries of the typical populations. Dicoma kurumanii can be distinguished from D. nachtigalii by its narrower leaves (8-12(-15) x 4-6(-8) mm) with spathulate shape including a conspicuously widened and flattened pseudopetiole. Other differential characteristics are the involucres, less than 12 mm long and totally covered with at least 20 subtending small leaves. Furthermore, the location from which the new species was collected is very far from the distributional areas of D. cuneneënsis and D. nachtigalii.
bibliographicCitation: Ortiz Nunez, S; Netnou, NC. 2005. A new species of Dicoma (Asteraceae, Mutisieae) from South Africa. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 147: 509-513. [All rights reserved]

description: E. pectinatus, the type of the genus, is very distinct and easily recognized on its grey tomentum and flat pectinate leaves. Features like the dense growth, the neat foliage, and the conspicuous flower-heads all contribute to give the plant a quite attractive appearance. It is not surprising that the species drew the attention of the early collectors at the Cape and that it was soon introduced into many European gardens E. pectinatus comprises two taxa, differing in leaf-shape and geographical distribution. They are here distinguished as subspecies.

description: The cypselas of Felicia martinsiana are highly characteristic, with pronounced surface wrinkles and sinuate margins that clearly distinguish this species from practically all other known species of the genus, which have smooth cypselas with straight margins. Within the genus, probably the most closely related group of species is that which has two rows of phyllaries and marginal cypselas without pappus. Within this group the most morphologically similar species appear to be F. bergeriana (Spreng.) O.Hoffm. and F. merxmuelleri Grau, which have cypselas with a slightly undulate surface; these species have a rather wide distribution in South Africa, the former from Namaqualand District (Northern Cape Province) in the north-west to the Cape Peninsula in the south, and also extending west in Western Cape Province, and the latter from Namaqualand to Ceres and Laingsburg in the Western Cape Province. Other species of this group can be easily distinguished from F martinsiana, for example F. heterophylla (Cass.) Grau by its plumose pappus and F. minima (Hutch.) Grau by its small involucre and black cypselas. Felicia annectens (Harv.) Grau, which may be only a depauperate form of F. bergeriana, can be easily separated from the new species by its glabrous phyllaries.Felicia martinsiana is readily distinguishable from F. bergeriana and F. merxmuelleri principally by its cypselas, which are markedly smaller, and which as noted have a conspicuously wrinkled surface and thickened sinuate margins. Furthermore, F bergeriana has opposite leaves with only eglandular hairs, while F. merxmuelleri has this same type of leaf indumentum and longer pappus than F. martinsiana.
bibliographicCitation: Ortiz Nunez, S. 2007. A new species of Felicia L. (Asteraceae, Astereae) from South Africa. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 154: 545-548. [All rights reserved]

description: This taxon is known from a single, but rich collection of eight sheets It is most similar to A. epaleata and A. vlokii but differs in a number of vegetative and floral characters. A. fallax resembles A. vlokii in habit, although the leaves are generally longer and narrower and more distinctly apiculate, and with slightly less revolute margins. The involucre offers the most readily observed distinguishing characters. The outer phyllaries are shorter and broader than in related species, and the petaloid inner bracts are woolly from the base, not basally glabrous as in A. vlokii, while the white petaloid portion is rather larger. The pappus bristles are also characteristic, with slender and thin bases, and rather thin and acute teeth, even apically in the male florets. An unusual feature is that some capitula are entirely male, lacking the female floret.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1996. Anderbergia B.Nord., a new genus of everlastings (Compositae-Gnaphalieae) from the Cape Province  . Ann. Naturhist. Mus. Wien 98(Suppl.B): 403-418. [All rights reserved]

description: A perennial herb, 1-4 dm high. The ray flowers are always white above, but underneath the colour varies somewhat, from purple-mauve-coppery. In older herbarium specimens it is often difficult to determine what colour the flowers were originally. The pubescence is quite variable. Some forms are provided with dense, pluricellular glandular hairs, 1 mm long, others again have very short glanduliferous hairs, hardly visible to the naked eye. The older leaves of the plant and the older parts of the stem and of the branches are sometimes glabrate.

description: E. virgineus is related to E. algoensis but clearly distinct by its deeper cleft leaves with narrower lobes, smaller capitula, and glabrous smooth achenes. The characteristic fan-shaped leaves vary in number of lobes between 3 and 7, often on the same specimen. The distinct stylophore of the disc-florets functions as a nectary, and the flowerheads are sweet scented. The disc-florets are sterile with shallowly lobed non-stigmatic styles. When in full flower the often compact shrubs are quite conspicuous with a profusion of brilliant yellow flowerheads.

description: S. glaberrimus is very closely allied to S. bupleuroides, being distinguished by its leaves, broader in relation to length than those of S. bupleuroides (mostly 2.5-4 times as long as broad, not mostly at least 10 times). They are sympatric and flower at the same time. Although nearly all specimens can be assigned to one or the other species, a few have leaves of intermediate length, that is, 6-7 times as long as broad e.g. Pietermaritzburg distr., Baynesfield, Billiard 2880 (NU), near Albert Falls, van der Merwe 2600 (NU), Lion's River distr., Nottingham Road, Hilliard 1966 (NU); Estcourt distr., Giant's Castle Game Reserve, Mckeown 65 (NU). The name S. inophyllus was given to plants with rigid rather than coriaceous leaves with all the nerves strongly raised, but there are numerous intermediate forms. S. swaziensis describes a tall coarse plant (from Mbabane and Hlatikulu districts, Swaziland) with very large, nearly round, coarsely toothed leaves. This too links through intermediate forms, some of which may possibly be of hybrid origin, to typical S. glaberrimus. Comparable variation in leaf texture and venation occurs in S. bupleuroides. This whole group demands close study, together with S. latifolius and its allies, as well as tropical African species such as S. pergamentaceus Bak. A very wide range of this variation is represented in the Itala Nature Reserve, Louwsburg, where S. scitus, S. latifolius and the radiate form of S. venosus also occur.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Very closely allied to S. gazensis S. Moore in the eastern highlands of Rhodesia and S. depauperata Mattfeld in the mountains between Lakes Tanganyika and Malawi, but distinctive among South African species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is similar to St. schultzii but can be distinguished by the presence of pappus, the prominent white involucral bracts, which are as long as the florets, as well as by pinkish-red florets.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2016. A monograph of Stoebe and Seriphium (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae) in southern Africa and neighbouring islands. Phytotaxa 242(1): 1-84. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.242.1.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Can be confused with S. affinis but that species is characterized by its stiff crowded stem leaves, and with S. albanopsis, distinguished by its turbinate heads on very scaly peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: H. allioides is characterized by its long narrow leaves, smooth above with traces of white wool often clinging to the veins, white-felted below. The tips of the inner involucral bracts are nearly always yellow, rarely creamy white. The rare specimens with broader leaves (but retaining the characteristic indumentum) have been recorded from Hluhluwe Game Reserve and Nfabanana in Zululand, and approach H. oxyphyllum both in this character and in the creamier-coloured involucral bracts. Some crossing may have taken place.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: One specific feature of A. vlokii is the absence of pubescence basally on the inner involucral bracts. The female florets are usually two in number, all other species of the genus having mostly a single one. In pappus characters and oxalate crystal morphology, A. vlokii resembles A. rooibergensis, but differs significantly by the diffuse and slender habit, the leaves lacking a prominent midvein on the lower side, the araneose rather than sericeous tomentum of the outer involucral bracts, the smaller petaloid tips to the inner phyllaries, and the almost glabrous cypselas. Besides, there seems to be a difference in corolla colour, viz. yellow in A. vlokii but white in A. rooibergensis.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1996. Anderbergia B.Nord., a new genus of everlastings (Compositae-Gnaphalieae) from the Cape Province  . Ann. Naturhist. Mus. Wien 98(Suppl.B): 403-418. [All rights reserved]

description: No material in PRE from EC.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The tuft of grey-woolly radical leaves is produced in the first season, the terminal flowering stem with glandular but not woolly leaves the following year, together with several woody runners each terminating in a new leaf rosette. The small heads with brown pointed bracts allied to the markedly discolorous radical and cauline leaves make this a very distinctive species.

description: Can be confused with V. dealbatum and Helichrysum indicum; distinguished from V. dealbatum by its broader heads in which ('bisexual') flowers outnumber ('female') by the involucral bracts, not or scarcely coloured red about the stereome and with white tips distinctly broader than the shaft; distinguished from H. indicum by its heterogamous heads (in H. indicum the heads are generally homogamous; only very rarely are 1 or 2 9 flowers present) and smooth, not crisped, involucral bracts.

description: Closely allied to and much confused with H. retortum but that is a coarser plant confined to the coast. See also H. lancifolium.

description: Steirodiscus speciosus is very similar to S. tagetes and was diagnosed against it by Pillans (as G. annua), and as having larger (±18 x 3.5-4.0 mm), more numerous (14-23) orange rays lacking a distinct annulus of papillae around the mouth of the tube and with more strongly exserted styles. Most of these characters do not hold, even in the type of S. speciosus, which has up to 15 rays that are no larger than are found in most populations of S. tagetes and also does not differ in the stylar characters.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Joubert, L. 2013. A taxonomic revision of the small Cape genus Steirodiscus (Asteraceae: Senecioneae). Bothalia 43(1): 109-119. [CC BY]

description: Easily confused with S. brevidentatus but distinguished by its differently shaped radical leaves and shorter involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: O. karrooicum differs from O. microphyllum inter alia by its longer leaves (c 2-4 times as long) and its acute, narrower, longer and more numerous involucral scales. In contrast to O. microphyllum, the material of O. karrooicum comprises several specimens with an abundance of fruits, so that one can get a good idea of the shape and variation of the achenes. The achenes are dimorphous, namely 3-winged and wingless. The winged achenes are much more numerous in each head than the others, and sometimes only winged achenes are formed. These achenes have rigidly membranaceous, often irregularly lacerate wings, and alwTays lack an apical cavity.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The ray flowers are white above except near the base, where they have a dark purple or violet zone. Beneath the colour shows a considerable variation: blue-violet-purple, often with an interspersion of copper, less often of brown or white colouring. The open flower heads are as a rule c. 4-6 cm in diam., but in some depauperated forms they measure little more than 2 cm in diam. and in luxuriant forms may reach 9 cm in diam. The ray achenes are usually more or less pronouncedly obpyramidal-3-angled with transversely rugose or tuberculate, rarely almost smooth sides, and with crenate or entire angles. In addition to these achenes there may be 1-3 terete or subterete, nearly smooth, more elongated achenes in a head. Forms also exist with narrow and elongated achenes. In contrast to the ray achenes, the disc achenes present only a slight variation in shape, being broadly obovate or obcordate according to whether the apex is clearly emarginate or not.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: O. dentatum is characterized by the lowermost and usually also the medial leaves of the stem being opposite.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Sometimes confused with H. cylindriflorum but distinguished by its involucral bracts, all with broad golden-brown subpellucid tips, not squarrose as in H. cylindriflorum (though the innermost are minutely radiating), and the consistently larger number of flowers in the head.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The white or pink and white heads make H. elegantissimum distinctive among its yellow-headed allies.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Cineraria aspera is a widespread species in South Africa that varies considerably in the breadth of the lobes of its leaves, the overall shape of its leaves (pinnatifid lobing to palmate outline), the combination of trichomes and the size of capitula. There appears to be a cline from the Eastern Cape to the more northerly provinces of South Africa (North-West, Gauteng, Northern Cape): involving an increase in width of lobes and a tendency towards a more palmate pattern of lobing northwards. The size of the capitula also increases in some northerly populations from Johannesburg have 13 involucral bracts). A detailed study of this variation revealed that there is a tendency for populations of C. aspera in the Eastern Cape to have narrow lobes, with broader ones occurring in the more northerly part of the range (viz. Gauteng, North-West Province and the north-eastern Free State). However, specimens with narrow lobes also occur in these more northern regions. Breadth of lobes and leaf size is also influenced by whether the plant is growing in the sun or the shade, with broader lobes and larger leaves being a feature of plants growing in shade. For example, Cron & Goodman 550 (J), growing in shade has a mean lobe width of 6.5 mm, while an adjacent plant, Cron & Goodman 551 (J), growing in sun, has a mean lobe width of 2.4 mm and a range of 1.6 to 2.5 mm. Linked to the increase in width of lobes is a tendency towards a more palmate pattern of lobing in the more northern range of the distribution as compared to the more pinnatisect lobing in the Eastern Cape specimens. Most specimens of Cineraria aspera have trichomes with c. 6 broadly-tapering basal cells and a long multi-celled apical appendage, in contrast to the fine trichomes that occur mainly (but not exclusively) in the Eastern Cape populations, commonly associated with specimens with very narrow-lobed leaves, as well as the type specimen. Certain specimens from Naval Hill, Bloemfontein, and Cron 12 (J) from Gaika’s Kop in the Eastern Cape) have fine trichomes on the dorsal surface of their leaves and the broader-based trichomes on the leaves’ ventral surface. In a study of variation in a population of Cineraria aspera in the Eastern Cape in April 1999, five collections at different altitudes along Naudé’s Pass near Rhodes were examined. In this single population, leaf lobe width varied considerably [from narrow (1 mm) to broad (9 mm)], as did the width of the midrib region (0.8-8.0 mm). The capitula tended to be larger at higher altitude, as reflected in the number of ray florets per capitulum: plants at 2600 m have 7 or 8 rays per capitulum vs. plants at 2200 m with only 5 rays per capitulum. In contrast, the number of involucral bracts appeared to be independent of altitude, with the range of 8-10 involucral bracts per capitulum occurring in all specimens. However, this altitudinal variation in the number of rays was not confirmed across the entire range of C. aspera. Specimens previously identified or cited as C. burkei appear to have leaves with a more palmate lobing and multi-celled trichomes, but no consistent differences could be found to warrant the maintenance of two separate species or even subspecies as there was no distinct regional pattern of variation. Similarly, C. hamiltoni falls within the range of variation seen in C. aspera. Hence a single species is recognised and C. burkei and C. hamiltoni are placed in synonymy with C. aspera. Cineraria aspera shows an affinity with C. erosa, but is distinguished from that species by having glabrous involucral bracts (with only a cobwebby calyculus), whereas C. erosa has cobwebby involucral bracts, usually glabrescent to some degree (but not glabrous). Cineraria aspera generally has larger capitula, with 5-8 rays and 8-10 (rarely as many as 13) involucral bracts. In contrast, C. erosa has smaller capitula with 3-5 rays and 8 involucral bracts. The tip of the ray limb in C. erosa is characteristically sculpted into 3 tips, matching the venation. The pattern of the lobing is distinctly palmate in C. erosa, giving the leaves a reniform outline, which differs from the more pinnatisect lobing of C. aspera, particularly those occurring in the Cape. The breadth of the lobes is larger in C. erosa than in C. aspera, and there is a typical subdivision of each lobe into three in C. erosa. Wells 3740 (K, PRE) and Stokoe s.n. sub SAM 60471 from the Prince Albert District and Moffett 183 (PRE) and Moffett 599 (PRE) from Cango Valley near Oudtshoorn in the Western Cape all have cobwebby involucral bracts as in C. erosa, yet the shape of their leaves is closer to that of C. aspera than C. erosa. They are at the east-west meeting point of the two species and could be the result of hybridization occurring between them. Cineraria aspera is listed as a problem plant as it may be competitive with desired vegetation, taint meat and milk [Collett 484 (K, PRE)] and be a seed contaminant. In addition to its more natural habitat amongst rocks on mountain slopes, it grows as a pioneer on roadsides and is reportedly grown as a fence around kraals in Lesotho.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: G. parva is a peculiar dwarf species. It appears to be uncommon, with a very restricted distribution area. It shows very little variation in general morphology. This nice little plant has not been introduced to European botanical gardens.
bibliographicCitation: Hansen, HV. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the genus Gerbera (Compositae, Mutisieae) sections Gerbera, Parva, Piloselloides (in Africa), and Lasiopus. Opera Bot. 78: 5-36. [All rights reserved]

description: E. rupestris is sometimes mistaken for a small-grown form of E. abrotanifolius, which it somewhat resembles in leaf-shape. The peduncles are lateral, however, not terminal like in the latter species. Furthermore, the involucral bracts are not strictly in one row, and the achenes are very different. From E. tenuissimus ssp. trifurcatus the species is well distinguished, i.a., by the peduncles being much longer than the leaves and by the sterile disc-florets. The styles of the sterile disc-florets are simple or shallowly lobed, but the style branches never become divergent and they lack stigmatic surfaces. The style only functions as a pollen-presenter. Two distinct types of achenes occur within the species. Both types have a fairly wide but somewhat different distribution. The local populations seem to be homogeneous, and no intermediates have been found. This forms a basis for dividing the species into two varieties. A parallel case occurs in the related species E. longipes var. rupestris is usually a shrublet less than 0.5 m high, growing in rock crevices at altitudes between c. 360 and 1800 m s.m.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is closely related to E. spinescens. These delicate, spinescent shrublets are very similar to E. ericoides during the active growing period. They differ from that species by the green-grey to silver-grey, small, imbricate leaves looking remarkably like a feather.
bibliographicCitation: Muller, MAN; Herman, PPJ; Kolberg, HH. 2001. Eriocephalus and Lasiospermum, Fl. S. Africa 33(4,1): 1-75. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209557#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Cineraria vagans is very similar to C. geraniifolia from which it is distinguished mainly by its diffuse straggling habit, forming small mats, with ‘stems rooting at the nodes and these somewhat tuberous’. The leaves are very shallowly lobed, less so than in C. geraniifolia, reniform with deeply cordate bases and only very rarely have pinnae, whereas lateral pinnae are more common in C. geraniifolia, especially in KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga. The leaves are almost exauriculate, with only the petiole widening slightly in the middle to upper leaves. Hilliard noted that the median veins in the disc corolla are pale (vs. reddish brown in C. geraniifolia), however this is not a reliable character. For example, Hilliard & Burtt 12393 (K, PRE), a good match of C. vagans from the type locality, has reddish-brown veins on the ray and disc floret corollas; in contrast Hilliard & Burtt 13228 (K) from the Boschberg has pale veins in disc florets of some capitula, but reddish-brown veins in florets from other capitula and matches C. geraniifolia well. The leaves of Cineraria vagans have only a few eglandular trichomes in the angles of their lobes and at the base of the lamina when young. These trichomes do not appear to be as long as the kind seen in C. geraniifolia. The number of ray florets in Cineraria vagans ranges from 5 to 8, most frequently 7 or 8. Cineraria geraniifolia, differs by having larger capitula commonly with between 8 and 13 rays, but some high altitude forms from the mountain peaks in the Eastern Cape have 5 rays. A number of morphological differences do exist between them, but C. geraniifolia is quite variable and this species may be a part of that variation. Molecular studies are needed to confirm that C. vagans is indeed a distinct species from C. geraniifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; Balkwill, K; Knox, EB. 2006. A revision of the genus Cineraria (Asteraceae, Senecioneae). Kew Bull. 61(4): 449-535. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/20443295] [All rights reserved]

description: E. pinnatipartitus is quite variable, especially in leaf-shape. Sometimes the leaves are very closely pectinate with flattened and spreading lobes, sometimes more laxly pinnatipartite with subterete and erecto-patent lobes. The two extremes look rather different at first sight, but they are connected by a continuous series of transitional forms. The tips of the leaf-segments are often bristle-pointed or shortly acuminate, but sometimes more mucronate. The peduncles are always short, seldom exceeding 5 cm in length, and young capitula may even appear almost sessile. The achenes afford very reliable diagnostic characters, too, by their densely tuberculatea surface. In herbaria the species is usually found under the names Gamolepis pectinata or G. pinnatipartita, but sometimes it is confused with E. abrotamfolius. Some forms of the latter are indeed almost indistinguishable from E. pinnatipartitus without an examination of pappus or achenes. The sterile disc-florets represent a fairly unusual condition within the genus, and they show an interesting variation in the shape of the styles. Sometimes the style is distinctly lobed with style branches up to 0.4 mm long. No distinct stigmatic areas are present, however. From this type all intergrades to completely undivided styles occur, often within the same capitulum. When simple, the style is tipped by a cone (similar to the condition in Othonna), which may be somewhat truncate or emarginate.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: D. nudicaulis is a perennial herb with one or several erect or ascendent stems, which are prolonged upwards into a scape-like peduncle. They are simple, and usually only furnished with leaves in their lowermost part, but seldom up to or somewhat above the middle of the stem. At the base the leaves are disposed more or less in the form of a rosette. The pubescence varies from densely and shortly hispid to sub-glabrous. The hairs are pericellular and glanduliferous, and feel rough at least when the plant is dried. In the main species the breadth and shape of the leaves varies very much even in one and the same individual, and the rosette of leaves consists of a large number of narrowly obovate to oblanceolate, sinuate-dentate or sometimes pinnatifid leaves. In addition, it usually has a few narrow, linear-lanceolate, sparsely denticulate or entire leaves. The ray flowers are white above, and beneath purple or violet, or else they have an interspersion of copper or other colouring.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Phymaspermum woodii shares the narrowly campanulate to urceolate involucres and flat, deltoid to ovate, closely appressed involucral bracts with P. argenteum but can be distinguished by the sparsely villous leaves with narrower lobes (<0.5 mm wide) and the 5-seriate, apically constricted involucres with at most indistinct brown margins. This species could also be confused with the spring flowering P. pinnatifidum with which it shares the smaller habit and narrowly lobed leaves but can be readily distinguished by the much narrower campanulate to urceolate, apically constricted involucres with closely appressed involucral bracts, the absence of a prominent membranous crown on the fruit and the later flowering time (late summer into autumn).
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: H. mixtum is aptly named, for it combines the foliage of H. cephaloideum with the loose inflorescence and acute involucral bracts of H. longifolium, as Kuntze himself pointed out, and it is not always possible to place specimens with certainty. In the Cape, despite the inner involucral bracts often being as obtuse as in H. cephaloideum, there is no difficulty in distinguishing H. mixtum with heads consistently larger than those of H. cephaloideum and loosely arranged. In KwaZulu-Natal and the Transvaal, however, the situation is not so clearcut. In KwaZulu-Natal, it is often difficult to decide whether a specimen is better placed as H. mixtum or H. cephaloideum or even H. longifolium. As suggested before (Hilliard l.c.), this may be due to crossing, or speciation in this whole difficult grpup may be incomplete. In the Transvaal, the situation is complicated by the presence of a plant that differs from H. mixtum in its larger heads with less glossy involucral bracts, and in its earlier flowering time. For convenience, it is accorded varietal rank, but experimental work on the whole group is highly desirable.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Bears a strong superficial resemblance to B. rhapontica var. exalata, but has long setose-acuminate pappus scales, very different from the short, acute or subacute pappus scales of B, rhapontica. Also the leaves are smooth above, not harshly pubescent, but this is a less reliable character than the pappus scales.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: A. lundgrenii is allied to A. arborescens (L.) Less, and A. laeve (Harv.) Lundgren, with both of which it shares the distinctly woolly achenes. It differs from both these species by the broader oblanceolate leaves, the fewer involucral bracts with a smaller white lamina, and the few-flowered capitula. The number of involucral bracts is 15-22 in A. arborescens and 18-25 in A. laeve. In A. lundgrenii the number is usually around 10, and not exceeding 13. The number of male florets seems to be constantly 2 in A. lundgrenii. In the two related species the number is always higher, viz. 4-5 in A. arborescens and 8-11 in A. laeve. In number of involucral bracts and florets the new species resembles A. virgatum DC, but the latter is very different in foliage, size of capitula, pappus structure, and especially achene surface, which is glabrous or sparingly puberulous. Further differences from A. arborescens are the pale colouring of the involucre and the extensive pubescence of the outer involucral bracts in A. lundgrenii, and the short pappus bristles in both types of florets further serve to distinguish the new species from A. laeve.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1988. A new species of Anaxeton (Asteraceae) from the south-western Cape Province. S. African J. Bot. 54: 631-632. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1988); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: E. munitus is well characterized by its curved and pinnatipartite leaves, usually with two or three pairs of lobes. Specimens from Union-dale Division tend to have rather small leaves, sometimes with only one pair of leaf-lobes. On the other hand, some collections from Port Elizabeth Division have comparatively large leaves, occasionally with as many as four pairs of leaf-lobes. In this character, as well as in the unusually big fruits, these specimens show some affinity to E. ursinoides, which grows in the same area (Van Staadens Mountains). A gene flow from the latter species, i.e. a case of introgression, might be suspected, and further investigations along this line may be rewarding. The length of the rays varies considerably, but apparently at random.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Very close to S. pterophorus, a largely Transkeian species with bigger heads (c. 13 rays), and S. juniperinus (with c. 13 rays and white-cobwebby at the base of the involucre).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Harvey's epithet polytrichoides very aptly describes the striking habit of this plant. There is a tendency towards monopodial branching further adding to the peculiar habit. This is brought about by the suppression of all but one branch at a ramification. The favoured branch then appears as a continuation of the mother branch, and often the original ramification is revealed only by the presence of a peduncle. This reversal of a (pseudo-)terminal position of the peduncle to a lateral condition must be regarded as a very advanced feature. Only in the closely related E. hypnoides (see below) the same tendency has been observed. It should be borne in mind that even the `terminal' position is derived, viz. from an originally lateral condition.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to S. bupleuroides.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Very near O. quinquedentata, but with thinner, less cuneate, more taper-pointed leaves, strongly decurrent at base, with usually more teeth. Drège’s specimens of O. grandidentata and pluridentata are from the same locality, and by me undistinguishable; the number of teeth is a most uncertain character.

description: M. muricata is recognized by its generally curved to hooked leaves, which are obtuse at the very apex; and by apically slightly carinate outermost to inner involucral bracts. It sometimes resembles M. densa, but the latter species has darker brown involucres due to the outer and inner involucral bracts being differently coloured. The outermost to inner involucral bracts in M. densa are flat apically, rather than slightly carinate. Occasionally M. densa has leaves that are apically curved to hooked, like those of M. muricata. M. umbelliformis is similar to M. muricata in foliage and features of the involucre, but is distinguished by its individually arranged capitula and apically appressed outermost and outer involucral bracts. M. muricata and M. umbelliformis are sister species. Specimens of low stature may resemble M. calcicola but that species has different foliage and involucral bracts which are thinner apically and hence not carinate. The features of the involucre are not always easily seen on old herbarium specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Karis, PO. 1989. Systematics of the genus Metalasia (Asteraceae-Gnaphalieae). Opera Bot. 99: 1-150. [All rights reserved]

description: Two chromosome numbers were found in E. oligoglossus, viz., 2n = 20 and 40, respectively. I have had one collection of each in cultivation, and they are distinguishable morphologically on a number of quantitative characters. The tetraploid has larger and more distantly spaced leaves, longer and somewhat thicker peduncles, bigger flower-heads, longer involucral bracts, larger disc-florets with longer anthers, and bigger pollen grains. The same differences are observable in the material collected in nature. The herbarium material available of E. oligoglossus could be sorted on the same characters with reasonable accuracy into two form series, probably representing two cytotypes. The two putative cytotypes are treated as subspecies in the present work. Although they are likely to be effectively isolated genetically, the morphological differences are small and of a purely quantitative nature. The two subspecies have different distribution ranges and possibly also a somewhat differing ecology. Further studies are needed, however, to clarify the variation, cytology, distribution, ecology, and interrelationship of the two subspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: This rare and imperfectly known species shows distinct affinities to E. othonnoides, e.g., in habit, indumentum, and achenes, but it is also allied to E. wageneri by characters of leaves, involucre, and ray-florets. The species thus takes a natural position in sect. Euryops, in spite of the peculiar, post-florally elongating pappus. Only very scarce flowering material has hitherto been collected, and it remains to ascertain whether the rays are always orange-coloured.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1968. The genus Euryops I. Opera Bot. 20: 7-409. [All rights reserved]

description: E. trilobus is quite variable in leaf-shape. Usually the leaves are three-lobed and obtuse, but in some specimens (Acocks 21050, Tyson 181) many or all leaves are entire and more acute. In spite of this variation E. trilobus is a well defined species, characterized, i.a., by the dense cushion-like growth, and the copious long pappus.

description: This species may only be confused with Cineraria aspera, but the lobes and pinnules of C. cyanomontana are essentially entire, whereas those of C. aspera are dentate. In addition, the auricles of C. cyanomontana are linear compared to the auriform, dentate auricles of C. aspera. The fine trichomes on the leaves of C. cyanomontana consist of two or three agranular, narrow basal cells with a long, multi-celled apical appendage. In C. aspera they commonly comprise the type with 4-6 tapering basal cells and a long apical appendage, although the fine type are present on some specimens. Cineraria cyanomontana is endemic to the Blouberg Mountain, in the arid northern region of South Africa, where it grows in the mist belt on the southern side of the mountain, near the summit. Despite searches by the authors and others, it has not (as yet) been found on the adjacent Soutpansberg range, which is about 50 km apart for the afromontane elements.

description: This new species resembles A. ramlowii but is distinguished by its shorter, darker and narrower rhizome scales, longer and broader fronds with the lowermost pairs of pinnae of a similar width or only slightly reduced towards the basal pair and by its larger, more dissected pinnae with distinct rounded pinnules. A. schelpei also shows some less obvious but nevertheless significant morphological affinities with A. splendens, which is a tetraploid species confined to South Africa. It shares with this species longer and broader fronds than those found in A. ramlowii and also larger, more dissected pinnae with rounded pinnules.
