description: Normally with a fine sericeous indumentum on floral parts, but subglabrous forms occur (e.g. Ngoni 130 from Zimbabwe). A rare form from Angola and Namibia (e.g. Menezes et al 3332, da Silva 2969, Kers 2844, Rautanen 157) has toothed vegetative leaves. This form also tends to have longer, wider and less hairy floral leaves and to have sparsely hairy sepals. But in the same areas there are intermediates with typical B. leendertziae (e.g. Pearson 2017, Teixeira 2615).
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: A very distinctive species which - despite a very different appearance - seems closest to B. fleckii with which it shares the spinescent petioles and hard leathery leaves with strongly raised white edges.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: Phyllopodium micranthum may at once be distinguished from P. capillare, to which it seems allied, by its different indumentum: the upper part of the stem is clad in small patent glandular hairs to the total or almost total exclusion of retrorse eglandular ones, while the entire stem of P. capillare is clad in this type of hair, more or less masking tiny glandular hairs that may also be present. There are other differences too: in P. micranthum, the lower leaf surface in particular is puberulous while the hairs are confined to the midrib and margins in P. capillare, and the corolla tube of P. micranthum is mostly shorter (1.5-2.5 mm versus 2.5-3.5 mm). Phyllopodium capillare is a plant of the lowlands; P. micranthum is a plant of the inland plateau.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: B. mitrata- as understood here - seems to contain a large number of slightly different forms. It is quite possible that detailed studies of populations in the field will result in the division of the species into a number of infraspecific taxa. At the moment - and without having studied the species in the field - I do not feel confident enough to attempt a division. The South African populations are generally less hairy than the Namibian ones, have fewer teeth on the leaves and have shorter spikes with fewer flowers.B. villosa s.str. is reasonably distinct from B. mitrata s.str. in the southern parts of its distribution where it differs in its longer inflorescences with longer peduncles and bracteoles. It also normally has white flowers. But if one compares the material from Namibia all these differences are eroded, and at the moment there is no justification for keeping B. villosa as a distinct species. B. mitrata is closely related to B, obmitrata, and the two are often difficult to separate. Not one single character will invariably separate all the collections, and one has to look at the combination of characters as given in the key to species. B. mitrata is normally a much more compact plant with usually very short internodes and with erect leaves hiding the spikes, the bracts are obovate with fewer generally longer teeth and the ventral sepal is generally shorter with shorter apical teeth. Taller forms (e.g. Merxmüller & Giess 28864) invariably have few bract-teeth of which the longest are always over 10 mm and always have the apical teeth on the ventral sepal less than 1.5 mm long. Dense compact forms of B. obmitrata have more than 5 large bract-teeth per side and have the apical teeth on the ventral sepal over 2 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: A very distinctive species which is not obviously close to any other species. The thin papery bracts with numerous flexible bristles combined with the trailing habit makes it immediately recognisable. It is the only species in the group with teeth on the petiole which has this growth form.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is isolated within the genus, and is easily recognized by its long leafy racemes, tiny flowers and possession of only two stamens. There is no indication of cleistogamy, but the reduction in number of stamens appears to be constant and to be associated with selfing: the stigma is never exserted, but curls round the anthers in the mouth of the corolla tube.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Differs most conspicuously from the related B. acanthodioides in the dense sericeous indumentum on floral leaves, bracts and sepals. It occurs in an area well known for several other narrowly endemic species of Acanthaceae, such as Ecbolium glabratum (Vollesen 1989) and Sclerochiton apiculatus (Vollesen 1991).
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: B. serrulata, drummondii and laevifolia are characterised by their often reddish tinged leaves with numerous fine forward-directed teeth.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: Schlechter remarked of his new species, Polycarena parvula, that it was distinguished from P. capillaris by its much smaller flowers. The corolla limb in Schlechter's specimens measures c. 2 mm across the lateral lobes, the posticous lip may be glabrous or have but a few hairs, and the anthers are also very small, with one pair only just exserted from the mouth. Other specimens over the geographical range of the species show similar traits, which probably indicate selfing. Despite variation in the size of the flowers, Phyllopodium capillare is easily distinguished from its allies by the very short ± curled white hairs thickly clothing the stems and inflorescence axes and more or less masking the tiny glandular hairs that are also present. There appears to be a local strain on the Cape Peninsula (e.g. Bolus 659, cited above) with very leafy stems, which appear to be prostrate; the typical plant is also on the Peninsula, and although the two differ in facies, I can find nothing else to distinguish them.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Known only from this collection. It is not immediately clear what is the nearest relative of this very distinctive species. It is the only species from northern South Africa with teeth on the petiole. It keys out next to B. mitrata, but this can at best be only a superficial similarity and it is more likely to be related to B. ilicina from Eastern Cape. The constantly 2-flowered spikes separate it from all other species in this group.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: The proper stems with whorled leaves are often almost absent, and most of the apparent 'stems' are the elongated peduncles. B. squarrosa is clearly related to the following two species where this condition has been taken to the extreme. It is also superficially similar to dwarfed specimens of B. capensis but, apart from the totally different area of distribution, it never has lateral branches in the axils of the bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: Leendertz s.n., Magaliesbergen, is a more robust plant than any other collection seen, with longer stems, larger leaves and larger bracts. These are the measurements in brackets in the description above. It is also generally more sparsely hairy. All this indicates that it may have been collected from a more shady habitat than normal for B. stainbankiae. But- mainly on account of its white corolla - it fits better into this species than anywhere else. Apart from this abnormal collection B. stainbankiae is normally easily recognised by the thin trailing stems and small wide leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: Differs from B. subvolubilis in the completely glabrous broader bracts, longer spikes with more flowers, broader glabrous bracteoles and longer anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2000. Blepharis (Acanthaceae), a taxonomic revision. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [All rights reserved]

description: B. diffusa can be distinguished from other members of Boerhavia in southern Africa by an indentation of the ribs near the apex. The plants often produce flowers and subsequent anthocarps on a short peduncle in the axis of the leaves, in addition to the typical inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Struwig, M; Siebert, SJ. 2013. A taxonomic revision of Boerhavia (Nyctaginaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 86: 116-134. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2013); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Very variable in size, in the thickness and amount of branching of the stem, in the length and width of the leaves, and in the extent of the inflorescence. While the more extreme forms appear distinct they are connected by all stages of intermediates. Many of the variations seem directly correlated with habitat conditions.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1959. The South African Species of Aizoaceae: VIII. Psammotropha. J. S. African Bot. 25: 51-68. [CC BY]

description: B. hereroensis is morphologically similar to B. deserticola in that both taxa have elliptic, lanceolate to ovate leaves with undulate margins, the lower coriaceous part of the flower is ovoid and the anthocarp is 5-ribbed and ellipsoid-clavate. It differs in having extremely glandular, hairy anthocarps, smaller, dark pink flowers and a diffuse habit.
bibliographicCitation: Struwig, M; Siebert, SJ. 2013. A taxonomic revision of Boerhavia (Nyctaginaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 86: 116-134. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2013); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: A peculiar feature of this species is the characteristic fimbriate or laciniate corona. Without flowers or fruit it is easily confused with B. mossambicensis, but the latter species, has leaves more or less evenly glabrous to pubescent on both surfaces, whereas the leaves of B. angustifolia var. corymbosa are much more densely hairy on the abaxial surface.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1970. Boscia, Fl. S. Africa 13: 150-159. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This complex species is not clearly understood and might need re-evaluation, particularly if material becomes available where the subspecies overlap geographically. B. microphylla is very closely allied and might have to be incorporated in this complex. At present the material is classified into four subspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1970. Boscia, Fl. S. Africa 13: 150-159. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Polycarena lilacina var. difficilis has all the characters of P. lilacina except the very short indumentum; instead, the hairs are up to 0.25-0.4 mm long. To assign varietal rank to this plant is a matter of expediency, a means of drawing attention to a variation that may seem trivial, but it assumes significance in the context of Polycarena as a whole where small differences in indumentum can often be used to distinguish species that are/easily separable on other characters. Typical P. lilacina is notable for its very short indumentum, a character that, combined with markedly different floral details, serves to distinguish it from P. capensis with which it shares the character of corymbose branching and leafy habit.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Hilliard & Burtt (1988) noted two rather distinct forms of P. montana in KwaZulu-Natal. The first form is characterized by plants on rock platforms that are low, rounded bushes, 0.3-1 m high, with the tips of the branches erect, whereas those of the second form inhabit valleys and are riverside bushes of up to 2 m high, with open branches and pendulous branchlets. The present study, taking the whole distribution range of P. montana into consideration, recognizes two forms. One, centred in the God's Window area of Mpumalanga, are rounded shrubs 0.5-2 m high, with many branchlets covered with smaller, decussate, imbricate leaves, bluish green in colour. The second form dominates in the Free State. Lesotho, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape. These plants are more robust, with open branches and larger, yellowish green leaves and inflorescences, which are tinged pink. However, the two forms are not geographically distinct and intermediates are common. Both forms unequivocally show the specific characters and therefore we do not propose to give them formal taxonomic recognition.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL; Van Wyk, AE. 2003. Taxonomy of the genus Passerina (Thymelaeaceae). Bothalia 33(1): 59-98. [CC BY]

description: The spikelets are too young to decide whether both or only one of the flowers will perfect a nut.
bibliographicCitation: Turrill, WB. 1925. Notes on Cyperaceae: II (New species etc. from Africa). Bull. Misc. Inform. Kew 1925(2): 67-76. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4107520] [All rights reserved]

description: The affinity is with T. stokoei, from which it is distinguished by the pale bracts and much larger, differently shaped female perianth.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1942. New species of South African Restionaceae. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 29(4): 339-356. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is very singular in appearance and quite distinct from all that are known to me. The soft fleshy compressed leaves, being united in pairs for about half their length into flattened obovate 2-lobed bodies, suggest a process of evolution where species of the type of M. bilobum have developed internodes between the successive growths and so developed into a shrublet. The oblique stripes on the leaves are not evident to all seasons of the year.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, NE. 1920. New and old species of Mesembryanthemum, with critical notes. J. Linn. Soc., Bot. 45: 53-140. [https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1095-8339.1920.tb00119.x] [All rights reserved]

description: The hairs which appear to arise upon the base of the ventral surface of the leaves may, in fact, arise upon a portion of the stem adhering to the leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: Protea namaquana is readily distinguished by its growth habit and foliage. Unlike P. sulphurea which assumes a procumbent, horizontally sprawling mode of growth, P. namaquana is an erect, compact, rounded shrub 1 to 2 m in height. The leaves are narrowly oblanceolate to linear-spathulate, 30-60 mm long and pale green in the live state, unlike the elliptic glaucous leaves, 11^40 mm long in P. sulphurea. The involucral bracts are dull carmine in contrast to the predominantly yellow bracts of P. sulphurea. Newly opened inflorescences emit a strong yeasty odour.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1990. A new species of Protea (Proteaceae) from Namaqualand with comments on the Kamiesberg as a centre of. S. African J. Bot. 56: 261-265. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1990); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: In leaf character B. corrugata resembles B. salviifolia very closely, being rugose on the upper surface, tomentose and reticulate below, with crenulate margins, but differs in the leaves being distinctly though shortly petioled, cuneate or rounded at the base (not cordate to auricled) and with only an interpetiolar ridge instead of stipules. It is also not so long acuminate to an acute apex as in B. salviifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Loganiaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 134-171. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Clustered, multiple flower-heads (usually a characteristic of P. welwitschii) are occasionally produced in P. gaguedi. These two species are best distinguished by the leaves which are glabrous when mature in P. gaguedi, while in P. welwitschii even the mature leaves are pubescent, or at least retain traces of pubescence along their midribs.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Hitherto it has been considered that Buttonia natalensis McKen ex Benth. and B. hildebrandtii Engl. represented two distinct taxa, but the material now available leaves little doubt that they are conspecific. Some of the Kenyan material named B. natalensis studied has leaves and flowers similar in size to some of the South African B. hildebrandtii and it would seem that the material used for the latter description was of a depauperate plant due to much drier and poorer local conditions. Here they are considered together under the earlier name.
bibliographicCitation: Philcox, D. 1990. 120. Scrophulariaceae: 35. Buttonia McKen ex Benth. In: E Launert & GV Pope (eds), Fl. Zambes. 8(2): 141-143. [CC BY]

description: This third species of Buttonia is closely related to B. natalensis McKen, but easily distinguished from it by the small, narrow spathulate bracteoles and the somewhat different and larger calyx. The corolla, too, seems somewhat larger in our species. From the other species, B. hildebrandtii Engl. of East Africa, it differs in the leaf shape and the much larger flowers, while the bracteoles are situated close to the calyx (in B. Hilde-brandtii they are remote).
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM; Obermeyer, AA; Bremekamp, CEB; Compton, RH. 1936. Plantae novae Africanae. Series VII. J. S. African Bot. 2: 145-169. [https://archive.org/stream/journalofsouthaf02unse#page/144/mode/2up] [CC BY]

description: Calodendrum capense is one of the few forest trees of South Africa with conspicuous flowers, and when the many-flowered panicles are at their best the trees stand out promin­ently as large lilac patches in forests. Trees may attain a height of about 60 feet with a stem diameter of 3 ft.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA; Letty, CL. 1948. Calodendrum capense (L.f.) Thunb. Fl. Pl. South Africa 27t.1041 [CC BY]

description: Capnophyllum africanum is vegetatively similar to C. leiocarpon and C. lutzeyeri but differs in that both the ovaries and fruit are covered with tubercles on the median and lateral ribs, as in C. macrocarpum. It differs from the latter species, however, in the larger number of rays per umbel (4 or more), the smaller fruit (less than 8 mm long) without a sterile apical portion and with the shortly conical stylopodium raised above the fruit apex.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM; Downie, SR. 2009. A taxonomic revision of Capnophyllum (Apiaceae: Apioideae). S. African J. Bot. 75: 283-291. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2009); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Capnophyllum leiocarpon differs from C. africanum and C. macrocarpum in the absence of tubercles on the ribs of both the ovaries and fruit. It can be distinguished from C. lutzeyeri by the longer styles of the mature fruit that become reflexed far beyond the base of the stylopodium, and the only very slightly concave commissural surfaces of the mericarps.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM; Downie, SR. 2009. A taxonomic revision of Capnophyllum (Apiaceae: Apioideae). S. African J. Bot. 75: 283-291. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2009); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: This complex species can easily be recognized by its characteristic leaves. The first and second pair of secondary veins are usually much longer and pronounced, and join the primary vein at a very acute angle. The flowers are usually slightly zygomorphic. The anterior sepal is usually saccate and the two adjoining petals are usually broader with a much more pronounced villose base. These hairs in the flowers are usually brown whereas those of the branches and leaves are brown, becoming greyish or sometimes greyish throughout. However, no definite pattern for this change of colour of hairs could be found. On the whole, C. fascicularis is very variable and several forms have been recorded. However, the South African material of the one form could not be assigned to either var. fascicularis or var. elaeagnoides as used by De Wolf (1964), because a complete range of 8-23 stamens, in a decreasing series from north to south is found. This makes it also impossible to uphold the two varieties var. transvaalensis and var. calvescens as distinguished by Marais (1964). C. zeylieri must also be linked to this species. Particularly in the vicinity of King William's Town and Bathurst, plants of var. fascicularis produce smaller flowers often borne on short axillary branches. Coppice shoots of the two forms are practically indistinguishable and produce straight thorns and spreading hairs. The var. zeylieri can only be distinguished by its lanceolate, acuminate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1970. Capparis, Fl. S. Africa 13: 144-150. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The habit, the many-ribbed stems and the leafless appearance make this an easily recognizable species.
bibliographicCitation: Hansen, OJ. 1975. The East African species of Sopubia (Scrophulariaceae). Kew Bull. 30(3): 543-558. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4103085] [All rights reserved]

description: Selago venosa has hitherto been confused with S. glomerata from which it can be distinguished by the raised venation on the backs of the leaves (often most easily seen in the primary ones) and the bracts; this feature suggested the trivial name. The bracts of S. venosa are also mostly broader than those of S. glomerata (lowermost 1.2-2 mm, versus 1-1.25 mm) and exceed the calyx, while both calyx and corolla tube are often shorter. The calyx is hairier in S. venosa than in S. glomerata and the cocci are almost flat on the inner face, not deeply concave.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago parvibractea is so-called because of its small somewhat obtuse bracts that are generally shorter than the calyx. Selago glomerata also has bracts mostly shorter than the calyx but the calyx of S. glomerata is longer (c.2.8-3.2 mm, not 1.7-2.4 mm) and the lobes are acute (not ± obtuse); also, the cocci of S. glomerata are deeply concave on the inner face, not almost flat as they are in S. parvibractea. Selago dolichonema has bracts similar to those of S. parvibractea, but its bracts are longer than the calyx and pubescent on the backs near the base, and its calyx lobes are sharply acute.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The leaves are chewed for an amphetamin-like stimulant action.
bibliographicCitation: Jordaan, M. 2019. Celastraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 768-785. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The distinguishing features of the species are the profusely branched inflorescence, the individual racemes with less than 20 flowers, the distinctly pedicelled lowermost flowers in a raceme distant, the calyx overtopped by the leaflike bract. The bract and calyx are minutely glandular all over, and usually there are few to many longer acute hairs as well; stem and leaves are similarly hairy. The primary leaves are relatively broad, frequently more or less toothed in the upper part, the 3-5 main veins conspicuous.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It is similar in fades to S. lamprocarpa (because of its short spreading leaves), but in floral detail more closely resembles S. oresigena; all three species are partially sympatric and they may hybridize, which is perplexing in an herbarium study. Field studies are much needed, particularly in the Baviaansberg where all three species occur, and on the Witteberg west of Laingsburg, where.S. lamprocarpa and S. perplexa have been recorded. Selago perplexa differs from S. lamprocarpa in its stem with recurved (not patent) hairs, bracts broader and often longer (lowermost c. 5-8 x 2-3.5 mm versus 3-5 x 0.9-1.3 mm) and strongly veined on the back (not veins invisible), calyx longer (3.3-4.5 mm versus 2-2.7 mm), corolla tube longer (c. 6-11.5 mm versus 2.3-3.8 mm), posticous anthers included or just visible in mouth (not all well exserted). Also, S. perplexa flowers in spring (mainly September and October), S. lamprocarpa in summer (mainly December, January). Selago oresigena also flowers in summer, and further resembles S. perplexa in its broad bracts, long corolla tubes and posticous anthers included or very nearly so. It differs in its stems, glabrous except for minute globular glands, largest leaves 4.5-12 x 1.4-2.8 mm (not 2.5-6 x 1-1.2(-1.5) mm), the internodes very short, the leaves strongly imbricated (not internodes longer so stem easily seen), and bracts either glabrous on the margins or with a few hairs to c. 0.2 mm long at the base (not hairs mostly 0.25-0.6 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: One of the distinguishing characters of S. pustulosa is its pustulate leaves; the pustules are probably raised stomata closely set all over the leaf surface, their pale colour often contrasting with the green of the surrounding tissue. The species is allied to S. dregeana, with which it is partly sympatric. Selago dregeana differs in the mostly longer hairs on the stems, mostly narrower leaves (0.5-0.9 mm, versus 0.8-1.7 mm) without raised pustules, calyx mostly shorter (2.2-3 mm, versus 2.8-3.5 mm), corolla tube mostly shorter (3-4.5 mm, not 4.5-6 mm).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago gloiodes is allied to S. eckloniana from which it is distinguished by its leaves with a median channel on the lower surface, the upper surface rounded (channelled above in 5. eckloniana), smaller raceme, and hairs on bracts and calyces not coarse. Stems, leaves, bracts and calyces are covered in minute glands that usually discharge heavily, making the plant very viscous, whence the trivial name (Greek for viscous).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the habit, narrow leaves, and especially by the fruit. In the past much confused with narrow leaved forms of C. glabrata.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: Selago dolosa derives its trivial name from the Latin for deceitful; it bears a deceptive resemblance to S. corymbosa and S. punctata. It can be distinguished from S. corymbosa by its leaves, of different shape and texture, and mostly shorter, broader and only glandular-punctate, also by its broader bracts; it differs from S. punctata, which has similar leaves, by its smaller, obtuse, bracts and shorter corolla tube. See further under S. corymbosa.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Centella annua is similar to C. capensis but differs in the annual habit, the presence of bisexual inflorescences, the male flowers which are shorter than the bracts and the inconspicuous stylopodia of the male flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1997. A revision of Centella series Capenses (Apiaceae). Nord. J. Bot. 17(3): 301-314. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago dolichonema is closely allied to S. venosa with which it is sympatric in the Cedarberg. It is distinguished principally by its bracts, narrower, often shorter, hairy on the lower part of the back, and the venation not raised. The bracts are occasionally hairy near the base in S. venosa in the Cedarberg (and northwards), but this may be due to introgression with S. dolichonema. The flowers tend to be smaller than those of S. venosa, the calyx being mostly shorter, and the corolla tube often so. The filaments are very long in relation to the size of the corolla tube, so that all four anthers are strikingly far exerted, even in this group of species where well exerted anthers are the norm. This suggested the epithet dolichonema (Greek, long thread).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to G. glabrata but differing in the habit, the long-petiolate lower leaves with 1 vein, the hairy petals, and the much longer bracts to the fruit. Originally described as a variety. The type material is incomplete; the later specimens collected at Klaver are much better.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: The affinity of S. baurii seems to lie with S. longipedicellata, S. immersa and S. innata (similar bract, pedicel, disposition of anthers, and cocci), but the calyx, irregularly 3-54obed, is distinctive but approaching that of S. longiflora.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: In facies, it is not unlike S. mucronata, which grows in the same general area, but it is easily distinguished by its leaves, obtuse and lacking the conspicuous recurved mucro seen in S. mucronata, by its longer calyx and corolla tube, and by the posticous anthers held in the throat or mouth. It is strikingly similar to specimens of S. glutinosa subsp. cylindriphylla from the southern part of its range, notably specimens collected at Constable (Compton 3756, BOL) and Karoo Poort (Compton 16066), from which S. albomontana differs in little more than the calyx being glabrous within, not glandular. Possibly it is no more than a form of subsp. cylindriphylla, but if so, it has remained constant between its first collection in 1926 and its latest in 1976, and needs recognition.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The relationship of S. adenodes lies with S. pulchra, with which it is sympatric. They differ in their bracts, lowermost 3-4 x 1.4-2.3 mm (not 2.3-3 x 1-1.3 mm), obtuse (not subacute), hairs 0.15-0.25 mm long on margins, minute glandular hairs all over both faces (not hairs up to 0.1 mm on margins otherwise glabrous), calyx with hairs 0.2-0.25 mm long on margins, minute glandular hairs all over outside (not hairs 0.1 mm long on margins, glabrous outside), cocci without spurious cells (versus cocci with two spurious cells).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Its relationship lies with S. rigida from which it is distinguished by shorter hairs on the stems, leaves mostly longer, bracts narrower and minutely glandular on both faces (versus glands on inner face only), and only sometimes with a few minute acute hairs on the keel (not with acute hairs scattered over the back), and calyx minutely glandular all over the outer face (not with acute hairs 0.1-0.25 mm long as well as globular glands).Both have the calyx irregularly 3-4 - 5-lobed, and both may produce only female flowers; S. chalarantha is unusual in that the staminodes are well exserted. The racemes of S. chalarantha (Greek: laxly flowered) are much laxer than those of S. rigida; this, combined with the longer leaves, contributes to the difference in facies between the two species, which are sympatric at least around Nieuwoudtville.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: A very variable species in size, leaf shape and texture, and in the degree of hairiness. Some of the variations are related to habitat and to season: plants growing on sand have larger and narrower leaves than those on clays, shade forms have broader and thinner leaves. Late in the season the basal leaves may wither away. The numerous varieties which have been based upon leaf form are of little value and quite impossible to disentangle satisfactorily. Many of them include both forms of this and of related species. Even the toothing of the leaves seems an accidental feature of no diagnostic value; it may be confined to the basal leaves (H. heterophylla Schinz) or occur in the upper leaves also (H. bupleurifolia var. tridentata E. & Z.). The varieties recognized here seem definite entities, some of them possibly specifically distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: Some forms may deserve species status.
bibliographicCitation: Winter, PJD. 2019. Apiaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 294-321. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species has hitherto been confused with S. corymbosa, from which it can be distinguished by its somewhat shorter leaves, broader in relation to their length (ratio length: breadth c. 7-8.5: 1 versus 10-24:1), hairy all over (not hairs confined to margins and midline on lower surface) and broader bracts (lowermost 0.9-1 mm broad versus 0.4-0.7 mm). There is probably also a difference in habit, S. corymbosa being a taller, bushier, plant, not stoloniferous at the base, but I have seen the root system of only two specimens of S. corymbosa (a simple taproot).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Judged by morphological similarities, the closest relative of C. glauca is C. macrocarpa, even though specimens have mostly been identified as C. linifolia or C. virgata in the past. Centella glauca is similar to C. macrocarpa but differs in the much larger habit, the glaucous leaves (hence the specific epithet) and the laminate, often toothed, coppice leaves. The mature leaves of C. glauca are acicular. Another distinct feature of C. glauca is that the rays of the functionally male and female umbellules may often be extremely long. The ribbed fruits are very similar in shape and surface sculpturing to those of C. macrocarpa, but are usually much larger. This new species forms an interesting morphological link between C. linifolia and the C. macrocarpalvirgata complex. The apparent isolation of C. linifolia from the series Virgatae Adamson is therefore reduced. The new species combines the glaucous leaf surface and distinct lamina of C. linifolia (at least in coppice shoots) with the acicular leaves and virgate habit of C. macrocarpa. The new species appears to be invariably resprouting, whereas C. virgata and some populations of C. macrocarpa are obligate reseeders. Further studies are in progress to examine relationships amongst these and related species.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1996. A new species of Centella. Bothalia 26(1): 50-52. [https://doi.org/10.4102/abc.v26i1.689] [CC BY]

description: Allied to C. eriantha but larger, usually more erect, and glabrescent except for the coarsely villous youngest parts.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: Selago michelliae is similar in facies to S. singularis and that is possibly where its relationship lies; it differs in the long shaggy indumentum on stems, leaves, bracts and calyces, the hairs all simple, not dendroid as they mostly are on the stems of S. singularis. Also the margins of the leaves are plane,' not so very strongly revolute that they are often confluent, and the bracts are longer. The calyx of S. singularis is always 5-lobed, that of S. michelliae is remarkably variable: of eight calyces examined, three were perfectly 3-lobed, two perfectly 5-lobed, and three were irregularly lobed.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Centella longifolia was previously considered to be a variety of C. montana. However there is sufficient evidence showing it to be a distinct species. C. longifolia is a tufted perennial with compressed internodes (rarely forming shoots). The linear-lanceolate, petiolate leaves originate from a central tuft. C. montana frequently forms shoots bearing elliptical, entire or sometimes dentate leaves on nodes separated by distinct internodes. Both species are pilose with a distinct red-brown colour also found in C. cryptocarpa. The extreme compression of nodes in C. longifolia creates the impression of a halo of shorter bisexual umbellules and longer functionally male umbellules arising from the base of the tufted plant. The umbellules of C. montana are borne on separate nodes but some degree of compression may occur.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1999. Three new species of Centella series Montanae. Nord. J. Bot. 19(4): 427-434. [All rights reserved]

description: The two species are readily distinguished by their bracts, hairy all over in S. inconstans, hairs confined to margins and midline of keel in S. monticola, calyx hairy all over in S. inconstans, hairs confined, or nearly confined, to margins in S. monticola, corolla tube usually longer is S. inconstans (c. 2.5 mm - 4 mm), only c. 1.7-2 mm in S. monticola. They differ too in habit, S. monticola being a few-stemmed, upright plant with a much larger, looser, compound inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the small parallel-sided fruit with acuminate bracts. Though originally described as a variety of C. glabrata, the differences in habit, leaves, petals, fruit and bracts are such that no very close affinity is indicated.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: Its relationship lies with S. ramosissima and S. thomii; it differs from both in its pubescent style. Selago ramosissima differs further in its calyx (glandular all over inside) and remarkably thick-walled cocci, while the bracts and calyces of S. thomii are not so conspicuously hairy as those of S. neglecta. All three species appear to be sympatric, though I have seen no specimen of S. thomii from precisely the same area as S. neglecta. Care is needed to distinguish them; all are small twiggy bushes with small inflorescences, and all dry blackish.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to C. glabrata but with quite different fruit and with much narrower leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: C. thesioides is similar to C. rupestris but differsmarkedly in its sparse inflorescences, which are borne well above the vegetative leaves (inflorescences congested, borne amongst the leaves in C. rupestris) and by the invariably acicular leaves which turn brown on drying (leaves invariable flat and linear, not turning brown on drying in C. rupestris). It is also similar to C. restioides but differs from this species in the terminal inflorescences (axillary in C. restioides), the persistent leaf bases (not persistent in C. restioides) and in the male umbellules, which have 3 male flowers in C. thesioides (5 to 7 male flowers in C. restioides), with a single pair of glabrous bracts (bracts in two pairs and villous in C. restioides) and in the obtuse apices of the fruit bracts (fruit bracts acuminate in C. restioides). The new species is geographically isolated from C. restioides and C. rupestris and is known only from the Riviersonderend mountain range.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1995. A taxonomic study of the Centella rupestris group. Nord. J. Bot. 15(3): 263-268. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from other herbaceous perennials by its relatively soft-textured, lyrate-pinnati?d or rarely simply oblanceolate basal leaves with softly puberulous, ± serrate blade. The epicalyx is sharply 4-toothed and the stigma is scarcely wider than the style.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Johns, A. 2014. A taxonomic review of Cephalaria (Dipsacaceae) in the Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 94: 195-203. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2014); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from C. attenuata and C. rigida by its pinnatisect or bipinnatisect leaves and sprawling or decumbent stems. The lobing of the leaves is very variable, with the upper leavers sometimes linear and lobed as in C. attenuata. We owe much of our knowledge of this rare species to the efforts of botanist Elsie Esterhuysen, who is responsible for the majority of the collections.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Johns, A. 2014. A taxonomic review of Cephalaria (Dipsacaceae) in the Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 94: 195-203. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2014); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Origin Amazon basin, declared weed (Category 1).
bibliographicCitation: Nonyane, FM; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Pontederiaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(3): 2104-2105. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species is often confused with the indigenous Euphorbia ingens but easily distinguished on account of the large fragrant flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Walters, M; Figueiredo, E; Crouch, NR; Winter, PJD; Smith, GF; Zimmermann, HG; Mashope, BK. 2011. Naturalised and invasive succulents of southern Africa. ABC Taxa 11: 1-370. [All rights reserved]

description: Bruyns (1985 points out that some plants identified as this species, might actually belong to C. linearis. He also suggests that C. cancellata may represent a hybrid between C. africana and C. linearis; future work should focus on testing this hypotheses.
bibliographicCitation: Nicholas, A; Glen, M; Shuttleworth, A; Bester, SP. 2019. Apocynaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 321-417. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Bruyns (1985) suggests that Ceropegia racemosa N.E.Br. subsp. setifera (Schltr.) H.Huber be sunk under C. carnosa E.Mey. The current author is of the opinion that shared common morphologies must be proved to be due to common ancestry (viz. homologous) before this can be done. If the morphologies of the two are due to convergent evolution (viz. analogous) they cannot be sunk into each other. More research is required.
bibliographicCitation: Nicholas, A; Glen, M; Shuttleworth, A; Bester, SP. 2019. Apocynaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 321-417. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The genus Securidaca can be separated from other Polygalaceae on the combination of one locular samaroid fruit, eight stamens and three petals.
bibliographicCitation: Johnson, CT. 1987. Taxonomy of the African species of Securidaca (Polygalaceae). S. African J. Bot. 53(1): 5-11. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1987); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Bruyns (1985 suggests it may be conspecific with the tropical Ceropegia meyeri-johannis Engl.
bibliographicCitation: Nicholas, A; Glen, M; Shuttleworth, A; Bester, SP. 2019. Apocynaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 321-417. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The hirsute fruits, truncate and pedicellate at the base, distinguish this species from all others in the genus. The small globose inflorescence composed of only four to five, four flowered involucres subtended by a lanceolate attenuate bract, are further diagnostic characters.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: This species is possibly most closely related to C. polyslachyos, but differs by the larger spikelets and the bulbous stem-base surrounded by fibres.
bibliographicCitation: Haines, RW; Lye, KA. 1983. The sedges and rushes of East Africa. East African Natural History Society, Nairobi. [All rights reserved]

description: The closest relationship is with C. geniculata, which occurs somewhat further east in the Ladismith area and extends nearly throughout the Little Karoo. Another relative is C. fimbriata, with which it was at one time confused, but that species is far removed to the east in the Fish River valley scrub and has a distinctive, dome-shaped corolla-canopy with long, pendulous, vibratile cilia. The inwardly directed long hairs from the corolla struts are the special feature of C. connivens.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: Variation is the keynote of most floral characters of this species: the corolla-lobes or struts are short and broad or long and narrow; long, purple, vibratile hairs are present on the short to medium length struts but absent from the most slender long lobes; the knee in the lobes varies in position from near the middle to near the base and its presence is the unifying character of the species concept; the outer corona-lobes vary in the length of the lobules. Speculations on the reason or reasons for the variability are bound to arise and it is merely pointed out that the closely allied species C. zeyheri, with long slender corolla-lobes, has been recorded from within the distribution range of C. geniculata, although only rarely. The next closest relative, C. connivens, with short broad struts, occurs only further west in the Worcester district. C. zeyheri and C. connivens have not been recorded together in the wild.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: Both C. barbata and C. filiformis differ from C. leptophylla by their broader leaves which are nearly flat above, with the margins slightly recurved, and in the corolla- lobes which are broad near the base and very slender above. In C. leptophylla the relatively short lobes are more or less uniformly broad and narrow abruptly to their point of fusion. Ceropegia leptophylla differs from the other two particularly in its outer corona. In both C. barbata and C. filiformis this is much longer than in C. leptophylla, and more deeply bifid, but each lobule terminates in a swollen, nearly spherical knob. In C. leptophylla the lobules are comparatively short and are not apically swollen. Ceropegia leptophylla somewhat resembles the widespread C. carnosa E. Mey. (including C. racemosa N.E.Br.) in corolla shape. However, this resemblance is only superficial. In C. carnosa the corolla-tube always becomes distinctly narrower around its mid-point and the gynostegium is fused into the sides of the corolla-tube around its base. In addition, the outer corona-lobes are excavated in their middle nearly to their bases in C. carnosa and their shape cannot be confused with that in C. leptophylla.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2003. Three new succulent species of Apocynaceae (Asclepiadoideae) from southern Africa. Kew Bull. 58(2): 427-435. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4120625] [All rights reserved]

description: C. macmasteri is most closely related to C. stentiae but is distinguished from this species by having linear, erect, bifid outer corona lobes and inner corona lobes conniving to form a central column. Furthermore, the yellow-green inner surface of the globose inflation of the corolla is densely purple-bullate, with a fringe of 1 mm long retrorse purple hairs at the constriction. The tube is glabrous within. C. stentiae has subquadrate, minutely three lobuled, ciliate outer corona lobes and erect, membranous inner corona lobes loosely conniving in the upper half and recurving at the apex. The inner surface of the globose inflation of the corolla is not bullate nor is the constriction fringed with hairs. The tube is sparsely villous within. C. stentiae is represented by three specimens from Naboomspruit and Pietersburg in Limpopo Province, ±1000 km north of C. macmasteri.
bibliographicCitation: Dold, AP. 2006. Ceropegia macmasteri (Apocynaceae-Asclepiadoideae-Ceropegieae), a new species from Eastern Cape, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 72: 144-146. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2006); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The bottle-shape of the inflated corolla with only a short neck subtending the relatively small, globose cage-like apex readily distinguishes this species. There is an unmistakable similarity with Ceropegia bonafouxii, which has a western distribution, but the colouration and shape of the terminal 'cage' differ markedly.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: Vegetatively it is indistinguishable from C. fimbriata or C. zeyheri and it lacks the roughening of the stems found in C. ampliata. The broadly inflated corolla-tube and the very slender inner corona-lobes of C. ampliata are not at all similar to the same structures in C. namaquensis. In C. fimbriata the corolla-lobes are always very much broader towards their tips where they remain fused into an umbrella-like structure some distance above the corolla-tube. In C. zeyheri the corolla-lobes are much narrower than in C. fimbriata and almost equal the tube in length. They remain fused at their tips but also become distinctly broader towards their tips than in the middle. The outside of the corolla is usually also papillate. In C. namaquensis the corolla-lobes are not significantly widened towards their apices and they do not remain fused there either.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2003. Three new succulent species of Apocynaceae (Asclepiadoideae) from southern Africa. Kew Bull. 58(2): 427-435. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4120625] [All rights reserved]

description: The range in size of flowers is very considerable and this is presumed to be related to soil conditions and variable rainfall. At one time it seemed possible to maintain C. pumila N.E. Br. as a subspecies but the variability in size within the complex made this of very doubtful value. There appear to be no other close relatives.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: C. gariepensis has the same habit as C. oblanceolata and C. gracilifrondosa Dinter ex J.J.A.van der Walt, but differs from them mainly in the shape of the leaves, in the morphology of the flowers and in the type of exudate. All three of these taxa have trifoliolate leaves, but C. gariepensis and C. oblanceolata have simple leaves in addition. Trifoliolate leaves in C. gariepensis have the lamina on terminal leaflets oblanceolate or rarely cultrate with up to 11 teeth on each side of the margin, whereas the lamina in lateral leaflets is narrowly elliptic, oblanceolate or cultrate to broadly cultrate with up to nine teeth on each side of the margin. In C. oblanceolata the lamina on both terminal and lateral leaflets is always oblanceolate, with up to 45 and 38 teeth respectively on each side of the margin. In C. gracilifrondosa, the linear or cultrate leaflets, very variable in size and form, distiguish it from the other two taxa. The leaves of some specimens of C. gariepensis and C. gracilifrondosa resemble each other superficially. However, the leaves of C. gariepensis are broader than those of C. gracilifrondosa for corresponding length. In C. gariepensis the flowers are borne in much reduced or short cymes up to 3.0 mm in length, in C. oblanceolata in thyrses or cymes up to 13 mm long and in C. gracilifrondosa on cymes up to 50 mm long. The flowers of C. gariepensis have 4-8 stamens per flower, whereas those of C. oblanceolata and C. gracilifrondosa have four stamens only. Unlike C. oblanceolata and C. gracilifrondosa, the latex of C. gariepensis is milky-watery (not watery) and does not squirt when branches or branchlets are damaged or cut. When without leaves or flowers, C. gariepensis is virtually indistinguishable from C. gracilifrondosa with which it shares the same habitat. The only notable difference then between the two taxa, is the milky-watery exudate which does not squirt in C. gariepensis, as opposed to being copious and only watery in C. gracilifrondosa. Although they share the same habitat throughout the known range of C. gariepensis. C. gracilifrondosa is common and much more widespread. Some specimens of C. gariepensis could easily be mistaken for C. oblanceolata due to the similarity of the leaves. However, the geographical distribution of the two taxa differs markedly. C. gariepensis being restricted to the Gariep Centre of Endemism and C. oblanceolata to the northern Central Namib and the Kaokoveld Centre of Endemism (Van der Walt 1986). Herbarium specimens of C. dinteri and C. gariepensis with leaves only, could also be confused. However, the leaves of C. dinteri are ± twice as broad as those of C. Gariepensis for corresponding length.
