description: The habit of this species varies according to the conditions under which it is growing, the branches eventually becoming decumbent in very exposed situations. Under these conditions the peduncles are almost absent and extreme cases, where they cannot be distinguished any longer, have been recorded. In the eastern parts of the distribution area the stems are often thin and wiry-woody, while west of Oudtshoorn they are usually carnose.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The species is obviously close to A. villosa ssp. villosa as pointed out already in the original description: 'Nahe verwandt mit A. cuspidata Mev. und A. umbellata W. [synonyms of A. villosa], von beiden durch den Kelch, vollstandig kahle Petalen und die, die Antheren sogar etwas iiberragen sterilen Stamina gut versebieden'. The most conspicuous feature of A. acuta is the narrow, lanceolate, more or less purple calyx segments which much exceed the mature capsule in length with the upper half usually involute so that they appear sharply acute to cuspidate. The staminodes are comparatively short, and the anthers much shorter than in A. villosa. The leaves are often loosely appressed, exposing the more or less convex dorsal side. The seeds are comparatively small and somewhat flattened laterally. The two collections from the French. Hoek Mts (the type collection and! 4744) are less extreme with respect to calyx characters and approach the rather distinct race of A. villosa ssp. villosa occurring at high altitudes on Landdrostkop and Somerset Sneeuwkop. True intermediates seem to the lacking, however, and for the time being. A. acuta is apparently best regarded as a separate species.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: Affinities obscure; A. dahlgrenii is a geographically and systematically isolated species possibly related to the A. villosa complex. It has the habit of a compact, rounded shrublet with robust branches, rather large, flat, conspicuously, glandular-punctate leaves, and flowers in few-flowered, condensed, loosely involucrate corymbs. The calyx is large with characteristically shaped segments, the petals are pinkish on both sides, the anthers are small with a comparatively large gland, the style soon becomes erect, and the mature capsule is much exceeded by the expanded calyx. The whole plant is glabrous or nearly so.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: Although this species has quite small flowers it is often a distinct feature of the vegetation on the Gifberg, Cedarberg range and Skurfteberge, because of its deep purplish red leaves. Plants on the Knersvlakte are usually much more robust, and their leaves are recurved and usually flat on the ground as in plants from the mountains from the Gifberg to the Skurfteberge. On the lower slopes a very abrupt transition occurs between the forms with long and with short leaves, but it could not be conclusively shown whether this was due to hybridization or to a cline. The isolated population of plants on top of the Helsberg in the Richtersveld is in most characters similar to plants from the southern Karoo. These northern plants are puberulous to pubescent.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A. fragrens is a distinct species, easily recognizable by its long, completely glabrous leaves, umbellate inflorescences, long pedicels, short, obtuse calyx segments, emarginate petals, etc.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: A white-flowered form of this species occurs on Potberg and near Cape lnfanta.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Small plants of C. columella might be confused with the common C. elegans subsp. elegans, but the latter is usually much branched and the leaf apices are not adpressed. C. columella superficially resembles C. plegmatoides, but the latter has coarse, usually rounded papillae on the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: C. compacta is very similar to some forms of C. capitella but is distinguished by its distinct style and transversely oblong squamae.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A. multiflora is a distinct and rather invariable species recognized by its erect, slender, much-branched habit, small, oblong leaves, and numerous small flowers which tend to aggregate in loose synflorescences. The calyx is very short with obtuse segments (less than half as long as the mature capsule). Contrary to most species in the genus, the petals are sometimes pink on both sides. All floral structures such as petals, staminodes, and stamens are noticeably small. The closest relative is apparently A. coriacea which is also characterized by bracteoles attached close to the calyx, short, obtuse calyx segments, papillate but eglandular ovary, and protruding capsule. A. multiflora differs in its erect habit, smaller and more sparsely glandular-punctate leaves, and much smaller and more numerous flowers. It is apparently restricted to altitudes between 500 and 1500 feet, whereas A. coriacea is a plant of rather high altitudes (2000-6000 feet).
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: A. mundiifolia is apparently most closely related to A. fragrans, from which it differs chiefly by its smaller, above dark green, dorsally eglandular or almost eglandular leaves and few-flowered umbels.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: West of the Fish River, plants of this species are usually very robust and with erect branches whereas to the east plants become progressively smaller with decumbent branches. A complete range of intermediates is found on the lower Fish River valley, e.g. Tölken 3721.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: C. cotyledonis is usually recognized by its coarse recurved hairs on the leaves, and particularly by the fact that if marginal cilia are recognizable they are not arranged in a single row.Usually the plants are rather robust and have broad leaves (up to 35 mm broad) but particularly in the western parts of the Little Karoo they are rarely broader than 15 mm. In extreme cases the squamae are oblong. Plants from south-western South West Africa/Namibia have spreading to recurved hairs on the leaves, which enhances the robust appearance of the plants.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The species is rather uniform except for a few collections where in some characters it approaches A. rotundifalia. The closest relative is apparently A. gummifera from which it can be distinguished by its shorter leaves, smaller flowers, less gummy heads, presence of staminodes, and tuberculate ovary. Its confusion with A. cuspidata is apparently merely a nomenclatural mistake; the latter is a synonym of A. villosa and thus only distantly related to A. obtusata.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: The shape and size of the leaves as well as the size of the petals vary greatly with the availability of water. Under dry conditions the corolla lobes are short and bluntly acute.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The globular part-inflorescences of C. cultrata are not as dense as in other species in this section and in cultivated plants the individual flowers are often quite separate.West of Port Elizabeth plants tend to be erect and have glabrous leaves while plants from localities to the north-east or east tend to have shorter internodes and become gradually more hairy.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The two collections of spontaneous material are very similar. A. schlechteri can be recognized by its slender habit, completely eglandular leaves (at least superficially), and rather rich-flowered, sub-umbellate inflorescences with villous, brownish- violet pedicels and calyces. The minute bracteoles are attached to the base of the pedicels, and the flowers are comparatively small. The cultivated specimens are slightly larger and more robust. No doubt A. schlechteri is most closely related to A. lasiantha from which it differs in having eglandular leaves and smaller flowers as well as in several floral details; for instance, the petals are glabrous with an elliptic rather than broadly cordate limb, and the anthers are much smaller.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: A. uniflora is obviously close to A. villosa from which it can be distinguished by its relatively soft leaves with revolute margins, solitary flowers, large, leaf-like calyx segments, and smaller anthers. Specimens from the mainland tend on the average to have somewhat smaller flowers than Peninsula material but are otherwise similar.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: The range of variation found in this species includes a number of local variants which are distinguishable by the size and shape of the free leaf apex. In some plants the hydathodes (spots on leaves) are more prominent than in others, but in most plants they become more pronounced under adverse conditions.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Usually ssp. biseriata is reasonably distinct and characterized by slender habit, small, elliptic to oblong, obtuse leaves, and pedicellate flowers with short and broad calyx segments.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: This plant is never common and rather difficult to find because it grow among much-branched karroid shrublets. By the time the plant is flowering the leaves on the erect branches have fallen off.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Typical specimens are found in the Steenbras and Gordon's Bay area. These are characterized by short and broad, more or less obtuse, conspicuously glandular-punctate leaves, subsessile, often solitary flowers, broad calyx segments, and nearly orbicular petal limbs. In leaf-shape ssp. orbicularis shows a certain similarity to ssp. sonderi, occurring in the southern half of the Cape Peninsula on the opposite side of False Bay.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: Typical specimens of ssp. sonderi such as found, for instance on Smitswinkel Flats, above Simonstown, in Fish Hock Valley, and also at low altitudes near Muizenherg, can easily he recognized by their broad, roundish leaves with conspicuous glandular dots beneath, large pedicellate flowers, and reddish, usually pilose calyces. There is considerable variation in leaf shape, however, and occasional specimens with longer and more acute leaves are also found in the above-mentioned areas.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: In South Africa the typical variety, var. gummifera occurs; specimens from a restricted area in Zambia have been described as var. cerifera (De Wilde, l.c. p. 264).
bibliographicCitation: De Wilde, WJJO. 1976. Passifloraceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 104-128. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A little known species which has been recorded from two centres in the Cape Province, near Vanrhynsdorp and between Matjiesfontein and Caledon. At present the two forms can be distinguished by the very strongly elongating pedicels and the less abruptly constricted squamae in the northern form. The species is, however, so rarely collected that one would not like to draw conclusions from it, especially as intermediate forms could occur on the rather poorly collected eastern slopes of the south-western Cape mountains.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The species was recently reinstated by Friedrich. The taxon should perhaps rather be placed at subspecific level under C. natans, as the differences between the two varieties of the latter species are greater than those between C. natans and the present species.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The flowers resemble those of A. glauca. The mostly early deciduous leaves often much resemble the simple leaves of A. fruticosa subsp. simplicifolia.
bibliographicCitation: De Wilde, WJJO. 1976. Passifloraceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 104-128. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished by the broad leaves, crowded flowers and the fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African species of Aizoaceae: I. Adenogramma and Polpoda. J. S. African Bot. 21: 83-95. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf21unse] [CC BY]

description: The contorted aestivation of the petals of this species is unusual in this section but when one notices that the petals are also asymmetrical, it becomes clear that it must be a pollination syndrome analogous to the Sphaeritis type.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Variable in size. The basal leaves wither before fruiting time. Much like A. glomerata and not easily distinguished in the absence of fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African species of Aizoaceae: I. Adenogramma and Polpoda. J. S. African Bot. 21: 83-95. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf21unse] [CC BY]

description: A very variable species, particularly in the shape and size of the leaves. Near Bredasdorp the flowers tend to be yellow and each ovary contains 6-8(-10) ovules while westwards the flowers tend to be cream or white with each ovary containing 14-22 ovules. Between these extremes a range of intermediates occurs.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The plants described as A. dregeana only differ in having larger flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African species of Aizoaceae: I. Adenogramma and Polpoda. J. S. African Bot. 21: 83-95. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf21unse] [CC BY]

description: Very distinctive in habit and leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African species of Aizoaceae: I. Adenogramma and Polpoda. J. S. African Bot. 21: 83-95. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf21unse] [CC BY]

description: This species had previously been included in C. vaillantii but the papillate sculpturing of the seed membrane distinguishes it well. The brood buds mentioned by Friedrich have only been observed on a few specimens and it has not been established whether they occur generally in this species or whether they are only induced by extreme conditions.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Although C. glomerata is usually easily distinguished by its dense inflorescences and papillae on the whole plant, including the characteristic apices of the petals, some plants are completely glabrous while others, particularly shade plants, have loosely pedicellate flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: This species, which is very similar to C. depressa, is known only from one collection, and until live material of the species has been found it cannot be ascertained whether the lateral appendage found consistently on the styles is a functional stigma.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A complete range from plants with glabrous leaves, to those covered with fine hairs and coarse rounded papillae can be observed from the south to the north. The form with coarse rounded papillae usually has few branches, mainly from the base, whlle the glabrous and hairy forms tend to be more branched. Depauperate individuals of the latter two forms can only be distinguished from C. elegans by their stiff, scarcely shrivelled old leaves, a character whlch is usually not observed in plants in cultivation. Similar depauperate forms with rounded papillae on the leaves, which were described as C. bakeri, approach the pointed-leaved form of C. deceptor, previously known as C. cornuta, from the Knersvlakte. However, apart from the geographic separation, C. grisea is distinguished by its pointed hair-like trichomes on the peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The most common species in Namaqualand which shows some local variation in the length of the stems and the amount of branching, the size and shape of the leaves and the number and intensity of purple markings thereon. It is a very robust plant with flat leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The leaves vary markedly in shape and size and the colour of the flowers also often varies from one locality to the other.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Characteristic of this species are the very much swollen calyx apices and the two pairs of leaves below the inflorescence which are usually the largest and have a very short internode between them.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A very delicate plant with leaves readily dropping when touched.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: C. inanis has never been found together with C. natans which grows in very similar habitats. The former is distinguished by its leaves being broader towards the base, and in vigorous plants more than one flower may occur in the axil of a leaf. Both plants often have perennial rhizomes growing in mud.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The leaves of this species are closely adpressed to one another and recurved under dry conditions and in young plants, whereas they are erect and cup-shaped under humid conditions and usually also when the plants are flowering. This species and C. socialis are the only species with reflexed styles.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A delicate plant somewhat like A. nanus but with extensively branched base forming mats up to 0.15 m in diameter.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The delimitation of the species and subspecific taxa is based on that of R. Fernandes but var. denticulata is raised to subspecific level. The three subspecies distinguished here were found to be ecologically and/or geographically isolated. The complex is not fully understood and in need of further detailed research and field observations with respect to lower subspecific categories as proposed by R. Fernandes.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Three subspecies need further research.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Thunberg's type specimen of Adromischus (Cotyledon) mammillaris was never re-investigated and consequently this name was misapplied for a very long time to this common plant. The type of subsp. marlothii is from an unusual specimen with subpetiolate leaves. Generally the plants of this taxon become more slender and prostrate eastwards. The number of the type collection of subsp. marlothii has previously been cited as Marloth 3861 cmstead of 2520.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: This species resembles C. cultrata superficially and has often been confused with it, but C. cultrata has an elongated inflorescence, differently shaped petals and different flowering times.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: C. macowaniana shows a great range of variation in the shape and size of the leaves, but even the plants may vary from shrubs up to 1.2 m to less than 0.2 m high. The latter form, which occurs in the area between Eksteenfontein (Richtersveld, Cape Province) and Port Nolloth, does not become much taller under cultivation, yet a range of intermediates was observed in the vicinity of Eksteenfontein. This miniature form is, however, easily distinguished from C. brevifolia subsp. psammophila and C. nudicaulis var. herrei by its sharply pointed leaves and rounded often almost circular sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species and although the flowers resemble superficially those of A. caryophyllaceus, the square squamae and the club-shaped trichomes, which are restricted to the area around the throat, indicate that A. leucophyllus should not be placed into the section Brevipedunculati.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The apex of the corolla lobes is the ellipsoid dorsal appendage, now in a terminal position, while the apices of the corolla lobes on the inside of this fleshy structure are no longer visible. This is similar to the structure of the corolla lobes in C. mesembryanthoides.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Only C. montana Thunb. subsp. quadrangularis in EC.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A rather rare plant with convex leaves in the south which tend to become very flat northwards in southwestern South West Africa/Namibia.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The leaves are very variable in their size, shape and surface texture. Many local forms exist but when a wide range is grown under similar conditions, a range of intermediates can be found. Pilbeam reinstated a number of names at the level of forma in order to retain a handle on these extreme forms for succulent collections. It is difficult, however, to accept his decision to maintain var. antidorcadum for plants with verrucose leaves and var. immaculatus only for plants with smooth leaves (pers. comm.) when this does not allow for changes due to ecological conditions. This division is not only completely artificial but might also prove to be ill-founded as it is not known whether the type of var. immaculatus had smooth leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A. phillipsiae is the only species in the genus which produces pendulous red flowers which seem to simulate the pollination syndrome of species of Cotyledon.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Three varieties in EC with only one endemic: C. muscosa L. var. polpodacea (Eckl. & Zeyh.) G.D.Rowley.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very delicate herb which may be confused with forms of C. dentata but C. nemorosa is distinguished by its grey-green leaves and its shallowly cup-shaped flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The shape and size of the leaves of this species are very variable and a number of local forms can be recognized. This is the most common species in the Little Karoo and adjoining areas and is easily distinguished from all other species by the curved apices of the buds.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A. trigynus is distinguished from A. umbraticola (below) and A. schuldtianus by the leaves which are remarkably uniform in shape and size on the same plant, usually convex above and with a horny margin right around them.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Although it is difficult to locate good key characters to separate this species from Acrolophia capensis and A. lamellata, it is clearly distinct by the simple, untidy inflorescence, with the long, slender, spreading pedicels, by the colour of the sepals, and by the texture of the perianth parts.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The leaves are usually narrowly oblong and the inflorescence is a much branched thyrse, but plants growing under adverse conditions will often produce short obovate leaves and a spike-like inflorescence. Local variation has been recorded in the shape and size of the squamae and the dorsal appendage on the petals as well as the presence or absence of marginal cilia on the sepals. Runners are usually only produced under favourable conditions, but some populations were observed where they never seem to be formed. This feature could not be linked with any other character nor with known distribution patterns.The species is unusual in this section in that the petals do not immediately recurve, whereas in others, they do. Seen side by side, such plants may appear to belong to different species. Plants from near Montagu usually have papillose ovaries, but unlike those found in C. pseudohemisphaerica, the papillae are not pointed.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The long, often woody adventitious roots (stilt roots) from the lower branches are an unusual feature of the species. They can be up to 0.2 m long before branching, which occurs when they touch the soil surface. Other species in this section, however, occasionally have shorter adventitious roots.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Similar to C. tenuicaulis, C. papillosa and C. expansa but differing in habit and habitat and especially in its distinctly papillose seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: C. alsinoides was reinstated as a separate species by Wickens & Bywater and later Wickens (pers. comm.) suggested that C. brachypetala should also be reinstated. In the interest of stability of names the earlier concepts are here maintained until the entire complex can be re-evaluated.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A. glochidiata can normally be distinguished even in the vegetative state from A. africana, its basal leaves being greyish, especially beneath, on account of the dense indumentum, not dark green as in the latter species. The inflorescence is also normally more branched. However, the wingless, glochidiate nutlets afford the easiest character for distinguishing the two species.
bibliographicCitation: Mill, RR. 1986. A revision of the genus Afrotysonia Rauschert (Boraginaceae). Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 43(3): 467-475. [CC BY-SA]

description: Three varieties endemic to EC: C. perfoliata L. var. coccinea (Sweet) G.D.Rowley, C. perfoliata L. var. minor (Haw.) G.D.Rowley, C. perfoliata L. var. perfoliata.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very variable species with leaves showing a range from ovate to lanceolate, with or without marginal cilia and with a more or less distinctly coloured horny margin. There is a form from the mountains along the Langkloof in which the length of the inflorescence may vary from very elongated to almost rounded, or very shortened and delicate. In extreme forms the whole plant is smaller and the leaves are fused almost in a ring around the branches. The smaller flowers and adpressed bracts at the base of the inflorescence do not allow confusion with similar vegetative features of some forms of C. rupestris.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Endemic to EC: C. perforata Thunb subsp. kougaensis Van Jaarsv. & A.E.van Wyk.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is very difficult to distinguish on herbarium material from Acrolophia cochlearis.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The affinity is with A. phillipsii Dummer but with the leaves convex above except for a furrow, and the ovary being glabrous.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1950. A revision of Agathosma. J. S. African Bot. 16: 55-177. [CC BY]

description: Plants from localities near Paarl and Stellenbosch are placed in this species by the sum of their distinguishing characters in spite of the presence of two lateral points on the trichomes, a feature characteristic of C. pustulata.Desfontaines (Tabl. Bot. edn 2, 187; 1815) based Crassula calycina, nom. nud. on a specimen of C. pruinosa, judging by a specimen in his herbarium. De Candolle included in the protologue of Dasystemon calycina an illustration of C. glomerata in addition to characters taken from a fragmentary specimen of C. pruinosa in his herbarium.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The leaves, when crushed, have a delightful smell similar to that of lemon-scented verbena and it was noted that the upper parts of the leaves were frequented by a small globose bug. There were, however, no small insects in the flowers but as the flowers are large and whitish in colour as well as being nectariferous, they are probably pollinated by some large insect, possibly moths at night. The plant inhabits an ecological niche similar to that of the more widely dispersed plant Teedia pubescens Burch. which bears fruits that are no doubt distributed by birds. In contrast, the seeds of this Agathosma are, as is usual in the genus, expelled by a catapult mechanism when ripe and must fall to the ground at the base of the cliff on which the plant is growing. As no plants are to be found on the ground below and as the seed has the usual elaiosomes, attractive to ants, one can only suppose that the seed is transported by some route up the cliff again to be lodged by the ants in crevices in the rocks. At the time when this plant was collected (1975) it was not realized that all the species in several genera of the Diosmeae were myrmecochorous and so no attempt was made to verify this supposition.

description: B.L. Burtt has observed of A gracilis and A longifolia: 'It has become increasingly clear that differences in bract shape are unreliable specific characters, and the limits between these species and their various varieties and subspecies recognised by Weimarck are quite unclear'. He has done signal service in so selecting lectotypes that A longifolia and A gracilis var. major are now homotypic. As anyone who has attempted to name tropical African Alepidea will recognise, both this latest revision by Weimarck and the account by H. Wolff are virtually useless. There is no hesitation in sinking all the subspecies of A longifolia recognised by Weimarck which occur in East Africa. A massaica has already been placed as a synonym of A longifolia by Agnew, and I entirely agree here. Even specialists have been unable to agree on determinations. A notable specimen at Kew is Lynes Dd139 (Njombe, Tanzania) which has several outer leaves narrowly cordate or truncate at the base. Although named as A longifolia subsp. swynnertonii by Weimarck on a determinavit slip at the top of the sheet, it also bears a Weimarck! alongside Norman's determination as A massaica at the bottom. Cited by Weimarck as subsp. swynnertonii in his revision, it is nevertheless to my eyes indistinguishable from other material named by him as massaica. A peduncularis was keyed out from A longifolia by Weimarck as having an involucre 20-30 mm in diameter and 10-15 involucral bracts (involucre 10-15 mm with 10 involucral bracts in longifolia). It is true that much Ethiopian material has a large involucre with long, taperingbracts; but material from Tanzania (e.g. Richards 9767 from the Poroto Mts.) is similar and grades into material from the same area with smaller, shorter bracts. Similarly, plants with smaller, shorter bracts occur in Ethiopia. It was found that bract number to 8-11 in Ethiopia as elsewhere, and have never seen as many as 15 bracts in a plant of this group. Of Wolffs fruit character ('ubique granulato-rugulosus' in A fischeri and 'depresso-squamulosus' in A peduncularis. It should be noted, too, that using Wolffs key the lectotype of A longifolia unquestionably comes straight out to A peduncularis.

description: Allocassine is an isolated monotypic genus not closely related to other southern African Celastraceae. It is maintained separately from the other Cassinoideae mainly on account of its flower, pollen, fruit and seed morphology, wood anatomy and bark structure. Its large elongated fruit and seed is particularly distinctive. Diagnostic characters for Allocassine include: pollen tectum perforate to smooth with conspicuous apertural duplication; leaf epidermis with sinuous anticlinal cell walls and depressions in cuticular flanges; flowers sessile; sepals coriaceous; fruit ellipsoid with relatively thin leathery pericarp, cell walls thick and cutinised; seed ellipsoid with thick black seed-coat; wood rays consisting of predominantly upright cells; bark with fibres, periderm persistent with no sequential periderm formation, hence phellem thick and well developed and rhytidome absent.

description: Cynoglossum obtusicalyx is characterized by a deeply lobed calyx, the lobes being oblong, with the apices broadly obtuse to truncate. Plants are hairy in all parts, the indumentum consisting of spreading and erect, thin unicellular hairs. The inflorescences are not as floriferous as in other members of the genus and the flowers are relatively large. Fornices are present in the throat of the corolla tube, with the stamens subsessile and situated below them. Nutlets of C. obtusicalyx are evenly covered with glochidia. The glochidia are well spaced, except along the margins of the nutlets where they are more densely arranged. The nutlets form animal-dispersed burrs. The new species appears to be most closely related to C. austroafricanum, showing similarity in fruit and calyx structure. The two species differ, however, in flower size and colour. The flowers of C. obtusicalyx are blue to white, with the corolla 5-7 mm long, whereas those of C. austroafricanum are bright blue to purple, with the corolla 2.75-4.25 mm long. The fruit stalks of C. austroafricanum are relatively short (usually < 5 mm), whereas those of C. obtusicalyx are relatively long (usually > 8 mm) and have a tendency to curve. With its few-flowered inflorescences and large, pedicellate flowers, C. obtusicalyx is quite different from C. lanceolatum, a species with characteristically divaricately bifid inflorescences with numerous, small, sessile or very shortly pedicellate flowers. The new species cannot be mistaken for C. hispidum, a species with the fruiting stalks distinctly curved and nutlets with glochidia swollen at the base. C. alticola Hilliard & B.L.Burtt has thick swollen glochidia, covering the whole nutlet and is therefore quite different from C. obtusicalyx. However, in leaf and floral characters, this species appears to be a close ally of C. obtusicalyx. In the case of C. coeruleum var. mannii, C. spelaeum and C. amabile, the glochidia are concentrated at the margins of the nutlets and joined at their bases.

description: Cysticapnos cracca is recognized by its lanceolate, blade-like capsules, 10-12 x 2-3 mm, containing numerous seeds in two peripheral rows. The pericarp dehisces from the base, with the two halves peeling away but remaining attached in the distal half. In general form and dehiscence they are very similar to those of C. pruinosa, but the latter has larger, ± quadrate capsules, 15-17 mm long, that are distinctly flexed upwards in the distal half, with obscurely scalloped margins. The racemes in C. cracca are almost invariably sessile, with flowers smaller than those of C. pruinosa (6.0-6.5 mm vs 7-8 mm) and generally fewer per raceme (mostly up to 15 vs more than 15). Vegetatively C. cracca is readily distinguished from C. pruinosa by its annual habit, less finely divided leaves, and yellow vs clear sap. Cysticapnos cracca is most likely to be confused with C. vesicaria, with which it co-occurs in parts of the southwestern Cape. Although typically smaller and more compact than C. vesicaria, C. cracca is otherwise almost indistinguishable in foliage, both species having broadly obovate, deeply 2- or 3-lobed ultimate leaf segments. The sap of C. cracca, however, is distinctly yellow, staining the skin bright orange, whereas that of C. vesicaria is clear. The two species are readily distinguished in flower and fruit, C. cracca having smaller, less prominently winged flowers and flattened, non-inflated capsules. Although C. cracca is typically found in heavier, clay soils, with C. vesicaria favouring deep coastal sands and gritty granite-derived soils, the two species have been recorded growing together in several places throughout their area of sympatry.

description: This species is similar to Anginon fruticosum but differs in the lateral racemes which terminate in simple umbels (compound in A. fruticosum) and also in the unbranched resin ducts of the petals (branched in A. fruticosum). description: The distribution overlaps with several other species. However, the large, numerous roots are characteristic and distinguish the species from A. burttii and A. nuda. description: It is very similar to A. grandiflora in distribution and leaf form but differs in having glabrous leaves; also, a single root is usually formed each year and the fruits are heteromorphic. It tends to be a smaller and less robust plant. The roots of A. nuda and A. burttii have a distinct sclerenchyma layer below the periderm; this is absent from all other species. Specimens from the eastern part of the distribution (Bredasdorp to Still Bay) differ from the typical form in the larger involucral and involucellar bracts, slightly larger fruits which tend to have sharp wings (tapering as seen in transverse section) rather than blunt-tipped as in the typical A. nuda. The leaves appear to be quite different; they are deeply dissected while the terminal segments are sparsely and coarsely dentate as opposed to the much broader segments with the more numerous shallower dentations of the typical A. nuda. Anatomically, the fruits appear almost identical. This form of the species needs to be investigated in more detail in future studies since it may possibly be a distinct taxon. The fact that this plant occurs on limestone soils is a further indication that it may differ genetically from the typical A. nuda but we find no distinct discontinuities to justify formal recognition of it.

description: D. holopetalus Turcz., united by Burtt Davy with D. aliens Ait., appears to lie between that species and D. bolusii Burtt Davy. It resembles D. bolusii in habit, particularly in the stout flowering stems and freely branched inflorescence and in the shape of the calyx-bracts, but is distinguished from it by the broader leaves, longer bracts at the base of the flowering stems, and smaller flowers with more or less entire, not fimbriate petals. The size of the flower, and the entire petals, link D. holopetalus with D. albens. In floral characters D. holopetalus is also similar to D. kamisbergensis (a plant still imperfectly known) from Little Namaqualand; D. kamisbergensis appears, however, to be much more slender in habit, to have scabrid stems and broader, less acuminate calyx-bracts. Turczaninow cited two collectings with the original description of D. holopetalus-Zeyher 78 and Ecklon & Zeyher 247. As Burtt Davy has pointed out, the Kew sheet of Ecklon & Zeyher 246 is a better match with Zeyher 78 and the original description than is Ecklon & Zeyher 247, which has fimbriate not entire or crenulate petals and a longer calyx. Ecklon & Zeyher 246 at Kew belongs either to D. bolusii or to D. holopetalus - probably the latter. Burtt Davy has suggested that the labels on the Kew sheets of Ecklon & Zeyher 246 & 247 have been wrongly assigned to the specimens. Transposing the labels as they now appear would provide the sheet of D. holopetalus with the locality of no. 247, Karreebergen Clanwilliam (now Van Rhyn’s Dorp Distr.), considerably further north than the other (Tulbagh and Malmesbury) localities.

description: Several features distinguish D. austromontana from the closely related Diascia barberae. Most obvious is the difference in the length of the spurs, particularly in relation to the size of the corolla limb. The difference between the two species is even more striking if the ratio of spur length to corolla limb length is considered. The other main distinction between D. austromontana and D. barberae is the shape and orientation of the pistils and filaments. The style of D. barberae curves upward in all of the populations In D. barberae the stigma is always surrouded by the coherent anthers, but in D. austromontana the style and stigma always emerge from the stamens without passing between the coherent anthers The filaments of D. austromontana are slightly longer than those of D. barberae with the morphologically lower one more curved. Also, the angle of the filaments in relation to the boss of the invaginated corolla tube is greater (155° vs. 110°) in D. austromontana than in D. barberae.

description: Diascia bicolor is very similar to D. cuneata in vegetative, capsule and seed morphology and has occasionally been confused with that species. However, the flowers are much larger than those of D. cuneata with an average limb length of ca. 16-18 mm vs. ca. 8-9 mm, and the ranges in limb length between the two species do not overlap. Unlike D. cuneata, the flowers of D. bicolor (in all but one population) possess well-developed sacs (52=1.7 mm) at the base of the upper corolla lobes that ascend behind the lobes and contain oil-secreting trichomes. While D. cuneata sometimes has a shallow depression in the corolla tube below each corolla lobe, these depressions are rarely more than 0.5 mm deep and if trichomes are present, they are only at the entrance to the sacs, not well inside them. Some plants in a population at the north-eastern range of D. bicolor also lack properly developed spurs, but their flowers are typical of D. bicolor in every other respect. The colour markings in the corolla tube also differ between D. bicolor and D. cuneata. In D. cuneata the tube below the upper and lateral corolla lobes is greenish-yellow, but in D. bicolor, only the boss and the sides of the sac openings are greenish-yellow, while the rest of that region is dark purple. Diascia bicolor is most easily confused with D. decipiens which has flowers of a similar size and colour pattern (yellow with a purple centre) and which occupies similar karroid habitats. It differs from that species in having corolla lobes that are yellow, not pale orange-yellow, stamens that project forwards, not upwards, trichomes that are long (ca. 1 mm) and yellow, not short (ca. 0.60 mm) and purple, a style that is more or less straight rather than curved upward, and sacs projecting upwards behind the upper corolla lobes rather than diverging and folding over at the tips.
