description: The material from Zimbabwe is quite disjunct from the main distribution. Most collections from Zimbabwe have white flowers, very conspicuosly glossy leaves and sericeous bract-indumentum. However, blue-flowered specimens have been collected from the same localities as white-flowered and the other characters are variable in South Africa. I have decided not to treat this form as a separate taxon. A handful of collections, all from the Pietersburg area of South Africa, are somewhat intermediate between B. subvolubilis and B. inaequalis. They show varying combinations of characters from the two, e.g. bract-and sepal-indumentum of B. subvolubilis combined with sepal-shape of B. inaequalis (Strey & Schlieben 8583, Codd 2967) or leaf-indumentum of B. subvolubilis combined with bract-and sepal-indumentum and sepal-shape of B. inaequalis (Leeman 60). Whether these forms are a result of repeated hybridisation or are merely extreme forms of B. subvolubilis remains to be studied in natural populations, but in their general 'gestalt' they are so much more like B. subvolubilis that I prefer to keep them here.

description: Alopecurus = a fox's tail; referring to the appearance of the leafy branches. E. alopecurus is easily recognized by its long spike-like inflorescence. Of the species of Erica occurring in the summer rainfall area there is none that in any way resembles this species. There is, however, a species, E. hippurus Salter, from the South-western Cape that is superficially similar to it. E. hippurus is endemic to the small Paardeberg feature just south of Malmesbury. E. alopecurus is widespread in its distribution, occurring on the Boschberg in the Somerset East District of the eastern Cape along the Drakensberg to the Soutpansberg in the northern Transvaal. Like several other Erica species occurring in this region it grows in mountainous or rocky country along streams frequently in deep kloofs. In Flora Capensis Guthrie & Bolus describe the var. glabrifiora from the Transvaal. The pubescence of the corolla is a variable character, specimens with pubescent and glabrous corollas occurring in the same areas.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This remarkable new species is unlike any other species in the genus on account of having, in the mature flowers, almost free corolla lobes which are spreading and then reflexed, with the alternate stamens reflexed between these lobes, and an exserted gynoecium. However, the species appears to be allied to species in the section Ceramia because of its habit, habitat preference and small pink flowers and open-backed leaves. In particular it superficially resembles species such as E. oligantha and E. planifolia L., but is different in a number of unique characters. The possession of almost free corolla lobes is very rare in the subfamily Ericoideae. It occurs in a few schizopetalous cultivars of European heathers. In southern Africa only four species share such a divided corolla, i.e. Erica lanuginosa Andr., E. occulta E.G.H. Oliver and E. bodkinii Guth. & Bol., but not to the same extent as in E. amicorum. Also they do not have the lobes reflexed in the mature flowers. This condition renders the flowers unique in that the complete androecium and gynoecium are exserted, thus giving the impression of an erica flower in which the corolla has been eaten away by some insect. The mature flower is also unique in having those stamens alternating with the corolla lobes totally reflexed between the lobes. The stamens are also rather unusual in being joined together at the base into a thickened collar. Fused or partially fused stamens are now no longer rare in the genus Erica because of the recent inclusion of the genus Philippia into Erica.Another striking feature of E. amicorum is the arrangement of the flowers which can be borne in a variety of ways on the branches from simple 1-3-nate terminal florescences to 1-flowered florescences on lateral absolute brachyblasts. These may then all be aggregated together into a loose synflorescence on a lateral branch. When the main branches are long, up to 1 m, they bear numerous lateral branches which themselves bear various combinations of florescences. In some cases the simple 3-flowered terminal florescence can look very similar to a terminal synflorescence. Examination of a florescence will show that flowers alternating with the leaves belong to a simple florescence whereas those opposite the leaves are terminal on absolute brachyblasts.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 1990. New species of Erica (Ericaceae) from the Cape Province. Bothalia 20(1&2): 41-48. [CC BY]

description: Erica anguliger is characterized by the accrescent calyx which is very variable in shape from obconic to tubular, and the 1-locular 1-ovulate ovary (G1/1). The fruiting calyx does not become deeply furrowed as in E. phaeocarpa or E. inflaticalyx and does not include the partly attached bracteoles as in E. inaequalis or E. kammanassiae. The species is clearly allied to the others in this group.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Leaves 4-nate; corolla hairy with a distinct swelling at the base; bract and bracteoles small, remote; anthers well exerted, muticous, long and narrow; sparse hairs on filaments and style; pedicel relatively long, 10-15 mm, with small, sticky, red glands; ovary densely hairy, cylindrical; leaves with very few sclereids. E. annalis could be related to several long-tubed species that occur in the region-E. wendlandiana Klotzsch, E. densifolia Willd. and E. abelii E.G.H.Oliv. and to a lesser extent E. maximilianii Bolus. The first three species have the narrow, elongated anthers which are included to slightly manifest, but these are appendiculate, they have the narrow cylindrical ovary but all of them are glabrous, and the hairy corolla. E. wendlandiana has the hairy filaments and style which can be present in E. densifolia but these are lacking in E. abelii. E. abelii differs in having a long bract and bracteoles which are approximate to the calyx, not small and remote. All three species differ from E. annalis in having 3-nate leaves and no similar basal swelling of the corolla. E. densifolia has spike-like synflorescences on the main stems. E. wendlandiana is remarkable in the genus for the large swelling at the base of the style and E. maximilianii differs in having a glabrous corolla and a glabrous, broadly obovoid ovary.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2002. Six new species and one new subspecies of Erica (Ericaceae) from Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 32(2): 167-180. [CC BY]

description: The nearest species to E. annectens is E. pinea Thunb. which, however, does not grow on the Cape Peninsula. Both species are very floriferous and striking when in full bloom. In the section Pleurocallis, E. annectens is unusual in possessing terminal or axillary flowers, a character that could equally place it in Evanthe.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica anomala is clearly allied to E. caespitosa, which may be found growing in the same area, but its spreading leaves and the aggregation of the glomerules of flowers into a pseudospike give it a different facies. The leaves are also larger and have marginal glands, not cilia. Florally the most striking difference in older specimens is the way the anthers are held together and are pushed up by the developing capsule so that they might seem to be exserted, but by the time this position is reached the filaments have been ruptured.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XI. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 227-260. [CC BY-SA]

description: Erica arachnocalyx is easily recognized by the dull-coloured flowers with stout, gland-tipped hairs particularly on the 4-partite calyx, four to eight stamens, the ovary mostly glabrous and the capitate enlarged stigma. The species is clearly allied to E. cereris, which occurs not far to the south and differs in the softer eglandular long calyx hairs and generally more stamens, which are always spurred.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: E. atrovinosa is a distinct species but bears a number of characters in common with E. inflata. It differs from the latter in having a less bushy habit, more crowded leaves which are terete and tremulous, and anthers with large pouched filaments and dark thick scabrid awns. Because of its unusual colour and abundance of flowers, E. atrovinosa is worth cultivating. The species is so rare it is even imperative that it should be brought into cultivation.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: In leaf character this species quite closely resembles Olea africana. Its leaves are very much the same shape and size and vary more or less to the same extent in these features. The lower surface has the same lepidote scales, only more plentifully, and the loops of the anastomosing veins run just within the margin as in those of Olea africana, but they are more prominent and obvious in Buddleia saligna. If the inflorescence is present these plants are easily distinguished for, besides the family differences in the flowers, B. saligna has a large terminal panicle with innumerable small flowers whereas in the Olea the panicles are axillary with fewer and larger flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Loganiaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 134-171. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica axillaris is characterized by its markedly funnel-shaped style/stigma complex with no distinct separate style and usually marked upper and lower halves of the fruit being irregularly wrinkled below and longitudinally ridged or angled above. The eight stamens vary in their fusion with almost free filaments to completely joined sometimes in the same collection. The ovary is mostly 2-locular, but 3- to 4-locular conditions can be found. In nearly all specimens there is one ovule per locule, but a few individual plants of some collections have shown a few flowers with two ovules.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: In leaf character this species resembles B. corrugata.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Loganiaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 134-171. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The short, fat leaves, which are wide-spreading and even recurved, give this species its distinctive appearance. The plants are generally small but always erect and covered with groups of 3 flowers. The grouping and arrangement of the flowers in 3-nate heads is very similar to that in the three species belonging to the section Amphodea. In many respects it resembles E. sexfaria Ait. but may be distinguished by its leaves. In its own section it may be mistaken when growing among low shrubs for E. placentae flora but on closer examination will be found to be quite different, especially in the leaves and corolla shape. In the flowers the corolla is pale pink and turns brown soon after opening. The sepals and bracts, which are white at first, gradually turn pink and even red with age and remain thus for quite a time after the corolla has faded.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica benthamiana is characterized by a 4-lobed slightly cartilagineous calyx, 2-lobed corolla and head-like synflorescences. It is easily distinguishable from E. labialis which has a 2-lobed corolla by the complex structure of its synflorescences and the constantly 4-lobed calyx. In the inflorescence character it is very similar to the following species, E. williamsiorum, but is distinguishable by its bract being non-recaulescent and calyx constantly 4-lobed without any sulcus or any groove opposite the lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Very near to the more glabrous forms of E. curviflora, of which it might, perhaps, he regarded as a variety. The angular attachment of the anther to the filament is, however, more marked than in any specimens of that which we have seen.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica blaerioides is closely related to Erica chionodes and E. oreotragus. It has spike-like synflorescences similar to those of E. chionodes, but differs in these being looser and much shorter, in having longer sepals, a differently shaped corolla which is more sparsely hairy with longer hairs, differently shaped ovary, stamens in a lower position in the corolla and very different seeds. It is also allied in many respects to E. oreotragus, but differs in the form of its inflorescence which is spike-like and not umbel-like, and by its subequal bract and bracteoles.This new species is divided into two subspecies on a number of characters, which show slight disjunctions- stamen number, size of the leaf sulcus, hairiness of the bract, bracteoles and sepals, and size of the sepals and anther appendages. The two taxa are allopatric. The type of the species and typical subspecies has been chosen from among the field collections made by the first author in the eastern populations.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2001. Five new species of Erica (Ericaceae) from the Swartberg Range, Western Cape, South Africa, and a no. Bothalia 31(1&2): 155-165. [CC BY]

description: E. bodkinii and E. grisbrookii have been placed together to show how two superficially similar species may easily be distinguished on closer examination. It will be seen that the major differences lie in the details of the anthers and in the nature and arrangement of the leaves. The soft delicate texture of the hairy flowers of E. bodkinii and the hard waxy texture of the smooth ones of E. grisbrookii; the lax arrangement of the flowers and the rigid close-set inflorescence borne on elongated branches in E. grisbrookii. E. grisbrookii tends to be found only among rocks on outcrops while E. bodkinii favours moist open slopes away from the rocks.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica bokkeveldia is characterized by a wide-open obconic pink corolla, the broadly orbicular scarious pink calyx-lobes, eight free stamens with long-spurred bilobed anthers and a 2-locular, 1-ovulate ovary (G2/1).
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: The four free stamens with broad free filaments and large pore, and the long distinct thin style serve to distinguish this new species. It also has a 1-locular, 1-ovulate ovary (G1/1) with only a few flowers having the 2-locular condition. This produces an indehiscent fruit with the mesocarp thickened and lignified whereas the endocarp is fairly thin and only slightly lignified as is the thin testa.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: This obscure species, quite distinct from any other, does not fit very well into any of the sections. Bentham placed it, with doubt, in § Polyodon, and it might almost equally well go into § Pyronium, Its spreading open-backed leaves, its struggling habit, and general viscidity, induce us to place it here [§ Ceramia].
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica bredasiana is very distinctive in the genus because of the ovary with its thickened walls, columella and septa. These become thicker and lignified in the fruiting stage. It is also characterized by completely fused filaments and partially fused anthers with very large pores and an internal hole connecting the two thecae, and by infrafoliar ridges which are very noticeable in the bark stage as greyish white, longitudinal, subfoliar flakes. The style is distinct from the stigma complex and the ovary and is as long as the ovary.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is readily distinguished by its tightly packed heads of creamy-white flowers. Further details that characterize it are the almost linear bracts and sepals and the conspicuous exserted anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: E. bruniades is most closely allied to E. villosa Wendl. which occurs at Hermanus, but may be distinguished by its broader sepals and finer denser hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica burchelliana is characterized by the multi-stemmed resprouting habit, fully recaulescent bract and bracteoles, large cyathiform to peltate stigma and thin papery pericarp with thick hard reticulate testa.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Coppice shoots of this species produce straight thorns up to 1 cm long and lanceolate leaves, truncate at the base and almost sessile. They can be distinguished from those of C. fascicularis by their white hairs and by the leaves which have crisped margins and are longer than 3 cm in C. brassii.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1970. Capparis, Fl. S. Africa 13: 144-150. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Material without flowers and fruits can easily be distinguished from that of C. sepiaria by the yellow tomentum covering the branches except in specimens from Natal where the pubescent young branches and spines often become more or less glabrous. In extreme cases, specimens from this area can only be identified when flowers are present. The sepals are always tomentose in C. tomentosa.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1970. Capparis, Fl. S. Africa 13: 144-150. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica calcicola is distinguished from other species in the Coccospermad group by the constantly 1-locular 1-ovuled ovary and four completely fused stamens. It also has characteristic hard incurved leaves and sepals and the flowers are virtually sessile. The pericarp is thinner and more papery in texture than in the other species.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: The most characteristic feature about the species is the turning back of the corolla-lobes at maturity. The lobes curl completely over, fitting exactly between the prominent sepals. This character is sometimes noticeable in E. lucida Salisb. which bears a strong resemblance to E. calycina but has much smaller flowers and lateral anthers. The turning back of the corolla-lobes displays the dark brown anthers which are partly exserted. They contrast well against the white of the corolla. The species can under favourable circumstances form fairly large and very floriferous bushes. This is also the case with the two varieties, periplocaeflora and fragrans, which have reddish-purple flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: E. cameronii is allied to E. tumida but can be distinguished, inter alia, by its 3-nate leaves and flowers, the ovoid-urceolate corolla and anthers without appendages. The habit and size of inflorescence in the two species are quite different.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is clearly closely allied to the preceding species, E. arachnocalyx, and may be distinguished by the long softer calyx hairs which are eglandular, the six to eight stamens, the pilose ovary and small simple-truncate stigma. The flowers are also white turning pink.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica cetrata is characterized by the scarious yellowish bract, bracteoles and calyx with a pink corolla, the eight free stamens, 2-locular ovary with 1 -ovulate locules, the peltate-cyathiform stigma and the lack of basal nectaries around the ovary.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: It is characterized in the section Orophanes by the combination of a corolla-limb rather large for the section and a very small cristate anther. They point out that the species bears a strong resemblance to some in the subgenus Platystoma. The description in Flora Capensis states that the leaves are always imbricate, as they are in the type, but recently collected material from Bain's Kloof shows that they are more often not or scarcely overlapping and about as long as the distance between them. Moreover the flowers are not consistently 4-nate as in other species in this section and are often 3-nate or clustered.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This species could be mistaken for C. malosana, but the latter has bigger leaves, > 40 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Kotze, M. 2019. Rhizophoraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 1381-1383. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Difficult to distinguish from other 2 species, possibly synonymous to C. filiformis. Occurs from Clanwilliam to EC.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL; Van Wyk, AE. 2019. Lauraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 1164-1167. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The rather large sepals give to the flowers a subcalycine aspect. They greatly resemble those of E. selaginifolia, E. acuta, and E. brevifolia in the § Trigemma, and the species is only separated from their neighbourhood by its axillary inflorescence. The whole aspect of the plant is, however, even more strikingly like E. seriphiifolia (§ Melastemon), but the flowers are very different.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is easily recognised by the large, burr-like fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM; Magee, AR. 2013. African Apiaceae: a synopsis of the Apiaceae/Umbelliferae of Sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar. Briza Academic Books, Pretoria. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is most closely related to E. curvifolia Salisb, in general appearance, but the latter species has no anther appendages and is confined to high altitudes on the mountains near Genadendal and Villiersdorp. E. cristata occurs mainly in the Kogelberg Forest Reserve area where it is extremely common in places.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Centella calcaria is a distinct species and differs from C. capensis and related species in the broad leaves and the densely tomentose vestiture. It also differs from all the other annuals and short-lived perennials in the pedunculate inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1997. A revision of Centella series Capenses (Apiaceae). Nord. J. Bot. 17(3): 301-314. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is similar in overall respects to the species of the Section Euryloma which is concentrated in the Caledon District of the south-western Cape. However, it is easily recognizable on account of the open, almost cup-shaped flowers which have a dark red colour like freshly dried oxblood.E. cunoniensis also bears some resemblance to material of E. squarrosa which does not occur in the same area but further east on the mountains east and north of the Grabouw Basin. Like E. gysbertii, E. squarrosa has flowers with a closed narrow ovoid-urceolate corolla with spreading lobes.In the latter two species, the basal portion of each flower (pedicel, bract, bracteoles and calyx) is much less hairy than in E. cunoniensis. The anthers of E. cunoniensis are similar in shape to those of E. squarrosa. In contrast to the free glabrous anthers of E.squarrosa, however, those of E. cunoniensis are united, due to lateral interlocking crisped hairs. E. gysbertii has arcuate anthers typical of another group of species in the section. The more open shape of the flowers is also distinctive and resembles the flowers of E. lananthera L. Bol. from the mountains around the mouth of the Palmiet River but this species too has arcuate anthers and very different leaves resembling those of E. retorta Montin.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 1990. New species of Erica (Ericaceae) from the Cape Province. Bothalia 20(1&2): 41-48. [CC BY]

description: Chiefly variable in the size of the flowers. Salisbury appears to have founded the species on the smaller size (corolla 4 lin. long) and Sprengel, his E. Zeyheri, on the larger (7-8 1/2 lin.). E. comptoniana., Andr. Heathery, t. 255, figured from a cultivated specimen, only differs slightly in the corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: In habit and leaf like G. affinis var. Richardiana but quite different in fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: There are very few species of Erica that can be regarded as having a scent. The most striking of these is E. cylindrica. Second place is probably taken by E. curvirostris, which gives off a distinct sweet scent which is quite noticeable in the surroundings near a large population of the species. A characteristic of this species is its habit of forming almost pure communities under certain ecological conditions. The plants tend to grow on dry slopes that are usually rocky. Where large slabs of rock come to the surface the plants grow in profusion in the shallow soil often to the exclusion of all other species. It is interesting to note that in addition to this preference for arid stony areas the species flowers in the driest and hottest months of the year. The feature of having a curved style is not always very pronounced and cannot be relied upon as a diagnostic character for identification. The possession of a rather wide-open white or pink corolla and the scent are useful in recognizing the species, as also is the type of habitat in which the plants grow.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica curvistyla is characterized by the obliquely 1-locular, 1-ovuled ovary (rarely 2-locular and erect) producing an indehiscent thin-walled fruit with a very thin-walled testa, the basally and apically curved style, bipartite anthers, recurved flattened leaves, subscarious white bract, bracteoles and calyx, and the sprawling to prostrate habit.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Centella cryptocarpa is similar to C. gymnocarpa but can be distinguished by its distinct red-brown colour (C. gymnocarpa is grey-white in colour) and by the large foliaceous bracts (up to 12 mm long) of the bisexual plants which enclose the fruit entirely and which are a unique character of the species (the bracts are shorter than fruit in C. gymnocarpa). There are separate male and functionally bisexual plants in C. cryptocarpa while C. gymnocarpa is invariably monoecious. The male umbels have one, three or five sessile flowers while those of C. gymnocarpa are always single-flowered.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1999. Three new species of Centella series Montanae. Nord. J. Bot. 19(4): 427-434. [All rights reserved]

description: The unusual narrow tube of the flowers of this species makes it easy to recognize. The nearest related species, E. infundibuliformis, is superficially very similar but has red or pink tubes, smaller corolla lobes and differently shaped anthers. E. cylindrica seems to be very local around the waterfall at Tulbagh where it is, however, plentiful. The species has also been recorded from Pic Blanche in the Worcester District, a locality some distance from the Tulbagh waterfall. The bushes may grow up to1.2 (4 ft) but remain rather open and straggly. The very pale yellow flowers make the bushes rather inconspicuous from a distance. The most striking feature of E. cylindrica is its powerful sweet scent. Flowering in two periods, March to May and August to October.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Diagnostic features: bracteoles positioned 1/2 way up pedicel to approximate to calyx, mainly much reduced but still leaf-like; corolla short to long, 1.5-5.5 x 2.2-4.0 mm; filaments very elongate, narrowly ovate with sub-apical S-bend, without a basal, spoon-like expansion; anthers appendiculate; ovary glabrous or hairy; fruit smooth not wrinkled. Variation in characters between the populations of E. cymosa are present. The most noticeable is in the size and shape of the corolla. There are however, two clear size groupings which occur in two disjunct distribution areas. These are also coupled with a difference in indumentum of the ovary. We have therefore decided to recognize these two regional variants at subspecific level.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2002. Six new species and one new subspecies of Erica (Ericaceae) from Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 32(2): 167-180. [CC BY]

description: Centella difformis is superficially very similar to C. brachycarpa and C. dolichocarpa and previously they have been regarded as a single species. All three species have dimorphic leaves: the basal leaves are mostly tridentate in the upper half while the upper leaves, which are borne on long shoots, are entire. However, there are important differences between them: C. difformis has fruit with distinct ribs and no distinct bulging of the commissure, while C. dolichocarpa and C. brachycarpa both have fruit without prominent ribs and with a distinct bulging of the commissure. We question Adamson's (1951) placement of C. difformis in the series Montanae and here propose a transfer to the series Glabratae. The fruit of C. difformis is often ribbed, a character found only in the series Glabratae and Virgatae and not in Montanae.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1998. Three new species of Centella series Glabratae (Apiaceae). Nord. J. Bot. 18(4): 461-469. [All rights reserved]

description: In this section E. daphniflora is the most variable in the shape, size and colour of the flowers. In several of its forms it can easily be confused with E. fastigiata and E. denticulata. Generally speaking the species can be distinguished from these by having its flowers in clusters, but not in all forms, and sometimes congested into large masses. From E. denticulata it differs in its sepals not being widest above the middle and not deeply toothed as in a comb. The species are not, as a rule, found growing in the same localities. In the past the numerous forms of E. daphniflora were regarded as being distinct and worthy of specific rank. As a result several additional species were described. Guthrie & Bolus in their treatment found that there were insufficient grounds on which to keep these species separate and so they treated them as varieties of E. daphniflora. Recently Dulfer has treated them as separate species again. In this work the views of Guthrie & Bolus have been followed on account of the degree of variation observed in the large amount of material gathered over the last thirty years. The variation in the colour, shape and size of the flowers is most striking in this species. The flowers can be yellow, green, pink, dark red, white or white and pink. Probably the showiest of them is the pink form which is the commonest and also the most floriferous. The most unusual form is var. pedicellata, which has relatively large flowers that are waxy and white, sometimes with a flush of pink. Flowers in July in eastern form.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: In floral characters very much like E. decipiens, but looks different; the branches more rigid; leaves usually longer, stouter, and more glossy; pedicels twice as long.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Very variable in leaf-size, the nature of the leaf edge, and in the degree of hairiness; var. glabrata Sond.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: It is closely allied to the §§ Gypsocallis and Ceramia, and might almost be placed in either.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Centella gymnocarpa is similar to C. montana but can be distinguished by its crowded habit and its monomorphic, widely ovate, sericeous, grey-green leaves (the leaves of C. montana are slightly dimorphic, elliptic to lanceolate, pilose and red-brown to green in colour). C. gymnocarpa is similar to C. cryptocarpa in that both species have congested nodes in the central part of the plant, with long trailing branches spreading from a central point. The attenuate and petiolate leaves of both species are usually covered with a dense indumentum. However the leaves of C. gymnocarpa are usually dentate and grey-green in colour while those of C. cryptocarpa are occasionally dentate and distinctly red-brown in colour. In C. gymnocarpa the male umbellules are mostly reduced to a single sessile flower, while in C. cryptocarpa they are made up of one to five sessile flowers each. C. gymnocarpa is a highly localized limestone endemic. It is superficially similar to another limestone endemic with sericeous grey-green leaves, C. calcaria (series Capenses) but the species differ significantly in the structure of the inflorescence and fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1999. Three new species of Centella series Montanae. Nord. J. Bot. 19(4): 427-434. [All rights reserved]

description: In collections this has been confused with G. villosa and with hairy forms of C. glabrata.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: P. drakensbergensis can easily be distinguished from P. evansii by the short pubescence on the leaves, sepals, ovary and stigma and also on the branches and branchlets which have in addition, stouter longer gland-tipped hairs. P. evansii, by contrast, has an abundance of gland-tipped hairs also on its leaves. The anthers of P. drakensbergensis are subbasally rather than basally attached and the pore is relatively smaller. The shape of the stigma in the new species is quite different, being funnel-shaped, whereas in P. evansii it is peltate. The flowers tend to be more densely clustered near the ends of the branches than they are in P. evansii. The most noticeable difference in the living state would be the stickiness of P. evansii plants.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 1985. Ericaceae: A new species of Philippia, from the Drakensberg. Bothalia 15(3&4): 550-551. [CC BY]

description: Rather variable in size, form, and hairiness. The plants described as H. alpina are merely rather slender forms of this species.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: Allied to C. flexuosa and distinguished chiefly on vegetative features. H. septemloba was stated to have tomentose fruits but differs in no other feature and cannot be maintained.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: The species is interesting because it is variable in the arrangement of the leaves and in the number of flowers per head, even on the same plant. It is placed in the section Pyronium and is nearest to E. deliciosa and E. simulans Dulfer (=E. decipiens Spreng.) although it is quite distinct from either, which both grow in the southern Cape.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This is very closely allied to E. inlervallaris, Salisb. and is, perhaps, not more than a variety of that species.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, HML. 1923. Novitates Africanae. Ann. Bolus Herb. 3: 159-184. [https://archive.org/details/annalsofbolusher03bolu/page/n189] [All rights reserved]

description: A well-marked species most nearly allied to E. salax, Salisb., next before which it may be placed. The corolla is of almost exactly the same shape but larger, while the limb-segments are proportionately shorter; the leaves also are different. The most important difference is the remarkable and apparently constant absence of bracts, a very rare character in the genus. In this respect, as well as by its muticous anthers, it differs also from the somewhat similar E. leucopelta, Tausch.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Kensit, HML. 1909. Contributions to the African flora. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 1: 147-163. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/181696#page/215/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to the last species, E. labialis, E. ecklonii is readily distinguished by its bract which remains leaf-like and mostly larger than the calyx in each whorl of the infloresence, the inflorescences themselves being very numerous and erect, not nodding. The flowers are pale pink and soon turn white after pressing whereas in E. labialis they remain pink for a long time and eventually turn brown. The shrubs of E. ecklonii are much woodier being stoutly stemmed and up to 1 m in height. From the common E. williamsiorum, which grows in the same area, it can be distinguished by the simple heads, not complex and compound, and the large leaf-like bract.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Centella pilosa is a distinct species with no obvious affinities. It differs from all other species in the co-occurrence of male, bisexual and heterosexual inflorescences. There is a similarity with C. montana but in the latter the inflorescences are all heterosexual and the commissure of the fruit is not bulging. It is also somewhat similar to C. difformis but differs in the uniformly pilose leaves and the rayed bisexual flowers (leaves dimorphic and pubescent, and bisexual flowers subsessile in C. difformis). The fruit of C. pilosa is smooth, with a distinctly bulging commissure, while those of C. difformis are ribbed and do not have a distinctly bulging commissure. C. pilosa is an annual or short-lived fireweed, while C. difformis is a perennial. C. pilosa furthermore is similar to C. glabrata from which it can be distinguished by the single-flowered male umbellules (male umbellules of C. glabrata with three to five flowers), the smaller fruit and the pilose indumentum (C. glabrata glabrous or rarely slightly villous). Thus C. pilosa is another species which clearly shows a link between C. difformis and C. glabrata.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1998. Three new species of Centella series Glabratae (Apiaceae). Nord. J. Bot. 18(4): 461-469. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is the smallest flowered species in the Ericeae and possibly the whole family with the corolla only 0.7 mm long. It shares this with some of the small flowered forms of E. muscosa and E. urceolata. It can also be distinguished by the free exserted stamens with wedge-shaped anthers without any internal hole connecting the thecae, and by being totally eglandular.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Much smaller than C. macrocarpa and quite different in fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the sub-genus Solandra of Centella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 1-48. [CC BY]

description: Erica eremioides is characterized by the four bipartite anthers, 2-locular 1-ovulate ovary (G2/1), and the straight style. The species is superficially similar to E. curvistyla which also possesses bipartite anthers but with eight of them. The latter also has a 1-locular oblique ovary with a distinctive curved style. The recurved, sometimes sparsely arranged, leaves of subsp. eglandula are very much like those in E. curvistyla. In E. eremioides the anticlinal walls of the testa cells are hardly visible (except in subsp. pubescens) and there are numerous elongated ribs. The anticlinal walls in E. curvistyla are clearly visible and there are no indications of pits or ribbing.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica eriocephala is characterized by the almost free narrow sepals half as long as the corolla (these always villous), the small sessile glands on adaxial surface of sepals, the four stamens, and a distinctly colliculate ovary. The fruit is unlike the others in having a hardish pericarp (not thin and papery) with a clear dehiscence line visible.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: The Graaff-Reinet and Zimbabwe records may yet prove to be erroneous.
bibliographicCitation: Winter, PJD. 2019. Apiaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 294-321. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Centella ternata is very similar to C. umbellata but differs in the axillary inflorescences with single, sessile rays (rays pedunculate and inflorescences leaf-opposed in C. umbellata), the serrate leaf margin (dentate in C. umbellata) and in the pubescent leaves, flowers and fruit (glabrous in C. umbellata). It is also similar to C. asiatica but differs from this species in the tufted, woody habit (stoloniferous in C. asiatica) and the serrate leaf margin (indistinctly dentate in C. asiatica). It differs from all other species of Centella in the three-flowered umbel lules, each with three bisexual flowers (umbellules with single bisexual flower in all other species).
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1995. Two new species of Centella (Umbelliferae) with notes on the infrageneric taxonomy. Nord. J. Bot. 15(2): 167-171. [All rights reserved]

description: Centella umbellata is similar to C. ternata but differs markedly in the structure of the inflorescences as described above and also in the dentate leaf margin and glabrous leaves and fruit. It differs from C. asiatica and all other species of Centella in the same characters as given under C. ternata. It is closely related to C. ternata but can easily be recognized by the glabrous leaves and the distinctly pedunculate, leaf-opposed inflorescences, each with several (two to five) rays.
bibliographicCitation: Schubert, MTR; Van Wyk, B-E. 1995. Two new species of Centella (Umbelliferae) with notes on the infrageneric taxonomy. Nord. J. Bot. 15(2): 167-171. [All rights reserved]

description: There are only two species in the section Bactridium and both have been included here owing to their striking appearance, E. fascicularis can easily be distinguished from E. massoni on the flower colour, leaves and general growth habit. The form with inflated tubular flowers from Riviersonderend has been described as var. imperialis.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: There are several species in this section which show a large amount of variation and are superficially similar. Some forms of E. fastigiata are very near to E. walkeria Andr. The latter is distinguished in the key as having shorter leaves, sepals that are wider above the middle and usually minutely toothed, and a more inflated corolla-tube. Although the typical forms of both species are easy to distinguish there are some intermediate ones that are difficult to differentiate with any certainty. Some of the long-tubed forms of E. fastigiata look similar to the shorter-tubed forms of E. infundibuliformis while var. coventryana may at first glance be mistaken for the spectacular E. vallis-gratiae Guthrie & Bolus from the Riviersonderend Mountains. E. fastigiata is a very common species with a rather limited distribution range. It grows mainly in damp places often near streams and can cover large areas. The species is not as spectacular and showy as E. walkeria when in full bloom but would be worth while having in a garden.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: E. feminarum is a very distinct species with its dark, wine-red flowers that appear almost black in direct sunlight, are very finely hairy, occurring singly on very short lateral branchlets, these often arranged in a pseudospike on the main branches, and have muticous anthers.There are indications that a relationship exists with the E. xanthina/cremea complex despite the difference in size of the corollas, the latter having long tubular flowers. All have a finely hairy corolla with non-spreading lobes, small broad sepals with similar appressed bract and bracteoles and similar anthers. They also have the same habitat preferences, namely seeps or moist gullies at high altitude. E. cremea Dulfer with cream-coloured flowers is a restricted endemic in the mountains of Bain's Kloof and E. xanthina Guthrie & Bolus occurs along the western part of the Riviersonderend Range. It has pale cream to pinkish flowers. There is also an alliance, but more remote, with the long-tubed E. kogelbergensis E.G.H.Oliv. with orange and yellow or plain yellow flowers from the Kogelberg area and E. colorans Andr. with white to pink flowers from the lower hills and flats in the Bredasdorp District.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 1999. Notes on African plants: Ericaceae. Two new species of Erica for Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 29: 95-98. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to Cephalaria pungens Szabó and C. oblongifolia in the ± crenulate epicalyx and distinguished by the linear or narrowly pinnatisect lower leaves, 2-12 mm wide with revolute mar- gins, and by the relatively broader and blunter receptacular bracts, suborbicular to ovate obtuse or sometimes acute. Collections of C. humilis from the CFR are clearly identi?able but further east the distinction between the three species, especially between C. humilis and C. pungens, becomes less clear-cut. As currently understood, C. pungens is characterised by the broader basal leaves, oblanceolate to elliptic, 10-25 mm wide and plane, and by the sharply pointed receptacle bracts, ovate to lanceolate and acuminate or cuspidate.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Johns, A. 2014. A taxonomic review of Cephalaria (Dipsacaceae) in the Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 94: 195-203. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2014); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to both C. humilis and C. pungens, with which it shares a similar lobed or crenulate epicalyx, C. oblongifolia is recognised by its relatively broad, usually simple, oblanceolate to obovate basal leaves, mostly 15-60 mm wide, always coarsely pubescent, at least towards the edges of the blades. The leaves in C. humilis are linear to narrowly lanceolate, 2-12 mm wide, and often pinnati?d, and the species has distinctive ovate, obtuse receptacle bracts. Both C. humilis and C. oblongifolia have glabrous stems and peduncles. The distinction between C. oblongifolia and C. pungens is more problematic. Generally the relatively broader, coarsely hairy leaf blades abruptly narrowed into the petiole serve to separate C. oblongifolia from C. pungens, which typically has oblanceolate leaves narrowed gradually into a petiole-like base although there are forms with distinctly petiolate leaves. Vestiture in the species varies from glabrous to pubescent, both on the foliage and on the stem and peduncles. Another useful character is provided by the leaf margins in the lower leaves, which in C. pungens are typically crenate or obscurely serrate but quite entire in C. oblongifolia. The two species appear to intergrade somewhat and their status requires further investigation.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Johns, A. 2014. A taxonomic review of Cephalaria (Dipsacaceae) in the Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 94: 195-203. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2014); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species, somewhat resembling E. triflora in external appearance, and unlike any other in this section.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: At first sight they seem as if they might be a small-flowered variety of E. parilis, Salisb. but the structure, of the flowers is quite different. It is not improbable that this may be either E. fallax, or E. festa, Salisb.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to C. attenuata and C. scabra in its subshrubby habit with cauline leaves and elliptic stigma, C. rigida is distinguished by its elliptic to oblanceolate, toothed leaves, ± hispid on the upper surface, at least along the margins. Plants from the Kleinrivier Mountains, a recent easterly range-extension for the species, are characterised by their smaller, spreading, subglabrous leaves with more coarsely and deeply serrated margins. Flowering in this population also appears to be later than usual, July or August rather than January to March.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Johns, A. 2014. A taxonomic review of Cephalaria (Dipsacaceae) in the Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 94: 195-203. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2014); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The plate of Andrews clearly does not depict the plant that was until now known as E. foliacea-it is now being described as E. ceraria. His protologue notes-'flowers nearly an inch long (± 25 mm), yellow, and transparent'. The many collections currently recognized under this name have flowers which are ±18 mm long, yellowish green and very hard, smooth and wax-like in texture, not the pure yellow with longitudinal stripes/ridges and do not have the ovary with bulbous upper lobes, as illustrated by Andrews. Guthrie & Bolus had only one of these collections, Bolus 6870, to which Andrews' name was applied thus setting the identification of all subsequent collections. All this material is here described as E. ceraria. Andrews' iconotype matches reasonably well the few collections that, until now, have been identified as E. foliacea var fulgens. This latter name in fact refers to a distinct variant based solely on the density of the synflorescences, the flowers being identical in all the collections of the species. These variants are recognized here at sub-specific level.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2005. The genus Erica (Ericaceae) in southern Africa: taxonomic notes 2. Bothalia 35(2): 121-148. [CC BY]

description: E. fontana, although similar in some respects to the two preceding species and to E. paludicola L, Bolus, differs in its habit and method of growth. Although confined to the southern tip of the Cape Peninsula, the species is to be found in several marshy places on the extensive flats west of Paulsberg. It forms an upright, sturdy plant trying to compete for existence with the other marsh flora. It is rather an untidy looking plant as it flowers practically the whole year round and always has a number of dead or dying flowers mixed with those in full bloom or in bud. E. fontana has been recorded to form hybrids with E. capensis Salter and E. laeta Bartl., both of which occur in the Cape of Good Hope Nature Reserve.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: E. formosa is a distinct species bearing a superficial resemblance to E. spectabilis Kl. which occurs west of its main distribution range. However, the two species cannot be mistaken for each other on close examination.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This subspecies is characterized by the 4-lobed corolla and the 2-locular ovary.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Characterized by the mostly 4-merous flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: This species has been much confused, and is often marked 'E. articularis' in herbaria. The 4-fid cruciform stigma is generally a diagnostic character, and was noted by Linumus.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The floral characters are fairly constant, including the important coronal structure, which was the deciding factor in holding the complex together. The closest ally of C. africana is C. barklyi, from which it is usually readily distinguished by the proportional lengths of corolla-tube to corolla-lobes: the lobes of C. africana are shorter.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: This species most closely resembles the tropical taxon C. denticulata K. Schum. var. brownii (Ledger) Bally, which Huber erroneously placed under C. nilotica. It still remains to be determined whether a climbing form exists.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: Great Karoo from which it differs mainly in the following respects: the corolla-lobes are free at the tips on opening, their shape is different and they are furnished with a distinctive pubescence, absent in C. filiformis. On the other hand the coronas are remarkably similar.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: E. hansfordii is distinguished by its delicate creeping habit, single-flowered florescences, by the flowers being small and pendulous with a clear yellow, smooth corolla, small broad ovate sepals, muticous anthers and a single spreading ovule per locule. This species is probably related to another localised species, E rehmii Dulfer, which occurs nearby in the mountains of the northeastern end of Bain's Kloof and is also confined to marshy seeps. The latter also has yellow flowers, similar sepals, bract/bracteoles, anthers and ovary, but differs in being much larger in stature (woody up to 1 m high), with prominent larger flowers which are erect and arranged in 4-flowered florescences.There are several Erica species that look very similar to E. hansfordii with the same distinctive habit, which is associated with marshy habitats dominated by short tufted restiads, but none occurs in the same region. E. myri-ocodon Guthrie & Bolus occurs in the Franschhoek area and has pale pink flowers, which are hairy with linear sepals, a longer pedicel, appendiculate anthers and a hairy ovary. The two very closely related species, E. limosa L.Bolus and E. salteri L.Bolus, both endemic in the Cape Peninsula also have similar muticous anthers and a glabrous ovary, but the flowers are hairy and are a dirty pinkish cream colour on a longer pedicel and with linear sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 1999. Notes on African plants: Ericaceae. Two new species of Erica for Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 29: 95-98. [CC BY]

description: Dyer (1983) maintains sororia as a subspecies in accordance with the accepted notion that subspecies should have some morphological differences and be allopatric. However, subspecies sororia can vary quite considerably.
bibliographicCitation: Nicholas, A; Glen, M; Shuttleworth, A; Bester, SP. 2019. Apocynaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 321-417. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica hebdomadalis is characterized by its low sprawling habit (maximum height 0.25 m), pendulous flowers with broadly cyathiform glabrous corolla, manifest anthers, and equally long style.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 1998. A new species of Erica (Ericaceae) from South Africa. Novon 8(4): 430-432. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/3391868] [All rights reserved]

description: Some difficulty arises occasionally in distinguishing between C. racemosa and C. carnosa. In addition to its generally smaller, subsucculent habit, C. carnosa has a 10-toothed or -lobuled outer corona.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: Heleo-marsh; -genus = born in; referring to the habitat. This is another of the typical marsh species with its slender, diffuse, often tortuous, stems and branches which are supported by the dense marsh vegetation. E. heleogena is very localized in its distribution. It occurs in a single large marsh in the Klaver Valley above Simonstown. In this marsh, however, it grows abundantly and is in no danger of being exterminated. It has been recorded as forming hybrids with E. laeta Barth and E. hirtifiora Curt., both of which occur in or near the marsh. The species is allied to E. paludicola L. Bolus and E. cyrillaeflora and may be distinguished from the former by being pubescent all over and in having longer sepals and from the latter by its elongate cup-shaped corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: E. hexensis is another of the small-flowered species in the section Arsace that bears a resemblance to the very common E. hispidula. From this it may be distinguished by the long soft hairs with long-forked tips on the branches, lack of glands except a few sessile ones on the branches, distinct white median line down the sepals, cyathiform corolla and papillate-verrucose ovary.From the more eastern E. glandulipila it differs in the lack of glands and anther appendages, the ovary surface and the cyathiform stigma, the latter having a subpeltate-capitate stigma. The type of hairs on the branches and the ovary indumentum serve to distinguish it further from E. hispiduloides.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 1995. Studies in the Ericoideae (Ericaceae). XVI. Six new species of Erica from the western Cape, South Af. Bothalia 25(1&2): 87-95. [CC BY]

description: Although allied to C. stapeliiformis in habit, shape of corolla-tube and, to some extent, in the corona, the opening of the corolla-lobes is markedly different: in C. stapeliiformis the tips of the lobes become free and spread apart, very rarely becoming twisted, while in C. cimiciodora the tips of the lobes become free but do not spread, the margins diverge laterally, leaving the sinuses as points of the star-shaped upper corolla (the spread of which is the same as that of the mature, but unopened, bud). This pattern of opening is to be seen in species where the tips of the corolla lobes are slightly united.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: The new species is apparently nearest in affinity to Ceropegia antennifera Schltr., an extremely rare species from the same general area in KwaZulu-Natal. The latter has unmistakable corolla lobes resembling antennae of certain insects in their distinctively expanded tips. Until the corolla opens completely, plants of the new species also bear superficial resemblance to Ceropegia dinteri Schltr., a species endemic to Namibia and from which it differs in size, shape and colour of the corolla and corona.
bibliographicCitation: Victor, JE. 2001. 430. Ceropegia craibii. Curtis's Bot. Mag. 18: 210-213. [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the Board of Trustees of the Royal Botanic Garden, Kew] [All rights reserved]

description: A clear distinction should be made between species with tubers and those with fleshy roots. It is noteworthy, however, that C. dubia, which possesses fleshy roots, superficially resembles species which bear tubers, such as C. cancellata, C. africana and C. linearis.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: This species is closely related to the common and widespread E. parviflora but can easily be distinguished by its broader, ovate, petaloid, pink sepals, finely hairy corolla and broad cyathiform stigma. The latter species has linear-lanceolate foliaceous sepals, a coarsely longhaired corolla and a small capitate stigma. The flowers of E. hottentotica are larger than those of E. parviflora although the form of the latter in the Hottentots Holland Mountains has fairly large flowers. E. parviflora is generally a scrambling plant in marshes, whereas the new species appears to form an erect sturdy shrub which may reach a height of 2.5 m (Stokoe 4009). There is also a resemblance to some forms of the common E. sitiens Klotzsch which has, however, a glabrous corolla, foliaceous sepals and a capitate stigma.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 1995. Studies in the Ericoideae (Ericaceae). XVI. Six new species of Erica from the western Cape, South Af. Bothalia 25(1&2): 87-95. [CC BY]

description: Alternative taxonomy: this species is presented in its narrow sense but forms part of a metaspecies or genetic complex. Bruyns (1985 has proposed an alternative hypothesis reducing C. geniculata R.A.Dyer and C. connivens R.A.Dyer to subspecies under this species. In his classification subspecies geniculata and connivens do not occur in the EC.
bibliographicCitation: Nicholas, A; Glen, M; Shuttleworth, A; Bester, SP. 2019. Apocynaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 321-417. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The two species E. placentaeflora and E. imbricata are often misidentified. More often than not E. placentaeflora is labelled as E. imbricata. This is understandable since some forms of the former species bear a very close resemblance to E. imbricata. The typical forms of the two species are distinct and easy to recognize. E. placentaeflora differs chiefly in having a globose-shaped corolla depressed in the middle and with the lobes tightly contracted round the stamens and a more lax habit. However, there are intermediate forms which are difficult to name and only a thorough field study of the two species will clear up the problems of identification.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The affinity with C. linearis is close but the deep corona-bowl, from the inside of which arise the linear inner lobes, is distinctive; the corolla-lobes taper to the apex as do the buds and there is no protrusion of the sinuses.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: Alternative taxonomy: Dyer (1977) placed this species under Ceropegia distincta subsp. haygarthii (Schltr.) H.Huber. This is generally no longer followed.
bibliographicCitation: Nicholas, A; Glen, M; Shuttleworth, A; Bester, SP. 2019. Apocynaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 321-417. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species has a superficial resemblance to E. obliqua in the section Pachysa. The latter species is distingusihed by its very much smaller and sparser growth and sticky flowers. The leaves, although they are on long petioles and are delicate, are not arranged to one side of the stem as is often the case in E. inflata. It is also closely related to E. sonora Compton from the Gifberg, Vanrhynsdorp, resembling it in habit of growth, leaves and inflorescence. The latter species differs, however, in having shorter pedicels, smaller flowers with a relatively broader globose corolla which is broadest above the middle and in having short and broad anther crests. In E. infiata the appendages are long and narrow.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Alternative taxonomy: several have been proposed to classify this polytypic species. Most current and useful is that of Bruyns (1985) who recognises 3 allopatric subspecies that have limited gene exchange. All 3 occurring in EC and have been recognised as distinct species by various authors. Probably a good example of a metaspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Nicholas, A; Glen, M; Shuttleworth, A; Bester, SP. 2019. Apocynaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 321-417. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is characterized by the remarkably enlarged calyx in the fruiting stage with the lobes becoming much inflated and cucullate, white and glassy, later thin and papery. The plants are erect, narrow, virgate up to 600 mm tall.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is unusual in having the innovation of new growth occurring from the apex of the current inflorescence, the scars of previous flowering inflorescences being clearly visible on old branches. This character is shared with only a few other species of Erica, but these are quite unrelated, such as E.fascicularis L.f., E. massonii L.f. and E. thimifolia Salisb. It may be distinguished in the group by the above character and also the possession of numerous long stiff erect hairs up the abaxial side of the anthers and the subapically papillate-aculeate filaments. The bracteole is also slightly different in this species in remaining green and relatively large up the whorls of an inflorescence. It is clearly allied to the species with 3-nate leaves, E. pulchelliflora and E. venustiflora, but differs in the above characters.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to C. linearis and C. woodii, but consistently distinct in its short corolla-lobes and small cage. Huber placed it under C. linearis subsp. woodii, but C. woodii.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: This taxon is chiefly remarkable for being more or less glandular-viscid in all parts except the androecium and for having rather remarkable anthers, as described. It does not appear to be closely related to any other species described in the section Hermes but rightly belongs there according to the definition of that section.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA. 1972. Two new species of Erica. J. S. African Bot. 38(2): 121-124. [CC BY]

description: Erica interrupta is characterized by the coriaceous corolla in the fruiting stage. The old corolla becomes shiny and reddish brown with age. This character is very unusual in the genus and may be likened to the coriaceous, but thinner and non-shiny, corolla in E. stokoeanthus. Other distinguishing characters are a single partially recaulescent approximate bract, the small almost fully divided calyx, the four stamens with hairy anthers and a shortly stipitate ovary which is 2-locular and 1-ovulate (G2/1) which produces a partially dehiscent fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: M. B. Bayer 745 and KG 162/73 were collected somewhat east of Hankey on the eastern Cape border. They are related to C. cancellata and C. woodii. They differ from the former in their subspathulate corolla lobes and show variability in their coronal structure: seed of the glabrous No. 745 produced pubescent seedlings and there was colour variation from the basic yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: E. involucrata is by far the most attractive of the three species, having its floral leaves coloured pink. In the other two species, E. senilis Kl. ex Benth. and E. eriophoros Guthrie & Bolus, the floral leaves are a dirty-white colour. The species may be distinguished from the others by having leaves edged with short bristles as opposed to long hairs. All the species are decumbent, forming dense mats, and grow on dry mountain slopes in the Ceres and Clan william Districts.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Very near to E. suffulta, and we retain the species with some doubt; but the sepals are broader, especially at the base, anthers much more obtuse; and the flowers larger.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: This species can be distinguished from most other members of this section by the 3-nate leaves, prognathous anthers and by the shape of the corolla which is not always typical of the section in which it is bottle-shaped with a tapering neck but is sometimes urn-shaped and not much inflated. E. irhyana is, however, closely related to E. shannonea and may be a miniature form of the latter. The habit and set of the leaves are different, the branches being straighter, more slender and longer. In E. irhyana the plants are generally taller and bear numerous heads of smaller flowers which are pink in colour. The dark red sepals make an effective contrast against the shiny bright pink corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: E. irregularis is allied to E. baccans L. in general structure and appearance. However, the-arrangement of the flowers on the branches is quite different; in the latter they are strictly terminal on short branchlets while in the former they are apparently borne in the axils of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: E. irrorata resembles most of the species in this section. It is, however, very similar to E. glandulifera Kl. which occurs in the same area. It may be distinguished from the latter species by having only two bracts, and wider, incised appendages to the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Jasminium = the jasmine; flora = flowers; referring to the shape of the flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica jonasiana is a very distinct species characterized by the fluted corolla with four large intercellular cavities, four stamens with hairy filaments and muticous anthers producing pollen in monads, a 1-locular 1-ovulate ovary with eccentric hairy-based style and a partially dehiscent fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: This new species clearly belongs to the group of species with enlarging calyces in the fruiting stage. It is easily distinguished by the markedly assymetrical 1-locular ovary with the style arising laterally. It is also the only species in the group without any basal nectaries around the ovary, with an expanded stigma and with large sessile glands on the edges of the calyx lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: The variation in the size of the flowers and in the spread and elevation of the canopy of the corolla, is such, that a form from Mozambique, Zululand and Natal with pendulous, purple cilia from the canopy was given specific rank as C. monteiroae. Schlechter even confused this form with C. fimbriata. To add to the complications, C. sandersonii is claimed to hybridize with such species as C. radicans and C. elegans Wall. (=C. similis N.E. Br), but as these hybrids are not produced in the veld.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1980. Asclepiadaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 27(4): 1-88. [CC BY]

description: This new species is most closely related to the widespread eastern Cape species, E. caespitosa Hilliard [= Philippia tristis Bolus], but may be distinguished by its single-stemmed reseeding habit, densely hairy pedicel with a hairy base to the calyx, always two free bracteoles, open broadly obconic corolla with the anthers clearly visible being half exserted and a very broadly cyathiform stigma.E. caespitosa, as its name suggests, is a low, multi-stemmed resprouter with a glabrous, or occasionally sparsely puberulous, pedicel and glabrous calyx, globose to broadly urceolate corolla with included anthers and obconic stigma. E. caespitosa occasionally possesses two bracteoles on the pedicel, but usually has none with the bract often fully recaulescent and forming part of the calyx in the philippioid condition.E. karooica has small insignificandy coloured flowers that are developed for wind pollination. At the type locality plants gave off small puffs of pollen into the wind when disturbed. The flowers are very similar at first glance to those in the minor genera of the Ericoideae like Salaxis Salisb. and Coccosperma Klotzsch, and therefore would probably not attract much attention among collectors. The flowers are unusual in that the corolla is a very translucent white with the red immature anthers clearly visible inside. Soon after the stigma appears beyond the corolla mouth, the corolla looses its colour, dries out and turns brown before the anthers have appeared and shed their pollen. I have not noticed this feature in any other species.The possession of an elaiosome on the seeds is a character that has never before been recorded in the Ericoideae. This is, however, not the only species that I have recently found, in the closer examination of Erica spp., to possess such an appendage. The biological implications of this character need some detailed field investigations.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 1995. Ericaceae: A new species of Erica from the Bredasdorp District. Bothalia 25(1&2): 242-244. [CC BY]
