description: Erica stokoeanthus is characterized by the 2-locular ovary with usually three pendulous ovules per locule, rarely two or six but sometimes four or five (G2/[2]3(4,5)[6]), a bract and two bracteoles, 4-partite calyx, an expanded stigma and no nectaries. The coriaceous corolla in the fruiting stage is unusual in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Its leaves and bracts is quite distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is closely allied to E. viridipurpurea, but is generally at once distinguishable by the acute interstices between the segments of the corolla-limb; the flowering season is also quite different.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: C. vendae is most closely related to Combretum nelsonii Dummer which occurs on the Makgabeng, Waterberg and Wolkberg, being both morphologically alike and occupying similar ecological niches. Within the Soutpansberg the C. vendae's nearest allies are Combretum kraussii and Combretum erythrophyllum. Within the Soutpansberg C. vendae is most closely related to C. kraussii. It differs from C. kraussii by having markedly raised net veining along the lower leaf surface and having scales on the upper leave surface that can be seen when the leaf is bent leaving a marked waxy white line. This character gives the leave a dull appearance were C. kraussii seen from a distance appears shiny glossy. Its leaves are also more leathery than C. kraussii. Nowhere in the distribution of C. vendae do the two species occur sympatrically. C. kraussii is confined to the higher rainfall regions and almost always occurs in or near Afro-montane forest along its entire distribution from the Cape to the Limpopo Province. C. erythrophyllum differs from C. vendae in being confined to river banks or areas with a shallow water table. C. erythrophyllum differs in habit from C. vendae in being a large single-stemmed tree, whereas C. vendae is usually a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Outside the Soutpansberg C. vendae is most closely related to C. nelsonii. C. nelsonii leaves are more similar to those of C. kraussii than those of C. vendae. C. nelsonii leaves differ from those of C. vendae by not having marked raised tertiary veins, the lower surface being glabrous and its lamina is also thinner not being markedly leathery.
bibliographicCitation: Hahn, N. 2012. A revision of the Combretum vendae complex. S. African J. Bot. 78: 147-149. [http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0254629911000950 ]

description: The unspecialized inflorescence, dense mat-forming habit, globose urceolate flowers with lanceolate sepals and distinctly visible corolla and the dark brown anthers serve to distinguish E. tegetiformis. This taxon was originally described by Dulfer as a variety of the Cedarberg species, E. senilis Klotzsch ex Benth., based on the single collection of Esterhuysen 28122 from Sonklip near Matroosberg. However, material recently collected and sent to me for identification, looked so different from E. senilis that I did not link the material with that species at the time and regarded it as a distinct undescribed species. Only when checking on possible alliances within the Section Chromostegia, particularly E. senilis and E. eriophoros Guth. & Bol. did I realise that Dulfer's variety was in fact this new species and that it bears only a superficial resemblance to E. senilis.E. tegetiformis undoubtedly belongs in the Section Chromostegia because of the prostrate habit and the compact heads of flowers even though in the new species this latter character is not very pronounced as is the case in E. senilis in which the leaves below the inflorescence as well as the bract and bracteoles, are enlarged and coloured giving an involucrate appearance to the inflorescence. This feature is far less developed in E. eriophoros and hardly so in E. tegetiformis. Similarities with E. senilis are not close, perhaps only in the relative size and shape of the anther. There is more affinity with E. eriophoros, but this in turn shows a closer affinity with E. senilis in many characters.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 1990. New species of Erica (Ericaceae) from the Cape Province. Bothalia 20(1&2): 41-48. [CC BY]

description: This species has more external resemblance to those of the § Desmia than to this section [§ Ceramia]; but the floral structure is different. The leaves are peculiar andunlike those of § Ceramia generally.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Many herbarium specimens of C. plumbagineus var. plumbagineus collected in South Africa have been incorrectly identified as C. decipiens. These two taxa are easily confused as they have a very similar growth form and both have white flowers. C. decipiens differs from C. plumbagineus var. plumbagineus in that C. depiciens is more pubescent in vegetative, but especially in the reproductive parts. The most obvious difference is that the lower coriaceous part of the flower of C. decipiens is clavate and covered with scattered sessile glands and hairs, while that of C. plumbagineus var. plumbagineus is cylindrical with ten, prominent sessile glands arranged around the apex and with only a few glands scattered over the surface below. The anthocarp of C. decipiens is clavate and the apex surrounded by five shortly stalked glands, with prominent glands and hairs scattered over the surface below the apex. The anthocarp of C. plumbagineus var. plumbagineus is fusiform with a ring of ten stalked glands around the apex and a few stalked glands grouped below the apex.
bibliographicCitation: Struwig, M; Siebert, SJ. 2013. A taxonomic revision of Commicarpus (Nyctaginaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 84: 44-64. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2013); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to E. lutea, and perhaps to be regarded as a variety of it. It is also allied to E. borboniaefolia, and all three resemble each other in floral structure, but differ in aspect.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: C. pentandrus is often confused with C. pilosus, but they differ in that the lower, coriaceous part of the flower of C. pentandrus is clavate while that of C. pilosus is elliptic. The anthocarp of C. pentandrus is clavate with five thickly stalked glands alternating with five smaller, less prominent glands around the apex while that of C. pilosus is elliptic-clavate with five shortly stalked glands around apex.
bibliographicCitation: Struwig, M; Siebert, SJ. 2013. A taxonomic revision of Commicarpus (Nyctaginaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 84: 44-64. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2013); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Erica terniflora is characterized by the anthers with basal hairs, broadly obovoid fruit with deep lateral grooves and short beak, hard endocarp and very thin testa.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica totta is characterized by the large white, scarious bract, bracteoles and free sepals, all with serrulate to fimbriate edges, the eight stamens, and the 4-locular 1-ovulate ovary (G4/1) producing a thin-walled, indehiscent fruit with seeds having a thin testa. It forms a low, grey-leaved, spreading shrublet with erect secondary branches, rarely erect and then usually when supported by other plants.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Somewhat intermediate between E. chrysocodon and E. setulosa, differing from the former by its sepals and corolla, and from the latter by its leaves and corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: It is characterized by its small dark mericarps without prominent ribs; only the Grecian species, C. divaricatum, shows a similar weak development of ribs, but it is easily distinguished by its larger mericarps (±4 x 1.5 mm) in which both pericarp and endosperm are strongly sulcate; in C. sphaerocarpum both are smoothly rounded.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Conium (Umbelliferae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 51: 465-474. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1985); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Erica uberiflora is characterized by the long tubular calyx which is longitudinally grooved with the grooves alternating with the small lobes, the obtuse angles opposite the lobes; the approximate subequal bract and two bracteoles in all flowers, and the narrow bipartite anthers with basal long appendages.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Delicate, brittle, pendulous shrub-let; leaves 3-nate, spreading (up to 90°), delicate; pedicel long (6-7 mm); flowers viscid; anther appendages long, narrow, zigzagged and irregularly toothed; ovary short-haired. This new species shares similarities with a range of viscid-flowered species such as E. carduifolia Salisb., E. nubigena Bolus, E. ixanthera Benth., E. wittebergensis Dulfer, and two undescribed species-one from the Kouga Mountains (Esterhuysen 10673, 27097), the other from the northern side of the Swartberg Pass (Schumann 798 and Vlok 2502). With these it shares long, 3-nate leaves mostly with sticky glands, often spreading and caducous, bract-like leaves at base of flowers and side branches, long pedicel with few to many glands, similar sized and positioned bract and bracteoles, large sessile marginal glands on the sepals, long anther appendages, and ovary with large placenta bearing numerous ovules producing small seeds. It differs in its growth form, being pendulous with thin, very brittle branches, much longer zigzagged and irregularly toothed anther appendages and short-haired ovary. Each of the species has rather specific leaves. Most of the other species grow in shaded, moist places often on southern slopes, E. nubigena and E. carduifolia at high altitudes, E. ixanthera, E. sp. nov. (Kouga) and E. umbratica at a much lower altitude. Erica sp. nov. from the Swartberg Pass is the odd one out as it grows on dry, rocky slopes in open veld on the northern side of the Swartberg and forms erect, woody shrublets. Erica umbractica has rather viscid flowers which easily collect dirt on them in the very windy conditions that prevail in Meiringspoort. This made Schumann in frustration, refer to this new species as Erica 'puersordidus'-the dirty boy, when trying to produce perfectly clean material for photographing.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2002. Six new species and one new subspecies of Erica (Ericaceae) from Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 32(2): 167-180. [CC BY]

description: There has been some confusion in herbaria between this species and E. inconspicua, Bartl.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is closely related to E. bruniaefolia but, though their floral characters are very similar, they have a very different appearance. In E. ustulescens the leaves are not incurved and the number of flowers in a head is far fewer. Unlike E. bruniaefolia, which is very variable in different localities, this species seems to be fairly consistent in its characters.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The extremely long, red pedicels, pendulous flowers and quadrangulate corolla serve to distinguish E. vallis-aranearum from all other species. The affinities of E. vallis-aranearum are not very clear. In the section Evanthe it is most closely related to Erica foliacea Andr., another greenish yellow flowered species from the same mountainous area, but occurring on drier open aspects. Both have very leafy twiggy branches and prognathous anthers though much more pronounced in the new species. It would seem probable that it has evolved from the common E. foliacea. Of similar structure are E. patersonia Andr. from the Hangklip flats and E. nana Salisb., which occurs close-by on the same mountain range.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Anderson, VF. 1973. Erica vallis-aranearum E.G.H.Oliv. Fl. Pl. Africa 42t.1680 [CC BY]

description: A fine and well-marked species, perhaps nearest to E. walkeria, but larger in all parts, and especially distinguishable by the straighter, more erect, longer leaves. It is also near to E. fastigiata, var. coventryana, but the sepals and the anthers are very different.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The section Leptodendron is one that is rather ill-defined and can incorporate a number of species from other sections. It is a type of `junk box' in the genus. It is most closely related to the section Orophanes, the number of leaves per whorl separating the two. In Orophanes the leaves are 4-nate; in Leptodendron 3-nate. E. vanheurckii belongs to Leptodendron on account of its 3-nate leaves but is very closely allied to E. rubens Thunb. in Orophanes. A thorough investigation of all the specimens of this complex occurring in the Cold Bokkeveld may show that the two species should be regarded as one. In habit and general form the species is similar to E. leptopus which, however, has a differently shaped corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to E. hirta, Thunb., but differs in the indument not being glandular, the broader sepals, the anthers attached to the filament almost at the middle, and the shorter awns.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, HML. 1918. Novitates Africanae. Ann. Bolus Herb. 2: 153-162. [https://archive.org/details/annalsofbolusher02bolu/page/152] [All rights reserved]

description: Erica velatiflora is unique in the genus for its involucrate almost hidden flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: E. ventricosa forms a complex with two species in this section, E. savilea Andr. and E. praecox Kl. both of which occur in the same area. The latter species can probably be regarded as a variety of E. ventricosa. Only a thorough investigation of all the available material and of populations in the wild will provide a satisfactory solution to the problem.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Its characters include a strong tendency toward singlehood, a certain squatness (except when seen after it has received abundant and excessive moisture), rounded windows (as seen from above and from the side), and white petals (though it can show purplish colours as well, particularly in the south). Always the bodies have a peculiar pliability.
bibliographicCitation: Hammer, SA. 1993. The genus Conophytum: A conograph. Succulent Plant Publications, Pretoria. [All rights reserved]

description: Vestitus = clothed; probably referring to the very crowded leaves which cover the branches. The colour variants of E, vestita are very striking and attractive. Closely allied to E. vestita especially in the formation of the leaves are E. nematophylla Guthrie & Bolus and E. filamentosa Andr., which are characterized by having much shorter flowers. All three occur together in the same areas. Some forms have a close resemblance to E. longijolia but may be distinguished by their longer and softer leaves with longer petioles.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: E. decora is very closely allied to E. viscaria L. and has been distinguished by having a larger corolla and anthers and peduncle over 3 mm long. Detailed study of field material may show that E, decora should be regarded as a large-flowered form of E, viscaria. The species is also closely related to E. axilliflora Bartl. from the Bredasdorp District. The latter species may be recognized by its corolla which widens more regularly from the base. The sepals and bracts are also entirely different. E. decora is also similar to E. conica Lodd. of section Pleurocallis which has, however, a more robust habit, different leaves and a hairy ovary. Both E. decora and E. viscaria occur on the Cape Peninsula where the latter is now regarded as rare. In this area E. decora is unusual in growing on the fairly moist mountain slopes on Noordhoek Peak and on dry hot clay ground on the lower northern slopes at Westlake.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is allied to E. calycina, Linn., from which it differs in the marked viscidity of the flowers. Its affinities place it naturally in § Eurystoma in spite of the viscidity.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM; Esterhuysen, EE. 1936. Plantae novae Africanae. Series VI. J. S. African Bot. 2: 47-64. [CC BY]

description: Erica viscosissima is characterized by the very viscid flowers which are agglutinated together in rounded many-flowered pendulous heads, the erect to subspreading leaves as long as the internodes and a pilose ovary.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica vlokii is distinct among the indehiscent-fruited species for its canescent branches with reflexed hairs, membraneous subpetaloid pink bract, bracteoles and sepals, eight manifest to exserted stamens, pollen in monads, 4-locular ovary with one ovule per locule (G 4/1) and fruit with a very hard, lignified endocarp and seeds with very thin testa.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to E. floccifera, Zahlbr. (E. floccosa, Bartl. non Salisb.), but differing by the characters enumerated above. It may be placed next after that species. E. affinis E. flocciferae, Zahlbr., differt foliis majoribus, bracteis laxioribus, sepalis lanceolato-ovatis acuminatis, corolla parum minoribus, antheris semi-ovatis angustioribus appendicibus brevioribus, ovario tomentoso.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Kensit, HML. 1909. Contributions to the African flora. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 1: 147-163. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/181696#page/215/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Erica zeyheriana is characterized by the fully recaulescent bract and bracteoles, papery yellow-brown corolla, broadly cyathiform to peltate stigma and berry-like fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: If the pressed material is scrappy or the collector's notes incomplete, specimens might be confused with K. albescens or K. breviflora. From the latter it differs in the longer perianth and from both in the buds being distinctly pendulous and scarlet in colour, and the bracts not as long-acuminate.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The variation may occur within a small area and the situation resembles the hybrid swarms reported under K. fibrosa. Here again it is assumed that the longer perianth and reddish colours are contributed by K. triangularis, which has dense, concolorous racemes, orange-red to coral-red in colour, with flowers 24-35 m long. Specimens with flowers about 30 mm long may be confused with K. ichopensis var. ichopensi, but the two can usually be separated on the basis of leaf width which, in K. angustifolia, does not exceed 5 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Fruits glabrous, not rostrate, rounded at apex.
bibliographicCitation: Jeffrey, C. 1978. 86. Cucurbitaeae. In: E Launert (ed.), Fl. Zambes. 4: 414-499. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, Glasgow. [CC BY]

description: The narrow, grass-like leaves of this species are similar to some forms of K. triangularis but are, in general, more nervose and fibrous. The floral characters of the two are also similar, though in K. galpinii the perianth lobes are not spreading and the raceme is bicolorous, with flame-red buds grading down to yellowish flowers. In K. triangularis the raceme is more or less concolorous, coral-red to orange-red in colour, and the perianth lobes are spreading.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: An extremely polymorphic species but all the variations intergrade so freely that it is not possible to divide it into satisfactory varieties. As regards pubescence, for instance, every stage exists between the form with numerous bulbous-based hairs on the leaves, represented by the type of C. arenicola, and the quite glabrous leaves of the type of C. serrifolios. See also notes under C. confusus.
bibliographicCitation: Wild, H. 1984. Tiliaceae, Fl. S. Africa 21(1): 1-44. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209546#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: In the herbarium it may be confused with the following species, K. baurii, which has some-what narrower, glaucous leaves, slightly shorter, more greenish flowers and a more inland distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Its nearest relative is K. breviflora from which it is distinguished mainly on perianth length which, in K. breviflora, is 7-11 mm. There are, however, occasional intermediates which suggest that K. buchananii might be better placed as a subspecies of K. breviflora. K. breviflora occurs more inland and at higher elevations than K. buchananii. For this reason K. parviflora var. albiflora A.Berger, based on J.M. Wood 4826 from Glencoe with flowers 6-7 mm long, is placed in synonymy under K. breviflora.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This species is very variable in leaf-shape, size, pubescence and, particularly if it is grazed or trampled, becomes semiprostrate and can be confused with C. asplenifolius. It is, however, always an annual, whilst C. asplenifolius is always a perennial.
bibliographicCitation: Wild, H. 1984. Tiliaceae, Fl. S. Africa 21(1): 1-44. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209546#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: It may be separated from the previous species, K. angustifolia by the slightly broader leaves nd narrowly funnel-shaped perianth. Its nearst affinity is probably K. pallidiflora Baker of Madagascar, which has more distinctly funnel-shaped flowers and longer pedicels. The Richards Bay specimens tend to have denser racemes and edtinged flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A spring-flowering species with globose racemes reminiscent of the following species, K. rooperi, but K. rigidifolia has erect, not spreading, yellow-green leaves and the buds are not erect and covered by the imbricate bracts as in K. rooperi. The two species are completely separated geographically.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: K. hirsuta resembles the following species, K. ritualis, in raceme, bract and perianth characters but is unique in the genus in having pubescent leaves. The only other species which approaches it in this respect is K. stricta which usually has scabrid papillae on the nerves.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A poorly known species.
bibliographicCitation: Burgoyne, PM; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Aizoaceae: Corpuscularia Schwantes. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 209-210. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unlike other species of Kniphofia in South Africa, the flowers do not become pendulous with age. Its closest relative is probably K. reynoldsii Codd from Malawi which, however, has a shorter perianth tube, up to 10 mm long, with spreading lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The large, ovoid fruits, 12-15 x 8-10 mm, carried erect on stout, arcuate pedicels up to 5 mm long, distinguish K. littoralis from related species. In the absence of fruits there may sometimes be difficulty in separating it in the herbarium from K. drepanophyll, K. baurii and from depauperate specimens of K. rooperi.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: K. linearifolia, K. rooperi and K. uvaria are closely related and intermediate specimens occur where their distribution areas overlap. The distinguishing characters are discussed under K. uvaria. There are also intermediate specimens linking K. linearifolia and K. tysonii, but the latter can usually be separated by the more elongate racemes with shorter flowers and well-exserted stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: K. laxiflora may be distinguished from other lax-flowered species, such as K. ichopensis and K. tabularis, by its broader bracts which are rounded or obtuse at the apex. A few specimens have, however, been seen with bracts of intermediate shape, which may be hybrids.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Related to K. baurii, but differs in the broader leaves which overtop the scape at the flowering stage, and the tapering raceme. The tapering raceme and the broader, rounded bracts distinguish K. latifolia from the next species, K. rigidifolia, which is restricted to Mpumalanga.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The leaves vary from linear to oblanceolate and are usually densely covered with glandular hairs. Plants with broader leaves and sparser tomentum should be treated with caution as these characters often indicate hybrid s with C. orbiculata. If the corolla of such specimens is orange and the lobes are recurved to recoiled, instead of reflexed and straight as in C. campanulata, this underlines their hybrid nature. Hybrids are quite frequently observed in the field but only extreme cases can be identified in herbarium material.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Annual, rosulate or branched, hispid herb. Leaves oblong to ovate, at least upper deeply pinnatifid and sharply dentate. Petals violet. Mericarps with apical pits eglandular and with I furrow, tail ±65 mm long. [The description is based on Acocks 19469 (K) and Webb & Chater].
bibliographicCitation: Venter, HJT; Verhoeven, RL. 1990. The genus Erodium in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 56: 79-92. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1990); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Annual caulescent, hispid to hirsute and glandular herb. Leaves broadly ovate to broadly deltate-ovate, margin usually shallowly lobed and obtusely dentate to serrate. Petals pinkish to purplish. Mericarps with glandular apical pits and without any furrow below pit, tail 30-40 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, HJT; Verhoeven, RL. 1990. The genus Erodium in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 56: 79-92. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1990); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The species is readily distinguished from C. woodii by the dwarf stature (2-15 cm) and sticky leaves of the new taxon. The new species also differs from C. woodii by bearing much longer compound inflorescences, more narrow corollas (5-6 mm in diameter) and squamae that are oblong, yellow, emarginate, and 1 x 0.75 mm in size. In contrast, C. woodii is always an erect shrub with usually solitary flowers whose squamae are transversely oblong, yellow and 0.8 x 2 mm in size. The leaves of C. woodii are most often glabrous although specimens with sticky, glandular hairy leaves have been rarely recorded on plants from the Kouga Dam. Cotyledon eliseae also somewhat resembles small-leaved forms of C. orbiculata var. orbiculata from the Little Karoo but the latter has glaucous, glabrous leaves and large transversely oblong, 1 x 1.5 mm squamae.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Koutnik, DL. 1997. New Cotyledon and Tylecodon species (Crassulaceae) from the Cape Province. Bradleya 15: 65-72. [https://doi.org/10.25223/brad.n15.1997.a8] [All rights reserved]

description: Erect to prostrate pilose and glandular herb. Leaves with petiole 25-165 mm long; lamina simple, broadly ovate to broadly deltate-ovate with base cordate to truncate, sparsely pilose with numerous sessile glands, normally soft-textured, margin serrate and usually only shallowly lobed. Petals violet or white. Mericarps with glandular pits and one furrow below pit, tail short, 20-30 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, HJT; Verhoeven, RL. 1990. The genus Erodium in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 56: 79-92. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1990); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Putative hybrids: C. orbiculata var. orbiculata x C. cuneata, C. orbiculata var. orbiculata x C. papillaris, C. orbiculata var. oblonga x C. velutina, C. orbiculata var. oblonga x C. papillaris.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Several of the various cultivated forms also occur as casual weeds.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W. 1970. Cruciferae, Fl. S. Africa 13: 1-118. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Putative hybrids: C. papillaris x C. campanulata and C. papillaris x C. orbiculata var. orbiculata.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Cotyledon pendens is at once distinguished from other Cotyledon species by its thin, flaccid, pendent stems of ± 2 mm in diameter, leaves and inflorescences on distinct, but short peduncles 30-40 mm long and with a single pair of leaf-like bracts. Its leaves are 18-25 mm long, crowded, elliptic to ellipsoid, conspicuously whitish grey-green, forming a loose cylindrical body up to 30 mm in diameter. Its vegetative parts are sparsely and inconspicuously glandular-hairy, becoming glabrescent with age. It has a relatively large corolla, 40-45 x 12-13 mm, in comparison to its small leaves. It comes closest to Cotyledon woodii, C. adscendens and C. orbiculata. C. adscendens is always a climber, occurring in dune thicket in a restricted area east of Port Elizabeth, with elongated branches bearing differently shaped greenish, obovate leaves which are usually concave at the top, and an erect thyrse, on a sturdy peduncle up to 200 mm long and 4-5 mm in diameter at the base with 1-3 dichasia. Leaves of C. woodii are somewhat similar to those of C. pendens, but they are flattened and only 4-6 mm thick. It is furthermore a much slower grower, has erect, woody branches and solitary flowers (rarely two), but always produced among the leaves on a much-reduced inflorescence. The flowers are slightly smaller (tube 15 x 8) than in C. pendens (20 x 13 mm). The apices of the calyx lobes in C. woodii become spreading and are usually not adpressed to the corolla as in C. orbiculata, C. pendens and C. adscendens. The squamae of C. pendens are transversely oblong, 2 mm high and 3 mm broad, the sides rounded and with a slight emarginate apex. It is the broadest measurement of squamae diameter recorded for any species of Cotyledon. They are also transversely oblong in C. woodii, but much smaller (0.8 x 2 mm). Another unique feature is the flowers on the inflorescence which open in succession and not all together as in other Cotyledon species. Cotyledon orbiculata is a very variable species which occurs sympatric (habitats not shared) with C. pendens, but local forms of Cotyledon orbiculata are always erect, with robust branches, much larger, ascending, green to grey-green leaves and an erect, much-branched inflorescence, 150 mm and longer (2-5 pairs of bracts). A form of C. orbiculata var. orbiculata with small ovoid grey-white leaves similar to C. pendens was described by Dinter as C. orbiculata var. oophylla from southern Namibia; it also occurs in the Alexander Bay region. This plant has similar small grey-white leaves but an erect rigid growth form, a distinct ascending inflorescence 150 mm high and a peduncle 4-5 mm thick. It is also a very slow grower.The vegetation consists of Subtropical Thicket rich in succulent plant species. Its pendent, flaccid stems, leaves and inflorescence are well adapted to life on the cliff face. The plants are rapid growers branching freely from the nodes. Cuttings grow ± 30 mm in length in a single year, becoming freely flowering shrublets 250 mm in diameter. In habitat the plants form conspicuous, dense, drooping mats from rock ledges on the south-facing cliff faces. C. pendens shares its habitat with other succulent plants such as Haworthia cymbiformis var. setulifera, Bulbine thomasiae, Crassula cordata, C. montana subsp. quadrangularis, C. perforata, Drimia anomala, Ceropegia sandersoniae (southernmost record), Albuca batteniana (easternmost record), Peperomia blanda, Rhipsalis baccifera, Ledebouria sp., Ornithogalum longibracteatum, Haemanthus albiflos, Plectranthus hadiensis var. hadiensis and Pelargonium acraeum (new record for the E Cape). Other non-succulent plants sharing the habitat include Ficus burtt-davyi, F. burkei, Scholia latifolia and Bauhinia bowkeri.The plants occur in an area that receives rainfall mainly spring to autumn (1000-1200 mm per annum) and the plants flower in summer (December and January). The Mbashe River has a number of endemic obligate cliff-dwelling plant species including Aloe reynoldsii, Bulbine thomasiae and our two new taxa.The small, neat, striking, whitish grey-green, pendent foliage and pendent inflorescences of large, red flowers (Red Group 39a, RHS Colour Chart) make Cotyledon pendens a handsome introduction to horticulture. The red tubular flowers suggest sunbird (Nectarinia) pollination. They last for up to 18 days. The rapid growth and freely branching habit make it an ideal plant for embankments, dry stone walls and hanging baskets. It grows very easily from cuttings and does well in containers.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: In these species the carpel bases are strongly lobed and are adorned with papillae. Although closely allied to L. ensifolia, L. sandersonii is easily distinguished by its smaller bulbs (10-30 x 10-15 mm versus 40-60 x 20-30 mm) and the absence of fusiform roots. In addition, the leaves of L. sandersonii are fewer (1-6 vs. 5-10), smaller and broader. Both maculate and immaculate forms of L. sandersonii occur, but mixed populations have never been encountered.
bibliographicCitation: Edwards, TJ; Venter, S. 2003. A revision of Ledebouria (Hyacinthaceae) in South Africa. 3. The reinstatement of L.ensifolia, L.galpinii and L. sandersonii. Bothalia 33(1): 49-51. [CC BY]

description: The most obvious distinguishing character of L. galpinii is the corrugated adaxial leaf surface, embossed with regular pits. L. cooperi is a plant on seepages and vleis, it is soboliferous and quickly forms dense populations. By contrast, L. galpinii is a plant of lithosols and while occasionally producing basal bulbs, is never soboliferous. Bulb morphology differs significantly, L. galpinii has ovate bulbs with truncate apices compared to the acuminate apices of L. cooperi. L. galpinii frequently produces 3 cataphylls but in L. cooperi cataphylls are always solitary. The leaves of L. galpinii are fleshy, flat, broadly ovate and humifuse, whereas those of L. cooperi are mesic, canaliculate, lanceolate and erect.
bibliographicCitation: Edwards, TJ; Venter, S. 2003. A revision of Ledebouria (Hyacinthaceae) in South Africa. 3. The reinstatement of L.ensifolia, L.galpinii and L. sandersonii. Bothalia 33(1): 49-51. [CC BY]

description: Putative hybrid: C. velutina x C. orbiculata var. oblonga.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The most distinctive vegetative feature of L. moniliformis is its rosette of numerous terete leaves, their upper two-thirds with prominent dark green, raised fleshy swellings.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: Euchaetis avisylvana is distinct on account of having villous-ciliate leaves tipped with a few hairs at the apex; lanceolate-acute, white, somewhat petal-like calyx lobes and acute petals. It differs from E. elata E. & Z. which has leaves, bracts, bracteoles and calyx lobes much shorter and ciliolate not villous-ciliate, and also the blade of the petal elliptic-apiculate not lanceolate-acute. The very short horns of E. avisylvana at once distinguish it from E. longicornis Williams which has very sharp pointed leaves; bracts, bracteoles and calyx lobes with scattered gland dots. The name is a latinisation of grootvadersbos, the locality where the type material was gathered.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1978. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 7. J. S. African Bot. 44(4): 329-362. [CC BY]

description: Euchaetis diosmoides is recognised as distinct having the disc open, sinuate-crenulate as in Diosma, the style at some stage deflexed, the stigma 0.3-0.5 mm diameter, and leaves acute, incurved-mucronate. It appears to be nearest to E. schlechteri which differs in having the style always erect with the stigma 0.6-1.0 mm diameter.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: In the centre of the distribution range on north-facing slopes in the vicinity of Jonaskop and Galgeberg, plants may be found with much broader leaves in which the gland dots are more conspicuous. Euchaetis flexiiis is recognised as distinct having the disc obvallate not closing over the ovary and not spreading, having no involucral leaves, having the style at some stage deflexed, haying petals only 3.6 mm long obtuse and having leaves obtuse with the apex sacculate with margins not villous ciliate but minutely ciliolate and broadly translucent. Sonder observed 'easily known by its smaller leaves with a wide hyaline margin, laxer inflorescence, and more obtuse calyces & bracts'.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: When ripe, the seeds, as is normal in the Diosmeae, are ejected by a catapult mechanism and may be thrown a distance of a few feet from the parent plant. Regeneration takes place after fires. The plant has a pleasant odour when crushed, reminiscent of aniseed. It appears to have a rather extended flowering period, the type collection, made in June, having both fruiting and flowering heads. Furthermore the florets in a single head are found to be in all stages of flowering. Pollination appears to be effected by small insects. In the early stages of flowering the style is bent to one side, and it only becomes erect at a later stage when the anthers, having shed their pollen, are withdrawn from the centre of the floret. Euchaetis glabra is recognised as distinct on account of its having orbicular-elliptic petiolate leaves with thin margins and in its being a completely glabrous plant.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1973. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 2. Euchaetis glabra Williams sp. nov. J. S. African Bot. 39(3): 229-232. [CC BY]

description: The plant is single stemmed at base and apparently will not regenerate after fires from the stump so that one presumes that it can only regenerate from seed. It differs from both Euchaetis scabricosta and Euchaetis meridionalis in having leaves that are always opposite with the midrib recurved, somewhat smaller, orbicular in outline with gland dots scattered and not just on midrib and margins. The shoots are dry without any trace of resin or wax.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1978. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 7. J. S. African Bot. 44(4): 329-362. [CC BY]

description: In the Caledon Division the bracts and calyx lobes are pale, almost white in colour, while those of the populations to the north are dark or reddened. This may be due to their exposure to sunlight at higher altitudes. Euchaetis linearis is recognised as distinct having the disc standing open as in Diosma and the style at some stage deflexed, having leaves linear-acute with a straight sharp point, quite glabrous, hyaline margins, serrulate or smooth and fruits with horns not more than 1.5 mm long. Another useful character is the almost petiolate shape of the petal. The numerous small gland dots in the leaves readily distinguish E. linearis from E. elata where they are much larger in size and fewer in number.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: This is one of the most complex species in the genus Crassula with a number of local forms, some of which are more or less geographically isolated. Yet each of these varieties shows some overlap with one of the other varieties, with the result that extensive hybrid populations often blur the already difficult delimitation even further. Much more field work is required to evaluate all the local forms.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: This plant is placed in the genus Euchaetis Bartl. & Wendl. because it possesses the following characters: (1) Flowers 1-3-nate. (2) Petals transversely bearded. (3) Staminodes vestigial. (4) Anther with a minute apical gland. (5) Disc well developed, exceeds the ovary. (6) Stigma capitellate. (7) Style short and glabrous. (8) Filament virtually glabrous. (9) Ovary 5-carpellate. Euchaetis longicornis is recognised as distinct on account of its having subulate leaves, sharply pointed bracts and bracteoles, acuminate calyx lobes and a fruit with exceptionally long horns, a character to which the name refers.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1975. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 5. J. S. African Bot. 41(3): 167-186. [CC BY]

description: It is nearest to Crassula perforata, a very variable taxon and with a wide distribution, occurring from Worcester in the Western Cape to central KwaZulu-Natal. It differs from that species by its much larger broadly ovate leaves and short rounded thyrse with pedicellate (2-5 mm) flowers. Although C. perforata is highly variable with many local forms (Tolken 1977, 1985) and C. badspoortense occurs sympatric with it, the latter is a distinct and rather invariable species with no hybrids observed between the two taxa. Crassula perforata and C. badspoortense are also related to C. sladenii Schonland which has a similar rounded thyrse and pedicellate flowers, but it is found only in the Richtersveld (Northern Cape) and southern Namibia.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2001. Crassula badspoortense Van Jaarsveld, a new species from the Western Cape Province. Aloe 38(1&2): 29-30. [All rights reserved]

description: Euchaetis tricarpellata is recognised as a distinct species because of its three-chambered ovary. It differs from E. dubia var. dregeana which has leaves and calyx lobes crisped ciliate and a 4-chambered ovary.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1975. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 6. J. S. African Bot. 41(4): 239-268. [CC BY]

description: The much-branched habit distinguishes C. barklyi from C. columnaris. Single branches of these species can only be distinguished by the leaves which are bulging and have a ridge along the main vein on the exposed surface in C. columnaris.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species readily distinguishable from the others when complete material is available. Leafy specimens of some forms of E. crispa var. ovata are, however, distinguishable vegetatively from E. coriacea but the flowers are quite different, the corolla of the former being cleft more than halfway down. Allied to E. tomentosa, of which the leaves are not undulate and elliptic to obovate.
bibliographicCitation: De Winter, B. 1963. Ebenaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 54-99. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: E. dewinteri is most closely related to E. crispa, especially in flower structure. Our species differs from E. crispa in (i) having the leaf blades ovate to elliptic and not obovate to lanceolate; (ii) not having leaf blades with undulate margins; and (iii) having much shorter peduncles than E. crispa. E. dewinteri differs from the other known species of the genus in growth form, being a virgate single- or multi-stemmed shrublet, 1-2 m high with divaricate branching at the end of the stems.
bibliographicCitation: Retief, E. 1986. Ebenaceae: A new species of Euclea from the Transvaal. Bothalia 16(2): 228-229. [https://doi.org/10.4102/abc.v16i2.1092] [CC BY]

description: Flowering material of this species is easily distinquished from C. saxifraga by its star-shaped flowers and by a few bracts subtending the branches of the subumbellate inflorescence. However, in the fruiting stage the corolla of C. capensis closes up and might be mistaken for tubular flowers; furthermore the bracts are caducous and care must therefore be taken when such specimens are identified.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Very closely allied to E. acutifolia from which it is almost indistinguishable vegetatively. The glabrous anthers of the male flowers and the long exserted style of the female flowers, which are arranged in lax not congested inflorescences, as well as the glabrous branches of the inflorescence distinguish this rather rare species from E. acutifolia.
bibliographicCitation: De Winter, B. 1963. Ebenaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 54-99. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very variable taxon which is distinguished from a number of similar species by its glabrous sepals which are rarely longer than 2 mm. Several local forms are distinguishable:1. Small plants with usually ovate leaves which are often 4-ranked, at least in the juvenile stage, occur widespread in the Great Karoo. An extreme form with strictly 4-ranked leaves is found mainly in the Baviaanskloof between Willowmore and Humansdorp.2. A glabrous form which was described as C. rhodogyna from south-eastern South West Africa/Namibia.3. A similarly glabrous form but with thick narrow leaves was described as C. nuda from the Little Karoo.4. Another extreme form of the narrow-leaved type reproduces vegetatively by its very brittle leaves which break off at the slightest handling. Often dense stands of these plants are found in the area between Graaff-Reinet and King William's Town and Greytown in central Natal.5. Some plants from near King William 's Town seem to simulate the flowers of subsp. capitella with a stiffly erect corolla, but the petal apex is not very fleshy, and the distinct style and small terminal stigma leave no doubt that these plants should be identified as subsp. thyrsiflora.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Related to E. tomentosa from which it can, however, be quite easily distinguished by the lanceolate to narrowly oblong boat-shaped bracts on the inflorescence, the rusty indumentum, and the shape of the leaves which tend to be elliptical. The bracts in E. tomentosa are ovate to rotundate, are large and fall off very soon, and the leaves are mostly obovate with a hoary indumentum. The distributions also differ, E. tomentosa being mainly found in the drier north-western Cape.
bibliographicCitation: De Winter, B. 1963. Ebenaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 54-99. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A species closely allied to E. schimperi from which it differs mainly in the leaf shape and texture and the hairy ovaries. Some robust specimens with large leaves are difficult to distinguish from E. schimperi and it is possible that hybridisation sometimes takes place where the species are in contact.
bibliographicCitation: De Winter, B. 1963. Ebenaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 54-99. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An isolated population in the mountains near McGregor has a similar habit and linear leaves, but the corolla is white, the squamae oblong and the leaves usually somewhat fleshy. These characters are more reminiscent of C. rubricaulis, but the length of the corolla suggests that the plant should be placed with C. cymosa.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Flowers arranged in whorls of three, with included, declinate filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: The shape and size of the leaves vary considerably from one locality to another; usually they become longer and narrower towards the north while they tend to be rather broad in the south-east.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The most distinctive feature of this species is that the lower leaves are borne in whorls of four. In depauperate plants the first leaves are usually entire whereas in vigorously growing plants the leaves soon become dentate. Such plants often bear small tubers in the axils of the leaves. These propagules break off and soon develop into new plants.Unusual in the range of variation is a hairy form recorded from the Cedarberg Tafelberg.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: In some areas two extreme forms can be distinguished, one with broad leaves (2-3 mm) and with a leaf sheath 1.5-3 mm long, the other with leaves rarely broader than 1 mm and with a leaf sheath up to 1 mm long. In other areas a range of intermediates between the two forms is found.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The size of the plant and the number of flowers as well as their size varies considerably according to environmental conditions. In addition some local variation can be observed in the colouration of the petals, which may vary from pure yellow to more or less orange around the throat and in the floral tube. The spreading lobes are rarely completely orange but even within a single population considerable variation is often found.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Only C. exilis Harv. subsp. cooperi in EC.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Some local variation in the shape and size of the leaves is found. While they are particularly broad on plants from the Cape Peninsula to Bredasdorp (3-5 times as long as broad), they are much narrower in the Koue Bokkeveld (6-8 times longer than broad).
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Most of the variation present in this species is due to environment. At times the leaves are as small as those of C. obtusa, but plants of C. fascicularis can always be recognised by the sessile flowers, by the base of each flower being partly covered by bracts, and by the narrow petal apices. Under particularly favourable conditions the leaves might be as much as 3-4 mm broad, which is within the range of C. coccinea but the latter species is easily distinguished as it usually has larger flowers and the leaves tend to be 2-3 times longer than broad.Some plants from the area between Du Toit's Kloof and Stellenbosch, and also the Cape Peninsula have white flowers instead of the more usual cream to pale yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The prominent, narrowly lanceolate white bracts (4-16 mm long) of L. longibracteata are longest in the upper part of the inflorescence and most conspicuous in the blue forms. The lower inner tepal is usually slightly shorter than the upper inner tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: Stands out amongst the members of section Lachenalia as the only species with yellowish- to deep brownish- maroon tepals. It is also unique within the genus in having prominent papery, bright white bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: Young plants of C. fusca usually have ovate leaves, but subsequent ones become gradually narrower until only the typical lanceolate leaves are produced.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The two syntypes are equally well recognizable as belonging to this species, but as it is not recorded on the sheets which specimen represents which collection it seems of little value to select a lectotype.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Under adverse conditions the plants usually produce only one seed per carpel and the aborted, usually lower ovule is easily overlooked when the pericarp breaks off the receptacle.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Plants from near the Olifants River mouth often show a great reduction in the number of hairs on the leaves, and occasionally completely glabrous plants are found.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: L. glauca has cernuous, oblong-campanulate perianths with well exserted, straight stamens and inflated scapes. L. glauca differs from L. violacea in its shorter perianth tube (1 mm long), greyish-mauve tepals, white or greyish-mauve filaments, heavy coconut scent, unmarked, usually narrower leaves and smaller globose seeds (0.9-1.0 x 0.9-1.0 mm), which have shorter inflated strophioles (0.5-0.6 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: C. maputensis differs from its neighbour C. expansa by the broader, flat, obtuse leaves, narrowing distinctly towards the base; by the flowers disposed from below to above along the stem and branches, while in C. expansa they are placed only along the upper half; by the thinner pedicels; by the relatively shorter sepals, usually only 1/3 as long as corolla whereas in C. expansa they are equal 1/2-2/3 as long; by the broader petals which are less connate at the base and, on account of this, somewhat spreading (they are nearly erect in C. expansa); and by the follicles being longer and more tapering into the styles.
bibliographicCitation: Fernandes, RMSB. 1983. 67. Crassulaceae, Fl. Zambes. 7(1): 3-74. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, London. [CC BY]

description: Differs from L. barkeriana in having lanceolate, prostrate leaves, a terete scape, longer inner tepals (10-13 mm long) and filaments that are not swollen in the upper half.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: The plants are very small with short leaves and irregular margins, rather different from those of F. felina.
bibliographicCitation: Groen, LE; Van der Maesen, LJG. 1999. Revision of the genus Faucaria (Ruschioideae: Aizoaceae) in South Africa. Bothalia 29(1): 35-58. [CC BY]

description: Study of the living material confirmed some relationship between F. nemorosa and F. subintegra. The reduction of the teeth in F. nemorosa is almost complete, being reduced to small tubercles. The fruits are similar, rather small, tightly attached on the plants and often broader than long. The scarce ecological data on F. subintegra indicate differences in habitat between the two taxa. F. subintegra is restricted to shallow hollows or crevices in bare sandstone rocks in full sun under very dry circumstances. F. nemorosa grows in soil in the understorey of shrubs in partial shade. SEM micrographs of F nemorosa show culicular folds which are also found in F subintegra, a common feature for Faucaria that is missing in Orthopterum.
bibliographicCitation: Groen, LE; Van der Maesen, LJG. 1999. Revision of the genus Faucaria (Ruschioideae: Aizoaceae) in South Africa. Bothalia 29(1): 35-58. [CC BY]

description: Intermediate plants have been found between F.felina subsp. britteniae and F. subintegra. The leaf shape was that of F. subintegra, the number and shape of the teeth those of F. felina subsp. britteniae It is unknown if these intermediate populations are the result of natural hybridisation.
bibliographicCitation: Groen, LE; Van der Maesen, LJG. 1999. Revision of the genus Faucaria (Ruschioideae: Aizoaceae) in South Africa. Bothalia 29(1): 35-58. [CC BY]

description: Some populations of F. felina subsp. britteniae at Hell's Poort, 35 km west of Grahamstown and near Fort Beaufort, look like F. tigrina because of the numerous large flecks on the leaves and the long bristles. However, the leaves of F. felina subsp. britteniae are larger, not pressed against each other and the number of teeth is reduced to 5 or 6. Forma splendens published by Jacobsen & Rowley in 1955, was recognised on the basis of its reddish leaves, typical for some populations. F. tigrina 'Superba' is a superfluous synonym, used in seed catalogues to differentiate good plants and seed, reintroduced by Mrs Dudley Ryder, from the usually inferior hybrids named F. tigrina.
bibliographicCitation: Groen, LE; Van der Maesen, LJG. 1999. Revision of the genus Faucaria (Ruschioideae: Aizoaceae) in South Africa. Bothalia 29(1): 35-58. [CC BY]

description: At a glance F. felina subsp. tuberculosa can be identified by the tubercles on the leaves which are unique in the genus. A typical plant is compact, with whitish dots and patches and resembles F. tigrina. Cultivated hybridised plants often show tubercles more prominent than in wild material.
bibliographicCitation: Groen, LE; Van der Maesen, LJG. 1999. Revision of the genus Faucaria (Ruschioideae: Aizoaceae) in South Africa. Bothalia 29(1): 35-58. [CC BY]

description: The rostrate petal apex without a dorsal appendage characterises this species within the section. It can be distinguished from the superficially similar C. subulata by its tuberous roots.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: C. natalensis has flowers rather similar to those of C. vaginata but they are white and flowering plants are readily distinguished by their distinct basal rosette as well as by the absence of a fleshy root stock. Invariably the short leaf sheath (up to 3 mm) will identify specimens of C. natalensis.While plants from low altitudes usually have marginal cilia with a swollen apex, the cilia are hair-like in plants from higher altitudes. Intermediate specimens usually show a whole range of variation on different plants as well as on the same plant.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: An often locally common species but often misidentified as it varies in size and habit according to environmental conditions.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: This species can be divided into three more or less clearly outlined forms which in extreme cases may be mistaken for distinct taxa:-1. Plants from the south are characterized by their long leaf sheath (3-5 mm long), but specimens from the Cape Peninsula and the Hottentotshollands Mountains usually have short leaves (up to 20 mm long) with cilia becoming reduced or lost from the apex downwards.2. East of Genadendal the leaves are longer than 20 mm and have distinct marginal cilia, and characteristically their corolla is 40-50 mm long.3. The northern population is characterized by its short leaf sheath (2-3 mm) in spite of their often long leaf blade (up to 50 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Herbarium material of this species is usually easily identified because older leaves tend to be covered with silvery scales in comparison to the powdery bloom of C. arborescens. The leaves vary considerably in size and shape and in the moister areas of Natal their size approaches that of C. arborescens, which occurs west of Prince Albert. In the field the characteristic flowering period helps to distinguish this species from forms with leaves covered with a bloom as they have been recorded from Natal.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The different organs show varying degrees of fusion with the central axis. This crust-like species with indehiscent fruits often remains visible for a long time on clayey soils.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The bulb is very similar to that of forms of L. revoluta from the Transvaal, but the leaves are more attenuate and much firmer-retaining their shape so that, after growth has commenced in spring, the previous season's dead leaves often persist. They are similar in texture to the leaves of Schizocarphus nervosus [as 'Scilla nervosa'], but the rigidity is given by collenchyma not sclerenchyma.
bibliographicCitation: Jessop, JP. 1970. Studies in the bulbous Liliaceae: 1. Scilla, Schizocarphus and Ledebouria. J. S. African Bot. 36(4): 233-266. [CC BY]

description: Very variable species, two subspecies widespread in EC.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although the species is obviously very similar to C. tetragona it is easily distinguished by its flat leaves and late flowering time.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Two subspecies endemic to EC: C. pubescens Thunb. subsp. radicans (Haw.) Toelken; C. pubescens Thunb. subsp. rattrayi (Schonland & Baker f.) Toelken.

description: It closely resembles F. polita subsp. polita, but differs from it in respect of the cuneate lamina base and the relatively long lamina which is up to three times as long as the petiole and two to three times as long as wide.

description: Plants of C. rogersii should not be confused with hairy forms of C. cultrata as its leaves are rarely longer than 25 mm, distinctly convex and without a sharp margin, and flowers are densely clustered in the part-inflorescences.

description: This species has a distinctive tall straight trunk with a whitish bark.
bibliographicCitation: Berg, CC. 1991. 156. Moraceae, Fl. Zambes. 9(6): 13-76. [CC BY]

description: This species is distinguished from the very similar C. pallens by the cilia on the leaves and sepals, its stringy bark and its more scrambling habit.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: L. atrobrunnea is related to L. viscosa Jessop which also has cylindrical bulbs and erect leaves. It is distinguished by its linear-lanceolate, non-viscid, twisted leaves and its hard purplish brown (hence the specific epithet) bulb scales.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, S; Edwards, TJ. 1998. A revision of Ledebouria (Hyacinthaceae) in southern Africa. 1. Two new species. Bothalia 28(1): 15-17. [CC BY]

description: C. saxifraga usually produces a branched rhizome with several tubers, a phenomenon which can also be observed in other species in this section. Each of these tubers will develop its own leaves and, in contrast to other species, the rhizome remains intact for more than one year in C. saxifraga.The size of the tubers varies greatly from 30-90 mm in diameter in semi-arid regions on the eastern slopes of the mountains between Worcester and Nieuwoudtville to rarely broader than 25 mm along the western and southern Cape coast. The leaves are usually produced after flowering in C. saxifraga, but in the mountains of the south-western Cape they are often found at the same time as the flowers. These plants are distinguished from C. capensis by the absence of the two bracts at the base where the inflorescence starts branching and by the tubular corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: L. aurioliae is a very variable, inconspicuous plant. The bulb is surrounded by hard, dark brown outer scales with distinctive fasciculate apices that are especially long in forms from the Tanqua Karoo. The broadly lanceolate to ovate, glaucous leaves are heavily spotted or banded with magenta on the leaf bases and the spicate or racemose inflorescence consists of urceolate, spreading to cernuous flowers arranged in distinct three-flowered whorls. Outer tepal colour varies from light blue to light grey with prominent brown apical gibbosities, and the inner tepals from translucent white to yellowish-green, with slightly recurved apices. The stamens are declinate, and included to shortly exserted.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: In contrast to the leaves of C. fusca those of young plants of C. sladenii are longer and often narrower than those produced on mature plants.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Very similar to Massonia pygmaea, with which it shares linear tepals not sigmoid-recoiled at the base, and outer and inner filaments of different lengths with blackish anthers, but differing in the fusion of the filaments into a short collar or column 1.5-2.5 mm long, whereas the filaments in typical M. pygmaea are fused only at the base for 0.5-1.0 mm. In addition, the ovary in M. dregei tapers imperceptibly into the style whereas the transition from ovary to style in M. pygmaea is more abrupt. The type of M. dregei and other collections from Lamberts Bay have the upper surface of the leaf mostly ornamented with distinctive pustules topped with several (rarely one) obtuse to acute trichomes, forming fascicles or short longitudinally elongated crests running along and between the main veins, typically with several shorter secondary trichomes or papillae on the crests as well. Investigation of wild plants at Lambert's Bay shows that there is variation in the leaf surface, most plants showing the characteristic crests or fascicles of papillae or setae but others with mostly a solitary seta per pustule and a few with completely smooth leaves lacking any excrescences or pubescence.

description: A coastal species of neutral or calcareous sandy flats, recognised by the tuberculate-pustulate leaves, often spotted or even entirely flushed purple, and the white or pinkish flowers with narrow perianth tube 2-3 mm diam., not occluded at the mouth by filament invaginations, with slender filaments (8-)12-17 mm long that are shortly connate at the base for up to 1.5 mm, and relatively small, yellow anthers 1.5-2.0 mm long at anthesis. The large, obovoid-cuneate, 3-winged capsules, (15-)20-30 mm long are also characteristic. Populations from De Hoop Nature Reserve are anomalous in their short filaments 8-10 mm long, but are otherwise florally and vegetatively consistent with the species.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2019. The genus Massonia Thunb. ex Houtt. (Hyacinthaceae: Scilloideae) in the Core Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 121: 329-354. description: Recognised by its yeast-scented flowers with broadly funnel-shaped perianth tube 8-13 mm long with a wide mouth 5-6 mm diam. and tepals that are sigmoid-flexed or -recoiled at the base, and relatively long filaments, 11-18(-20) mm long and connate at the base for 1-3 mm in a pale or reddish collar, with diagnostic large anthers 3-4 mm long at anthesis. The leaves are either smooth or sparsely to more densely papillate or even echinulate, sometimes only distally. Rarely the leaves may be verrucose with the epidermal cells forming fascicles of papillae on each verruca.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2019. The genus Massonia Thunb. ex Houtt. (Hyacinthaceae: Scilloideae) in the Core Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 121: 329-354. description: The subspecific taxa recognized by Tölken and R. Fernandes are not adopted here and only the following three forms are outlined. These were found to be linked by ranges of intermediates: 1. The typical form from the central Transvaal never has very elongated branches so that the plants consist of one to several rosettes. 2. From near Barberton through Swaziland and into northern Natal the plants are very similar to the previous form except that their leaves are glabrescent to glabrous. 3. Along the escarpment from north of Barberton to the Soutpansberg plants tend to be more delicate and have elongate branches but in several areas intermediates to the typical form can be observed.

description: Although this species seems to combine the characteristics of C. exilis and C. capitella subsp. thyrsiflora it has a different distribution to these two species.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Massonia latebrosa can be distinguished by the leaves streaked longitudinally with purple and covered by inflated, spheroidal to ellipsoidal trichomes bearing a smooth surface.

description: Distinguished from both M. plumbea by having the leaves fully developed and flat on the ground at flowering time.

description: Readily diagnosed by the ñobconic perianth tube 10-12 mm long with an open mouth 4-5 mm diam., tepals that are sigmoid-recurved basally, and strikingly bicoloured filaments, (11-)15-22 mm long and whitish for most of their length but connate at the base in a thick, obsidian-green or bluish black collar 2-5 mm long, and with relatively large anthers, 2.5-3.0 mm long at anthesis. The leaves are usually tuberculate-pustulate but are smooth in some collections The large, obovoid-cuneate, emarginate, 3-winged capsules, 20-30 mm long, are also diagnostic.

description: C. tuberella is very similar to C. inanis but is distinguished by its erect altogether more delicate habit- even in standing water the branches remain erect, 1(-3) flowers per leaf axil and by the underground tubers at the end of the rhizomes. As Friedrich states, the distribution areas of the two species overlap. They were, however, never found growing together and are therefore considered to be distinguished by both habit and habitat.

description: Court (1982) includes F. angustifolia K.Schum. as a synonym of F. comaru, while Bruyns & Klak (2006) maintain F. angustifolia as a separate more northern species.

description: Plants growing in exposed positions often form an almost flat disc rather reminiscent of C. pageae, but if conditions change subsequently, the younger internodes will elongate. It is interesting to note that the pedicel will elongate up to 15 mm even in depauperate plants.

description: Tölken mentioned three elements which can be discerned within the species. These have now been described as different species by Friedrich, a status accepted here although more research is needed to delimit the taxa clearly.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The two species C. muricata and C. whiteheadii have very similar shrubby habit and produce succulent root tubers, but the latter is distinguished by the distinct dorsal petal appendage, the presence of cilia on the leaves as well as the sepals and the anthers which are at least 1 mm long.

description: In EC this plant has long been called C. nanum (E.Mey. ex Benth.) Engl. This name was sunk under C. plantagineum by Fischer (1992) but this may be incorrect, especially as there is a large gap in the distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Linderniaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 1173-1174. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Leaves in adult plants of F. pulchra are longer (15-25 mm) than in F. humilis (shorter than 15 mm ). Leaf colour also varies slightly between the two species, those of F pulchra having a bluish tinge, whereas those of F. humilis are tinged brown or purple. The windowed tips of the leaves, however, differ conspicuously between the two species. Windows of F. pulchra are convex when turgid, slightly concave when flaccid and those of F. humilis are concave even when turgid, with crenulate markings along the margins. These leaf differences were also noted by Zimmermann (1996). Flowers of F. pulchra are bright magenta with a white or light yellow centre and are 25-35 mm in diam. Those of F. humilis are white with a yellow centre, sometimes tipped with pale pink, and are generally smaller (15-20 mm diam.). Occurs west of Pretoria in the Rustenburg area (F. humilis E of Pretoria).
