description: In this species the peduncle is more or less oblique, while the raceme is erect. There is thus a distinct angle at the base of the raceme. The leaves are flat to D-shaped in section and the flowers are pinkish brown. Plants may be stemless or caulescent. In A. spicata, the only species with which A. vryheidensis is likely to be confused, the leaves are channelled, the raceme is narrower and the flowers are greenish yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Glen, HF; Hardy, DS. 2000. Aloe. In: G Germishuizen & E du Plessis (eds), Aloaceae (first part), Fl. S. Africa 5(1,1): 1-167. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209564#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: In inflorescence characters, the Wolkberg form is almost identical with the Zoutpansberg form of A. sessiliflora, but from all forms of A. sessiliflora it is distinguished by having a much stouter stem, shorter thicker and much more fleshy leaves, which are arcuate-erectly incurved and form much more compact rosettes. The buds are also less obscured by their bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Reynolds, GW. 1974. Aloes of South Africa, 3rd ed. A.A. Balkema, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Although superficially similar to A. greatheadii, this species is useless to bees as the flower is too narrow to admit them.
bibliographicCitation: Glen, HF; Hardy, DS. 2000. Aloe. In: G Germishuizen & E du Plessis (eds), Aloaceae (first part), Fl. S. Africa 5(1,1): 1-167. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209564#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Usually recognizable in the section by its exceptionally elongate inflorescence, and more calycine flowers, the sepals being longer in proportion to the corolla than in the other species.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica albertyniae is characterized by the distinctive 3-nate adpressed, small, ovate leaves which are as long as or shorter than the internodes, the shallowly grooved calyx, the smooth corolla, and the 2-locular 1-ovulate ovary (G2/1) without an enlarged columella in the fruit. The species is probably most closely allied to the more widespread E. glabella subsp. laevis which grows in the same region. It differs in the distinctive 3-nate leaves (not 4-nate) and the shallower angles to the calyx. The testa sometimes has scattered pits which are lacking in the latter species.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: The flowers show considerable natural variability, both in size and colour. The perianth varies from deep rose pink to nearly white and is 7-11 cm long. Some of the forms have been afforded varietal and even specific rank but field observations do not support this treatment. The peduncle of A. belladonna persists for a lengthy period after the ripening of the seeds. This contrasts with the collapse of the peduncle just above the bulb of species of Brunsvigia and Crossyne ['as Boophone'] for example, whose ripe inflorescences are rolled about the veld by wind during seed dispersal.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA; Letty, CL. 1955. Amaryllis belladonna L. Fl. Pl. South Africa 30t.1200 [CC BY]

description: E. alnea is most closely related to E. cupuliflora on account of the bulbous joined base of the calyx but differs in having a broadly ellipsoid corolla, muticous anthers placed on short broad filaments and with short stout setae on the adaxial edges of the thecae, a glabrous ovary and far exserted cyathiform stigma. Dulfer's (1963) species has an open cyathiform flower, scabrid anthers with long awns, a sparsely pubescent ovary and subcapitate-cyathiform stigma which is included. He likened his species to E. micrandra Bolus but that species has remarkable small anther thecae with relatively large narrow crests, and also to E monantha Compton which has aristate leaves and belongs to the E. longipedunculata Lodd. complex. The species could also be mistaken for E. tenuis Salisb. or E. leptopus Benth. which have the same general facies but simple stigmas.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 1995. Studies in the Ericoideae (Ericaceae). XVI. Six new species of Erica from the western Cape, South Af. Bothalia 25(1&2): 87-95. [CC BY]

description: In structure this species is nearest to E. acuta Andr. but there are many differences in detail and dimension. The rather peculiar anthers are, however, similar.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA. 1971. Taxonomic notes on Erica. J. S. African Bot. 37(3): 169-176. [CC BY]

description: In floral structure this is near to E. maesta, but it is separated by its much longer and 4-nate leaves, and different habit; also to E. coarctata.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Bracteoles basal, leaf-like; corolla short (± 3.5 x 3.5 mm); filaments broadish, straight or with slight S bend subapically, with slight spoon-like base; anthers muticous; ovary woolly; fruit smooth, not wrinkled.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2002. Six new species and one new subspecies of Erica (Ericaceae) from Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 32(2): 167-180. [CC BY]

description: Erua amatolensis is most closely related to the morerecently described E. passerinoidcs and E. hillhurttii.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F; Brown, NE. 1909. Ericaceae: III. Ericinella. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 318-319. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15242#page/332/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: This species connects this section [§ Amphodea] with Oxyloma, approaching to E. cumuliflora, which it much resembles, but differing by its 3-nate flowers in fewer-flowered heads, and its appendiculate, less distinctly lateral, anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The plants rarely grow higher than 60 cm (2 ft) and are sparsely branched. Each branch terminates in a set of 3 or 4 flowers which do not always mature at the same time. Under cultivation the plants may be induced to form a bushy shrublet and to produce many more flowers. The flowers are somewhat variable in different localities both in length and in the amount of swelling in the lower part but, in its best form, the flower is the perfect example of the ampule or flask-shape referred to in the introduction. In Flora Capensis Bolus describes the var. obbata. It is separated from the type on the shorter and fatter corolla. The variations mentioned above do not allow for this variety to be regarded as a separate and distinct species.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Unique in Aponogeton with inflorescences resembling Ranunculus flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Cook, CDK. 2004. Aquatic and wetland plants of southern Africa. Backhuys Publishers, Leiden. [All rights reserved]

description: This new species is characterized by its compact, dense habit, glabrous leaves, white flowers with erect to spreading lobes, pedicel mainly with simple hairs and very few plumose hairs admixed and a capitate-peltate stigma. It is a high altitude species. It is most similar to the widespread and common E. calycina, especially the Cederberg form, which differs in having larger appendages on the anthers (about twice the size), many more plumose hairs on the stem and pedicel, a hairy ovary with truncate stigma, finely hairy leaves, and in growth is woody and erect up to 1 m tall. Several of the collections of the new species were originally identified as being E. calycina.It is also similar to E. laxa [= E. lucida var. laxa] which differs in having dense plumose hairs on the stem, leaves and pedicel and pink flowers. It is a coastal endemic on recent sands of the west coast, north of Cape Town. The typical E. lucida is widespread along the mountains of the western region from Cape Town to the Kamiesberg in Namaqualand, and forms sparsely branched, fastigiate shrubs, up to 1.5 m tall.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2001. Four new species of Erica (Ericaceae) from Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 31(1&2): 1-8. [CC BY]

description: Brilliant orange or sulphur-yellow flowers with a dark eye make it instantly recognisable among all other Colchicaceae.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P; Condy, GS. 2011. Baeometra uniflora (Jacq.) G.J.Lewis. Fl. Pl. Africa 62: 2-9, t.2261 [CC BY]

description: Erica angulosa is characterized by the extreme length of the calyx relative to the corolla (mostly as long as the corolla tube); the deeply grooved calyx; the enlarged cyathiform to peltate stigma; the lack of any basal nectaries of the ovary. The species is clearly related to some forms of E. uberiflora in habit, general form of the calyx and the short corolla and was at one stage considered by myself to be just an inland form of that species. However, it can be distinguished by the very short corolla in relation to the calyx, the enlarged stigma and lack of nectaries. The only variable characters found in the species are the degree of hairiness of the calyx lobes and the occasional loss of anther spurs.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Boophone haemanthoides differs from B. disticha in the following : The perianth tube is shorter. The perianth segments remain erect or sub-erect until they wither. The spathe valves are larger. The perianth is cream-coloured becoming reddish only with age.
bibliographicCitation: Gerstner, J; Leighton, FM; Levyns, MRB. 1947. Plantae novae Africanae. Series XXVII. J. S. African Bot. 13: 53-64. [CC BY]

description: Stem glaucous, green when young; capsule 4-6 mm long, valves emarginate, without a little horn at the external point of the nectary.
bibliographicCitation: Muller-Doblies, D; Muller-Doblies, U; Reid, C; Ward-Hilhorst, JE. 1990. Bowiea gariepensis Van Jaarsv. Fl. Pl. Africa 51t.2007 [CC BY]

description: B. comptonii is distinguished by the densely macropapillate upper surface of its few, small leaves, its small inflorescence with short pedicels, 10-25 mm, obsolete perigone tube, <0.5 mm long, and upwardly flared tepals, 15-27 mm long. Other features of the flower are variable. Plants from the inselbergs between Ghaamsberg and Pofadder have filaments that are more markedly declinate than elsewhere. Plants from northern Bushmanland and central Bushmanland also occasionally have translucent, lateral wings (up to 5 mm long) near the base of both filament whorls. These may be apically pointed or ± smoothly tapering towards the apex. In southern Bushmanland , near Langberg , in the Tanqua Karoo and near Matjiesfontein, appendages are occasionally present near the base of the filaments as minute, lateral thickenings.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 2012. A revision of the Brunsvigia radula-group (Amaryllidaceae: Amaryllideae) of species in South Africa, including the description of Brunsvigia gariepensis a new species from Bushmanland in Northern Cape. S. African J. Bot. 79: 106-116. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2012); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Erica areolata is characterized by the ovary being mostly 1-locular, 2-ovulate, relatively unsculptured and with a distinct narrow glabrous style, four to six stamens which are mostly fused throughout the length of the filament, short calyx relative to the corolla and large hard red fruits remaining on the plants for some time. The species is similar to E. parviporandra from the Klein Swartberg, but there are no cilia on the corolla lobes, the anther thecae are differently shaped with pores larger and more basally attached and the filaments are broader when not fused.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Characters which assist in distinguishing the species are, the broad, obtuse scarcely undulate perianth segments, the stamens which are arranged in two very distinct rows, the short ones being only half as long as the rest, the few erect to spreading leaves, and the large bulb with the neck exposed above ground.
bibliographicCitation: Barker, WF. 1963. Two new species of Amaryllidaceae. J. S. African Bot. 29: 163-166. [CC BY]

description: Allied to E. marifolia and resembling it in miniature; but differing in the sepals, corolla, and the anthers, the latter being both shorter and broader; also to E. hirta, to the flowers of which (especially the short-sepaled form) it is very near; but the habit, pubescence and anthers are different. The pubescence appears to be more silvery than in either of the two species above named.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica artemisioides is easily recognized by the assymmetrical 1-locular 1-ovulate ovary with a subapical style which is distinct and flexed and also by having mostly six stamens which have connate anthers but free or only basally fused filaments and with the thecae apically strigose.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: It is well recognised now that the Cape Peninsula plant has velvety leaves when fresh. Professor R. H. Compton writes: 'B. orientalis, the Cape Peninsula species, with velvety leaves, normally has the bulbs completely (or almost so) below the surface of the sandy ground in which it grows, and the leaves spread out flat on the surface.' The leaves may be slightly roughish on the upper surface when dry. There has been quite a degree of confusion at various times between the names B. orientalis and B. josephinae, perhaps because of the general similarity in the irregular flowers, but there are marked differences in detail and the bulbs and leaves are also very different.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1951. A review of the genus Brunsvigia Heist. Pl. Life 7(1): 45-64. [All rights reserved]

description: Differs from the other species in having erect perianth segments.
bibliographicCitation: Barker, WF. 1963. Two new species of Amaryllidaceae. J. S. African Bot. 29: 163-166. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species, with the aspect of plants of the § Hermes, from which it is separated by its strictly terminal inflorescence. Wood’s 693 appears to be a short-stamened form of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Jacquin in 1797 explicitly stated that B. radula has a pair of thick-textured leaves, which are rough with short, hard trichomes on the adaxial surface. Inserted on large pustules and densely covering the adaxial surface, the ±2 mm long, ivory-coloured trichomes remain remarkably rigid and upright, even in pressed specimens. The leaf margins are thick and tough and fringed with similarly hard, short, curved bristles. Florally B. radula is difficult to separate from B. comptonii and B. namaquana, as all three species have similar, small, pink, few-flowered inflorescences. Although flowering specimens of B. radula have not often been collected, the flowers are not known to have appendages at the base of the filaments. In the wild only a small number of plants seem to flower each season.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 2012. A revision of the Brunsvigia radula-group (Amaryllidaceae: Amaryllideae) of species in South Africa, including the description of Brunsvigia gariepensis a new species from Bushmanland in Northern Cape. S. African J. Bot. 79: 106-116. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2012); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by the extreme fineness of its leaves. This species must not be confused with E. aspalathifolia, Bolus.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: These plants seem to hold together in a natural group, but at the same time show a fairly wide range in time of leaf production, in their surface and also in the size and shade of flower. Out of this assemblage one could quite conceivably have sorted out a number of specimens and given them specific rank, but this would not for long have successfully masked our ignorance. In the Orange Free State with low and late summer rainfall the leaves are absent at the time of flowering, whereas in Natal, with medium rainfall, they are produced with the inflorescence (the peduncle arising outside the new leaves). This difference in time of leaf production is probably due to habitat conditions. Some specimens have the leaves rough-granular on both surfaces, others are rough on the upper surface alone, but very rarely smooth on both surfaces. There are many other variations; for instance, concerning specimens from the neighbourhood of Fauresmith in the Orange Free State, a collector recorded: ' I am sending you today another Brunsvigia. The bracts are quite different from all I have seen up to now. In this plant they are red and fleshy, not pink or membranous. The colour of the perianth is more red than the previous specimens.' Several other similar examples of variation could be cited.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1951. A review of the genus Brunsvigia Heist. Pl. Life 7(1): 45-64. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to E. podophylla, which is somewhat remarkable from the fact that their native localities are so far apart. The strongly nerved corolla of the present species would alone serve to distinguish it, and is very unusual in the genus. This species affords a transition to the § Gypsocallis, and might almost equally well have been placed there on account of its partially axillary inflorescence, but the anthers are not fully exserted, and it has hardly the appearance of that section.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica atromontana is characterized by the non-accrescent, rather rigid calyx which is large relative to the corolla, with the sepals being fused for about half their length, the short thick anther appendages, the 2-locular ovary (G2/1) and the minutely capitate to cyathiform stigma. It is most similar to E. montis-hominis which differs in having an almost free calyx, 1 -locular ovary (G1/1) which is acute and anthers with minute appendages.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is allied to E. conica and to E. viscaria. From the former it is distinct by its less robust habit, its leaves usually fewer in the whorl, and always shorter and less acuminate.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: A well-marked species, allied to E. tegulaefolia, differing in corolla and anthers. Salisbury says the leaves are sometimes 3-nate; we have not seen such. It is also allied to E. irregularis.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Botanically this species is interesting as, although it is closely related in habit to several species in the section Ephebus, it is entirely glabrous as a rule and on that account was placed in the Section Leptodendron. It could also be classified with the marsh-loving species in section Ceramia. It has, however, been placed among the species in Ephebus by Dr. Dulfer in Ann. Nat. Hist.Wien 68 : 72 (1965), In the present work the species has been placed in Ceramia next to Ephebus.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: If the plant is held up by the tuber, the erect leaves detach from the tuber without any external pressure. The leaves are extremely delicate and bruise at the slightest pressure.
bibliographicCitation: Williamson, G. 1996. New Bulbine species (Asphodelaceae) from the northwestern Cape. Haseltonia 4: 13-23. [All rights reserved]

description: At first glance this species looks very much like many other pink-belled species. A closer examination shows that it possesses a feature unique in the genus, namely completely reflexed sepals. This character alone serves to distinguish E. bergiana from all other species.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: B. lavrani is distinguished from other Bulbine species by the coal-black, carrot-shaped tubers and single succulent, 3-4 mm broad, erect, terete to subterete leaf. At present, of the known species, only B. monophylla is unifoliate but differs from the new species in that the tuber is almost ovoid, there are at least two basal leaf bracts, the leaf is much longer, ca. 180 mm and proportionately narrower and the inflorescence is more robust. B. lavrani flowers during the hottest summer months, end of February into March, before the leaves develop. The flowers open before the sun rises and remain open all day. In horticulture the leaf elongates unnaturally and occasionally a second leaf appears. An interesting feature is the strongly carnation-scented flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Williamson, G. 2006. New species of Bulbine Wolf (Asphodelaceae) from the Northern and Western Cape Provinces of South Af. Aloe 43(4): 91-95. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica binaria is characterized by having most floral organs not hairy (excluding margins), the calyx lobes triangular and abaxially flat, mostly eight stamens with hairs at the base of the anthers, and a 2-locular 1-ovulate ovary which produces an elliptic fruit with a number of irregular longitudinal grooves.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: E. blandfordia is similar superficially to E. sitiens of this section but can in no way be misidentified as such on account of its yellow flowers and different distribution range.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Bulbine meiringii is characterised by its oblong tubers bearing slightly fusiform roots and by the slender, linear-lanceolate, glaucous leaves. In contrast, B. cremnophila has shorter, much more fleshy leaves, and lacks the oblong tuber and fusiform roots. B. meiringii is also closely related to B. rupicola occurring towards Klipplaat in the north-east. The latter has ovoid tubers and short, ascending, green, somewhat channelled leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2003. Four new cliff-dwelling Bulbine taxa (Asphodelaceae) from the Eastern and Western Cape. Aloe 40(1): 4-7. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica bolusanthus is characterized by the small flowers with relatively short calyx which is not accrescent, the usually 2-locular ovary, far-exserted stamens, usually enlarged stigma and the hard pustulate fruit with distinct slit-like grooves.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: E. borboniaefolia belongs to that group of species in the section Lamprotis in which the leaves are opposite and not whorled as is the case in most species of Erica, In this respect it is similar to E. lutea and E. tenuifolia L., which, however, have much smaller flowers. The species is similar to the form of E. pycnantha Benth. that has been recorded from the Hottentots-Holland Mountains but not yet described.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The new taxon is well distinguished by the vegetative growth form and ovoid tubers. The leaves emerge as a rosette, are very succulent and terete to basally subterete.
bibliographicCitation: Williamson, G. 2000. Four new, succulent Bulbine species (Asphodelaceae) from the Western and Eastern Cape Provinces of the Republic of South Africa. Bradleya 18: 31-40. [https://doi.org/10.25223/brad.n18.2000.a3] [All rights reserved]

description: A distinct species, although it is difficult of location. In general appearance and in its small inconspicuous dull-coloured flowers, it resembles species of the § Arsace but is separated by the exserted anthers. It approaches E. demissa, but is smaller and more slender in habit and the corolla and sepals are quite different.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Bulbine truncata has some affinity with B. diphylla but differs in that the short leaves are distinctly truncate and subtended by a short, tight sheath.
bibliographicCitation: Williamson, G. 1996. New Bulbine species (Asphodelaceae) from the northwestern Cape. Haseltonia 4: 13-23. [All rights reserved]

description: Niven, 74; Burchell 7300, 7333; Borcherds in Herb. Bolus 5958; Galpin, 3608; also cultivated specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Bulbinella barkerae may be confused with B. caudafelis, but is separated from that species by a number of features, especially the spreading leaves with regularly ciliate margins, the smaller greyish green fruits, the seeds with a broadish wing extension and also the strong-smelling flowers. B. barkerae is easily separated from the other species with ciliate margins, B. ciliolata, on locality and also on the broader and fewer leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Perry, PL. 1999. Bulbinella in South Africa. Strelitzia 8: 1-78. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is allied to the common and widespread E. globiceps with which it shares the 4-nate leaves and 3-merous flowers. It can easily be distinguished by the enlarged stigma and lack of any sulcus on the lobes. These latter characters it shares with E. erina which occurs slightly further west but which has the calyx angles opposite the lobes and 3-nate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: The section Apoecus contains only two species, E. brownleeae and E. caffrorum, which are characterized by having 4-nate leaves and very large imbricate sepals. E. brownleeae is separated from the latter species by its larger flowers and broad-crested anthers. Both species form large shrubs up to 3 and 4 metres high (10-13 ft) and grow in moist areas on the higher mountains of the Eastern Cape. In many cases the plants grow near forests and form part of the forest edge. Neither of the species has been recorded from the area of the Cape Flora proper, i.e. west of Port Elizabeth. This section is thus the only one in the genus that is not represented in the south-western and southern Cape. Flowering from December to March, but also at other times during the year.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Superficially the species appears to be distinct but is, however, closely related to E. propinqua Guthrie & Bolus and E. excavata L. Bolus. The latter two species are erect shrublets with bright pink flowers. The anther awns in E. calcareophila are straight while in the other two species they are sharply curved and spreading. The leaves of the former are recurved, sometimes markedly so, and in the others they are erect and straight.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Those forms which have been collected northwards towards Clanwilliam diverge from the others by a poorer growth and smaller leaves and flowers, the result probably of climatic influences; but the floral structure differs little.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: E. canaliculata is one of the few species of Erica that may be classed as a `tree heath', since it may grow to a height of 1.9 m (6 ft) and more under favourable conditions. In this respect it is like E. caffra L. which may grow up to 20 and 30 ft alongside mountain streams. Flowering at all times of the year but mainly in summer.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Two other species, Bulbinella divaginata and B. trinervis, are of similar size and have narrow leaves similar to those of B. triquetra, but their leaves are almost terete and without denticulations, not trigonous and with finely denticulate margins as in B. triquetra. They are both autumn-flowering species with leaves in an early stage of development at anthesis, whereas B. triquetra is spring- to early summer-flowering with the leaves having completed development at flowering. B. trinervis has white flowers, whereas B. divaginata and B. triquetra have yellow flowers, but the two last-named species are clearly separated by the sheathing leaf bases in B. triquetra, whereas in B. divaginata the fibrous sheath is formed from separate cataphylls.
bibliographicCitation: Perry, PL. 1999. Bulbinella in South Africa. Strelitzia 8: 1-78. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to E. bruniades, this species grows on dry sandy flats and is becoming very rare due to the spread of housing estates and of alien vegetation in the Cape Peninsula.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Characterized by the 2-locular 1-ovulate ovary, four stamens which have bipartite anthers, two to twelve whorls of flowers per inflorescence which is umbel-like, the fruit with very thin papery pericarp, and seeds with a very thin transparent testa.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Essential characters; the hard, woody roots, knobby rhizome, flattened scape, small dark bracts, pedicels articulated near the base and very short filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: The typical plant (cultivated) had wide leaves; those from moist areas also have them but some from around Pretoria and several other localities have a much narrower lamina, a xerophytic adaptation. The very long, subulate bracts and the flowers congested on the simple raceme are typical for the species. Although there are usually about 15 ovules per cell, the type plant was said to have 20-30 ovules. The doubling of one or both rows of ovules occasionally occurs. C. ntagnificum Weimarck from Southern Rhodesia seems to be a wide-leaved luxuriant form of C. bowkeri.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: Bracteoles basal, leaf-like; corolla long, ± 9 x 4.5 mm; filaments narrow straight with spoon-shaped base; anthers muticous; ovary glabrous; fruit with large, irregular wrinkles/folds.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2002. Six new species and one new subspecies of Erica (Ericaceae) from Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 32(2): 167-180. [CC BY]

description: Characteristic of this species are the leafy tufts at the apices of the racemes. These bend down to earth because of their weight and take root. In this way they multiply very rapidly and cover vast stretches in the undergrowth of the eastern Cape forests. The plants however do not always produce these leafy rosettes. Those seen from the northern Transvaal never had them.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: An extremely variable species, chiefly as to pubescence, leaves, and size of corolla. The species is one of the most widely spread in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The size of the bracts varies from small and green to large, white and membranous; the type (form a) according to the description, has the large bracts, a common form in the Drakensberg area. It is very similar in appearance to A. capitatum which Baker separated because of the papillate (not smooth) filaments. I suspect that this variation in the filaments may be the result of hybridization, possibly with A. saundersiae. The Transvaal and eastern Cape specimens show a form with small, green bracts, somewhat more lax inflorescence and fairly short, falcate leaves (form b). This form agrees with A. pachyphyllum Bak. It was not practicable however, to maintain these forms as separate species.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: Flowering at any time during the year.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: E. meianihera is closely allied and similar in appearance to E. chamissonis. The chief differences between the two species are several. In E. chamissonis the leaves are quite different in appearance, being more or less open-backed and bearing long hairs, the peduncles and sepals are densely villous not merely pubescent and the anthers are not or scarcely produced beyond the pore. The two species occur in different areas which do not overlap and flower at different times of the year. In distribution E. melanthera is interesting in that it is confined to moist slopes along the entire length of the Langeberg and Outeniqua Mountains and on Swart berg Range further inland with records from the isolated mountains in the Little Karoo. In this respect it is an excellent example of the link between the floras of the moister southern mountains and the drier Swartberg Range. Flowering at any time during the year, but mainly in spring.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica chionodes is distinguished by the long, dense, spike-like synflorescences with pure white, finely hairy flowers, partially open-backed leaves, long, narrow, pendulous anther appendages and hairy ovary. It is closest to E. oreotragus E.G.H.Oliv. which is common along the full length of the Swartberg Range and has flowers in terminal 6-8-flowered heads on main branches (not in spike-like synflorescences), glabrous, mostly shorter pedicels, longer sepals which are about half the length of the corolla and have fewer longer hairs, relatively long corolla lobes, and anther appendages shorter than the thecae and broader and hairy. It is also allied to the new species, E. blaerioides.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2001. Five new species of Erica (Ericaceae) from the Swartberg Range, Western Cape, South Africa, and a no. Bothalia 31(1&2): 155-165. [CC BY]

description: Related to the tropical African species C. gazense Rendle, C. laxum R. Br. and C. petiolatum Bak.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species, somewhat anomolous by its inflorescence in this or any of our sections. It was placed by Bentham in § Plalyspora, but is unlike that by its calycine flowers. Bentham had not seen mature seeds, nor have we.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily distinguished from the related species C. undulatum because of its solitary, long leaf, and from C. lewisae which has several short leaves and a bulbous rhizome.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: Like A. longistylum Bak. and A. haygarthii, this species also has narrow-leaved forms.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: This new species is distinguished by the dense compound synflorescence, the leaves of which are longer than the lateral flowers, the bracteoles often fully recaulescent as the lateral segments of the calyx, the short anther spurs which are partially decurrent along the apex of the filament, and the absence of nectaries. The pseudospicate, columnar synflorescences give the species its name, columnaris = pillar- or column-like. Several species show alliances with E. columnaris based on the long erect tightly packed synflorescences with small corolline flowers and stems with infrafoliar ridges. E. regerminans with a very similar habit and method of branching, differs in its slightly larger, more conspicuous dark pink flowers that are longer than the leaves, its corolla being ellipsoid with a longer pedicel and in the long anther spurs which are not decurrent. E. dodii differs in having a soft delicate growth form, corolla more open cyathiform to campanulate, anthers small and delicate with spurs much longer but slightly decurrent, style included, flowers pink not dark purplish pink and larger and more visible. E. coarctata Wendl. differs in the flowers being slightly smaller and more cyathiform and greenish cream-coloured sometimes tinged pink, the anthers lacking spurs, the stigma peltate-cyathiform and far exserted and the ovary not emarginate.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2000. Notes on African Plants: Ericaceae. Two new species of Erica from Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 30(1): 49-53. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species, the flowers somewhat too coralline for this section, but difficult to place elsewhere. Its nearest ally seems to be E. lachneaefolia Salisb.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The roots are very typical and distinguish it from all other species.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: Clivia mirabilis is distinguished by its straight, actinomorphic, bicolored (orange/yellow) tubular corolla, long drooping pedicels, 25-40 mm long, that are orange-red at anthesis and green when fruiting; the distinctive single median white striation on the upper surface of the leaves with smooth cartilaginous margins; and irregularly shaped glebulose-gongyloid berries. The basal part of the leaves forming the leaf sheath is flushed a deep carmine maroon, unlike any other Clivia except C. nobilis, which occasionally produces similarly coloured leaf bases. The orange-red coloration of the pedicels in this species during anthesis is a unique character in the genus Clivia.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 2002. Clivia mirabilis (Amaryllidaceae: Haemantheae) a new species from Northern Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 32(1): 1-7. [CC BY]

description: Two subspecies are recognized based on the corolla length and colour. Both share the distinctive sepals of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2005. The genus Erica (Ericaceae) in southern Africa: taxonomic notes 2. Bothalia 35(2): 121-148. [CC BY]

description: This rare species is well marked by the one large bract, the minute sepals, and thick rough corolla. It has a general resemblance to E. trichadenia.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Differs chiefly in aspect, the floral characters being almost identical. The anther varies unusually, both in size and shape.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: One of the easiest species to identify on account of its highly congested inflorescence axis with extremely elongate pedicels, the flowers thus apparently borne on 1-flowered peduncles rather than in a raceme. The raceme is never branched, and up to a maximum of 9 flowers are produced, thus very much fewer than in other species. The flowers are strongly enantiostylous, and either white to pale pink with uniformly yellow anthers, or pale yellow with maculate anthers. These colour morphs, which are geographically segragated, are correllated with the position of the bracteole on the pedicels, and are segregated as three subspecies. The large, ellipsoid capsule, 13-15 mm long, is unique in sect. Cyanella, resembling those of C, cygnea and C. orchidifromis in sect. Trigella.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. A revision of Tecophilaeaceae subfam. Tecophilaeoideae in Africa. Bothalia 42(1): 21-41. [CC BY]

description: The species is very variable but may be recognized by its clustered flowers at the ends of the branches and by the large sepals that almost completely cover the corolla. Another feature that is distinctive is the rapid ageing of the lobes of the corolla. Very soon after the flower opens the pale-pink lobes turn brown. Considerable variation occurs in the size of the flowers from the common small-flowered form which is rather insignificant to the very attractive large-flowered form from the Hottentots-Holland Mountains in which the flowers are as large as those in E. taxifolia. The plants of this latter form are generally small and compact. The plants of this species are otherwise erect and rather sparse and do not bear many flowers. A small-flowered form with numerous flowers with large spreading pink sepals occurs in the Riviersonderend Range and is very showy.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to Cyanella orchidiformis, with which its shares characteristically mottled flowers and large, ovoid-ellipsoid capsules ± 15 mm long and greyish or purple markings or speckling on the anthers. C. cygnea typically has smaller flowers, with tepals 8-10 vs (8-) 10-15 mm long but is best identified by its stamens. The strongly geniculate-sigmoid filaments of the posterior (upper) stamens are bulbous at the base and filiform in the distal half, giving them a characteristic flexuous form, with the outer pair slightly longer than the median. All three anthers in the posterior cluster are subequal in size, 1.5-2 mm long, and the lower anthers are equally larger, 2.5-3.0 mm long. In contrast, the upper stamens in C. orchidiformis are ± uniformly thick except at the extreme apex and not evidently flexuous, the outer anthers are slightly smaller than the median, and the lower anthers are larger 5-6 mm long, sometimes with the median larger than the laterals. The distributions of the two species are largely complimentary, with C. cygnea occurring to the north and west of C. orchidiformis but they overlap around Steinkopf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. A revision of Tecophilaeaceae subfam. Tecophilaeoideae in Africa. Bothalia 42(1): 21-41. [CC BY]

description: E. corydalis is a rather twiggy little shrub with unusually shaped flowers which resemble those of E. thunbergii. The flowers, which are white, soon turn brown when picked and have slightly viscid sepals and bracts. The anthers' shape, besides being very complicated, is somewhat variable and difficult to describe. The anthers are also covered with a strange white fungus-like substance.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Near to some forms of E. copiosa.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Cyanella pentheri has mostly been treated as conspecific with C. hyacinthoides, essentially because of the confusion between true C. pentheri and what we regard as pubescent forms of C. hyacinthoides. Florally, the two species are certainly alike in their moderately dense, branched racemes of spreading, white or mauve to blue flowers with 5 + 1 arrangement of stamens with the filaments connate for ± half their length or more, but they differ significantly in their foliage. The leaves of C. pentheri are consistently linear and canaliculate-involute, mostly 1-4 mm wide, with margins that are conspicuously ciliate only towards the base with long, shaggy hairs 2.0-3.0 mm long. Similar, long cilia also fringe the upper catapyll, which is funnel-shaped, and strikingly pigmented with deep purple along the edges and veins, giving it a characteristic fenestrate appearance. The leaves of C. hyacinthoides, in contrast, are mostly lanceolate and 4-15 mm wide, rarely narrower, with margins either smooth or ciliolate-pubescent along their entire length, with much shorter hairs 0.2-1.0 mm long, and the upper cataphyll is usually unmarked. Pubescent forms of C. hyacinthoides from central Namaqualand have leaves that are variously puberulous to villous but never with the long cilia characteristic of C. pentheri.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. A revision of Tecophilaeaceae subfam. Tecophilaeoideae in Africa. Bothalia 42(1): 21-41. [CC BY]

description: In general appearance, and in the flowers, resembling E. myriocodon, but distinct by its constantly 3-nate and broader leaves, and its larger oblong anthers. Also very near to E. planifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The species should not be confused with two closely related species. E. seriphiifolia Salisb. has shorter, erect to incurved leaves, smaller flowers and three bracts and E. tetrathecoides Benth. has a much more open habit with flowers in looser umbels, scattered leaves and is entirely glabrous. All three species occur in the same area and in the same type of habitat. E. seriphiifolia does however tend to grow in drier places. E. cubica occurs abundantly in very wet marshes, seepages or bogs along the Southern Cape coast. It has been recorded from scattered localities as far north as Zululand. The form from the summer rainfall area is described as var. natatensis. Flowering mainly from September to November but also at other times during the year.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The crowded globose flowering heads of E. cumuliflora make the species easily recognizable. The first impression of the `flower' is a single large globose white flower which is in fact a densely packed head of 5 to 12 flowers, each with its set of exserted black anthers. The corolla possesses lobes that are long compared with the tube and are unusually shaped. The corolla is white but the lobes are brown in colour. This resembles the condition in E, genistaefolia to which E. cumiluflora is most closely related. It can be distinguished from the former by its 4-nate leaves and dense capitate flowering heads.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is apparently rather variable as populations have been studied in which the flower colour ranges from red, through red with yellow lobes to orange and clear yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: The current concept of the genus Cyrtanthus includes both Vallota Herb, and Anoiganthus Baker. The latter was originally separated on the anthers being sagittate and basifixed rather than dorsifixed. This has proved to be fictitious. Both Vallota and Anoiganthus differ from most species of Cyrtanthus in having the perianth tube shorter than the lobes. However, in C. guthrieae L. Bolus, C. thorncroftii C. H. Wright and C. bicolor R. A. Dyer tube and lobes are described as more or less equal in length, and in the recently published C. montanus R. A. Dyer the perianth is said to be divided for about two-thirds of its length. Clearly the reduction of Vallota and Anoiganthus is justified. Cyrtanthus brachysiphon is interesting because at first sight it looks more like the usual run of Cyrtanthus than do the plants previously placed in Vallota and Anoiganthus. The subsequent observation of its short perianth tube, which seems to place its affinity with these other short-tubed species, came as a surprise. It is thus fair to say that C. brachysiphon provides a final link justifying the current concept of the genus.In the recently published account of the genus (C. Reid & R. A. Dyer, A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus, 1984) C. brachysiphon runs down to C. bicolor R. A. Dyer, but differs from it, in addition to the shorter perianth tube, in having broader blunter leaves (in C. bicolor they are only 4-5 mm broad and gradually narrowed to an acute tip).
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1986. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XII. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 43(2): 189-228. [CC BY-SA]

description: The robust form (corresponding to C. breviflorus, sensu stricto) and the slender form (corresponding to C. luteus).
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: It is sometimes confused with another 'fire-lily', C. tuckii, although the perianth shape, dimensions and colouring are different in that species.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: As in C. montanus, the bulbs produce large numbers of bulbils which take two to three years to flower in cultivation. Within populations the flower colour can be rather variable. The normal colour is bright crimson but forms have been found in which the base or entire perianth is white. Pink forms also occur.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: The author of C. erubescens was faced with the problem of where to place the species-in Cyrtanthus or Anoiganthus. The characters used by authors to distinguish the two genera, namely relative length of the perianth tube to the segments (Phillips, 1951), and position of insertion of the anthers (Baker, Handb. Amaryllid. ix. 1888), did not hold, and consequently he placed the species in Cyrtanthus, sensu lato. In addition, Gouws (1949) and Wilsenach (1963), found that the ideograms of the two genera were more or less identical. Anoiganthus was eventually sunk by Gordon-Gray and Wright (1969).
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: This species (named 'eucallus' for the beauty of its flowers) is evidently closely related to C. sanguineus. The flowers, however, are much smaller and the perianth segments spread widely but do not recurve as in C. sanguineus; the anthers are also differently placed. The entire plant is more luxuriant with up to six flowers per umbel and longer, broader leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: Cyrtanthus flammosus appears to be most closely related to C. guthiieae (endemic to elevated, rocky habitats in the Bredasdorp district) and C. elatus (known from moist ravines of the George, Knysna, Uniondale and Humansdorp districts), and shares with these species erect flowers, uniseriate stamens and obovate, outspread tepals which give the flowers a flat-rimmed appearance. However, it is distinguished from these species by its thick-textured, lorate leaves which taper and thicken proximally. These characteristically tapering leaves also occur in C. sanguineus and C. galpinii but these are not as thickened. Furthermore, the flowers of C. sanguineus and C. galpinii differ by having a curved perigone tube and biseriate stamens which are distinctly declinate in C. sanguineus.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA; Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Ward-Hilhorst, JE. 1995. Cyrtanthus flammosus Snijman & Van Jaarsv. Fl. Pl. Africa 54: 100-103, t.2120 [CC BY]

description: The species is distinguishable from others in this difficult section mainly by the sepals being broader above the middle and being deeply toothed or denticulate like a comb. The flowers are also somewhat inflated. It approaches very near to a variety of another very variable species E. daphniflora. The flowers are usually arranged in distinct clusters up the branches. In colour they are usually pure white varying to creamy-white or greenish-white. Occasionally, pinkish and yellow forms are recorded. Despite the apparent delicate appearance of the flowers, the species lasts well when cut. The corollas are hard and wax-like and not soft like many other species.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is one of the showiest in this section of the genus. The bright yellow flowers are usually sweetly scented.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinct in the section by its long corolla, and the long (3/4-1 lin.) petioles of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Flowering from February to August but chiefly in late summer and autumn.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to E. Nabea, of which it has somewhat the appearance in miniature; but the sepals are much smaller, and the corolla larger and differently shaped.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: This attractive species is evidently closely related to C. sanguineus, which is of more robust habit and in which the broad part of the perianth tube is proportionally much longer. C. galpinii ranges in colour from red to pink.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: In the description, Mrs. Bolus mentions that the species is a connecting link with Vallota, which has subsequently been transferred to Cyrtanthus.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: This species differs from C. clavatus mainly in its spirally twisted leaves. The habitat is also somewhat drier than that of C. clavatus. The adaptive significance of twisted leaves is not known; it is certainly common in plants of arid habitats and is not always constant in those species of Liliaceae and Iridaceae which exhibit the phenomenon.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is distinguished by the presence of a bract and two bracteoles in all flowers, the thick obconical calyx which is shallowly lobed, the smooth corolla and the considerably enlarged columella in the fruit. It is most closely allied to E. piquetbergensis and E. dregei and to E. glabella subsp. laevis.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: It is closely allied to E. dominans, with which it is at least partially sympatric, but, along the face of the Drakensberg, E. dominans may be found on Cave Sandstone platforms and rocky grass slopes, as well as in stream gullies, to which E. dissimulans is confined. Typical E. dominans from the summit plateau has leaves mostly 2-3 mm long and between 0-75 and 1 mm broad; these are erect and closely appressed; but along the face of the escarpment, not only do the plants grow taller, and bear slightly larger flowers, but also the leaves are often longer, and then they may be recurved, as in E. dissimulans. However, the leaves of E. dissimulans are proportionately narrower than those of E. dominans; for example, a leaf of E. dissimulans 3-5 mm long will be 0-5 mm broad, but a leaf of E. dominans of the same length will be 1 mm broad. Furthermore, the leaf margins in E. dissimulans are clad in small glands, which may soon fall; the leaf margins of E. dominans are clad in coarse hairs that are often forked; these may fall to leave stubs, so it is best to examine young leaves, especially the margins in the lower half of the leaf. The styles in E. dissimulans scarcely exceed 1 mm in length; those of E. dominans are usually 1.5-2.25 mm long: plants with slightly shorter styles may occur on the summit plateau, but then the leaves are small and appressed, and no confusion can arise.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XI. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 227-260. [CC BY-SA]

description: The shape of the corolla is nearly that of E. pusilla; but the habit (usually more divaricately-spreading), inflorescence, size of the anthers, and the shape of their appendages, are different. The latter closely resemble those of E. pubescens and E. hirtiflora.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely allied to the next [E. regerminans, Linn.]; distinguishable by its spreading not virgate habit, its shorter and narrower pseudo-spikes, corolla not at all constricted at the throat, besides some minor characters.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The bulbs produce numerous offsets.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica dolfiana is characterized by 4-nate leaves with relatively long petioles; relatively large bract and bracteoles about the size of the sepals, but remote from them, sepals white with long-stalked red marginal glands, urceolate glabrous white corolla, which is relatively small for the genus, glabrous anthers with long narrow appendages and thin filaments, enlarged subpeltate to peltate stigma, and the standard reticulate/alveolate ericoid-type seed.E. dolfiana shows no close affinity to any other species. It may, however, be related to E. lignosa H.A.Baker, a widespread Swartberg species, and 'to E. jugicola E.G.H.Oliv. ined., a more restricted new species. Both have similar long-stalked red glands on the bract, bracteoles and sepals, but both have larger, pink flowers (very much larger in the latter) which are mostly finely hairy. They also have larger anther appendages and a small simple stigma. All three species are sympatric on the genus, glabrous anthers with long narrow appendages and thin filaments, enlarged subpeltate to peltate stigma, and the standard reticulate/alveolate ericoid-type seed.E. dolfiana shows no close affinity to any other species. It may, however, be related to E. lignosa H.A.Baker, a widespread Swartberg species, and 'to E. jugicola E.G.H.Oliv. ined., a more restricted new species. Both have similar long-stalked red glands on the bract, bracteoles and sepals, but both have larger, pink flowers (very much larger in the latter) which are mostly finely hairy. They also have larger anther appendages and a small simple stigma. All three species are sympatric on the Blesberg.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2001. Five new species of Erica (Ericaceae) from the Swartberg Range, Western Cape, South Africa, and a no. Bothalia 31(1&2): 155-165. [CC BY]

description: C. loddigesianus is definitely not the same as C. helictus, which has spirally twisted leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is distinguished from others in this section by its longhaired ovary, the others having short-haired ovaries. The description here gives the corolla length as varying from 10 to 14 mm. It seems likely, according to Esterhuysen (Journ. S. Afr. Bot. 29 : 52 (1963)) that E. phillipsii L. Bolus is just a short-tubed variety of this species. E. phillipsii occurs on the mountains of the Tulbagh and Ceres Districts.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: West of the main centre of distribution there occurs a form with darker salmon-pink flowers. This group (C. clavatus, C. loddigesianus, C. speciosus, C. helictus and C. smithiae) are, apart from relative differences in size and the presence of spirally twisted leaves in the latter two species, very similar. Here, population studies are essential to determine whether the differences are merely environmentally induced or whether they remain stable in cultivation.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: C. epiphyticus, C. obrienii, C. junodii and possibly C. rectiflorus and C. rhododactylis all probably represent forms of C. macowanii. It is evident that C. macowanii should be regarded as a widespread, variable species occupying a range of habitat.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica dregei is characterized by the lack of bracteoles, the pilose calyx being obscurely 8-angled and rounded, and a 2-locular ovary (G2/1). It is closely allied to E. piquetbergensis and to E. dispar. The secondary ridge running down the midrib below the calyx lobes is markedly increased in this species and causes the deep grooves present in the other species to become somewhat obscured. It is clearly a late summer-flowering species whereas the nearby E. piquetbergensis is a spring flowering species. This is surprising as the low-altitude habitat of E. dregei, being situated in the strictly winter-rainfall region, must be very much drier than the habitat of E. piquetbergensis on the upper mountain slopes in late summer.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: No authentic specimens have been seen. This probably represents a form of C. macowanii Bak.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: This is another species in which, as the name implies, the flowers are fragrant.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: No authentic specimens of this species have been seen. From the Bot. Mag. plate it appears to be related to C. macowanii Bak.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is superficially similar to E. rufescens Kl. which occurs in the same mountain range. A close examination shows that the latter species has a finely hairy corolla and free anthers. Flowering in summer.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The flowers apparently emit a strong scent of cloves, also described as 'nutmeg and pepper'. This species and C. rotundilobus are distinguished from the remainder of the C. macowanii group by the presence of a solid peduncle. This character is of unknown significance.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: A conspicuous feature is the large green spathe-valves which remain erect and green at anthesis in contrast to C. contractus, in which they are usually withered at this time.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica erina is a very distinct species in the genus with its long exserted style with small peltate stigma and a single relatively long stigmatic process. It also has no sulcus on the hirsute calyx lobes which have the distinct calyx ridge opposite them. The species is clearly allied to the widespread E. similis with the calyx ridge opposite the lobes and not alternating as in most other species, the reduction in the calyx sulci and the hirsute calyx.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: A conspicuous feature is the large green spathe-valves which remain erect and green at anthesis in contrast to C. contractus, in which they are usually withered at this time.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: The identity of this species is not certain. Authentic specimens have not been seen.
bibliographicCitation: Reid, C; Dyer, RA. 1984. A review of the southern African species of Cyrtanthus. American Plant Life Society, La Jolla Stanford. [All rights reserved]

description: The highly zygomorphic lower flowers in which the outer tepals are greatly exaggerated in size make this species instantly recognizable. It is also characterized by large floral bracts that are persistent and papery in fruit. D. aurea occurs in two colour forms, the more common one a brilliant red and the other canary yellow. Populations are typically uniformly coloured, although red populations will often contain occasional yellow morphs, whereas yellow populations may include a few plants in which the tepals are flushed reddish at the tips. The yellow populations consistently come into flower one or two weeks before the red but the fruits appear to take much longer to ripen. The prominent papery bracts that are characteristic of the species are particularly conspicuous in fruit, serving as sails that assist in the wind dispersal of the infructescences.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Merwe, AH. 2002. Systematics of the genus Daubenya (Hyacinthaceae: Massoniae). Bothalia 32(2): 133-150. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished from other species in which the filaments are fused into a long, narrow column by the peculiar disc that occludes the mouth of the column and through which the style protrudes via a narrow pore.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Merwe, AH. 2002. Systematics of the genus Daubenya (Hyacinthaceae: Massoniae). Bothalia 32(2): 133-150. [CC BY]

description: This has somewhat the habit and appearance of E. bicolor, but the flowers are usually fewer and less prominent. It is very distinct in this section by its anthers; none of those which are muticous being so small and few even of those which are appendiculate.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the well-exserted conical inflorescence of strongly scented, yellow flowers with linear tepals and free filaments. A distinct feature of D. namaquensis is the bilabiate lower flowers in which the upper side of the perianth tube is prolonged for ± 2 mm beyond the lower side, resulting in a distinct sinus between the three upper and three lower tepals. This differential in the tube length rapidly becomes less evident higher up the inflorescence and the upper flowers are quite actinomorphic.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Merwe, AH. 2002. Systematics of the genus Daubenya (Hyacinthaceae: Massoniae). Bothalia 32(2): 133-150. [CC BY]

description: The species is isolated in distribution and relationship. Although it has a flower similar to E, physodes it has a number of very distinctive characters. The leaves are rough-edged, very thick and out-curved and around the flowers form a type of involucre completely hiding the peduncles and bracts. The flowers are characteristically borne in a tightly packed nodding head.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Living plants of D. zeyheri are readily recognized by the conspicuous purple centres to the flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Merwe, AH. 2002. Systematics of the genus Daubenya (Hyacinthaceae: Massoniae). Bothalia 32(2): 133-150. [CC BY]

description: Said by Bentham to resemble in habit E. marifolia, but to be more rigid and more branched. It is closely allied to the three next [E. setosa, E. straminea and E. lerouxiae]; but our material, with the single exception of E. lerouxia, is too scanty to enable us to decide satisfactorily whether or not they should all be regarded as varieties of this, or be maintained as distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: In many respects it is similar to the following species E. thimifolia. The latter may be distinguished by its non-sticky flowers, broad leaves with a bristle at the tip, the broad-based filaments and exserted anthers with minute appendages. E. filiformis is distinguished from the other species in the section by having exserted anthers without appendages, leaves that are linear and not open-backed and by having sticky flowers. The species is interesting botanically because of the variation in the number of stamens. The number, which is not constant but usually the same on one plant, varies from 4 to 8. Those plants with only 4 stamens would, technically, be classed as members of the genus Blaeria in which this is a feature. As most of the specimens have been recorded with 8 stamens, the species has been placed in the genus Erica.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Similar to Drimia convallarioides, but separated by very short filaments, 0.3-0.5 mm vs 1-2 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species. The shape of the corolla is somewhat like that of E, filiformis, but other differences are great. The filaments with their wide spoon-bowl-shaped base are something like those of E, thimifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by its elongate raceme of moderately small flowers, with tepals recurved from near the base, 5-6 mm long and connate for ± 1 mm, and the solitary (rarely two), cylindrical leaves usually present at flowering and mostly 3-5 mm diam. The leaf blade withers from the apex in sections separated by a distinct transverse abscission layer, thus is generally truncate and dry at the apex. The partially sheathing leaf bases have broad, papery, chestnut brown margins, and persist to form a conspicuous collar or neck of papery segments above the bulb. The bracts are small, 1.0-1.5 mm long, the lower with a short spur 1-2(-5) mm long. The capsules are remarkably small for the size of the inflorescence, 4-6 mm long, and contain small, strongly angled seeds 1.5-2.0 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very different from any other species in this section by the peculiar indumentum on its sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The tall flowering stems of Drimia capensis are similar in size to those of D. altissima, but the pedicels in D. capensis are much shorter, 2-6 mm long, giving the raceme a tight, poker-like form unlike the columnar or cylindrical raceme in D. altissima, which has wiry pedicels (8-)10-25(-30) mm long. The floral bracts in D. capensis are much shorter, the lower 3-5 mm long vs 5-10(-15) mm long in D. altissima, but the flowers are larger in all details, the tepal lobes 8-14 mm long vs 5-8 mm long, the filaments 8-10 mm long vs 4-7 mm long, and the style 7-9 mm long and 1.5-2.0 times as long as the ovary vs 2-4 mm long and ± as long as the ovary. The distribution of the two species is complimentary, with D. altissima occurring further east and north. Drimia capensis may be confused with robust forms of D. elata, notably on the Cape Peninsula and around Port Elizabeth where they co-occur, but that species typically has longer floral bracts, up to 25 mm long, without an associated bracteole, a caducous perianth with the tepals connate at the base for 3-6(-7) mm long, thus one fourth to one half their length, smaller anthers ± 1 mm long, and a longer style, 9-13 mm long. Although the leaves are typically glabrous, plants on the Kamiesberg have densely villous leaf margins. This deserves further investigation although similar variation in leaf vestiture is also seen in D. elata.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]
