bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: One of the most characteristic species of the genus, easily recognized by its large flowers with very long filaments and styles. The perianth is usually bi-coloured in contrasting tones of white or rose-pink and deep-purple or maroon. The filaments are slender, usually white-coloured, sometimes rosy, and only occasionally purple-tipped. The undulate character of the leaves is taxonomically virtually useless, since entirely flat-leaved single specimens, or even whole populations, are by no means uncommon. The nectary margin also varies in shape. It is often more or less straight (like in O. vulgare) but not seldom prolonged into a short tongue, which may be entire, emarginate or bilobed. Similar tongue-like projections of the nectary margin also occur in two other species, viz. O. gracile and O. calcicola.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1982. A monograph of the genus Ornithoglossum (Liliaceae). Opera Bot. 64: 5-51. [10.1111/j.1756-1051.1983.tb01058.x] [All rights reserved]

description: The plain white perianth-segments and especially the small club-shaped, echinulate seeds show affinity with the Cape species.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: Allied to E. inclusa, but differs a good deal in appearance by its stouter habit, much longer and acuminate leaves, larger flowers, differently coloured sepals, and aristate (but otherwise very similar) authors. Has been confused with E. holosericea from which, however, it is even more distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: In comparison with the other subspecies its bulbs most readily form bulblets, contributing to the abundance of individuals in most populations. Throughout its range it varies quite considerably in size. The spathe valves of some individuals are as short as 20 mm or as long as 60 mm, while the leaves range from 10 mm to 60 mm across; however, it is always characterised by the dense pubescence on the adaxial surface and the flat leaf blades.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1984. A revision of the genus Haemanthus L. (Amaryllidaceae). J. S. African Bot.: 1-139. [CC BY]

description: This species is somewhat variable in the length, though little in the width, of the corolla, and also in the shape of the anthers. It may generally be distinguished, when in the living state, from all others of this section [§ Hermes], except E. flavicoma, by its yellow corolla. From the latter it may be known by its quite different leaves and sepals, as well as by its anthers; the corolla only, both in shape and colour, is very similar.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The typical variety is characterised by the generally smaller plants, narrower stems and branches, and by the larger cladoles, which are always linear and more than 1 mm long. The flowers are sweetly scented.
bibliographicCitation: Jessop, JP. 1966. The genus Asparagus in southern Africa. Bothalia 9(1): 31-96. [CC BY]

description: This species is characterized by having mostly six or seven stamens which are fused only at the very base or the basal half of the filaments, by its distinctive anthers with very small pores and the strigose apex to the ovoid to subquadrate thecae. The small anther pores, sometimes only 1/8 of the theca, are in contrast to the larger size in the other species of the Coccospermad group. The style is also more distinct than in the first two species. The ovary has four distinct ridges in the upper half and is neither verrucose nor rugose. In the group the species has the largest adaxial calyx lobe-as long as or longer than the corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: The variety galpinii is a xerophytic form, fairly uniform in appearance and is common around Barberton, the type locality, and elsewhere in the Lowveld.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: The leaf in subsp. capense is sub-erect, ovate and entirely glabrous. The abaxial surface frequently has bands of red corresponding to the longitudinal veins. Tubers may be multiple and sometimes produce stolons. The flowering season seems to vary with locality from west to east, starting in November/December in the Ceres Karoo and finishing in February in the eastern Cape.
bibliographicCitation: Perry, PL. 1994. A revision of the genus Eriospermum (Eriospermaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 17: 1-320. [CC BY]

description: Tepals in var. cooperi are a uniform colour in both whorls, being either white or pale green with a darker green midnerve and sometimes with red stippling towards the apex.
bibliographicCitation: Perry, PL. 1994. A revision of the genus Eriospermum (Eriospermaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 17: 1-320. [CC BY]

description: Plants of subsp. mackenii are always entirely glabrous. The 2-4(5) leaves are broadly ovate and the amplexicaul contemporary leaf sheath is usually not exserted above ground. In the more northerly parts of its range, leaves tend to be narrower and may be extended into a distinct leaf sheath.
bibliographicCitation: Perry, PL. 1994. A revision of the genus Eriospermum (Eriospermaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 17: 1-320. [CC BY]

description: This species is easily distinguished by its umbel-like inflorescences with widely divaricate flowers, the flowers being tuberculate-colliculate always with a small bract and two bracteoles approximate to the calyx and by the filaments being aculeate apically and the anthers having large pores 1I2 to 4/5 the length of the thecae. It is closely allied to the rare E. niveniana which is similar in many respects, but does not possess aculeate filaments, has anther pores less than half the length of the thecae and has imbricate leaves and forms a woodier, more erect shrublet.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: This subspecies is distinguished by its 4-angled calyx tube which is distinctly glabrous except for patches of short hairs on the areas between the angles and just below the expanded lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Seeds smooth, papillate or sparsely prickly; inner filaments filiform to broadly subulate or expanded below: plants flowering in spring; Richtersveld southwards to the vicinity of Worcester.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: Allied to E. rhodantha, Guthrie and Bolus, but differs in having longer leaves, the flowering branchlets scarcely developed so that the 3-flowered tufts appear to be lateral, longer pedicels, and manifest anthers. In general appearance recalls E. lacandulifolia, Salisb.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, HML. 1918. Novitates Africanae. Ann. Bolus Herb. 2: 153-162. [https://archive.org/details/annalsofbolusher02bolu/page/152] [All rights reserved]

description: In the Clanwilliam area this variety of the species is represented mainly by slender plants with distinctly lobed corms and simple, few-leaved stems. Further to the north, especially in Namaqualand, stouter forms are predominant, often with simple corms and branching stems. Some of these forms have rather numerous leaves and bracts which overtop the flowers, whereas others are more sparsely leafed, with few and comparatively large flowers. The latter are classified as O. parviflorum mainly because of their short anthers, and in other respects are difficult to distinguish from small-flowered forms of O. vulgare. It is possible that introgression occurs in the border areas where related taxa meet. This may also be the case along the southern limit of its distributional range, where O. parviflorum meets O. viride. Specimens from the eastern part of the distributional area (e.g. Calvinia and Laingsburg Divisions) also deviate in some respects, possibly due to similar causes. The perianth colour also varies, from predominantly green (as in O. viride) to dark maroon or almost black. The claw and the filaments, however, are always light-coloured, at least basally and, together with the light-coloured styles, provide a contrast to the dark tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1982. A monograph of the genus Ornithoglossum (Liliaceae). Opera Bot. 64: 5-51. [10.1111/j.1756-1051.1983.tb01058.x] [All rights reserved]

description: Pec finis = comb; referring to the comb-like leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Many populations have constantly dark-margined perianth segments, whereas others have mixed concolorous and margined flowers. The dark margins are especially distinct in the Clanwilliam-Piketberg area.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: Umbel loose, hemispherical; spathe valves 4-7(-10); flowers rose-pink to white; perianth 7-16(-18) mm long, tube 1-6(-7) mm long, segments 4-10(-14) mm long; stamens equalling the perianth segments or exserted by up to 5(-8) mm.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1984. A revision of the genus Haemanthus L. (Amaryllidaceae). J. S. African Bot.: 1-139. [CC BY]

description: Flowering from December to April and also in the Cold Bokkeveld, Ceres District, flowering in September.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Flowers predominantly deep red; habitat moist (damp partly shaded cliff faces or rock flushes).
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1978. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: VII. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 36(1): 43-76. [CC BY-SA]

description: The nearest species to E. perlata is E. barbata Benth. Of the latter Guthrie & Bolus state `The only absolute character distinguishing this from the preceding is the anther-crest, which can hardly be regarded as of specific value. The plants have, however, a somewhat different aspect, and we follow Bentham, though with doubt, in keeping them separate.' Flowering in early summer.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The specific epithet indicates a resemblance between this species and Chortolirion angolense (or Haworthia angolensis), a member of the Asphodelaceae.
bibliographicCitation: Glen, HF; Hardy, DS. 2000. Aloe. In: G Germishuizen & E du Plessis (eds), Aloaceae (first part), Fl. S. Africa 5(1,1): 1-167. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209564#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The species forms a variable complex with E. macowanii and E. leucotrachela. All three occur in the Betty's Bay/Kleinmond area with the latter two on the mountains. Only careful examination of the flowers can provide the distinguishing characters with corolla colour being a problem-easily noticed in fresh material, but not always recorded in dried herbarium material.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2005. The genus Erica (Ericaceae) in southern Africa: taxonomic notes 2. Bothalia 35(2): 121-148. [CC BY]

description: Gasteria brachyphylla var. brachyphylla is very variable in leaf size. The plants are readily distinguished from G. disticha by their smooth, darker green leaves with acute apices (see under the species).
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 1994. Gasterias of South Africa: a new revision of a major succulent group. Fernwood Press, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Gasteria carinata var. carinata is variable, grading into the other varieties; intermediates are often encountered. In the typical form the leaves are triangular, tuberculate and keeled. At the western end of its distribution they tend to be more distinctly tuberculate than they are further east.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 1994. Gasterias of South Africa: a new revision of a major succulent group. Fernwood Press, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The variety pillansii is very variable in floral and leaf characters.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 1994. Gasterias of South Africa: a new revision of a major succulent group. Fernwood Press, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This very distinct variety differs from the typical in its more luxuriant growth, being about twice the size of Haworthia angustifolia. In the shade it becomes a lighter green and the leaves are much more spreading. Compared with var. albanensis it is a much heavier plant with many more leaves, which are much longer (up to twice as long), and broader. The pedicels are 3 mm long as against the almost sessile flowers of v. albanensis and the perianth is slightly shorter.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, GG. 1943. Some new species and varieties in the genus Haworthia. J. S. African Bot. 9: 93-107. [CC BY]

description: Erica phacelanthera is easily distinguished by the large sessile flattened gland at the apex of the leaves and calyx lobes, by the included anthers adhering to the corolla tube and also laterally and by the beaked ovary with short style and the thin fragile fruit with very thin-walled seed.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: It is quite distinct from H. bolusii, not only because of the distance of its locality, but also because of the floral and leaf characteristics. The rosette is in most cases half the size of H. bolusii. The leaves are very narrow, dark green in colour and opaque, without any translucent marks. The margins and keels bear fine white hairs. The flowering time is 2 months earlier than that of H. bolusii. The inflorescence is much smaller and with less flowers than H. bolusii. It is a delicate species.
bibliographicCitation: Breuer, I. 2003. Beschreibung einiger neuer Haworthia-taxa. Avonia 21(3): 45-65. [All rights reserved]

description: In rosette and leaf shape it somewhat resembles Haworthia cymbiformis v. multifolia Triebn., but the leaves are larger, not as numerous, not as pellucid and the rosettes are larger.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, GG. 1944. Some new species and varieties in the genus Haworthia II. J. S. African Bot. 10: 11-24. [CC BY]

description: The floral characteristics are much the same as for H. picta as are size and shape of the leaves, but the surface of the end area is smooth, more opaque with a coloration resembling that of H. splendens. The most important reason to treat it as a variety is its distinct locality.
bibliographicCitation: Breuer, I. 2003. Beschreibung einiger neuer Haworthia-taxa. Avonia 21(3): 45-65. [All rights reserved]

description: Its nearest affinity is with H. comptoniana from which it differs by the straight to rounded, nearly reticulate, face lines on the end-area; there are also differences in flowering times, and small differences in the reproductive organs.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: The color varies in a fully expanded flower from Tangerine Orange (R.H.S. color chart 9/3) to somewhat deeper, depending on the light exposure.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, JR. 1965. Notes on Haworthias. Cact. Succ. J. (Los Angeles) 37(5): 127-128. [All rights reserved]

description: It is a distinct species and readily separable from other Haworthias which occur in the Barrydale district. Its nearest affinity is with H. serrata from which it is distinguished by the smooth margins and longer end-awn of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: It has been distributed under the name of H. arachnoidea var. setata because it looks like H. setata at a first glance. It is an intermediate form between H. setata and H. mucronata sensu Bayer, concerning the floral characters as well as the leaf characters.
bibliographicCitation: Breuer, I. 2003. Beschreibung einiger neuer Haworthia-taxa. Avonia 21(3): 45-65. [All rights reserved]

description: The plants grow, flat, with the retused surface level with the ground, and although found in dense patches, they are all single. Compared with the species, this variety has a long persistent end-awn, the end-area is rough with small concolorous tubercles, has more face lines, the margins and keel have many small teeth and the peduncle is much thicker and with a short dense raceme.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, GG. 1946. Some new species and varieties in the genus Haworthia. V. J. S. African Bot. 12: 1-14. [CC BY]

description: Near Haw. retusa (L.) Haw. but the end-faces of the leaves are not as retuse, are more acuminate and the color is a paler green.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, JR. 1969. Notes on Haworthias. Cact. Succ. J. (Los Angeles) 41(1): 57-59. [All rights reserved]

description: There is considerable variation in the length of the corolla with most of the long-tubed variants flowering in late summer/autumn and the short-tubed variants flowering in spring/early summer.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2005. The genus Erica (Ericaceae) in southern Africa: taxonomic notes 2. Bothalia 35(2): 121-148. [CC BY]

description: It is nearest to H. retusa var. solitaria G. G. Smith, but is a larger and taller growing plant, the leaves are somewhat less retused, and the end-awn is longer.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, GG. 1946. Some new species and varieties in the genus Haworthia. V. J. S. African Bot. 12: 1-14. [CC BY]

description: This distinct species is distinguished by its very hairy flowers in all parts including the adaxial surface of the sepals with stalked glandular hairs intermixed (both ab- and adaxially), and also the filaments. The calyx segments are free and as long as the corolla or just longer and are sulcate for their full length.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: It is nearest to H. comptoniana.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Leaves soft, keeled, 500-800 x 5-10 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Leaves relatively broad (up to 35 mm), usually serrulate; buds usually spreading, orange-red to pinkish red: flowers spreading to pendulous, yellow to yellow-green. Related to K. linearifolia but the raceme is more oblong to subcylindrical, and the flowers are shorter with well-exserted stamens. However, intermediate specimens are encountered which may be difficult to allocate with certainty. Typical subsp. tysonii occurs in Eastern Cape [Transkei] to southern and central KwaZulu-Natal. It has relatively broad, yellow- green leaves and the buds tend to be orange-red in contrast to the pinkish red of K. linearifolia and the dull blood-red, imbricate buds of subsp. lebomboensis. Further north, in the districts of Melmoth, Nkandla and Nqutu, specimens are found with pinkish red buds resembling those of K. linearifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Erica plumosa is characterized by the four stamens having markedly bipartite anthers with broad thecae; 2-locular ovary with one pendulous ovule per locule; the distinctive corolla with a bulbous base, a narrow middle and a broad cyathiform mouth.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: A very distinct and well-marked species. Bentham placed it in § Leptodendron; but it seems to fit better here [§ Ephebus].
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: This species does not come very happily into this or any section. Though distinct, it is allied to E. lachnaeoides (E. Lachnaea, var. purpurea, Andr., as figured in Andr. Heathery, t. 170).
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Chiefly distinguished from E. savilea by its longer leaves, narrower and muticous anthers with larger pore, and more evidently stipitate ovary; the pubescence on the younger parts is also generally more copious. Our material, though good, is not copious enough to afford good evidence that these small differences ure constant.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: This can hardly be a variety of E. walkeria. It is indeed nearer to E. fastigiata, but seems to be sufficiently distinct. Bentham, to whom Tausch's species was, apparently, unknown, quoted it with doubt, and says 'an species propria?' In general appearance it has some resemblance to E. denticulata var. grandiflora, but is immediately distinguishable by the different sepals besides the less inflated corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Its nearest relative is, probably, E. maderi but it differs largely from this by being procumbent, having widely crested anthers, gland-tipped hairs on the bracts and sepals, much wider filaments and being much more hirsute. It will be seen from the details of the distribution that the species is fairly well distributed in the area and has been collected several times before, even as far back as 1912, but has for some reason remained undescribed until now.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is characterized by the 4-lobed calyx and corolla, the four stamens and 3-nate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: In this respect, except for the colour, the species resembles E. empetrifolia L. of this section. In the latter, however, the appendages on the anthers are much narrower. Those in E. pyxidifiora are outstandingly broad and in Flora Capensis are described as looking like `bats' wings'. Despite their delicate appearance the flowers are hard and wax-like and vary from pale pink to dirty white.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This species shows great variability in habit and foliar morphology, and this led Sprague to create 10 species and 4 varieties. Aubreville and Sillans recognised later only one species with 3 varieties: Kigelia africana var. africana, var. aethiopica (Decne.) Aubrev. ex Sillans and var. elliptica (Sprague) Sillans, for W. Africa. Although we recognise that the specimens growing in woodlands and in forests present a tendency to produce large leaflets with acute apices, entire margins, dense indumentum and weak consistence, as opposed to the tendency in specimens from open areas, to produce smaller leaflets, with rounded apices, toothed margins, glabrescent and coriaceous consistence. We noticed all steps of variability to occur, and thus believe that they are mere ecoforms.
bibliographicCitation: Diniz, MA. 1988. 124. Bignoniaceae, Fl. Zambes. 8(3): 61-85. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, London. [CC BY]

description: Superficially the species is very like E. mauritanica L. (=E. viridipurpurea L.) which is a commonly cultivated species. The latter species is characterized by having the angle between the corolla-lobes distinctly rounded, which feature is easily seen in the bud stage and is unique in the genus. In E. quadrangularis the angle is acute (V-shaped). In habit E. quadrangularis forms a more spreading bush and has shorter leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: It is characterized by a calyx joined only halfway (not three-quarters), a few sessile glands around the margins of the lobes adaxially rendering the corolla shiny or sometimes very slightly viscid, by the prostrate creeping habit and limestone habitat. The inflorescence is also umbel-like and not a condensed raceme with distinct internodes, and the bract is recaulescent and approximate to the calyx.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: One of several long-tubed, pink-flowered species of Hesperantha in eastern southern Africa, H. brevicaulis is distinguished by the soft-textured, trailing leaves, and short, usually trailing stem, 100-250 mm long. The comparatively large flowers typically have a perianth tube 18-35 mm long and tepals 20-25 mm long, the open flower thus 40-50 mm diam. The flowers are adapted for pollination by long-proboscid flies. Plants from the Wolkberg and Serala in Limpopo apparently represent this species but flower earlier in the season, beginning to bloom as early as the middle of February. They also have flowers with a somewhat shorter perianth tube, 13-16 mm long. These shorter-tubed plants are provisionally included in H. brevicaulis. Plants from Serala, south of the Wolkberg, also differ from populations to the south in having anthers 5.0-6.5 mm long vs. 7-10 mm elsewhere. Also puzzling are plants from Mt Prospect near Lydenburg, collected in early flower in mid-February. They have long-tubed mauve flowers with a tube 30-32 mm long, tepals ± 18 mm long, short filaments about 3 mm long, and anthers 6 mm long. The four leaves have well-developed blades and there is no sign of a largely sheathing upper leaf. The plants have blades with a firm texture, an apparently drooping flowering stem, and a spike of five flowers. The plant thus fits poorly in Hesperantha brevicaulis because of the firm leaves, absence of a sheathing upper leaf, spike with more than four flowers, short filaments, and relatively short anthers. Additional material of this plant is needed.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Generally distinguishable by the virgate habit, and the closely-set inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised in sect. Radiatae by the flexuose stem, leaves with unusually short, plane blades, 20-30 mm long, and bract margins united around the axis only at the base. Unlike related H. radiata, the short perianth tube, 6-8 mm long, is ± straight rather than curved at the apex, and the flowers are thus suberect or half-nodding vs. nodding to almost pendent.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the moderate-sized to fairly large usually pink to mauve-pink but occasionally white flowers with tepals mostly 15-20 mm long, perianth tube 7-12(-14) mm long, and anthers 5.0-7.5 mm long. At flowering time in late winter or early spring the leaves are sometimes dry at the tips or scorched by veld fires. The flowering time is important in distinguishing the species, although the somewhat fleshy leaves, often with obtuse tips, aid identification. Hesperantha candida is separated from the late winter-spring-blooming H. longituba by its shorter perianth tube and diurnal flowers. In H. longituba the perianth tube is 14-22 mm long and the apparently consistently white flowers are crepuscular. The leaves of H. candida are typically sword-shaped with a raised main vein and margins and an otherwise smooth surface but some collections from Eastern Cape have oblong to nearly ovate leaves that appear to lack thickened margins, whereas other collections from the area are intermediate, having the lowermost leaf sword-shaped and the other basal leaves oblong, leaving no doubt that broader-leaved plants are H. candida. Whatever the shape of the leaves, the surface between the margins and midrib is always plane and smooth, with secondary veins not visibly thickened. Plants from Grahamstown, at the southwestern extremity of the range, have the smallest flowers in the species, tepals ± 12 x 6 mm, and some specimens from there also have more flowers per spike than recorded elsewhere. They have 4 to 6 flowers per spike instead of the more usual 1 to 3 in populations further north. These plants are puzzling but more likely represent a southern and lower elevation morph of H. candida than an undescribed species. The name Hesperantha candida has been mistakenly associated with the narrow-leaved but summer-blooming H. leucantha. This fairly slender, pale pink-mauve-flowered species of the Drakensberg and nearby has, like H. candida, diurnal but generally smaller flowers, with tepals 12-15 x 3-5 mm long and anthers 4.5-5.5 mm long, whereas those of H. candida have tepals mostly 15-20 x 6-9 mm and anthers 5.0-7.5 mm long. Leaves of H. leucantha are usually quite slender, mostly 1.5-2.5 mm wide, with only lightly thickened midribs and margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Among the Coccospermad group E. remota is easily distinguished by the 1-locular, 1-ovuled ovary, mostly five or six stamens with partially fused filaments, the beak on the unsculptured fruit and the longish distinct style. The pericarp and the testa are thinner than they are in the other species.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the relatively large, white flowers mostly with the outer tepals red outside and usually 12-20 x 6-10 mm, and the large asymmetric corms up to 14 mm diam. with imbricate tunics. The flowers are crepuscular, usually opening after 16:30 and then sweetly scented. Well-grown plants have at least four leaves, the lower three basal and with long, plane blades up to 10 mm wide. Populations from the Bokkeveld Mtns growing on sandstone pavement are often shorter in stature, with a slightly longer perianth tube, 10-12 mm vs. 6-10 mm, and shorter anthers, 4-5 mm vs. 6.0-8.5 mm, and perhaps merit taxonomic recognition. The style branches reach the tips of the anthers in these plants because the anthers are relatively short, whereas the style branches reach to between the base and middle of the anthers in other populations. Plants from the southern Roggeveld with spikes of fewer flowers (mostly two or three) and the outer tepals brown outside (red elsewhere), and growing in wet habitats are referred to Hesperantha palustris.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the stem, curved outward above the base and then suberect, Hesperantha curvula has moderately long-tubed, bright magenta-pink flowers, the tube 18-25 mm long, with spreading tepals ± as long as the tube. Hesperantha pulchra, from lower elevation grassland in the Eastern Cape, has a comparably long tube but pale pink flowers and erect stems. Hesperantha scopulosa, which co-occurs with H. curvula in part of its range, has a longer perianth tube mostly 32-42 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An unspecialised species, Hesperantha erecta is recognised by the relatively short stature, rarely exceeding 150 mm, small corm with the tunics fragmenting into elliptical segments, and pale yellow to creamy white flower open during the day, the outer tepals only lightly pigmented grey to light brown outside. Although the flowers are white to creamy yellow, they are not, as might be expected in the genus, crepuscular as far as known and have been recorded opening ± midday and at 14:00 and closing at ± 16:00, thus before sunset.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In floral structure allied closely to E. floribunda, yet with certain differences, and especially in its general aspect.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: One of the most common and widespread species of the genus in the winter-rainfall zone, Hesperantha falcata is recognised in sect. Hesperantha by the three or four, usually falcate, basal leaves and one more cauline and largely sheathing leaf, and white, creamy white or yellow flowers. Other white-flowered species of the section have smaller flowers, in H. spicata a perianth tube 4-6 mm long and tepals 4-7(-9) mm long. Hesperantha laxifolia has a similarly short perianth tube ± 5 mm long, only two foliage leaves (and one or two more entirely sheathing) and unusually short style branches ± 2.5 mm long. In H. laxifolia the style and style branches remain included in the perianth tube and in H. cedarmontana both style branches and stamens are included. In the rare white-flowered H. dolomitica from the Knersvlakte and H. eremophila from the Richtersveld, the narrow tepals remain half cupped in fully open flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very often this species may be overlooked because of its superficial resemblance to the common E. corifolia. The two species often grow in the same area but do not necessarily flower at the same time for a comparison of the flowers In habit and appearance E. rhopalantha is more striking than the small-flowered form of E. corifolia. The latter species forms a rather sparse, erect bush usually with not many flowers which are mostly pale pink. In E. rhopalantha the bush is small with numerous rather slender branches giving it a neat compact appearance. The flowers are borne in profusion at the ends of the branches and are a striking maroon-pink colour.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This very variable species is characterized by the fused anthers often remaining in a ring around the style in the fruiting stage, with relatively large pores which face slightly upwards and with a large pore in the septum between the thecae, the acute ovary with a short beak to the fruit and the distinct style longer than the ovary. The fruit has a thick sclerified endocarp and the seeds a thin testa.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: One of several long-tubed and pink-flowered species of Hesperantha in eastern southern Africa, H. grandiflora stands out in its zygomorphic, nodding flowers with the perianth tube, usually 40-55 mm long, curved outward near the apex and about 1.5x as long as the tepals, which are oriented ± vertically, while the stamens are unilateral and declinate, arching downward to lie above the lowermost tepal. The anthers are dark purple to red-brown, only rarely encountered in the genus. Hesperantha stenosiphon, with a similarly long perianth tube but much smaller tepals, also has dark anthers, as does short-tubed H. hutchingsiae, but both have radially symmetric flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: E. rivularis which has a large foliose bract on the main axis, not on the pedicel, should therefore be placed in section Hermes. The long sepals, which make the flowers of E. rivularis subcalycine, however, suggest that E. rivularis should be placed in section Trigemma. In spite of this discrepancy, it has been decided that E. rivularis should be placed in section Hermes, because of the close relationship to E. thodei, which fits well into section Hermes.
bibliographicCitation: Davidson, LE. 1989. A new species of Erica (Ericaceae) from the eastern Transvaal. S. African J. Bot. 55(5): 473-475. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1989); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: One of three closely allied acaulescent species of the western Karoo, Hesperantha hantamensis has white flowers with a slender perianth tube 14-20 mm long and spreading tepals 8-12 mm long. The flowers are crepuscular, opening in the late afternoon, 16:30 and strongly fragrant, closing after dark. Related H. flava has larger, yellow flowers and H. humilis even larger, pink to rose flowers with a dark throat.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica rosacea is a widespread and common species characterized by a 4-locular, 1-ovuled ovary, four free stamens, a fruit with a thin pericarp and seeds with a thick testa.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: One of several species of eastern southern Africa with long-tubed, pink to purple flowers, Hesperantha hutchingsiae appears to be allied to the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal species H. pulchra. It is distinguished from that species by the shorter, narrower leaves 1.5-2.0 mm wide, 2- or 3-flowered spikes, and rosy-purple flowers. Hesperantha pulchra has leaves 3.0-5.5 mm wide, and spikes with mostly 5 to 11 bright pink flowers. Hesperantha hutchingsiae also stands out in the brown cataphyll sheathing the base of the stem, and in the dark brown anthers and pollen, both unusual in the genus, although dark brown to purple anthers also occur in the pink-flowered H. grandiflora and H. stenosiphon, both of which have flowers with a substantially longer perianth tube, 40-55 mm long in H. grandiflora and 45-60 mm long in H. stenosiphon; and in H. mtamvunae, with much longer anthers 11-12 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the pale pink flowers with an elongate perianth tube, typically 30-39 mm long, and large yellow anthers, 7-10 mm long. Plants have fairly broad, flaccid, drooping leaves, a suberect to drooping stem, and usually a cormlet in the axils of the lower leaves. The seeds of H. huttonii are distinctive, mostly 2.5-3.5 x ± 1.25 mm wide, with membranous wings at either end, the wings each ± half as long as the seed body which is up to 1.5 mm long. Plants from coastal northern Eastern Cape province, some 250 km to the east of the main range, best match the species, but one of the collections from there appears to lack axillary cormlets and has a perianth tube 23 mm long, while another collection has flowers with a tube only 15-17 mm long. The coastal plants are provisionally included in H. huttonii until more information becomes available.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: E. roseoloba is a very distinct species which clearly belongs in the group of closely related sections comprising Polycodon and Melastemon, with their coloured petaloid sepals, open cyathiform corollas and anthers tending to be produced beyond the pore. There is, however, no clear alliance with any species in particular. Within the same region E. humifusa Salisb. occurs but possesses an ovate (not lanceolate), petaloid, approximate pherophyll and approximate bracteoles. The species is unusual in retaining on the plants, numerous dehisced capsules from the previous flowering season together with the current season's flowers. The species is also unusual in having no nectaries at the base of the ovary. This feature is associated with a wind pollination syndrome in Ericaceae and yet the flowers are brightly coloured - whitish with bright pink lobes, hence the name. The stigmas are also slightly enlarged with unusual spreading stigmatic lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 1996. Studies in the Ericaceae (Ericoideae) XIX. Two new species of Erica from southern Africa. Feddes Repert. 107(5-6): 305-310. [All rights reserved]

description: With unremarkable, white or sometimes pale pink flowers, Hesperantha hygrophila is recognised primarily by the distinctive pale green leaves with the main vein, margins, and a secondary pair of veins quite clearly thickened. The main vein is raised and flattened into wings that arch over the leaf surface and even the secondary veins are visibly thickened when seen alive. The flowers are diurnal with a record of opening between 8:30 and 9:00 and closing by 12:30. The species has been confused with white-flowered H. inconspicua, a generally more robust species with ± plane leaves and more flowers per spike (up to 16 in some plants), and sometimes with the stem branched in the axil of the third leaf. Hesperantha hygrophila may also be confused with the creamy white to pale yellow-flowered H. lactea, which grows in drier, well-drained grassland at altitudes of up to 800 m, rather than in wet habitats. Hesperantha lactea has dull yellow to light brown anthers that tend to dry dark brown, a feature which conveniently separates it from H. hygrophila in which the creamy white anthers remain pale when dry. The differences in leaf venation also separate the two but this feature is not always easy to see in dry specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: E. rubiginosa resembles E. scytophylla superficially but may be distinguished by its glabrous branches, longer leaves and peduncles and by its anthers which have no appendages.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Readily recognised by the smooth, terete leaves, outer bracts united around the spike axis in the lower half to one third, and white flowers with a straight perianth tube only 5-6 mm long. The flat-based corm and bracts united around the spike axis are typical of sect. Radiatae. Related H. radiata has plane and often somewhat succulent leaves, the outer bracts united for ± half their length, and a longer perianth tube mostly 7-15 mm long, curved in the upper half. Unusual for white-flowered species of the genus and section, the flowers open early in the morning and close at ± 16:00.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Still incompletely known, Hesperantha karooica is distinguished by the large, ± globose corm with overlapping tunics, a low stature, seldom exceeding 80 mm in open sites, narrow leaves, 3-4 mm wide, and relatively large, uniformly yellow flowers, with tepals ± 20 x 9-10 mm. The general appearance and yellow flowers recall H. vaginata, also restricted to the Calvinia District, but this taller species has broader leaves, 7-10 mm wide, and the flowers usually have large, dark brown makings on larger tepals, 30-35 x 12-17 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively tall species sometimes up to 500 mm high or more, with pale, creamy white to pale yellow flowers with a tube 6.0-8.5 mm long, and spreading tepals 14-20 mm long. The anthers, 5-7 mm long, are discolorous, usually brown or dull yellow, an unusual feature among white-flowered species of the genus. Like other white to pale yellow-flowered Hesperantha species of eastern southern Africa, the flowers are diurnal, with records of opening 11:45-12:30 and closing 16:40-17:15. This contrasts sharply with most white-flowered species of the genus from the southern African winter-rainfall zone, the flowers of which are crepuscular to nocturnal, opening in the late afternoon and closing after dark.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is closely related to the previous one in having no distinct narrow style and eight stamens with fully fused filaments and mostly 2-locular ovaries. It can be distinguished by the ovary being always 2-locular and the fruit being glabrous and longitudinally grooved and horizontally slightly so, and never distinctly verrucose. In E. rugata the endocarp is slightly lignified and clearly visible, whereas in E. subcapitata it is extremely thin with the cells hardly visible.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the relatively large white flowers that open in the late afternoon and close after dark, Hesperantha longituba has tepals 15-22 mm long and a perianth tube usually 14-22 mm long. The leaves are broad and leathery with prominent, raised margins and midrib. The large corms, up to 18 mm diam., have overlapping tunics notched into segments below, like those of several western Karoo species, including H. cucullata, H. humilis and H. vaginata and on this basis H. longituba appears allied to these species rather than to those of eastern southern Africa. Hesperantha longituba is sometimes confused with a second spring-flowering species from eastern southern Africa, H. candida, and has at times been included in that species. The two differ mainly in the length of the perianth tube, mostly 14-22 mm long in H. longituba vs. 10-12 mm long in H. candida. The flowers of the latter, as far as are known, are diurnal (confirmed by notes on some herbarium collections) whereas those of H. longituba are crepuscular. Plants from the Aliwal North and Stutterheim areas of Eastern Cape are intermediate in perianth tube length and make the distinction between the two species sometimes seem arbitrary but those from further west, at Cradock, Somerset East, and Graaff-Reinet always have a longer perianth tube, up to or even exceeding 22 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica viminalis is characterized by its tall growth (3 to 1.5 m [as '5 ft'] according to Esterhuysen) with fast-growing willowy branches, (hence the epithet, viminalis = bearing long flexible shoots/branches or willowy), 4-nate leaves with 0-2 sclereids around the midvein, the numerous (± 30) ovules per locule (a large number for a small-flowered species) and the long thin anther appendages.It is most similar to several species in the section Orophanes. It shares with E. gracilis the 4-nate leaves, the similar corolla and sepal shape and size, and the glabrous ovary and leaves with few sclereids, but that species has much smaller leaves and darker pink flowers and forms a dense, small, delicately branched shrub. With E. leucantha it shares the white flowers, similar anther appendages, glabrous ovary, similar stigma type and 4-nate leaves having few sclereids, but it does not have the glabrous leaves and stems, and the narrow cyathiform corolla. It is also similar to E. sitiens in many of the above characters but that species has much larger flowers with a short pedicel and only 6 ovules per locule and forms smaller fastigiate shrublets up to 1 m tall.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2001. Four new species of Erica (Ericaceae) from Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 31(1&2): 1-8. [CC BY]

description: Hesperantha luticola stands out in sect. Hesperantha as one of only two acaulescent species of the section. The white flowers have large purple blotches at the bases of the outer tepals and a remarkably long perianth tube, mostly 30-45 mm long. The tube has thick walls that tightly clasp the style so that nectar is forced into the top of the tube where it is accessible to insect visitors with short mouth parts. The corm, with short, radiating spines most closely resembles the corms of H. latifolia and H. pauciflora and it seems reasonable to infer that these are the closest relatives of H. luticola.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to the species in the section complex Polycodon/Melastemon. It is most closely related to E. chamissonis Klotzsch from the Eastern Cape, but differs in having the calyx lobes longer in relation to the corolla (more than half the length of corolla) thus rendering the corolla far less evident, the pherophyll and bracteoles more recaulescent (in upper half, not lower half of the pedicel), a larger (1.2 mm long, not 0.4 mm), capitate (not subsimple), stigma, a darker coloured corolla and the exserted anthers especially noticable in dried material. The anthers in E. saptouensis are more exserted than in the smaller flowered E. chamissonis var. polyantha (Benth.) Dulfer whereas in the larger flowered typical variety they are totally included within the corolla. The flowers are erect in this species whereas they tend to be mostly nodding in E. chamissonis.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 1996. Studies in the Ericaceae (Ericoideae) XIX. Two new species of Erica from southern Africa. Feddes Repert. 107(5-6): 305-310. [All rights reserved]

description: Sometimes confused with Hesperantha baurii, H. modesta is a late winter-spring-flowering species, usually with three leaves, the lower two basal and with well-developed linear blades of soft texture and the upper one (or two) cauline and largely sheathing (H. baurii usually has four, sometimes five leaves). The flowers are relatively large, in the middle of the range for H. baurii, but the available collections show it to be unusual in usually having only two to four flowers per spike. There is confusion about the type locality of H. modesta as the isotype at the KwaZulu-Natal Herbarium has the locality, Umlaas Location, whereas the sheet at K with the same number and date is purportedly from the Bevaan River, in the interior in the Vryheid District, which is evidently incorrect. Hesperantha subexserta, from Botha’s Hill and also based on a Medley Wood collection, flowering in October, has provisionally been treated as a synonym of H. modesta. The type plants have two basal leaves, and one or two cauline, sheathing leaves of the soft texture typical of H. modesta, but the spike of one of the plants of the type collection has up to eight flowers and a short lateral branch in contrast to the two or three, or at most four flowers per spike of specimens of H. modesta. A collection from Eshowe, Zululand (Lawn 1179), well to the north of other collections of H. modesta is provisionally included here. The poor condition and crowded mounting of the specimens makes them difficult to identify for certain but the flowering time, October, and marshy habitat, suggest this species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the moderate-sized crepuscular flowers, white with the outer tepals red outside, with tepals 14-16 mm long and as long as to slightly longer than the perianth tube. Plants bear four leaves, the lower two basal and largest, often prostrate or nearly so and the upper leaves small and sheathing the flowering stem. Plants mostly have two to four flowers per spike but plants with up to eight flowers are known.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Largest-flowered species of sect. Radiatae, Hesperantha muirii has white to pale pink flowers with a perianth tube up to 25 mm long, curved at the apex, and spreading, ± vertically oriented tepals up to 25 mm long. The stamens are ± unilateral and pendent and the long style branches are twisted and sometimes tangled together, an unusual feature in the genus but one shared by pink-flowered H. kiaratayloriae, in which the style divides near the tips of the coherent anthers and the style branches are held erect.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very distinct in the section by its small leaves and flowers. The anther-cells are very similar in shape and size to those of E. lachneaefolia, and E. floccosa, but there are considerable differences in other respects. Schlechter's specimens show not a few flowers with 6-lobed corollas, 11 or 12 stamens and a 6-celled ovary; and it is his plants, also, which have the smaller elliptic aristate anthers, mentioned in the description; these occur in the normal, as well as in the abnormal, flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the ovoid corm with prominently flattened side and relatively large pale pink to nearly white flowers with perianth tube 13-17 mm long and slightly shorter tepals 10-15 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: E. gibbosa forms a large robust shrub up to 1.5 m (5 ft) and is chiefly remarkable in this large section for its leaves which are covered with coarse, often gland-tipped, hairs and have a swollen tubercle at the base and also for its more or less ovate sepals. These characters serve to distinguish it from a closely related species, E. scabriuscula Lodd., which also occurs in the same area. This latter species is glandular-ciliate all over and has whitish flowers. Both species appear to be fairly common in the George and Knysna Districts. The only other species in this section with roughly hairy leaves is E. bergiana which has already been pointed out as being unique in the genus for having completely reflexed sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Variable in flower colour and phenology, Hesperantha pilosa can readily be recognised by the sparsely hairy stem and three leaves, the lower two basal and the third largely sheathing the stem. The leaf blades are hairy to minutely ciliate and the stem, usually unbranched, bears a scale-like bract in the upper third. Usually plane and without raised margins, the leaf blades of some interior populations have raised margins or may be ± terete and grooved with minute cilia on the groove edges. Variation in flower pigmentation and timing of opening and closing has resulted in recognition of two subspecies. Subsp. pilosa has white (occasionally pale pink or lilac) flowers with dark markings on the reverse of the outer tepals and flowers are crepuscular, opening ± 18:00; and subsp. bracteolata has blue or deep pink (or rarely white) flowers often darkly veined on the reverse of the outer tepals and flowers are diurnal, opening in the morning and usually closing in early afternoon. The two subspecies have complimentary geographic ranges. Hesperantha pilosa is closely related to H. pseudopilosa and the two are often so similar that the latter was originally described as subsp. latifolia of H. pilosa. Both have hairy stems and leaves but very different capsules and seeds and can also be distinguished by leaf width, up to 10 mm in H. pseudopilosa, which also has a longer scale-like bract 8-20 mm long on the upper part of the stem.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Poorly known, Hesperantha pubinervia is readily recognised by the ± linear basal leaves scabrid-hairy on the margins and veins, and the relatively long-tubed flowers of an unusual dull salmon-pink colour. The perianth tube, 20-25 mm long, is unusually slender and completely occluded by the style. The flowers do not produce nectar and are evidently pollinated through deceit, offering no reward to its pollinator, a long-proboscis fly. Hesperantha pubinervia is also somewhat unusual in having relatively short, ascending style branches ± 6 mm long, rather than spreading over the tepals as in most species of the genus. The distinctively coloured flowers contrast markedly with the deep pink to magenta flowers of sympatric and co-blooming H. baurii and H. scopulosa, and with the pale pink flowers of H. brevistyla and H. leucantha.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A late-flowering species, Hesperantha pulchra is recognised by the bright pink flowers with a perianth tube of intermediate length, mostly 15-20 mm long (14-28 mm), and relatively short filaments, 3-6 mm long. Plants from KwaZulu-Natal, north of the Tugela River, with a tube 15 mm long (Gerstner 6713, PRE) and ± 12 mm (Fakude 3, NH) fit uncomfortably in this otherwise Eastern Cape species. Plants from Mt Thomas, near Stutterheim in Eastern Cape (McMaster s.n., NBG), collected in later flower on 11 February, with ripe capsules at the base of the spike, resemble H. pulchra except for the early flowering. These plants have narrowly elliptic capsules 25 mm long that contain large seeds, up to 4 mm long with the wings at either end ± 1 mm long and the seed body ± 2 mm long. Capsules of H. pulchra are described by Hilliard & Burtt (1986) as 10-17 mm long with seeds ± 1.25 mm diam., with weakly or strongly developed wings. We need to know more about both the Zululand and Mt Thomas plants. Additional collections, especially in fruit, will be helpful in understanding the range of variation in this species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica serrata is a very distinct and unique species in the Ericeae on account of the partial fusion of the corolla, filaments and ovary, which is difficult to ascertain even with a microscope. Besides this feature the species can be distinguished by the 2-locular ovary with two ovules per locule (G2/2), the beaked ovary and the laterally adhering anthers. The plants have a hard siliceous texture and often dull greyish green colour which features can often be used to identify plants not in flower - a rare feature in Ericeae!
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Readily recognised by the red-purple flowers, the lower tepals with even darker markings, and slender perianth tube ± 20 mm long. The relatively large asymmetric corms with overlapping tunics suggest a relationship with H. cucullata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Reliably identified by the distinctive chestnut-brown cataphylls and white flowers with a particularly short perianth tube, 2-3 mm long. Plants consistently have two spreading, pale, relatively broad basal leaves and a largely sheathing upper leaf which is quadrangular in cross section. Observations on one population indicates that the flowers open at 16:00-16:30 and then produce a sweet, rose-like fragrance but the tepals close again at nightfall, and the flowers are completely closed by 19:30.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised in sect. Radiatae by the outer bracts united around the spike axis for at least half their length, Hesperantha radiata has nodding to half pendent flowers with a perianth tube of modest length, mostly 6-15 mm long, and tepals spreading to slightly reflexed when fully open near or after sunset. The leaves are unremarkable, although often slightly fleshy and thicker in the centre, sometimes even hollow near the midline. The corms, typical of the section in their horizontal to oblique flat base are somewhat variable, the outer layers splitting from the base into rounded to acute segments. Two subspecies are currently recognised: the taller, more robust subsp. radiata with broader leaves, larger flowers, and blooming in the winter-rainfall zone mainly in August and September; and subsp. caricina, usually a smaller plant, typically with a collar of fibres around the base, and a crowded spike of overlapping bracts 10-13 mm long, and blooming mainly from September to December in the winter-ranfall zone.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Sessiliflora = flowers without peduncles, i.e. sessile. The ease with which this species is recognized and its wide distribution make it a well-known plant to many people. Both the flowering and fruiting stage are very distinct and as a result the plants can readily be identified at any time of the year. The greenish flowers are packed tightly into short spikes at the ends of the branches. When the flowers dry and shrivel up, the sepals remain green and alive and increase slightly in size thus protecting the developing ovaries which in this species take considerably longer to mature than in most other species of Erica. After a time the hard sepals turn red and remain thus in a tight `fruiting head' which may last on the shrub for several years even after the seed has been shed. It is these persistent `fruiting heads' that make E. sessiliflora so easily recognizable. Occasionally one comes across plants growing under very dry conditions. When not burnt the plants may attain quite a size. Some have been recorded reaching a height of 2 m (6 1/2 ft). Under cultivation they reach even greater sizes. It is certainly a species worth cultivating if it can be grown in masses when it makes an effective display, especially when young.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: A fairly robust species, sometimes standing 450-500 mm high, Hesperantha rupestris most closely resembles pink-flowered H. baurii in general aspect and is distinguished by the white to creamy white flowers with outer tepals flushed dark pink to red on the outside. Plants usually have four leaves, the lower two basal, narrowly lanceolate and reaching to about the base of the spike. The firm-textured blades have the margins and main vein thickened. As in other eastern southern African Hesperantha species with white flowers, these are diurnal and have been reported as opening in the morning.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is allied to E. ampullacea and E. lagenaeformis Salisb. but may be distinguished by its leaves which are 3-nate and narrower.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica similis can be distinguished from the other species in this subgroup by its simple stigma and longer, more oblong, 4-nate leaves. These plants appear very distinct with their densely hirsute, almost lanate, greyish leaves which could be an adaptation to the inland high altitude where the conditions are very harse in the winter months.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: A distinct species; recognized by the inflated, almost narrow-ovoid, corolla, and its peculiar long bristly yellow hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Flowering mainly in spring and summer.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Readily recognised by the almost white flowers suffused pale pink outside, an elongate perianth tube 35-40 mm long, filaments ± 15 mm long and exserted ± 11 mm, and prominent anthers 5-6 mm long. Blooming late in the season, the leaves are usually withered and dry when flowering commences. Shorter-tubed, pink-flowered I. longituba, has shorter filaments exserted 5-7 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its pale purple flowers with small, dark eye, Ixia brevituba has relatively broad, blackish anthers that dehisce laterally so that the light-coloured pollen forms a contrasting pale margin to each anther, and short style branches that are ± as long as the filaments, thus scarcely projecting from between the filaments. The lovely amethyst-coloured flowers are borne on inclined spikes so that they face directly upward in an elegant, arching spray. I. brevituba falls among a small group of species that are endemic or near-endemic to the Roggeveld Escarpment and Klein Roggeveld, including I. curvata, I. rigida, and I. trifolia, all of which share relatively unspecialized, longitudinally dehiscent anthers 3-5 mm long. Among these species I. brevituba appears to be most closely allied to I. trifolia on the basis of their unusual, inclined spikes, and lateral branches that are decurved and nodding when young. All other species have spikes that are erect from bud to fruit. The two species also share a perianth tube 2-3 mm long. I. brevituba differs from I. trifolia in its blackish purple anthers and purple perianth tube, which gives the flowers a small, dark central eye, consistently narrower leaves 1.5-2.0 mm wide, and medium-textured corm tunics drawn into a well-developed neck. I. trifolia, like all other species in sect. Dichone, has yellow anthers, although the filaments may be pale mauve, and a pale perianth tube, giving the flowers a well-defined whitish central eye. The leaves of I. trifolia are broader than in I. brevituba, (2.5-)5.0-12.0 mm wide, and the tunics are more coarsely fibrous, with the lower fibres developed into woody claws but not drawn into a neck above. In addition, the style branches of I. trifolia are longer than the filaments, 4-5 mm long, and project conspicuously between them. In view of its narrow range there is concurrence with Raimondo et al.’s (2009) conservation status of vulnerable (Vu), but it is also noted that the entire range of I. brevituba falls within the Tanqua National Park and future disturbance seems unlikely.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: The species is easily recognizable from its red tightly-packed heads of flowers with their prominently exserted black anthers and unusual appearance of the bracts and sepals, which condition gives the species its name. It is closely allied to E. sexfaria Ait. which has ovate, acute corolla lobes and white or pale pink flowers and also to the other species, E. amphigena Guthrie & Bolus, which is rare and has obovate-oblong bracts as opposed to the broad-ovate bracts of E. spumosa.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the narrow, linear leaves up to 2 mm wide, corm tunics of fine, netted fibres and a main spike with 1 to 3 flowers. Branchlets when present are very short and 1- or 2-flowered. The pale blue or occasionally creamy yellow flowers have a perianth tube ± 5 mm long, enclosed by the translucent floral bracts, 6-8 mm long, the flowers, excluding the ovary, are ± 20 mm long. The plants typically have a prominent dark brown cataphyll, a feature more prominent in the northern populations of the species and the upper leaf sheathes the stem for ± half its length. The type material is readily matched by plants from the Western Cape mountains, long known by the name, that have filaments exserted 1-2 mm and anthers held in a column 4.0-4.5 mm long and a style dividing opposite the upper third of the anthers into short branches 1-2 mm long. Ixia capillaris is most likely to be confused with I. exiliflora, specimens of which were often included in the past as that species. Whereas I. capillaris has flowers with a perianth tube 4-7, rarely 8 mm long, and tepals about twice as long as the tube, I. exiliflora has a perianth tube 8-10 mm long, and tepals about as long as the tube. The bases of the anthers of I. exiliflora are included in the tube but those of I. capillaris have anthers that are normally exserted 1-2 mm, or rarely barely exserted on included filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ixia collina is easily distinguished from other members of ser. Dichone by the unusual branching pattern: the relatively short branches extend outward horizontally and curve upward distally as well as by an unusual floral feature. The filaments are unique in the section in being filiform below, curved at right angles in the distal 1 mm and broadened so that they are as wide as the anthers. With so narrow a range Raimondo et al. (2009) regard the species as endangered (EN).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the orange flowers with a brown centre often edged in green, united filaments, erect, contiguous anthers and an elongate, filiform perianth tube, 10-15 mm long, substantially exceeding the bracts, 7-12 mm long. Unlike the superficially similar I. maculata, which has orange or yellow flowers but a perianth tube mostly 5-8 mm long, about as long as the bracts, the corms of I. curta do not produce stolons and the bracts are pellucid, sometimes speckled with brown distally, rather than partly to entirely rust-brown.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised among the species of sect. Ixia with yellow or orange (occasionally red as in the synonym I. frederickii) flowers by the pale but semi-translucent floral bracts often flushed and veined pink and a moderate-sized flower with tepals mostly 12-15 mm long. The flowers have a comparatively small, brown to purple stain in the centre about one quarter the length of the tepal. The filaments are comparatively long, 5-6 mm long, darkly coloured and the style divides at or close to the anther bases so that the yellow style branches arch outward between the lower half of the divergent anthers. The outer floral bracts either have a single prominent median tooth or three small teeth, the central one more prominent than the laterals. Filaments of I. dubia are typically free (or rarely basally united) and the perianth tube is usually 6-9 mm long, but ± 12 mm long in plants from the Tulbagh Valley. Plants are usually of moderate height, rarely exceeding 300 mm, are seldom branched and although the narrowly lanceolate leaves reach to about the middle of the stem, plants growing in dense undergrowth have longer and narrower, sometimes almost linear leaves. Flowers are pollinated by hopliine beetles, different species of which have been captured at different sites. Historically Ixia dubia has often been confused with orange-flowered I. maculata, but that species has very different, large floral bracts, rust-brown in the upper half or entirely, partly to entirely united filaments and the corms bear stolons. Yellow-flowered plants with corm tunics of particularly fine fibres or papery layers and bearing stolons sometimes included in the past in I. dubia and also treated as I. polystachya var. lutea are I. sarmentosa, a species of wet habitats in Western Cape. Although superficially similar to I. dubia, I. sarmentosa typically has a larger central stain (up to one third the length of the tepals), and a short, dark style dividing at the mouth of the perianth tube so that the style branches extend between the base to middle of the filaments. The filaments diverge slightly and are relatively short, up to 2.5 mm long (3-5 mm long in I. dubia).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively small species, Ixia erubescens is immediately recognized by the fine corm tunics, the 4-6 narrow, deeply undulate and crisped leaves, usually unbranched stem, and the vertically oriented flower with the stamens unilateral and slightly pendent when fully open. Both Lewis (1962) and De Vos (1999) regarded the flowers as fundamentally actinomorphic with symmetrically arranged stamens and noted that only late in anthesis do the anthers become unilateral and pendulous, simply due to gravity. Our own observations counter this: the stamens are unilateral immediately the flower buds open. We assume that I. erubescens is most closely allied to I. scillaris, which typically has medium to coarse corm tunic fibres, broader leaves, usually with plane margins, and somewhat to substantially larger flowers, also with unilateral stamens, but with a perianth tube up to 4.5 mm long and tepals up to 14 mm long (vs. tube 2-3 mm long and tepals 11-12 mm long). Occasional populations of I. scillaris with undulate or crisped leaves are readily distinguished from I. erubescens by their broader leaves, larger flowers, and coarser corm tunic fibres. The conservation status of I. erubescens is listed by Raimondo et al. (2009) as (LC), least concern, although its range has been historically much reduced through agriculture, especially in the Swartland and Boland.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: Strigilis - a short, rigid, bristle-like hair; referring to the hairs on the leaves. Erica strigilifolia and the following species, E. pectinifolia, are closely related species that were separated by Salisbury. They were retained as separate species by Guthrie and Bolus in Flora Capensis but were reduced to one species by Dulfer (1965). He regarded E, strigilifolia as being a variety of E. pectinifolia.
