The two species are being kept separate in this book. A thorough field study of the two will be necessary in order to make a final decision as to their status. The basic difference between the two species is in the shape of the sepals which, in E. pectinifolia are unique in possessing a distinct claw at the base, like the handle of a hand-mirror. The upper portion is broad and flat. The sepals in E. strigilifolia are long and narrow and have no claw at the base. Both species are characterized by the bristles on the edges of the leaves, bracts and sepals and the shaggy hairs on the upper portion of the corolla. E. strigilifolia has muticous anthers, occasionally minutely aristate, whereas in E. pectinifolia they are always aristate. The size of the flower varies considerably in E. strigilifolia from 5 mm on specimens from Ladismith to 15 mm on specimens from the Swartberg Pass area. Bolus described a variety rosea based on the shape of the sepals and the softer hairs on the calyx and shortly aristate anthers. The distribution ranges of the two species are different but overlap in the Uniondale and Willowmore area. E. strigilifolia appears to be confined to the tops of mountains in its range, which is limited to the Swartberg Mountains with outliers west at Montagu and on the Anysberg and east on the Kammanassie Mountains. E. pectinifolia on the other hand is typically a lowland species growing in dry arid areas especially in the Humansdorp District. It has only been recorded at high altitude on the mountains east of Uniondale. In colour the species overlap to a certain degree. In E. strigilifolia the predominant colour is rosy-pink with occasionally white. In E. pectinifolia white is the usual colour but often the flowers may have a tinge of pink. In the plates illustrating the species here both are shown white. The plates must therefore be examined more closely to find the distinguishing features.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its small flowers, among the smallest in sect. Ixia, I. flexuosa has a perianth tube typically 5-6 mm long and tepals, mostly 10-14 mm long, thus about twice as long as the tube (occasionally perianth tube only ± 4 mm long and tepals ± 8 mm long). Coloured white to pink or light purple with fine, dark longitudinal veining on the lower half of the tepals, the flowers have a penetrating, honeysuckle-like scent. The style is relatively long, usually dividing between the base and middle of the anthers, rarely just below the anther bases. The stem may have up to four short, erect branches seldom bearing more than six flowers, whereas the main spike has up to 15 flowers. The leaves are linear to narrowly sword-shaped, mostly 2-5 mm wide and often less than a third as long as the wiry stems. Somewhat unusual in the section, the outer floral bracts usually have three prominent veins terminating in three short, sometimes acute teeth. Smaller-flowered morphs of I. polystachya are easily confused with I. flexuosa but have outer floral bracts with a single prominent central tooth and flowers almost always with a solid, darker centre. Lacking dark pigment in the centre of the flower, Ixia flexuosa fits uncomfortably in sect. Ixia, especially as the perianth tube is slightly flared near the apex for ± 1.5 mm and the flowers are conspicuously scented. Despite its predominantly filiform perianth tube, typical of sect. Ixia, I. flexuosa, most closely resembles I. orientalis (sect. Hyalis), which has a narrowly funnel-shaped perianth tube, almost filiform in the lower half. Only close examination of the outer floral bracts and filaments makes it possible to separate the two. In I. flexuosa the filaments are broadened basally, whereas I. orientalis has uniformly slender filaments decurrent on the tube and the outer floral bracts have a single central tooth, sometimes with a shorter lobe or tooth on either side of the central cusp. The style of I. flexuosa, usually reaching to between the base to middle of the anthers (rarely slightly below the anther bases), also often differs from that in I. orientalis, where the style typically divides close to the filament apices or opposite the anther bases. Ixia flexuosa is the only member of sect. Ixia known to produce nectar. It is probably most closely related to I. patens, which also has slender, wiry stems, and flowers lacking a dark central stain, but this species has larger, deep pink (to dull red) flowers that lack the dark longitudinal streaking in flowers of I. flexuosa. Floral scent in the two species appears identical, although of weaker intensity in I. patens. The flowers of I. patens lack nectar.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica subcapitata is characterized by the very distinctive verrucose ovary and fruit which is 1- or sometimes 2-locular. The style/stigma complex is elongated funnel-shaped with no distinct narrow stylar portion present.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: A striking species in bloom, Ixia gloriosa has a bright magenta perianth with a small, glossy, almost black centre, and purple-black stamens and style branches. The leaves are particularly narrow, typically 2-3 mm wide and the corm tunics are composed of fine fibres. The species is also distinctive in having up to three short branches held close to the main axis, each usually bearing fewer blooms than the 4 to 6 on the main spike. Plants give the illusion of having a particularly long, lax spike with flowers scattered along its entire length but some of the open flowers are borne on the branches. The pale floral bracts, ± 6 mm long, have prominent purple veins, the outer with three short, acute teeth. When described by Lewis (1962), I. gloriosa included I. superba and the original description is an amalgam of the two species. The anthers, 5-7 mm long and slightly more than twice as long as the filaments, were originally described as connivent at the tips, but there is no evidence of this in available preserved material. The style divides at or just above the bases of the filaments and style branches are unusually long, reaching up to 5 mm and exceeding the shorter filaments. Among other differences, I. superba has a longer style, dividing above the bases of the anthers, but shorter style branches 2-3 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the relatively large, deep pink, purple, mauve-pink or blue-mauve flowers usually with a relatively well-developed perianth tube, (7-)10-18(-23) mm long that gradually widens toward the mouth, and spreading tepals 13-20(-23) long. The long stamens have filaments exserted 6-8 mm from the tube and anthers 3-5 mm long. The floral bracts are mostly 8-10 mm long and distinctive in having narrowly acute teeth. The two basal leaves are usually fairly broad, 10-18 mm, but occasionally only 5 mm wide. The third leaf sheaths the stem for its entire length. Plants with short, somewhat twisted, rather than straight, lateral branches and slightly smaller flowers, described by G.J. Lewis (1962) as var. curviramosa, are now included in I. latifolia. The degree of twisting and length of the branches is not consistently correlated with any other character, and is often difficult to determine because plants with shorter, ± straight branches, conform to neither taxon. Flower size is unusually variable. Both the northernmost populations of I. latifolia in the arid Tanqua Basin and the easternmost near Oudtshoorn are exceptional: the Tanqua populations, growing in perhaps the most arid habitat for the species, have the largest flowers with a tube 20-23 mm long and tepals up to 21 x 10.5 mm. In contrast, the Gamkaberg populations have flowers with a tube 7-8 mm long and tepals 13-15 x ± 7 mm, among the smallest in the species. But plants from several other localities have flowers almost as small. The plants from the Tanqua Karoo reverse the usual trend for smaller stature and flower size in the driest habitats and merit further study. Ixia latifolia is probably most closely related to I. divaricata, a plant of wet, sandstone habitats in the Cold Bokkeveld and surrounding mountains, which has long, slender, straight lateral branches with flowers crowded in the upper half and a smaller perianth with a tube 8-11 mm long, tepals 11-14 mm long, and filaments 4-5 mm long reaching 1-2 mm beyond the mouth of the perianth tube or sometimes only to the mouth of the tube. Ixia divaricata typically has pale pink or white flowers and narrow leaves, thus very different from the larger, deep pink-mauve or purple flowers with well-exserted filaments, and broad, fairly short leaves of I. latifolia. Plants with broader leaves may be the result of crossing with I. latifolia, and plants of that species with particularly long branches may be the result of occasional crosses with I. divaricata at sites where the habitats of the two are close together.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied both to E. leptopus and to E. crateriformis.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: A striking plant in full bloom, Ixia leipoldtii has large, predominantly white flowers with tepals up to 22 mm long, and a dark purple central blotch with pale greenish throat. Apart from the unusual flower colouring, I. leipoldtii is readily distinguished by the translucent brown bracts, broadly ovate to almost orbicular tepals, and filaments included in the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This very distinct species is unique in the genus for the form of the anther appendages which are broad, very irregularly shaped crests which, in some anthers, may be absent on one side. They are remarkable in sometimes being larger above the point of attachment to the theca and therefore totally ascending. The superficial fades of the calycine, open-mouthed flowers with manifest stamens would place the species in the section Eurystoma of Flora capensis where it shows some resemblance to several species which occur in the same area: E. calycina, E. brevicaulis and E. costatisepala H.A. Baker. These latter species have complex dendroid hairs on many parts of the plant and have long pedicels. E. tarantulae has a sparse complement of short fine simple hairs and almost subsessile flowers. The style is also unusual in being apically papillate, a condition found only in the section Platyspora.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 1995. Studies in the Ericoideae (Ericaceae). XVI. Six new species of Erica from the western Cape, South Af. Bothalia 25(1&2): 87-95. [CC BY]

description: Typical of sect. Ixia, I. leucantha has the filiform perianth tube and filaments inserted at the tube mouth diagnostic for the section, but the flowers lack the dark centre of most species of the alliance. The species was included by De Vos (1999) with I. patens, which has larger, deep pink (rarely red) flowers usually somewhat darker in the centre and relatively narrow tepals, whereas I. leucantha has white flowers. It differs additionally from I. patens by the longer style dividing opposite the lower third of the anthers and short style branches 2.3-3.0 mm long. In I. patens the style typically divides opposite the anther bases and the style branches are unusually slender, ± 4 mm long. Significantly, I. patens flowers from late August to mid-September, whereas I. leucantha flowers from late October to November and possibly even into early December.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished among the longer-tubed species of sect. Hyalis by the pink flowers with filaments exserted 5-7 mm, anthers 4-6 mm long, and well-developed style branches 3-5 mm long. Perianth tube length is remarkably variable, mostly 12-33 mm long, but as short as 10 mm and occasionally as long as 35 mm. Two subspecies are recognised, subsp. longituba for plants with a perianth tube (10-)12-23 mm and subsp. macrosiphon for those with a tube 25-35 mm long. Subsp. macrosiphon comprises the northern populations of the species, all close to the foot of the Riviersonderend Mtns. However, plants from the south of its range, near Bredasdorp may have a perianth tube 22-23 mm long. There appears to be pattern of tube length across the range from south to north. Historically, Ixia longituba was confused with I. bellendenii but this species has white flowers, a longer perianth tube 35-40 mm long and filaments exserted up to 11 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In general appearance E. taxifolia resembles E. corifolia, especially the large-flowered forms of the latter species. It differs mainly in having 3-nate spreading leaves and sepals that clasp the corolla rather than spreading from it. The shape of the appendages on the anthers is also different. As is the case in E. corifolia the size of the flowers in E. taxifolia varies. This variation seems to be correlated with the altitude, the large-flowered forms occurring at higher altitudes.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by orange or sometimes yellow flowers with a small dark brown, star-shaped or round centre. The central dark part of the flower is slightly cupped with only the distal 2/3 of the tepals outspread. The yellow filaments are united in the lower half or completely, with the style dividing above the bases of the anthers. Particularly unusual are the short, branched stolons produced from the corm base, each branch bearing a small cormlet. Similar branched stolons are also found in I. stolonifera of sect. Ixia and in I. purpureorosea (sect. Hyalis). The stem is usually unbranched and the linear to narrowly lanceolate leaves are mostly 2-7 mm wide. Ixia maculata is one of few species of sect. Ixia with large dry floral bracts rust-brown in the upper half or entirely. Ixia maculata was initially broadly circumscribed, thus including several species with flowers of various colours but with a dark centre.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica taylorii, here described de novo as a distinct species, is related to the group of species which is characterized by plumose hairs and large, coloured, petaloid bract and bracteoles. The group includes the E. goatcheriana L.Bolus complex, E. modesta Salisb. and the recently described E. schumannii E.G.H.Oliv. and E. kirstenii E.G.H.Oliv. E. taylorii differs in having very few, relatively short (not numerous and dense), plumose hairs on the pedicel, and flowers in one, sometimes up to three whorls. This latter character relates the species to two species with plumose hairs and umbel-like inflorescences, namely E. cernua C.V.Montin and E. sphaerocephala J.C.Wendl. ex Benth. The former has a globose corolla and larger anther appendages, whereas the latter has much reduced bracteoles and sepals (not large and petaloid), and long-aristate leaves, bract, bracteoles and sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Oliver, IM. 2001. Five new species of Erica (Ericaceae) from the Swartberg Range, Western Cape, South Africa, and a no. Bothalia 31(1&2): 155-165. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its short perianth tube, 2.5-4.0 mm long, and stem bearing several short, few-flowered, wiry branches, Ixia marginifolia also has unusually broad, short, leathery leaves with strongly thickened margins. It is sometimes confused in herbaria with I. rapunculoides, which is similar in general aspect, including flower colour and leaves with thickened margins, but the latter has short filaments included in the perianth tube, whereas I. marginifolia has the filaments exserted (1.5-)3.5-4.0 mm so that the anthers are prominently displayed. Ixia marginifolia displays an unusual pattern of variation in flower colour. Populations in the northeast of its range have a pink perianth, but to the southeast in the Calvinia area flowers are pale blue-mauve, the same shade as equally common I. rapunculoides with which it is easily confused from a distance. On the northern and central Roggeveld Escarpment plants have either blue-mauve or white flowers, occasionally both colours occurring together, but at the southern end of the escarpment populations are uniformly white-flowered, as is also reported for the Nuweveld population. Plants from the southern end of the range have violet flowers. White flowers remain open long after nightfall, whereas those of other colours close shortly after sunset. Variation in the number of flowers per branch is notable: while 2 or 3 flowers is most common, plants with predominantly or only single-flowered branches occur throughout the range of the species, perhaps a reflection of poor growing conditions rather than genetically based. A few collections, e.g. from the base of the Voetpadsberg near Pietermeintjies Siding in Western Cape, consist of plants with smaller flowers than are considered typical for I. marginifolia, with tepals ± 7 x 5.5 mm (vs. 10-12 x 6-8 mm), short filaments exserted ± 1.5 mm from the tube (vs. 3.5-5.0 mm). These plants also have 1-flowered branches; both this and the smaller than normal floral features may again result from of poor growing conditions that particular season. Plants from near Matjiesfontein a short distance to the east of the Pietermeintjies site and collected in another year have flowers typical in size for the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the pale pink, lilac or pale to deep mauve flowers, the tepals with an irregularly shaped, small, dark red or purple mark or ring at the base surrounded by a white zone and a dark spot in the lower midline. The obovate tepals remain slightly cupped even when the flowers are fully open, showing pale, nearly white stamens with erect filaments enclosing the style, and divergent anthers. The style divides opposite the base or lower third of the anthers. Added to the flowers, which are unusual for sect. Ixia, the leaves are linear to narrowly lanceolate, up to 6 mm wide, and the plants may have a well-developed collar of fibres around the base (sometimes not collected when plants are not extracted with care from the ground). Plants produce one or more relatively large cormlets at the base of the main corm and/or thick, rhizome-like stolons that terminate in a large corm. Ixia metelerkampiae is closely allied to I. campanulata but differs in its taller stature, reaching up to 700 mm, and flowers differently coloured and marked (flowers usually ± uniformly red, less often white, in I. campanulata) and short, colourless bracts, 4-5 mm long, with inconspicuous cusps. Both also have an unusually short perianth tube for sect. Ixia, 2-4 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: I. micrandra stands out in the group in its long, narrow, almost linear filaments and its style branches, which are unusually long at 2.0-3.5 mm, and straight or slightly arched, thus extending between the bases of the anthers. I. confusa has similarly slender but somewhat shorter filaments, slightly shorter anthers, and shorter, strongly arched style branches, 1.5-2.0 mm long. The leaves of I. confusa have plane, usually wider blades up to 4 mm wide (vs. 0.5-1.5(-2.0) mm) and without the prominently thickened main vein of M. micrandra. The style branches are also strongly arched in I. minor but that species has unusual flattened, lanceolate filaments, narrowed and kinked at the tips. The ranges of I. micrandra and I. minor are almost complementary, that of I. micrandra extending east of I. minor, but the two have been collected growing and flowering on the same day in the Houw Hoek Mtns, where their distributions overlap. The only significant variant of Ixia micrandra we have seen is from near Bot River (MacOwan in Herb. Norm. Austr. Afr. 262). Plants of this population have unusual thick, fleshy leaf blades, but the flowers and other features accord with the species. Largely montane, we see no current threat to the species and endorse Raimondo et al.’s (2009) (LT), least threat, status.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: The most important characters that separate E. tenella from the other species are the anther shape and its appendages. The anthers are more or less equilaterally triangular in sideview with rounded corners about as broad as long and the anther appendages are crests, even though they are somewhat narrow in some specimens. Superficially the species is easily mistaken for E. sitiens. However the latter species forms a more robust plant and has flowers that are characteristically curved. The flowers of E. tenella vary in colour like those of E. sitiens. Usually they are white or rosy-pink. The colour form with bright salmon-pink flowers is most attractive especially as the flowers are produced in profusion on the small shrublets.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: One of only two species of the genus that extend outside the Greater Cape flora region (the other being Ixia marginifolia), I. orientalis is a relatively unspecialised species lacking any outstanding features, thus difficult to diagnose. It can be identified by the combination of branched stems, spikes often with seven or more flowers, four to six leaves (rarely only three), none completely sheathing the stem, and small, pink or white flowers. The perianth tube, 8-12 mm long, is narrowly funnel-shaped with the proximal half to two thirds always extremely narrow. Well-grown specimens have stems with 2 to 4 branches and the main spike usually bears 7 to 12, rarely up to 16 flowers, although in plants from the mountains of the southern Cape the stems may be unbranched and the spikes have fewer flowers. Typical plants from Eastern Cape have the largest flowers, with the tube 12 mm and tepals ± 14 mm long, but to the west, particularly around Caledon, flowers are smaller, sometimes with a tube only 8 mm long and tepals ± 10 mm long, but there seem to be no other differences and the pattern of variation lacks clear discontinuities so that it is impossible to recognise infraspecific taxa. Late flowering, I. orientalis is seldom seen before the middle of September, although there are records as early as August. It may be most closely related to the largely montane Western Cape species, I. odorata, which typically has slightly smaller flowers, usually yellow, rarely white, with a strong sweet scent and distinctive, relatively short filaments up to 3 mm long (measured to the base of the anthers), and the style dividing between the base and apex of the filaments. This contrasts with longer filaments, up to 6 mm long, and a style usually dividing between the base and upper third of the anthers (rarely shortly below the filaments) in I. orientalis. It is also difficult to distinguish from I. flexuosa (sect. Ixia) without careful dissection. Both may have a perianth tube of similar length, with a relatively short, wider distal portion, a style often dividing opposite the bases of the anthers, and many-flowered spikes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognizable by its pallid branches, oblong leaves, long pedicels and muticous anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinctive in its fairly tall stature and remarkably long-tubed flowers, the tube usually 40-65 mm long, with the darkly coloured anthers included in the tube (sometimes partly or rarely fully exserted). The perianth is pale yellow to pale beige with the undersides of the tepals often flushed with pink or red. Plants from inland in the north of its range, from Piketberg to the Bokkeveld Mtns, have tubes 45-65 mm long, those from the coast north of Cape Town are consistently long-tubed, 65-75 mm long, but those from the Cape Peninsula and the False Bay Coast have shorter tubes 35-55 mm long. Collections from the Cape Flats stand out in their pale anthers and style dividing ± 2 mm beyond the anther tips. In other populations the style divides between the lower and upper third of the anthers, exceptionally opposite the anther tips. The anthers, usually dark brown or almost black, are typically 5.0-6.5 mm long and half exserted but sometimes fully included. The Cape Flats plants are particularly unusual, not only in the short perianth tube and long style but the pale anthers are only 4.5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ixia pauciflora typically has just one or two flowers on slender, often unbranched stems, or with one or two (rarely to four) short branchlets. The flowers are relatively large, having tepals 16-18 mm long, ± as long as the flared perianth tube, long filaments exserted 2-6 mm from the tube, and anthers 4-6 mm long. The stamens on fully open flowers are unilateral and are held horizontally with the anthers facing the dorsal tepal, a feature impossible to determine from pressed specimens. Vegetatively, the species is virtually identical to the more common I. capillaris in its two linear leaves, small corms with finely fibrous tunics, a collar of fine fibres around the underground part of the stem, and dry, chestnut-brown cataphylls. Blooms of I. capillaris are radially symmetric and have a perianth tube 4-8 mm long, ± half as long as the tepals, and filaments ± 5 mm long, usually exserted 1-2 mm from the tube. Ixia pauciflora also closely resembles the local Villiersdorp endemic, I. reclinata, in its flower, including the unilateral stamens, extended horizontally with declinate anthers, but the latter has longer filaments, exserted 8-10 mm (vs. 2-6 mm in I. pauciflora). Ixia reclinata also lacks the collar fibres around the stem base present in I. pauciflora, the stems typically have one or two branchlets, and the cataphylls are green or partly membranous when alive and not dry and brown. Ixia reclinata also differs in having the bracts and prophylls subtending the branchlets short and obtuse to subacute, quite different to the fine, thread-like bracts and prophylls of the remaining species of the I. capillaris group.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the purple-pink flowers with the tepals white at the base, sometimes edged with pale pink, and a perianth tube dark red-purple to brown outside. A particularly striking feature of I. purpureorosea is the presence of one or more broad stolons produced from the corm base. Unique in the genus, the stolons are thick and fasciated, up to 60 mm long, branching distally with each branch bearing a small terminal cormlet.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica thamnoides is a very distinctive species with its 1-locular 4-ovuled ovary which produces a partially dehiscent capsule, its funnel-shaped calyx with adaxial sessile glands, approximate relatively large bract and bracteoles and basifixed anthers with small spurs arising from the apex of the filament.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: E. thimifolia forms diffuse little plants which are often straggling and matted in a form like those of E. filiformis. The species is not very common but occurs over a fairly wide area and grows in small populations often in a pure stand. It may be found on the edge of a seepage area, on moist disturbed clay ground or under rocky overhangs, usually at lower altitudes. It is distinguished from E. planifolia L. with which it is often confused by its leaves and anthers. In the latter species the leaves are much broader and very long-ciliate and the anthers are included and have longer appendages.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: With narrow, sublinear leaves 2-6 mm wide, flowers crowded terminally, Ixia rouxii is distinguished primarily by the flowers with large, dark central stain, almost black stamens and distinctive, short lateral branches extended outward almost horizontally and curving upward at the tips. The tepals range in colour from purple to deep pink or blue-mauve (rarely white), always with a dark brown to purple-black central stain covering ± one third their length. Spikes bear relatively few flowers, often only 4 to 6 on the main spike (sometimes more), and fewer on the branches and the bracts are ± papery and pale below, becoming brown distally and the outer may have one tooth or three ± equal teeth, this varying even in the same population. Somewhat unusual for sect. Ixia, the corms bear short, relatively slender stolons, the remains of which can be seen on most herbarium specimens. Ixia rouxii has been regarded as allied to I. polystachya, which typically has two or more ascending to upright branches, many more flowers per spike, floral bracts usually pale throughout and the corms do not produce stolons. The style in I. rouxii divides at or shortly above the filament bases, occasionally opposite the middle of the filaments. The central stain of dark pigment is often less pronounced in I. polystachya, which also usually has the style dividing opposite the filament bases. Both Lewis (1962) and De Vos (1999) remarked that the tepals are unusually narrowed below into short claws (tepals unguiculate or subunguiculate according to Lewis), but there seems little merit in this distinction. Notable features of Ixia rouxii are the black anthers, the thecae of which are separated from one another to expose a narrow strip of connective on the abaxial (outer) surface. Anthers in the type from Porterville, and in a collection said to be from ‘near Hopefield’ have particularly prominent connectives, ovate in shape. This recalls the condition in I. atrandra, suggesting a possible relationship between them. The use of this feature in circumscribing I. rouxii is limited because anthers from the southern end of the range at Stellenbosch and nearby have nearly parallel thecae with the connective not, or barely exposed. The pollen, a bright yellow colour, contrasts with the black anther tissue in dehisced thecae.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The most common and widespread species of sect. Dichone, Ixia scillaris is recognised primarily by the nodding flowers with vertically oriented tepals and unilateral, slightly pendent and often relatively long anthers, combined with a fan of 3 to 7 basal leaves, (3-)6-20 mm wide. Related I. erubescens has narrow, ± falcate leaves, 2-4(-6) mm wide, with closely crisped margins, and is a smaller plant with smaller flowers, the tepals 8-11 x 4-6 mm and anthers 2.0-2.5 mm long vs. tepals mostly 10-15 x 5-9 mm and anthers 3-4 mm long in I. scillaris. Apparently closely allied I. simulans, with half to fully nodding flowers and unilateral stamens with pendent anthers, has a single basal, ± linear foliage leaf and a second leaf sheathing the stem for most of its length.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The most common and widespread species of sect. Dichone, Ixia scillaris is recognized primarily by the nodding flower with vertically oriented tepals with unilateral, slightly pendent and often relatively long anthers, combined with a fan of 3-7 basal leaves, (3)6-20 mm wide. Related I. erubescens has narrow, ± falcate leaves, 2-4(-6) mm wide, with closely crisped margins, and is a smaller plant with smaller flowers, the tepals 8-11 x 4-6 mm and anthers 2.0-2.5 mm long vs. tepals mostly 10-15 x 5-9 mm and anthers 3-4 mm long in I. scillaris. Apparently closely allied Ixia simulans, with half to fully nodding flowers and unilateral stamens with pendent anthers, has a single basal, ± linear foliage leaf and a second leaf sheathing the stem for most of its length. Ixia tenuis from the Piketberg is a particularly slender species with small corms with finely fibrous tunics, just three, narrow, soft-textured leaves and relatively small flowers with dark magenta tepals. I. tenuis grows in a habitat unique for species allied to I. scillaris, seeps on sandstone rocks, growing in moss in soils less than 10 mm deep. Variation: Typical Ixia scillaris from Darling and Tulbagh to the Cape Peninsula has (4)5-7 relatively narrow leaves, mostly 5-8 mm wide, with 3-5 secondary veins conspicuous only when dry, mostly branched stems (rarely with up to 7 branches), and moderately dense spikes with flowers spaced 8-12 mm apart. The flowers are relatively small, with tepals 8-10 x 4-5 mm and ± symmetrically arranged, although the lowermost tepal is held slightly apart and recurved, and anthers 2.0-2.8 mm long. In contrast, plants from the Olifants River Valley and low elevations in the Cedarberg ranging into the Bokkeveld and Spektakel Mtns are always taller, with 2-4, broader leaves mostly 15-20 mm wide, usually with at least two conspicuous secondary veins in addition to the main vein, stems simple or with 1(2) branches, and lax spikes with flowers distantly spaced, 15-25 mm apart. The flowers are larger, with tepals 14-16 x 5-9 mm, the upper tepals overlapping and separated from the three lower tepals, and anthers 3.2-4.0 mm long. A third set of divergent populations occurs on the Gifberg-Matsikamma Mtn complex. These consist of unusually small plants, seldom exceeding 150 mm in height, with small flowers (tepals ± 8 x ± 4 mm, anthers ± 2 mm long), thus like those of the southern populations of Ixia scillaris but with just three leaves (rarely two in depauperate individuals), recalling the northern populations, at least in leaf number, although the leaves are shorter and narrower. The taxonomic solution to the variation in Ixia scillaris is to recognize the three sets of populations as separate subspecies, those of the larger-flowered, northern populations as subsp. latifolia and the Gifberg-Matsikamma populations as subsp. toximontana.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species unlike any other in floral character, or in aspect, with the single exception of E. flavisepala.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the pink flowers with a relatively long, nearly cylindric perianth tube mostly 14-22 mm long and by the partly included (rarely just exserted) anthers. Well-grown plants may reach as much as 400 mm high. Ixia stohriae appears to be most closely allied to I. fucata of the western Langeberg and Hex River Mtns to the west and they are virtually identical vegetatively. Ixia fucata has either white or pink flowers, the filaments are exserted 2-5 mm from the tube, and the style branches are consistently longer than in most collections of I. stohriae, 2.0-2.5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the unusual floral bracts with setaceous cusps, the outer bracts with three to five veins and three ± equal cusps, and by the distinctive stolons produced from the corm bases. The stolons are broadened distally and shortly branched, each branch terminating in a tiny cormlet, at most 2 mm diam. The flowers are relatively small and cupped, with a pale mauve-pink perianth with a small, dark purple stain in the centre, a perianth tube 2-4 mm long, and tepals mostly 10-12 mm long. The style divides close to the bases of the anthers. Like almost all species of sect. Ixia the open flowers are crowded together, close to the spike apex.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The colour combination of the flowers in E. thunbergii is most strikingly beautiful, the bracts and sepals being bright yellow and the corolla limb orange-red. This is only found in one other species, E. flavisepala Guthrie & Bolus, from the same area and the most closely related species. Because of the bright garish colours E. thunbergii is referred to locally as the `Malay Heath'.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The distinctive leaves with raised and winged margins, thus ± H-shaped in cross section, combined with a perianth tube 8-10 mm long and the unusual, warty ovary and capsules make Ixia thomasiae unmistakable. The leaf shape and warty ovary and capsules are not known elsewhere in Ixia except in related I. alata. Flowers of I. thomasiae are pale blue-mauve and slightly larger than those of I. alata which has pale pink flowers. The two species are evidently most likely allied to the I. marginifolia group with which they share a funnel-shaped perianth tube and partly exserted filaments and fully sheathing uppermost leaf. The particularly large anthers of I. thomasiae, ± 6 mm long, and style branches, up to 2 mm long, are consistent with other species of the group.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This is most nearly allied to E. passerinae (§ Gamochlamys), and is a connecting link between the present and that section. It may be readily known from that species by its different indumentum, larger and flatter leaves, longer pedicels, and more deeply divided calyx. It is also related to the preceding [E. nervata].
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: I. trinervata is readily recognized by the presence of just one foliage leaf, the blade narrowly sword-shaped and with three ± equally conspicuous veins and unthickened margins. A second leaf is largely to entirely sheathing, although relatively broad. The flowers are an intense, bright mauve pink or red-magenta. This species is considered most closely related to usually pale pink-flowered I. stricta, which blooms later in the season, at which time its 3-5 leaves are usually dry. Both species favour clay or clay loam soils. The new I. bifolia recalls I. trinervata in its single foliage leaf, but the leaf blade is much narrower than in I. trinervata, with a single main vein embedded in the leathery-succulent leaf tissue. When dry the leaf margins appear particularly thickened, unlike those of I. trinervata. The flowers of I. bifolia are slightly smaller than those of I. trinervata and have unusual, almost straight, deep pink style branches in marked contrast to the pale pink, falcate style branches of I. trinervata. Agreement with Raimondo et al.’s (2009) estimate of near threatened status (NT) for I. trinervata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the presence of just one foliage leaf, the blade narrowly sword-shaped, mostly 6-10 mm wide, with three ± equally conspicuous veins and unthickened margins. A second leaf is largely to entirely sheathing, although relatively broad. The flowers are an intense, rose-pink also described as red-magenta. Related I. bifolia recalls I. trinervata in its single foliage leaf, but the leaf blade is much narrower, usually only 3-5 mm wide, with a single main vein embedded in the leathery, almost succulent leaf tissue. When dry the leaf margins appear moderately thickened, unlike those of I. trinervata. The flowers of I. bifolia are slightly smaller than those of I. trinervata and have unusual, almost straight, deep pink style branches in marked contrast to the pale pink, falcate style branches of I. trinervata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in the twisted blades of the three or four basal leaves with tightly undulate to crisped margins, Ixia vanzijliae has attractive brick-red to salmon-pink flowers with a small, dark central eye. Plants are usually relatively short, up to 200 mm high but may reach up to 400 mm under favourable conditions. The filiform perianth tube is 8-12 mm long and the dark purple style divides opposite the lower to middle third of the anthers. The floral bracts are pale except for a brown flush toward the tips.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A species singularly interesting as being an outlier from the great central home of heaths; and as curiously resembling E. leptoclada, from the station of which it is separated, by some 800 miles, while both appear to be rare. It is distinguishable from that, species by its broader leaves, its approximate (not basal) bracts, and its apparently stouter and stranger habit; yet the shape of the corolla, and the shape and size of the anthers are almost exactly the same.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: This lovely plant, with its extraordinary green to turquoise, or sometimes grey-blue flowers usually with maroon to almost black centre, is unmistakeable. Added to the unique flower colour is an elongate spike with large blooms open at the same time and spaced well apart from one another. The particularly long anthers are mostly 9-13 mm long (occasionally only 5-7 mm long) and always suberect and the style divides at or shortly above the bases of the free filaments. The elongate spike is unique in the genus Small-flowered populations with a pale centre, including the anthers, are recorded from Romans River Farm and from Weltevrede Farm near Botha, along with typical large-flowered, dark-centred populations. These anomalous populations may represent pollination ecotypes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: As far as we can determine this is an autogamous species which is prone to the development of local forms varying in flower size, especially perianth tube length and tepal dimensions, several of which were described as distinct species. Among the southern African material we are able distinguish two more-or-less distinct entities, smaller flowered plants corresponding to Radinosiphon leptostachya and larger-flowered, outbreeding plants which we treat as R. lomatensis. Typically, R. leptostachya has flowers with the perianth tube 15-30 mm long, and narrow, almost linear lower tepals 8-12 x 1-2 mm, with the upper tepals at most 3 mm wide. The small capsules, 4-6 mm long, contain just one or two seeds per locule (up to five in tropical African material). The species appears to have a very distinctive means of vegetative reproduction through the development of thick, scaly rhizomes. These do not always elongate, resulting in the formation of clusters of corms.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species is similar in appearance to E. cerinthoides, E. cameronii and E. oatesii. The latter species, however, occurs some 1,000 miles away in Natal and the Transvaal. The relationship with E. cameronii is discussed under that species. E. cerinthoides occurs in the same areas as E. tumida but differs in its leaves and less inflated corolla and in its completely different habit and inflorescence. The flowers of E. tumida vary considerably in colour through various shades of red. The var. minor from the Cedarberg closely resembles species in the section Ephebus.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied by its exserted anthers to § Pyronium, and by its capitate inflorescence to § Pseuderemia; but best placed, as by Bentham, in this [§ Ephebus] section.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The plant has much external resemblance to Blaeria ericoides.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The dark blackish purple tepals distinguish Klattia partita from the other species of Klattia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia anceps is readily recognised by the combination of short floral bracts 5-10 mm long and white to ivory-coloured flowers flushed pink on the outside of the tepals and tube, usually with a relatively long perianth tube, mostly 50-80 mm but occasionally only 20-40 mm, and narrow tepals 3-4 mm wide (sometimes the dorsal up to 5 mm). The lower tepals usually have a claw-like projection just above the base. The bell-shaped corms have either bluntly lobed or minutely serrated basal rims.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to E. filiformis, from which it differs by its fewer flowers in the whorl, and its appendiculate anthers. The corolla is singularly like it in shape and texture, except that the limb in this is considerably longer.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Lapeirousia violacea shares dark violet flowers with reddish to purple and white markings on the lower tepals with L. jacquinii, but they differ markedly in their floral bracts and corms. The corms of L. jacquinii are bell-shaped without the long spiny, laterally projecting teeth typical of the obconic corms of L. violacea, which has inflated outer bracts folded or slightly keeled, thus very different from the shorter, typically two-keeled bracts of L. jacquinii. The two species share pollinators but hybrids between them are unknown in the wild.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia pyramidalis is immediately recognised by the broadly ovate to deltoid bracts with obtuse to retuse apices, combined with a relatively long perianth tube 25-55 mm long. In profile the bracts do not taper to a point but curve outward and have blunt tips. The flowers have shortly clawed, subequal tepals with broadly oval to rounded limbs.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia arenicola is distinguished by its small size, pale beige-pink, slender-tubed flowers with narrow tepals. Perhaps most easily confused with L. macrospatha which has similarly coloured flowers, L. arenicola has a uniformly narrow, cylindric perianth tube 17-33 mm long and tepals 10-11 x 3-4 mm whereas L. macrospatha has a wider tube, 25-35 mm long, expanded toward the apex and considerably larger tepals, the uppermost ± 20 x 7 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia exilis is distinguished by the short, usually underground stem and tufted habit, and pale blue flowers with a perianth tube up to 25 mm long. The flowers are zygomorphic, with white and darker blue markings only on the lower tepals, and unilateral stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica urceolata is a very distinctive species forming a finely and densely branched shrub characterized by the leaves being open-sulcate at the base, the very small flowers with the corolla inflated in the middle, the very small ovary with long style and relatively very large cyathiform stigma, three included free stamens with anthers broader than long and flattened with small pores which are almost forward facing, and the papillate/colliculate fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: E. urna-viridis closely resembles E. physodes when in a dried condition on a herbarium sheet. In the field, however, the species is unmistakable in its habit and distinctively coloured flowers and longer peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Early collections of Lapeirousia spinosa were first included in the broadly similar L. divaricata and flowers of the two species are alike in their white (or palest pink) colour, short perianth tube, and general shape, with the lower three tepals united with the upper laterals for several millimetres and ornamented with a tooth-like median ridge. The flowers of L. spinosa are larger, with a perianth tube 9-12 mm long and a dorsal tepal 18-23 mm long vs. a tube 7-10 mm long and dorsal tepal 14-16 mm long in L. divaricata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowers in L. simulans and L. arenicola are so similar in tube length and general size and markings that they can be distinguished only with difficulty, and their flowering times overlap although that of L. simulans is generally somewhat later in the season, usually mid- to late September, by which time the last flowers of L. arenicola are often depauperate, and have shorter tubes and duller colouring than earlier in the season. The two species are most readily distinguished by the underground part of the stem. The corms of L. arenicola lie 35-55 mm below the surface on a straight stem that lacks axillary cormlets but the underground stem of L. simulans is 55-85 mm long so that the corm lies at a greater depth than in L. arenicola, and each of the two underground nodes consistently bears a large cormlet.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica vallis-fluminis is characterized by the hairy, narrow to open-cyathiform corolla, small bract and two bracteoles, four stamens with bipartite anthers and pollen in tetrads, and by the ovary being bilocular with a single ovule per locule (G2/1). The fruit is very hard with a thick sclerified endocarp and thin testa.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: This species has been confused with E. leptopus, Benth., bat the corolla is quite different in shape. The anther, as also the filament, is much more copiously bearded in Ecklon & Zeyher's specimens than in Schlechter's; but of these latter only his 10223 appears to have a few fully developed flowers, and those showing them clearly as described.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The acaulescent Lapeirousia montana is allied to the widespread L. plicata, which it replaces in the southern Roggeveld, and is distinguished from that species by the larger flower with longer perianth tube, mostly 32-45 mm long, and tepals 10-15 mm long, always with ± straight margins. The anthers are ± white and 3-4 mm long. Lapeirousia plicata has smaller flowers with a perianth tube 12-30 mm long, tepals 7-9 mm with undulate margins, and anthers usually blue and mostly 1.8-3.0 mm long. The upper leaves and floral bracts are typically crisped in L. plicata vs. with straight margins in L. montana.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Characterised by pale, uniformly coloured flowers with a long perianth tube expanded and curving outward distally, Lapeirousia littoralis can usually be recognised by its white flowers and relatively low stature with short branches from near the base. Plants mostly bloom in late winter or spring soon after the first rains of the season and are usually 100-150 mm high, and sometimes congested. The flowers have acute tepals ± 20 mm long and 2.0-2.5 mm wide and the floral bracts are usually 15-20(-25) mm long. Lapeirousia littoralis is closely related to L. caudata and the two have at times been united, but the latter is readily distinguished by the long slender branches, the main stem and branches up to 300 mm tall, and the creamy yellow to buff-brown or maroon flowers with particularly long, narrow, attenuate tepals 25-30 mm long and ± 1.3 mm wide. As the flowers fade and dry the tepals appear virtually filiform.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica venustiflora is distinguished from the rest of the group by the combination of the slightly expanded stigma (not simple and truncate), the distinctly sulcate calyx lobes (not esulcate with just a puberulous patch), tubular corolla not much contracted within the calyx and inflorescences which are non-innovating. It is the only species in the group in which the lowest whorl of flowers in an inflorescence can have two distinct bracteoles.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Erica vemicosa can be distinguished by the 2(3)[4]-locular, papillate, emarginate ovary, the more conspicuous, pilose calyx and the prostrate matted habit with rooting occurring along the main branches. The flowers are less viscid than in the first two species, but nevertheless well coated with a shiny layer, hence the specific epithet.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Although vegetatively there is little to distinguish Moraea macgregoriorum from related species, including M. saxicola and it allies, in the solitary, rather narrow undulate leaf, branched stem and ± dry spathes, the flower is, however, striking: the pale blue-lilac tepals are held well apart from one another and have long, very narrow claws, narrow, spreading to reflexed limbs and characteristic orange nectar guides. Particularly distinctive are the elongate filaments ± 15 mm long and disproportionately short anthers ± 4 mm long (M. saxicola has filaments 12-14 mm long and anthers 6-9 mm long). As in other members of sect. Deserticolae the ovary is included in the spathes. Molecular phylogenetic studies show that M. macgregoriorum is closely allied to M. saxicola and M. bolusii.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by the small, violet to pale blue flower with feathery or fringed style crests, unique in Moraea and reminiscent of the related genus Ferraria. The species also recalls Ferraria in the stigmatic surfaces located at the lateral tips of style branches. Both floral morphology and molecular phylogenetic studies place M. lugubris close to the base of phylogenetic trees, in some it is retrieved as sister to the remaining species of Moraea. The corm is of the Moraea type, thus consisting of a single internode with an apical bud and enclosed by well-developed tunics. The tunics of coarse fibres loosely enclosing the corm body are, however, unique in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the so-called ‘peacock moraeas’, Moraea loubseri is readily recognised by the striking dark blue-violet flowers with the outer tepal claws and proximal parts of the limbs densely covered with dark blue-black hairs. The flowers are relatively large with outer tepals 24-30 x 12-18 mm. As in several other species of the M. villosa alliance, the solitary, linear leaf is velvety-hairy on the outer surface and the stem is minutely velvety. The inner tepals are 3-lobed with a particularly long, slender central lobe spreading to laxly reflexed and the style branches and crests are unusual in spreading horizontally rather than ascending as in other species of the M. villosa group.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to the well-known and widespread Moraea ciliata and occurring entirely within the range of this species, M. macronyx can be distinguished by its larger flowers with the outer tepal claws one and a half to twice as long as the limbs. The larger outer tepals are 40-60 mm long with the claws 25-40 mm long and the style branches are ± 20 mm long with crests up to 25 mm long. The outer tepals of M. ciliata are mostly 25-35 mm long with the claws 12-15 mm long, thus about half as long as the limbs, and the style branches are typically 8-15 mm long. Vegetatively M. macronyx and M. ciliata are nearly identical although the corm tunics may differ, those of M. macronyx sometimes unusual in being entire and peculiarly soft, of an almost spongy, pith-like texture. Some populations, however, have fibrous corm tunics no different from those of M. ciliata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea margaretae has the brown, ± woody corm tunics, leathery rhipidial spathes with brown tips and flowers with finely brown-veined yellow tepals characteristic of subg. Umbellatae, and is distinguished in the subgenus by its habit and flowers with well-developed style branches and prominent style crests. The leaves and branches (when present) are crowded close to ground level and the aerial stem and branches comprise a single internode. The species is tetraploid, 2n = 40 (two populations counted), one of the few exclusively polyploid species known in Moraea. Moraea margaretae seems to be most closely related to M. orthrosantha of central Namaqualand but this species has aerial stems of three or four internodes, with two or three branches at the aerial nodes. The flowers of the two are similar in size and colour but those of M. margaretae have shorter filaments ± 5 mm long vs. filaments 8-9 mm long in M. orthrosantha. Both species have red anthers and pollen. Hybrids between M. margaretae and M. intermedia occur at a site west of Springbok.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Spring-flowering Moraea marionae is an inconspicuous plant and even in bloom the small, white to pale blue flowers are difficult to spot in the resprouting grass. As a result it remains poorly documented over its relatively wide range. The outer tepals are only 10-20 mm long, the limbs rarely longer than 12 mm, and the inner tepals are 3-lobed with small, rounded lateral lobes and a linear central cusp that is coiled inward. The terete leaf is often absent or just emergent at flowering time and attains its full length during the summer after the capsules have ripened. No plants with fully developed leaves are known. Its relationships are most likely with M. trifida, also of eastern southern Africa but with larger, brown to greenish flowers, also with 3-lobed inner tepals, but a channelled leaf present at flowering.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Viridis = green; with green flowers. In Flora Capensis Guthrie & Bolus described this species as having dry, i.e. not sticky, flowers and they placed it in the section Didymanthera in which all the species are dry. The species is best placed in this section and is, therefore, an exception. E. viridiflora is a very sticky species with flowers of a vivid emerald green colour. It occurs on the mountains of the Mossel Bay, George and Knysna Districts and may be seen on the Robinson and Outeniqua Passes. In the former locality it grows with E. viridescens Lodd. (= E. unicolor Wendl.) and in the latter locality with E. hebecalyx Benth., both of which are green-flowered species but easily distinguishable from E. viridiflora. In the wild E. viridiflora forms untidy, scraggly bushes which do not produce a good show of flowers. Under cultivation the plants may form more shrubby growth and bear a greater profusion of flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinctive in its acaulescent habit and yellow, long-tubed flowers. The combination of a flower with long perianth tube and underground stem is unique in subg. Umbellatae but the brown corm tunics, yellow flowers with brown-veined tepals, and outer rhipidial spathes free and diverging distally, are consistent with this placement. The species bears more than a passing resemblance to M. cooperi, also with a perianth tube but with a well-developed aerial stem.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Apart from its unusual habitat, Moraea huttonii is distinguished among the several yellow-flowered species of the subgenus by the conspicuous purple to brown blotches on the style crests. The flowers are typical of subg. Grandiflorae in their large size, yellow colour and well-developed style branches and crests. Plants typically grow in clumps, as does the related M. spathulata, but M. huttonii usually has narrower leaves mostly 4-10 mm wide (rarely to 25 mm) and usually deeply channelled. Unlike most species of the subgenus, stems of M. huttonii are occasionally branched from the upper nodes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Longifolius - with long leaves. Flowering at various times during the year depending on the locality. On account of the variation much subdivision has taken place in the past. In Flora Capensis five separate varieties were recognized. Most of these overlap in characters and run into each other and it is therefore considered not worth retaining most of them. In the case of var. maritima there are good grounds for retaining it as a variety. The length of the leaves is a variable character. Generally they are long but not shimmering as in E. vestita. Occasionally they can be quite short, only 8 mm long, which may mislead one into thinking that it is not E. longifolia. One of the attractions of E. longifolia is the great variety of colour forms that occur. Only a few of these are shown on the plate. Others that occur are red, brown, yellow-green, pink, orange and yellow, and purple. This species is easily recognized from its relatively long, narrow and crowded leaves which are not versatile or loose and from the narrow leaflike bracts and sepals. This latter character distinguishes E. longifolia from the closely related E. onosmaeflora Salisb. in which the sepals are wide and have a long linear tip narrowing gradually upwards.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the combination of a dry (or absent) foliage leaf at flowering, a fairly short stem up to 250 mm high, and small, pale blue-mauve to lilac flowers. Only the outer tepals bear nectar guides and the style branches are relatively well developed and bear short, erect crests ± 3 mm long. The foliage leaf, also distinctive, is emergent at or soon after flowering, and has a terete, prominently ribbed blade with a thickened apex. Ultimately the leaf may be up to 600 mm long or longer, then trailing through low, grassy vegetation. At the end of the growing season the leaf turns dry and brown and the flowering stem to which it is attached begins to elongate in preparation for flowering the following spring. Flowering at the end of the dry season, the rhipidial spathes and sheathing leaves are, like the foliage leaf, usually dry and brown. Moraea stricta is one of relatively few polyploid species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Somewhat variable across its wide range, Moraea spathulata typically forms large tufts, thus it is not unusual to see several flowers open at once. Each flowering stem bears a single broad leaf, shallowly channelled to almost flat. The species can be distinguished by its large yellow flowers, the outer tepals up to 50 mm long, tall stems, and clump-forming habit. Plants flower in late winter and spring along the coast but in summer and autumn inland. The species comprises numerous local races, but owing to the small differences between them, it is difficult to define many of them. Four subspecies were described in Goldblatt (1973) but are not currently recognised.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erica williamsiorum is characterized by the spike-like synflorescences with a calyx mostly 2-lobed, subglabrous to sparsely pubescent and by the 2-lobed corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: With its open, poppy-like flowers, either bright orange-red or creamy green with a brown centre, Moraea insolens is one of the most striking species in the genus. The filaments are united in a smooth, dark brown column and the large anthers, ± 8 mm long are closely appressed to and exceed the narrow style branches with their tiny crests. The inner tepals closely resemble the outer in colour and orientation and are only slightly smaller. Moraea insolens is probably most closely related to M. lurida, a species of sandstone soils which usually has dark maroon flowers, sometimes with contrasting white markings, and similarly reduced style branches and crests but smaller inner tepals often with 3-lobed limbs. The two species share an unusual karyotype, unique in sect. Vieusseuxia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in having several foliage leaves, all inserted well above the ground just below the first branch, large yellow flowers with bright red anthers that extend beyond the stigmas, and nodding capsules. The large corms of M. indecora are particularly deep seated, buried at least 200 mm below the ground, partly wedged in bed rock. The nodding, soft-walled capsules and fibrous corm tunics recall M. vegeta, perhaps its closest ally. The chromosome number of 2n = 16 is unusual in subg. Moraea (x = 10) but at least M. papilionacea (n = 9 and 8) also departs from that base number.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea incurva has blue to violet flowers with the inner tepals either 3-lobed with the inner lobe linear and 18-20 mm long, or entire and thus exceptional but not unknown in subg. Vieusseuxia. The inner tepal limbs are abruptly curved inward (hence the name incurva) on suberect claws. The species otherwise conforms to subg. Vieusseuxia in the solitary basal leaf, modest size of the flowers, and in the filaments united in a slender column with only the tips free. The filament column, 10-11 mm long, raises the anthers above the bases of the inner tepal limbs and the orange anthers are thus prominently displayed. The immediate relationships of M. incurva are uncertain but molecular studies place it close to M. unguiculata and M. tripetala. The entire to 3-lobed inner tepals with incurved limbs and long filament column recall M. barkerae and the two species may be, on this basis, closely related.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very widespread species, E. woodii is closely allied to E. hispidula and can easily be mistaken for it, but differs chiefly in having a capitate stigma instead of a plate-like or cup-shaped one, the flowers usually all in the leaf axils and in having appendiculate anthers. However, the difference in their distribution would ensure that the two species could not be collected in the field together. E. hispidula occurs in the winter rainfall area whilst E. woodii grows in areas receiving rain in summer.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, HA; Oliver, EGH. 1967. Ericas in southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Although confused in the past with Moraea natalensis, which has a similar habit with the leaf inserted on the stem just below the inflorescence, M. inclinata is taller and more robust, sometimes up to 900 mm tall, with the inner rhipidial spathes 34-40 mm long and the outer only about half as long. Other differences include the globose capsules, ± 5 mm in diam., and the larger flowers with outer tepals 25-30 mm long vs. capsules club-shaped, up to 10 mm long, and outer tepals 15-20 mm long in M. natalensis.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is very distinct in the genus for its densely lanate-ciliate leaves, bract, bracteoles and sepals, adaxial glands on sepals rendering the corolla viscid, and the very large anther pores.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: Up to 600 mm tall, Moraea pubiflora is a fairly robust species of sect. Vieusseuxia and most easily distinguished by inner tepals divided into 3 subequal slender, spreading, brown-speckled lobes, the outer two expanded at the tips and obtuse, and the inner slender with a ± acute apex and curving upward distally. The outer tepal limbs are typically white but the claws, inner tepals and style branches and crests are densely dotted with dark brown on a pale yellow to greenish background. A particularly unusual feature of the species is the scabrid to velvety surface of the outside of the outer tepals. Similar in flower structure, although smooth or papillate on the outside of the outer tepals, M. brevistyla has similarly coloured but much smaller flowers, the outer tepals 18-20 mm long and the filaments just 5-7 mm long compared with outer tepals 25-30 mm long and filaments 13-15 mm long in M. pubiflora.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unmistakable in having two opposed, strongly coiled leaves, each with a broad, translucent central band along the midline. The translucent, prominently veined spathes and subsessile, cylindric ovary with a sterile tubular beak are typical of sect. Gynandriris, in which the large, dark blue to violet flowers with broad reflexed inner and outer tepal limbs, the latter 21-30 x 10-15, are also distinctive. Moraea pritzeliana and M. contorta share an unusual feature, viz. as the capsules mature at the end of the growing season the stem becomes loosely coiled.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Rarely exceeding 120 mm in height, Moraea tortilis is distinguished by tightly coiled, corkscrew-like leaves terete in section. Plants are usually branched and the flowers, violet or sometimes white with yellow nectar guides, are distinctive in the broad, half reflexed tepal limbs. The ovary and capsules remain enclosed in the spathes as in the closely allied M. serpentina, which has loosely coiled to twisted leaves, the blades channelled or flat, and predominantly yellow or white flowers with erect or suberect, spathulate inner tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The inflated, tubular, falcate leaves are diagnostic for Micranthus tubulosus, the spikes and flowers of which differ hardly at all from those of M. alopecuroides. A particularly distinctive feature of the leaves is the prominent brown mucro at the obtuse to ± truncate apices. The leaves are often ± dry at flowering time.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by its small, predominantly white flowers with outer tepals up to 27 mm long, and dark purple style branches and crests, Moraea modesta is a low-growing species, seldom reaching more than 200 mm in height. The vestigial inner tepals are 5-6 mm long, either hair-like cusps or obscurely 3-lobed at the apex. It is one of several species that flower after the foliage leaf, produced the previous summer, is dry and dead. The leaf is sometimes retained at flowering, still attached to the base of the flowering stem but more often has decayed and is no longer evident. A new, emergent leaf is sometimes present at flowering, extending well above the stem later in the growing season. Populations from near Machadodorp in central Mpumalanga have more-or-less free filaments, unusual for the species, and require additional study. In other populations the filaments are united for at least half their length.
