bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The close affinity between K. breviflora and K. buchananii has been discussed under the latter species above. They are separated mainly on the basis of the shorter perianth of K. buchananii. At the other end of the scale, K. breviflora is related to the following species, K. albescens, which forms more robust plants with leaves 8-15 mm broad, and longer perianth, 11-15 mm and bracts 7-9 mm long. The latter species also has a more northerly distribution, extending into Mpumalanga but, where the two overlap in northern KwaZulu-Natal, it is sometimes difficult to distinguish between them with certainty.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: For differences between this species and the related K. breviflora, see notes after the latter species. In perianth length, K. albescens approaches K. fibrosa and K. crassifolia, but these two species are much less robust, with narrow grass-like leaves and serrulate margins.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Widespread and relatively common in interior southern Africa, Moraea polystachya is recognised by the combination of several foliage leaves, branched stem, and large blue-mauve to violet flowers. The limbs of both tepal whorls are half reflexed but only the outer tepals bear nectar guides, and the tepal claws form a narrow cup enclosing the filaments and broad style branches, leaving the style crests prominently displayed. An unusual and particularly distinctive feature of most populations is the red veining on the ovary, this absent in plants from the Little Karoo. Once regarded as an ecological variant of M. polystachya, M. venenata is now regarded as a separate, but closely related species. A shorter plant, M. venenata has somewhat larger flowers with inner tepals usually held ± erect, the ovary also typically red-veined. The larger capsules, up to 16-20 mm long, are nodding when mature and contain larger seeds, ± 2 mm long. Capsules of M. polystachya are held erect, are 9-16 mm long and the smaller seeds are 1.2-1.6 mm long. Both M. polystachya and M. venenata are poisonous to stock. Moraea polystachya in the Little Karoo is distinctive not only in lacking red veining on the ovary but in having blue rather than violet flowers with the inner tepals held erect for most of the flowering cycle. No other features appear to distinguish these plants, which flower in the winter months rather than in late summer and autumn.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It somewhat resembles K. breviflora but has broader leaves and broader, obtuse bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Related to the following species, K. fibrosa, but differs in the characteristic serrulation of the leaf margin. Although a search has been made in the type area, no further material has been forthcoming.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Flower colour varies according to the three localities indicated above: (a) in the typical form, known from only a small area on the western extremity of the Waterberg (Kransberg), the buds are coral-pink shading to creamy white or ivory as the flowers mature; (b) on the highest point of the Blouberg, the plants tend to be smaller with orange-yellow buds, becoming pale yellow in open flowers; (c) in the Soutpansberg to Wolkberg area, the plants tend to be more robust than the typical form, with orange-scarlet buds changing to orange-yellow towards the base of the raceme, bearing a superficial resemblance to K. linearifolia, but differing in the narrower leaves and lanceolate-acuminate bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Related to the former species, K. typhoides, but smaller in stature with shorter and narrower leaves and somewhat smaller flowers, 4-5 mm long. The bracts are ovate, acute, whereas in K. typhoides they are rounded at the apex. The only other species with such small flowers is K. buchananii, but in this species the flowers are white, the bracts are lanceolate, acuminate, and the leaves are grass-like, 400-600 x 2.5-4.0 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Virtually identical to the relatively common Moraea stricta in vegetative features and life history, M. thomsonii is distinguished only by the flowers. The blue-mauve tepals have nectar guides on both the outer and inner tepal limbs and the inner tepals, ± 7 mm wide, are broader than in M. stricta. The style branches are poorly developed and have vestigial crests shorter than the stigma lobes. In M. stricta the style crests are 3-4 mm long and held erect above the nectar guides and the inner tepals are only 3-4 mm wide. As in M. stricta, the leaf is terete, usually dry and broken at flowering time and the sheathing leaves and spathes are more-or-less dry.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A spring-flowering species related to K. littoralis, but the globose racemes are flame-red at the apex, grading down to yellow flowers and the smaller, globose fruits are borne on short, spreading pedicels. Unlike K. littoralis, it grows among sandstone rocks.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The affinity of K. citrina is with the K. uvaria complex, a variable group showing several evolutionary trends. One of these trends has been towards reduction in stature, size of inflorescence and length of perianth, combined with shorter and narrower leaves. Its distribution overlaps with K. uvaria and intermediate specimens are found, suggesting that separate species rank for K. citrina is scarcely justified.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Its nearest affinity is probably with the following species, K. bruceae, from which it differs in its shorter perianth and pedicels and somewhat narrower leaves. The flowers are usually orange-yellow with red-tipped buds, but around Sabie, in Mpumalanga, the flowers lack red pigment and are greenish yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The large yellow or yellow and orange flowers of Moraea ochroleuca are distinctive in their wide cup formed by the tepal claws and spreading tepal limbs. The species is unusual in having nectar secreted from veins over the claw surface rather than from discrete nectaries at the tepal bases as in most other Moraea species. The style branches, relatively well developed and up to 6.5 mm long but only ± as wide as the anthers that are appressed to them, terminate in bilobed stigma lobes but lack discrete crests. The tall plants, up to 750 mm high, typically have a solitary foliage leaf but plants with two, or even three foliage leaves are known, these mostly from higher elevations. Flowers of M. ochroleuca last three days, opening in the morning on the first day and fading gradually during the third day. The flowers have a strong, rather sickly sweet, slightly fermenting odour.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to K. northiae, but distinguished by the narrower leaves which are V-shaped in cross section.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: K. porphyrantha is relatively small in stature with small racemes, pale to lemon-yellow in colour, tinged with red at the apex; the leaves are flaccid, yellow-green in colour with smooth margins. In the herbarium it is not always easy to distinguish it from certain other species with acute to acuminate bracts but, with fresh material, the above characters provide a basis for separating K. porphyrantha from the following: (a) K. triangularis subsp. ob-tusiloba, which has concolorous, coralred to orange-red racemes and spreading perianth lobes; (b) K. galpinii, with its predominantly scarlet racemes and narrower, grass-like leaves; (c) K. thodei with the unusual brownish red and white coloration of its racemes and the usually denticulate leaves; and (d) K. fluviatilis, which resembles K. porphyrantha in the colour of the raceme but has longer flowers (42-50 mm) and the leaves tend to be broader, more glaucous and are V-shaped in cross section.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Moraea umbellata has the vegetative morphology typical of subg. Umbellatae, viz. a stem comprising a long basal internode, leaves clustered well above ground at the first aerial node where branching occurs, and several subequal branches clustered in semi-umbellate manner. Plants can be robust, reaching as much as 450 mm in height and can often be distinguished by size alone. The flowers are also distinctive with the tepal claws 5-7 mm long and enclosing the filaments, which are either united entirely or free near the apex, and reduced and narrow style branches appressed to but shorter than the anthers and lacking crests. The outer inflorescence spathes may be entirely sheathing or free distally as in several other species of the subgenus. The fugaceous flowers last only a few hours, opening in the late afternoon, fading in early evening and completely collapsed by 19:00. Individuals of three of four populations so far examined cytologically are triploid, 2n = 30, hence sexually sterile, and only one diploid population is known, 2n = 20. It seems likely that many populations of the species are triploid as plants often fail to set seed, and most collections lack developing capsules. Reproduction in the sexually sterile plants is evidently by the numerous tiny cormlets produced around the base of the mother corm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: K. parviflora is unique in the genus in usually having a secund raceme. As the flowers start to open, the inflorescence leans to one side and the flowers turn in that direction. In the bud stage the raceme is narrowly cylindrical and may be confused in the herbarium with K. breviflora, but K. parviflora has longer racemes, greenish yellow to pale greenish brown flowers and broader, more ovate bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Poorly known, Moraea unibracteata is one of the smallest members of subg. Grandiflorae. It can always be recognised by the stem bearing a single sheathing leaf, this inserted in the upper half of the stem and usually reaching or overlapping the rhipidial spathes. The pale yellow to almost white flowers are unremarkable in the subgenus, although relatively small, with outer tepals 30-45 mm long and anthers 7-9 mm long. The tepals are reported to have dark veins, especially evident when dry.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: These small, depauperate plants may be confused with K. littoralis and K. drepanophylla. It is considered that the type of K. longicollis Baker is probably a small specimen of K. rooperi; although the bracts are not an exact match of K. rooperi, they come nearer to that species than to K. littoralis. The plant illustrated in Curtis's Botanical Magazine t. 7623 (Baker 1898a) as K. longicollis is not that species but is probably a form of K. praecox. It is also doubtful if the plant figured as K. rooperi in Curtis's Botanical Magazine t. 6116 (Hooker 1874) is correctly named. The raceme is too elongate for K. rooperi and it appears to be a form of K. linearifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A fairly clear-cut species showing affinity to the Limpopo species, K. coralligemma, from which it differs in its longer bracts, somewhat shorter, broader and more glaucous leaves, shorter peduncles and in the flowering time.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: K. ritualis has conspicuously long, narrow bracts like those of K. sarmentosa but is distinguished from the latter by its markedly serrulate leaves and longer perianth, which is 25-30 mm long, as against 20-25 mm in K. sarmentosa.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The two to four leaves are straight, firm-textured, erect, hollow and round to oval in section, ± 2-3 mm diam., and reach or shortly exceed the spike. When alive the leaves are smooth with the veins evident as paler, translucent lines. On drying, the veins appear hyaline and the veins at the adaxial and abaxial poles are somewhat more prominent. The stem is often branched, and as many as four (exceptionally nine) short branches may be produced shortly below the base of the main spike, these seldom exceeding half the length of the main spike. The lower flowers of the spike are often replaced by cormlets [as many as five may be present in an axil.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Resembling Moraea villosa in its velvety stems and outer leaf surfaces, M. tulbaghensis typically has bright orange flowers with navy blue to glossy, emerald green nectar guides. The flowers are usually somewhat smaller than those of M. villosa, the outer tepals 22-40 mm long, but the species is most easily distinguished by the anthers, 7-10 mm long and exceeding the style branches and often overtopping the particularly short crests ± 2 mm long. Western populations, recognised as Iris pavonia and later named M. neopavonia, sometimes have small, elliptic to obscurely three-lobed rather than the strongly tricuspidate inner tepals that characterise other populations, and are diploid, whereas the species is tetraploid elsewhere. Tepal markings in these populations are either navy blue or consist of small dark spots. Populations from Voëlvlei and at Elandsberg Nature Reserve have dark red rather than the more common orange flowers. Even more unusual, a white-flowered population occurs on the slopes of Kasteelberg.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The leaves of K. stricta are U-shaped in cross section, rigid, erect and strongly nervose, often with the margins tending to be inrolled. When herbarium specimens are prepared, the leaves become flattened and the characteristic shape is not always apparent. Along the nerves there are often minute papillae, making the leaf surface scabrid to the touch, which may lead to confusion with the following species, K. hirsuta, in which the leaves are hispid and V-shaped in cross section.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished by its relatively large white to pale yellow flowers, the outer tepals with narrow, deep yellow nectar guides, and the much reduced inner tepals, hair-like cusps just 5-7 mm long, usually entire, or obscurely 3-lobed at the apex. One of the taller species of eastern southern African species of sect. Vieusseuxia, it stands up to 600 mm high.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Herbarium specimens of K. thodei without notes on flower colour may be confused with either K. porphyrantha or K. triangularis. Fresh specimens may be recognized by the unusual colour combination in the raceme, with buds dull red to brownish red often tipped with white, and open flowers whitish in colour. In K. porphyrantha the raceme is lemon-yellow tinged with red at the apex and the leaves are yellow-green with smooth margins. K. triangularis has concolorous coral-red to orange-red racemes and the leaves are usually longer and more fibrous in texture than in K. thodei.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 2005. Asphodelaceae (First part): Kniphofia, Fl. S. Africa 5(1,2): 1-94. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209560#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised in Moraea by the yellow, finely veined flowers and perianth of only three tepals, united basally in a short perianth tube. In addition, the narrowly fusiform ovary is included within the spathes and the compressed seeds are winged at both ends. The relationships of M. cooperi remain puzzling and it is provisionally included in subg. Umbellatae, with which its brown corm tunics, pale yellow, finely veined tepals and chromosome number, n = 10 are consistent. A perianth tube is also found in M. longiflora of the subgenus and the two species were placed together in sect. Tubiflorae of subg. Moraea in earlier studies. Molecular phylogenetic studies do not place M. cooperi among other species of subg. Umbellatae but show it to be isolated, at least with the plastid DNA loci so far sequenced. The presence of a floral tube prompted Foster (1939) to transfer both Moraea cooperi and M. longiflora to Gynandriris (now sect. Gynandriris of Moraea) but the members of sect. Gynandriris do not actually have a perianth tube but rather a tubular extension of the ovary and are not closely related to M. cooperi.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively short species, 200-400 mm tall, characterised by its white flowers with laxly spreading tepals marked with nectar guides only on the outer tepal limbs, a strong, rich floral scent, and well-developed style crests. Confusion is perhaps possible with Moraea inconspicua but that species has a smaller flower, occasionally with white tepals but more often yellow to brown or creamy pink, with the tepal limbs always sharply reflexed, at least to 45º and more often to ± 90º.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Annual prostrate hispid herb. Leaves oblong to ovate, upper deeply pinnatifid and sharply dentate. Petals pink to pale violet. Mericarps with eglandular apical pits and 2 furrows below the pit, tail 50-110(-200) mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, HJT; Verhoeven, RL. 1990. The genus Erodium in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 56: 79-92. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1990); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Annual prostrate hispid to hirsute and glanduliferous herb. Leaves ovate to elliptic, pinnate; pinnae pinnatifid to pinnate, but always divided for more than half-way to midrib. Petals purplish-pink to whitish. Mericarps with eglandular apical pits, furrow below pit absent, faint or distinct, tail 10-70 mm long. Webb and Chater recognize three subspecies in E. cicutarium, viz. subspecies cicutarium, bipinnatum Tourlet and jacquinianum (Fisher, CA. Meyer & Ave-Lall.) Brig. Although much variation occurs in E. cicutarium in southern Africa all the specimens examined belong to E. cicutarium subsp. cicutarium (G.G. Guittonneau, University of Orleans, Orleans, France, pers. comm., 1987).
bibliographicCitation: Venter, HJT; Verhoeven, RL. 1990. The genus Erodium in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 56: 79-92. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1990); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: One of several species of the ‘peacock moraea’ group of species, characterised by their particularly broad, spreading outer tepals marked with large, contrasting markings, Moraea villosa is distinguished by the velvety stems and abaxial leaf surfaces, large flowers with outer tepals 28-40 x 20-25 mm and 3-lobed inner tepals with a long, spreading central lobe, and the well-developed style branches 6-8 mm long with crests 3-8 mm long. The anthers are usually shorter than the style branches, though occasionally slightly longer. The closely related M. tulbaghensis, which has orange to red (rarely white) flowers, has anthers exceeding the shorter and narrower style branches and significantly smaller flowers (outer tepals 28-31 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea vegeta with its several characteristic glaucous leaves, velvety stem, and somewhat pendulous capsules is not easily confused with related species with similar flowers such as M. papilionacea and M. gawleri (the latter its closest relative according to molecular data). Moraea indecora, restricted to northern Namaqualand, has similar drooping capsules but rather different habit and flowers, and may be immediately related but molecular evidence on the question is lacking. Moraea vegeta is one of the few species of the genus that has adapted to human settlement and it is most common, almost weedy, in parts of the Constantia area of the Cape Peninsula where it thrives under the naturalised oaks and pines. Moraea vegeta is also one of few species of Moraea that is self-compatible and autogamous in the absence of insect-mediated pollen transfer. The dull-coloured and inconspicuous flowers are consistent with this mode of reproduction.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely resembling Moraea fugax in general appearance except smaller in all features, M. filicaulis has a slender, almost filiform stem ± 1 mm in diam., and one or more often two subequal or unequal, filiform, narrowly channelled leaves inserted at the first above ground internode. The flowers are usually white, but occasionally pink or blue-mauve or even violet, and have outer tepals mostly 20-35 mm long (occasionally longer) and inner tepals 18-30 mm long. Flowers of M. fugax have outer tepals mostly 30-45 mm long and inner tepals 25-35 mm long. The inner rhipidial spathes, a useful measure of plant size, are 20-35(-40) mm long in M. filicaulis but 40-65 mm long in M. fugax. Moraea filicaulis has been treated as a subspecies of M. fugax and an important reason for recognising it as a separate species is that it sometimes co-occurs with typical M. fugax but always showing slightly different habitat preferences.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowers are yellow, the petals and filaments often tinged with purple on fading. Flowering time is apparently entirely dependent on rainfall. This species can be confused with Sisymbrium turczaniuowii but differs in the 1-nerved valves and the ± conical beak of the fruit and in the ovary generally being glabrous at anthesis. It can also be recognized by the retrorse hairs on the basal part of the stem.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W. 1970. Cruciferae, Fl. S. Africa 13: 1-118. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowers are white, produced from August to October. Phillips describes the cotyledons as transversely 2-folded.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W. 1970. Cruciferae, Fl. S. Africa 13: 1-118. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the solitary leaf inserted on the stem well above ground, the stem flexed above the sheath of the foliage leaf, and yellow or pink flowers with the tepal claws forming a narrow cup including both filaments and anthers. The capsules are unusually long, even for sect. Homeria, typically 30-40 mm long and have a short blunt beak ± 1 mm long. It is often difficult to distinguish in herbaria from several other solitary-leaved species of sect. Homeria, in particular M. minor and M. flaccida. In M. minor the shorter anthers are 3-5 mm long, the style branches are 5-6 mm long and divide 2-3 mm above the anther bases, the ovary is shorter, up to 10 mm long, with capsules 18-28 mm long. Taller, more robust M. flaccida has tepals 35-40 mm long with claws that diverge to form a wide cup, elongate capsules, typically 30-55 mm long, with an acute beak ± 2 mm long. Natural hybrids between Moraea collina and M. flaccida have been recorded from the Cape Peninsula.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: L. ensifolia differs from other species of Ledebouria in having fusiform roots. L. cooperi and L. revoluta (L.f.) Jessop are commonly misidentified as L. ensifolia but both have bracteoles and smooth carpel lobes; the latter also has elongate styles (±6 mm). In addition, the torn leaves of L. revoluta reveal `threads' (from unravelling xylem), no such `threads' occur in the leaves of L. ensifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Edwards, TJ; Venter, S. 2003. A revision of Ledebouria (Hyacinthaceae) in South Africa. 3. The reinstatement of L.ensifolia, L.galpinii and L. sandersonii. Bothalia 33(1): 49-51. [CC BY]

description: Usually easy to recognise by the long basal internode with the leaf or leaf pair inserted at the first node above ground, Moraea fugax has a few- to several-branched stem and relatively large flowers. Also distinctive, the ovary and capsules are included in the spathes and have a short beak, conspicuous in fruit. The species includes three main morphs. The typical form with yellow flowers and relatively broad inner tepal limbs is often early flowering, mainly in August to the middle of September, and occurs mostly on stony sandstone slopes. A second morph has white to blue flowers with narrower inner tepals and is largely coastal, occurring in deep sands and extending from Namaqualand to Hermanus but inland for some distance and occasional in the Olifants River Valley. A third morph from interior southwestern Cape has smaller, white flowers with unusually narrow inner tepals. The tall, white to blue-flowered morph has been recognised as M. longifolia (or as M. edulis var. longifolia) [under the assumption that M. edulis represented yellow-flowered plants]. Another unusual variant is represented by yellow flowered plants from the Pakhuis Mtns and nearby flowering in late September and October, with inner tepals erect (unique in the complex) and particularly slender stems and filiform, tightly rolled leaves. Not only is M. fugax diverse morphologically but chromosome numbers are strikingly varied, with diploid numbers ranging from 2n = 20 to 10, the lower numbers usually associated with yellow-flowered populations. Further investigation at population level is necessary to resolve variation in the complex into a more refined taxonomy.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small, tufted plant seldom reaching 60 mm when in flower, producing several smooth, falcate leaves, sometimes with ciliate margins, surrounding one or more sessile inflorescences, the spathes of which differ hardly at all from the leaves except by their position subtending the fugaceous blooms. The flowers are white with prominent yellow nectar guides on the outer tepals and dark purple or sometimes grey markings on the inner tepals and frequently dark purple on the lower half of the otherwise white style crests.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The rare M. galpinii is distinguished by the single, slender foliage leaf, usually barely emergent at flowering time but ultimately exceeding the stem. The blade appears at first to be terete but has a narrow adaxial groove separating the two closely appressed leaf halves. The flowers, fairly typical of subg. Grandiflorae, are bright yellow and have outer tepals 40-50 mm long with spreading limbs and erect inner tepals ± 35 mm long. Particularly distinctive is the collar of hard, blackish vertical fibres enclosing the base of the stem and extending a short distance above ground. This feature is shared with M. robusta, which is distinguished by paler, larger flowers with erect to spreading inner and outer tepal limbs. Young plants not yet of flowering age have rather soft, unbroken ± membranous cataphylls.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively small plant, Moraea gawleri is most easily recognised by its short rhipidial spathes, the inner seldom more than 20 mm long and the outer about half as long, and the two or rarely solitary foliage leaf, the blades sometimes loosely coiled and the margins undulate to crisped, although plane-margined forms (var. rectifolia Baker) occur, often in moister habitats. The small flowers are unexceptional except for their variable colouring, sometimes brick-red, white or yellow or combinations of these colours. Both morphology and molecular studies show the species is closely allied to other members of subg. Moraea, in particular M. vegeta and M. vlokii. This last species is almost identical to M. gawleri vegetatively but has flowers with reduced style branches that lack crests, and usually a solitary foliage leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Pollination is most probably by insects and the ripe seeds are ejected by the usual catapult mechanism. Regeneration from seed takes place after fires. The leaves have a faint smell of turpentine or eucalyptus when crushed. This plant appears in most respects to be atypical Euchaetis. (1) The flowers are in pairs. (2) The petals are transversely bearded. (3) Staminodes are vestigial. The anther possesses a small apical gland which is rather larger than normal. The disc is well developed and exceeds the ovary. (6) The stigma is capitate. (7) The style is short. (8) The filaments and style are glabrous. (9) The ovary is 5-carpellate. Euchaetis albertiniana is recognised as distinct from E. burchellii in that it is destroyed by fires whereas E. burchellii develops a stout rootstock from which it may regenerate after fires. Unfortunately this valuable character is seldom noted on a herbarium sheet. Among other characteristic differences one may, however, see that the leaves in E. albertiniana are often adpressed, ciliolate with an apical callus, whereas those of E. burchellii are never so. The anther in E. albertiniana possesses a small pointed gland, but that of E. burchellii is minute. E. albertiniana is also closely related to Euchaetis laevigata Turcz. but differs in that the leaves of E. laevigata are complicate, orbicular, spreading and somewhat more recurved towards the apex. The apical gland on the anther in E. laevigata is minute as in E. burchellii but not in E. albertiniana. E. burchellii is found in sandy soil fairly near the coast from near Great Brak River in the east to Uilenkraal River near Gans Baai in the west. E. laevigata occurs on limestone hills near Bredasdorp. The name refers to the locality where this species occurs.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1975. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 5. J. S. African Bot. 41(3): 167-186. [CC BY]

description: It is perhaps closest to E. albertiniana Williams which however is a fairly diffuse shrub, single-stemmed at base with leaves sometimes adpressed and with a small apical callus. It differs from E. laevigata Turcz. which has leaves sub-complicate, orbicular and spreading and is found growing upon limestone to the east of Bredasdorp.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: Euchaetis cristagalli is most easily recognised as distinct from other species of Euchaetis with linear-lanceolate leaves because of its having the longest petals. It has been observed that these petals very readily fall away. E. cristagalli may be distinguished from E. elata which has leaves sessile, pubescent on the adaxial surface and flowers sessile ± 3-nate with the style at some time deflexed; from E. glomerata which has broader leaves and smaller flowers in multi-florous heads; from E. flexilis which has leaves with sacculate apices and broad translucent margins. It is perhaps nearest in appearance to E. linearis which however has leaves with only two rows of gland dots, flowers in many flowered heads with small petals and a disc that stands open, not obvallate. The name refers to the locality where this plant occurs.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1979. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 8. J. S. African Bot. 45(2): 147-184. [CC BY]

description: Unique in subg. Vieusseuxia, the diminutive Moraea fergusoniae has 3 to 6 foliage leaves, all basal, and the short stems consist of only one or two aerial internodes. The flowers are usually white to creamy white but very attractive blue-flowered populations occur in the vicinity of Swellendam. The flowers are long-lived and have either entire and lanceolate or 3-lobed inner tepals, then with a longer acute central cusp and short lateral lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive among the eastern southern African species of sect. Vieusseuxia in its attractive dark purple flowers with yellow nectar guides, and 3-lobed inner tepals, the linear central lobe shorter or sometimes longer than the lateral lobes which have rounded, expanded tips.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Towards the north, where the populations occur at higher altitudes, plants appear to have broader distinctly petiolate leaves with the margins becoming crisped ciliate; on the broadest leaves two extra rows of gland dots appear along the margins, one to either side. Young leaves become decidedly pubescent in the most northerly populations and the sparse pubescence on the adaxial surface of the leaves seems to disappear. Euchaetis elata is recognised as distinct having the disc obvallate, surrounding the ovary but neither closing over it nor spreading, having flowerheads without conspicuous involucral leaves as in E. longibracteata, with the flowers opening first at the apex of the inflorescence, having the style at some stage deflexed, with petals obtuse 3.8 mm long, not as long as 5.5 mm in E. cristagalli, having leaves linear-lanceolate, inflexed, obtusely mucronate, not flat, with margins ciliolate or crisped ciliate, not villous ciliate as in E. avisylvana, and having fruits with horns less than 1 mm long not 3.5 mm long as in E. glomerata. The leaves of E. linearis are seen to differ in having more numerous gland dots that are also very much smaller in diameter, and the leaves of E. flexilis clearly differ in their sacculate apices.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: Although vegetatively typical of subg. Visciramosae, Moraea elsiae is immediately recognised by the flowers with subequal tepals, all with nectar guides at the bases of the limbs, and the reduced style branches with vestigial crests overtopped by the anthers. Flowers of M. elsiae are usually yellow but white-flowered plants have been recoded at Kleinmond and near Elim, the latter with flowers slightly smaller than elsewhere.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Euchaetis elsieae is recognised as distinct on account of its having linear-elliptic obtuse leaves, somewhat thickened at the apex, flat on the adaxial surface (concave when dried) and rounded on the outside, with the flowers borne usually in pairs. It differs from Eucaetis glomerata Bart & Wendl. Euchaetis elata Eckl. & Zeyh., Euchaetis linearis Sond. and Euchaetis flexilis Eckl. & Zeyh., all of which have flowers aggregated into multiflorous heads and leaves varying from linear to lanceolate. It is nearest to E. flexilis but differs in that the apex of the leaves in E. elsieae is thickened whereas in E. flexilis it is sacculate.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1974. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 3. Euchaetis elsieae Williams sp. nov. J. S. African Bot. 40(2): 85-89. [CC BY]

description: Euchaetis ericoides is recognised as distinct because of having leaves that are rather flat with a tendency to curl upwards, i.e. sub-secund. Other distinguishing characters are: the disc closes over the ovary at first, the fruit is 5-carpellate with horns not cleft at the apex, the leaves are lanceolate, fairly flat, glabrous, opposite or alternate and not gibbous behind the apex.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: Euchaetis esterhuysenae is recognised as distinct having leaves small, ovate, glabrous, sessile, alternate and spreading, and small flowers with petals that soon fall away.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1979. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 8. J. S. African Bot. 45(2): 147-184. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the two or more foliage leaves, the blades linear, channelled and up to 6 mm wide, and the relatively small, Moraea-type flower with well-developed, broad style branches and prominent, erect crests. The stems have several branches in mature plants in seasons of adequate rainfall and the flowers are usually blue to blue-mauve with yellow nectar guides only on the outer tepal limbs, the outer tepals 16-30 mm long and the inner 14-25 mm long. Plants from the Perdebont Valley in the southern Little Karoo near the northern end of Robinson Pass have pale yellow flowers otherwise exactly like those of blue-flowered plants. This is a striking exception not only for M. bipartita but for the entire sect. Polyanthes. Closely related Moraea polyanthos is virtually identical vegetatively to M. bipartita but has subequal tepals, the limbs of both whorls spreading horizontally and bearing small white to yellow nectar guides, and the style branches, ± as wide as the anthers, lack crests. The filaments of M. polyanthos are united in a slender column whereas those of M. bipartita are free in the upper third. Hybrids between M. bipartita and M. polyanthos have been recorded where the two species co-occur, and plants with a range of flowers intermediate between the two indicate introgression among the hybrids. Moraea polystachya has flowers of similar form to those of M. bipartita, thus with broad style branches and crests, but plants are larger as are the flowers, the outer tepals 36-55 mm long. The ovary is often veined dark red in M. polystachya but is uniformly green in M. bipartita.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Late-flowering Moraea saxicola is recognised by the solitary foliage leaf with thickened, straight to undulate margins, and relatively large flowers with outer tepals 34-45 mm long and the limbs of both whorls half reflexed. The tepals are usually pale blue in the north of its range, white to palest yellow elsewhere, and the outer tepal limbs bear pale yellow nectar guides. The foliage leaf is fairly broad and slightly undulate with occasionally slightly crisped margins. Unusual for Moraea, the juvenile leaves are narrow and sometimes terete and coiled near the apex. By the time these plants reach flowering age, the leaf is usually broad, channelled and trailing. Moraea saxicola is allied to the yellow-flowered M. bolusii of northern Namaqualand, which also has an undulate leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unusual in subg. Vieusseuxia in the pale pink (sometimes almost white) flower, the outer tepals with white or pink nectar guides with broad purple edges, and the unusually long filaments, united in a slender column 10-15 mm long and free for 5 mm, thus raising the anthers well above the tepal limbs so that the bright, orange-red pollen is clearly visible. The well-developed inner tepals, ± 15 mm long, are held almost erect, the limbs curving inward and with attenuate apices or sometimes obscurely 3-lobed, with the central lobe particularly prominent and the lateral lobes no more than small obtuse lateral projections. The slender, typically unbranched stem and often nearly entire inner tepals suggest a possible relationship with violet-flowered M. incurva, which shares these features, as well as having unusually long filaments and the anthers prominently displayed above the outer tepal limbs.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A slender species standing up to 300 mm tall, Moraea barnardii is immediately distinguished by the white flowers faintly blue-veined on the underside, with broad, spreading to laxly reflexed outer tepal limbs with undulate margins and nectar guides consisting of a ring of dark blue edged with radiating blue lines. Flowers lack inner tepals and have short filaments 8-9 mm long, united in the lower third, dark blue anthers and red pollen. Plants are usually unbranched. The immediate relationships of M. barnardii are with the Caledon Swartberg endemic M. longiaristata and the several differences between then are discussed under that species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to Moraea tricuspidata and often difficult to distinguish from it as dry specimens, M. bellendenii is a taller plant often exceeding 1 m in height with yellow flowers darkly spotted in the centre. The flowers have broad outer tepal limbs laxly spreading and curving upward distally, and 3-lobed inner tepals. As in white- to pale creamy yellow-flowered M. tricuspidata, the inner tepals have short, obtuse lateral lobes and a linear central cusp-like lobe that curves inward obliquely. The inner tepals of M. bellendenii are 8-10 mm long, whereas those of M. tricuspidata are 10-12 mm long. The two may also be distinguished by the filaments, 6-7 mm long in M. tricuspidata vs. 3-5 mm in M. bellendenii.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: E. glomerata is recognised as distinct having the disc obvallate, neither closing over the ovary nor spreading, having the style at some stage deflexed and petals obtuse only 2.8 mm long, having leaves lanceolate, acute, sessile, adpressed, with margins serrulate and rigidly ciliate, and having fruits with horns 3.5 mm long. In the flower heads the first flowers open at the base of the head and the last at the apex.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: E. intonsa is a distinct species having leaves alternate, elliptic, sparsely pubescent and ciliate, with bracts, bracteoles and calyx lobes pubescent and with petals small with the midrib glabrous on the inside. It differs from E. burchellii, E. laevigata and E. scabricosta which have opposite leaves, glabrous bracts and glabrous calyx lobes. Although E. meridionalis, a more glabrous plant, is found nearby and may also have 4 or 5-ranked leaves, it differs from E. intonsa which has smaller, sparsely pubescent, leaves and pubescent bracts, bracteoles and calyx lobes. The epithet 'intonsa' refers to this hairiness.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1978. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 7. J. S. African Bot. 44(4): 329-362. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from its allies in subg. Visciramosae by its relatively large, usually yellow flowers with spreading to half-reflexed tepals with only the outer bearing nectar guides, and by the large, often obtuse spathes, 25-40 mm long. Confusion between M. bituminosa and M. bubalina is possible as the latter has equally large tepals and spathes, but the spathes in M. bubalina are acute with the outer spathe half to two-thirds as long as the inner (subequal in M. bituminosa). In addition, M. bubalina, from dry areas in the Western Karoo and Clanwilliam District, has dull buff- to khaki-coloured flowers, the tepal claws forming a wide cup, and relatively short style crests only 2-3 mm long. Currently included in M. bituminosa, plants from the Tulbagh Valley and Jonkershoek have larger flowers than are typical of the species and a blue-mauve perianth with white nectar guides. The taxonomic status of these plants remains to be established.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Euchaetis longibracteata with its conspicuous involucral leaves is easily recognised as distinct. It should be noted that it falls into the group in which the disc is obvallate, not closing over the ovary and not spreading.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: Euchaetis pungens is recognised as distinct with its rigid prickly habit, having the anther cuneiform-ovoid in shape, the disc closing over the ovary with a 5-sided aperture fitting the 5-sided stigma, having evanescent staminodes and having a fruit with the horns deeply divided. It has also been noted that the calyx lobes are unusually deeply divided.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: Distinct in subg. Visciramosae in having more than two leaves and acute rhipidial spathes, features it shares with M. striata and M. vespertina but it differs from these species in the buff-coloured to brown perianth with spreading claws forming a wide cup, the subequal tepals all bearing nectar guides, and the relatively short style branches and crests.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Fruits ripen mostly in November and December. At first glance it would almost appear that this flower, with its stigma and anthers in close proximity, completely hidden between the densely bearded petals, must be self-pollinating. However the following factors may indicate that this is not the case: The disc exudes nectar apparently to attract insects. The limb of the petal spreads widely displaying a small but nevertheless obvious flower. The stigma is never really in contact with the anthers and the style lengthens to elevate the stigma only after the anthers have discharged their pollen. The pollen is somewhat sticky and does not fall upon the stigma when the anther splits open. In flowers examined, the pollen has all vanished by the time that the stigma has been raised to its highest position. The flowers are inhabited by small insects, up to 1.3 mm long, in various stages of development who apparently live on the nectar and pollen therein. These do not, however, appear to be the pollinating agents which must be very much larger. The seeds when ripe are ejected from the capsule and may be thrown up to 1 m from the plant. Regeneration would only appear to take place from seed and normally only after fires. The leaves have an odour reminiscent of cedar when crushed.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1974. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 4. J. S. African Bot. 40(4): 275-290. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the mauve-lilac to almost pink or whitish flowers with 3-lobed inner tepals, and broadly ovate outer tepals limbs with small, yellow or black nectar guides. Unlike most other members of the section the leaves and stems are usually glabrous, but at least a population from the Grootwinterhoek Mtns has conspicuously velvety stems, and somewhat larger flowers, seemingly confirming the relationship of M. caeca to the M. villosa alliance. Moraea caeca is the only montane species of sect. Villosae. It is distinguished from M. villosa by its smaller flowers with reduced nectar guides.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It seems to be rather rare and when found very few plants are to be seen. It may have possibly been largely eliminated by cultivation. Euchaetis schlechteri is a distinct species most readily distinguished by the disc being open sinuate-crenulate as in Diosma and the capitate stigma 0.6-1.0 mm diam. The lanceolate, often pungent leaves up to 1.5 mm long, without obvious gland dots, also make it easy to recognise. It may be distinguished from E. diosmoides which has a much smaller stigma 0.2-0.5 mm diam.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 10. A review of the genus Euchaetis. J. S. African Bot. 47(2): 157-193. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf47unse] [CC BY]

description: With relatively small, blue to violet flowers and orange-red pollen, Moraea algoensis is distinguished primarily by the characteristic inner tepals, often dark violet to brown, with a broad, relatively short limb, sometimes entire or 3-lobed with a long, incurved central lobe. The filaments are united in the lower 2/3 in a slender, smooth column, arching outward distally, and bearing pale blue anthers with bright orange pollen. Flowers of some populations may be confused with M. unguiculata, but that species rarely has blue flowers and more strongly reflexed outer tepal limbs, the inner tepals darkly speckled on a yellow to white background, and a consistently trilobed inner tepal limb with the longer, narrow central cusp coiled inward. Bright red to orange pollen is not known in M. unguiculata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Euchaetis vallis-simiae is recognised as distinct because of having prominently-nerved, elliptic leaves which, with the bracts, bracteoles and calyx lobes, are conspicuously gibbous behind the apex and scabro-tomentose on both sides. It also has an erect style bearing an unusually large capitate stigma.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1979. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 8. J. S. African Bot. 45(2): 147-184. [CC BY]

description: A clump-forming species, Moraea alticola is distinguished by its habit and broad, more-or-less plane foliage leaf 14-15 mm wide, both features shared with M. spathulata. Despite its occurrence in an alpine area, at high elevations in the Drakensberg, it is easily the largest, most robust species in the genus. Although size alone makes M. alticola easy to recognise it is also distinctive in its uppermost cataphyll, which forms a well developed, pale, basket-like network well above the ground. Similar net-like cataphylls are found in some other species of subg. Grandiflorae but never as well developed. The pale, watery yellow flowers have rather narrow nectar guides on the outer tepals, unlike the large, yellow to orange nectar guides of most of the many forms of M. spathulata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is very similar to E. crispa subsp. ovata but the leaves of the latter are usually opposite and the fruits are smaller, only about 5 mm in diameter. The corolla tube of E. coriacea is only slightly lobed at the mouth whereas that of E. crispa subsp. ovata is divided into lobes for at least half its length.
bibliographicCitation: Coates Palgrave, K; Coates Palgrave, M. 2002. Trees of southern Africa, 3rd ed. Struik, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the virtually free filaments (united for < 0.4 mm), inner tepals reduced to hair-like cusps up 2.5 mm long, and the distinctive mode of vegetative reproduction in which the parent corm is often replaced annually by two new corms. Plants also often have a cormlet in the leaf axil and as a result form clonal colonies. This unusual characteristic is only evident if the plants are carefully extracted from the ground. The species is most likely to be confused with M. grandis, which also has nearly free filaments but is larger in all features, notably the ovary, 10-12(-15) mm vs. 6-9 mm long in M. amabilis and anthers 9-11 mm long, ± twice as long as the filaments vs. 4.5-7.0(-8.0) mm and up to half again as long as the filaments in M. amabilis. The corms of M. amabilis have pale (rarely dark) brown, coarsely fibrous tunics with prominent vertical elements in contrast to the finer tunic fibres in M. grandis. Apart from smaller flowers, M. amabilis often has white pollen in contrast to the consistently bright red-orange pollen of M. grandis. Capsules of M. amabilis, typically 11-16 mm long, contain relatively small, sharply angular seeds, ± 2 mm at longest axis, with a prominent, pale, spongy micropylar crest, whereas capsules of M. grandis are significantly larger, up to 19 mm long, with a thickened apical ridge and the large, dark brown seeds are up to 3 mm long. The velvety to pilose pubescence is universal on the leaves, stem and spathes of western Karoo populations of M. amabilis but those from the Bokkeveld Mtns, Gifberg and Cederberg-Olifants River mtns usually have glabrous leaves although there are some exceptions in the area. Only moderate confidence can be placed in the pubescence character as some other members of the M. tripetala complex occasionally have hairy leaves (notably M. mutila) although M. grandis is consistently glabrous. In the Nieuwoudtville area M. amabilis and M. grandis are sometimes difficult to distinguish, most likely due to hybridization. Plants from near Worcester included in M. amabilis have unusual, buff-yellow or dusty pink flowers and those from the Rabiesberg, not far distant, also with velvety stems and leaves, were described as having brown (we assume buff-brown) flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea anomala can usually be distinguished from its close allies by the stem bearing two sheathing leaves (rarely one) and with nodes smooth rather than sticky, as well as by the pale yellow flower with filaments united for at least 2 mm and usually 4-8 mm long. Flowers usually open in the late morning, and last till ± 17:00 the same day, but those of the Cederberg populations only to open at ± 16:00 and evidently represent a distinct race of the species. It is most easily confused with M. angusta which has similar nectar guides but usually a single sheathing leaf on the stem and filaments united for ± 1 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A species which, on the whole, is much less variablet than is usually found in Euclea. Intermediate forms between E. crispa var. crispa and E. divinorum are frequently found and very probably represent hybrid forms. A broad-leaved form of the species occurs in tropical Africa and has been described as E. keniensis Fries and E. katangensis de Wild. It cannot be regarded as more than a subspecies or variety of E. divinorum. This broad-leaved form is sometimes difficult to distinguish from E. schimperi, from which it differs, however, by the strigose corolla lobes of the flowers, bristly ovaries and the leaves which are broadest at or below the middle, never above the middle as in E. schimperi. E. huillensis Guerke, based on Baum 33 (represented in Kew and Vienna), also belongs in this broad-leaved form.
bibliographicCitation: De Winter, B. 1963. Ebenaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 54-99. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The only blue-flowered member of subg. Grandiflorae in southern Africa, Moraea ardesiaca is immediately recognised by the large flowers either slate-blue to blue-mauve. Confusion with M. carnea is possible but this species has pale pink flowers with darker pink to purple style crests and smaller, narrower tepals 55-60 mm long vs. 65-70 mm in M. ardesiaca. Moraea carnea also occurs along streams on open slopes at relatively high elevations, usually above 2300 m, whereas M. ardesiaca is generally found at lower elevations along streams and drainage lines.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is significant that the Transvaal plants are the only ones which are in contact with the related E. crispa, from which it mainly differs in the narrow linear leaves and quite glabrous twigs and inflorescences. The Cape and Rhodesian plants of E. linearis occur outside of the distribution of E. crispa. It seems probable therefore that the variability of the Transvaal specimens, where both species occur, can be attributed to hybrid influences. Sterile specimens can be confused with E. pseudebenus but the different habitat and more coriaceous leaves of the latter sufficiently distinguish them to make identification possible even in the sterile state.
bibliographicCitation: De Winter, B. 1963. Ebenaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 54-99. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its solitary habit and relatively large flowers with the outer tepals 60-75 mm long. Populations from KwaZulu-Natal are usually only 250-400 mm high and the stem bears a single sheathing leaf but Eastern Cape populations, treated as subsp. notata, are usually taller, up to 600 mm high, with two or three sheathing leaves, and the style crests stained with mauve near the bases, thus bicoloured. Subsp. graminicola may be confused with M. unibracteata which also has a single sheathing leaf and flowers early in the season but in M. unibracteata the foliage leaf is 2-10 mm wide, the sheathing leaf is inserted close to the base of the inflorescence, leaving the lower part of the stem visible, and the flowers are smaller than those of subsp. graminicola, the lower tepals 30-45 mm long and anthers 7-9 mm long vs. ± 13 mm in M. graminicola.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Living plants of Moraea simulans are readily recognised by their distinctive flowers with the tepals speckled throughout with darker mauve to violet blotches on a pale blue-lilac background, a feature unique in the section but unfortunately not visible when dry. The flowers are moderate in size, having outer tepals 17-28 mm long and both inner and outer tepals are rather narrow with laxly spreading to half reflexed limbs. Flowers open in the middle of the afternoon, usually after 15:30 and last just a few hours, collapsing after 19:00. Despite its several synonyms, M. simulans is not particularly variable except in height and the number of branches, features dependent on growing conditions rather than genetically determined. The species is evidently polyploid but chromosome numbers are known from only two collections, one tetraploid, 2n = 24, and the other hexaploid, 2n = 36.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With a relatively open flower, Moraea patens has tepal claws inclined gently upward forming a wide, shallow cup that includes the filament column and with the tepal limbs extending laxly outward. The filaments are united in a cylindric column 7-8 mm long and papillate in the lower half, and the diverging anthers are held well above the tepal cup. Moraea patens may be most closely related to the widespread M. minor but the two have quite different flowers, the tepal claws in M. minor forming a narrow cup completely including both the filaments and the suberect anthers. Moraea vallisbelli, occurring to the north on the Bokkeveld Mtns, is probably also closely allied but differs in its well-formed tepal cup, reduced style branches, and ovary and capsules enclosed by the accrescent rhipidial spathes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Despite its several synonyms, Moraea pallida is relatively uniform both in the small yellow flowers and low stature with a solitary leaf clasping the lower half of the stem. The flowers have spreading tepal limbs 16-24 mm long and erect claws, ± 3 mm long, clasping the lower part of the filament column. Somewhat unusually for the genus, the filaments are free and diverging distally for 1-2 mm, a feature shared with M. cookii to which it appears to be closely related. The relatively short style branches reach only to the middle of the anthers but have short crests, either erect or curving inward. Populations from KwaZulu-Natal differ somewhat in having numerous small cormlets around the base of the parent corm and even in the axils of the foliage and sheathing leaves. Plants bloom in spring to early summer usually at the end of the dry winter, before the onset of the summer-rainfall season.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Broadly resembling the widespread Moraea cookii in the solitary broad leaf clasping the lower half of the stem, M. marlothii is a taller plant with slightly smaller, usually half nodding flowers with spreading to half reflexed tepals 27-34 x 11-17 mm and nearly equal vs. outer tepals 30-43 x 14-18 mm and markedly larger than the inner in M. cookii. The filaments are completely united whereas those of M. cookii are free in the upper 1-2 mm. A striking feature of M. marlothii is the slender, curved ovary up to 20 mm long. Moraea marlothii co-occurs on the Hantamsberg with vegetatively similar M. reflexa, which has pendent flowers with the tepals fully reflexed and a top-shaped ovary only 7-8 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A fairly typical member of subg. Homeria, Moraea louisabolusiae has flowers with subequal tepals, all bearing nectar guides, short, erect tepal claws, and filaments largely united in a slender column but free in the distal 0.5-1.0 mm. The style branches are ± 2.5 mm long, shorter than the anthers, and bear short crests up to 1.5 mm long. Plants have a solitary, narrow foliage leaf inserted well above ground level and the stem is flexed outward above the sheathing part of the leaf. Apart from the single foliage leaf, the stem bears only sheathing leaves with attenuate apices. The flowers open early in the morning, at first light, and fade between 13:00 and 14:00. Molecular studies place M. louisabolusiae close to M. patens, which also has a solitary foliage leaf and the stem flexed above the leaf sheath but somewhat different flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the tall stature and relatively large white or pale blue flowers, the outer tepals 40-45 mm long, and the well-developed style branches and style crests, Moraea vespertina is also distinctive in subg. Visciramosae in having 4 to 6 foliage leaves, a characteristic shared in the subgenus with M. bubalina and M. striata, the three species constituting sect. Multifoliae. The remaining species of subg. Visciramosae have two foliage leaves and comprise sect. Visciramosae. The populations in the Calvinia area have white flowers, sometimes flushed blue on fading and bloom late October to November whereas plants from the Tanqua Basin have a slate-blue perianth, slightly larger flowers and bloom in September (possibly into October).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A slender plant with solitary, narrow leaf, 1.5-2.0 mm wide, Moraea deltoidea is allied to M. unguiculata and M. tricuspidata and significant differences between them are restricted to the flowers. Moraea deltoidea has oblanceolate inner tepals with a broad claw and short, somewhat attenuate limb extending outward or reflexed to the same degree as the outer tepal limbs. In M. unguiculata the inner tepals consistently have a fairly narrow claw and trilobed limb consisting of two shorter, obtuse lateral lobes and a slender, tapering central lobe that coils inward. The style crests of M. unguiculata are usually well developed and lanceolate, thus longer than wide whereas in M. deltoidea they are deltoid, thus wider than high. Moraea deltoidea may also be confused with M. tricuspidata, which has larger, creamy white flowers with 3-lobed inner tepals in which the lateral lobes are fairly broad and obtuse and the narrow central lobe curves inward obliquely.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Evidently closely related to the widespread M. brevistyla but the two are readily distinguished when alive. They grow within a few metres of one another on the slopes of The Sentinel where M. brevistyla grows on deeper soils on grassy slopes and M. vigilans is confined to basalt outcrops. The most striking difference between them is the broadly ovate to orbicular outer tepal limbs of M. vigilans, spreading or ascending up to 30°, whereas the narrower, oblanceolate-obovate outer tepal limbs of M. brevistyla are weakly to strongly reflexed and the limbs are usually pinched downward in the proximal third. Less apparent are the shorter outer tepal claws of M. vigilans, 7-9 mm long, and shorter filament column and style branches, the latter reaching opposite the apex of the outer tepal limb. The short, brownish crests extend upward above the base of the tepal limbs for up to 4 mm. The outer tepal claws of M. brevistyla are 9-11 mm long, the filaments and anthers are longer than those of M. vigilans (11-12 mm combined length in M. brevistyla vs. ± 8.5 mm in M. vigilans), and the style branches usually exceed the outer tepal limbs by up to 3.5 mm, while the white style crests extend upward a further 5 mm. Vegetatively the two species appear virtually identical but the stems of M. vigilans are somewhat willowy and incline toward the ground, whereas the stems of M. brevistyla are usually stiffly erect.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Specialised in subg. Homeria in having the branches of the style almost or entirely suppressed, the style either dividing near the apex of the anthers, with very short branches, 1-2 mm long, or essentially undivided with three apical stigmatic lobes. In other respects the species broadly resembles M. collina and particularly M. minor in the tepal claws forming a narrow cup including the stamens. In M. minor the style divides at or below the midline of the anthers, and the well-developed style branches are fairly broad and at least 3 mm long, bearing distinct crests. The ovary and capsules of M. longistyla are usually well-exserted from the spathes, while those of M. minor are typically enclosed, at least during development, although the ripe capsules are usually exserted. Moraea longistyla and M. minor have complementary distribution ranges, with M. minor always in sandy soils from the Cape Peninsula northward along the west coast into the Olifants River Valley.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species often closely resembles E. divinorum but differs from it in the glandular not hairy ovary, the smaller leaves and fruits, the usually glabrous corolla and the less dense not compound inflorescence. The vernacular name used for both varieties is Guarrie or Gwarrie. The fruits have been reported as edible in both varieties but are not very palatable. The leaves of var. undulata as well as var. myrtina are reported to be browsed by cattle and the var. myrtina by kudu in South West Africa.
bibliographicCitation: De Winter, B. 1963. Ebenaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 54-99. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Typically has slightly twisted leaves with undulate margins, and the outer inflorescence spathes are free distally and curve outward. The flowers of M. knersvlaktensis, which open early in the morning and fade after 12:30, are pale yellow with relatively prominent nectar guides bordered in pale grey-green, and the tepal claws, up to 2 mm long, clasp the base of the filament column. Closely related to M. schlechteri, the two species, as well as M. flexicaulis, are unusual for subg. Homeria in that every stem axil bears a foliage leaf, whereas other species bear attenuate, entirely sheathing leaves resembling the rhipidial spathes at the upper nodes. All three species have filaments with the apices free and diverging, and relatively well-developed style branches with relatively prominent crests.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the solitary foliage leaf inserted well above the ground, sparsely branched (rarely simple), flexuose stem, and yellow flower with the erect tepal claws forming a narrow cup ± 10 mm long completely enclosing the stamens. The filaments are entirely united in a cylindric column 4-5 mm long relatively densely hairy in the lower half, and the anthers, 5-8 mm long, are usually slightly shorter than the style branches. The nearly erect style branches, ± 5 mm long, bear short, horizontal crests, hardly visible in pressed flowers. Moraea pyrophila may be most closely related to M. autumnalis, which has the foliage leaf inserted close to ground level, and deeper yellow flowers with a floral cup including the filaments and only the bases of the anthers. Moraea pyrophila may also be confused with M. collina but that species has a longer leaf, usually trailing distally in contrast to the very short, apically thickened leaf of M. pyrophila, which seldom exceeds the stem.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the solitary foliage leaf inserted on the stem well above ground, main stem and branches flexed above the sheaths of foliage or sheathing leaves, and a pink or yellow flower with the tepal claws diverging to form a relatively wide cup that includes the filaments. The filaments are united in a narrow column that is velvety in the lower half, and the diverging anthers slightly exceed the style branches, the crests of which are vestigial. It is apparently related to the more widespread M. minor of the Western Cape Atlantic Coast and Olifants River Valley and the two are easily confused, especially when dried. However, in M. minor the tepal claws form a narrow cup including both filaments and anthers and the short style branches have larger, clearly visible crests. Both species are diploid but M. minor is autogamous and M. vallisbelli is self-incompatible.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Relatively poorly known, Moraea fuscomontana has flowers resembling those of M. miniata except that the filament column is cylindric rather than bulbous below. This and the solitary foliage leaf and flexuose stem separate it from that species. Moraea fuscomontana may be most closely related to salmon-pink-flowered M. brachygyne, which also has the rhipidial spathes enclosing the developing capsules, but a longer, prominently papillate filament column ± 8 mm long, held well above the tepals, vs. 6 mm long and velvety below in M. fuscomontana. Moraea fuscomontana is also easily confused with M. demissa and M. flavescens, which are similar in size and vegetative morphology but differing in their flowers, especially in having divergent anthers and style branches with short crests.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the purple flowers with a purple-black centre and spreading rather than cupped tepals, and the partly united filaments, free in the distal 1-2 mm. The yellow anthers exceed the unusually broad style branches. Moraea barnardiella is vegetatively almost identical to M. melanops but the latter has shallowly cupped tepals, free to partly united filaments diverging distally, and the style exceeds the anthers and has fairly narrow branches.
