bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the flexuose stem, two or three foliage leaves with the lowermost inserted on the stem well above ground, and relatively large, pale yellow flowers. Particularly unusual, the style branches are relatively well developed for subg. Homeria, ± 2.5 mm long with visible crests 0.5 mm long with the margins of both the style branches and crests serrated. The tepal claws, ± 5 mm long, form a wide cup that includes the lower part of the filament column while the tepal limbs spread outward, often slightly below the horizontal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In the arid northern parts of its range in the southern Richtersveld and Namaqualand, the flowers of L. mutabilis are predominantly spreading, with dull yellowish-green tepals and brownish-green or light blue rachis apices; towards the central and southern parts from Vanrhynsdorp southwards, the flowers tend to be slightly to strongly cernuous with brighter yellowish-green, light to bright yellow or light to deep mauve outer tepals. Forms in the Citrusdal and Clanwilliam areas have narrower, longer racemes with intense, electric blue rachis apices. A form with inflated scapes from Sewefontein in western Namaqualand and another from the Gifberg south of Vanrhynsdorp are exceptional in having fertile flowers with distinct pedicels 4 mm long and exserted stamens. A particularly attractive bright yellow form occurs just north of Calvinia and in the southern Tanqua Karoo.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: Evidently one of the least specialised species of subg. Homeria, Moraea schlechteri has several foliage leaves, the lower longest, but even those on the upper nodes normally have expanded blades. The flowers are pale yellow and have small darker yellow nectar guides on all tepals, these with short, poorly differentiated claws ± 1 mm long. The filaments are united in a slender column but are free in the upper 0.5-1.0 mm, and the well-developed style branches are slightly wider than the anthers and have prominent crests 2 mm long. Closely related M. knersvlaktensis has a similar vegetative form, though with broader, undulate leaves, the lowermost inserted well above the ground and even the outer rhipidial spathes are somewhat leafy, sheathing the inner spathes only in the lower half. The flowers of the two species are structurally nearly identical but the nectar guides are more prominent in M. knersvlaktensis, the tepals claws 2 mm long, and the filament column sparsely and shortly hairy. Both M. schlechteri and M. knersvlaktensis have morning flowers that fade soon after midday.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised but the moderate-sized to small white, sometimes blue to mauve flushed flowers, the outer tepals only 16-30 mm long and with a spreading to half reflexed limb 9-20 mm long, and characteristic inner tepals with the limbs consisting of three linear, subequal lobes with the inner lobe spreading and arching upward distally. It is closely allied to the Mpumalanga and Eswatini M. pubiflora, with strikingly similar but substantially larger white flowers, the outer tepals 25-30 mm long and disproportionately long filaments with a column ± 13 mm long vs. 4 to 9 mm in M. brevistyla. Moraea pubiflora also has unusual scabrid or velvet outer surfaces of the large outer tepals, whereas in M. brevistyla the reverse of the outer tepal claws is smooth or minutely papillate. The ranges of the two overlap in the Wakkerstroom area of the Mpumalanga-KwaZulu-Natal Border, but the two species remain distinct morphologically. Moraea brevistyla is parapatric in the Sentinel area of the northern high Drakensberg with the very similar M. vigilans.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea kamiesmontana stands out in subg. Galaxia not only in its particularly small size but in the structure of its flowers. In other species of the subgenus the flowers have flaccid, widely cupped tepals that lack distinct claws, but in M. kamiesmontana the ascending tepal claws form a narrow cup enclosing the filaments and the limbs are sharply flexed at right angles to the cup, thus extended horizontally. The chromosome number, 2n = 18, is the ancestral number for the subgenus, and we interpret Moraea kamiesmontana as a relict species, surviving in specialised, seasonally moist, montane habitats.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely resembling the common and widespread Moraea gawleri in all vegetative features, notably the strongly vertically ribbed corm tunics, and short rhipidial spathes with the outer much shorter than the inner, M. vlokii usually has a single foliage leaf (occasionally a second much shorter one), always with straight margins, and pale yellow flowers with short tepal claws less than one quarter as long as the limbs, and vestigial style branches shorter than and concealed by the anthers and lacking crests. By contrast, M. gawleri has tepal claws only slightly shorter than the limbs and style branches with prominent, petaloid crests. Both species have broadly obovoid to almost globose capsules. Flowers open in early morning and collapse at ± 13:00, whereas those of M. gawleri open in mid- to late morning and last through late afternoon.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished among the yellow-flowered species of subg. Homeria by the solitary, broad, glaucous leaf, the lower portion clasping the stem, and the half to fully pendent flowers with reflexed tepal limbs. The tips of the tepal claws clasp the thickened filament column but are slightly bowed toward the bases, which contain nectar. The style branches are relatively well developed and bear broad stigmatic lobes and straight linear crests. Moraea reflexa may be confused with superficially similar M. marlothii, a taller, more robust species that occurs widely across the western Karoo, but the tepals in that species, either yellow or pink, spread horizontally or are sometimes half reflexed, the filament column is usually narrow and cylindric or only slightly thickened below, and the ovary is long and slender and curved outward, whereas the shorter ovary of M. reflexa is straight, top-shaped and widest near the apex. Although the flowers of M. marlothii are comparable in size to those of M. reflexa, it has much larger anthers 8-11 mm long compared with anthers ± 6 mm long in M. reflexa.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The wet habitat is distinctive for Moraea stagnalis, which has flowers almost identical with those of other members of ser. Galaxia but with the filaments usually free in the upper third. The style divides opposite the anthers and the stigmatic fringes of the style branches are always in contact with the anthers and pollen. The narrow, shallowly channelled leaves have smooth to minutely ciliate margins. Moraea stagnalis is polyploid, 2n = 36, and in the laboratory is autogamous. The species is most easily confused with M. fugacissima, which has larger flowers with a perianth tube mostly 15-24 mm long, anthers up to 4 mm long, and the style usually exceeding the anthers rather than tangled among them. The filaments of M. fugacissima are usually completely united whereas those of M. stagnalis are typically, though not invariably, free in the upper third.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Coastal populations of M. bulbillifera are unmistakable for the strongly cormiferous habit, but even plants lacking cormlets in the aerial axils are fairly easy to distinguish from other solitary-leaved species by their flowers with the narrow tepal cup enclosing only the filaments, with the anthers and well-developed style branches and crests extending well above the cup. The foliage leaf is usually inserted at or very close to the ground but plants from the drier valleys at the northern edge of its range are often confusing as the leaf may be inserted rather high above ground. Two subspecies are recognised. The typical subsp. bulbillifera is coastal and always found on sandy or limestone substrates. It is usually robust and has a well-developed cormiferous habit. Subsp. anomala occurs inland, mainly in renosterveld, on the rolling clay plains of the southern Cape, extending into the sandy and rocky valleys of the Langeberg and Riviersonderend Mtns. Sometimes as robust as subsp. bulbillifera, it is more often a much smaller plant, especially in drier habitats, with the dwarfing extending to the flowers as well.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Often confused with other single-leaved species of subg. Homeria, Moraea britteniae is immediately recognised by the basal foliage leaf sheathing the lower half of the stem and the creamy white (to pale yellow) flowers. The tepal claws form a narrow cup including the filament column and sometimes the base of the anthers, with the apices of the filaments free for up to 1.5 mm. The ovary is relatively long, 15-24 mm, giving rise to capsules mostly 25-45 mm long. The apically free filaments and leaf sheathing the stem for some distance correspond with the critical features of the M. cookii-M. pallida group, although the long floral cup is unknown elsewhere in the group.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unusual in the genus in its early flowering time, April to June (autumn and early winter), Moraea autumnalis is recognised by the solitary foliage leaf inserted close to the base of the sparsely branched (rarely simple) and slightly flexuose stem, and yellow flowers with the tepal claws ± erect and forming a narrow cup 9-10 mm long enclosing the filament column and bases of the anthers. The filaments are entirely united in a cylindric column minutely papillate in the lower half, and the anthers, 5-7 mm long, are twice as long as the style branches and arch inward after dehiscence. The style branches bear short, horizontal crests. When described M. autumnalis was thought to be closely allied to M. pyrophila (as Homeria galpinii) because they have a similar vegetative morphology and broadly similar flowers, but the claws of the pale yellow tepals of M. pyrophila form a cup enclosing both filaments and anthers, and the shorter filaments, 4-5 mm long, are conspicuously pubescent in the lower half. The anthers are usually shorter than the style branches, which bear short crests as in M. autumnalis. It is probably significant that the flowering in M. pyrophila is also relatively early in the season, mostly in July and August but as early as March and April.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Resembling Moraea unguiculata, M. rivulicola has larger, pale, creamy green, yellow-green or beige flowers, the outer tepals up to 28 mm long with limbs typically held at 60° below horizontal and smooth claws. The inner tepals are also distinctive in having the central lobe of the typically 3-lobed limb drawn into a slender, obliquely coiled cusp, while the lateral lobes are rounded and very short. The ovary is oblong-cylindric and 11-14 mm long, and gives rise to large cylindric capsules 25-32 mm long. Moraea unguiculata has smaller flowers with the outer tepals seldom exceeding 16 mm and with densely pubescent or bearded claws. The inner tepals, 7-10 mm long, are also 3-lobed but the long central cusp is coiled inward symmetrically. Flower colour in M. unguiculata ranges from white to creamy white, brownish, and even blue, and the outer tepal limbs may be half reflexed or, in some populations outside Namaqualand, may be completely reflexed. A population from the rocky hills west of Bitterfontein and south of Kotzesrus stands out in the particularly large flowers with the inner tepals ± 19 mm long, and with an ovate-attenuate limb. Other organs are also larger, with the filaments united in a column up to 10 mm long and free for an additional 2.5 mm and the anthers are 5.5-6.0 mm long. This population represents a significant variant and distinctive race, perhaps deserving of infraspecific recognition.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the small, pale yellow flowers with subequal tepals, all with short, ascending claws and small, deeper yellow nectar guides at the bases of the tepals, Moraea maximiliani also has short, reduced style branches appressed to the anthers with the stigmatic tips extending between them. The slender, almost filiform leaves are crowded at the top of the elongated based internode. The outer rhipidial spathes clasp the inner only in the lower half and arch outward distally.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Flowers of Moraea nana are of the Hexaglottis-type and closely resemble those of Moraea sect. Hexaglottis in their spreading, subequal tepals with short erect claws and style branches reduced to paired filiform arms, but the resemblance is convergent and M. nana has a vegetative form almost identical to that of some species of subg. Umbellatae, with leaves and branches crowded together above the ground. Chromosome number n = 10, also matches subg. Umbellatae (subg. Hexaglottis has x = 6). Moraea nana is probably most closely allied to M. maximiliani and the two can only be distinguished by examination of the floral parts: M. maximiliani has tepal claws ± 6 mm long, entirely united filaments, and short, apically diverging style branches partly hidden by the short erect and contiguous anthers, whereas M. nana has shorter tepal claws, 2-4 mm long, filaments free in the upper half, and filiform, spreading style branches extending between the filaments. Moraea nana and M. maximiliani are interfertile but neither can be crossed with species of sect. Hexaglottis. Flowers typically open after midday, ± 12:30 and collapse after 18:00 but in plants from the Pakhuis area of the northern Cederberg flowers open at ± 8:00 and deliquesce at ± 13:00. Flowers of these populations are slightly smaller than is typical but otherwise do not appear to differ significantly.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the three well-developed foliage leaves, relatively soft textured and loosely coiled distally, together with softly velvety, flexuose stems. Although always salmon-pink, the flowers are similar to those of M. miniata in having short, erect claws enclosing the base of the filament column, itself swollen above the base and densely velvety in the lower half. The two species are, however, easy to distinguish from vegetative morphology as M. miniata has straight, leathery leaves and a nearly straight, glabrous stem.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of three species of the Roggeveldia group of sect. Pseudospicatae, Moraea fistulosa has the characteristic blue to violet flowers of the alliance with subequal, ± spreading tepals all bearing yellow nectar guides, free stamens, and filiform style branches extending between the stamens. Of the three species of the group, M. fistulosa is recognised by the straight, hollow, terete leaf blade, ± 3 mm in diam. and relatively tall stem, up to 500 mm high. The smaller M. monticola also has a terete leaf, but only ± 1 mm in diam., solid internally and slightly smaller flowers, the tepals 13-15 mm long (vs. 16-18 mm in M. fistulosa). As in allied species in sect. Pseudospicatae, the flowers open in the later afternoon, after 16:00 and fading and collapsing at dusk, usually between 18:00 and 19:00.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A slender plant with a solitary, narrow, channelled leaf and small, fugaceous flowers, Moraea exiliflora is recognised primarily by flower size, the outer tepals 14-17 x ± 4.5 mm and the inner 12-14 x ± 2 mm with the limbs of both whorls spreading to laxly reflexed up to 30º. The rhipidial spathes are proportionately small, the inner 22-32 mm long and, like all members of sect. Pseudospicatae, are long-attenuate with brown tips. Moraea lazulina, has similarly proportioned but larger flowers with the outer tepals 22-27 x 8-9 mm, the tepal limbs being reflexed more than 45º, the inner sometimes more so than the outer.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by its low stature, mostly 40-80 mm in height with stem underground or barely exserted at flowering, single narrow, falcate to trailing foliage leaf, and elongate, included ovary, 17-22 mm long. The capsules are even longer, up to 36 mm long and remain largely included in the spathes. Apart from the unusually long ovary, the flowers differ little from those of M. fugax and M. filicaulis and it has the beaked ovary of those two species. Capsules of M. filicaulis are usually 8-15 mm long and those of M. fugax typically 15-27 mm long vs 18-36 mm in M. macrocarpa. The tepals of M. macrocarpa are either blue-mauve, the outer with deep yellow nectar guides at the bases of the limbs edged in dark purple or in subsp. virginea white, also with yellow nectar guides, but lacking dark edges.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the pink to lilac flowers with outer tepals 27-30 mm long, and 3-lobed inner tepals 16-18 mm long. The inner tepals have a narrow, channelled claw but the 3-lobed limb consists of an erect central cusp ± 9 mm long and shorter rounded lateral lobes. The filaments are 7-8 mm long with a papillate or smooth column, The species is clearly allied to the widespread southern African winter-rainfall M. unguiculata, a remarkably variable species, both as regards perianth colour and size, but its critical features are inner tepals 10-12 mm long and trilobed with the central cusp linear and coiled inward, filaments usually 3-5 mm long with the column lightly to densely papillate, and the outer tepals are typically 12-16 mm long, rarely up to 24 mm long in northern Namaqualand populations. The stems in M. unguiculata are almost always branched unless depauperate due to environmental conditions but typically unbranched in M. lilacina. The outer tepals of M. unguiculata may be white to cream-coloured, brown, violet, or even dull yellow and usually have a contrasting mark at the base of the limb, and the style branches are narrow and spreading as in M. lilacina, but with erect crests 2.0-4.0(-5.5) mm long vs. 5-8 mm in M. lilacina.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea cantharophila has the solitary, long, channelled foliage leaf and branched stem typical of the subg. Vieusseuxia but unlike most species of the subgenus the inner tepals are not tricuspidate but broadly lanceolate with an entire, acute apex. The filaments are united to the apex, also uncommon in the subgenus. The dark central streak on the inner tepals is distinctive and is directly related to the pollination by hopliine beetles. Moraea cantharophila is evidently most closely related to M. lurida and M. insolens, both of which also have entire inner tepals with well-developed limbs. Fly-pollinated M. lurida typically has dark maroon flowers in which both the inner and outer tepals produce nectar over the entire inner surface of the claws, and the outer tepals are usually without contrasting markings. It has relatively long tepal claws, 13-17 mm that exceed the limbs, compared to claws ± 10 mm in M. cantharophila, thus shorter than the limbs. The tepal cup is thus deeper in M. lurida and includes both stamens and style branches, whereas the anthers are partly exserted in M. cantharophila. There is considerable variation in M. cantharophila, the type population from Sandy’s Glen with larger inner tepals, 12-15 x 9-11 mm, with a broad brown central band on the claws, whereas plants from Sir Lowry’s Pass have smaller inner tepals, 8-9 x 5-6 mm, and lack the prominent band of colour on the claws. Possible hybrids between M. cantharophila and M. lurida have been recorded near Elgin.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the large, deeply cupped, pale blue to white flowers with subequal tepals, 30-36 mm long, horizontally spreading tepal limbs, and long conspicuous, erect and contiguous anthers. It most closely resembles M. speciosa, which has somewhat larger flowers of similar morphology with tepals 36-45 mm long, and several broad leaves up to 40 mm wide unlike the two or three narrow foliage leaves of M. deserticola, only 2-3 mm wide, with the margins often tightly inrolled. The ovary of M. deserticola is veined dark purple whereas M. speciosa has a uniformly green ovary.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Resembling the more common and widespread Moraea crispa in both flower structure and general aspect, M. pseudospicata has pale blue-mauve flowers with subequal tepals with short erect claws that form a short, narrow cup including the lower part of the filament column. The anthers are nearly erect and so concealing the narrow and short style branches, whereas in M. crispa the anthers and style branches diverge, exposing the style branches. Moraea pseudospicata differs also in its taller stature, up to 400 mm high, sessile lateral inflorescences with dry, chaffy sheathing leaves and rhipidial spathes, and in its globose capsules with almost membranous walls, apparently dehiscing irregularly rather than along the locule sutures. Flowering middle to late summer in an area of summer drought, the leaves are usually dry and broken at flowering time.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This may be only a variety of E. minuta, but it conspicuously differs by the middle series of corona-lobes being shorter than the style and very much less deeply divided. The figure of E. hastata in Engl, and Prantl, Pflanzenfam. iv. ii. 234, fig. 68 N-P, may possibly be intended for this plant; but the lateral segments of the middle series of corona-lobes are not represented as being auriculate at the base.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, NE. 1908. Asclepiadeae. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4(5): 673-864. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: L. zebrina is considered to be allied to L. buchubergensis and L. nordenstamii. These species share solitary lanceolate leaves, which are heavily banded on the lower surface, and broadly winged, obcordate capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the large, usually pale yellow (rarely pale salmon-pink) flowers with short, erect tepal claws and broad spreading limbs mostly 25-35 mm long. The claws either clasp the filament column or form a narrow cup including the lower part of the filament column. The filaments are free distally for 1-2 mm, a feature shared with few other species of subg. Homeria, notably the closely related M. elegans. The broad leaves are grey-green and usually 15-25 mm wide (occasionally narrower) and clasp the lower part of the stem. The species is heteroploid, with diploids and tetraploids in the Karoo and interior but hexaploid in Western Cape.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A tall species up to 1 m high with at least three well-developed leaves and the upper leaves with short, expanded blades, Moraea cedarmonticola is unmistakable even before flowering. The large yellow flowers have subequal tepals ± 40 mm long, the claws forming a narrow cup including the filament column but with the anthers exserted.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ezosciadium capense is a highly distinctive species, easily distinguished from all other annual species by the pilose vegetative and reproductive organs, the sessile compound umbels with a few, markedly unequal rays, the non-inflexed petal tip, the relatively small, highly inflexed stamens which appear almost sessile, and the prominent bifid carpophores, one half of which persists on the plant.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM; Downie, SR. 2008. Ezosciaium (Apiaceae): A taxonomic revision of yet another early diverging South African apioid genus. Pl. Syst. Evol. 276: 167-175. [DOI 10.1007/s00606-008-0086-z] [All rights reserved]

description: A striking and unusual species both in flower and vegetative morphology, Moraea atropunctata has dull coloured flowers with broad outer tepal limbs reddish brown outside, and 3-lobed inner tepals with the longer median lobe laxly spreading. The nectar guides consist of small dark spots at the bases of the outer tepals while the claws are dark brown. The leaves are relatively short, not or hardly exceeding the stems, and unusually broad, with prominently ciliate-hairy margins. Although evidently related to the M. tricuspidata and M. unguiculata groups in general, the foliage and flowers easily separate it from the several species of these alliances. The unusually large, inflated capsules, 25-35 mm long, are also unusual for these two groups and recall the M. villosa species group.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the combination of small, pale blue-violet flowers with subequal tepals 10-13 mm long, all bearing yellow nectar guides, and short tepal claws ± 1.8 mm long diverging to form a wide, shallow cup around the filament bases. The filaments are united in a smooth column and diverge only near the tips. In general the flowers resembles those of M. crispa and its close allies, both in form and in the short style branches that lack crests and are appressed to the subtending anthers but it differs from that species in having sessile lateral rhipidia and unusual capsules, ± spindle-shaped with a short sterile beak, unique in sect. Pseudospicatae. The solitary foliage leaf is linear, narrowly channelled and usually more-or-less trailing distally, thus typical of the section.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An inconspicuous plant, Moraea albiflora has the fringed style branches characteristic of ser. Galaxia and is recognised by its small white flowers with a yellow cup, the tepals only 9-12 mm long, and style dividing below the apex of the anthers so that the fringed stigma lobes are tangled in the anthers. The leaves are ± straight and spreading to nearly prostrate, with finely ciliate, hyaline margins. Moraea albiflora is autogamous, the pollen shed directly onto the stigmatic surfaces during the few hours that each flower remains open. Despite its autogamy, hybrids with M. fugacissima have been recorded where the two co-occur on Rondebosch Common on the Cape Peninsula.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Micranthus alopecuroides is distinctive in its plane, sometimes very broad lanceolate to linear or falcate, basal leaves sometimes up to 12 mm wide or exceptionally up to 15 mm. Exceptions are numerous and there are populations with ± linear leaves 3-5 mm wide and only up to 25 mm long. The flowers are typically dark blue but also pale blue, with a perianth tube ± 5 mm long. The spikes of 40 or more flowers are often unusually congested with the internodes ± 1.5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The yellow flowers with a short perianth tube only 1-2 mm long distinguish Moraea brevituba from close allies in sect. Hexaglottis, particularly the widespread M. virgata, which has similar vegetative morphology but flowers with a well-developed perianth tube some 4-7 mm long, and the ovary entirely included on short pedicels 4-6 mm long. The ovary of M. brevituba is often partly exserted and the pedicels are (4-)7-10 mm long. Like other species of the section, the flowers open in the middle of the afternoon and last just a few hours.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowers of Moraea lewisiae are typical of sect. Hexaglottis in the yellow tepals with short erect claws and it is distinguished mainly by the capsules either cylindric but triangular to 3-lobed in section and 11-20 mm long or ovoid-ellipsoid and round in section, 8-15 mm long, and usually with a short beak up to 1 mm long. The tepal limbs bear yellow nectar guides at their bases dotted with fine, green to black spots. Taller M. longifolia has paler yellow tepals of similar size but lacking spotted nectar guides and the flowers have none or little scent and slightly shorter style branches, and characteristic obovoid, club-shaped capsules with obviously truncate apex and larger seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Nivenia parviflora is an autumn-flowering species distinguished by the dark brown and much wrinkled floral bracts, and relatively small flowers with tepals 5-6 mm long and tube ± 5.5 mm long, and blue anthers. The brown, wrinkled floral bract and blue anthers are shared with N. binata and N. stenosiphon, but these two species have larger flowers with longer perianth tubes, usually 10-15 mm long in N. binata and 32-38 mm long in N. stenosiphon. The spathes in N. parviflora are 3-4 mm long and the floral bracts ± 5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Nivenia argentea is distinguished by its congested, compound, ± raceme-like inflorescence with lanceolate-attenuate subtending spathes that entirely brown and dry. The ultimate branches bear single-flowered rhipidia, each flower surrounded by a tubular, dry, membranous bract 18-25 mm long, usually silvery-transparent in the upper half and brown below but sometimes entirely shining brown. The species is heterostylous and the flowers have a perianth tube 14-25 mm long with the anthers exserted on filaments either 4-5 mm long (thrum flowers) or 1.0-1.5 mm long (pin flowers). The style branches are slender and typical of most other species in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Faucaria felina subsp. britteniae is unique in the genus because of the (partially) whitish grey epidermis. This taxon deserves the rank of subspecies by the presence of numerous very small dots on the leaves, papillate bristles and restricted area of distribution. Additional features are the large number of teeth and the size. The most characteristic specimens with many, but rather small teeth are found at Ecca Pass, north of Grahamstown.
bibliographicCitation: Groen, LE; Van der Maesen, LJG. 1999. Revision of the genus Faucaria (Ruschioideae: Aizoaceae) in South Africa. Bothalia 29(1): 35-58. [CC BY]

description: Nivenia stokoei has the largest flowers in the genus, with relatively crowded inflorescences of pale to deep blue flowers with a perianth tube 27-37 mm long. The large flower size is reflected in the bracts and spathes so that the species can also be identified after flowering. Each inflorescence normally comprises 20 to 40 flowers although there may be as few as 12 flowers in depauperate plants. The flowers are not heterostylous but the style varies in length in different plants. The flowers are solitary in the binate rhipidia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Nivenia levynsiae is recognised by its low, tufted, often cushion-like habit, and pale blue, particularly short-tubed flowers with widely cupped tepals. It is the only species of the genus in which the tepals are substantially longer than the perianth tube, and one of only two species with ± cupped tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The growth form of Nivenia fruticosa is unmistakable, but herbarium specimens can also easily be recognised by the slender stems, narrow leaves 2.0-2.5 mm wide, and inflorescence of a single flower pair. The flowers are unusual in their long perianth tube and relatively short tepals ascending below and ultimately recurved, unlike the horizontally extended tepals of most other species of Nivenia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the smaller species in the genus, Nivenia concinna rarely exceeds 200 mm in height and has dark blue flowers with a relatively short perianth tube, ± 15 mm long, and unusually long, ascending style branches. The inflorescence is apparently a reduced pseudopanicle and homologous to the multi-flowered inflorescences of N. corymbosa and N. dispar. The species is not heterostylous but is evidently derived from heterostylous ancestors and the flowers are solitary in the paired spathes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its flowers with large purple or violet blotches in the throat, inner bract usually with brown-streaked membranous margins (sometimes colourless), and corms with an almost cicular basal ridge.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species in the section with an oblique corm by the pink flowers with conspicuous violet or purple blotches in the throat of a yellow cup. Similarly coloured and marked flowers are characteristic of Romulea hirsuta and may indicate a relationship between them (De Vos 1972) but the corm in R. hirsuta is bell-shaped with a circular basal rim. Plants from the foot of the Gifberg have smaller yellow cups than those from the Biedouw Valley.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to the widespread African Romulea camerooniana and sharing with it a corm with a small, narrowly toothed basal ridge but distinguished by the often larger flowers with finely veined bracts and short stamens and style, not reaching the middle of the perianth and thus included in the floral cup.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Diagnosed by the hemispherical corm with broadly crescent-shaped basal ridge not wider than the corm itself, subterranean stem, leaves that are unifacial in the lower half, canary-yellow flowers with golden-yellow cup, usually with brown markings around the throat, and inner and outer bracts that are submembranous in the basal half but green and subherbaceous above. Romulea austinii is difficult to separate from forms of R. tortuosa lacking strongly compressed corms with a wide, fan-shaped basal ridge but that species typically has entirely papery or membranous bracts and more numerous leaves, bifacial almost to the tips and usually flexuous or twisted and sometimes conspicuously ciliate. Although De Vos (1972) cited the relatively shorter anthers in R. austinii as another character separating it from R. tortuosa, this is not infallible as some populations of R. tortuosa have similarly short anthers. The two species are largely parapatric, with R. tortuosa ranging to the north and west, from Namaqualand onto the Bokkeveld, Cold Bokkeveld and Roggeveld as far south as Worcester, thus overlapping with R. austinii on the Bokkeveld Plateau between Nieuwoudtville and Calvinia, and below the escarpment in the western Great Karoo between Matjiesfontein and Laingsburg.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to R. autumnalis.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This rare species, found only recently (27-7-1982), has bracts similar to the brown-streaked bracts of R. atrandra and R. luteoflora. The flower and leaf anatomy approximate that of R. atrandra var. esterhuyseniae, but the corm is similar to that of R. cruciata and R. eximia.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The bulb is similar to that of L. revoluta and L. marginata but the pink colour tends to be present as a uniform wash rather than as spots and the bulbs divide to form two cohering daughter bulbs more frequently than in the other two species. The erect very glaucous leaves, which usually lack spots are also characteristic. At flowering the attenuate apices of the leaves are often all that show of the leaf, but the narrowing of the leaf towards the base contrasts with the broader base of the other two species.
bibliographicCitation: Jessop, JP. 1970. Studies in the bulbous Liliaceae: 1. Scilla, Schizocarphus and Ledebouria. J. S. African Bot. 36(4): 233-266. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its corm with a pointed base, very slender flexuose or recurved leaves, bright yellow flowers and bracts which are largely membranous. The species is seemingly not closely related to any other species of Romulea. It may perhaps form a link between the R. atrandra and R. cruciata species groups.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its stemless habit and small, mostly pale mauve flowers, the tepals 4-9 mm long, submembranous outer bracts finely speckled with rusty brown throughout and inner bracts with prominently brown-spotted margins, and corm with a high, almost spathulate basal ridge. Romulea sinispinosensis from coastal sands north of Lamberts Bay on the West Coast has larger, white flowers, the tepals 10-12 mm long, pale bracts, and bracteoles with weakly spotted margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A rare species with 2 or 3 filiform leaves and magenta flowers with yellow cup, and diagnostic style dividing well below the anthers into purple or blackish, antler-like branches that are further once or twice divided, thus with 12 or more stigmas. The species co-occurs with R. komsbergensis and may be overlooked but the latter has more numerous leaves and flowers with a characteristic brown stain at the bottom of the cup and once-forked style branches, and is ecologically separated by its preference for seepages and marshy situations.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differs from all other known species of Ledebouria in having viscid leaves and in the shape of both the leaves and the bulbs. Although other collectors have recorded the viscid nature of the leaves and although the leaves of both herbarium specimens and specimens examined in the field by the author have large numbers of sand particles adhering, it was found that the leaves are not actually sticky to the touch. Whether the stickiness is a feature of the leaves only at certain times of the year or at certain stages of development has not been ascertained.
bibliographicCitation: Jessop, JP. 1970. Studies in the bulbous Liliaceae: 1. Scilla, Schizocarphus and Ledebouria. J. S. African Bot. 36(4): 233-266. [CC BY]

description: A large, polymorphic species in which four largely interfertile varieties are recognized, with some inter-mediates between the varieties. The flower colouring, which varies from deep old-rose to yellow, without any bluish tints, distinguishes this species from R. rosea; also the recurved flexuose peduncles and the 2n chromosome number of 22.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The hairy leaves render it unmistakable Its silky haired leaves resemble those of some species of Hypoxis.
bibliographicCitation: Jessop, JP. 1970. Studies in the bulbous Liliaceae: 1. Scilla, Schizocarphus and Ledebouria. J. S. African Bot. 36(4): 233-266. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Romulea rosea by the somatic chromosome number 2n = 22 (2n = 18 in R. rosea), the presence of some degree of yellow pigmentation in the tepals (distal to the cup), the flowers ranging from yellow through apricot-, terracotta-coloured and salmon-pink to rosy-pink, with a greenish yellow to orange-yellow cup, and the fruiting peduncles remaining widely spreading on drying. Flowering plants without careful colour notes are impossible to assign between the two species with any accuracy. Yellow-flowered forms resemble R. monticola from the Bokkeveld and Matsikamma-Gifberg Mtns, but the flowers are duller in hue with proportionally longer outer bracts more than half as long as the flowers, inner bracts with membranous margins distinctly narrower than the central green portion, and peduncles widely spreading in fruit. Romulea obscura is best known historically from the West Coast between Saldanha and the Cape Peninsula but is now less often encountered as a result of increasing urbanisation. The species is polymorphic for flower size, colour and markings.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to R. obscura and distinguished chiefly by its bright golden-yellow flowers on brownish subterete peduncles which remain suberect or bend only slightly in the fruiting stage. The flower can be confused with that of the sympatric R. montana but R. monticola differs in its corm, less green bracts, leaf anatomy with fibre bundles along the margins of the leaf ribs, and in chromosome number.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its usually pink flowers with very little yellow in the base, and with maroon filaments (rarely yellow) inserted just above the middle of the rather long perianth tube. Variation occurs in the length of the flower and its parts, especially the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The epigeal bulb and somewhat spreading leaves distinguish this species from the smaller members of the L. cooperi complex.
bibliographicCitation: Jessop, JP. 1970. Studies in the bulbous Liliaceae: 1. Scilla, Schizocarphus and Ledebouria. J. S. African Bot. 36(4): 233-266. [CC BY]

description: Variable in colour and distinguished by the narrowly funnel-shaped perianth tube with the filaments inserted at or above the middle, often black or reddish, with very little yellow in the cup. The leathery bracts are closely ribbed and often keeled in the upper part. Forms with glossy rose-coloured to coppery salmon-pink or brick-red flowers are especially attractive.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of two truly aquatic species with more than four longitudinal grooves in the leaves, Romulea multisulcata is characterised by two basal leaves, the upper usually sheathing the stem, funnel-shaped perianth tube with filaments 4-6 mm long and anthers 6-8 mm long, style dividing near the top of the anthers, and widely spreading fruiting peduncles elongating slightly in fruit and ultimately 50-90 mm long. The type and other collections from around Nieuwoudtville on the northern Bokkeveld Escarpment have yellow flowers but populations from the southern Bokkeveld and from the flats below Vanrhyn’s Pass around Vanrhynsdorp have white flowers with a yellow cup.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In the east of its range it merges with the smaller forms of L. cooperi. The leaf-form does not always provide adequate grounds for separation, but the laxer inflorescence in L. ovalifolia can generally be regarded as diagnostic. Confusion with L. revoluta is also possible, but the shape of the base of the leaf, the smaller bulb and form of the inflorescence provide characters for separation.
bibliographicCitation: Jessop, JP. 1970. Studies in the bulbous Liliaceae: 1. Scilla, Schizocarphus and Ledebouria. J. S. African Bot. 36(4): 233-266. [CC BY]

description: The type and all subsequent collections from the Bokkeveld Plateau are diagnosed by the filaments fused into a stout, smooth, cylindric column, but collections from the Roggeveld have oblong, closely appressed but free filaments bearded basally. These populations may be confused with R. sabulosa, but that species has the filaments triangular in section and distinctly tapered above, and ± terete peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very closely related to R. sabulosa. It is interfertile with R. sabulosa, the F1 hybrids resembling the latter in their free filaments (De Vos, I.e. 1970). Probably some specimens, distinguished as R. sabulosa, are hybrids.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the most distinctive species in the genus, Romulea hantamensis has salver-shaped, pink to purple flowers with the tepals strikingly marked and veined with purple with white streaks, and a cylindric perianth tube 30-70 mm long, partially concealed by long bracts 28-35 mm long. The diploid chromosome number 2n = 30 is unique in sect. Roseae although recorded for several species in sections Romulea and Aggregatae.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: L. parvifolia is closely related to L. cooperi but differs in producing appressed leaves with longitudinal rows of broad-based hairs on their adaxial surfaces. Both L. cooperi and L. parvifolia produce a single basal cataphyll, a character not found elsewhere in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, S; Edwards, TJ. 1998. A revision of Ledebouria (Hyacinthaceae) in South Africa. 2. Two new species, L.crispa and L.parvifolia, and L. macowanii re-instated. Bothalia 28(1&2): 179-182. [CC BY]

description: L. crispa is allied to a number of species with prominent bulb necks and lacking extendable xylem `threads' in their torn leaves. L crispa is distinguished from its allies by its diminutive size, synanthous leaves with crispate margins, epigeal bulbs and solitary inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, S; Edwards, TJ. 1998. A revision of Ledebouria (Hyacinthaceae) in South Africa. 2. Two new species, L.crispa and L.parvifolia, and L. macowanii re-instated. Bothalia 28(1&2): 179-182. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the solitary, narrowly grooved basal leaf with pilose median ribs, and orange flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species recognised by the narrowly funnel- or salver-shaped, magenta-purple flowers with perianth tube 17-25 mm long with relatively short, glabrous filaments 4-5 mm long inserted in the upper half of the tube and included within it. The inner and outer bracts are unusually similar in texture for the genus, both green and leathery with the inner differing only by their relatively broader, colourless membranous margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinghuished by its long perianth tube which is longer than the segments, with stamens and style included in the tube.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from allied species in the series with herbaceous outer bracts with prominent membranous margins by its yellow flowers, sometimes streaked or blotched with brown, and style not exserted above the anthers. Plants from the Roggeveld have thicker, shorter leaves. The fruiting peduncles coil up when ripe Romulea luteoflora may be confused with R. diversiformis but the latter is readily identified by the longer style well exserted beyond the anthers, more numerous (6 to 12) leaves, and preference for marshy soils in seepages and around seasonal pools. It has also been confused with R. monticola from the Bokkeveld Mtns and R. obscura from the Cold Bokkeveld, both of which have the outer bracts less firmly herbaceous below and the inner bracts with finely brown-speckled membranous margins. The fruiting peduncles in Romulea monticola are slender and reddish brown, and remain suberect or are curved in fruit, whereas they are typically thicker in R. obscura and spread widely in fruit. Both species differ from R. luteoflora anatomically in lacking rib marginal veins in the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: L. macowanii is closely allied to L. socialis but differs in its hypogeal bulbs and prominent nectariferous ridges on the carpel bases.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, S; Edwards, TJ. 1998. A revision of Ledebouria (Hyacinthaceae) in South Africa. 2. Two new species, L.crispa and L.parvifolia, and L. macowanii re-instated. Bothalia 28(1&2): 179-182. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to Romulea tabularis and sharing with it the yellow pigmentation extending onto the lower half of the tepals but occurring mostly inland of that species [both species are recorded around Piketberg] and separated from it by the mostly two basal leaves, generally larger, white to cream-coloured flowers with tepals mostly more than 5 mm wide, and the firm-textured inner bracts. It can be confused with white-flowered forms of R. schlechteri but that species has inner bracts with unmarked membranous margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very closely related to R. tabularis.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its light grey, spreading to suberect, oblong-campanulate flowers with strongly recurved inner tepals, well-exserted, recurved filaments and relatively large, ovoid seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: Varying in the length of the stem, number of basal leaves, flower colour, and length of the style but generally recognised by the lavender-blue (rarely white) flowers with orange or golden-yellow cup extending onto the basal half of the tepals, mostly solitary basal leaf, and often somewhat submembranous inner bracts with brown-flecked membranous margins. The species is closely allied to Romulea leipoldtii, which is distinguished by its invariably two basal leaves, generally larger, white or cream-coloured flowers with tepals 18-35 x 5-8 mm, the outer tepals not marked on the reverse, and inner bracts that are green and leathery in the centre. Specimens with two basal leaves may also be confused with Romulea schlechteri from drier situations, which has the yellow pigment restricted to the cup itself and not extending onto the lower half of the tepals, and inner bracts without brown flecks on the membranous margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the undulate and crisped, sclerotic margins of its leaves, which are only present in one other Lachenalia species, L. nervosa. The green apical gibbosities and median keels stand out against the cream background of the outer and inner tepals and the declinate, well-exserted filaments are prominent in their light magenta upper parts. The solitary bulb is distinctive in having numerous cartilaginous outer tunics that are produced into a thick, fasciculate neck.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: The only member of ser. Bicarinatae with pink flowers with a yellow cup, Romulea subfistulosa is also readily distinguished by the several, subfistulose leaves 2-5 mm wide, either X-shaped and widely 4-grooved or more usually ± H-shaped with the median ribs winged.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Superficially, L. arbuthnotiae resembles L. lutea, which has a similar spike of narrowly oblong- campanulate, heavily sweet-scented, yellow flowers, but the latter differs in its non-curved, shorter perianths, with the inner tepal apices acute and flat, and in its flower orientation, which is usually strongly suberect.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: The common, yellow-flowered Romulea species of central Namaqualand, Romulea citrina, is relatively undistinguished among the yellow-flowered members of sect. Romulea, and is diagnosed by the crescent-shaped basal ridge, two basal leaves when the stem is exserted, and lemon- or canary-yellow flowers lacking dark blotches or streaks in the throat. The leaves are distinctive in the development of marginal fibre strands in the ribs, a feature also of the Namaqualand species in ser. Namaquana.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to R. atrandra. Characters intermediate between R. atrandra and R. komsbergensis. It was at first thought to be a hybrid between these two species; it produces, however, well developed seeds.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: L. dolomiticola is a close relative of L. atrobrunnea and L. viscosa which also possess cylindrical bulbs, erect leaves and prominent shoulders on the carpel apices. L. dolomiticola is distinguished from both by its epigeal bulbs and from L. viscosa by its non-viscous leaves and from L. atrobrunnea by its membranous dead bulb scales.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, S; Edwards, TJ. 1998. A revision of Ledebouria (Hyacinthaceae) in southern Africa. 1. Two new species. Bothalia 28(1): 15-17. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the white flowers with orange-yellow cup, the outer tepals flushed green or pink on the reverse, and the bell-shaped corm. The presence of secondary veins in the leaf ribs appears to be unique in the section. In the field the species is easily confused with another Gifberg endemic, Romulea toximontana, unless excavated, when the latter is readily identified by its laterally compressed, oblique corm with wide basal ridge. The two species differ slightly in their flowers, with the bright yellow anthers in R. sladenii partially exserted from the cup on filaments 5-7 mm long and the cream-coloured anthers of R. toximontana included in the cup on shorter filaments 3-5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to R. hirsuta from which it differs as follows: Leaves filiform, glabrous, 0.5-1 mm diam., grooves narrow. Distinguished by its bell-shaped corm and bright golden yellow or rarely white flowers, without any red colouring. Some herbarium specimens are not easily distinguished from R. hirsuta var. cuprea which, however, has some anthocyanin in its perianth.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species without evident close allies, readily recognised by its distinctive H-shaped leaves, usually variously pubescent on the wing-margins, the pubescent peduncles and outer bracts, which have relatively broad membranous margins and apices, and the relatively small, lilac to magenta (rarely white) flowers with yellowish or violet cup. The leaves are often relatively short, not longer than the flowering stems. Both yellow-flowered Romulea hirta (sect. Roseae) and orange-flowered R. pilosa (sect. Aggregatae) have developed remarkably similar 4-winged leaves The species is variable in the colouring of the floral cup, anthers and pollen, and in the length of the style.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its large, carmine- or deep rosy-red flowers with a white or rarely yellow cup finely lined with black and with black blotches in the throat, and bell-shaped corm with small fibril clusters on the basal rim.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the characteristic corms, splitting at the basal ridge into longitudinal strips that are finely split at the tips into clusters of converging fibril-like teeth, and by the inner and outer bracts paler and submembranous in the lower half. The membranous margins of the inner bracts are spotted with brown rather than flecked, as in R. gigantea, which also differs in its corm tunics splitting into slender parallel teeth.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of a small group of Namaqualand species with prominent, brown-flecked membranous apices to the outer bracts, distinguished by the stemless habit and yellow, funnel-shaped flowers. This group shares similar leaf anatomy, notably the development of sclerenchyma vascular girders and rib marginal fibre strands, and absence of phloem caps on the secondary bundles.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very closely related to R. amoena.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A polyploid species closely allied to Romulea minutiflora from more southerly and inland locations, which has smaller, mostly pale lilac or mauve flowers with tepals 4-9 x 1.5-2.5 mm, often with a dark ring in the throat, finely rust-coloured speckled outer bracts, and inner bracts with membranous margins only inconspicuously brown-spotted or -speckled near the tips.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognised by a rostette of up to 12 linear, canaliculate, spreading leaves and erect filaments that are distinctly swollen in the upper half.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: A spring-flowering species recognised by the scabro- or echino-tuberculate leaves with tubercles topped by a minute, pointed, conical trichome, and yellowish green or reddish flowers with short, broad perianth tube, 4-6 x 3-4 mm, ovate to lanceolate tepals 4-6 mm long with a weak sigmoid curvature at the base, and short, subulate filaments 3-5 mm long, connate at the base for 1.0-1.5 mm in a shallow, open collar that exposes the ovary to view. The anthers are relatively large, 2.5-3 mm long at anthesis.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2019. The genus Massonia Thunb. ex Houtt. (Hyacinthaceae: Scilloideae) in the Core Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 121: 329-354. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2018.11.015] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2019); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [All rights reserved]

description: Massonia echinata can be easily distinguished by the relatively small leaves covered by distinct conical emergences with a declined trichome on top bearing a smooth surface; perigone-filaments tube 5-7 mm long, subcylindrical at the base and widening at the upper portion into a funnel that exposes the gynoecium; free portion of perigone segments at anthesis strongly reflexed with a sigmoid, but not strongly inrolled, curve at the base; filaments reddish and basally connate for ca. 1-1.5 mm above the perigone; and ovary sub-oblong, green with a reddish flush, truncate to the style.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Pinter, M; Crespo, MB; Slade, JM; Deutsch, G; Wetschnig, W. 2015. Clarification of Massonia echinata and some other frequently misunderstood Massonia species (Asparagaceae, Scilloideae), with the description of M. pseudoechinata and M. roggeveldensis. Phytotaxa 239(2): 101-129. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from Romulea schlechteri by the very slender, almost wiry stems, mostly smaller, usually deep pink flowers with golden-yellow cup, and shorter stamens 6-8 mm long. The two species differ also in chromosome number (De Vos 1972). Romulea saxatilis may also be confused with R. vinacea, which has the outer tepals dark plum-coloured or wine-red on the reverse, and distinctly ciliate leaves and peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very closely related to R. schlechteri.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to Romulea flava in the solitary, often rather thick basal leaf and submembranous inner bracts, and distinguished by the large, cadmium to golden-yellow (rarely cream-coloured) flowers with broad tepals, and the slightly firmer-textured inner bracts. The central portion of the inner bracts is sometimes spotted with brown, and plants with cream-coloured tepals and a golden-yellow cup may be confused with R. leipoldtii but that species has two basal leaves and narrower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of three species in ser. Bicarinatae with large, glossy red to orange, cup-shaped flowers, Romulea sabulosa is distinguished from R. unifolia by the several, narrow leaves ± 1 mm diam. and scarlet to currant-red flowers, and from R. monadelpha by the free stamens, widened toward the base and tapering above. It is ecologically separated from these two species, both restricted to heavy clay soils derived from dolerite, by its preference for loamy tillite.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognized by its hirsute leaves with hairs or bristles 0.5-2.0 mm long, and especially the distally ciliate-bristly inflorescence bracts recurved at the tips that are diagnostic for the species. The ovary that tapers gradually and imperceptibly into the style, and the black anthers with blue pollen are characteristic of the group of species centred on M. pseudoechinata but none of these species have hirsute bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2019. The genus Massonia Thunb. ex Houtt. (Hyacinthaceae: Scilloideae) in the Core Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 121: 329-354. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2018.11.015] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2019); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the well-developed brownish or brown-flecked membranous margins to the outer bracts and the large, carmine-red flowers with anthers longer than the filaments. The membranous bract margins and the leaf anatomy (sclerenchyma strands present along the groove margins and sclerenchyma girders developed on the main vascular bundles) associate it with a small group of Namaqualand species including white-flowered Romulea maculata and R. rupestris, and yellow-flowered R. pearsonii.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from R. rosea, which has somewhat similar flowers, in its firmer green bracts with closely spaced veins and prominent membranous margins and tips, in the sharply bent, grooved teeth of the corm tunics, and in chromosome number. Three varieties occur which differ mainly in leaf width, and size and colouring of the perianth and anthers.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from yellow-orange-flowered Romulea setifolia by its white or pink to magenta flowers and distinctive corm tunics, the converging clusters of basal fibrils rather soft in texture and separated by small woody teeth that are grooved apically over the basal ridge. In R. setifolia, as in all other members of sect. Aggregatae, the converging fibrils are woody and not different in texture from the rest of the tunic. The species was originally known only from one or two pink-flowered populations from the Cold Bokkeveld but we include in it additional populations from Ceres and the northern slopes of the Hex River Mtns with white flowers but the same distinctive corms with soft fibril clusters.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Occurring north of Romulea syringodeoflora and distinguished from it by the longer, suberect and softly villous leaves with hairs up to 1 mm long and white, salver-shaped flowers with perianth tube 30-33 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species with large, yellow flowers with dark brown blotches on the inner tepals and unique, flattened bell-shaped corm much wider than high.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very similar to M. echinata from the Bokkeveld around Nieuwoudtville, with which it shares similar flowers with short, broad perianth tube, 4-6 x 3-4 mm, ovate to lanceolate tepals 4-6 mm long with sigmoid flexure at the base, and short, subulate filaments 4-6 mm long, connate at the base for 0.5-1.5 mm in a shallow, open collar that exposes the ovary to view. The anthers are relatively large, 2.5-3 mm long at anthesis. Both species are spring-flowering and are distinguished essentially by the nature of the trichomes on the leaves, those in M. echinata sharply pointed and conical or almost uncinate and those of M. latebrosa blunt and ellipsoid to globular.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2019. The genus Massonia Thunb. ex Houtt. (Hyacinthaceae: Scilloideae) in the Core Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 121: 329-354. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2018.11.015] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2019); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [All rights reserved]

description: A high altitude species of the mountains in the extreme southwestern Western Cape, recognised by the mostly papillate or tuberculato- to muricato-pustulate leaves, and especially the flowers with slender perianth tube 6-13 mm long, spreading tepals without a marked sigmoid flexure at the base, and unequal filaments with the inner series 1.5-2.0 mm longer than the outer. All of the inner filaments in some flowers are not always markedly longer than the outer. The anthers are dark purple or blackish and the pollen either turquoise blue or sometimes yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2019. The genus Massonia Thunb. ex Houtt. (Hyacinthaceae: Scilloideae) in the Core Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 121: 329-354. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2018.11.015] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2019); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [All rights reserved]

description: An early flowering species instantly recognised by its solitary (rarely two), sticky leaf with adhering sand grains, sticky bracts, and lilac flowers without a yellow cup and with concolorous stamens. A similar, later flowering species from the Cederberg, Romulea cedarbergensis, is even smaller, with mostly two leaves without adhering sand grains and smaller, white to pale pink flowers with golden-yellow cup and stamens, the tepals only 7-16 mm long and filaments 4-6 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Related to the white-flowered form of R. schlechteri and to the yellow R. saldanhensis, but differing in the shape of the perianth segments and the more pilose filaments; and from the latter also in its two basal foliage leaves and greener inner bract.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to R. longipes.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The only species in the genus that includes plants with yellow as well as pink flowers, Romulea dichotoma is recognised by its characteristic basal leaf, the median ribs reduced and much smaller than the marginal ones and the blade thus almost I-shaped in section. The median ribs are flange-shaped or winged and curve over and partially conceal the marginal veins, which are rounded in section and lacking secondary veins (visible only under the microscope). Plants with pale orange flowers can be confused with R. jugicola from the inland mountains ranges unless the leaves are examined carefully. That species has terete leaves with all four ribs subequal in size and form. Similarly, plants at the east of the range with pale flowers may be confused with R. longipes, but that species has two basal leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Romulea hirsuta essentially by its more slender habit and smaller, pale pink to salmon-coloured flowers with tepals 12-18 x 3-5 mm. It may represent merely a small variant of that species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species can be recognised by the relatively long stipules (1.5-4.5 cm long, up to 8 cm long on new flush).
bibliographicCitation: Berg, CC. 1991. 156. Moraceae, Fl. Zambes. 9(6): 13-76. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the solitary, often rather swollen basal leaf, the cauline leaves typically with wide sheathing bases, the entirely membranous or submembranous inner bracts, and the canary-yellow or white to pale blue flowers. A common, widely distributed and polymorphic species varying greatly in size, growth form, leaf thickness and ciliation, and flower colour. Flower colour is genetically determined but growth form is at least partly influenced by growing conditions.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Sharing a pointed corm and acute, ± beaked capsules with Romulea cruciata and distinguished from it by the larger, (35-)40-50 mm long [vs. 22-35 mm long], old-rose to terracotta-coloured flowers (i.e. with a yellow admixture to the pink) with a pale or greenish yellow cup [vs. magenta to rose-pink with golden- or orange-yellow cup]. Anatomically it is also distinguished by the smaller, thickened leaf epidermal cells. The two species share the somatic chromosome number 2n = 18 but hybrids between them are only partially fertile (De Vos 1972). True R. cruciata is absent from range of R. eximia and the two taxa are thus parapatric. The species is florally very similar to the often sympatric Romulea hirsuta with bell-shaped corm and often exserted stem but has a pale or greenish yellow vs. golden- or orange-yellow cup.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The large old-rose flowers with their maroon blotches resemble those of the sympatric R. hirsuta and R. obscura var. blanda, but R. eximia is distinguished by a pale greenish yellow perianth cup with dark blotches and corm with a pointed base and straight basal teeth.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]
