description: Unmistakable in its unique, T-section leaves with two broad grooves separating a narrower and a broader rib and white flowers with large black blotches outlined with yellow in the throat. The solitary basal leaf and entirely membranous inner bracts ally it to Romulea flava.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognised by the distinctively marked flowers, purple anthers coiled around the style, red-brown pollen, and unusually broad style branches. The common form with salmon-pink flowers occurs in the Nieuwoudtville area, with the white-flowered form in the south of its range. The two colour morphs usually occur in pure stands, but white morphs mixed with the salmon-coloured are known from a few sites. The shift from salmon- to white-flowered populations is abrupt.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This Cape species is closely related to F. hirsuta. It is closely related to F. pomonensis, endemic in the Namib, but the latter forms small bushes and bears fewer and smaller flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1976. Frankeniaceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 32-36. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the large flowers with a particularly large, erect dorsal tepal, 20 x 12 mm, held vertically above the small, spooned and down-curved lower tepals. The flowers are usually strongly scented. The finely fibrous corm tunics accumulate in a dense mass around the corm and base of the stem, and the somewhat obtuse leaves are speckled with red to purple at the base. The capsules are unusually small for the genus, 5-8 mm long and contain at most 4 seeds per locule (compared with as many as 8 to 10 per locule in S. villosa and 10 to 12 in S. metelerkampiae). Based on morphology alone, S. galeata has been considered most closely allied to S. roxburghii, which has similar finely fibrous corm tunics that form a collar around the stem base, usually speckled leaf bases, and a prominent, erect dorsal tepal. Flowers of S. roxburghii are differently coloured, and have a perianth tube 20-30 mm long compared to 12-15 mm in S. galeata. The molecular-based phylogeny suggests that S. roxburghii is more closely allied to S. auriculata, but all three species are clearly related and share unusually small, rounded capsules with up to four seeds per locule.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowers of Sparaxis caryophyllacea most closely resemble those of S. villosa, but the similarity may be because this is the ancestral flower type in the genus rather than an indication of close relationship. It can be distinguished by the relatively large flower size alone, the dorsal tepal 24-28 mm long compared with 12-16 mm in S. villosa, and in addition the pale yellow perianth is conspicuously striped with black in the throat and strongly carnation scented. Another diagnostic feature is the red to purple speckling on the sheaths of the lower leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The large flowers of Sparaxis variegata are either yellow with the dorsal tepal pale violet or predominantly violet with the lower tepals either yellow or white, tipped with violet and the throat white streaked with purple lines. The typical violet-flowered form occurs in the south of the range, notably at Rondegat, south of Clanwilliam. The larger size of the flowers, including the tepals and anthers, a style that divides near the anther apices, and often the predominantly yellow perianth, distinguish S. variegata from closely allied S. metelerkampiae. The longer style with the branches arched above the anthers makes self-pollination unlikely, but in any event, the species is genetically self-incompatible. The capsules, up to 11.5 mm long, typically contain 8 to 10 seeds per locule. Like its close relative S. metelerkampiae, S. variegata has corms with coarsely fibrous tunics and flowers with a long perianth tube with a strong bend at the apex of the slender, cylindric part of the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the radially symmetric yellow flowers with a dark centre and long-cuspidate bracts with the lateral margins slightly and irregularly serrated. The bracts are almost identical to those of S. fragrans, which also has a radially symmetric flower, leaving no doubt that the two are immediately related. Sparaxis fragrans is consistently a more slender plant with linear to narrowly lanceolate (or falcate) leaves, 2-8 mm wide and predominantly yellow to buff-coloured flowers with narrower tepals, ± 7 mm wide, sometimes with small dark marks at the tepal bases. The flowers of S. fragrans mostly have a slightly unpleasant, acrid odour, whereas those of S. maculosa lack scent.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species recognized by the usually echino-tuberculate leaves with declinate, rugulose trichomes, and small flowers with short, obconic perianth tube 2.5-7.0 mm long, lanceolate tepals without a sigmoid flexure at the base, and short, subulate or triangular filaments 3.5-7.5 mm long. The filaments are free or shortly connate at the base for up to 0.5 mm, the anthers are purple with yellow pollen, and the ovary is sharply contracted above into the style. The rugulose trichomes appear to be unique to the species.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2019. The genus Massonia Thunb. ex Houtt. (Hyacinthaceae: Scilloideae) in the Core Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 121: 329-354. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2018.11.015] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2019); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised among the other summer-rainfall species in sect. Syringodea with a narrowly funnel-shaped perianth tube by its relatively large, pale to deep violet flowers with a white throat.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A species of loamy soils recognised by leaves that are variously echinulate or scabrid to hispid above, either persistently so or glabrescent, and flowers with the perianth tube occluded at the mouth by invaginations of the staminal column between the base of the filaments, with yellowish anthers and pollen, and the ovary abruptly contracted above into the style.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2019. The genus Massonia Thunb. ex Houtt. (Hyacinthaceae: Scilloideae) in the Core Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 121: 329-354. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2018.11.015] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2019); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [All rights reserved]

description: Distinctive in sect. Saxatiles in its several to numerous, often loosely coiled or helically twisted leaves mostly less than 2 mm diam., and relatively small flowers with perianth tube 15-25 mm long and tepals 8-15 x 3-8 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species, with pale lilac flowers with notched or bifid tepals and a uniquely cylindric perianth tube 60-100 mm long and not widening at the throat.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Related to S. longituba and S. derustensis and differs mainly in its single, strongly curved leaf which is unifacial and terete in its upper half and ciliate on the margins in the lower. Young plants which have not yet flowered have the whole leaf unifacial and terete, and not ciliate.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unique in the genus in its solitary, falcate leaf with short, unifacial and subcylindric blade. The leaf in juvenile plants is entirely unifacial and terete. The close association of daughter corms with the parent may result in adult plants appearing to produce more than one leaf per corm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowers of Sparaxis auriculata resemble those of the common southwestern Cape S. villosa in general appearance but are substantially larger in all respects. In S. auriculata the dorsal tepal is ± 25 x 18-20 mm and the anthers 7-8 mm long, compared with a dorsal tepal 14-19 x 10-12 mm and anthers 3-4 mm in S. villosa. Furthermore, the style in the latter species divides near the anther bases, the style branches are ± 3 mm long, rarely reaching beyond the middle of the anthers, and the lower tepals are inclined slightly below the horizontal and without auriculate basal lobes, whereas S. auriculata has longer anthers, style branches dividing just below the anther tips, ± 4.5 mm long and exceeding the anthers. The downward-directed lower tepals bear unusual prominent auriculate lobes above the base. Sparaxis auriculata can also be distinguished by vegetative features: the corms are narrowly conic with tunics of medium-textured fibres, the leaf sheaths are liberally spotted with dark purple, and the leaf blades are unique in Sparaxis in the prominent submarginal vein that makes the margins appear thickened. The corms of S. villosa differ substantially being globose with coarse, netted fibres, the vertical elements of which are thickened into claw-like ridges below, and the leaves lack the dark spotting so marked in S. auriculata. The narrow, conical corms and soft corm tunics are characteristic of only two other species of Sparaxis, S. galeata and S. roxburghii, both occurring in northern Western Cape. The underground part of the stem is enclosed by a thick collar of fine fibres and the leaves have speckled sheaths but the two differ from S. auriculata in floral details. Sparaxis galeata has short-tubed, extremely sweetly fragrant flowers with a reflexed dorsal tepal, and prostrate, obtuse leaves, and it favours dry, stony, clay flats and slopes. The rare S. roxburghii has long-tubed flowers (perianth tube 20-25 mm long), otherwise resembling those of S. galeata, and is known from a few populations in the mid-Olifants River Valley on stony slopes. Neither species has the submarginal vein of S. auriculata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Tritoniopsis bicolor is recognised by its moderately-sized, bright yellow flowers with the bicoloured lower tepals maroon in the lower third and joined at the base for up to 1.5 mm without forming a well-defined lower lip. The perianth tube is short, 2-5 mm long, and the filaments are 6-7 mm long, with the base of the tepals and mouth of the tube minutely papillate. The leaves are conspicuously petiolate with a narrowly lanceolate blade 6-10 mm wide, with 1 or 2(3) veins, and the capsules are conspicuously inflated.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Glabrous except for scattered appressed hairs on the youngest parts. Leaves gray or gray-green, thinner, usually folded upwards, very finely papulose. Flowers axillary, not on lateral branches, usually in groups of 3, the lateral on branchlets 2-5 mm. long. Perianth segments 4, papulose on the back. Styles 4.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1956. The South African species of Aizoaceae: III. Galenia L. J. S. African Bot. 22: 87-127. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf22unse/page/n113/mode/2up?view=theater] [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its one or two distinctly petiolate leaves with terete pseudopetiole, simple or branched stems with relatively soft-textured, acute bracts 10-12 mm long and pink flowers with moderately long, slender perianth tube 20-21 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Tritoniopsis revoluta is recognised by the long-tubed pink flowers with slender perianth tube (25-)40-70 mm long and ± as long as or usually much longer than the dorsal tepal, 20-40 mm long, and the long bracts, the outer (12-)15-50 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The most common species in the genus, recognised by the basal fan of lanceolate leaves, 8-20 mm wide, and the yellowish or pinkish to red flowers with dimorphic perianth tube 25-40 mm long, and narrowly spathulate to oblanceolate-spathulate tepals, the dorsal 22-30 x 4-7 mm, and arising either at the same level as the other tepals or below them. The capsules are somewhat to markedly inflated.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of two species with a solitary, petiolate basal leaf and long-attenuate cauline leaves, Tritoniopsis triticea is a robust species with stems 400-750 mm high and compact spikes of red flowers with dimorphic perianth tube 25-40 mm long. The mouth of the tube is not evidently oblique and the tepals are not markedly unequal, the dorsal and often the laterals only slightly larger than the lower three. All the tepals are ultimately strongly reflexed and often twisted during the female phase of flowering. The relatively small, woody capsules 12-14 mm long are also distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to the largely sympatric Tritonia marlothii, with which it shares similar narrow, leathery leaves without evident secondary veins and spikes of long-tubed flowers with short, often largely herbaceous bracts and unusual lower tepals minutely puberulous on the upper surface. They are distinguished by details of the flowers, T. delpierrei having fragrant, pale creamy yellow flowers with a perianth tube 12-22 mm long and T. marlothii with odourless, pale to deep purple flowers with a longer tube 28-42 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its short stature, tight fan of usually falcate or strongly curved, leathery leaves with the cauline leaves seldom visible above the basal fan, and short, inclined spike of large, funnel-shaped flowers with a sharply bent perianth tube 25-32 mm long and about twice as long as the tepals. The stem is shortly exserted above the leaves and the fragrant flowers are pale creamy to dull orange, with conspicuous dark veins, and long, bright yellow ridge or crest-like calluses less than 1 mm high on the lower tepals extending into the throat. The congested fan of recurved, leathery leaves, short stem, and large, funnel-shaped flowers with long, crest-like calluses, and large capsules all suggest a relationship with Tritonia florentiae from the Tanqua and western Great Karoo. Flowering in the winter in May and June, acaulescent T. florentiae has bright yellow flowers without conspicuous veins and a perianth tube about as long as the tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to T. delpierrei, also from the Richtersveld, and shares with it similar narrow, leathery leaves without evident secondary veins and spikes of long-tubed flowers with short, often largely green bracts and unusual lower tepals minutely puberulous on the upper surface, especially toward the base. The two species are distinguished by the flowers, T. marlothii having odourless, pale to deep purple flowers with a perianth tube 28-42 mm long and style branching between the base and middle of the anthers, and T. delpierrei having fragrant, pale creamy yellow flowers with a perianth tube 12-22 mm long and style dividing between the middle and apex of the anthers. Plants of the disjunct population in Bushmanland differ in their smaller size, softer-textured leaves and flowers with slightly broader, obovate tepals, the style branching shortly below the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A slender species distinguished by its narrow, linear leaves, 1.5-3.0(-4.0) mm wide with a prominent submarginal vein, and widely funnel-shaped, red to deep pink flowers with a yellow blotch at the base of the lower tepals, these surrounding small, triangular calluses 1.0-1.5 mm high. Tritonia drakensbergensis can be confused in the dried state with narrow-leaved forms of T. disticha, which has similarly shaped and coloured flowers, also with a yellow spot at the base of the lower tepals, but that species lacks calluses (represented at most by a low, ridge-like thickening) and the leaves are narrowly lanceolate and (5-)8-12(-20) mm wide. Tritonia disticha typically occurs at lower altitudes in drier grassland on dolerite or sandstone.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from spring-flowering T. securigera and its allies with similar short-tubed, orange flowers by its later flowering, from late (rarely mid-) summer to early winter, and by its characteristic capsules, ellipsoid and much larger than in other species of the genus, (12-)15-22 mm long and appressed to the axis. The stiffly erect, often elongate spike is distinctive, and the species often (?always) produces short or long stolons terminating in a solitary cormlet. In other species the cormlets are subsessile. Tritonia laxifolia is replaced in the northern provinces of South Africa by T. nelsonii, a generally taller and more slender plant with narrower, linear-striate leaves (1-)2-4(-6) wide, and shorter, subglobose capsules 7-10 mm long. Both species bloom from midsummer to early winter.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from the other members of sect. Pectinatae by its linear-lanceolate leaves with slightly concave blade with margins inrolled but never crisped, and by its salver-shaped flowers with relatively short tube up to 25 mm long, spreading, subequal tepals, the lower three slightly smaller and marked with two short red lines near the bases, and short filaments 6-7 mm long. Both Tritonia undulata, with crisped leaf margins, and T. cooperi with winged leaf margins, have more markedly bilabiate flowers with longer tubes, usually more than 30 mm long, and filaments 8-12 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species with white, long-tubed flowers by its narrowly lanceolate, often spreading, soft-textured leaves, typically about half as long as the flowering stem and mostly 10-15 mm wide with a prominent main vein and the ± 3-toothed outer bracts mostly 7-10(-15) mm long. The lower three or only the median tepal often has a yellow ridge-like or low, oblong callus near the base. Rarely, especially in the plants on the Rooiberg and Gamkaberg, the calluses are enlarged into obliquely square teeth up to 2 mm high, as found in sect. Montbretia. Populations near Robertson are distinctive in having longitudinal red streaks near the bases of the lower tepals. Plants with a shorter perianth tube, 30-35(-45) mm long vs. 45-65(-70) mm long, were segregated as subsp. tayloriae by De Vos (1983). Shorter-tubed populations are recorded from the western and eastern periphery of the range of the species, between Robertson and Montagu, and north and south of Calitzdorp. They do not differ in any other way from typical plants, and short- and long-tubed populations display a similar variation in the development of a callus on the median lower tepal. In the absence of any clear geographical pattern we regard the short-tubed populations as local variants. Tritonia pallida can be confused with the parapatric T. flabellifolia, which ranges from the Riviersonderend Mtns eastward along the foot of the coastal ranges as far as Riversdale, but that species has distinctive attenuate-aristate bracts mostly 15-40 mm long and stiffly erect, linear to linear-lanceolate, attenuate leaves mostly 4-10 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An extremely variable species, but readily distinguishable from G. gerrardii.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB; Robson, NKB. 1976. Clusiaceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 14-23. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species in sect. Pectinatae by the linear to lanceolate leaves that develop broad wings on the edges typically rendering them H-shaped in section. The wing edges are smooth or ciliolate. The flanges or wings are flattened when pressed, making it difficult to establish the form of the leaves in herbarium specimens. The species resembles Tritonia undulata closely in its flowers but lacks the inrolled and crisped or undulate leaf edges characteristic of that species. Plants from the Riviersonderend Mtns have broader leaves with poorly or incompletely developed wings and look vegetatively remarkably like T. lancea but the flowers are clearly bilabiate with longer tubes, 30-55 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by its stiff, linear leaves (1-)2-5 mm wide with the main vein, submarginal and intervening veins moderately thickened, the blades thus striate, and the dark red flowers drying blackish purple. The lower median tepals bear a yellow, axe-shaped callus and evidently smaller, dark calluses on the lower lateral tepals. It has a superficial resemblance to Tritonia disticha but this species has broader leaves, (5-)8-12(-20) mm wide, and orange to red flowers without evident calluses on the lower tepals. It is more likely to be confused with T. drakensbergensis, which has similarly narrow (but not striate) leaves and red flowers with yellow calluses on the lower tepals, but this is a high altitude species from basalt soils and the calluses are lower and triangular in shape.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unique in the genus, Tritonia dubia has perfectly radially symmetric flowers with erect, centrally placed stamens surrounding the style. The stamens are inserted near the top of the perianth tube which thus widens only in the upper 2-3 mm. In other species with a regular perianth the stamens are inserted in the lower half of the tube and the flowers thus have a prominent gullet. Plants appear to set seed readily and completely, and are thus evidently autogamous, an observation consistent with the branching of the style below the anthers where the stigmas will become dusted with self pollen. The capsules are unusually large and elongate for the genus, ellipsoid and 15-25 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the bright orange, bowl-shaped flowers with a star-shaped yellow marking in the throat, often outlined with red. The prominent yellow throat or gullet and the lack of hyaline zones along the margins of the tepal claws separates Tritonia deusta from both orange-flowered T. crocata and pink-flowered T. squalida. It is often also smaller in stature and flower size than either of these species. Hybrids are recorded with both T. crocata and T. squalida. Tritonia deusta varies in the number, size and shape of the dark markings on the tepals: populations west of Swellendam typically lack dark markings on the outer tepals, although unmarked plants are also found further east, whereas plants east of Swellendam mostly have a prominent dark reddish black blotch at the base of the outer tepal limbs. The prominently marked forms conform to the type of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from the florally similar Tritonia pallida from the Little Karoo by always lacking calluses on the lower tepals, which are marked with a red or yellow and red streak, and by its stiffly erect, narrowly lanceolate-attenuate leaves, mostly 4-10 mm wide, and distinctive attenuate-aristate bracts mostly 15-40 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unique in the genus in its very short perianth tube, 1.0-1.5 mm long and entirely included in the floral bracts, the outer bracts only 3-5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised in the wild by the ± falcate leaves, the lowermost mostly 3-7 mm wide and usually much shorter than stem, with a more-or-less distinctive pseudomidrib, and magenta or deep pink flowers with pale yellow anthers on filaments 3-4 mm long. The flask-shaped capsules, 6-8 mm long, are highly diagnostic, and the fusiform seeds have a hooked, thread-like chalazal extension ± twice as long as the seed body.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its compact, subcapitate spike of actinomorphic, white or pale lilac (rarely midblue) flowers with filiform, straight perianth tube, 7-12(-15) mm long and up to 0.5 mm diam., tightly clasping the style for most of its length and abruptly dilated only in the distal 1 mm, with the filaments thus completely exserted. The stamens are symmetrically arranged, with ± horizontally spreading anthers, and the filaments occlude the mouth of the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the filiform-terete leaves and lax spike with distant bracts, the lower internodes 3-5 times longer than the bracts. Uniquely in the genus, the inner bracts are as long as or slightly longer than the outer and similar in texture, both leathery and green with dry, papery apices - in other species the inner bracts are smaller than the outer and ± membranous.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Tritonia securigera and its allies with similar short-tubed, orange flowers by the presence of a conspicuously thickened submarginal vein within 0.5 mm of the leaf margins. These are typically more prominent than the lightly thickened midrib. Similar leaves are characteristic of sect. Subcallosae but these species lack the quadrate calluses and conspicuous yellow mouth to the perianth tube characteristic of T. securigera and its allies.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished in sect. Pectinatae by the plane, lanceolate to sword-shaped leaves with closely crisped and undulate, often ciliate margins. The only other species with crisped leaves and long-tubed flowers, Tritonia tugwelliae from the western Great Karoo, has plane, falcate leaves and uniformly pale bracts, thus evidently not immediately related to the species of sect. Pectinatae in which it was once included. The length of the perianth tube in Tritonia undulata varies widely across its range, with a trend for longer tubes, 60-85 mm long, in populations in the north and west, from the Olifants River Valley along the coast to the Cape Peninsula, and shorter tubes, 22-50 mm, inland and to the south, from Tulbagh to Gordon’s Bay.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very little known. The very short, thick wide leaves with obtuse tips suggest a connection with the N. laticoma group but the slender terete scape and the shape and size of the flower are clearly related to N. humilis.
bibliographicCitation: Norris, CA. 1974. Part II: The genus Nerine. Nerine Society Bulletin 6: 7-31. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from other species with similar, relatively small, pink flowers with narrow tepals, by the stiff stems, mostly 2-3 mm diam., bearing numerous dingy or brownish pink flowers from near the base of a long spike much longer than the non-flowering part of the stem, and by the conspicuously apiculate bracts that are hard and cartilaginous at flowering time.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from similar short-tubed, pink-flowered species by its mostly larger, candy-pink flowers, the dorsal tepal 23-33 x 5-8(-12) mm and the filaments 15-20 mm long with conspicuously apiculate anthers, and the relatively long style branches 3-4 mm long. The tepals are clawed in the basal half and recurved distally, giving the flowers a rather open appearance, with the lower tepals almost as wide as the upper. The stems are mostly 300-600 mm high and unbranched (rarely with a solitary short erect branch).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geranium amatolicum has been known for about 150 years, but it has always been confused with G. ornithopodon, which can be distinguished immediately by its leaves being differently cut and never glandular below.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: A very distinctive species, 500-1100 mm high, with relatively long spikes of creamy white to pale yellow flowers with a slender, subcylindric tube 30-40 mm long and relatively short tepals 9-13 mm long. The sweetly scented flowers are pollinated by sphinx moths. Unlike other species in the genus, in which the tepals start to gape several days before the flowers open fully, the tepals in Tritoniopsis nervosa remain joined at the tips until anthesis.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its small, short-tubed, pale yellow to creamy white flowers, sometimes flushed pinkish, with tepals 9-13 mm long and short filaments (3-)4-7 mm long. The capsules are moderately to well inflated, 15-20 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species with a short, compact spike of long-tubed, pink flowers with long, attenuate bracts 25-35 mm long. The solitary basal leaf, dry at flowering, has a conspicuous long false petiole and relatively small, elliptic to ovate-lanceolate blade 30-55 mm long with crisped or undulate margins. The cauline leaves are linear-attenuate, ± overlapping and concealing the stem, closely sheathing below with the distal free portion involute and appearing terete. The uppermost cauline leaves are closely associated with the flowering spike and grade into the floral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species with dense spikes of moderate-sized, pink, funnel-shaped flowers and coarse, dry, brown, overlapping bracts by its densely clumped habit, with the stems inclined at the base and then sharply erect below the spike. The bracts are greenish straw-coloured with noticeably darker brown margins and pale venation. Watsonia canaliculata has similar pale bracts but is a solitary-growing species with erect stems and channelled leaves; W. pulchra has dark brown bracts and broad leaves, (10-)15-30 mm wide with heavily thickened margins; and W. lepida is a shorter, solitary-growing species, with the lowermost leaves dry and broken at flowering, and uniformly dark brown bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other pink-flowered species with declinate stamens and purple anthers by the long perianth tube, 30-50 mm long with the lower part 26-40 mm long and a short upper part 5-8 mm long, and the long bracts, mostly 30-50 mm long, usually diverging from the stem, and the relatively short filaments 6-12 mm long. Watsonia strictiflora from south of Wellington has slightly shorter bracts, (15-)20-25(-33) mm long, and a longer upper part of the perianth tube, 8-14 mm long, with proportionally longer filaments, 13-15 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small, orange-flowered species up to 500 mm high, with the upper part of the perianth tube narrowly trumpet-shaped, 10-12 mm long and slightly shorter than the tepals, and short filaments ± 10 mm long just included in the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily distinguished by its slender stems up to 2 m tall, short bracts 6-12 mm long, and short perianth tube with the upper part 4-8 mm long but relatively long filaments 12-15 mm long, thus ± twice as long as the upper part of the tube. Watsonia wilmaniae from much the same habitats and location and with similar short bracts has the upper part of the perianth tube 15-20 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small species with narrow, linear leaves 4-5 mm wide, laxly spaced cauline leaves, and pale pink flowers with funnel-shaped tube, the upper part ± as long as the tepals, and arcuate stamens with yellow anthers 8-9 mm long. Watsonia distans from marshy sites in the Hottentots Holland Mtns has unbranched stems with mostly fewer flowers with shorter anthers, 5-6 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species with similar flowers by its short stature, mostly less than 400 mm high, and relatively long, herbaceous bracts, 20-25 mm long, the inner as long or slightly longer than the outer and barely forked apically. The bracts remain relatively soft in texture and do not turn dark brown on drying. The capsules are large and leathery, 20-25 mm long. Watsonia meriana is a larger species, 500-2000 mm tall, usually branched, with broader leaves 12-35 mm wide and slightly longer flowers, the filaments 35-45 mm long. Watsonia humilis has white to pink flowers with relatively short filaments 10-20 mm long included or scarcely exserted from the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species is sometimes confused with G. canescens, which has similarly cut leaves, but these are usually more markedly discolorous than those of G. harveyi, and the indumentum is thinner (the leaf blade is often visible through the hairs on the lower surface in G. canescens; it is completely obscured in G. harveyi). Also, G. canescens always has gland-tipped hairs on the upper parts (they are very rare in G. harveyi, and then confined to the pedicels and lower part of the sepals), and the petals are usually white (rarely flushed pink), not deep pink nor purple, 8-11.5 x 4-5 mm, not 12-15 x 6.5-9 mm. The two species are allopatric.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: One of several species with dense spikes of moderate-sized, pink, funnel-shaped flowers and coarse, dry, brown, overlapping bracts and distinguished by its solitary habit and comparatively short, stout, erect stem up to 650 mm tall with the basal leaves dry and withered at flowering time. It is most likely to be confused with Watsonia confusa, often a taller plant up to 1500 mm tall with the leaves green at flowering and broader bracts, 14-18 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species with broad, bright green leaves, 30-60 mm wide, and long-tubed, dull red to maroon flowers with the upper part of the perianth tube subcylindric, 18-24 mm long and slightly shorter than the tepals. Watsonia gladioloides from the Eastern Cape Drakensberg has similar, orange to scarlet flowers but narrower leaves, less than 18 mm wide, and bracts completely dry at flowering.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by its glabrous, transversely ridged carpels and deeply notched petals.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: It is allied to the widespread G. schlechteri, but differs in its more deeply cut leaves (the free part of the midlobe in proportion to the joined part being about 8-16:1, not 2-5:1); it is also markedly less glandular than G. schlechteri; and when gland-tipped hairs are present, they are very short (up to ±0.3 mm, not mostly 0.5-1.5 mm).
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: Recognised by the narrow leaves, 3-15 mm wide and unbranched stem of tubular, dark red flowers, the upper part of the tube subcylindric, (20-)25-30 mm long and slightly longer than the tepals, and dry, brown bracts. The filaments are 25-35 mm long, exserted 5-7 mm from the perianth tube. Watsonia latifolia from northern KwaZulu-Natal and southern Mpumalanga with similar long-tubed, red flowers has broad, bright green leaves, 30-60 mm wide, and the upper part of the perianth tube 18-24 mm long and slightly shorter than the tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The most striking feature of the plant is its peltate leaves, which are unknown elsewhere in the genus in southern Africa. The leaves alone serve to distinguish it from its ally, G. flanaganii, but where we saw them growing together near the Molweni river, we were at once struck by the differences in indumentum between the two species, the delicate spreading hairs on the stems and petioles of G. ornithopodioides often reaching 3 mm in length, more than twice the length of those in G. flanaganii.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: A tall species, 1500-2000 mm high, with herbaceous bracts 15-20 mm long, and pale pink flowers, the upper part of the perianth tube ± 22 mm long and tepals 20-22 mm long. The yellow anthers are diagnostic. The capsules are unknown. Watsonia meriana, the only other species of Watsonia recorded on the Kamiesberg, has slightly longer bracts, bracts (18-)24-30 mm long, and reddish orange flowers with tepals 21-26 mm long, and violet anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by its deeply dissected leaves and transversely ridged, glabrous carpels.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: Distinguished from other species with dense spikes of moderate-sized, pink, funnel-shaped flowers and coarse, dry, brown, overlapping bracts by its comparatively short, erect stem, 300-450 mm tall, and narrow leaves, 4-7 mm wide, with the margins curved inward so that the leaves are markedly channelled or sometimes sigmoid in section. Watsonia lepida, also a solitary-growing species, has flat leaves 5-15 mm wide, the lowermost dry and broken at flowering, and uniformly dark brown bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is a very distinctive plant, yet it is frequently misidentified as either G. incanum, G. canescens, or G. harveyi, none of which is shrubby, and all differ further from G. robustum in other characters. Geranium robustum is allied to G. pulchrum, which replaces it on the Natal side of the Drakensberg, though G. pulchrum possibly demands wetter sites than G. robustum.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: Distinguished from other species with dense spikes of moderate-sized, pink, funnel-shaped flowers and coarse, dry, brown, overlapping bracts by its comparatively tall, erect stem, 600-1200 mm tall, lanceolate leaves (10-)15-30 mm wide, with strongly thickened margins but only weakly thickened midrib, and dark brown bracts without paler venation.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A delicate species with 1 or 2 narrow, basal leaves and a mostly unbranched stem with pink flowers with narrowly subcylindric perianth tube, the upper part 12-16 mm long, and purple anthers. Watsonia distans has funnel-shaped flowers with the upper part of the perianth tube flared and 9-12 mm long, and evidently yellow anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The type specimen of G. sparsiflorum came from the Zuurberg, near Weza in southern Natal, and subsequent collections have come from nearby Ixopo and Mount Currie districts, as well as from Magwa Falls and Mateku in Lusikisiki district, Pondoland, that part of the Transkei lying immediately south of Natal. The type of G. alticola, which was also collected by Schlechter, reputedly came from Van Reenen, in northern Natal, but the species has never been re-collected there. Schlechter's number, 6994, is not listed in the account of his itinerary in South Africa (Jessop, in J.S. Afr. Bot. 30:137, 1964): his 1891-95 tour ends with no. 6992, collected at Van Reenen in March 1895. The isotype of G. alticola (Schlechter 6994) at the Albany Museum bears a Schlechter printed ticket with the collector's number only written in by Schlechter himself; the locality has been added much later by another hand (the isotype of G. sparsiflorum, Schlechter 6590, GRA, has number, locality and date all written in by Schlechter). It seems possible that, at the end of his tour, Schlechter found himself with a few specimens that he numbered but did not localize; the locality 'Van Reenen' was added later, in consequence of no. 6992 having been collected there. The localities of other Schlechter specimens can be questioned (see Jessop, loc. cit.). The deeply and sharply cut leaves with their spreading hairs are distinctive, bearing some resemblance only to those of G. contortum, a plant differing from G. sparsiflorum in habit among other characters. It can also be confused with G. subglabrum: see under that species.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: Geranium subglabrum is similar to G. caffrum in leaf indumentum, but the leaf lobing is different and so is the indumentum on the peduncles (spreading gland-tipped hairs richly developed in G. subglabrum, wanting in G. caffrum). It can also be confused with G. sparsiflorum, but the leaf cutting is different as is the indumentum.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: Although it was described forty-five years ago, the name has never been taken up, and the species will be found in herbaria commonly misidentified as G. ornithopodon, sometimes as G. canescens. It is at once distinguished from both these species, as well as from G. schlechteri, by its narrow deeply notched petals (they are entire or shallowly notched in the other three species). The hairs on G. wakkerstroomianum are usually eglandular; however, throughout its range, occasional specimens, even in a single collection, may have some gland-tipped hairs particularly on the pedicels, peduncles and upper parts of the stems. There is also some variation in degree of development of hairs: plants are generally well clothed in spreading hairs, but when the pubescence is more scanty, the hairs may be shorter and retrorse.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: Recognised by the small bracts, 5-8 mm long and dry at flowering, and the dull red, tubular flowers with the upper part of the perianth tube 12-15(-20) mm long, and relatively small tepals, 12-15 x 5-8 mm. The small flowers separate it from the southern Cape Watsonia wilmaniae, which has the upper part of the perianth tube 15-20 mm long and tepals 18-22 mm long. Watsonia angusta also has larger flowers with the upper part of the perianth tube 20-22 mm long, tepals 19-25 mm long, and filaments 30-38 mm long; and characteristic fusiform capsules 25-35 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species with similar long-tubed, red to orange flowers by the relatively short bracts, (10-)14-18 mm long and the oblong-fusiform capsules tapering at the tips. Watsonia angusta is a generally taller species, with dull red flowers with narrower tepals mostly 4-8 mm wide and a longer upper perianth tube, 20-22 mm long. Watsonia fourcadei is likewise a more robust species with much longer, typically rather drooping flowers with the upper part of the tube 22-26 mm long, and deeply forked inner bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the long bracts, (20-)25-35 mm long, and especially the very long lower part of the perianth tube, 25-30 mm long, with a narrowly funnel-shaped upper part ± 15 mm long. Watsonia occulta has even longer bracts, 35-55 mm long, and similarly long-tubed flowers with a much shorter upper part of the tube, just ± 6 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Tendrils bifid near apex; leaves glabrous; anther connective without a spur-shaped appendix; styles 3.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other summer-rainfall species with similar pink, funnel-shaped flowers by the unbranched stems with narrow bracts not or hardly clasping the stem below, relatively large flowers with attenuate tepals 20-25 mm long, and more northerly distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Tendrils bifid near apex; leaves tomentose on lower surface; anther connective with a spur-like appendix; style 1, short, conical.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished from other species with similar, long-tubed orange flowers by the strongly inflated cauline bract leaves and the large, oblong-truncate capsules 20-30 mm long. The floral bracts are relatively short, 10-15 mm long, with the inner as long as or slightly longer and forked apically for up to 3 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very distinctive but inconspicuous species, with a spike of 3 to 7 pale pink flowers largely concealed by unusually long bracts, 35-55 mm long. The flowers are long-tubed, with the lower part of the perianth tube 30-50 mm long and the upper part relatively short, ± 6 mm long. Watsonia wilmsii is a larger, more conspicuous species with similarly long-tubed flowers but with a much longer upper part of the tube ± 15 mm long, and shorter bracts (20-)25-35 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A particularly robust species readily recognised by its broad leaves, (33-)55-85 mm wide with the midrib poorly defined but the margins heavily thickened, somewhat inflated bract-like cauline leaves, dry, lacerate floral bracts 25-45 mm long and large, long-tubed red flowers, the tube alone up to 50 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unique in the genus in its pale, dry bracts and actinomorphic flowers with short, narrowly cupped perianth tube 7-12 mm long. Forms with lateral branches are highly floriferous, the branches appressed to the main axis and giving the appearance of a single, densely-flowered inflorescence. The peg-like callus at the base of each tepal is distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A short species, up to 450 mm high, with distinctive, narrow perianth tube 25-34 mm long and ± 4 mm diam. at the mouth, with spreading tepals and filaments 15-20 mm long and barely exserted from the perianth tube. Watsonia fergusoniae from limestone habitats is taller, usually more than 400 m high, with larger flowers, the tube 35-50 mm long and mostly ± 6 mm diam. at the mouth, and longer filaments 25-35 mm long well exserted from the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species with similar flowers by its large stature and relatively long, herbaceous bracts, (18-)24-30 mm long, the inner as long or slightly longer and acute or barely forked apically. The bracts remain relatively soft in texture and do not turn dark brown on drying. The capsules are large and leathery, 22-30 mm long. Watsonia coccinea is a shorter species up to 400 mm tall, often unbranched, with narrower leaves mostly 2-8 mm wide and slightly smaller flowers, the filaments 25-30 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the lanceolate leaves, 25-40 mm wide, and the long-tubed pinkish purple flowers with the upper part of the perianth tube 20-30 mm long, and declinate stamens with purple anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the glabrous stem and leaf, rather than velvety or hairy as in M. villosa, and by the white flowers with striking nectar guides of dark purple or turquoise green. The outer tepals are up to 35 mm long with the limbs almost orbicular, thus nearly as wide as long, and the tepal claws are heavily bearded. Moraea aristata is diploid with 2n = 12 in contrast to most populations of closely related M. villosa, which are tetraploid.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea abyssinica is readily recognised by the compressed, 2-winged stem, comprising a long terminal internode bearing a subterminal leaf subtending one or two flower clusters.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very variable in the size and width of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1961. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IX. Glinus. J. S. African Bot. 27: 125-130. [CC BY]

description: Globulariopsis obtusiloba is remarkable among its congeners for its calyx with all five lobes obtuse (the anticous lobes are obtuse in G. montana), and for the lack of hairs on both surfaces of the bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its robust habit with a relatively open, branched flowering stem bearing relatively large flowers with tepals up to 20 mm long, and most significantly, elongate capsules 15-25(-30) mm long, thus oblong in outline but with broad, narrow vertical wings. The capsules contain 2 or 3 (occasionally more) flat seeds per locule, each seed always with a fringe of papillae along the margins. The inflorescence spathes and bracts are dry, papery and rust-brown and usually minutely hairy to scabrid on the abaxial (outer) surfaces.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea biflora is readily recognised by the large, pale blue to mauve flowers 50-60 mm diam. with the outer tepals asymmetric about the midline and each with a pair of transparent to slightly bronzed windows near the base. Seen from above the windows appear dark green or brown depending on lighting.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea bracteata is readily recognised by the relatively large flower clusters enclosed by large, more-or-less dry, firm-textured, ovate, spoon-shaped spathes 10-18 mm long. Both the spathes and floral bracts are minutely hairy, papillate or scabrid.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differences in leaf shapes, expression of teeth, width and length, used to distinguish species in the past, occur within populations as well, suggesting the present wider circumscription of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Hartmann, HEKO; Golling, H. 1993. A monograph of the genus Glottiphyllum (Mesembryanthemum, Aizoaceae). Bradleya 11: 1-49. [https://doi.org/10.25223/brad.n11.1993.a1] [All rights reserved]

description: The flattened stem with a pronounced main axis, straight, stiff lateral branches, soft-textured leaves 8-12 mm wide and the shorter spathes and bracts less than 9 mm long separate it from the taller, round-stemmed A. flexicaulis.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea cuspidata is recognised by the comparatively slender, usually unbranched stem bearing several sessile flower clusters or the lower clusters sometimes on short stalks, with relatively prominent spathes, initially green but soon turning rust-brown. The spathes and bracts are usually rough and minutely scabrid.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea ensifolia is distinguished by the strongly compressed and winged stem, often with a few branches but with sessile lateral flower clusters, relatively small flowers and elongate, often drooping capsules 35-50 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea flexicaulis is immediately recognised by the tall stature, some individuals exceeding 1200 mm high, with stems divaricately branched in the upper quarter. Some of the branches bear sessile lateral flower clusters plus one or two sessile axillary flower clusters.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea galpinii closely resembles A. grandis from coastal KwaZulu-Natal in its large flower clusters, each containing 8 to 12 flowers and subtended by a prominent spathe, initially green below but aging rust-brown from the apex. Aristea galpinii is a shorter and less robust species, up to 650 mm high (although the type is less than 300 mm high), with narrower leaves up to 9 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species is robust, up to 950 mm tall, and has leaves 10-16 mm wide. The distinctive flowering stem may bear up to 6 large flower clusters, each with up to 16 flowers in a complex arrangement. The inner floral spathes and bracts are greenish to translucent below, light red-brown above, and closely resemble those of A. galpinii and A. schizolaena. Most significantly, the angular seeds have a smooth surface, in marked contrast to those of most other eastern southern African species, which have foveate sculpturing.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The half-nodding, dark blue flowers of Aristea inaequalis are unique in the genus in having unequal stamens, the lower filament being ± 2 mm longer than the other two. The species is also distinctive in the laxly branched flowering stem, the branches bearing shortly stalked and sessile flower clusters.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea lugens has upright, predominantly white to blue flowers with the small outer tepals dark brown or black on both surfaces. The inner tepals are obovate and outspread, and the outer tepals, ± half as long as the inner, are suberect and curved inward distally.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Despite its height, up to 1 m but usually only 500 mm, and robust habit, Aristea palustris is typical of sect. Aristea in the nearly dichotomous branching pattern, largely translucent spathes, and broadly winged capsules. Pollen is likewise consistent with the section, the large grains with specialised trisulcate apertures. The dry, silvery spathes and bracts with a narrow dark keel most closely resemble those of A. oligocephala, which is common throughout the Caledon and Bredasdorp Districts of Western Cape, and we assume the two species are immediately related. A shorter plant, A. oligocephala has firm-textured, fibrous leaves 1.5-3.0 mm wide, whereas those of A. palustris are sword-shaped, relatively soft-textured and 4-9 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The relatively small flowers with subequal tepals 15-22 mm long and short anthers 3-4 mm long resemble those of most species of Aristea whereas other species of sect. Pseudaristea often have longer anthers, mostly 4.5-6.0 mm long. The leaves of A. pauciflora are unique in the section in their rounded margins lacking the typical marginal anatomy of translucent, thickened marginal epidermal cells of other members of subg. Pseudaristea, in which the margins have acute edges that become hyaline when dry. Aristea pauciflora is most easily confused with A. simplex, which has either pale or sometimes deep blue flowers of similar proportions but half to fully nodding, and plane leaves with acute margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Broadly similar to the more common and widespread Aristea africana, A. recisa shares with that species distinctive dry-papery, prominently fringed spathes and floral bracts. The two might easily be confused but the bracts of A. recisa are rusty brown along the margins, the leaves are often broader, up to 5 mm wide, and soft-textured, and the flowering stems are usually held well above the leaves, whereas the stems in A. africana are usually (but not invariably) not much longer than the leaves. The critical distinction between the two species lies in the spathes and bracts, which in A. recisa are fringed for less than a third of their length, whereas in A. africana they are fringed for half their length or more, as well as usually being uniformly coloured.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea rigidifolia is a tall species with a much-branched stem, readily distinguished in having only two basal leaves, the blades narrow, 1.5-3.0 mm wide, and more-or-less elliptic in section with rounded margins of solid green tissue.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It has tufts of leaves at ground level and produces persistent aerial stolon-like stems that root at nodes some distance from the parent plant, a feature unique in Aristea, and in a sense it is a trailing plant. The slender flowering stems, produced from leaf clusters, are usually dichotomously branched and bear pendent flower clusters the rounded, ± doughnut-shaped seeds with a depression at the chalazal end are quite unlike the tangentially flattened, lamellate seeds of other members of subg. Aristea. The seed funicle is persistent and fleshy, forming an irregularly lobed body.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea teretifolia is distinguished in subg. Pseudaristea by the narrow, fibrous leaves either terete or plane and up to 2 mm wide, and by its relatively large flowers, 50-58 mm diam., and largely pale lilac, mauve or creamy yellow, with the outer tepals marked with a dark bronze-brown blotch in the lower half edged in pale blue or turquoise. The outer tepals are obovoid and relatively small, ± 20 mm long, compared with the inner which are fiddle-shaped and 24-28 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised primarily by the distinctive spathes and bracts, these dark green below edged reddish brown and grading unevenly into broad translucent margins darker along the veins thus giving them a feathered appearance. The pale edges of the spathes and bracts become torn and irregularly fringed with age. The spathes are fairly large, especially those of the lower flower clusters. The flowering stem bears several sessile lateral flower clusters and is often unbranched or the lower fertile nodes may bear one or more, short erect branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea zeyheri is distinguished by the slender habit, growing singly (not in tufts as originally suggested) with an unbranched stem and terete leaves, and broadly lobed, style with fringed stigmatic lobes. The relatively large flowers, up to 35 mm diam., are evidently nodding and unusual in the elongate ovary as well as the fringed stigmatic lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the dark blue perianth with relatively broad, subequal tepals held in a shallow cup enclosing the stamens and style. The perianth is inverted so that the dorsal tepal and arched stamens face the spike apex, unusual in Babiana, shared with few other species. The lower tepals of the darkly pigmented perianth have blackish or occasionally dark red spear-shaped marks in the lower midline and this together with the blackish anthers gives the flowers a distinctive appearance. The flowers are often visited by hopliine scarab beetles, sometimes seen resting for long periods in the base of the floral cup, and these beetles may be the primary pollinators of B. angustifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Babiana attenuata has attractive blue-violet flowers borne on crowded horizontal spikes close to ground level. It is most easily recognised by the moderately long perianth tube, 25-35 mm long, about as long as or slightly longer than the bracts and tepals, and the strong sweet violet floral fragrance. It is easily confused with the vegetatively virtually identical B. curviscapa, which extends from Steinkopf in the north to Bitterfontein in the south, thus including the entire range of B. attenuata. They are separated primarily by the length of the perianth tube, substantially longer in B. curviscapa and usually 36-43 mm vs. 25-35 mm in B. attenuata. Flowers of B. attenuata are always strongly fragrant and have tepals usually 26-35 mm long, whereas the flowers of B. curviscapa are only faintly scented or lack a floral odour completely and the shorter tepals are 20-23 mm long. In the north of its range B. curviscapa has magenta to cherry-red flowers but elsewhere they are blue as in B. attenuata. Despite its relatively long perianth tube, B. attenuata is pollinated by anthophorine bees with mouthparts about 10 mm long. Plants from the southern Kamiesberg with erect, linear leaves up to 150 mm long and conspicuously long-hairy, appear rather different to other populations of B. attenuata and may represent a local variant or possibly a separate species but the flowers match those of other populations of the species in critical details.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the strongly deflexed stem and blue-mauve flowers with yellow markings on the lower tepals and auricular lobes at the base of the lower lateral tepal limbs. Although included in sect. Babiana because of the ovary hairy on the ribs, the inner bracts are not divided to the base but are joined in the lower third by membranous tissue. At first B. auriculata appears to be a smaller form of B. mucronata, but that species has the inner bracts clearly divided to the base, a densely hairy ovary, and the lower tepals lack auricular lobes. The auricular lobes of the lower tepals recall sect. Antholyzoides but the partly hairy ovary is inconsistent with that section, as are the membranous inner bract margins and midline. Apart from their incomplete separation, the inner bracts are otherwise typical of sect. Babiana in their membranous margins and rust-coloured tips. The narrow claws of the lower tepals suggest that B. auriculata is most closely allied to B. unguiculata, which also has narrowly clawed lower tepals. The nearly horizontal spike axis with the flowers facing the stem apex is another striking feature of Babiana auriculata, and one shared with a few other species of section Babiana.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The large-flowered Babiana blanda with its bright rosy pink, radially symmetric perianth is now unfortunately on the brink of extinction in the wild. Never common, its specialised, seasonally wet habitat has now all but disappeared, and the remaining known wild plants are seriously threatened by encroachment of alien Acacia species and pasturage. It appears to be most closely related to B. villosula, which has similar, though generally smaller, radially symmetric flowers but blooms earlier in the season. The two may be distinguished by flower size and colour, the tepals of B. villosula are 20-30 x 8-13 mm and blue to blue-mauve (rarely white) with a small white centre, whereas those of B. blanda are 23-33 x 14-20 and rosy pink, and unscented, unlike B. villosula. The style branches of B. villosula are filiform with small expanded tips, whereas those of B. blanda have prominent, broad apices. The leaf blades of B. blanda also tend to be oriented more obliquely to the sheaths than in related species, but this character is variable and cannot be relied upon alone. Lewis (1959) described several hybrids between B. blanda and B. villosula. Populations that we have seen on low sandstone outcrops between Klipheuwel and Joostenberg are variable between the two species in flower colour, tepal shape and style length, and presumably represent hybrid swarms.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Superficially resembling the widespread and well-known Babiana ambigua in the narrow leaves and acaulescent habit, B. cedarbergensis has inner bracts divided only in the upper third, whereas B. ambigua has the inner bracts divided to the base. Other differences between these two species are the thick fibrous neck around the base of the stem, stiff, straight leaves, and hairy ovary of B. cedarbergensis, whereas B. ambigua has a poorly developed neck of fibres around the base, firm but not rigid leaves, and a hairless ovary. The resemblance to B. ambigua is presumably convergent. Babiana cedarbergensis is restricted to higher elevations in the Cederberg and is endemic to the Northwest Centre of the Cape Floristic Region. The hairy ovary of B. cedarbergensis is unusual in section Teretifolieae.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The most common long-tubed species of Babiana in Namaqualand, B. curviscapa blooms from late August to the end of September, depending on elevation, plants on the Kamiesberg flowering the latest. It appears to be most closely allied to B. attenuata, which is vegetatively virtually indistinguishable in its short, somewhat twisted leaves but with strongly scented violet flowers with a shorter perianth tube, 25-35 mm long, and adapted for pollination by large-bodied long-tongued anthophorine bees, whereas the longer-tubed flowers of B. curviscapa are pollinated by long-proboscid flies. Although the two species flower at a slightly different time, B. curviscapa mainly in September and B. attenuata from late July to late August, flowering times may overlap at some sites, creating the possibility for hybridisation. Possible interspecific crossing between the two species is the reason they can sometimes be difficult to distinguish.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The very distinctive Babiana dregei has striking, hard-textured, lanceolate leaves with a prominent, spiny, piercing apex and is a robust species, plants reaching up to 350 mm in height and producing numerous flowers on branched stems. The leaves have prominent, pale fibrous veins at the angles of the folds or pleats and are usually smooth but sometimes finely hairy.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although typical of sect. Babiana in its branched, aerial stem and inner bracts divided to the base, B. ecklonii is remarkable for its tall stature when well grown, the stem largely sheathed by the bases of the erect leaves, and for its elongate perianth tube, 35-47 mm long. The blue-violet flowers have large white markings on the lower lateral tepals and unusual stamens, which are initially parallel, but after dehiscence the filaments diverge, leaving the anthers widely separated from one another. Variation across the range of Babiana ecklonii is puzzling. It is fairly uniform in the Olifants River Mtns, where it has blue-violet flowers with very discrete and prominent white to pale yellow nectar guides on the lower lateral tepals, an erect stem, fairly attenuate floral bracts, and style branches terminating in small stigmatic lobes. At the northern edge of its range, at Klawer and on the Gifberg, plants have narrower, more densely pilose leaves and also have flexed and inclined stems. While the type form of B. ecklonii has the ovary densely hairy above the base, plants from sites west of the Olifants River Mtns may have the ovary hairy only on the ribs.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the hairless or nearly hairless stem and the woolly or cobwebby cataphylls and bases of the leaf sheaths, Babiana fimbriata has leaves 3-4 mm wide with the blades slightly twisted. The dark purple to almost brown flowers have greenish yellow lower lateral tepals with prominent auriculate lobes at the limb bases.
