The upper lateral tepals of B. fimbriata are directed forward or are slightly curved inward in the proximal half, a feature unique in the genus. Babiana spiralis, which has been confused with B. fimbriata, has smooth cataphylls and leaf sheaths, a velvety stem, and bright pink or blue flowers, also with auriculate lobes on the lower tepal limbs. The upper lateral tepals of B. spiralis curve outward shortly above the base in conventional subpatent orientation.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Known only from the type, Babiana foliosa is a puzzling plant, with radially symmetric flowers closely resembling those of winter-flowering B. villosula from west of the Hottentots Holland Mtns. At first it seems merely to be an eastern form of that species but its flowers have substantially longer filaments, ± 10 mm long vs. 4-6 mm in B. villosula, and a stouter perianth tube. The more numerous leaves, for which the species was named, and green bracts without dry rust-coloured tips, also make it easy to distinguish B. foliosa from other species of sect. Babiana with actinomorphic flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the well-developed aerial stem, smooth ovary, and outer bracts dark rusty brown at the tips and rather irregularly lobed or torn. Among the species of series Patulae, B. fourcadei is recognised by the well-developed and usually repeatedly branched stem, and fairly large pale blue to violet flowers with a perianth tube, 20-30 mm long, dorsal tepal 25-30 mm long, and the completely smooth ovary. Babiana patula, often confused with B. fourcadei, always has a shorter, ± decumbent stem, and thus seldom exceeds 100 mm in height, and the ovary in most populations is minutely hairy on the ribs (plants with a completely hairless ovary are unusual but are reported in the literature). The perianth of B. patula ranges from either pale blue to mauve, purple, or pale yellow to white, typically with large yellow or cream-coloured markings on the lower lateral tepals. The flowers are slightly smaller, the tube 10-14 mm long, the dorsal tepal mostly 20-25 mm long, and the bracts acute and often only light brown.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Most easily identified by its short stem, reaching no more than 20 mm above ground, tight fan of basal leaves, and ± erect spike with silky bracts 40-50 mm long. The flowers are deep violet-blue and have an elongate perianth tube 60-70 mm long, slightly curved at the throat. The lower tepals have bold white markings in the midline outlined in darker blue or red and the tepals are relatively narrow, 5-9 mm wide, and spread almost at right angles to the tube when the flowers are fully open. The stamens are held erect with the filaments exserted ± 10 mm from the tube and the anthers are 7-9 mm long. Babiana framesii is well known from the immediate vicinity of Nieuwoudtville, where it is often difficult to distinguish from the long-tubed B. sambucina subsp. longibracteata. The latter has a straight perianth tube, broader tepals mostly 8-12(-16) mm wide, and even when the flowers are fully open, the tepals may overlap one another and remain slightly ascending, unlike the outspread, widely separate tepals of B. framesii. The perianth tube of B. sambucina subsp. longibracteata is 30-55 mm long, shorter than that of B. framesii.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Low-growing and virtually acaulescent, Babiana geniculata is distinctive in its flowers with a long slender perianth tube 35-45 mm long and bent at a sharp angle just below the apex, the ovary hairy above the base, and the divergent rather than parallel filaments with the anthers held well apart from one another. The style is also unusual in dividing opposite the middle of the filaments, thus below the bases of the anthers. The style branches, the longest in the genus, 11-13 mm long, are slender and barely expanded at the tips. The flowers are adapted for pollination by long-proboscid flies. The inner bracts, forked in the upper third, are consistent with sect. Teretifolieae in which the inner bracts are usually forked only near the apex, whereas superficially similar Babiana ecklonii is a taller plant with the inner bracts divided to the base, a feature diagnostic for sect. Babiana. Babiana curviscapa from Namaqualand, also with short leaves and a decumbent spike of long-tubed flowers with the perianth tube sharply bent below the apex, has conventional arcuate and parallel stamens, a hairless ovary, and the style divides close to the anther apices into short branches, ± 4 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognised by the unusual leaves, borne on pseudopetioles sometimes up to 30 mm long, with the expanded, lanceolate to oblong blades prominently 3- or 4-ribbed, scarcely pleated, and held horizontally at right angles to the sheaths. The flowers typically have lilac outer and yellow inner tepals but may also be entirely yellow. The immediate relationships of B. horizontalis are uncertain, but it seems to be allied to the several dwarf, acaulescent species of Namaqualand, all of which have a smooth ovary and similar inner bracts forked at the apex.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species at first glance appears similar to Gnidia polycephala (C.A.Mey.) Gilg which also has alternate leaves, a terminal, indeterminate, bracteate umbel with involucral leaves much broader than the cauline leaves and yellow sericeous flowers. It, however, differs from G. polycephala by the usually well-developed peduncle, the coriaceous involucral bracts which are glabrous abaxially and the four-merous flowers with four, fleshy, petaloid scales. In G. polycephala there is no well-developed, naked peduncular region, the papery thin involucral bracts are adpressed hairy abaxially, the flower is pentamerous and the petaloid scales are absent.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2002. Thymelaeaceae: A new species of Gnidia from the Knersvlakte, Western  Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 32(1): 79-81. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its actinomorphic flowers with erect, symmetrically arranged filaments enclosing the style and bearing linear, white or yellow anthers. It may be most closely allied to B. villosula, which also has radially symmetric flowers and the two are easily confused. Babiana villosula has pale blue to mauve flowers with a small white centre, and usually bluish to mauve anthers, whereas B. leipoldtii has violet flowers darker in the centre and white or yellow anthers that contrast with the perianth colour. Both species have short filaments included in the upper part of the perianth tube and the anthers held at the mouth of the tube. Apart from the flowers, B. leipoldtii is distinguished from most other species with an actinomorphic flower by the relatively tall, aerial stem and somewhat lax spike. Related species have the stem extended only a short distance above the ground.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in the short, oblong leaf blades held at right angles to the short, erect pseudopetioles, a softly hairy stem of short stature, up to 150 mm high, and relatively long, sparsely hairy floral bracts 15-20 mm long. The greenish yellow flowers have a short perianth tube, 10 mm long, a dorsal tepal ± 25 mm long, and lower tepals ± 20 mm long with short, well-developed claws. Babiana salteri, also with short spreading leaves, has hairy, soft-textured leaves, inner bracts divided to the base, and a densely hairy ovary. The similarity of the short leaf blades held nearly at right angles to the sheaths is best seen as convergent. Babiana lewisiana is most likely allied to the group of species in sect. Antholyzoides that have a pubescent stem and lack the cobwebby to woolly hairs on the cataphylls and lower leaf sheaths. These include B. spiralis and B. stenomera but it should not be confused with either of these species because of the plane leaves with broad, oblong blades extending almost horizontally, unlike the narrow, distally coiled leaves of the latter two species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is a dwarf suffrutex, much tufted and branched, very floriferous, and is at the peak of its flowering in October. The flowers are solitary in the leaf axils over nearly the whole length of each branchlet, which makes it easy to distinguish from its allies, G. baurii and G. fastigiata, in which the flowers are borne only in the upper leaf axils. Furthermore, the flowers are always paired in G. baurii; in G. fastigiata there are usually two to several in each axil, rarely only one, and in that species, the flowering tips are soon overtopped by new long sterile shoots, giving it a facies quite unlike that of G. renniana.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1986. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XII. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 43(2): 189-228. [CC BY-SA]

description: Recognised in sect. Babiana by the rigid, narrow, suberect, deeply plicate leaves, several-branched stem with short bracts, and zygomorphic, markedly bilabiate flower with the dorsal tepal erect and the lower tepals united below to form a prominent lip. Plants typically grow in dense colonies in damp sandy sites where the pale blue-mauve flowers make a display unusual for the genus. The fairly short-tubed flowers are adapted for pollination by anthophorine bees and Apis mellifera workers, which visit the flowers for their nectar. Babiana lineolata is evidently most closely related to B. mucronata and it is easily confused with this species. The paler coloured flowers with a perianth tube 8-15 mm long and bracts 7-12 mm long, easily separate it from the taller subsp. mucronata which has a tube 15-25 mm long, bracts 15-25 mm long, and broader, more softly textured leaves 7-15(-20) mm wide. The shorter B. mucronata subsp. minor is not likely to be confused with B. lineolata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With blue flowers with yellow markings on the lower tepals, Babiana lobata is recognised by the simple or dichotomously branched stem with flowers borne on the upper side of horizontal spikes, the lower tepals with auricular lobes at the bases of the limbs. The plants are hairless throughout and the floral bracts are short, 5-8 mm long, dry distally with the inner forked in the upper third. Somewhat unusual, the dry remains of past season’s leaves are twisted around the base of the stem. Babiana lobata has been associated with two related species, B. fimbriata and B. spiralis from central Namaqualand, both also with auriculate lobes on the lower lateral tepal limbs. Babiana fimbriata has leaves twisted distally, woolly-cobwebby cataphylls, and lightly hairy bracts 12-14 mm long, much exceeding those of B. lobata. The related B. spiralis has velvety hairy stems but smooth cataphylls and leaf sheaths, and bracts 8-10 mm long. The hairless habit, short floral bracts, and more-or-less divaricate branching suggest that B. tritonioides is most closely related to B. lobata. Centred in the Komaggas area of northwestern Namaqualand, B. tritonioides has short, relatively broad leaves, the blades borne at right angles to the sheaths and twisted or folded back on themselves in concertina fashion and is typically a shorter plant, 100-150 mm high.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Winter-flowering Babiana minuta remains poorly known and inadequately documented but is more widespread than originally believed and is even locally quite common. The reddish mauve to violet flowers are typical of the short-tubed species of sect. Teretifolieae and surprisingly large for the small leaves: a single open flower may be larger than the rest of the above ground parts of an individual. Plants grow in small tufts with adult, flowering individuals surrounded by the narrow juvenile leaves of young plants derived from cormlets produced from the base of mature corms.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the unusual, coarsely fibrous corm tunics that form a distinctive hard, cylindric collar around the stem base, Babiana montana has blue-mauve flowers with unequal filaments, the median one longer than the other two. In addition, the style branches have prominent orbicular tips, a character rare in the genus. The smooth ovary also stands out in sect. Babiana but this feature is shared with a few other species, including B. ambigua and B. fourcadei. Babiana montana can also be distinguished from B. ambigua by the thick collar of fibres about the underground part of the stem, a feature lacking in the latter, as well as the unequal stamens. Plants from limestone habitats west of Bredasdorp have smaller bracts than is usual, 12-14 mm long, and smaller flowers about 40 mm long, but have the unequal stamens typical of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although surprisingly common in the Richtersveld, Babiana namaquensis is seldom seen for it flowers early in the season, mostly in June or July, when little plant exploration is undertaken. Leaf morphology of B. namaquensis is unusually variable. Younger plants produce narrow leaves, twisted or coiled above, while mature plants have narrowly lanceolate leaves loosely twisted distally. The leaf morphology recalls that of B. torta, a similarly acaulescent species of central and southern Namaqualand that also has coiled to twisted leaves. In B. torta the leaves are usually densely hairy, while the slate-blue or rarely white flowers have a perianth tube 20-22 mm long, and the bracts are prominently veined and silky hairy or rarely sparsely velvety. In contrast, B. namaquensis has sparsely hairy to smooth leaves, consistently smooth bracts, and a pale mauve to white perianth with a tube 25-28 mm long. Babiana torta appears to be confined to granitic substrates, mostly growing in cracks in granite outcrops, and it flowers mainly in May or early June, whereas B. namaquensis favours limestone substrates and flowers somewhat later, in late June or July.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The moderate-sized blue, violet, or sometimes purple to pink flowers marked with white or pale yellow on the lower tepals of Babiana nana are a striking sight in spring along the coast of the Western Cape Province, and are rendered even more attractive at close range by their intense, rosy violet perfume. The species appears to have a combination of the most unspecialised characteristics of Babiana, including green floral bracts becoming dry at the tips, inner bracts forked only at the tips, and zygomorphic, bilabiate flowers. In addition, it is one of relatively few members of the sect. Teretifolieae that has an aerial (though short) stem that is often branched. The relatively short, funnel-shaped perianth tube and blue perianth are likewise ancestral features for the genus. A few other species of the section also have an aerial stem but appear specialised in their leaf morphology, notably B. pilosa and B. rubella.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by a combination of zygomorphic flowers with a moderately long, slender perianth tube 20-30 mm long, dark blue, usually arrow-shaped anthers (sometimes linear) and a densely hairy ovary. The flowers are pale blue to mauve, sometimes largely white, with the lower lateral tepals partly cream-coloured to yellow. The floral bracts range from 12-18 mm in plants from the west to up to 30 mm long in the east where it may possibly be confused with long-tubed but acaulescent B. sambucina (section Teretifolieae) but B. patersoniae always has the inner bracts divided to the base. In the west, B. patersoniae may be confused with B. purpurea, which also has dark anthers and inner bracts divided to the base but a pink to purple perianth, and longer tepals relative to the tube, which is narrow below and only wider in the upper third, whereas the tube of B. patersoniae has a wider diameter and is gradually flared in the upper half. Confusion is also possible with B. fourcadei, which also has bracts divided to the base, but a smooth ovary, and is often a more robust plant, usually bearing 3 to 5 short lateral branches. The intensely fragrant flowers of B. fourcadei have white lower lateral tepals edged distally in pale blue, long slender style branches not so obviously expanded at the tips, and a generally larger flower with the dorsal tepal 25-30 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The subspicate, usually long and dense racemes with pointed bracts and perianth-segments on sturdy peduncles are typical for the species, although the unequal stamen-whorls may vary.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: Flowering in June, soon after the first winter rains have fallen, Babiana pauciflora is recognised by the violet flowers with relatively long perianth tube, 35-45 mm long, smooth ovary and large green bracts, 35-55 mm long, with the inner forked apically. It lacks any obvious specialisations that would help determine its possible relationships. The perianth tube, about as long as or slightly longer than the dorsal tepal, suggesting a possible relationship with the yellow-flowered B. vanzijliae of the section. Also from the Bokkeveld Mtns and Plateau, B. vanzijliae blooms later, in August and September, whereas B. pauciflora blooms in June.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the narrow leaves with a long pseudopetiole and the light magenta-pink perianth, an unusual colour in the genus. Both the stem, leaves and floral bracts bear slightly retrorse hairs, also rare in the genus. The pink flower colour is known in a few other species, notably the densely hairy B. rubella, also from Namaqualand, which has short, relatively broad leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished among the species with truncate leaves by the slender perianth tube, ± 50 mm long, sharply bent below the apex, and the relatively narrow tepals 15-20 mm long and 5-7 mm wide. Although said by Lewis (1959) to occur from Garies southward to Mierenkasteel (near Nuwerus) in southern Namaqualand, B. pubescens has only been reliably reported from Komaggas, southwest of Springbok, and in the vicinity of Garies. Despite being increasingly threatened by overgrazing and especially the heavy stocking of goats, B. pubescens remains relatively common locally.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Babiana purpurea has pink or purple flowers that at first glance appear to be radially symmetric but the stamens are unilateral and erect and the anthers are parallel, facing the lower tepals, which usually have contrasting markings near the base. The dark blue to blackish anthers are arrow-shaped, suggesting a relationship with B. nervosa and B. villosa of sect. Babiana. Unlike these species, however, the anther connectives are not visibly expanded. The flowers are evidently adapted for pollination by large anthophorine bees that visit the flowers in search of nectar, quantities of which are secreted from septal nectaries into the base of the perianth tube. It can be distinguished from B. nervosa by the pink to red-purple perianth colour, perianth tube 18-28 mm long, and unusual style branches, broadly lobed at the tips and held above the anther apices. Babiana nervosa has white to creamy yellow or blue to blue-mauve flowers with creamy white markings on the lower lateral tepals, a perianth tube 10-18 mm long, and fairly short style branches up to 3 mm long, less prominently expanded at the tips, and usually dividing opposite the lower half to middle of the anthers. Although Lewis (1959) described the flowers of B. purpurea as sometimes having symmetrically disposed stamens, this condition is evidently rare and not representative of the species. Babiana purpurea is sometimes confused with a second species of clay soils in the southern Cape, B. patersoniae, which extends from Napier and Riviersonderend to Port Elizabeth and Alexandria in Eastern Cape. That species has flowers with a longer perianth tube, 20-30 mm long, lightly flared from the base and curved near the apex, a bluish or mauve to nearly white perianth, and a strong sweet fragrance with a strong clove component.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: G. fruticosus subsp. decipiens is easy to confuse with eastern populations of G. tomentosus but the presence of a falcate tooth on the upper margin of the corona lobe clearly argues for placement within G. fruticosus. Some material of G. tomentosus (e.g. Ngoni 501 & Leach & Noel 117, both from Botswana), show hints of a tooth, but this is never well developed. The follicle of subsp. decipiens is more abruptly tapered than in G. tomentosus.
bibliographicCitation: Goyder, DJ; Nicholas, A. 2001. A revision of Gomphocarpus R.Br. (Apocynaceae: Asclepiadaceae). Kew Bull. 56(4): 769-836. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/4119297] [All rights reserved]

description: The unusual flower of Babiana ringens, one of the most distinctive species in the genus, is adapted for sunbird pollination. Its specialisations include the red colour, stiff stamens and style, and elongate perianth tube with a wide throat. Apart from the flower itself, the most striking adaptation of Babiana ringens is the sterile main stem, which acts as a perch for visiting sunbirds. Closely related, but smaller-flowered B. avicularis, shares this feature but differs from B. ringens in the falcate leaves elliptic in section and in the smaller flowers with a perianth tube 16-21 mm long, with the narrow basal part 4 mm long and kinked at the apex and dorsal tepal 15-18 mm long vs. tube 22-45 mm long and dorsal tepal 18-50 mm long but mostly 20-45 mm in B. ringens. The two species are allied to B. hirsuta, which has similar red flowers with a channelled dorsal tepal enclosing the filaments and style, but a multi-branched stem, the main axis of which bears a typical spike of several flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is very closely allied to G. semilunatus and G. kaessneri, sharing the characteristic growth form of a principal upright stem and many side shoots rather than the more bushy habit of the G. fruticosus group. The G. physocarpus group also has similar preferences for seasonally flooded meadows. The species of this group can generally be distinguished by the form of the corona. The calyx of G. physocarpus is also much shorter than in G. semilunatus.
bibliographicCitation: Goyder, DJ; Nicholas, A. 2001. A revision of Gomphocarpus R.Br. (Apocynaceae: Asclepiadaceae). Kew Bull. 56(4): 769-836. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/4119297] [All rights reserved]

description: Babiana secunda is one of a handful of species of Babiana with inverted flowers, that is, with the spike inclined and the flowers facing upward, with the dorsal tepal and the unilateral stamens facing the spike apex. It can be distinguished by the smooth, dry, often torn floral bracts, the outer tricuspidate with a long central awn and hairless ovary, the latter unusual for sect. Babiana. Babiana secunda blooms unusually late in the season, usually in October or November. In the other species with inverted flowers, B. angustifolia, B. inclinata, and B. rubrocyanea, the ovary is densely hairy, the bracts remain partly green at flowering, are usually velvety and lack a pronounced awn although they do tend to be tricuspidate. The anthers and pollen are pale to deep blue or violet (or sometimes white) in B. angustifolia and B. inclinata, whereas the anthers and pollen of B. secunda are yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the most distinctive species of the genus, Babiana sinuata can be recognised immediately by the twisted and broadly undulate leaves with thickened, crisped margins and woolly to cobwebby cataphylls and leaf sheaths; the upper (adaxial) margins also bear fine long hairs. The moderate-sized, pale blue-mauve flowers have the upper tepals at first arching over the stamens but later becoming erect and the lower median tepal has a prominent violet central mark on a pale yellow background. Most remarkable, however, are the long, arched stamens with anthers joined together, a feature unique in the genus. The woolly cataphylls and crisped, undulate, and twisted leaves suggest a close relationship with B. striata, with which it has been confused. Flowering earlier in the year, B. striata is easy to distinguish by the more compact inflorescence of smaller flowers with the anthers parallel but not joined together, and the corm tunics of particularly coarse fibres.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Babiana torta flowers early in the season, mainly in late autumn, when little collecting is normally done. Plants are most often seen growing in cracks in granite outcrops with the narrow, coiled juvenile leaves mixed with the broader, less hairy leaves of mature individuals. Although plants usually have softly hairy leaves and bracts, the leaves may occasionally be almost smooth and the bracts sparsely hairy. Flowers are usually pale to mid-blue with white to pale yellow on the lower tepals, but may occasionally be white or even greenish mauve. Babiana torta appears to be related to a group of early winter-flowering, dwarf species of Namaqualand and the adjacent western Karoo, including B. crispa, B. minuta, B. namaquensis, and B. tanquana. These all have few-flowered spikes borne at ground level and variously undulate, twisted or crisped leaves. Among this group, B. torta may be most closely related to B. minuta, also a species of rock outcrops and shallow soils that occurs in the western Karoo and adjacent southern Namaqualand. Babiana torta may also be confused with B. namaquensis and their differences are discussed in detail under the latter species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The short floral bracts, 6-8 mm long, strongly inclined, secund spike and flowers with narrow tepals suggest that Babiana tritonioides is closely allied to the Richtersveld species, B. lobata, and the two seem somewhat isolated taxonomically within sect. Antholyzoides. The species is especially distinctive in the ± horizontal and distally twisted leaf blades, but the lower tepals have auriculate lobes above the base characteristic of the section. Based on morphology, B. lobata and B. tritonioides appear closely related and evidently represent a northern species pair of sect. Antholyzoides. The short leaves of B. tritonioides with relatively broad blades, mostly 40-60 x 6-10 mm, held nearly at right angles to the sheaths and twisted or folded back on themselves in concertina fashion, and short stature make the species easy to distinguish from the taller B. lobata, which has stems 120-250 mm high and erect, linear to narrowly sword-shaped leaves 2.5-4.0 mm wide, only lightly twisted in the upper half.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the creamy white to creamy pink flowers, usually flushed pink to red outside, with prominent red markings on the lower tepals, and the elongate perianth tube 65-105 mm long, usually expanded in the upper 8-20 mm in a wide gullet. It is often confused with white (or creamy white to pink)-flowered B. tubiflora, a widespread coastal species that typically has narrow, ± linear, pilose leaves, a similarly elongate perianth tube, mostly 60-80 mm long but slender throughout or only slightly expanded in the upper 5-7 mm; in addition, it has shorter filaments 13-16 mm long, a short style usually dividing opposite the base to middle of the anthers (sometimes exceeding the anther tips), and style branches 3-4 mm long. The larger flowers of B. tubulosa have filaments 20-22 mm long and style branches ± 6 mm long prominently displayed above the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The fairly small, yellow flowers, hairy ovary, and inner bracts divided almost to the base of Babiana unguiculata are consistent with sect. Babiana. In the type collection the narrow leaf blades are tightly pleated, appearing to be ribbed, but other collections have softer-textured leaves, only moderately pleated, densely short-hairy but long-hairy along the adaxial margins. The general appearance of the flowers and the short floral bracts recall B. auriculata and B. lineolata in particular but both have blue rather than pale yellow flowers. Flowers of B. unguiculata lack the auriculate lobes on the lower tepal limbs so characteristic of B. auriculata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the radially symmetric flowers with large black or purple, arrow-shaped anthers with a broad connective, widest in the lower third. The flowers range in colour from brilliant scarlet-red to dark purple or deep pink, with a moderately long, slender perianth tube, mostly 16-28 mm long but in some populations up to 36 mm, and an unusually short style, dividing opposite the anther bases. Scarlet-flowered plants are restricted to the upper Tulbagh Valley but elsewhere flowers are deep purple, or on the Paardeberg near Malmesbury to the west, are pink. The latter plants have the longest tube in the species, up to 30-36 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the radially symmetric flowers typically with a pale blue perianth and white throat, or rarely uniformly white (or mauve-pink), short stamens with filaments up to 6 mm long, and usually pale blue or mauve (rarely whitish) anthers held in the mouth of the tube that contrast with the white throat. The anthers are usually linear with parallel lobes but occasional populations have the connective slightly expanded below and the lobes slightly diverging.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An acaulescent species, Babiana virginea has densely hairy, lanceolate leaves exceeding the typically white but sometimes pale mauve flowers. The flowers are large, with a tube up to 65 mm long and dorsal tepal 35-40 mm long, and have a strong, clove-like fragrance suggesting moth pollination. Babiana virginea is perhaps most closely related to the widespread, blue-flowered B. sambucina, also acaulescent, and can be distinguished from that species by the leaf vestiture, usually almost smooth or sparsely scabrid. The lowermost outer floral bract in B. sambucina is produced upward as a small leaf, a feature sometimes weakly developed in B. virginea.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the fibrous spathe-like bract subtending the synflorescence, usually greyish and inconspicuous but sometimes with a long foliar tip, and the dense, globose inflorescence of 16 to 60 rhipidia characteristically grouped in fascicles of 2 to 6. The rhipidial bracts are grey or brown and much shorter than the straw-coloured inner spathe. The capsules are typically prominently rugose or tubercled but are smooth in populations from the Elandskloof Mtns in the south. Bobartia fasciculata is closely allied to Bobartia rufa, sharing with it a similar fibrous bract subtending the synflorescence and ± tubercled (or smooth) capsules, and remarkably narrow inner tepals, ± half as wide as the outer. The two species are sympatric on the Olifants River Mtns and are readily confused there. B. rufa is distinguished by its ± flat-topped, obconical synflorescence with attenuate, dark red outer rhipidial bracts closely overlapping and concealing the inner rhipidial spathe.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small, slender species up to 550 mm high but often less, typically with a solitary rhipidium (rarely two or three) on a slender, plane, linear or subterete stem up to 1.5 mm diam. The stems and leaves are faintly striate but lack fine, stomatiferous furrows. Larger plants with two or three rhipidia are difficult to separate from Bobartia gladiata, and the two species may hybridise.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although vegetatively similar to Ornithogalum thyrsoides in its small bulb with pale, membranous tunics and slender, suberect leaves clasping the stem at the base, O. ceresianum is distinguished by the large, dark olive central eye that covers the basal third of the tepals, the glossy black ovary, and by having all six filaments expanded and winged in the lower two thirds. The inner filaments are more broadly winged than the outer and in some individuals may be petaloid with a dark base. In O. thyrsoides the outer filaments are at most slightly expanded, the dark centre of the flower is much smaller, covering no more than the base of the tepals, and the ovary is ovoid and matt. In addition the racemes are typically longer, with the lower pedicels shorter in fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB. 2007. A revision of Ornithogalum subgenus Aspasia section Aspasia, the chincherinchees (Hyacinthaceae). Bothalia 37(2): 133-164. [CC BY]

description: The species is close to O. hispidum, but its small size, usually corymbose inflorescence and the peculiar acute angle of the peduncle below, separate it from this species. Possibly the flowers open at night, for the majority had the perianth more or less closed.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: Usually readily recognised by the linear, flattened stems and leaves and the compressed inflorescence, but some forms have subterete or rarely terete leaves and stems. The stems and leaves are striate but lacking fine, stomatiferous furrows. Although microscopic, this character is reliable for separating terete-stemmed forms of the species from other, superficially similar species. Smaller, more delicate forms with only 3 rhipidia are difficult to distinguish from Bobartia filiformis. Highly variable in size.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unique in the genus in the laxly branched stem and blue to blue-mauve flowers. The terete or subterete flowering stem, with conspicuously viscid or sticky patches below the nodes, is well differentiated from the plane leaves. The lowermost cauline leaf or spathe is inserted in the lower 1/3 of the flowering stem and is leaf-like, with a short unifacial blade. The only other species with a similar laxly branched stem with sticky internodes, Bobartia paniculata, has yellow flowers and a bract-like spathe inserted in the upper 1/3 of the stem at the top of a conspicuously elongated internode.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is curious that no one seems to have observed that the characteristic rusty red hairs occupying a large part of each loculus in the capsule develop from the capsule sutures and not from the seed. Watt (1907, pi. 51) even illustrates the seed ‘showing floss’. His illustration (same plate) of the seed '(floss removed)’ shows all the hair that actually grows from the seed coat.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, JB. 1947. Notes on the classification and distribution of genera related to Gossypium. New Phytol. 46(1): 123-141. [https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/j.1469-8137.1947.tb05075.x] [All rights reserved]

description: One of two species in the genus with the ovary included in the rhipidial spathes, and the capsules remaining concealed by the bracts, Bobartia macrospatha is distinguished from B. anceps by its terete or subterete leaves and stem, the mostly dry and fibrous bract subtending a relatively small synflorescence of up to 15 suberect rhipidia. The bract is ± expanded at the base and sheaths the relatively small inflorescence. The inner spathes of the suberect rhipidia are (13-)15-20 mm long. The capsules are ovoid and 8-10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small, slender species, 150-500 mm tall, with 2 to 7 rhipidia in a narrow, cylindric synflorescence ± completely enclosed by an erect, broad, fibrous, dark reddish or chestnut-brown subtending bract. The species resembles small forms of Bobartia macrospatha but is distinguished by the exserted ovary and capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ornithogalum dubium is defined by the firm-textured, dark brown to black bulb tunics, spreading, rather blunt leaves, seldom up to half as long as the infloresence and typically densely ciliate on the margin, and corymbose to subcorymbose raceme of white, yellow or orange flowers, usually with a dark centre. The filaments are at least partially concolorous with the tepals, often with a dark zone in the middle or upper part, and the dark-coloured ovary typically narrows into the style, which may be shorter than or subequal to the ovary. The seeds are minute, 0.5-1.0 mm long, and echinulate. Yellow- or orange-flowered plants with dark outer bulb tunics and ciliate leaves are readily assigned to Ornithogalum dubium but white-flowered individuals may pose some problems. The dark tunics, relatively short, spreading leaves and corymbose inflorescence serve to distinguish such plants from O. thyrsoides and O. strictum, which also have larger seeds, 1.5-2 mm long. O. pruinosum, from further north in Namaqualand, has similar dark tunics and small seeds but the leaves are distinctly glacous and usually glabrous or minutely puberulous on the margins. O. corticatum from the Roggeveld Escarpment is distinguished by its thick, almost corky bulb tunics, leaves that are distinctly pubescent on the upper surface near the ends, plain white tepals and filaments, and yellow ovary. On the Cape Peninsula, O. conicum is recognized by its large bulb and linear-filiform filaments and larger seeds. In the Eastern Cape, white-flowered O. dubium is distinguished from O. synanthifolium by its deciduous habit, shorter leaves with ciliate margins, subcorymbose inflorescence and much smaller seeds (0.5-1.0 mm vs 2-3 mm).
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB. 2007. A revision of Ornithogalum subgenus Aspasia section Aspasia, the chincherinchees (Hyacinthaceae). Bothalia 37(2): 133-164. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the obconical, ± flat-topped synflorescence partially sheathed by a pair of grey, fibrous spathe-like bracts, the rhipidia with conspicuous, acuminate, dark reddish brown bracts and lower rhipidial spathe not much shorter than the straw-coloured inner spathe and concealing it. The capsules are either smooth or tubercled. Bobartia rufa is clearly closely allied to B. fasciculata, sharing with it a similar fibrous spathe and ± tubercled capsules, and remarkably narrow inner tepals, ± half as wide as the outer. The two species are sympatric on the Olifants River Mtns and may be confused there. Bobartia fasciculata is distinguished by its globose inflorescence with more clearly fasciculate rhipidia with greyish or brown outer rhipidial spathes much shorter than the inner rhipidial spathes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished from the other species by the dwarf, compact habit and the narrow, linear, glabrous leaves. The flowers are smaller and, because of the short internodes, appear close together near the centre of the small cushions. The plants are inconspicuous and are easily overlooked except during their short flowering period in spring.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1964. Scrophulariaceae. Bothalia 8(2): 176-177. [https://doi.org/10.4102/abc.v40i2.210] [CC BY]

description: A unique species because of its xerophytic distichous leaves with fimbriate margins.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the globose corm, unlike the almost disk-like corm of its two congeners, the slender flower with small lateral and lower tepals, the green colour of the lower lateral tepals and the yellow underside of the tube, and the short style branches, ± 3 mm long. The strongly drooping apex of the spike, evident even after the lower flowers have opened, is also distinctive. The spike is usually straight before the first flower buds open in C. aethiopica and C. floribunda. Chasmanthe bicolor appears to be most closely related to the more robust C. floribunda, which has a particularly large corm, and larger, bright orange-scarlet flowers with style branches 7-10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowers open in the late afternoon and close during the night. The nectaries appear to be well developed. Young buds adopt a drooping position.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: With broad leaves ciliate on the margins and flowers on long pedicels much exceeding the bracts. The plants varied greatly in stature and in the number of flowers in an inflorescence; it seems that young plants flower readily.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM; Burtt, BL. 1988. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XV. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 45(2): 179-210. [CC BY-SA]

description: The tallest species in the genus, Crocosmia paniculata reaches well above 1 m sometimes almost 2 m tall and has broad, deeply pleated leaves and erect several-branched stems. The spikes arch outward, becoming almost horizontal so that the bright to dull orange or reddish flowers are displayed above the spike axes, forming two rows facing outward. The flowers have an elongate perianth tube 33-40 mm, narrowed in the lower portion, and large dorsal tepal 15-18 mm long, well exceeding the lateral and lowermost tepals, only 6-12 mm long. The flowers are pollinated by sunbirds. Plants from the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands, for example, near Hilton, Howick and Nottingham Road, have dark red flowers with a shorter perianth tube, only 26-28 mm long. They are seldom seen in truly wild situations but are either cultivated in gardens or found near abandoned dwellings, road verges and ditches. The first record of this form appears to have been collected at Pietermaritzburg in 1909, and it is possibly an old cultivar no longer available in the trade, although similar plants appear to be wild in the Karkloof.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The most characteristic feature is the funnel-shaped nectary, Some variation in the shape of the nectary is also observed in other regions. The nectary opening may be somewhat elongated and its margin may be irregularly incised, sometimes with a deep adaxial slit. In general appearance the species most closely resembles O. vulgare, though the morphology of the nectary region of the latter is very different.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1982. A monograph of the genus Ornithoglossum (Liliaceae). Opera Bot. 64: 5-51. [10.1111/j.1756-1051.1983.tb01058.x] [All rights reserved]

description: Crocosmia pottsii is distinguished by the small, funnel-shaped flowers with a perianth tube 14-20 mm long, and a dorsal tepal up to 15 mm long. The leaves are sword-shaped and plane, with a prominent main vein.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With a short perianth tube, ± 2.5 mm long but relatively long tepals, 11-13 mm long, Geissorhiza alticola appears to be allied to the G. hesperanthoides complex (including G. nubigena and G. umbrosa as well). It is similar to these species in general appearance and leaf morphology but has unbroken, papery rather than fibrous corm tunics. It can be distinguished from other high mountain species by its short, funnel-shaped perianth tube and fairly large blue-violet flower. Normally only the lowermost leaf is produced to any extent, while the two upper leaves sheath the stem for most or all of their length.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Diminutive, white-flowered Geissorhiza bolusii is unusual in the genus mainly in the several plane, more-or-less sword-shaped leaves usually prostrate or arching toward the ground, the several, small cauline, sheathing leaves, and the presence of two kinds of stems. Some produce no flowers but develop a cormlet in the axil of each flower bract, while others bear small white flowers but no capsules, and a cormlet later develops in place of each aborted bloom. Most populations comprise plants of both kinds, and it never reproduces by seed. Reproduction is exclusively by the small axillary cormlets. Geissorhiza bolusii is probably most closely related to G. ovalifolia, which grows in similar habitats and also has small, white flowers but usually has none or only one cauline leaf or bract and produces one or few cormlets in its leaf axils. Fruit development is evidently fairly rapid and immature capsules can be seen in some collections in which fading blooms are present at the tips of spikes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species belongs to Sect. Pluriovulatae Burret, Subsect. Apodogynae Burret, but illustrates the somewhat artificial nature of the two subsections Apodogynae and Podogynae Burret in that the species is really more closely related to G. caffra Meisn. of the Podogynae than to any species in the other subsection. In other words the androgynophore is not elongated above the node, but in all other respects the affinities of G. gracillima are with G. caffra. The presence or absence of the lower glabrous portion of the androgynophore, corresponding to the presence or absence of a nectariferous claw to the petal, is, usually at least, of no taxonomic significance in the genus Greiuia, since both forms are frequently found in the one species, as in G. monticola Sond. and G. microcarpa K. Schum. for example. There is no evidence, however, that this is so with the presence or absence of an extension above the lower portion of the androgynophore. The presence of the extension in Subsect. Podogynae and some spec’es of Sect. Greivia (=Sect. Oppositiflorae Burret) for instance seems to be a perfectly constant and reliable character. If this were not so a good deal of Burret’s classification of the genus would fall down. This being so there is no doubt that G. gracillima is a good species but that although it falls artificially in the Apodogynae it is nearer G. caffra than to G. carpinifolia Juss., G. holstii Burret or G. flavescens Juss. which are typical of the Apodogynae. This view is further reinforced by the fact that in G. gracillima the androgynophore is rounded at its apex, not shallowly cupular as in the specif just quoted.
bibliographicCitation: Wild, H. 1956. New and little known species from the Flora Zambesiaca area III. Bol. Soc. Brot. 30: 81-97. [All rights reserved]

description: The semi-aquatic Geissorhiza brehmii is recognised by the two or three leaves, all with terete, usually 4-grooved blades, the uppermost with an inflated and prominently ribbed sheath, a corm with imbricate tunics, and white to creamy yellow flowers, occasionally with a dark centre. The perianth tube is 5-9 mm long and the tepals 15-26 mm long. The leaf blades are typically slightly succulent and usually somewhat inflated and possibly hollow, and in most plants are terete but occasionally flattened and few-ribbed, these difficult to distinguish from narrow-leaved individuals of G. imbricata. Gessirohiza brehmii has been confused at times with G. hispidula and with G. geminata but both these species have corms with concentric tunics. Also an aquatic species, G. geminata has two to four, well-developed basal leaves, plane when dry but possibly terete when alive, with a slightly thickened and raised main vein but without thickened margins. Capsules of G. brehmii appear to be unusually small, globose in shape and ± 6 mm long. Although poorly documented, capsules of G. geminata are obovoid and longer, mostly ± 8 mm long in dry specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Seemingly a small shrub. The older branches are naked, with a rough, dark coloured bark. Leaves 3/4-1/8 inch long, 1/2 inch wide, roundish or elliptical, sided, unequally toothed; the veins prominent on the underside. Peduncles shorter than the leaves, scale of the petals and gynophore crowned with dense, white bristles; ovary similarly setose. Very unlike any other Cape species.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1860. Tiliaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Ranunculaceae to Connaraceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 1: 223-229. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15231#page/279/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the weak, inclined to trailing stem and inclined to horizontal spikes of up to 10 small white flowers with tepals just 8-10 mm long. The stems are hairless and the stamens unequal. It bears the closest resemblance to the widespread montane species, G. ramosa, the two having similar small flowers with short unequal stamens but G. ramosa is a ± erect plant with 2- to 4-branched stems, blue to mauve or purple flowers, and leaves with strongly thickened margins and midrib.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Related to G. monticola but has smaller leaves and fruits. The narrow bracts are 2-3-fid but are shed early and so are not present in fruiting specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Wild, H. 1984. Tiliaceae, Fl. S. Africa 21(1): 1-44. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209546#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A climbing shrub. Leaves much larger and broader than in any other S. African species, 2 1/2-3 1/2 inches long, 2-2 1/2 inches broad, minutely netted and (when dry) finely wrinkled on the upper surface, which is hispidulous in the younger, and smooth in the older leaves. Allied to G. Asiatica, and still more nearly to G. villosa, W. & A. but differing from both in its flowers, the character of pubescence, and rugulose reticulation of leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1860. Tiliaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Ranunculaceae to Connaraceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 1: 223-229. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15231#page/279/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by its low stature, up to 120 mm high, linear leaves with heavily thickened margins and midvein, minutely ciliate stems, and small white flowers with a perianth tube ± 1.5 mm long, tepals 6-7 mm long, and unequal stamens. The corm tunics are soft-textured and not firmly fixed in position but evidently imbricate.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small, delicate plant mostly 30-90 mm high, Geissorhiza delicatula has simple or 1- or rarely 2-branched, slender stems and small flowers, with tepals 7-12 mm long and a short perianth tube, 3-4 mm long, included in the bracts. It is apparently related to G. inconspicua and G. foliosa, both larger plants with larger flowers and spikes typically with at least 3 and up to 7 flowers. The plane leaves are soft-textured leaves and often prostrate or decumbent.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species was stated by its authors to be related to G. madandensis J.R. Drummond (= G. bicolor Juss.) which is in section Axillares Burret. Although the inflorescences are certainly not opposite the leaves, they are in fact somewhat extra-axillary and, what is much more important in this connection, the ovary and fruit are very deeply 4-lobed; it is better placed, therefore, in section Grewia (= section Upposuijiora Burret) tor the time being although it is obviously somewhat intermediate between the two sections.
bibliographicCitation: Wild, H. 1984. Tiliaceae, Fl. S. Africa 21(1): 1-44. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209546#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: It is one of the forms common in G. bicolor and G. monticola with the basal glabrous portion of its androgynophore lacking. Belongs to section Axillares.
bibliographicCitation: Wild, H. 1984. Tiliaceae, Fl. S. Africa 21(1): 1-44. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209546#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The large-flowered Geissorhiza erosa is vegetatively almost indistinguishable from G. inflexa, but the spikes usually have fewer flowers, usually 2 to 4, with larger tepals, 18-24 x 8-10 mm, and often broader leaves. Consistent with the larger flower, the anthers are 7-10 mm long and the outer bracts are 18-20 mm long vs. tepals 10-15(-17) x 5-7 mm and anthers 4-6 mm long in G. inflexa. Generally the bracts of G. inflexa are dry and brown at flowering but in G. erosa the bracts are often green, turning light brown with age. The tepals are brilliant scarlet in popoulations from the upper Tulbagh Valley but pink to almost white or purple elsewhere.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small-flowered species of sect. Ciliatae, Geissorhiza erubescens is recognised by the unusual collar of fibres around the stem base (at least in older individuals), strongly winged leaf margins, and relatively small flowers with tepals 8-12 mm long and equal stamens. The flowers are creamy white with the outer tepals bright red on the outside and the stem is ciliate-pubescent, less so in the upper half. It may be most closely allied to the smooth-stemmed southwestern Cape G. inflexa, or larger-flowered G. leipoldtii or G. nutans, the latter with unequal stamens and somewhat larger white flowers with tepals 14-16 mm long without the deep red markings on the reverse of the outer tepals characteristic of G. erubescens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the strikingly coloured flowers, dark blue with a deep red centre, and with broad, conspicuously hairy stigmas. The leaves are relatively broad and strongly multi-ribbed. Geissorhiza radians, which has similarly coloured flowers but with the red centre edged with a narrow white band, is immediately distinguished by its narrower leaves. Geissorhiza eurystigma was confused in the past with G. mathewsii and was treated for a time as G. eurystigma subsp. mathewsii. The latter has similar blue flowers with a red centre and broad style branches but differs in its much shorter perianth tube, only ± 2.5 mm long, and anthers held above the style branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the leaves with winged margins held at right angles to the blade but the main vein hardly raised, the leaf thus H-shaped in cross section, and by the large, cream-coloured to pink flowers with perianth tube 40-80 mm long, usually well exserted from the bracts, and narrowly obovate tepals, 26-35 x 4.5-6.0 mm. The stems are sometimes short and entirely sheathed by leaf bases. Geissorhiza tenella has a similar leaf morphology but usually smaller flowers with a perianth tube 20-40(-50) mm long and slightly shorter, narrower tepals 13-23 x 2.0-4.5 mm. Plants from the Bokkeveld Mtns stand out in having bracts rather shorter than elsewhere, 30-35 mm long and matching those of Geissorhiza confusa but the leaves in these populations are quite typical of G. exscapa. Populations from the Pakhuis Mtns and some from the Piketberg have the perianth tube shortly exserted from the bracts, giving the specimens an unusual appearance. Again, the leaves are typical of the species and there seems no reason to treat them as separate taxa. In the absence of leaves, however, these plants can barely be distinguished from G. confusa, in which the tube may occasionally be up to 50 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Flowers much smaller than in G. tenuifolium; the petals less than an inch long, bright yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1862. Rosaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Leguminosae to Loranthaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 2: 285-305. Lovell Reeve & Co. Ltd., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by its 5 to 7, characteristically short, lanceolate leaves, Geissorhiza foliosa has relatively large pink to purple flowers with tepals 13-17 mm long and a short perianth tube ± 5 mm long. It is perhaps most easily confused with G. inconspicua but this species has smaller, violet to purple or white flowers, with shorter tepals mostly 8-11 mm long and longer leaves reaching at least to the base of the spike.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the wetland habitat, white flowers, and corms with concentric tunics, Geissorhiza geminata also has an unusual branching pattern: when branched, the stem forks into two ± equal axes, thus in dichotomous fashion, the main stem then hardly different from the branch. Geissorhiza geminata is superficially similar to G. brehmii, which is also semi-aquatic and has fairly large white flowers, but G. brehmii has the imbricate corm tunics of subg. Geissorhiza and also differs in having terete leaves, whereas G. geminata has plane or possibly hollow terete leaves without visible or raised margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Near O. niveum Ait., but differs by the ciliate leaves, stouter peduncles, and the denser 8-16 flowered racemes.
bibliographicCitation: Fourcade, HG. 1932. Contributions to the flora of the Knysna and neighbouring divisions. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 21(1): 75-102. [All rights reserved]

description: Geissorhiza humilis is recognised by the relatively large, bright or pale yellow flowers with tepals 16-22 mm long, and three leaves, the blades with thickened margins and midribs, thus narrowly 2-grooved on each surface. Both the leaves and the floral bracts are sticky and usually have grains of sand adhering to them. Populations on the Cape Peninsula always have bright, golden yellow flowers but elsewhere the species may have pale yellow flowers, with or without a green or dark tube. Geissorhiza humilis and the related but smaller flowered G. hispidula grow together at several sites on the Cape Peninsula, and often flower at the same time, when it is clear that they are quite different species although vegetatively they are almost identical. Not surprisingly, they have often been confused and their taxonomic history is intertwined. Geissorhiza hispidula can be distinguished by the smaller, creamy white flowers with short perianth tube 3-4 mm long and tepals 10-15 mm long, the outer marked red on the reverse, and spikes usually with 2 to 5 flowers, often fewer than in G. humilis. Geissorhiza darlingensis, restricted to the Darling area to the north of Cape Town, is closely allied to G. humilis and also vegetatively almost identical but has somewhat larger flowers with tepals 23-26 mm long, a tube 9-11 mm long vs. 5-8 mm in G. humilis, and longer filaments 8-9 mm long. The flowers also have a conspicuous dark centre.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The long-lived leaves (persisting for over two years), are almost black in colour and are semi-terete in section with a narrow groove along the upper surface and weak longitudinal ribs on the abaxial surface, occasional, scattered white trichomes are found throughout. The entire leaf surface is rugose with ± parallel, undulating, transverse grooves within which fine sand particles are held firmly, giving the leaf a dry, dusty appearance, not easily removed even with washing.
bibliographicCitation: Dold, AP; Hammer, SA. 2003. Hyacinthaceae: A new species of Ornithogalum from Eastern Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 33(1): 112-115. [CC BY]

description: Ornithogalum rupestre is one of the most recognizable species in the section, identified by the few to many, subterete, glabrous leaves. It is typically less than 100 mm high, with pure yellow or orange flowers with linear to lanceolate filaments and a very short style. O. rupestre shares glabrous leaves, mostly yellow or orange flowers with a rudimentary style, and minute, rugulose seeds with O. maculatum. The flowers of O. rupestre are typically bright yellow or orange but populations from Langebaan and the Cold Bokkeveld have pale yellow flowers, and plants with cream-coloured flowers have been collected around Pakhuis Pass. The flowers of populations from the Vredenburg Peninsula are uniformly white or pinkish.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB. 2007. A revision of Ornithogalum subgenus Aspasia section Aspasia, the chincherinchees (Hyacinthaceae). Bothalia 37(2): 133-164. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished mainly by the ribbed leaves, the uppermost with an inflated, ribbed sheath and actinomorphic flowers, usually white to creamy white but occasionally yellow and in some populations with a dark centre. Shorter-tubed populations are regarded as subsp. imbricata and those with longer tubes are segregated as subsp. bicolor.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza inaequalis is evidently closely related to common and widespread Western Cape species G. aspera, and they can be difficult to distinguish when dry. Both have a similar habit, flat, sword-shaped leaves and minutely velvety stems. Geissorhiza aspera typically has deep blue-violet, less often white or purple flowers, and at flowering time the upper parts of the floral bracts are often dry and rusty brown. The stamens are only slightly unequal or nearly equal, whereas G. inaequalis has larger, pale purple flowers, and green or pale, membranous bracts at flowering time, the brown colouration developing only after the flowers fade. It also has one filament about half as long as the others and even one anther may be slightly shorter than the other two. Geissorhiza inaequalis may also be confused with G. heterostyla, which is similar in habit and has one short filament. The latter, however, has leaves that are ciliate along the raised margins and main vein, and a short, dry scale-like bract in the upper part of the stem. Dry material must be examined carefully to avoid misidentification.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by its long style, which exceeds the ovary in length and the softer and longer cilia forming an untidy leaf border.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza inconspicua can usually be distinguished by its 3 to 5 comparatively short leaves clustered at the base of the plant and typically well-branched stems with several-flowered spikes held well above the leaves. Flowers are either white or violet to purple. It is sometimes difficult to separate from the Langeberg species, G. foliosa, but this species has shorter and often relatively broad leaves in contrast to the longer, narrowly sword-shaped to linear leaves of G. inconspicua, and larger flowers with tepals 13-17 mm long and anthers 4-6 mm long vs. tepals mostly 8-11 mm long (rarely up to 15 mm) and anthers 3-4 mm long in G. inconspicua.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the relatively small, creamy white flowers, often lightly flushed pink to red outside, inflexed stem, and narrowly sword-shaped leaves with raised and narrowly winged margins. The flowers have tepals mostly 10-15 mm long but exceptionally up to 18 mm in populations on the Cape Peninsula and nearby, and stamens with the anthers 4-6 mm long. The edges of the marginal wings, the main vein and sometimes secondary veins are ciliate to obviously hairy but the stem is quite smooth. Geissorhiza inflexa is closely allied to G. erosa and the two species have at times been united. The latter has larger, pink, red, purple or sometimes white flowers with tepals 18-24 x 8-10 mm, longer anthers 7-8 mm long, and usually broader leaves 5-10 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Evidently allied to Geissorhiza leipoldtii and sharing with it a papillate to ciliate stem and three leaves, the lower two basal and the upper cauline and largely sheathing, G. ixioides is recognised by its mauve-pink flowers with a dark purple centre, relatively short, equal filaments, and short, purple style dividing opposite the middle third of the anthers. Geissorhiza leipoldtii has larger, pure white flowers with longer stamens with equal filaments 7-8 mm long and anthers 6.5-8.0 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its deep blue flowers, paler in the throat, with an elongate perianth tube, 18-25 mm long, shortly exceeding the long floral bracts. The style is relatively short, dividing opposite the lower third of the anthers. The stem and leaves have a heavy, almost velvety, pale pubescence. Both G. namaquensis and G. namaquamontana are vegetatively similar, with puberulous stems and leaves with raised and winged margins, but their flowers are paler blue to blue-mauve, with a shorter perianth tube only 6-11 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in having half nodding flowers solitary on stems or branches, of which up to four may be produced on each plant. The glossy violet-purple flowers are large and attractive and unusual in being zygomorphic with unilateral, declinate stamens, while the tepals are subequal and symmetrically arranged. Plants have four to six narrow, linear leaves inserted at the base, up to 1.8 mm wide. Geissorhiza karooica appears to be allied to two western Karoo species, G. corrugata and G. spiralis, which have radially symmetric flowers also borne singly on each branch but with spirally coiled leaves, and are also distinctive in having the style dividing near the anther bases into unusually long branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the hard woody corm tunics, and large, violet-purple flowers with tepals 15-20 mm long and relatively short perianth tube 7-8 mm long. The anthers are yellow. Plants typically have three leaves, the lower two basal and with linear blades with the margins and main veins heavily thickened.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other Ornithogalum species by its grey-white epigeal bulbs bearing a rosette of dense linear-lanceolate green leaves with 6 rows of marginal cilia. Another unique feature is the ovary which is distinctly tuberculate in the upper part.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 1994. Ornithogalum sardienii, a new dwarf succulent bulb from the Little Karoo. Bradleya 12: 33-35. [All rights reserved]

description: Geissorhiza mathewsii has been confused in the past with G. eurystigma, both of them with similarly coloured deep blue flowers with a red centre and broad style branches, and multi-ribbed leaves, but the structure of the flowers is quite different. Those of G. mathewsii have a short perianth tube 2-3 mm long, and anthers articulated on the filaments so that they lie almost horizontally and are held above the broad flat style branches. Geissorhiza eurystigma has flowers with a perianth tube 6-9 mm long and a long style with the broad style branches held above upright anthers. The style branches of G. eurystigma are conspicuously hairy, whereas those of G. mathewsii are evidently smooth, at least to the naked eye. The distinctive flower colouring of G. eurystigma is also found in G. radians, but that species is easily distinguished by the pitted markings on the tepals, narrower leaves up to 1.5 mm wide with 2-grooved blades, and a longer perianth tube 6-8 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The dwarf Geissorhiza minuta stands up to 120 mm high although is more often shorter than that. The white flowers are among the smallest in the genus, with a perianth tube ± 1 mm long and tepals 7-8 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Hitherto specimens of this species have been identified as Maytenus heterophylla s. l. but it differs in having thick leathery leaves with indurate margins, stamens in male flowers and style in female flowers protruding well beyond the petals, rather than being slightly shorter than the petals, and trilocular capsules with a verrucose rather than a rugose, smooth or ridged surface. G. arenicola is a gnarled shrub or small tree with a specific habitat preference, namely coastal sand dunes. The leaves have a yellow midrib which is prominent below in dry specimens. The verrucose surface of the red capsules is unique among species of Gymnosporia.
bibliographicCitation: Jordaan, M; Van Wyk, AE. 1999. Systematic studies in subfamily Celastroideae (Celastraceae) in southern Africa: Two new species of Gymnosporia from the Maputaland Centre of Endemism. S. African J. Bot. 65(5&6): 315-320. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1999); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: A dwarf species, Geissorhiza nana rarely reaches up to 80 mm high and has tiny creamy white flowers with a perianth tube 1.0-2.5 mm long and spreading tepals 3-6(-8) mm long. It is closely allied to and easily confused with G. bracteata, which has somewhat larger flowers with a perianth tube 2.5-5.0 mm long and tepals 8-12 mm long, rarely smaller. Geissorhiza setacea is very similar in general appearance to G. nana but is larger in all features, having flowers with a tube ± 6 mm long and tepals mostly 8-12 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In the herbarium and in the field G. devenishii can easily be confused with a sympatric species, G. mossambicensis (Klotzsch) Loes. (=Maytenus mossambicensis). They resemble each other superficially in habit and leaf characters, but their fruits are quite different. G. mossambicensis has semi-fleshy, round, smooth capsules which dehisce completely, the valves becoming reflexed and the inside turning purplish. The new species has prominently sulcate, coriaceous fruits which dehisce incompletely. This is the only known species of Gymnosporia with distinctly sulcate fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Jordaan, M; Van Wyk, AE. 2000. Systematic studies in subfamily Celastroideae (Celastraceae) in southern Africa: Two new species of Gymnosporia from KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape. S. African J. Bot. 66(1): 10-14. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2000); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Unusual in flowering in the summer, Geissorhiza nubigena is distinguished by the fibrous corm tunics, rose-pink flowers with a relatively long perianth tube, typically 12-18 mm long, exserted from the bracts when fully open. The flowers are held nearly horizontally, thus almost nodding with the tepals spreading at right angles to the tube. It is allied to the vegetatively similar G. hesperanthoides, which has violet to blue-purple flowers held upright with somewhat cupped tepals and a shorter perianth tube 5-8(-10) mm long. Both species have corms with fibrous tunics, and three leaves, the lowermost of which is longest, and blades with heavily thickened margins and main vein.
