bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small plant, Geissorhiza parva is recognised by the creamy white to pale yellow flowers with a perianth tube 3-4 mm long, tepals 6-8 mm long and by the three or four, short, inclined to prostrate leaves mostly up to 20 mm long (but occasionally up to 45 mm). Populations occurring north of the Hex River Mtns can often be distinguished by having four leaves, in contrast to the southern populations, which normally have only three, but the difference is not without exception. Some northern populations of G. parva can be difficult to distinguish from the related G. ovalifolia, but this species has white flowers, softer-textured leaves and usually an axillary cormlet in one or more of the lower leaf axils. Hybrids have been recorded between G. parva and the taller and larger-flowered G. ovata near Caledon, and are intermediate between the two species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This poorly known taxon comes closest to O. undulatum, which it resembles in the undulate leaves (although this is not a constant feature of O. undulatum), in having relatively long filaments and a laxly corymbose inflorescence, and in its flowering time. The most obvious distinguishing character is afforded by the narrow, greenish-coloured tepals. Furthermore, the flowers are borne higher above the leaves and the filaments usually have a distinct hump-like swelling below the middle.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1982. A monograph of the genus Ornithoglossum (Liliaceae). Opera Bot. 64: 5-51. [10.1111/j.1756-1051.1983.tb01058.x] [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the hard, woody, concentric corm tunics, three narrow leaves, the lower two with thickened margins and main vein, and ciliate edges, and light to dark purple flowers borne on an inclined, flexuose spike. The leaves are ± oblong in cross section with two broad channels on each surface between the margins and main vein. It is perhaps most closely related to G. juncea, but that species has somewhat smaller, white to yellow flowers and terete leaves. Plants from well-drained, stony, south-trending slopes of the Piketberg appear to belong here but are unusual in having broader leaves, up to 5 mm wide, and flowers with a somewhat longer perianth tube, ± 6 mm long, compared to populations to the south and west, which have leaves only 2-3 mm wide and a perianth tube 3-4 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This variety may form a separate species intermediate between G. angularis and G. nemorosa. The material available is insufficient to warrant a new species being formed on it, and it appears wiser to retain this as a variety of G. angularis as the inflorescence is very similar, until more complete material has been seen.
bibliographicCitation: Davison, JD. 1927. Celastraceae R.Br. Bothalia 2(1-3): 289-346. [CC BY]

description: Relatively rare today, Geissorhiza purpureolutea has ribbed leaves with the uppermost leaf cauline and largest, and relatively small, pale to deep yellow flowers with a dark brown to purple centre. The perianth tube is 2-4 mm long and the tepals mostly 10-17 mm long. It is closely related to G. imbricata and almost identical with that species vegetatively but G. imbricata has larger flowers with a perianth tube 2-8 mm long and white to pale yellow tepals only occasionally with a dark centre.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although its general morphology suggests a close affinity with the widespread Gymnosporia buxifolia, G. macrocarpa can easily be distinguished by its larger, rugose, woody capsules (12-15 mm long), well-developed brachyblasts up to 20 mm long, and restricted geographical distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Jordaan, M; Van Wyk, AE. 2000. Systematic studies in subfamily Celastroideae (Celastraceae) in southern Africa: Two new species of Gymnosporia from KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape. S. African J. Bot. 66(1): 10-14. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2000); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: G. markwardii is a rhizomatous geoxylic suffrutex, sometimes without spines, leaves are glaucous and discolorous; flowers have exserted stigmas and anthers. The taxonomic affinities of this species are uncertain. Macromorphological characters such as the mostly alternate rather than fasciculate leaf arrangement, discolorous glaucous leaves, bilocular ovaries, dark red or purplish capsules and seed with a white aril, suggest a relationship with G. senegalensis (Lam.) Loes. On the other hand, certain leaf anatomical characters, such as the presence of a hypodermis rather than a multiseriate epidermis, show affinity with species in the G. buxifolia group (the former Maytenus heterophylla complex).
bibliographicCitation: Jordaan, M; Van Wyk, AE. 1999. Systematic studies in subfamily Celastroideae (Celastraceae) in southern Africa: Two new species of Gymnosporia from the Maputaland Centre of Endemism. S. African J. Bot. 65(5&6): 315-320. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1999); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the concentric corm tunics, zygomorphic flowers with vertically oriented tepals and unilateral, declinate stamens, Geissorhiza roseoalba has relatively large white to pink-flushed tepals, the lower with pink to red markings near the base. At one stage included in the genus Engysiphon, now sect. Engysiphon, G. roseoalba differs markedly from the other species of that section in having three to five fairly soft-textured leaves with a plane blade in contrast to the one to two firm leaves with heavily thickened and viscid margins of species of sect. Engysiphon.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: G. mossambicensis is a distinct species, quite different from G. harveyana with which it has been considered conspecific for more than 30 years. It lacks the conspicuous thread-like stipules of G. harveyana and has lax inflorescences usually much longer than the leaves, and grows at lower altitudes in hot, mixed woodland or thicket. G. harveyana has much shorter inflorescences and is a species of temperate Afromontane Forest.
bibliographicCitation: Jordaan, M; Van Wyk, AE. 2003. A taxonomic revision of the Gymnosporia mossambicensis group (Celastraceae: Celastroideae). Kew Bull. 58(4): 833-866. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4111200] [All rights reserved]

description: Geissorhiza rupicola stands out in the genus in its unusually long perianth tube, 16-23 mm long, slightly longer than the tepals. A tube of this length is also known in G. grandiflora but this species has longer tepals and unequal stamens with one filament shorter than the other two. The soft, papery corm tunics becoming torn into narrow vertical strips, ultimately almost fibrous, and accumulating with cataphylls as a fibrous collar around base are also distinctive for G. rupicola, the relationships of which are uncertain.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza scopulosa superficially resembles G. ramosa in the small, short-tubed flowers and general appearance but is a smaller plant with ciliate-papillose stems and is rarely branched, whereas G. ramosa has smooth stems and is almost invariably branched, sometimes with up to three or four branches. Geissorhiza scopulosa is vegetatively more like the small-flowered species of sect. Ciliatae, in which most species also have ciliate-papillose to puberulous stems. The leaves of G. scopulosa have the margins raised into broad wings but the main vein hardly thickened, the blade thus H-shaped in section, a feature also consistent with several species of the sect. Ciliatae.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A dwarf species 40-80 mm tall, Geissorhiza setacea is most easily recognised by its fairly large, relatively long-tubed flowers usually borne singly on short stems. The flowers are usually white and have a perianth tube ± 6 mm long and tepals 8-12 mm long. Also short in stature, G. nana has similar but smaller flowers with a perianth tube 1.0-2.5 mm long and tepals 3-6(-8) mm long. Although usually white-flowered, populations of G. setacea have pale yellow flowers with a blackish centre in the north of its range at Elandsberg Nature Reserve near Gouda.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With blackish imbricate corm tunics regularly notched below into blunt triangular segments, Geissorhiza silenoides is a typical member of subg. Geissorhiza, in which it stands out in the scabrid-puberulous stems, short leaves with heavily thickened margins and midribs, thus with two narrow grooves on each surface, and distinctive, pale pink flowers with long perianth tube, 15-17 mm long, and unequal stamens, each filament being of a different length.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza subrigida stands out in its comparatively large blue to violet flowers, strongly ciliate-pubescent leaves, and a divaricate branching pattern. It is closely allied to the more widespread G. divaricata, which is similar in vegetative morphology, also with a divaricate branching pattern, but has smaller, white to pale mauve flowers. The leaves of G. subrigida and G. divaricata, with raised and flattened margins and the raised and winged midrib, both ciliate on their edges, are similar to several other species of sect. Ciliatae, in which the two species stand out in their divaricate branching, the presence of a bract-like scale on the stem, and equal stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Evidently somewhat isolated taxonomically, Geissorhiza sulphurascens has relatively small, creamy white to almost yellow flowers borne on relatively crowded spikes, the perianth tube 3-4 mm long and tepals 13-18 mm long. The leaves are linear with thickened margins and main vein, thus 2-grooved on each surface. The uppermost of the three leaves is usually largest and sheaths the lower 2-3 of the stem, the sheath somewhat inflated and several ribbed as are the upper leaves of all members of sect. Geissorhiza.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the white or pale pink flowers with unusually narrow tepals 13-23 x 2.0-4.5 mm, Geissorhiza tenella has a perianth tube remarkably variable in length, mostly 30-40 mm long but as short as 20 mm and occasionally as long as 50 mm. The leaf blades are H-shaped in cross section with the margins raised into broad wings held at right angles to the blade. It is allied to the long-tubed Atlantic Coast species G. exscapa and to the Cape Peninsula endemic G. bonaspei, with which it shares the distinctive leaf with winged margins and H-shaped in cross section. Geissorhiza bonaspei has slightly larger, deep pink flowers with relatively broad tepals mostly 24-27 x 5-7 mm. Flower size is unusually variable in G. tenella. Plants from the east of its range, in the Caledon and Bredasdorp Districts as far east as Still Bay (as well as some from the Cape Flats), have a relatively short perianth tube, some 24-30 mm long and tepals 12-15 mm long. In contrast, most populations from the Cape Flats and along the Atlantic Coast usually have much larger flowers with a perianth tube 40-50 mm long and tepals up to 23 mm long. Such specimens approach G. exscapa in their flower size and this is probably related to their pollination biology.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the branched stems, each branch bearing just a single flower, a small corm with soft corm tunics and plane, trailing leaves. The pink flowers are zygomorphic and have a short perianth tube 9-13 mm long and subequal tepals 20-22 mm long. The single-flowered branches and unilateral declinate stamens recall G. fourcadei, but this has a longer perianth tube, (8-)17-20 mm long, xeromorphic, terete, 4-grooved leaves and larger corms with persistent firm-papery corm tunics.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An inconspicuous species, Geissorhiza umbrosa has small, white flowers with a perianth tube up to 4 mm long and tepals 10-13 mm long. The ± linear leaves have thickened margins and main vein and are 2-grooved on each surface, and the corm tunics range from soft and papery to fibrous. Its relationships are obscure.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The aerenchymatous tissues of the bulb tunics are very typical for the species. They no doubt are able to absorb moisture. In plants from the northern areas the leaf tuft may be present at flowering time, although apparently on the verge of withering.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: Devia xeromorpha is recognised by the several, linear leaves dry at flowering time and a slender spike of small, relatively inconspicuous, dusty pink flowers. Plants are moderate in size, 500-700 mm high, and form dense tussocks resembling associated clump-forming grasses. The flowers are radially symmetric except that the style is twisted to lie off-centre while the stamens are rotated anticlockwise, a feature unknown elsewhere in the family. The leaves are unusual in having a pair of narrow longitudinal grooves on each surface, and the margins have columnar epidermal cells with thickened walls. The subglobose capsules are lightly warty and each locule usually contains two rounded to lightly angled seeds which have the ovular vascular trace excluded.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The bulb is usually poorly developed as a result of the moist habitat.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: A clump-forming species with pendulous spikes of magenta-pink flowers, characteristic bracts with 6 to 9 lateral veins each side of the main vein and with the intermediate veins strongly developed, the veins all coalescing toward the base into solid tissue. The primary spike has 7 to 11 flowers. Dierama dracomontanum has the veins well-spaced with thinner tissue between them, and mostly fewer flowers in the main spike, 4 to 7, with a shorter perianth tube 5-7 mm vs. 6-10 mm long. Occasional hybrids between the two species are known from the Zuurberg and Ngeli Mtns where they co-occur.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Seeds densely prickly; inner filaments with pointed expansions; plants flowering in midsummer; Peninsula and vicinity.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1978. Ornithogalum: A revision of the southern African species. Bothalia 12(3): 323-376. [CC BY]

description: Occurring as solitary stems or small tufts with rather blunt, pure white bracts, rarely with a few flecks, and bell-shaped, mostly white or ivory-coloured (rarely mauve-pink) flowers with a perianth 18-30(-35) mm long. Populations from lower elevations up to ± 900 m have smaller flowers, the perianth mostly 18-25 mm long with tube 4-6(-7) mm long, and those at higher elevations larger flowers, the perianth mostly 25-35 mm long with a longer tube ± 7-12 mm long. Dierama pallidum from between Pietermaritzburg and Durban, also with creamy white to pale yellow flowers sometimes tinged pinkish, has acuminate bracts and smaller, more closed flowers, 15-18 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Endemic to Eastern Cape, occurring as solitary stems or small tufts, 750-1250 mm tall, with moderately sized, dark maroon to purple-black (rarely light purple) flowers, the perianth 21-32 mm long, and bracts flecked all over and appearing pale brown to the eye.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A clump-forming species with pendulous (or rarely suberect) spikes of moderate-sized, mostly rose-coral-pink flowers with perianth 19-25(-29) mm long, the primary spike with 4 to 7 flowers. Dierama dissimile has the stems solitary or a few in small tufts, narrower leaves mostly 2.0-3.5 mm wide and smaller flowers with perianth 18-22 mm long, and flowers mainly August to October. Dierama floriferum has the clumped habit of D. dracomontanum but mostly smaller flowers with perianth 15.5-20.5 mm long, and 4 to 9 lateral spikes per stem with 4 to 9 flowers each.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Occurring as solitary stems with white or lightly flecked bracts, and remarkable for its very small, dark purple-red flowers often shorter than the bracts, the perianth 14-18 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A clump-forming species with stems more than 1.5 m tall, leaves 6-12 mm wide, and erect spikes with partly solid bracts. The flowers are subrotate with a well-marked red and yellow eye at the base of each tepal. Dierama insigne, also with partly solid bracts, has the stems solitary or a few in small tufts, narrower leaves 2-6 mm wide, and pendulous spikes with fewer laterals, mostly 2 to 4.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A solitary or tufted species with stems 450-1350 mm tall and pendulous spikes of moderately-sized pink flowers with perianth 16-31(-34) mm long and tube 5-8(-9) mm long. Dierama pendulum has broader bracts, 8-13 mm wide and generally larger flowers with perianth tube 9-13 mm long and longer anthers 8-9 mm long. The two species co-occur at Grahamstown. Dierama igneum is also sympatric with D. pulcherrimum, which is distinguished by its mostly larger, bell-shaped perianth 35-54 mm long, and the two species appear to hybridise in the Amatole Mtns.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A clump-forming species with pendulous spikes of moderately large, widely funnel-shaped, pale lilac flowers with perianth 25-28 mm long and broad tepals 8-12 mm wide. Dierama dracomontanum has slightly smaller, pink to almost red flowers with perianth 19-25 mm long and tepals 5-8 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Pauridia longituba is distinguished by an elongated perigone tube, at least three times longer than the tepals, and the virtual absence of a pedicel which contributes to its pronounced dwarfed habit. Both P. longituba and P. minuta occur on the Witteklip, a massive granite dome on the outskirts of Vredenburg where they superficially resemble one another. Plants of the two species, nevertheless, differ consistently in both pedicel and perigone tube length. Since the pedicel in P. longituba is either entirely lacking or extremely short (up to 2 mm), the flowers are only partially exserted above ground, mainly due to the presence of an elongated perigone tube. Conversely, the flowers in P. minuta are short-tubed and each is held aloft by a well-developed pedicel. Subtle differences in floral fragrances also separate the two species in this area. P. longituba has an unpleasant, acrid odour, whereas the scent in P. minuta is faint but sweet. Despite the distinctly long perigone tube, the various insects seen visiting the flowers of P. longituba are all short-tongued, mainly muscid flies, which apparently feed on the minute amounts of exudate that collects on the downwardly hooked style lobes within the perigone throat.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 2014. A taxonomic revision of the genus Pauridia (Hypoxidaceae) in southern Africa. Phytotaxa 182(1): 1-114. [All rights reserved]

description: Occurring as solitary stems or small tufts with large, translucent bracts, 24-32 mm long, and 3- to 6-flowered spikes of large, rather closed, white to creamy yellow flowers, the perianth 30-50 mm long with the anthers and style deeply included. Dierama argyreum has mostly 6- to 9-flowered spikes of smaller, widely flared flowers with perianth 18-30(-35) mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A dainty species 300-750 mm tall with leaves 1-4 mm wide and short, dense spikes of small, mauve to magenta flowers, the perianth 13-18(-20) mm long. The short bracts, (10-)14-16 mm long, are lightly to densely flecked but always with whitish margins. Dierama floriferum differs in its clumped habit and more numerous coflorescences (mostly 4 to 9 vs. 2 or 3).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Endemic to Mpumalanga and Eswatini, occurring as solitary plants or small tufts up to 1500 mm tall, with relatively small, magenta-pink to deep wine-red flowers, the perianth 16-20 mm long, and lateral spikes borne on strikingly long peduncles, usually 90-230 mm long. The bracts have 4 or 5 veins each side of the main vein. Dierama pictum has similar flowers but the plants are mostly shorter, usually barely up to 1000 mm tall, with shorter peduncles 60-125 mm long, and dark brown bracts with sharply contrasting white shoulders and 6 to 8 veins each side of the main vein. The two species may hybridise in Eswatini.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A solitary-stemmed or tufted species, 800-1000 mm tall, with diagnostic obovate bracts, 12-18 x 5-9 mm, solidly to heavily flecked brown and with 6 to 8 lateral veins each side of the main vein. Dierama pictum, which flowers from November to February, has similar bracts with more sharply contrasting white shoulders, and slightly smaller flowers with a perianth 15-23 mm long (vs. 20-29 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Occurring as solitary stems or small tufts with acuminate, pure white bracts, and small, rather closed, creamy white to pale yellow (rarely tinged pink or mauve) flowers, the perianth 14-18 mm long. Dierama sertum from northern coastal KwaZulu-Natal has similar flowers but bracts well flecked in the lower part and along the midline. Dierama argyreum, also with white bracts, has larger, bell-shaped white or ivory-coloured flowers, and the perianth 18-35 mm long with flaring tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Occurring either as solitary plants or small tufts, the stems rarely more than 1000 m tall, with relatively small, pale to magenta-pink or deep wine-red flowers, the perianth 15-23 mm long, with characteristic bracts, with dark brown base and sharply contrasting white shoulders, rather closely veined with 6 to 8 lateral veins each side of the main vein. The species may hybridise with Dierama mobile in Eswatini.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Occurring as solitary stems or up to three in small tufts, with pure white or lightly flecked bracts appearing silvery white, and dark wine-red flowers with perianth 17-30 mm long. Dierama dubium has much smaller flowers usually shorter than the bracts, the perianth 14-18 mm long. Purple-flowered forms of D. latifolium are distinguished by the markedly clumped habit and often broader leaves, 5-15 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A solitary-stemmed or tufted species with pendulous spikes of moderately sized, creamy white to pale pink flowers, the perianth (24-)26-35 mm long with a tube (7-)8-12(-13) mm long. Dierama latifolium from lower elevations forms large clumps and usually has silvery white bracts. Dierama cooperi is distinguished by its closely veined bracts and mostly smaller, often bright pink flowers but probably hybridises with D. robustum in northern Lesotho and eastern Free State.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small, early-flowering species with foliage leaves produced on a separate shoot alongside the flowering stem and often not fully formed at flowering, and flowers with spreading tepals three times as long as the perianth tube. The small, 3-toothed bracts, 6-14 mm long, are also diagnostic. Dierama trichorhizum is unique in the genus in the well-developed basal internode between the corm and the lowest cauline leaf on the flowering stem, and in producing cormlets in the lowest leaf axil. Dierama nixonianum has a similar habit, producing the foliage leaves on a shoot alongside the flowering stem, but lacks the pronounced basal internode and axillary cormlets, and has rather more closed flowers with tepals only twice as long as the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A clump-forming species with erect spikes of pale to deep pink flowers with perianth 19-23 mm long, and translucent, lightly flecked bracts. Dierama galpinii from southern Mpumalanga and northern KwaZulu-Natal has similar spikes but longer stems 1.0-1.5 m tall in smaller tufts, and more flowers on the lateral spikes, mostly 6 to 13.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Taxonomically isolated, Dietes bicolor is distinguished by the dichotomously branched flowering stem and pale yellow to white flowers, the outer tepal limbs usually bearing dark brown nectar guides at the bases. The tepal limbs are rounded, with the inner tepals overlapping the outer. Dietes bicolor is the only polyploid species of the genus and is more closely related to the Lord Howe Island species, D. robinsoniana, than to any of the other African species. Both share a similar dichotomous branching pattern.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its very broad leaves, mostly 30-50 mm wide, Dietes butcheriana has white flowers closely resembling those of D. iridioides but with white rather than blue-purple flushed style branches. The large capsules, up to 35 x 20 mm, are pendent and have a smooth surface and rounded apex quite different from the beaked and wrinkled capsules of D. iridioides and are indehiscent, the walls slowly decaying to release the seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its relatively small white flowers usually with pale blue-mauve to violet style branches, usually uniformly white inner tepals, and elongate capsule with a short beak. The capsules are roughly fissured longitudinally and usually tardily dehiscent, sometimes appearing indehiscent. Plants often produce new clusters of leaves at the tips of old flowering stems, these arching to the ground where they take root. Plants in the southern part of its range, in southern Western Cape between the Riviersonderend Mtns and Humansdorp have filaments united in the lower half and form a bulbous column towards the base. Further north in Eastern Cape, plants have filaments with similar broad bases but these are free although contiguous. Elsewhere filaments are narrower, with only slightly expanded bases and usually not contiguous.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An affinity of H. humifusa E. & Z., but differing as follows: -Leaves more elongate and less lacerate. Peduncles shorter. Bracts very much smaller, sheathing. Petals cream-coloured or more rarely dull pink, the limb much longer than the claw. Filaments narrower across the lobes, the lobes nearer the base. Ovary more globose. It differs from H. chloroleuca Diels (ex desc.) in the colour of the flowers, not white suffused with green, in the much smaller floral parts and in the calyx, which bears stellate hairs. It is superficially like H. collina Schltr., but the upper part of the filaments (above the lobes) is not sigmoid as in that species.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1946. Some notes on the genus Hermannia, with descriptions of five new species. J. S. African Bot. 12: 95-103. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in Ferraria, the leaves of F. brevifolia form a tight, 2-ranked fan, with elongate sheaths 40-80 mm long, much exceeding the short, ovate, obtuse blades, 7-15 mm long. The blades, usually less than half as long as the sheaths, have relatively thick margins and oblique, acute or apiculate, hooked tips. The pale yellow flowers are virtually identical to those of F. macrochlamys, with a narrow floral cup, ± 12 mm deep, and tepal limbs, 22-28 mm long, with crisped, light brown or rarely reddish brown margins. The flowers produce a faint, slightly sweet scent. They can be distinguished from those of F. macrochlamys, if at all, by their somewhat longer outer tepals with long, tapering loosely coiled tips.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the growth habit, with stems produced well above the ground and bearing numerous branches crowded in the upper half, Ferraria crispa has a flower with a wide, shallow cup and an ovoid to ellipsoid capsule rounded or acute at the apex and lacking a beak. The sword-shaped lower leaves and shorter cauline leaves have a definite main vein and form two opposed ranks. The strongly scented flowers have tepals speckled or blotched dark brown to dull purple on a cream-coloured to pale yellowish background, or occasionally predominantly dark brown, always with pale crisped margins, these sometimes almost golden yellow when the tepals are otherwise brown. The tepal claws each bear a large, glistening nectary, often covering almost half the surface. The nectaries produce minute droplets of concentrated nectar scattered over the entire surface.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Are variable: the tepal limbs may be uniform in colour except for the margins, and range from light to chocolate-brown with paler margins or dull yellow-brown, then with little or no colour difference at the margins. The tepal claws are creamy white to palest yellow with fine, dark, longitudinal streaks and usually a dark median stripe. A second species, F. variabilis, has been confused with F. divaricata but is typically a low-growing, usually ± tufted plant, mostly 100-200 mm tall. It has similar flowers but more varied in colour. The vegetative differences are correlated with differences in the seeds. Those of F. divaricata are globose with a wrinkled surface and concave epidermal cells, whereas other Ferraria species, including F. variabilis, have angular seeds with 5 or 6 flattened facets separated by thickened ridges. Flowers of F. divaricata last a single day whereas those of F. variabilis last two or sometimes three days.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The aggregate species is characterized by the rather small, velvety tomentose, mostly entire leaves, the leaf-like stipules and the nodding, often secund flowers which are axillary and occur singly or in pairs on fairly short peduncles. The tomentum is made up of fringed scales intermingled with fine stellate hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: Vegetatively, Ferraria foliosa can be distinguished by the long, linear basal leaves much thickened in the midline, thus ± diamond-shaped in cross section, and sometimes dry by flowering time. The basal leaves differ markedly from the shorter, broader cauline leaves, the blades also thickened in the middle and arching outward, ultimately spreading horizontally. Successive leaves are opposed but collectively the leaves have a spirally two-ranked arrangement. This is also reflected in the short lateral branches, which are crowded in the upper half of the stem, the successive ones rotated slightly in a clockwise direction. The flowers differ little from those of closely related F. crispa in their darkly mottled pigmentation, broad tepal claws with large nectaries, and wide, shallow floral cup. Whereas the flowers of F. crispa are usually shades of dull yellow, buff-coloured and brown, those of F. foliosa are mottled dull purplish, or brownish maroon on a paler grey-purple background.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differing from all other southern African species of the genus in the sticky stems, open branching habit, and rhipidia with several (usually 4 to 6) flowers. The capsules are subglobose and flat-topped, unlike capsules of the remaining southern African species. Flowers are variously coloured, ranging from almost uniformly brown to dark purple or maroon with pale yellow to light brown crisped margins to partly marked with yellow streaks or bands.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An easily recognisable species distinguished from other adaxially-glabrescent, evergreen species with suberect to spreading leaves by the long petioles (longer than or equal to the lamina), the sparsely crenate to dentate leaf margins and the fruits without a prominent median rib. There are two collections from an aberrant Nuweberg population (Mc Donald 609, NBG; Haynes 523, NBG) which are unusual in having adaxially densely lanate leaves and involucral bracts, but in all other aspects are typical for the species. These can be distinguished from other adaxially non-glabrescent species by the lanate rather than felty adaxial indumentums, smaller leaves and umbels.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; De Villiers, BJ; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2015. A revision of the South African genus Hermas (Apiaceae). Syst. Bot. 40(1): 352-365. [DOI 10.1600/036364415X686639] [All rights reserved]

description: Typically with a tufted habit, Ferraria uncinata has flowers with a narrow floral cup 8-12 mm deep, the tepals either deep blue to violet edged with dull yellow-green or in the north of its range buff-coloured to dull yellow with violet speckles and yellow-brown margins. The leaf margins are thickened with at least the edges of the lower leaves crisped and undulate. The margin surface itself is smooth. The hooked tips of the leaves and spathes, the character for which the species was named (uncinatus = Latin for hooked), is frequent, though not constant, not only in F. uncinata but in several other species of the genus. The yellow-flowered central Namaqualand species, Ferraria macrochlamys has at times been included in F. uncinata, but is now understood to be a separate species differing not only in the pale yellow flower colour but in the fine structure of the thickened leaf margins, which resemble those of F. uncinata only superficially. In F. macrochlamys subsp. macrochlamys the marginal thickenings are usually densely ciliate and irregularly serrulate or crenulate, as well as sometimes being slightly crisped. The tepal limbs of F. uncinata are at least 1.5 times as long as the claws and up to three times as long in the northern populations, and the tepal apices are unusually extended. In F. macrochlamys the tepal limbs are slightly shorter to ± 1.5 times as long as the claws and are less prominently attenuate.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Mostly readily recognised by its relatively short, blunt or subacute leaves, often borne in a prostrate fan, and by its ± horizontal inflorescence, typically with rather large bracts. The white flowers are flushed with purple and marked on some or all of the lower tepals with golden-yellow blotches that turn brown as the flowers age, and appear in late autumn or winter, from April to June, rarely into July. Forms with narrower, suberect leaves and flowers with just the median lower tepal marked with yellow occur on coastal limestones around Bredasdorp and may represent introgression with Freesia leichtlinii subsp. leichtlinii. Similar plants from coastal outcrops at Onrus and Hermanus have been treated in F. leichtlinii subsp. alba but they lack the characteristic axillary cormlets of that species. Individuals in these populations with very narrow leaves approach F. praecox but tend to have fewer leaves than that species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The suffrutescent habit distinguishes this species from H. arborescens and H. papulosa. It differs from other suffrutescent species by being virtually glabrous throughout, in the rather few (10-)14-19(-25), thin rays up to 5 cm long, the lax inflorescence, and in the ovary which is more than twice as long as the stylopodium.
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E; Winter, PJD. 1996. A revision of the genus Heteromorpha (Apiaceae). Kew Bull. 51: 225-265. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from other early-flowering species of sect. Viridibractea by its narrow, glaucous, almost grass-like leaves, 4-5 mm wide, and 3-toothed bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Evidently closely allied to Freesia grandiflora and sharing subglobose-conical corms, suberect spikes of brilliant scarlet flowers (pale bluish in subsp. azurea), and seeds that are bright orange or red when fresh. Both species are restricted to forest or savanna in regions of summer rainfall. The flowers in F. laxa are generally smaller, with a relatively longer perianth tube more than twice as long as the tepals (9-15 mm long), and very short filaments, 3-4 mm long and scarcely exserted from the tube. The species reproduces vegetatively by sessile cormlets.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its deeply buried corms with finely fibrous corm tunics and suberect leaves with the lower always bearing cormlets in their axils along the subterranean portion of the stem. The white to pale yellow flowers are produced in spring, mainly between August and late September.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from the similar Freesia refracta and F. corymbosa by its obtuse or subacute leaves, typically shorter than the flowering spike, flowers with rather blunt tepals, and brown-tipped bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A slender shrub, with rodlike branches and a very close-pressed and short, but rigid pubescence. Leaves 1/2-3/4 inch long; petioles 1/4 inch. Peduncles about twice as long as the leaves; flowers bright crimson, 1 1/2 inch across, with narrow, cuneate petals. The leaves in the specimens seen can scarcely be called 3-lobed, but there is a tendency to such division and, notwithstanding the short petioles, the habit reminds us of some depauperated forms of H. pedunculatus.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1860. Malvaceae Juss. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Ranunculaceae to Connaraceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 1: 157-177. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15231#page/213/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from Freesia corymbosa and F. occidentalis, which it resembles in its bracts and flowers, by its mostly dull yellowish or greenish perianth, uniformly pale bracts without brown tips, and leaves mostly as long as the stem.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This plant is allied to H. cannabinus L. and H. asper Hook. fiI. Its leading characteristics are: -Stem erect, aculeate. Leaves palmatisect, the middle lobe oblong or oblong-oval; petiole aculeate. Involucral bracteoles very narrow, generally furcate near the apex. Fruiting calyx 17-18 mm long, lobes lanceolate acuminate, verrucose on the back; capsule very hairy.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, EG. 1939. New Malvaceae from Angola. J. Bot. 77: 17-22. [All rights reserved]

description: A distinctive species with obtuse, often somewhat succulent leaves and large, pale creamy yellow flowers, 50-70 mm long, with broadly elliptical or suborbicular lower lateral tepals, 11-12 mm wide, and elongate filaments 27-33 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A highly distinctive species with several vegetative and floral specialisations, notably the flattened and winged stems, the small, greenish or brown flowers with strongly curved perianth tube and included stamens, and the one-banded pollen operculum. The species is self-fertile and facultatively autogamous.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the long lower leaf with x-shaped blade and the obliquely tubular flowers with dimorphic perianth tube 40-52 mm long, the upper lateral tepals ± half the size of the dorsal and the lower tepals reduced to small triangular scales 3-6 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its small, tubular, pale greenish to white or yellowish flowers with strongly recurved tepals with tapering acuminate tips. The perianth tube 16-30 mm long is relatively long for so small a flower. The anthers are barely exserted from the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A spring-flowering species recognised by the short leaves seldom exceeding the lower third of the stem and the ± funnel-shaped flowers with perianth tube 28-40 mm long and relatively small tepals, the upper three 25-30 mm long and the lower three 17-23 mm long. The plants produce separate leafy shoots from the corms toward the end of the flowering season. In this respect it resembles Gladiolus aurantiacus Klatt from east of the escarpment, which has larger, orange flowers, the perianth tube 44-70 mm long and the dorsal tepal usually 35-45 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With its rounded and hardly angled, almost ‘furry’ stems which are often densely packed into mats, H. pillansii is one of those stapeliads that is always immediately recognisable, whether flowers are present or not. The stems are almost cylindrical and the tubercles are arranged very vaguely into anything between 10 and 16 rows, which often form spirals up the stem. As in several other species, the stems are extremely variable in length and relative thickness. They may be short (15-30 mm long) and nearly as thick as tall and then form dense, tightly packed mats, but they may also be quite long and slender and gathered into quite diffuse clumps. In H. pillansii (and H. longii) the number of angles rises rapidly on the primary stem from the initial number of four to the level typical of mature stems. Each tubercle is attenuated into a soft, bristle-like leaf-rudiment which tends to wear off with age. In H. pillansii the flowers have long, narrowly deltate lobes which taper to a fine point and are usually at least three times as long as broad. There is a relatively short, cupular tube. The inner surface is cream, finely spotted with red (rarely uniformly red) and from a distance this has the appearance of being pale brown all over. It is covered with papillae which are of a similar size over the whole surface, though they decrease slightly in length towards the tips of the lobes. Inside the tube is a very darkly coloured gynostegium. This has relatively long outer lobes adpressed to the base of the tube and fairly long, erect inner lobes which end in a swollen and noticeably bristly apex. Although the flowers of H. pillansii are unusual within the genus, they are similar to those of H. longii. These two species differ mainly in that H. longii has a distinctly rhizomatous habit and, while the stems are also cylindrical, the tubercles are more clearly arranged into far fewer rows in H. longii. The slender bristles on the tubercles of H. pillansii are replaced in H. longii with a much shorter leaf-rudiment. Flowers of H. longii are similarly coloured but have distinctly shorter corolla lobes. The stems of H. pillansii are also reminiscent of those of Stapelianthus pilosus. However, where S. pilosus is very unusual in this respect in Stapelianthus, in Huernia there is a gradation from 4-angled stems right through to the more or less cylindrical shape with large numbers of obscure angles that are found in H. pillansii. There is no similarity in the flowers, though, between H. pillansii and S. pilosus and the similarity of the stems appears to be purely coincidental.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 1. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: A spring-flowering species recognised by the short leaves not forming a basal fan, and the narrowly funnel-shaped flowers more-or-less strongly flecked or blotched orange, with an elongate perianth tube 44-70 mm long, slender in the lower half and abruptly expanded and cylindric above. The dorsal tepal is ascending to nearly horizontal and usually 35-45 mm long. The plants produce separate leafy shoots from the corms toward the end of the flowering season. In this respect the species resembles Gladiolus antholyzoides from the highveld, but this has smaller, mostly yellowish flowers with a narrowly funnel-shaped perianth tube 28-40 mm long and upper tepals 25-30 mm long. The narrow flowers of G. aurantiacus distinguish it from G. dalenii, which has a funnel-shaped perianth tube up to 50 mm long and concave dorsal tepal arching over the stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its superposed, hairy leaves and small, bright yellow flowers with funnel-shaped perianth tube 19-24 mm long with the lower part filiform, and nearly equal tepals about as long as the tube, with the filaments just reaching the top of the tube or shortly exserted.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An autumn-flowering species with only three leaves on the flowering stem and few-flowered spikes of pale pink to salmon-pink flowers with long, slender perianth tube 50-70 mm long, the filaments mostly included and exserted just ± 2 mm. Non-flowering plants produce a single long leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Flowering in late spring, Gladiolus brachyphyllus is distinctive in the foliage with short, largely sheathing leaves, and relatively large, deep pink flowers with dark red throat and violet anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the short, bladeless leaves on the flowering stem and relatively small, usually unscented pink to mauve flowers with short perianth tube 11-13 mm long. The solitary, linear-lanceolate and pubescent vegetative leaf produced in the winter is distinctive and dried remains from the previous season should always be sought for positive identification. In the absence of these remains the species is best separated from other superficially similar small-flowered species with bladeless leaves by the coarsely fibrous corm tunics. The species is most usually confused in flower with Gladiolus martleyi, typically from deep sands, which has almost identical but usually fragrant flowers and a soft, fleshy corm with softly membranous or finely fibrous tunics. The terete, 4-grooved leaf developed in G. martleyi later in the season is quite different from that of G. brevifolius.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An extremely variable species in habit, leaf shape and size, flower size and colour and density of punctate glands.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB; Robson, NKB. 1976. Clusiaceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 14-23. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A slender species with soft-textured, linear leaves, unusual ovate bracts, subequal tepals and subrotate, orange flowers with very short perianth tube, 2.5-4.0 mm long, enclosing the short, unilateral filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An attractive plant with large, yellow flowers, known as the Forest Primrose or Curry Bush, because of the curry-like odour given off by the leaves, particularly when crushed.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB; Robson, NKB. 1976. Clusiaceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 14-23. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A summer-flowering species characterised by its long spikes of narrowly tubular flowers, the upper part of the tube cylindric with comparatively short tepals, especially the lower, and disproportionately long bracts reaching at least to the top of the perianth tube and sometimes to the top of the flower.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its four, rarely three, linear leaves with overlapping bases completely sheathing the stem to near the apex, the attenuate and ribbed bracts, and the one or two large, bell-shaped blue flowers with short, sharply bent tube 10-16 mm long. The lower tepals are marked with yellow lateral blotches or a transverse yellow band edged with purple.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the lower leaf blade, 3-7 mm wide with broad marginal wings, thus ± H-shaped in section, and the relatively short-tubed, pale blue flowers with obtuse tepals, the lower spotted with dark blue. Gladiolus gracilis from clay soils further inland has narrower leaves 1.5-2.5 mm wide with the marginal wings curved over the blade, and variously coloured flowers with acute tepals, the lower streaked and spotted.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the relatively large, white or pinkish flushed flowers with a moderately long perianth tube (16-)25-40 mm long and the basally spurred or tailed anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is distinguished by the narrowly elliptic lip in the lower position, the glabrous filaments, the verrucose, tuberculate seeds and the 'boomerang-shaped' cystoliths.
bibliographicCitation: Balkwill, K; Getliffe Norris, FM. 1985. Taxonomic studies on the Acanthaceae: The genus Hypoestis in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 51: 133-144. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1985); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the conspicuously mottled cataphylls, three linear leaves with lightly thickened midrib, and relatively large, funnel-shaped flowers, usually pale to mid-blue but rarely pink or yellowish, the dorsal tepal 24-38 mm long. Blue-flowered plants are most common and are widespread through the coastal areas; yellow-flowered plants are largely restricted to montane and interior areas. Winter-flowering Gladiolus griseus from neutral and calcareous sands along the southwest coast has smaller, greyish flowers with perianth tube 6-10 mm long and dorsal tepal 16-26 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: an autumn-flowering species recognised by the reduced foliage and moderately large, funnel-shaped, carmine flowers with perianth tube 30-35 mm long. It has been confused with vegetatively similar Gladiolus stefaniae on the Potberg, but that species has larger, usually red flowers with perianth tube 35-45 mm long, dorsal tepal 53-58 mm long and filaments 30-42 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Corona longer than the free filaments, free filaments less than 2 cm long, anthers less than 10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Bjornstad, I. 1973. A revision of the genus Pancratium L. (Amaryllidaceae) in Africa south of the Sahara. Norweg. J. Bot. 20: 281-291. [All rights reserved]

description: A robust species with leaves 20-45 mm wide, large, long-tubed pink flowers with a perianth tube 40-50 mm long and firm-textured, green bracts 50-70 mm long. Gladiolus cataractarum has a general resemblance to G. saxatilis, but that species has unmarked flowers with shorter bracts, 40-50 mm long, that turn rusty brown at flowering.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the dense spike of small flowers with overlapping bracts ± two internodes long and the basal fan of tough, fibrous leaves with the margins and midrib plus one or more pairs of secondary veins thickened and hyaline. The flowers vary greatly in colour but are most frequently pink to salmon or dull purplish with darker nectar guides highlighted with yellow. Plants with orange to coral-pink flowers occur locally in Mpumalanga. The species is often confused with Gladiolus densiflorus, which occurs mainly to the east and at lower elevations, but their distribution overlaps along the Mpumalanga Escarpment, where G. crassifolius typically flowers slightly later. The flowers in the two species are very similar, although the perianth in G. densiflorus is sometimes finely speckled, but the two are most reliably separated by their foliage: the leaves in G. densiflorus are characterised by numerous, fine, closely spaced tertiary veins uninterrupted by evident secondary veins between the margins and main vein. Some plants may, however, be difficult to place. Gladiolus serpenticola from near Barberton can also be confused with G. crassifolius but is typically a taller plant with erect stems 750-1500 mm high, less fibrous leaves, and mostly shorter bracts 12-16 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Specimens of Q. acutiloba form clumps up to 300 mm in diameter. Vegetatively they are not readily distinguishable from most other members of this section, although the stems are often rather irregularly 4- or 5-angled with the angles slightly spiralling and they never have the minute stipular denticles alongside the teeth on the tubercles that most of the others regularly have. However, Q. acutiloba is always easy to recognise when in flower. The buds are characteristic and unmistakable with their broadly and shortly deltate shape and the very short pedicels that hold them close to the stem. The corolla is usually around 10 mm across and is practically without a tube. On the inside it is glabrous and entirely smooth. In this species the flowers are quite variable in the extent to which the lobes spread out. They are usually quite flat but occasionally they only open slightly so that the corolla has a more or less campanulate appearance. They are extremely variable in colour and may be found from dark, practically uniform purple-black to intensely or faintly spotted with purple-black on yellow-green or, on rare occasions, they are plain yellow-green. The somewhat cup-like corona is also relatively flat and broad. The outer lobes fill the gaps between the inner lobes and each is usually divided into two very short, deltoid lobules. The inner lobes are narrow and they cover the anthers at least partly. This whole structure is usually dark red (becoming darker when the corolla is darker) but it is bright yellow when the flower is plain yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the three leaves with centric, X-shaped blade with four longitudinal grooves or furrows and unscented, salver-shaped flowers with cylindric perianth tube (25-)35-52 mm long, the lower tepals with dark diamond-shaped markings, and relatively short filaments 7-8 mm long. Related Gladiolus inflatus has funnel- or almost bell-shaped flowers with longer filaments 12-18 mm long and a shorter perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The two species Q. arenicola and Q. armata are rather similar. Both have a clump-forming habit with the side-stems rooting readily at their bases, which is an unusual feature among these more robust, relatively large-flowered taxa. In Q. arenicola, which has a more easterly distribution on the edge of the winter-rainfall region and the western margin of the Great Karoo, the ascending to spreading tubercles on the stems are arranged fairly exactly into four neat tiers, the stems are uniformly grey- to purple-green and the leaf-rudiment may be subtended by a pair of stipular denticles surrounded by a few ‘hairs’. The flowers are borne on peduncular patches at more or less any height on the stems but with a preponderance towards the base.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the large flowers with the upper tepals 35-50 mm long and much exceeding the recurved lower tepals, the dorsal tepal concave and arching over and concealing the stamens. The species is variable in flower colour and flowering time. Madagascan populations of the species are diploid but most of those from continental Africa are polyploid.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the mostly four (rarely three) linear leaves with lightly thickened midrib and margins, striate or ribbed bracts, and white flowers marked with red on the lower tepals and often flushed pinkish on the reverse, with a cylindric perianth tube (10-)15-22 mm long expanded only near the top. The markings on the lower tepals include chevrons, diamonds or streaks and lines in regular patterns, and the base of the throat is also marked with a ring of red. Populations from the Hottentots Holland Mtns have the smallest flowers, with the lower tepal marking reduced to a small red diamond; plants on the Cape Peninsula have flowers marked with V-shaped chevrons; and those from Hermanus to Bredasdorp are marked with paired spots and streaks. Gladiolus variegatus from limestone hills on the Agulhas Peninsula has mostly three leaves, smooth bracts, and unevenly spotted lower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowers are typically small and cream, produced in small, but often dense clusters along the stems.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: In Q. linearis the plant forms a small and usually compact shrub. This mostly does not exceed 150 mm in height and diameter and roots by the central stem only, though cuttings are readily rooted. The young stems are exceptionally dark in colour and may be practically black. Although the tubercles are a little more prominent than in Q. ramosa, they are rounded and still quite obscure, and are joined into obtuse angles along the stem. Unlike in Q. ramosa, in Q. linearis each tubercle bears a quite obvious, albeit minute tooth, which is flanked by two even tinier stipular denticles. The flowers arise on small inflorescences towards the tips of the stems and are produced in unusually modest numbers for this section: they are frequently solitary or in lax groups of only two or three. The corolla lobes are tightly folded for most of their length so they are slender, only widening suddenly at the base. For most of their length they are a dark red-purple and this changes suddenly on the widened basal part to white. This white colour continues into the short, but quite deeply cup-shaped tube. The entire corolla is made of a relatively thin fabric which is devoid of bristles or papillae inside. The flowers emit a faint, unpleasant, excrement-like odour. In the base of the tube, well separated from its sides, is the gynostegium. The outer corona lobes are fused together into a deep cup while the inner lobes are more unusual: initially adpressed to the anthers, they rise in the centre in a short column and then spread out. This arrangement is unique in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: This species has stout, often quite attractively mottled stems which form substantial clumps up to 0.5 m in diameter. The tubercles are also stout and tipped with a hard and often quite sharp tooth. Their somewhat disorganised arrangement on the stems makes it easily separable from Q. arenicola. However, it is not so readily distinguished vegetatively from Q. armata, and the plants can look very similar. One very large plant of Q. multiflora seen south-east of Calvinia had longer stems than usual and looked similar to Q. mammillaris. Here only the more spreading habit and the roots that were produced on a few of the side-branches suggested its real identity, which was confirmed once flowers appeared. In Q. multiflora the flowers are produced in dense clusters of up to 30 per inflorescence towards the tips of the stems. Most of the flowers in a cluster open more or less simultaneously. From the point of view of the colour of the inside, these flowers are similar to most of the larger-flowered species. They have the typically dark, often purple-black lobes and whitish tube with a few dark spots mainly near the mouth which are found in most of them. They also emit an unpleasant odour. Very occasionally the dark colour of the lobes is speckled with yellow but usually their dark colour only begins to break up towards the mouth of the tube. The outside is smooth and often rather shiny but the inside is velvety and covered, or rather ‘encrusted’, around the mouth of the tube with a growth of quite large papillae. From all the similar species Q. multiflora is easily distinguished by the shape of the corolla lobes, which are either parallel-sided or widen gradually to a broader, abruptly acute, incurved tip. This shape in the lobes can usually be detected in the buds which, instead of narrowing from the base of the lobes towards the apex, are somewhat club-shaped. The corona is usually purplish towards the tips of the lobes and white lower down. The outer lobes are each bifid into small, deltoid, erect teeth and these, together with the similarly shaped dorsal ridge on the inner lobes, form a cup-like structure. The inner lobes are quite long. Initially they are pressed to the anthers, after which they rise in the centre into a slender column which nearly reaches the mouth of the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from glabrous or subglabrous forms of Gladiolus sericeovillosus by its shorter stature, 400-600 mm high, with the basal fan of leaves typically reaching no higher than the base of the spike and with distinctive venation, the margins strongly thickened but the midrib and other veins fine and closely set. Gladiolus elliotii also flowers earlier in the season, mainly November to January or early February.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In subsp. gracilis the flowers are generally held facing upwards. They have an unusual colour pattern in that towards the centre the corolla is usually white and speckled with purple-brown, with the purple-brown sometimes coalescing further out as in subsp. swanepoelii. The flower is made considerably more striking by the fact that the tips of the lobes (which are slightly thickened) may be brown or deep to pale yellow and this then forms a strong contrast against the colours lower down. In this respect the colour scheme differs from that in subsp. swanepoelii. However, in one specimen seen the lobes were initially purple mottled on white and after a day or so the tips faded to a pale yellow so that in this specimen they began with the colouring of subsp. swanepoelii and faded to something more like subsp. gracilis! Other differences between the two subspecies lie in the constriction of the corolla lobes near their middle in subsp. gracilis (this is visible in the bud which is broad at the base then distinctly narrower above and almost beaked) and the ascending pedicel which is 3 -5 mm long. However, none of these differences is constant and reliable and, in particular, plants have been collected where the lobes are not so narrow, the pedicel is ascending and the striking apical change of colour on the lobes is absent. In these cases it becomes difficult to separate this subspecies from subsp. swanepoelii. The corona is raised usually on quite a long stipe and is mostly dark purple. The outer lobes are slender but only slightly bifid at the tips and the inner lobes sometimes possess a small dorsal projection.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the three, largely sheathing and overlapping leaves with reduced blades, the lowermost sheathing the lower two thirds of the stem, and the white to cream-coloured flowers with long, slender tube (22-)40-60 mm long, produced in autumn.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Quaqua pillansii is probably the most handsome and striking member of a genus where the plants are generally rather dull-looking. The robust stems are up to 300 mm long and form a substantial shrub sometimes nearly half a metre in height and even more in diameter, which roots only on the main central stem (though cuttings are readily rooted). The imposing size of these plants is only exceeded occasionally in Q. mammillaris. The stems are beautifully mottled with purple-brown on a grey-green background. They have large, deltoid, laterally flattened tubercles which are joined into four broad wings along the stems. Each tubercle is tipped with a blunt but hard tooth. Nevertheless, despite the size of the plants, they are not always particularly easy to find. Plants are, for one thing, often very few and far between but, in addition, the jagged teeth and mottling of the stems break up their outlines to provide an effective camouflage which enables them to blend in remarkably with their surroundings of sandstone rocks and bushes. The flowers are also unmistakeable. They are produced in dense, more or less simultaneously-opening clusters and they emit a strong, somewhat fruity, unpleasant odour. Outside, the corolla is dark and often somewhat shiny but inside the flower is covered by a very rich combination of cream mottled with roundish spots and transverse markings of purple-brown or maroon. The lobes are broad and ovate and usually spread out only slightly so that the flower is distinctly campanulate. In the centre there is a small but relatively deep, cupular tube whose mouth is slightly constricted by the thickened tissue of the corolla. The interior is covered with papillae, in some plants densely and extensively but in others these are found only around the mouth of the tube. Each papilla has an elongated apical bristle and these bristles are longest in the tube and around its mouth. The corona is seated on a short stipe right in the base of the tube. It has short, blunt outer lobes united into a cup around the anthers and inner lobes which are broad and usually rise somewhat in the centre, rather above the level of the anthers. The whole structure varies from nearly entirely dark purple to dark on the outer lobes and paler yellow on the inner.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by its low stature, seldom more than 400 mm high, with a fan of relatively short, often slightly twisted leaves not exceeding the spike. The leaf blades have thickened margins and midrib with fine, closely set tertiary veins between. The flowers are slightly larger than those of Gladiolus densiflorus, which has similar leaf venation, especially the perianth tube, 14-16 mm long vs. 12-14 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the three, linear to almost filiform, short-bladed leathery leaves without thickened midrib and margin, and funnel-shaped pale blue to whitish flowers with the perianth tube shorter than the dorsal tepal. Related Gladiolus mutabilis from the south coast has four leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Specimens of Q. ramosa form shrubs rooted by a central stem and may reach 300 mm tall and broad. In this species branches will root in cultivation, but this happens slowly and with difficulty. Plants are usually densely branched somewhat above the base. The stems of Q. ramosa are most unusual and their unmistakeable shape was very accurately portrayed by Masson, who figured this species for the first time in his book Stapeliae Novae. The four thick and rounded continuous angles are made up of obscure, rounded and rather ‘mammose’ tubercles which are practically devoid of an apical tooth. Young stems are greenish but soon they become grey and most of the plant has this grey colour, looking rather like pieces of old wood. It is from this that the popular name ou ram or ‘old goat’ is derived. In Q. ramosa the flowers are produced towards the apices of the stems on quite conspicuous peduncular patches and they usually open together in dense clusters. They have a strong and unpleasant smell of sheep or buck urine. The corolla lobes are strongly folded down the middle but rarely spread out very far, mainly because of congestion in the inflorescence. They are dark purple-black both inside and outside with the outside fairly shiny. On the inside they are not at all shiny, becoming densely papillate towards their bases and in the mouth of the tube. The tube, which is cup-shaped and about twice as deep as the height of the gynostegium, is white with dark spots and is slightly thickened around the mouth. In Q. ramosa the gynostegium is broader than tall, with very small outer lobes along the sides and with the inner lobes just covering the anthers. Quaqua ramosa is clearly closely related to Q. mammillaris and Q. arenicola and all these species have flowers which are hard to distinguish between. They are most easily separated vegetatively, with the unusual stems of Q. ramosa making it unmistakeable.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the long lower leaf with x-shaped blade and the relatively small flowers with dimorphic perianth tube 35-46 mm long, the upper tepals yellowish green flushed and veined with dusky red, and the smaller lower tepals ± half as long as the upper.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A winter-flowering species with conspicuously mottled cataphylls, three linear leaves with lightly thickened main veins, and small, greyish flowers with short perianth tube 6-10 mm long and dorsal tepal 16-26 mm long.
