Gladiolus carinatus from acid sands along the coast and inland has larger, blue to pink or yellow flowers with a perianth tube 13-16 mm long, dorsal tepal 24-38 mm long and filaments 11-15 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Usually recognised in the field by its very vivid flowers and bright green erect leaves, which are only slightly hairy. The larger forms are much taller plants than those of R. baurii. Herbarium specimens can be distinguished by groove over the midrib which does not continue right to the tip of the leaf, whereas it does so in R. baurii. No ovary beak. Flowers held on pedicels and capules ripen in this position.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1978. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: VII. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 36(1): 43-76. [CC BY-SA]

description: Leaves triangular-filiform, subglabrous, outer perigone segments 5-9 mm long, ovary, subterranean, joined to the perigone by a distinct beak, beak 7-15 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1978. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: VII. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 36(1): 43-76. [CC BY-SA]

description: Flowering in autumn and winter, Gladiolus guthriei is recognised by the superposed, glabrous or villous leaves and relatively long-tubed, strongly clove-scented, dull pink to brownish flowers, with the perianth tube ± as long as the dorsal tepal and 20-27 mm long. The northern populations have glabrous or sparsely hairy leaves whereas those from the south are relatively densely hairy.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the hairy, superposed leaves, usually with relatively short, lanceolate blades 3-8(-13) mm wide, and the moderate-sized, weakly scented, pink to mauve flowers with red-streaked and spotted nectar guides on the lower tepals and perianth tube 15-26(-40) mm long. The filaments are 11-13 mm long. A collection from the Kogelberg is anomalous in its large flowers, 75 mm long with perianth tube 40 mm long. Gladiolus caryophyllaceus has broader leaves, 10-27 mm wide, with the margins thickened and often flushed pink or red, and large, strongly scented flowers with perianth tube 35-40 mm long and longer filaments 22-27 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Leaves triangular-filiform, subglabrous, outer perigone segments 8.5-20 mm long, ovary, subterranean, joined to the perigone by a distinct beak, beak 14-37 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1978. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: VII. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 36(1): 43-76. [CC BY-SA]

description: Notobubon sonderi is distinguishable from N. gummiferum by the long-pedunculate inflorescence which is often branched, the fewer-rayed primary compound umbel (12–20 rays), the more finely dissected leaflets as well as the smaller stature of this species with the stems becoming decumbent (see notes under N. gummiferum). Together with the previously mentioned characters it can be distinguished from N. tenuifolium by the discolorous leaves (adaxial surface green to dark green, abaxial surface silvery and glaucous) and the larger elliptic fruit (5.0–6.5 mm long). It differs from N. ferulaceum in the much larger leaves (usually more than 110 mm long) that are congested or irregularly arranged up the decumbent stem, the ultimate leaflet segments that are always flat and laminate, and the broad commissural vittae in the fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2009. A taxonomic revision of the woody South African genus Notobubon (Apiaceae: Apioideae). Syst. Bot. 34(1): 220-242. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the linear lower leaf with heavily thickened margins and midrib, and moderate-sized, dull-coloured flowers with upper tepals 23-30 mm long and perianth tube 25-36 mm long, with the lower lateral tepals obliquely twisted away from the lower median. The broad transparent lower edges of the dorsal tepal are striking. Gladiolus liliaceus has larger flowers, the upper tepals 40-45 mm long and the perianth tube 40-53 mm long, with the lower lateral tepals not obliquely twisted.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An early-flowering species resembling Gladiolus wilsonii in the white to mauve flowers with short perianth tube 9-12 mm long but with subsucculent leaves, oval in section when fresh but largely withered at flowering.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Even though it is in some cases difficult to distinguish the var. cordata from the var. scabrida, it is here kept distinct. The var. cordata is a more common plant and a more important constituent of the vegetation where it occurs than the rarer var. scabrida, which in reality probably is only an offshoot of the former variety.
bibliographicCitation: De Winter, B. 1963. Ebenaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 54-99. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Leaves small, no larger than 3.5 x 3 cm.
bibliographicCitation: Coates Palgrave, K; Coates Palgrave, M. 2002. Trees of southern Africa, 3rd ed. Struik, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the rather triangular, white to pale pink flowers, the outer whorl of tepals lanceolate-attenuate and much larger than the inner whorl (including the dorsal tepal), and the lower lateral tepals narrowly involute with a broad greenish yellow band. The slender stolons are characteristic of several species in the series.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the long basal leaf with terete, finely 4-grooved blade, and pale blue-lilac flowers with darker speckling, the narrowly clawed lower tepals with abruptly expanded limbs coloured pale yellow at the base, and the obliquely ovate upper laterals forming a window with the dorsal tepal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the horizontal spikes of long-tubed, cream-coloured flowers with narrow, spreading tepals, the lower three with small yellow and red markings near the base, the perianth tube long, straight and subcylindric, 35-40 mm long, and the filaments short, ± 8 mm long and exserted from the tube for about half their length.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its slender, whip-like leaves and long-tubed, cream-coloured to pale yellow flowers with attenuate tepals, the lower lateral tepals much smaller and marked with a median purple streak, and a slender perianth tube, 45-50 mm long, more than twice as long as the bracts and longer than the dorsal tepal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Strumaria barbarae, like its close ally S. phonolithica, has the largest flowers in the genus, with tepals 30-40 mm long. Strumaria barbarae is additionally distinguished by its somewhat trumpet-shaped flowers, which, like those of S. hardyana and S. truncata are pendulous and clustered.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: Diagnosed by the ± X-shaped or terete lower leaf with heavily thickened and raised margins and midrib, and the long-tubed, trumpet-shaped flowers, cream-coloured or ± mottled with brown, the dorsal tepal 25-32 mm long and the upper laterals up to 45 mm long, and the perianth tube 45-110 mm long, with the filaments entirely or mostly included and 5-13 mm long. The bracts are relatively short and blunt, 35-65 mm long. Gladiolus tristis has longer filaments, (15-)18-25 mm long, and occurs mostly west of Port Elizabeth but has also in the Swartberg Mtns.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The delicate habit of S. pygmaea places it close to S. tenella. Both species have filiform leaves and the smallest flowers in the genus, however, S. pygmaea has only two to three leaves (up to 80 mm long) and a sheathing cataphyll, whereas S. tenella has up to six leaves per annum (70-380 mm long) and lacks a cataphyll. A novelty, is the extremely slender, wiry and more or less spirally twisted scape which bears contrasting stout, green pedicels. The infructescence persists throughout the vegetative phase, with the green pedicels apparently functioning as assimilatory structures.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: A summer-flowering species from the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg with poorly developed corm, recognised by the soft-textured leaves without thickened margins, and the small, pale lilac-pink flowers with prominent, dark veining on the lower lateral tepals, these much shorter than the lower median tepal, and a very short perianth tube ± 5 mm long. The slender stolons are characteristic of several species in the series.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Strumaria tenella subsp. tenella is usually smaller than S. tenella subsp. orientalis, particularly in the diameter of the stylar swelling. Furthermore the stylar swelling is typically indented above, whereas in S. tenella subsp. orientalis it is consistently dome-shaped.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: As the specific epithet suggests, the distinctly clawed tepals are diagnostic for the species. In addition, the abrupt broadening of the tepals above the proximal claw creates characteristic 'windows' between adjacent tepals at the base of the flower. The leaves also readily distinguish the species and are charateristically broad (usually 30-60 mm across), thin-textured, with the edges somewhat undulate or conduplicate. The closest ally is 5. karoopoortensis, which occurs as an isolated population in the more arid Tanqua Karoo to the south east.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: Very similar to Gladiolus woodii and co-occurring with it at the type locality but taller, 550-700 mm high, with sparsely villous or glabrous lower leaf sheaths and slightly larger, blue-mauve flowers with the upper tepals 28-30 mm long. The tunics accumulate in a mass around the stem base. Gladiolus woodii is usually less than 500 mm tall, often with more densely villous leaves, and smaller, lilac, yellow or brownish flowers with the upper tepals 17-27 mm long. The corm tunics do not accumulate.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An unmistakable species with villous leaves, the blades X-shaped, and pale blue, bell-shaped flowers with darker speckles and strongly clawed lower tepals with pale yellow nectar guides outlined with darker speckles on the limbs.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An autumn-flowering species recognised by the softly papery or finely fibrous corm tunics, the foliage reduced to three, ± entirely sheathing leaves on the flowering stem, and pink to mauve, funnel-shaped flowers with transverse yellow bands or spear-shaped marking edged with red on the lower tepals. The solitary foliage leaf, produced from a separate bud later in the season, is terete and 4-grooved. Gladiolus jonquilliodorus from the Cape Peninsula and nearby Atlantic Coast has similar pale yellow or pearly grey flowers produced in midsummer, and two or three foliage leaves. Gladiolus subcaeruleus from clay soils has coarsely fibrous corm tunics forming a collar around the base of the stem and pale blue flowers with a slightly longer perianth tube, 15-17 mm long, and a thinly hairy foliage leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Strumaria karoopoortensis is most closely related to S. unguiculata. Both species have the broadest leaves (up to 50 mm or more across) and the longest (10-14 mm) and broadest tepals (3.5-6.5 mm wide) of all the stellate-flowered species of Strumaria. Several differences separate S. karoopoortensis from S. unguiculata, including the yellowish inner tunics of the bulb and the flaccid leaves. Furthermore the flowers are scentless and the tepals, which are slightly undulate along the edges, lack the basal windows found in S. unguiculata and are conduplicate apically. With age the pink pigmentation of the tepals is accentuated, whereas in S. unguiculata the ageing flowers become translucent.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinctive in its pubescent leaves and orange or yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers with dimorphic perianth tube 35-43 mm long, the lower part narrow for 11-18 mm and abruptly expanded into a wide horizontal cylindric upper part 22-25 mm long, with subequal, broadly obovate to suborbicular tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the three linear leaves with short, subsucculent blades without thickened midrib and margins, and the long-tubed, cream-coloured to pink flowers, the tube 40-48 mm long and slender and subcylindric in the lower half and widely cylindric in the upper half. Orange-flowered Gladiolus priorii from the west and southwest coast has narrower, oblong upper lateral and lower tepals 9-12 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the distinctive flowers, pale to deep salmon-orange with darker tepal midlines and a distinctively shaped perianth tube, 50-65 mm long and divided into a narrow lower part and a broader cylindric upper part ± 30 mm long, and the relatively long filaments, 35-37 mm long. Related Gladiolus floribundus has a narrowly funnel-shaped perianth tube, cream-coloured to yellow-green flowers and shorter filaments, 20-22 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Gladiolus ochroleucus by the larger, consistently pink flowers with longer perianth tube, 30-45 mm long. Gladiolus mortonius can be confused with forms of G. oppositiflorus, but that species has a markedly 2-ranked spike and distinctive floral bracts, somewhat inflated below with the margins of the inner bracts connate and tubular around the ovary and the apices drawn into long, brown-tipped cusps.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the linear, villous leaves with thickened veins, and usually branched stem with pale pink flowers with clawed tepals, the lower laterals with a yellowish green, heart-shaped blotch at the base of the limb.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the elongate-obconic corm with four, linear, sometimes short-bladed, leathery or subsucculent leaves with the midrib and margins not thickened or raised, and the funnel-shaped flowers with perianth tube shorter than the dorsal tepal. Gladiolus exilis from the mountains on the West Coast has three leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In comparison to the closely allied pubescent-leaved species with white-fleshed bulbs and stellate flowers (S. chaplinii & 5. leipoldtii), S. discifera has consistently long, narrow lanceolate leaves, distinctly channelled tepals and a bulbiform to discoid swelling at the base of the style.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: Like S. chaplinii, S. discifera and S. leipoldtii, this species has the apomorphic character state of retaining the long soft pubescence on the leaves into maturity. The leaves of S. villosa, which are appressed to the ground, are softly villous on only the adaxial surface and characteristically glaucous. Unlike the other pubescent-leaved species of section Gemmaria, S. villosa has the derived character state of yellow inner bulb tunics, which suggests a close affinity to S. merxmuelleriana: a species which becomes hairless at maturity and co-occurs with 5. villosa near Kosies in the grid area 2917BA. Although close morphologically, S. villosa and S. merxmuelleriana occupy distinct habitats and they retain their vegetative differences in cultivation.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: Of all the species of subgenus Gemmaria, S. aestivalis is remarkable in having wide nectar wells formed by the fusion of the lateral margins of the inner filaments to the sharp edges of the triquetrous style. This specialised characteristic is also well developed in subgenus Strumaria and indicates parallel development in the two groups. Vegetatively, S. aestivalis most closely resembles S. pubescens, in having yellow-fleshed bulbs and broadly lorate pubescent leaves; both are derived characters, which points to a close alliance between the species.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: An obligate pyrophile recognised by the unusual, abrasive leaves with minute recurved-scabrid hairs on the veins and the trumpet-shaped flowers with dimorphic perianth tube 46-55 mm long, the lower 18-20 mm narrow and abruptly expanded into a wider cylindric upper part 24-35 mm long. The lower tepals are significantly smaller than the upper, about half as long, and rarely more than 15 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Strumaria salteri is undoubtedly the most showy species in the genus. The widely funnel-shaped flowers and bifoliate leaves, appressed to the ground, place it close to S. watermeyeri, from which it is easily distinguished by its minutely ciliate leaves and somewhat broader tepals which are free from the stamens. Known populations at the northern and southern limits of the narrow distribution belt show a trend towards floral dimorphism. Specimens from the Pakhuis Pass have stamens which more or less equal the length of the tepals, whereas in the north the stamens exceed the tepals by up to 4 mm. If further data corroborate these initial observations, the formal recognition of subspecies may become justifiable in future.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its relatively short, soft-textured leaves with lightly thickened margins and midrib, and the moderately sized flowers, in combination with its wetland habitat and early flowering. Gladiolus paludosus is most likely to be confused with G. crassifolius, a summer-flowering species of drier, often stony habitats, that has longer leaves with thickened margins and prominent secondary veins, and longer spikes of smaller flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Florally, S. picta is recognised by its widely campanulate flowers; the broad brownish red median band on the abaxial surface of each tepal; the broadened filaments and ovoid style. Vegetatively, the species is differentiated by its spreading, lorate, glaucous leaves with the margins densely fringed with minute cilia. Strumaria picta is the only species in the genus in which one to three leaves with reduced leaf blades remain hidden in the bulb. These are considered not to be comparable to the cataphylls of other species as they do not occur in a regular sequence from year to year.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from yellow-flowered forms of Gladiolus woodii by the glabrous lower leaf sheaths and the strongly clawed upper tepals. Non-flowering plants ultimately develop three leaves, unlike the solitary leaf developed in G. woodii. The two species are allopatric, with G. woodii occurring east and south of the range of G. pardalinus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A dwarf species with wiry stems and reduced foliage, the lowermost leaf sheathing the lower half of the stem with a villous, often slightly inflated sheath and vestigial blade, and the upper leaf reduced to a minute scale inserted just below the spike. The flowers are pale pink with a sub-actinomorphic perianth and short tube 5-7 mm long. Similar Gladiolus pubiger is a taller plant with two or three leaves, the upper not inserted immediately below the spike, and larger flowers with attenuate tepals and slightly longer tube, 7-8 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the three leaves with narrow, terete blades and fragrant, bluish to grey or cream-coloured, bell-shaped flowers with sharply bent perianth tube 10-15 mm long, the lower tepals with a transverse yellow band outlined with darker colour. Gladiolus inflatus from the western and southwestern mountains has unscented, pink to mauve flowers with dark spear- or spade-shaped markings on the lower tepals and a curved perianth tube 12-30 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Strumaria truncata is the only species of the genus with an exserted, reddened cataphyll which sheathes the mostly twisted foliage leaves. With respect to the size, shape and position of the flowers it is extremely similar to S. hardyana which lies to the north of its range. Flowers vary considerably in colour and range from deep pink to white colour forms before subsequently ageing to a deeper pink after anthesis. Other variables are the extent to which the filaments are adnate to the style, the length of the filament tube and the dentition on the confluence between the outer filaments and the style. The plasticity of these floral features is such that they may vary among the flowers of a single inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its slender, terete and 4-grooved leaves and small, short-tubed, lilac to pink flowers, the lower tepals with a pale, transversely spade-shaped mark outlined with purple, and the subglobose capsules with completely wingless seeds. The relatively shorter perianth tube, 11-14 mm long separates it from Gladiolus filiformis from around Zeerust, characterised by its longer perianth tube, 25-40 mm long and longer than the dorsal tepal. Gladiolus rubellus from eastern Botswana and northern Namibia has linear leaves with thickened midrib and margins, bright orange-red flowers, and partially winged seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the three smooth to pubescent leaves with a pair of thickened and raised veins on one side but with the margins unthickened and bell-shaped, yellow flowers with short, sharply bent perianth tube 11-12 mm long. Gladiolus delpierrei has similar leaves but softly fibrous corm tunics and funnel-shaped, pale yellow to cream-coloured flowers with a very short perianth tube ± 8 mm long. Gladiolus sufflavus from the Bokkeveld Escarpment has X-shaped leaves with thickened margins and midrib, and greenish flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the conspicuously mottled cataphylls, three linear leaves with lightly thickened midrib, and radially symmetric, mauve to pink (rarely white) flowers with darker veins. The flowers close tightly in mid-afternoon.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Vegetatively similar to Gladiolus vinosomaculatus and distinguished from it by the pure white to pale lilac flowers with slightly shorter anthers, 9-10 mm long but longer style branches, 6-8 mm long. The two species are allopatric, with G. rehmannii occupying subtropical habitats in drier bushveld and savanna to the north of G. vinosomaculatus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to Gladiolus caryophyllaceus and G. hirsutus and distinguished by its summer-flowering habit and long-tubed flowers with perianth tube 25-36 mm long and cylindric for most of its length, flaring only in the upper 5-7 mm, and the more definitely lozenge-shaped nectar guides on the lower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A variable species with three to five linear leaves with the margin and midrib lightly thickened, rarely solidly oval in section, and inflated, bell-shaped, mauve to blue flowers with a short, sharply bent perianth tube 12-19 mm long. The lower tepals are typically marked with a white to yellow transverse band outlined with dark blue or purple.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very distinctive species, with narrow, 4-grooved leaves, pale bracts with brown tips and margins, and pale, short-tubed flowers densely speckled with red. The spikes bear up to 30 flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the pale pink flowers with relatively narrow, spreading tepals, the upper ± 8 mm wide, lower tepals with cream-coloured and reddish markings, and relatively long filaments ± 25 mm long, well exserted from the perianth tube and papillose toward the base.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the sweetly scented, dull yellowish to brownish flowers with the upper tepals windowed in profile, ± erect leaves, unspotted upper cataphylls and woody corm tunics clawed at the base and orange when young. The parapatric Gladiolus venustus has abruptly deflexed lower tepals with the lower laterals strongly auriculate at the base of the limbs and suberect upper lateral tepals not forming windows with the dorsal in profile. The two species intergrade along the Vanrhynsdorp-Calvinia axis and discrimination between them may be difficult there.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Resembling Gladiolus permeabilis subsp. edulis in the habit and in the form of the flowers, but distinguished by the much longer perianth tube, 25-35 mm long and red streaks on the tepals. The scaly suckers produced by the corms are also distinctive and not present in G. permeabilis.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of three allopatric species with similar, large red flowers with white marks on the lower tepals, distinguished by the evergreen habit, numerous, relatively soft-textured leaves and the rhizome-like rootstock with well-developed, scaly stolons.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its stiffly erect stems with three or four leaves, the lowermost or lower two subbasal with a centric blade, terete or X-shaped in section and the remainder largely sheathing with softly villous sheaths, and nodding, pale yellow to yellow-green, bell-shaped flowers with a sharply bent perianth tube 14-15 mm long. Gladiolus pritzelii has bright yellow flowers, often conspicuously marked with brown on the lower tepals, and plane leaves with one or two raised veins but unthickened margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Diagnosed by the ± X-shaped lower leaf with heavily thickened and raised margins and midrib, and the pink, funnel-shaped flowers with subactinomorphic perianth with a very short tube, 8-12 mm long and short filaments ± 7 mm long scarcely exserted from the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from allied species in the series with similar flowers by the terete leaves, 1-2 mm diam., with the main vein and margins heavily thickened and thus with four fine longitudinal grooves. Gladiolus watsonius from west of the Hottentots Holland Mtns has linear leaves, mostly 4-6 mm wide with two furrows on each surface, and G. quadrangularis from inland near Ceres has centric blades that are x-shaped in section and 2.5-4.0 mm diam., and softer corm tunics.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Diascia pusilla differs from its nearest relative, D. collina, in corolla size, shape of the posticous filaments, size and shape of the corolla sacs, and habitat. The difference in flower size between the two taxa is not simply a function of plant vigour, since small plants of D. collina at Postberg, with only a few leaves, have much larger flowers than robust plants of D. pusilla, with many large leaves and long thick stems, at Droogerivier. Corolla limb length of D. pusilla reaches 13.5 mm, but averages 11.5 mm, whereas limb length of D. collina ranges from 13.3 to 23 mm, but averages 17 mm. The corolla sacs of D. pusilla are about half the size of D. collina sacs (2.1 mm vs 4.4 mm long) and are parallel or only slightly divergent near the tips. They are not strongly divergent like those of D. collina. The shapes of the filaments also differ between these two species. D. pusilla lacks the protuberance on each posticous filament that is present in D. collina.
bibliographicCitation: Steiner, KE. 2009. Three new species of Diascia (Scrophulariaceae) from the Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 39(1): 11-17. [CC BY]

description: A poorly collected taxon resembling Gladiolus permeabilis subsp. permeabilis in the form of the flower but with a larger dorsal tepal 28-32 x 15 mm and longer perianth tube (22-)28-35 mm long. The habitat on sandstone in fynbos, flowering after fire, also differs.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Vegetatively similar to Gladiolus carneus but distributed mostly north and west of that species and distinguished by the consistently paler flowers with longer perianth tube, 52-75 mm long, about twice as long as the bracts and longer than the dorsal tepal, and the attenuate, ± strongly undulate or crisped tepals. The distinction between the species is especially difficult between Wellington and Paarl, where their distributions overlap.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the plane, subsucculent and usually ± falcate leaves, and the strongly purple-veined flowers with a large, suberect dorsal tepal. The production of slender, naked stolons is characteristic for the species. Gladiolus ceresianus and G. virescens have similar flowers but corrugate or grooved to terete leaves with thickened and raised veins and margins, and sessile or subsessile cormlets.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the mostly three (rarely four) linear leaves with lightly thickened main vein and margins, striate or ribbed bracts, and white to pale pink flowers irregularly spotted with red on the lower tepals, with a cylindric perianth tube 14-20 mm long expanded only near the top. Gladiolus debilis from sandstone slopes has mostly four leaves, ribbed bracts, and symmetrically marked lower tepals, mostly with diamond-, spade-, or chevron-shaped markings.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the fragrant, yellowish flowers tipped mauve to bright pink, the upper lateral tepals suberect and partially overlapping the dorsal tepal, the lower tepals abruptly deflexed and pinched together at the base and the lower laterals strongly auriculate at the base of the limbs. Most populations have the tepals tipped dull purple to mauve but populations in the Olifants River Valley and around Worcester have bright pink tips. The parapatric Gladiolus scullyi has the upper lateral tepals forming a more-or-less pronounced window with the dorsal tepal in profile, and the recurved lower tepals not strongly auriculate at the limb bases. The two species intergrade along the Vanrhynsdorp-Calvinia axis and discrimination between them is problematic there.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Nemesia aurantia is most closely related to N. versicolor, but has orange rather than blue or yellow flowers, lacks a conspicuous spur, and has a bilobed palate on the lower lip that is less prominent. The only other saccate Nemesia species with orange flowers is N. strumosa Benth. Plants of N. aurantia are typically shorter than N. strumosa (up to 410 mm vs up to 730 mm) with smaller flowers (corolla limb 13-19 mm vs 17-35 mm long). The sac of the corolla in N. aurantia is less than half the length, on average, of N. strumosa and the raised palate and divergent bosses on the lower lip of N. aurantia are absent in N. strumosa.
bibliographicCitation: Steiner, KE. 2009. Two new species of Nemesia (Scrophulariaceae) from arid areas of the Northern Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 39(1): 67-72. [CC BY]

description: Nemesia suaveolens is easily recognized by its yellow and magenta flowers with a ± straight spur and a prominent yellow rectangular spot (nectar guide) at the base of the upper corolla lip. It is most closely related to N. euryceras, but differs from that species by having a lower lip that is yellow rather than white with pale violet margins, an upper lip with a conspicuous yellow rectangular patch, just above the corolla opening, a spur that is ± equal to the length of the lower lip, not half the length of the lower lip, and a hypochile that is yellow rather than dark violet. Nemesia suaveolens often grows in close proximity to N. karroensis Bond and has been confused with that species. It is similar in coloration to N. karroensis, especially when both are pressed and dried, but differs in having a short, straight, downwardly oriented spur instead of a long (8.9-12.3 mm), backwardly projecting one that is usually strongly recurved in its distal half.
bibliographicCitation: Steiner, KE. 2009. Two new species of Nemesia (Scrophulariaceae) from arid areas of the Northern Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 39(1): 67-72. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the mostly four linear leaves with lightly thickened midrib and margins, striate or ribbed bracts, and long-tubed, pale pink flowers with a cylindric perianth tube 35-40 mm long expanded only near the top. The lower lateral tepals are strongly marked with red, spade-shaped nectar guides. Somewhat similar Gladiolus debilis, which also occurs on the Cape Peninsula, has ribbed bracts and a shorter perianth tube, (10-)15-22 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The specific epithet refers to the distinctly ericoid leaflets. Unlike Erica leaves, however, the leaflets of O. ericifolia are rolled adaxially, and almost completely enclose an unusually papillate adaxial epidermis. Other diagnostic characters of this species include the filiform petioles, the swollen articulation on the peduncle, the wine-red filaments and petal-bases, and the very short claw.
bibliographicCitation: Oberlander, KC; Dreyer, LL; Curran, HR. 2009. An unusual new species of Oxalis (Oxalidaceae) from the Knersvlakte, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 75: 239-245. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2009); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the conic corms, four leaves with unusual 3-angled blades with the adaxial margin winged at right angles to the blade proper, and distinctive purple-streaked flowers with attenuate tepals. The attenuate tepals and puberulous upper cataphyll suggest a relationship with yellow-flowered Gladiolus comptonii from the Heerenlogement Mtn near the coast.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the four linear leaves with lightly thickened main veins and margins, striate or ribbed bracts, and relatively long-tubed, pink flowers with lanceolate-attenuate tepals and red, chevron-shaped nectar guides on the lower tepals. Allied Gladiolus blommesteinii has a lightly shorter, gently flared perianth tube, 17-24 mm long, and streaked or spotted nectar guides on the lower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Superficially this species resembles the sympatric species O. flava but O. saltusbelli lacks the distinct basal petiolar articulation and papery bracts at the leaf bases that characterise O. flava. The sticky, blackish-brown tunics of O. saltusbelli are also very different to the papery, pale brown bulb tunics produced by O. flava.
bibliographicCitation: Dreyer, LL; Roets, F; Oberlander, KC. 2009. Oxalis saltusbelli: A new Oxalis (Oxalidaceae) from the Oorlogskloof Nature Reserve, Nieuwoudtville, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 75(1): 110-116. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2009); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the purple and white mottled, often puberulous cataphylls and the relatively short, usually twisted leaves, sometimes with finely puberulous sheaths, and the hard corm tunics separating into claws at the base. The flowers are dull green to yellowish brown with purple highlights and intensely fragrant.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the ribbed and scabridulous leaves, and the characteristic greenish to creamy white flowers with a translucent, boat-shaped dorsal tepal hooded over the stamens, and darkly veined, heart-shaped upper lateral tepals. The lower tepals are predominantly yellowish green except at the tips. The flowers are exceptionally cryptic and often most easily located by their strong and penetrating fragrance.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea majubensis is recognised by the weakly compressed stem (sometimes lightly angled but not winged) becoming terete in the upper half, subdivaricate branching with lateral branches usually simple (rarely with 1 or more sessile lateral flower-clusters), and the comparatively short, partly transparent, entire or lightly torn spathes and bracts, 7-8 mm long The style is relatively long and the stigmatic lobes are fan- to wedge-shaped. Plants in fruit (and herbarium specimens) are almost uniformly black, less so distally.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Subsp. imbricata is distinguished by the somewhat smaller flowers, either white or creamy white to pale yellow and always uniformly coloured. The tepals are mostly 10-15 mm long and the perianth tube 2-4, rarely up to 6 mm long vs. mostly 5-8 mm long in subsp. bicolor. A certain amount of overlap in the flower features is to be expected between subspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Subsp. ornithogaloides is distinguished from subsp. flava only by the corms, ovoid-ellipsoid and tapering at both ends, this typical of subg. weihea and the ancestral type in Geissorhiza ornithogaloides. The bell-shaped corm of subsp. flava is specialised and derived. In all other features, the two subspecies are essentially identical, although there are several populations of subsp. ornithogaloides on the edges of the range of this subspecies that have smaller flowers than any found in subsp. flava.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This variety resembles R. cruciata var. intermedia in its flowers, but the corms are distinct.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from R. rosea var. australis by its more erect, narrower leaves and flower colouring. Some indifferent herbarium specimens can, however, be confused.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A. galpinii sometimes flowers when leafless and then specimens may be difficult to distinguish from A. nigrescens in the same condition. The differences between the two species are given under A. nigrescens.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Subsp. grandiflora is recognised by the plum-red flowers white in the throat and tube (occasional white-flowered morphs have been recorded in some populations) with spathulate tepals broadest in the upper third.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its white to cream-coloured flowers with a longer perianth tube, mostly more than 30 mm long and up to 65 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Subsp. spicata, often low in stature but up to 200 mm tall, has plane, strongly falcate leaves with undulate to crisped margins, and a spike with up to 12 flowers, but often fewer.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of a small group of species in sect. Roseae with ± membranous or papery outer and inner bracts, and yellow flowers, among which it is distinguished by the rounded corm, numerous (7 to 9) leaves, and flowers with a golden-yellow cup marked with dark blotches and streaks around the throat.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowering stem of A. nana is almost always unbranched and bears leaves only near the base. The terminal internode is several times longer than the rest of the stem and terminates in a single inflorescence of 2(3) flowers. Particularly striking are the well-developed pedicels of the flowers, 10-12 mm long, and the ovoid ovary 4-6 mm long, quite different to the short pedicels, ± 2 mm long and triangular-columnar ovary 12 mm long of A. pusilla.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An easily recognized species, even in sterile condition, particularly when leaves are simple or once ternate. The cordate leaflet base tends to be less pronounced in leaflets of higher order. It resembles A. anemonoides in habit, but it differs from this species by the glabrous fruits, less compound leaves, and by the distribution and length of hairs on the leaf blade.
bibliographicCitation: Rasmussen, H. 1979. The genus Knowltonia (Ranunculaceae). Opera Bot. 53: 1-44. [All rights reserved]

description: Seemingly relatively unspecialised in the section, B. fragrans is recognised by the subequal, spreading tepals, the dorsal only slightly longer than the lower, and small pale markings edged in darker blue or purple on the lower tepals. The perianth tube is about as long as or slightly longer than the dorsal tepal and the erect, usually branched stem bears spikes of up to 10 flowers. The suberect stamens are unilateral and the anthers parallel and contiguous, and usually dark blue. The soft-textured, hairy leaves are lightly pleated and often oblong rather than the usual sword-shape in sect. Babiana. The flowers have a strong, pleasant scent, likened to carnations. Somewhat variable across its range, B. fragrans from the interior southwestern Cape has a more strongly bilabiate flower with the dorsal tepal up to 5 mm longer than the lower and the upper lateral tepals are united for a short distance with the lower, thus forming a more pronounced lip than is evident in plants from the Cape Peninsula and nearby.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of five species of Babiana with abruptly truncate, wedge-shaped leaves, B. praemorsa is recognised by its flowers with a straight, cylindric perianth tube 40-60 mm long and firm, narrow, spreading tepals, 18-22 mm long. The perianth is deep violet rather than blue as in the apparently related long-tubed B. pubescens of the central Namaqualand. Babiana praemorsa can be distinguished from it and B. cuneata, the other long-tubed species with wedge-shaped leaves, by its short filaments, 8-9 mm long, exserted 4-5 mm from the perianth tube, tepals spreading at right angles from the nearly straight tube of uniform diameter, and short style branches ± 3 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognised by its actinomorphic flower with broad, ovate, overlapping tepals that form a shallow cup, and coloured dark blue with a deep red centre. The stamens are arranged symmetrically around the short style that divides below the level of the linear anthers and the anthers bear reddish brown pollen. It was initially regarded merely as a colour form of B. nervosa, but that species has a zygomorphic flower with blue to mauve, white or cream-coloured, spreading tepals, the lower distinguished from the upper by different markings, unilateral stamens, sagittate anthers with an expanded connective and a style dividing at the base of the anthers. Babiana rubrocyanea from Darling, also with bowl-shaped purple flowers with a red centre, is distinguished by its mostly unilateral stamens with the anthers facing the spike apex, and the unusually short style branches with very broad tips.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This subspecies differs from ssp. anemonoides by the usually more slender habit, the often irregularly cleft and lobed leaflets, the smaller flowers with fewer ovaries, and by the small stamens, which never have elongated connectives. The colour of the flowers is reported to be yellowish-green in contrast with the white flowers of ssp. anemonoides. However, this character seems to vary. Specimens with short scape can be distinguished from A. knowltonia by the fewer ovaries, the shape of the torus, which is steeply conical to columnar in A. knowltonia, and by the indumentum. The leaves of A. knowltonia become more hairy above than beneath with age, while in A. anemonoides the lower side is always the more hairy.
bibliographicCitation: Rasmussen, H. 1979. The genus Knowltonia (Ranunculaceae). Opera Bot. 53: 1-44. [All rights reserved]

description: Drimia flagellaris is recognised by its clumped, evergreen habit with characteristically keeled bulbs, rather flaccid leaves commonly exceeding 500 mm in length, and long racemes with up to 90 flowers on pedicels 17-25 mm long. The inflorescence persists for some time, remaining green and photosynethetic after the seeds have been shed, a characteristic sometimes also found in D. calcarata, which is characterised by its smoothly rounded bulbs, often shorter racemes, mostly 3- to 30(40)-flowered, and shorter pedicels 1-14(-22) mm long. Drimia flagellaris is sympatric at Kranzkloof with a grassland form of D. calcarata (Edwards et al. 2005) with subterranean bulbs and deciduous leaves, but evergreen forms of D. calcarata with semi-epigeal bulbs are known from elsewhere. Further investigation is required to clarify the distinction between the two species.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Annesorhiza calcicola is easily distinguished by its small stature (inflorescence less than 0.3 m and leaves less than 150 mm long), the hysteranthous, pilose leaves that are completely absent at flowering (dead or dying at flowering in other species, and usually glabrous), and by its unique greyish-black, pilose inflorescence (yellowish-brown and glabrous in other species). It approaches A. grandiflora (Thunb.) Hiroe (which also occurs in the area), in its pilose leaves and homomericarpic fruit but differs from that species in its whitish petals (yellow in A. grandiflora), smaller fruit (< 5 mm long vs 6-7 mm in A. grandiflora), and in its solitary, vertical, active root, which appears to abscise distally. A. grandiflora, like other species in the genus, has a cluster of several roots and flowers in mid-summer, unlike.

description: Recognised by the tufted habit and small, pale yellow flowers with a narrow floral cup and divaricate anther thecae.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its fairly low, tufted habit, rarely exceeding 200 mm in height, with the relatively few branches crowded near the base, combined with fairly large flowers with broad tepal claws forming a deep, relatively wide bowl in which nectar accumulates in a pool. The spreading tepal limbs vary considerably in colour and marking. In the north of its range, in Namaqualand and southern Namibia, flowers have light brown tepal limbs with a dark purple longitudinal band toward the base and light brown margins, while the claws are pale greenish cream-coloured with a narrow darker band running down the midline. The nectaries in the northern populations are fairly large and green or less often purple-black. In the western and southern Karoo and the southern Cape, populations have greenish yellow or pale to middle brown tepal limbs, usually darker in the midline, and with small or medium-sized spots in the lower 1/3 or when brown then often with spots irregularly scattered across the limb and the margins sometimes slightly darker coloured. The claws are pale, usually with a darker streak in the midline and have a small dark nectary at the base or on the inner tepals, shortly above the base. Perianth colour can vary as much within a population as across the entire southern Cape and western Karoo. Ferraria variabilis is heteroploid, the northern populations are diploid, 2n = 20, whereas the southern are tetraploid, 2n = 40, this based on several counts across its range. A notable variant from the Olifants River Valley and adjacent mountains has leaves broader and more succulent than found elsewhere, up to 20-22 mm wide (versus typically 4-12 mm for most other populations), and the rest of the plant is also larger, thus the outer spathes are 50-70 mm long and the inner may reach 85 mm. Plants form circular mats in stony ground, which suggests spreading by vegetative means. Populations from the Tanqua Basin and nearby hills stand out in having the nectaries located in prominent pouches in the middle of the tepal claws, rather than at the bases of the claw. The anthers in these populations and some others from nearby have the anther thecae held ± parallel, although joined together only at the tips, as they are in plants from other parts of the range, which have widely diverging anther thecae.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: D. humile shares the non-succulent leaves and only slightly prominent fruit ribs with D. capense, D. grandicarpum, D. hispidum, D. perennans and D. tenue but is distinguished from these species by the broader ultimate leaflet segments 2-3 mm broad (< 1 mm in the other species). Among the other species mentioned, only the widespread D. hispidum is known to extend into the Eastern Cape. Dasispermum humile can be further differentiated from this species by the glabrous fruit, the fibrous ridges on the dorsal surface of the fruit ribs, and usually by the lack of involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Downie, SR; Magee, AR; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E. 2010. A taxonomic revision of the South African endemic genus Dasispermum (Apiaceae, Apioideae). S. African J. Bot. 76: 308-323. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2010); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Resembling Freesia caryophyllacea in its prostrate, ± obtuse leaves and early flowering but distinguished by the ± glaucous leaves with inconspicuous main vein but prominent submarginal vein, clearly visible in both fresh and dried leaves as a translucent line ± 0.5 mm in from the leaf margin.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With small, pale pink flowers, the outer tepals pale greenish pink on the outside and veined dark green, Hesperantha brevistyla has unusually small white anthers, 2.2-4.0 mm long and remarkably short, suberect style branches that reach only to the base or middle of the anthers, unlike the longer, spreading style branches typical of the genus Hesperantha brevistyla may be most closely allied to a second small-flowered Drakensberg species, H. exiliflora, which has pink flowers with a perianth tube 3.5-5.0 mm long, tepals 6-8 x ± 2.5 mm, yellow anthers 2.5-3.3 mm long, and style branches 3.0-3.5 mm long, reaching to between the middle of the anthers or just beyond their tips in the closed flower. The flowers of H. exiliflora dry purple whereas those of H. brevistyla dry pale pink.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A slender, rather delicate plant, Hesperantha debilis is recognised by the small corms 4-5 mm diam., soft-textured, linear leaves 1-2 mm wide, and a slender, branched stem bearing one or two flowers per branch. The white flowers have a short, straight perianth tube 4-5 mm long, and spreading tepals 12-14 mm long, thus more than twice as long as the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to the widespread Hesperantha pilosa and initially appearing to be a depauperate form of that species, H. glabrescens can be distinguished from its ally in several features. The leaves are sparsely hairy, unlike the fairly densely hairy or even downy leaves of H. pilosa, and the spikes are mostly 1- or rarely 2-flowered, whereas H. pilosa typically has several, sometimes up to 10 flowers per spike. Notable is the small size of the plants, only 30-50 mm high, shorter than recorded in H. pilosa. The flowers are magenta and quite small, with a perianth tube ± 3.5 mm long and tepals ± 8 mm long. Flowers of H. pilosa are always larger, usually white (subsp. pilosa) or blue or rarely deep pink (subsp. bracteolata), with a perianth tube mostly 6-8 mm long and tepals 9-16 mm long. The decision to recognise H. glabrescens was made in part because of the consistently different morphology from H. pilosa and because H. pilosa subsp. bracteolata grew nearby and was always taller, up to 120 mm high, and with 2 to 4 flowers per spike. These plants had plane, densely pilose leaf blades, in contrast to those of H. glabrescens. The flowers of the two species were, however, nearly identical in pigmentation and almost so in size at this site, although they could be distinguished by differences in perianth tube length.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Assigned to Hesperantha pilosa when first collected because it has sparsely hairy leaves, H. malvina actually bears little further resemblance to that species. The flowers are in general larger, with broadly elliptic tepals up to 14 mm long and 4-5 mm wide, while the leaves are linear-oblong and somewhat obtuse at the tips. In H. pilosa the tepals are seldom as long as 14 mm, rarely more than 3 mm wide, and the leaves are usually linear or linear-lanceolate and acute. The habitat, rocky sandstone cliffs, also differs from that of H. pilosa, which grows on granitic or sandy flats or lower slopes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Dasispermum perennans is vegetatively most similar to D. hispidum and D. suffruticosum but differs from D. hispidum in the perennial habit and permanent woody stem, and from D. siffruticosum in the subterete coriaceous, waxy green leaves (vs succulent, glaucous leaves in D. suffruticosum), papillose petals (vs glabrous) and fruit with only slightly prominent ribs (very prominently ribbed or winged in D. suffruticosum).
bibliographicCitation: Downie, SR; Magee, AR; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E. 2010. A taxonomic revision of the South African endemic genus Dasispermum (Apiaceae, Apioideae). S. African J. Bot. 76: 308-323. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2010); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the trailing stems, linear leaves up to 2.2 mm wide, and spikes of only 2 to 5 white flowers with tepals 11-16 mm long. The stamens are comparatively short, with filaments up to 3 mm long and anthers about 4 mm long. Hesperantha saxicola has been confused with H. leucantha, which has upright stems and smaller, pale pink flowers. A collection from Mt. Sheba, a short distance to the north of Long Tom Pass, appears to belong here but the flowers have tepals lightly flushed with purple outside, leaves less than 1 mm wide, a perianth tube about 7 mm long and tepals ± 11 mm long, smaller than in populations to the south.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Hespernatha sufflava at first appears to be intermediate between the common, usually white-flowered H. falcata and the rarer H. spicata, but at the type locality H. spicata grows together with H. sufflava and is obviously quite different in its secund spike of small, pure white flowers with slightly curved perianth tube 4-6 mm long and smaller tepals 4-7 mm long. Moreover, flowers of H. spicata open at about 18:30 when they release a strong, sweet, narcissus-like scent with a strong clove component. Flowers of H. sufflava are pale yellow and open at about 15:00 and have a quite different, slightly acrid, pyrethrum-like odour. Particularly unusual are the long style branches about 12 mm long that divide in the middle of the perianth tube, with only the upper 7 mm exserted. In nearly all Hesperantha species the style divides just below the mouth of the tube and not within its narrow part. Although easily confused with Hesperantha falcata the flowers of H. sufflava are somewhat smaller, with tepals 7-10 mm long but a substantially longer perianth tube, usually 12-16 mm long, and always longer than the tepals. In H. falcata the tepals are usually 12-18 mm long, exceptionally only 9-11 mm in southern Cape coastal populations, and the perianth tube is 4-9 mm long, thus usually shorter than the tepals. Apart from the flowers, H. sufflava is distinctive in always having only three leaves, all basal or the uppermost one subbasal, and the stem often has a branch produced from the axil of the upper leaf. Most populations of both H. spicata and H. falcata have three (rarely more) foliage leaves and one short, largely or entirely sheathing upper leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Glia pilulosa is distinguished by the pilulose vestiture of the leaf margins, veins and petioles as well as the small flowers and small fruits borne in extensive panicles. The lateral branches of the inflorescence almost invariably have the terminal umbel plus three lateral umbels in a racemose arrangement and not single as is often the case in G. prolifera and mostly (always?) in G. decidua (and some species of Anginon). The mericarps are isodiametric, resulting in a schizocarp that appears to be laterally compressed.
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM; Magee, AR. 2010. A revision of the genus Glia (Apiaceae, tribe Heteromorpheae). S. African J. Bot. 76: 259-271. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2010); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Flowers of subsp. anomala are usually smaller than those of subsp. bulbillifera with outer tepals rarely reaching 35 mm in length. The foliage leaf may be basal as in subsp. bulbillifera but is more often inserted shortly to well above the ground. Plants will on occasion produce one or two cormlets at some nodes, but this development is much less noticeable than in subsp. bulbillifera, where the many cormlets break through the bases of the sheathing leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Particularly variable, subsp. secunda usually has two foliage leaves and produces 1 to 3 long branches from the base. It may be a tall plant up to 600 mm high, but plants from the dry foothills of the Bokkeveld and Koebee Mtns may be only 200 mm high and have only a single leaf. Also unusual, flowers in these populations open later than elsewhere, usually after 16:30. Plants from dolerite outcrops in the Calvinia District may have up to four leaves and appear very different vegetatively.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The growth habit, corm tunics, characteristic branching with sticky internodes, and the free but parallel and coherent filaments all place Moraea simplex firmly in subg. Visciramosae but its simple filiform, apically stigmatic style branches extending outward between the top of the filaments, and short, suberect tepals claws ± 2 mm long are unique in the subgenus and remarkable in Moraea, in which just two species of subg. Polyanthes have similar style branches. Vegetatively, M. simplex may be mistaken for the common and widespread M. inconspicua in both habit and the short rhipidial spathes, but the flowers of M. inconspicua, although small, conform to the conventional type in the genus in their flattened style branches bearing paired erect, style crests.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species resembles T. muricata but the roots are few, tuberous and short. It differs from T. tortilis in that the root tubers are not fused, the leaves pubescent, the raceme much branched and the pedicels erect in fruit. The leaves may show some transverse folds when young.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: A mountain grassland species resembling T. saltii but distinguished by the long, reflexed tawny hairs, which are characteristic especially on the young racemes emerging from between the leaves. The thin, untidily straggling pedicels are also typical. In drying the plants usually turn black.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: Takes five or more years to reach the flowering stage.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA; Burges, EK. 1944. Retzia capensis Thunb. Fl. Pl. South Africa 24t.942 [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the relatively few (2 to 4), filiform leaves, submembranous bracts, and yellow or pale apricot-coloured flowers with narrowly funnel-shaped tube 10-13 mm long. Possibly most closely allied to Romulea malaniae, another species with few leaves and pedicels coiling in fruit but with smaller flowers with shorter perianth tube. Anatomically, the leaves are unusual in lacking secondary veins on either side of the main veins and in having a subdermal sclerenchyma layer joining the main and marginal bundles.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from the closely related I. purpurea and I. indica by its sepals with narrow elongate green tips much longer than the body and sepals which are hispid-pilose on the back, the hairs mostly with swollen bases.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Strumaria prolifera is easily recognized by its pink, funnel-shaped flowers, which enclose the stamens. Only two other species have similarly shaped flowers with short, included stamens, namely S. barbarae Oberm. from southern Namibia and the eastern Richtersveld, and S. pubescens W.F.Barker from the Roggeveld escarpment and Laingsburg District. Based on the stamen and style morphology, S. prolifera shows greatest affinity with S. barbarae, which belongs to subgenus Strumaria. In both species the filaments form a proximal tube up to 3-5 mm long and through the fusion of the outer stamens to the three-winged style base, the tube is divided into three separate hollows, where nectar collects from the peristylar pores on the ovary dome. Thus insects seeking nectar are forced to probe each hollow consecutively. Moreover, both species have drooping, scented flowers. The perigone in S. barbarae, however, is longer (28-38 mm) and mostly white when fresh, unlike the shorter (18-20 mm long), distinctly pink perigone in S. prolifera. More divergent is S. pubescens, belonging to subgenus Gemmaria, that has spreading to erect flowers in which all six stamens are adnate to the narrowly trigonous style base. Nectar therefore discharges and collects as three small droplets in the sinuses between the inner filaments and style.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 2005. Three new species and a new synonym in Strumaria (Amaryllidaceae: Amaryllideae) from southern Africa. Bothalia 35(1&2): 21-27. [CC BY]

description: Resembling Thereianthus minutus in the moderately long bracts 6-8 mm long and perianth tube 22-27 mm long but differing in the narrower, linear leaves less than 3 mm wide, the lower mostly longer than the stem, and in the purple perianth with concolorous anthers on relatively longer filaments 6-8 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to Trachyandra zebrina in the usually coiled leaves, large cataphylls (up to 30 mm long) and upcurved styles, but differs in that the cataphylls are not striped (transversely striped in T. zebrina), the leaves are transversely plicate (spirally coiled in T. zebrina), and the fruiting pedicels recurved.

description: Following Codd (1963); Kupicha (1985) recognised C. bispinosa subsp. bispinosa only, comprising both varieties described by Codd.
bibliographicCitation: Nicholas, A; Glen, M; Shuttleworth, A; Bester, SP. 2019. Apocynaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 321-417. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to C. bispinosa, but differs in the shorter and more rounded corolla lobes. The shorter and more elliptic-ovate leaves and the purple to black fruits are also helpful in separating C. haematocarpa.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1963. Apocynaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 244-296. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In habit, C. burchellii can be very similar to C. scabra; it is, however, easily distinguished by its ovaries/ fruits which have only one fertile ovule/seed.
bibliographicCitation: Puff, C. 1986. Paederiaceae, Anthospermae, Rubieae, Fl. S. Africa 31(1,2): 1-75. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209569#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Different in habit from the other species of this genus, and somewhat resembling Merciera brevifolia, A. DC. Buek, in describing it, noted it as “a singular plant, most likely constituting a distinct genus.” Harvey distinguished it as a Rubiacea, but, probably from want of good specimens, proceeded no further. The old specific name fits its present position; for it differs from its congeners by its 4 nearly equal calyx-lobes, and by its 6-7-lobed corolla. The peculiar hook with which the corolla-lobes are tipped is entirely on the upper, not on the underside.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H. 1896. Contributions to the flora of South Africa. J. Bot. 34: 16-25. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/35905#page/28/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: The 2 pendulous collateral ovules show affinity to Bulbinella, which it does resemble superficially. In Bulbinella however, the perianth is star-shaped and persistent whereas our species has a typical Trachyandra perianth, for in fading the segments fuse above the ovary, and it then drops off, where the pressure of the expanding capsule tears it apart. The species resembles T. tabularis but this species has a branched inflorescence and 6 ovules per cell to mention but a few differences.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: The rough woolly pubescence and the erect fruiting pedicel easily distinguish it from T. ciliata and T. hispida.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: Has long been confused with C. scabra, Sond (type Anthospermum scabrum, Thunb.) a species superficially very much like it. C. scabra has a 2-chambered ovary with two rugulose whitish-grey seeds, one in each chamber, the calyx lobes vary from 5 to 7 and the leaf pairs are only very shortly connate at the base.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1937. Notes on some species in the family Rubiaceae in the Cape Peninsula. J. S. African Bot. 3: 109-116. [https://archive.org/details/journalofsouthaf03unse/page/126] [CC BY]

description: The horned capsules are unusual.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1962. A revision of the South African species of Anthericum, Chlorophytum and Trachyandra. Bothalia 7(4): 669-767. [CC BY]

description: It differs from T. succulenta in its simple filiform trichomes (as opposed to the dendroid trichomes of T. succulenta), its laxer inflorescences and its pink flowers. It differs from T. media in its much smaller, crenate leaves (those of the former are 35-65 x 25-35 mm and entire), short petioles, congested panicles and lilac-pink corollas All have scentless, narrow corolla tubes about 20 mm in length with pilose hairs covering the inner surfaces around the lower style and ovary. The lower corolla lips are fleetingly porrect but soon become reflex, suggesting a hovering vector. Their anthers are exserted to about 5 mm. The flowers of T. succulenta are pale bluish mauve with darker spots and nectar guides on the petal lobes, T. media has lilac corollas with purple markings and the new species has lilac-pink flowers with purple markings.
