description: Aspalathus abbottii keys out to Dahlgren's informal group 33. Calcicolae. It is most similar to the Eastern Cape species Aspalathus frankenioides DC. and A. gerrardii H. Bol. (both grassland species from the Transkei area in Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal). The new species is characterised by its rigid spreading habit, few bright yellow flowers per flowering branchlet, glabrous bracts and bracteoles, densely villous yellowish green seasonal shoots and pale brown to tan older branches with a blackish lattice of peeled bark. A. frankenioides differs in its allopatric distribution, decumbent and ascending habit; shorter (20-50 cm) and fewer (less than 10) semi- incurving leaflets; pale lemon yellow flowers with purple shades; and hairy, linear-subulate shorter bracts (1.5-3.8 mm). A. gerrardii differs in its erect, cattail-like habit; greenish leaves, white woolly or sericeous branches; pale lemon flowers; and pubescent bracts and bracteoles. The other KwaZulu-Natal species are the widespread and very variable, multi-stemmed resprouter A. chortophila Eckl. & Zeyh.; A. simii Bolus, an erect, branched shrublet scattered from the Eastern Cape to coastal KwaZulu-Natal, and finally the widespread A. spinosa L., a rigid, erect to ascending spiny shrub. A. chortophila is easily separated by its distinct habit; spreading, glabrous (occasionally with scattered spreading hairs) leaflets; long floral 'pseudospikes' of many large bright yellow flowers; pubescent bracts, bracteoles, and keel blades; and narrow woolly fruits. A. spinosa is an erect to ascending shrub easily distinguished by its densely branched, rigid thorny and spiny stems; flattened leaflets; and stiff and rigid yellowish flowers with glabrous petals. A. simii is easily distinguished by its linear, needle-like leaves and terminal head-like umbels with small (up to 5 mm long) yellow flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Stirton, CH; Muasya, AM. 2011. Aspalathus abbottii (Fabaceae: Crotalarieae), a new species from KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 77: 675-679. [doi:10.1016/j.sajb.2011.02.006] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2011); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: A puzzling species of sect. Babiana, plants are nearly acaulescent and have blue flowers borne close to ground level, thus broadly resembling B. ambigua, from which B. arenicola differs markedly in having a fairly prominent hairy ovary, narrow, deeply pleated, stiff leaves 3-6 mm wide, and straight perianth tube, ± 30 mm long. The style is also unusual in dividing below or shortly above the base of the anthers into slender branches 5-6 mm long. By contrast, B. ambigua has firm, but less rigid leaves, 3-10 mm wide, a curved perianth tube, 10-19 mm long, wider in the throat, arched filaments, and the style dividing opposite the anther tips.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species shares the straight leaf rachis and pinnae, the branched resin ducts in the petals, and the broadly winged, elliptic to narrowly ovate fruits in dorsal view with Annesorhiza bracteosa, but can be distinguished by the reduced scale-like peduncular bracts (prominently foliose in A. bracteosa), the smaller involucel bracts, ? 2 mm long (? 4 mm long in A. bracteosa), and the acute to tridentate calyx lobes (calyx lobes truncate in A. bracteosa).
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Vessio, N. 2011. A taxonomic revision of the Annesorhiza triternata Group (Apiaceae, Apioideae): The transfer of Peucedanum triternatum and P. filicaule and the description of five new species. Syst. Bot. 36(2): 508-519. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/23029026] [All rights reserved]

description: Babiana gariepensis remains poorly collected and somewhat puzzling. The large bracts, 23-35 mm long, with the inner forked near the apex place B. gariepensis in sect. Teretifolieae. The broad, sparsely hairy, lightly plicate leaf and moderately long perianth tube, 20-22 mm long, with a sharp curve below the throat suggest a possible relationship with the central Namaqualand B. attenuata. The flowers seem distinctive also in the relatively long, narrow tepals, the dorsal 28-32 x 5 mm. Additional material in flower is needed to better understand this apparently rare southern Namibia and Richtersveld endemic.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species shares the ternately divided leaves, the 2- or 3-sect ultimate leaflets with linear segments, the unbranched resin duct in the petals and the winged marginal ribs of the fruits with A. filicaulis and A. radiata. It differs most notably from both of these species in the very prominent to narrowly winged dorsal ribs of the fruits (dorsal ribs filiform to somewhat evident in A. filicaulis and A. radiata). While the fruits are usually broadly winged and twice as long as broad, some poorly developed fruits may appear somewhat narrowly winged and therefore superficially similar to the geographically isolated A. filicaulis. However, in the latter the fruits are consistently narrowly winged and three times as long as wide. Annesorhiza laticostata can be further distinguished from A. radiata by the sub-erect unequally rayed umbels which as a result appear obtriangular in outline, the narrowly conical stylopodium and the fleshy pencil-like roots.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Vessio, N. 2011. A taxonomic revision of the Annesorhiza triternata Group (Apiaceae, Apioideae): The transfer of Peucedanum triternatum and P. filicaule and the description of five new species. Syst. Bot. 36(2): 508-519. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/23029026] [All rights reserved]

description: Annesorhiza elsiae shares the ternately divided leaves, 2- or 3-sect ultimate leaflets with linear segments and branched resin ducts in the petals with A. triternata but can be distinguished by the much branched synflorescence bearing more than 6 secondary and tertiary umbels all of which are composed of hermaphroditic flowers (as opposed to synnflorescence sparsely branched and consisting of a single primary umbel and up to 3 secondary umbels with the tertiary umbels, if present, composed of functionally male flowers in A triternata), the few rayed primary umbels with only 2 or 3 rays (4 to 18 cm A. triternata), and the marginally ribbed fruits (marginal ribs broadly winged in A. triternata).
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Vessio, N. 2011. A taxonomic revision of the Annesorhiza triternata Group (Apiaceae, Apioideae): The transfer of Peucedanum triternatum and P. filicaule and the description of five new species. Syst. Bot. 36(2): 508-519. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/23029026] [All rights reserved]

description: Resembling Babiana odorata in the relatively broad leaves and pale yellow flowers, B. noctiflora has a taller but inclined stem, up to 300 mm long, and inclined spike. The flowers stand out in having an elongate perianth tube 33-50 mm long, compared with 10-14 mm in B. odorata. It is also late flowering, from mid-September until mid-October, which contrasts with the early spring flowering of B. odorata in July and August. The flowers have the typical features of ser. Mucronatae, having inner bracts divided to the base, a densely hairy ovary and linear anthers. The flowers are adapted for pollination by night-flying moths and they remain open and scented all night.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the ± acaulescent habit, and radially symmetric, blue-mauve flowers with dry, membranous floral bracts with attenuate awn-like tips. It is most closely related to the taller, short-tubed B. scariosa, which has bilabiate flowers but similar dry floral bracts, also shared with long-tubed B. spathacea, both of which also occur in the immediate vicinity of Nieuwoudtville. The radially symmetric flower of B. papyracea is a striking contrast to the zygomorphic flowers of its two relatives.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: So named for the leaf blades narrowed below into a terete, petiole-like base above the sheaths, the remainder of the blades of Babiana petiolata are oblong to lanceolate. The distinctive leaves are inclined toward the ground and the blades are concave, especially when young or on immature plants, which have only one or two leaves versus three or four in mature individuals. The species is evidently most closely related to the widespread B. ambigua and is readily confused with this species. Both have the inner floral bracts divided to the base, and smooth ovary, and the underground part of the stem lacks a collar of fibres. It is distinguished from B. ambigua by the consistently pseudopetiolate leaves with smooth or sparsely papillate to scabrid blades, small flowers with a perianth tube ± 11 mm long, a pleasing Iris-like scent, and its early flowering time, mainly late June and July. Leaves of B. ambigua often appear petiolate but the apparently narrow base of the blade is actually the leaf sheath extending upward, and is normally clasping the leaf above; the blades are also obviously pleated and usually prominently hairy. The larger flowers have a tube 12-19 mm long and a spicy, acrid scent with undertones of violet. Babiana ambigua extends from Strandfontein north of Lambert’s Bay to Riversdale in the southern Cape and co-occurs with B. petiolata near Lambert’s Bay and then their differences become evident.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Striking in its deep violet flowers, Babiana rigidifolia is recognised by the elongate perianth tube, 45-50 mm long, lower tepals joined to the upper laterals and forming a prominent lip 5-7 mm long, and rigid, velvety to almost smooth leaves with pungent tips. The leaves are fairly broad, up to 16 mm wide, strongly pleated and are held in a tight, erect fan. With their firm tips the leaves recall those of the Namaqualand B. dregei, but that species has smooth to glabrescent leaves with cartilaginous hyaline veins and margins and a particularly horny, pungent tip. The flowers are similar but somewhat smaller, with the dorsal tepal 18-28 x 8-10 mm, and the lower lateral tepals have prominent white median blotches. On drying, the major veins and margins of the leaves of B. rigidifolia appear prominent and hyaline, plants then even more closely resembling those of B. dregei.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The affinity is with T. laxa from which it is easily distinguished by the absence of tubercles from the calyx-tube which is remarkable for its furrowed surface.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: Usually acaulescent Babiana tanquana is distinguished by the almost plane leaves with light pubescence on the blade surface and long-hairy on the margins, a spike borne at or shortly above ground level, and flowers with dark purple upper tepals, pale lilac on the edges, and the pale yellow lower lateral tepals. The inner floral bracts are forked only near the apices and the ovary is hairless. Babiana tanquana most closely resembles the western Karoo B. salteri in general aspect, particularly the broad leaves held obliquely to the sheaths and short spike, but that species has inner bracts divided to the base and a densely hairy ovary. The attractive flowers have a distinctive acrid-musky scent characteristic of several other species of the genus. Babiana tanquana keys closest to B. minuta, the tepals of which also have pale margins, but this species has narrow leaves and the inner bracts shorter than the outer, whereas in B. tanquana the inner bracts exceed the outer by 2-5 mm. The species remains poorly documented.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is similar to L. procumbens H. Bol. but differs from this species by the less woody habit, the long inflorescence axis, the widely spaced bracts, the fusion of the bracts to the pedicels and by the upper lobes of the calyx. The upper lobes of L. difformis are much shorter than the lower three (upper lobes are similar to the lower ones in L. procumbens and in all other species of Lipozygis). It is also similar to L. It is also similar to L. corymbosa (E. Mey.) Benth. and related species, but differs from these by the structure of the inflorescence, the very large foliaceous bracts, the large bracteoles and the structure of the calyx as mentioned above.
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E. 1989. Studies in the genus Lotononis (Crotalarieae, Fabaceae). VIII. A new species of the L. corymbosa group and notes on the taxonomy of the section Lipozygis. S. African J. Bot. 55(5): 528-532. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1989); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Allied to T. laxa, but distinguished by its hispid leaves and ovate petals. Upper parts of the plant resemble the more slender growths of Lycopodium clavatum L.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: Colchicum asteroides is clearly allied to C. roseum, with which it shares a multifoliate, rosette habit and more or less flat or shallowly concave tepal limbs lacking prominent basal auricles. It is distinguished from C. roseum by the broader, lanceolate leaves with the blades usually at least 10 mm wide towards the base and smaller, pure white flowers that do not protrude much above the crown of the plant. The tepal claws are oblong, 6-8 mm long and the limbs ovate, 8-9 x 4-6 mm. A roseum is characterized by linear-lanceolate leaves up to 5 mm wide and pinkish or pink-streaked flowers that protrude conspicuously above the crown of the plant. The tepal claws are narrowly oblong, 10-12 mm long and the narrowly oblong-elliptic limbs are 13-16 x 3-4 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2001. Colchicaceae: A remarkable new species of Androcymbium from Northern Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 31(2): 203-205. [CC BY]

description: The affinity is with L. myrtoides from which it differs in the calyx-lobes being more united and the petals less united. In this and other species of the genus Lonchostoma the ovary is incompletely bilocular; the loculi being incompletely closed on the adaxial face. This is best seen on separating the loculi.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: The affinity is with N. fragarioides from which it is distinguished by much smaller differently shaped hairy calyx-lobes, much smaller floral parts, and by the almost total absence of hairs from the top of the ovary.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: The affinity is with R. stokoei from which it is distinguished by the glabrous calyx-tube and longer styles.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: The nearest affinity is with P. cordata from which it differs by the leaves normally having a more convex lower surface, the calyx-lobes being more united, and by much longer petals.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: Hall (2001) regards this taxon as a subspecies of Brunia (= Raspalia) angulata (E.Mey. ex Sond.) Class.-Bockh. & E.G.H.Oliv. from SW Cape, but molecular analyses place them in 2 well-separated clades; a detailed investigation of the taxa is urgently needed.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Classen-Bockhoff, R. 2019. Bruniaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 715-718. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The affinity is with R. microphylla Brongn. from which it is distinguished by longer, differently shaped and ascending leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: This species and R. oblongifolia, the species following next, are distinguished from all others by their leaf-characters.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: The most striking is the three-lobed lip. The lateral lobes of the lip combine with the basal anticous petal lobes in forming a “platform” flanking the stigma, rather similar to the situation in Disa purpurascens Bolus.
bibliographicCitation: Hitchcock, AN; Linder, HP. 2006. Disa remota, a remarkable new orchid species from the Western Cape. S. African J. Bot. 72: 627-629. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2006); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Remarkably luxuriant growth occasionally appears on plants of normal growth producing erect-spreading leaves up to 7 mm. long, less concave on the ventral surface and more pilose on the dorsal surface.
bibliographicCitation: Pillans, NS. 1947. A revision of Bruniaceae. J. S. African Bot. 13: 121-203. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the stellate, fugacious white flowers on long pedicels 15-18 mm long, with anthers 3 mm long and connivent in a tight cone around the style, and the filaments 3.5 mm long and connate for most of their length into a staminal collar 2.5 mm long. The leaves are 1.5-3.0 mm wide, semiterete and shallowly channelled above and lightly grooved beneath. The inflorescence is persistent and photosynthetic long after the seeds are dispersed. Superficially similar Drimia cyanelloides has softer, linear, keeled leaves 3-8 mm wide, shorter pedicels 7-8 mm long, and slightly shorter filaments free to the base with much longer anthers 5-6 mm long. The inflorescence in D. cyanelloides is not persistent after the seeds are shed and the flowers last two days.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Gasteria tukhelensis grows prolifically from the base, forming clusters on the sheer southwest-facing cliffs above the northern bank of the Tukhela River, east of Ngubevu near Kranskop, and is distinguished from G. Batesiana by its much larger rosettes of falcate, dark green leaves, often becoming recurved, with a shiny, faintly spotted surface and by its leaf margin which is minutely denticulate to almost entire. Furthermore, the perianth of G. tukhelensis is 40-43 mm long in contrast to the shorter, 35-40 mm long perianth found in G. batesiana. The slender pedicels are 10-17 mm long, compared to 6-12 mm in G. batesiana. The fruiting capsules also differ from those of G. batesiana, being more slender and 23-32 mm long compared to 16-20 mm in G. batesiana. The inflorescence may be a simple raceme with up to 11 flowers opening at the same time, but with a pair of side branches in adult plants. G. tukhelensis is distinguished from G. pendulifolia by its shiny leaf surface, slightly tuberculate when young. Its long, slender perianth comes closest to G. acinacifolia from the coastal Eastern Cape and the eastern extreme of Western Cape.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2005. Asphodelaceae: Gasteria tukhelensis, a new species form KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Bothalia 35(2): 164-166. [CC BY]

description: Ledebouria cremnophila is related to the widespread L. revoluta, a species which also has purple-spotted, spreading, lanceolate leaves, flaccid inflorescences and well-developed bracts and bracteoles. The new species is at once distinguished by three prominent features: the bulbs are semi-epigeous to epigeous; the bulbs are cylindrical with hard, dark brown bulb scales; and the filiform floral bracts form a distinct coma which is very prominent in the young inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, S; Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2006. Ledebouria cremnophila (Hyacinthaceae), a new cliff-dwelling succulent bulbous species from the Barberton region, South Africa. Aloe 43(4): 78-79. [All rights reserved]

description: Ledebouria venteri is related to L. concolor. Both are evergreen species, with epigeous bulbs and fleshy leaves without spots, usually confined to cliff faces and steep slopes. The new species is at once distinguished by its succulent, unspotted, linear-lanceolate leaves with a white, minutely denticulate margin and tepals that are free and fully reflexed. The flowers of L. venteri are much smaller than those of L. concolor and the flower stalks, stamens and stigma are distinctly maroon-red. L. concolor, on the other hand, is a much larger species, its leaves are ovate-lanceolate, with a distinctly undulating margin, and the tepals are much larger, fused at the base and reflexed only towards the tip.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2006. Ledebouria venteri (Hyacinthaceae), a new cliff-dwelling species from the Gouritz River, Western Cape. Aloe 43(4): 75-77. [All rights reserved]

description: The short lower lip, from which the specific epithet is derived, and the broadly obtrullate upper lip are distinctive characteristics.
bibliographicCitation: Edwards, TJ. 2005. Two new Plectranthus species (Lamiaceae) and new distribution records from Pondoland Centre of Plant Endemism, South Africa. Bothalia 35(2): 149-152. [CC BY]

description: Plectranthus porcatus is distinguished from all other southern African Plectranthus species by its peculiarly ribbed stems. The origin of these ridges is not clear, but they appear to be associated with the petiole base. A possible explanation is that they are protruding bundle sheaths associated with deeper-lying leaf traces. Its raised leaf scars are quite distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Winter, PJD. 2005. Lamiaceae: Plectranthus porcatus, a new species endemic to the Sekhukhuneland Centre of Plant Endemism, Limpopo Province, South Africa. Bothalia 35(2): 169-173. [CC BY]

description: L. globulosa is similar to L. pentaphylla (E. Mey.) Benth. and L. bolusii Dummer but differs in the very large, broadly ovate bracts, the slightly larger flowers, the suborbicular (not oblong) standard petal and in the consistently 3-foliolate leaves (always at least some leaves 5-foliolate in L. pentaphylla and L. bolusii). It is particularly similar to L. laticeps B-E. van Wyk, but differs from this species in the globose (not discoid) inflorescences, the larger bracts, the more hirsute vestiture, the longer standard petal, the wider calyx lobes and the two upper calyx lobes, which are wider than the lower lobes (upper lobes as wide as the lower lobes in L. laticeps).
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E. 1990. Studies in the genus Lotononis (Crotalarieae, Fabaceae). 9. Four new species of the L. pentaphylla group, section Lipozygis. Bothalia 20(1): 1-7. [CC BY]

description: Allied to L. polycephalum, of which it has the inflorescence and calyx, but from which it remarkably differs in pubescence, in the shape of the vexillum, the long earlike appendages of the lower petals, and in minor characters.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1862. Leguminosae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Leguminosae to Loranthaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 2: 1-285. Lovell Reeve & Co. Ltd., London. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.821] [All rights reserved]

description: L. longicephala is a distinct species with no obvious affinities. It is similar to L. pentaphylla and L. bolusii, but differs from these and all related species in the consistently 3-foliolate leaves, the much smaller and oblong (not globose or discoid) heads, the much smaller flowers and the much smaller pods. It differs from L. globulosa and L. laticeps also in the inconspicuous, linear bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E. 1990. Studies in the genus Lotononis (Crotalarieae, Fabaceae). 9. Four new species of the L. pentaphylla group, section Lipozygis. Bothalia 20(1): 1-7. [CC BY]

description: Together with H. canescens and H. linearis, the three species form a closely related group with almost identical floral characters and small inconspicuous bracts. H. canescens may be distinguished on the basis of the dense, short and often crisped pubescence on stems and leaves and is distributed more on the high plateau formed by the northern Cape and south-western and central Transvaal, but extending to eastern Transvaal (where the two may overlap), Swaziland and Natal. In H. linearis the leaves are linear to filiform and the leaves and stems are glabrous or with a few scattered long hairs. It overlaps with H. petrensis in Angola, Zimbabwe, S.W.A./Namibia and Botswana and occasional intermediates may be found.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Resembles H. elliottii in the entire, grey tomentose leaves and the entire (or almost entire) stigma, but the calyx and corolla are considerably larger and the stamens well exserted.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Diagnostic features are the linear, subglabrous leaves and the subglabrous to sparingly villous stems which have a somewhat varnished appearance. See also notes after H. canescens and H. petrensis.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: It is sometimes confused with another dwarf grassland species, H. thorncroftii, but the latter usually has narrower leaves, 4-6-flowered verticils, and a persistent coma of colourful bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Allied to H. rugosifolia but has smaller, more ovate leaves, smaller, less conspicuous apical bracts and whiter, more dendroid pubescence. In H. rugosifolia the pubescence consists mostly of short, simple hairs with a few stellate hairs intermingled.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: An anomalous species with narrow corolla tube and persistent bracts similar to those of H. pretoriae but the upper bracts are colourful; the upper stamens are attached near the base of the corolla tube and the filaments are pubescent for almost their whole length; and the filaments of the lower pair of stamens are united for only about 0.5 mm at the base.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Very distinct by its long narrow flowers and its long-stalked ovary. In the only flower I dissected the stipes was 1 x 3 centim. in length. The whole plant is a silvery white, and the flowers light yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H. 1889. Contributions to South-African botany.-Part IV (with a revised list of published species of extra-tropical South-African Orchids). J. Linn. Soc., Bot. 25(170): 156-210. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/8381#page/210/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: An anomalous species in which the bracts subtending the verticils are persistent and leaf-like, the corolla tube and lips are relatively long and narrow resembling Orthosiphon, and the upper two stamens are included in the corolla tube. However, the united lower stamens, which are shortly exserted, and the large upper tooth of the calyx, indicate that it belongs in Hemizygia.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Closely related to the previous species, H. modesta, but grows at lower altitudes forming a taller soft shrub up to 1.2 m tall, and tends to have smaller flowers. It superficially resembles the small-leaved form of H. transvaalensis, but the latter has 4-6-flowered verticils and a persistent coma of colourful bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: L. solitudinis superficially resembles one-flowered forms of L. prostrata, Benth. and L. varia, Steud., but the entire glabridity of the plant easily distinguishes it from either; the stipules are also very minute, while the calyx is comparatively short; its isolated inland distribution from a section, which is more or less geographically confined to the coastal regions, has suggested the specific name. Like L. macrocarpa, Eckl. and Zeyh., the plant dries a dark brown or black.
bibliographicCitation: Dummer, RA. 1913. A synopsis of the species of Lotononis, Eckl. and Zeyh., and Pleiospora, Harv. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 3: 275-336. [All rights reserved]

description: L. acuticarpa is similar to L. calycina (E. Mey.) Benth. but differs in the smaller habit and leaves, the much smaller and narrower flowers and particularly in the shape and size of the fruit. The fruit are much longer than the calyx (as long as the calyx in L. calycina), flat (not turgid as in L. calycina) and the apices are acute and curved upwards (not obtuse and curved downwards as in L. calycina). It is also similar to L. adpressa N. E. Br. but differs from this species in the smaller and annual habit, the glabrous adaxial surface of the leaflets and in the much longer, more acute and slightly falcate fruit.

description: See also the closely related H. subvelutina for differences between the two. These two species have certain characteristics which set them apart from most other species, for example: the simple, not branched inflorescence; the leaf-like bracts which persist for the entire length of the inflorescence; the tubular corolla tube; and the shortly exserted stamens. Somewhat similar characteristics are shown by H. pretoriae in which the two upper stamens are not exserted, and H. persimilis, in which the bracts, though persistent, are more colourful.

description: Dried specimens may be confused with those of the tropical Asian species J. humile which is also found in cultivation. The flowers of J. humile, however, are yellow and the leaves alternate.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The two species J. fluminense and J. angulare are closely related and are best distinguished from each other by the very small calyx of J. fluminense, usually not over 2 mm long, its broad inflorescence borne clear of the leaves, and short pedicels. The distribution is distinct, J. fluminense being a tropical species reaching only as far south as the north eastern Transvaal and northern Zululand (Ingwavuma) whereas J. angulare occurs commonly in the Cape and as far north as Volksrust in the Transvaal and Utrecht in Natal.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very variable perennial, erect or prostrate, easily recognised by the winged stem and branches, and the cylindraceous capsule. Leaves subfleshy, 1-2 inches long, the upper much smaller. Flowers blue, small. Calyx glabrous or pubescent. Capsule 4-6 lines long.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Zaluzianskya regalis is an annual herb with retrorsely-haired stems and relatively large, dark pink to deep magenta flowers marked in the mouth with a yellow star surrounded by conspicuous red diamonds. The perianth tube is 35-40 mm long and covered in long, soft, acute hairs mixed with minute, gland-tipped hairs, and both pairs of stamens are usually developed. The retrorse hairs on the stem of Zaluzianskya regalis are diagnostic of a small group of closely allied species in subsection Zaluzianskya centred on the Roggeveld and Hantam Plateau. Z. regalis is distinguished in the alliance by having the largest and brightest flowers, with a corolla tube 30-40 mm long, limb 15-18 mm in diameter, and style 30-35 mm long. The dark pink or magenta limb is boldly marked with a starshaped yellow patch around the mouth, the rays bifid and extending shortly up the sinuses to enclose a conspicuous dark red diamond- or spade-shaped patch that covers most of the shaft of each corolla lobe. Both Z. pilosissima and Z. violacea have smaller, pink or pale mauve flowers with inconspicuous red flecks around the yellow eye (occasional pale yellow-flowered plants with a darker eye have also been recorded in Z. violacea). The corolla tube in both species is 10-25 mm long, the limb 7-12 mm in diameter, and the style 9-18 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2010. Two new species of Limoselleae from western South Africa: Trieenia occulta and Zaluzianskya regalis. Bothalia 40(1): 84-90. [https://doi.org/10.4102/abc.v40i1.195] [CC BY]

description: Perennial, rigid, stronger than L. setacea, 1-2 feet and more high, branched in the upper part. Leaves filiform, callous at the apex, 4-6 lines long. Pedicels 2-3 lines long, often shorter, rarely longer, erect. Calyx-lobes 1.5-2 lines long. Corolla blue; lobes oblong. Anthers hairy, hirsute at the apex. Capsule as large as a pea.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Species nova ab Lobelia thermali Thunb. caulibus manifeste alatis ascendentibus et foliis 15-22 mm longis inciso-dentatis dentibus patentibus differt. The new species is characterized mainly by its ascending, distinctly winged stems which are not rooting at the nodes, its longer leaves with longer, more outwardly directed and often recurved teeth (hence the specific epithet), and its usually somewhat smaller flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Thulin, M. 1983. Some tropical African Lobeliaceae. Chromosome numbers, new taxa and comments on taxonomy and nomenclature. Nord. J. Bot. 3(3): 371-382. [DOI: 10.1111/j.1756-1051.1983.tb01952.x] [All rights reserved]

description: Characteristic features of W. capensis are the small size of the plant and the flowers, the few-flowered narrow spike, and the peculiarly hooked styles, which are unique in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: The new species is no doubt close to W. angustifolia, but differs, inter alia, in leaf-shape. Instead of being flat with inrolled margins, the basalleaf is thickish and sometimes almost semiterete with a concave upper surface, i.e. more or less reniform in transect. The cauline leaves are also more or less semiterete above the broader basal portion. The spike is few-flowered with somewhat larger flowers than in W. angustifolia and with more spreading segments. The perianth is almost pure white without nectar blotches. The anthers are purplish red to brown and somewhat larger than the yellow anthers of W. angustifolia. Finally, the pistil is more oblong with less recurved and more slender styles with smaller stigmas.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1978. The genus Wurmbea in Africa except the Cape region. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 36(2): 211-233. [CC BY-SA]

description: Unusual in its small size and especially in floral morphology, the tepals being connate only basally and not forming a distinct tube.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: A very distinct species, by the creeping stems, the habit of Veronica agrestis, and the variable size of calyx-lobes. Root annual. Stems 0.3 m [as '1 ft.'] and more long; branches shorter. Leaves 3-5 lines long, 3-4 lines wide, obtuse, crenate; upper sometimes oblong. Peduncles 1 inch and more long, hairy or glabrous. Calyx-lobes lanceolate-subulate, 1.5 line long, and ovate, 2-3 lines long, 1 line wide in the same branch. Corolla blue; tube pale or whitish. Anthers hairy, the 2 lower bearded.

description: The pink flowers with distinctly exserted stamens are unique in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: Many perennial stems, 0.5-1 foot high, more or less branched, sometimes simple. Leaves 0.5-1 inch long. Pedicels 6-8 lines long. Flowers blue, 0.5 inch long, lobes oval or elliptical. Anthers hirsute at the apex, hairy on the back. Very near L. linearis and only distinguished by the hemispherical, obtuse calyx-tube.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: This small-flowered and rather inconspicuous species is characterized by the creamy to greenish white perianth with more or less erect segments. They have usually purple marks close to the pocket-shaped nectary, and the anthers are always small and yellow. The leaves are narrowly elongate and normally straight, and the solitary basal leaf has inrolled flat margins, which are finely scabrid with little protuberances.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1978. The genus Wurmbea in Africa except the Cape region. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 36(2): 211-233. [CC BY-SA]

description: Closely resembling the southwestern Cape W. gracilis, with which C. nutans shares nodding flowers with apically connivent anthers dehiscing through introrse, subapical pores and sometimes prickly stems, pedicels and abaxial leaf midribs but distinguished by its free-standing, mostly unbranched stems, leaves without tendril-like tips, and unmarked, white or pink to pale blue tepals. The stems, pedicels and underside of the leaf midribs may be smooth or variously armed with recurved prickles but these are more delicate, almost bristle-like and mostly < 1 mm long, and the anthers are mostly yellow, with the purple and grey banding restricted to the apical third. This contrasts with W. gracilis, which has well-branched stems, more robust prickles 1.0-1.5 mm long, the upper leaves distinctly cirrhose and drawn into coiled, tendril-like tips, white tepals marked with a purple blotch at the base, and anthers that are yellow only in the lower half. The presentation of the flowers is also subtly different in the two species. The pedicels in W. nutans are essentially suberect up to the level of insertion of the bracteole in the upper third or quarter, at which point the pedicels are sharply decurved, whereas the bracteoles in W. gracilis are mostly inserted ± midway along the pedicels, which are therefore more arcuate. The seeds of W. gracilis are also distinctive in being essentially smooth in the basal half (apart from the trichome-tufts) with a dense apical cluster of suasage-like papillae, unlike those of W. nutans, which are entirely papillate, with the apical papilla only slightly longer.

description: Perennial 1 foot or more high. Branches filiform. Leaves 0.5-1 inch long and wide. Petiole as long or longer than the leaf, ciliolate. Raceme 2-6-flowered. Calyx-tube 1 line long. Corolla blue or whitish. Capsule hemispherical, half superior.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Easily recognized on its stellate purple flowers. It can only be confused with another purple-flowered species, W. recurva. The eastern populations (from Caledon to Rivers-dale) tend to have narrower and more acuminate perianth segments, longer filaments and smaller anthers, and also narrower leaves than specimens from the western parts of the distribution area. The largest flowers are found in the Mamre area in Malmesbury Division.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: A rigid shrub, 1-1.5 ft. Stem nodulose, leafless at the base; branches closely leafy. Leaves imbricate, 0.5-1 inch long, nearly 1 line wide, upper ones smaller. Peduncles 1-2 inches long, rarely longer, 1-3-flowered. Calyx-tube short; lobes 1.5 lines long. Corolla blue; lobes of the lower lip oval or obovate.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Recognizable by the lax spike with truncate perianth tubes and narrow, rather widely separated segments. It may be confused with W. hiemalis, which differs by the denser spike and the perianth segments being closer and margined down to the base. In W. monopetala the perianth segments are characteristically margined in the distal two-thirds only. Another distinct feature of W. monopetala is the swollen and somewhat spongy inside of the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: 1-1.5 foot high, more slender than L. spartioides and leafy. Leaves about 1 inch long, not 1.5 line wide, acute, quite entire or minutely denticulated towards the apex. Racemes forming a terminal panicle. Pedicels 4-5 lines long. Calyx acute at the base 10-nerved, 1 line long; lobes 4-times shorter than the blue corolla, which has oval lobes. Capsule broadly ovate-turbinate, longer than the erect calyx-lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: This rare and little known species possesses some unique features, such as the long and much exserted filaments and styles. It somewhat resembles W. elongata, but the spike is twice as broad, the flowers much larger, and the stamens often overtopping the perianth segments. The dark and thickish margins of the segments are reminiscent of W. spicata var. ustulata.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: Clearly allied to W. marginata, with which it shares the red or deep purple perianth with contrasting yellow anthers. The spike is narrower, however, due to the smaller perianth with shorter and re-flexed segments. There is some variation in flower colour, from deep purple or red to a lighter brownish tinge. The light colour in some forms may be due to introgression from other species, such as W. inusta, which apparently hybridizes with W. recurva, occasionally forming hybrid swarms.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: The long perianth tube is very characteristic, although there is considerable variation in its length. One of the more showy species, and it also has a sweet and pleasant scent.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: A characteristic species with moderately dense spikes, usually easily recognized on the rather long perianth tube (though shorter than in W. dolichantha). Furthermore the perianth has nearly always small spots of a brownish-orange colour. These speckles are elongated on the perianth tube and more rounded on the segments. The dots are most easily seen in mature flowers and especially on dried material. The perianth tube is variable in length, but usually somewhat longer than the segments or about equal in length. The species may be confused with W. dolichantha, which has a distinctly longer, concolorous tube.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1986. The genus Wurmbea (Colchicaceae) in the Cape region. Opera Bot. 87: 5-41. [All rights reserved]

description: Amphistomatic and dorsiventral with two to three layers of long palisade cells containing long rectangular crystals, spongy tissue between lateral vascular bundles with thickened walls; adaxial surface slightly undulated, inconspicuous median adaxial groove and narrow abaxial furrows. Epidermis with upright cells, on adaxial side generally with thickened walls, on abaxial side only outer wall thickened, within furrows with coronulate and (towards furrow opening) cylindrical papillae; hypodermis with one layer of slightly thickened prismatic cells; small cells between bundle sheath and sclerenchyma girder with cubical crystals; sunken leaf glands few or absent.

description: Xerophyta longicaulis shares all anatomical characters with X. viscosa, but is distinct by its longer decumbent stem, length of stigma relative to style, and its rbcL sequence.
bibliographicCitation: Behnke, HD; Hummel, E; Hillmer, S; Sauer-Gurth, H; Gonzalez, J; Wink, M. 2013. A revision of African Velloziaceae based on leaf anatomy characters and rbcL nucleotide sequences. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 172: 22-94. [All rights reserved]

description: Blades amphistomatic, only weakly dorsiventral with two layers of small palisade cells (cell length about 1.5 times their width), amphistomatic; lateral vascular bundles with partial abaxial Y- or ?-shaped girder.
bibliographicCitation: Behnke, HD; Hummel, E; Hillmer, S; Sauer-Gurth, H; Gonzalez, J; Wink, M. 2013. A revision of African Velloziaceae based on leaf anatomy characters and rbcL nucleotide sequences. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 172: 22-94. [All rights reserved]

description: Corolla up to 6 mm diameter at the mouth; corolla lobes up to 1.5 mm long; anthers about 1 mm long; capsule up to 10 mm long; teeth sometimes present on lowest third of leaf margin.
bibliographicCitation: Phillipson, PB. 1986. Taxonomy of Monopsis (Lobeliaceae): M.simplex, M.debilis and a new species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 93(4): 329-341. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is closely related to the European Z. noltii Hornem. and could perhaps be considered a southern population as suggested by Dandy. The two taxa are however completely isolated. The African plants appear to be larger, the leaf apex is asymmetrical, the retinacula are broader and the testa of the nut is distinctly striate. Z. nana Roth is an illegitimate name for Z. noltii Hornem.
bibliographicCitation: Obermeyer, AA. 1966. Order: Helobiae. In: LE Codd, B De Winter & HB Rycroft (eds), Fl. S. Africa 1: 56-112. BRI & Nat. Bot. Gdns, Pretoria & Cape Town. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209551#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The species M. heterophylla occurs plentifully in central Texas and southwards to certain areas in Mexico. D. Oliver writes in 1884 that N. E. Brown of Kew was the first to identify the South African plants with the Texan species. In 1932 Steyermark in his 'Revision of Menodora' agrees that the South African specimens are not specifically distinct but owing to certain morphological differences he describes them as a variety of the New World species. The main difference is in the size of the leaves, which in the Texan plants are up to 4 cm long and 3 cm broad while in our plant they are seldom even half that size. In South Africa this variety is very close to M. africana and differs principally in the leaves being lobed rather than bipinnatisect, and the segments not being subulate. The calyx segments are usually simple and only occasionally lobed, instead of being usually multipartite; the habit also is rather more erect and rigid. But owing to the variation in size and shape of the leaves of M. heterophylla var. australis, it is not always easy at first sight to distinguish between it and M. africana.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Habitat and distribution information based on Acocks 16269 and Galpin 5772 (PRE), quoted by Jessop (1976) as Drimiopsis maxima Baker. Description according to Jessop (1976).

description: The lower leaves of M. scabra sometimes become distinctively deflexed and incurved, whereas in the other species of the genus the lower leaves are normally erect or spreading. Fruiting pedicels deflexed near the middle; capsules inverted, subglobose; fertile nodes often clustered along the stem; hypanthium and sepals usually with 1 mm long hairs; corolla 10-19 mm long ochreous yellow.

description: Monopsis unidentata subsp. laevicaulis is distinctive within the genus with its thick erect stems commonly reaching 400 mm in height, sub-whorled linear leaves, and brownish corolla lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Phillipson, PB. 1989. Taxonomy of Monopsis (Lobeliaceae): M. scabra and M. unidentata. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 99(3): 255-272. [https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1095-8339.1989.tb00403.x] [All rights reserved]

description: This is a very variable species and a number of forms sometimes exist side by side. It has not been deemed practicable to subdivide the species.

description: Calyx and capsule sub-globose; calyx lobes usually reflexed at anthesis; leaf margins strongly thickened on abaxial surface It is usually quite distinct from the other varieties with its sub-globose calyx and capsule, and characteristic leaf margin.
bibliographicCitation: Phillipson, PB. 1986. Taxonomy of Monopsis (Lobeliaceae): M.simplex, M.debilis and a new species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 93(4): 329-341. [All rights reserved]

description: The branchlets of O. exasperata are rough with numerous raised lenticels and prominent leaf-scars. Its leaves resemble those of O. africana in the tendency for the margins to roll backwards but the lower surface in O. exasperata appears minutely and densely pitted, not scaly as in O. africana. The terminal inflorescence of O. exasperata is another distinguishing character between these two species.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is very close to A. inapertus subsp. intermedius, but the very short tube precludes it from being placed in that species.
bibliographicCitation: Leighton, FM. 1965. The genus Agapanthus L'Héritier. J. S. African Bot.: 1-50. [CC BY]

description: But closely related to the tropical African species O. welwitschii (Knobl.)Gilg. & Schellenb., O. hochstetteri Bak. and O. guineensis (Gilg)Gilg & Schellenb.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The cultivated olive, O. europaea L and its subspecies and varieties, have most of the characteristics of O. africana and is distinguished by the larger, broad-based and more fleshy fruits. These features may have come about through ages of selection and cultivation but they are today established and reproduced in the progeny. Some authorities suggest that O. africana in the broadest source of the cultivated olive, but others favour treating O. ferruginea Royle, an Asian from O. africana and look upon it as the possible ancestor.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species is readily distinguished by the bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the genera Prismatocarpus and Roella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 93-166. [CC BY]

description: Albuca caudata can be easily identified by its bulb mostly solitary covered by brownish papery scales usually disposed at different heights and bearing long thick tuberose roots, its long and narrow canaliculate or infolded leaves, its inclined raceme, with usually all pedicels patent and erect, giving a unilateral appearance to the inflorescence, and its white erect flowers with a median green stripe.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB; Dold, AP; Barker, NP. 2011. The identity of Albuca caudata Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae) and a description of a new related species: A. bakeri. PhytoKeys 5: 5-19. [doi: 10.3897/phytokeys.5.1166] [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the short leaves, the rigid toothed bracts and calyx lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the genera Prismatocarpus and Roella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 93-166. [CC BY]

description: It differs in the larger leaves; squarrose or reflexed bracts; hairy calyx, and more deeply lobed corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1951. A revision of the genera Prismatocarpus and Roella. J. S. African Bot. 17: 93-166. [CC BY]

description: Allied to W. robusta, Sond., according to the description, but differs in having sessile leaves widened at the base and usually lobed, the corolla-tube 2-3 times as long as the segments, and the calyx-segments sometimes much longer than the valves of the capsule. The corolla is a deep blue and very fugitive (fide Dr J. Muir).
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, HML. 1915. Novitates Africanae. Ann. Bolus Herb. 1: 185-197. [https://archive.org/stream/annalsofbolusher01pear#page/185/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: It is distinguished from the closely related W. virgata by its 3-locular ovary and larger leaves, and differs from W. androsacea by its absence of a basal leaf-rosette, its reticulate testa and by the position of the stylar glands. However, in South Africa the situation is more complicated. Several related forms occur and a large number of names, especially from the work of von Brehmer, have been applied to them. Characters like a 2-locular or almost superior ovary, leaves approaching the form of W. virgata, or a corolla up to 3 cm long occur for example in various combinations. I have not taken a position as regards the taxonomic status of all the forms in southern Africa, but I am convinced a much wider species concept than that of von Brehmer is necessary for a sound specific delimitation.
bibliographicCitation: Thulin, M. 1975. The genus Wahlenbergia s. lat. (Campanulaceae) in tropical Africa and Madagascar. Symb. bot. upsal. 21(1): 1-223. [All rights reserved]

description: Doubtfully distinct from A. setosa.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Hyacinthaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(3): 1771-1810. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The nearest ally of W. rhytidosperma perhaps is W. schwackeana, a species only recorded, as far as I know, from Minas Gerais in Brazil. These species are very similar in habit and also agree very well in shape and size of leaves, stamens, style and capsule. Furthermore they both have a 3-merous gynoecium, alternate leaves in the inflorescence region and non- reticulate seeds. Nevertheless the two species are quite distinct. The inflorescences of W. schwackeana apparently are always one- flowered and the testa is almost smooth. Only at a high magnification short, shallow, mostly longitudinal depressions are visible on the seeds. Furthermore the corolla-tube in W. schwackeana is less than 1 mm long and only about a quarter of the length of the corolla (in W. rhytidosperma about half the length). A more vague difference is found in the texture of the leaves which are thin and brittle in W. rhytidosperma as opposed to the more cartilaginous ones in W. schwackeana.
bibliographicCitation: Thulin, M. 1978. Wahlenbergia rhytidosperma (Campanulaceae), a new species from Transvaal. Bot. Not. 131: 67-70. [All rights reserved]

description: In 1915 W. von Brehmer published an extensive revision of African Wahlenbergia (Bot. Jahrb. 53: 9-143) and in this he recognised no less than 30 “Artengruppen” (which we refer to henceforth as ‘series’). Within this elaborate taxonomic structure it is impossible to find a place for W. pulvillus-gigantis, and it is clear from von Brehmer’s diagram of growth-forms that he did not know any cushion-forming species. His key is divided primarily into three sections with leaves alternate, opposite or rosulate. The ‘rosulate’ heading sounds attractive, but proves to include only a single series of herbs with a basal rosette of flat petiolate leaves. Despite their close congestion the leaves of the new species are spirally arranged, not opposite. The only dwarf plants are the very different procumbent forms with sessile flowers: We can only seek a distant affinity for W. pulvillus-gigantis amongst caulescent species and here we are led to the series Squamifoliae. There are only two species placed here, W. epacridea Harv. and W. squamifolia v. Brehm. Both have the erect stem closely invested with small hard leaves. No fundamental differences have been observed in flower or fruit and we can only suggest that W. pulvillus-gigantis may possibly represent a very distant alpine cousin of these species.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1971. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: II. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 31(1): 1-33. [CC BY-SA]

description: Near L. huttoni, Sond. and L. unidentata, Sond.; from the former it differs in having toothed leaves and from the latter it may be distinguished by having a glabrous calyx and corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Phillips, EP. 1917. description: Taller, stouter and more rigid than most of the species. Distinctive in habit, leaf, and inflorescence. Previously confused with L. nodosa and L. diffusa.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African species of Lightfootia. J. S. African Bot. 21: 155-218. [CC BY]

description: A. aculeata differs from A. petricola in having many-nerved, not 3-5-nerved, bracts which are shorter than in the latter species. The pedicels and flowers in A. aculeata tend to be longer than those of A. petricola, though there is overlap in these characters.
bibliographicCitation: Glen, HF; Hardy, DS. 2000. Aloe. In: G Germishuizen & E du Plessis (eds), Aloaceae (first part), Fl. S. Africa 5(1,1): 1-167. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209564#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Allied to L. calcarea but differing in habit, colour, the short calyx lobes which are not rolled, long corolla tube, and ovary as wide as long.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African species of Lightfootia. J. S. African Bot. 21: 155-218. [CC BY]

description: Much like L. juncea, distinguished by the longer narrower leaves, the larger flowers on long pedicels, and the larger fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African species of Lightfootia. J. S. African Bot. 21: 155-218. [CC BY]

description: A. africana is a very distinctive species and could hardly be confused with A. ferox, even when not flowering. In A. africana the leaves are thinner, narrower, and more spreading to recurved, whereas in A. ferox they are more fleshy and more compact. In inflorescence characters, A. africana can always be recognised by its racemes which are cylindric-acuminate, 40-60 cm long, about 10-12 cm broad at base and tapering to 3-4 cm diameter at the apex. The flowers are very distinctive, averaging 50 mm in length; they are slender, cylindric-curved, with the mouth so markedly upcurved as to be almost at right angles to the base of the flower. When the flowers are shorter, straighter and somewhat enlarged at the middle, a cross with A. ferox (of which there are many) could well be suspected.
bibliographicCitation: Reynolds, GW. 1974. Aloes of South Africa, 3rd ed. A.A. Balkema, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Its nearest ally in size and leaf is A. saundersiae which differs in having narrower greener leaves, and smaller flowers with regular mouth. A. albida is nearest allied in floral characters to A. myriacantha but the latter is a much larger plant with dull pinkish flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Reynolds, GW. 1974. Aloes of South Africa, 3rd ed. A.A. Balkema, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Like L. namaquana but shorter.
