description: Unmistakable in its 2- or 3-flowered spikes of uniformly red-purple flowers with a perianth tube up to 35 mm long, and long, narrow tepals 15-18 x 3 mm. The plants are quite small, mostly less than 80 mm tall, with narrow, falcate leaves 2-3 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very similar to S. albicans and S. bechuanicus, which have inflorescences wider than 5 mm; S. virginicus, which has lower glume 2/3-3/4 as long as spikelet and a wider inflorescence, 6-7 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC; Fish, L. 2015. Sporobolus R.Br. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 635-656. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to S. festivus, which lacks woolly hairs between the basal sheath fibres; S. englerii, an annual; and S. nebulosus, which does not have a fibrous base.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC; Fish, L. 2015. Sporobolus R.Br. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 635-656. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the pale yellow, diurnal flowers with a relatively long perianth tube mostly 16-22 mm long, and narrow tepals that remain slightly cupped even when fully open. The small corms, up to 6 mm diam. and with several small cormlets at the base, mostly closely resemble those of H. bachmannii and the two species also share soft-textured, slightly flaccid leaves. On this basis we consider them to be closely related. The crepuscular flowers of H. bachmannii are, however, very different, with white tepals and a curved perianth tube, thus facing toward the ground. The flowers of H. pallescens open shortly after 12:00 and close after 17:30, and have been found to be self-compatible, but pollination of the species remains to be studied.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The rachilla extension in this species is unique for the genus. Similar to S. conrathii, which has a fibrous base; and S. welwitschii, which has an inflorescence with only a few hairs in the inflorescence branch axils.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC; Fish, L. 2015. Sporobolus R.Br. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 635-656. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Typical pink to purple-flowered Hesperantha pauciflora is recognised by the flat-based, bell-shaped corms with radiating marginal spines and an aerial stem up to 200 mm high. The flowers are large and attractive with tepals 18-26 mm long and a short perianth tube 6-11 mm long. Plants from Namaqualand have dark pink to purple flowers with a white throat, stamens with filaments 4-8 mm long, anthers 6.5-9.0 mm long, and the style branches reaching the anther tips or exceeding them by up to 2 mm in the closed flower. On the Bokkeveld Escarpment, ± 100 km south of the nearest Namaqualand populations, the flowers are either uniformly pale to deep pink, or often with darker pigmentation at the base of the tepals and in the throat, and the stamens in these populations have filaments only 2-3 mm long, with anthers 7-9 mm long, and the style branches barely reach the anther tips or up to 2 mm below them. Plants with pale yellow flowers from the south of its range at Papkuilsfontein south of Nieuwoudtville are included here, expanding the range of variation in H. pauciflora. They appear to differ in no other significant way from the pink-flowered populations and have identical bell-shaped corms with prominent radiating spines, spikes of only 2 to 4 flowers, and submembranous bracts, dry near the tips. The flowers also have the same daily opening and closing pattern. The flowers of Hesperantha pauciflora open on warm days after 13:00 and close again after 17:00.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to S. conrathii and S. subtilis, which have inflorescences with many hairs in almost all the axils, glumes ± equal and 1/2 as long as spikelet.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC; Fish, L. 2015. Sporobolus R.Br. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 635-656. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Hesperantha pseudopilosa has the hairy leaves and stem of H. pilosa but differs in the broader foliage leaves, up to 10 mm wide, a longer scale-leaf 8-20 mm long. The larger capsules are 8-9 mm long and contain larger seeds, 2-3 mm long, with a loose testa. Capsules of H. pilosa are typically 6-8 mm long and the seeds are sharply angular and ± 1 mm diam. The crepuscular white flowers open relatively late in the day, mostly after 18:00, and then produce a strong sweet scent.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to S. namaquensis, which has all three awns plumose and shorter more pungent leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Stipagrostis Nees. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 665-687. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although not particularly distinctive in its white, relatively large flowers, Hesperantha rivulicola is recognised by the small corms with concentric tunics and unusual, pale green leaves with slightly inflated blades without raised veins or margins. In cross section the leaves are oval to almost rectangular with rounded margins and internally have large, spongy cells. The uppermost leaf has an unusually long sheath, enclosing a good part of the stem with a short free apex. The flowers are pollinated by large anthophorine bees when they open after 16:00 and after dark by a range of settling moths.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Hybridises with S. namaquensis, (De Winter 3266).
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Stipagrostis Nees. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 665-687. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily mistaken for the more common and widespread Hesperantha spicata, H. saldanhae differs in its longer perianth tube, 9-10 mm long, thus ± twice as long as in H. spicata, filaments only 1 mm long and anthers 2-3 mm long, both shorter than in H. spicata. In addition, the style divides near the middle of the perianth tube with the short style branches barely reaching the mouth of the tube, and the base of the anthers. Flowers of H. spicata are fairly typical of the genus with the style dividing close to the mouth of the tube with the style branches spreading over the tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Crocus-like Hesperantha schelpeana typically flowers on a short stem, the leaves of which are dry or absent, and is distinguished in addition by the short-tubed, relatively small flowers that appear in dry grassland. The perianth tube is up to 10 mm long and the tepals 14-22 mm long, thus ± twice as long as the tube. The flowers are usually white or pale pink with the outer tepals feathered red-purple outside but plants from The Sentinel on the Free State-Lesotho Border in the Drakensberg, at the northern limit of the species, have pink flowers, shading darker at the tips of the tepals and with the throat dark brown, providing a stark contrast to the deep yellow anthers and pollen. The reverse of the outer tepals is so strongly feathered with brown as to appear nearly uniformly pigmented. New, green leaves are sometimes emergent at flowering, usually two in number and produced on a shoot separate from the flowers. The leaf blades are solid and oval in cross section when alive but appear flat with a prominent main vein when dry. The occasional presence of leaves at flowering time makes it possible to confuse Hesperantha schelpeana with H. candida, which flowers at the same time of year and has living, green leaves present on the flowering stem (unless destroyed by fire or grazing). Properly developed plants of H. candida have four leaves, two basal, a third subbasal and partly sheathing, and a short, sheathing leaf in the upper part of the stem. Hesperantha schelpeana, however, never has more than three leaves, the lowermost slender and exceeding the stem (when still present at flowering and then dry), the second much shorter, often largely sheathing, and a third, short, sheathing leaf usually present on the upper part of the stem. The leaf blades also differ, those of H. candida fairly broad and plane with thickened and raised margins and midrib.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to S. geminifolia, which is usually smaller than 300 mm, the inflorescence as long as wide and the lower part enclosed in the swollen upper leaf sheath, and spikelet fascicles densely clustered.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Stipagrostis Nees. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 665-687. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of several pink-flowered species of the genus, Hesperantha schlechteri is recognised by the relatively short perianth tube, 5-7(-10) mm long, anthers mostly 4.0-4.5 mm long, and typically 5 leaves, the lower 3 with extended blades 2-4 mm wide. The flexuose stem has a pronounced loop above the sheaths of the upper leaves. Plants from Mariepskop with four or five leaves, the blades only about 1 mm wide, may not be correctly placed in H. schlechteri. Plants from near Mac-Mac Falls are also puzzling, the plants having blades of the lower leaves 4-6 mm wide, unusually broad for any Hesperantha species in Mpumalanga. The flowers are quite small, with tepals ± 7 mm long and a tube ± 5 mm long. They may be depauperate H. schlechteri or an undescribed species. A few other collections, including some from Dullstroom, also represent this variant.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Among the long-tubed Hesperantha species of the Drakensberg, H. scopulosa stands out in its rocky habitat, curved and often trailing stems, falcate leaves and mauve to magenta-pink flowers. The perianth tube is typically 30-42 mm long and 1.5-2.0x as long as the tepals, 16-25 mm long. Seeds of H. scopulosa, are striking in the genus, ovoid, ± 1.3 mm long, with a pale, irregularly twisted persistent funicle several times longer than the seed body. The chalazal end of the seed has what appears to be a vestigial wing.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the relatively small, white flowers with perianth tube ± 4 mm long and tepals as long as to 1.5x as long. The anthers, articulated on the filament tips spread horizontally over the tepals. The corms, usually ± bell-shaped or obconic, often have a flared margin and sometimes lack the serrated or spiny margins common in sect. Hesperantha. The seeds are notable, having a white, spongy coat, not known in other species of the genus. Variation in leaf morphology, correlated to some extent with height and number of flowers per spike, led to recognition of three subspecies: subsp. graminifolia with plane leaves with straight margins and often a taller plant; subsp. fistulosa with terete, hollow leaves; and subsp. spicata with strongly falcate leaves with undulate to crisped margins, a shorter stature and fewer-flowered spikes. Recent records of subsp. fistulosa in full bloom growing in a wet seep and subsp. spicata in fruit nearby in deep sand expands our understanding of this plant. The situation seems inconsistent with separation at subspecies rank and an alternative treatment as a separate species for subsp. fistulosa seems equally acceptable.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in the centric, ± terete, minutely grooved, hollow leaves with the surface between the grooves densely covered by minute papillae or extremely short, cilia-like hairs (visible only at 10x magnification). The white flowers open late in the afternoon, mostly after 16:30, and are then sweetly scented. The flowers, typical of the genus in form, are creamy white with a perianth tube 9.5 mm long, slightly shorter than the elliptic tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its unusually short, relatively broad basal leaves with blades no more than 20 mm long and up to 8 mm wide. The upper, cauline leaf is slightly inflated, up to 80 mm long and sheaths the stem for its entire length. The stem also bears a short, scale-like bract shortly below the spike, a feature of H. pilosa and several related species, all of which differ from H. truncatula in their longer leaves, usually hairy or ciliate. The flowers, typical of the genus, have a relatively short perianth tube ± 7 mm long and tepals 1.5x as long as the tube. The pale blue-purple flowers are crepuscular, opening in the late afternoon and closing after dark.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by the large yellow, cup-shaped flowers, in most populations strikingly marked with large brown markings on the tepals. Occasional populations are known with uniformly yellow flowers (matching the type of H. stanfordiae) or with both marked and unmarked flowers. The perianth tube is relatively short, 5-8 mm long, but the tepals, 30-35 x 12-17 mm, are among the largest in the genus. The tepals unfold in the early afternoon after 14:30 on warm sunny days and close about three hours later. Closely related H. karooica also has bright yellow flowers but never with contrasting markings, and the tepals are considerably smaller, ± 20 x 9-10 mm. Usually a smaller plant, H. karooica seldom exceeds 80 mm unless growing through bush, and has narrower leaves 3-4 mm wide vs. 7-10 mm in H. vaginata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to S. ciliata var. capensis, which has culm nodes with long spreading hairs and is more common and widespread.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Stipagrostis Nees. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 665-687. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of a handful of long-tubed, pink-flowered species of Hesperantha in eastern southern Africa, H. woodii is a relatively tall species, reaching up to 450 mm, with radially symmetric flowers, and is recognised by the perianth tube mostly 20-38 mm long, only slightly curved near the mouth, and the ascending rather that fully spreading tepals. Vegetatively similar H. grandiflora has a strongly curved perianth tube (26-)33-55 mm long, and zygomorphic flowers with vertically oriented tepals and unilateral stamens and style branches, and red-brown anthers and pollen, which are in marked contrast to the conventional yellow anthers and pollen in H. woodii.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Typical Ixia abbreviata is recognised by the relatively large flowers crowded near the top of the spike, either white to creamy yellow or deep pink to red-purple, with a dark brown to green or purple centre. The style divides at the mouth of the tube into short, curved branches, usually pale violet in colour. The floral bracts are typically brown distally, the outer with a prominent central cusp and the inner are forked to about the middle. The bracts are often relatively long, 10-12 mm, but plants from Elandsberg Nature Reserve have bracts only 7-8 mm long. Unusual for the species, a population from Darling Nature Reserve has uniformly pale bracts but with brown veins. Over much of its range Ixia abbreviata has white to creamy yellow flowers (also described as pale yellow) with a brown central eye, but plants from Porterville and the Tulbagh Valley have deep pink to purple flowers with a dark purple centre. Although treated as separate varieties in the past, the two colour morphs are merely colour variants differing in no other features and are not recognised taxonomically.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its acaulenscent habit, short leaves without thickened midrib or margins, and long-tubed yellow flowers with subterranean ovary. Corms are wedged in rock crevices and are very difficult to extract undamaged. The capsules are typical of the genus but are borne at ground level. Ixia macrocarpa, a second acaulescent species, is thought to be closely allied to I. acaulis as it has similar leaf morphology but the yellow flowers have brown markings at the base of the tepals, filaments inserted at the mouth of the tube, a longer style dividing opposite the middle of the anthers, and unusual, large capsules, ± 20 mm long and sterile in the upper third, unique for the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Not well differentiated from subsp. zeyheri, which is apparently limited to the winter rainfall area.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Stipagrostis Nees. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 665-687. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in the terminally crowded flowers with pink or creamy white tepals with a large dark centre, tepals narrowed near the base ± into short claws and arrow-shaped, black anthers, broadest at the base, and with the connective visible on the abaxial surface. The connective bears small, rounded, blue deposits, evidently an epidermal secretion. Ixia rouxii, which also has an exposed anther connective, likewise has these surface deposits and also has tepals somewhat narrowed below and on these grounds they have been considered immediately allied. Both species have the style dividing at or just above the bases of the filaments and 3-toothed outer floral bracts, the teeth very short in I. atrandra.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ixia aurea has bright yellow-orange flowers in crowded spikes and has been confused with I. dubia (sect. Ixia), because of the general resemblance to that species, despite the lack of a dark central mark to the flowers. The flowers of I. aurea have a narrowly funnel-shaped tube, tightly enclosing the style in the cylindric lower half but containing nectar in the upper third unlike I. dubia, in which the perianth tube is cylindric and closely clasping the style almost to the apex and the filaments are basally coherent or connate, thus occluding the mouth of the tube. In I. aurea the filaments diverge from the base and do not block the tube. The relationships of I. aurea lie with the short-tubed species, possibly I. odorata, flowers of which are sweetly scented, smaller, pale yellow or white and have tepals up to 15 mm long (vs. 16-23 mm in I. aurea).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The hygroscopic awns of the florets intertwine, thereby detaching the florets from the panicle in clusters and making this a good aid for seed dispersal.
bibliographicCitation: Nembudani, MT. 2015. Streblochaete Pilg. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 688-689. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its pale mauve flowers with small, dark eye, and relatively broad, blackish anthers that dehisce laterally, the light-coloured pollen then contrasting with the dark anther tissue. The style is ± as long as the filaments and the short branches 2.0-2.5 mm long scarcely project between them. The flowers are borne on inclined spikes and they face directly upward. Ixia brevituba falls among a small group of species that are endemic or near-endemic to the Roggeveld Escarpment and Klein Roggeveld, including I. curvata, I. rigida and I. trifolia, all of which share conventional longitudinally dehiscent anthers. Ixia brevituba appears to be most closely allied to I. trifolia on the basis of their distinctive, inclined spikes that are decurved and nodding when young. Other related species have spikes erect from bud to fruit. The two species also share a perianth tube 2-3 mm long but the pink (or mauve) flowers of I. trifolia have a pale central eye and yellow anthers. The leaves of I. trifolia are broader than in I. brevituba, (2.5-)5.0-12.0 mm wide, and the tunics are more coarsely fibrous, with the lower fibres developed into woody claws but not drawn into a collar above. In addition, the style branches of I. trifolia are longer than the filaments, 4-5 mm long, and project conspicuously between them.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by its unusually dark floral bracts, which although membranous and semi-translucent, are a glossy dark chestnut-brown. The pale pink or white flowers have a funnel-shaped perianth tube 5-7 mm long and spreading tepals 10-15 mm long. An unusual feature of the species is the production of stolons from the base of the corm, each bearing a small cormlet. The production of cormlets on stolons is relatively rare in Ixia; the only other species of sect. Morphixia that have stolons, I. oxalidiflora and I. sobolifera, both allied to I. rapunculoides, appear to have evolved this capacity independently and both favour heavier soils of clay or clay loam.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very narrow, sword-shaped to almost linear leaves, an unusually sturdy stem, relatively few flowers crowded at the spike apex and usually with uniformly brilliant red, glossy tepals are diagnostic for I. campanulata. The perianth tube is unusually short, 2-3 mm long, even for sect. Ixia. Another aid to identification is the style, which divides opposite the middle to upper third of the anthers, sometimes even exceeding them. A white-flowered form is known, evidently occurring in uniform stands. The short floral bracts, up to 3 mm long, are half as long to almost as long as the spike internodes and the outer has three short, subequal teeth. Spikes typically have 2 to 4 flowers but there are examples of white-flowered plants with up to 8-flowered spikes. Lewis (1962) regarded I. campanulata as most closely related to I. metelerkampiae, which also has a short perianth tube, 3-4 mm long, narrow leaves and obovate tepals, these however, pale pink, lilac or blue-mauve but with a dark red to purple throat and markings, and is a taller plant, reaching up to 700 mm, and colourless bracts with inconspicuous cusps. In I. campanulata the bracts are white or deep pink and have prominent, dark veins and usually prominent cusps. Both species usually have a well-developed collar of fibres around the base.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in sect. Hyalis in the deep pink flowers with a narrowly funnel-shaped perianth tube mostly 12-18 mm long, at least four, and up to seven, narrow, fairly firm leaves, and in the presence of a fibrous collar around the stem base. The relatively long and narrow perianth tube is reminiscent of I. fucata and I. stohriae, also montane species, but occurring to the north and east, in the Hex River Mtns and Langeberg. These two species have broader, soft-textured leaves and shorter stamens, the filaments exserted only 2-5 mm in I. fucata and up to 1 mm in I. stohriae, compared with the longer filaments of I. cochlearis, which are exserted up to 6 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily distinguished from other members of ser. Dichone by the unusual branching pattern: the relatively short branches extend outward horizontally and curve upward distally, as well as by an unusual floral feature. The filaments are unique in the section in being filiform below, curved at right angles in the distal 1 mm and broadened so that they are as wide as the anthers. As in I. scillaris, the flowers are zygomorphic and have unilateral stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Relatively low growing, Ixia curvata is a small plant, seldom exceeding 200 mm (although taller plants are known) and has nodding, pink flowers with vertically oriented tepals with horizontal stamens. Like other members of ser. Euanthera, the anthers split completely. The four or five leaves are typically falcate and leathery rather than fibrous. Other species of the series have upright flowers with tepals spreading horizontally. The plants are notable for the thick collar of fibres around the base and chestnut-brown cataphylls.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Relatively low growing, Ixia curvata is a small plant, seldom exceeding 200 mm in height (although taller plants are known) and has nodding, pink flowers with tepals held vertically with stamens borne horizontally. Like other members of ser. Euanthera, the anthers split completely. The four or five leaves are typically falcate and leathery rather than fibrotic. Its immediate relationships remain uncertain. Other species of the series have upright flowers with tepals spreading horizontally. The plants are notable in the thick collar of fibres around the base and chestnut-brown cataphylls. Raimondo et al. (2009) regarded the conservation status as of Least Concern (LC) noting the relatively modest range of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: A relatively small plant, Ixia erubescens is immediately recognised by the fine corm tunic fibres, 4 to 6 narrow leaves with deeply undulate and crisped margins, usually unbranched stem, nodding, pink flowers with vertically oriented tepals and the stamens unilateral and slightly pendent when fully open. Ixia erubescens is evidently closely allied to I. scillaris, which typically has medium to coarse corm tunic fibres, broader leaves, usually with plane margins, and somewhat to substantially larger flowers, also with unilateral stamens, but with a perianth tube up to 4.5 mm long and tepals up to 14 mm long (vs. tube 2-3 mm long and tepals 11-12 mm long). Occasional populations of I. scillaris with undulate or crisped leaves are readily distinguished from I. erubescens by their broader leaves, larger flowers, and coarser corm tunic fibres.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Can be confused with I. odorata, normally a taller plant with multi-flowered spikes, but I. esterhuyseniae has a shorter and sometimes wider perianth tube, 4-5 mm long and ± 4.5 mm wide at the mouth (vs. (7-)8-12 mm long and 3-5 mm wide at the mouth in I. odorata), the tepals thus about twice as long as the tube. The style divides opposite the middle of the anthers into branches ± 2.5 mm long, whereas in I. odorata the style divides below the anther bases (sometimes opposite the bases of the filaments), and the style branches are up to 5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Morphologically variable; closely related to T. obliterum.

description: The type of Ixia fucata is an illustration of a species of Ixia with a white flower, pink on the outside and with small red streaks at the base of the tepals. The yellowish tube is narrow but well developed, and there are five narrowly sword-shaped (± sublinear) leaves, the uppermost of which sheaths the stem for about 2/3 its length. The name is now associated with plants from the Hex River Mtns. Ixia fucata is somewhat variable: plants from the Langeberg have pink flowers, with the bases of the tepals red, the outside of the tube and tepals are dark pink, and unusual for Ixia, the stamens are unilateral and declinate. The parallel anthers thus lie in one plane and face upward toward the top of the spike. In contrast, plants from the Hex River Mountains have symmetrically disposed stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Rigid shrub, readily known from A. kraussii by its smaller, fascicled leaves; short, one-flowered peduncles; and smaller, glabrous, funnel-shaped corolla, with narrow segments and long anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1859. Thesaurus capensis, Vol. 1. Hodges, Smith & Co., Dublin. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.2117] [All rights reserved]

description: Immediately recognised by its solitary long, narrow foliage leaf, mostly 1.0-2.0 mm long, almost linear filaments, and unusually long style branches 2.0-3.5 mm long either straight or slightly arched, extending between the bases of the anthers. Ixia confusa has similarly slender but somewhat shorter filaments, slightly shorter anthers, and shorter, strongly arched style branches, 1.5-2.0 mm long. The leaves of I. confusa have plane, usually wider blades up to 4 mm wide (vs. 0.5-1.5(-2.0) mm) and without the prominently thickened main vein of I. micrandra. The style branches are similarly strongly arched in I. minor but that species has unusual flattened, lanceolate filaments, narrowed and kinked at the tips. The ranges of I. micrandra and I. minor are almost complementary, that of I. micrandra extending east of I. minor, but the two have been collected in flower on the same day in the Houw Hoek Mtns, where their distributions overlap.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A striking species, Ixia monadelpha has grey-blue to light purple or even pink flowers (rarely white to grey-yellow), dark purple, iridescent green to almost black in the centre edged with a light brown to green halo. The stamens are also darkly coloured and even the pollen is blue to grey. The species was named for the united filaments, sometimes for only half their length, unusual in the genus, and even the anthers are erect and contiguous. The pale floral bracts are minutely speckled brown or red distally but are distinctive in the somewhat thickened, twisted, almost black cusps, the outer with the central cusp more prominent than the laterals. Added to these unusual features are a perianth tube 10-18 mm long and a stem usually bearing two or more branches held at right angles to the main axis and curving upward distally. Ixia monadelpha has often been associated with orange-flowered I. curta, which also has united filaments, contiguous anthers and an unusually long perianth tube, and the two have at times been treated as a single species. The two may well be closely related but can be separated not only by flower colour, but I. curta has corm tunics of fine, soft fibres, a markedly thicker perianth tube and the stem is rarely branched.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The spikelets in this species are usually glabrous, but individuals with hairy spikelets can be separated from T. capensis, which has hairy culms.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Tricholaena Schrad. ex Schult. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 717-720. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the hard, coarse corm tunics, the fibres extending upward as a collar around the base of the plant, Ixia mostertii also has relatively large flowers, somewhat crowded apically and with a prominent dark central eye. The flowers are either pink, mauve-pink or white with the central mark dark blue or iridescent green. Notably, the style is long, dividing opposite or above the bases of the anthers. It has been suggested to be allied to I. vinacea on account of the coarse collar of fibres around the base and flowers with a dark centre, but I. vinacea has linear leaves up to 3 mm wide and exceeding the spike, very different from the shorter, broader leaves of I. mostertii. It also differs in the relatively few-flowered spike and short style dividing opposite or slightly above the base of the filaments. The prominent anthers, up to 9 mm long (before anthesis), remain straight and suberect as the flower ages, another important feature of I. mostertii and useful in distinguishing plants collected without corms from I. polystachya, the anthers of which spread widely, often becoming somewhat twisted and almost horizontal after anthesis.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The length of the glumes and spikelets vary considerably. Previously two varieties, var. grandiglumis and var. minor, were distinguished on spikelet length (5.3-14.0 mm and 5.3-8.2 mm respectively), and ratio of awns to floret (longer than and shorter than the floret respectively). No clear separation of specimens is given by these two characters and pending further investigation, these varieties are not upheld here.
bibliographicCitation: Nembudani, MT; Fish, L. 2015. Trichoneura Andersson. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 720-723. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Habit similar to Eragrostis volkensii, which can be distinguished vegetatively by the blades being blue-green, wider (up to 8 mm) and stiff.
bibliographicCitation: Moeaha, J. 2015. Trichopteryx Nees. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 723-724. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished in the I. rapunculoides complex by the longer perianth tube, mostly 13-16 mm long, short branchlets bearing 1 or 2 flowers each, and corm with tunics of coarse, netted fibres. The flowers are relatively large with tepals mostly 14-16 mm long and anthers 3.5-4.5 mm long. The proximal halves of the tepals form a floral cup that fully encloses the stamens. The flowers are usually sweetly scented but are appear unscented in the Bokkeveld Mtns. Pink-flowered plants with a perianth tube 16-20 mm long from Hex River Pass and nearby identified in the past as I. namaquana are a different species, I. oxalidiflora, distinguished by the longer perianth tube, suberect rather than horizontally oriented flowers, fully included anthers, and most significantly by the corms with papery to finely fibrous tunics and bearing ribbon-like stolons. The type of Ixia namaquana from Klipfontein near Steinkopf in northern Namaqualand has particularly large flowers, with the tube up to 18 mm long, and the style divides opposite the anther tips with the branches extending above them. The northern populations need additional study.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Well named for its particularly sweetly scented flowers crowded at the top of the short spike. Typical I. odorata has the following characteristics: bracts 6-7 mm long; perianth tube 7-12 mm long; tepals 9-11 x ± 5 mm; filaments 2.5-3.0 mm long, exserted 1-2 mm; anthers 5-6 mm long. Populations of short, few-flowered plants from middle and upper elevations in the Hottentots Holland-Jonkershoek Mt complex are now treated as a separate species, I. esterhuyseniae, this very different in stature from the taller, fairly small-flowered I. odorata, but they share outer floral bracts with a single main vein and usually a single tooth, in contrast to the more common 3-veined and 3-dentate outer bracts of the genus. Apart from its low stature, I. esterhuyseniae has style branches dividing above the bases of the anthers, usually opposite the middle third of the anthers, thus unlike I. odorata in which the style divides below the anthers, sometimes within the tube and opposite the bases of the filaments. Plants treated as I. odorata var. hesperanthoides Lewis (1962) remain puzzling. The type collection has white flowers with a perianth tube only ± 5 mm long, tepals ± 8 mm long, and anthers 3.5-4.5 mm long, all smaller than in typical I. odorata. Other features accord with typical I. odorata, although the length of the style branches is also shorter than the normal 4-5 mm of the species. The type collection was said to have flowers opening in the late afternoon, unlike ± 11:00 for typical, yellow-flowered I. odorata, indicating that some white-flowered populations, as the type of var. hesperanthoides, represent a separate race, possibly even a separate species. Additional research is needed to assess their status. Ixia odorata is sometimes mistaken for the southern Western Cape and Eastern Cape I. orientalis and the two can be confused when flower colour is not known, although the latter is almost always branched, whereas I. odorata is rarely so. White- or pink-flowered I. orientalis has a perianth tube of similar dimensions, and with a filiform lower portion but the style typically divides opposite the base of the anthers (rarely just below them), and it has longer filaments 5-6 mm long (vs. 2.5-3.0 mm) exserted 2-4 mm (vs. 1-2 mm), and unscented or only weakly scented flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ixia patens comprises two morphs, one with narrow, almost linear leaves, a slender stem, and pink or red-purple flowers; the other has broader, lanceolate leaves with somewhat thickened margins and dull red flowers. Both have terminally crowded flowers, outspread tepals, erect filaments, yellow anthers and a style dividing opposite the bases of the anthers. Diagnostic features are the long, yellow anthers 6-8 mm long, pale yellow style dividing opposite the base or lower third of the anthers, a stem occasionally with one or two short branches, a perianth tube 3-5 mm long and tepals connate basally for up to 2 mm. The outer floral bracts are variable, sometimes prominently 3-cusped and flushed with pink in the upper third or 1-cusped and uniformly pale and opaque.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the pale beige to creamy white flowers (sometimes described as pale yellow), a cylindric perianth tube (22-)25-35 mm long, and narrow tepals 11-15 x 3.0-4.5 mm, spooned at the tips. The filaments are ± 3 mm long and exserted ± 2 mm from the tube, and the style divides close to or opposite the anther tips so that the style branches arch over the anthers. The species is readily distinguished from I. dolichosiphon in herbaria by the very coarse-textured corm tunics, longer floral bracts, (6-)8-9 mm long, longer perianth tube (15-18 mm in I. dolichosiphon, which has bracts 5-6 mm long, white flowers flushed pale lilac, and veined purple outside). The shorter style divides opposite the middle of the anthers with the style branches extending between them. The two species also differ in flowering time and habitat: I. dolichosiphon blooms in August and early September and favours south-facing sandstone slopes, whereas I. paucifolia grows on clay and shale slopes and blooms in late September and October.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by moderate-sized flowers crowded together at the top of the spike, and a stem typically with two or three short, ascending branches. Flowers range from white to pink or blue-mauve with a relatively small darker blue, purple or grey centre and have tepals 9-18 mm and a perianth tube 6.5-11.0 mm long and half as long as the tepals. Added to this, the floral bracts are usually pale translucent and the outer has a prominent central vein and an acute central cusp, sometimes with a pair of small lateral lobes. The style typically divides at the mouth of the perianth tube with the style branches extending between the bases of the filaments. Plants also usually have dark anthers and as the flower ages the anthers spread outward to become almost horizontal and slightly twisted. The specific epithet, polystachya (many-branched), is misleading for although stems sometimes have one, two or even three branches (as in the type illustration), this character is not consistent and plants are sometimes unbranched. Curiously, plants sometimes have an unusually long style dividing shortly below to shortly above the base of the anthers. Such plants are most common on the Cape Peninsula but also occur in populations from the Olifants River Mtns. The short-styled plants are most frequent at lower elevations between Cape Town and Tulbagh. Style length may even vary within some populations. Plants referred in the past to var. lutea are now regarded as a separate species, Ixia sarmentosa, which has pale yellow to white flowers with a large central stain and corms usually bearing stolons (not present in I. polystachya).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Specimens without tubercle-based hairs on glumes and lemmas are found in the Eastern Cape.-(3129 BC): Port St. Johns, Ntsubane, R. C. Strey 8998; Ntsubane Forestry Station: near Fraser fall, F. Venter & P. Vorster 44.-(3129BD): Mkambati Nat. Reserve, C. Shackleton 41; main camp at Msikaba River mouth, L. Smook 5481. Specimens with filiform leaves have been found in the Wakkerstroom area. More specimens and research are needed to establish whether these belong to a new species/taxon or if it is due to variation within the species.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Tristachya Nees. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 729-733. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its low stature, the plants seldom exceeding 150 mm, and unusually coloured dull reddish flowers with pale brown, opaque bracts. The filaments are exserted ± 4 mm from the perianth tube and the dark purple style divides opposite the middle of the anthers. The ovary and capsules are unusual in the genus in their minutely warty surface.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the half to fully nodding, mostly blue flowers with a yellow cup (locally pale pink with a white cup), short perianth tube mostly 5.5-8.0 mm long, short filaments 2-3 mm long and anthers 2.3-3.5 mm long and half included in the perianth tube. In the vicinity of the Hantamsberg the species co-occurs with I. robusta, which was distinguished at the varietal level by Lewis (1962) by the presence of a short collar of fibres sheathing the base of the stem, and three or sometimes four, rather than the usual two leaves with expanded blades. A significant variant of I. rapunculoides from the Keiskie Mtns south of Calvinia has long narrow tepals ± 18 x 4 mm, a perianth tube 8.5 mm long and filaments inserted ± 4 mm above the tube base and ± 4 mm long. Elsewhere flowers of I. rapunculoides have broader tepals 11-15 x 4.5-6.0 mm, a perianth tube rarely more than 8 mm long, filaments inserted 2-4 mm above the tube base and 2-3 mm long. The anthers of the Keiskie population are also longer, ± 4 mm, compared with 2.3-3.5 mm for I. rapunculoides. These plants merit further investigation.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Close to the annual U. trichopus, which has lower glume 3-nerved, stiff hairs on the back, and the perennial U. oligotricha with the lower glume 5-nerved.

description: Distinguished by the slender perianth tube 27-30 mm long, expanding gradually and uniformly from base to apex, dull reddish or deep pink perianth, and fully included stamens. The floral bracts are unusual: the outer of the pair is truncate and obscurely 3-veined, whereas the inner is fairly typical in having 2 veins and is shallowly forked at the tip. It has been assumed to be closely related to the more widespread I. paniculata, which also has a long perianth tube and included stamens. Flowers of I. paniculata are pale yellow to beige, sometimes almost white, and also have partly to fully included stamens, but the anthers are usually dark and the perianth tube is cylindric and usually longer, up to 75 mm but only 35-50 mm at the southern end of its range, compared to the gradually flared tube 27-30 mm long and yellow anthers of I. splendida. In addition, the outer floral bracts of the two differ substantially. Those of I. paniculata are elongate and attenuate, with a single prominent vein, whereas those of I. splendida have 3 veins and are truncate or obscurely 3-lobed apically.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Typically flowering late in the year, in November and December, the foliage of Ixia stricta is often more-or-less dry at flowering. Not particularly distinctive, the pink flowers are radially symmetric and have short, erect stamens. It is identified in ser. Dichone by a combination of the rotate flowers and a basal fan of (3)4 or 5 sword-shaped leaves with a prominent main vein and thickened margins. The sweetly scented flowers have a filiform tube about half as long as the tepals and particularly short style branches ± 1.5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from V. bromoides and V. muralis only by the key characters.

description: While not particularly distinctive in its radially symmetric flowers with short, erect stamens, Ixia stricta is identified in ser. Dichone by a combination of the rotate flowers and a basal fan of (3)4 or 5 sword-shaped leaves, the blades with a prominent main vein and thickened margins. The sweetly scented flowers have a filiform tube about half as long as the tepals and a particularly short style ± 1 mm long. Blooming late in the season, in November and December, the leaves are often dry or partly so, a feature unusual in the genus. Raimondo et al. (2009) suggest a conservation status of (LC), least concern, but (NT), near threatened, is suggested to be more appropriate.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: Readily identified not only by the relatively long perianth tube, (12-)15-19 mm, particularly narrow in the lower half, and short floral bracts, 6-8 mm long, but by the unbranched stem and firm, leathery, straight leaves. The floral bracts are distinctive in being ± opaque, pale in the lower half and rust-brown above. The flowers, either deep salmon-pink, orange-red or yellow to orange, usually have a dark brown or reddish centre.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ixia trifolia is recognized by the combination of bright pink, rarely mauve flowers, white to yellow edged with dark pink in the centre, always held upright on inclined spikes, and two or three, relatively broad foliage leaves plus one (or two) more sheathing the stem. The specific epithet trifolia refers to the three foliage leaves, thus ignoring the presence of the upper, entirely sheathing leaf. Like other species of sect. Dichone from the Western Karoo, the style branches are slender and nearly straight and the anthers dehisce completely. Unique to this species in the section is that the filaments may be united basally for up to one quarter of their length, and the style is exserted up to 1.5 mm from the filiform part of the perianth tube. Ixia trifolia is perhaps most closely allied to I. brevituba, which has similarly oriented, upright flowers on an inclined spike but with narrower leaves, up to 1.5 mm wide and violet flowers darker in the centre. Both species stand out in the section in having the spikes drooping in bud.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the combination of two or three, relatively broad foliage leaves plus one (or two) more sheathing the stem and bright pink, rarely mauve flowers, white to yellow in the throat edged with a narrow dark pink line, always held upright on inclined spikes. Like other western Karoo species of sect. Dichone the style branches are slender and nearly straight and the anthers dehisce completely. A unique feature for the section, the filaments may be united basally for up to one quarter of their length and the style is exserted up to 1.5 mm from the filiform part of the perianth tube. Ixia trifolia is perhaps most closely allied to I. brevituba, which has similarly oriented, upright flowers on an inclined spike but with narrower leaves, up to 1.5 mm wide, and mauve flowers darker in the centre. Both species stand out in the section in having the spikes drooping in bud.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively short plant, seldom exceeding 300 mm, Ixia versicolor is distinguished primarily by the narrowly lanceolate leaves, the blades somewhat twisted and with thickened and raised, partly crenulate margins. The terminally crowded flowers are purple or white with a prominent dark centre, the colour variation present even in a single population. The dark stamens are free and the anthers are erect or curving inward distally. The anthers are important in distinguishing I. versicolor from I. polystachya, which sometimes has flowers almost identically coloured, but anthers usually widely diverging and almost horizontal. Both species have outer floral bracts with only a prominent central cusp and the style dividing at the mouth of the perianth tube, the branches thus extending between the bases of the filaments (the latter feature is variable in I. polystachya, the style occasionally reaching the bases or lower third of the anthers).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Particularly distinctive in sect. Ixia, I. vinacea has linear, firm, somewhat fibrous leaves up to 3 mm wide, the lowermost one or two of which are unusual in exceeding the spike. The corm tunics consist of coarse fibres that extend upward, forming a prominent collar around the stem base. Not only are the leaves and corm tunics unusual but the few, terminally crowded flowers are deep red with a dark purple to navy blue centre. The style divides opposite the base to middle of the filaments. On the basis of the coarse corm tunics, fibrous basal collar and dark centre of the flower I. vinacea has been considered closely related to I. mostertii, but that species differs significantly in having relatively broad leaves, differently coloured flowers and a longer style dividing opposite the lower third to middle of the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Radinosiphon leptostachya by its larger flowers, with longer perianth tube, (25-)30-45 mm long, broader tepals, the uppermost 12-15 x 3-7 mm, slightly longer filaments 6-7 mm long, and anthers 5-6 mm long. Plants of R. lomatensis reproduce vegetatively by slender, naked stolons quite different from the thick, scaly rhizomes developed in R. leptostachya. The species is evidently outcrossing, producing larger capsules with up to 8 seeds per locule, unlike autogamous R. leptostachya, which produces small capsules, 4-6 mm long, containing just 1 or 2 seeds (rarely up to 5 in tropical Africa) per locule.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Klattia stokoei is immediately recognised by the large red bracts enclosing the inflorescence, and the bright red tepals. The leaves are also distinctive, comparatively wide, mostly 7-14 mm wide in the midline and usually somewhat falcate.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Klattia flava is distinguished from the other species of Klattia by its bright yellow perianth and straight, somewhat glaucous, relatively narrow leaves, (3-)5-8 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The acaulescent Lapeirousia oreogena is distinguished from its allies of similar habit by its large dark blue to violet flowers with slightly reflexed tepals and a perianth tube 50-60 mm long. The tepals are almost black at the base with white, triangular to arrowhead-shaped marks. The centrally placed purple anthers form a ring around the style and have dark purple pollen. Like some other acaulescent members of sect. Sophronia, the leafy outer bracts extend well above the flower buds and have wavy to crisped margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aloe hahnii differs from A. swynnertonii in the shorter bracts, pedicels and perianths. as well as flowers that are a glossier scarlet-red and more decurved It is distinguished from A. vogtsii Reynolds, with which it occasionally grows sympatrically in the central regions of the Soutpansberg mist belt, by the latter species having buds that are borne horizontally in more elongated (not capitate) racemes.
bibliographicCitation: Klopper, RR; Smith, GF. 2009. Asphodelaceae: Aloe hahnii, a new species in the Section Pictae, in the Soutpansberg Centre of Endemism, Limpopo Province, South Africa. Bothalia 39(1): 98-100. [CC BY]

description: This attractive species has odourless, long-tubed, usually 50-55 mm long, white flowers with red, round to heart-shaped marks on one or more of the three lower tepals, and flushed red on the reverse of the tepals and tube. The plane tepals, and fairly long and comparatively narrow bracts with deflexed apices are distinctive. Lapeirousia verecunda belongs to the group of species in sect. Chasmatocallis with bell-shaped corms that are ridged or regularly lobed on the basal rim. Lapeirousia silenoides has similar bracts but cerise flowers with spoon-shaped lower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia lewisiana has magenta-red (also sometimes described as purple) flowers, the lower three tepals with prominent white, median streaks in the proximal third, and the perianth tube is typically 40-45 mm long, and the basal foliage leaf is finely but sparsely hairy.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia dolomitica is recognised by its distinctive, obconic corms with blackish, rough-surfaced tunics bearing prominent spines extending outward from the base, and by the somewhat inflated bracts with only weakly developed keels. When seen alive the bracts are unusual in having alternating longitudinal bands of pale translucent and dark opaque colouring. The flowers are pale blue or lilac (recorded in some collections as violet), with pale yellow markings at the bases of the lower tepals and sometimes also short tooth-like, basal ridges. Among the long-tubed species of Lapeirousia, it has a perianth tube shorter than usual, mostly 25-35 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Named for its uneven and widely angled (divaricate) branching pattern, Lapeirousia divaricata is readily recognised by its short-tubed, white to pale pink flowers, a stem normally branched well above the ground, and short floral bracts that are white to translucent on the sides. The lower tepals bear a conspicuous tooth-like ridge in the lower midline, a feature shared with only a few other species of the genus. The bell-shaped corm has finely toothed margins with the teeth directed downward. The relatively small capsules of L. divaricata are ridged with apically auriculate locules.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The purple to violet perianth and relatively short-tubed flower combined with a broadly conical corm with well-developed basal teeth distinguish Lapeirousia barklyi. The floral tube, 15-25 mm long, is normally shorter than to about as long as the rest of the flower. This contrasts with L. macrospatha, which has a cream-coloured to beige perianth flushed pink on the reverse, and a tube 30-35 mm long and one and a half times as long as the rest of the flower.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is very closely allied to D. natalensis.
bibliographicCitation: De Winter, B. 1963. Ebenaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 54-99. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia tenuis and L. divaricata share corms with spiny basal rims and comparatively small bracts but have markedly different flowers. In L. divaricata (and allied L. spinosa) the lower tepals are united with the upper laterals for some distance and the lower tepals have large, tooth-like median ridges whereas the flowers of L. tenuis have narrow tepals that spread ± uniformly from the apex of the perianth tube. The lower tepals appear to be united for a short distance but are not fused to the upper tepals at all, and they have claw-like basal cusps rather than tooth-like median ridges.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The bright magenta to cerise flower with darker colour in the centres of the lower tepals and cream-coloured streaks or blotches on the lower tepal bases instantly identify Lapeirousia silenoides over most of its range. To the south, in the Vanrhynsdorp and Clanwilliam districts, L. pyramidalis may be similarly coloured, though more often purple to violet, but the two species can be separated by their different bracts, narrow to fairly broad and acute with an upturned apex in L. silenoides but broad and often retuse with the apex curving downward in L. pyramidalis.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Smallest of the several acaulescent species of sect. Sophronia, the tufts of Lapeirousia plicata seldom reach 50 mm including the flowers. The perianth tube ranges from 12-20 mm long in southern and western populations, to as much as 30 mm in the northeastern populations. A distinctive feature of L. plicata is the orientation of the stamens, the filaments of which are initially erect but arch outward during anthesis, so that the dehisced anthers come to lie in a ± horizontal position.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the narrow leaves and spikes of creamy pink or pale salmon-pink flowers with slender perianth tube 30-55 mm long and longer than the relatively shorter tepals. It broadly resembles autumn-flowering Gladiolus bilineatus from the southern foothills of the Langeberg, but that species has just three, mostly slightly wider leaves on the flowering stem and a slightly longer perianth tube 50-70 mm long, with the filaments shortly exserted only ± 2 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its bright yellow, strongly windowed flowers with suberect upper lateral tepals and sharply deflexed lower tepals, the lower laterals strongly involute and auriculate at the base of the limb. The corm tunics are relatively soft-textured or papery. Gladiolus venustus has similar, mostly purple or pink flowers with yellow markings but woody corm tunics and obovoid-retuse capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its long, slender, relatively soft-textured leaves and two-ranked spikes of moderately long-tubed, pale pink flowers with dark red centre, purple anthers and lanceolate-attenuate tepals, the lower three streaked with red. The perianth tube is 33-35 mm long. The margins of the inner bracts are connate below forming a tube enclosing the ovary, and both outer and inner bracts exude drops of photosynthate from the tips that attract ants. The tubular inner bracts are otherwise characteristic of ser. Oppositiflori, where similar exudates are produced by G. dolomiticus and G. pole-evansii.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The flowers of Lapeirousia fabricii are among the largest in the genus, with a long perianth tube and often wide throat. The perianth tube ranges from 30-65 mm long and is usually expanded in the upper 5-10 mm in a short to long cup or gullet. The tepals are shortly clawed, particularly the lower three, which are united basally for ± 2 mm and the erect claws form the upper part of the floral cup. When fully open the lower and sometimes the upper tepal limbs spread at right angles to the tube, or the dorsal is suberect. The lower tepal claws often bear claw-like cusps that arch forward over the limb bases, but these cusps are sometimes absent and represented by thickened median ridges. Vegetatively, L. fabricii has distinctive flattened, narrowly winged stems, the wings usually minutely crisped or serrated. The well developed outer floral bracts are ribbed and have crisped to serrated keels.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia jacquinii is easily distinguished in flower and in fruit by the prominently 2-keeled outer floral bracts (occasionally 1-keeled, especially the lowermost). The stems are conspicuously 3-angled with the angles winged and undulate and sometimes minutely toothed. The long-tubed flowers are deep violet (rarely white) with darker violet or red markings outlined in white on the lower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia macrospatha is recognised by its large flowers with a long, slender perianth tube 30-35 mm long, widening noticeably toward the apex and white to ivory-coloured flushed red on the outside and with red markings on the lower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lapeirousia caudata is characterised by uniformly coloured, pale dull yellow, yellow-brown or maroon flowers with a long perianth tube, mostly 30-45 mm long, expanded and curving outward distally. The relatively long tepals, 25-30 mm long, are up to 2 mm wide and as the flowers fade and dry the tepals appear filiform and less than 1 mm wide. The habit is also distinctive, and well-grown plants have several (up to 12) long branches 200-300 mm high, produced from near the base, and relatively lax spikes with short bracts, 10-18(-23) mm long. The tepals spread outward from the base in somewhat lax fashion with the dorsal tepal ± erect and the lower three arching toward the ground.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Attenuate bulb scales, leathery leaves with dull surfaces and thickened margins, solitary erect inflorescence with a smooth rachis and fleshy deltoid bracts with bracteoles. L. coriacea is not closely allied to other Ledebouria species.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, S. 2008. Synopsis of the genus Ledebouria Roth (Hyacinthaceae) in South Africa. Herbertia 62: 85-155. [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the International Bulb Society] [All rights reserved]

description: The cylindrical bulb with truncate apices to the dead bulb scales, long basal stem, leaves (2-4) fully developed at anthesis, with threads when torn, leathery, dull glaucous with purple stripes and blotches, purple cross-bars at base of leaf, 1-2 dense and erect inflorescences that are shorter than the leaves, rachis ridged, bracts and bracteoles membranous and the filaments slightly flattened at base.
bibliographicCitation: Hankey, AJ; Hahn, N; Buys, MH. 2014. Ledebouria caesiomontana A.J.Hankey & N.Hahn (Hyacinthaceae: Hyacinthoideae): A new species from the Blouberg centre of endemism, Limpopo, South Africa. Bothalia - ABC 44(1,a119): 1-4. [http://dx.doi.org/10.4102/abc.v44i1.119] [CC BY]

description: L. papillata is closely related to L. galpinii but differs in having longitudinal rows of papillae on the adaxial leaf surface, purple cross bars on the petiole, erect inflorescences, and papillate peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Hankey, AJ; Hahn, N; Buys, MH. 2014. Ledebouria caesiomontana A.J.Hankey & N.Hahn (Hyacinthaceae: Hyacinthoideae): A new species from the Blouberg centre of endemism, Limpopo, South Africa. Bothalia - ABC 44(1,a119): 1-4. [http://dx.doi.org/10.4102/abc.v44i1.119] [CC BY]

description: Cannot be confused with any other Ledebouria species. The long, thin petiole is unique in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Hankey, AJ; Hahn, N; Buys, MH. 2014. Ledebouria caesiomontana A.J.Hankey & N.Hahn (Hyacinthaceae: Hyacinthoideae): A new species from the Blouberg centre of endemism, Limpopo, South Africa. Bothalia - ABC 44(1,a119): 1-4. [http://dx.doi.org/10.4102/abc.v44i1.119] [CC BY]

description: Variable in flower colour and to some extent in tepal shape, the perianth of Moraea lurida is typically an unusual dark liverish maroon and unpleasantly scented but is sometimes marked with yellow, through orange, violet, brown to creamy white. Both the dark and the lighter coloured flowers, the latter evidently unscented, seem equally attractive to muscid, dung and game flies that visit them in large numbers and are likely the legitimate pollinators. Also unusual in Moraea, the bases of the tepal claws lack discrete nectaries and nectar is secreted over the claw surface along vein lines. While the outer tepals are fairly uniform in shape, with the limbs shorter than the claws, the inner tepal limbs vary from fairly broad and entire to truly tricuspidate with a fairly long coiled central cusp and shorter, obtuse lateral lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to Moraea deserticola from the Knersvlakte, M. tanquana is distinguished by the three linear foliage leaves up to 5 mm wide, pale blue to mauve flowers with subequal tepals ± 22 mm long, united filaments, and short, contiguous anthers, 4-5 mm long that exceed the style branches and enclose them. The style divides opposite the lower third of the anthers so that the stigmatic tips of the short style branches, ± 1 mm long, emerge from between the middle of the ± contiguous anthers, and the branches lack crests. A smaller plant, M. deserticola has narrow foliage leaves 2-3 mm wide, tepals 30-36 mm long, and anthers 6.0-6.5 mm long (shrinking after anthesis to 5 mm) that remain contiguous around the style with their bases held within the floral cup. The ovary is conspicuously veined with dark red in M. deserticola but uniformly green in M. tanquana.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Satyrium situsanguinum is recognized by its urceolate- campanulate cauline leaf sheaths, white flowers with spurs longer than the ovary, and a rostellum with lateral viscidia. None of these characters is unique within Satyrium but their combination is not matched among other known species. S. lupulinum Lindl. differs in having cream to dull yellowish green flowers tinged dull purple instead of white flowers, leaf sheaths that are more closely adpressed to the flowering stem instead of clasping the stem loosely, often slightly shorter spurs (15-18 mm vs. 15-21 mm), and having a laterally complanate rather than subglobose labellum. Also, although S. lupulinum is relatively widely distributed throughout the southwestern mountains of the CFR, it is has not been recorded from the Slanghoek and adjacent Du Toit's Kloof mountains, or indeed from the same quarter degree grid square (3319CA) as S. situsanguinum. Another species resembling S. situsanguinum is the highly variable S. longicauda Lindl. Apart from several localities in the eastern parts of the CFR, this species is widespread in the moister highlands of the southern African summer-rainfall region. The two species differ in several respects, (although given the highly variable nature of S. longicauda none of these seem consistent). The labellum flap of S. longicauda is mostly puberulous, whereas it is glabrous in S. situsanguinum. The sepals and petals are fused at the base for a small portion in S. situsanguinum, whereas the sepals are ± free to the base in S. longicauda and the leaves of the latter are typically borne on a separate shoot, whereas they are part of the flowering shoot in S. situsanguinum. Satyrium humile Lindl. differs in that the spurs stand away from the ovary instead of being parallel to it, and the rostellum possesses terminal instead of lateral viscidia. Satyrium acuminatum Lindl. differs by its sepals and petals forming a U-shaped entrance to the wide labellum galea instead of having the sepals and petals arranged ± horizontally, and in having kidney-shaped instead of globose viscidia. Finally, Satyrium stenopetalum Lindl. differs in having erect bracts instead of reflexed bracts and the tips of the sepals and petals, including the labellum flap, being acuminate instead of truncate.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Niet, T; Liltved, WR; Oliver, EGH. 2009. Satyrium situsanguinum (Orchidaceae): a new species from the Western Cape, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 75: 22-26. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2009); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Allied to H. incana but the leaves tend to be smaller with darker upper surfaces and the calyx and corolla are smaller. The next species, H. elliottii, differs from H. cinerea in having a distinct coma of mauve-purple bracts at the apex of the inflorescence, the calyx is stellate tomentose, not villous, and the stigma is capitate, not shortly bifid; it is also a species of the hot, dry savanna areas rather than of high altitudes. Also related to H. stenophylla, which occurs further south and at lower altitudes, and which has somewhat longer leaves with revolute margins, colourful bracts at the apex of the inflorescence and a glandular-hispid calyx.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Trachyandra sanguinorhiza is similar to T. thyrsoidea in its membranous bracts and upcurved styles, but the roots differ in that they are bulbous and have red inner tissues. In T. thyrsoidea the roots are white, finger-like and swollen towards the ends.
bibliographicCitation: Boatwright, JS; Manning, JC. 2010. Notes on the genus Trachyandra (Asphodelaceae: Asphodeloideae) 1: A review of the T. thyrsoidea group (section Trachyandra), including three new species from the Northern Cape. S. African J. Bot. 76: 499-510. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2010); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Flowers are pink to lilac with the form of the flowers like S. longifolia, but they bear a saccate spur.
