bibliographicCitation: McDonald, GJ. 2008. A review of the genus Stenoglottis Lindley. Orchids South Africa 39(2): 6-12. [All rights reserved]

description: With the smallest flowers in subg. Visciramosae, Moraea inconspicua is distinguished by its flowers with fully reflexed tepals, the outer mostly 12-18 mm long (rarely up to 25 mm), the limb at least twice as long as the claw. In addition the rhipidial spathes are short, usually less than 28 mm long and sometimes only 18 mm. Flower colour is variable, mostly yellow or partly to completely brown, but white-flowered morphs occur in the Biedouw Valley near Clanwilliam and on the Agulhas Plain near Elim, the latter with the smallest flowers recorded in the species. In Namaqualand flowers are sometimes ivory-coloured or pink, but also yellow or brown as elsewhere. The foliage leaves are usually straight and erect below but often trailing distally, and have channelled blades, but plants from Namaqualand have distinctive spirally coiled leaves with a plane surface and on this basis have been segregated as subsp. namaquensis. Populations from the northern Cederberg and Biedouw Valley have unusually large flowers for the species, the outer tepals up to 25 mm long, thus matching those of closely allied M. bituminosa. The narrow leaves, short style crests and almost fully reflexed tepal limbs conform to M. inconspicua. Superficially similar Moraea viscaria, is a white-flowered species with spreading tepals 15-23 mm long, a strong floral odour, and relatively well-developed style crests up to 6 mm long, half as long to ± as long as the style branches. Moraea saldanhensis may also be confused with M. inconspicua but has slate-blue flowers with the tepal claws as long as to slightly longer than the limbs, the latter usually reflexed to ± 45º.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the distinctive foliage and flowers, the half-epigeal bulbs with imbricate, truncate scales, the inner with small, linear to narrowly lanceolate blades 12-26 x 1.0-1.5 mm, the upper surface minutely longitudinally scabridulous and the undersurface smooth but glaucous distally; and the shallowly campanulate flowers with dimorphic tepals, the inner broader than the outer and conspicuously fringed except at the base.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Particularly tall for sect. Hexaglottis and standing up to 2 m high, Moraea longifolia is distinguished by the pale yellow flowers with faint nectar guides without dark spotting, comparatively short style branches, 4-6 mm long, and large, obovoid to club-shaped capsules. Moraea longifolia is tetraploid and known to be self-compatible and autogamous, whereas the other species of the section are diploid and self-incompatible (compatibility relations are not known for M. brevituba). Closely related and similar M. lewisiae has cylindric 3-lobed capsules, slightly larger, deeper yellow flowers with prominently spotted nectar guides, and style branches 6-7 mm long. Also sometimes confused with M. longifolia, M. riparia has smaller capsules and bright yellow, strongly scented flowers, and is self-incompatible.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the taller species in the genus, plants often exceeding 1 m in height, and exhibits such ancestral features as multiple foliage leaves and an unspecialised yellow flower. Notably the filaments are free or barely united at the base, evidently a derived condition. Peculiar to the species are the hard, spiny roots that enclose the corm and hundreds of cormlets produced around the base. The spiny roots probably have a protective function but they evidently do not prevent massive depredation by baboons and porcupines that uproot large numbers of plants in search of the edible corms. The survival of such populations is assured by the production of cormlets which are shed in large numbers from the base of the main corm and also from the lower aerial nodes. The corm tunics, often decayed at flowering, consist of firm, leathery, brown layers that split from the base.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to D. aggregata, but may be distinguished by its paniculate-cymose inflorescence, shorter spathes and larger spikelets.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, HML. 1923. Novitates Africanae. Ann. Bolus Herb. 3: 123-146. [https://archive.org/details/annalsofbolusher03bolu/page/n151] [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to the widespread Moraea spathulata, the flowers of M. reticulata are almost identical in size and general aspect but the plants themselves differ in being almost invariably solitary. Moraea spathulata occurs in the same areas as M. reticulata but blooms from November to January, whereas M. reticulata flowers later, from March to May. The species is also recognised by the distinctive cataphylls, the uppermost of which extends well above the ground as a grey or brown basket-like network around the base of the leaf and stem. Occasionally also seen in M. spathulata, the cataphylls are never as prominently developed.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its deep yellow flowers with exceptionally broad tepals and a dark, maroon-black central eye. The perianth tube, 3-4 mm long, is relatively short in comparison to the tepals, 12-15 mm long. The species recalls G. inconspicua and G. foliosa in vegetative morphology, but the flowers are larger than in both of these species and very different in colour. Geissorhiza foliosa has pink to light purple flowers with a tube ± 5 mm long and tepals 13-17 mm long, and G. inconspicua has blue-violet, pink or white flowers with a perianth tube 4-6 mm long and tepals 8-11, rarely up to 15 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Spikes of 1 or 2, large, pale yellow, cup-shaped flowers and terete, four-grooved leaves set Geissorhiza sufflava apart in sect. Angustifoliae. It falls closest to the widespread, small-flowered G. juncea and the southwestern Cape endemic G. furva, both of which have similar foliage. Geissorhiza furva has deep yellow flowers with a perianth tube 3-5 mm long and tepals 15-22(-28) x 5-8(-9) mm, thus usually smaller than those of G. sufflava. The two species appear to differ in ecology and distribution, with G. furva from the Swartland south of the Piketberg, between Hermon and Paarl, occurring on stony, often seasonally waterlogged clay flats and slopes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the smallest of the yellow-flowered species of subg. Grandiflorae, Moraea muddii stands 150-600 mm tall and is normally a solitary plant with soft, brown, irregularly broken cataphylls. The pale yellow flowers have tepals up to 50 mm long, thus of moderate size for the subgenus. Similar M. unibracteata is also of relatively low stature but has slightly smaller flowers and is easily distinguished by its single sheathing leaf inserted in the upper part of the stem, leaving the lower half visible vs. two or three overlapping sheathing leaves in M. muddii. Plants from Eastern Cape flowering somewhat later in the season and currently included in M. muddii probably represent a separate subspecies or even species but too little is known about them to permit an informed decision about their status. The leaves stand out in having a V-shaped keel instead of the rounded keel elsewhere in subg. Grandiflorae.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished in subg. Grandiflorae by its solitary habit, long, narrow, channelled leaf 11-15 mm wide, often with a grey blush, and very large, pale yellow to white flowers. The outer tepals are up to 75 mm long and the inner up to 60 mm long. It is most easily confused with M. spathulata, some forms of which are similar, but the two can usually be distinguished by the solitary habit of M. moggii compared with typically clump-forming M. spathulata, which has broader leaves often flat or very widely channelled and usually darker yellow flowers. Apart from this, M. moggii is generally a late flowering species, while M. spathulata flowers in spring or summer, except for some southern KwaZulu-Natal populations that also flower late in the season. Two subspecies are recognised, northern subsp. moggii, with pale yellow flowers, and southern subsp. albescens which typically has white or creamy yellow flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Identified by the narrow, sublinear to falcate leaves with the margins and central vein raised and extended into prominently ciliate wings, combined with a smooth stem, and flowers with equal filaments. Leaf morphology places the species in sect. Ciliatae, in which it appears to be most like G. inflexa. This species is an altogether larger plant with corms 7-12 mm diam., leaves mostly at least 3-4 mm wide, and flowers with tepals at least 8 mm long and more often 10-18 mm long. The stamens of G. inflexa are also larger, the filaments 4-7 mm long, the anthers mostly 3-6 mm long, and the style branches 4-5 mm long. Whereas G. inflexa favours clay or loam slopes and flats in renosterveld, G. exilis is a plant of sandy slopes in fynbos habitats.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to the common and widespread Geissorhiza aspera, G. demissa is a smaller plant rarely reaching 120 mm in height. It has the plane leaves with margins and main vein only lightly thickened, puberulous stem, and unequal stamens consistent with G. aspera but the smaller flowers have tepals only 7-10 mm long and anthers 2-3 mm long. The variable G. aspera typically has dark blue to violet flowers although northern populations from the Cederberg and Gifberg have white or bicoloured white and blue flowers. Geissorhiza aspera is typically larger in all respects and almost invariably branched, with leaf blades 2-7 mm wide, 2- to 7-flowered spikes, and stems that are puberulous up to the base of the spike, even in the northern, white-flowered populations. The unbranched stems of G. demissa are subglabrous below the spike and the leaves are never more than 1 mm wide. The flowers of the two species are similar in shape, but those of G. aspera are larger and nodding with horizontally oriented stamens and tepals 11-15 x 4-6 mm and anthers 2-5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The dark brown, overlapping corm tunics and unequal filaments place Geissorhiza reclinata in subg. Geissorhiza, where it was initially compared with the Cape mountain species G. pseudinaequalis and G. scopulosa of sect. Monticolae partly because of the zygomorphic flowers with unilateral, declinate stamens and style and the upper tepals with dark markings near the base. However, it has pollen grains with specialised apertures known only in sect. Ciliatae, where it may be allied to G. heterostyla subsp. heterostyla, also with zygomorphic flowers. The sparsely short-hairy stems and leaves with the margins and central vein winged with ciliate wing edges likewise are consistent with G. heterostyla and other species of sect. Ciliatae. Unusual in subg. Geissorhiza, the basal leaves are prostrate and the stamens are unusually long, the two long filaments 10-12 mm long. The relatively large flowers have a perianth tube ± 2 mm long and tepals 14-16 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the most inconspicuous species of Geissorhiza, G. platystigma stands just 25-50 mm high with the main stem and branches each bearing a single small flower. The style branches, its most distinctive feature, are short, ± 1.5 mm long, broad and densely covered in prominent hairs much longer than the width of the branches. The corm closely resembles that of G. ornithogaloides subsp. flava in its bell shape with flat base and minutely serrated margins. Seemingly immediately allied to this widespread species of the southern Cape and interior, G. platystigma differs from it in flower size and details; G. ornithogaloides has a perianth tube 2-3(-4) mm long, tepals (6-)7-12(-18) mm long, much larger anthers 3-6 mm long, and the style branches are slender, 2-3 mm long, and thread-like as is typical of the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Resembles P. clavata in its robust, congested raceme of pale, greenish white, tubular flowers but differs sharply from it in the shape and orientation of the flowers, and in the much larger bracts and bracteoles. The flowers of P. liliiflora spread ± horizontally and are sharply upcurved at the tips (this is very evident in bud), with the mouth of the tube facing upwards.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC; Williamson, G. 2009. Hyacinthaceae: Pseudogaltonia liliiflora (Ornithogaloideae), a new species from the Richtersveld, Northern Cape. Bothalia 39(2): 229-231. [CC BY]

description: Stands out in the solitary basal leaf with a long, narrowly channelled blade, straight margins and relatively large, blue or white flowers. Typical of sect. Deserticolae, the ovary is included in the spathes and as far as known, the capsules are beaked, a feature of some members of the M. saxicola complex. When described only white-flowered plants were known but the population from near Port Nolloth has blue-mauve flowers somewhat larger that those of those from Namibia, the outer tepals up to 47 mm long and the inner up to 40 mm long. Other features of the Port Nolloth population are similarly slightly larger that previously recorded, particularly the style crests, up to 25 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A diploid, self-compatible and autogamous species, Moraea minor has fugaceous flowers, opening in the late morning and fading in the middle of the afternoon of the same day. The flowers are similar to but slightly smaller that those of M. collina, having tepal claws forming narrow cup including the stamens and style branches, but the capsules are smaller, 25-28 mm long and without a beak, whereas the longer capsules of M. collina are typically 30-40 mm long, with an obtuse beak. On the Cape Peninsula, where both M. collina and M. minor occur, the species are separated by a difference in flowering times, although they may be sympatric and have similar soil preferences. Moraea minor flowers in late August and September there, while M. collina blooms from June onwards and is usually in seed by August. Moraea minor is closely allied to M. longistyla, which occurs east of the range of M. minor and usually on clay or rocky ground, and their differences are discussed under that species. Flowers of M. minor are fugaceous, whereas those of M. collina and M. longistyla last two or three days.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Superficially like Moraea angusta (subg. Monocephalae) in its pale yellow flowers with lanceolate, entire inner tepals, stamens united only near the base, and unbranched stem, M. thomasiae otherwise has a single channelled leaf inserted near the stem base and long-lasting flowers. These two features, as well as the chromosome number, 2n = 12, accord best with subg. Vieusseuxia and molecular phylogenetic studies also place M. thomasiae among the species of this subgenus but without close relatives. Most other species of the subg. Vieusseuxia have reduced inner tepals, most often with 3-lobed limbs, sometimes a linear cusp, or even lacking.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Most remarkable for its small size, Moraea alpina stands no more than 120 mm high and is distinguished by the solitary, terete basal leaf, which is absent or emergent from a separate shoot at flowering, as in M. stricta. That species blooms early in the season before the new leaf has emerged, and the leaf attached to the flowering stem is dry or absent. Moraea alpina has deep blue to violet flowers somewhat larger than those of M. stricta and ± globose capsules ± 5 mm long, whereas capsules of M. stricta are club-shaped and up to 10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of several species of subg. Homeria with nearly identical flowers with short erect tepal claws clasping or enclosing the bulbous lower part of the filament column, spreading tepal limbs, and erect, contiguous anthers concealing the style branches, Moraea miniata is distinguished by its two, or more usually three, straight, linear leaves and several-branched stem. Flowers vary in colour, most often pink, especially in the south of its range, or yellow, or white in the immediate Vanrhynsdorp area. Plants in the Olifants River Mtns and valleys of the Cederberg are distinctive in their rather small, deep pink to almost orange flowers and shorter stature. Plants from the Upper Karoo are the most robust, reaching up to 600 mm high. Moraea miniata has become a serious weed in the southwestern Cape where it is often difficult to distinguish wild from adventive populations, the latter obvious on road verges and in overgrazed pastures. Plants reproduce readily from axillary cormlets and eradication is difficult. Some plants in old fields are obviously sterile, and these produce much larger numbers of cormlets than the wild plants.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished by the hairy to velvety stems and usually hairy undersides of the leaves with long-ciliate margins, and its fugaceous, yellow or deep salmon-pink flowers, sometimes pink with yellow style branches. Plants have at least two and sometimes three or four foliage leaves, the two longest inserted at the base or at the first above-ground node. The remaining foliage leaves are much shorter, the uppermost subtending the branch or branches at the uppermost aerial node. Plants are typically branched and the stem consists of just two well-developed internodes above the lowermost leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by its low stature, no more than 50 mm high when in bloom, an unbranched stem, solitary foliage leaf, and blue, fugaceous flowers. The flower itself is unexceptional and helps little in understanding its relationships. The species was originally assigned to sect. Polyanthes (now subg. Polyanthes), but its chromosome number 2n = 20 is inconsistent with that placement. Molecular study places M. nubigena in an isolated position but embedded among species with the same chromosome number. It is provisionally placed in sect. Polyphyllae of subg. Moraea, where it is notable for being the only blue-flowered species of the subgenus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished when alive from M. angusta by its bright yellow flower with nectar guides consisting of longitudinal lines of black dots across the lower third of the outer tepal limbs. It can also be recognised by its usually sticky nodes, single sheathing leaf, and style crests usually slightly shorter than the style branches. It is frequently the most robust member of the alliance with stems up to 500 mm tall (although sometimes much shorter).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With moderate-sized, blue-mauve to violet flowers, only the outer tepals with nectar guides, and well-developed style branches and crests, Moraea natalensis has unexceptional flowers for subg. Polyanthes but stands out in having a solitary foliage leaf inserted well above the ground on a stem with a long basal internode. The leaf is green at flowering and narrowly channelled, sometimes with the margins tightly inrolled and thus apparently terete. The few to several branches are short and somewhat crowded above the axil of the foliage leaf. This distinctive growth form is shared among the eastern southern African species of the subgenus only with M. inclinata, a taller plant, usually with darker violet flowers, green rhipidial spathes with the outer only about half as long as the inner, and nearly globose capsules. In M. natalensis the rhipidial spathes are often almost dry at flowering with the outer spathe only slightly shorter than the inner, and the capsules are obovoid to club-shaped.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differs consistently from all morphs of the very variable M. fugax in its distinctive extended stem, multi-branched habit, and smaller pale blue to almost white flowers, the outer tepals 20-30 mm long. The rhipidial spathes are also relatively short, the inner spathe, 25-40 mm long, and the capsules are only ± 10 mm long. Timing of anthesis is also different in the two species. Flowers of M. gracilenta open ± 15:30 and last until 19:00, whereas those of M. fugax open between 11:00 and 13:00 and collapse by 18:00. The flowering phenology of M. gracilenta appears to vary hardly at all in wild populations.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Leaves variable in shape, generally rather smaller and narrower, apex tapering to rounded, and margin slightly wavy.
bibliographicCitation: Coates Palgrave, K; Coates Palgrave, M. 2002. Trees of southern Africa, 3rd ed. Struik, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: A slender plant with one of the smallest flowers in subg. Vieusseuxia, the outer tepals typically 12-18 mm long with limbs ± 8-10 mm long. Flowers are unusually varied in tepal orientation and colour. The most common morph has outer tepal limbs half reflexed and white to creamy yellow, darkly speckled near the base, but populations in the Ceres area of the Western Cape have attractive dark blue-violet tepals. A second morph, corresponding to the synonym, M. tenuis, has the outer tepal limbs fully reflexed and the tepals dull pinkish brown with pale yellow, velvety nectar guides. These morphs may represent separate taxa but so far attempts to refer all herbarium collections to one or other morph have failed owing to the presence of apparent intermediates. Plants consistently have filaments united in a slender, smooth column with only their tips free, comparatively narrow style branches, short narrow crests, and 3-lobed inner tepal limbs, the longer central lobe linear and symmetrically coiled inward. Evidently closely related, M. bellendenii and M. tricuspidata have larger flowers, also with 3-lobed inner tepals but with the central lobe asymmetrically coiled. Also easily confused with M. unguiculata, M. rivulicola has somewhat larger flowers of very similar structure but with outer tepals up to 24 mm long, unbearded tepal claws, and a larger ovary and capsule, the latter 25-32 mm long vs. 13-15 mm in M. unguiculata. The two species co-occur at some sites in Namaqualand in slightly different habitats. An odd variant of Moraea unguiculata from the Kamiesberg of central Namaqualand has linear, filiform inner tepals but otherwise seems to conform to the species. Typical M. unguiculata with 3-lobed inner tepals also occurs in the Kamiesberg.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to P. viscidula, a more western species with a different base.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Our new species is very similar in general to R. zuluensis: the spikelet structure is the same, the sheaths look identical, and the culms are a similar dimension and color. The most striking difference is in the underground parts: R. zuluensis has a very well developed rhizome (which is very unusual in the genus Restio), while R. mkambatiae spreads with stolons. There are also differences in the texture of the spathes and bracts of male and female inflorescences. In R. zuluensis these are papery, while in R. mkambatiae they are cartilaginous or coriaceous.
bibliographicCitation: Linder, HP. 2011. New species and combinations in the African Restionaceae. S. African J. Bot. 77: 415-424. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by blue to violet flowers with inner tepals reduced to hair-like, filiform cusps mostly 2-4 mm long (rarely up to 6 mm long), and filaments united for up to 1.5 mm and occasionally free. The outer tepal limbs are broadly ovate, longer than wide and oriented ± 45° below horizontal. The corm tunics are dark brown to grey and usually composed of medium-textured fibres. The production of cormlets is not known in M. tripetala. Nectar guides are often yellow edged with dark blue or purple, but occasionally white, then dotted with blue to purple. The seeds are small, and typical of the complex in being 5(6)-sided with the facets slightly wrinkled and showing the brown colour of the seed body. The angles are raised into narrow wings of paler colour. Related species including M. amabilis, M. cuspidata and M. grandis have larger seeds of more complex structure.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of several eastern southern African species of sect. Vieusseuxia with 3-lobed inner tepals, Moraea trifida is distinguished by the dull-coloured, pale yellow to creamy brown flowers, dotted brown to green. The outer tepal limbs are strongly reflexed and the foliage leaf is distinctive in being inserted well above ground. The dull flower colouring recalls some morphs of the winter-rainfall species, M. unguiculata, but the resemblance is superficial. The foliage leaf in M. unguiculata is basal and the flowers are usually smaller.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the large orange flowers with tepals slightly cupped even when fully expanded and a solid, red to brown centre, partly to entirely united filaments, also dark in colour, and dry floral bracts rust-brown in the upper half. The relatively broad leaves are usually twisted distally and the corms have softly fibrous tunics and bear long white stolons from the base, each terminating in a single, relatively large cormlet Ixia maculata has flowers with narrower tepals and a small dark central eye, the corms produce short, branched stolons bearing small cormlets and the filaments and anthers are yellow. Ixia calendulacea bears a striking resemblance to I. curta, which has a slightly longer perianth tube, bracts usually paler but with dark brown tips and conical corms without stolons.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. natalense differs from C. zoutpansbergense, which is so far the only other species of this subgenus, in the greater width of the leaves, the shorter pedicels and the shorter corolla tube. C. natalense is a rather variable species.
bibliographicCitation: Bremekamp, CEB. 1952. The African species of Oldenlandia L sensu Hiern et K. Schumann, Vol. 48. North-Holland Publishing Company, Amsterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Readily distinguished in sect. Vieusseuxia by the comparatively large, white or sometimes pale creamy yellow flowers with spreading, comparatively broad tepal limbs forming a wide cup. The inner tepal limbs are 3-lobed with rounded lateral lobes and a slender central lobe up to 5 mm long, usually obliquely coiled inward (sometimes straight in subsp. parviflora). Closely allied to M. bellendenii and sometimes barely distinguishable from it without knowledge of flower colour, M. tricuspidata is a shorter plant, rarely exceeding 500 mm in height, whereas M. bellendenii has deep yellow flowers and is a taller, more slender species, 500-1000 mm high. Slight but apparently consistent differences in size of floral parts can usually be relied upon to distinguish them. Although they have somewhat different habitat preferences and flowering times, the two occasionally grow close to one another at sites on the Cape Peninsula, where hybrids between the two occur, these intermediate in height and with pale yellow flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its broadly triangular style crests 8-10 x 5 mm and relatively short style branches, up to 5 mm long, ± half as long as the crests. In the Atlantic Coast forelands of Western Cape flowers are either predominantly deep pink to brick-red (flower colour in the type of the species) or yellow or, in the Saldanha area, violet, and have virtually hairless leaves and spathes. In the Caledon District plants grow in renosterveld on clay ground and have pale purple flowers, and the leaves and spathes are velvet. Added to these differences is a difference in chromosome number, 2n = 18 in the west but 20 in the Caledon District. Populations further east in the De Hoop area and near Still Bay have yellow flowers and resemble the western populations morphologically but bloom earlier in the year, in May and June versus July to September in the west.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Morphologically very variable.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unmistakable in its relatively straight stems with strongly diverging lateral branches, and tepals united in a relatively long perianth tube 4-7 mm in length. Associated with the development of a perianth tube, the ovary is entirely included in the spathes and borne on a short pedicel 5-6 mm long. The capsules remain included in the spathes even as they ripen. Related M. brevituba has a much shorter perianth tube only 1-2 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea venenata has the several leaves, a branched stem, and blue-violet flowers much like those of M. polystachya, but is a more robust species, although often not as tall. The flowers have outer tepals 40-60 mm long with the claws 22-30 mm long, and as far as known the inner tepals are erect. The widest of the several leaves are up to 30 mm wide near the middle [vs. 6-12(-20) mm in M. polystachya] and the outer spathes are up to 60 mm long and the inner about half as long but with unusually broad, translucent margins, free almost to the base, an unusual feature among the southern African members of the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to P. curvifolia, which has swollen leaf margins.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A variable species and delimitation from P. oreodoxa, P. glandulosa and P. ampla is often difficult.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its robust, several- to many-branched stem and characteristic flowers with the tepal claws widely diverging to form a shallow dish including the filaments and bases of the anthers. The tepals are usually salmon-pink with a yellow cup but populations with uniformly yellow flowers are not uncommon. When dry the shape of the flowers is often lost but its large size makes identification fairly easy. The tepals, ovary, filaments, anthers, and capsules are amongst the largest in the genus. The outer tepals are usually 35-40 mm long, and the filaments are ± 8 mm long with the anthers up to 11 mm long. The ovary, initially 17-20 mm long, elongates after fertilization and the capsules may reach a length of 55 mm. The capsules are notable in having a pointed beak some 2 mm long. Earlier-flowering Moraea collina has been confused in the past with M. flaccida but is a shorter, few-branched species, the flowers with suberect tepal claws forming a narrow cup enclosing both filaments and anthers. The tepals of M. collina seldom exceed 35 mm, the filaments are 6-7 mm long, and the anthers are slightly shorter, 5?6 mm long. The ovary in M. collina is often as long as that of M. flaccida and the capsule may attain a length of over 35 mm. Capsules of M. collina, however, have a shorter, rather obtuse beak ± 1 mm long. Although M. flaccida flowers relatively late in the season, by which time M. collina is usually in fruit, their flowering times may overlap and natural hybrids have been recorded between the two species on the Cape Peninsula.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to P. horrida, specimens of which were previously placed in P. rigidissima, differs with anthers 2.1-2.8 mm long and a different micro-habitat.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With one of the largest and most striking flowers in the genus, Moraea gigandra has dark blue-purple, or rarely white or orange flowers with broad, shortly clawed outer tepals up to 45 mm long and 30-35 mm wide, the limbs spreading horizontally and with dark blue to turquoise, crescent-shaped nectar guides. The flowers are distinctive not only in size but also for their extraordinarily long anthers, 13-15 mm long and exceeding the style branches. The style crests are barely developed and are about as long as the stigmatic lobes. The single, channelled leaf is usually hairy on the abaxial surface and the stems are velvety. Like other species in the M. villosa alliance the inner tepals are 3-lobed, with an elongate spreading to trailing central lobe. The species is comparatively late-flowering. Moraea gigandra was evidently once common north of the Berg River but is now on the verge of extinction.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very variable species, seven morphological forms can be distinguished, but the variations are very complex and further studies are needed.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of several species of sect. Pseudospicatae, Moraea crispa has small, pale blue-mauve flowers with small yellow nectar guides at the bases of the limbs of both inner and outer tepals, and short tepal claws forming a cup around the bases of the filaments. The style branches are much reduced, 2-3 mm long, appressed to and reaching only to about the middle of the anthers. The single foliage leaf is unusually variable, usually channelled and somewhat twisted, occasionally with undulate and even crisped margins (the type form from near Calvinia), sometimes ± filiform and tightly rolled with straight margins or somewhat twisted. White-flowered plants from the Baviaanskloof open at ± 18:00 in contrast to ± 16:00 for blue-flowered plants and need further investigation. Moraea crispa is unusual in being heteroploid. Populations from the Western Karoo are mostly diploid, 2n = 12, but tetraploid and hexaploid populations have been recorded from the Cederberg and Cold Bokkeveld and these plants have the longest anthers in the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A slender plant, Moraea debilis has small flowers initially violet, fading to pale blue-mauve and becoming mottled, spreading to reflexed outer tepal limbs and trilobed inner tepals. The filaments are united for half their length in a column ± 2.5 mm long. Somewhat unusual in sect. Vieusseuxia, the linear leaf is softly hairy on the outer surface and the margins are usually ciliate.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the large flowers with predominantly yellow tepals spreading from the base, the tepals oblong and broadest in the lower half with the outer tepals strikingly marked with large green or green and orange blotches in the distal half. Plants have a solitary foliage leaf and bear few to several branches. The anthers, 8-10 mm long, are borne on a sturdy filament column wide at the base and tapering to a narrow apex, and exceed the style branches, an important distinction between M. elegans and closely allied M. comptonii, which has shorter anthers, either uniformly yellow or salmon to orange flowers with a yellow cup with or without green markings, these at the base of the spathulate or fiddle-shaped outer tepals, thus in the middle to lower third of the tepals. Moraea elegans and M. comptonii have complementary ranges in the Caledon and Bredasdorp Districts and are generally easy to distinguish, although some populations of M. comptonii approach M. elegans in appearance.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished on a number of characters: Flowers white and magenta, not spotted versus purple brown in the rear half and white to cream to green in the front half and variously purple spotted; Flowers noticeably larger than those of D. obtusa subsp. hottentotica and subsp. picta, the galea 7-9 mm long versus 4-7 mm long; Spur 1-1.5 mm long and as long as to broader than long, parallel sided, emarginate, always 2-tubed versus spur variable in shape and length, 0.2-2.2. mm long but distinctly longer than broad, when short then V-shaped, obtuse, straight to strongly decurved, 1-tubed or only slightly 2-tubed; Lower point of attachment of spur to galea indented versus rounded and convex; Rostellum arms prominent, erect, parallel in a U-shaped arrangement, 1 mm long versus divaricate in a V-shaped arrangement and shorter, 0.5-0.6 mm long; Dorsal sepal deeply and narrowly canaliculate forming almost a partition on the inside of the galea versus dorsal sepal shallowly and broadly canaliculate; Lateral sepals more spreading at an angle of 60-80o between lip and sepal versus 45o or less; Galea opening suberect and patent versus galea mostly facing downwards; Stigma positioned in front of the galea versus stigma included in the galea; Raised front margin of stigma purple versus colourless/white; Flowers mildly scented versus pungently scented Plants at first compact and conical with densely packed flowers, the lower whorls just opening, elongating later on with the flowers becoming more spaced versus tightly packed and elongated inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Liltved, WR; Bytebier, B. 2011. Disa albomagentea (Orchidaceae), a new species from the Hottentots Holland Mountains in the Cape Floristic Region, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 77(2): 313-318. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2010.08.010] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2011); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: With relatively small flowers, Moraea elliotii currently includes plants from the Mpumalanga highveld with a linear leaf inserted high up on the stem but not immediately under the inflorescence, as well as those with a more-or-less basal leaf. The leaf is channelled but sometimes with margins tightly inrolled and appearing subterete or terete (the type of the synonym M. juncifolia). Plants from Gauteng, Mpumalanga and Eswatini mostly flower from December to March, whereas those from the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands generally flower in late spring, and those in the Eastern Cape may bloom as early as September. The flowers are small, with outer tepals 20-30 mm long and those from the north of its range are blue to violet with yellow-orange nectar guides and have inner tepals with half reflexed limbs. Populations from KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape are variable in colour, sometimes pale violet to lilac or even white, often with the inner tepals spreading almost from the base and twisted through 90º and the filaments united for only ± 1 mm, vs 2.0-2.5 mm elsewhere. There appear, however, to be no consistent floral differences between the southern and northern populations and this makes formal recognition of subspecies impossible. Populations of Moraea elliotii with the leaf inserted high on the stem can be confused with M. natalensis, but the latter is a more slender plant usually with smaller flowers, and the leaf is inserted higher on the stem at the base of the crowded branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to and easily confused with P. aurea, which has a different base.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Relatively common in northern Namaqualand, Moraea bolusii is distinguished by its solitary, fairly broad, undulate and loosely twisted leaf with somewhat thickened margins, and pale yellow flowers with relatively broad tepals up to 12 mm wide, both the inner and outer tepals limbs reflexed to ± 45º. The inner tepals, style branches and crests are typically paler than the outer tepals, often almost white. Flowers of related M. saxicola are usually white, sometimes pale blue, and open later than those of M. bolusii, between 15:00 and 16:00, also collapsing at sunset. The range of M. bolusii falls entirely within that of M. saxicola.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This taxon may be confused with Pentameris basutorum, which has long, lax hairs covering the lemma.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Mashau, AC. 2015. Tenaxia N.P.Barker & H.P.Linder. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 692-695. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Male spathes overtopping spikelets. Female tepals acuminate.
bibliographicCitation: Linder, HP. 2011. New species and combinations in the African Restionaceae. S. African J. Bot. 77: 415-424. [CC BY]

description: Flowers of Babiana avicularis resemble those two other predominantly red-flowered species of the genus, B. hirsuta and B. ringens, except that they are almost half the size. Like B. ringens, the main axis is sterile and, as in B. ringens it serves as a perch for birds taking nectar from the flowers but their flowers differ in some important respects apart from their smaller size. Flowers of B. ringens subsp. ringens have a perianth tube 28-40 mm long, a dorsal tepal 25-45(-50) mm long, enlarged lower lateral tepals ± 20 mm long, and the upper tepals are recurved. In addition, the filaments are 37-70 mm long, the anthers 5.0-7.5 mm long, and the style divides opposite the upper half of the anthers or shortly beyond their tips. Subsp. australis has slightly smaller flowers with the dorsal tepal 18-30 mm long and filaments 24-34 mm long. In contrast, flowers of B. avicularis have a tube 16-21 mm long and distinctive in the lower cylindrical part of the tube 4 mm long and kinked below the apex. All three lower tepals are pale green and directed forward. In both species, as well as in B. hirsuta, the margins of the dorsal tepal curve inward and enclose the filaments and style with only the distal third or quarter expanded and slightly recurved. The filaments of B. avicularis are 25-32 mm long, the anthers 3.5-5.0 mm long and the style divides below the bases of the anthers. The leaves of B. ringens are lanceolate to sublinear but firm to rigid in texture with almost pungent tips, in contrast to the longer, linear, arching, softer leaves of B. avicularis The floral bracts of Babiana avicularis are notable in two respects: they are rust-coloured at the tips and prominently mucronate, and the shorter inner bracts are divided for about 3?4 of their length, with the two halves strongly divergent, whereas in both B. hirsuta and B. ringens, the inner bracts are divided in the upper third to half and do not notably diverge. The two coastal populations of B. avicularis are sympatric and co-blooming with B. hirsuta, but no hybrids have been recorded at either site.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In its subterete leaves and crowded, decumbent spikes of extremely long-tubed flowers, Babiana teretifolia superficially appears to be merely a variant of B. brachystachys, a species centred in coastal Namaqualand and extending south to near Lambert’s Bay in Western Cape. The flowers, however, differ in several respects, especially in the remarkably narrow, channelled, spreading and twisted tepals, with the dorsal tepal hardly differentiated from the remaining five. The dorsal tepal is ± 30 × 4 mm and the remaining tepals ± 26 × 2.5 mm, whereas typical B. brachystachys has oblong-lanceolate, ± plane tepals, the dorsal tepal 20-24 × 6-8 mm and the lower three tepals 15-18 × 4-6 mm. These differences extend to the stamens: in B. teretifolia the filaments are ± 12 mm long and exserted ± 9.5 mm from the tube and the anthers are 5.5-6.0 mm long and white, as is the pollen, whereas B. brachystachys has filaments 4-5 mm long, exserted 1-3 mm, and anthers 4-5 mm long and usually pale violet to purple when fresh, as is the pollen, but occasionally white. In addition, the style of B. teretifolia divides opposite the anther tips so that the style branches, ± 5 mm long, arch above the anthers and can readily be seen to be notched at the tips. In B. brachystachys the style divides opposite the upper third of the anthers and the style branches are only ± 2.5 mm long. Added to the floral differences are the sparsely hairy leaf sheaths and flowers spaced ± 1.5 mm apart, in contrast with the woolly leaf sheaths and flowers set 3-6 mm apart in most populations of B. brachystachys. The extraordinarily long, linear and twisted tepals, compared to the more conventional oblong-lanceolate tepals of B. brachystachys, mark B. teretifolia as a specialised, geographic segregate of its already highly specialised sister species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With the typical features of the subgenus, viz. a solitary foliage leaf with a terete blade and narrowly 3-winged ovary, Moraea angusta is recognised by darkly veined yellow to almost brown flowers with prominent nectar guides edged with dark pigment, filaments that are united basally for ± 1 mm, and relatively narrow style crests ± as long as but usually slightly longer than the style branches. The stem usually bears a single sheathing leaf (rarely two) and is not normally sticky below the upper nodes. Related M. neglecta also has filaments united only near the base but the firm-textured tepals are not darkly veined and the nectar guides consist of longitudinal lines of dark dots. In addition the style crests are ± half to 2/3 as long as the style branches. In M. anomala the filaments are united for (2-)4-8 mm and the stem almost always has two sheathing leaves and is rarely sticky below the nodes. The red pollen colour of M. angusta is shared with M. anomala but M. neglecta has yellow to white pollen. Unusually small-flowered plants collected on the Langeberg may be confused with Moraea vallisavium from the Klein River Mtns but can be recognised by the relatively short, stiff, terete leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea amissa has broad, spreading, outer tepal limbs reminiscent of M. villosa but the pale blue flowers are much smaller and the inner tepals are either entire or imperfectly 3-lobed, thus inconsistent with M. villosa. The stems and leaves are glabrous, in contrast to the condition in most members of the M. villosa alliance.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar in habit to C. cincta, which has tufted hairs on the lemma.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC; Fish, L. 2015. Capeochloa H.P.Linder & N.P.Barker. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 150-153. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A tree with elliptic or ovate leaves varying considerably in size with margins usually entire, but sometimes serrate-crenate and with circular and linear pellucid dots scattered over the blade. The flowers are small and arranged in dense, axillary fascicles. The terminology relating to the structure of the flowers is not consistent, thus Phillips (l.c.) and Hutchinson (1967) refer to 'calyx lobes', Wild (l.c.) to 'sepals' and Sleumer (l.c.) to 'tepals'. Similarly Phillips, Hutchinson and Wild refer to 'staminodes', while Sleumer refers to 'disc lacinia'.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished in sect. Gynandriris by its low stature and small flowers. The blue-mauve flowers have orange and white nectar guides on the outer tepals, 12-18 mm long, and the limbs of both outer and inner tepals are half reflexed. The small flower size is reflected in the short filaments 3.5-6.0 mm long and short anthers up to 4 mm long. The flowers open between noon and 13:00 and fade shortly before sunset. Several populations examined for chromosome number are diploid, 2n = 12, and plants have been found in the greenhouse to be reproductively self-compatible and autogamous. They thus produce ample seed wherever they occur. This mode of reproduction is unusual in Moraea but explains its success as a weed.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small plant, Moraea serpentina rarely attains 200 mm in height and 90-120 mm is usual. It is readily distinguished by the typically three, rarely two or four foliage leaves, the blades channelled or flat and always at least loosely twisted, sometimes tightly so. The flowers are either partly yellow with pale yellow or white style branches and crests or white with the inner tepals and style branches flushed with violet. The inner tepals are held erect, a striking feature of the species. In the Kamiesberg populations the leaves are hairy on the margins or abaxial surface. Closely related M. tortilis, restricted to northern Namaqualand, has a broadly similar appearance but the leaf blades are terete and tightly coiled in corkscrew fashion, and the violet or white flowers have both outer and inner tepal limbs invariably half reflexed. Populations of Moraea serpentina from the western Knersvlakte, north of Vredendal, stand out in having consistently smaller, pale blue-violet flowers and two or even a single leaf but evidently do not otherwise differ from white-flowered plants. One- or two-leaved plants are occasionally found elsewhere across its range.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Among the smallest of the southern Africa species of subg. Grandiflorae, Moraea carnea stands no more than 500 mm high. It is also the only pink- to creamy pink-flowered species of the subgenus and is also unusual in having darker pink to purple style crests and sometimes darker inner tepals. Moraea ardesiaca is a larger plant up to 700 mm tall with larger, slate-blue to blue-mauve flowers. The two species also differ in relative anther length, shorter than the filaments in M. carnea but longer than the filaments in M. ardesiaca.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished in subg. Acaules by the often pubescent leaves and spathes, and most frequently blue flowers with relatively slender inner tepals, either linear-spathulate or narrowly lanceolate, and slender style crests. The capsules of Moraea ciliata are the longest in the subgenus, 10-28 mm long, and the seeds are more-or-less globose or somewhat angled by pressure and ± 2 x 2-3 mm. Two additional subspecies are recognised, yellow-flowered subsp. lutescens and white- or pale pink-flowered subsp. cuprina. The subspecies have separate but complimentary ranges and are weakly differentiated from one another. Moraea ciliata is easily distinguished from M. tricolor, which has broad style crests longer than the style branches, and tepal claws shorter than the limbs. Closely related M. macronyx has the tepal claws much longer than the limbs, whereas in M. ciliata the claws are slightly shorter than to about as long as the limbs.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A particularly distinctive member of the Moraea spathulata complex, M. hiemalis is unusual in flowering in winter, July and August. It is distinguished by its cylindrical leaf with the margins tightly inrolled, and its solitary habit. The plants are also generally smaller in most features than typical M. spathulata and its immediate allies, the outer tepals 45-50 mm long and the inner ± 40 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the most common species of subg. Galaxia, Moraea galaxia has the yellow flowers and fringed style lobes typical of ser. Galaxia and is best distinguished by the broad, ± ovate leaves prostate or nearly so and with thickened, usually densely ciliate margins. The filaments are united in a bottle-shaped column with the sessile anthers appressed to the style. Over most of its range M. galaxia is tetraploid, 2n = 36, but diploid plants, 2n = 18 occur in the southeast of its range in the Caledon District.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Two forms in EC: Thicket form short (up to 5 m high) sometimes has more than one thick stem, fewer branches, leaves paler green. Forest form high (up to 30 m high), mostly single stemmed, multibranched, leaves darker green.
bibliographicCitation: De Villiers, BJ. 2019. Araliaceae: Cussonia Thunb. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 418-420. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differentiating characters for C. transvaalensis are the glaucous colour of the multidigitately compound leaves, primary leaflets which are particularly compound, leaflets without a prominent midrib, entire leaflet margins, the absence of stipellae on the articulations and a single hypsophyll subtending each flower. In extreme cases the primary leaflets may have up to four articulations and tertiary leaflets are present.
bibliographicCitation: Reyneke, WF. 1984. A new species of Cussonia (Araliaceae) from the Transvaal. S. African J. Bot. 3(6): 368-374. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1984); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The purple flower with a dark centre and shallowly cupped tepals recall particularly Moraea barnardiella, and it is to that species that M. melanops is evidently most closely allied. Vegetatively, they appear to be identical but M. melanops has free to partly united filaments diverging distally and the style exceeds the anthers and has fairly narrow branches, whereas M. barnardiella has filaments free in the upper 1/3 and strongly diverging above, and the style divides opposite the apex of the filament column, with broader branches than in M. melanops.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Broadly resembling the more common Moraea miniata, M. karooica may differ in leaf number, usually single (rarely two or three) vs. two or three in M. miniata, but more fundamentally in the flowers. Moraea karooica has ascending tepal claws that together form a shallow cup and a cylindric filament column, whereas in M. miniata the short tepal claws clasp the base of the bulbous filament column. Moraea karooica may be most closely allied to the rare M. fenestrata of the Tanqua Basin, which has a similar habit but consistently two or more leaves, and tepals conspicuously narrowed at the base, thus usually forming a windowed cup. Populations of M. karooica with more than one leaf are from the Koedoes Mtns and Verlatenkloof near Sutherland.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In its vegetative form Moraea fragrans is nearly identical to M. bifida, both with a glaucous, falcate leaf with the lower half sheathing the stem almost to the base of the first branches. The flowers are, however, very different. The flowers of M. fragrans are nearly always pale yellow with darker yellow central cup and tepal claws ± 8 mm long, diverging to form a relatively wide cup that includes the stamens. The deep yellow nectar guides are edged with a band of grey-green. In M. bifida the tepal claws are short, only ± 2 mm long, erect and clasp the bulbous base of the filament column. Despite their different floral morphology, the two are likely closely related and hybrids have been recorded between them where their ranges come together. Greenhouse studies have shown the hybrids to be sterile.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct but apparently a quite local species.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, NE; Hutchinson, J; Prain, D. 1920. Euphorbiaceae. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Thymelaeaceae-Ceratophylleae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 5(2-3): 216-516. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15244#page/3/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Although vegetatively resembling several other species of sect. Homeria in the solitary, somewhat glaucous leaf inserted above the ground and the few-branched stem, Moraea radians is so distinctive in its floral structures that it was at first referred to a separate genus, Sessilistigma. The beige-yellow flowers, with short, erect tepal claws and spreading limbs, are remarkable for the subgenus in their free stamens and almost vestigial style ± 1 mm long, dividing into three, flattened branches forked for half their length. Other species of subg. Homeria have filaments partly to entirely united and enclosing a well-developed style, the branches of which are each appressed to the opposed anther. The style branches of M. radians lack crests and are stigmatic at the tips of each lobe.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Seemingly a typical member of ser. Galaxia, Moraea angulata has relatively small flowers with tepals 13-19 mm long, and is distinctive in the short, terete, fleshy leaves, usually grey in colour, and unique corm tunics of soft, pith-like material with wide vertical wings, for which the species is named. The filaments are completely united in a column enclosing the style, which divides above the tips of the diverging anthers into fringed stigmatic lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species is very close to Disa bivalvata and hybridises with it.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished primarily by the relatively long, grass-like, linear leaves up to 80 mm long and usually terete distally. The fugaceous flowers are typical of ser. Galaxia, having a yellow perianth, filaments usually entirely united, and fringed style branches. Occasionally the filaments are free in the upper third and the style may divide opposite the anthers rather than above them, possibly a developmental abberration. Moraea fugacissima is most easily confused with M. stagnalis but that species has broader leaves and smaller flowers with a perianth tube 5-10 mm long, a short style dividing opposite the anthers, and filaments typically free in the upper third.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Disa atrorubens is closely related to D. ophrydea by its purple colouration, but may be distinguished by the shape of its lip. A putative hybrid has been recorded with D. sabulosa as the second parent.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Largest member of ser. Galaxia, Moraea kamisensis has large yellow flowers, the perianth tube up to 25 mm long and tepals 22-30 mm long. The spreading to nearly prostrate foliage leaves have conspicuously thickened, ± translucent margins (hyaline when dry) that are fairly densely ciliate, similar to those of leaves of M. galaxia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very variable in several characters over the whole distribution range.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The ovate to oblong, ± prostrate leaves of Moraea luteoalba are like those of the more common M. galaxia but it has sharply different flowers with tepals deep yellow in the centre typically grading to creamy white distally or sometimes uniformly yellow, and filaments united only in the lower third and diverging distally. Moraea galaxia always has uniformly yellow flowers with the filaments united entirely in a bottle-shaped column, with the anthers appressed to the style.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively small plant, Moraea pilifolia has pale yellow flowers with a perianth tube up to 10 mm long and tepals 6-10 mm long, otherwise typical of ser. Galaxia, thus with united filaments, sessile anthers and short, fringed style branches. The leaves are distinctive in their oblong shape with thickened, densely long-ciliate margins. It most closely resembles M. galaxia, which has broader, usually prostrate leaves, the margins with short cilia, and larger flowers with tepals 16-20 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the tallest species of subg. Homeria, standing up to 750 mm, Moraea pendula has several, glaucous-grey foliage leaves and bright yellow, nodding to completely pendent flowers that are unusual in having the tepal limbs tightly reflexed against the pedicels. The filaments are fully united in a column abruptly swollen above the base and tapering to a narrow apex, and the tepal claws, ± 4 mm long, clasp the bulbous part of the filament column. Typically the anthers and pollen are orange-red and provide a contrast to the yellow tepals. Moraea pendula is evidently closely related to the widespread M. miniata, which has smaller, spreading tepals but a similar filament column swollen at the base. Both occur in the Kamiesberg but M. pendula blooms later in the year and grows in wetter sites than M. miniata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The smallest species of subg. Homeria, Moraea demissa has a solitary leaf, flexuose stem, and yellow flowers with tepals only 9-12 mm long. The tepal claws are suberect and form a narrow cup that includes the lower half of the filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The only yellow-flowered species of ser. Eurystigma, Moraea citrina has relatively large flowers with tepals usually 20-28 mm long and rarely wider than 10 mm. The glossy leaves are channelled and have straight margins. It is one of just two species of the series with sessile anthers, the other being M. versicolor. Orange-flowered plants are known from the Bokkeveld Mtns at the northern end of its range. Hybrids have been recorded near Ceres between M. citrina and M. variabilis. These plants have larger flowers in a range of colours, mostly pale orange, not recorded in either species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the smallest species of subg. Galaxia, Moraea fenestralis has falcate, terete leaves with a transparent band of tissue on the upper (adaxial) surface. Plants bloom early in the season, mostly in June but also July, and the small flowers have tepals ± 15 mm long. An unusual feature of the flowers is that the inner tepals are joined to the filament column for ± 2 mm. The short style branches bear broad stigmatic lobes with entire, undulate margins, the ancestral condition for the subgenus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With very small, white flowers, Moraea minima has nearly prostrate leaves with flat or shallowly channelled blades and style branches with entire stigmatic lobes. The flowers have a perianth tube only 7-10 mm long and tepals 9-12 mm long. Possibly most closely related to M. melanops or M. versicolor, both of which have larger, pink to purple flowers, M. minima differs significantly in having a short style so that the stigma lobes reach only to the middle of the anthers, the pollen thus in direct contact with the stigmas, and the species is self-compatible and, under greenhouse conditions, autogamous. The similarity of the small white flowers of M. minima to those of M. albiflora, which is also autogamous, is superficial and M. albiflora has the fringed style branches typical of ser. Galaxia. Moraea minima has a unique chromosome number in subg. Galaxia, a derived diploid number of 2n = 12, the lowest number in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With a reddish purple flower with yellow cup, Moraea variabilis most resembles M. versicolor but differs in the glossy, dark green leaves, channelled with straight margins, filaments usually united entirely or rarely free for less than 1 mm, thus with the anthers sessile or almost so, and the style dividing just above the anther tips. Moraea versicolor has the leaves usually glaucous and with wavy margins, the filaments free and diverging in the upper 1.0-1.5 mm, and the style dividing 2-3 mm above the tips of the anthers. The ranges of the two species are complimentary. Apparent hybrids with Moraea citrina have been recorded at a few sites and have large orange or pink flowers. The variation in flower size and colour among the hybrids suggests that they are interbreeding.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea versicolor has pink to purple flowers with tepals forming a cup in the lower half, usually with a yellow centre but populations with a blue to violet centre occur locally. The leaves are usually somewhat glaucous and widely channelled and often somewhat twisted, with undulate margins. The filaments are free and diverging in the upper 1.0-1.5 mm and united in the lower part, usually forming a bottle-shaped column wider in the lower half but populations with a cylindric filament column occur in the Breede River Valley. The style divides above the anthers, often exceeding them by 3-4 mm. Moraea variabilis has similarly coloured flowers but glossy, channelled leaves with straight margins, and filaments united entirely or rarely free distally for less than 1 mm, with the style dividing just above the anther tips. The species is variable for chromosome number and most populations have a diploid number of 2n = 16 but plants from the northern Cape Peninsula and from the Tulbagh Valley have 2n = 14.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A putative hybrid, known as Disa x brendae, has been recorded with D. uniflora. A hybrid has also been reported with D. tripetaloides as the second parent, and was formally named D. x nuwebergensis.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Stands out in its slender, terete leaf, often loosely spirally coiled, and in the small, violet flower with subequal tepals with spreading to reflexed limbs and short, almost vestigial style branches lacking crests. The flower is subsessile and the perianth is raised above the spathes on a sterile, tubular extension of the ovary, a structure that is paralleled in sect. Gynandriris. Moraea herrei is allied to two southern Namibian species, M. graniticola and M. rigidifolia, both of which have a shortly beaked ovary with the beak much shorter than in M. herrei. Moraea graniticola differs additionally in having a true perianth tube and a stem barely reaching above ground.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea brachygyne has a solitary, narrow leaf up to 4 mm wide, with the stem sharply flexed above the sheath, and small, salmon-pink flowers with short tepal claws and a slender filament column 6-8 mm long prominently papillate in the lower half. Yellow-flowered M. fuscomontana seems closest to M. brachygyne but has a shorter filament column ± 6 mm long, velvety in the lower two-thirds. The flowers themselves differ little from those of M. miniata except for the cylindric, rather than flask-shaped, filament column, but M. miniata is also readily distinguished by its multi-leaved habit.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species may be readily identified by the slender beetroot-red plant with minute flowers with saccate spurs.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the solitary foliage leaf sheathing the lower half of the stem, short lateral branches borne in the upper half of the stem, and pink or yellow, star-like flowers with short tepal claws and spreading tepal limbs. The filament column is swollen and bulbous just above the narrow base and tapers in the upper third to a narrow apex. The tepal claws, ± 2 mm long, are erect and clasp the bulbous part of the filament column. The flowers are virtually identical to those of the widespread M. miniata but the latter is very different vegetatively, having at least two and often three or four foliage leaves, not clasping the stem for any distance. The two species can occasionally be found growing nearby but no intermediates are known and experiments have shown they cannot be crossed. The distinctive vegetative form of M. bifida is shared with M. fragrans but the flowers are rather different, the latter with tepal claws diverging from the base to form a shallow cup. Hybrids have been found in the wild between these two species in the Nieuwoudtville area where the two are common though confined to different soils.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]
