description: Distinguished in subg. Vieusseuxia by the comparatively large, dark violet-purple flowers, the outer tepals 26-40 mm long with unusually long claws 10-12 mm long, and narrow, either ± linear or 3-lobed inner tepals. It is closely related to M. unguiculata, which has smaller flowers and almost always trilobed inner tepals with a large incurved central cusp and small but broadly obtuse lateral lobes. The slender filament column and narrow style branches are also characteristic of the M. unguiculata group of species. Typical plants south of De Rust have violet flowers but a collection from south of Oudtshoorn with pale blue flowers may also belong here.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Disa filicornis is very closely related with D. tenuifolia with which it also hybridizes.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: One of three species of subg. Polyanthes with filiform, undivided style branches extending between the anthers, Moraea monticola is distinguished by the single, falcate to trailing foliage leaf with a terete blade. Related M. marginata has a broad, channelled leaf with thickened margins and slightly smaller flowers, the tepals 9-13 mm long vs. 13-15 in M. monticola.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Relatively poorly documented, Moraea flavescens is rather variable as circumscribed at present. Plants in the south have smaller flowers than those in the north of its range and specimens from this area bear the manuscript name H. klawerensis L.Bolus. The species is characterised by its pale, watery yellow flowers with a wide tepal cup and emarginate outer tepals, and flat style branches shorter than the anthers. Populations from the southern Cederberg have the unusual diploid number of 2n = 9, and form complex heterozygotes at meiosis. Moraea flavescens is closely related to a second Cederberg-Gifberg endemic, M. demissa, which also has unusual chromosome cytology with diploid numbers of 2n = 10, 9 or 8. Moraea demissa has smaller flowers, also pale yellow, but the tepal claws are suberect and form a narrow cup around the lower half of the filament column. Flowers of M. flavescens open in the morning while those of M. demissa open after midday and last through the late afternoon.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A remarkable member of subg. Vieusseuxia, Moraea worcesterensis has small, star-like, violet-purple flowers with spreading outer and inner tepals both with small yellow nectar guides at the limb bases. The style branches, held well above the tepals, are much reduced, < 1 mm wide and ± as wide as the anthers, and lack true crests. The purple filaments are united in a cylindric column but free distally and the purple anthers slightly exceed the style branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: So unusual is Moraea flexicaulis that when first described it was assigned to a separate sect. Flexuosae of subg. Moraea, but molecular studies have shown it to be deeply nested in subg. Homeria, in which its chromosome number, 2n = 12, and karyotype of exclusively acrocentric chromosomes are consistent, as are the largely united filaments forming a sturdy, cylindric column. Moraea flexicaulis is now considered to be most closely allied to two Namaqualand species of subg. Homeria, M. schlechteri and M. knersvlaktensis, all three with several leaves, even those in the upper part of the stem with free blades, and filaments free and diverging distally. The species remains a very distinctive member of the subgenus. Its particularly well-developed style branches and crests are exceptional in subg. Homeria but both its presumed close allies have style branches bearing moderately well-developed crests although they have much shorter style branches. Blooming early in the season, in late June and July, Moraea flexicaulis comes into flower three to four weeks after the first soaking autumn or winter rains fall in this arid area of the southern African northwest coast. As with many plants of arid areas, plant size is very variable depending on rainfall. Plants from the base of the Ploegberg in the Richtersveld are unusually robust compared to other collections, up to 150 mm tall (vs. < 100 mm elsewhere) and with larger rhipidial spathes (45-50 mm vs. 20-40 mm) and broader leaves, leaving open the possibility that they may be a separate species but this remains uncertain until more material is available.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species may be confused with Disa purpurascens, from which it is readily distinguished by the subclavate spur, down-curved lip margins and the later flowering time. A natural hybrid with D. ferruginea as the second parent has been described as Herscheliodisa vogelpoelii.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is highly variable in flower colour and the degree of laceration of the lip, often within populations.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Like its apparent close relative, Moraea galpinii, M. robusta has distinctive coarsely fibrous corm tunics forming a collar around the stem base but it differs from M. galpinii in its larger, white or pale yellow flowers with the limbs of both the inner and outer tepals at length spreading to laxly reflexed, the outer tepals 55-65 mm long vs. ± 40 mm in M. galpinii. The leaf is channelled and wider than in M. galpinii, 4-10 mm wide but in some populations the margins are closely inrolled. Populations on the slopes of The Sentinel in the northern KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg have the upper portion dry and broken suggesting emergence before winter, whereas the lower portions are green, evidently having emerged in the spring. The narrowly ellipsoid capsules are up to 45 mm long and up to 10 mm at the widest. The capsules contain numerous angular seeds arranged in two rows per locule. The narrow capsules with a prominent beak and angular seeds stand in marked contrast to the ± ovoid capsules and flattened, discoid seeds of M. spathulata and other species of the subgenus for which these characters are known.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Resembles M. villosa in its velvety stems and outer leaf surfaces but differs in its clear blue to blue-mauve flowers, usually lacking markings on the tepal limbs and with dark, almost black tepal claws. Moraea calcicola is a more slender plant than M. villosa and has closer set outer tepals with darkly bearded claws 8-10 mm long and relatively short filaments 2-3 mm long. Moraea villosa has large dark nectar guides and contrasting yellow tepal claws 8-12 mm long, and filaments 4-5 mm long. The dark-coloured hairs on the outer tepal claws of M. calcicola are reminiscent of M. loubseri, which has outer tepals with a heavy beard covering the claws and proximal part of the limb, and the inner tepals are similarly coloured.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the tallest and most robust species of sect. Gynandriris, stems of Moraea hesperantha may reach up to 650 mm high and bear several, short lateral branches. The two long, suberect, channelled leaves trail distally. The dark violet flowers recall those of M. pritzeliana but have suberect inner tepals vs. reflexed in M. pritzeliana, which has characteristically coiled leaves and is a much shorter plant. Moraea hesperantha stands out in particular in being evening blooming: the flowers open at 16:00-16:30, about the time that flowers of M. pritzeliana begin to fade, and the flowers last till well after dark, usually collapsing by 19:30. The evening blooming habit is unique in sect. Gynandriris.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Large-flowered Moraea comptonii is distinguished by the fiddle-shaped to spathulate tepals weakly divided into claw and limb, with the lower halves forming an open cup and upper halves spreading. The flowers are particularly strongly and sweetly scented and either entirely yellow, or salmon-pink to orange with a yellow cup, often with dark green markings in the lower third. Like its close relative M. elegans, plants have a solitary leaf, a partly to fully included ovary, and the inner rhipidial spathes become enlarged to enclose the developing capsules. Also like M. elegans, the filaments are fully united in a column tapering from a wide base but the anthers are usually shorter than the style branches in contrast to M. elegans, in which the anthers exceed the style branches. Another difference between the two is that the tepals of M. elegans are more-or-less ovate, widest in the lower third, and the tepal markings are confined to the outer tepals in the upper third, whereas tepals of M. comptonii are widest in the distal third and are either unmarked or have markings at the bases of the tepal limbs of both whorls.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An unusual species, Moraea linderi has the brown, woody, initially entire corm tunics and outer rhipidial spathes free distally, that characterise subg. Umbellatae but stands out in having a well-developed basal leaf (leaves in the subgenus are often inserted well above ground) and filaments united for ± 1 mm (± one sixth of their length). The flowers have well-developed style branches and prominent crests ± 10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea longiaristata and M. barnardii have a superficially similar flower but the inner tepals of M. longiaristata are linear and erect, ± 15 mm long and the outer tepals have claws 12-16 mm long, whereas M. barnardii lacks inner tepals entirely, and the outer tepal claws are ± 7 mm long and shorter than the tepal limbs. Associated with the longer tepals claws, the filaments of M. longiaristata are up to 15 mm long but only 8-9 mm long in M. barnardii. In other respects, including broad, white outer tepal limbs with undulate margins, nectar guides consisting of dark blue spots, the short, purple anthers and red pollen, the two species are very alike.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although evidently a member of subg. Monocephalae, Moraea vallisavium has some unusual features for the alliance, particularly the finely fibrous corm tunics, the persistent old corms that accumulate beneath the current corm, and the leaf blade compressed and unifacial rather than terete. Also unusual, the margins of the sheathing leaf and outer rhipidial spathes are free to the base, whereas those of other species of the subgenus are united basally for a short distance. Like other members of the subgenus M. vallisavium has a solitary foliage leaf, an unbranched stem and fairly large yellow flowers. The seeds are unusual for subg. Monocephalae in their relatively large size ± angular shape, quite unlike the flattened discoid seeds of other species of the subgenus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With flowers typical of the genus, Moraea namaquamontana has moderate-sized, yellow flowers with outer tepals up to 28 mm long and inner up to 25 mm long, both whorls with half reflexed limbs. It stands out particularly in having several, mostly basal, relatively broad leaves, falcate and slightly twisted. The stems usually have one or two branches, these subtended by short, partly sheathing bract-like leaves. The fairly short rhipidial spathes, the outer about one third as long as the inner, recall those of M. gawleri and the corms of the two species are similar, having relatively coarse fibres with prominent vertical members.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the flexuose stem, sharply flexed above the sheaths of the two to four leaves, the lowermost of these inserted well above ground level. All nodes of the stem bear foliage leaves except for the terminal which bears the inflorescence. The pink (rarely yellow) flowers have a yellow cup formed by the diverging tepals claws, often so narrow at the base that the edges are gapped, the cup thus windowed near the base. Plants from the Koedoes Mtns lack these windows but in other respects match the type except that some plants have uniformly yellow flowers. The flowers have filaments united in a slender column, only slightly wider toward the base, and contiguous anthers, with the stigmatic tips of the forked style branches extending between the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Disa ophrydea is related to D. atrorubens by the purple colour, but is readily distinguished by the narrow lip.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the large dark blue flowers with relatively broad tepals, the outer 21-26 x 10-12 mm long, with the claws ± a third as long as the limbs, Moraea contorta is most closely related to the more widespread M. pritzeliana and its range falls entirely with that of the latter. The flowers of M. contorta have a strong sweet, coconut-like scent while those of M. pritzeliana, often darker in colour, are apparently unscented. Vegetative differences are more pronounced, and M. contorta typically has a single, linear, channelled leaf in contrast to the very distinctive pair of opposed, helically coiled leaves of M. pritzeliana. The two species share a unique feature, as the capsules ripen and the stems dry out they become loosely coiled.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by its bell-shaped corm with the woody corm tunics splitting from the basal point; wiry, divaricately branched stem with spreading, scalloped spikes of small, cream-coloured to pale yellow flowers with lanceolate-attenuate tepals and an obsolete perianth tube; and distinctive depressed-cordate, deeply 3-lobed or -winged capsules with finely papillate surface.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With yellow flowers typical of sect. Hexaglottis, Moraea riparia is distinctive largely in its small obovoid to club-shaped capsules and comparatively slender, often willowy stems. The capsules, 6-10 mm long (occasionally up to 12 mm long in robust plants), recall those of M. longifolia but this species has much larger capsules, usually 16-23 mm long. Moraea riparia is diploid, 2n = 12, whereas M. longifolia, usually a taller plant, is tetraploid, 2n = 24. The flowers of M. riparia are deep yellow and scented in contrast to the pale yellow, usually odourless flowers of M. longifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished in sect. Gynandriris by the relatively large flower, the outer tepals 23-30 mm long and style crests 8-12 mm long, M. australis otherwise closely resembles the widespread M. setifolia. The latter, an autogamous, weedy species has smaller flowers with outer tepals 12-18 mm long and style crests 4-7 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: There is some superficial similarity to Disa scullyi, with which it may be confused in the Eastern Cape. The species is somewhat variable over its range.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Stands out in sect. Hexaglottis in the spreading to prostrate basal leaves, undulate and twisted leaf blades with crisped margins, and branched stem with all lateral inflorescences stalked. Other species have linear, upright leaves with straight margins and sessile or very shortly stalked lateral inflorescences. The flowers are virtually identical with those of M. lewisiana and M. rupicola except for their slightly smaller size, with tepals ± 20 mm long. The capsules are ellipsoid and well exserted from the spathes. Moraea lewisiana growing nearby at the type locality has linear leaves and tall stems but no intermediates between the two species are known.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species belongs to the long, slenderspurred group, and is easily distinguished by the leathery green bracts, and the petals and sepals forming a floral 'tube'.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Is readily distinguished from all others by the geniculate spur and bifid petals.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the relatively small, white flowers, Moraea cedarmontana has outer tepals 24-27 mm long and the inner 20-25 x 3-5 mm, relatively narrow in proportion to the length. Plants are usually fairly slender and up to 300 mm tall.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Nivenia stenosiphon, which flowers in the autumn and early winter, closely resembles the late spring-flowering N. binata in the form of the inflorescence and in the long, wrinkled flower bracts, and the blue anthers and pollen. The flowers in both species are heterostylous and paired within the binate inflorescence units, and there seems little doubt that they are immediately related. They are distinguished by the phenology and dimensions of the floral bracts and perianth tube, the bracts 8-9 mm long and the perianth tube 32-38 mm long in N. stenosiphon.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The large, congested and flat-topped compound inflorescence of single-flowered rhipidia in Nivenia dispar closely resembles that of N. corymbosa and the two species can be distinguished only by comparison of flower size. Both species are heterostylous, but flowers of N. corymbosa are consistently smaller, with the perianth tube 11-13 mm long and tepals 9-11 mm long versus the perianth tube 16-20 mm long and the tepals 11-14 mm long in N. dispar.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The heterostylous Nivenia corymbosa can easily be recognised by its relatively small, dark blue flowers in large corymb-like compound inflorescence often comprising more than 100 flowers. The binate rhipidia bear a single flower each, and the two style morphs are quite different, with the filaments either prominently exserted ± 8.5 mm from the tube (thrum flowers), or nearly sessile with the anthers placed immediately above the mouth of the perianth tube (pin flowers).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This subspecies is very variable, both within and between populations. The common form is large-flowered, a pale reddish or greenish colour, with well-developed lateral lip lobes and patent lateral sepals, while there is a rarer form which is smaller-flowered, has a purplish colour, with very short lateral lip lobes and the lateral sepals usually held erect in front of the galea entrance. Although most individuals can readily be referred to one of these forms, the existence of numerous intermediates precludes the formal recognition of separate taxa.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The paired flowers in large corymbose inflorescences and long, brown, wrinkled bracts are the most distinctive features of Nivenia binata. The flowers have a relatively short perianth tube and are heterostylous. The unusual dark blue anthers and blue pollen are shared with N. parviflora and N. stenosiphon, restricted to the Klein Swartberg and adjacent Touwsberg, just east of the range of N. binata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This generally lowland species, as well as the closely related montane R. campanuloides, differs from R. rosea, R. eximea, and R. cruciata which have somewhat similar flowers, in the small ridge at the base of the corm, and inner bracts with colourless membranous margins; also in flowering period (late summer and autumn) and in chromosome number.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Quite distinct in this section by the yellow colour and the long apiculi.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: A diminutive species separated from Romulea rosea by its one or two filiform leaves up to 0.5 mm diam., and solitary, white to pale pink flowers with golden-yellow cup and anthers ± half as long as the filaments. An allied, winter-flowering species from the Cold Bokkeveld, Romulea lilacina, has a solitary, sticky leaf and larger, lilac flowers without a yellow cup, the tepals 16-20 mm long and filaments 8-9 mm long, produced in May and June. Anatomically, the leaves lack secondary veins and have highly reduced fibre strands in the rib margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to Romulea autumnalis from lower altitudes in the Eastern Cape and sharing with it a corm with a small, narrowly toothed basal ridge but distinguished by the mostly smaller flowers with closely ribbed bracts and longer stamens and style, typically more than half as long as the perianth and thus exserted from the floral cup.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is variable in the size of the flowers, the length of the apiculi and the degree of crenulation of the petals, lip and median sepal. Although there is some geographical basis to this variation the various characters are not correlated.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The only member of ser. Bicarinatae with yellow flowers, distinguished from other species in the genus with yellow flowers blotched with brown in the throat by the large size of the flowers and by the strongly ribbed inner and outer bracts, the inner bracts 2-keeled with the keel veins stouter than the others. The black-chequered bract margins are characteristic.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the basally pointed corm, conspicuous membranous tips to the outer bracts, and magenta flowers with yellow cup. Similar corms occur in several species in sect. Roseae but the immediate relationships of the species appear to lie with Romulea atrandra and other species with strongly veined outer bracts with prominent membranous tips, rather than with other pink-flowered species with pointed corms and lightly veined outer bracts lacking prominent membranous tips, such as R. cruciata. The species may be confused with R. atrandra in the Little Karoo and examination of the corms is necessary to separate R. vlokii, with straight basal teeth converging to a basal point, from R. atrandra, with a rounded corm with basal teeth curved or bent over a basal ridge.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in the genus in its mostly solitary leaf (rarely with an additional one or two much reduced leaves) and large, orange to reddish orange flowers with black and yellow markings in the cup. The basal leaf is thick and subfistulose, 2-4 mm wide and broadly 4-grooved.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: There is substantial geographical variation in this species, in the size of the plants, in the shape of the tepals, and the colouration. Yellow forms occur occasionally, and a white albino has also been reported.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: This species may be difficult to distinguish from Disa racemosa. White albino forms have been recorded.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Usually a tall plant, sometimes reaching 650 mm, Sparaxis pillansii has lax spikes of large flowers coloured old rose to dull pink with a small yellow centre edged with red to purple. The shape of the radially symmetric flowers closely resembles that of S. tricolor, a shorter plant seldom exceeding 350 mm with bright orange flowers with a larger yellow centre. Molecular phylogenetic analysis shows S. pillansii and S. tricolor to be immediately related and sister to S. elegans. The species occupy very different soil types and their ranges complement one another. In some populations the anthers are very slightly twisted, a feature otherwise unknown in the genus, except for the exaggerated twisting of the anthers of S. elegans.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised but its ± cup-shaped, radially symmetric, brilliant orange flowers with a yellow centre edged in dark red-brown to almost black. The dark markings enclosing the yellow extend as a narrow line almost to the base of the tepals. The yellow stamens are erect and surround the style, which divides opposite the lower third of the anthers into short branches 2-3 mm long. The ± narrowly deltoid-ovate bracts of S. tricolor and allied S. elegans and S. pillansii differ from those of other species in the genus in lacking obvious veins, and the outer are initially entire and acute, later becoming irregularly torn. The bracts, also crinkled and flecked with dark brown streaks, are quite different to the cuspidate bracts of other species of the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small and inconspicuous member of ser. Atrandrae distinguished by the 1 to 3 leaves, ± membranous inner and outer bracts, and unmarked, pale yellow flowers with tepals 8-20 mm long and short anthers 3-4 mm long. The short, stout peduncles have a characteristic knee-bend just below the flower.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Related to the R. atrandra group of species and distinguished by its small, pale yellow flowers on rather stout peduncles which recurve with an almost knee-like bend even before the flowers fade, often pushing the developing capsules underground. The dry capsule again appears above ground when the peduncle coils up.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of a handful of species with basally pointed corms, distinguished by the soft inner bract, subherbaceous only in the upper half, and with wide membranous margins and tips, and the golden-yellow flowers with darker veins in the throat.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Disperis cardiophora and D. renibractea are closely related and characterized by the single leaf near the stem base, secund inflorescence and reni-form bracts with pellucid margins. In D. cardiophora the flowers are smaller and the petals are orientated so as to obscure their inside when the flower is viewed from the front.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Very closely related to R. komsbergensis.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: D. x duckittiae, a putative hybrid has been reported with D. villosa as the second parent.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from other members of sect. Roseae with rounded corms by the golden-yellow flowers, usually with dark veins in the cup, dark reddish brown, subterete peduncles not spreading or coiling in fruit, and subherbaceous outer bracts with relatively narrow, finely brown-speckled margins. Closely resembling yellow-flowered forms of Romulea obscura from the Olifants River Valley but distinguished by its brighter yellow flowers with proportionally shorter bracts less than half as long as the perianth, inner bracts with broader membranous margins ± as wide as the central green portion, and the peduncles remaining suberect or curved in fruit. The flowers in R. obscura are mostly dull yellow (to salmon-pink) with the bracts more than half as long as the flowers, the membranous margins of the inner bracts distinctly narrower than the central green portion, and peduncles widely spreading in fruit. Romulea monticola may also be confused with R. luteoflora, which typically has more strongly herbaceous bracts with whitish margins and apices marked with larger, dark flecks, and peduncles that ultimately coil up in fruit. Neither R. obscura nor R. luteoflora have been recorded from the Bokkeveld and Matsikamma-Gifberg. It is also superficially similar to R. montana (sect. Romulea), which usually has dark markings on the tepals, bracts without visible membranous margins, and corms with a crescent-shaped basal ridge.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Disperis disiformis is closely related to D. micrantha but is easily recognized by the deflexed spur on the median sepal.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Resembling white-flowered Romulea toximontana in the wide, scalloped basal ridge on the corm but distinguished by its bright yellow flowers, usually with dark blotches or streaks in the throat. The species is essentially identical in flower to the Bokkeveld endemic R. discifera, but that species has a conspicuously depressed corm with a complete, circular, similarly scalloped basal rim. Another common, yellow-flowered species, R. monticola (sect. Roseae), has flowers without dark markings, bracts with narrow, brown-speckled markings, and corms with coarse, bent teeth.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to R. fibrosa.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species is closely related with Disperis cardiophora from which it is distinguished by the larger flowers and large anterior petal lobes which are strongly marked on the inside.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: One of three species in the genus with similar, 4-winged leaves, often hairy on the wing margins, but the only one with this leaf type in sect. Roseae and also the only one with pale yellow flowers. The flowers often have an indistinct dark band in the throat but are only rarely (a single collection from the Nieuwoudtville Wildflower Reserve) marked with distinct black blotches. The exact relationships of the species are not clear. There is a tendency for the bracts to develop prominent membranous apices as in ser. Atrandrae, and specimens with dark markings have been confused with Romulea luteoflora.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A putative hybrid between this species and D. cucullata is known from three localities in the Darling district of the Western Cape, and is known as D. x duckittiae.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Very closely related to R. atrandra.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from allied species in ser. Atrandrae with magenta flowers by the conspicuous brown stain covering the base of the floral cup and filaments, and cytologically in a having 2n = 20 rather than 22. The orange-yellow cup is rimmed with a purple or blue transverse band and the tepals often fade bluish at the tips. The species typically has a short style dividing near the base of the anthers but populations around Middelpos in the north of the range have the style well exserted, up to 4 mm beyond the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from R. atrandra by its less rigid, more membranous bracts, incurved or circinnate anthers, acuminate style branches, and perianth cup with a brown base. One or two of the style branches are sometimes split, thus forming more than six stigmas.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished by the very shortly pedunculate, yellow flowers with relatively long, funnel-shaped perianth tube, (13-)20-65 mm long, and correspondingly long, submembranous bracts, 20-60 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species in the section with aerial stems by its mostly two basal leaves with narrow grooves, white or pale yellow to pale apricot-coloured flowers, and more easterly distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species recognised by its one or two filiform conduplicate leaves and small, violet to purple, salver-shaped flowers with stamens inserted at the mouth of the tube, and entirely membranous bracts outer and inner bracts. Its relationships are obscured by the highly derived flowers but the absence of secondary veins in the leaves is an unusual character found in relatively few species in the genus, typically in members of sect. Tortuosae which also have a tendency for conduplicate leaves but which are uniformly yellow-flowered, and have the derived chromosome number 2n = 30 or 32. A more likely alliance is with species such as R. vinacea, with similar leaf anatomy and lilac flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the rounded corm, arched or abruptly spreading, smooth or shortly ciliate leaves and pink to magenta, salver-shaped flowers with perianth tube 15-22 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An early-flowering species allied to Romulea atrandra and resembling thick-leaved forms of that species but separated by its winter-flowering and pale lilac or wisteria-blue flowers with orange-yellow cup, and outer bracts with acute, triangular herbaceous basal portion.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species recognised by the obliquely hemispherical corm, solitary leaf up to 200 mm long with adhering sand grains, and one or two golden-yellow flowers with both outer and inner bracts submembranous and flushed purple in the lower half and also with adhering sand grains. The corm, partially bifacial leaf, submembranous outer and inner bracts, yellow flower, and chromosome number 2n = ± 30, 32 all indicate a relationship with Romulea tortuosa and its allies but the solitary leaf with mucilage secretions is diagnostic.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Related to R. hirsuta.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished by its exserted stem, ± unmarked golden-yellow flowers (rarely white with a yellow cup), and bell-shaped corm. White morphs are known only from near Stanford, and the populations in the Overberg near Caledon are unusual in having the outer tepals flushed dark brown on the reverse - all other populations have the tepals yellow on both sides. Plants with ± bicoloured tepals in which the outer half is tinged salmon-coloured or orange are referred to Romulea hirsuta subsp. cuprea.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of two species in ser. Ciliatae with a wide, fan-shaped basal ridge on the corm and green bracts, Romulea toximontana is distinguished from yellow-flowered R. montana, which occurs on the Bokkeveld Mtns and Cederberg but is absent from the Gifberg, by its white or cream-coloured flowers with pale yellow anthers and a chromosome number 2n = ± 28. It is readily confused in flower with another Gifberg endemic, R. sladenii, which has a bell-shaped corm with circular basal ridge and more widely spreading peduncles diverging at ± 180o.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to R. hirsuta.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by tree habit, smooth, pale bark, strongly discolorous leaves and usually ovoid, ribbed fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Chippendale, GM. 1988. Eucalyptus, Fl. Australia 19: 1-448. Australian Govt Publishing Service, Canberra. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely related to E. lehmannii, but a small, smooth-barked tree with larger buds and fruits. This and E. lehmannii are the only species with fused hypanthia.
bibliographicCitation: Chippendale, GM. 1988. Eucalyptus, Fl. Australia 19: 1-448. Australian Govt Publishing Service, Canberra. [All rights reserved]

description: A very tall tree with smooth bark usually in coloured patches, discolorous leaves, 7-flowered umbels, and fruits which are ovoid or subglobular.
bibliographicCitation: Chippendale, GM. 1988. Eucalyptus, Fl. Australia 19: 1-448. Australian Govt Publishing Service, Canberra. [All rights reserved]

description: A large tree with grey flaky-fibrous bark, 7-flowered umbels, usually sessile buds and large, campanulate or cylindrical fruits. The hemispherical operculum clearly wider than the hypanthium is distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Chippendale, GM. 1988. Eucalyptus, Fl. Australia 19: 1-448. Australian Govt Publishing Service, Canberra. [All rights reserved]

description: In morphological features this species shows relationship with both R. minutiflora and R. rosea var. australis, the corm, especially, being intermediate between the two. It might well have originated from these as an amphidiploid, as is indicated by its chromosome number of 2n=44. It has often been mistaken for R. rosea var. australis, but it differs from the latter in its corm and somewhat greener bracts.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very tall tree with rough fibrous bark to about halfway up trunk, then smooth, white or grey-green bark above, with umbels paired in leaf axils.
bibliographicCitation: Chippendale, GM. 1988. Eucalyptus, Fl. Australia 19: 1-448. Australian Govt Publishing Service, Canberra. [All rights reserved]

description: Leaves broadly rounded to subacute at apex. Leaves coriaceous, up to 4-6 x 3 cm, base usually subcordate or broadly rounded.
bibliographicCitation: White, F; Kupicha, FK. 1978. 74. Myrtaceae. In: E Launert (ed.), Fl. Zambes. 4: 183-212. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, Glasgow. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from R. citrina by its bracts with pronounced brown streaks on the margins and tip, and from R. luteoflora by its corm and its ripe capsules which are on almost straight peduncles on an elongated stem.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An enigmatic species unique in the genus in its entirely red flowers without a paler cup. It might be considered a colour form of R. amoena but also differs from that species in the incomplete basal rim on the corm and in its glabrous, reddish filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very closely related to R. minutiflora. Might be considered as a slightly larger form of R. minutiflora distinguished by slightly larger flowers with slightly wider perianth segments, longer anthers and style, and by the faint marks on the margins of the inner bracts. The morphological features and chromosome number indicate a possible amphidiploid origin from R. minutiflora and some other species of Romulea.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A mostly acaulescent, rarely short-stemmed species with filiform leaves, usually colourless (rarely brown-flecked) membranous margins to the inner bracts, and yellow to apricot-coloured flowers with a yellow cup, sometimes with dark blotches in the throat. Romulea setifolia is highly variable in the dimensions and markings of the flowers and in the relative lengths of anthers and filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The broadly concave sac in the lip lamina readily distinguishes this taxon from all other southern African species of Eulophia.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely related to R. flava.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The large, broadly rounded sac at the base of the lip, the broad, truncate midlobe, and the rhomboid crests at the distal rim of the lip sac make this species distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: In general appearance this species resembles some forms of Eulophia clavicomis which differ in lacking an abscission layer in the leaves, in having the lip crests vestigial on the side lobes, the lip narrow at the base and the leaves and sheaths lacking purple spots.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The most common species in the genus, diagnosed by the rounded corms and magenta to lilac-pink or white flowers with greenish or golden-yellow cup, often with a violet zone in the throat but without distinct blotches, herbaceous outer bracts with narrow membranous margins and apices, and peduncles curving after flowering but straightening and ± erect as the capsules dry out. It is distinguished from Romulea obscura by the lack of yellow pigmentation in the tepals (apart from the cup), the flowers thus either white or pink with a bluish cast, fruiting peduncles straightening in fruit, and a somatic chromosome number 2n = 18. Romulea rosea is a polymorphic species with a number of variants and forms, often connected by intermediates.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The central species in ser. Atrandrae, Romulea atrandra is highly variable in size, flower colour and markings. It is diagnosed by the rounded corm, firm-textured and closely ribbed outer bracts with conspicuous brown-flecked membranous tips, and white, pale blue or lilac to magenta flowers with white to golden-yellow cup, with or without dark blotches around the cup or dark lines in the cup. The most striking form, occurring over much of the Roggeveld, has large, bright magenta flowers with a pale yellow or whitish cup boldly striped with black on the veins, and banded with black in the throat. Other populations have white or pale blue to pink or magenta flowers with unstriped cups, either pale or golden-yellow and with or without dark markings in the throat. Populations along the south coast have small, unmarked, white to pale blue flowers and may be confused with forms of R. rosea, from which they differ in the closely ribbed bracts with conspicuous brown-flecked tips, and anatomically in lacking veins in the rib margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of a pair of allied aquatic species with more than four longitudinal grooves in the leaves, Romulea aquatica is recognised by its solitary basal leaf, cup-shaped perianth tube with short filaments, 2-3 mm long, short anthers 3-5 mm long, and short, suberect fruiting peduncles, 10-30(-50) mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Related to R. multisulcata.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of a small group of Namaqualand species with prominent, brown-flecked membranous apices to the outer bracts, distinguished by the stemless or short-stemmed habit, large white flowers with outer tepals feathered purple on the reverse, and the purple upper cataphyll conspicuously and finely speckled with white above ground.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from similar pink or lilac-flowered species such as Romulea schlechteri and R. saxatilis by the strongly discolorous outer segments glossy dark plum-coloured or wine-red on the reverse, contrasting strongly with the pale inner tepals. Additional features of the species are leaves with ciliate rib margins, peduncles with ciliolate angles, and inner bracts with the margins brown-flecked along the edge.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to Eulophia macowanii, which differs in having numerous slender papillae on the central third of the lip, generally narrower leaves (10-30 mm broad) and the lip white with only the main lateral nerves purple near the base.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Usually readily recognised by the several, often flexuous leaves bifacial to the tips and sometimes conspicuously ciliate or pilose, the yellow flowers subtended by ± entirely membranous inner and outer bracts, and the often strongly vertically flattened corm with broad, fan-like basal rim. Some forms of Romulea tortuosa have been confused with R. austinii, but that species has fewer leaves, 2 to 4(6) that are unifacial in the upper half and never more than sparsely ciliolate, and only partially membranous inner and outer bracts that are green and herbaceous or subherbaceous in the upper half. Romulea tortuosa varies greatly in the size and markings of the flowers, which range from less than 25 mm long and pale yellow with conspicuous dark black or brown blotches to over 40 mm long and golden-yellow without markings.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Often misidentified as Eulophia speciosa, which differs in having the convexity on the midlobe distant from the gynostemium, the spur saccate to shortly conical, and the petals lacking reddish brown markings.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Readily distinguished by the solitary basal leaf, well-exserted stem with cauline leaves clustered at the apex, outer bracts with brown-flecked membranous margins and inner bracts with very wide, brown-flecked membranous margins, and white to pale mauve flowers with pale yellow cup. Superficially resembling Romulea tabularis, a coastal species extending north to Hondeklip Bay with similar aerial stem, solitary basal leaf, and pale blueish but generally much smaller flowers, the tepals 10-28 mm long, and shorter bracts 8-16 mm long with scarcely visible membranous margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Sometimes misidentified as Eulophia streptopetala which differs in having the lip very convex between the side lobes, the sepals about as long as the petals, and the leaves thin-tissued with emergent veins and an abscission layer near the base.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the plain yellow flowers, the outer tepals narrower than the inner and lime-green on the reverse with distinctive brownish flecks along the margins, and the green inner bracts with narrow, colourless membranous margins widened only at the base. Superficially similar yellow-flowered species of Romulea with two basal leaves have inner bracts with broad, brownish or brown-flecked membranous margins and inner tepals coloured differently on the reverse.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by its bright yellow, unmarked flowers with relatively broad, obovate tepals, the inner notably broader than the outer, and the long style, exserted 3-6 mm beyond the anthers. The numerous leaves and the whitish or colourless membranous margins to the inner and outer bracts are also distinctive. The species has been confused with Romulea luteoflora, but that species has fewer leaves (2 to 6), brown-flecked membranous margins to the inner and outer bracts, and a shorter style not exserted beyond the stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Frequently misidentified as Eulophia clitellifera, which differs in having a cylindrical spur 2.5-4 mm long, crests consisting of low verrucose ridges produced chiefly on a convexity on the midlobe, and no calli on the inner surface of the mentum.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: A putative hybrid of this species with Eulophia ovalis subsp. bainesii has been reported.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely related to R. hirsuta. May perhaps be regarded as a small montane variety of R. hirsuta, with smaller, paler flowers and narrower perianth segments.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differing from other species in its elongated connectives and therefore longer anthers.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Instantly recognised by the unique anthers, sagittate at the base with the connective produced apically well beyond the thecae as an attenuate membranous appendage. The white to pale lilac flowers are relatively large, with ± acuminate tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It seems, therefore, reasonable to distinguish the present plant as a distinct species differing from E. Morinii, as described by Berger, in its spineless, coarsely toothed, broad-ribbed stems and sessile flower-heads. I have contrasted it also with E. polygona, as it is known in gardens. It is, however, doubtful whether this is the E. polygona which Haworth described in his Miscellanea, 184 (1803), as a plant with closely set (contigui) spreading black spines, about 12 mm long, minute leaves, entirely of the nature of spines (omnino natura s'pinarum), solitary peduncles and involucres with bifid lobes. No specimen or figure of Haworth’s plant having been preserved the species remains for the present a “species dubia.” E. anoplia belongs to a group of cactoid euphorbias characterized by the extreme reduction of their leaves, which are moreover not accompanied by stipules, and the very general presence of spines which morphologically are modified axes of inflorescences; hence the name of the group, Anthacantha. Some of the earliest introductions of South African euphorbias from the Cape belong here as E. cereiformis (1679), E. mamillaris (1703), E. heptagdna (1717) and others. The spines of these species may be barren or they may start as flower-bearing peduncles, then harden and persist after the fall of the flowers or fruits. The extent to which a specimen is armed with such spines varies in certain species, but without continued observation it is difficult to say how far gaps in the armature or general scantiness of spines are due to the casual or zonal suppression of the flowering axes or to their reduction to sessile flower-heads which would ultimately disappear without leaving a spine behind. In some species sessile flower-heads and spines occur simultaneously. In E. anoplia the latter have disappeared entirely. In that respect it conforms with the group of E. meloniformis and E. obesa, but here the body is so rounded off in all directions as to exclude the suggestion of close affinity with E. anoplia. E. anoplia is like its allies, dioecious.
bibliographicCitation: Stapf, O. 1923. Euphorbia anoplia. Curtis's Bot. Mag. 148t.8947 [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the Board of Trustees of the Royal Botanic Garden, Kew] [All rights reserved]

description: A montane species distinguished by the corm tunics splitting longitudinally into narrow, fringed strips with a well-developed fibrous neck above, and the pink to purple flowers. The species may have 1 or 2 basal leaves, and colourless or ± densely brown-flecked membranous margins to the outer and inner bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very closely related to R. longipes. Specimens without corms or with young corms can only be distinguished from R. longipes by their flower colouring and their more membranous bracts. R. fibrosa differs from R. dichotoma in usually having 2 basal leaves with the four ribs subequal in width.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to R. flava.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The large white flowers of Sparaxis bulbifera are easily confused with those of white flowered S. grandiflora subsp. fimbriata, and they are indeed strikingly similar in their radially symmetric perianth but unilateral stamens and unilateral style with long slender style branches. The tepals of S. bulbifera are narrowly ovate to lanceolate, whereas those or S. grandiflora subsp. fimbriata tend to be broader, usually widest in the upper third and sometimes spathulate. The two species are more easily distinguished by vegetative features: S. grandiflora produces branches from the base; thus close to or below ground level, whereas branching in S. bulbifera is aerial and even when unbranched, the stems of this species have one or more aerial nodes, each bearing a leaf, and after flowering a cluster of small cormlets. Differences in habitat also help separate the two: S. grandiflora favours clay ground, sometimes waterlogged in winter but relatively well drained, whereas S. bulbifera is rarely encountered away from wet, sandy flats. The two species are evidently immediately related and, not surprisingly, hybrids between the two have been recorded where their habitats overlap.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: E. cumulata is allied to E. mammillaris Berger, E. ferox Marloth, E. capitosa N.E. Br. and E. aggregata. The outstanding differences to all these are it method of spreading by means of rhizomes and its consistently unbranched stems.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1931. Notes on Euphorbia species of the Eastern Cape Province with descriptions of three new species. Rec. Albany Mus. 4: 64-110. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the small yellow to buff-coloured, mostly unpleasantly scented flowers borne in few-flowered spikes, symmetrically disposed stamens and narrow, acute leaves. It shares virtually identical, fringed bract margins and radially symmetric flowers with S. maculosa, evidently its closest relative, but the latter has larger, unscented blooms boldly marked at the base of the tepals with large maroon-purple markings divided longitudinally by a pale yellow line.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by a combination of the unilateral orientation of the stamens but radially symmetric perianth and the branching produced only from the base, typically below ground level. Unlike other Iridaceae with unilateral stamens, the filaments are not parallel with contiguous anthers but are divergent and held well apart from one another. Only S. bulbifera has similarly unilateral stamens and a radially symmetric perianth, but it always bears cauline leaves and branches arise on the upper part of the stem. After flowering in S. bulbifera, numerous small cormlets are produced at the aerial nodes in addition to larger cormlets at the underground nodes. The tepals are also consistently ovate-elliptic in S. bulbifera but are often slightly spathulate in S. grandiflora.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: E. Bergii resembles E. rudis and E. braunsii in the elongation of the main stem and the uniform growth of all the branches, which produce an even cushion-like mass, but the cushions formed by E. bergii are rather more flat at the surface and thus less distinctly hemispherical than those of the other two species. The relationship of the new species appears to be nearer to E. rudis, because the branches are relatively slender at the upper part and quite unlike the more chunky ones of E. braunsii. On the other hand the cyathia are solitary, whereas in E. rudis they tend rather to cluster in small cymes. The tips of the tubercles are not at all recurved, thus differing again from E. rudis; and finally the united portion of the styles is very much shorter, hardly exceeding one-third of their length. As the species now stands, it is well distinguished from E. rudis as well as from E. braunsii, and its claim to be considered distinct from both seems amply justified. However, should further investigation reveal some overlapping of its habitat with that of either of the two other species, with the presence of intermediate forms, it would perhaps be advisable to reduce it to varietal rank. This cannot be done on the basis of present knowledge.
bibliographicCitation: White, AC; Dyer, RA; Sloane, BL. 1941. The succulent Euphorbieae, Vol. 1, 1st ed. Abbey Garden Press, Pasadena (California). [All rights reserved]

description: Parapatric with Syringodea concolor and distinguished from it (De Vos 1974) by the yellow or orange throat and brown seeds with coarsely sculptured testa with 5 or 6 interstitial cavities per mm. The larger flowers, mostly more than 16 mm diam., distinguish it from S. flanaganii.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its comparatively small flowers with an erect to slightly hooded, dorsal tepal usually ± 16 mm long, much exceeding the yellow lower tepals, ± 10 mm long. The distinctive coarse corm tunic fibres are also shared with the rare S. caryophyllacea, but this species has larger flowers, the dorsal tepal ± 20 mm long. The two long-tubed species, S. metelerkampiae and S. variegata, also have similar corm tunics but the long perianth tube immediately sets them apart. These distinctive corm tunics define the lineage comprising these four species. A particularly small-flowered variant of S. villosa occurs on granite outcrops at Vredenburg, the dorsal tepal ± 10 mm long and perianth tube ± 12 mm long. These plants might easily be misidentified as S. parviflora were it not for the distinctive woody tunics.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by its tiny flowers, the smallest in the genus, with white or mauve upper tepals and yellow lower tepals with white or mauve tips, and the finely fibrous corm tunics. The small flowers have a dorsal tepal 9-10 mm long, and the three lower ± 8 mm long. The plants are also fairly small, usually less than 150 mm tall and more often less than 100 mm, and the leaves are seldom more than 12 mm wide. In contrast, the seeds are the largest in the genus, up to 2.8 mm in diameter. In shape and colour the flowers are most like those of S. calcicola, but this species has much larger flowers, 20-22 mm long. Some forms of S. villosa have particularly small flowers, the upper tepal ± 10 mm long, and confusion between them is best avoided by examination of the corm tunics, those of S. villosa being coarsely fibrous and ± clawed below, contrasting starkly with the finely fibrous tunics of S. parviflora.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The finely fibrous corm tunics forming a neck around the stem base and the erect to reflexed, rather than hooded, upper tepal suggest that Sparaxis roxburghii is most closely related to S. galeata, from which it is distinguished by the elongate perianth tube, 20-30 mm long vs. ± 15 mm in S. galeata. Molecular studies, however, suggest that S. roxburghii is most closely related to S. auriculata, which has a funnel-shaped rather than largely cylindric perianth tube ± 18 mm long. All three species have unusually small and nearly globose capsules containing only 2 to 4 seeds per locule.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its 3 to 5, linear to lanceolate leaves 3-6 mm wide and showy flowers with perianth tube 25-35 mm long and obovate tepals 15-20 x 8-10 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to S. bifucata, differing mainly in the smaller size of all the organs.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Retained as distinct from Syringodea bifucata, with which it shares a perianth tube marked with yellow or orange in the throat, on the basis of its much smaller flowers less than 16 mm diam., with tepals 5-10 x ± 2 mm and style branches 1-2 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Sparaxis metelerkampiae has long-tubed, purple flowers with the lower tepals each with a white longitudinal streak, at the centre of which is a pale yellow or reddish mark. The tepals are smaller than those of immediately related S. variegata, the dorsal tepal 15-20 mm long vs. 25-30 in S. variegata, and the style is short, dividing below or opposite the lower third of the anthers and has branches 2-3 mm long. In S. variegata the longer style divides close to the anther tips and the branches are 4-5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its relatively large, bright yellow flowers with the lower tepals not heavily bicoloured with purple, and shortly joined at the base without forming a well-defined lower lip. The perianth tube is short, 4-5 mm long, and the filaments are ± 10 mm long with anthers 4-5 mm long. The leaves are subpetiolate below with a narrowly lanceolate blade mostly 4-8 mm wide, with 2 or 3 veins. The fruits are unknown.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised among species with similarly shaped, red flowers by its characteristic carmine to deep pinkish red or purple perianth with broad, oblong to obovate tepals arising ± at the same level, the dorsal 8-10 mm wide, and its relatively short filaments, 20-23 mm long and only shortly exserted from the tube, with apiculate, purple anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its soft corm tunics without a collar and narrow, linear-lanceolate leaves, 5-7 mm wide with 2 or 3 veins, and long-tubed red flowers with oblanceolate tepals. The capsules are unique for the genus, relatively small and only slightly inflated, 7-10 x 6-9 mm, with conspicuously wrinkled-warty walls.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar in habit and closely allied to E. trichadenia, Pax, but evidently distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, NE; Hutchinson, J; Prain, D. 1920. Euphorbiaceae. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Thymelaeaceae-Ceratophylleae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 5(2-3): 216-516. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15244#page/3/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished from Tritonia securigera by the pale to bright yellow flowers, sometimes flushed apricot, with proportionally longer perianth tube, (18-)20-28 mm long and about twice as long as the dorsal tepal, and vegetatively by the more wiry tunics thickened into claws at the base. The tunics in T. securigera are always fine-textured and the mostly orange flowers have a shorter perianth tube more-or-less as long as the dorsal tepal or rarely slightly longer but never twice as long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This is very similar to E. ericoides, Lam., but may be easily distinguished from that species by its acute leaves, larger involucre and more united bifid styles. It is variable in appearance, and some specimens resemble E. epicyparissias, E. Meyer, from which it is distinguished by its numerous shorter and usually simple or once or twice umbellately branched stems. E. epicyparissias is 2-5 ft. high and much branched.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, NE; Hutchinson, J; Prain, D. 1920. Euphorbiaceae. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Thymelaeaceae-Ceratophylleae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 5(2-3): 216-516. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15244#page/3/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: A very distinct species with long, striate, firm-textured, terete or subterete leaves often taller than the inflorescence and with a dense fibrous collar around the base. The lax spikes bear zygomorphic, ruby-redor purple, somewhat Freesia-like flowers with a funnel-shaped perianth tube 16-20 mm long. The small, leathery bracts are dry and papery only near the tips.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Tritonia securigera and its allies including T. laxifolia with similar short-tubed, orange flowers by its taller, more upright habit, the plants mostly 300-600 mm tall, and the stiffly erect, linear-striate leaves, (1-)2-4(-6) wide, with the main vein and 3 or 4 secondary vein pairs ± equally prominent. Other members of the group have the midrib and sometimes submarginal vein thickened and prominent but not the intervening secondary veins, the blades thus not conspicuously striate.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Introduced weed.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2019. Euphorbiaceae: Euphorbia L. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 905-919. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised among the pale-flowered, long-tubed species of Tritonia by its slender, straight leaves, terete to elliptic in section without an evident main vein, and almost symmetrical, salver-shaped perianth with a slender, curved tube, the flowers tilted backward so that the anthers face upwards. The long-tubed species of sect. Pectinatae have plane leaves with a thickened main vein and zygomorphic, bilabiate flowers facing outward, with arcuate stamens held under the arching to horizontal dorsal tepal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A dwarf species, Tritonia florentiae, the only acaulescent member of the genus, has a tight fan of recurved, leathery leaves and large, fragrant, bright yellow flowers with long, crest-like calluses on the lower tepals. The species exhibits some highly unusual features, presumably associated with its ecology and habit. The inflorescence is reduced to several short, one-flowered branches, a development that has evolved several times in acaulescent members of several different genera of Crocoideae, including Crocus, Duthiastrum and Syringodea. The large, inflated capsules are unique in the genus. Tritonia florentiae resembles spring-flowering T. karooica in general habit, notably the tight fan of recurved, leathery leaves, and large flowers with long, crest-like calluses on the lower tepals, but the latter has an aerial stem, cream-coloured to dull orange flowers with conspicuous dark veins and a relatively longer, sharply bent perianth, about twice as long as the tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The central flower of the umbel 5-glandod, the lateral flowers 4-glanded as in E. ornithopus, the flowers nearly half? inch in diameter. Lobes of involucre tomentose, the glands horizontal, 2-lipped as in E. globosa, the upper lip square, the lower lip with 3 fingers just below its outer rim. Each finger is formed of a linear lobe, green on the upper side, and white tomentose at the margin and on the back. As the margins are bent upwards until they meet here and there, the green colour of the upper side of the finger remains visible only at intervals, and it is at these spots that the nectar is accessible to the insect visitors. The ovary is borne on a pedicel as in the other species and finally projects from the flower sideways. It differs from the other species by bearing 6 tufts or ridges of wool.
bibliographicCitation: Marloth, HWR. 1931. Euphorbias III, section Dactylanthes. S. Afr. Gdng Country Life 21: 127-127. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its lanceolate leaves (5-)8-12(-20) mm wide with a prominent submarginal vein and funnel-shaped, red, orange-red or pink flowers, sometimes darkly veined, lacking well-developed calluses. The lower tepals, especially the median, are marked at the base with a small yellow blotch outlined with red. It is closely allied to and largely sympatric with T. gladiolaris, which blooms earlier, mainly August to November (rarely into December), and has cream- to straw-coloured or pale yellow flowers, sometimes flushed pale apricot-coloured, usually with prominent dark veins.
