Plants with ± 3-toothed or irregularly toothed bracts, the lower bracts sometimes acute, were separated as subsp. rubrolucens from typical T. disticha with obtuse to acuminate or sometimes 3-toothed bracts, recorded mainly from the coastal Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from the two other species with large, bowl-shaped flowers with spathulate tepals and diverging filaments by the broad, orange to red tepals with hyaline margins on the claws, the lower 3 tepals with a narrow median yellow stripe in the throat, sometimes raised as a low ridge. Orange-flowered Tritonia deusta lacks the hyaline margins to the tepals and has a distinct, large yellow star-like marking in the throat of the tube and often a large dark blotch on the outer tepals, and T. squalida has pink to mauve, often narrower tepals, also with hyaline margins on the claws. Hybrids between T. crocata and T. deusta have been recorded between Riversdale and Albertinia where the ranges of the two species overlap.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species with the leaves terete or elliptic in section and without evident veins, and deep purple to violet, sideways-facing flowers with a curved perianth tube 7-15 mm long and tepals with prominent, darkly mottled veins. The filaments are declinate and relatively long, 8-10 mm long. The anthers are usually white, but some populations have purple anthers with brown pollen.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from the other species with strongly ribbed leaves by the moderately long perianth tube, (12-)15-18(-25) mm long, usually curved outward slightly near the tip and dilating gradually and evenly from base to apex, elliptic-oblanceolate tepals, 10-18 x 3-5 mm, and filaments 3-4 mm long. Although usually glabrous, the leaves in some plants are scabridulous along the ribs and margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Separated from all other species in the genus by its unusually long perianth tube, 25-40 mm long and 2.0-2.5 times longer than the tepals. The flowers vary in colour from pale pink or almost white to purple-pink, with darker tube and purple, chevron-shaped markings on the lower tepals. The species may be confused with longer-tubed forms of T. spicatus, but the perianth tube in that species is shorter, mostly less than 20 mm long (rarely up to 25 mm) and always less than twice as long as the tepals, and also narrower, at most 1.5 mm diam. at the mouth.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Introduced.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2019. Euphorbiaceae: Euphorbia L. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 905-919. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively small plant, Tritonia parvula is distinguished from T. securigera by the narrower, linear leaves mostly 1-2(-3) mm wide, sometimes as long as the flowering stem. Some individuals are difficult to place, notably those growing in crevices in sandstone cliffs and with trailing leaves. Tritonia parvula most closely resembles T. cedarmontana from the Cederberg in habit but that species lacks calluses on the lower tepals and has shorter filaments 4-5 mm long with the anthers half-included in the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of three closely allied species with almost symmetric, bowl-shaped flowers with more-or-less spathulate tepals and weakly diverging filaments, Tritonia squalida is distinguished by its pale to deep or dusty pink to mauve tepals, the claws with broad hyaline margins. It is separated from orange-flowered T. crocata from shale soils in the same region primarily by flower colour, but it seems that the style also branches slightly lower down and the tepals are never as broad as seen in some plants of T. crocata. The two species have different soil preferences and no intermediates between them have been found in the wild. Putative hybrids between T. squalida and T. deusta have been recorded near Albertinia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Die Pflanze dürfte am nächsten mit der in Natal vorkommenden F. venosa (Hochst.) K. Sch. verwandt sein, weicht aber auch von dieser ab durch ihre deutlich vierkantigen Stengel sowie ihre nicht abgestumpften, unterseits schwach behaarten Blätter.
bibliographicCitation: Krause, K. 1907. Rubiaceae africanae. Bot. Jahrb. Syst. 39: 516-572. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/701#page/535/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: The central species in a taxonomically difficult group that is characterised by similar two-lipped, orange flowers with an obliquely funnel-shaped tube conspicuously yellow in the throat and about as long as the tepals (sometimes slightly longer), the lower tepals each with a yellow blotch near the base bearing a quadrate or axe-like callus 1-4 mm high. Within this group, Tritonia securigera is applied to plants with plane, lanceolate or linear-lanceolate leaves, usually forming an erect fan up to half as long as the stem, the main vein raised and the margins thickened and without a prominent submarginal vein. The perianth tube is usually 10-15 mm long, with the narrow basal portion 3-6 mm long. Plants from Kommadagga are variable in tube length, the tube in some individuals up to ± 20 mm long with the narrow basal portion 15 mm long. Introgression with T. chrysantha may be indicated here. Tritonia nelsonii from Gauteng, Limpopo and Northwest is usually taller with narrow, stiffly erect leaves with numerous prominent veins; T. strictifolia from interior Eastern Cape around Grahamstown, is distinguished by the prominent submarginally veined leaves; and T. laxifolia from Eastern Cape and subtropical Africa, flowers in late summer and autumn and has larger capsules 12-15 mm long closely appressed to the stem. Two other taxa are less clearly separated: T. parvula from the central and eastern Little Karoo, is a mostly smaller plant with linear leaves, mostly 1-2(-3) mm wide; and T. watermeyeri from the western Little Karroo, has more-or-less spirally twisted leaves with the margins often undulate or crisped.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: G. bredasdorpense seems to be a close ally of G. capense (ssp. capense), but clearly differs in having very short internodes (frequently shorter than the minute leaves), short, ovate-lanceolate leaves (vs. long, linear in G. capense) and highly reduced inflorescences with leaf-like bracts and smaller flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Puff, C. 1978. The genus Galium L. (Rubiaceae) in southern Africa. J. S. African Bot. 44: 203-279. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species with a remarkable superficial resemblance to Freesia verrucosa, and recognised by the fan of falcate, acuminate leaves with crisped or undulate margins and the dense, horizontal spike of long-tubed, white flowers with cylindric perianth tube 10-30 mm long, compressed in the gullet, with the upper lateral tepals sharply reflexed behind the spreading dorsal tepal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A short, relatively stout species with a basal fan of broad, lanceolate leaves, 8-25 mm wide with 4 to 6 veins, and shortly branched flowering stems up to 350 mm tall, with pale to creamy pink flowers, the lower tepals marked with a red median streak or line, and tube 8-10 mm long. The yellow anthers are 5.0-5.5 mm long and shortly apiculate. The broad leaves with overlapping sheaths distinguish Tritoniopsis latifolia from others with similar pink flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A somewhat variable species, Tritoniopsis dodii typically has a short, compact spike but includes forms with more lax, subsecund spikes. It is recognised essentially by its unbranched stems and short-tubed, pink flowers with narrow tepals clawed in the lower two thirds, the dorsal tepal 20-23 x 3-5 mm, the anthers only shortly apiculate, and the style branches up to 2 mm long. The flowers are typically rather dingy pink, with the tepals erect below and recurved only in the distal third, thus essentially like those of T. elongata, which is distinguished by its much longer spike, the flowering portion much longer than the non-flowering stem.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although the morphological distinction between the polymorphic ssp. namaquense and ssp. capense may occasionally become rather difficult (sometimes indumentum is the only “good” separation character), it was decided to follow Ehrendorfer’s (1952, unpublished) suggestions on sheets from the herbaria K and P to treat “namaquense” as a subspecies of G. capense. Its distinct and ± closed area of distribution (with hardly any overlap with ssp. capense) supports the subspecies rank rather than varietal status (the latter would possibly have been more appropriate if the taxon had been sufficiently scattered geographically).
bibliographicCitation: Puff, C. 1978. The genus Galium L. (Rubiaceae) in southern Africa. J. S. African Bot. 44: 203-279. [CC BY]

description: Unique in the genus in its bright red, actinomorphic, almost salver-shaped flowers with slender perianth tube 18-28 mm long, and spreading tepals forming a shallow bowl. The style is relatively short, dividing just below the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A robust species with stout, shortly branched flowering stems a metre or more tall, and a basal fan of overlapping, lanceolate leaves, 9-25 mm wide with 5 to 7 veins. The short-tubed, bright yellow flowers have the lower tepals marked with a brown median streak or line. The yellow anthers are 7-9 mm long, with a bifid apiculus ± 1 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Var. dregeanum seems to be much rarer than var. mucroniferum. G. mucroniferum and G. subvillosum constitute a very closely related species pair sharing, among others, the following characters: tetraploidy, very pronounced protandry, flowers with stamina nearly as long as the corolla lobes (long, thin filaments), and reduced snyflorescences consisting of few groups of 3 flowers (G. subvillosum) or 2 flowers (G. mucroniferum) on the paracladia. All these characters distinguish this group from the remaining Southern African Galium species. The two species, however, are, in addition to synflorescence differences, easily kept apart by their leaves (short, wide: G. subvillosum vs. long, narrow: G. mucroniferum). They may virtually grow side by side in the field [cf. Puff 760908-6/2 (NU, WU) and -6/3 (WU)], but, according to my field observations, do not hybridize.
bibliographicCitation: Puff, C. 1978. The genus Galium L. (Rubiaceae) in southern Africa. J. S. African Bot. 44: 203-279. [CC BY]

G. mucroniferum and G. subvillosum constitute a very closely related species pair sharing, among others, the following characters: tetraploidy, very pronounced protandry, flowers with stamina nearly as long as the corolla lobes (long, thin filaments), and reduced snyflorescences consisting of few groups of 3 flowers (G. subvillosum) or 2 flowers (G. mucroniferum) on the paracladia. description: Recognised by its moderately sized, yellow flowers with bicoloured lower tepals flushed maroon or purple in the lower third and joined at the base for 3-4 mm to form a well-defined lower lip. The perianth tube is short, 3-4 mm long but the filaments are relatively long, 12-14 mm long and strongly arched. The base of the tepals and mouth of the tube are minutely papillate.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A short species up to 300 mm high, with the stem simple or often with up to three short suberect branches, and a spike of salmon- or rose-pink flowers with a moderately long perianth tube (10-)15-17 mm long and dark blackish brown, leathery bracts. The basal leaves are narrowly lanceolate, usually with 1 or 2 (rarely 3) veins, and the lowermost cauline leaf resembles the basal leaves in having a well-developed blade. We have seen only a single collection of capsules and these are highly distinctive, inflated and irregularly wrinkled-warty.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

G. mucroniferum and G. subvillosum constitute a very closely related species pair sharing, among others, the following characters: tetraploidy, very pronounced protandry, flowers with stamina nearly as long as the corolla lobes (long, thin filaments), and reduced snyflorescences consisting of few groups of 3 flowers (G. subvillosum) or 2 flowers (G. mucroniferum) on the paracladia.
