description: Although only known from the type collection, I have no doubt that G. rourkei is a “good' new species. It is allied to both G. subvillosum and G. mucroniferum, primarily on account of the similar, reduced inflorescences (3-or 2-flowered partial inflorescences) and flowers with stamens (filaments) almost as long as the corolla lobes. Also similar habitat conditions (sheltered, cool, moist) and corresponding average pollen diameters, larger than those of other Cape species of Galium (except for G. undulatum, an unlikely ally which markedly differs in floral and inflorescence structure), suggest an affinity. The large average pollen diameter may, furthermore, indicate poly-(?tetra)ploidy, which has been documented for both G. subvillosum and G. mucroniferum (Puff, 1978). G. rourkei differs from both species in having its leaves arranged in whorls of 4 or 5 (6 leaves per whorl are the exception), shorter and broader leaves (leaf size and shape of some forms of G. subvillosum may ± overlap with those of G. rourkei. but the former has always 3- rather than 2-flowered partial inflorescences), much more delicate stems and usually shorter internode
bibliographicCitation: Puff, C. 1983. Galium rourkei (Rubiaceae): A new species from the South Western Cape. J. S. African Bot. 49(3): 185-188. [CC BY]

description: A variable species with moderately sized pink flowers with perianth tube 7-15(-20) mm long and narrow tepals, the dorsal 20-28 × (3-)4-6 mm and the lower tepals 3-5 mm wide. The capsules are diagnostic for the species, being unusually small, (6-)8-12(-15) × 8-10 mm, and pale or greenish with dark bands along the sutures. Flowering plants are sometimes less easily identified. Typical forms with laxly branched stems are readily recognised but unbranched plants are more difficult to place. It is separated from T. laxa by the generally smaller flowers with narrower tepals; from T. pulchella by the mostly shorter perianth tube and more slender stems; and from T. dodii by the usually softer bracts and the conspicuously apiculate anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Shows considerable variability in growth form, leaf size and shape; narrow-leaved, weakish plants and atypical, ± glabrescent forms should not be confused with G. capense subsp. garipense. In the eastern Cape the two taxa are occasionally difficult to distinguish.
bibliographicCitation: Puff, C. 1986. Paederiaceae, Anthospermae, Rubieae, Fl. S. Africa 31(1,2): 1-75. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209569#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Resembling Watsonia amabilis Goldblatt and W. rogersii L.Bolus in its short, simple stems and funnel-shaped pink flowers but distinguished from them by its arcuate stamens with shorter, yellow anthers 5-6 mm long. The funnel-shaped flowers with short upper portion of the tube, 9-12 mm long, distinguish it from the vegetatively similar W. paucifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Diagnosed by the lanceolate leaves without strongly thickened midrib and margins, the branched spike with relatively short bracts 9-14(-16) mm long, and long-tubed red flowers with narrow tepals 4-8(-10) mm wide, and fusiform capsule 25-35 mm long. Watsonia stokoei, with remarkably similar flowers, has small, obovoid capsules up to 10 mm long containing angular seeds only 5 mm long. Watsonia zeyheri, also with fusiform capsules, has the upper part of the perianth tube 16-20 mm long, and broader, slightly cupped tepals 8-11 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: G. undulatum is undoubtedly very closely allied to G. tomentosum with which it shares the following characters: (usually) very wide, oblanceolate or obovate leaves with reversed prickles on the margins (otherwise glabrous), flowers with very short stamina, and large fruits. Of the two, G. tomentosum (dioecious, “sex-dimorphism”) clearly is the more derived species.
bibliographicCitation: Puff, C. 1978. The genus Galium L. (Rubiaceae) in southern Africa. J. S. African Bot. 44: 203-279. [CC BY]

description: This species is fairly uniform in the Old World but New World specimens often have up to 5-flowered (and only rarely 1-flowered) inflorescences and hence a rather different appearance. Possibly the Old World material could form a subspecies with a name based on G. reniformis. Muller mentions that the fruits turn black but no other reference to this has been found. I am unable to agree with Hepper that G. lancistipula Hiern (in F.T.A. 3: 221 (1877); F.W.T.A. 2: 128 (1931) type from Gabon?.) is a synonym of G. repens; it differs in having dark blue hairy fruits, pyrenes of a very different shape and somewhat differently shaped leaf blades.
bibliographicCitation: Verdcourt, B. 1989. 94. Rubiaceae (tribe Rubioideae), Fl. Zambes. 5(1): 1-210. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, London. [CC BY]

description: A relatively short species with funnel-shaped, white or pale pink to mauve or rarely orange flowers with declinate stamens and short, pale yellow (rarely purple) anthers 4-5 mm long. The broad-based bracts, pale and dry above with netted venation, and the fusiform capsules are also distinctive. The flowers are mostly pink to mauve (rarely orange near Heidelberg) and broadly funnel-shaped with the upper part of the perianth tube flared and 7-10 mm long but up to 15 mm long in some populations. Populations in the upper Breede River Valley between Montagu and Worcester represent a distinct variant with consistently bright orange, narrowly funnel-shaped flowers with the upper part of the perianth tube scarcely or only weakly flared and 15-25 mm long, thus ± 1.0-1.5 times as long as the tepals, and often purple anthers. Some of the longer-tubed forms may also indicate introgression with that species. Watsonia aletroides has ± tubular flowers with the tepals less than half as long as the upper part of the perianth tube. Both species have similar bracts and unusual, fusiform capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species with similar long-tubed flowers by the mostly pink to purple (only rarely red) perianth, the lower part of the tube 12-20 mm long and the upper part 17-20(-24) mm long, the mostly unbranched stem, and the herbaceous bracts (12-)14-20(-24) mm long. Populations from the mountains around George, especially Ruitersberg at Robinson’s Pass, are unusual in their dry bracts, suberect tepals and shorter filaments only shortly exserted from the tube. Closely related Watsonia pillansii has consistently orange flowers with bracts (19-)23-33(-40) mm long, and a perianth tube with both the lower and upper parts 17-25 mm long, the filaments thus slightly longer, 30-40 mm long. The two species hybridise extensively along the southern Cape coast, notably near Prince Alfred’s Pass and Kareedouw Pass but also elsewhere.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from similar species with long-tubed, red flowers by the flowering time, autumn and winter, at which time the foliage is dry and withered, and by the deeply forked inner bracts, divided up to half their length. The leaves are unusually narrow, up to 10 mm wide but usually less.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its short stature, up to 300 mm high, relatively long, herbaceous bracts, (15-)20-30 mm long and recurved apically, and moderately to long-tubed, white to pink flowers with relatively short filaments, 10-20 mm long, not or shortly exserted up to 5 mm from the perianth tube. The bracts remain relatively soft in texture and do not turn dark brown on drying. Watsonia coccinea has red to pink flowers with longer filaments, 25-30 mm long, well exserted from the perianth tube, and narrower leaves 2-8 mm wide. Watsonia stenosiphon from east of Gordon’s Bay also has flowers with short filaments 15-20 mm long but an orange to salmon-pink perianth, and the bracts are not recurved apically.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the combination of acute to attenuate, moderate-sized bracts, 10-18(-25) mm long, the inner deeply forked apically for 3-6 mm, and the very long flowers, typically rather drooping, with the lower part of the tube (20-)25-30 mm long and usually well-exserted from the bracts. The obconic, tapering capsules are diagnostic. Watsonia angusta has acute or shortly bilobed inner bracts and smaller flowers, with the lower part of the tube (15-)18-22 mm long and narrower tepals 4-10 mm wide, and elongate, fusiform capsules. Watsonia schlechteri, also with entire or shortly forked inner bracts and shorter lower and upper parts of the perianth tube, 15-20 mm long, has subglobose to obovoid capsules up to 10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively small species seldom more than 500 mm tall, the leaves with unthickened midrib and margins, green bracts, and scarlet-red flowers with the upper part of the tube 20-25(-30) mm long and (4-)6 mm diam. at mouth, with filaments 25-35 mm long, and unusual yellow anthers. Watsonia stenosiphon from sandstone habitats has the upper part of the tube 13-16 mm long and ± 4 mm diam., and shorter filaments 15-20 mm long, only shortly exserted from the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Habenaria bicolor and H. laevigata are closely related and share the erect midlobe of the lip, the filiform spur tapering to the tip, the peg-like, fleshy rostellum with median keel and vestigial anther canals.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: A robust species with bright apple-green leaves and well-branched stems more than 1000 mm tall, with funnel-shaped, pink flowers, the perianth tube flared in the upper ± half and 20-40 mm long. The filaments vary in orientation from arcuate-horizontal to decumbent.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The scarlet-red flowers are unique in the genus in having the stamens and style included in the perianth tube, the filaments reaching to ± the middle of the upper part of the tube with the anthers reaching almost to the mouth, and the style branching below the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of three early flowering, locally endemic species with pink, funnel-shaped flowers restricted to the southeast coast around the Mtamvuna River Gorge, distinguished by its linear leaves, 3-4 mm wide and usually dry and broken at flowering, the plants thus sometimes apparently leafless, the ± dry bracts, and the small flowers with tepals 14-16 mm long. Watsonia pondoensis from marshy sites has leaves 4-14 mm wide, ± herbaceous bracts, and larger flowers with the lower part of the tube 15-20 mmm long and tepals 20-22 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species with similar dry, clasping bracts and pink, funnel-shaped flowers with included filaments, by the relatively few-flowered spike with non-overlapping bracts 10-16 mm long, and small flowers with tepals 15-18 mm long and anthers 5-6 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its clump-forming habit, erect, unbranched stems, and relatively lax spike of dark pink or mauve, funnel-shaped flowers with largely herbaceous bracts 17-25 mm long, and the relatively long lower part of the perianth tube, 15-20 mm long. Watsonia inclinata from drier grasslands in the same region has pale green leaves and inclined stems of slightly larger flowers with tepals 24-28 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its inclined, unbranched stem and relatively lax spike of pink, funnel-shaped flowers with largely herbaceous bracts 18-27 mm long. Watsonia pondoensis from marshy habitats in the same region forms small clumps, with stiffly erect stems, glaucous leaves, and slightly smaller, purple flowers with tepals 20-22 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other summer-rainfall species with similar pink, funnel-shaped flowers by the relatively short bracts mostly 1.0-1.5 internodes long and thus not closely overlapping, and often green and leathery in the lower half at flowering. The stems are simple or branched and the anthers are moderately large, 6-8 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small species with linear to lanceolate leaves and pink flowers with funnel-shaped perianth tube 16-27 mm long, and declinate stamens with relatively short, purple anthers 7-8 mm long. Watsonia rogersii is superficially similar, but has longer anthers 9-13 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of several species with dense spikes of moderate-sized, pink, funnel-shaped flowers and coarse, dry, brown, overlapping bracts and distinguished by its comparatively tall, erect stem, 500 to 1500 mm tall. The bracts are broad, 14-18 mm wide, and usually noticeably darker in the upper half, and the flowers are often large, with tepals (22-)25-32 × 8-11 mm. It is most likely to be confused with Watsonia lepida, a shorter species up to 650 mm tall, with the leaves dry and withered at flowering, and with narrower bracts, mostly occurring above 1000 m.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species has invariably been confused with Habenaria ciliosa because they share distinctively hispid sepals and bracts and strongly barred basal leaf sheaths. H. pseudociliosa differs in the characters in the key and is more widely distributed, but the two species appear to be largely allopatric.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: A small species with short bracts 8-14 mm long and relatively small, orange-red flowers, the upper part of the perianth tube 9-10 mm long and slightly shorter than the tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively short species distinguished by its ± pendent, tubular reddish or purple flowers with short, barely spreading tepals ± 10 mm long and less than half as long as the upper part of the perianth tube, and declinate filaments with short, yellow anthers 4-5 mm long. The broad-based bracts, pale and dry above with netted venation, and the fusiform capsules are also distinctive and are shared with Watsonia laccata, which has funnel-shaped flowers with the tepals ± as long as or longer than the upper part of the perianth tube, and shorter filaments up to 20 mm long. The two species hybridise in the wild, producing a range of fertile intermediates.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species can be confused with the more widespread Habenaria lithophila but is recognizable by the horizontally held flowers with the narrow median sepal reflexed to expose the gynostemium, the twisted upper petal lobes, and the longer lower petal lobes and lip side lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Characterised by the short bracts, 7-12 mm long, long-tubed flowers with the upper part 15-20 mm long, and obovoid capsules 10-12 mm long. Watsonia angusta from similar habitats has slightly longer bracts, 9-16 mm long, and characteristic fusiform capsules, 25-30 mm long, with longer seeds 9-10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species readily recognised by the one or two linear basal leaves and dense spikes of small flowers, the upper part of the perianth tube 7-9 mm long and the tepals 10-18 mm long. The flowers are typically and uniquely pale yellow to cream-coloured, but maroon-flowered populations occur around Mankayane in southwestern Eswatini.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its long spikes of relatively small, pale pink flowers with the upper part of the perianth tube 6-7 mm long and tepals 17-19 mm long, and short, ± dry floral bracts 9-14 mm long, not clasping the stem. Watsonia transvaalensis from the escarpment north of Graskop has mostly narrower leaves, 8-20(-25) mm wide, with moderately thickened margins, and mostly unbranched stems with larger bracts, 13-28 mm long, and larger flowers with tepals 20-25 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other pink-flowered species with declinate stamens and purple anthers by the longer perianth tube, 30-50 mm long with the lower part 20-35 mm long and the upper part 8-14 mm long, and comparatively short bracts, mostly 15-30 mm long. Watsonia dubia from Wellington and Tulbagh has slightly longer bracts, mostly 30-50 mm long enclosing all or most of the lower part of the perianth tube, with the upper part of the tube relatively short, 5-8 mm long, and proportionally shorter filaments usually 6-12 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species with small bracts up to 12 mm long by the heavily thickened leaf margins and branched, multi-flowered spike of relatively small flowers with the upper part of the perianth tube 14-18(-22) mm long, and deeply forked inner bracts. Watsonia fourcadei is a superficially similar species with forked inner bracts but larger flowers, the upper part of the tube 22-26 mm long, and elongate, tapering capsules 18-20 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The squamules or stout hairs on the leaves of this species and the reflexed hairs on the scape are similar to those of Holothrix cernua. However the lip lobes are much shorter and relatively broader than the linear lobes of H. cernua.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: In H. exilis the side lobes are either absent or up to 0.4 times the length of the midlobe while in H. villosa (both varieties) they are from 0.6 times to equal to the length of the midlobe.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: A short species up to 500 mm high with bracts 20-40 mm long and large, strongly bilabiate, red to orange flowers with acute tepals 30-35 mm long. The perianth tube is markedly oblique at the mouth, the lower three tepals separating ± 3 mm before the upper three tepals and strongly recurved. Watsonia coccinea has slightly shorter bracts 20-25 mm long, and smaller flowers with ± obtuse tepals 16-23 mm long, the lower not strongly recurved, and filaments 25-30 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the long-tubed, orange flowers with the lower part of the perianth tube 17-20 mm long and the upper part 22-30 mm long, filaments 35-45 mm long, and reddish, mostly herbaceous bracts 18-30 mm long. Watsonia pillansii from further east and along the coast has similar bracts and flowers, often with longitudinal ridges inside the perianth tube between the bases of the filaments, and mostly broader leaves, (7-)12-18 mm wide, with moderately thickened midrib and margins. The two species converge in the Langeberg between Cloete’s Pass and Riversdale, and plants from this area are difficult to identify with confidence. Watsonia fourcadei may have similar red to orange-red flowers but typically has shorter bracts, 13-18(-25) mm long, attenuate and somewhat scarious with the inner strongly forked, and diagnostic, obconic capsules tapering above.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively small species, up to 500 mm high, with narrow leaves, 5-10 mm wide with strongly thickened midrib and margins, and pink flowers with a funnel-shaped perianth tube 20-25 mm long, and decumbent stamens with purple anthers 9-13 mm long. Watsonia borbonica is a larger species, 1000 mm or more tall, with broader, apple-green leaves 20-40 mm wide. The two species co-occur along the foot of the Hottentots Holland and Kleinrivier Mtns, and may hybridise.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This small uncommon species is similar to Holothrix orthoceras which reaches the southern limits of its distribution adjacent to the area where H. macowaniana occurs. H. macowaniana, however, is usually smaller (though the small number of collections available might distort the figures), and the lip lobes are less well defined without an outer pair of longer lobes. The leaves are not silver-veined as is the case in H. orthoceras.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the long-tubed, orange flowers with the lower and upper parts of the perianth tube 17-25 mm long, the filaments 30-40 mm long, and the mostly herbaceous bracts (19-)22-35(-40) mm long. The perianth tube usually bears internal longitudinal ridges between the lower part of the filaments. Populations from the Hogsback-Katberg mountains represent a distinct race of tall plants with up to 35 flowers per spike, and unusually short inner bracts up to ± half as long as the outer. Watsonia knysnana has mostly pink to purple (rarely red) flowers with the lower part of the perianth tube 12-20 mm long, the filaments thus 16-28 mm long, and bracts (12-)14-20(-24) mm long. The two species hybridise extensively along the southern Cape coast, notably near Prince Alfred’s Pass and Kareedouw Pass but also elsewhere. Watsonia schlechteri from further west and inland has similar bracts and flowers but lacking the ridges inside the perianth tube and mostly narrower leaves 6-15 mm wide with heavily thickened midrib and margins. The two species converge in the Langeberg between Cloete’s Pass and Riversdale, and plants from this area are difficult to identify with confidence.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This rare species is similar to Holothrix incurva, but is smaller, has a slightly denser spike, a different distribution and a different flowering time.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: This is one of the smallest species in the genus in southern Africa and the only one with a condensed inflorescence. It is very similar to Holothrix aspera in the lip structure but the condensed inflorescence, the smaller flowers and the straight spur will easily distinguish it.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Resembling Xenoscapa grandiflora in its unscented, moderately sized, pink flowers with contrasting darker nectar guides on the lower tepals, but distinguished by the dark pink perianth with shorter tube 20-28 mm long and tepals 6-7 mm long. Hybrids with Xenoscapa fistulosa have been recorded on Sneeukop where the two species grow near one another.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the relatively small, fragrant, mostly white (rarely pale pink in the Richtersveld and southern Namibia) flowers without markings on the lower tepals and a slender perianth tube up to 1.5 mm diam. at the mouth. In most populations the main stem is relatively long, up to 180 mm, exceeding that of other species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The circinnate spur and the petals being adnate to the lip at the base are characteristic of this species and will distinguish it from all those species having membranous petals.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The flowers of Lapeirousia angustifolia, like those of L. pyramidalis subsp. pyramidalis, are white to pale lilac or mauve in colour and also pleasantly, if not as strongly sweet-scented, but are readily distinguished by the shorter perianth tube, 13-15 mm long vs. 25-40 mm, and the claw-like cusps on the lower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea africana stands 100-150 mm high and is readily distinguished by the prominently fringed, silvery-translucent spathes and bracts, sometimes brown at the tips and appearing almost woolly.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although broadly similar to A. abyssinica, it is distinguished by the sturdier stem and the longer, firm-textured, rusty brown spathes and bracts ± 15-20 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The glabrous leaves and the petals being adnate to the base of the lip will distinguish this species from others having a 5-lobed lip and carnose petals.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Although it has a flower very similar to that of Holothrix exilis, H. thodei has squamules on the scape as in H. cernua. It also has a quite different distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Aristea cantharophila has sessile lateral inflorescences, a cylindric ovary and elongate capsules 50-60(-75) mm long, longer than any other species of the subgenus. The flower colour is distinctive, pale lilac, mauve, or whitish with a dark greenish black central eye 6-7 mm diam. grading to turquoise at edges. Both the filaments and style are also dark greenish black. The relatively large tepals are 22-26 x 12-15 mm with the outer three slightly smaller than the inner, and the large anthers, ± 5.5 mm long, bear orange pollen.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The tall, robust Aristea capitata with flowering stems up to 1.5 m high and bearing a crowded compound inflorescence of hundreds of flowers is one of the most easily recognised members of the genus. The spathes are also distinctive, being dry-membranous, lanceolate, and translucent with narrow, dark keels extending upward as a short cusp. The relatively short, narrowly winged capsules are 8-12 mm long and contain one or two lamellate seeds per locule The distinctive spathes, together with the compact, columnar and crowded compound inflorescence, make A. capitata unlikely to be confused with other species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A doubtful taxon, specimens at PRE not matching the original description well.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL; Makgakga, CM. 2019. Rosaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 1384-1398. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The cushion-like habit, tuft of narrow basal leaves, and dichotomously branched stem make Aristea dichotoma easy to recognise.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea ecklonii is recognised by the compressed and relatively broad, sharply 2-winged flowering stem, rust-coloured floral bracts and sometimes spathes, and the relatively long, cylindric ovary (up to 8 mm long). The species is unmistakable in fruit as the elongated capsules are up to 20 mm long and deeply 3-lobed, showing the outline of the seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Much more glabrous and more robust than A. capensis, with palmatifid long-stalked leaves. Stems 2 feet long or more. Petioles 2-2.5 inches long; leaves 1.5 as broad as long, the lobes cut at least halfway to the base, round topped.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1862. Rosaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Leguminosae to Loranthaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 2: 285-305. Lovell Reeve & Co. Ltd., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Aristea fimbriata is distinguished by the regularly fringed spathes and floral bracts, minutely notched style, and relatively long, narrowly winged capsules up to 15 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the smallest species in the genus, Aristea glauca forms diffuse low tufts up to 150 mm high, and as the name suggests, has grey-glaucous leaves, mostly 2-3 mm wide. The flowering stems are relatively stout, conspicuously flattened, and often simple or 1- to 3-branched.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Harvey's description of this species is satisfactory, but his specification of the size of the leaflets is somewhat exaggerated. He also remarks that C. obovata comes close to C. marginata and, according to my opinion, he is quite right.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The receptacle of C. polygonifolia has a rather interesting shape. It is furnished with three broad, inclinate wings. At first sight the receptacle seems to be broad and complanate and equipped with shallow furrows, although, in reality, it is narrowly fusiform. The shape of the leaflets is rather varying. C. polygonifolia itself has, as a rule, entire and oblong leaflets.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Aristea juncifolia rarely reaches 300 mm in height and has terete, mostly unbranched stems and relatively large, boat-shaped, rhipidial spathes 12-18 mm long, green with broad transparent margins. The rigid, somewhat twisted leaves are elliptic or nearly round in section and without true margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. aculeata is a morphologically very unique type within the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1946. Further notes on the genus Cliffortia. Bot. Not. 1946(4): 407-420. [All rights reserved]

description: Evidently allied to Aristea torulosa, A. montana has similar dark green spathes and bracts with broad pale margins irregularly grading to darker colour and becoming irregularly fringed with age. The two are often difficult to distinguish, but A. montana, a high mountain species, is relatively low in stature, seldom exceeding 250 mm. They can best be distinguished by the stem, which is at most weakly compressed in A. torulosa and bears several, relatively laxly spaced flower clusters, those at the lower nodes sometimes on short branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is morphologically closely allied to C. cuneata and C. phillipsii. It differs from C. cuneata, among other features, in its acute, green laminas. In its up to 5 mm long stipides and in its rubiginose receptacles. As to form and colour of the leaves C. acutifolia corresponds more to C. phillipsii, from which it, however, differs in the glabrous receptacles. No [male]-specimens are known.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. alata is a very characteristic species, differing from all other Cliffortia-species by its broadly two-winged receptacles. Even when sterile it is easily recognised. The leaflets are mucronate, have strongly revolute margins and are sparingly-rather densely pilous.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: A relatively short plant, seldom exceeding 200 mm, Aristea oligocephala has a few-branched or rarely simple stem bearing large flower clusters up to 20 mm long. The spathes and bracts are papery and shiny-translucent with narrow dark keels. The firm, fibrous leaves are about half as long as the stem and up to 3 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea parviflora has well-branched stems (one or two orders of branching) and the smallest flowers in the genus, the tepals ± 6 mm long and the flower thus ± 12 mm diam., and correspondingly short filaments, ± 2.5 mm long. The globose capsules up to 4 mm long are also distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. burgersii is similar to C. alata, but differs in the more branched compact growth form, the smaller yellow-green blunt glabrous leaves (bluish grey-green, distinctly red mucronate and crisped puberulous all over in C. alata), the larger number of stamens, 10-11(-13) (6-8 in C. alata), the size of the fruit, (8)9 x 10(11) mm [(5)6 x (6)7 mm in C. alata)]; the colour of the fruit, green and reddish pink (red all over in C. alata) and the number of wings in the fruit, 3-4 (2-3 in C. alata). In situ, C. burgersii is fairly conspicuous due to the very noticeable reddish pink fruits which cover the ultimate branches of the plants. These fruits remain on the plant for several months during the winter period gradually drying and turning brown by summer. In C. burgersii five different patterns can be seen in the arrangement of the fruit wings. Two opposite wings interspersed by two opposite combs occur very rarely. A Y-shaped arrangement of three wings is more frequent. Equally frequent is the arrangement of three wings, where two are opposite and the third at right angles to these. Four equally spaced wings occur more commonly. Most commonly the fourth wing is replaced by a comb. In C. alata the two-winged form is the most prevalent, the three-winged form occurring only occasionally. Other winged species in the Section Alatae are C. teretifolia L.f. And C. semiteres Weim. These species have small, inconspicuous, narrowly winged, dull coloured fruits quite unlike those of C. alata and C. burgersii. The only other species with narrow straight wings is C. phyllanthoides Schltr. in the Section Bifoliolae. Other winged species occur in Section Inflexae, but there the wings are all curved and the fruits small and hidden in contrast to the showy exposed fruits of C. alata and C. burgersii.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH; Fellingham, AC. 1991. Rosaceae: A new species of Cliffortia from the south-western Cape. Bothalia 21(1): 60-62. [CC BY]

description: The closest ally to C. conifera is C. arborea. C. conifera possesses female flowers borne in condensed cone-like structures, in a different position to those of C. arborea. A detailed examination of the cones of both species showed that they are very similar in their structure and differ mainly in their position on the main branches. In C. arborea the primary axis of the cone is the main relative branch which elongates beyond the cone and also laterally via sterile, lateral, secondary branchlets within the cone, whereas in C. conifera the primary axis of the cone is a secondary lateral branch which is determinate in growth and devoid of any lateral vegetative branching. Further differences in the cones occur between the secondary cone leaves. In C. conifera they are mostly obovoid in shape with a stiff, apical, adaxially pointing subula. They are at first softish, but become woody and remain intact in the cone for the life of the cone (± 6 years). In C. arborea they are widest at the middle with the upper portion narrowing, foliaceous and reflexed and with an apical, more or less erect subula. They are softish, not becoming very woody and after several seasons abscise at the top of the sheath. Thus in C. arborea the old cones retain only the flattened bases of the secondary cone leaves and are considerably narrower than the flowering and fruiting cones. Apart from the differences in the cones, the leaves in C. conifera are visibly very different from those in C. arborea which are much wider and erect-spreading.
bibliographicCitation: Fellingham, AC; Oliver, EGH. 1994. A new serotinous species of Cliffortia (Rosaceae) from the southwestern Cape with notes on Cliffortia arborea. Bothalia 24(2): 153-162. [CC BY]

description: Characteristic features of C. ericifolia are the simple ericoid leaves, which are clustered on the greatly abbreviated bractyblasts. The inner side of the vaginas have brownish grey pilosity with short, less prominent hairs above the vagina. The brachyblasts constitute almost necklace-like swellings in the gracile branchlets.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: All five species belonging to the section Complanatae have the transverse section of their receptacles more or less flat, while the two ovoid or oblong achenes are firmly enclosed by the sides of the receptacle. In C. polygonifolia the receptacles, however, are but seemingly complanate. In reality they are narrowly fusiform, the three declined wings being placed in such a manner that at first sight one has the impression that the receptacle itself is flat. A very characteristic feature of C. hantamensis is its very dense branchings, thickly leafed, very short brachyblasts and its long, densely greyish-white woolly leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The very distinctive Aristea platycaulis resembles the widespread A. ecklonii in general aspect, notably the modest stature, compressed, 2-winged stem and fairly soft-textured leaves, but the small flowers are crowded in shortly stalked or sessile flower clusters and have a short, papillate ovary that develops into a conspicuously warty, deeply 3-lobed capsule only 3.5-4.0 mm long and slightly wider than high.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A dwarf plant, typically 80-120 mm high but sometimes shorter, Aristea pusilla is readily recognised by its soft-textured, sword-shaped leaves and compressed and narrowly 2-winged flowering stem, 1.5-2.0 mm wide, bearing one or more leaves along its length. The stem is often unbranched with a single terminal flower cluster but particularly robust plants may have one or two sessile lateral flower clusters. The flower clusters have at most two flowers and the lateral clusters often just a single flower. The flowers are contained within relatively long, green spathes and are ± sessile and carried on elongate ovaries above the spathes. The ovary is triangular in cross section, but mature capsules, (14-)20-25(-30) mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea racemosa, frequently seen in flower after fire in montane habitats, it is one of a group of three species of sect. Racemosae of similar low stature with boat-shaped, rust-brown spathes with broad membranous margins, and sessile rhipidia, the lower sometimes shortly stalked. It is readily recognised in the alliance by the relatively short spathes, inconspicuous bracts subtending the rhipidia, and the stiff, fibrous leaves, terete or elliptic in section without differentiated margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea rupicola is distinguished by its low stature, dichotomous branching pattern, and prominently 3-lobed to -winged capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The relatively tall and slender Aristea schizolaena broadly resembles the more widespread A. torulosa in its few-branched or unbranched stem with several sessile lateral flower clusters but is distinguished by the spathes and bracts subtending the flower clusters, these membranous distally and red-brown even before the first flowers open.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Superficially similar to Aristea spiralis and often confused with it, A. simplex has narrower leaves and significantly smaller, pale to deep blue flowers with tepals 15-20 mm long versus white or pale blue flowers with tepals 30-35 mm long in A. spiralis. The ovate to broadly elliptic stems of A. simplex and narrow, ± linear, leathery leaves, 2-4 mm wide, also contrast with the compressed, prominently winged stems of A. spiralis and its broader, sword-shaped, softer-textured leaves, 4-7 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea spiralis is recognised by the large, half to fully nodding flowers, mostly white with light purple markings near the bases of the tepals but an attractive pale blue in the southern part of its range in the Langeberg and the mountains around Hermanus and Bredasdorp.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is very distinctive on account of its unique growth habit: a single stem often up to 3 m tall with short branches all the way up, spreading at right angles to the main stem. The leaves are also diagnostic, being held at right angles and almost circular in outline with a leaf-like stipule formed by fusion of the two separate ones on the reverse side of the stem.
bibliographicCitation: Whitehouse, CM. 2004. New species in the section Multinerviae of Cliffortia (Rosaceae). Bothalia 34(2): 77-85. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the acaulescent habit, stem lacking a collar of fibres around the base, rather soft-textured fibrous corm tunics and floral bracts divided to the base. The relatively large flowers are predominantly dark blue to violet with white to creamy white markings and have a sweet or spicy scent. It is often confused with a second coastal species, B. nana, and the two sometimes occur together, B. nana flowering somewhat later in the season than B. ambigua. Hybrids between the two species have been described by Lewis (1959) from the Cape Peninsula and on the Atlantic Coast to the north. Although similar in general appearance, B. nana usually has a short aerial stem and larger and more intensely fragrant flowers, the perianth often a deeper colour and, most importantly, the inner bracts are undivided. Lewis (1959) also reported hybrids between B. ambigua and the related and similar B. scabrifolia from the Olifants River Valley. Babiana grandiflora is also easily confused with B. ambigua, but this species from coastal Namaqualand has the inner floral bracts only notched apically, and considerably larger flowers with the dorsal tepal 45-55 mm long vs. 28-40 mm in B. ambigua.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Burchell’s specimen of this species was included within C. ilicifolia by Weimarck (1934) on account of its broad, toothed leaves. However, in other characteristics it is closer to C. dregeana, with which it has generally been placed in herbaria. The broadly oblong, few-toothed leaves, combined with the limited distribution range, make this species easily distinguishable. However, in the south of its range, specimens that are more intermediate in character with C. dregeana do occur.
bibliographicCitation: Whitehouse, CM. 2004. New species in the section Multinerviae of Cliffortia (Rosaceae). Bothalia 34(2): 77-85. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the subterranean stem and inflorescence, the flowers thus arising shortly below ground level, and by its narrow, upright leaves, associated with blue-mauve to violet flowers with white markings on the lower lateral tepals edged in darker blue. The flowers have a perianth tube 40-55(-70) mm long and subequal tepals, the dorsal usually about as long as the tube, or slightly shorter when the tube exceeds 50 mm. The narrow leaves are linear to sword-shaped, erect and 15-25 mm long, thus much exceeding the flowers. Plants are often difficult to see among the grass where they grow, but when in bloom can often be located by their particularly strong sweet scent. Available evidence indicates that the flowers are pollinated by large-bodied bees. A peculiar feature of this and the allied Babiana hypogaea is the underground inflorescence, a spike but with the lower flowers borne on short stalks, these sometimes resembling lateral branchlets, each bearing one or two flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unmistakable in the linear to nearly terete leaves with narrow longitudinal grooves, and the horizontal spikes bearing pale pink flowers with an elongate, slender perianth tube 70-75 mm long, Babiana brachystachys is a remarkable plant. The unusual flowers suggest pollination by long-proboscid flies, which pollinate flowers of several species with this shape and colour. Apart from the evident close relationship to B. teretifolia, its affinities are uncertain and we suggest that it may be allied to the large group of Babiana species with a similar largely underground stem, decumbent spike and inner bracts divided in the upper third. The cobwebby to woolly cataphylls of B. brachystachys are remarkable for the sect. Teretifolieae and recall the predominantly Namaqualand sect. Antholyzoides. Although known originally only from the sandveld east of Hondeklipbaai near Wallekraal, B. brachystachys has since been recorded at several localities to the south, including near the Groen River Mouth, Brand-se-Baai, Vredendal and Lambert’s Bay.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Babiana crispa has relatively large flowers and large bracts, with the inner forked only at the tips, and is evidently allied to a group of early flowering species with short-tubed, scented flowers that extend across the dry northern interior of Western and Northern Cape from the western Karoo to northern Namaqualand. Among these species, all of which have few-flowered spikes borne at ground level, B. crispa can be recognised by the narrow leaves, 3-6 mm wide on mature flowering individuals, the blades undulate or lightly crisped, hardly or not at all pleated, and lightly twisted in the upper half.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Previously classified with C. intermedia, this species actually bears closer resemblance to the Langeberg endemic, C. lanceolata but lacks the hairs on the anthers that are diagnostic for that species. C. prionota has a very narrow range, being endemic to the Kogelberg, and for that area the long, narrowly lanceolate leaves on a clonally, spreading erect shrub, prevent confusion with any other species. However, the species is comparatively variable within its range, from having leaves that are tough, rigid and entire to ones that are relatively soft and flexible and bearing numerous small teeth. This degree of variation may be the result of introgression with other species, such as the sympatric C. heterophylla (e.g. Levy ns 7042).
bibliographicCitation: Whitehouse, CM. 2004. New species in the section Multinerviae of Cliffortia (Rosaceae). Bothalia 34(2): 77-85. [CC BY]

description: Among the five species of Babiana with truncate, ± cuneate leaves, B. flabellifolia is distinguished by the sweetly scented flowers with subequal tepals and a perianth tube of short to moderate length, 12-36 mm long. The tube is largely or entirely included in soft-textured bracts 15-30 mm long. The flowers remain open at night and are then strongly scented of carnation. The relatively short perianth tube has comparatively thick walls in the lower half when the tube exceeds 20 mm, so that nectar is forced into the upper part of the tube where it is accessible to long-tongued solitary bees and moths, the presumed pollinators. Plants are often hairless, or sparsely hairy on the leaf margins or bracts, but the feature is variable, and some collections from near Springbok have lightly hairy leaves. The type collection of B. flabellifolia is somewhat puzzling because the leaves and bracts are conspicuously hairy. The exact origin of the type is unknown but Reverend Whitehead, who collected it, was stationed at the Anglican Mission at Modderfontein, close to Springbok and the presumption is that the type of B. flabellifolia was collected there or nearby. The long-hairy leaves and bracts of the type are not matched in any other specimen with truncate leaves and it is possible that they represent a taxon separate from the hairless or sparsely hairy plants that occur widely in southern Namaqualand as well as north of Springbok. More information on the variation in the type population and those growing nearby would be helpful in dealing more critically with the question about the status of the type of B. flabellifolia relative to other collections assigned to the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: At first sight, this species can be mistaken for a member of the genus Anthospermum (Rubiaceae). However, on closer examination the alternate arrangement of shoots becomes evident. Morphologically it appears closest to Cliffortia ramosissima Schltr. but the habit of that species is lower and spreading, not upright as in C. anthospermoides. Furthermore, the leaves of C. anthospermoides are larger and more tightly packed on the stems and the species generally has more stamens in the male flowers: 9-12, as opposed to C. ramosissima, which has fewer than nine. The distributions of the two species do not overlap.
bibliographicCitation: Whitehouse, CM; Fellingham, AC. 2007. New species and notes on the genus Cliffortia (Rosaceae). Bothalia 37(1): 9-22. [CC BY]

description: The leaves of this species appear most similar to Cliffortia arcuata Weim., but that species is only found on the mountains surrounding the Little Karoo. Related species that occur in the vicinity of C. perpendicularis include C. ramosissima and C. falcata L.f. The leaves are generally longer and more curved than C. ramosissima and more sharply pointed than C. falcata. However, the most distinctive feature about C. perpendicularis is the very sparse branching (excluding the brachyblasts). It has a spindly, lax habit, so much so that often only a couple of long branches exist and the main stem is unable to bear the weight of the plant, resulting in its sprawling amongst the surrounding vegetation. This is in contrast to C. arcuata and C. falcata, which have erect ascending branches, and C. ramosissima which has an intricate divaricate branching pattern. The distinctive branching pattern is accentuated by the brachyblasts, which appear to project from the stem at right angles.
bibliographicCitation: Whitehouse, CM; Fellingham, AC. 2007. New species and notes on the genus Cliffortia (Rosaceae). Bothalia 37(1): 9-22. [CC BY]

description: Both Babiana hypogaea and B. bainesii are acaulescent plants with the long-tubed flowers arising below the ground, but those of B. hypogaea have a tube 30-40 mm long and shorter, often sparsely hairy to almost smooth leaves, sometimes with inclined to prostrate blades. The blades are often visibly constricted and apparently flexible at the base, which suggests an inclined to prostrate orientation even when they appear upright in pressed specimens. In contrast, B. bainesii has larger, blue-mauve to violet flowers with prominent white markings on the lower lateral tepals edged in darker blue, as well as nearly erect, usually densely hairy leaves, mostly 15-25 mm long. The flowers also have a tube (40-)50-60(-70) mm long, contrasting with the shorter tube of B. hypogaea. The shortly stipitate ovary of B. hypogaea and B. bainesii are typical of species of several genera of Iridaceae with an inflorescence borne at or below ground level and occur in other acaulescent species of Babiana, notably B. sambucina.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is very similar in many respects to Cliffortia eriocephalina but differs on account of its longer, narrower, stiffer and pointed leaves. The leaves are similar in form to the unrelated lowland species, C. stricta, but are much more hairy and grey in appearance. C. eriocephalina and C. weimarckii grow sympatrically in some places such as Matroosberg, where they can be easily distinguished. However, some specimens from the Baviaansberg (Stokoe 4537, Esterhuysen 29806) and Cederberg Langberg (Bond 1383) have leaves of intermediate length, and without field observations on the populations, they are only tentatively attributed to this species.
bibliographicCitation: Whitehouse, CM; Fellingham, AC. 2007. New species and notes on the genus Cliffortia (Rosaceae). Bothalia 37(1): 9-22. [CC BY]

description: Differs from B. ecklonii in its unusual style branches conspicuously enlarged at the tips, purple flower colour with narrow white nectar guides on the lower lateral tepals, blue-black anthers, and obtuse apiculate tepal tips. Flowers of B. ecklonii are violet with broad white to pale yellow nectar guides, the anthers are pale violet, and the tepals are narrow and acute. The style divides opposite the anther apices in B. latifolia and the style branches are ± 4 mm long with the tips unusually broad and undulate. In B. ecklonii the point of division of the style and length of style branches is variable, in different individuals, dividing variously below the anthers and ± 2 mm long, or opposite the middle or close to the anther apices and up to 4 mm long, but in both cases the style branches are slender, widening gradually toward the tips. Vegetatively the two also differ: in B. latifolia the leaf and stem pubescence is velvety but in B. ecklonii the pubescence is longer and sparser, and the erect stem is largely sheathed by the leaf bases, whereas the stem of B. latifolia arches outward and is free of the leaf bases for at least half its length.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the most common species of the interior valleys and lower mountain slopes of the western half of Western Cape, Babiana mucronata is recognised among species of sect. Babiana with a densely hairy ovary by the pale to deep violet flowers with white to pale yellow blotches on the lower lateral tepals. The anthers are pale yellow to lilac or sometimes turquoise and the flowers usually have an acrid to metallic odour or occasionally apparently odourless. Most other blue-flowered species of sect. Babiana from this area are more-or-less acaulescent, have leaves taller than the stem, and a smooth or sparsely hairy ovary, except for the relatively tall B. lineolata, which favours wet sandy ground and is easily separated by the rigid, narrow, deeply pleated leaves and short floral bracts, mostly 7-10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The attractive Babiana odorata is a common species of the loamy clay or granitic soils of the Swartland north of Cape Town and is a pleasant sight in lightly disturbed renosterveld in early spring around Malmesbury and Moorreesburg. Plants have short, velvety stems or are almost stemless, the flowers then borne close to ground level. The flowers may be pale creamy yellow with bright yellow lower tepals or rarely flushed pale mauve, but are always intensely fragrant, with a spicy to pleasant violet odour, the scent varying with ambient temperature and age of the flowers, which each last three days. Babiana odorata is most easily confused with the vegetatively similar B. patula, which occurs in similar habitats to the east, in the Breede River Valley and across the low hills of the southern Cape. Most readily distinguished by the ovary smooth or lightly hairy on the ribs vs. densely hairy in B. fragrans, B. patula has dull yellowish or white or more often pale mauve to blue or dull purple flowers with yellow markings and a particularly strong fragrance, often of violet or freesia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in the relatively small, strongly fragrant flowers, Babiana patula is typically low growing and often has an unusually coloured perianth. While the flowers may be white to creamy yellow, they are more often violet or light mauve to purple with the lower lateral tepals deep yellow and tipped with purple or mauve. The affinities of B. patula seem to lie with the southern Cape B. fourcadei, a taller plant with blue to violet flowers marked with white, a longer perianth tube 20-30 mm long, often a quite different, spicy acrid fragrance, and a completely smooth ovary. The ovary of B. patula, unusual in sect. Babiana but typical of other members of series Patulae, is usually sparsely hairy on in the ribs. The character readily separates it from the superficially similar B. odorata, which also has strongly scented, cream-coloured and yellow flowers, sometimes flushed with mauve, but always has a densely hairy ovary. Babiana patula may also be confused with Babiana ambigua, a typically acaulescent or short plant of sandy habitats. Flowers of B. ambigua are dark blue, rarely mauve, and have white nectar guides. The ovary of B. ambigua, like that of B. patula, is smooth or sparsely hairy on the ribs, but the outstanding difference is that B. ambigua lacks a well-developed fibrous collar around the stem base present in B. patula.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the pinnate, usually 7-foliolate, subglabrous leaves, pruinose hairy stems, and small pinkish petals.
bibliographicCitation: Sochor, M. 2018. Biosystematic revision of the native and naturalised species of Rubus L. (Rosaceae) in the Cape Floristic Region, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 118: 241-259. description: The general aspect of Babiana pygmaea suggests an affinity with the B. nana group of species of sect. Teretifolieae, which have a similar vegetative morphology but conventional zygomorphic, more-or-less bilabiate blue to violet or purple flowers with the lower lateral tepals bearing nectar guides. One aspect of B. pygmaea that does not entirely accord with section Teretifolieae is the short, erect aerial stem and erect, rather than inflexed or decumbent spike. This feature may be associated with the actinomorphic flower, which is best displayed on an upright stalk. The apparently related B. nana also has a short, suberect aerial stem and only slightly deflexed spike.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the deep blue flowers with a dark red centre, and unusual red-brown anthers and pollen. The tepals are subequal and symmetrically arranged but the stamens and style are usually unilateral with the anthers facing the spike apex. The style also has unusually short style branches with very broad tips. Babiana regia has superficially similar, dark blue flowers with a red centre but the stamens are symmetrically arranged in the centre of the flower, and the style banches below the anthers into filiform branches that are not or barely expanded apically. Babiana rubrocyanea is most likely allied to the B. angustifolia group of species and possibly most closely to B. angustifolia. That species has similarly cupped, subequal tepals, flowers borne on a strongly inclined stem, and outer floral bract bidentate with a central mucro. The latter recall the trilobed to obscurely tricuspidate bracts of B. rubrocyanea. Also, the unilateral stamens with the anthers facing the spike apexes of B. rubrocyanea have exactly the same orientation in B. angustifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The dwarf Babiana salteri is recognised by the low stature, up to 100 mm high, and leaves with broadly lanceolate to ovate blades held almost at right angles to the sheaths enclosing the erect stem. The relatively small, pale blue-mauve flowers have a short perianth tube ± 9 mm long, dorsal tepal ± 23 mm long and lower tepals 13-15 mm long tapering toward the base, although not distinctly clawed. The short, horizontally oriented leaves recall those of the Richtersveld endemics, B. gariepensis and B. horizontalis, as well as those of the southern Namaqualand B. lewisiana but none of these species has bracts divided to the base.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the smooth spike borne at ground level, a distinctive lowermost outer floral bract that is extended upward into a short blade, and flowers with a long, straight perianth tube and nearly equal tepals. The leaves and bracts are often almost hairless or at best velvety but are sometimes sparsely long-hairy, and with silky pubescence at the top of the leaf sheaths. The perianth is pale to deep blue or violet and the lower lateral tepals each have a prominent white mark edged in dark blue and sometimes red. The tepals are relatively large, usually 30-35 mm long, only slightly shorter than the tube, mainly 35-55 mm long, or sometimes equalling the tube. Flowers of most populations are strongly and sweetly scented of violets, a particularly characteristic feature of the species Babiana sambucina can be confused with the widespread B. bainesii (long misidentified as B. hypogaea) of summer-rainfall southern Africa. The latter differs most significantly in the spike being borne just below the ground so that the flowers arise at about ground level, whereas in B. sambucina the spike is carried slightly above the ground. The leaves of B. bainesii are longer and normally narrower than in B. sambucina, usually 3-10 mm wide, and roughly hairy, but the degree and type of leaf pubescence is variable in both species. The perianth tube of B. sambucina, normally 35-55 mm long, is similar to that of B. bainesii, but the tepals, 20-60 x 6-12 mm, are proportionally narrower than in B. sambucina and do not overlap one another in the lower half as in B. sambucina. In addition, the perianth tube of B. bainesii has a wide throat and the lower tepals are joined to the upper laterals, forming a prominent lip not found in B. sambucina, which has the tube cylindric or gradually expanded from the base and the tepals arise at more-or-less the same level. Among the species of the southern African winter-rainfall zone, Babiana sambucina may be most closely allied to B. framesii of the Bokkeveld Plateau and we find it difficult to separate the two when dry. Babiana framesii has, like B. sambucina, a long straight perianth tube, although somewhat curved below the throat, but the somewhat smaller tepals are proportionally narrower and spread almost at right angles to the tube, and the flowers are at most only lightly scented.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Most easily recognised by the underground stem, often branched at ground level, and usually forming small tufts, and the fairly large, pale blue to blue-mauve flowers, which have a pleasing sweet scent and contrast both in the scent and large size with those of B. mucronata, which is also common in the Olifants River Valley. That species typically has an erect, usually well-developed aerial stem, while the flowers have a densely hairy ovary and produce a rather harsh acrid-spicy odour. Young plants do not have the narrow, twisted to coiled immature leaves of B. scabrifolia that surround the parent plants. It reproduces amply by cormlets and it is common to see mature flowering plants with their broad, soft-textured leaves surrounded by the linear, twisted to coiled leaves produced by immature plants.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the blue flowers with white to yellow markings, a perianth tube of intermediate length, mostly 12-15 mm (but up to 20 mm in the type) combined with distinctive dry, brown to translucent floral bracts. Plants can be relatively tall for the genus, up to 500 or even 800 mm but plants from the Bokkeveld Plateau are consistently shorter, mostly ± 300 mm tall. Babiana scariosa is most closely allied to acaulescent B. papyracea, which has a radially symmetrical, short-tubed flower, but similar dry, membranous floral bracts. It may also be related to B. spathacea of the western Karoo, which also has similar floral bracts, but the flowers of this species are creamy beige with red markings on the lower tepals and have an elongate perianth tube. Hybrids between this species and B. scariosa may be found where the two co-occur on the Bokkeveld Plateau south of Nieuwoudtville.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by the long-tubed, usually creamy beige to ± white flowers with dark red to purple markings near the bases of the lower three tepals, a perianth tube 35-45 mm long and dorsal tepal ± 25 mm long. The dry, membranous, long-cuspidate floral bracts, which prompted the name spathacea, are distinctive only in combination with the perianth characters. Two other species also have similar floral bracts, B. scariosa, which has bilabiate, blue flowers with a relatively short perianth tube, 12-20 mm long, and the acaulescent B. papyracea, which has large, radially symmetric flowers. South of Nieuwoudtville plants included in B. spathacea are unusually variable, some having pale lilac-blue flowers with purple markings, a somewhat smaller perianth with the tube 30-36 mm long and the dorsal tepal 13-23 mm long. These plants also sometimes have longer style branches, up to 4 mm long, unusual for the species, in which 1.8-2.0 mm long is typical. It seems likely that hybridisation with Babiana scariosa, which also grows there and in the same habitat, is the source of the bluish colouring, shorter perianth tube, and longer style branches. Closer to Nieuwoudtville plants have white flowers with red markings, flushed lilac on the tube and reverse of the tepals, and the anthers and pollen are dark purple. Flowers are smaller and have a tube ± 30 mm long and a dorsal tepal ± 15 mm long, but the style branches in these plants are 2.0-2.5 mm long, which is typical of B. spathacea.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Babiana spiralis is perhaps most closely related to B. fimbriata of central Namaqualand and it has often been confused with that species. The brightly coloured, attractive flowers, velvety hairy stem, and leaves twisted or coiled above and hairless except for a few long hairs on the margins distinguish it from B. fimbriata, which has dull coloured flowers, somewhat rigid, only weakly twisted leaves, a sparsely hairy or smooth stem, and upper lateral tepal limbs curving inward, very different from the ± patent tepals of B. spiralis. The lower lateral tepals of B. fimbriata also lack the auriculate lobes at the base of the limbs characteristic of most species of series Exohebeoides, including B. spiralis. Instead, the lower lateral tepals are obscurely lobed at best. The leaf sheaths and cataphylls of B. spiralis are not woolly or cobwebby as they are in B. fimbriata, and the leaf blades may have fairly well-developed terete pseudopetioles, sometimes up to 40 mm long with the broad part of the blade abruptly expanded. The ranges of the two species overlap in central Namaqualand, but B. spiralis has the wider distribution, extending westward to the sandy coast south of Hondeklipbaai and south to the Nardouw Mtns in Western Cape.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Cliffortia apiculata resembles externally certain forms of C. polygonifolia rather much but is readily distinguished from the latter species by the glabrous leaves. The type of the flowers and the fruits is however systematically more significant. According to the features in question C. apiculata obtains its natural place within the sect. Costatae H. Weim. and belong to the vicinity of C. glauca H. Weim.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1946. Further notes on the genus Cliffortia. Bot. Not. 1946(4): 407-420. [All rights reserved]

description: C. atrata is very similar to C. paucistaminea and C. pterocarpa (see also C. dodecandra) and is not easily distinguished from them in a sterile state. All three species have more or less densely pilous branchlets and needle-shaped leaflets, on the upper side somewhat flat. C. pterocarpa has, however, broader leaflets, which are very often to a smaller or larger extent connate at the base. In C. paucistaminea the midrib of the leaflets is thicker and more prominent on the under side than in C. atrata. When fertile, C. pterocarpa has 15, C. atrata 12 and C. paucistaminea only 3 or 4 stamens. The receptacle in C. pterocarpa is brown and has high and usually sharp-edged ribs, in C. atrata it is black-darkly brownish black and has low, rather broad and rounded ribs, and in C. paucistaminea again, the receptacle is brownish green and has narrow low ribs.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the floral bracts 15-20 mm long, the inner of which does not have rust-coloured, acuminate tips, and the ascending leaves are 4.0-5.5 mm wide. Babiana stenomera is evidently most closely related to a second Namaqualand species, B. fimbriata, but that species has narrower leaves, up to 3.5 mm wide, tapering and lightly twisted in the upper half, a smooth or at best sparsely hairy stem, and prominent long hairs on the edges of the leaf sheaths. The bracts of B. stenomera in particular, mostly 15-20 mm long, are beyond the expected range for B. fimbriata or for the related B. spiralis which has narrow, coiled leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Winter-flowering Babiana striata is recognised primarily by the unusual inclined leaves with undulate and tightly crisped margins, smooth or at most ciliate on the margins with the entire blade loosely twisted. The fairly small flowers are borne on an inclined to horizontal spike facing the spike axis, and the tepals are pale yellow, flushed light purple outside. Like most species of sect. Antholyzoides, the cataphylls and leaf bases are cobwebby. The species is most often confused with blue-flowered B. sinuata, which also has similar undulate and twisted leaves but is otherwise very different. The leaves of B. sinuata differ in having long hairs on the margins of the sheath and upper margin of the blade, the flowers are larger, with the dorsal tepal ± 28 mm long (versus 20-25 mm in B. striata), and are pale blue with pale yellow lower tepals with pale blue tips, and the lower laterals have a conspicuous dark violet median mark. Even more distinctive are the stamens of B. sinuata, which have filaments ± 20 mm long and connate anthers, a feature that persists even in pressed specimens. The stamens of B. striata have filaments ± 15 mm long and the anthers free from one another. Surprisingly, given their dull colouration, the flowers of B. striata appear unscented, at least in the live plants examined from near Kotzesrus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]
