description: This species is particularly characterized by the spherical, berrylike receptacles, and the name, C. baccans, indicates this peculiarity. Even in a sterile state the species is easily distinguished from other Cliffortia-species by the short, at most 3.5 mm long, needle-shaped leaflets.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. brevifolia stands, morphologically, close to C. ericifolia. The following differences may be emphasized: C. brevifolia has slightly glossy laminae 1.5-2 mm long, [male] bracteoles about 1 mm long, filaments about 2.5 mm long and receptacles about 1.8 mm long. C. ericifolia, on the other hand, has opaque laminae 4-5 mm in length, [male] bracteoles 0.5-0.6 mm long, filaments 3-3.5 mm long and receptacles 2-2.5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Usually a small plant, typical Babiana tubiflora is recognised by the relatively small, white to creamy white flowers, often with small red or pink markings at the base of the lower tepal limbs, an elongate perianth tube, and often narrow, linear leaves. The perianth tube is uniformly slender or very gradually expanded toward the apex and usually 60-80 mm long but sometimes shorter or longer. The filaments are 13-16 mm long and the style branches are 3-4 mm long and often not reaching the anther tips. Babiana tubiflora is closely related to a second long-tubed species, B. tubulosa, and often confused with it. This local endemic of the Atlantic Coast and near interior of Western Cape has creamy beige to pink flowers usually flushed pink outside, prominent red markings on the lower tepals limbs, and a perianth tube 65-105 mm long that is expanded distally into a wider gullet 5-12 mm long. The longer stamens have filaments 20-22 mm long with longer anthers, and the style divides opposite or slightly beyond the anther tips with the style branches ± 6 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of just a handful of yellow-flowered species of Babiana, B. vanzijliae is recognised primarily by the yellow flowers with a long perianth tube mostly 25-50 mm long. In the south, at Papkuilsfontein and Lokenberg, the perianth may be a dull creamy yellow or flushed pale bluish mauve and the perianth tube is often shorter, 18-25 mm long. The shorter-tubed plants with mauve flowers may be the result of introgression due to occasional crossing with short-tubed, violet-flowered B. mucronata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively slender species mostly less than 700 mm tall, with a narrow, shortly pedunculate synflorescence of 3 to 10 rhipidia subtended by a narrow, leaf-like spathe with terete blade often greatly prolonged and appearing as an extension of the stem, the synflorescence thus apparently lateral. The ± papillate ovaries develop into tuberculate capsules 8-13 mm long. The Langeberg populations are anomalous in their smooth ovaries and capsules. The species is superficially similar to Bobartia gracilis, which is distinguished by its smaller, smooth, subglobose capsules 5-8 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The long needle-shaped leaflets, the large amplectant bracteoles, and the erect sepals of the female flowers, which remain till the fruits are mature, are very characteristic features in C. burchellii. As to the last mentioned character the species corresponds with C. erectisepala, which, however, has simple leaves. The style is very short, and the stigmas project only very little outside of the sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Cliffortia carinata comes morphologically near C. glauca and C. marginata. The species differs from these types i.e. by its pronouncedly keeled i.e. sepals and its pilous twigs.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: C. geniculata comes near C. obovata E. Mey. and C. glauca Weimarck. It differs from these species by its pilous twigs and larger flowers, from C. glauca, moreover, by its thin leaflets and from C. obovata by its larger receptacles.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: C. castanea belongs to the group of Cliffortia species which have 3-foliolate leaves with acicular leaflets, 'the juniperina group'. Distinguishing features of this species are above all the semiterete, densely verruculose leaflets with no visible ribs and the oblong, brown-castaneous receptacles.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Superficially similar to Bobartia aphylla and distinguished by its small, smooth, subglobose capsules, 5-8 mm long. A poorly understood species that can also be difficult to separate from forms of B. orientalis but typically with fewer, longer rhipidia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from similar species with a narrow, leaf-like spathe subtending the synflorescence by the characteristically long, trailing leaves, much longer than the flowering stem. The dense, globose synflorescence of several to many, narrow rhipidia is subtended by two horizontally spreading, narrow, rigid, leaf-like bracts or spathes, the lowermost longest and the other much shorter and almost awl-like. The pedicels are characteristically densely villous distally. Bobartia indica is probably most closely allied to B. orientalis, which has leaves ± as long as the flowering stem, diagnostic short rhipidia with inner spathes 10-18 mm long and small, subglobose capsules mostly 4-6 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. crenata is the largest species within this section and cannot be confused with any other Cliffortia-species. The leaflets are kidney-shaped or sometimes nearly orbicular. The stipules are connate, constituting an ovate-almost circular leaflike structure. The midrib of the leaflets is stronger and more marked than the lateral veins and has 2-5 pairs of lateral evanescing nerves.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: A poorly understood species superficially resembling Bobartia longicyma subsp. longicyma but distinguished from it by the rhipidia borne on a short common peduncle above the spathe.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Bobartia macrospatha, the only other species in the genus with the ovary not exserted from the rhipidial spathes, by its flattened or subterete leaves and stem, 3-6 mm wide, mostly spreading, leaf-like spathe not expanded or enclosing the synflorescence, and the more numerous, spreading rhipidia densely clustered in a rounded head. The individual rhipidia are relatively small, with the inner spathe 13-15 mm long, and the capsules are also small, subglobose to broadly oblong, 4-8(-10) mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the hemispherical, paniculate inflorescence with sticky internodes and relatively small, yellow flowers. The basal internode of the stem is conspicuously elongated, with the inflorescence thus clearly borne at the tip. This is intermediate between the inflorescence type in Bobartia lilacina, in which the two or three lower internodes are subequally developed, and the remaining species in the genus, which have only the lowermost internode elongated and a congested inflorescence. The stem lacks stomatiferous furrows and is thus smooth when fresh but the presence of peripheral longitudinal sclerenchyma strands causes it to become slightly striate when dry.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A large, often clump-forming species with robust stems 3-6 mm diam. and a dense, obovoid synflorescence of 8 to 40 suberect rhipidia and ± papillate ovary scarcely exserted from the rhipidial spathes. The large flowers have tepals, 20-32 mm long and the large capsules, 7-18 mm long, are conspicuously rugose or verrucose to muricate. Bobartia aphylla, also with usually verrucose capsules, is a smaller, more slender species mostly less than 700 mm tall, with a narrow, green, leaf-like spathe subtending a narrow, ellipsoid synflorescence of up to ten rhipidia. Old individuals form large, rush-like tussocks.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by its comparatively short stature, the spike seldom reaching more than 500 mm in height, unbranched flowering stem, and inclined to almost horizontal spike. The 10 to 16 flowers are borne in a single congested row on the upper side of the spike axis. The flowers are distinctive in the perianth tube being abruptly expanded above the narrow cylindric lower part, the wider upper part of the tube is lightly expanded into three pouches, and the lower part of the tube is twisted through 360°. Although all Chasmanthe species have orange seeds, only those of C. aethiopica have a fleshy coat when first exposed after the capsule walls split. The seed coat later becomes dry and wrinkled. The inside of the capsules is often flushed reddish to purple. Thus both vegetatively and in flower and fruit C. aethiopica stands apart in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished from its congeners by the relatively large flowers, branched stem and erect spike, Chasmanthe floribunda has uniformly coloured, bright orange-scarlet flowers borne in an erect, two-ranked spike. It has long been confused with C. aethiopica, a shorter plant with an unbranched flowering stem and inflexed spike, either strongly inclined or nearly horizontal, with the flowers borne in a single row on the upper surface of the flowering axis.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Crocosmia fucata is a tall plant with fairly narrow, plane leaves, and a flowering stem usually with 2 to 4 branches diverging at a wide angle from the main axis and a strongly arching spike. The flowers are predominantly scarlet with the lower 3 tepals each with a narrow red median streak and the tube yellow in the underside and in the throat. The long-tubed flowers are similar to those of species like C. paniculata and C. pearsei, with a narrow cylindric lower portion and a wider, also cylindric upper part but both of these species have strongly pleated leaves. In detail, the flowers can be seen to be somewhat different from those of C. paniculata, which has the outer whorl of tepals noticeably smaller than the inner three, and a slight but unmistakable pouch where the lower part of the perianth tube expands into the wider upper portion.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. drepanoides comes very close to. C. falcata but there is no difficulty in distinguishing one from the other.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Perhaps the loveliest of all Crocosmia species, C. masoniorum, the swan crocosmia, is recognised by the broad, pleated leaves, and the brilliant orange flowers borne on inclined stems with crowded spikes held horizontally. The flowers have a perianth tube 18-25 mm long and spreading, somewhat flaccid tepals, with the rather stiff, diverging stamens prominently displayed.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Crocosmia mathewsiana is readily identified by the combination of strongly pleated leaves, multibranched flowering stem, drooping, flexuose spikes, and relatively short-tubed, brilliant orange-scarlet flowers. We assume its relationships lie with the three other pleated-leaved species of the genus, and it is perhaps most closely allied to C. paniculata, which also has a multibranched flowering stem and strongly flexuose spikes. Vegetatively the two are almost indistinguishable, although the stem and branches of C. mathewsiana are more slender and strongly nodding in bud. The spikes are also less prominently flexuose and the flowers of the two species differ considerably, those of C. paniculata having an elongate perianth tube 33-40 mm long (vs. 20 mm).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the slender stem seldom reaching 1 m in height, often unbranched or at most with 1 or 2 short branches, unlike the strongly branched C. paniculata with which it may be confused. The spikes in both species are strongly flexuose, with the flowers borne in two opposed rows, facing away from one another. The flowers of C. pearsei are larger, some 60-70 mm long, with a perianth tube 40-45 mm long and a dorsal tepal ± 20 mm long, whereas typical C. paniculata has flowers with a perianth tube 33-40 mm long and a dorsal tepal 14-18 mm long. The two species occupy quite different habitats, C. paniculata being a plant of wet sites, growing in deep, rich soils at moderate elevations, unlike the high-altitude, well-drained basalt slopes and cliffs favoured by C. pearsei.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. exilifolia resembles C. paucistaminea Weimarck and C. filifolia L. fil. rather much. The species differs from C. paucistaminea by the leaflets, which have smooth margins and convex under-side with no prominent midrib, and by the number of the stamens (in C. paucistaminea 3 or 4). From C. filifolia it deviates by its pubescent twigs, sessile leaflets and much smaller bracteoles.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the puberulous stem (usually smooth below), two basal leaves with thickened margins and raised and thickened central vein, minutely ciliate on the edges and slightly sticky on the raised surfaces. The third leaf is largely sheathing, the sheath slightly inflated and distinctly ribbed. The flowers are usually deep blue and relatively large, with tepals mostly 12-15 mm long, and the filaments are unequal. Populations in the southern Bokkeveld Mtns are unusual in having uniformly white flowers. Geissorhiza arenicola is most easily confused with the more widespread and usually smaller-flowered G. aspera but is apparently related to the dark blue-flowered G. splendidissima, with which it shares a puberulous stem, a strongly ribbed and grooved upper leaf sheath, short perianth tube, and basal leaves with strongly raised margins and midrib, the edges of which are usually lightly ciliate.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. falcata is very uniform and varies only in the length of the petioles and the leaflets.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Often locally common, Geissorhiza aspera is recognised by the minutely puberulous stem, plane leaves with slightly thickened margins, and typically glistening, dark blue (sometimes white) flowers with a greenish yellow throat, usually with slightly unequal filaments. The floral bracts are green in bud but as the flowers open they become dry and turn rusty brown at the tips. Plants vary greatly in size depending on soil fertility and available moisture, and may grow up to or even over 300 mm high, or be stunted and less than 100 mm. Although most often blue, plants in the Olifants River Valley and to the north often have partly or entirely white flowers. The stamens are sometimes described as being equal, but careful examination of live plants shows that one filament is usually slightly shorter, and in populations in the north of its range the filaments are clearly unequa.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by the zygomorphic flowers borne on inclined to nearly horizontal spikes, the tepals remaining somewhat cupped even when the nodding flowers are fully open. The pale yellow flowers have large purple-black markings on the lower third of the outer or all tepals, a perianth tube 7-8 mm long, and tepals 22-30 mm long. The unilateral stamens are decumbent, thus held above the lowermost tepal and the filaments are unequal, one ± 5 mm shorter than the other two. It is evidently allied to and almost identical vegetatively to the more widespread G. imbricate, which has smaller, radially symmetric flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the unusual leaf morphology and relatively large, pink flowers with a perianth tube 20-30 mm long and tepals 24-27 mm long and up to 7 mm wide. It is sometimes difficult to separate from closely allied to G. tenella, but that species has flowers white or faintly flushed pink, with a perianth tube 30-40 mm long and narrow tepals 14-22 x 3.0-4.5 mm. The leaves of both species are H-shaped in cross section with the margins raised into wings at right angles to the blade surface, the wings curving inward.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its relatively small size, several plane leaves often inclined toward the ground or even prostrate, and small white flowers mostly 1 or 2, rarely 3 per spike. Branches, when present, are typically produced from the base of the stem. The flowers have a perianth tube up to 5 mm long and tepals up to 12 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The large, leaflike stipules, distinguishing this species from the other Cliffortia-species are very characteristic. The [male]-flowers are tetramerous and have 8 stamens. The [female]-flowers are also tetramerous and the receptacle is very small, only one mm long, or slightly longer, quite smooth and lacking every trace of furrows or ridges.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Geissorhiza brevituba is distinctive in sect. Engysiphon in the relatively short perianth tube, ± 8 mm long, substantially shorter than the floral bracts, these 15-20 mm long, relatively short for the section. Despite this the tepals are 25-30 mm long, in the normal range for the section. The leaves with thickened margins and main vein and large, more-or-less nodding, zygomorphic flower with declinate stamens and style are typical of sect. Engysiphon.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Striking when in flower, Geissorhiza burchellii has relatively large deep purple to violet flowers with a short perianth tube, only 4-6 mm long and about one third as long as the spreading to slightly reflexed tepals. The stamens are unequal, typical of the section, and the corm tunics are of the imbricate type but are of soft, papery rather than woody texture. The stems are hairless and usually branched and the leaves have the margins and main vein thickened, rendering the leaf surfaces two-grooved.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With relatively large, pink flowers that are darker at the base of the tepals, Geissorhiza callista is recognised also by the elongate perianth tube 22-25 mm long and unilateral stamens and style. The stamens extend well beyond the mouth of the perianth tube, and the particularly long style divides up to 6 mm beyond the anther tips. The stem is usually inclined and the leaves falcate to trailing from steeply sloping ground. Like most members of sect. Monticolae, the leaves have thickened margins and main vein and are thus shallowly 2-grooved or channelled on each surface. The species was previously included in G. grandiflora, but that species differs in its erect stems and smaller flowers, the perianth tube up to 18 mm long and the tepals 20-22 mm long, a shorter style dividing opposite the upper third to apex of the anthers, and slightly longer style branches 4-5 mm long, contrasting with the longer style and shorter style branches, ± 3 mm long, in G. callista.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza cataractarum is unusual in its habitat and in its particularly delicate, almost membranous corm tunics that seldom accumulate, instead decaying entirely within a year. The flowers are unremarkable, and typical of the genus in their blue-mauve colour, perianth tube 4-6 mm long, and spreading tepals. Plants have three leaves, the lower two longest and with trailing blades with thickened margins and main vein, thus are shallowly two-grooved on each surface.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza cedarmontana and the poorly known G. esterhuyseniae stand out in the genus in having stamens and style branches included within the relatively long perianth tube. Geissorhiza cedarmontana is recognised by its very short filaments, ± 1 mm long, inserted ± 2 mm above the base of the perianth tube, and a similarly short style less than 1 mm long, with three short poorly defined branches. The pink to almost white flowers have a red mark at the base of each of the spreading tepals. The leaves are also modified, having much thickened margins and main veins, thus with two longitudinal grooves running the length of each leaf surface. In contrast, G. esterhuyseniae has uniformly white flowers with filaments ± 3 mm long, inserted ± 2.5 mm above the base of the perianth tube, and better developed style branches some 2 mm long. The leaves of G. esterhuyseniae are flat, with only slightly raised margins and main veins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. concinna belongs to sect. Costatae and may be closely allied to C. geniculata and C. obovata. Especially characteristic are the leaves, greyish-green on both sides and having only the mid rib distinct. The mid rib projects in a short, marked point. The leaves are densely crowded on the brachyhlasts.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1953. Two new Cliffortia species from the Cape Province . Bot. Not. 106(1): 78-80. [All rights reserved]

description: C. graminea is perhaps, from a morphological point of view, the most peculiar of all Cliffortia species. It may easily be mistaken for a grass. The vagina is up to 6 cm long, foliaceous, many-nerved and in all respects similar to the blade. As regards texture and colour, the stipules are also leaf-like. The blade may reach 15 cm in length with a breadth of only 6 mm. The margins are almost smooth or else furnished with more or less conspicuous teeth. The sepals of the [male]-flower are up to 14 mm long and at most 2 mm wide. As in other species within the genus the sepals have a small spot of dense papillae on the inner side of the tip.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The variety differs from C. grnminea by its much more gracile habit and its shorter vaginas and laminae. The margins of the leaves are entire and firmer in texture, the number of the stamens is smaller and the sepals of the female flowers are shorter, only 1-1.2 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: C. graminea var. convoluta is a form which in some respects differs widely from C. graminea. The variety has slightly shining, convolute leaves and has also another organization of branching. C. graminea has exclusively elongated branches, whereas var. convoluta has strongly marked brachyblasts. Only male or sterile specimens are known. A curious thing is that the pollen grains seem to be imperfectly developed. Thus, it may be suspected that var. convoluta in reality represents a hybrid.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: A very peculiar feature of this species is the occurrence of two quite different types of leaf. All leaves, except those growing close to the top of the branches and stems, are lanceolate and uniform in breadth, are evenly and finely toothed and have filiform stipules up to 20 mm in length. The leaves towards the top of the stems and branches, on the other hand, are triangularly lanceolate-oblong or ovate and are often slightly and inconspicuously toothed and have no, or very short, stipules. Only [female]-flowers are known.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: With large creamy white or beige to almost yellow flowers, Geissorhiza confusa is one of the most conspicuous species in the genus. Vegetatively, the long basal leaf with thick margins and main vein and the large corm with woody tunics are typical of sect. Engysiphon but the perianth tube, mostly 35-50 mm long, is one of the longest in the section. The species has been much confused historically with G. exscapa, which has a comparably long perianth tube but usually pink flowers and different leaf morphology, the blades appearing terete but actually ± H-shaped in section with margins raised into wings that curve inward over the main vein, which is only slightly thickened.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza corrugata stands out in its small size, up to 50 mm tall, including the flowers, and in its loosely spirally coiled leaves. The bright yellow flowers and borne singly on the stems, and have a short perianth tube up to 3 mm long, spreading tepals, and a style dividing ± opposite the bases of the anthers. It shares these distinctive leaf and style features with G. spiralis, which has purple to deep pink flowers with a longer perianth tube. Greenhouse-grown plants have shown that flowers of G. corrugata are self-compatible and autogamous. The short style and spreading branches facilitate self-fertilization. Plants are often exceedingly common locally and can make a striking display, the yellow blooms visible from a considerable distance.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A striking species, Geissorhiza darlingensis has large pale yellow flowers with a purple-black centre. Allied to G. humilis of the Cape Peninsula and adjacent West Coast, it has a longer perianth tube 9-11 mm long and tepals 23-26 mm long vs. perianth tube 5-8 mm long and tepals mostly 16-22 mm long in G. humilis. Both species have linear leaves with thickened margins and midribs and are sticky, usually with sand adhering to the surface. The ciliate edges of the leaf margins and main vein of G. darlingensis are evidently lacking in G. humilis. The distinction between the two species is not always clear where their ranges approach.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza divaricata is apparently very closely allied to G. subrigida, also restricted to the Bokkeveld Mtns. The two are distinctive in having a sheath of fibres around the stem base, smooth stems, ciliate to pubescent and ribbed leaves, divaricate branching, and brown, membranous stem bracts. These shared similarities have tended to obscure their differences. Geissorhiza divaricata has small white to pale mauve or blue flowers with a perianth tube 1-2 mm long and tepals ± 10 mm, while G. subrigida, a shorter plant, has larger blue to violet flowers with perianth tube 3-4 mm long and tepals 12-17 mm long. Both grow in rocky sandstone ground but have not been recorded growing together. Plants included in G. divaricata from the Gifberg collected to date have either simple or 1-branched stems and lack the distinctive dry stem bracts found in those from the Bokkeveld Mtns.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. hirta is rather similar to C. eriocephalina, C. stricta and C. nitidula var. pilosa but differs by exhibiting longer and thicker pilosity on the branchlets, very long-hairy leaves, large [male]-flowers with about 20 stamens; it has also a bigger receptacle than the other species of the same group.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Geissorhiza elsiae is distinguished by its large, purple flowers with tepals 15-20 mm long, 1- to 4-flowered spike, and few-branched habit; branches, when present, are produced from the upper nodes rather than from near the base. It is probably most closely allied to the more widespread southern Cape species, G. inconspicua which has smaller flowers, usually violet or white in colour.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: On account of its peculiar and quite different appearance from other Cliffortia-species C. ilicifolia has in only a very few cases been mistaken for other species or given new names. The form of the leaves and the number of the teeth vary rather much. Some of the most extreme and, from the main type, strongly deviating forms are treated as varieties.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: One of the most remarkable species in the genus, Geissorhiza esterhuyseniae has both stamens and style included within a relatively long perianth tube up to 16 mm long. This set of characters is known elsewhere in Geissorhiza in the northern Cederberg species, G. cedarmontana, and in G. adriaanii (sect. Engysiphon) from Piketberg. Corms are not known for G. esterhuyseniae and it is included in subg. Weihea because of its morphological similarity to G. cedarmontana. This species has a perianth tube 13-15 mm long, comparable with that of G. esterhuyseniae, but shorter filaments 1 mm long and the white flowers have red at the tepal bases, whereas G. esterhuyseniae has uniformly white flowers with filaments ± 3 mm long. Both species grow in similar sheltered, south-facing rocky situations.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in the genus in the persistent bases of leaves and cataphylls which accumulate in a collar around the stem base and in the spike and its branches always bearing just one flower. It is also notable in having the corms of past seasons often persist instead of decaying, so that a series of old corms accumulate behind the current one. Geissorhiza fourcadei seems isolated in the subgenus but is best referred to sect. Weihea in which there is a tendency for the reduction of the number of flowers in the spike. It is also distinctive here in its terete, 4-grooved leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza furva is a relatively short specuies, rarely exceeding 120 mm in height, with terete, 4-grooved leaves, and large deep, golden-yellow flowers. The flowers are unusual in turning a blackish colour on drying. The small corms, up to 9 mm diam., with concentric tunics that fragment vertically into irregular sections are typical of subg. Weihea. Geissorhiza furva is probably mostly closely related to the more common and widespread G. juncea, which has smaller, white to pale yellow flowers, the tepals mostly 8-12 x 3.0-5.5 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza grandiflora has one of the largest flowers in the genus, comparable in size with those of some species of sect. Engysiphon (subg. Weihea). The flowers are deep pink and zygomorphic with stamens and style both unilateral and lying above the lowermost tepal. The light brown, imbricate corm tunics are papery in texture but otherwise match those of subg. Geissorhiza and are regularly notched along the lower margin. The unequal stamens and branched stems are characteristic of the sect. Monticolae, in which it most closely resembles G. burchellii, a generally smaller species with leaves with heavily thickened margins and midrib, and dark purple, radially symmetric flowers with a shorter perianth tube 4-6 mm long. The two species are occasionally sympatric or nearly so and both have been collected on the Cossacks and Slanghoek Mtns. A collection from the Grootwinterhoek mtns, provisionally assigned to G. grandiflora, has somewhat smaller flowers than are typical and their colour is uncertain.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. integerrima stands morphologically close to C. theodori-friesii. The differences between the two species will be found under that species.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Geissorhiza hesperanthoides is unusual in the genus in having fine, fibrous corm tunics, shared only with G. nubigena and G. umbrosa and evidently a specialised character in Geissorhiza, where hard woody concentric tunics are likely the ancestral state. Flowers of G. hesperanthoides have broad, somewhat cupped, violet-blue tepals and a perianth tube 5-8 mm long, extending to 7-10 mm in older flowers, and typically not or barely exserted from the bracts. Geissorhiza nubigena, with which G. hesperanthoides has been confused, has pink flowers with narrower tepals that extend at right angles to the longer tube, which is well exserted at anthesis and 10-18 mm long, becoming even longer in older flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geissorhiza heterostyla was based on plants from Whitehill in the western Karoo, individuals of which were variable for style length, hence the specific epithet. Plants had variously long styles dividing beyond the apex of the anthers, medium styles dividing at anther level, or short styles, dividing below the anthers. Other distinguishing features are the puberulous stem, submembranous sheathing, bract-like scale on the upper part of the stem, and leaves with raised, narrowly winged, ciliate margins (leaves I-shaped in section). Flowers are half to fully nodding and zygomorphic with the stamens unilateral and lying above the lower tepals or more-or-less upright with ascending, symmetrically arranged stamens. The stamens are consistently unequal, one filament 1-2 mm shorter than the other two, and the style arches downward to lie beneath the stamens. Collections from near the type area and elsewhere either consist of plants with unequal styles or all plants in the population have long styles but otherwise match the species. Populations mixed or uniform for style length have now been collected across the western half of its range and while it appears likely that populations with uniformly long styles are the same species, the variation in style length is remarkable. All populations from the eastern end of the range examined have long styles.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Cliffortia hermaphroditica differs from all Cliffortia species hitherto known by the feature that most flowers are bisexual and apparently perfectly fertile in both sexes. Several cases are known within the genus, it is true, where flowers occasionally contain both male and female organs, but then the females are weakly developed and obviously sterile. The occurrence of bisexual flowers within Cliffortia is of a certain interest, for the genus Cliffortia has in all probability evolved from forms with bisexual flowers. The bisexual condition may for that reason be regarded as a primary feature.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Geissorhiza hispidula has small corms with concentric tunics, just three leaves, these with a sticky surface and thickened margins and main veins, and relatively small, creamy white flowers with a narrow perianth tube 3-4 mm long and narrowly elliptic tepals 10-15 x 5-8 mm. It has often been confused with G. humilis, with which it sometimes grows and flowers and then their differences are quite evident. Geissorhiza humilis has bright yellow flowers with broader tepals, 16-22 x 12-14 mm and a perianth tube 5-6 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. linearifolia comes near to C. serpyllifolia. As already mentioned under C. serpyllifolia C. linearifolia has very narrow leaflets, with sharply revolute margins and a thick midrib running between the marginal edges. The bracteoles and sepals of the [male]-flowers are larger than in C. serpyllifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The leaflets are linearly lanceolate, somewhat broader towards the apex, obtuse or mucronulate. C. obovata, C. glauca and C. marginata are morphologically closely related. C. glauca has 15 stamens, whereas C. obovata and C. marginata have 12.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: A small, inconspicuous plant, Geissorhiza intermedia stands out in its densely ciliate stem, an unusual character in subg. Weihea and is otherwise undistinguished in its white flowers with a short perianth tube 2-3 mm long and narrow leaves with strongly raised margins and main vein. It can easily be mistaken for the similar and probably closely related G. hispidula, which has a largely lowland distribution, and has narrower, sticky leaves and bracts and invariably a smooth stem. Geissorhiza intermedia may also be confused with G. similis, which is alike in general appearance but has imbricate corm tunics, a longer perianth tube, and also has smooth stems.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Comes morphologically rather close to C. serpyllifolia Cham. et Schldl. and C. browniana Burtt Davy. Very characteristic are the leaves with their very broad and thick ribs which fill up almost all the blade. The top of the leaves is broad and furnished with 3-5 obtuse teeth. Remarkable are also the very small flowers, especially the female ones, which are hardly visible without a magnifying lens.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, H. 1940. Cliffortia micrantha H. Weimarck spec. nova. Bot. Not. 1940: 97-99. [All rights reserved]

description: The fairly common Geissorhiza juncea is recognised by its slender habit, with two basal leaves, the blades terete but with thickened margins and main vein and four narrow grooves between them, and small, white to pale yellow, star-like flowers with a perianth tube 2-3 mm long and tepals typically 8-12 mm long. It is is allied to a group of species including G. humilis and G. hispidula which have small corms with hard concentric tunics and narrow leaves with raised and thickened margins and midribs but can be readily distinguished from these species by its terete leaves and particularly short perianth tube. It is perhaps most closely allied to G. furva, with similar narrow, terete leaves but larger, deep yellow flowers with tepals 15-22(-28) mm long. This is also typically a shorter plant than G. juncea, mostly 60-120(rarely to 180) mm high, and the flowers are distinctive when dry as they turn an unusual blackish colour with age.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. mirabilis varies with respect to differentiation of the leaves in a similar way to C. varians. Many leaves have 2 entire leaflets, others have 2, one of which is more or less deeply cleft, others have 3 leaflets. C. mirabilis on account of this peculiar variability falls between sect. Bifoliolae and the trifoliolate sect. Costatae. Within sect. Bifoliolae the species exhibits great similarity to C. crenata L. fil., but differs from this species -besides the leaf formation discussed above -by the number of the stamens and the appearance of the receptacle.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its ciliate stem and only two basal leaves, the margins with narrowly, ascending wings minutely ciliate on the edges, Geissorhiza leipoldtii has large, upright to slightly nodding, pure white flowers with tepals 19-26 x 7-11 mm. The stamens are relatively long and usually equal (or one filament slightly shorter) with anthers up to 8 mm long, bright yellow and bearing yellow pollen. In the past G. leipoldtii included plants from the Olifants River Valley and nearby with nodding flowers and markedly unequal filaments, but these are now recognised as G. nutans, as well as mauve-pink flowered G. ixioides, now also recognised as a separate species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the relatively large, dark, blue-violet flowers with a pale, yellow-green throat, tepals 15-20 mm long, and unilateral, decumbent stamens with unequal filaments. The stem is minutely puberulous but the leaves are smooth except for the raised margins, which are usually minutely ciliate. It appears to be most closely related to G. aspera with which it is sometimes sympatric, but it is always distinguished by the larger flower size, unilateral, declinate stamens and style and more intense blue-violet pigmentation than G. aspera, the nodding flowers of which have tepals 11-15 mm long, and shorter, horizontally oriented stamens. Both species have one filament slightly shorter than the other two. Geissorhiza lewisiae occurs in two disjunct sets of populations, a northern one around Citrusdal in the Olifants River Valley, and a western set along the Western Cape Coast, from Steenberg Cove on St Helena Bay to Saldanha Bay. Although typically associated with granite outcrops, it also occurs on limestone pavement and calcrete in the vicinity of Saldanha Bay. It has been included in G. monanthos, but this species has flowers with a pale, translucent centre surrounded by a dark blue to purple or red zone, and curved, bicoloured filaments that are pale in the lower half but dark violet distally. The median filament in G. lewisiae is always conspicuously shorter than the others by some 1.5 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. hirta, C. eriocephalina, C. stricta and C. montana constitute a group of closely allied species, pointing towards C. nitidula. Among these species C. hirta stands somewhat more isolated, characterized as it is by about 20 stamens and by other diverging morphological attributes. All the other species have 6 stamens and show great correspondence to one another even with regard to vegetative characters. C. montana differs from the other species within this group in having very short, only 2.5-5 mm long, leaflets. In pilosity it agrees with C. stricta.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinctive in sect. Engysiphon in its moderate-sized, white or pale pink flowers with a relatively short perianth tube 14-20(-25) mm long and narrow, often almost linear tepals 17-27 x 5-9 mm. It is sometimes confused with G. confusa, which is similar in overall appearance but is usually taller in stature and has larger, creamy white to beige flowers with the tube 25-40 mm long and mostly broader tepals 28-40 x 7-10 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A member of the Geissorhiza imbricata group, G. louisabolusiae has narrow, often almost terete, several ribbed and grooved leaves, the uppermost largest and with an inflated, strongly ribbed sheath. The flowers are uniformly bright yellow, have a short perianth tube 4-6 mm long, and usually slightly unequal stamens, two filaments ± 2 mm longer than the third.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is however possible with the material at present at our disposal to form an opinion of the shape of the receptacle in mature state and to ascertain that it is quite different from pungens, so closely allied to it in other features. With regard to the difference between the two species the reader is referred to the comparison given under C. pungens.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: With a bell-shaped corm with a somewhat oblique, flat base with toothed margins, Geissorhiza malmesburiensis closely resembles G. ornithogaloides subsp. flava in habit, corm and leaves. The pale yellow flowers are, however, somewhat larger, with a perianth tube ± 4 mm long, tepals mostly 15-25 x 4-7 mm and remaining cupped when fully open, and longer filaments, 7-10 mm long. Geissorhiza ornithogaloides has smaller flowers with the perianth tube 2-3(4) mm long, tepals (6-)8-15 mm long, rarely up to 18 mm, and shorter filaments, 2-4 mm long. Also, robust plants of G. ornithogaloides are often branched and have spikes of more than one flower each.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Usually low growing and seldom reaching more than 160 mm in height, Geissorhiza monanthos is recognised by the distinctively coloured flowers, violet with a glossy translucent white centre broadly edged with a band of darker violet or red, and filaments that are white below but violet in the upper 2?3. The flowers are nodding and zygomorphic with decumbent stamens strongly curving upward distally so that the anthers are suberect. As its name suggests, the inclined to horizontal spikes bear few flowers, often only one but occasionally up to four. Geissorhiza monanthos may be most closely related to G. lewisiae, a taller species with spikes of 2 to 5 flowers that are violet with the bases of the tepals and throat yellow-green to white. The stamens of G. lewisiae are unilateral but nearly straight, with the filaments uniformly coloured, thus very different from those of G. monanthos. In addition, the leaves of G. monanthos have slightly raised margins and midvein and are always smooth, whereas those of G. lewisiae have raised and narrowly winged margins and central veins. The pollen of G. lewisiae is pale mauve or ± white but G. monanthos usually has red-brown or occasionally white pollen.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. discolor comes near C. hirsuta Eckl. et Zeyh. The species differs from C. hirsuta by the more roundish leaves, which are hairy beneath only in the nerves but are glabrous and white-greyish white in the inter-spaces; the teeth are acute but not cuspidate.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: One of three species of Geissorhiza endemic to Namaqualand, G. namaquensis is recognised by the well-developed perianth tube, mostly 8-11 mm long, minutely velvety stem, and leaves with raised, narrowly winged margins and main vein, both ciliate on the edges. The flowers are bright blue to blue-mauve with tepals 14-18 x 4 mm. Closely related G. namaquamontana, from the Grootberg and Kamiesberg, has smaller flowers with a perianth tube 6-7 mm long, tepals (6-)8-10 x 1.5-2.0 mm, and anthers 2-3 mm long. Long-tubed G. kamiesmontana, which is restricted to the Kamiesberg, has a longer perianth tube, 18-25 mm long, and dark violet flowers with longer, narrower tepals 16-20 x 3 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Even sterile C. paucistaminea may be recognized by its very closely arranged brachyblasts and leaves. Furthermore, the leaflets are markedly keeled on account of the prominent, thick midrib. In the fertile state C. paucistaminea is characterized by the brownish green, not very strongly ribbed receptacles and by the [male]-flowers, which have only 3 or 4 stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. phillipsii stands close to C. cuneata and hydridizes with that species. It differs, however, in several morphological features from C. cuneata. In C. phillipsii the blades are lanceolate, acuminate and have 1-2 large, acuminate teeth on either side, on the upper side they are slightly glossy and the stipules are up to 5 mm in length. In C. cuneata the blades are cuneate, truncate and furnished, as a rule, with 4 or 5 teeth at the top; they are dull on both sides and the stipules are only 1 mm long. Further, C. phillipsii has a densely and canescently pilous receptacle about 10 mm long, whereas the receptacle in C. cuneata is only 7 mm in length and quite glabrous.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinctive in its short-tubed blue-purple flowers, the perianth tube 2-3 mm long and much longer tepals 14-16 mm long, Geissorhiza nigromontana has spikes of only 2 or 3 flowers. The style branches are unusually long, 4-5 mm long, and the corm tunics are softly papery. Notably the stem is prostrate at the base and becomes abruptly erect above. It is most probably closely related to G. foliosa, a species of the Langeberg foothills, which blooms mainly in October and November and it has the broad flat leaves typical of that species, but G. foliosa has a perianth tube 5-6 mm long, a spike of up to 7 flowers and style branches up to 3 mm long. Geissorhiza nigromontana is also distinctive in bearing cormlets in the lower stem axils, a feature rare in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species differs from all known species of Cliffortia by the very long pedicels of its [male]-and [female]-flowers. C. pedunculata, as Schlechter himself emphasizes, varies greatly with regard to the shape of the leaflets. Broadly lanceolate and wholly coarsely dentate leaflets occur side by side with linear, slightly dentate or simply entire ones even on the same specimen. The narrower leaflets are frequently more or less sickle-shaped, a fact confirming the opinion that C. pedunculata is related to C. falcata and C. drepanoides.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: A dwarf and typically slender species, Geissorhiza ornithogaloides is recognised by the mostly solitary, bright yellow flowers, unusual in the genus. It is morphologically variable and even within populations plants may be more robust and have much larger flowers than others, the extremes seemingly almost different species. The vegetative morphology is, however, quite uniform, with plants always having spikes with either one or two flowers, two narrow, plane, basal leaves and two cauline and partly sheathing leaves. The corms are of two types: the interior and eastern populations, subsp. ornithogaloides, have small ellipsoid corms with concentric tunics of the type characteristic of subg. Weihea, whereas the southwestern populations, subsp. flava, have bell-shaped corms with a flat base and minutely serrated margins. The two sets of populations otherwise appear identical. Geissorhiza ornithogaloides is most closely related to G. malmesburiensis, which is broadly similar to subsp. flava in the yellow flowers and bell-shaped corms, but differs in having somewhat larger, cupped flowers, the perianth tube ± 4 mm long, tepals mostly 18-20(-25) mm long and filaments 7-10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. pilifera is rather similar to C. odorata. It differs from this species in several morphological features. It is in all parts more gracile and more slender. The branchlets are thin, the flowering ones are almost filiform, the flowers are solitary in the axils, the laminas are thin and furnished with broad teeth, which are at the apex abruptly contracted and extended in a long hair-point. (See also C. reticulata.)
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: On account of the margins being strongly revolute the leaflets seem to lie terete and the species has a pronounced, external resemblance to C. teretifolia. C. polita differs, however, from all other species within the section Costatae by cylindric-6-angular receptacles, which are only slightly larger than the leaflets and are for that reason easily overlooked. The glabrous or finely pilous twigs and the number of the stamens (6) may be pointed out as other characteristic features.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Evidently most closely related to Geissorhiza roseoalba, G. outeniquensis has, like that species, a zygomorphic flower with declinate stamens and style. The flowers have a perianth tube 10-13 mm long vs. 8-10 mm in G. roseoalba and it also differs in its riverine habitat, soft-textured corm tunics and four to several, soft-textured, often trailing leaves. Geissorhiza outeniquensis has an unusual caespitose habit: the main plants produce short runners which sprout to form new stems and leaf clusters close to the parent plant. It seems to have lost the deciduous habit of the genus and does not die back and become dormant during the later summer and autumn.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Characteristic of C. pterocarpa are the relatively broad leaflets, 15 stamens and the brown receptacle, furnished with high, usually sharp-edged ridges. (See also under C. atrata.)
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The diminutive and small-flowered Geissorhiza ovalifolia is distinguished by the stem prostate at the base and erect distally, and four or five plane leaves, at least the lower three or four prostrate and ovate to oblong. Plants often produce a cormlet in the axils of the basal and even cauline leaves. The flowers are white with a pale yellow throat and have a perianth tube 2-3 mm long and tepals 6-8 mm long. It is often confused with the more widespread and common G. bolusii, which occurs in similar habitats in the Western Cape mountains. Geissorhiza ovalifolia is evidently sexually fertile, and capsules develop rapidly after blooming whereas the triploid G. bolusii is sexually sterile and reproduces by the production of cormlets in all basal and cauline leaf axils as well as in the axils of the floral bracts after flowering. The two can sometimes also be distinguished by the number of cauline sheathing leaves, one in G. ovalifolia but usually several in G. bolusii, however the difference does not always hold.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognised by the pair of ovate or oblong basal leaves, prostrate or nearly so, and the stem prostrate near base, Geissorhiza ovata has long-tubed white flowers marked with red in the centre and red to brown on the reverse of the tepals. The perianth tube, mostly 10-18 (rarely up to 30) mm, is well exserted from the bracts and the spreading tepals are typically 10-13 mm long. It is allied to G. parva, a smaller species with a similar habit with short, prostrate or semi-prostrate leaves but smaller yellow to creamy-white flowers, with a perianth tube 3-4 mm long. Geissorhiza ovata is quite variable as to height and flower size, and although the perianth tube is typically 10-18 mm long it is up to 30 mm long in plants from the Klein River Mtns. Plants from near the eastern end of its range near Swellendam have the smallest flowers with tepals ± 7 mm long, although the perianth tube is of normal length.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A rare and local endemic of southwestern Western Cape, South Africa, known from near Ceres, Highlands near Caledon and the Riviersonderend Mtns in the east; in sandy ground. Diagnosis: evidently closely allied to Geissorhiza hispidula and very similar in leaf morphology, G. pappei is a smaller plant with smaller, white flowers with a perianth tube 2.5-3.5 mm long and tepals 6-9 mm long. The larger, usually creamy white flowers of G. hispidula have a perianth tube 3-4 mm long and tepals 10-15 long. Geissorhiza pappei is poorly known and requires additional study.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. pulchella has very peculiar leaves. They are circular or kidney-shaped, the upperside being glossy and concave. The ribs are pseudodichotomous and the final branchings reach right up to the margins of the leaf. When the leaves have fallen off, the short stalks remain and thus give the branches an almost step-like appearance. The flowers are concealed among the leaves and not always easy to find, especially on herbarium specimens, in which the leaflets are pressed with the surfaces towards one another, in this way concealing the flowers in the hollow made by the concavity of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: One of several species of Geissorhiza that occupy specialised niches in the mountains of southwestern Western Cape, G. pseudinaequalis is distinguished by its papery corm tunics, smooth stem and markedly unequal stamens, with the longer two filaments 8-12 mm and shorter one 4-6 mm long. It also has relatively large, blue to violet (rarely blue-purple) flowers with tepals 12-17 mm, rarely up to 20 mm long. Geissorhiza pseudinaequalis is sometimes confused with G. inaequalis (sect. Planifoliae) because of its unequal stamens and flat leaves but that species has woody, imbricate tunics and puberulous stems. Geissorhiza pseudinaequalis is probably related to other montane species with similar soft-textured imbricate corm tunics, including G. burchellii and G. tabularis, both of which also have unequal stamens but differ in their larger size and in their leaves with strongly raised margins and midrib.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. repens has simple, needle-shaped and, in the margin, scabrid laminae, which vary in length and breadth. C. repens has in the herbaria been confused to a great extent with other species of Cliffortia, especially C. filifolia, C. juniperina and C. linearifolia. All these species, however, have 3-foliolate leaves, whereas C. repens has simple leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. ramosissima is characterized by a very close ramification. The leaflets are almost flat; the midrib is very slightly prominent on the underside. The leaf-margins are markedly scabrid-finely serrulate. The flowers are trimerous: 3 sepals and 6 stamens, and very often the receptacles are 6-ribbed.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. reticulata is closely related to C. odorata and to C. pilifera. With regard to pilosity, texture of leaves and the nearly filiform branches it is very similar to C. pilifera. It can be said to a certain extent to be intermediate between the said two species and may perhaps prove to be a hybrid between them. C. reticulata differs from C. odorata, inter alia, in the thin, sparsely pilous leaves, its glabrous or only sparsely pilous stems and branches and also in having the last branches very gracile. It differs from C. pilifera, on the other hand, in that its branchlets are nearly always straight and that the teeth of its leaves are abruptly mucronate, not as in C. pilifera elongated to a long hair-point.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Evidently taxonomically isolated, Geissorhiza pusilla stands out in subg. Weihea in its plane, softly hairy leaves with ciliate margins and small blue to blue-mauve flowers. It closely resembles the common G. aspera, which has ± black, imbricate corm tunics characteristic of subg. Geissorhiza, a puberulous stem and usually unequal stamens with one shorter filament. Geissorhiza pusilla has light brown concentric corm tunics, a hairless stem, and the stamens are equal in length.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: One of the most striking species in the genus, Geissorhiza radians is immediately recognised by the large flowers with deeply cupped tepals, deep blue with red in the lower third edged with a narrow white band and each with a dark pit-like depression in the middle. The leaves are linear (sometimes almost terete) with thickened margins and main vein. The flowers are zygomorphic with the stamens unilateral and declinate, the style lying beneath them above the lowermost tepals. Geissorhiza eurystigma and G. mathewsii have similarly coloured flowers but lack the pitted tepal markings, and have unusual, broad style branches, and broader, ribbed leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the small, dark blue to violet or purple flowers with tepals 5-9 mm long and unequal stamens with anthers up to 3.5 mm long, and by its normally 2- to 4-branched, hairless stem. The unequal stamens are typical of most other species of sect. Monticolae. Depauperate plants may be less than 200 mm tall and without branches making identification uncertain.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The following features are characteristic of C. ruscifolia. The young parts of stems and branches are shortly and densely pilous with greyish white hairs. The leaves are clustered closely together in, usually, very much abbreviated brachyblasts, not more than 10 mm long. The vagina of the leaves is very short and carries insignificant, sometimes hardly visible, stipules. The blade is on the upper side sparsely pilous, or quite glabrous, with usually inconspicuous nervature; on the other hand, the underside of the blade, at least when young, is more or less densely covered with canescent hairs; sometimes these hairs are very long, quite white and almost silky. The nerves are not very prominent, often inconspicuous with the midrib stronger and with weaker lateral nerves.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. robusta is externally rather similar to C. curvifolia, but the leaves have no prominent midrib underneath, the stamens are fewer in number (in curvif. ca. 25) and the receptacle -although young -does not seem to become fusiform. Furthermore, C. robusta has glabrous twigs.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Fairly typical of sect. Engysiphon, Geissorhiza schinzii is distinguished by the relatively large, nodding flowers with a perianth tube of intermediate length, 24-32 mm long, and tepals 35-40 mm long, exceeding the length of the tube. The flowers are zygomorphic with unilateral, decumbent stamens and style. Like other species of the section, the leaves have thickened margins and main vein and are sticky, usually with sand adhering to the surface.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. serpyllifolia varies rather much with regard to the habitus. In the western part of its area, as e.g. seen from the type specimen from Cango, it has acute leaflets with plane margins. In the eastern districts of Cape Province (Kaffraria) and in Natal almost all leaflets of the examined material have more or less revolute margins. Some specimens are not unlike C. linearifolia, although this species differs from the former in having still more revolute margins, tightly pressed towards the thick prominent midrib. This is never the case in C. serpyllifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The distinctive Geissorhiza scillaris has imbricate corm tunics, small white to blue flowers, and just two foliage leaves, the lower with a long free blade and the upper sheathing the stem for most of its length. Plants usually have an inconspicuous green or transparent, sheathing bract a short distance below the spike. The blade of the lowermost leaf is terete with heavily thickened margins and main vein, thus cross-shaped in section and with 4 longitudinal grooves. Both the sheath and blade are sticky and usually have sand adhering to the surface. The star-like flowers are small, with a tube up to 1.5 mm long, spreading tepals 7-9 mm long, and usually white or pale grey-blue but some populations in the Cederberg and Cold Bokkeveld have clear blue flowers with a white centre. Geissorhiza scillaris has often been confused with G. juncea, which is broadly similar in appearance but with three foliage leaves, the lower two basal, slender and terete, and corm tunics of the concentric type.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: As to habit the resemblance between the two species Cliffortia subsetacea and C. setifolia is very striking. However. C. subsetacea always has acuminate leaflets, the new species on the other hand obtuse. Furthermore C. subsetacea has 8 stamens, 2 mm long or longer receptacles, furnished with 4 higher and 4 lower ridges (sometimes even somewhat winged), whereas C. setifolia has 4 stamens and only 1 mm long, quite smooth receptacles. C. setifolia belongs to sect. Costatae and comes morphologically close to C. paucistaminea and C. subsetacea.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, H. 1937. A new Cliffortia species. Bot. Not. 1937: 337-340. [All rights reserved]

description: Already in a sterile state C. stricta is distinguished from more related species by its mucronate, adpressedly hairy-almost glabrous leaflets.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the imbricate corm tunics that are brown rather than almost black as more typical of subg. Geissorhiza, white to creamy white flowers, and long basal leaf with thickened hispid margins and main vein, the remaining two leaves much shorter and largely sheathing. The leaf sheath and basal blade are sticky, and in this, as well as the white flowers, G. similis resembles the apparently unrelated G. hispidula, which has different corms with concentric tunics. Without corms it is difficult to separate the two species, although G. hispidula has well-developed blades on the cauline leaves and sticky floral bracts. Taller and more slender specimens of G. similis may also be confused with G. umbrosa (subg. Weihea) in the absence of corms, but that species normally has somewhat larger flowers and the leaves are smooth, without the ciliate to hispid and sticky margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its four (rarely three) twisted leaves, solitary-flowered spikes, and style dividing opposite the base of the anthers. These features are also characteristic of G. corrugata, which has bright yellow flowers with a perisanth tube ± 3 mm long whereas G. spiralis has purple to deep pink flowers marked white and red-purple at the base of the tepals and a perianth tube 4-5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by the glossy, dark blue flowers with dark red-brown pollen, Geissorhiza splendidissima has imbricate corm tunics typical of subg. Geissorhiza. Its affinities seem to be with sect. Ciliatae as it has similar leaf morphology, with strongly raised and winged margins ciliate on the edges. The puberulous stem is also consistent with the section, but the zygomorphic flowers with unilateral, declinate stamens and dark red-brown pollen are unusual, as is the somewhat ribbed sheath of the uppermost leaf. This character is shared with the apparently allied G. arenicola, a character that sets these two species somewhat apart in the section.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A remarkably long and slender perianth tube 40-50 mm long and narrow terete leaves make Geissorhiza stenosiphon unmistakable. Another unusual feature of the species is the style that divides at or below the base of the anthers. The flowers are actinomorphic with relatively small white tepals, 12-14 mm long, spreading horizontally. The vegetative morphology, especially the terete, 4-grooved leaves and apically dry floral bracts, is consistent with sect. Angustifoliae in which the short style and elongate perianth tube are unique.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. subdura belongs to sect. Inflexae and is distinguished from the earlier known 5 species within this section by its glabrous, rather stiff folioles, which on the upper side are green and glossy, and on the underside are dull and greyish green. Externally C. subdura resembles C. rigida (sect. Costatae) but is recognized by its receptacles. The branchlets in C. subdura are villous, in C. rigida glabrous, and this fact may be a help to botanists in their determination work.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1959. Four new Cliffortia species. Bot. Not. 112(1): 73-79. [All rights reserved]

description: Geissorhiza tabularis was for many years included in the smaller-flowered G. ramosa and the two are no doubt closely related. Geissorhiza tabularis is distinguished by the larger flowers with tepals 15-18 mm long vs. 5-9 mm in G. ramosa and longer stamens. The two species share a smooth stem, often more highly branched in G. ramosa, a short perianth tube, and unequal filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. grandifolia has the largest leaves of all the species of Cliffortia. The leaves reach 10 cm in length and 3 cm in breadth. The teeth of the margins are very large and strong and are sparsely but evenly distributed along the margin. Only [male]-flowers are known in the main species, and they are larger than those of any other form of Cliffortia.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. triloba has its short petiole in common with C. falcata and C. drepanoides. At leaf-fall these petioles remain and, standing straight out from the branches, the plant acquires a somewhat thorny appearance.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: One of the most striking species of the genus, Geissorhiza tulbaghensis has large white flowers marked in the centre with maroon-red to brown. The flowers are half nodding and zygomorphic with the stamens and style unilateral and decumbent. Although similar vegetatively to G. radians and sharing with it very similar large zygomorphic flowers with declinate stamens and style, they are evidently unrelated: G. tulbaghensis has plane leaves and a puberulous stem typical of sect. Planifoliae whereas G. radians has the linear, 2-grooved leaves and ribbed leaf sheaths characteristic of sect. Geissorhiza. Geissorhiza tulbaghensis is distinctive not only in its flower coloration, but in the flat leaves with a slender petiole-like base.
