bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. tuberculata var. muricata differs from the main species by having somewhat longer receptacles, which are besides acute at the top and have denser and smaller muricate warts. As to habitus the variety is very similar to the main species and is hardly distinguished from the latter in a sterile state.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Characteristic for this species are the plain, pine-like, at the tip claw-like, curved leaves and the elongated, ovately cylindrical receptacle.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily recognised by its single basal foliage leaf, minutely ciliate stem 50-100 mm high, and tiny flowers with tepals up to 5 mm long. The remaining one or two leaves are short and largely to entirely sheathing. The leaf sheath and cataphyll are sticky and have sand adhering to them. The papery, rather than woody corm tunics are concentric and fairly typical of subg. Weihea. The relationships of G. unifolia are uncertain but the ciliate stem recalls G. intermedia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. uncinata var. recta differs from the main species on account of its broader, uncurved leaves, straight at the tip. In other morphological properties it agrees entirely with C. uncinata.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: A solitary-stemmed or tufted species with stems up to 1.2 m high, leaves mostly 3-5 mm wide, and 8- to 10-flowered terminal spikes with 5 to 7 lateral spikes, and mauve to magenta flowers with perianth 15-21 mm long. Dierama gracile is a clump-forming species with generally shorter stems, 300-750 mm tall, with fewer lateral spikes, 1 to 5 per stem, and delicately veined bracts with just 3 or 4 lateral veins each side of the main vein.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species is characterized by the cordate -broadly cordate blades, which are evenly toothed. The teeth are squarrous or more or less reflexed.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. viridis comes near C. discolor Weimarck, C. hirsuta Eckl. et Zeyh. and C. odorata L. fil. but differs from these species by the leaves being glabrous when developed, by the glabrous, attenuate stipules and by the glabrous stems and branches. The leaves are thicker and more rigid, at least when dry, the sepals and bracteoles larger than in C. odorata, from C. hirsuta, furthermore, the species differs by the much more slender stems and branches and by the ovate sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: A solitary-stemmed or tufted species with pendulous spikes of relatively small, often bright pink flowers, the perianth 16-23 mm long with a tube 5.0-7.5 mm long and characteristic bracts with ± 6 secondary veins each side of the main vein and well-developed intermediate veins, the veins all parallel and so close together that the base of the bract appears almost solid. The primary spike has 8 to 13 flowers. Dierama robustum has the bract veins further apart and mostly paler, slightly larger flowers, the tepals 17-26 x 7-12 mm and the tube 7-12 mm long. The two species probably hybridise in northern Lesotho and neighbouring Free State.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A solitary-stemmed or tufted species with pendulous spikes of relatively small, pale to deep pink flowers, the perianth 18-22 mm long with a tube 5-7(-8) mm long. Dierama dracomontanum, with which it is sympatric, has a clumped habit and slightly larger flowers with perianth 19-29 mm long, and flowers slightly later, mainly November to February.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A short, strongly clump-forming species with stems 400-750 mm high barely exceeding the leavers and spikes of relatively small, pale pink to purplish flowers with perianth 15.5-20.0 mm long. Flower colour varies within a single colony and there is also significant variation in the flecking of the bracts among populations, some with lightly flecked to almost pure white bracts. Die-rama dracomontanum from mostly higher altitudes has larger flowers 19-29 mm long and generally fewer lateral spikes with fewer flowers in each, mostly 2 to 5.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A clump-forming species with stems 750-1650 mm tall, leaves mostly 6-10 mm wide, and large flowers with the perianth 26-37 mm long. The bracts are 20-25 mm long and usually heavily flecked reddish brown, with the veins often very closely set in the lower part. Other species from the Mpumalanga Escarpment are mostly solitary-stemmed or form small tufts, with shorter bracts and smaller flowers. Dierama tyrium, usually with darker purple flowers, typically has more flowers in the terminal spike and more numerous coflorescences, 8 to 11, narrower bracts 5-8 mm wide, and a shorter perianth tube 6-8 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A tufted species with erect inflorescences 1.0-1.5 m tall of pale to deep pink flowers with perianth 17-25 mm long, and translucent, lightly flecked bracts. Dierama tysonii from southern KwaZulu-Natal with similar inflorescences is more strongly clump-forming, with shorter stems up to 8.5 m tall, and fewer flowers on the lateral spikes, mostly 4 to 7.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A clump-forming species with relatively short stems 300-750 mm tall and short, delicately veined bracts with just 3 or 4 lateral veins each side of the main vein.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Restricted to the mountains near Graaff-Reinet and Somerset East and occurring as solitary stems or small clumps with stems ± 1500 mm tall, leaves 4-8 mm wide, and pendulous inflorescences of large, dark pink flowers with funnel-shaped perianth (30-)50-70 mm long, the tips of the tepals characteristically folded together, recurved and twisted.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Growing as solitary plants or in small tufts with stems mostly less than 1.5 m tall, leaves 2-6 mm wide, and pendulous spikes with partly or mostly solid bracts. The flowers are bell-shaped and pale to magenta-pink. Dierama erectum from Ngome, also with partly solid bracts, is a clump-forming species with taller stems 1.50-1.65 m tall, leaves 6-12 mm wide, and erect inflorescences with more numerous coflorescences, and subrotate flowers with conspicuous red and yellow markings at the base of the tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Characterised by the conspicuously clumped habit, typically broad leaves, 5-15 mm wide, and pink or rarely dark wine-red flowers with white or faintly speckled bracts. Dark-flowered plants are sympatric with Dierama reynoldsii but that species grows as solitary stems or in small tufts of up to three stems, with narrower leaves 3-6 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A tufted species with stems up to 1000 mm tall and leaves 1.5-4.5 mm wide, and relatively lax spikes of mauve to magenta-pink flowers with perianth 18-25 mm long. The bracts are very delicate and usually speckled but sometimes pure white. Dierama medium, which is sympatric with D. mossii in southeastern Mpumalanga and Eswatini, has more crowded spikes of mostly smaller flowers, the perianth mostly 13-18 mm long with anthers 4.5-6.0 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small, early-flowering species with foliage leaves produced on a separate shoot alongside the flowering stem and often not fully formed at flowering, rather closed flowers with tepals only twice as long as the perianth tube, and short bracts, 8-15 mm long. Dierama trichorhizum has a similar habit, with the current season’s foliage leaves on a shoot alongside the flowering stem, but with a characteristic long internode between the corm and the lowest cauline leaf on the flowering stem, cormlets in the lowest leaf axil, and widely funnel-shaped flowers with spreading tepals three times as long as the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A small, clump-forming species 300-600 mm tall, with narrow leaves 1-4 mm wide and delicate, few-flowered spikes of funnel-shaped, pink to reddish flowers with characteristic small, rusty red bracts 12-18 mm long, with 6 to 8 veins each side of the main vein. The perianth is 20-28 mm long, with narrow tepals 4.5-8.5 mm wide. Dierama nebrownii, also with brown bracts with 6 to 8 veins each side of the main vein, is a taller species with mostly solitary stems 800-1000 mm tall.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Restricted to the southern coastal and near inland areas, and occurring as solitary stems or small clumps with stems ± 1-2 m tall, leaves 6.0-8.5 mm wide, and pendulous spikes held well above the leaves, bearing moderate-sized to large, purplish pink flowers with funnel-shaped perianth 28-48(-50) mm long. Dierama igneum from Grahamstown eastward has narrower bracts mostly 5-8 mm wide and a mostly shorter perianth, 16-34 mm long with the tube 5-8 mm long, and spikes nodding down to reach the tips of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Occurring as solitary stems or small clumps with stems 900-1800 mm tall, leaves 4-11 mm wide, and pendulous inflorescences of moderately large, magenta to purple flowers with a rather closed perianth 35-54 mm long. The species is easily recognised in the living state by the characteristic flowers, with suberect tepals from a conical base. Dierama pendulum, with widely spreading tepals from a rounded base, has a more southern distribution. Forms with dark red flowers occur in areas of sympatry with dark-flowered Dierama atrum (Dohne, Stutterheim, Pirie and King William’s Town) and D. reynoldsii (Baziya-Engcobo), suggesting possible hybridisation. Hybridisation with D. igneum in the Hogsback area is also a possibility.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Occurring as solitary stems, with very narrow, almost needle-like leaves, 1.0-2.5 mm wide, solid brown or heavily flecked bracts, and small, pale creamy yellow, rather closed flowers, the perianth 13-19 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Petioles winged and expanded to resemble leafy stipules, these decurrent on the stem.
bibliographicCitation: Gonçalves, AE. 2005. 119. Solanaceae, Fl. Zambes. 8(4): 1-124. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [CC BY]

description: Occurring as solitary stems or small tufts with brown-flecked bracts, and small to moderately sized, rather closed, creamy white to pale yellow (rarely pale pink) flowers, the perianth 16-19(-25) mm long. Dierama pallidum from south-central KwaZulu-Natal between Pietermaritzburg and Durban has similar flowers but pure white bracts. Dierama argyreum, also with white bracts, has larger, bell-shaped white or ivory-coloured flowers, the perianth 18-35 mm long with flaring tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Calyx campanulate, 10-ribbed. Corolla salviform, with face expanded relative to the throat and generally with ± rounded lobes; stamens arising from the corolla mouth, adnate around the style.
bibliographicCitation: Gonçalves, AE. 2005. 119. Solanaceae, Fl. Zambes. 8(4): 1-124. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [CC BY]

description: Occurring as solitary stems or small tufts, 1200-2100 mm tall, with moderately sized, dark magenta to purple flowers, perianth 22-31 mm long, and bracts partly or ± entirely flecked with reddish brown. Dierama mobile and D. pictum, also from Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal have similar coloured but smaller flowers, with perianth 15-23 mm long. Dierama atrum from Eastern Cape is a shorter plant, 750-1250 mm tall, with fewer, darker maroon flowers in the terminal spike, mostly 4 to 8, and slightly broader bracts, 8-11 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Discolorous leaves, mostly recurved prickles, large yellow fruits. Poisonous, used medicinally.
bibliographicCitation: Gonçalves, AE. 2005. 119. Solanaceae, Fl. Zambes. 8(4): 1-124. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to the widespread Dietes iridioides and easily confused with it, D. flavida has pale yellow flowers of much the same size and proportions and the outer tepals with brown-spotted nectar guides. The style branches are usually also creamy yellow or rarely very lightly flushed with purple, and the leaves have a greyish waxy covering. The capsules of D. flavida are ± ovoid, nodding to pendent, with a completely smooth surface and dehisce irregularly instead of along the carpel sutures. The ± cylindric capsules of D. iridioides are usually distinctly beaked, with an irregular, fissured surface, and eventually dehisce from the apex downwards for some distance, sometimes seemingly indehiscent.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The largest-flowered species of the genus, Dietes grandiflora is easily recognised not only by the larger flowers, which last three days in contrast to those of other members of the genus, but also by the floral markings. The white outer tepals are conspicuously marked with a velvety, yellow nectar guide at the base of the limbs, and a yellow velvety band in the centre of the claws while the inner tepals have dark brown lines either side of the pale midline. The flowers in well-grown plants may be up to 100 mm in diam.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ripe fruit vermillion, 20-40 mm in diam., flesh thick, white, spongy; seeds winged.
bibliographicCitation: Welman, WG. 2003. The genus Solanum (Solanaceae) in southern Africa: subgenus Leptostemonum, the introduced sections Acanthophora and Torva. Bothalia 33(1): 1-18. [CC BY]

description: Early flowering and relatively rare, Ferraria densepunctulata is distinctive in the narrow basal leaves, oval in cross section, and rather different from the shorter, broader cauline leaves, and in the unusually coloured flowers, minutely dark blue to purple spotted on a pale greenish to grey-blue background, but with the limbs of the inner tepals so densely speckled as to appear solidly coloured, either maroon or dark slate blue. The flowers are also unusual in having the tepal limb margins undulate instead of closely crisped. Small bilobed nectaries are located at the base of the outer tepals but in the midline of the inner tepal claws, the lower halves of which are linear and ± 1 mm wide. Like other members of sect. Ferraria, the stigmas are terminal on the arms of the style branches and the ovary is not beaked. The flowers are unique in the section in lasting two days instead of a single day. The leaves of non-flowering plants are so strikingly different from those of mature, flowering individuals that they appear to represent a different species. Four to six in number, they are held in a close, 2-ranked fan and the blades are dark green, terete and hollow. The early flowering habit of Ferraria densepunctulata is matched in the genus by F. ornata and F. ovata, both of which also have the narrow basal leaves differentiated from the shorter and broader cauline leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Coarse red-brown stellate pubescence on calyx, stems, young parts, main veins on underside of leaves; deeply stellate white flowers, 20-50 mm in diam.
bibliographicCitation: Welman, WG. 2003. The genus Solanum (Solanaceae) in southern Africa: subgenus Leptostemonum, the introduced sections Acanthophora and Torva. Bothalia 33(1): 1-18. [CC BY]

description: Prickles mostly present. Leaves white floccose-tomentose below. Inflorescence an unbranched or paniculiform cyme. Anthers 2-4 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Welman, WG. 2008. The genus Solanum (Solanaceae) in southern Africa: subgenus Leptostemonum, section Giganteiformia. Bothalia 38(1): 39-47. [CC BY]

description: Unarmed shrub. Leaves thin, soft, dark green, glabrescent, lanceolate to obovate. Seeds very large.
bibliographicCitation: Welman, WG. 2008. The genus Solanum (Solanaceae) in southern Africa: subgenus Leptostemonum, section Giganteiformia. Bothalia 38(1): 39-47. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the linear basal leaves, quite different from the shorter cauline leaves, the stem usually partly exposed, and with red-flushed and white-speckled cataphylls and lowermost leaf sheath. The large flowers have a deep and relatively narrow floral cup, 17-20 mm deep and ± 12 mm wide at the mouth. The flowers are usually shades of turquoise-grey to pale slate-blue with a pale yellow nectar guide lightly speckled with darker colour on the limbs of the outer tepals. The flowers have a faint sweet odour, often with spicy overtones of almond, cinnamon or vanilla, unique in the genus. Ferraria ferrariola has been confused with F. parva, which has flowers of similar shape with a narrow floral cup but much smaller, with a floral cup ± 6 mm deep and outer tepals 18-22 mm long compared to (30-)35-40 mm in F. ferrariola. The sheaths and cataphylls of F. parva also lack the red flush and white speckling characteristic of F. ferrariola.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The parallel anthers, wide and shallow tepal cup, spindle-shaped ovary without a beak, and stigmas terminal on the style arms, place Ferraria ovata in sect. Ferraria where it is unusual in the few-branched or simple stem and strongly dimorphic leaves, the basal linear and the cauline bifacial, short and spoon-shaped. The relatively small flowers are strikingly coloured yellow and glossy dark brown. The nectaries are bilobed or paired well above the bases of the tepal claws. Ferraria ovata is one of three winter-flowering species in the genus, the others being the coastal species F. densepunctulata and F. ornata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unlike the flowers of the related species, Ferraria crispa and F. foliosa, those of F. schaeferi sometimes have, at least to the human nose, a pleasant, sweet scent reminiscent of violets, but with a slightly sour undertone. The flowers otherwise resemble those F. crispa and F. foliosa, having widely spreading tepals, the broad claws forming a shallow cup, ± 8 mm deep and some 12 mm wide at the rim. The tepal claws bear large heart-shaped nectaries, while the limbs have a creamy pale yellow ground colour speckled with small dark brown spots, the same colour as the crisped margins. In vegetative form, F. schaeferi most closely resembles F. foliosa, which also has the leaves and branches arranged in a two-ranked spiral, and the leaf blades are similarly thick and leathery with a weakly defined central vein. In addition to the differently coloured perianth, the ovary and capsule have a pronounced beak up to 8 mm long. This readily separates F. schaeferi from F. foliosa. In its sandy habitat, plants spread vegetatively by long runners produced from the base of the stem that can extend below the ground a metre or more from the parent plant, each terminating in a corm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Freesia andersoniae has an erect, almost smooth stem and thin-textured, membranous or papery bracts, and large, fragrant white flowers, 50-60 mm long, marked with characteristic purple chevrons in the tepal sinuses.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Inflorescences to 10 cm long, many-flowered. Corolla yellow. Calyx enlarged in fruit, with dense, sharp, long, yellow prickles. Berries black.
bibliographicCitation: Henderson, MD; Anderson, JG. 1966. Common Weeds in South Africa: Mem. bot. Surv. S. Afr. 37. Mem. Bot. Surv. South Africa: 1-440. Government Printers, Pretoria. [All rights reserved]

description: Resembling both Freesia refracta and F. occidentalis in its bracts and flowers but distinguished by the usually obtuse bracts prominently tipped with dark brown for up to 0.5 mm, and often more brightly coloured flowers, mostly pale to deep yellow but also pink, or rarely white. The flowers are typically pale yellow with a darker throat and lower tepals but are deep yellow around Port Elizabeth, and rose- or deep pink-flowered populations occur in the Long Kloof, near Haarlem, Joubertina and Zuurbron, and near Hankey.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Usually readily recognised by the fragrant, pale yellow flowers with prominent orange markings on the lower tepals. The spikes are held well above the leaves, which are typically prostrate and obtuse but in some populations may be suberect and acute. Erect-leaved plants of Freesia fergusoniae are most likely to be confused with yellow-flowered F. leichtlinii subsp. leichtlinii, but that species is restricted to coastal sands or sandy loam and has deeply buried corms with fine to medium-textured tunics, and produces axillary cormlets along the subterranean portion of the stem. Populations from Soetmelksrivier, southeast of Riversdale with cream-coloured or white flowers and a prostrate flower spike are easily confused with Freesia caryophyllacea, but the more numerous leaves (9 to 12 vs. 5 to 7) and later flowering (mid- to late July) are consistent with F. fergusoniae.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: All parts covered with glandular hairs and orange-red to yellow-brown prickles up to 20 mm long. Flowers white, cream, bluish. Fruit bright red, shiny.
bibliographicCitation: Henderson, MD; Anderson, JG. 1966. Common Weeds in South Africa: Mem. bot. Surv. S. Afr. 37. Mem. Bot. Surv. South Africa: 1-440. Government Printers, Pretoria. [All rights reserved]

description: Leaves markedly grey- or yellow-tomentose below at maturity, Prickles mostly present. Inflorescence an unbranched or paniculiform cyme. Anthers 4-7 mm long. Seeds 2.5-3.8 x 2-3 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Welman, WG. 2008. The genus Solanum (Solanaceae) in southern Africa: subgenus Leptostemonum, section Giganteiformia. Bothalia 38(1): 39-47. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other gullet-flowered species by its slender, white flowers with narrow tepals up to 5 mm wide and narrowly funnel-shaped tube with the slender, lower portion 12-15 mm long and ± as long as or slightly longer than the upper part.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Prickles straight. Leaf lobes shallow, obtuse to acute. Flowers mostly white. Fruits large yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Vorontsova, MS; Knapp, SD. 2012. A new species of Solanum (Solanaceae) from South Africa realated to cultivated eggplant. PhytoKeys 8: 1-11. [doi: 10.3897/phytokeys.8.2462] [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the spreading or prostrate fan of short, obtuse leaves, and the declinate or horizontal spike of pink, ± salver-shaped flowers with slender tube 15-20 mm long and short bracts 4.0-5.5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Notobubon galbaniopse is most easily distinguished from N. galbanum by the long pedunculate inflorescence which is often well-branched, the fewer-rayed primary compound umbel, usually with less than 28 (-48) rays and the heteromorphic fruit. The ultimate leaflet segments are often distinguishable from those of N. galbanum in being irregularly-toothed, so that the lamina between the teeth appears concave and the lamina is often prominently revolute along the margins. Hybrids with N. ferulaceum (Magee et al. unpublished data) are known from around Kirstenbosch [Pillans 20064 (K)].
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2009. A taxonomic revision of the woody South African genus Notobubon (Apiaceae: Apioideae). Syst. Bot. 34(1): 220-242. [All rights reserved]

description: It is interesting that the seedling leaves as well as the upper (mature) leaves are invariably simple. This character enables the plant to be easily identified (once it has been spotted). The single species is exceptionally variable, especially in overall size, leaf size and calyx shape. It is the only African species that has spiny calyx lobes although this character occurs only sporadically.
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM; Magee, AR. 2013. African Apiaceae: a synopsis of the Apiaceae/Umbelliferae of Sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar. Briza Academic Books, Pretoria. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished among the species with ridged or winged stems and large, predominantly orange flowers with yellowish green markings on the lower tepals by the narrow, ribbed or corrugate leaves, suberect dorsal tepal, and pubescent filaments and style. Gladiolus meliusculus is vegetatively similar but typically has pink (rarely orange) flowers with broader, oblanceolate lower tepals with reduced yellow markings heavily edged with dark red, and shorter filaments ± 15 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Gladiolus maculatus, in which it was once included a subspecies, by the unmarked, white to cream-coloured flowers with mostly longer perianth tube, (35-)45-65 mm long and well exserted from the bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by a combination of a relatively long perianth tube, 20-25 mm long, and small to moderate-sized corms with finely fibrous corm tunics. Most populations have white flowers, pale yellow in the throat, but those with pale pink tepals have been recorded. Flowers are sweetly scented and remain open at night. Some white-flowered plants were included by Lewis (1962) in I. paucifolia but that species is distinguished by falcate leaves, coarsely fibrous corm tunics and typically beige flowers with a perianth tube mostly 25-35 mm long. Flowers of I. cedarmontana have ovate tepals 10-16 x 5-8 mm, thus about twice as long as wide, and filaments reaching the apex or exserted up to 4 mm from the perianth tube. The flowers of I. paucifolia are always unscented, have narrower tepals, 12-15 x 3.0-4.5 mm, thus about three to four times as long as wide, and the filaments are consistently exserted 2-3 mm. Because the flowers are scented and remain open at night, moth pollination is inferred for I. cedarmontana. In contrast, flowers of I. paucifolia, a plant of relatively dry, well-drained open clay and shale slopes, are unscented, close at night and are pollinated by long-proboscid flies. Relatively tall plants from the Great Winterhoek Mtns and Bokkeveld Tafelberg, up to 500 mm high, and with deep pink to pale cherry-red flowers and leaves 4-8 mm wide included in the past in Ixia cedarmontana are now regarded as a separate species, I. seracina.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from closely allied Gladiolus carneus and G. undulatus by the combination of a very long perianth tube, (45-)65-110 mm long, and relatively short tepals, the dorsal 32-40 mm long with the lower tepals markedly shorter. Lowland populations along the Atlantic Coast have especially long perianth tubes. The geographical variation in perianth tube length is associated with similar variation in the length of the proboscis of the local long-proboscid flies that are the pollinators.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its relatively long perianth tube, 15-18 mm long, white or pale lilac-flushed perianth and short filaments ± 2 mm long, included or exserted up to 1.5 mm from the tube. It is closely allied to, and most easily confused with beige-flowered I. paucifolia, a species of shale slopes in the dry interior valleys of the southwestern Cape. That species has flowers with a perianth tube (22-)25-34 mm long, slightly constricted at the apex, spreading tepals 12-15 x 5 mm, filaments ± 3 mm long, exserted 2-3 mm from the perianth tube and anthers ± 4 mm long. Although confined to cooler, south-facing slopes, I. dolichosiphon flowers from late August to mid-September, earlier than any population of I. paucifolia. It differs from I. paucifolia not only in its white or pale lilac-flushed flowers, veined purple on the outside, and shorter perianth tube, but in the tepals, stamens and style. The tepals are 9-13 mm long, the anthers are ± 3 mm long and the style divides opposite the middle of the anthers with the style branches emerging between them in contrast to the longer style of I. paucifolia that divides close to the anther tips with the style branches arching above the anthers. As in I. paucifolia, the filaments of I. dolichosiphon are decurrent almost to the base of the tube, dividing the interior of the tube into three compartments.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The broadly obconic corm with dark brown, rugose tunics spiny along the rim of Lapeirousia kamiesmontana are shared with L. dolomitica and L. lewisiana, from which it is distinguished by white flowers with distinctive red markings on the lower tepals, and a perianth tube mostly 45-60 mm long. The earlier-blooming L. lewisiana has dark red-purple to magenta flowers with white markings and a perianth tube (35-)40-48 mm long. The distinctive, somewhat woolly indumentum on the basal leaf is also shared in the genus only with L. lewisiana, but the ranges of the two species do not overlap, and the flowering times, even at the same elevation, are separated by at least two to three weeks in any particular year.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Among the three species with basally spurred anthers, Gladiolus appendiculatus is recognised by its short-tubed, white or pale pink flowers with perianth tube ± 15 mm long. The species includes two distinct forms. Taller plants, more than 450 mm tall, with narrow leaves 2.5-8.0 mm wide reaching to the middle of the spike and with up to 25 flowers per spike, are known from Eswatini and near Lydenburg in Mpumalanga. Shorter plants with broader leaves 8-12 mm wide not reaching the base of the spike and with 5 to 12 flowers per spike have been recorded from Pilgrim’s Rest and Barberton to Wakkerstroom and Vryheid. Intermediates occur near Lydenburg and Barberton.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the reduced, rhizome-like rootstock with a basal fan of four to six, relatively soft-textured leaves, and pale mauve-pink flowers with perianth tube 34-40 mm long and slightly longer than the dorsal tepal. The oblong or slightly sigmoid seeds are unusual in the series.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from superficially similar species such as Gladiolus scullyi by its early flowering, softly papery or membranous corm tunics, and finely pubescent leaf sheaths and blade midrib and margins. The distinctive puberulous leaf sheaths are sometimes also encountered in G. viridiflorus, another winter-flowering species distinguished by its woody corm tunics, strikingly mottled cataphylls and often twisted leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the ± conical corms with papery to somewhat fibrous corm tunics, four linear leaves with the margins and midrib moderately thickened, and deep mauve to violet, funnel-shaped flowers with darker streaks on the lower tepals. The thickened midrib and margins distinguish the species from Gladiolus mutabilis, which has characteristic subsucculent leaves without evidently thickened midrib and margins, and G. inflexus has just three leaves and subglobose corms with woody tunics.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: his species is now divided into the three species: A. chortophila, A. kougaensis and the alpine A. congesta which occurs far west of A. chortophila. It probably comes closest to A. kougaensis and may represent a high-mountain derivative of this, with glabrous foliage. It is quite distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Dahlgren, RMT. 1988. Papilionoideae: Crotalarieae (Aspalathus), Fl. S. Africa 16(3,6): 1-430. BRI, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209549#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The species is closely allied to A. retroflexa, but has smaller leaflets and flowers and a differently shaped keel.
bibliographicCitation: Dahlgren, RMT. 1988. Papilionoideae: Crotalarieae (Aspalathus), Fl. S. Africa 16(3,6): 1-430. BRI, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209549#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the four linear leaves with slightly thickened main vein and margins, striate or ribbed bracts, and funnel-shaped, pink to mauve flowers with lanceolate-attenuate tepals, typically with darker veins and with purple-streaked nectar guides. Gladiolus virgatus has a slightly longer perianth tube, 22-27 mm long and ± abruptly flared above, and chevron-like red markings on the lower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A. kougaensis has previously been treated as a subspecies of A. chortophila, with which it is probably very closely allied. The A. kougaensis complex is, however, so characteristic and geographically well separated that specific distinction is justified.
bibliographicCitation: Dahlgren, RMT. 1988. Papilionoideae: Crotalarieae (Aspalathus), Fl. S. Africa 16(3,6): 1-430. BRI, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209549#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Like A. chortophila but leaves grey-hairy and flowers pale lemon-yellow.

description: This species has turned out to be more distinct from A. linearis than originally thought. In the regions where the two species overlap, they are different and distinct. The eastern forms are rather small-flowered.
bibliographicCitation: Dahlgren, RMT. 1988. Papilionoideae: Crotalarieae (Aspalathus), Fl. S. Africa 16(3,6): 1-430. BRI, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209549#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Previously included in A. hispida (A. thymifolia) and A. ericifolia, but distinct from both. Distinguished from A. ericifolia by the very slender bract and bracteoles, and the tapering, often slightly recurved calyx lobes, and from A. hispida in the larger, yellow flowers and the puberulous pubescence.
bibliographicCitation: Dahlgren, RMT. 1988. Papilionoideae: Crotalarieae (Aspalathus), Fl. S. Africa 16(3,6): 1-430. BRI, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209549#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This is the subspecies of A. shawii which most closely approaches A. joubertiana both morphologically and geographically.
bibliographicCitation: Dahlgren, RMT. 1988. Papilionoideae: Crotalarieae (Aspalathus), Fl. S. Africa 16(3,6): 1-430. BRI, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209549#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: One of three allopatric species with similar, large red flowers with white marks on the lower tepals, Gladiolus cardinalis is distinguished by the well-developed foliage, small corm, and habitat, trailing from wet cliffs. Autumn-flowering Gladiolus sempervirens from the Outeniqua and Tsitsikamma Mtns is a more leafy, evergreen species with a rhizome-like rootstock and scaly stolons.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Habit and leaf-shape suggest affinities to E. algoensis DC., E. virgineus (L.f. DC. and E. latifolius B.Nord. (Nordenstam et al. 2009.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to H. adpressa Schulz but differs in the shape of the buds, the larger, broader petals and the bigger appendages of the petals and filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W. 1970. Cruciferae, Fl. S. Africa 13: 1-118. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A polymorphic species, varying in most features, especially flower shape, colour and markings but recognised by the moderately soft-textured leaves and the large, white to pink flowers with the perianth tube ± as long as the dorsal tepal and usually slightly exserted from the bracts. Plants from the Langeberg and Outeniqua Mtns have paler flowers with more strongly crisped tepals, whereas those from the west are usually pink with less undulate tepals. Populations from coastal marshes between Rooi Els and Kleinmond have unmarked flowers with the lower tepals spooned, although similar floral morphs occur elsewhere as well. Gladiolus carneus is especially difficult to distinguish from forms of G. pappei, a slender species with narrow, superposed leaves and 2 to 4 dark pink flowers, and from G. undulatus, a hygrophilous species with cream-coloured, attenuate and crisped tepals, and a perianth tube longer than the dorsal tepal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by the bright yellow, sweetly scented flowers and typically stemless habit, with well-grown plants bearing 3 or 4 main branches arising below the ground and with numerous rhipidia set closely together. The several broad, firm to rigid leathery leaves, up to 300 x 20 mm, recall those of F. divaricata, which has aerial stems and larger, usually predominantly brown flowers (but sometimes dull yellow) with a wider floral cup. The flowers of F. flava resemble those of F. macrochlamys and its immediate allies in having a relatively narrow floral cup but are larger, with tepals ± 30 x 10 mm and claws ± 15 mm long, and last a single day, unlike those of the F. macrochlamys group, which have smaller tepals with claws 10-14 mm long, and last two days.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Resembling Gladiolus hirsutus in its superposed, villous leaves but with broader blades 10-27 mm wide, the margins thickened and often flushed pink or red, and the large, strongly scented flowers with perianth tube 35-40 mm long and longer filaments 22-27 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Stemless and with the tepal claws unusually narrow in the lower part, thus forming a windowed cup, Ferraria ornata is easily recognised by these features, as well as its small size, flowering individuals standing only 50-80 mm high. The apparently scentless flowers are unique in the fleshy crests bordering the distal margins of the nectaries, which are situated in the middle of the tepal claws and secrete miniscule quantities of sticky, sweet nectar. The short, concave cauline leaves of flowering plants contrast with the long, cylindric leaves of juvenile and non-flowering individuals. Both the early flowering and unusual, concave cauline leaves of flowering plants suggest it is most closely allied to F. ovata, which has a similar growth strategy of early flowering and small, concave cauline leaves on a taller flowering stem. Replacement corms of flowering individuals are absent at flowering and develop later as the capsules ripen.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the dark, fibrous corm tunics, the three overlapping leaves concealing the stem between the second and third leaves, the lowermost leaf terete and 4-grooved, and the strongly purple-veined flowers with more-or-less erect dorsal tepal. Gladiolus virescens has similar flowers but the uppermost leaf is always slightly distant from the second leaf, thus exposing a section of stem, and the corm tunics are softly papery becoming finely fibrous.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Individual heads of flowers are flat-topped and form pseudanthia with the orange patches on the posticous lips turned towards the centre of the inflorescence and simulating anthers. Melanospermum transvaalense is closely allied to M. foliosum: see discussion under that species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the four narrow leaves and the canary-yellow flowers with attenuate tepals, the upper laterals characteristically strongly recurved. The attenuate tepals and puberulous upper cataphyll suggest a relationship with mauve-flowered Gladiolus violaceolineatus from the Cederberg and adjacent mountains.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Trieenea schlechteri is easily recognized by its very lax racemes, sometimes forming few-branched panicles, and small narrow bracts, which are often adnate only to the extreme base of the pedicels; at the tip of the inflorescence, where the pedicels may be much abbreviated, the bract may be adnate nearly to the top of the pedicel.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Vegetative material of T. wallichii and T. cacalioides cannot be distinguished as the phyllopodia on the stems of both species may vary in length from more than 10 mm to 0 mm (see T. papillaris under Species insufficiently known).
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A summer-flowering species with linear leaves, 1-3 mm wide with two main veins on one side, floral bracts 24-33 mm long, and deep pink flowers with undulate or crisped tepals, the lower three marked with median red chevrons and speckles toward the base. The species may be confused with local populations of Gladiolus oreocharis, but that species has mostly wider leaves (1-)2-6 mm wide and shorter, obtuse bracts mostly 13-20 mm long, and flowers with lozenge-shaped nectar guides on the lower tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its relatively soft-textured leaves, trailing stems and large, scarlet flowers with white transverse chevrons near the base of the lower tepals, the dorsal tepal horizontal but the others ± spreading from a narrow perianth tube ± 28 mm long. The filaments are ± 40 mm long and well exserted.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its scarlet flowers with spathulate-concave dorsal tepal flanked by suberect, ear-like lateral tepals, and highly reduced, scale-like lower tepals flexed upward to form a small cup-like structure enclosing a tooth-like projection at the base of the median filament. Allied to and allopatric with Gladiolus splendens and G. saccatus, all sharing similar, bright red, highly bilabiate flowers with an enlarged, spathulate upper tepal partially adnate to the upper lateral tepals and reduced lower tepals with a thickened tooth or crest at the base of the median filament, ± versatile anthers, and involute style branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: When in flower this is a very elegant species.
bibliographicCitation: Lamarck, JBAPdeM de. 1791. Tableau encyclopédique et méthodique des trois règnes de la nature. Botanique, Vol. 1. Pancoucke, Paris. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/6086#page/1/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the three linear leaves, the lowermost with one or two veins thickened and raised and the margins lightly thickened, and small, funnel-shaped, pale creamy yellow flowers with a red throat and red streaks at the base of the upper and lower lateral tepals, with a very short perianth tube ± 8 mm long. Gladiolus pritzelii has similar leaves, with two veins thickened and raised and the lower tepals also puberulous in the lower midline, but coarsely fibrous tunics and bell-shaped, yellow flowers with a sharply bent perianth tube 11-12 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Highly variable in size and flower colour and recognised by the fan of leaves with thickened margins and main vein and fine, closely set tertiary veins between, and the generally tall, dense spike of small, short-tubed flowers. The flowers are plain or speckled and variable in colour. The species is superficially similar to Gladiolus crassifolius and the two may be confused where they co-occur along the Mpumalanga Escarpment. They are distinguished by details of the leaf venation: the leaves in G. crassifolius are more fibrous, with one or more pairs of secondary veins thicker and more conspicuous than the tertiary veins developed on each side of the main vein.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unmistakable in the almost regular, dark blue flowers on a scalloped, nearly horizontal spike, purple and white spotted upper cataphyll, and coarsely fibrous corm tunics. The lower lateral or all lower tepals are creamy white in the lower third.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the pubescent cataphylls, stem, leaves and bracts, and the moderately-sized pale pink flowers with lanceolate-elliptic tepals, perianth tube 18-27 mm long, and relatively short anthers, 4-6 mm long. The leaves are fibrous and the inner bracts are tubular below.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The shorter terminal inflorescences (25.3 ±9.4 mm) of I. origanoides separate it from I. woodii (56 ±21 mm), I. glandulosissima (42 ±22 mm) and I. ovata (66 ±22 mm). The flowers of I. origanoides are longer (13.8 ±2.3 mm) than those of I. ciliata (12.3 ±2.5 mm), I. delicatula (10.8 ±1.6 mm), I. pondoensis (9.9 ±1.3 mm) and I. gracilenta (9.4 ±1.4 mm). In addition, the calyx lobes are densely fringed with white hairs and the upper internodes of the stems are densely hairy with long white eglandular hairs. I. prolixa differs by having glandular hairs with five or more stalk cells on the bracts and calyx lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Balkwill, K; Sebola, RJ; Poriazis, DL. 2017. Taxonomic revision of white-flowered Isoglossa Oerst. (Acanthaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 108: 48-80. description: A relatively low-growing species with a fan of short, often rather blunt leaves 15-53 mm wide borne at ground level, the main vein hardly thickened, other veins fine and close-set, and an inclined spike of finely speckled flowers with large, imbricate and keeled floral bracts. The flowers are short-tubed, the perianth tube 14-20 mm long. The species is variably in flower size and in the colour, degree and intensity of the speckling on the perianth. Populations around Dullstroom are especially attractive, with relatively large almost entirely pink or reddish flowers. The species can be confused with Gladiolus vinosomaculatus, but the latter has longer, narrower, ± glaucous leaves 4-12 mm wide with longer sheaths forming a pseudostem, and shorter filaments, 7-12 mm long, with longer anthers, 10-13 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An autumn-flowering species with the foliage reduced to two sheathing cauline leaves and distinctive, long-tubed, fragrant flowers with a slender perianth tube 32-45 mm long abruptly curved or bent near the top.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Based on morphological similarity, Ixia pavonia must be regarded as most closely allied to the widespread western Karoo species I. marginifolia and like that species, it has three leathery basal leaves with thickened margins and main vein, a stem bearing three or more, short lateral branches, and a flower with a short perianth tube ± 3.5 mm long. Unlike the uniformly blue-mauve, white or pink flowers of I. marginifolia, I. pavonia has a blue-mauve perianth with a black centre surrounded by a broad red zone. Accompanying the colour difference in the perianth are purple-black filaments and style. Although the perianth tube and tepals are about the same dimensions as in I. marginifolia, the filaments in that species are 5-7 mm long and typically exserted 3.5-5.0 mm from the tube. The short filaments of I. pavonia, only 4 mm long and exserted ± 1.5 mm stand in sharp contrast.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very much like I. thomasiae in its tall stature, stem with half nodding branches, half to fully nodding flowers and, in particular, the long narrow leaves with broadly winged margins. The two differ, however, in flower size: the perianth tube of I. alata is just 5-6 mm long and the tepals 13-16 x 5-8 mm compared with a tube 8-10 mm long and tepals 14-20(-25) x 5.0-6.5(-8.0) mm. The perianth tube in particular is significantly shorter, and the tepals only slightly shorter but about as wide as those of I. thomasiae. Added to these differences are a main spike of 4 to 6 flowers and floral bracts 6-8(-10) mm long in I. alata compared with spikes of 7 to 10 flowers and floral bracts 9-12 mm in I. thomasiae. While I. alata blooms from mid-September to early October, I. thomasiae growing a short distance away, does not come into flower until the end of September and sometimes not until the second week of October. Both species have slightly warty capsules, not known in other species of Ixia.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The asymmetric corm with brown, ± woody corm tunics, relatively blunt, brown-tipped rhipidial spathes, and yellow, darkly veined tepals place Moraea intermedia in subg. Umbellatae. The long basal internode with leaves clustered at the first aerial node recalls M. nana of the subgenus, but the flowers have typical Moraea-like style branches with terminal, transverse stigma lobes and prominent, paired petaloid style crests. Unlike the typical Moraea flower, however, all six tepals of M. intermedia have short claws clasping the base of the filament column, the claws all bearing basal nectaries, and the limbs each have a nectar guide at the base. Other Moraea-type flowers have inner tepals lacking both nectaries and nectar guides. The similarly marked inner and outer tepals recall the Homeria-type flower as found in subg. Umbellatae in M. maximiliani and M. umbellata, whereas M. cooperi, M. linderi, M. longiflora and M. margaretae have more-or-less typical Moraea-type flowers. The remaining member of the alliance, M. nana, has spreading, subequal tepals with short claws clasping the base of the filament column but the style branches are reduced to paired filiform arms extending between the anthers. At the type locality, Moraea intermedia is parapatric with the closely related M. margaretae, which favours somewhat wetter sites, and a range of hybrids between the two species occurs there.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the broad, falcate lower leaves widest near the tips and with reddish, heavily thickened margins and large, bright orange to scarlet flowers with hooded dorsal tepal. The filaments are smooth.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to P. setifolia, which is awnless; P. oreodoxa and certain forms of P. pallida.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the fibrous leaves with poorly developed secondary veins, and unbranched spike of white to pink flowers with relatively short perianth tube 13-16(-20) mm long and dry, rusty brown bracts 20-30 mm long. Gladiolus ferrugineus is closely related to G. varius, distinguished by its mostly larger flowers with longer perianth tube 30-50 mm long. Hybrids between the two species occur on the upper slopes of Long Tom Pass. Gladiolus ferrugineus comprises two, more-or-less distinct forms that we interpret as ecological races: an early-flowering form from the lower escarpment with slightly broader leaves 6-15 mm wide and flowers with a short perianth tube, mostly 12-16 mm long, flowering from late November to early February; and a later-flowering form from the upper escarpment with narrow, heavily thickened and often twisted leaves 3-6 mm wide and flowers with a slightly longer tube 18-25 mm long, flowering in March and April.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its slender, terete and 4-grooved leaves and long-tubed mauve to pinkish flowers, the lower tepals with pale, spade-shaped markings outlined with purple, and the perianth tube 25-40 mm long and longer than the dorsal tepal. The seeds are unevenly winged with the lateral and lower wings reduced or vestigial. Gladiolus pretoriensis is separated by the shorter perianth tube, 11-14 mm long, and subglobose capsules with wingless, angular-prismatic seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the fan of stiff leaves, and thick-textured carmine-red flowers with a rather closed, urn-like shape and somewhat sigmoid perianth tube 35-45 mm long. The lower tepals are each marked with a median white streak outlined with dark red.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from allied species by the pale flowers with longer, narrowly funnel-shaped perianth tube, 40-60(-70) mm long, and lower tepals markedly shorter than the upper. Gladiolus miniatus with salmon-pink to orange flowers has a differently shaped perianth, 50-65 mm long, divided into a narrow lower part and a broader cylindric upper part ± 30 mm long, and much longer filaments, 35-37 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A robust species, mostly more than 0.8 m tall, with seven to nine leaves and multi-flowered inflorescences of pink to purple flowers, the perianth tube 30-40 mm long and the dorsal tepal 40-55 mm long. Gladiolus carneus, which is not recorded east of Knysna, is a smaller plant, seldom more than 600 mm tall, with 4 or 5 leaves and mostly smaller flowers with the dorsal tepal 28-40(-50) mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the narrow, marginally winged lower leaf blade, 1.5-2.5 mm wide and ± H-shaped in section with the margins curved inward over the midline, and the relatively short-tubed, funnel-shaped flowers with acute tepals, the lower streaked and spotted. Gladiolus caeruleus from coastal limestones on the Atlantic Coast, has broader leaves, 3-7 mm wide with the marginal wings at right angles to the blade, and pale blue flowers with obtuse tepals, the lower spotted with dark blue.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With the spreading, ± fringed stigmatic lobes of ser. Galaxia, Moraea vuvuzela stands out in its pale yellow flowers with brown or purplish markings at the top of the darker yellow floral cup. Most of the remaining members of the series have uniformly bright yellow flowers. The corm tunics of M. vuvuzela are ± woody with prominent, thickened longitudinal ribs only partially separated from one another by transverse fibres. The corm tunics in most other species are less woody, with the longitudinal ribs separated by transverse fibres, with the exception of M. angulata, which has unique, woody or corky tunics with wing-like longitudinal ribs.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Separated from short-tubed Gladiolus rudis by the slightly longer perianth tube, usually 27-35(-50) mm long, the longer filaments, 14-22 mm long, and the different markings on the lower tepals, reddish median streaks rather than yellowish spade-shaped blotches outlined with red or purple. The white mottling on the cataphylls is not raised. Gladiolus grandiflorus may be difficult to separate from shorter-tubed forms of G. floribundus but that species usually has a longer perianth tube, 40-70 mm long, with the lower tepals markedly shorter than the upper. Populations from calcareous sands along the coast near Stilbaai have pink flowers with crispulate tepals. Populations from near Port Elizabeth have almost actinomorphic flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is characterized by the usually ovate-lanceolate leaves, with acute apices. In addition the costa in cross-section is usually broadly elliptic at midleaf with 4-6 guide cells disposed in a single layer and the lamina is uni- to irregularly bistratose, with a yellow to orangish yellow colour in KOH. The marginal laminal cells are scarcely differentiated, and in the revolute part are slightly thicker walled and with lower papillae than the juxtacostal cells. Most of the Australian and South African collections studied of this taxon were labeled under Pseudocrossidium hornschuchianum. Both species share some characters such as the excurrent costa forming a mucro or awn, the acute leaf apex and differentiated perichaetial leaves. However, the two species are easily distinguished because the crosssection of P. adustum is usually elliptical with 4-6 guide cells whereas in P. hornschuchianum it is semicircular with 2 guide cells. In addition, the leaves of the latter species are triangular to ovate-triangular rather than ovate-lanceolate to oblong in P. adustum Among Pseudocrossidium species, the Chilean endemic P. chilense R.S. Williams seems to be the most similar to P. adustum. Both species share the color of the lamina in KOH, partially bistratose lamina, and the shape of the costa in cross-section. However, P. chilense differs in having a regular bistratose lamina near costa (unistratose or partially bistratose in P. adustum), percurrent costa and upper and median juxtacostal laminal cells with longer papillae (5-8 µm high). In addition when dry, the leaves are rather erect in P. chilense compared to appressed and spirally twisted in P. adustum.

description: Pilularia dracomontana differs from P. americana in both vegetative and sexual characters, and is smaller in several respects. Mature sporocarps of P. americana have a mean diameter of 2.67 mm and contain 12-20 megaspores per sorus, whereas the corresponding values for P. dracomontana are 1.58 mm, and 3-5 megaspores respectively. The apical papilla-like laesura (acrolamella) of the megaspores of P. dracomontana is proportionately much longer (at ± 23 %) than its equivalent in P. americana, which has been documented as ± 12.5 % of the total spore length. Leaf lengths of P. americana range from 15-50(-100) mm, whereas leaves of the new species are no longer than 14 mm, on average attaining < 12 mm. The leaves of P. americana from North America exhibit obvious circinate vernation, but this feature is yet to be observed in P. dracomontana; additionally, more than one leaf per node has been observed in P. americana, whereas P. dracomontana invariably produces only one per node. Internode lengths recorded for P americana are up to 11 mm and up to 30 mm; the maximum observed in P. dracomontana is only 4.2 mm. Comparison of the Drakensberg species with the two other 4-locular pillworts, P. novae-zelandiae Kirk and P novae-hollandiae A.Braun, reveals real differencesin the size of fronds, pedicels, sporocarp diameters, megaspores per sporocarp, and spore dimensions.

description: The littoral habitat is unique among southern African Gladiolus species and this, combined with the narrow, glaucous and subsucculent leaves and subactinomorphic, purplish flowers with white nectar guides, are diagnostic for the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The important characters that in combination distinguish this genus from similar genera (especially Syntrichia Brid.) in the Pottioideae are small plants, gregarious, orange; stem only 0.05 cm long, with central strand apparently absent; leaves strongly reflexed to squarrose when moist, usually curved longitudinally in different directions on each side, 1.2-1.5 mm long, leaf bases very broad for the length of the leaf and sheathing, margins plane throughout, occasionally dentate above, often irregularly and weakly bordered in 1(-2) rows with somewhat thick-walled, less papillose cells, these often elongate 2:1; costa usually of nearly homogeneous cells with epidermal cells sometimes with wider lumens; upper laminal cells medially rounded-quadrate to rhomboid, rather small, ca 12-15 mm in width, 1:1, with evenly thickened walls, papillae large, simple to bifid, 1-2 per lumen; hyaline, short-rectangular basal cells grading to elongate, thick-walled cells medially; paroicous; seta absent; capsule cleistocarpic, globose and short- apiculate with a mitrate calyptra. There was nothing found with these trait combinations in the literature or in collections at BOL or MO.

description: Diagnostic characters. Psoralea fleta differs from the rest of the P. aphylla group by its filiform leaflets (9-11 mm long) borne on its flowering shoots. In habit it ranges from tall willowy shrubs to small slender trees, with drooping branches when in full flower producing a mass of intensely sweet-smelling flowers. Each flower is subtended by a trifid cupulum. Psoralea fleta is similar to P. gigantea in that they both have seasonal shoots emerging on upper parts of tall bare branches, filiform, unifoliolate leaves in seasonal shoots, inflorescences borne in the uppermost axils of seasonal shoots and calyx lobes that are shorter than the calyx tube. However, P. gigantea can be separated by its distinct tree habit when mature, densely sericeous hairy young shoots, bilobed cupulum with one of the lobes slightly bilabiate, mauve standard petals without darker veins and with just a small purple flash above the paired callosities, pale mauve wing petals, and narrowly triangular calyx lobes.

description: Distinguished from related species with similar small flowers by the relatively longer perianth tube, 18-30 mm long and ± as long as or longer than the dorsal tepal. This character serves to separate it from species such as Gladiolus crassifolius, G. densiflorus and G. serpenticola.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the long lower leaf with x-shaped blade and the large, orange flowers with dimorphic tube 50-53 mm long marked with characteristic red longitudinal lines, and the reduced lower tepals ± half as large as the upper.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the linear, grass-like leaves as long as the flowering stem or longer, 1-2 mm wide and dry at flowering, and inclined spikes of white, long-tubed, zygomorphic flowers with low, greenish yellow, ridge-like calluses on the lower tepals. The corms bear short, fasciated stolons and many small cormlets. The species flowers in summer, in December, at which time the leaves are dry and withered. The flowers are almost indistinguishable from those of Tritonia pallida and the two may comprise a vicariant species pair. That species, centred in the western and central Little Karoo, has lanceolate leaves mostly 8-15 mm wide and about half as long as the flowering stem, and occurs on shale slopes, primarily in renosterveld or transitional vegetation types, flowering from mid-September to late October. The long, linear leaves of Tritonia linearifolia may lead to confusion with the partially sympatric T. bakeri, a long-tubed species widespread through the Little Karoo from Ladismith to the Long Kloof, but the leaves of T. bakeri are highly characteristic, fleshy and semi-terete in section when fresh, without thickened main vein or margins. Flowering is also somewhat earlier, mainly October to November, at which time the foliage is still green. The two species are florally very different, although this is best seen when alive. Tritonia linearifolia has zygomorphic flowers with arcuate stamens whereas the perianth in T. bakeri is almost actinomorphic and salver-shaped, with the flowers inverted, curved or slightly twisted at the base, so that the dorsal tepal is lowermost and the stamens almost central with the anthers facing upwards.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: When dry the stems and branches are curved, giving the plants a distinctive appearance. The serrate upper leaves, short and double costa and strongly differentiated alar cells help to identify specimens of N. gracile. The branch leaves have a few scattered prorate cells on the upper dorsal surface. The papillae are obvious, even at lower magnifications, in micropreparations and should also aid in identifications.

description: Recognised by the three leaves with narrow, terete blades and unscented, funnel-shaped flowers with perianth tube 12-25(-30) mm long, the lower tepals with dark spear- or spade-shaped markings. The species is variable for tube length. Late-flowering plants from the higher mountains around Ceres with pale pink flowers have the longest perianth tubes, up to 30 mm long. These may be confused with Gladiolus cylindraceus but this species has salver-shaped flowers with a cylindric perianth tube and shorter filaments, 7-8 mm long. Gladiolus patersoniae has consistently short-tubed, sweetly scented flowers with a sharply bent tube 10-12 mm long, the lower tepals with a transverse yellow band.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the woody tunics, three linear leaves, and flexuose stem with purplish, narrowly funnel-shaped flowers, the lower tepals streaked and spotted. Gladiolus gracilis has similar flowers but mostly four leaves, these H-shaped in section with winged margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unmistakable in its falcate, H-shaped leaves 4-6 mm wide with villous, winged margins, villous bracts, and orange flowers with conspicuous yellow cup extending onto the lower third of the tepal limbs. Similar leaves are otherwise known only in yellow-flowered Romulea hirsuta (sect. Stellanthe) and pink-flowered R. tetragona (sect. Roseae).

description: Diagnosed by the linear lower leaf with heavily thickened and raised margins and midrib, and relatively large, dull, trumpet-shaped flowers with upper tepals 37-45 mm long and perianth tube 40-53 mm long. The lowermost bracts are conspicuously attenuate. Similar Gladiolus hyalinus has smaller flowers, the upper tepals 23-30 mm long and the perianth tube 25-36 mm long, with the lower laterals obliquely twisted away from the median. Gladiolus tristis has X-shaped leaves and mostly cream-coloured to yellowish flowers with shorter, acute to obtuse bracts up to 50 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Phyllopodium cordatum typically has a few pairs of ovate petiolate leaves confined to the lower part of the stem, the upper part running out into a long nude scape bearing the terminal inflorescence. Sometimes the leaves tend to be more elliptic than ovate, and sometimes they may be more numerous and run up the scape, diminishing rapidly in size. The leaves and bracts are pubescent on both surfaces and this, together with the pale flowers devoid of colour patterning as well as the creamy-coloured seeds, will distinguish the species from P. heterophyllum (see also under that species). Phyllopodium cordatum is easily confused with P. mimetes, which also has the leaves crowded near the base of the plant and solitary heads on long peduncles; discriminating characters are given under P. mimetes (below).

description: Readily recognised by the narrow leaves and long-tubed, white to pale salmon-pink flowers with attenuate tepals, slender perianth tube 40-45 mm long, and basally spurred anthers.

description: Recognised by the three or four linear leaves with short, subsucculent blades without thickened midrib and margins, and the fragrant, mottled flowers with narrowly funnel-shaped perianth tube 23-35(-48) mm long and longer than the dorsal tepal. The flowers are highly variable in colour and intensity of mottling Gladiolus albens from Port Elizabeth to Alexandria has unmarked white flowers with a mostly longer perianth tube (35-)45-65 mm long.

description: This species is characterized by a dull orange-yellow corolla with large lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Retief, E; Reyneke, WF. 1984. The genus Thunbergia in southern Africa. Bothalia 15(1&2): 107-116. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the narrow, ribbed or corrugate leaves and pink to orange flowers with suberect dorsal tepal, oblanceolate lower tepals yellowish only toward the base edged with dark red, and relatively short, pubescent filaments ± 15 mm long and pubescent style. Gladiolus alatus has consistently orange flowers with narrower lower tepals yellowish for most of their length except at the extreme apices, and longer filaments 20-26 mm long.

description: Characterized by its hastate leaf base.
