description: Recognised by its drooping spikes of long-tubed pink flowers with slender perianth tube 35-40 mm long, attenuate tepals with the outer whorl subequal and notably wider than the inner whorl. The cataphylls and leaves are minutely pubescent. The habitat on wet cliffs and rocks is characteristic.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Related to but readily separated from Gladiolus brevifolius and other small-flowered, autumn-blooming species with reduced leaves and pale pink flowers by the longer perianth tube, 22-30 mm long and longer than the dorsal tepal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The variation in this species is difficult to analyse satisfactorily. In the Zambezi valley, from where the type of the specific name comes, plants are uniformly vigorous perennial herbs or subshrubs with large leaves with a very characteristic shape which we have described as subpandurate (with a narrow truncate base and concave lower margins. Similar plants (var. africanus) also seem to occur in the Limpopo valley, but here they intergrade completely with plants of a quite different facies which are low branching perennial herbs to subshrubs with small elliptic leaves (var. limpopoensis). The subpandurate leaf shape is found also in plants of east-central Tanzania, which we therefore also refer to var. africanus. Here, however, it is difficult to make a confident distinction from plants from further west and north in Tanzania which have a low-growing inter-twining habit and usually elliptic and auriculate leaves (var. masaicus). These in turn are difficult to key out from var. limpopoensis, though the more branching habit and smaller non-auriculate and non-apiculate leaves of the latter usually enable a distinction to be made at a glance. Finally plants from the Ruaha National Park, although similar in facies to the nearby var. masaicus, have a very characteristic bract shape with a broad lateral veinless flange and we keep them as a fourth variety (var. ruahae). The lack of clear-cut exclusive distribution patterns, and the presence of many intermediates where taxa meet, argue for varietal rank rather than subspecies, despite the fact that the extremes of variation have a very different facies which might well suggest different species.

description: Recognised by the crowded, subcapitate spike of scarlet or reddish orange, funnel-shaped flowers with subequal tepals 19-22 mm long and ± straight perianth tube 25-31 mm long, almost entirely including the stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the three leaves with relatively short, terete, longitudinally grooved blades and the white, narrowly funnel-shaped flowers with red median markings on the lower tepals, moderately long perianth tube, (17-)20-25 mm long, and purple anthers. Flowering in midsummer and autumn.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: B. integrifolia var. integrifolia can be superficially close to forms of B. maderaspatensis with solitary flowers, but is easily recognised by the presence of bracteoles with long straight mucro and by the blue corolla. The material from Uganda and Congo has appressed indumentum or is subglabrous and has no long pilose hairs on the leaves. The material from Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda and Tanzania has spreading indumentum and long pilose hairs on the leaves. However, in South Africa, plants with appressed and spreading indumentum occur in the same area, and it seems doubtful whether any infraspecific taxa can be recognised on this basis. In South Africa the plants with long spreading hairs (var. setosa, s. str.) also tend to have narrower leaves, but again this is not an absolute character as almost glabrous plants with linear-lanceolate leaves have been seen. In the Indian material the bracteoles often have 1-2 bristles per side while this is only rarely seen in Africa and here only in South Africa (see note after var. clarkei). Bracts, sepals and corollas in the Indian material are also always at the lower end of the size-variation, and it is rare for Indian collections to have distinctly 'shouldered' dorsal sepals. Small flowers are also met with in Africa, and sepals without 'shoulders' - although rarely seen - do occur here, especially in South Africa. Gillett 13663 from Kenya, Moyale differs from all other collections in having scattered stalked capitate glands on bracts and sepals and also has very long.

description: Recognised by the reduced foliage, the flowering stem bearing two or three glabrous leaves with reduced or vestigial blades, and the erect spike of pale mauve, strongly bilabiate flowers, the lower tepals clawed with oblong blades and usually slightly shorter than the median, the nectar guides transverse median chevrons of pale colour edged with purple. The species is closely allied to Gladiolus atropurpureus from tropical Africa but pale-flowered forms of that species can be distinguished from G. oatesii by their broader, spade-shaped lower tepals, the laterals ± as long as or slightly longer than the median and with nectar guides a solid, median blotch, and the shorter filaments 6-8 mm long.

description: This variety is distinguished from H. aristata var. alba by its shorter bract tails, larger purple flowers, larger fruits and different geographic distribution. It is neither succulent nor is it restricted to sand dunes as is H. aristata var. thiniorum.

description: Recognised by the basal fan of lanceolate leaves and smallish, short-tubed flowers with relatively long, green bracts 25-50 mm long and perianth tube 15-20 mm long. The leaf margins are often ciliolate or scabrid. Plants from the northern and central parts of the range, in southern KwaZulu-Natal and Transkei [Eastern Cape], have creamy yellow flowers, while those from south of the Kei River are mostly bright pink. A dark purple form occurs near East London. Gladiolus mortonius from slightly higher elevations inland has a considerably longer perianth tube, 30-45 mm long, and firmer, more fibrous leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the two-ranked spikes of large, long-tubed flowers, the perianth tube (28-)40-55 mm long, the bracts ± inflated and the inner tubular below. The stem, leaves and bracts are either smooth or more often puberulous. The typical form of the species from the coastal Eastern Cape is tall with markedly two-ranked spikes of bright pink to mauve flowers. Plants from higher elevations inland are shorter with salmon-pink flowers in less markedly two-ranked spikes. Gladiolus oppositiflorus is most likely to be confused with G. mortonius, but that species has the leaves in a short fan not reaching above the base of the 1-sided spike, and the inner bracts are open to the base and not drawn into cusps above.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the several plane leaves and characteristic greenish to purplish flowers with narrow, strongly arched dorsal tepal 3-6 mm wide, and broad, spade-shaped upper lateral and lower median tepals. Populations from the Atlantic Coast have almost turquoise green flowers but elsewhere the flowers are greyish to dull purple.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: I. delicatula has an interrupted inflorescence with inflorescence nodes that are half as long to almost as long as the calyx and two flowers at a node. Bracts are from two thirds as long as the calyx to a bit longer than the calyx. The calyx lobes have eglandular hairs together with dense glandular hairs with three stalk cells. Although there are many similarities between some material of I. delicatula and I. woodii (e.g. plant height, inflorescence length, long petioles and long patent hairs on the petioles), I. delicatula has slender, linear bracts (4.5 ±2.3 mm wide) whereas I. woodii has very characteristic broad bracts (8.7 ±2.7 mm wide) with acuminate tips.

description: A summer-flowering species with narrow leaves, 2-6 mm wide and typically with two main veins, short, obtuse floral bracts, mostly 13-20 mm long, and small, pink flowers with lozenge-shaped nectar guides and perianth tube 15-24 mm long. The upper cataphyll is sometimes hispidulous. Gladiolus crispulatus from the Langeberg has linear leaves 1-3 mm wide, mostly larger bracts, 24-33 mm long, and undulate or crisped tepals, the lower marked with median red chevrons and speckles toward the base.

description: A shrub 3.7-4.9 m [as '12-16 ft.'] high.

description: Recognised by the soft, membranous corm tunics, three linear leaves, and pink, broadly funnel-shaped flowers with moderately short tube, 18-20 mm long, the lower tepals each with a white lozenge-shaped marking outlined with red.

description: The rounded leaf bases together with prominent midveins and lateral veins and long (30-118 mm), mostly terminal inflorescences are characteristic of I. ovata. The bracts have only eglandular trichomes. All other species of Isoglossa are found on forest floors, along forest edges or in savanna whereas I. ovata is mainly found in grassland.

description: Readily recognised by the markedly inclined spike of relatively large, nodding, bell-like flowers with prominent nectar guides on the lower tepals and sharply curved perianth tube 18-20 mm long. The relatively small corm has papery tunics. Plants spread vegetatively by means of long stolons.

description: Difficult to separate from slender forms of Gladiolus carneus but diagnosed by its very narrow leaves, 1.6-3.0 mm wide, and few-flowered spike of one to four, mostly dark pink flowers with relatively short, lanceolate tepals, a preference for marshy habitats, and the very small corm, ± 5 mm diam. description: Evidently restricted to dolomite outcrops and distinctive in its long, relatively soft-textured leaves and short-tubed, pale shell-pink flowers with a conspicuous dark red mouth and purple anthers. The slender stolons are characteristic of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the narrow leaves and small, short-tubed, usually dull-coloured flowers with a wide gap or window between the bases of the dorsal and upper lateral tepals when viewed in profile. The corm tunics are finely fibrous and the capsules are ovoid-ellipsoid. Similar flowers with longer tubes 22-35 mm long, distinguish Gladiolus uitenhagensis and G. sekukuniensis. In the extreme west of the range it can be confused with G. scullyi which has woody, clawed corm tunics and obovoid, retuse capsules.

description: Diagnosed by the branched stems up to 750 mm high, relatively soft-textured leaves 6-20 mm wide, and the small, dark pink flowers with short perianth tube 18-20 mm long, and lower tepals each with a white lozenge-shaped nectar guide outlined with red. The corms develop characteristic short, fasciated stolons bearing clusters of small cormlets.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by puberulous cataphylls, stems, leaves and bracts, and the relatively small, pale flowers with short perianth tube ± 15 mm long. The bracts are short, 16-25 mm long, usually no more than one internode long, and the inner bracts are tubular in the lower half. The bracts and bracteoles exude photosynthate from the tips that attract ants onto the inflorescence, a remarkable feature otherwise known only in Gladiolus dolomiticus Oberm. and G. reginae.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the three or four linear leaves with short, subsucculent blades without thickened midrib and margins, and the long-tubed, red to nearly orange flowers, the tube 30-46 mm long and slender and subcylindric in the lower half and widely cylindric in the upper half. With cream-coloured to salmon-pink flowers, Gladiolus meridionalis from the south coast has broader, ovate tepals 15-23 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Diagnosed by the two (rarely three), largely or entirely sheathing leaves, the lowermost villous and sheathing the lower half of the stem and the remaining one or two hairless and much smaller, and the almost actinomorphic perianth with lanceolate-attenuate tepals and the short stamens well concealed in the flower. Mauve-pink-flowered Gladiolus parvulus from southern KwaZulu-Natal is a smaller species with the upper leaf reduced to a bract-like scale inserted at the base of the spike, and smaller, acute but not attenuate tepals. Gladiolus pubiger typically has lemon-yellow flowers, but the Eswatini and some Mpumalanga populations have blue-mauve, slightly larger flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the plane leaves without thickened or raised veins, and salmon-pink to orange flowers with a suberect dorsal tepal and conspicuously hairy filaments. Gladiolus speciosus, with similar leaves, has a concave dorsal tepal that is strongly arched over the stamens, and almost glabrous filaments; it also produces characteristic long, slender stolons from the base of the corm. Gladiolus alatus has similar flowers but strongly ribbed or corrugate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very distinct in Pseuderanthemum with its red flowers and seeds with two different surfaces. In these characters it seems to tend towards Ruspolia. The pale yellow to reddish brown glossy bark and protruding leaf bases are also distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 2010. 36. Pseuderanthemum, Fl. Trop. E. Africa, Acanthaceae (2): 478-484. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from allied species in the series with similar flowers by the softer corm tunics and centric leaves, 2.5-4.0 mm diam., x-shaped in section with main vein raised on either side of surface into wing-like ridges. Gladiolus watsonius from the western lowlands has linear leaves, mostly 4-6 mm wide with two furrows on each surface, and G. teretifolius from the Overberg has terete leaves, 1-2 mm diam., with the main vein and margins heavily thickened and thus with four fine longitudinal grooves. Both of these species have hard, clawed corm tunics.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Corolla-tube 9-13 mm long; capsule puberulous or sparsely so all overor apically only; seed 5-6 x 4-5 mm; inflorescence-axes with non-capitate glandular hairs and longer capitate glands.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 1989. A revision of Megalochlamys and Ecbolium (Acanthaceae: Justicieae). Kew Bull. 44(4): 601-680. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the narrow, marginally winged lower leaf blade, ± 2 mm wide and ± H-shaped in section with the margins curved inward over the midline, and the relatively long-tubed flowers with crisped, attenuate tepals, the lower streaked and spotted, and the perianth tube 27-36 mm long. Gladiolus gracilis has obliquely funnel-shaped blue, rarely pink, flowers with a shorter perianth tube, 12-18 mm long and ± acute tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the white or pale lilac flowers with long, narrow tube 28-44 mm long, with the filaments included or very shortly exserted, and ovate tepals with the dorsal smaller than the upper laterals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An autumn-flowering species with short, linear leaves and large, pinkish flowers with relatively long perianth tube, 36-44 mm long and slightly longer than the dorsal tepal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from other species in the series with similar short stems and thickly fibrous tunics accumulating in a mass by the short-tubed flowers with perianth tube 18-21 mm long and lower tepals with a yellowish, spade-shaped marking outlined with red or purple, and the short filaments 12-14 mm long. The raised white mottling on the cataphylls is also distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Hybridises with S. columbaria.
bibliographicCitation: Welman, WG. 2019. Dipsacaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 852-855. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Whole plant clothed with appressed silky hairs; stem suffruticose, branched and leafy at the base; leaves sessile, lyrately- or cuneate-spathulate, serrato-dentate from the middle, quite entire at the base; peduncles elongated; heads of fruit subglobose; corollas radiant, 5-fid; crown about 20-nerved; bristles of calyx 5, 2-3-times longer than the crown.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Dipsacaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 41-44. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/47/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: A plant from the same area, Nuzu plateau, fl. & fr. iii.1935, Gilliland 1615, (BM; K) appears to have affinities with S. tysonii L. Bolus, in its very leafy appearance, with broadly ovate terminal segments of the leaves right to the top of the stem, and small capitula. The specimen consists only of the top part of the plant, but in view of its hollow stems and robust nature it is best considered here, rather than to regard it as an extension of the range of S. tysonii from S. Africa.
bibliographicCitation: Cannon, MJ; Cannon, JFM. 1983. 96. Dipsacaceae, Fl. Zambes. 7(1): 77-85. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, London. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its scarlet flowers with only the dorsal tepal well developed and spathulate-concave, the remaining tepals reduced and scale-like. The upper portion of the perianth tube forms a sac-like spur enclosing a tooth-like crest at the base of the median filament. Allied to Gladiolus cunonius and G. splendens, all sharing similar, bright red, highly bilabiate flowers with an enlarged, spathulate upper tepal partially adnate to the upper lateral tepals and reduced lower tepals with a thickened tooth or crest at the base of the median filament, ± versatile anthers, and involute style branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished in having the branches uniformly leafy throughout, with no radical leaves, and the very short bristles of the calyx.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, HML. 1918. Novitates Africanae. Ann. Bolus Herb. 2: 95-111. [https://archive.org/details/annalsofbolusher02bolu/page/94] [All rights reserved]

description: Most leaves usually longer than 3.5 cm.
bibliographicCitation: Coates Palgrave, K; Coates Palgrave, M. 2002. Trees of southern Africa, 3rd ed. Struik, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinctive in its large, nodding, scarlet flowers with horizontal to drooping dorsal tepal and strongly recurving lower tepals splashed with white on the lower half. The perianth tube is strongly curved, 33-37 mm long, and the anthers are well-exserted on filaments 30-50 mm long. The unusually long style branches, 7-8 mm long, are distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by its broad, moderately soft-textured leaves, (12-)18-35 mm wide and relatively large, pale pink flowers with perianth tube 30-40 mm long, and rusty red-brown bracts 38-48 mm long. The leaves lack the fine, closely set tertiary veins of species such as Gladiolus ferrugineus and G. varius.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the scabridulous stems, leaves and floral bracts, and the long-tubed, pink flowers with slender perianth tube 35-40 mm long. Gladiolus microcarpus has similar long-tubed, pink flowers but hairless, drooping stems and attenuate tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The whole plant has a somewhat shining silvery-grey appearance, yet not quite glabrous. It is very near E. media.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: This species was placed by Bentham in the § Ephebus, to which, without doubt, it is allied, and to which it affords a transition; but it seems better included here [§ Myra]. It has also affinities with E. tumida, Ker.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: A very distinct species, with the aspect of plants of the § Hermes, from which it is separated by its strictly terminal inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: It is noticeable by its persistent flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the markedly two-ranked spikes of rather dull coloured, often greenish flowers with inflated, pleated bracts. The narrow, fibrous leaves often form a distinct pseudostem, the blades arising well above the ground, with strongly thickened midrib, margins and one or more pairs of other veins. Plants flower in the late summer and autumn.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from allied species by its tall stature, 750-1500 mm high, narrow glaucous leaves 7-10 mm wide, and small, dry, brittle floral bracts 12-15 mm long. The short-tubed flowers resemble those of Gladiolus densiflorus and G. crassifolius and the three species are best distinguished vegetatively: G. crassifolius has strongly fibrous leaves with more heavily thickened midrib and margins plus at least one pair of secondary veins, and G. densiflorus has leaves with fine, closely set tertiary veins. Some plants in Mpumalanga, where the distribution of the species overlaps, may be difficult to place.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very distinct species and generally recognizable at once by its clustered flowers and rather large, coarse leaves. The anther-crests are almost exactly those of E. pubescens, L., and E. distorta, Bartl.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: A relatively late-flowering species recognised by narrow, linear to falcate leaves with plane blades, and bright orange flowers, the upper laterals often predominantly yellow on the reverse, with hooded dorsal tepal arched over the stamens. The conspicuous, slender stolons are diagnostic among the small group of species with angled to winged stems and orange flowers. Gladiolus pulcherrimus with similar leaves, has flowers with a suberect dorsal tepal and conspicuously hairy filaments and the corm lacks stolons.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its scarlet flowers with spathulate-concave dorsal tepal flanked by suberect, ear-like lateral tepals, the lower lateral tepals reduced and scale-like and the lower median boat-shaped and deflexed above the short, cup-like upper portion of the perianth tube enclosing a tooth-like projection at the base of the median filament. Allied to and allopatric with Gladiolus cunonius and G. saccatus, the group sharing similar, bright red, highly bilabiate flowers with an enlarged, spathulate upper tepal partially adnate to the upper lateral tepals and reduced lower tepals with a thickened tooth or crest at the base of the median filament, ± versatile anthers, and involute style branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Gladiolus cardinalis and G. sempervirens with similar, large red flowers by the upright habit, mottled cataphylls and reduced leaves with the blades shorter than the sheaths or lacking. Typical populations from the Langeberg are bright scarlet but those from the Potberg are carmine. The latter form especially resembles G. carmineus from coastal scrub between Pringle Bay and Cape Infanta and has been identified as that species in the past, but G. carmineus has smaller, more cupped flowers with perianth tube ± 30 mm long, dorsal tepal ± 35 mm long, and filaments 21-26 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in its drab white to pale lilac, radially symmetric flowers with a star-like perianth and erect, symmetrically arranged stamens and style. It is probably closely allied to G. permeabilis and G. wilsonii, both of which have bilabiate flowers with unilateral stamens distinctive in its drab white to pale lilac, radially symmetric flowers with a star-like perianth and erect, symmetrically arranged stamens and style. It is probably closely allied to G. permeabilis and G. wilsonii, both of which have bilabiate flowers with unilateral stamens. The flowers open only in the mornings, closing tightly at midday.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very distinct from E. fascicularis by its habit and its hairy, usually close-pressed leaves; the anther is also different.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Unmistakable in its nodding, scarlet flowers with obovate, cupped tepals. The reduced, bract-like and softly hairy leaves on the flowering stem distinguishes it from the unrelated, summer-flowering Gladiolus insolens from the Piketberg, which has remarkably similar flowers but a basal fan of smooth, well-developed leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An autumn-flowering species recognised by the fibrous corm tunics forming a collar around the base of the stem, three or rarely four, ± entirely sheathing leaves on the flowering stem, and pale blue, funnel-shaped flowers with transverse yellow bands or spear-shaped markings edged with purple on the lower tepals. The solitary foliage leaf, produced from a separate bud later in the season, is terete and 4-grooved, with scattered long hairs along the edges of the grooves. Gladiolus martleyi from sandy soils has softly papery or membranous corm tunics and pink to mauve flowers with slightly shorter perianth tube, 11-12 mm long, and a glabrous foliage leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Most nearly allied to E. cryptanthera, and E. thymifolia. It is more robust than the former and distinguished from the latter by its shorter corollas and included anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the woody tunics, three linear leaves, and small, purplish flowers with darker veins, the lower tepals streaked and spotted with purple on pale yellow nectar guides.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the woody corm tunics, three leaves with slender, oval to terete and 4-grooved blades, and the creamy white to yellow, weakly zygomorphic flowers with funnel-shaped perianth tube 16-20 mm long and subequal tepals, the lower deeper yellow toward the base and with dark purple lines or streaks in the throat. White-flowered plants occur in the Hottentots Holland Mtns and around Bredasdorp.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Diagnosed by the ± x-shaped lower leaf with heavily thickened and raised main vein and thickened margins and relatively large, cream-coloured to pale yellowish, trumpet-shaped flowers, sometimes ± shaded with grey-brown on the reverse of the tepals, upper tepals 22-28 mm long and perianth tube 40-63 mm long. The bracts are relatively short and blunt, (25-)40-50 mm long. Gladiolus liliaceus has linear, grooved leaves and mostly brownish-mottled flowers with longer bracts, 55-115 mm long, those of the lower flowers always long-attenuate and much longer than the perianth tube. Gladiolus longicollis has shorter filaments, 5-13 mm long, and occurs mostly east of Port Elizabeth but also occurs in the Swartberg and Kammanassie Mtns.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the two bladeless leaves, the lowermost sheathing the lower two thirds of the stem and the upper reduced to a sheathing bract or scale. The funnel-shaped flowers are pale blue to white, with a perianth tube shorter than to ± as long as the dorsal tepal. The stem and sheathing leaves remain green and photosynthetic throughout the winter months.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the almost tubular, bright red flowers with elongate perianth tube 35-45 mm long, cylindric in the upper part, with ± connivent upper tepals and small, linear lower tepals. The mottled cataphylls and slender stolons are characteristic of several species in the series.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the narrow, fibrous leaves up to 9 mm wide with strongly thickened margins and midrib, and the moderately large, long-tubed pink flowers with perianth tube (27-)37-50 mm long, and large, rusty brown bracts (25-)30-70 mm long. The narrow, thickened leaves distinguish the species from Gladiolus saxatilis. Shorter tubed plants may be confused with G. ferrugineus, with mostly paler pink flowers with perianth tube 12-16(-25) mm long. Hybrids between the two species are recorded from the upper slopes of Long Tom Pass.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A winter-flowering species with linear, grooved leaves dry at flowering, and pale pink to cream-coloured flowers with yellow markings on the lower tepals, and obliquely spathulate upper lateral tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the narrow, glaucous leaves 4-12 mm wide, forming a pseudostem at the base, large glaucous bracts up to 120 mm long partly concealing the flowers, pale tepals spotted of blotched red or purple and short filaments, 7-11 mm long and anthers 10-13 mm long. Gladiolus ecklonii, with similarly but often more finely spotted flowers, has a basal fan of bright green leaves and often smaller flowers with longer filaments, 12-15 mm long, and shorter anthers, 7-10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the soft corm tunics, the ribbed or grooved and often scabrid leaves, the uppermost separated from and not overlapped by the leaf below it, thus exposing a portion of the stem, and the strongly veined flowers with suberect dorsal tepal. The flowers are variable in colour, usually yellowish to greenish with purple veins but sometimes pinkish with darker pink veins. Plants from the Swartruggens are unusually robust, with branched stems and relatively small, pinkish flowers. Gladiolus ceresianus has similar flowers but invariably three leaves, the lowermost terete and 4-grooved, the sheaths of all three leaves overlapping and completely concealing the lower part of the stem, and characteristically dark, fibrous corm tunics forming a neck around the base of the stem.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from allied species in the series with similar flowers by the linear leaves, mostly 4-6 mm wide, with the main vein and margins heavily thickened, the blade thus with four longitudinal grooves. Gladiolus teretifolius from the Overberg has narrow, terete leaves 1-2 mm wide, and G. quadrangularis from inland near Ceres has centric blades x-shaped in section and softer corm tunics.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The closest relationships of A. incurvifolia are not fully understood.
bibliographicCitation: Dahlgren, RMT. 1988. Papilionoideae: Crotalarieae (Aspalathus), Fl. S. Africa 16(3,6): 1-430. BRI, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209549#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the basal fan of linear leaves, 1-3 mm wide, with the midrib area thickened but not the margins, and the rather closed, white to greenish flowers with short perianth tube 6-13 mm long. Gladiolus inandensis from higher elevations and further north has very similar flowers produced in winter and spring at which time the current season’s leaves are mostly dry and withered - the fresh leaves are subsucculent and distinctly oval in section.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the villous cataphylls and basal leaf sheaths, and the strongly bilabiate flowers with the upper tepals 17-27 mm long, the dorsal more-or-less hooded, and the lower tepals shortly clawed with auriculate limbs. Taller Gladiolus malvinus has sparsely hairy or glabrous leaves and larger, blue-mauve flowers with the upper tepals 28-30 mm long. The species is highly polymorphic for flower colour, with an associated variation in floral scent. The distribution of the colour forms has no clear geographic pattern.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: B. acuminata is easily recognised by the predominantly unifoliolate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E; Venter, M; Boatwright, JS. 2010. A revision of the genus Bolusia (Fabaceae, Crotalarieae). S. African J. Bot. 76: 86-94. [doi:10.1016/j.sajb.2009.08.010] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2010); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Unless dwarfed by poor seasonal rains, subsp. mucronata is an erect plant with an aerial stem usually at least 150 mm high. It grows in a variety of habitats, and may be found on sandstone outcrops, stony clay slopes, and sometimes on the shale band of the Table Mountain series of the Cape System.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This variety differs from the typical variety in having thicker, hairier stems with a tendency of becoming woody, with pubescent to densely velvety leaflets that often have very prominent venation, and the strongly asymmetrical lateral leaflets.
bibliographicCitation: Moteetee, AN; Le Roux, MM. 2016. The Rhynchosia totta complex (Phaseoleae, Fabaceae) in Southern Africa, including the description of a new variety and new species. Bothalia - ABC 46(1,a2041): 1-19. [http://dx.doi.org/10.4102/abc.v46i1.2041] [All rights reserved]

description: Subsp. nana is recognised by the broad leaves, held obliquely to the sheaths and often more-or-less horizontally. Flowering mainly in September, plants are often seen at the Hopefield and Darling wild flower shows where their form and wonderfully rich, violet-like scent can be admired comfortably. It is readily distinguished from the narrow-leaved subsp. maculata of the southern Cape coast by leaf shape.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Stems glabrous to sparsely pubescent. Leaflets 0.8-4.4 x 0.3-1.1 cm, glabrescent or sparsely pubescent, the surface never obscured by hairs, the margins ciliate and venation raised on both surfaces. Calyx 5-6 mm long. Standard 7-9 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Verdcourt, B. 2001. 61. Leguminosae (Papilionoideae): Tribe 8. Phaseoleae: 61. Rhynchosia Lour., Fl. Zambes. 3(5): 168-210. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the bell-shaped corm and moderate-sized to large flowers with the distal part of the tepals ranging in colour from magenta through salmon-pink to coppery orange or pale apricot-coloured, with or without dark markings around the cup. The presence of some pink anthocyanin pigment in the tepals is essentially what separates Romulea hirsuta from yellow-flowered R. triflora [see further under subsp. cuprea]. Romulea hirsuta is relatively common in the lowlands and coastal mountains of the Western Cape, and is highly variable in habit, width and vestiture of the leaves, and in the size, colour and markings of the flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Can be distinguished from S. flanaganii by the leaves which are somewhat rhombic in shape with an acuminate apex, 5 or 6 pairs of veins and reddish petioles and the sessile, solitary flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: According to a note on Moll & Nel 5608 the foliage is pendent with the young leaves dark pink and highly conspicuous and the slash is pale pink. A variable species as regards leaf size, texture, margin and pubescence of ovary.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the presence of a large reddish black blotch or transverse band on the outer tepals at the base of the limb.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With the appearance of a Scolopia, but differing in its opposite leaves, 2 or 3-ovuled ovary and capsular fruits. Pseudoscolopia polyantha bears some resemblance to Cassipourea flanaganii (Schinz) Alston of the family Rhizophoraceae with which it has sometimes been confused.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Subsp. baurii is usually taller than subsp. formosa and mostly 350-500 high, with slightly smaller bright pink flowers with tepals 12-18 mm long. The spikes also have several to many more flowers than subsp. formosa, as many as 15 to 18 vs. 2 to 6. Although intermediates between the two subspecies have been recorded, the presence of both at one site is puzzling indicating a need for additional research.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The leaves of young coppice shoots are much thinner than the adult leaves, the petioles are shorter and the hairy pockets in the leaf axils are more conspicuous. In the southern part of the Kruger National Park there is a form with densely tomentulose leaves and branchlets represented by Codd 5257, Codd & De Winter 5161, Van der Schijff 2507, etc. This form resembles H. chasei Wild from Rhodesia in its pubescence, but has the paniculate inflorescence of H. dentatum. According to a note on Hutchinson 1848 the flowers of H. dentatum 'smell like sweet chestnut.'
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A clear-cut species with smaller leaves than H. dentatum.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognised by the large, pale blue-mauve flowers with a deep, wide, pale yellow floral cup that includes the filaments, these entirely united in a cylindric column. The anthers are initially contiguous and appressed to the style, later becoming slightly divergent distally. The style divides opposite the middle of anthers and the slender branches lack crests and do not reach the tips of the anthers. Plants have several, relatively broad leaves up to 40 mm wide, trailing distally and with undulate margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the branched stem bearing two to four foliage leaves, and moderate-sized, blue to blue-mauve, violet or rarely white flowers with style branches as narrow and as long as or slightly longer than the anthers and lacking style crests. The ascending tepal claws diverge slightly to form a relatively narrow cup that includes the filaments and the lower part of the anthers or all of the anthers, and the tepal limbs spread more-or-less horizontally. The filaments are united in a slender, smooth column usually 7-9 mm long. A notable variant of the species from near Albertinia and Herbertsdale in southern Western Cape has slightly smaller, white or pale blue flowers with the filaments only 5-6 mm long, and both filaments and anthers are included in the floral cup whereas the anthers are usually fully excluded from the cup in typical M. polyanthos. The species is closely allied to M. bipartita, which has conventional Moraea-type flowers with broad style branches with prominent crests but the two are identical in vegetative features. Hybrids between these two species have been recorded where they co-occur.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Aristea cistiflora is evidently most closely related to A. teretifolia, which also has the outer tepals with dark markings, the markings extending to the middle of the tepals in A. teretifolia versus close to the base in A. cistiflora. Aristea teretifolia is additionally distinguished by the leaves sometimes terete or linear and up to 2 mm wide, the flowering stem bearing at most two lateral flower clusters (versus up to six in A. cistiflora), and by the slightly smaller flowers with ascending tepals, the outer ± 20 mm long and the inner 24-28 mm long, thus substantially longer than the outer. In A. cistiflora the inner tepals are only 1-2 mm longer than the outer.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is recognised by its low stature, combined with relatively broad stem and leaves, these rather firm and more leathery, and by the long, angular ovary and elongate capsules 20-30 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Among the species with truncate foliage, Babiana cuneata is distinguished by the elongate perianth tube, 40-60 mm long, more-or-less equal, ascending tepals 26-30(-40) mm long, and a pale blue to violet, fragrant or apparently odourless flower. The stamens are openly displayed, with filaments 15-18 mm long and exserted 9-10 mm. The point of division of the style varies. In the type population the style branches opposite the base of the anthers but in plants to the south, below the Roggeveld Escarpment, it reaches the anther apices before branching. Flowering occurs from early August to late September. Babiana flabellifolia has, in contrast, strongly scented bilabiate flowers with an arched dorsal tepal more-or-less concealing the stamens, a perianth tube 18-36 mm long, and often dry, submembranous, or occasionally green, leafy bracts. In specimens where it is possible to see floral details, the style divides opposite the anther apices. Flowering in B. flabellifolia occurs from late June through July, rarely in early August in seasons when the rains are late or conditions are particularly cold. The flowers of B. cuneata closely resemble those of B. sambucina, which is widespread across the dry interior of the Cape Floral Region, but absent from the Roggeveld. Plants at the southern end of the range, in the Klein Roggeveld south of Komsberg Pass, have unusually large flowers with the dorsal tepal ± 40 mm long, the anthers 9-11 mm long, and the style is also unusual in dividing opposite the anther apices rather than opposite their bases. Plants also seem unusual in the blue-grey colour of the leaves, often 20-30 mm wide, likewise exceptional for the species. At present, however, there appears no reason to recognise these as a separate taxon.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Babiana planifolia has nearly plane leaves, occasionally lightly undulate toward the base, and corm tunics of relatively fine texture. Plants have cobwebby to woolly cataphylls and lower leaf sheaths and the leaf blades are sparsely long-hairy on the veins or are virtually hairless. Like B. striata the stem and bracts are usually hairless and the lower lateral tepals appear to lack the prominent auriculate lobes typical of most other species of sect. Antholyzoides, including B. striata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A little known species very closely related to S. rara. Acocks 17290 from Lokenburg, Calvinia, is closest to S. membranacea in external appearance, but the anthers are without glands, the style is 3.5-3.75 mm long with a small stigmatic swelling below the middle. The calyx-segments have broad wings which are somewhat papillose along the margins.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W; Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Gentianaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 171-243. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Bulbine retinens is at once distinguished from the other dwarf, cluster-forming, cliff-dwelling Bulbine species by its erect linear leaves arising from a short neck, its ovate tubers covered with fibrous, reticulate remains of leaf bases, and its peculiar mode of seed-retention.
bibliographicCitation: Hammer, SA; Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2005. Bulbine retinens, a new cliff-dweller from the Eastern Cape. Aloe 42(1&2): 14-15. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the loosely aggregated bulb scales that are narrowed or stalked below, and the linear, stiffly spreading leaves up to 2.5 mm wide that are channelled above with thickened, colliculate-cartilaginous margins.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: S. albidiflora (Labill.) F.v.M. from Australia is very closely related to S. minutiflora.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W; Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Gentianaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 171-243. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Its short, broad leaves (35-80 x 14-25 mm) and perianth with a globose to globose-ovoid, gasteriform portion of 6-8 mm in diameter, immediately separate it from G. bicolor var. liliputana and G. baylissiana.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2004. Gasteria doreeniae: A new species form the Eastern Cape. Aloe 41(4): 81-83. [All rights reserved]

description: Evidently allied to the two other southern African Drakensberg species that flower early in the season at which time the foliage leaves are dry or withered, with the new season’s leaves appearing on separate shoots later in the year, Hesperantha crocopsis and H. schelpeana. It is most like H. schelpeana in its fairly large flowers but differs in having a perianth tube 20-27 mm long and uniformly creamy white perianth, whereas H. schelpeana has whitish or pink flowers with the outer tepals flushed to uniformly darker pink to purple on the outside, and a perianth tube 5-10 mm long. Hesperantha crocopsis has smaller flowers, the tepals only 6-7 mm long but a perianth tube 9-14 mm long, and like H. schelpeana, the outer tepals are red to purple on the outside. Foliage leaves are lacking on flowering specimens, but plants from ridges west of Thaba Ntlenyana in Lesotho that appear to be H. altimontana have a distinctive, falcate leaf with a plane blade like no other known member of the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Poorly collected and often confused either with the widespread Hesperantha radiata or the related western Karoo species H. marlothii, H. decipiens is distinguished by the few-flowered, flexuose spike with the outer bract margins united around the axis only near the base, and corms without prominent lateral spines. Hesperantha decipiens has the flexuose, few(or several)-flowered spike of H. marlothii but the outer bract margins in that species are united for up to 4 mm, ± a third of their length. The corms in H. marlothii bear prominent lateral spines, whereas those of H. decipiens closely resemble H. radiata in their scalloped, lightly fringed lobes. Close examination of the flowers shows that the style branches of H. decipiens usually exceed the anthers by 1-2 mm and the anthers are 5-7 mm long. Robust specimens of H. marlothii have anthers 6-8 mm long and the style branches reach only to about the middle of the anthers. Less robust specimens have anthers 4.5-6.0 mm long but the style branches are still slightly short of the anther apices. Hesperantha radiata has the outer bract margins united for ± half their length, and a straight spike usually bearing >8 flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unexceptional in its vegetative aspect and flowers, Hesperantha inconspicua stands out among the eastern southern African species in its relatively tall stature, mostly 400-600 mm high, and white perianth (sometimes faintly flushed pink on the reverse of the outer tepals). Among the few other white- or cream-flowered species of eastern southern Africa, H. inconspicua can be confused with the coastal KwaZulu-Natal species H. lactea, which has creamy yellow flowers and dull yellow to brownish anthers and pollen. The leaves of the two species are virtually identical, both having thickened margins and a lightly raised, rounded midrib, with the other veins obscure and not visible when alive. The related H. saxicola, which also has white flowers, often fading pink, stands out both in its shorter stature and unusual habitat, rock outcrops and cliffs. These plants have drooping leaves and stems 100-180 mm long, and flexuose spikes of up to five large flowers with tepals mostly 15-16 x 7 mm and anthers ± 4 mm long. Hesperantha inconspicua often has smaller flowers with tepals 12-15 mm long but longer anthers, 6.5-8.0 mm long, and 6-12 flowers per spike. Hesperantha hygrophila, also with white flowers, has very different leaves with the margins thickened and main vein raised and flattened into wings held parallel to the blade surface.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its short stature, up to 50 mm tall, soft-textured, spreading to drooping leaves, and a 1- to 3-flowered spike of moderate-sized white flowers. The relatively large corms have an oblique flat side and ± concentric tunics, and most closely resemble those of H. acuta, suggesting a possible relationship with this interior Western Cape and western Karoo species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Among the elongate-tubed and pink-flowered species of Hesperantha of eastern southern Africa, H. ste-nosiphon stands out in the radially symmetric flowers with a nearly straight perianth tube 45-60 mm long, and dark brown to nearly back anthers but yellow pollen. The filaments are comparatively short, ± 3 mm long whereas the anthers are 9-10 mm long. It is probably most closely allied to long-tubed H. grandiflora and H. woodii and shares with them linear leaves with lightly to moderately thickened margins and midribs as well as the pink perianth. Hesperantha grandiflora has nodding flowers with vertically oriented tepals and unilateral, declinate stamens and style branches, filaments 8-14 mm long, and red-brown to purple anthers and pollen; and H. woodii has similarly large, but nearly upright, radially symmetric flowers with filaments 6-8 mm long and yellow anthers and pollen.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Decumbent, much-branched, rose-scented subshrub. Lamina 3-5-palmatilobate to 3-5-palmatipar-tite, crisped, villous to densely villous. Pseudo-umbels capitulum-like, with 8-20 flowers each. Flowers pale pink to dark pink-purple, pedicels much shorter than hypanthium. P. capitatum is closely related to P. vitifolium (L.)L'Herit. and the differences between these two species are tabulated under P. vitifolium. The villous leaves of P. capitatum can also be confused with those of P. tomentosum Jacq., but they have a completely different odour, the leaves of P. capitatum being rose scented and those of P. tomentosum having a peppermint scent. Furthermore, the inflorescences and flowers of these two species differ markedly.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the relatively crowded spike of large flowers and the pink perianth with a large, glossy black centre. Unusual for sect. Ixia the black bases of the tepals are united in a wide cup ±3 mm deep. The stamens and style branches are also darkly pigmented with the erect filaments clasping the style and the anthers diverging. Significantly, the style divides above the bases of the anthers. The lower two leaves are lanceolate and comparatively broad, up to 10 mm wide and the third leaf sheathes the stem for its entire length. It has been confused with I. gloriosa and was at first included in that species, perhaps due to the flower colour, although I. gloriosa has deep magenta flowers with a blackish centre when seen alive. Differences between the two, apart from perianth colour, include leaf width (leaves of I. gloriosa are linear and only up to 3 mm wide), shape of the flowers and the short, erect branches of I. gloriosa in contrast to the spreading branches of I. superba. The style of I. gloriosa divides opposite the bases of the filaments unlike that in I. superba. Both species have the outer floral bracts 3-toothed, sometimes with the central tooth somewhat more prominent.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Time has been considered a form of P. grossularioides (Linn.) Ait., but is distinguished from that in all the leaves being tripartite, the smaller flowers, and the broad fruit with very short rostrum.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1932. Notes on the Flora of southern Africa: II. New or noteworthy plants. Bull. Misc. Inform. Kew 1932(9): 443-450. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4113490] [All rights reserved]

description: Ornithogalum juncifolium var. emsii is at once distinguished from the typical variety by its proliferous production of bulbils at the base of the bulb and its flowering time which is from December to January. Var. juncifolium flowers from spring to early summer and has slightly smaller flowers (tepals 7-10 mm long) and does not have the dense basal proliferation of small bulbils.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2005. Hyacinthaceae: Ornithogalum juncifolium var.emsii, a new cliff-dwelling Ornithogalum from Eastern Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 35(1): 82-84. [CC BY]

description: This has much the look of the South African Plectronia spinosa, Klotzsch, among other points of difference being the lanceolate leaves, the smaller ovary and corolla hairy at the throat. From spinous forms of P. ventosa, Linn., which it still more closely resembles, it can be easily told by the fasciculate (not corymbose) inflorescences and the smaller flowers with exserted stigma.
bibliographicCitation: Swynnerton, CFM; Rendle, AB; Baker, EG; Moore, SLM; Gepp, A. 1911. A contribution to our knowledge of the flora of Gazaland: Being an account of collections made by C.F.M. Swynnerton. J. Linn. Soc., Bot. 40(275): 1-245. [All rights reserved]

description: Erect shrublet; branches thin; bark pale, waxy, often with vertical stretch markings; spines dark brown to almost black, thin and perfectly straight. Leaves entire, glaucous, apex emarginate to obcordate. Sepals with a mucro longer than 2 mm. Petals slightly longer than broad, cadmium lemon to pyrethrum yellow. Mericarp: base longer than 13 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Moffett, RO. 1979. The genus Sarcocaulon. Bothalia 12(4): 581-613. [CC BY]

description: Superficially P. anethifolium resembles some forms of P. triste (Linnaeus) L'Heritier on account of the division of the lamina into very narrow linear segments; but it is readily distinguished by the lamina being less than 2x instead of at least 2x as long as wide, by the indumentum of the lamina being inconspicuous to the naked eye instead of mostly densely hirsute (at least in narrow-segmented forms), and having 6 instead of 7 fertile stamens. In P. multiradiatum Wendland the lamina is also divided into linear segments; but in that species the segments are conspicuously wider (up to 3 mm wide), and the plant is altogether much larger with lamina up to 450 x 450 mm and up to 15 or even 30 flowers per pseudo-umbel. In addition, at least the lowermost regments branch off the rachis at close to a right angle, whereas in P. anethifolium they branch off at an acute angle. In P. multiradiatum we observed only 5 fertile stamens per flower, in contrast to 6 in P. anethifolium. The flowering period is much shorter than in P. triste, which flowers almost throughout the year.
bibliographicCitation: Maggs, GL; Vorster, PJ; Van der Walt, JJA; Gibby, M. 1999. Taxonomy of the genus Pelargonium (Geraniaceae): the section Polyactium   3. The subsection Polyactium. S. African J. Bot. 65(3): 115-143. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1999); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: C. suberosum is allied to C. ventosum (L.) S. Moore, of which C. inerme (L.f.) Kuntze is regarded as a synonym, but differs in several respects. C. ventosum shows a tendency to be scandent with longish internodes and spine-like branchlets, and the bark on the older twigs is smooth and longitudinally wrinkled, somewhat waxy and not powdery or corky, while the bark on the main trunk never becomes thickly corky; the leaves are more or less ovate, in outline, obtuse at the base and acute to acuminate at the apex and are relatively thin in texture; and the inflorescence is usually branched and many-flowered. C. suberosum, on the other hand, is never scandent, but has thickish, brittle branches with shorter internodes and more conspicuously thickened nodes; the bark on the older twigs is scurfy, cracking into a more or less rectangular network while on the main trunk the bark often becomes conspicuously corky with age; the leaves are elliptic to oblanceolate-obovate in shape, cuneate at the base and obtuse to rounded at the apex, greyish and relatively thick in texture; and the inflorescences are few-flowered and subsessile. There is also a difference in distribution with C. ventosum scattered from the Cape Peninsula, through the eastern Cape Province, Natal, Swaziland and the eastern and northern Transvaal to Rhodesia and Mozambique, while C. suberosum is essentially a species of the wooded quartzite and granite formations of the central Transvaal plateau, with outliers in western Swaziland.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1967. Rubiaceae: A new species of Canthium. Bothalia 9(2): 345-346. [CC BY]

description: Erect to decumbent, branched to much-branched, non-aromatic shrub or subshrub. Lamina circular to broadly elliptic to ovate, flat, veins depressed, margin rather coarsely dentate to serrate. Pseudo-umbels with 2-6 relatively large, pink to purplish flowers each, pedicel usually longer than hypanthium. There is a resemblance between the flowers of P. betulinum and P. cucullatum (L.) L'Herit., but their leaves differ markedly, those of the latter species being larger, hairy and more or less hood-shaped. A natural hybrid between these two species has been recorded. Superficially, the flowers and leaves of P. betulinum resemble those of P. elegans (Andr.) Willd. of the section Campylia, but the habit of these two species differs completely. Whitish flowers of P. betulinum have been recorded from plants occurring in Llandudno on the Cape Peninsula, and also from those growing on the hard, lime-rich dunes of De Hoop Nature Reserve near Bredasdorp. Plants collected in the Mossel Bay-Knysna areas, show a much coarser leaf margin than those from the south-western Cape.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: The erect, fan-shaped leaf arrangement and dorsifixed anthers of S. luteoloba are sufficiently distinctive to place the species in subgenus Strumaria, but unlike most species in the subgenus, the filaments of S. luteoloba are not proximally fused into a tube. Like S. phonolithica the new species has narrow, closely imbricate tepals. However, S. luteoloba is easily recognized by the tepals being deeply channelled and sharply reflexed from ± halfway along their length, and by the outer tepal whorl reflexing 2-4 mm below the inner whorl so that the perigone has a distinctive biseriate appearance. The flower colour is also unique in the genus. The perigone is pinkish red near the base and pale lemon- to cream-coloured in the distal half. S. gemmata Ker Gawl., belonging to subgenus Gemmaria, is the only other species with lemon- or cream-coloured flowers but these are stellate and concolorous.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 2005. Three new species and a new synonym in Strumaria (Amaryllidaceae: Amaryllideae) from southern Africa. Bothalia 35(1&2): 21-27. [CC BY]

description: Canthium vanwykii is a clear-cut species easily distinguished by a combination mainly of inflorescence and floral characters. These include the multiflowered inflorescences, predominantly pentamerous (rarely tetramerous or hexamerous) flowers, a relatively short corolla tube with the mouth not constricted - thus rendering the whole disc visible from above - and relatively long corolla lobes exceeding the length of the tube. The leaves are usually broadly ovate or broadly elliptic and distinctly petiolate. Pubescence is largely confined to the petiole, the midrib and usually also to some of the larger secondary veins. The hairs, however, are minute and scarcely visible to the unaided eye. Domatia are usually present. Although some of the aforementioned characters are present in other southern African species of Canthium, none displays the above combination. The wide mouth of the funnel-shaped corolla tube is perhaps the most noticeable character by which to separate C. vanwykii from all the other southern African members of the genus. Vegetatively, C. vanwykii superficially resembles C. ciliatum (Eckl. & Zeyh.) Kuntze. Both species are spinose and may occasionally be found in close proximity in the veld. However, C. vanwykii prefers a sunny habitat and in the forest is very rarely encountered away from the margin. C. ciliatum is not as strictly confined to the forest margin and often occurs as an undercanopy component in shady conditions. In an anatomical study of Canthium s.l. in southern Africa (Tilney 1986), it was found that C. vanwykii resembles in some respects certain specimens of C. ciliatum - a species showing blade. In the 21 specimens of C. ciliatum examined the range obtained was (70 - )130-190(-440)pm, whereas in C. vanwykii the range was (170-)220-310 pm. Apart from the midrib and principal lateral veins, the lamina is nearly always glabrous in C. vanwykii. Characteristically the whole lamina surface is pubescent in C. ciliatum. Studies of the pollen grains (Anastassiades 1983; Tilney 1986) did not reveal any significant differences between C. vanwykii and C. ciliatum. The grains of these species are similar in many respects to the other native members of Canthium s.str. C. vanwykii is the third member of the Rubiaceae known to be endemic to the southern Natal/Pondoland sandstone region. The other two species are Tricalysia africana (Sim) Robbrecht and Anthospermum streyi Puff. Although not an endemic, the monotypic grassland suffrutex, Eriosemopsis subanisophylla Robyns, has its centre of distribution in this region.
bibliographicCitation: Tilney, PM; Kok, PDF. 1987. A new species of Canthium (Rubiaceae) from southern Natal and Pondoland. S. African J. Bot. 53(1): 98-102. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1987); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Decumbent to procumbent subshrub, lamina sericeous, greyish-green, trilobate to trisect to trifoliolate with the terminal segment/pinna much larger and variously incised. Pseudo-umbels with 1-4 flowers each. Flowers with 4 white to pink petals, posterior two with dark red markings, anterior two with a pink blotch, fertile stamens 5.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA; Boucher, C. 1986. A taxonomix revision of the section Myrrhidium of Pelargonium (Geraniaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 52(2): 438-462. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1986); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Closely similar to P brevirostre, but differs in their allopatric distribution, peduncle lengths, and flower characters. Pelargonium capituliforme occurs in Lesotho and surrounding areas in South Africa, and has relatively short peduncles [9-21(-27) mm long], hypanthia equal or shorter than the pedicels, and pink-reddish calyx lobes, whereas P. brevirostre occurs further south in the Western and Eastern Cape, the peduncles are (24-)35-92 mm long, hypanthia invariably longer than the pedicels, and the calyx lobes green-coloured.
bibliographicCitation: Le Roux, MM. 2019. A taxonomic revision of the southern African species of Pelargonium section Peristera (Geraniaceae). Phytotaxa 418(2): 119-157. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.418.2.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Erect, much-branched, strongly lemon-scented shrub. Lamina palmatifid to palmatisect, sparsely hirsute to hispid. Flowering branches profusely branched. Pseudo-umbels with 5-8 pinkish-purple flowers each, pedicel usually longer than hypanthium. P. citronellum exhibits many leaf characters which are intermediate between those of P. scabrum (L.) L'Herit, and P. hispidum (L.f.) Willd. The leaves of P. citronellum are less scabrous and more strongly lemon-scented than those of P. scabrum. Those of P. hispidum are aromatic but not lemon-scented, and less scabrous, than those of P. citronellum. Most of the herbarium specimens of P. citronellum collected by previous workers, have been identified as P. scabrum. This error could be ascribed to the similarity which exists between the leaves of the two species. However, the flowers of these two species differ considerably. The flowers of P. citronellum are much larger and darker in colour than those of P. scabrum. The latter is a very variable species with a large distributional range stretching from the north-western Cape to the southern Cape. The southern Cape form of P. scabrum resembles P. citronellum much more than the western Cape form, and it is possible that P. citronellum evolved from this form. P. scabrum is also known as a species which hybridizes easily with other species, and it is therefore also possible that P. citronellum originated as a natural hybrid between P. scabrum and P. hispidum. A natural hybrid between P. citronellum and P. hispidum has been recorded (Van der Walt, 1124 in STEU).
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Often shorter than subsp. edulis and distinguished by the mostly darker flowers with acute or very shortly attenuate tepals. Gladiolus uitenhagensis has very similar flowers, pale in colour with a longer perianth tube, 22-35 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is named after Matt Buys, University of Stellenbosch, who accompanied the first author on several field trips, on one of which the new species was collected. Since Jacquin's description of Pelargonium columbinum, all resembling specimens were included in this species. This resulted in P. columbinum being regarded as a species with a high morphological variability. However, although closely related to P. columbinum, P. buysii is a distinct species. Although both exhibit a rosulate growth form, P. buysii is more compact, prostrate and richly leaved. The flower-bearing stems of P. buysii are prostrate whereas those of P. columbinum are almost erect. Furthermore, the leaves and bracts of P. buysii are thinner and more incised. The two species also differ in flower and fruit sizes: the purple and well-developed hypanthium off! columbinum is 1.5-4(-6) mm long, the petals (6-7 x 1.5-2 mm) are distinctly longer than the sepals, and the androecium and gynoecium are up to 4.5 mm long. In contrast, the hypanthium of P. buysii is only 0.5-1.5 mm long, and the petals (3-4 x 0.8-1 mm) do not overtop the sepals. The androecium and gynoecium are also smaller in sizes (2.5-3 mm). Finally, P. buysii is characterized by the white stigma branches, which are in strong contrast to the purple ones of P. columbinum. P. buysii (Van der Walt 1628) and P. columbinum (Albers 2156) have the same chromosome number (2n=22) and a similar karyotype length, but artificial cross pollination was undertaken without success, although successful hybridization attempts between different species of Pelargonium do occur. These two autogamous annuals are predominantly sympatrically distributed in the Western Cape and show similar demands to the habitats. Nevertheless, P. columbinum is more common and can also be found at higher altitudes (200-1 900 m).
bibliographicCitation: Albers, F; Hellbrugge, D; Vorster, PJ. 1996. A new small-flowered Pelargonium species (Geraniaceae) from the Western Cape Province, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 62(3): 143-145. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1996); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Strongly lemon-scented subshrub or shrub. Lamina reniform, 3-palmatilobate to 3-palmatisect, crisped, strigose, base cordate. Pseudo-umbels with 1-2(-3) flowers each. Flowers white to dark pink or almost purple, anterior petals much narrower than posterior ones, pedicel usually shorter than hypanthium. The relationship between P. crispum and P. hermanniifolium (Berg.) Jacq. is discussed under the latter species. The leaves of P. crispum can also be confused with those of P. englerianum Knuth. Differences between these two species are tabulated: P. crispum - 1. Leaves lemon-scented. 2. Leaves strigose. 3. Lamina crisped and relatively small. 4. Young stems green. 5. Flowers relatively large. P. englerianum - 1. Leaves rose-camphor-scented. 2. Leaves hispid. 3. Lamina less crisped and larger. 4. Young stems purplish. 5. Flowers relatively small.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Erect, much-branched, non-aromatic shrub. Lamina circular, reniform or triangular in outline, with or without shallow angular incisions, villous or strigose, flat to hood-shaped at base. Pseudo-umbels with (1-)3-6(-13) flowers each. Flowers relatively large, pale pink to dark pinkish-purple, pedicel usually as long as hypanthium.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Erect, much-branched, balm-scented, viscid shrub. Lamina pinnatisect to palmatisect with pinnatisect segments, segments narrow and adaxially grooved, apices acute, apices of teeth acute, sparsely strigose. Peduncles distinctly articulated, pseudo-umbels with 3-9 flowers each. Flowers relatively small, pinkish-purple, pedicel shorter than hypanthium. Inflorescence and floral characters indicate a very close relationship between P. denticulatum and P. glutinosum (Jacq.) L'Herit. The leaves of these two species are both viscid and they have the same balm scent.
