However, the leaves of P. glutinosum are less divided (pinnatisect) and the leaf segments consequently much wider than those of P. denticulatum. The leaves of P. denticulatum could also be confused with those of P. radens H.E. Moore. The differences between the leaves of these two species are tabulated under P. radens.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Pelargonium dispar is rather distinct in its upright, herbaceous habit. It is most closely related to P mossambicense Engler (1895: 225) (also subgenus Parvulipetalum and unassigned at sectional level), but differs in having an upright, smaller habit (up to 0.2 mm in diam.), and an allopatric distribution where it is endemic to South Africa [P mossambicense has a decumbent, spreading habit, up to 1 m in diam., and occurs in southern Zimbabwe and Mozambique]. Both these taxa somewhat resemble P album, but this species has a succulent habit, and compound pseudo-umbellate inflorescences, whereas P. dispar and P. mossambicense have herbaceous habits, and simple inflorescences
bibliographicCitation: Le Roux, MM. 2019. A taxonomic revision of the southern African species of Pelargonium section Peristera (Geraniaceae). Phytotaxa 418(2): 119-157. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.418.2.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Erect to decumbent, much-branched, rose-camphor-scented subshrub, young stems purplish and villous. Lamina reniform, more or less crisped, hispid. Pseudo-umbels with 2-5 flowers each. Flowers white to pinkish-purple, relatively small, pedicel longer than hypanthium. In the past, most herbarium specimens of P. englerianum have been erroneously identified as P. crispum (Berg.) L'Herit. These errors can be ascribed to the similarities which exist between the leaves of the two species. The differences between P. englerianum and P. crispum are given under the latter species.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Forms with less distinctly recurved leaf blades should not be confused with the allied C. vaginellata. C. heteromorpha is easily distinguished by the rather long whitish hairs on the stipular sheaths and lower half of the leaf blades, by having flowers with unusually long corolla tubes and by its ± round fruits crowned by 4 long calyx lobes; both flowers and fruits are usually hidden amongst the dense foliage and plants give the impression of being permanently in a vegetative state.
bibliographicCitation: Puff, C. 1986. Paederiaceae, Anthospermae, Rubieae, Fl. S. Africa 31(1,2): 1-75. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209569#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This species is undoubtedly closely related to those of the subsection Polyactium, as manifested by its basic chromosome number of x=11, the morphologically similar flowers, the unusual dusk-scentedness of the flowers, and the pale yellow pigmentation of the petals. Yet its unusually strong stem development above ground level, which lends the plant a shrubby appearance, and its lack of an underground tuber, places it apart from the other species, for which reason we retain it in a separate subsection.
bibliographicCitation: Maggs, GL; Vorster, PJ; Van der Walt, JJA. 1995. Taxonomy of the genus Pelargonium (Geraniaceae): the section Polyactium   2. The subsection Caulescentia. S. African J. Bot. 61(4): 173-179. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1995); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: It is similar to P. grossularioides, but differs in the consistent pubescent-pilose indumentum, lobed leaves, and short pedicels (0-3 mm long). Pelargonium grossularioides has a pubescent or puberulous indumentum or it is glabrous, the leaves are variously lobed and incised, and the pedicels are 2-9 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Le Roux, MM. 2019. A taxonomic revision of the southern African species of Pelargonium section Peristera (Geraniaceae). Phytotaxa 418(2): 119-157. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.418.2.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Erect, much-branched, strongly balm-scented, viscid shrub. Lamina 3-palmatilobate to pinnatisect, glabrescent. Peduncles distinctly articulated, pseudo-umbels with 1-8 flowers each. Flowers pale pink to dark pink, pedicel shorter than hypanthium. It is an extremely variable species, both as far as the leaves and flowers are concerned. Three forms can be distinguished: (a) Plants from the western part of the distribution area have deeply incised leaves and pale pink flowers. The flower buds are distinctly pear-shaped. This form was described as P. erectum by Knuth. Plants from northern Transvaal show a strong resemblance to this form, although the flowers are smaller and the hypanthium, especially, is much shorter. (b) Plants from the Karoo regions have less incised leaves and pink flowers. (c) Plants from the eastern part of the distribution area have shallowly incised leaves with dark pink flowers. The distribution of these three forms is by no means disjunct and a continuous variation pattern of leaf and floral characters occurs. It is therefore not possible to recognize infraspecific taxa although considerable differences exist between the extreme forms. The leaves of P. denticulatum Jacq., P. panduriforme Eckl. & Zeyh. and P. quercifolium (L.f.) L'Herit. are also viscid and emit the same balm scent as P. glutinosum. Inflorescence and floral characters-indicate a very close relationship between P. glutinosum and P. denticulatum.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Superficially, C. scabra often closely resembles C. vaginellata but the latter is distinguished vegetatively by its long, funnel-shaped stipular sheaths [(1.5-)2-3(-4) mm vs. 0.5-1 mm long].
bibliographicCitation: Puff, C. 1986. Paederiaceae, Anthospermae, Rubieae, Fl. S. Africa 31(1,2): 1-75. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209569#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Erect, much-branched, non-aromatic to aromatic shrub. Lamina cordiform, shallowly 3-(5-8)-pal-matilobate to palmatipartite, hirtellous and with long hairs interspersed. Pseudo-umbels with 2-9 flowers each. Flowers white to pale pink, anterior three petals much narrower than posterior two, pedicel relatively thin and longer than hypanthium. P. greytonense is probably of hybrid origin with the sympatric P. hermanniifolium (Berg.) Jacq. and P. papilionaceum (L.)L'Herit. as possible parent species. Many characters of P. greytonense, such as the shape and indumentum of the leaves, are intermediate between these two species. There is also evidence of backcrossing between P. greytonense and P. hermanniifolium. The habitat requirements of P. greytonense are also between those of the two putative parent species: P. papilionaceum growing in a rather moist, semi-shaded habitat and P. hermanniifolium in drier situations with direct sunlight.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: T. barberae and its close allies appear to have evolved allopatrically in river gorges of the eastern seaboard of South Africa. An undescribed subspecies of T. barberae occurs along the Bashee River in the Eastern Cape. T. barberae grows along the Fish River Valley as a xerophyte in karroid scrub (the type locality is recorded as ‘Orange River Colony’ but this is very improbable. Similarly, T. tuberosa is restricted to Valley Bushveld of incised dry gorges of the KwaZulu-Natal midlands.
bibliographicCitation: Edwards, TJ. 2006. Notes on the Lamiaceae: A new Tetradenia and a new Thorncroftia from South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 72: 202-204. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2006); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: P. lucidus is closely related to P. verticillatus (L.f.) Druce and P. strigosus Benth. (section Plectranthus series Plectranthus), it is distinguished by its 2-flowered verticillasters and short corolla (9-11 mm) of which the lower lip margins are conspicuously inrolled. In both P. strigosus and P. lucidus the corolla is constricted at the throat, unlike P. verticillatus where the corolla is linear. It shares its habitat with other shade-loving coastal plant species such as P. madagascariensis and Scadoxus membranaceus.
bibliographicCitation: Edwards, TJ; Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 1997. Notes on Plectranthus (Lamiaceae) from southern Africa. Bothalia 27: 1-6. [CC BY]

description: Characterized by the long pedicels, (80-)100-200 mm long, with the bracteole inserted between one third and three-quarters along, and white or pale pink flowers flushed darker pink on the reverse. the anthers are uniformly yellow anthers, with the upper cluster free or coherent. Plants are often well grown, producing 3-9 flowers. The position of the bracteoles in the distal half of the pedicels distinguishes the subpsecies from subsp. minor from the Tanqua Basin to the south, which has the bracteoles sub-basal.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. A revision of Tecophilaeaceae subfam. Tecophilaeoideae in Africa. Bothalia 42(1): 21-41. [CC BY]

description: Related to Aloe soutpansbergensis I.Verd. from which it is distinguished by its slightly glaucous bluish-green subterete leaves and dense clusters of smaller shortly racemose or sub-capitate inflorescences, subclavate perianth 25 mm long and floral bracts 8-9 x 4 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2006. Aloe challisii, a new cliff-dwelling aloe from Mpumalanga, and a checklist of the obligate cliff-dwelling aloes in South Africa and Namibia. Aloe 43(2&3): 36-41. [All rights reserved]

description: Evidently most closely related to the other long-tubed Babiana species of sect. Teretifolieae, B. carminea has a spike borne at ground level, finely and shortly hairy leaves, floral bracts 40-50 mm long, and flowers with an elongate perianth tube, 56-60 mm long. The primary distinction between the long-tubed species of this alliance is in the flowers, which closely reflect their pollination ecology. Babiana dregei and B. framesii have dark blue to violet flowers with white markings, and a slender, straight or curved perianth tube of narrow diameter and both are pollinated by long-proboscid flies. In contrast, the flowers of B. carminea are red to reddish purple with a perianth tube that is slender below and wide and cylindric above.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A dwarf species, Babiana cinnamomea has distinctive, broadly ovate leaves with undulate and crisped margins unique in the genus, and the floral bracts are unusual in being largely dry, thinly papery in texture, and pale straw in colour with minute light brown flecks over the surface. Even in full bloom B. cinnamomea is inconspicuous, for the pale bluish green to pale yellow flowers are borne close to the ground and are easily overlooked. The flowers have a particularly strong, sweet, spicy scent, reminiscent of cinnamon and clove, produced during the day and at night, a feature more noticeable than the drab flower colour and suggesting moth pollination. Like many other species of Babiana with highly modified leaves, the juvenile foliage is very different. Seedlings and plants with immature corms have slender, linear leaves that bear a few long soft hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Pelargonium lobatum is a distinctive species, and this is reflected in its limited synonymy. It belongs in the section Polyactium DC, which is characterized by having a series of massive underground tubers. Three groups of species can be distinguished in this section, viz. the P. luridum complex with pink, white, or yellowish petals and occurring in the temperate summer rainfall area of southern Africa; the P. schizopetalum group of species which have fimbriate petals and occur in the summer rainfall areas along the east coast of South Africa (e.g. P. bowkeri Harv.); and finally the group of mainly winter rainfall species to which the subject of this plate belongs. Within the last-named group, P. lobatum is distinguished by its lobed to pinnate, more or less procumbent, pronouncedly herbaceous and sericeous leaves. The colour of the petals is variable: in some specimens the dark pigmentation in the centres of the petals may extend almost to the margins, leaving only the narrowest yellowish outline round the petals, whereas in other specimens the dark pigmentation is almost absent so that the petals are of a dirty fleshy yellow colour. The shape of the leaves also varies in the degree of lobing. Little-lobed leaves are often the first leaves of the current growing season, and may bear little resemblance to the deeply lobed or pinnate leaves formed later in the season. It bears some resemblance to P. pulverulentum Sweet, a species with leathery, glaucous leaves from the eastern summer rainfall area of South Africa of which the taxonomic delimitation is still obscure. Although the present author could not detect it, the flowers are said to emit a distinctive cinnamon-like scent at dusk, hence the vernacular name Kaneelblom. This suggests that it is pollinated by a dusk- or night-flying insect, probably a moth with a long proboscis which can be inserted down the nectar tube.
bibliographicCitation: Vorster, PJ; Kimpton, J. 1986. Pelargonium lobatum (Burm.f.) L'Hér. Fl. Pl. Africa 49t.1924 [CC BY]

description: Procumbent to decumbent subshrub; lamina glabrous to pubescent to sparsely hirsute, green, pinnatifid to bipinnatisect. Pseudo-umbels with 2-6 flowers each. Flowers with 4 or 5 white, pink, lilac to pinkish-purple petals, hypanthium 4-10 mm long, fertile stamens 5 or 7.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA; Boucher, C. 1986. A taxonomix revision of the section Myrrhidium of Pelargonium (Geraniaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 52(2): 438-462. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1986); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from B. nana by the larger flower with a longer perianth tube 23-30 mm long, subequal tepals, longer anthers, 8-9 mm long, and sparsely hairy to smooth, often glaucous leave.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A dwarf plant, seldom reaching more than 100 mm above the ground, Babiana engysiphon is recognised by its elongate perianth tube, mostly 35-40 mm long, violet perianth with large white markings on the lower lateral tepals and horizontal spike. The several leaves, narrow and almost linear to narrowly sword-shaped and usually lightly pleated or nearly plane and velvety, arch toward the ground and are often close to horizontal. Its immediate relationships are uncertain. The softly hairy ovary and bracts divided to the base or nearly so conform to ser. Mucronatae of sect. Babiana Plants co-occur in some places with Babiana mucronata subsp. minor, which has short-tubed, scented flowers adapted for pollination by anthophorine bees, whereas the odourless flowers of B. engysiphon are pollinated by long-proboscid flies. Despite the difference in pollination system, some hybridization between the two is evident. These plants have a tube of intermediate length and pale yellow rather than white markings on the lower tepals. Babiana engysiphon also co-occurs with B. rigidifolia, but this more robust, broad-leaved plant grows in a different habitat, with the corms wedged in crevices in sandstone pavement.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Schlechter placed this species in the section Cortusina DC. because of its supposed resemblance to Pelargonium echinatum Curt. Although there is an undoubted similarity between these two species, P. magenteum resembles much more closely P. reniforme Curt. (Plate 672 in this series) from the eastern Cape, also in this section and likewise with underground tubers. P. reniforme is, however, clearly distinguished from P. magenteum by its larger leaf blades and much longer petioles, by having more flowers per pseudo-umbel and by the joint between pedicel and hypanthium being exposed above the bracts subtending the pseudo-umbel. It is noteworthy that there is no profound structural difference between P. magenteum, on the one hand, and species such as P. plurisectum Salter, P. abrotanifolium (L.f.) Jacq. and P. exstipulatum (Cav.) L'Herit. of the section Ligularia (Sweet) Harv., on the other. Perhaps this is an indication that the infrageneric classification of Pelargonium should be reconsidered.
bibliographicCitation: Vorster, PJ; Scott, M. 1987. Pelargonium magenteum J.J.A.van der Walt. Fl. Pl. Africa 49t.1947 [CC BY]

description: Closely resembles P minimum, but differs in the plain white flowers, densely appressed pubescent hairs on the calyx, hypanthia that are shorter than the pedicels, 5 fertile stamens, ca. sessile stigma, and smaller, condensed habit (up to 0.45 m in diam.). Pelargonium minimum has white to pink flowers with darker pink venation on the posterior petals, spreading pubescent-villous hairs on the calyx, hypanthia equal or longer than the pedicels, 7 fertile stamens, a style of ca. 2.5 mm in length, and a large, spreading habit (up to 1 m in diam.). There is variation in the leaf shape as was illustrated by Hellbrugge (1997); some populations have leaves that are almost entire and lobed (not incised, e.g. in the Seven Weeks Poort, Koedoesberg and Lykso-Kuruman areas), but others are pinnately or bipinnately incised. Some populations in the Eastern, Northern, and Western Cape have deeply bipinnately incised leaves with leaflets somewhat conduplicate, appearing ‘feathery’ (e.g. Middelburg, Kimberley, Colesberg, and Touws River areas). There is no clear geographical correlation in leaf variation. Populations with bipinnately incised leaves sometimes resemble that of P minimum, but the flower characters are clearly different and can be used to distinguish these the two species.
bibliographicCitation: Le Roux, MM. 2019. A taxonomic revision of the southern African species of Pelargonium section Peristera (Geraniaceae). Phytotaxa 418(2): 119-157. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.418.2.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Currently included in sect. Teretifolieae, which comprises species with apically forked inner bracts, often a more-or-less underground flowering stem and a smooth ovary, Babiana grandiflora is distinctive mainly in its large flower, the perianth tube 18-20 mm long and dorsal tepal 45-55 mm long. The flowers have a strong odour of violets mixed with a spicy acrid odour, a common scent in the genus. Despite the large flowers, the stamens are disproportionately short, with the filaments ± 10 mm long, so that the anthers are held within the floral cup and largely hidden from view inside the funnel-shaped perianth. It may be most closely allied to the Western Cape coastal species, B. nana, but is easily distinguished from that species by the narrow, erect leaves with short, velvety pubescence and the mostly unbranched spikes borne at ground level and bearing 2 to 5 flowers. Babiana grandiflora has in the past been confused with the widespread B. ambigua of deep sands in coastal and inland sites in Western Cape, and although B. grandiflora resembles that species superficially, B. ambigua has inner bracts divided to the base, somewhat smaller flowers with the dorsal tepal 28-40 mm long and longer filaments 13-16 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to P minimum, but differs in having a short, compressed habit in which branches do not spread (as in P. reniforme and P. sidoides), petioles that are only up to 43 mm long, inflorescences upright and always longer than the leaves, and hypanthia 6-8 mm long. The entire plant is covered in a dense pubescence giving it a glaucous-silver appearance. Pelargonium minimum has a procumbent or spreading habit, petioles up to 100 mm long, inflorescences as long as or longer than the leaves with a pubescent-tomentose indumentum, and hypanthia only 2-4 mm long. Pelargonium nelsonii is also similar to P. malacoides, but differs in the erect habit, long hypanthia (longer than the pedicel), and the presence of pink venation on the petals, whereas P malacoides has a spreading habit, hypanthia usually as long as or much shorter than the pedicels, and lacking venation on the petals.
bibliographicCitation: Le Roux, MM. 2019. A taxonomic revision of the southern African species of Pelargonium section Peristera (Geraniaceae). Phytotaxa 418(2): 119-157. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.418.2.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Babiana inclinata has been confused with the vegetatively similar B. angustifolia, which also has inverted flowers, but B. inclinata has a more widely cupped flower, unequal tepals that do not form a cup, a dorsal tepal 22-24 mm long and held well apart from the others, and the anthers are purple to lilac or white rather than almost black. The lower tepals are shortly united with the upper laterals for about 2 mm to form a distinct lower lip, and the free parts are 12-15 mm long. While the anthers of B. inclinata are the same size as in B. angustifolia, 5-6 mm long, the filaments are longer, 12-15 mm versus 8-10 mm in B. angustifolia. The tepals of B. angustifolia are ± equal, 20-22 mm long and overlap one another forming a cup and the filaments are 12-15 mm long. In the inverted flowers of the two species the unilateral stamens lie above the dorsal tepal and face the top of the spike.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: An early flowering species, Babiana karooica is recognised in sect. Teretifolieae by the acaulescent habit, blue to violet flowers with perianth tube 20-35 mm long and puberulous in the throat, and violet anthers. The style divides beyond the anther tips. The species is easily confused with larger-flowered B. sambucina, which blooms later, mostly in August and September, but that species has a straight perianth tube 35-65 mm long and at least 1.5× as long as the dorsal tepal in length, and the tepals are broader, mostly 30-35 x 5-12 mm. In addition, the perianth tube is smooth inside, the anthers are cream-coloured to pale yellow, and the style typically divides opposite the base to middle of the anthers. Babiana karooica also lacks the distinctive leafy outer bract of the lowermost flower of the spike characteristic of B. sambucina. Babiana karooica may also be confused with B. bainesii but this species always has the spike underground, the flowers thus arising below ground level. A widespread species of the southern African summer-rainfall zone, B. bainesii typically flowers in late summer, mainly February to April, but later, in July and August in colder parts of the high mountains of the Great Karoo. Babiana karooica has broader and shorter leaves than B. bainesii, usually sparsely hairy on the veins and margins, slightly smaller flowers, and green floral bracts tipped rust-brown.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With relatively small flowers, although with a relatively long perianth tube, ± 24 mm long, Babiana lanata has a dorsal tepal ± 17 mm long and the lower tepals only slightly smaller. The upper three tepals are pale yellow or maroon with yellow edges, an unusual colour for the genus, while the lower tepals are pale creamy yellow with a pale maroon central streak. The most striking feature of the species is the leaf, the blade abruptly truncate, widest about the middle and the apex serrated, with the surface covered with long silky hairs as are the spike axis and bracts. The truncate leaf blades recall those of B. flabellifolia and its immediate allies but B. lanata is probably not immediately related to this group of species, which always has fairly large, blue to mauve or purple flowers, less conspicuous vestiture, and leaves more obviously truncate, usually widest at the apex. The long silky pubescence and leaf blades set obliquely to the sheaths recall B. rubella, also from coastal Namaqualand, but that species is readily distinguished by its magenta-pink perianth, hooded dorsal tepal and acute leaf tips.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erect, branched, strongly balm-scented, somewhat viscid shrub. Lamina panduriform to cordiform in outline, pinnatilobate to pinnatipartite, abaxially sparsely villous to lanate and greyish-green. Peduncles distinctly articulated, pseudo-umbels with 2-20 relatively large flowers each. Flowers pale pink to pink, pedicel shorter than hypanthium. P. panduriforme is closely related to P. quercifolium (L.f.) L'Herit. Erect, much-branched, strongly balm-scented, viscid shrub. Lamina 3-palmatisect to pinnatisect with the segments irregularly pinnatifid to pinnatisect, almost scabrous. Peduncles distinctly articulated, pseudo-umbels with 2-6 flowers each. Flowers pale pink to dark pinkish-purple, relatively large, pedicel much shorter than hypanthium. P. quercifolium and P. panduriforme Eckl. & Zeyh. are closely related species and the following characters can be used to distinguish between them: P. quercifolium - 1. Leaves 3-palmatisect to pinnatisect with the segments irregularly pinnatifid to pinnatisect. 2. Leaves almost scabrous and abaxially sometimes villous but never lanate. 3. Leaves usually viscid. 4. Pseudo-umbels with 2-6 flowers each. 5. Posterior petals up to 25 mm long. P. panduriforme - 1. Leaves pinnatilobate to pinnatipartite with the segments occasionally shallowly lobed. 2. Leaves usually soft to the touch and abaxially villous to lanate. 3. Leaves occasionally somewhat viscid. 4. Pseudo-umbels with 2-20 flowers each. 5. Posterior petals up to 35 mm long. There is evidence that hybridization takes place between sympatric populations.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Readily recognised by the white flowers with red V-shaped markings on the lower tepals, a straight, nearly cylindric perianth tube 22-40 mm long, and long, narrow leaves with sharp, pungent tips. The flowers are typical of those adapted for pollination by long-proboscid flies. When not in flower the stiff, sharply pungent leaves of B. lapeirousioides are easily confused with young plants of blue-flowered B. dregei, which grows in similar habitats in granite outcrops at higher elevations in the Kamiesberg.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Babiana melanops has long been confused with related B. villosa, which also has radially symmetric flowers and prominent, blackish stamens with arrow-shaped anthers but it differs in its suberect stem, tepals spreading horizontally when fully open, and narrowed at the base more-or-less into claws so that the perianth has small windows between the bases of adjacent tepals. The flowers of typical B. melanops are either dark blue or mauve with a dark, almost black centre.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Pelargonium pulchellum falls in Knuth's section Ligularia which is distinguished by the combination of seven fertile stamens and the two upper petals which taper towards their bases. Within this section, P. pulchellum can be recognized as being the only species of which the stipules are adnate to the stem, the stem is short and fleshy and the flowers are white with red markings. The contracted stem and deeply lobed leaves indicate that it is a relatively specialized species which is adapted to harsh environmental conditions. In his original description Sims stated that only five stamens are fertile, but this is incorrect. In the sketch of the staminal column it can be seen that two of the fertile stamens are very short; when these have lost their anthers they can easily be mistaken for staminodes.
bibliographicCitation: Vorster, PJ; Merwe, AH. 1973. Pelargonium pulchellum Sims. Fl. Pl. Africa 42t.1669 [CC BY]

description: Due to the remarkable variability of its foliage, P. pulverulentum is often confused with other species in the subsection. The densely pubescent form can be confused with the consistently velutinous P. lobatum, but in that species the base of the lamina is never decurrent. The more common glabrous form can be confused with P. pillansii, but is easily distinguished by the ciliate leaf margins; furthermore P. pulverulentum is an Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal species while P. pillansii is known from the Western Cape only.
bibliographicCitation: Maggs, GL; Vorster, PJ; Van der Walt, JJA; Gibby, M. 1999. Taxonomy of the genus Pelargonium (Geraniaceae): the section Polyactium   3. The subsection Polyactium. S. African J. Bot. 65(3): 115-143. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1999); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the radially symmetric flower with a pink-purple perianth, the tepals forming a shallow bowl, and short style with the branches extending between the lower parts of the anthers. The stem is subterranean, only the spike is held above ground, and the linear leaves are 2-4(-7) mm wide, usually bearing fine long hairs. The large soft, pale green floral bracts, the inner of which is forked apically, and smooth ovary place the species in sect. Teretifolieae, where it may be most closely related to the widespread B. sambucina. That species has broader, noticeably pleated leaves, usually shortly hairy to scabrid leaves and zygomorphic flowers, usually blue to violet with the lower lateral tepals boldly marked in the centre with white blotches outlined in darker blue or rarely red-purple. The radially symmetric flower of B. radiata is an independent development in the section.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erect, much-branched, strongly balm-scented, viscid shrub. Lamina 3-palmatisect to pinnatisect with the segments irregularly pinnatifid to pinnatisect, almost scabrous. Peduncles distinctly articulated, pseudo-umbels with 2-6 flowers each. Flowers pale pink to dark pinkish-purple, relatively large, pedicel much shorter than hypanthium. P. quercifolium and P. panduriforme Eckl. & Zeyh. are closely related species and the following characters can be used to distinguish between them: P. quercifolium - 1. Leaves 3-palmatisect to pinnatisect with the segments irregularly pinnatifid to pinnatisect. 2. Leaves almost scabrous and abaxially sometimes villous but never lanate. 3. Leaves usually viscid. 4. Pseudo-umbels with 2-6 flowers each. 5. Posterior petals up to 25 mm long. P. panduriforme - 1. Leaves pinnatilobate to pinnatipartite with the segments occasionally shallowly lobed. 2. Leaves usually soft to the touch and abaxially villous to lanate. 3. Leaves occasionally somewhat viscid. 4. Pseudo-umbels with 2-20 flowers each. 5. Posterior petals up to 35 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive both in the densely long-hairy stem and leaves, and in the pink to light purple perianth with pale yellow lower lateral tepals. The flowers are of moderate size with a perianth tube 12-15 mm long, a dorsal tepal 28-30 mm long, and have a pleasant sweet, rose-like scent and the leaves have short, oblong-ovate blades held nearly horizontally to the sheaths. Superficially B. rubella resembles a second Namaqualand endemic, B. horizontalis, in the unusual pink flower colour, but that species has almost hairless leaves and bracts, and the stem reaches only shortly above ground. Babiana pilosa also has pink flowers and is densely hairy, though with retrorse hairs. Both B. nana, a species of coastal sandveld in Western Cape, and B. rubella may have a branched aerial stem, suberect to weakly inclined spikes, and relatively short, broad leaves, often held nearly at right angles to the sheaths but the flowers of B. nana are usually blue to violet with white markings.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in the spreading, velvety leaves, lightly coiled at the tips, Babiana toximontana typically has short, branched stems with horizontally arching, secund spikes, and fairly truncate bracts, the inner divided to the base. The flowers are moderately sized and pale to deep blue marked with white blotches and red streaks on the lower tepals. It is evidently closely allied to B. salteri, which also has oblique, rather spreading leaves and dense, horizontal spikes and also flowers early in the season, in late June and July. Babiana salteri has broader, more widely spreading leaves that are firm-textured and never twisted or coiled at the tips, and smaller flowers (tube ± 9 mm vs. 12-14 mm long and dorsal tepal 23 mm vs. 28-30 mm long) with the lower lateral tepals mostly or entirely yellow and the upper lateral tepals narrower and recurved. The two species favour different habitats, with B. salteri restricted to quartz patches on clay soils in succulent karoo scrub, and B. toximontana favouring sandstone-derived soils in arid fynbos. Babiana salteri is known for certain only NE of Vanrhynsdorp, whereas B. toximontana occurs in several populations in the foothills and lower slopes of Gifberg and Matsikamma.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Erect, much-branched, rose-scented shrub. Lamina palmatisect to pinnatisect, segments pinnatisect, narrow, apices usually obtuse, margins revolute, almost scabrous. Pseudo-umbels with 3-8 flowers each. Flowers pale purple to pinkish-purple, pedicel as long as hypanthium.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Bulbine suurbergensis differs from other cliff-dwelling species by its long, pendent, dichotomous, sparsely branched stems up to 700 mm long, characteristically curving upwards and by its soft, linear-lanceolate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2017. Bulbine dewetii, a new cliff-dwelling Bulbine species (Asphodelaceae) from the Western Cape. Haseltonia 23: 53-56. [https://doi.org/10.2985/026.023.0108 ] [All rights reserved]

description: P. radulifolium is distinguished by its erect, pinnate to 2-pinnatifid leaves of which the lamina is 2 to 3 times as long as wide, membranous, not glaucous, and adaxially often densely strigose to hirsute. In P. pillansii the lamina is also pinnate to pinnatifid; but almost as long as wide, leathery, glaucous, and glabrate.
bibliographicCitation: Maggs, GL; Vorster, PJ; Van der Walt, JJA; Gibby, M. 1999. Taxonomy of the genus Pelargonium (Geraniaceae): the section Polyactium   3. The subsection Polyactium. S. African J. Bot. 65(3): 115-143. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1999); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Erect, much-branched, aromatic shrub. Lamina 3(-5)-palmatilobate to 3(-5)-palmatifid, hirtellous, apices of lobes mostly obtuse. Flowering branches profusely branched. Pseudo-umbels with 6-12 flowers each. Flowers white, anterior three petals much narrower than posterior two, hypanthium prominently thickened at base, pedicel as long as hypanthium. P. ribifolium resembles P. scabrum (L.) L'Herit. in its habit, and there is some resemblance in the shape of the leaves. The flowers of P. scabrum, however, are seldom white, and the thickening at the base of the hypanthium is less conspicuous. Furthermore, the lobes of the leaves are acute instead of obtuse, as is mostly the case in P. ribifolium.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: It is related to both P. zonale Willd. and P. inquinans Ait., and has some important features in common with P. acetosum Ait., another eastern Cape Province species. A possible clue to its origin is an unnamed specimen in the National Herbarium, Pretoria, collected in 1892 among rocks near Komgha by H. G. Flanagan (No. 1294).
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA; Burges, EK. 1945. Pelargonium salmoneum R.A.Dyer. Fl. Pl. South Africa 25t.971 [CC BY]

description: Erect to decumbent, branched, non-aromatic subshrub, young stems wine-red, villous to hispid. Lamina 3-palmatisect to pinnatisect with the segments irregularly incised, margins coarsely serrate-dentate and wine-red, almost scabrous. Pseudo-umbels with 3-5 flowers each. Flowers white to pale pink-purple with darker markings, pedicel as long as hypanthium. The wine-red young stems with long hairs and typical leaf structure of P. scabroide distinguish it from other species of the section. P. scabroide has many characters in common with P. sublignosum Knuth and P. englerianum Knuth, and they undoubtedly are closely related. It is, however, easy to distinguish between these three species by leaf characters.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: The species of this section are distinguished from one another mainly by the morphology of their leaves. The mature leaves of Pelargonium schizopetalum are oblong-ovate, with a cordate base, the lamina deeply incised almost to the midrib and the margins are unevenly crenate. P. amatymbicum, in the past regarded as a subspecies and even a synonym of P. schizopetalum (Vorster pers. comm.), differs in having cordate to elongately cordate leaves which are lobed only to half the distance between the margin and midrib. The leaves of P. caffrum are digitately or pinnately dissected into linear segments, and those of P. bowkeri are obviously pinnately compound with fine linear segments. This species is a geophyte, possessing a tuber which is often branched. The flowers are pale yellow or yellow-green with red or purple stripes. These colours, as well as the presence of a long, nectar-filled, tubular hypanthium, the unpleasant scent which is noticeably stronger at night and the personal observation that the flowers tend to open most widely at night, indicate that this species is probably pollinated by a nocturnal hovering moth, such as a hawk moth. However, no pollination studies have yet been carried out in the field. The anthers mature and dehisce approximately three to four days before the stigmas. This protandry ensures the transfer of pollen from one flower to another, and prevents pollen transfer within one flower. The flowers in the observed specimen did not mature synchronously within an inflorescence, and it is therefore possible that pollination within a plant can take place. Upon maturity, the fruit dehisces into individual mericarps. Each is provided with a long, spiralled awn from which hairs or bristles protrude. This structure is light and fluffy when dry, and is wind-dispersed.
bibliographicCitation: Barker, NP; Condy, GS. 1990. Pelargonium schizopetalum Sweet. Fl. Pl. Africa 51t.2019 [CC BY]

description: Style 3.0-4.5(-5.0) mm long, all around papillose, sometimes sparsely so; claw of tepals (4-)5-7(-9) mm long; leaves 5-21, of which the lower 4 have a stem-clasping insertion (rarely the 5 lower leaves are amplexicaul, but then at least a total of 10 leaves present); plant not rarely two-flowered (occasionally up to 4-flowered).
bibliographicCitation: Muller-Doblies, D; Muller-Doblies, U. 1990. Zur kenntnis der gattung Androcymbium (Colchicaceae) im südlichen Afrika: 2. Androcymbium exiguum hat doch Artwert. Willdenowia 19(2): 453-470. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/3996654] [All rights reserved]

description: Procumbent, perennial subshrub; lamina green, sparsely pilose to villous, pinnatilobate to pinnatisect or bipinnatilobate to bipinnatisect; stipules relatively large (±10 x 8 mm). Pseudo-umbels with 3-6 flowers each. Flowers with 4 or 5 white to yellowish or dark pink-purplish petals, posterior two with dark red markings, fertile stamens 7.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA; Boucher, C. 1986. A taxonomix revision of the section Myrrhidium of Pelargonium (Geraniaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 52(2): 438-462. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1986); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: P. triste is distinguished by its lamina being at least twice as long as wide, usually conspicuously pubescent, divided into linear segments which are usually about 1 mm wide but may be up to 8 mm wide in leaves in which segmentation is poorly developed, and 7 fertile stamens per flower. In the only other species in this subsection in which the lamina is divided into linear segments, P. anethifolium and P. multiradiatum, the lamina is almost as wide as long and at least adaxially the indumentum is inconspicuous. Furthermore, P. anethifolium has only 6 fertile stamens, and P. multiradiatum only 5.
bibliographicCitation: Maggs, GL; Vorster, PJ; Van der Walt, JJA; Gibby, M. 1999. Taxonomy of the genus Pelargonium (Geraniaceae): the section Polyactium   3. The subsection Polyactium. S. African J. Bot. 65(3): 115-143. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1999); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: This species was initially considered a geographic colour form of Disa montana, a rare high altitude species of the Eastern Cape which is allopatric from D. vigilans. D. montana differs in its larger stature, broader leaves (±6 mm vs 2-4 mm broad), longer ovaries (20-26 mm vs 12-18 mm) and much broader perianth segments, the dorsal sepals in particular. In D. montana the dorsal sepals are flattened and usually orbicular, 10-18 x 9- 16 mm, whereas those of D. vigilans are oblong, galeate, and 10-14 x 5-7 mm. The species also differ in the size and shape of the lip. In D. montana the lip is ovate-acuminate, oblong or rounded and 10-15 x 3-5 mm. In D. vigilans the lip is oblan- ceolate, broadest in the distal third, and 10-14 x 3 mm. In D. montana the lateral sepals are broader, 12-17 x 4.0-6.5 mm. In D. vigilans the lateral sepals and droop are obliquely patent and narrow, 11-14 x 3.0-3.5 mm. D. vigilans is sympatric with its close ally Disa amoena. Both are very narrow endemics limited to the Mt. Mauch-Mt. Anderson area, although the latter is locally fre quent. D. amoena is a larger species 300-600 mm tall with longer leaves and larger inflorescences. The flowers are deep pink in D. amoena and all the segments are larger (dorsal sepals 15-20 x 6-9 mm vs 10-14 x 4-7 mm; lateral sepals 13-20 x 6-10 mm vs 11-14 x 3.0-3.5 mm; lip 15- 18 x 3-4 mm vs 10-14 x 3 mm). The spur of D. amoena is also considerably longer (25-35 mm vs 12-16 mm).
bibliographicCitation: McMurtry, DM; Edwards, TJ; Bytebier, B. 2006. A new species of Disa (Orchidaceae) from Mpumalanga, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 72: 551-554. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2006); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Resembling small forms of Drimia physodes in its subcapitate-racemose inflorescence, longitudinally puberulous scape and minute bracts, but distinguished by its shorter pedicels, (3.0-)5.0-6.5 mm long, and pigmented ovary, white with yellow shoulders edged with purple speckles. The development of a terminal bulbil on the roots (sic.) (?stolons) is evidently diagnostic for the species. The bulbil forms at the end of the new growth after the parent bulb breaks dormancy, but is readily detached.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Its most distinctive features are the very large solitary leaf cylindric corollatube, which is more conspicuous than the limb, a patent indumentum onthe corolla and ovary, and very long capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1971. Streptocarpus: an African plant study. Univ. of Natal Press, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: It is readily recognized by its flat rosette of very glandular leaves, widely tubular flowers, which are prettily coloured violet, cream and yellow, andits relatively short capsules. S. meyeri and S. rexii could combine to givethese characters.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1971. Streptocarpus: an African plant study. Univ. of Natal Press, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: The flowers of S. pogonites are small and white, in size and ground colour not at all unlike those of S. pusillus and S. rimicola.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1971. Streptocarpus: an African plant study. Univ. of Natal Press, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by the combination of stellate, blue-violet flowers with subequal tepals, free stamens and undivided, filiform style branches, Moraea marginata also has a solitary, linear, channelled leaf with conspicuous, maroon margins that are very conspicuously thickened when dry. As with related M. fistulosa and M. monticola, the style branches are filiform, undivided and extend between the stamens. The leaves of M. marginata are dry and withered at flowering, and the attractive, blue-violet flowers, 20-25 mm in diam., open in early summer in the late afternoon for just a couple of hours, withering near sunset, a phenology shared with several other species of the M. crispa alliance.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is easily recognized by its small white tubular flowers and by its habit of producing a second flowering leaf from near the apex of the stalk of the main leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1971. Streptocarpus: an African plant study. Univ. of Natal Press, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: S. rimicola very closely resembles S. pusillus. The flowers of S. rimicola are slightly smaller than those of S. pusillus, but they are otherwise distinguishable largely because the anthers of S. pusillus are bearded and the connective is often toothed (one or other character is always present, sometimes both), while neither of these characters is present in S. rimicola.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1971. Streptocarpus: an African plant study. Univ. of Natal Press, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: In its typical form it is a small, erect, branched plant about 0.3 m tall with stems often arising annually from a burnt base. In the eastern Transvaal some plants may have straggly stems, which grade into P. mutabilis while, in the Eastern Cape, it is not always easy to separate it from var. madagascariensis. Its nearest affinity appears to be P. hadiensis var. hadiensis, and the two are separated mainly on size of leaf, with some specimens from Natal and the Waterberg being intermediate between the two.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 23. Plectranthus. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 137-172. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: S. wilmsii is easily recognized by its single leaf that is generally more or less heart-shaped and its very open inflorescences of white, tubular flowers, yellow on the floor of the tube and there spotted violet.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1971. Streptocarpus: an African plant study. Univ. of Natal Press, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Plectranthus stylesii strongly resembles P. verticillatus but is distinguished from this procumbent species by its thick, rigid, erect stems and bushy habit; plants grow up to 0.6 m tall without support from adjacent vegetation. The leaves of P. stylesii are much larger (50-80 x 40-80 mm) than those of P. verticillatus (16-40 x 12-40 mm). The corolla of the new species is distinctly constricted at the throat, whereas that of P. verticillatus is only slightly narrowed.
bibliographicCitation: Edwards, TJ. 2005. Two new Plectranthus species (Lamiaceae) and new distribution records from Pondoland Centre of Plant Endemism, South Africa. Bothalia 35(2): 149-152. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species with narrowly funnel-shaped, mauve to lilac or pink flowers with yellow tube 10-13 mm long, and uniquely long filaments, 8-9 mm long inserted in the lower half of the tube and exserted ± 2 mm. In other species with a long perianth tube the elongation is of the lower portion of the tube below the filaments, which remain short and are inserted near the top of the tube. The wide, scalloped basal ridge on the corm suggests a possible relationship with Romulea toximontana.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In habit, ecology and distribution within our area it resembles H. petrensis, but may be distinguished by the conspicuous coma of large whitish to rose-purple bracts and by the usually whitish corolla which is slightly shorter than the mauve to violet corolla of H. petrensis.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A good deal of variation is included in H. canescens, from linear leaves (3-4 mm broad) in the dry western extremity of its range in the Mafikeng region to lanceolate and ovate-lanceolate in more mesophytic areas. It is diagnosed by the short often crisped tomentum of stems and leaves. See also notes after the following species, H. linearis and H. petrensis. Superficially H. canescens and H. petrensis are very similar, but the latter has long villous hairs on the stems, though the pubescence of the leaves is often similar. H. petrensis is a more western species, entering the northern and eastern Transvaal lowveld. However, two specimens from the Waterberg in S.W.A./Namibia, Boss sub TRV 35003 and De Winter 2799, have pubescence resembling H. canescens.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A remarkably aromatic plant, smelling of mint and coconut. Allied to H. canescens, but has more ovate leaves, longer petioles and longer corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Hermas villosa shares the stiffly toothed, adaxially glabrescent and shortly petioled leaves and basally-winged median fruit ribs with H. quinquidentata but is readily distinguished by the larger, stout shrubby habit (to 60 cm tall), the larger primary umbels (more than 40 mm in diameter), the larger leaves (lamina more than 60 mm long) that are regularly serrate to dentate with numerous teeth and the sepals with a single prominent vein.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; De Villiers, BJ; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2015. A revision of the South African genus Hermas (Apiaceae). Syst. Bot. 40(1): 352-365. [DOI 10.1600/036364415X686639] [All rights reserved]

description: Resembles H. rehmannii but has slightly narrower, more lanceolate leaves and a tuft of conspicuous mauve-purple bracts at the apex of the inflorescence. H. cinerea, which occurs in the Natal Drakensberg at higher altitudes and also lacks the conspicuous coma of bracts, has more elliptical leaves and the calyx is distinctly villous.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Hermas intermedia shares the large, adaxially felty leaves with H. gigantea and H. lanata. It can be distinguished from H. gigantea by the densely felty or lanate involucral bracts, involucellar bracts and penduncle, as well as having only the sepals maroon (entire umbels maroon in H. gigantea). It can be distinguished from H. lanata by the maroon sepals (cream in H. lanata), less rigid, adaxially short lanate leaves (rigid, long lanate, matted and shaggy in H. lanata) with usually truncate bases (prominently cordate in H. lanata).
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; De Villiers, BJ; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2015. A revision of the South African genus Hermas (Apiaceae). Syst. Bot. 40(1): 352-365. [DOI 10.1600/036364415X686639] [All rights reserved]

description: H. teucriifolia, to which H. subvelutina is closely related and of which it could be regarded as a subspecies. H. subvelutina tends to have narrower, more ericoid leaves, shorter intemodes and a yellowish tomentum, but there appear to be some intermediates in the Kaapsche Hoop area. H. teucriifolia is mainly a Natal species which extends to the Barberton mountains in the Transvaal.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 30. Hemizygia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 193-212. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This species has previously been incorrectly treated as synonymous with H. quinquidentata, with which it shares the basally-winged median fruit ribs, but can be distinguished by the densely lanate adaxial leaf indumentums, the sepals with one prominent vein (lateral veins when present inconspicuous) and the soft, crenate and slightly undulate leaf margins, which are not involute. It shares the felty to densely lanate upper leaf surface indumentum and glabrous involucellar bracts and bracteoles with H. gigantea but is easily distinguished by the smaller leaves (less than 70 mm long), the cream-coloured sepals with a single prominent vein and the fruit with basally-winged median ribs.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; De Villiers, BJ; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2015. A revision of the South African genus Hermas (Apiaceae). Syst. Bot. 40(1): 352-365. [DOI 10.1600/036364415X686639] [All rights reserved]

description: This species is easily distinguished from H. quercifolia by the glabrous upper leaf surface, the stiff coarsely serrate leaves with strongly involute margins and the sepals with three prominent veins. It shares the stiffly toothed, adaxially glabrescent and shortly petioled leaves with H. villosa but is readily distinguished from this species by the much smaller habit (dwarf shrublets less than 20 cm tall), the smaller leaves (lamina less than 45 mm long) that are coarsely serrate with only 5 to 10 teeth and the sepals with three prominent veins.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; De Villiers, BJ; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2015. A revision of the South African genus Hermas (Apiaceae). Syst. Bot. 40(1): 352-365. [DOI 10.1600/036364415X686639] [All rights reserved]

description: Recognised by its lanceolate leaves (5-)7-10(-18) mm wide, with a prominent submarginal vein, and funnel-shaped, cream- or straw-coloured to pale yellow or pale apricot-flushed flowers usually with dark veins and lacking well-developed calluses. Flowering is from spring to early summer, mainly August to November, rarely into December. Tritonia gladiolaris is closely allied to and largely sympatric with T. disticha, which flowers in mid- to late summer, mainly December to February or March, rarely earlier in November, and has red, orange-red or pink flowers, the lower tepals, especially the median, marked at the base with a small yellow blotch outlined with red.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A. macowani differs from A. amatymbica by its lobed leaves, the lobes of which have 2-3 teeth, by its much larger sepals, longer styles and by its involucral segments being subecpial. In the material investigated the vittae are wider than is the case in amatymbica but no fully ripe fruits have been available in A. macowani.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1949. A revision of the genus Alepidea. Bot. Not. 4: 217-268. [All rights reserved]

description: A small plant with relatively large flowers, Tritonia watermeyeri is distinguished from T. securigera by the narrow, more-or-less spirally twisted leaves, 1.5-4.0(-5.0) mm wide, with the margins often tightly undulate or crisped. The corm tunics are always wiry with the fibres thickened at the base into flattened claws. Tritonia watermeyeri occurs west and northwest of the range of T. securigera. Populations between Montagu and Barrydale are readily recognised by their tightly twisted and crisped leaves but populations from the Anysberg are less distinctive, with plane, only loosely twisted leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species resembles J. tortuosum Willd. of the Eastern Cape in that the leaflets are long and narrow and without acarodomatia, but in J. tortuosum the leaves are always 3-foliolate whereas in J. quinatum they are mostly digitately 5-foliolate and only occasionally with some leaves 3- or 7-foliolate. The habit of the latter is a low shrublet forming a fairly dense growth from a creeping rootstock whereas J. tortuosum is a high climber, and the area of distribution is distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In the Flora Capensis this species is partly confused with J. glaucum (L.f) Ait., and the type number of J. multipartitum, Krauss 458, is cited under J. glaucum. J. multipartitum is also closely related to the subtropical species J. stenolobum Rolfe. The main difference between these species is the obvious pubescence of J. stenolobum and the less conspicuous but characteristic short dense pubescence of J. multipartitum. Among the tropical species, J. multipartitum is nearest to J. meyeri-johannis Engl, as defined in the Flora of Tropical East Africa (1952). The main difference is the constantly 3-flowered inflorescence of the tropical species, and there is a slight difference in the size, texture and venation of the leaves. The fruits of J. multipartitum were tested at the laboratories of the Division of Veterinary Services, Pretoria, where 2 doses of 20 grams each were given to rabbits with negative results.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Monopsis simplex is peculiar in lacking the densely penicillate anthers of other species of Monopsis.
bibliographicCitation: Phillipson, PB. 1986. Taxonomy of Monopsis (Lobeliaceae): M.simplex, M.debilis and a new species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 93(4): 329-341. [All rights reserved]

description: Resembles S. graciliflora but is a more robust plant with denser indumentum on the leaves and stems, more finely toothed leaf margins and more slender, elongate inflorescences. Also related to S. kuntzei, in which the upper leaves tend to be sessile, the bracts are broader, the calyx tube is longer in relation to the teeth, which are markedly spine-tipped, and the rhachis and calyx are glandular-pubescent.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 13. Stachys. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 51-78. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A little-known species closely related to S. natalensis but distinguished from that species by the densely matted-villous lower surface of the leaves. Further material is required in order to determine how meaningful this distinction is. A specimen from northern Natal, near Luneburg, Galpin 9870, has this type of tomentum but differs in having petioles up to 7 mm long. Until more material is forthcoming, it is referred to S. sessilifolia with some hesitation; from 5. malacophylla it differs in having 2-flowered, not 4-6-flowered verticils.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 13. Stachys. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 51-78. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: In South Africa J. stenolobum is most like J. multipartitum from which it is mainly distinguished by the conspicuous pubescence on the twigs, leaves and calyx. The pubescence is mostly rather dense, tomentulose, with spreading or recurved, often crisped, hairs which vary somewhat in density and length. J. multipartitum on the other hand appears to be glabrous but is persistently, minutely and densely puberulous, at least on the twigs.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: There is a good deal of variation in size and shape of leaves, density of indumentum and size of corolla. It is sometimes confused with S. chamelaeagnea which has a coarser, glandular pubescence, shorter hairs on the calyx and deciduous bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 14. Salvia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 79-102. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: J. abyssinicum is closely related to J. fluminense, from which it can be distinguished principally by the slightly larger calyx and the axillary as well as terminal inflorescences. In the South African specimens it can also be distinguished by the usually rather larger leaves which are thinner in texture and glabrous, and the acarodomatia which, when present, occur in the axils of upper as well as basal veins. One or other of these features may occasionally be found in eastern forms of J. fluminense, but then the size of the calyx will be decisive, or the shape of the inflorescence, which is more or less flat-topped in J. fluminense and rather oval in outline in J. abyssinicum.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The leaves vary considerably in size, texture and degree of crenation but the species is readily distinguished from the other shrubby South African species by the leaves being truncate to cordate at the base. Its nearest ally appears to be S. dominica L. of the eastern Mediterranean area.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1985. Lamiaceae: 14. Salvia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 28(4): 79-102. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209555#page/9/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This species is confused in the Flora Capensis with J. multipartitum. The specimens cited there from the south-western Cape are J. glaucum (L.f.) Ait. and those from outside the winter rainfall area are J. multipartitum Hochst. These closely related species are distinguished by the completely glabrous plants of J. glaucum with glaucous leaves which are usually about 3 times as long as broad, and the inflorescence being normally 3-flowered, as opposed to J. multipartitum which has puberulous branchlets, green leaves which are variable in size but seldom 3 times as long as broad, and normally a 1-flowered inflorescence. Among tropical African species, J. glaucum is closest to J. kerstingii Gilg which occurs in West Africa It differs in the plants being glabrous instead of distinctly pubescent as in J. kerstingii.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Oleaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 100-128. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although always recognizable by its small flowers and characteristic nectary, the species may vary much in appearance. Further north it is replaced by O. parviflorum, which is doubtless its closest relative.
bibliographicCitation: Nordenstam, RB. 1982. A monograph of the genus Ornithoglossum (Liliaceae). Opera Bot. 64: 5-51. [10.1111/j.1756-1051.1983.tb01058.x] [All rights reserved]

description: Annual, exactly resembling Cyphia Phyteuma, with the inflorescence of L. spicata. Leaves 1.5-2 inches long, 1-1.5 inch wide, entire or obscurely crenulated. Scape with one small leaf near the base, 1 foot high, the spiked raceme 4 inches long. Flower 3 lines long. Lobes of the upper lip erect, linear-acuminated; lobes of the lower lip ovate, acute.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Sub-shrub, very like the preceding, but not tomentose, and the leaves usually broader and serrato-pinnatifid, spreading, hairy or glabrous, flat or concave above. Peduncles 1-5-flowered. Flowers large, sometimes 1 inch long, blue. Valves of capsule as long or longer than the base.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Internodes about 1.7 cm, petioles 5-7 mm, leaf-blades about 7 cm, sepals about 1.75 mm, claw of petals 2 mm, blade of petals 6 mm, stamens (which ripen successively) about 8 mm, filaments 6 mm, ovary 3 mm, fruit 1 cm long. Style 3 mm long and 1/2 mm thick.
bibliographicCitation: Schonland, S. 1914. On some new and some little known South African plants. Rec. Albany Mus. 3: 52-64. [All rights reserved]

description: Habit of L. patula, but different by the obovate, cuneate leaves, and smaller flowers. Larger leaves 1 inch long, 4-5 lines wide, with 2-4 equal teeth on each side, glabrous or hairy on the nerve beneath. Pedicels 3-4 lines long. Corolla blue, lobes of the lower lip oblong, glabrous. Capsule hemispherical.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Annual (not perennial, as indicated by authors), very similar to the largest forms of L. bellidifolia, and only distinguished by the pubescence, commonly larger, roundish leaves, and white flowers. Stem 1 foot or more high, flexnous; branches ascending, filiform. Leaves 4~i inch long, the lower 6-10 lines wide, on broad petioles 4-8 lines long, petioled; middle leaves usually somewhat narrower and shorter, petiolate; upper ones lanceolate or linear, toothed or entire. Pedicels drooping or spreading, 1-1 J- inch long, minutely pubescent, or villous as the calyx. Corolla with a narrow tube; lobes of the lower lip oblong. Capsule 4 lines long.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Perennial. Petioles 1-2.5 inches long, with spreading hairs. Leaves 6-8 lines in diameter with blunt teeth or lobes. Flower blue, not 1 inch long.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: A highly variable species, especially with respect to leaf size. V. obscurum var. longifolium and V. obscurum var. brevifolium are based on atypical leaf types which appear sporadically and do not appear to be geographically consistent. Var. brevifolium is apparently a form common on exotic species (Salix) to which it could probably not have become adapted since their introduction. These leaf variations thus seem likely to reflect variations in the host or the ambient environment and as such should not receive taxonomic recognition.
bibliographicCitation: Wiens, D; Toelken, HR. 1979. Loranthaceae and Viscaceae, Fl. S. Africa 10(1): 1-56. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Annual herb. Small specimens 3-4 inches high, simple; larger ones 1-2 feet, with filiform branches. Lower leaves 0.5-1.5 inch long, 3-6 lines wide, often smaller and roundish, toothed or subserrated. Petioles short. Upper leaves sessile. Flowers racemose or subpanicled. Bractea linear. Pedicels 4-8 lines long, pubescent or glabrous, compressed. Calyx-lobes 1.5-2.5 lines long, entire or with 1 or 2 acute teeth. Corolla blue or violet, glabrous. Lobes of the upper lip linear; the 3 segments of the lower lip oval or obovate, with 2 white lines or spots near the base. Capsule 2-4 lines long.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: A small annual, 4 inches high. Radical leaves suborbicular, 2-3 lines long and wide, equal in length to the petiole; stem leaves 4-10 lines long, 2-3 lines wide, with 6-8 short teeth above the middle, obtuse, sessile or narrowed into a petiole; upper leaves and bractea 4 lines long, 1 line wide. Calyx at flowering time 1 line long; lobes acute. Corolla blue; lobes of the lower lip oblong. Capsule obconical.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Stem shrubby, terete; branches fastigiate. Leaves 6 lines long, toothed near the apex, rarely towards the base, densely tomentose, greyish. Peduncles filiform, glabrous or with appressed hairs, 3 inches to 1 foot long. Corolla blue or violaceous, 6-8 lines long.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Closely related to T. quinquenervius and possibly best considered as conspecific with it. The taxon differs from T. quinquenervius by its shorter and broader calyx tube and both the colour and pattern of its corolla markings. In T. bolusii the red is bright instead of dark and a very light green is substituted for the white.
bibliographicCitation: Wiens, D; Toelken, HR. 1979. Loranthaceae and Viscaceae, Fl. S. Africa 10(1): 1-56. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Herb densely tufted, pale green; branches 2-4 inches long. Leaves 2-4 lines long or smaller. Calyx scarcely 1 line long. Corolla purplish, 2 lines long. I have only seen a few and not very perfect flowers, in one of which I observed a 3-parted corolla, with 2 distinct petals, representing the upper lip; the lower lip is 3-fid. It may be the type of a new genus or a Dobrowskya.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1865. Campanulaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Rubiaceae to Campanulaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 3: 530-605. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15235#page/536/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Die Lappung der Blätter wechselt von kaum ein Viertel bis über die Hälfte der Spreite, mit tief geteilten Seitenlappen, so daB die Blätter fast 5-lappig erscheinen. Die von Schlechter gesammelten Pflanzen besitzen auffallend kleine und stark gelappte Blätter. Auch Gueinzius n. 423 hat stark geteilte Blätter. Der Fruchtbau, Behaarung, Blüte und alle sonstigen Merkmale stimmen vollkommen mit der Drègeschen Originalpflanze.
bibliographicCitation: Ulbrich, OE. 1920. Monographie der afrikanischen Pavonia-Arten nebst Übersicht über die ganze Gattung  . Bot. Jahrb. Syst. 57(1): 54-184. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/720#page/61/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: This species is rather variable in habit, leaf-shape and degree of pubescence, so that it has been described several times. The larger-leaved plants from E. Africa, referred by Ulbrich to P. mollissima (Garcke) Ulbr., do not seem to be more than luxuriant forms of P. leptocalyx.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1960. 28. Malvaceae (part 1), Fl. Zambes. 1(1): 475-511. Crown Agents for Oversea Governments & Administrations, London. [CC BY]

description: Die Art nimmt innerhalb der Gattung ihren sehr anffälligen Blattschnitt und die groBen Früchtechen eine besondere Stellung ein.
bibliographicCitation: Ulbrich, OE. 1920. Monographie der afrikanischen Pavonia-Arten nebst Übersicht über die ganze Gattung  . Bot. Jahrb. Syst. 57(1): 54-184. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/720#page/61/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: The type specimen has no ripe capsules, and the characters given in the above description were taken from Britten 5545. H. aridus is evidently a comparatively rare endemic species limited to the dry karroid scrub from Uitenhage to Albany and Bathurst Divisions. It is distinguished by its large dark yellow flowers on long peduncles, ovate or ovate-orbicular leaves, stellate-hispid on both surfaces, and lanate seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1933. Notes on the Flora of southern Africa: IV. Miscellaneous new species. Bull. Misc. Inform. Kew 1933(9): 459-462. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/4113465] [All rights reserved]

description: A slender undershrub, clothed with very minute, yellowish stellulate pubescence. Leaves 1-1 1/2 inches apart. Petioles 3-4 lines long. Lamina 3/4-1 inch long, 1/2-3/4 inch wide. Flowers an inch across, bright scarlet or crimson. Staminal column antheriferous in the middle. Very unlike any Cape Hibiscus; but closely related to H. denudatus (Benth! Sulp. p. 7. t. 3.), a native of Lower California and New Mexico, from which it scarcely differs save in the more minute pubescence, the smaller flowers, and the glabrous seeds. It is also allied to H. micranthus, L., a native of North Africa and tropical Asia; but differs in pubescence, want of involucel, and in the glabrous seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Harvey, WH. 1862. Addenda and corrigenda to the first volume. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 2: 583-599. [All rights reserved]

description: O. woodiana resembles O. africana in that it also bears axillary inflorescences. description: The protologue of M. bachmannii was presumably based on material housed in B and later destroyed during World War II. No duplicates have been found in other herbaria, including KIEL where Bachmann’s collections are mainly deposited (Dr Martin Nickol, pers. comm., 29 November 2018). We thus follow Van Wyk’s (1983) neotype designation for M. bachmannii, as well as his treatment of M. grandiflorum as a taxonomic (heterotypic) synonym of M. bachmannii. The type of M. grandiflorum has nearly orbicular leaves, but this form occurs sporadically throughout the geographic range of M. bachmannii (e.g., at Egosa, Khebenge, Umtamvuna, Oribi Gorge, and near Paddock) and appears to be part of the normal range of variation. Memecylon bachmannii is clearly distinguished from M. natalense by its larger, subsessile, broadly ovate to suborbicular, basally rounded to subcordate leaves (vs leaves smaller, distinctly petiolate, ovate-acuminate and basally cuneate); cymes <1 cm long on peduncles to 4 mm (vs cymes to 2 cm long on peduncles to 7 mm); bracteoles persistent (vs rapidly deciduous); larger flowers (10 mm in diameter with petals 6 x 6 mm vs 5-7 mm in diameter with petals 5 x 4 mm); and fruits ovate (vs subglobose).
