description: In the past the name E. atrovirens (Desf.) Steud. (widespread in tropical Africa to India and Philippines) was used, but this species is not rhizomatous. Resembles E. lappula and E. hierniana, which have palea keels hairs longer than 0.3 mm; and E. chapelieri, which has palea margins not touching and spikelets reddish-brown.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L. 2015. Eragrostis Wolf. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 281-338. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Although P. sulphurea should be easily recognised by its large, pendulous, shallowly bowl-shaped flower-heads, there are some geographical variants. The Kamiesberg form differs in that the leaves are markedly longer and linear-spathulate as well as lacking the heavy glaucescence of the more southerly form. Slight differences in bract colour also occur, particularly towards the eastern end of the species' range along the north slopes of the Swartberg, where forms with uniformly wine-red bracts are found.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: In floral structure, P. venusta is most closely allied to P. punctata and P. lacticolor although its procumbent growth habit at first belies this relationship. Actually, some plants of P. venusta have a tendency to produce erect bushy stems up to about 70 cm in height, suggesting that the procumbent growth form may have been developed from an erect shrubby habit, perhaps in response to harsh growing conditions at high elevations.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. witzenbergiana may be distinguished from related species by its prostrate growth habit, the long foliaceous appendages on the outer involucral bracts and the short needle-like leaves (15-55 mm long)? each tipped with a prominent backwardly deflected spine, but most especially by the sparse pubescence on the young stems and leaves. Unfortunately, this characteristic pubescence tends to rub off with age but is usually easily observed in young growth flushes.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Among the species of Leucospermum characterised by a distally inflated perianth tube, L. erubescens is distinguished by the prominently pedunculate slightly asymmetrical inflorescences, the obliquely spheroidal to conical-depressed involucral receptacle sharply differentiated from the peduncle and the uniformly velutinous perianth.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: Similar to E. x pseudobtusa, which has the lower part of palea keels broader and projecting from the upper part and ending in a round or shallow notch at the top.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L. 2015. Eragrostis Wolf. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 281-338. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The inflorescence is so reduced as to consist of between four and seven (usually five) flowers, arranged in a radially symmetric manner so as to form an apparent whorl, with the styles of each flower all strongly curved inwards. Leucospermum hamatum is probably both the most reduced and the most specialised species in the genus. In each inflorescence the involucre is either absent or reduced to a mere three or four bracts, while the floral bracts subtending each flower are enlarged to form a cup-like 'pseudo-involucre' clasping the perianths.The specific epithet 'hamatum' draws attention to a character unique in Leucospermum and in fact in the whole of the South African Proteaceae; namely, the presence of minute, retrorsely directed barbs in the subterminal region of the style.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1983. A remarkable new Leucospermum (Proteaceae) from the southern Cape. J. S. African Bot. 49: 213-219. [CC BY]

description: In the section Leucospermum, L. hypophyllocarpodendron is distinguished by its prostrate growth habit, the trailing stems with secundly arranged linear canaliculate to narrowly oblanceolate leaves which may be pubescent or glabrous and by the broadly ovate involucral bracts, 5.0-7.0 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: The cuneate to very broadly obovate leaves, 7-17 toothed at the apex, distinguish L. mundii from all other species in the section Crinitae.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. patersonii may be distinguished by its arborescent growth habit, the large, broadly oblong leaves with 3-8 teeth, the lanate perianth claws and the obliquely turbinate pollen presenter. The inflorescences are usually held erect.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: This species and the perennial E. superba are the only species in Eragrostis in the FSA region in which the spikelets disarticulate below glumes at maturity, and fall as entire units.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L. 2015. Eragrostis Wolf. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 281-338. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Among the prostrate species of Leucospermum with a conic involucral receptacle and infundibuliform perianth tube, L. profugum is distinguished by its long style, 4.5-6.2 cm in length and the large (2.9-5.2 cm long) glabrous to glabrescent, obovate to oblanceolate leaves, usually with 3 or 4 teeth at the apex.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. prostratum is distinguished from L. pedunculatum by its diffuse prostrate growth habit, the slender, rarely branched trailing stems which arise from a stout subterranean rootstock, the small globose inflorescences 2.0-2.5 cm in diam., the cylindric obtuse to clavate styles and the perianth colour, bright yellow on opening, becoming deep orange with age.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: Resembles forms of E. curvula, which has basal sheaths densely hairy.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L. 2015. Eragrostis Wolf. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 281-338. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Among the species of the Sect. Diastelloidea with styles 1.2-1.9 cm long and clavate to cylindric-obtuse pollen presenters, L. royenifolium is distinguished by its procumbent growth habit and the glabrous to glabrescent patent leaves. Although nearly always glabrous, the bright green leaves are very occasionally sparsely hirsute but soon become glabrous.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: The narrowly cuneate to linear leaves, narrowed towards the base, often with involute margins, the lanceolate acute bracteoles and the pale green colour of the perianth distinguish L. saxatile from related species.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: The infundibuliform perianth tube, the very narrowly conic-acute pollen presenter (scarcely differentiated from the style) and the oblanceolate-elliptic leaves very attenuate to petiolate at the base, serve to distinguish L. saxosum from related taxa.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. secundifolium is unlike any other species in the genus and may readily be distinguished by the glabrous, distinctly petiolate, narrowly elliptic, obtuse leaves secundly arranged and the very small (1.0-1.5 cm in diam.) few flowered inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. truncatum may be distinguished by its oblanceolate cuneate leaves, 0.8-1.5 cm wide, the style, 1.8-3.8 cm long, the cylindric obtuse to clavate pollen presenter, the villous to lanate perianth claws and the perianth tube which is sharply narrowed proximally. It is conned to limestone formations.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: Similar to E. pilosa and E. aethiopica, which have the lemmas on same side of rachilla overlapping the lemma above.

description: Although L. winteri cannot be counted among the most handsome of the 'pincushions', it is certainly one of the most interesting taxonomically. This is because its peculiar morphology suggests that it could represent a type ancestral to two sections in the genus. Several well defined sections were upheld by the author in a recent revision of Leucospermum, but it is impossible to accommodate L. winteri comfortably in any of them. The uniformly cylindric perianth, short style and clavate pollen-presenter, point to an affinity with Leucospermum sect. Diastelloidea, but the broadly obovate, multidentate leaves suggest a connection with L. mundii in Leucospermum sect. Crinitae. However, in all the species in the sections mentioned above, the involucral receptacle is so reduced as to be almost flat, a character not shared by L. winteri, in which the receptacle is not reduced but is usually obliquely conic to obovoid.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP; Anderson, VF. 1979. Leucospermum winteri Rourke. Fl. Pl. Africa 45(3&4)t.1781 [CC BY]

description: L. wittebergense is distinguished by the short style, 12-19 mm long, the clavate to cylindric-obtuse pollen presenter and the crowded ascending imbricate leaves beset with a short, dense, greyish-silvery indumentum.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. album is readily distinguished from all other species by it's linear leaves and silvery appearance. Another useful character is the plumed perianth which acts in the dispersal of the ripe fruit. In L. album the perianth segments are connate for a short distance just above the membranous lower portion of the perianth as is the case in L. argenteum and L. rubrum (L. plumosum R.Br.) but in L. album the 'plumes' are about half the size of those in L. argenteum and L. rubrum. In L. dregei the perianth segments are plumed and free above, as in L. album, but not connate except in the lower membranous portion surrounding the fruit. The 'parachute' in this case carries the fruit but is not able to slide up the style as in L. album.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. arcuatum is a very distinct species not closely related to any other, distinguished in being the only species with a large nut fruit to have many stems and a persistent rootstock. It also has spathulate, obtuse, glabrous and rather thick leaves, narrowly triangular basal bracts and globose male heads. It differs from L. loranthifolium which is an erect shrub, with branches developing from a single stem below, with ovate basal bracts and the male heads flattened above. L. bonum Williams, a rare species from Gideon's Kop, has rather similarly shaped spathulate leaves and also many acute basal bracts but differs in arising from a single stem at the ground and in having silvery-pubescent leaves and pubescent basal bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: Leucadendron barkerae can be distinguished from those species which are nearest to it, by the elliptic sub-glaucous tomentose leaves, by the linear 'aterally ciliate male floral bracts, by the truncate bifid abortive stigma and by the fruits with ridged margins but above all if the plant can be observed in the bud stage up to several months before flowering, the buds will be seen to be Quite unlike those of any other closely related species.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. cadens is a small sprawling shrub with leaves narrowly oblanceolate and sub-secund, with, in the male plant, basal bracts sub-orbicular, floral bract 1.05 cm long, glabrous, perianth tube 9.5 mm long, limb 2.8 mm long and style 1.1 cm long, with hypogynous scales vestigal in the female plant and with the mature female head 2.7 cm long. It differs from Lglaberrimum (Schlectr.) Compton in its having a more decumbent habit, in the leaves being less narrowed to the base, in the floral bract of the male being very much longer, broadened towards the apex and quite glabrous, in the floral bract of the female being narrow and minutely refuse, in having hypogynous- scales vestigal in the female flower and in having the mature female head somewhat larger and more conicaL.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. chamelaea is an erect glabrous shrub with straight branches and linear-oblanceolate, obtuse leaves. The bracts in the mature female head are obovate, not connate, with adjacent bracts arranged in five spirals. The fruit is narrowly winged with the abaxial surface ventricose. It differs from L. globosum and L. elimense both of which have broader leaves and larger male inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. comosum is a species with distinctly dimorphic foliage and dark red flowers. It often bears the longest cones in the genus. It is nearest to L. platyspermum but differs in having a smaller leaf which is acute at the apex, a male floral bud somewhat clavate, mature cone bracts thinner at the edges and a very much less broadly winged fruit. It grows on the Langeberg, Outeniqua and Swartberg mountain ranges and is never found, as is L. platyspermum, at low altitudes in the Caledon or Bredasdorp Divisions.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. coniferum differs from all others in the shape of the male abortive stigma Which is constricted below the apex. In general appearance it resembles L. eucalyptifolium Buek ex Meisn. which however differs in having a leaf with a short blunt mucro. It differs also from L. meridianum Williams which has leaves more obtuse usually with a somewhat silvery adpressed pubescence. Both L. eucalyptifolium & L. meridianum have very much smaller fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. cordatum is most closely related to L. tinctum Williams and was in fact considered conspecific by Drège (1844). A reliable character which immediately separates these two taxa is found in the position of the head; in L. cordatum the upper part of the branch is sharply bent alowing the head to hang downwards; in L. tinctum the lower part of the branch is often sharply bent, around the previous years inflorescence, thus holding the head erect. The leaves in L. cordatum are broadly elliptic whereas those of L. tinctum are more oblong.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. coriaceum is easily recognised in the field by having a persistent root-stock from which it coppices after fires and in having small, obovate, glabrous leaves narrowing to the base. It is also unusual in having hairs 2 mm long on the lower half of the male style.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. cryptocephalum appears to be closest to L. laureolum (Lam.) Fourcade (= L. decorum R.Br.) but differs in being a much smaller shrub, paler in colouring and flowering about two months earlier. Its most distinctive feature is indicated by the specific epithet (cryptocephalum) which is a character that distinguishes this species from all others in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: The boundary between E. viscosa and E. amabilis, which has the inflorescences eglandular or with non-sticky glands, is not always sharp and intermediates are found. Similar to E. arenicola, which has the inflorescence contracted; and E. ciliaris, which has lemma keel with long hairs.

description: L. discolor is a species distinguished by having broad ovate leaves. The male plant has large reddish heads, glabrous floral bracts and a broadly clavate abortive stigma. It is apparently nearest to L. procerum (Salisb.ex Knight) Williams which has narrower leaves and smaller heads in the male plant. It also differs from L. strobilinum (L. ) Druce which has densely pubescent floral bracts in the male and very much larger cones in the female.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. ericifolium is in many ways a most unusual plant. It has dimorphic leaves in both sexes. The male plant has a very large number of flowering heads which besides being pedunculate, have only twelve florets in each. These florets are unusual in that the perianth tube and the style are connate and there are no hypogynous scales. In the female plant the head, which may be axiliary or terminal, is unique in the genus in having only a single flower which is subtended by a single floral bract. The hypogynous scales are also absent in the female flower.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: The long narrow glabrescent leaf with a small blunt mucro is characteristic of L. eucalyptifolium. The only other species with a somewhat similar leaf is L. coniferum (L. ) Meisn. (= L. sabulosum Salter) in which however the leaf is apiculate and glabrous. Furthermore they are also geographically separated. L. eucalyptifolium also differs from L. xanthoconus (O.Ktze) K.Schum. (= L. salignum R.Br.) which is a much smaller shrub with thinly adpressed-pubes-cent linear leaves and from L. salicifolium (Salisb.) Williams (= L. strictum R.Br.) which has narrower apiculate leaves and male heads that are very much smaller and more numerous.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. flexuosum appears to be very localised, as distinct from L. salignum Berg (= L. adscendens R.Br.) which is widespread and is to be found in abundance, with L. flexuosum but blooming a little later in the year. It differs further from L. salignum Berg in having fewer and longer stems not hidden by the leaves and in the smaller, more erect green leaves and from the Longkloof form of L. salignum Berg in the involucral leaves not being so much broadened. It differs from L. lanigerum Buek ex Meisn. in the leaves which are neither pubescent nor scabrous, and from- var.laevigatum in its time of flowering, which is in April/May, whereas var.laevigatum flowers much later in September.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. floridum is a species distinguished by having villous branchlets, with silky-pubescent, apiculate leaves which are rounded at the base, with the male limb pubescent, with a tubular perianth in the female flower and with trigonal fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. gandogeri is a glabrous species with large oblanceolate or elliptic leaves and a wide open involucre. It is distinguished from L. laureolum which has an enveloping involucre, ciliate basal bracts and short-pubescent female bracts. It differs from L. microcephalum which has conspicuous sticky brown basal bracts and sticky cones. It also differs from L. strobilinum which has more numerous cone bracts and often strongly ciliate leaves, and from L. spissifolium which has ciliate basal bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: Typical L. lanigerum is very closely related to L. modestum Williams and L. lanigerum var. laevigatum Meisn. but it differs in having a large persistent rootstock with several stems arising therefrom. L. modestum is a somewhat smaller shrub usually found in dense stands. In L. lanigerum var. laevigatum the leaves are more smooth and the habit more erect.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. loeriense can be distinguished from L. uliginosum R.Br, by being a low shrub, never tall, by having leaves with an erect and not adpressed pubescence, by having a reddish not a silvery appearance and by having fruits that are broadly (not narrowly) winged towards the apex. L. radiatum Phillips & Hutch, has leaves that are very much more twisted.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. loranthifolium is readily distinguished from all others by its glaucous leaves and greenish flower heads. L. roodii, which is very closely related, may be distinguished by its sacculate basal bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. meridianum is a compact shrub with sub-verticillate branches, with silvery pubescent leaves, with a glabrous perianth, with the abortive male stigma clavate, with mature female cone bracts ciliate and with flat winged fruits. It is most closely related to Lconiferum (L. ) Meisn. (= L. sabu/osum Salter) which however has larger glabrous leaves, larger cones with eciliate floral bracts and the abortive stigma somewhat hoof-shaped and constricted towards the apex. It also differs from L. u/iginosum R.Br, which is a tall straggly shrub, with scattered branchlets, with a smaller more silvery leaf, with a pubescent perianth and with trigonal fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. nitidum is especially distinct in its nut which is smooth, greyish and shining with a vertical dorsal ridge caused by a double fold in the exocarp. Also unique is the male perianth tube, which is connate with the lower part of the style. This is correlated with the absence of hypogynous scales. Only L. sericeum (Thunb.) R.Br, has a similar fruit and perianth, but this species is distinguished by being very much smaller in stature and in leaf size.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. nobile is easily distinguished from all other species of Leucadendron by its tall habit, long needle-like leaves and spicate heads. It is closest to L. teretifolium (Andr.) Williams (L. abietinum R.Br.) which is in every way smaller and to L. muirii Phillips which has thick broad leaves and grows on limestone.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. pubibracteolatum is closely related to L. tinctum which it resembles in the shape and attitude of its leaves, and also to L. orientale which it resembles in having numerous reflexed-adpressed basal bracts and fruits with the perimeter ridged. However L. pubibracteolatum differs from L. tinctum in having the male floral bract pubescent not glabrous, in having a fruit with a ridged perimeter and in having a broad based cone with the bracts recurved or standing fairly open. It differs also from L. orientale which has leaves that are more erect, never deflexed, which has involucral leaves that closely imbricate the base of the head, particularly so in the female and which has the male floral bract and the male perianth tube very sparsely pubescent.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: Lradiatum is quite distinct on account of its small size, dense habit and small twisted leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. remotum is easily recognised by being a shrub up to 1.5 m tall with leaves in the male plant 2.9 cm long, 6.5 mm broad, in the female plant 4.2 cmj long, 8 mm broad, in both sexes strap-shaped or oblanceolate-linear, obtuse, sub-glaucous, glabrescent, erect, imbricate towards the base, with basal bracts ovate, acute, imbricate, dusky, shining, with the male style glabrous and with the ovary pubescent towards the apex.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. sheilae is a small shrub up to 1 m tall, glaucous and glabrous, with short, slender branches, with narrowly oblanceolate leaves, with a small, greenish flowered, foetid inflorescence, with varnished, eciliate, reddish basal bracts, with the floral bract of the female broadly ovate obtuse and pubescent below, with the mature female head 1.6 cm diam., and a nut 5.5 mm long, 8-9 mm broad, 4.5 mm thick. This species is very similar to L. roodii Phillips and L. loranthifolium (Salisb. ex Knight) Williams but differs in being a much smaller shrub with much smaller leaves, flowers and fruits. It differs from L. glaberrimum (Schlechter) Compton which has thicker leaves, which are less glaucous and more narrowed to the base with a greater difference in size between male and female leaves, ciliate basal bracts and yellow flowers with a faint but pleasant smelL.

description: L. stellare may be recognised by being a shrub with many stems arising from a persistent rootstock, and with small linear-lanceolate imbricate leaves narrowing to the apex. It differs from L. thymifolium (Salisb. ex Knight) Williams which is a plant which developes from a single stem and which has shorter elliptic leaves. L. stellare is also readily distinguished from L. levisanus (L) Berg which has obovate leaves narrowing towards the base and from L. brunioides Meisn. which has linear leaves that are somewhat longer.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: Intergrades with H. rufa, which has exserted racemes and more awns, 7-14; and similar to H. gazensis, which has slender culms and fewer awns, 4-5 and H. finitima, which has a narrow pungent callus.

description: L. stelligerum is a slender shrub up to 1.3 m tall with few stems, arising from a single stem below, with leaves 2.3-2.8 cm long, 7-8 mm broad, obtuse or sub-acute, fairly smooth, erect, not twisted and with a conspicuous starry involucre. It is most closely related to L. modestum which however is a much smaller shrub with smaller leaves and a less conspicuous involucre. It is also related to L. lanigerum Buek ex Meisn. which is a smaller shrub with many stems arising from a persistent rootstock and rough twisted leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: Related to H. collina, H. tamba and H. rudis, from which it may be distinguished by its densely tufted habit and very many short awns.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Hyparrhenia E.Fourn. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. description: L. strobilinum is a stout shrub with short purplish stems clothed with a fairly long, rather widely spaced, erect pubescence, with dark green, glabrous leaves remaining conspicuously ciliate for a long time, with the apical callus not deeply immersed, with somewhat ivory white involucral leaves, with male heads depressed globose and female heads with many florets and with fruits which are quite flat and narrowly winged. It differs from L. laureolum (Lam.) Fourc. which has branches with a short dense erect somewhat matted pubescence, with thinly ciliate becoming eciliate leaves which are somewhat pubescent and narrower, with yellow involucral leaves which more or less conceal the head, with male heads more elongated and female heads with fewer bracts and florets and with broadly winged fruits. It also differs from L. microcephalum Gandoger which has almost glabrous branches, narrow glabrous and eciliate leaves, basal bracts which are conspicuous oily and brown in colour and fruits with the perimeter sharply ridged with a rough excrescence on the median ridge. Futhermore it differs from L. gandogeri Shinz ex Gandoger which has branches with a short dense erect rather matted pubescence, narrower leaves which are glabrous and eciliate except when young with the callus somewhat longer and more deeply immersed at the apex shewing as a distinct notch like mark and with broadly winged fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: Forms a bridge between var. filipendula and H. hirta and H. anamesa.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Hyparrhenia E.Fourn. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. description: L. thymifolium is distinct in being a plant developing from a single stem at ground level with elliptic-oblong leaves, with hypogynous scales, with thiniy pubescent cone bracts and with mature cones dehiscent. It differs from L. stellare which has many stems and leaves linear-lanceolate narrowing to th? apex, and from L. levisanus which has leaves obovate-spathulate narrowed tc the base and indehiscent mature cones. L. thymifolium differs also from L. dubium which has no hypogynous scales and densely pubescent mature cones.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. tradouwense is an erect shrub with glabrous branches, with leaves erect not spreading, with the male floral bract glabrous, with mature female heads 1.3-1.6 times longer than broad and with their bracts very broad, obtuse, not oily and not recurved. It differs from L. tinctum a less erect shrub, which has pubescent branches with spreading and deflexed leaves, and with the mature female head very nearly as broad as long and with their bracts narrower and oily. It also differs from L. pubibracteolatum which has pubescent male floral bracts, and with mature female heads always broader than long with recurved oily bracts. Furthermore it differs from Lorientale which has thinly pubescent branches, female heads much larger with many more basal bracts and mature female heads with recurved bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: This species links H. hirta, which does not have deflexed racemes and H. nyassae, which has yellow raceme hairs and it may be a product of introgression between these species.

description: Polystichum dracomontanum may be confused with P. monticola, which occurs in the same region and often in similar habitats. It can, however, be separated from it in the decumbent rhizome that produces slender stoloniferous branches, in the stipe that becomes near glabrous with age, and in the ovate lamina. Other diagnostic features are the entire rhizome paleae that evidently always terminate in a short thin-walled cell, in contrast to the often acicular apical cell in P. monticola. Paleae from the stipe, rachis, pinna-rachis and abaxial lamina surface appear to terminate more often in a thin-walled cell in contrast to those of P. monticola, where the apical cell appears to be largely acicular. The adaxial surface of the pinnules is largely glabrous but a few filiform paleae may occur proximally along the costa. These paleae always terminate in an acicular apical cell. Paleae from the abaxial surface of the pinnules largely terminate in an acicular apex, but paleae terminating in a short thin-walled cell are not unknown. The smaller paleae in P. dracomontanum are stramineous and membranous. The coriaceous lamina and somewhat revolute pinnule margins are also diagnostic. Micromorphological characters separating P. dracomontanum from other taxa are the small, almost square, adaxial epidermal cells with almost straight anticlinal walls and the almost circular stomata that are visible at a x 12 magnification.

description: The ripe seeds are ejected in the normal way by a catapult mechanism. As far as can be seen regeneration takes place only from seed. The leaves, when crushed, are almost without any smell. This species has been placed in the genus Macrostylis Bartl. & Wendl. because each one of the following characters, which it possesses, helps to exclude it from some other genus in the Diosmeae. (1) Heads multiflorous, up to 6. (2) Petals villous, mostly down the midrib. (3) Staminodes vestigial. (4) Anthers with a minute apical gland. (5) Disc encloses the ovary. (6) Stigma capitellate, larger than usual in the genus. (7) Style & filament long, exceeding the petals. (8) Style & filament glabrous. (9) Ovary 3-carpellate. (10) Fruit with fairly short horns, 2 mm long, which is unusual in the genus. Macrostylis cauliflora is recognised as distinct on account of being a pseudo-cauliflorous shrub with leaves gland-dotted only on the midrib and margins, with leaves, petals, style and filaments all smaller than usual and with the stigma rather larger than usual. It is, in appearance, most like Macrostylis crassifolia Sond. but differs in that the leaves of Macrostylis crassifolia are gland-dotted all over, not only on the midrib and margins. The name is an allusion to the habit of this plant of bearing the flowers below the leafy branchlets.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1975. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 5. J. S. African Bot. 41(3): 167-186. [CC BY]

description: Macrostylis ramulosa is recognised as distinct on account of being a semi-decumbent shrub with many branchlets sprouting towards the base, with linear-lanceolate pubescent leaves without any prominent midrib, with pubescent bracts 2.5-4.5 mm long, with bracteoles and calyx lobes pubescent at their tips, and with the fruit pubescent. It is nearest to M. decipens which is a much more glabrous plant with the ability to coppice from the root after fires.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, I. 1978. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 7. J. S. African Bot. 44(4): 329-362. [CC BY]

description: In only one case (Esterhuysen 21156) has it been noted that leaves which are normally alternate, may be found to be opposite. Without apparent reason leaves may be glabrous, scabrid, clothed with a short spiky pubescence or quite hairy. Although in most cases the leaves are spreading-erect, they may also be found to be adpressed (Esterhuysen 17991) or spreading (Esterhuysen 22550). Fruits usually have very long horns. The longest are on specimens from the Giftberg (7 mm, Esterhuysen 22126) at the northern limit of distribution and the shortest on specimens fron the Hex River Valley (1.5 mm, Bolus 13080) at the southern limit of distribu tion. Macrostylis tenuis is recognised as distinct being a shrub arising from a single stem at ground level, not coppicing after fires, having branchlets spreading-erect, leaves elliptic or ovate, obtuse with gland dots scattered and on margins, with the apex thickened, the style simple and fruits 2 or 3-carpellate. It differs from M. decipiens which coppices after fires, has erect branchlets, lanceolate leaves and fruits always 3-carpellate. It differs from M. cauliflora which has capitellate style.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 11. A review of the genus Macrostylis. J. S. African Bot. 47(3): 373-403. [CC BY]

description: Macrostylis villosa is recognised as distinct being one of only two Macrostylis species that coppice after fires, having the stigma capitellate and having leaves lanceolate acute 4-13 mm long with the apex trunculate.

description: When describing Salvadora australis the author, Schweickerdt, contrasted it with the nearly related species S. persica Linn. and S. oleoides Decne. The last mentioned is an Indian species which does not occur in Africa. Evidently Schweickerdt was not aware of S. angustifolia Turrill, a Madagascan species, which agrees very well with the South African S. australis and which the author, Turrill, states is nearest S. oleoides Decne. A study of material from Madagascar showed that the South African specimens differed from those from Madagascar only in the persistent short dense pubescence of the branchlets and leaves and Schweickerdt's species was therefore reduced to varietal rank under S. angustifolia Turrill.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Salvadoraceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 128-134. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Thesium alatum was first collected in 1930, but it has been persistently misidentified as T. angulosum A.DC. of section Imberbia, from which it immediately distinguished by its bearded perianth segments and almost sessile stigma, as well as by its more robust habit and differently disposed flowers. In A. W. Hill's account of the genus (in Flora Capensis 5(2): 136, 1915) it runs down to T. cytisoides A. W. Hill, which has been reduced to a synonym of T. utile A. W. Hill by N. E. Brown. This is where its affinity lies. Thesium alatum is common on steep grass slopes along the face of the Drakensberg from Royal Natal National Park (Bergville district) in the north to Bushman's Nek (Underberg district) in the south. The plants are a dull yellowish green and often form conspicuous stands though individually well-spaced. The flowers, too, are dull yellowish green outside, but white inside with snowy white tufts of hairs at the tips of the perianth segments.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM; Burtt, BL. 1983. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: X. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 41(2): 299-319. [CC BY-SA]

description: The general aspect of T. albomontanum is distinct from that of any other species and recalls that of certain Euphorbias; the low bushes are densely and intricately branched and the stems are thick and rigid. The flowers are very similar to those of T. commutatum Sond. in form and size, but they are borne in larger numbers in the cluster and are slightly more fleshy; the bracts, moreover, have quite entire margins, whereas those in T. commutatum are fimbriate. My plants were reported upon at Kew as 'T. commutatum Sond., though stems thicker than sp. in Kew Herb.' I have carefully compared the plant with Wolley-Dod 3015, Bolus 8000, and Schlechter 10235, in the Herb. Bolus, all vouched for as T. commutatum by Dr. A. W. Hill, and I conclude that my plant is quite distinct. Schlechter 10235 is from a similar locality (Cold Bokkeveld, 5800 ft.) and would be expected to approximate to mine if an identical species.
bibliographicCitation: Compton, RH. 1931. The Flora of the Whitehill District. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 19: 269-326. [All rights reserved]

description: Thesium durum is a distinctive plant forming dense hard cushions on basalt sheets or in hard stony ground. The older parts of the stems appear to be leafless, but this is not so: the leaves are scale-like, closely appressed and distant. On young twigs the leaves are imbricate and are easily seen because the upper parts are spreading, imparting a spiky look to the twigs. The flowers are borne on much abbreviated dwarf lateral shoots arranged in spikes; here the leaves, which resemble the bracts, are closely imbricate, so that the flowers appear to terminate short scaly peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM; Burtt, BL. 1983. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: X. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 41(2): 299-319. [CC BY-SA]

description: Chevalier, in Cafeiers du Globe 3: 219 (1947), included the nomen C. klaurathii De Wild. (in Ann. Jard. Buitenz., Suppl. 3, 1: 372 (1910) under the synonymy of C. racemosa. Since the specimen on which C. klaurathii was based (Klaurath s.n., Bt) came from Iringa in Tanzania, this association is highly unlikely. This species is very polymorphic, especially with regard to the size, shape and number of corolla lobes. The leaves also vary in texture and in the type of domatia, but this may be due (in part at least) to the stage of growth at which they were collected. This coffee has been referred to as ‘Inhambane (or Inyambane) Coffee’ and is reputed to have been used by local settlers. Numerous collections from Mozambique are reported from cultivation.
bibliographicCitation: Bridson, DM. 2003. 94. Rubiaceae: 70. Coffea L., Fl. Zambes. 5(3): 452-463. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [CC BY]

description: Two taxa have previously been confused under the epithet C. zanguebariae, namely this species and C. pseudozanguebariae Bridson from Kenya and Tanzania. Loureiro described the flowers of C. zanguebariae as being “polynatus” and having a 6-7-lobed corolla; this species has 2-5 flowers per axil while C. pseudozanguebariae has 1-2(3) individually borne flowers per axil; both have 6-8 corolla lobes. Furthermore, Loureiro’s description of the fruit agrees with this species rather than with the small-seeded, distinctly beaked fruit of C. pseudozanguebariae, which would seem less likely to have been cultivated, as mentioned by Loureiro, or so extensively used, as suggested by Cheney. The fact that no gatherings of C. pseudozanguebariae are known south of latitude 8°S further substantiates the choice of this taxon as being the correct C. zanguebariae, because the related species, C. racemosa, also based on a Loureiro type, was also collected from Mozambique. Chevalier’s (1949) inclusion of this species in South Africa (Pondoland) was most likely incorrect.
bibliographicCitation: Bridson, DM. 2003. 94. Rubiaceae: 70. Coffea L., Fl. Zambes. 5(3): 452-463. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. [CC BY]

description: With corms with fine, netted tunics and narrow, leathery leaves of the Ixia capillaris type, I. dieramoides is recognised mainly by the larger flowers with a tube 13-18(-22) mm long and with filaments and often the bases of the anthers included in the tube. The smaller flowers of I. capillaris have a tube (4-)5-7(-8) mm long, tepals spreading from the base and filaments typically exserted 1-2 mm. Unlike I. capillaris, the flowers are often faintly scented. Well-grown plants usually reach 600 mm high, thus extending substantially above the surrounding vegetation, which may be only 350 mm high. In dry, stony ground in poor soils, plants may be just 250 mm high, have one or two flowers and may be unbranched. Seen from a distance, the flowering spikes nodding in the breeze resemble species of Dierama. Ixia dieramoides from the Cederberg has short, included filaments 2.5-5.0 mm long, as well as shorter anthers and style branches.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: At first appearing to be a slightly smaller-flowered variant of the widespread, short-tubed Ixia capillaris, I. exiliflora is distinguished by the longer perianth tube 8-10 mm [vs. (4-)5-7(-8) mm in I. capillaris] and anthers partly included in the tube, whereas the filaments are usually exserted ± 2 mm in I. capillaris. The partly included anthers recall the I. rapunculoides complex of species but the very different, narrow leaves and small corms with finely fibrous tunics, as well as the smaller flowers, make it clear that the included filaments are convergent. Plants from near Simonskloof, west of Koo, stand out in having white flowers with a yellow cup, but otherwise closely resemble blue-flowered I. exiliflora and have the characteristic short stamens and partly included anthers of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ixia reclinata has linear leaves typical of the I. capillaris group but considerably larger flowers with a perianth tube up to 15 mm long and spreading tepals forming a flower ± 40 mm in diameter. The style divides just below to opposite the bases of the anthers and has branches ± 5 mm long, unusual for the complex. This contrasts with blue-mauve (or pale yellow) flowers with a tube up to 8 mm long, flower diameter of ± 20 mm, style dividing opposite the upper third of the anthers and with branches < 1.5 mm long in I. capillaris. The flowers of I. reclinata are white, suffused with blue-mauve and zygomorphic, having unilateral stamens with parallel filaments extended horizontally with the anthers held closely together and facing upward. Unilateral stamens are rare in Ixia but are known in I. pauciflora of the I. capillaris group, to which I. reclinata appears to be most closely related. In I. pauciflora the stems are usually unbranched, the pink flowers have filaments exserted only 2-5 mm and the style usually divides opposite the lower third of the anthers. Stems of I. pauciflora are typically sheathed below by a collar of fibres, a feature uncommon in Ixia, but also present in the I. capillaris group in I. dieramoides.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is characterised by leaves which do not look glossy, and which are slightly rough to the touch. This roughness is due not to pubescence but to minute asperities along the venation. In addition, typical plants show no spots on the leaves, but a purple flush on their lower surface. When the plant grows in unusually shady places, the leaves may be very big, and rather more glossy. In addition, the purple stain is not inevitably present; and very rarely colonies of plants are encountered with spotted leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Merwe, FZ; Burges, EK; Dyer, RA. 1944. Scilla asperifolia F.van der Merwe. Fl. Pl. South Africa 24t.944 [CC BY]

description: Ledebouria confusa is similar to L. atrobrunnea but the plants are gregarial. The dry bulb scales have many thickened horizontal ridges and the leaves are partly emerged at anthesis, also much broader and non-spiral.

description: Included under T. racemosum Bernh. in F.C. 5, 2: 149, is a Natal sp. of stouter habit, different appearance and smaller fls. The measurements of typical T. racemosum (Krauss 386) are: cal.-tube 0.7 mm l.; lobes 1.2-1.3 mm l.; style 0.7 mm l. The measurements of gracilentum are: cal.-tube 1.5 mm l.; lobes 1.2-1.5 mm l.; style 2 mm l. The cal.-lobes of the type are fringed with papillae, but the specimen collected by Rogers (22054) has them fringed with distinct hairs, otherwise there seems to be no distinction. The apical tuft of hairs is absent from this sp.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, NE. 1932. 1. Thesium L. In: J Burtt Davy (ed.), A manual of the flowering plants and ferns of the Transvaal with Swaziland: 455-462 Longmans, Green and Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Ledebouria pardalota is related to L. floribunda but differs in the leaves lacking threads when torn, revolute leaf margin, inflorescence longer than the leaves, fleshy flower bracts without bracteoles, ovoid ovary with raised apex shoulders and papillate dorsal lobes. From L. revoluta it differs in the bulb scales and leaves with no threads when torn, pruinose abaxial leaf surface 1(-2) inflorescences, scape compressed at base, fleshy flower bracts and papillate basal lobes.

description: Thesium gypsophiloides is often confused with T. gracilarioides and T. resedoides where their distribution ranges overlap in northern KwaZulu-Natal but is easily distinguished by its thick (up to 10 mm diam.) woody stems that grow up to 2 m tall, the absence of vegetative scales, large linear-lanceolate leaves (7)9-19.5(25.5) x 0.6-2 mm, and compound monochasial cymose inflorescences with long peduncles (2.7)5.7-17.5 mm long tending towards the arrangement of scorpioid cymes. Thesium gracilarioides has slender stems up to 5 mm diam. growing to a maximum height of 1 m, with vegetative scales on the root and lower parts of the stems, smaller linear or linear-lanceolate leaves 3.0-14.5 x 0.3-1.0 mm, and short racemose inflorescences. Thesium resedoides has similar slender stems up to 3 mm diam. growing to a maximum height of 0.4 m, vegetative scales on the root and lower parts of the stems, smaller, linear leaves 4.5-22.5(26.0) x 0.3-2.3 mm, and racemose inflorescences with short pedicels (0.0)0.5-3.0 mm long. Thesium gypsophiloides and T. gracilarioides are also altitudinally separated as they occur between 152-610 m a.s.l. and 1640-1890 m a.s.l., respectively.

description: Dr. A. W. Hill (to whom I dedicate this species) examined the material and confirmed my opinion that it was new. African species in the section) principally in the arrangement of the flowers.T. penicillatum: Flrs, arranged in fairly dense terminal corymbs; perianth segments linear lanceolate. description: Flowering in mid-winter in May and June, Moraea longipes has the general aspect of M. ciliata and M. tricolor except that the stem is not subterranean at flowering but extends up to 180 mm above ground. Like most species of subg. Acaules the ovary is retracted to the base of the inflorescence spathes after flowering. The flowers are most like those of M. ciliata but have slightly broader style crests, triangular with the base 2.5-3.0 mm wide (± linear in M. ciliata) and the filaments are united basally for ± 1.5 mm, about one fifth of their length, as are those of most other species of subg. Acaules. The anthers of M. longipes are the longest in the subgenus, 7.5-9.0 mm long (5-8 mm in M. ciliata) and are held above the nectar guides on filaments as long as the tepal claws. A notable feature of M. longipes is the collar of fibres around the underground part of the stem, uncommon but not unique in the subgenus. The species flowers early in the season, May to early July, and grows in places where M. ciliata has been found in bloom six to eight weeks later. Flower colour in M. longipes is either pale, watery yellow or translucent white, then with the edges of the outer tepal limbs and the inner tepal limbs a pale coppery pink colour and with the tepals flushed the same colour outside.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Flowering in the dry season, the solitary, long, trailing leaf up to 1 m long is dry or almost so when flowering begins. The relatively small, blue flowers are distinctive, resembling those of sect. Hexaglottis in having subequal tepals with short erect claws, free stamens, and style branches divided to the base into filiform arms extending between the stamens. Plastid DNA data confirm an alliance with Moraea crispa and M. pseudospicata, both of which have small, blue flowers with partly united filaments and flattened style branches forked at the tips and appressed to the subtending anthers. The leaf of M. pearsonii is linear and narrowly channelled when fresh, but with the margins tightly inrolled on drying so that the leaf then appears to be terete. The main stem and branches bear sessile rhipidia at the upper nodes, a pattern found in several species of the section, including M. pseudospicata and M. verecunda, both Western Karoo endemics.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: There are four species of Thorncroftia: T. longiflora, T. media, T. succulenta and T. thorncroftii, known from Mpumalanga and Limpopo Provinces in South Africa and from Swaziland. Thorncroftia greenii always has entire leaves, whereas the leaves in the other species are usually crenate or obscurely so. T. greenii and T. longiflora have smaller leaves (maximum length 20 mm) as opposed to a minimum of 25 mm in all other species. While T. greenii is morphologically similar to T. longiflora, it shows differences in trichomes and corolla length. T. longiflora has coarse eglandular trichomes and almost inconspicuous capitate glandular hairs, whereas T. greenii has very thin (fine) eglandular hairs with conspicuous fine capitate glandular hairs. The corolla is shorter (28-32 mm) in T. greenii than in T. longiflora (35-48 mm). The species are allopatric, making identification easier. T. thorncroftii is easily distinguished from the other species in the genus by its small flowers (shorter than 180 mm) and prostrate, herbaceous habit.

Our species further differs from the unkeeled-leaf form of Aloe cooperi Baker in having much shorter flowers presented in a denser, capitate raceme, and the flower colour is not orange.

Drimia platyphylla, which is widespread through the western half of South Africa and has also been recorded from central and southern Namibia, differs from D. oliverorum in its usually paired leaves, distinctly pendent, urn-shaped flowers with papillate-puberulous filaments and sagittate anthers with basally diverging thecae barbellate at the base, and in the very short style, markedly shorter than the ovary.

description: Thesium procerum is a large, much-branched, spreading shrub up to 1.5 m tall, which is characterized by its sparsely leafy (5 to 10(16) leaves per 50 mm at middle of stem) and terete stems, racemose inflorescences with abundant 2- or 3-flowered monochasia and occasional 3-flowered dichasia, flowers with stamens inserted at the base of the tepals, twisted placental columns and stipitate fruits. Thesium gracilarioides and T. gypsophiloides are the only other species in the complex that grow taller than about 0.3 m. Thesium procerum is geographically separated from T. gypsophiloides which is restricted to KwaZulu-Natal and differs in its moderately leafy (4 to 12 leaves per 50 mm at middle of stem) and sulcate stems, compound monochasial and dichasial cymes which resemble scorpioid cymes, flowers with stamens inserted in the perianth tube, straight placental columns and sessile, or occasionally shortly stipitate fruits. Thesium gracilarioides occurs sympatrically with T. procerum and has a similar inflorescence structure but its leafy (14 to 40 leaves per 50 mm at middle of stem) and sulcate stems, flowers with stamens inserted in the perianth tube, straight placental columns and sessile fruits separates it from T. procerum.

description: A comparison of the three species T. virgatum, T. pseudovirgatum and T. commutatum seems desirable as superficially they are much alike. T. virgatum is widely distributed on the Cape Peninsula and appears to be the only one of the three species occurring North of Constantia Nek. The other two range from Constantia Nek southwards, and south of Smitswinkel Bay they are much more common than T. virgatum. The habit is similar but T. commutatum is usually much more densely branched than the others. In T. virgatum the inflorescence is somewhat corymbose but in the others the cymules do not reach a common level. The flower in T. virgatum has a definite pedicel, in T. pseudovirgatum it is almost sessile and in T. commutatum the pedicel is entirely absent. The bracts and bracteoles are relatively large in T. commutatum where they exceed the perianth tube in length. In T. virgatum they are yet smaller. Good diagnostic characters are provided by the perianth. In both T. virgatum and T. commutatum the lower part of the perianth is saucer-like. In T. pseudovirgatum it is more like a cup. On the outside of the perianth glandular patches are present in all three species but they are much more conspicuous in T. virgatum than the others. Both T. virgatum and T. pseudovirgatum have well developed humps on the back of the perianth lobes at the apex. This hump is only slightly developed in T. commutatum. The stamens have short filaments in T. virgatum and T. commutatum, but long, well developed filaments in T. pseudovirgatum. The length of the style bears a direct relation to the length of the stamens in all three species. The long style of T. pseudovirgatum is a useful diagnostic feature in distinguishing this species from the other two. The fruits afford good means of identifying the species, but a word of caution is necessary. In dried herbarium material the veins on the fruit usually become prominent and these are often used as a specific character. In fresh material these veins may be quite obscure and only become evident after drying. As most species of Thesium shed their fruits before they are completely dry, the fruits found on any particular specimen gathered for identification will not necessarily have characters in the fresh fruit such as will become evident after drying. As descriptions of almost all South African species of Thesium have been drawn up from herbarium material, it follows that these descriptions do not always fit the fruit when fresh. For instance in the three species under consideration all have prominent veins when dried but in both T. virgatum and T. pseudovirgatum these are obscure in the middle portion when fresh. The fruits illustrated were ripe fruits, ready for shedding but not completely dry. They are all drawn to the same scale. In T. virgatum and T. pseudovirgatum a prominently 5-ribbed pedestal is present. In T. commutatum this pedestal is relatively shorter and though it may be obscurely lobed, the well-marked ribs of the other species are never present. Ten conspicuous ribs with minor irregular ridges running between them are usually evident on the body of the fruit when it is ready for shedding in T. commutatum. In T. virgatum the ten ribs are either absent or just visible when the fruit is shed and the intervening ridges are not evident. T. pseudovirgatum has a similar fruit but here only five of the ribs are eventually seen to run from the pedestal to the perianth, the five intermediate ribs being incomplete. In all cases drying brings the ribs into prominence so that descriptions based on herbarium material alone would give all fruits as ribbed with reticulations between the ribs. In T. commutatum a depression is formed below the junction of adjacent perianth segments. This depression is completely lacking in the other two species and affords a sure means of identifying T. commutatum.

description: Distinguished by its small size and underground stem, Geissorhiza lapidosa has a corm with concentric tunics and smooth, ± plane, falcate leaves. It differs from other dwarf species of subg. Weihea in its high mountain habitat and unusual leathery, falcate leaves at most 1 mm wide. The short-tubed, white flowers have an unusually short style dividing opposite the lower half of the anthers. Similar flowers are found in G. nana and G. setacea, both lowland species: G. nana occurs in renosterveld vegetation in the Overberg between Caledon and Swellendam and has broader, thin-textured leaves up to 2 mm wide and even smaller flowers with the tepals mostly 3-6 mm long, and very short filaments ± 2 mm long; G. setacea grows in seasonally wet places on flat sandy or loamy ground in Western Cape between Gouda and Caledon and has similarly narrow but linear leaves, 0.5-1(-2) mm wide but larger flowers with tepals 6-8 mm long, a longer tube ± 6 mm long, and the style branching opposite the tips of the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its large, zygomorphic flowers solitary on the branches, Geissorhiza monticola has a nodding blue perianth and well-exserted, declinate stamens The flowers have a short perianth tube ± 3 mm long and tepals 14-18 mm long. The plane leaves are prostrate with slightly thickened margins and main veins. Its relationships presumably lie with G. delicatula of the Langeberg and Swartberg and its allies, with which it shares an oblique corm, several plane leaves with the marginal vein set slightly away from the margin itself, and solitary flowered spikes. Geissorhiza delicatula has much smaller, cup-shaped flowers held upright, with elliptical or obovate, pale mauve tepals mostly 7-10 mm long, erect stamens with filaments 3-5 mm long, and a central style of similar length with short style branches up to 1.5 mm long, thus less than half as long as in G. monticola. Geissorhiza nigromontana may also be confused with G. monticola, but it has a stem ± prostrate toward the base, a spike of 2 or 3 flowers (flowers always single in G. monticola), bears cormlets in the leaf axils, shorter leaves with blades 4-10 mm wide vs. 2-3 mm in G. monticola, and the flowers are, as far as known, upright and radially symmetric.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: With its five or six relatively short leaves, the basal with horizontally spreading blades, low stature and 1- or 2-flowered spikes, Geissorhiza altimontana appears most closely allied to the Swartberg species, G. nigromontana and G. uliginosa. Geissorhiza uliginosa is essentially aquatic, growing in streams and waterfalls, and has reduced corms, but G. nigromontana has a similar habitat to G. altimontana, viz.; damp, mossy ledges in shallow soil and south-facing slopes, and both species flower in the summer months of January and February. The longer perianth tube, 7-8 mm long, and tepals ± 14 mm long, readily separate G. altimontana from G. nigromontana, which has a very short perianth tube, 2-3 mm long, and tepals 14-16 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In its general aspect Geissorhiza helmei recalls species of sect. Engysiphon, most members of which have fairly large corms with concentric tunics that fragment into sections that taper above into short bristles, and a single long basal leaf, always with thickened and winged margins and central vein, and with the surface of the margins glandular and with sand adhering to them. It and G. adriaani stand out in the section in having actinomorphic flowers, whereas other species have zygomorphic flowers with decumbent stamens and style. Most other members of the section also have flowers with a longer perianth tube although G. brevituba has a short tube, ± 8 mm long, thus comparable to the tube of G. helmei, ± 6 mm long. Geissorhiza brevituba, also endemic to the Piketberg, has larger flowers with tepals 25-30 mm long and spikes typically with only one to three flowers with the style dividing well beyond the anther tips. The main spikes of G. helmei have up to 10 flowers with tepals ± 10 mm long.

description: Recognised by the combination of a hairy stem, leaves with the margins and central vein winged with pilose wing edges, and small, white to pink flowers with unequal filaments. Its immediate relationships are uncertain although it evidently falls in sect. Ciliatae. Pollen grains with specialised, complex apertures place the species closest to G. exilis and G. inflexa, but the filaments of both these species are equal in length. The low stature and small flowers recall G. minuta of the Gifberg and Pakhuis Mtns, but that species has a smooth stem, equal stamens, and the thickened leaf margins and central vein lack the wings with ciliate edges of G. saxicola.

description: Distinguished by the two basal leaves with narrowly winged margins and a raised and winged central vein exactly like those of its presumed immediate relative G. heterostyla, and it also has the derived pollen grains with complex aperture and operculum often found in that species. In living plants, the glistening purple-pink flowers with a dark purple centre, purple filaments and a short purple style are unmistakable. The style, ± 3 mm long, divides opposite the lower third of the filaments and the nearly straight style branches are unusual in the subgenus and probably associated with its pollination by hopliine beetles, species of which have been captured on the flowers. Vegetatively almost identical, widespread Geissorhiza heterostyla is particularly difficult to distinguish from G. cantharophila in the herbarium but alive the blue to mauve or almost white flowers, pale yellow to green in the throat and tube usually edged in darker blue or mauve, and ± white stamens and style branches make it easy to separate the two species.

description: Thesium vahrmeijeri is routinely misidentified as T. resedoides but is easily recognised as the only annual herbaceous species in the T. goetzeanum complex. Plants have a slender branched root system, lacking vegetative scales on the roots and lower part of the stems, which are slender and often spreading, with stipitate fruits. Thesium resedoides is a suffrutex with a thick woody rhizome, with vegetative scales on the roots and lower parts of the stems, robust erect or sub-erect stems, and sessile fruits. Thesium vahrmeijeri is also spatially separated from the rest of the T. goetzeanum complex as its distribution is restricted to coastal regions in northern KwaZulu-Natal at elevations lower than 152 m a.s.l.

Lamarck's name T. virgatum has been restored for the species so long known as T. paniculatum. It is unfortunate that Sonder in taking up T. virgatum included specimens referred by De Candolle to T. juncifolium. T. virgatum embraces a wide range of forms which merge into one another, and it has not been found possible to keep up T. dregeanum, A.DC., as a distinct species.

description: It is partial to damp sandy places, and on the Cape peninsula reaches 2000 ft. (Wolley Dod).
bibliographicCitation: Hiern, WP. 1904. XCV. Scrophulariaceae. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4(1-3): 121-420. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15241#page/129/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: Previously specimens were included under P. rigidissima, which has anthers 1.4-1.8 mm long and forms small tufts, never rings.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species was sunk into P. eriostoma by Linder & Ellis, but Galley & Linder now recognise P. juncifolia as a separate species. P. eriostoma is woolly hairy on sheath and the sheath mouth, does not form neatly defined tussocks in the field, and occurs on shales and sandstones.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Specimens with forked corolla lobes are often confused with M. silenoides, but M.fragrans is easily distinguished from both M. silenoides and M. praeterita by the minute glandular pubescence on stem and leaves (not hairs 0.1-0.3 mm long, with balloon-tipped hairs also present especially on the inflorescence axes). The petiolar part of the leaf is often much longer in M. fragrans than in the other two species, and the pedicels are mostly shorter.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Balloon-tipped hairs characteristic of the genus as a whole on the lower stem, leaves and corolla tube. These hairs will distinguish M. glandulosa from M. leiostachys, as Phillips pointed out, but the species is probably more closely allied to M. laxa, which also has balloon-tipped hairs, but M. laxa is grey, well grown plants are more branched than those of M. glandulosa, the leaves are often entire, the flowers often solitary and tending to be smaller than those of M. glandulosa, with corolla tube up to 9 mm long, limb up to 8 mm in diameter and anticous lobe 2-3 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Variable, especially in size, and two forms can be distinguished: a tall, soft lowland form and a small, purplish high altitude form.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is allied M. dregei and M. platystigma, also montane in their distribution, but occurring much further east in the Drakensberg massif. The grey indumentum will at once distinguish M. incana, but it differs further in floral detail, particularly in its longer calyx tube and the disposition of the clavate hairs in the throat.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Manulea laxa is characterized by its grey stems and leaves, these more or less obtuse with mostly entire to subentire margins (occasionally sparingly toothed), short indumentum, the hairs mostly balloon-tipped (though in the southern part of its range gland-tipped hairs may be intermixed) and delicate inflorescences in which the flowers are either solitary or in very few-flowered monochasial cymules. On the other hand, M. leiostachys (with which M. laxa is often confused) is green often drying brown with mostly longer indumentum (hairs to 0.6-1 mm though they may be much shorter), serrate leaves, and coarser inflorescences with up to 15 flowers in each dichasial cymule.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Manulea minor has been much confused with M. exigua, from which it is easily distinguished by its scapose stems, much less markedly toothed leaves and glandular pubescence. Its relationship seems to lie with M. praeterita, from which it is distinguished by the longer hairs on the stems (up to 0.2-0.3 mm versus 0.1 mm) and leaves (up to c. 0.3-0.4 mm versus 0.25 mm), and the entire corolla lobes (not distinctly lobed).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Not easily mistaken for any other species except M. schaeferi, known from north and east of the area of M. nervosa.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Similar to P. tysonii, which has the lateral awns not reaching glume apices.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Nembudani, MT; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Pentameris P.Beauv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 517-559. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: I have seen nothing to match this plant precisely. It is allied to M. tomentosa, and resembles the lax form of that plant, but it is at once distinguished by the entire or subentire leaves clad in a mixture of glandular and eglandular hairs, and by the monochasial cymes. In facies and in size of flowers it most closely resembles some of the plants mentioned under M. caledonica (viz. Maguire 29 and Martin 340) as possibly having been influenced by M. tomentosa, but the long hairs on the stems and leaves of these specimens are distinctly obtuse (almost balloon-tipped), whereas in M. obtusa they are acute, as in M. tomentosa.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Manulea robusta appears to be a more rigid plant than M. dubia, less leafy, with differently shaped leaves (much narrower in relation to their length than those of M. dubia and with a much less well marked petiolar part) and these rapidly smaller upwards, the lowermost floral bracts always linear (never leaf-like) and the flowers often smaller, particularly in length of calyx lobes and size of corolla limb; the flowers may also differ somewhat in colour, but this needs confirmation.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Aloe neilcrouchii belongs to A. sect. Leptoaloe and represents the largest of the known species of this group. Its closest affinity appears to be A. boylei Baker, especially A. boylei subsp. major Hilliard & Burtt. However, it differs from that species by its long, sprawling, leafless stems that branch from the base or form offshoots along its length, its shorter but broader, elongated-deltoid leaves that are copiously covered with white tuberculate spots on both surfaces and its taller inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Klopper, RR; Smith, GF. 2010. Asphodelaceae: Aloe neilcrouchii, a new robust Leptaloe from KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Bothalia 40(1): 93-96. [CC BY]

description: The stems of M. turritis are leafy throughout, which character, as well as the leaves themselves (elliptic in outline and with distinctly doubly serrate margins), will at once distinguish the species from both M. rubra and M. leiostachys, with which it has been confused. Furthermore, in M. rubra there are strong bands of clavate hairs in the throat; in M. turritis, the throat is glabrous or nearly so, as it is in M. leiostachys.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Manulea schaeferi has been much confused with M. nervosa, which it resembles in habit and in its almost regular corolla limb, but it is readily distinguished by the calyx, which is lobed almost to the base whereas in the markedly bilabiate calyx of M. nervosa the two lips are each lobed less than halfway. The flowers of M. schaeferi are mostly smaller too (e.g. anticous lip of calyx 3.5-4.8 mm long versus 4.6-8.5 mm, and corolla limb 10-14 mm in diameter versus 14-20 mm) and the calyx lobes are narrower in relation to their length.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The essential features of typical M. tomentosa are its villous (hairs acute) stems and inflorescence axes, obtuse leaves running up to the base of the dense many-flowered inflorescence, corolla tube hairy all over outside and with strong longitudinal bands of clavate hairs inside the throat, and corolla lobes almost or quite as long as broad with rounded tips (the true breadth often obscured by the revolute margins).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It is easily recognized by its large colourful flowers with radiating dark lines around the mouth of the corolla tube, relatively narrow leaves, and rather sparse indumentum, particularly on the ovaries and capsules. This last character will at once distinguish it from the closely allied L. formosa; see under that species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It is closely allied to P. cuneifolium; the differences between them are detailed under that species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]
