description: The species is sometimes confused with the allied P. bracteatum, with which it is sympatric, but P. bracteatum differs in facies (very lax inflorescences with the lowermost flowers in the axils of the uppermost leaves with an imperceptible gradation to leaflike bracts, in contrast to the dense racemes of P. cuneifolium with a more or less abrupt transition from leaves to bracts; even when the lowermost flowers are widely spaced, as they sometimes are, the change from leaves to bracts is evident) as well as in floral detail: P. cuneifolium has bracts 0.5-3 mm broad in the upper part (versus 2.5-9 mm), anticous calyx lobes 1.5-2 mm long (versus (2.25-)3-4 mm, corolla limb (4-)5-7 mm across the lateral lobes, and mauve (versus 3-4.5 mm, and white), anticous lobe 2.5-4 mm long (versus 1-2.1 mm).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Similar to T. purpureum, a rhizomatous perennial that has longer lemma hairs (1.8-2.2 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Tribolium Desv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 707-717. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to T. tenellum, an annual with shorter lemma hairs (0.5-1.2 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L; Moeaha, MJ. 2015. Tribolium Desv. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 707-717. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: P. cephalophorum can be recognized by its shaggy white indumentum, narrow toothed leaves and masses of small round heads corymbosely arranged, the bracts characteristically glabrous to puberulous at the tips and becoming shaggy in the lower half. It is often confused with P. capitatum. Phyllopodium cephalophorum is closely allied to P. phyllopodioides and in areas where they are sympatric they may be difficult to distinguish.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Phyllopodium multifolium and P. elegans grow together on the Potteberg, where the obvious difference in flower colour (mauve in P. multifolium, white in P. elegans) has induced collectors to take both. In this locality (and also further east, at Silver River) P. multifolium tends to have much broader basal leaves than P. elegans (up to 12 mm broad, seldom exceeding 3 mm in P. elegans). There are also differences in indumentum, P. multifolium being more glandular than P. elegans and this often shows up well on the bracts; the corolla limb of P. multifolium tends to be larger than that of P. elegans (4.5-7 mm across versus 4-5 mm), reflected in the size of the lobes (e.g. anticous lobe 2-3.2 mm long in P. multifolium, 1.75-2 mm in P. elegans).Both species are readily mistaken for Selago, especially `S. heterophylla E. Mey.' of Rolfe's account in Flora Capensis 5(1), but they are of course easily distinguished by their ovaries, multiovulate in Phyllopodium resulting in a many-seeded capsule, biovulate in Selago, which produces two 1-seeded cocci.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Polycarena pubescens is however a well-marked and easily recognized species distinguished by its relatively broad, entire bracts and heads of almost sessile flowers with a small limb.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It is easily recognized by its delicate habit and relatively long racemes with minute widely-spaced flowers borne on conspicuous filiform pedicels up to 5 mm long. No other species of Polycarena has a regular corolla limb with very acute lobes. The frequent reduction of the stamens from four to three or two suggests that selfing may take place, but in all cases both anthers and style are exserted.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is characterized by the small tight knots of vegetative buds at the crown, by its wiry spreading, branching stems, narrow spreading leaves and few-flowered inflorescences. The corolla lobes are mostly glandular above at least near the base (when we described the species, we were mistaken in thinking that the type material is eglandular).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It differs from T. guthrieae by the larger, wider, more or less orbicular flowers, in which the tepals are exserted next to the floral bracts, and by the absence of sterile branches at the nodes of older, mature culms. This new species is also found far to the east of the nearest currently known populations of T. guthrieae from the Langeberg at Garcias Pass.
bibliographicCitation: Linder, HP. 2011. New species and combinations in the African Restionaceae. S. African J. Bot. 77: 415-424. [CC BY]

description: Zaluzianskya benthamiana is very glandular on stems, leaves, bracts and calyx, and this feature, in combination with the long patent acute hairs, relatively long, narrow, entire or subentire leaves, and rounded corolla lobes make it easily recognizable. Its closest ally appears to be Z. pusilla, with which it is partly sympatric; Z. pusilla differs not only in having four stamens, but it is also a much less glandular plant, with ± retrorse hairs on the stems, and a shorter corolla tube.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: There is remarkable variation in the width of the leaves and they may be entire to prominently toothed, irrespective of width. The degree of hairiness is also variable, from almost shaggy to nearly glabrous, with corresponding indumentum on the bracts and calyx. In the western part of the range, indumentum is usually well developed, but nearly glabrous plants also occur, while along the southern coast, hairs on leaves, bracts and calyces are nearly confined to margins and midlines.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Zaluzianskya diandra is a most distinctive species, both in habit (well-grown plants are bushy) and in the flowers: the strongly reflexed narrow orange lobes with revolute margins are more like those of many species of Manulea than any Zaluzianskya, but the two well exserted, disproportionately large, anthers are unique.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Zaluzianskya distans is closely allied to Z. ovata, from which it differs in habit (tufts of simple or subsimple stems, not a well branched shrublet) and in its generally much laxer inflorescence. The two species are sympatric on Platberg, where these differences, as well as the differences in the type of habitat that is favoured, are strikingly demonstrated.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Zaluzianskya inflata is an odd-looking plant with the relatively huge bracts and calyces seeming to weigh down the stems, which, when they attain any height, have dried contorted and bent. The small corolla limb is all out of proportion to these large organs and the long corolla tube. The species has been much confused with Z. pumila, which has a mostly smaller calyx, and larger corolla limb with a distinctive raised orange 'star' around the mouth, and larger anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: There is remarkable variation in the size of the corolla limb, which is nevertheless the most distinctive feature of the species. The flowers open in sunshine and the limb is held vertically; it is strongly zygomorphic, glandular both above and below, and the mouth is glabrous or very nearly so. This contrasts with the actinomorphic limb in Z. natalensis and Z. spathacea, which is held horizontally and opens at dusk. These two species, like Z. microsiphon, produce a single stem from a mass of undeveloped buds on the crown of the rootstock, and favour similar habitats; Z. microsiphon and Z.spathacea are partly sympatric.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Its distinguishing features are the mass of undeveloped buds on the crown and the tightly congested inflorescence, the axis invisible even in fruit. This latter character will at once distinguish it from its ally, Z. spathacea; its growth habit distinguishes it from Z. maritima, an annual herb with which it has been much confused.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Harvey's figure (loc. cit.) clearly shows the elongation of the spike that is characteristic of Z. pachyrrhiza and helps to distinguish it from Z. natalensis, in which the spike remains short and thick. Zaluzianskya pachyrrhiza has a thick woody rootstock often without any vegetative buds on the crown, in contrast to the crown of Z. natalensis with its thick tuft of vegetative buds. The corolla tube of Z. pachyrrhiza is often shaggy with long acute hairs mixed with shorter glandular ones; sometimes glandular hairs predominate and acute hairs may occur only near the base of the tube; the tube of Z. natalensis is usually glandular, the hairs up to 0.25 mm long, rarely with a few eglandular hairs as well, up to 0.25 mm-0.4 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The species varies a great deal in its pubescence. The unarmed form with relatively glabrous leaves has in the past been separated as D. tristis, while D. zeyheri is described as being spiny and having pubescent leaves. Intermediates are, however, so common that the step taken by Wild (l.c.) to merge the two species is supported. Following Sleumer (l.c.), D. revoluta is treated here as a local form of D. zeyheri with glabrous leaves and papillose-puberulous ovaries and fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Langenegger, JE. 1976. Flacourtiaceae: Dovyalis, Fl. S. Africa 22: 84-90. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The calyx, only very shallowly bilabiate and almost always puberulous or pubescent, is a good distinguishing character; allied to the glabrous mouth, it will at once distinguish Z. peduncularis from Z. collina, with which it has been much confused and with which it is partly sympatric in Namaqualand. However, its relationship is with Z. elgonensis and Z. rubrostellata: Z. elgonensis has much smaller flowers (corolla tube only 10-12 mm long) and different colour-patterning; the patterning in Z. rubrostellata (a distinct star-shaped scarlet 'eye') also marks it off from Z. peduncularis, but it is further distinguished by differences in foliage and corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It differs chiefly in the higher percentage of citronellal, and hence the more fragrant lemon-scented leaves, and in its non-rostrate operculum and somewhat smaller fruits. Its leaves are often narrower.
bibliographicCitation: White, F; Kupicha, FK. 1978. 74. Myrtaceae. In: E Launert (ed.), Fl. Zambes. 4: 183-212. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, Glasgow. [CC BY]

description: The growth habit of the plant (a cushion of leaf rosettes, whence the trivial name) is a valuable diagnostic feature. There is considerable variation in leaf form: plants with narrowly linear leaves look strikingly different from plants with broader, spathulate leaves. Narrow-leaved plants seem particularly common in the northern part of the range (though not to the exclusion of broad-leaved plants), for example, at Leribe (Lesotho), on Qua Qua Mountain and Platberg in the Orange Free State, on parts of the low Drakensberg in northern Natal (Bezuidenhout's Pass, Manyanyeza Mountain, Itala), and between Badplaats and Lake Chrissie in the Transvaal, where the leaves are remarkably long and narrow.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: An acaulescent herb with radical, rosulate, bullate leaves dark green and shiny above and paler below, with flowers mostly hidden under the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Achariaceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 128-134. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Zaluzianskya rubrostellata is allied to Z. peduncularis and their areas abut on the western margins of Lesotho, but Z. peduncularis is always at lower altitudes than Z. rubrostellata, on the sandstone, not the basalt. The leaves of Z. rubrostellata are thicker in texture than those of Z. peduncularis and usually extend further up the stems, the colour patterning around the mouth is markedly different (always starshaped in Z. rubrostellata, merely a neat ring in the throat of Z. peduncularis), the limb mostly larger, with broader lobes (10-15 mm in diam. versus 5-10 mm with lobes 3.2-5 mm broad at the tips versus 1-3.2 mm), and the anthers are larger (anticous anthers 1.4-1.7 mm versus 0.4-1.4 mm, posticous ones 2.3-2.8 mm versus 0.6-1.8 mm). Unlike Z. peduncularis, Z. rubrostellata gives no indication of either cleistogamy or autogamy.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Its closest ally is Z. angustifolia, which differs in its sprawling well-branched stems, vegetative buds on the crown, mostly fewer flowers in an inflorescence, and the limb of the corolla larger (lobes mostly 5-8 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Despite its diminutive size, it has relatively large and somewhat fleshy rhomboid leaves and bracts increasing in size upwards; this feature, as well as the spreading glandular hairs on the stems, make it a most distinctive species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It is distinguished by its bifid corolla lobes, two stamens, and leaves and bracts more or less obtuse, margins of at least the leaves usually distinctly toothed, and both surfaces clad in short dense pubescence, longer hairs also being present particularly on the lower margins and lower backs. The whole plant generally, but not always, dries dusky. From Langebaan north to Velddrift, Aurora and Sauer, the hairs on leaves and bracts may be sparser and longer and the tips of both rather more acute. Some of these plants dry dusky, others are greenish: they begin to approach Z. affinis in the shape of leaf and bract, but the leaf margins are toothed as in Z. villosa and the indumentum is closer to that of Z. villosa than that of Z. affinis. They are therefore included in a broad circumscription of Z. villosa. See further under Z. affinis, Z. sanorum and Z. pilosissima, all of which have been confused with Z. villosa because they share the characters of bilobed corolla lobes and stamens reduced to two. The corolla limb may be white to various shades of mauve and usually has a yellow 'eye' that darkens to orange or red as the flower ages.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Zaluzianskya violacea is normally easily recognized by the combination of retrorse hairs on the stems, finely pubescent corolla tube, mauve limb with bifid lobes, a deep yellow 'eye', and four stamens. The two anticous (exserted) stamens are occasionally completely aborted, apparently throughout a whole population; the two posticous stamens are then shortly exserted.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The salient features of the species are the finely pubescent leaves, bracts and calyces (almost velvety in the western part of the range, coarser in the eastern), the conspicuously pedunculate racemes loosely panicled, narrow bracts, and the corollas usually mauve.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Rolfe reduced S. capituliflora to synonymy under S. albida, but S. capituliflora differs from that species in its much less hairy leaves, bracts and calyces, its large lax panicles, shorter corolla tube, and style glabrous or nearly so.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Specimens are frequently misidentified as S. fruticosa, but S. aspera bears scant resemblance to that species (which has divaricately branched stems and much shorter inflorescences); in facies it strongly resembles S. pinea and S. grandiceps. Both these species differ in having strongly glandular bracts and calyces (eglandular hairs far outnumber glandular in S. aspera); also, the hairs on the stems of S. pinea are distinctive, being relatively long and strongly appressed, and the corolla is violet. Selago grandiceps differs from S. aspera not only in its strongly glandular bracts and calyces but also in its mostly longer calyces and corolla tubes and posticous anthers only briefly exerted. See also under S. nigrescens.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Among its close allies, the distinguishing features of S. atherstonei are its stems clad in simple acute patent hairs often underlain by minute glandular ones, short hairy fascicled leaves in which only the midrib is clearly visible, bracts scarcely longer than the calyx, calyx 2-3 mm long. In his key to the species of Selago, Rolfe (1901) distinguished S. muddiiirom S. atherstonei by 'heads solitary' versus 'heads not solitary'. The solitude of the heads depends on the age of the stem carrying the inflorescence: in young stems such as those sprouting anew from the caudex, heads are initially solitary, but subsequent branching eventually produces loosely panicled heads. Only S. procera has stems with patent hairs like those of S. atherstonei. It is easily distinguished by its much larger primary leaves with the 3-5 main veins clearly visible, its large profusely branched panicle, at least the lowermost bracts in each raceme far exceeding the calyx, and often longer calyx (3-4.4 mm). The area of S. atherstonei lies wholly within that of S. procera. Selago atherstonei is very closely allied to S. lydenburgensis with which it may hybridize.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It has been confused in herbaria with both S. galpinii and S. capitellata; it is easily distinguished from the latter by its flowers with a much longer corolla tube, and from S. galpinii by its much shorter and blunter bracts and mostly shorter calyx.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The type specimens of S. bolusii and Hilliard & Burtt 10735, which came from very nearly the same locality, have more acute leaves and bracts than the other material now included within the circumscription of the species, and the calyces are very irregularly 3-5-lobed, but I can see nothing to separate them at specific level.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Its characteristic features are the stem clad in coarse patent hairs, tufts of short thick glossy apiculate leaves, short broad spikes (c.15-20 x 10-12 mm), often solitary, sometimes associated (usually very loosely) with up to five (rarely more) subsidiary spikes borne on unbranched peduncles, both bracts and calyx hairy, the hairs on the backs of the bracts almost scabrid, and the cocci, deeply concave on the inner face (other species in this group with similar cocci are S. glomerata and S. nigromontana, probably S. karooica as well, but no ripe cocci have been seen). In herbaria, it is often confused with S. luxurious.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The relationship of S. burkei possibly lies with S. capitellata, from which it differs in its leaves, shorter and mostly narrower, margins revolute, both surfaces clad in minute (less than 0.1 mm) hairs, longer calyx, corolla limb always white. Also, the stems and inflorescence of S. burkei are often more branched than those of S. capitellata.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The characteristic features of S. curvifolia are its short, narrow, spreading-recurved leaves, loosely panicled short narrow racemes, narrow bracts, calyx glandular inside, short corolla tube, all anthers well exerted, style pubescent. The outside of the calyx is often clad all over in patent hairs (as in the type), but in many specimens these are few or wanting.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The salient features are the pale bark, short divaricate branchlets bearing small glomerules, their tips becoming spinescent when the flowers fall, and tufts of fascicled leaves spaced out along the branches; stems, leaves, bracts and calyces often all minutely puberulous, but leaves and bracts varying to almost glabrous. Characteristically, each primary leaf is strongly reflexed and is much larger than the axillary leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The characteristic features of S. eckloniana are the very short hairs on the stem often but not always confined to longitudinal bands, leaves longitudinally channelled above at least in the lower half, plane or somewhat rounded below, flowers distinctly pedicellate, bracts lanceolate and nipped in near the base to embrace the pedicel (lowermost few bracts sometimes leaflike; ignore them), calyx very glandular inside (globular glands easily seen except when oozing and then sticking to the corolla tube). The globular glands on stem, leaves, bracts and calyces often ooze so that these parts look varnished. Selago eckloniana is frequently misidendfied as 'S. spinea', that is, S. pinea, which is easily distinguished by the relatively long glandular hairs on stems, bracts and calyces.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago elongata is a distinctive species whose relationship probably lies with S. trinervia from which it differs sharply in its more or less fascicled leaves, inflorescence of sessile or nearly sessile flowers crowded into long spikes (not flowers on long pedicels loosely arranged in racemes), and its short broad rugulose cocci with a pair of incipient spurious cells (not long narrow and smooth without any trace of spurious cells).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The plant is distinctive by virtue of its dense glandular pubescence, the relatively long glandular hairs on the margins of the bracts and calyx lobes not matched in this group of species, nor the patent glandular hairs on the stem. Selago acocksii is also very glandular but the hairs are much shorter, and those on the stem are mostly masked by retrorse hairs, lacking in S. ferruginea.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The affinity of S. flanaganii seems to lie with S. immersa and S. innata, which it resembles in habit, flat leaf-like bracts, floral details, and pairs of cocci that do not separate; it differs, inter alia, in its very short pedicels (see key). The pairs of cocci of S. flanaganii are almost round and as hard as stone.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Characteristic features of S. fruticosa are the more or less divaricate branching with many short lateral branchlets mostly terminating in an inflorescence, the spikes rounded or oblong and remaining congested in fruit, relatively broad bracts and relatively long corolla tube, and the calyx glabrous inside. S. fruticosa is sometimes confused with S. triquetra, at once distinguished by its virgate branching, narrower spikes and shorter corolla tube.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Disa bifida is often confused with D. inflexa, to which it is closely allied, but it can generally be distinguished by the larger flowers, the broader median sepal and the slender, tapering, ascending spur. It also flowers earlier, and at lower altitudes than D. inflexa.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is very similar to Disa atricapilla, but recognizable by the shape and colour of the lateral sepals. D. bivalvata hybridizes with D. atricapilla. A posªsible hybrid with D. racemosa was also recorded.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: In herbaria, S. hermannioides is sometimes confused with ,S. namaquensis, which is easily distinguished by its much less hairy leaves, bracts and calyces; also, S. hermannioides dries greenish, S. namaquensis often blackish.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Disa bolusiana may be difficult to separate from D. comosa, and intermediate forms exist. The two can only be reliably separated on the leaf characters.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The species readily sets seeds and was shown to be self-pollinating.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: In herbaria, S. lamprocarpa has sometimes been confused with the plant here enumerated as S. perplexa.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It shares with S. canescens the characters of hairs in bands down the stem and nearly glabrous leaves and bracts; they differ inter alia in the structure of their compound inflorescences. Each side branch in S. linearis terminates in a simple raceme, whereas in S. canescens the side branches bear mostly racemes of racemes, the calyx tube is hairier and the cocci are narrower (0.8-1.2 mm broad vereus 1.5-1.7 mm) because the two spurious cells are not visible externally (they clearly bulge out on either side of the fertile part in S. canescens). Specimens of S. linearis tend to dry black, of S. canescens, greenish.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: In facies, S. longicalyx most resembes S. foliosa from southernmost Natal and nearby Transkei, a bushier plant with broader leaves and more spreading inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: In herbaria, the species is frequently confused with S. innala, which is similar in facies, but differs inter alia in its much more shallowly toothed calyx.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: A putative hybrid with Disa rhodantha was described as D. x paludicola J. Stewart & J.C. Manning.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago namaquensis is sometimes mistaken for S. hermannioides.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Most of the specimens now before me have been misdetermined as either S. dregei or S. scabrida. Among its close allies, S. polystachya is readily distinguished by its stems, the young parts being very narrowly winged down the centre of each decurrent leaf base, this part being either glabrous or less hairy than the rest of the stem, which is clad in recurved hairs (the overall degree of hairiness on both stems and leaves is variable), and by its inflorescence composed of relatively short broad spikes either arranged in a crowded corymb or running back down the stem to form a narrow panicle. It is easily confused with S. scabrida, which is distinguished by its stems, wingless and hairy all round, mostly longer and narrower spikes (in well grown specimens crowded at the apex of the stem, and not running back down the stem as they may do in S. polystachya), and mostly shorter corolla tubes. The two species are partially sympatric and it is not unlikely that they hybridize though their flowering periods scarcely overlap.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago ramosissima is characterized by its closely branched habit, small leaves closely appressed to the stem, innumerable small inflorescences, shaggy calyx glandular inside as well as out, and relatively broad cocci composed of bone hard tissue flanking the small fertile part that constitutes only roughly one third of the coccus. Several species partially sympatric with S. ramosissima are similar in facies: S. thomii is distinguished by its less conspicuously hairy bracts and calyces, calyx tube always glabrous inside, the lobes either glabrous or with a few minute glands at their tips, and narrower cocci with the seed occupying the whole of the interior (this is visible very early on, when the ovary begins to swell after fertilisation).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: This wide-ranging species is variable in the shape of the petal apices, the lip and the lateral sepals. Some of this variation is geographical, but there does not appear to be any correlation between the variable characters, so division of the species is not possible. It is one of the very few orchids that occurs in both winter- and summer-rainfall regions.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Among the group of species with deeply and subequally 5-lobed hispid or scabrid calyces and bracts, S setulosa is distinguished by its stems clad in long patent hairs and short, relatively broad, leaves hispid mainly on the margins and often liberally sprinkled with round white 'scales'. The calyx is usually at least 3 mm long, but in three of the westernmost specimens seen (Hugo 1715, NBG, Klein Hagelkraal, and Lewis 4143, SAM, Leighton 2535, BOL, Hagelkraal) the calyx measures only c. 2.2 mm and the leaves are mostly very small (measurements given in parentheses in the formal description). This may be an undescribed species, allied also to S. seticaulis.The closest ally of S. setulosa is S. prostrata, which has similar patent hairs on the stems and similar leaves, but which differs in its divaricate branching and longer spikes.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: This species varies in the width of the floral segments, the shape of the tepal apices, the degree of petal exsertion from the galea and the plant size. Much of the variation follows an altitudinal cline, with high altitude plants having narrow, acute floral segments and low altitude plants having wide, obtuse floral segments. There is also some differentiation between the midlands plants from KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape. These populations have been much reduced by farming activities.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Its general affinity is with S. foliosa and allies, but its distinctive calyx sets it apart.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago trinervia is without close allies (except perhaps S. elongata) but the sparingly toothed leaves, flat bracts adnate to a conspicuous pedicel as well as the calyx tube, and included posticous anthers indicate the general affinity of S. longipedicellata and its allies. The species is easily recognized (flat leathery leaves not crowded in fascicles and long racemes of pedicellate white flowers often overtopped by the bracts) despite its considerable variability in indumentum on leaves, bract, calyx and corolla, in the length of the bract, and in depth of lobing of the calyx. Leaves, bract and calyx range from almost glabrous to scabrid-pubescent.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is closely allied to S.canescens, from which it may be distinguished by its stems clad in mostly longer hairs, longer calyx and longer corolla tube; there is possibly also a difference in habit, S.villicaulis appearing to be a smaller, less bushy, plant than S.canescens, but there are too few adequate collections for me to be certain.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It is not easily confused with any of its allies except S. swaziensis to which it is very closely allied. Both species have long spreading hairs on stems, leaves, bracts and calyces, and relatively broad leaves, but whereas S. villosa is stoloniferous, S. swaziensis has a woody caudex, the leaves of S. villosa are nearly always entire, those of S. swaziensis very often toothed, thicker (c. 0.4-0.5 mm in a leaf cut midway, versus c. 2 mm), and perhaps always ascend rather than spread as in S. swaziensis; the glomerules of S. villosa are often solitary or subsolitary, those of S. swaziensis are usually borne in a narrow panictdate inflorescence. Moreover, specimens of S. villosa dry greenish, those of S. swaziensis blackish. The two species may be regarded as vicariads, one in the Barberton Mountains, the other about 40 km to the south on the high ground around Mbabane.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago ciliata is a well-marked species not easily confused with any other.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago decipiens is very closely allied to S. cinerea from which it is most easily distinguished by its lax rather than compact corymbose panicles; also, the leaves are devoid of hairs on the margins (except sometimes very minute ones at the base), and the posticous anthers are in the mouth or very nearly so. The two species appear to be allopatric.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago densiflora is allied to S. paniculata from which it is distinguished by its stems, 1 floriferous only in the upper part (not nearly to the base), panicles profusely branched, the individual racemes on leafy peduncles c. (10 -) 15-50 (- 100) mm long (not simple or sparingly branched, peduncles up to 10 mm long), largest primary leaves on mature stems ormv 0.5-1 mm broad, to 1.5 mm on very young stems (versus 1.2-2.1 mm broad, up to 4-5 mm on very young stems), bracts acute or subacute with conspicuous white membranous margins c. 0.2 mm broad, tapering upwards (versus obtuse or nearly so, without membranous margins). Only where the areas of the two species meet, along the Cape border.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Specimens of S. geniculata dry either blackish or greenish, which gives them a superficial dissimilarity, but it is not uncommon for the parts of a single collection to have dried differently. Among its allies, the diagnostic features of S. geniculata are the very short hairs on the stem, very long narrow spikes, bracts with rather abruptly acute to shortly acuminate incurved tips, backs of bracts glabrous except for tiny hairs sometimes present at the extreme base, the base pouched and transversely wrinkled, calyx 3-5-lobed, hairs on margins and outside up to c. 0.2 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: There is much variation in the size and shape of the leaves, but the species is easily recognised by its twiggy habit, hairs on the stems confined to longitudinal bands, leaves not fascicled, leathery, glandular-punctate, only occasionally with hairs on the margins, relatively long corolla tube, limb bright magenta-pink, and the coccus with two very large spurious cells.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago paniculata is distinguished by its short peduncles, relatively short leaves, glandular-punctate and either with few very small coarse hairs on margins and midline on lower surface or otherwise glabrous, bracts thick - textured, wrinkled when dry, obtuse, without white membranous margins, globular glands on lower part of back, calyx with broad anticolateral lobes clad in short coarse hairs and globular glands, and the pairs of cocci ovoid in outline.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is highly variable in its colour, ranging from a deep plum-purple to almost red. It is sometimes difficult to distinguish from Disa versicolor, although the shape and orientation of the petals and the degree of spur curvature will separate most collections. In addition, the sepals in D. versicolor turn brown at anthesis, while those of D. hircicomis do not.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago rotundifolia is relatively easily recognized despite a good deal of variation in indumentum on the stems and in shape of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: In herbaria, it is sometimes confused with S. recurva [S. albanensis].
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The distinguishing marks of the species are the narrow leaves, flowers in small glomerules c. 3-6 mm long (these aggregated into the terminal corymb), pedicels scarcely reaching 0.5 mm (occasionally 0.8 mm) in length, and the relatively broad bracts. The stems usually have long hairs throughout their length, but these hairs are entirely wanting in specimens from the environs of Makapan's Gat. The species is often confused in herbaria with T. natalensis, which also has narrow leaves, but the short pedicels, crowded glomerules and broader bracts will at once distinguish it.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: This taxon is probably of hybrid origin, the putative parents being Disa versicolor and D. hircicomis. Although the available collections indicate that recognizing three species is the best solution, more material from more collections should be investigated.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: A putative hybrid with Disa pulchra has been described.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The lip length is highly variable with populations in the Cederberg and Swartberg having much shorter lips than in the rest of the distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Striga elegans shows considerable variation in corolla size and color that does not seem to correlate with geography. This beautiful species resembles S. asiatica and the two are sympatric in East Africa (see notes under S. asiatica), but it can be distinguished from S. asiatica by its relatively short, dense inflorescence with opposite flowers and large brilliant scarlet corolla lobes. Authentic crop loss from this parasite has not been reported.
bibliographicCitation: Mohamed, KI; Musselman, LJ; Riches, CR. 2001. The genus Striga (Scrophulariaceae) in Africa. Ann. Missouri Bot. Gard. 88(1): 60-103. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2666132] [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the Missouri Botanical Garden Press, St. Louis.] [All rights reserved]

description: Knepper et al. showed that some populations of S. forbesii are distylous. Flowers either had styles strongly exserted from the corolla tube exposing the stigma, or stigmas were among or just below the epipetalous stamens, with increasing possibilities of self-pollination. Striga forbesii resembles S. latericea. Both are sympatric in East Africa, occupy wet habitats, and have unique salmon-pink corollas. No work has been done to demonstrate interfertility between these two species. Striga forbesii is distinguished from S. latericea by its annual habit, stiff hairs that give the plant a harsh texture, coarsely toothed and broader leaves, and shorter corollas with smaller lobes and a brighter salmon-pink color. The corolla color is darker in S. latericea.
bibliographicCitation: Mohamed, KI; Musselman, LJ; Riches, CR. 2001. The genus Striga (Scrophulariaceae) in Africa. Ann. Missouri Bot. Gard. 88(1): 60-103. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2666132] [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the Missouri Botanical Garden Press, St. Louis.] [All rights reserved]

description: It does not extend north into Mozambique where the similar S. pubifilora occurs. The two species may have different ecological requirements. Striga junodii is also morphologically similar to the Asian species, S. masuria; however, S. junodii has a characteristic notch on the lower corolla lobes. The current status of S. junodii remains unknown. We are unaware of extant populations. Collectors in Mozambique and South Africa should be aware of its presence.
bibliographicCitation: Mohamed, KI; Musselman, LJ; Riches, CR. 2001. The genus Striga (Scrophulariaceae) in Africa. Ann. Missouri Bot. Gard. 88(1): 60-103. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2666132] [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the Missouri Botanical Garden Press, St. Louis.] [All rights reserved]

description: It differs from H. sanguinea, as from all the other known South African species, in having the lowest calyx segment very much shorter than the others.
bibliographicCitation: Phillips, EP; Lansdell, KA. 1923. Hyobanche fulleri E.Phillips. Fl. Pl. South Africa 3t.89 [CC BY]

description: Disa physodes could be confused with D. cernua, but is distinguishable by a spur less than 10 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: A putative hybrid with Disa montana has been recorded.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: This species could be confused with Disa graminifolia but is distinct by the conical spur, up-curved lip margins and earlier flowering time. Occasional white-flowered forms have been recorded.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The relationship of M. annua clearly lies with M. arabidea and its allies. It can be distinguished from M. arabidea not only by its bearded posticous filaments but also by its longer pubescence and mostly larger flowers (anticous calyx lobes 2-4 mm long versus 1.25-2 mm, corolla tube 4-7 mm long versus 2.75-4 mm). Manulea paucibarbata can at once be distinguished by the scant short hairs in the throat and glabrous filaments.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The characteristic features of the species are its elliptic to obovate, serrate, leaves, glandular-hispid on both surfaces, and the thick-textured corolla limb, shades of orange-brown to dark brown above, with thin-textured pale margins. The flowers are remarkably similar to those of J. burkeana, whose area lies mostly west of that of J. accrescens, but where they are sympatric, in the Zoutpansberg, at Makapan near Potgietersrust, and near Ohrigstadt, they hybridize. Normally, the species are easily distinguished by differences in the shape and indumentum of the leaves; also, in J. accrescens, there are almost always glistening glands on the upper surface of the corolla limb around the sinuses (J. burkeana rarely has glistening glands on the upper surface of the limb, and then they are along the upper margins). The putative hybrids have leaves more or less intermediate between those of the two species (± shape of those of J. accrescens, but margins more boldly and irregularly toothed, upper surface with few hairs), and there may or may not be glistening glands around the sinuses of the corolla limb.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Its distinguishing marks are its leaves, only once divided into lobes that are mostly entire, its short pedicels up to 10 mm long, its relatively long corolla tube and style (6.3-10 mm, style 5-7 mm, the longest in this group) and its golden-yellow limb, the lower lip not porrect.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Subsp. rhodesiaca (Summerh.) Summerh. is a larger plant with longer and broader leaves and many-flowered inflorescences of lilac or purple flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Summerhayes, VS. 1968. Orchidaceae. In: E Milne-Redhead & RM Polhill (eds), Fl. Trop. E. Africa (1): 1-236. Crown Agents, London. [CC BY]

description: Jamesbrittenia albanensis is characterized by its bluntly lobed leaves, glandular-pubescent on both surfaces, flowers borne in pseudoracemes, and mauve to magenta corolla limb. In foliage, it resembles forms of J. filicaulis, which differs in its leafy inflorescences and white corolla limb. In leaf cutting, inflorescence and flower colour, it resembles J. foliolosa, but that species is distinguished by the indumentum on the leaves: lower surface thickly clad in glistening glands, minute glandular hairs present or not, upper surface either glabrous or minutely glandular-pubescent. Jamesbrittenia foliolosa possibly hybridizes with J. albanensis in the Grahamstown area.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The salient features of the species are the very minute glandular hairs on the stems, inflorescence axes and pedicels, the ± spathulate leaves, either entire or bluntly few-toothed, the lower surface thickly covered in glistening glands, the upper glabrous or with a few scattered glands, and the white corolla limb.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The distinguishing features of J. amplexicaulis are its habit (weak stems tufted from a woody caudex), the stems terminating in long crowded inflorescences, leaves sharply ascending, imbricate, the lowermost much reduced in size, then more or less abruptly larger, again diminishing in size on the floriferous part of the stem (this is of course not always visible, not only because only the upper part of a stem may be present on the sheet, but also because the lower leaves may have fallen), the short corolla tube and small bilabiate limb.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Jamesbrittenia argentea shows considerable variation in the size and toothing of the leaves, but the plant is unmistakable: wiry, straggling habit, ultimate branchlets often short and almost patent, densely leafy, flowers borne on spreading filiform pedicels in the axils of the leaf-tufts and not running up into discrete racemes, corolla limb white. The leaves are often cuneate in outline and 3-toothed at the apex, but large leaves are often rhomboid to oblong with several pairs of coarse teeth. They are glabrous above, densely clad in glistening glands below (which possibly suggested the epithet argentea, that is, silvery); the calyx lobes too are clad only in glistening glands. Hiern misdetermined specimens of J. integerrima and J. foliolosa as Sutera argentea, and subsequently the name has scarcely ever been correctly applied; much material will be found in herbaria under Sutera pedunculala. The habit of Jamesbrittenia argentea is similar to that of J. kraussiana, but they are easily distinguished by their leaves, elliptic in J. kraussiana (not rhomboid, cuneate nor oblong), glandular-puberulous above (not glabrous or with a very few glistening glands) and glandular-pubescent calyx (not glistening glands only).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Somewhat similar to Disa virginalis.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Its area thus lies mainly south of that of its ally J. megadenia, but they are known to be sympatric between roughly Warmbad and Upington; Pockenbank lies west of the area of J. megadenia. Both species have a white corolla limb patterned round the mouth in orange and violet, but the corolla lobes are much more deeply notched in J. aridicola (c. 0.8-1.6 mm) than in J. megadenia (up to c. 0.3 mm), and J. aridicola lacks the relatively huge glands that are a notable feature of J. megadenia (care must be taken because sand and dust stick to glandular heads and may give a false impression of size).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The distinguishing features of the species are its small narrowly oblong to spathulate leaves (ratio of length to breadth 2.5-7:1), mostly entire, some of the primary leaves occasionally with a pair of small teeth near the apex (rarely a plant will produce an occasional leaf as much as 7 x 3 mm with two pairs of teeth), the normally very short indumentum on stems, leaves and pedicels (a mixture of glistening glands and minute gland-tipped hairs that often ooze and give these parts as well as the calyx a varnished look, the individual hairs then often invisible), often longish pedicels, the calyx clad predominantly in large glistening glands, and the corolla limb usually shades of pink, mauve or blue, possibly always yellow in the throat (collector's notes often meagre or wanting) and, once, a red spot was recorded at the base of each lobe; this is not visible in the dried specimen. Jamesbrittenia aspalathoides is often confused with a variety of other microphyllous species; Philcox (in Fl. Zam. 8(2): 3, 1990) went so far as to reduce it to synonymy under Sutera atropurpurea, but Jamesbrittenia atropurpurea is at once distinguished by its flowers: corolla tube c. 15-24 mm long, either glabrous or very minutely puberulous, limb shades of brown, the margins of the lobes revolute giving the lobes a peculiarly narrow appearance, the texture thick, venation invisible on the upper surface.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: In leaf-characters this species very nearly resembles the South African N. melisscefolia Benth., but is a far less robust plant apparently annual and with flowers of only about half the size.
bibliographicCitation: Rendle, AB. 1932. African notes II. J. Bot. 70: 89-96. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is characterized by its longhand often relatively broad primary leaves, conspicuously stalked flowers, narrow, curved, obtuse and more or less hooded bracts, narrowanticolateral calyx lobes, and the pair of cocci reniform or cordate in outline. It is easily distinguished from S. paniculata by its narrow bracts and anticolateral calyx lobes, shorter corolla tubes, and smaller, differently shaped, cocci.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago cecilae is a much coarser plant than S. densiflora leaves more scabridulous, mosdy larger (typically 10-18 x 1.2-1.8 mm versus 5-10 x 0.5-1 mm, but ignore leaves on young stems, which can reach 1.5 mm in width), crowded panicles with most peduncles up to c. 10 mm long (not c. 15-50 mm), calyces longer (1.25-1.8 mm versus 1.1-1.2 mm). Its typically long leaves will help to distinguish it from S. paniculata, also its bracts with white membranous margins (wantmgin S. paniculata) and granular (not smooth) cocci. It differs from S. lacunosa by its broader bracts (0.8-1 mm versus 0.3-0.6 mm), longer calyces (1.25-1.8 mm versus 0.8-1.1 mm) with broader anticolateral lobes (0.5-0.8 mm versus 0.2-0.4 mm), longer corolla tubes (1.5-2 mm versus 0.8-1.1 mm), and larger cocci (1.1-1.4 x 0.8-1 mm versus 0.6-0.8 x 0.5-0.7 mm), the pair ovoid in oudine (not reniform nor cordate).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: M. acuminata var. acuminata is sometimes confused with M. forbesii, which has more or less the same habit and partly the same distribution. These taxa are mainly distinguished by the shape and length of the epicalyx-bracts around the length of the style. According to Wild, M. velutina sensu Exell & Mendonca in Conspectus Florae Angolensis is partly M. acuminata.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1981. Revision of Melhania in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(3 & 4): 263-273. [CC BY]

description: In the Transvaal this species is very common between Potgietersrus and Pietersburg. The form which occurs here agrees with the description of M. albicans, but no grounds can be found for separating it from M. burchellii in spite of the disjunct distribution and the difference in habitat. In the Transvaal it grows on a heavy gravelly loam soil which is very different from the loose sand in which it is found in the north-western Cape. It may be noted that the type locality of M. albicans is given as Pilgrims Rest. The Rev. William Greenstock, who collected the original specimen, spent some time with Edward Button at Eersteling Mine, between Potgietersrus and Pietersburg, before proceeding to Pilgrims Rest. The plant has not been found at Pilgrims Rest again and it is considered that Greenstock collected this specimen in the neighbourhood of Eersteling. Several similar cases are known where species based on Greenstock specimens have been attributed to Pilgrims Rest, but subsequent investigation has shown that they were without doubt collected in the Eersteling area. In the Flora Capensis under M. burchellii Miss Owen’s specimen is cited as coming from ‘Zooloo Country’; this is probably another case of the several instances where Miss Owen’s specimens, collected after she had left Zululand (that is, after the Dingaan massacre), were labelled as from Zululand, whereas they probably were from the Kuruman or Zeerust Districts. Regarding another citation in the Flora Capensis, namely Zeyher from the ‘Aapies River’, it is doubtful whether this locality is correctly cited, since this species has not been found near Pretoria. Although none of the syntypes of M. dinteri has been seen, the description best fits the specimens in this taxon.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1981. Revision of Melhania in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(3 & 4): 263-273. [CC BY]

description: The entire, velvety-tomentose leaves, together with the long style and large petals, characterize the species. It resembles M. randii Bak. f. from Zimbabwe in the entire leaves but differs, among other things, in the pubescence on the upper surface of the leaves, the larger flowers and the ovate-cordate epicalyx. The specimen from Abel Erasmus Pass is not quite as velvety as the Wolkberg specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1981. Revision of Melhania in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(3 & 4): 263-273. [CC BY]

description: This is the first known record of a species of Melhania with polygamous flowers. The essentially male flowers are more showy with longer petals, large stamens and an aborted style. The female flowers have short petals, small stamens and a style with long, stout branches. The broad ovate-trullate leaves, that is, leaves, which are usually broadest about a third of length above the base, are a distinguishing feature.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1981. Revision of Melhania in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(3 & 4): 263-273. [CC BY]

description: A putative hybrid with Disa filicornis as the second parent has been recorded.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The decision to follow the authors of Flora Zambesiaca and put M. linearifolia Sond. into synonymy under M. prostrata and not as a variety of M. didyma as Szyszylowicz did, was made after seeing the type specimen of the former. This specimen compares well with the type of M. prostrata from Griqualand West and the many specimens of this species found throughout the Transvaal and in parts of Natal. M. prostrata is closely related to M. didyma, but may be distinguished by the much narrower leaves with entire margins (very rarely a single leaf shallowly lobed in part). The pubescence on the upper surface of the leaves is, when present, like that of M. didyma of rather long usual single subappressed hairs, but in M. prostrata the upper surface is early glabrescent. Where the distribution of these two species overlap, intermediates are found. It is not clear whether these intermediates are of hybrid origin or whether the two taxa are fairly recent segregates from a common stock. The specimen of Schlechter 4322 in the Transvaal Museum Herbarium, now in the National Herbarium, is a mixture of M. prostrata and M. transvaalensis. The latter has the upper surface of the leaves distinctly stellate throughout. When Burchell collected the type of this species, he evidently thought it was a Dombeya, for in his catalogue he has listed it as Dombeya prostrata.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1981. Revision of Melhania in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(3 & 4): 263-273. [CC BY]

description: A study of Rehmann’s route when he collected the type of this species shows that the locality ‘Elands-river Drift’ was most probably in the northern part of the Pretoria District, north-east of Rust de Winter. The herbarium sheet of Schlechter 4322 from the Transvaal Museum, now in the National Herbarium, Pretoria, has mounted on it a mixture of this species and M. prostrata. Another sheet of the same number, Schlechter 4322, which has been in the National Herbarium for many years, is purely M. transvaalensis, i.e. all the leaves are crenate-dentate and coarsely stellate on the upper surface (not entire with simple subappressed, long hairs or glabrous on the upper surface). In Engler’s Monographieen Afrikanischer Pflanzen, K. Schumann describes M. transvaalensis Szyszyl. as having the upper surface of the leaves ‘appresse pilosis’ which describes those of M. prostrata. It is difficult to explain this for he cites only Rehmann 4940, the type number. The sheet in the Kew Herbarium of Rehmann 4940 has the leaves stellate-pubescent on the upper surface as described by Szyszylowicz, the author of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1981. Revision of Melhania in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(3 & 4): 263-273. [CC BY]

description: The confusion that existed between this species and M. rehmannii is understandable for, until one has recognized the features that distinguish them, these species look very much alike. The specimen on which Bolus based the greater part of his description of M. griquensis, i.e. Orpen sub Bolus 6015, is a mixed gathering. Four of the portions have the linear-subulate epicalyx bracts as described by Bolus, and the fifth, on the left hand side of the sheet, the ovate bracts of M. rehmannii. The distribution of these two species overlap in the northern Cape and parts of the Transvaal. A further distinguishing feature is that the peduncles in M. virescens are short (usually shorter than the petiole) and suberect and the pedicels, if present, are also short and suberect, whole in M. rehmannii the peduncles are somewhat longer (about as long as or longer than the petiole) and the pedicels, if present, longer, thinner and cernuous. With regard to the distribution, as mentioned above, these species overlap in the northern Cape and the Transvaal, but M. virescens extends further westward in South West Africa. According to collectors’ notes M. virescens is restricted to limy soil, while M. rehmannii is not so restricted and is much more widespread. The specimens added by N. E. Brown to Bolus’s original description of M. griquensis, namely Burchell 2385, Holub s.n. Rehmann 5220 are all M. rehmannii.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1981. Revision of Melhania in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(3 & 4): 263-273. [CC BY]

description: There is substantial variation in flower shape and colour in this species - this is consistent with the wide distribution of the species. In addition, a recessive yellow form is known from Transkei (Eastern Cape). The species has been reported to hybridªize with Disa caulescens.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The commoner form of this typical variety, in the adult stage, is conspicuous during early spring because of its profuse white (rarely pink) flowers borne on almost leafless, rough-barked trees. The same variety on the central plateau of South West Africa/Namibia and in occurs as a bushy shrub, only here and there reaching tree form, and flowers at any time from spring to autumn, the flowers and leaves appearing together.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC; Herman, PPJ. 1986. Revision of the genus Dombeya (Sterculiaceae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 16(1): 1-9. [CC BY]

description: Resembles H. comosa in some respects but is readily distinguished by the consistently deeply divided leaves. H. abrotanoides is characterized by the silvery stellate pubescence, together with the inflated calyx which is appressedly stellate-pubescent, the hairs fine and many from a silvery central scale, some very shortly stalked as well and these are readily caducous. H. pulverata has the same silvery stellate pubescence and resembles H. abrotanoides in the divided leaves but it can be distinguished mainly by the calyx which is not inflated.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: Characterized by the usually stellate-tomentose leaves, the indurating branchlets, and the long, pilose horns on the capsules. H. affinis, as defined here, varies considerably, but it can, nevertheless, be recognised as an entity and distinguished from related species. The two species with which it has been very generally confused are H. spinosa and H. helianthemum. From H. spinosa it can be distinguished, among other details, by the branchlets being stellate- tomentose and becoming indurated or spine-like, whereas in H. spinosa the branchlets are sparsely stellate-pubescent or glabrous and it is usually the persistent, enlarged peduncles which become spikelike. H. helianthemum differs considerably from H. affinis, for it has long, slender branchlets which do not become indurated but terminate in raceme-like inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: Three not clearly defined groups can be recognized, (1) a fairly robust, suberect to erect form with normal internodes, (2) a form with more or less the same habit but with short internodes, and (3) a prostrate form with flowers rather smaller and petals only slightly longer than the calyx. All three these forms are represented in LINN: the typical form by Cat. No. 854.5, the form with short internodes by 854.6 and the prostrate form with short petals by 854.7. All forms are characterized by numerous small flowers, suborbicular cuneate leaves which are stellate-tomentose on both surfaces, the lower usually whitish tomentose, and the rather thin calyx which is usually laxly stellate-pubescent, with the stellate hairs occurring mainly on the nerves.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: The pubescence varies considerably in this species, from densely and smoothly to roughly and thinly tomentose.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: The distinguishing characters are found mainly in the flowers. The parchment-like calyx is distinctly 5-angled, the angles extending from the sinuses to the base of the calyx with the portion between being concave. The calyx is broad at the base and the lobes do not spread nor reflex at any time. The shortly exserted petals are strongly twisted and lemon -yellow grading into orange-red. Characteristic too is the blade of the petal which is broadly oblong and several times longer than the basal claw.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: The concept of this species is rather unsatisfactory, as it is intermediate between D. hians and D. baurii, as well as between D. hians and D. barbata. Further research may well indicate that it may be better included in one of these taxa.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Previously considered a white form of Disa maculata.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Characterized by the roughly stellate-pubescent calyx and capsule.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: H. bryoniifolia is characterized by the ovate-oblong leaves which are lobulate-crenate and fairly coarsely stellate-pubescent. The flowers and capsules are small.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: The species appears to be commonly cleistogamous. Due to their diminutive size plants of this species are probably often overlooked. Disperis bodkinii is closely related to D. macowanii.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: H. comosa is a variable species and several putative hybrids have been noted. The feature which probably suggested the specific epithet, namely the stalked tufts of hairs which are commonly found on the calyx, is not completely diagnostic. These comas fall readily and appear to be absent on some plants. There is also considerable variation in the density of the fine, stellate pubescence that covers all parts of the plant and often gives it a silvery grey sheen.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: This recently described species is characterized by the leafy branches with regularly arranged, rather stiff leaves. The stipules are leaf-like and usually more than half as long as the leaves. They can be distinguished from the leaves by their shape which is more or less oblong and not clearly narrowed towards the base. The leaves and stipules, which appear to be glabrous, are minutely stellate-pubescent. H. concinnifolia has, to date, been found only in Coastal Fynbos on limestone formations in the Bredasdorp district and eastwards to Riversdale. It can be distinguished from the nearly related species H. rudis and H. flammea principally by the more densely leafy branches with regularly arranged leaves. Compared with H. rudis it is also less roughly pubescent and from H. flammea it can be distinguished by the flowers being more compactly disposed, not in elongated racemose cymes. In the case of H. flammea the petals are usually dark red, at least on the outside, and on herbarium specimens they dry darker than the calyx. This is not usually so in H. concinnifolia which has been described as having yellow petals. Colour, however, often varies in most species of Hermannia and cannot be relied on as a diagnostic feature.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: This aberrant variety seems to lack many features which are of importance in the pollination biology of the species, and may represent an inclination to autogamy.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: The species is characterized by the long spreading hairs, especially conspicuous on the young flowers and the glomerate inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: H. cordifolia is nearest H. rugosa, but differs in being a more robust, erect plant with larger leaves, calyces and capsules, and in having a clustered inflorescence and a calyx which is suburceolate to campanulate, not somewhat salver-shaped as in H. rugosa.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: Characterized by the short calyx lobes, the 5 prominent ribs on the calyx (outside), the fine, short, stellate tomentum, the three prominent basal nerves on the under surface of the leaves and the stellate-tomentose capsule with very short horns.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: This species is closely related to H. involucrata having the same type of pubescence and leaf-shape and the same non-inflated calyx which is densely stellate-pubescent with yellow hairs. It differs from that species in the smaller leaves and flowers and the leaves being more erect and fairly closely appressed to the stem.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: This species is characterized by the consistently decumbent habit, the practically leafless, ascending inflorescence with clustered flowers, and the hairs on the calyx and parts of the inflorescence which are longer and more obvious than on most other parts of the plant. It is nearest to H. althaeifolia, having the same semi-inflated calyx and large stipules, but it can be distinguished by the more or less leafless inflorescence with long, spreading, matted pubescence on the calyx and the usually glabrescent stipules. The areas of distribution are adjacent but do not overlap. H. althaeifolia is recorded from the Peninsula and northwards to beyond Calvinia and eastwards to Uniondale and northern Mossel Bay; it is generally found just to the north of the Coastal Fynbos in which H. decumbens occurs.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: The almost straight rostellum arms of Disperis concinna are shared in this group only with D. stenoplectron but the two species differ greatly in the shape of their lip and appendage.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Characterized by the fine, pale, stellate pubescence, the semi-inflated, shallow calyx, 5-gibbose at the base, the indurating twigs and suborbicular leaves, which are cuneate into a petiole and crenate-dentate.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: Although the areas of distribution of the varieties overlap to some extent and are approximate, the typical variety seems to favour higher regions in karroid shrub, whereas var. graciliflora is found at lower levels in Coastal Renosterveld or Fynbos.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: In var. diversistipula the fringed scales are usually larger, the leaves, which hardly exceed the stipules, are often lobed at the apex and the flowers are usually found in the axils of only the upper three to five leaves. In var. graciliflora the fringed scales are minute, the leaves which overtop the stipules by about half are entire at apex and flowers usually arise in the axils of leaves along the upper half or two-thirds of the branchlets.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: Disperis micrantha is closely related to D. disaeformis which has a very similar lip appendage. The two species are ecological vicariants, and occupy different habitats and flower at different times of the year.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: H. floribunda is characterized by the long branches which arise near the base of the plant; these may be erect or sprawling and are stellate-pubescent not canescent-tomentose; they bear short, floriferous lateral branchlets. The specific name is apt, because in the axils of the leaves and at the apices of both the main and lateral branches, several cymes with flowers of different ages are clustered, with several grey, subglobose buds in each group.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]

description: Distinguishing features are: abbreviated, slender, congested shoots bearing small, persistent bracts in lower half, and leaves and flowers above; long, indurated branchlets, minutely papillose (not stellate- pubescent) becoming glutinose; peduncle short, persistent; pedicels longer and stellate-pubescent; petals longer than calyx, margins inrolled on claw, not thickened, glabrous on inner face; capsule with five laterally compressed carpels free to the axis; horns 10, long, pilose, spreading and recurved.
bibliographicCitation: Verdoorn, IC. 1980. Revision of Hermannia subgenus Hermannia in southern Africa. Bothalia 13(1&2): 1-63. [CC BY]
