description: R. multifida specimens are distinguished by the following characters: 1, The thalli are markedly feathery, with rather crowded and generally very regular, pinnate branching; 2, The ultimate anti lateral pinnules are thin, linear and paralled-sided, with the outer 3 cell rows unistratose and translucent on either side of the thicker, opaque, median region; 3, The ultimate pinnules have crenulate distal margins, with the marginal cells bulging externally and smaller than the intramarginal cells; 4, The oil bodies are mostly absent from the marginal and epidermal cells of the median region, hut present in the internal cells; 5, The epidermal cells of the median part are generally narrower than in allied species, i.e. 25.0-37.5(-55.0) µm wide: 6. The plants are rarely synoicous.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2001. Studies in the liverwort family Anueraceae (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 2. The genus Riccardia and its type species, R. multifida, with confirmation of its presence in the region. Bothalia 31(2): 183-187. [CC BY]

description: Cliffortia cristata H. Weim. has been given this name alluding to the high cocks-comb-like ridges which ornament the receptacle. The species comes near C. dodecandra H. Weim. and C. pterocarpa (Harv.) H. Weim. C. cristata differs from these and other species within the sect. Costatae by the form and colour of the receptacle. In conformity to C. dodecandra the species has pilous leaves. The pilosity is however much denser in C. cristata: young leaflets are covered by greyish white, woolly hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1946. Further notes on the genus Cliffortia. Bot. Not. 1946(4): 407-420. [All rights reserved]

description: It is distinguished by its somewhat leathery appearance, conspicuous, pendant, marginally serrate scales, and by occasional oil cells.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The species can be recognized by the large, mostly regular, yellowish green rosettes, often tinged with red along the thallus margins; the spores are characteristically bi- or trichoto-mously ridged on the distal face.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The species can be distinguished from the other southern African species with shiny black scales, by its generally smaller size, by scales that are closely appressed and do not extend above the thallus margins and by the dark brown dorsal colour of the thallus.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The most remarkable feature of C. cuneata is the form of the leaves. They are, as the name indicates, cuneate and have a truncate apex, furnished with 4 or 5 teeth, but occasionally the number of the teeth is smaller or greater. The receptacle is deeply furrowed and quite glabrous. By means of the last-mentioned feature the species differs, among other things, from the allied C. phillipsii and from the hybrid between the two species, which have densely, canescently pilous receptacles.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The thickened dorsal cell walls provide the most useful diagnostic character for separating this species from other southern African Riccia species and it can always be recognized by this. The spores, ornamented with numerous granules on the proximal face and with larger central alveoli and tall spinous processes at the nodes on the distal face, are also quite distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: When fertile, T. hypophylla is recognized by the ventrally displaced capsule contained in a shiny black pouch at the apex of the thallus; sterile plants are distinguished by their dark green, somewhat leathery appearance, the conspicuous white-encircled air pores and reddish to purple-black, obliquely triangular ventral scales with a single appendage.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: This species is recognized by its mucronate leaves and the production of numerous, stalked, leaf-like propagulae. The Southern African specimens differ from the North American plants in the absence of the minute apical teeth only. The species is related to S. fragilis and S. laevipila; differences are discussed under those species.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: The South African plant usually has thinner cell-walls than the European ones, probably only an ecological variation.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: The receptacle is fusiform and up to 12 mm in length, a type, which is found also in C. densa. The two species are also in other respects morphologically closely allied. The differences between them are to be seen under C. densa.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. cymbifolia resembles C. ruscifolia L. but differs from this species by its smaller, narrower and glabrous leaves, its glabrous bracteoles, fewer stamens (in C. ruscifolia ca. 12) and smaller receptacles. The species is also rather similar to C. subulata but differs i.e. by its brachyblasts and by its shorter stipules.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Brachiolejeunea phyllorhiza is easily recognized by the densely imbricate and usually squarrose, suborbicular leaves with broadly rounded apex and with a very broad, somewhat truncate lobule with 2 widely spatiated, small teeth, by the large, rounded under leaves with recurved margins, by the 3-keeled perianths with winged-cilate keels, and by the short-specialized male branches which are usually present somewhat lower down on the female shoots.
bibliographicCitation: Gradstein, SR. 1994. Lejeuneaceae: Ptychantheae, Brachiolejeuneae, Fl. Neotrop. Monogr. 62: 1-216. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4393845] [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the New York Botanical Garden Press] [All rights reserved]

description: C. densa and C. curvifolia are closely related. They have strongly curved leaflets and peculiar, fusiform receptacles. They are, however, markedly distinguished. In C. densa the leaflets in transverse section are almost square with rounded angles; the underside is slightly convex, and the thick margins are furnished with a shallow furrow. In C. curvifolia, on the other hand, the midrib is prominent and takes the shape of a strongly arched keel, and the margins are somewhat revolute. C. densa has shortly acuminate bracteoles, 15 stamens and a 6 mm long receptacle (not quite mature), whereas C. curvifolia has c. 25 stamens and a 10-12 mm long receptacle in mature state. The sepals and stigmas of the two species are unknown.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: R. boryana is a very distinct, large species,easily recognised in the field, and unlikely to be con-fused with any other when well-grown. Small formscan, however, be similar to R. appressa (see under thelatter species). However, the several layers of small,very thick-walled cortical cells (stem section) in R.boryana are highly characteristic.
bibliographicCitation: Jones, EW. 2004. Lepidoziaceae Limpr. - Notothyladaceae (Milde) Müll.Frib. ex Prosk. In: MJ Wigginton (ed.), E.W. Jones's liverwort and hornwort Flora of West Africa: 102-424 National Botanic Garden (Belgium), Meise. [All rights reserved]

description: Willdenow (1. c.) puts C. dentata immediately after C. obcordata, remarking that the two species are very similar but, nevertheless, different. As regards size and habitus they show, in fact, very great resemblance. However, they must be put into different groups on account of the fundamental differences in the development of the flowers and of the fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: R. stenocalyx resembles R. flaccida in mostrespects, but differs in the shape of the lobule, which is oblong rather than rhombic and not prolonged at the apex, and in the gemmae being discoid (rounded to their attachment with the leaf, not reniform-incised). The gemmae are less freely produced than they are in R.flaccida, sometimes very rare in a collection, and are much less conspicuous. However, in the absence of gemmae, the form of the lobule will serve to separate the two species.
bibliographicCitation: Jones, EW. 2004. Lepidoziaceae Limpr. - Notothyladaceae (Milde) Müll.Frib. ex Prosk. In: MJ Wigginton (ed.), E.W. Jones's liverwort and hornwort Flora of West Africa: 102-424 National Botanic Garden (Belgium), Meise. [All rights reserved]

description: Cliffortia dispar comes morphologically near C. eriocephalina Cham. It differs a.o. from this species in the following features: the leaves are often simple, especially in the flowering twigs, the pilosity of the leaflets is less patent, the sepals of the male flowers are pilose on the whole outside, the stamens are 9 in number (in C. eriocephalina 6), the stigmata are only thinly ramified.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1946. Further notes on the genus Cliffortia. Bot. Not. 1946(4): 407-420. [All rights reserved]

description: C. dodecandra comes morphologically rather close to C. atrata. It differs from the latter in that the leaflets on the underside are densely verruculose and, when young, furnished with long white hairs; the midrib is less prominent than in C. atrata. In C. dodecandra the bracteoles of the [female]-flower are narrower, leaving a greater part of the receptacle free than is the case in C. atrata, while the receptacle is rufescently black-brown. The two species have 12 stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: In such a wide ranging species one would expect some local variation. A Sim specimen, PRE-CH 1491, from Table Mountain has bistratose wing margins, and medianly there are four layers of cells. The determination was kindly confirmed by Dr Grolle. Arnell (1963) regarded the size of the marginal teeth in S. podophylla as having no taxonomic significance, nor the thickness of the walls in the marginal cells. He also did not find distinct differences between the erect and procumbent forms, there being a continued gradation between the two. In a comparison of transverse sections taken at the middle of the apical lobes of specimens of S. podophylla and of S. hymenophyllum from Juan Fernandez. Arnell (1956) stated that the thickness of the ‘nerves’ and the size of the teeth in the margin of the thalli vary but little. Arnell (1963) also compared specimens of S. hymenophyllum from Tristan da Cunha and Inaccessible Island as well as from Reunion and from Kilimanjaro, with numerous specimens of S. podophylla from the Cape (e.g. Thunberg’s collections) and could not find any real difference between them. On the other hand, Gottsche et al. (1846) distinguished S. podophylla from S. hymenophyllum by the ‘frondis laciniis basi attenuatis subpetiolatis’ of the former Symphyogyna podophylla is a less common and smaller plant than S. brasiliensis. It can be distinguished by: its growth form which is generally flabellate from an erect stalk arising from a creeping rhizome; the lobe margins which are toothed and hardly undulate; it rarely fruits and the spore ornamentation is characterised by broad, flat, roughened, irregular ridges, sometimes forming ‘loops’, and not by narrow, erect ridges as in S. brasiliensis. Symphyogyna podophylla and S. brasiliensis are the only two species of Symphyogyna occurring in southern Africa and are placed in the subfamily Symphyogynoideae (Trev.) Grolle.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1993. The hepatics, Symphyogyna podophylla and Pallavicinia lyellii (Pallaviciniaceae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 23(1): 15-23. [CC BY]

description: Cliffortia dregeana stands morphologically rather close to C. theodori-friesii and C. integerrima. The species has glabrous stems and branches, no brachyblasts and more or less pronouncedly canaliculate, 1.5-3.5 cm long, lineary lanceolate-lanceolate, smooth-margined or on each side one-toothed blades, which run out in a long, pungent apex. The species differs from C. theodori-friesii and C. integerrima in the form of the leaves and in the receptacle, which reaches 8 mm in length.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The narrowly elliptical leaves, extension of basal leaf cells up the margins and paroicous condition will help to identify this species.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: The macroscopic resemblance of this species to Barbula is superseded by the Tortula-like peristome and costal anatomy. The differentiated marginal leaf cells would place this species in Pseudocrossidium sensu Zander (1979); see note under P. replicatum.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: Differs from the main species only in having 2-4, often stout, teeth on each margin. All kinds of transitions, however, are to be seen, from forms with quite entire margins to those having toothed margins. The boundary between the forms is thus vague. The mutual connection of the different forms can hardly be determined until crossings have been made.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is recognized by its long reddish awn, more or less smooth leaf cells and large, minutely spinose spores.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: The relatively long, oblong leaves and short-excurrent costa of P. subplanomarginata will separate it from the other Southern African species. The description and illustration of P. verrucosa strongly suggest that the type (B) was P. macowaniana, however, the specimen at NH! is P. subplanomarginata.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: Morphologically C. erectisepala is closely related to C. repens. It differs from that species, among other things, in its considerably longer bracteoles, which are nearly twice as long as the receptacle. In C. erectisepala the receptacle is smooth, in C. repens it is furnished with low ridges. The calyces are upright and with the edges stuck together, and finally fall off as a whole, while in C. repens they are quite free from one another and spread out.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The peristome of Syntrichia amphidiacea is unusual, being irregularly twisted and crumpled when dry but widely spreading or reflexed when moist. The species has a distribution disjunct between the southern Appalachians and Mexico, similar to that of a number of other mosses (including S. fragilis) and flowering plants that appear to be relicts of an ancient tropical flora. Sporophytes are known only from southern Mexico and southwards. Syntrichia amphidiacea is a rare species in the southeastern United States but common in Mexico.
bibliographicCitation: Mishler, BD. 2007. 33. Syntrichia Bridel, Fl. N. Amer. 27: 618-627. New York Botanic Garden, New York. [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the New York Botanical Garden Press.] [All rights reserved]

description: Concerning the differences between C. eriocephalina and C. hirta. C. montana, C. nitidula and C. stricta see under these species.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Cliffortia esterhuyseniae stands morphologically rather isolated within the section. Especially characteristic are among other features the excurved or declinate leaves, situated on very short brachyblasts. and the [female] flowers, the sepals of which are linear and only about 0.2 mm broad. The form of the leaf laminae varies within wide limits.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: The species will be recognized by its habit, branching patterns of the stem, leaf shape and areolation. A. drakensbergense can be distinguished from A. filiforme by the percurrent costa, entire leaf margins, shorter and wider upper laminal cells and reduced peristome.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1987. Bryaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,2): 335-393. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Sterile specimens can be distinguished from A. muscicola by the compactness of the assimilation tissue and from A. wilmsii, by its smaller size and the lanceolate appendages (occasionally double) of the purple or reddish purple ventral scales and from A. marginata by its generally purple, not wide, black thallus margins and by its mostly summer rainfall distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: It can be distinguished from the others by the single, ovate or roughly triangular, large-celled appendage of the ventral scales, by the distinctly lobed disc of the carpocephalum, with purple paleae protruding from the notches and by the slightly broader-based paleae (up to 7 cells wide).
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia albolimbata is characterized by its large, frilly, hyaline or white ventral scales, frequently encrusted with deposits of calcium carbonate, by the dorsal covering of the sporangia turning chalk-white and spongy and by the spores which are generally incompletely reticulate on the distal face with the outer ridges radially elongated.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia congoana differs from the other black-scaled Riccia species in southern Africa by the large size of the green to blue-green thalli, very obliquely sloping flanks covered by large, shiny black or deep purple-red, generally crescent-shaped scales and by the subglobular, apolar spores with angular, thin-walled alveoli.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Differences in the spore ornamentation between R. concava. R. albomarginata Bisch. ex G.L. & N., and one or two new. as yet undescribed species in the section, are sometimes quite difficult to discern, even on SEM micrographs, nor are radiating ridges on the distal face altogether distinctive. Moreover, the spores of R. concava can be quite variable, even when from the same sporangium. R. concava often grows in association with other Riccia species of section Pilifer and with the moss species
bibliographicCitation: Jones, EW. 2004. Marchantiaceae (Bisch.) Lindley - Lepicoleaceae R.M.Schust. In: MJ Wigginton (ed.), E.W. Jones's liverwort and hornwort Flora of West Africa: 46-100 National Botanic Garden (Belgium), Meise.

description: The great variability within C. ferruginea, especially with respect to the development of the stems and the form of the leaves, has caused several authors to describe new species or varieties with more or less extreme forms as types.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Riccia microciliata is distinguished from the other southern African ciliate species by the small size of the thalli and by the arching, deeply channelled cilia. Its spores are wingless, the triradiate mark poorly defined and the alveolar walls smooth, never granulate.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: In contradistinction to C. filicaulis the var. octandra has usually an adscendent or erect stem. The hairs are usually longer and denser, the leaflets are larger and more cuneate, the flowers are also larger and have longer filaments. The differences, however, are not very constant.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Species in the R. fluitans complex are difficult to distinguish, as the gametophytes are highly sensitive to different environmental conditions and the habitat can vary from terrestrial to aquatic. Nevertheless, R. stricta can generally be recognized by its mostly smooth dorsal surface, through which the large air chambers are faintly to fairly clearly visible, by small ventral scales and by smallish spores with large, deep-walled alveoli containing a central boss on the distal face and, on the proximal face, a prominent triradiate mark.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: As to habitus it comes very close to C. filicaulis but differs in its sterile state from this species by the curved main petiole of the leaves, which remains on the plant, even when the leaflets fall off.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The taxon is vegetatively similar to A. abyssinica (C. Mull.) Flow., but sporophytically it is more closely related to A. menziesii (Turn.) Par. The presence of a peristome excludes this taxon from A. abyssinica.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1987. Mniaceae to Bartramiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,2): 395-438. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. filifolia is rather similar to C. tuberculata, especially as to the leaves. Even as sterile the two species can easily be kept apart, C. filifolia has a very short, although marked, petiole on the top of the vagina, whereas C. tuberculata has sessile leaves. They are still more different in the fertile state. C. filifolia has 6, while C. tuberculata has 12 stamens, and the receptacle in C. filifolia is slightly furrowed -almost smooth, in C. tuberculata, however, verrucose.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. glauca is closely related to C. obovata and C. marginata. C. obovata, however, has thin and, at the apex, roundish-obtuse leaflets, smaller flowers and only 12 stamens. C. marginata has very characteristic transparent leaf-margins, narrower and usually obtuse leaflets and sepals of the [female]-flowers only about 1 mm long. The form and the nervation of the leaflets vary in C. glauca rather much, but the species is very characteristic on account of its thick, coriaceous, mucronate, greyish and obscurely veined leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Rosulabryum capillare can be recognized when dry by leaves that are spirally twisted around the stem. The leaves are mostly ovate to oblong in shape, with rounded apices, inconspicuous and narrow borders, smooth to slightly denticulate margins and strongly excurrent costae forming smooth awns. Brown tubers are produced in abundance and sporophytes are rare. In some specimens (Magill 5074, Russell 2669, Van Rooy 709) the leaf border is weak to absent but the plants conform well in other characters to R. capillare. The only fruiting specimen collected so far (Schelpe 2135), differs from sterile plants of B. capillare in being lax, with reddish green, oblong-spathulate leaves, distantly spaced along the red stem. The specimen is placed in R. capillare on the basis of the leaf and upper laminal cell length, the inconspicuous and narrow leaf borders, the entire to slightly denticulate leaf margins and the rounded leaf apices. No tubers could be found in the specimen. For differences between R. capillare and R. torquescens (Bruch & Schimp.) J.R. Spence see note under that species.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1987. Bryaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,2): 335-393. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the solid thallus, monoicous sexual condition and spore ornamentation.
bibliographicCitation: Van Rooy, J; Retief, E; Meyer, NL. 2017. Anthocerotophyta. In: E Retief & NL Meyer (eds), Plants of the Free State: Inventory and identification guide, Strelitzia 38: 108-108. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Plagiochasma eximium is a rather variable species, but can be distinguished by its robust, yellow-green thalli with large, deep pink to wine-red ventral scales narrowed above into (1)2 or 3 tapering appendages which are only a little constricted or pleated at the base. Ventrally the flanks are wrinkled and deep red, not dark purple. Elaters from the few spore-bearing plants studied are bispiral.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The species is veryvariable, especially in respect of the dentition of theleaves and the degree of crisping of the ventral leafbase, and three varieties have been described from Africa. In West Africa, var. squamulosa seems to be thepredominant form, chiefly characterised by short lateralbranches, and leaf margins with spiniform teeth. The two other varieties are known from East Africa.Var. sinuosa (Mitt.) Vanden Berghen is very closelyallied to var. squamulosa, from which it differs chieflyin having leaves with shorter teeth (triangular ratherthan spiniform, and of shorter cells 18-24(-28) µm long). In addition, the plant is usually more closely andregularly pinnate or bipinnate, with longer lateralbranches, the ventral crest is more open, particularly onbranches, and the ventral leaf margin sometimesstrongly undulate. Var. crispulo-caudata (Gottsche) Vanden Berghen is also very closely allied to var.squamulosa, differing from it in its more shortly dentateleaves, the more open branching with longer segments,and the ventral margin and ampliate part of the ventralbase not undulate, forming a well defined ventral crestwhich conceals the longly decurrent, highly crispedventral wings. Var. crispulo-caudata is mainly EastAfrican, but has been reported from Cameroon. Anotherspecies in this group, P. cambuena Steph., has beenreported from Ivory Coast, and is otherwise known onlyfrom East Africa. It is mainly characterised by the verystrongly undulate and crisped ventral leaf margin andbase. It is similar in size to P. pinniflora, the leaf mar-gins of P. cambuena also lacking dentition. P. squamulosa differs from P. pinniflora in its largersize, and the dentate leaves with an undulate andstrongly crisped decurrent ventral wing. I have not seenintermediates between P. pinniflora and P. squamulosa,and from present evidence it seems that the altitudinalranges of the two species do not overlap, though there has been insufficient collecting in the critical areas ofCameroon and Uganda, where both species occur, toprove that this is always so.
bibliographicCitation: Jones, EW. 2004. Lepidoziaceae Limpr. - Notothyladaceae (Milde) Müll.Frib. ex Prosk. In: MJ Wigginton (ed.), E.W. Jones's liverwort and hornwort Flora of West Africa: 102-424 National Botanic Garden (Belgium), Meise. [All rights reserved]

description: C. hexandra differs from the two closely related species C. polygonifolia and C. sericea by means of its very small, only 2.0-2.5 mm long leaflets, its 6 stamens and the narrowly winged receptacle.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: The abrupt distal rounding of one blade of the vaginant laminae and its strong termination on the costa will separate F. marginatus from all other Southern African species except F. simii. The size and shape of leaves and laminal cells will separate the latter.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Sphagnaceae to Nanobryaceae, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 23-70. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Pterobryopsis acutifolium is somewhat variable in plant size and leaf shape. The plants can be very short and compact or larger and full. The leaves, which exhibit some variation in shape of the lamina and apex, are occasionally crisped when dry. The plants are identified by their large size, single costa, entire leaf margins, and smooth, strongly thickened and pitted leaf cells.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1998. Erpodiaceae to Hookeriaceae. In: OA Leistner & E du Plessis (eds), Fl. S. Africa (1,3): 445-622. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/171731#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The suberect plants, large leaf cells, single costa and strong leaf borders should place specimens of var. mniifolium. The strongly differentiated basal leaf cells are reminiscent of the cancellinae of Calymperaceae. The small number of specimens examined seems to indicate that the variety is quite variable.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1998. Erpodiaceae to Hookeriaceae. In: OA Leistner & E du Plessis (eds), Fl. S. Africa (1,3): 445-622. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/171731#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: In such a wide ranging species one would expect some local variation. A Sim specimen, PRE-CH 1491, from Table Mountain has bistratose wing margins, and medianly there are four layers of cells. The determination was kindly confirmed by Dr Grolle. Arnell (1963) regarded the size of the marginal teeth in S. podophylla as having no taxonomic significance, nor the thickness of the walls in the marginal cells. He also did not find distinct differences between the erect and procumbent forms, there being a continued gradation between the two. In a comparison of transverse sections taken at the middle of the apical lobes of specimens of S. podophylla and of S. hymenophyllum from Juan Fernandez. Arnell (1956) stated that the thickness of the ‘nerves’ and the size of the teeth in the margin of the thalli vary but little. Arnell (1963) also compared specimens of S. hymenophyllum from Tristan da Cunha and Inaccessible Island as well as from Reunion and from Kilimanjaro, with numerous specimens of S. podophylla from the Cape (e.g. Thunberg’s collections) and could not find any real difference between them. On the other hand, Gottsche et al. (1846) distinguished S. podophylla from S. hymenophyllum by the ‘frondis laciniis basi attenuatis subpetiolatis’ of the former Symphyogyna podophylla is a less common and smaller plant than S. brasiliensis. It can be distinguished by: its growth form which is generally flabellate from an erect stalk arising from a creeping rhizome; the lobe margins which are toothed and hardly undulate; it rarely fruits and the spore ornamentation is characterised by broad, flat, roughened, irregular ridges, sometimes forming ‘loops’, and not by narrow, erect ridges as in S. brasiliensis. Symphyogyna podophylla and S. brasiliensis are the only two species of Symphyogyna occurring in southern Africa and are placed in the subfamily Symphyogynoideae (Trev.) Grolle.
bibliographicCitation: Jones, EW. 2004. Lepidoziaceae Limpr. - Notothyladaceae (Milde) Müll.Frib. ex Prosk. In: MJ Wigginton (ed.), E.W. Jones's liverwort and hornwort Flora of West Africa: 102-424 National Botanic Garden (Belgium), Meise. [All rights reserved]

description: The two species, C. odorata and C. hirsuta, are however quite different from one another. They form a sterile hybrid which is a beautiful intermediary between the two progenitorial species. The specially characteristic features of C. hirsuta in contradistinction to C. odorata are its much more robust stems and branches, which when young are covered with long and very thick yellowish grey hairs. Further, the vaginas and stipules are furnished with the same kind of hair as that on the stems and branches; the leaf-laminae are thick, coriaceous, sparsely pilous on the upperside, densely greyish white tomentose on the underside. The teeth of the leaves are acuminate and stiff, almost prickly.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Resembles P. haumannii Herz. from Ruwenzori, but is much smaller and has smaller cells.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinct in habit and in spores and in being dioecious.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: C. incana may be taxonomically allied to C. stricta but differs from this species in that the leaves are less rigid with a whitish-green colour and the branches and branchlets have a much longer and denser hairiness.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1953. Two new Cliffortia species from the Cape Province . Bot. Not. 106(1): 78-80. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be distinguished from R. crystallina and R. cavernosa, the other two rather similar species with spongy thalli, by being dioicous and heterothallic, by the characteristic 'butterfly' shape of young thalli, and by never developing a reddish or purple tint on exposure to the sun, as in R. cavernosa. The spores can be recognized by the very prominent arms of the triradiate mark on the proximal face, the thick wing and foveolate ornamentation.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: C. intermedia is rather similar to C. integerrima, C. theodori-friesii and C. dregeana. It differs from the two first-mentioned species by the 25-30 mm long, 5-6 mm broad and oblong-lanceolate, by 9-10 mm long [male]-and c. 4 mm long [female]-sepals. In addition the species is distinguished from C. dregeana by the above-mentioned features and by plain, not canaliculate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Can be distinguished from it by its almost white colour when dry, the larger size of the thalli, the less pronounced and generally shorter groove and the many exposed, hexagonal air chambers. There is a good deal of overlap in the size of the spores of the two species, but in R. garsidei there are generally fewer and larger alveoli.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia limbata can be distinguished from other southern African Riccia species with shiny black scales by its generally more 'fleshy' thallus, especially toward the apex and, more reliably, by its quite large spores, up to 130 µm diam., and ornamented on the nearly smooth proximal face by fovea and on the distal face, by spiralling ridges surrounding the central alveoli.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Differs from O. denudatum by the shape of the leaves and the thick-walled gemmae.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: Difficult to distinguish; living material is mostly required for identification, as the dorsal cell pillars, a critical character, cannot be reconstituted in dried herbarium specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The most conspicuous characters distinguishing C. juniperina from allied species are the following: the bark of the younger branches and branchlets is densely covered with warts and are never pilous. The number of the stamens is about 20, whereas the morphologically allied species never have more than 15.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. lanceolata is rather similar to C. dregeana with regard to the shape of the leaves. In C. dregeana, however, the blades are thicker, more coriaceous and more or less canaliculate, whereas in C. lanceolata the leaves are quite plain. Another very characteristic feature of this species is the occurrence of acuminate and, when young, sparsely-densely pilous stipules. As far as I know, C. lanceolata is the only species of Cliffortia which has the connective of the stamens furnished with hairs. These hairs are very short and apparently fugacious.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. lepida comes close to C. pedunculata Schltr. The former species has however, shorter, thinner pedicels, smaller [male] flowers with only 12 stamens (in pedunc. ca. 50), shorter petioles and smaller, entire or usually 2- or 3-lobed leaflets. The species also resembles C. triloba Harv., but this species on the other hand has shorter petioles and much shorter pedicels. C. lepida may be said to keep an intermediate position between C. pedunculata and C. triloba.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: The species can be recognized by the smallish, hardly robust, Ungulate branches of the lime-green to yellowish thalli. In some respects it is rather similar to small plants of R. bullosa and of R. garsidei , but the branches are narrower and more delicate, sometimes forming a rosette. The smaller, narrow-winged spores with poorly defined, triradiate mark and rounded alveoli with distinctly wider walls, scarcely raised at the nodes, also differ from those of R. bullosa and of R. garsidei.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The very tall, shiny dorsal cell pillars, triangular scales, apically split into loose, filamentous strands which mingle with the epithelial hairs at the margins and the quite large, dull brown, incompletely reticulate spores, distinguish this species from other members of section Pilifer.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia schelpei is characterized by the somewhat greasy appearance of the dorsal epidermis when fresh, with air pores surrounded by a ring of smaller, fragile cells superimposed over thicker-walled cells, giving it a mottled appearance; on drying out, the dorsal face turns yellowish and parchment-like, the groove is deep and the margins winged.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The differences between C. strobilifera and C. longifolia are very great. C. strobilifera has brachyblasts only a few mm long, [male]-flower bracteoles about 3 mm long, lanceolate and glabrous, while C. longifolia, on the other hand, has brachyblasts 10-30 mm long and linear, densely bristly bracteoles about 15 mm in length.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Specimens of M. berteroana are easily distinguished by the tiny marginal cells of the median scale appendages, by the cruciate dorsal pores and by the lobulate thallus margins. The membranous margins of the rays of the male receptacle also have very small cells. Otherwise it is quite similar to M. polymorpha, except for the latter having papillae on the rays of the carpocephalum. The ornamentation of their spores is also quite similar.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: L. helenae is probably identical with L. saccatiloba Sl. from W. Africa, it is, however, necessary to compare living plants and also to cultivate them together to be sure.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: C. tenuis is very similar to C. marginata. It differs from the latter in its leaflets, which are lacking the transparent leaf-margin. It has very small stipules, whereas C. marginata has no stipules at all or has them united to a semicircular structure, and its receptacles are finely verrucose. Furthermore, C. tenuis has 6 stamens, C. marginata 12.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: In several aspects, the gametophyte, with its prostrate stem (or axis) and delicate, 2-ranked, succubously inserted leaf-like lobes, resembles Fossombronia species, but so-called ‘angle’ leaves at the fork of dichotomies, as described by Proskauer (1954) and Schuster (1992), have not been observed by me in the present study, although I. am familiar with them from my work on the Fossombroniaceae (Perold 1999a).
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2000. Studies in the Sphaerocarpales (Hepaticae) from southern Africa. 2. The genus Sphaerocarpos and its only local species, S. stipitatus. Bothalia 30(1): 17-24. [CC BY]

description: Oxymitra cristata is distinguished by its large, obliquely triangular, shiny, dark red scales and by the row of archegonia enclosed in an irregular, but continuous, crest-like, fleshy ridge of tissue.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Fertile plants of M. capensis can be distinguished quite readily from other members of the Marchantiales by the stalked, domed and unlobed carpocephala, lacking a pseudoperi-anth. Sterile specimens are more difficult to distinguish, particularly from Targionia hypo-phylla and small Asterella plants. In T. hypo-phylla, however, the dorsal air pores are larger, and, when dry, white-encircled; in Asterella species, with the exception of A. muscicola, the air pores and air chambers are generally difficult to detect from above, fresh or dry.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: C. monophylla somewhat resembles C. filicaulis externally, but differs from it in having simple leaves. Morphologically it belongs to that group associated with C. odorata. Specially characteristic for this species are the small cordate -oval leaf-laminae, about 4 mm in length, the remaining triangular stipular teeth and the greyish white pilosity of all young parts.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Gemmae only on dorsal surface of thallus, discoid and oval; costa very broad.
bibliographicCitation: Phephu, N; Van Rooy, J. 2013. Studies in the liverwort family Metzgeriaceae (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 1. Metzgeria nudifrons stephani and a a key to the species. Polish Bot. J. 58(2): 449-455. [DOI: 10.2478/pbj-2013-0045] [All rights reserved]

description: C. multiformis is very singular owing to the varying shape of the leaves. On the same branchlet the blades can be simple and lanceolate or ± deeply lobed or 2-3-parted right down to the base. All transitions between these extreme forms are represented. From a morphological point of view the species thus forms a unique type connecting sect. Multinerviae and the sections with three leaflets. -The leaflets of C. multiformis, however, have more than one nerve, even when the blade is divided to the base. This feature indicates that the species should be referred to sect. Multinerviae. Within this section C. multiformis and C. ruscifolia alone have brachyblasts, whereas all other species have only elongated branches.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Exormotheca holstii can be distinguished from other species in the genus by its large size, its tall air chambers, basal V5-V3 occupied by chlorophyllose filaments, and laterally adjoined except for the apical 250 um toward the centre of the thallus and marginally for the apical ± 500 um; by the large, hyaline, triangular scales with long filiform appendages and its subsessile gynoecia. Tubers were not found.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: C. obcordata varies with respect to the relative size of the leaflets. Sometimes the mid-leaflet is small and the lateral ones larger, sometimes the middle one is the largest. The form of the mid-leaflet, however, is very characteristic, and C. obcordata may be readily distinguished from other species.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. odorata varies rather much with respect to the form and size of the leaves and to the pilosity of the branches and leaves, especially on the underside of the latter. The hairs can here be localized almost entirely to the veins of the leaves while the interspaces are quite smooth. Usually the interspaces are sparsely pilous but occasionally the whole of the underside is covered with long, dense, white, somewhat silvery hairs. A characteristic feature of the species, however, is, as Harvey also points out, that 'the pubescence is never persistent'.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. ovalis is a very striking species. The shape of the leaves is rather similar to that of C. ilicifolia but the margins are furnished with rather small cuspidate teeth. Only elongated branches are developed.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Riccardia compacta specimens are distinguished by the following characters: 1. The plants grow in dense, thick cushions of several layers of intricately inter twining branches, mostly at high altitudes: 2. The thalli are narrow and small, only up to ± 15 mm long, with irregularly branched, lateral branches, their margins generally parallel and unwinged: 3. From above the dorsal cells of the ultimate segment of the main axis are thick-walled, and in cross section, so are the medullary cells; 4. The antheridial branches in South African plants are usually short and have conspicuous marginal cells; and 5. The corona of the calyptra is smooth and the cells thick-walled.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2002. Studies in the liverwort family Aneuraceae (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 3. Riccardia compacta. Bothalia 32(1): 15-19. [CC BY]

description: A variable species.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is similar to Chorisodontium aciphyllum (Hook, f. & Wils.) Broth, and C. dicranellatum (Dus.) Roiv. but differs in the falcate, secund leaves, strongly serrate subulae, coarsely mammillose dorsal costa and costal anatomy.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: The narrow costa, differentiated alar cells, bordered leaves and smooth leaf cells of this species are characteristic. It is distinct from the other Southern African species by its non-porous, shortly rectangular leaf cells and oblong alar cells.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: The species can be distinguished by the 'ruched', lobed leaves, which are mostly wider than long, the tuberous stem apices, the completely or incompletely reticulate spores and by the occasional to frequent presence of some hyaline rhizoids. The tuberous apices of the stems bear some resemblance to those of F. spinifolia (Perold 1997b), which has markedly dentate leaves in the male plants, spores with 6 or 7 short irregular ridges, and which is only known from Genadendal.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1998. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 5. A new species from Northern and Western Cape. Bothalia 28(1): 1-5. [CC BY]

description: Riccia alatospora is the smallest species in section Pilifer. Its size, reddish pink scales and wide-winged, highly ornamented, large spores, distinguish it from other species in this section. It is closely related to R. hantamensis (, which is, however, a much larger plant, but with similarly ornamented, though smaller spores.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia alboporosa is easily recognized by its widely, but regularly spaced air pores, encircled by dorsal epithelial cells, the inner parts of which rapidly become white on drying. The species differs from the other white-scaled species by its inconspicuous scales, heavily encrusted with calcium salts, by the puffy appearance of the dorsal surface in the dry plant and by the finely reticulate spores.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: As to size C. phyllanthoides mostly agrees with C. pulchella and C. crenulata. From the other species within the section the plant differs in the leaflets, which, at the base, have only 2-3 inconspicuous ribs and relatively broad transparent margins. The narrow, curved mid-leaflet is also characteristic. The receptacle has three, at the margins undulate, transparent wings, while the other species have the receptacles not furnished with wings.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Vegetatively R. albornata is not easily distinguished from R. albolimbata , but it never grows in rosettes; the scales are generally larger and frillier; the dorsal epithelial cells are somewhat larger and the air canals are wider, enclosed by six columns of cells; the spore ornamentation is also markedly different with numerous small, irregular alveoli and convoluted ridges on both faces.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia angolensis differs from the other black-scaled species of Riccia from southern Africa by its generally rather thin thalli and sometimes irregularly shaped branches.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia tomentosa differs from other Riccia species by the unique, long, vertical, hair-like, cellular outgrowths from many of the epidermal cells, often basally slightly raised in support, by the well-spaced stomata, as well as by the papillose to verruculose spores in permanent tetrads.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia hantamensis is closely related to, but distinguished from R. alatospora, on account of its much more robust thalli, the inconspicuous, hyaline scales on the ventral face, the rounded apical cells in the loose dorsal cell pillars, and the much smaller, but similarly ornamented, and far more numerous spores. Spores collected from the same population during a dry season, appear to be more highly ornamented and rather smaller than those collected in a wet season.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished between cilia and hairs ('poils'), the latter being thin-walled and stouter.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: As appears from the diagnosis of C. propinqua this species has a slightly flattened, pubescent receptacle with two developed achenes, whereas C. serpyllifolia has in cross-section a round, glabrous receptacle with only one achene.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Fossombronia spinosa can be recognised by its rather small size, frilly, angularly lobed leaves and finely spinose spores, of which some spines coalesce to form short ridges. F. leucoxantha, also from the Western Cape, has similar finely spinose spores, but mostly with papillae interspersed between the spines, and has ‘incised-dentate’ leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 8. F. elsieae and F. spinosa, two new Western Cape species with spinose spores. Bothalia 29(1): 25-33. [CC BY]

description: F. marindae can be recognised by usually split-open pseudoperianths with undulating margins at the mouth; they are often situated very close to the stem apices and sometimes on short shoots which are apically slightly raised. The most important character, however, is the very elaborate spore ornamentation with 7 or 8 ridges across the distal face and numerous spinules between. It is surely one of the most beautiful in the entire genus and not to be confused with that of any other species.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 10. Three new species from Northern and Western Cape. Bothalia 29(1): 83-93. [CC BY]

description: Vegetatively F. monticola is quite a variable species, but it can generally be distinguished by somewhat fan-shaped leaves that are 2- or 3-lobed and mostly wider above than below; the upper margin is undulating, and has several short spinous projections topped with a papilla; the pseudoperianth is campanulas, its mouth is divided into 11 or 12 lobes and the margin has up to 35 spinous projections; the distal face of the spores is covered with 9-11 irregular ridges, up to 5 pm apart and sometimes joined by fainter transverse walls to form areolae.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 10. Three new species from Northern and Western Cape. Bothalia 29(1): 83-93. [CC BY]

description: Var. mucronulata differs from the main species only by the form of the leaflets, which have a cordate base and are mucronate at the apex.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. pungens and neglecta are habitually much alike, while at the same time they need never be confused. The most conspicuous distinguishing features of the two appears from the following comparison: C. pungens: bark smooth; leaves glossy; leaves with narrow, deep furrow on the upperside; receptacle prismatic, hexagonal.; C. neglecta: bark, at least on young branches, pilous; leaves dull; leaves plane on upperside or with shallow, slight furrow; receptacle ovoid.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Generally, the species can be distinguished by being larger than M. debilis and by lacking a dark median line on the dorsal surface of the thallus; its median scale appendages are large and often marginally toothed, with the inner cells large, presenting a 'loose' appearance; its cupules have longer cilia; the female receptacle is shortly divided into rays and the involucral margin is ciliate; androgynous branches in the female receptacle are sometimes present.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Pelekium ramusculosum resembles both P. varians and P. chenagonii and has often been confused with these species. However, the characters of the sporophyte, the paraphyllia, and the papillae on the leaf cells serve to distinguish it easily. Some collections of P. ramusculosum are more robust than P. varians (as Dixon stated in his diagnosis of Thuidium sublaevipes) but as a rule the plants of P. ramusculosum are intermediate in size between P. varians and P. versicolor.
bibliographicCitation: Touw, A. 1976. A taxonomic revision of Thuidium, Pelekium and Rauiella (Musci: Thuidiaceae) in Africa south of the Sahara. Lindbergia 3: 135-195. [All rights reserved]

description: Pelekium versicolor and Thuidium torrentium were both created by C. Mueller and based on collections from the Cape Province, Republic of South Africa. He stressed that they are closely related, but that P. versicolor has longer leaves, and he described these as narrowly ovate-acuminate (unfortunately, without mentioning whether stem leaves or branch leaves were meant). The stem leaves of T. torrentium were described by him as having an ovate base and a short slender acumen, whereas the branch leaves were described as elliptic and short curved-acuminate. Judging from the numerous South African collections P. versicolor s. s. and T. torrentium arc forms of a single species. In P. versicolor s. s. the branch leaves are longer (up to 0.4 mm) than in T. torrentium (up to 0.35 mm), and the majority of the branch leaves are triangular-ovate with an acute to weakly acuminate apex. Towards the end of the branches and along the branchlets the leaves are comparatively shorter and more abruptly narrowed to a more or less rounded-acute apex. In T. torrentium the same leaf shapes are found, but the latter type predominates. Many collections show intermediate features, and both forms show the same distribution area and appear to grow in the same habitat; P. versicolor s. s. shows some preference for slightly wetter places. I have been unable to find any other differences.
bibliographicCitation: Touw, A. 1976. A taxonomic revision of Thuidium, Pelekium and Rauiella (Musci: Thuidiaceae) in Africa south of the Sahara. Lindbergia 3: 135-195. [All rights reserved]

description: C. rigida exhibits a certain external resemblance to forms of C. polygonifolia but differs from this species above all in its receptacles being costate and not winged, in its twigs and leaves being glabrous and in its leaflets having a pungent top. Most characteristic is, however, the differentiation of the leaves. Some of them are 3-foliolate with oblong-lanceolate leaflets, others united a longer or shorter part of their length, others again are simple and 3-lobed in the top. The simple leaves have 3 nerves about equally strong and agree very well with those of certain species of sect. Multinerviae. C. rigida thus holds an intermediate position between sect. Costatae and sect. Multinerviae with regard to the differentiation of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Although related to R. rubricollis, which was collected by Duthie in 1929 at Knysna, this new species differs from it by being more delicate and by totally lacking any purple colouration due to anthocyanin pigmentation on the dorsal surface of the thallus, as well as in the antheridial necks. Furthermore, the spores of R. sibayenii have double rows of granules along the wing margins and on the alveolar walls on the distal face. The proximal face is ornamented with spinose granules and not with smooth-walled alveoli, which are present in R. rubricollis on both faces (Perold 1991). In addition, R. sibayenii grows in the subtropics, which has summer rain, not in the temperate southern Cape, known for its fynbos and rain almost all year round.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2001. Studies in the genus Riccia (Marchantiales) from southern Africa. 25. A new species in subgenus Ricciella, section Ricciella. Bothalia 31(2): 151-154. [CC BY]

description: Differs from all other S. African species of Lophocolea by the almost entire mouth of the perianth and by the small cells from all other species except L. fragrans.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: Differs from all other African species of the genus by the absence of amphigastria and by the hyaline border of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: It is recognized as a new species mainly by the unique spore ornamentation which is characterized by exceptionally heavy ridges, and is referred to section Pilifer because of the free-standing cell pillars dorsally on the thalli. The specific epithet was chosen because of the radiating ridges on the distal face of many of the spores, quite different from those previously studied.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2004. Studies in the genus Riccia (Marchantiales) from southern Africa. 26. A new species in section Pilifer, Riccia radiata, is descrtibed. Bothalia 34(1): 23-26. [CC BY]

description: C. semiteres is known only in one collection. No [male] flowers are known, and the female flowers occur only in a voting stage. The receptacles have 3 low but conspicuous wings. The species is on that account here referred to sect. Alatae.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is most easily recognized when it forms large, loose tufts on boulders or tree limbs. The julaceous stems are ± erect and have few branches. The leaves are ecostate, but have a pronounced group of elongated basal cells in the lower centre of the leaf. It is similar to the North American species, L. julaceus (Hedw.) Sull. which differs by having the upper laminal cells papillose on the dorsal surface. Specimens of P. assimilis are frequently confused with Braunia secunda. However, that species has weakly plicate leaves, generally hyaline and papillose leaf tips, and gymnostomous capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1998. Erpodiaceae to Hookeriaceae. In: OA Leistner & E du Plessis (eds), Fl. S. Africa (1,3): 445-622. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/171731#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: It is easily recognized by the rather flattened round discs of the carpocephala, by horizontally protruding pseudoperianths, their rather short segments becoming free at the tips before the capsules dehisce.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: C. lanata is a distinct type very much deviating from the other species of the section. The leaflets are entire and densely lanate with greyish white hairs. The species is on that account rather similar to certain forms of C. eriocephalina, a feature mentioned by the discoverer. The fruits are not fully ripe. As in C. polygonifolia and allied species the receptacles have 3 high, recurved wings. Furthermore, there occur 3 low wings alternating with the higher ones.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: Cliffortia spathulata has here been distinguished as an independent species different from C. browniana. No transitional forms have been found. The interpretation of the two types as different species is moreover supported by the fact that typical specimens of the two species have been collected in one and the same area: Cathedral Peak. C. browniana has entire or very scantily serrulate, oblong leaflets, prominently costate receptacles and cinereous-blackish pilosity on the twigs, whereas C. spathulata has much broader, spathulate leaflets toothed in the broad, truncate or roundish top, indistinctly costate receptacles and dense, ferruginous pilosity.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1948. The genus Cliffortia, a taxonomical survey. Bot. Not. 90(2): 167-203. [All rights reserved]

description: The small plants and smooth leaf cells separate Z. dixonii from other Zygodon species in southern Africa.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1998. Erpodiaceae to Hookeriaceae. In: OA Leistner & E du Plessis (eds), Fl. S. Africa (1,3): 445-622. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/171731#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: C. strobilifera is above all characterized by the linearly lanceolate, smooth-margined or occasionally serrulate leaves. The stem-leaves lose their laminae at an early stage, only the wide, usually grey -greyish green vagina remaining, crowned by the two stipules. The receptacle is peculiar. It has a length of only about 1.5 mm and has an unusually wide opening at the upper end.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Triquetrella mxinwana differs most saliently from the majority of congeners by its low, bifid laminal papillae several occurring over each lumen. Furthermore, it is smaller, with stems to 2 cm, not 7 cm, in length; the central strand is never present; leaves are entire, never weakly serrulate above; the seta is 0.9-1.0 cm long while the seta of other species is generally 1.5-2.3 cm in length; and the theca is shorter, 1.0-1.2 mm as opposed to1.6-2.1 mm in length.
bibliographicCitation: Hedderson, TAJ; Zander, RH. 2007. Triquetrella mxinwana, a new moss species from South Africa, with a phylogenetic and biogeographic hypothesis for the genus. J. Bryol. 29: 151-160. [All rights reserved]

description: The small plants, with ovate-lanceolate to spathulate, red-awned leaves, bearing immersed cupulate to short-cylindric capsules (in the wet state) with a very long-conic operculum and an evertable annulus are diagnostic.
bibliographicCitation: Hedderson, TAJ; Zander, RH. 2007. Ludorugbya springbokorum (Pottiaceae) a new moss genus and species from the Western Cape Province of South Africa. J. Bryol. 29: 222-227. [DOI: 10.1179/174328207X229742] [All rights reserved]

description: Although Rosulabryum rubens was originally considered related to Gemmabryum subapiculatum, morphology as well as recent molecular work support a position near R. capillare.
bibliographicCitation: Spence, JR. 2014. 42. Bryaceae Schwagrichen, Fl. N. Amer. 28: 117-185. New York Botanic Garden, New York. [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the New York Botanical Garden Press] [All rights reserved]

description: Leaf margins recurved in upper portion, commonly weakly bordered with narrow, somewhat thicker- walled cells near apex; costa narrow above midleaf, mostly 25-35 µm wide, weakly papillose; synoicous or paroicous; seta short but distinct, 0.10-0.20 mm; spores spiculose-papillose.
bibliographicCitation: Hedderson, TAJ; Zander, RH. 2009. Acaulonopsis, a new moss genus of the Pottiaceae from Western Cape Province of South Africa, and comments on Vrolijkheidia. J. Bryol. 31: 234-239. [All rights reserved]

description: Leaf margins mostly plane, sometimes weakly recurved above, unbordered; costa broad above midleaf, mostly 40-50 µm in width, strongly papillose; rhizautoicous; seta extremely short or nearly absent, 0.015-0.040 mm; spores smooth or weakly low-papillose.
bibliographicCitation: Hedderson, TAJ; Zander, RH. 2009. Acaulonopsis, a new moss genus of the Pottiaceae from Western Cape Province of South Africa, and comments on Vrolijkheidia. J. Bryol. 31: 234-239. [All rights reserved]

description: This species may be confused, vegetatively, with Acaulon. Sporophytically, V. peraristatum is distinct in the exposed, elliptical-rostrate capsules, differentiated exothecial cells and cucullate calyptra.The species was described as having smooth leaf cells, however all subsequent collections examined from Southern Africa, have several fine, C-shaped papillae on the upper laminal cells. Since these papillae were detected on specimens mounted in Hoyer's medium, it was believed that the papillae had been overlooked when the species was described. Unfortunately the type has not been located.A specimen recently examined from Kenya is similar to the Southern African specimens except that it has smooth leaf cells. It may, therefore be more similar to MacOwan's collection than the papillose specimens from the western Cape. The taxon is considered to include both 'facies', however the papillose specimens may represent an undescribed variety.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: The short, only 3-5 mm long, semicircularly curved leaflets are very characteristic. As distinguished from C. filifolia the species has, moreover, 4 sepals, 8 stamens and, usually, 4 high and 4 low ribs on the receptacle.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. teretifolia is markedly distinguished from the other species within the section. It is especially characterized by elongated branches with uniform interspaces between the closely leafed brachyblasts. Stems and branches are glabrous, and the younger portions are darkly redbrown and shining. Of special interest is the form of the sepals, which on the exterior surface, immediately below the rounded top, are furnished with a long spine. The receptacle is 3-or 4-winged, and the wings are broad and transparent.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Spinously, patently hairy; leaves variable in size; calyx lobes 12 x 6 mm in fruit; apices of corolla lobes long and acuminate; nutlets ovoid-cup-shaped with distinct serrate, raised margins and a concave, glochidiate inner face.
bibliographicCitation: Retief, E; Van Wyk, AE. 2002. The genus Trichodesma (Boraginaceae: Boraginoideae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 32(1): 151-166. [CC BY]

description: Multistemmed greyish green suffrutex; stems glabrous or with setae with prominent discoid, multicellular bases; flowers drooping; calyx brownish purple; corolla white with a light brown rim at apices of lobes; fruit a hairy, discoid nutlet.
bibliographicCitation: Retief, E; Van Wyk, AE. 2002. The genus Trichodesma (Boraginaceae: Boraginoideae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 32(1): 151-166. [CC BY]

description: The most remarkable features of C. theodori-friesii, as distinguished from the relatively similar C. ruscifolia and the hybrid between the two species, will be found under the hybrid. As a matter of fact the form of the leaves of the two species is so similar that they have been considered to represent one and the same species. The intermediate forms, represented by the hybrid, have obliterated the boundary line between the two species, which, however, are not so closely related. On the other hand C. theodori-friesii stands near to C. integerrima. The principal differences between them are the following. C. theodori-friesii has blades 10-14 mm long, and 3-5 mm broad, evenly tapering towards the apex, about 5 mm long bracteoles, 6-7 mm long [male]-flower sepals, about 20 stamens and [female]-flower sepals about 1.5 mm long. C. integerrima, on the contrary, has blades 12-20 mm long, 7-10 mm broad and abruptly contracted at the apex about 3 mm long bracteoles, [male]-flower sepals about 5 mm long several stamens and [female]-flower sepals 2.5-3 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: C. tricuspidata is, as mentioned by Harvey (1. c., p. 300), rather similar to C. filicaulis Cham, et Schldl. The main type of that species has, like C. tricuspidata, slender, trailing stems and canescently pilous branches and leaves. The differences between the two species are, on the other hand, so great that they must be referred to different sections. C. tricuspidata is in addition to the already discussed features also characterized as follows: The blades have at their apices three, or occasionally only two, usually strongly claw-shaped teeth; the stamens are as a rule 6 in number, and the receptacle, about 2.5 mm long, is smooth without any furrows but furnished with reticular nervature. Morphologically the species stands dose to C. ferruginea and C. monophylla.
bibliographicCitation: Weimarck, AH. 1934. Monograph of the genus Cliffortia. Hákan Ohlsson, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: A variable species, especially in indumentum, shape of leaves and in the shape of the fruit, i.e. the relationship between the length of the valves and the length of the beak. The beak varies from about 0.5 as long to nearly as long as the valves.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W. 1970. Cruciferae, Fl. S. Africa 13: 1-118. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Cliffortia verrucosa is a member of sect. Multinerviae and comes morphologically close to C. ruscifolia. As well as in this species the leaf-blades in verrucosa are pilous on the underside but the hairs are shorter than in C. ruscifolia. The leaf-blades are smaller than in any known form of C. ruscifolia, broader in proportion to the length, and many of them are more or less deeply lobed thus exhibiting a certain similarity to small-leafed forms of C. ilicifolia. C. verrucosa deviates from all known species of the section by its receptacles which are provided with small verrucae, conformable to those in C. tuberculata (sect. Costatae).

description: C. varians is very similar to C. crenulata but differs by its entire leaflets, glabrous twigs and bracteoles. Transitional types occur: some leaves have the middle leaflet reduced in size, in others it is more or less united with one of the lateral leaflets. Trifoliolate leaves agree very much with those of C. glauca and C. obovata of the sect. Costatae.

description: Because of the weakly developed root system and the absence of woodiness at the base of the stem, N. deflexa could easily be mistaken for an annual, and in most situations (e.g. the type locality), it almost certainly behaves as one. However, given adequate water and nutrients, plants are capable of surviving the hot, dry summer period of the western Cape (at least in cultivation). This is in contrast to the situation for most, if not all, spring-flowering annual Nemesia species. They do not survive the high temperatures associated with summer drought even when supplied with ample water and nutrients. It is not known whether plants of Nemesia deflexa ever survive for a full year or more in the natural environment. It is probable that in most situations, they survive the dry season solely in the form of seed which is produced in fairly large amounts. The seeds germinate readily as soon as they are shed if sufficient moisture is present.

description: The plant is a dwarf shrublet, the many branches densely leafy, but the terminal floriferous parts nearly nude because of the sudden gross reduction in leaf-size. The leaves are borne in closely set pseudofascicles. They are small (up to c. 11 mm long), spathulate in outline, nearly always conduplicate, the margins in the upper part deeply cut into 1-4 pairs of ± oblong lobes; only the largest lobes are occasionally toothed; the smallest leaves may be entire. The backs of the leaves are thickly beset with large glistening glands; these are absent from the upper surface, which may or may not produce scattered minute glandular hairs. Similar minute hairs are often present on the petiolar part of the leaves, but they are usually very inconspicuous. The corolla limb is usually shades of purple, blue or mauve, rarely white. The capsules have glistening glands confined or very nearly confined to the sutures, with tiny glandular hairs elsewhere, though these may disappear with age.

description: Jamesbrittenia fruticosa is distinguished from its allies primarily by its leaves: the cauline leaves are nearly always elliptic, tapering at both ends (ratio of length: breadth 2-4.8:1) and spread nearly at right angles to the stem; only the uppermost leaves subtending flowers are sometimes ovate and broad-based. The pubescence on the leaves is often (but by no means always) shorter than in allied species; it is useful to examine the margins, where the hairs are easily seen in profile. The pedicels are short (up to 10 mm, but 4-5 mm is more usual), the calyx lobes mostly less than 1 mm broad (occasionally up to 1.5 mm), the corolla tube long (mostly 20-26 mm, occasionally as short as 16 mm) and only lightly bearded with short clavate hairs that scarcely extend onto the base of the lower lip. The whole plant often blackens on drying.
