description: Lessertia sneeuwbergensis and L. cryptantha closely resemble one another, but are separated by a number of morphological differences and by their distribution. L. cryptantha occurs in the Klinghardts Mountains in central Namibia and L. sneeuwbergensis occurs in the Sneeuwberg Mountain range and Lootsberg in the central Cape Province.
bibliographicCitation: Germishuizen, G. 1992. Lessertia sneeuwbergensis, a new species from the Middleburg disctrict of the central Cape Province. Bothalia 22(2): 189-190. [CC BY]

description: Lachnaea elsieae superficially resembles L. penicillata, a distantly related species, but differs in having a pseudobracteate umbel, with up to four open flowers at a time, and a glabrous style.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: I. prolixa has inflorescences in which there is often only one flower at each node. In addition, the internodes of the inflorescence may be as long as or slightly longer than the calyx. The margins of the bracts and calyx lobes have glandular trichomes with stalks of five or more cells and these distinguish I. prolixa from other species of Isoglossa, where the glandular hairs on the margins of the bracts and calyx lobes have stalks with four or less cells. The leaves of I. prolixa have a slight greyish bloom.
bibliographicCitation: Balkwill, K; Sebola, RJ; Poriazis, DL. 2017. Taxonomic revision of white-flowered Isoglossa Oerst. (Acanthaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 108: 48-80. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2016.09.013] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2017); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The affinities of L. coleorum are still unclear. The nearest match for its seeds and fruits is found in L. werneri. If these taxa are closely related, this suggests a very large disjunction, some 1300 kilometres. However, L. werneri consistently shows the fine red markings ('rubri-cations' sensu Cole) characteristic of its Namibian neighbours, L. pseudotruncatella (Berger) N.E.Br, and L. gracilidelineata Dinter, whereas L. coleorum lacks them. Also, the three Namibian species have a characteristically slow maturation, retaining a short juvenile fissure for several years. Other possible relatives - L. gesineae De Boer from the Tiras Mountains in central Namibia, and L. terricolor (N.E.Br.) N.E.Br, from the western Cape (both taxa lack rubrications and have a window structure roughly comparable to that of L. coleorum) - would still present very large disjunctions, otherwise unknown in Lithops.
bibliographicCitation: Hammer, SA; Uijs, R. 1994. Lithops coleorum S.A. Hammer & R. Uijs sp. nov., a new species of Lithops N.E.Br. from northern Transvaal. Aloe 31(2): 36-38. [All rights reserved]

description: Lachnaea oliverorum can be distinguished from its sister species, L. funicaulis, by having 18-22-flowered umbels, larger flowers (up to 9 mm long), a villous- tomentose indumentum on the flowers and the cupshaped upper portion of the hypanthium.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The broadly ovate or obovate bracts with a markedly acuminate tip are diagnostic of this species. There are long and short eglandular hairs on the bracts and calyx and dense glandular hairs with up to three cells in the stalk. The long patent hairs on the long petioles are unusual in the genus, but are shared by many specimens of I. delicatula, which has much narrower bracts (1.3 ±0.9 mm wide in I. delicatula and 6.5 ±0.3 mm wide in I. woodii). I. woodii has 5 to 7 lateral veins in the leaf whereas I. glandulosissima has 3 to 4. The mature inflorescences of I. woodii are longer than those of I. origanoides (56 ±20 mm rather than 25 ±9 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Balkwill, K; Sebola, RJ; Poriazis, DL. 2017. Taxonomic revision of white-flowered Isoglossa Oerst. (Acanthaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 108: 48-80. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2016.09.013] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2017); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: This species is allied to Lachnaea funicaulis which has a similar flower structure but also differs in several aspects. L. greytonensis has a pseudobracteate umbel, the upper portion of the hypanthium is cup-shaped, narrowing into a very short tube at the base, which is villous-tomentose outside and villous-hirsute within, and the sepals are abaxially villous-tomentose. In L. funicaulis the umbel is bracteate, the upper portion of the hypanthium is funnel-shaped, tomentose-sericeous outside and adpressed hairy inside, and the sepals are abaxially tomentose-sericeous.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lachnaea pusilla is closely allied to L. leipoldtii but differs in that the basal portion of the hypanthium outside is covered with obtuse hairs in the upper half and the stigma is very narrowly conical and papillate.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: L. alpina subsp. alpina can be distinguished from L. alpina subsp. multiflora (Eckl. & Zeyh.) B.-E.van Wyk by the thick and robust branches, larger leaves and stipules, and the smaller flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Boatwright, JS; et al. 2019. Fabaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 926-1066. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: B. amajubica is closely allied to B. glabrescens and could be confused with the latter species but for its prominent indumentum, elongate bracts and larger calyx lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Edward, TJ; Getliffe Norris, FM. 1990. Notes on the genus Buchenroedera (Fabaceae) in Natal. S. African J. Bot. 56(3): 275-284. [https://doi.org/10.1016/S0254-6299(16)31055-9] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1990); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: R. viminea is closely allied to B. amajubica but is distinguished by its taller stems, compound inflorescence and villous indumentum. In addition B. viminea produces larger, porcelain-white flowers opposed to the gentian-blue flowers of B. amajubica.
bibliographicCitation: Edward, TJ; Getliffe Norris, FM. 1990. Notes on the genus Buchenroedera (Fabaceae) in Natal. S. African J. Bot. 56(3): 275-284. [https://doi.org/10.1016/S0254-6299(16)31055-9] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1990); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The species is closely allied to L. tenuiflora, but it is a more robust plant, mostly broader in the leaf than L. tenuiflora (ratio of length: breadth c.2-3: 1 versus 4-5: 1) with longer pedicels (lowermost c. 18-23 mm, not 4-11 mm), and larger, hairier ovaries and capsules. The corolla limb is white (shades of pink and mauve in L. tenuiflora) and the colour-patterning around the mouth more pronounced.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The type has not been seen, but from the description it is considered to belong near J. petiolaris; the locality fits that of subsp. incerta sensu meo.
bibliographicCitation: Immelman, KL. 1995. 5. Justicia. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 30(3,1): 18-46. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lachnaea pendula is a sister species of L. penicillata based on two shared characters: inflorescence borne on the main flowering branches and a pubescent style. L. pendula can easily be distinguished by its small, pendulous, bractcate inflorescences and the pale gold- coloured pubescence on the abaxial side of the sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinct species, similar to L. pachycarpa but differs in the slender, linear leaflets, the inconspicuous stipules, the shorter and more closely appressed vestiture and the oblong-linear and only slightly inflated pods. It is also similar to L. falcata, but differs from this and related species in the long slender pedicel (much longer than the calyx) and the linear, densely silky-strigillose leaflets.
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E. 1990. Studies in the genus Lotononis (Crotalarieae, Fabaceae). 9. Four new species of the L. pentaphylla group, section Lipozygis. Bothalia 20(1): 1-7. [CC BY]

description: M. hamata is closely related to M. revoluta, with which it shares general appearance and-more importantly-the glandular-glochidiate seeds. It differs from subsp. revoluta-which is in habit the closest-in longer petioles, wider leaves, longer bracteoles, longer corolla and longer filaments. From subsp. cognata, which has a more or less sympatric distribution, it also differs in the spreading indumentum.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 1989. A revision of Megalochlamys and Ecbolium (Acanthaceae: Justicieae). Kew Bull. 44(4): 601-680. [All rights reserved]

description: L. filiformis is very closely related to L. azurea Eckl. & Zeyh. but differs in the very long, slender and sparsely branched habit, the slender linear leaflets, the oblong (not triangular) calyx lobes, the smaller narrower fruit and particularly in the minutely strigillose vestiture of the twigs, leaves, calyx and fruit (not sparsely pilose as in L. azurea). It is also geographically isolated from the latter and has a more western distribution, known only from the northern slopes of the Outeniqua Mountains. The narrow calyx lobes are very similar to those of L. azurea var. lanceolata Harv. (based on Ononis villosa Thunb.), with which L. filiformis has previously been confused. I have examined the Thunberg type specimen of Ononis villosa, but the long, sparse and spreading hair covering of the latter is very different from the dense and minutely strigillose vestiture of L. filiformis.
bibliographicCitation: Van Wyk, B-E. 1990. Studies in the genus Lotononis (Crotalarieae, Fabaceae). 10. L. esterhuyseniana, a new species from the south-western Cape. Bothalia 20(1): 70-73. [CC BY]

description: M. kenyensis has been widely confused with M. revoluta and M. hamata with which it shares the glandular-glochidiate seeds. In the herbaria it has most commonly been identified as a form of M. revoluta, but in my opinion it deserves to be treated as a distinct species. It differs from M. revoluta and M. hamata in the longer spikes with the bracts clasping the capsules and in the long-stalked shiny capitate glands on bracts and calyces.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 1989. A revision of Megalochlamys and Ecbolium (Acanthaceae: Justicieae). Kew Bull. 44(4): 601-680. [All rights reserved]

description: M. revoluta can be divided into three subspecies which have allopatric distributions. The division is mainly based on indumentum characters.
bibliographicCitation: Vollesen, KB. 1989. A revision of Megalochlamys and Ecbolium (Acanthaceae: Justicieae). Kew Bull. 44(4): 601-680. [All rights reserved]

description: Lachnaea grandiflora is closely related to L. uniflora. Their inflorescence and floral structure are similar. The narrow-leaved form of L. grandiflora has in the past been confused with L. uniflora. L. grandiflora is multistemmed at the base, resprouting after fires, whereas in L. uniflora two distinct forms have been identified, namely a single-stemmed reseeder and a multistemmed resprouter. Although the hypanthium of both species is sericeous on the outside, the trichomes of the basal portion of the hypanthium in L. uniflora are blunt (obtuse), whereas those in L. grandiflora are acicular, similar to those on the upper hypanthium.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lachnaea filicaulis is distinguished from L. axillaris by the upper portion of the hypanthium being cup-shaped without a basal invagination, the hypanthium and sepals being sericeous on the outside, and by the conical, papillate stigma.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lachnaea laxa is easily distinguished from the other solitary-flowered species with a decussate leaf arrangement and cream to pink flowers, by the upper portion of the hypanthium being funnel-shaped and the floral scales arising at the mouth of the hypanthium.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lachnaea stokoei resembles L. ericoides in general facies in that it has alternate, narrowly elliptic to ovate leaves with involute margins and tufts of hairs at the apices and the inflorescence which is an ebracteate umbel with up to three open flowers at a time, but the flower structure differs. The antesepalous stamen whorl is exserted, the antepetalous one semi-exserted, the floral scales arise abaxially ± a third of the way down the upper portion of the hypanthium and the stigma is conical and elongate-papillate.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lachnaea rupestris is allied to L. eriocephala and L. naviculifolia, but is easily distinguished by its low straggling habit. It is superficially very similar to L. marlothii from which it can be distinguished by the thin pubescence of the branches, glabrous leaves, dorso-ventrally flattened pedicels, which are abaxially produced beyond the point of attachment of the flower, by the antesepalous stamens which arise at the base of the sepals and by the narrowly ellipsoid or narrowly obovoid floral scales.
bibliographicCitation: Beyers, JBP. 2001. The Cape genus Lachnaea (Thymelaeceae): A monograph. Strelitzia 11: 1-115. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Passerina montivagus is easily distinguished from P. filiformis by its more robust and luxuriant habit. Furthermore, for some distance below the inflorescences, the foliage leaves are expanded at the base and the bracts are ovate to obovate. narrowing gradually into a sturdy, leaf-like point, with margins along their distal half conspicuously fringed by strong white trichomes. P. montivagus could also be confused with P. falcifolia. but it is distinguished from the latter by the apical beard on the young leaves regarded the species as 'useless' and advised that it should be eradicated by hand, as it was not dense enough to burn without additional fuel. This Fynbos species, distributed along the Great Escarpment has not been reported as undesirable or invasive and is currently not regarded as a threat, although it might be a dominant species in restricted areas.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL; Van Wyk, AE. 2002. Taxonomy of the Passerina filiformis complex (Thymelaeaceae). Bothalia 32(1): 29-36. [CC BY]

description: R. alata differs from R. vlokii and R. elliptica in the smaller, procumbent, mat-like habit and the large, wing-like extensions between the calyx lobes (extensions absent in R. vlokii and R. elliptica).
bibliographicCitation: Campbell, GJ; Van Wyk, B-E. 2001. A taxonomic revision of Rafnia (Fabaceae, Crotalarieae). S. African J. Bot. 67: 90-149. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2001); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Leaves elliptic, 3-8 cm long, lateral veins often indented above.
bibliographicCitation: Coates Palgrave, K; Coates Palgrave, M. 2002. Trees of southern Africa, 3rd ed. Struik, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: R. acuminata is similar to R. amplexicaulis but differs in the prostrate, trailing habit (R. amplexicaulis is a large, erect, robust woody shrub) and the proximally narrow pod (the pod is proximally broad and the upper margin convex in R. amplexicaulis). R. acuminata is distinguished from the remaining species by its cordate, reticulately veined leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Campbell, GJ; Van Wyk, B-E. 2001. A taxonomic revision of Rafnia (Fabaceae, Crotalarieae). S. African J. Bot. 67: 90-149. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2001); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The niche and vegetative form of S. hilburtianus is similar to S. galpinii J. D. Hooker, but they are distinguished by pedicel length and corolla morphology. In S. hilburtianus the pedicels are consistently shorter, 10-14 mm long, compared to 25-90 mm long in S. galpinii. The corolla of S. galpinii is distinctive for the genus, being short and open with a violet purple limb and a white patch, often colored with yellow, at the base of the lower lip. In contrast the new species has a cylindrical corolla tube usually with two chevrons of deep mauve flanking the medial lobe of the lower lip. The pollen of S. hilburtianus is unique in the genus. The tectal ornamentation is very similar to that of the S. rexii aggregate but the grains are spheroidal and not prolate.
bibliographicCitation: Edwards, TJ. 2003. Two new species of Streptocarpus (Gesneriaceae) from South Africa. Novon 13(2): 185-188. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/3393515] [All rights reserved]

description: Dryopteris lewalleana is often confused with D. inaequalis and D. pentheri, to which it is undoubtedly closely related. From D. inaequalis it can be distinguished by its firmer lamina texture (herbaceous to firmly herbaceous vs. thinly herbaceous to herbaceous), the thicker, short- decumbent rhizomes, the basal pinna pairs generally not shorter than the pair above and the indusia always being eglandular. From D. pentheri it differs in the lamina axes and more frequently eglandular veins, and if glandular, then more sparsely so. The glands are mostly clavate and not oblong as in D. pentheri. Also the shorter gland length [(46-)95(-166) µm vs. (60-)137(- 260 µm], the guard cells [(30-)41(-62) µm vs (34-)53(-72) µm], and the absence of 2-celled hairs from the lamina axes and veins separating them.
bibliographicCitation: Roux, JP. 2012. A revision of the fern genus Dryopteris (Dryopteridaceae) in sub-Saharan Africa. Phytotaxa 70(1): 1-118. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.70.1 ] [All rights reserved]

description: This is very distinct by its peculiar inflorescence, which resembles that of Stoebe cinerea, Thunb., and by its very small broad anther.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Passerina drakensbergensis is characterized by appressed leaves, up to 6.5 mm long. The bracts are lanceolate, up to 7 mm long, the apex is obtuse to acute without a leaf-like point and membranous wings are absent. It may easily be confused with P. montivaga and P. montana, both occurring in the northern KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg area. P. montivaga has longer leaves (up to 8 mm) and bracts with the midrib extended, forming a straight or filiform, leaf-like point. The wings are ovate with margins hairy in the distal half, or obtrullate, narrowing abruptly into the midrib. P. montana can be separated by its terminal subcapitulate spikes and short leaves (up to 4 mm long), which are linear to lanceolate, with a dilated base and with a prominent median vein in the upper third of the leaf, incurved at the acute apex. The bracts are ovate to obovate in outline.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL; Van Wyk, AE. 2003. Taxonomy of the genus Passerina (Thymelaeaceae). Bothalia 33(1): 59-98. [CC BY]

description: The larger-flowered form is very distinct in this section; there is. However, a certain resemblance in the flower to E. vallis-gratiae and E. alfredii, but the sepals and bracts in each of these are much wider and longer, besides other differences.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Polycarena formosa can be recognized by its narrow, sparsely but sharply toothed leaves, linear to oblong bracts and the large creamy-white flowers vividly marked with orange (whence the specific epithet). The species has generally been confused with P. aurea, to which it is certainly allied; see under P. aurea for distinguishing characters.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The trivial name tarachodes refers to the confusion that has prevailed over the identity of this species, previously determined as either.S. woodii (that is, S. peduncularis) or S. hyssopifolia; see under S. hyssopifolia for details of the original collections made by Drège and bearing the name S. hyssopifolia.Selago tarachodes is probably more closely allied to S. peduncularis than to S. hyssopifolia (which is easily distinguished inter alia by its smaller flowers). The flowers of S. tarachodes and S. peduncularis are similar, and the pedicels in S. tarachodes are sometimes as long as those in S. peduncularis, but the two species have strikingly different inflorescences; the individual racemes of S. tarachodes are composed of up to c. 10 flowers and are arranged in a compact corymbose panicle; the individual racemes of S. peduncularis are many-flowered, and the primary terminal raceme may eventually be overtopped by lateral branchlets each bearing a terminal raceme; in well-grown specimens the whole forms a loose panicle. In S. tarachodes the hairs on the leaves are more or less confined to the margins and the midlines either on both surfaces or the lower surface only; in S. peduncularis, hairs are scattered all over the upper surface.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: In subsp. tentaculata, although the flowers may be as little as 12 mm across, they are usually quite a bit larger and may even reach 25 mm in diameter. The corolla lobes are tightly folded except right at the base and this makes them long, slender and rather spidery or tentacle-like, which gave rise to the name of this subspecies. The corolla is cream to white both inside and outside when it finally opens, despite being bright green outside often till quite late in its development. The corolla tube is usually pentagonal and is cup-shaped on the outside but inside the mouth is distinctly constricted by thickened tissue. Flowers of this subspecies have been observed to emit a weak but unmistakeably sweet, honey-like scent. The corona is indistinguishable from that of subsp. hottentotorum and, as in that subspecies, is raised on a stipe above the base of the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to E. Baurii, but a stronger, more woody plant, with larger and differently shaped corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Three usually remote bracts, small inconspicuous sepals, and small urceolate corollas, with a cyathiform or peltate stigma.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Its relationship seems to lie with Z. divaricata, from which it is at once distinguished by the conspicuous patent glandular hairs on stems, leaves and bracts, by the almost entire bracts, and flowers with a much shorter corolla tube and limb lacking any colour patterning.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is so near to some forms of E. parviflora, that we admit it with some doubt. Yet even as a variety of that species it would be well marked by its usually larger and more membranous sepals, its much less hairy leaves, sepals, and (usually quite glabrous) corolla, its pseudo-racemose inflorescence, and its more virgate graceful habit.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: The white-woolly calyx and bracts white-woolly on the lower half, green and very shortly pubescent on the upper, are unmatched in the genus. The orange-yellow, entire corolla lobes each marked with an orange bar point to its being in the general affinity of Z. collina, but the relationship is not close.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Zaluzianskya marlothii has the aspect of Z. bella but can be distinguished not only by its entire corolla lobes, but also by the dense fine pubescence underlying the long coarse hairs particularly on the backs of the bracts and the petiolar part of the leaves, this composed of both glandular and eglandular hairs (both leaves and bracts in Z. bella lack any glands); the anthers of Z. marlothii may be longer than those of Z. bella but this needs confirmation on more material (anticous anthers 0.8 mm versus 0.4-0.7 mm, posticous anthers 1.5-1.6 mm versus 1-1.4 mm). Its true relationship possibly lies with Z. minima, from which it is easily distinguished by its longer corolla tube and larger limb with broadly spathulate lobes, and well-bearded mouth.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Somewhat resembling E. pusilla but with longer and narrower corollas.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Zaluzianskya sanorum is readily distinguished from Z. affinis (Z. villosa var. glabra) by its glabrous to sparsely pubescent stems, the hairs up to 0.2 mm long and ± retrorse (not villous with patent hairs up to 0.4-2 mm long), hairs on margins of bracts up to 0.4-1 mm long (not 1.5-3 mm) and corolla tube distinctly pubescent with a mixture of glandular and eglandular hairs, one or the other often predominating, glandular hairs less than 0.1 mm long, acute hairs up to 0.2-0.25 mm (not minutely puberulous to nearly glabrous). The corolla limb of Z. sanorum seems always to be coloured rich shades of red-violet, contrasting with the bright yellow or orange 'eye'; that of Z. affinis is frequently white, sometimes mauve, also with a contrasting 'eye'. The area of Z. affinis lies west and south of that of Z. sanorum, mostly at lower altitudes. Their areas appear to meet west of Steinkopf.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The indumentum around the mouth, a band of clavate hairs giving way to tiny glands on the shaft of the lobes, is similar to that in Z. pumila and.Z. inflata. The plant has the facies of Z. pumila, but can at once be distinguished by the lack of a thick-textured orange 'star' around the mouth. It differs from Z. inflata not only in aspect but also in its much smaller calyx and corolla, as well as, possibly more significantly, in its longer anthers (anticous ones 1.25 mm long (versus 0.4-0.8 mm), posticous ones 2.5 mm (versus 1.5-1.8 mm)).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It may be distinguished from Z. venusta, which it most resembles in facies, by the shorter indumentum on the stems (acute hairs up to 0.8 mm long versus 1-1.4 mm, the glandular hairs also being shorter than those of Z. venusta), corolla lobes white (not mauve to purplish pink) above, with the rays of the yellow to orange star-shaped patch around the mouth very short and scarcely reaching the base of the lobes, whereas in Z. venusta the rays reach well up the shaft of the lobes. The two species appear to be sympatric only in the Ladismith area, whence Z. venusta spreads north north east, Z. synaptica west and east. In Z. venusta, the corolla lobes are mauve to bright purplish-pink above and possibly always shades of orange below; in Z. synaptica they appear to be mostly white above, occasionally orange, and shades of orange below.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Zaluzianskya vallispiscis is allied to Z. crocea from which it is distinguished by its flower spikes, laxer in fruit than those of Z. crocea, the bracts oblong-lanceolate and roughly 3-5 times as long as broad (not spathulate and 2-3 times as long as broad; examine the lowermost bracts); it is also more glandular than Z. crocea with hairs up to 0.4-0.5 mm long on the corolla tube (up to 0.15 mm in Z. crocea).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It has been much confused with Z. violacea, whose area lies to the west and north west of that of Z. venusta (mainly around Calvinia) and which is easily distinguished by its stems with retrorse appressed hairs, and corolla tube finely pubescent with long (up to 0.3-0.4 mm) acute hairs. It is closely allied to Z. bella.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: E. stenoma Tausch appears to be this species or near to it, but the type is too small for satisfactory examination.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, H; Guthrie, F. 1909. Ericaceae: I. Erica. In: WT Thiselton-Dyer (ed.), Vacciniaceae to Gentianeae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 4: 2-315. Lovell Reeve & Co., London. [All rights reserved]

description: Similar to P sessiliflorum, but differs in the longer length of the pedicels [0.5-2.0(-4.0) mm long] and hypanthia [3-9(-11) mm long], discolorous, larger leaves (11-57 x 13-60 mm), and tomentose indumentum. In P sessiliflorum the flowers have sessile or subsessile flowers (pedicels 0-0.5 mm long) and very short hypanthia (0-1.5 mm long) that are sometimes difficult to distinguish, smaller leaves (10-21 x 11-23 mm) that are not clearly discolorous, and a pubescent-villous indumentum.
bibliographicCitation: Le Roux, MM. 2019. A taxonomic revision of the southern African species of Pelargonium section Peristera (Geraniaceae). Phytotaxa 418(2): 119-157. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.418.2.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Although O. obovata was first described as a variety of insignis it seems to be a distinct species so far as the forms of that species occurring in eastern Africa are concerned. However plants from the coastal provinces of western Africa, such as Heudelot 67 and Sieber 33 from Senegal, which are treated as Heeria insignis in F.W.T.A. (1958) and which, although not actually cited, appear to be included in her O. insignis subsp. latifolia (Engl.) R. Fernandes var. intermedia by R. Fernandes in Garcia de Orta 14: 28 (1966), are hardly distinguishable from exceptional forms of obovata such as Kirk s.n. from Bagamoyo T6 and Butler 19 and Rawlins 654 from K7 in which the leaves are unusually narrow, often widest below the middle and pointed. It must be left to future research to decide how this anomalous situation should best be resolved.
bibliographicCitation: Kokwaro, JO. 1986. Anacardiaceae. In: RM Polhill (ed.), Fl. Trop. E. Africa: 1-60. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [CC BY]

description: Cultivated for dune reclamation, firewood, invades dunes, watercourses, roadsides, fynbos; origin Australia, declared invader (Category 2).
bibliographicCitation: Boatwright, JS; et al. 2019. Fabaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 926-1066. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It closely resembles O. lusoafricanum but is clearly differentiated from it by the spores with their conical lumina, and the short, ellipsoid rhizome. The apex of the trophophore is generally sharply apiculate compared to the acute apex of O. lusoafricanum. O. gracillimum is separated from O. caroticaule by its trilete and smaller spores, 27-38 µm in equatorial diameter, and its much narrower and slightly falcate trophophore.
bibliographicCitation: Burrows, JE. 1993. Nomenclatural changes and additions to the genus Ophioglossum in  Africa (Ophioglossaceae: Pteridophyta). Bothalia 23(2): 185-190. [CC BY]

description: It can be confused with P. gilioides sens, strict., from which it may be distinguished by its glabrous (not pubescent) corolla tube, which is 8-12(-25) mm long (versus 7.5-10 mm) with limb 7-13.5 mm across (versus 5-8 mm), and both tube and limb often flushed purple outside (not so in P. gilioides). There is some difference too in the arrangement of the flowers, the raceme being very lax in P. gracilis, congested in P. gilioides and elongating only slightly in fruit. P. gracilis and P. gilioides may interact where their areas overlap, but the lax inflorescence and particularly the glabrous corolla tube of P. gracilis are good distinguishing characters.The relationship of P. gracilis possibly lies with P. aemulans, which has lax racemes and corolla tube and limb flushed purple outside, but P. gracilis may be distinguished by its relatively narrower upper leaves (6-30 x 0.25-1.5(-2) mm, linear or narrowly oblanceolate, versus 6-15 x 1-3 mm, spathulate), calyx 4-6 mm long (versus 2.5-4 mm), corolla tube glabrous (not pubescent), limb 7-13.5 mm across (versus 3-9 mm), stamens always 4 (not often reduced to 2 or 3).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Ixia ramulosa has the narrowly funnel-shaped perianth tube and moderately to well-exserted anthers of its allies but is distinguished by the perianth tube 7-9(-10) mm long and several, short, wiry, lateral branchlets each bearing 1 or 2 or occasionally 3 flowers. The species normally has just three leaves, the two lowermost with well-developed blades, and the upper one largely to entirely sheathing the stem. Ixia ramulosa is best known from central Namaqualand in the vicinity of Kamieskroon and nearby Grootvlei and Skilpad farms where plants have brilliant, dark purple (also described as magenta) flowers with a white throat. Plants from higher elevations in the Kamiesberg east of Kamieskroon have pink or blue-mauve flowers with a yellow throat and also differ in perianth tube length, 7-8 mm long vs. 8-9(-10) mm for purple-flowered plants from lower elevations. Their later flowering, in October to early November, may be explained by the higher elevation. Among these Kamiesberg populations some consist of particularly tall, slender plants up to 650 mm high with long narrow leaves 5-6 mm wide, very different from the short-leaved populations and possibly explained by their marshy habitat. Alternatively these plants may represent a separate taxon. Provisionally, plants from the Bokkeveld Mtns to the south are included in Ixia ramulosa. Like typical I. ramulosa, these plants have stems with several short, filiform, few-flowered lateral branches and bracts sometimes flushed rust-brown distally, but a perianth tube 8-9 mm long and filaments ± 8 mm long (longer than in typical I. ramulosa), exserted ± 5 mm from the tube. These southern populations have branchlets with one to three flowers and white or pale blue-mauve flowers with a yellow cup and may be exceptionally robust, up to 750 mm high.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Near S. flavescens Gilg., the narrower, not imbricated leaves and the very small flowers with bracteoles but little shorter than the calyx are points of easy recognition.
bibliographicCitation: Moore, SLM. 1919. Alabastra diversa - Part XXX (cont.). J. Bot. 57: 112-119. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/35891#page/130/mode/1up]

description: A. nigrescens sometimes flowers when quite leafless and may then be difficult to distinguish from A. galpinii which sometimes does the same. A. galpinii may be distinguished by its shorter (0.75-1.25 mm long) usually ± puberulous calyx and by the corolla-lobes which are usually puberulous outside. In A. nigrescens the calyx is 1.5-2.2 mm long and glabrous, as are the corolla-lobes.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Anginon swellendamense is easily recognized by the thick, robust, primary stem which is unbranched at the base but branched higher up, and the thick, divided or junciform leaves, densely arranged from the base of the plant upwards. The mature parts (stems, leaves and inflorescences) are invariably glaucous.
bibliographicCitation: Allison, I; Van Wyk, B-E. 1997. A revision of the genus Angnion (Apiaceae). Nord. J. Bot. 17: 561-577. [All rights reserved]

description: Stalks of the sporocarps usually branched; conceptacles lacking basal teeth.
bibliographicCitation: Jones, DL. 1998. Marsileaceae. In: PM McCarthy (ed.), Ferns, Gymnosperms and allied groups, Fl. Australia 48: 166-173. ABRS/CSIRO Publishing, Melbourne. [All rights reserved]

description: R. schlechteriana is distinguished from the other species of Rafnia by the leaves on the flowering branches which are invariably opposite, the large basal leaves that are distinctly cartilaginous and much larger than the upper leaves and sometimes acuminate, the inflorescences that are secondarily aggregated towards the branch ends into large, pyramidal flowering branches, the symmetrically truncate keel petal (as in R. capensis subsp. pedicelata) and the broad, obliquely lanceolate, sessile pod which is broadly winged on the upper suture. R. schlechteriana and R. ovata are easily confused on herbarium sheets, but the flowers differ markedly.
bibliographicCitation: Campbell, GJ; Van Wyk, B-E. 2001. A taxonomic revision of Rafnia (Fabaceae, Crotalarieae). S. African J. Bot. 67: 90-149. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2001); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: A suffrutex with flexuous branches. The young foliage is silvery, the leaflets are lanceolate.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, EG. 1923. Revision of South African species of Rhynchosia. Bothalia 1(1-3): 113-138. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognized by the terete, scandent, cinnamon-coloured, hirsute or tomentose stem, and very lax 2-5-flowered racemes.
bibliographicCitation: Baker, EG. 1923. Revision of South African species of Rhynchosia. Bothalia 1(1-3): 113-138. [CC BY]

description: Rhynchosia totta var. totta differs from var. rigidula in the herbaceous habit, long rachises and leathery, glabrescent leaves (woody with short rachises and often slightly silver-felted leaves that are not leathery are found in R. totta var. rigidula). This variety also resembles the new species, R. pedunculata, but differs in the trailing, twining or spreading habit and inflorescences that are not distinctly longer than the leaves or leaves orientated horizontally(prostrate habit with inflorescences much longer than the leaves and invariably standing upright in R. pedunculata).The typical variety includes those taxa with a woody base and herbaceous stems, and unifoliolate or trifoliolate leaves with leaflets that are ovate to lanceolate in shape. There are some specimens with long petioles and linear-lanceolate leaflets (formerly R. totta var. graciliflora), but, given the lack of any other morphological features to distinguish these collections from the typical form, the variant is included in R. totta var. totta.
bibliographicCitation: Moteetee, AN; Le Roux, MM. 2016. The Rhynchosia totta complex (Phaseoleae, Fabaceae) in Southern Africa, including the description of a new variety and new species. Bothalia - ABC 46(1,a2041): 1-19. [http://dx.doi.org/10.4102/abc.v46i1.2041] [All rights reserved]

description: Corolla at least 8 mm diameter at the mouth; corolla lobes at least 3 mm long; anthers at least 1.5 mm long; capsule up to 7 mm long; teeth not present on lowest third of leaf margin.
bibliographicCitation: Phillipson, PB. 1986. Taxonomy of Monopsis (Lobeliaceae): M.simplex, M.debilis and a new species. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 93(4): 329-341. [All rights reserved]

description: A. lophantha favours river banks, forest margins and wooded ravines. It is the only species of Albizia in our area with a spicate inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: In this variety leaf shape is very variable, particularly on coppice shoots, and it seems as if the plant goes through a few developmental stages before the leaf of the mature plant is produced.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1970. Capparis, Fl. S. Africa 13: 144-150. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is characterised by its densely branched, compact woody habit (vs open spreading to erect shrubby habit with virgate seasonal shoots), retention of the previous season’s short shoots (vs loss), broader glabrous leaves with visible glands (vs narrower minutely puberulous to glabrescent leaves with scarcely visible glands), small stumpy white flowers with a broad purple and yellow streaked triangular nectar guide and tufted bracts (vs ebracteate lilac flowers), sparsely blackhaired calyces (vs glabrous to densely white sericeous), and khaki seeds with brown blotches (vs chestnut brown).
bibliographicCitation: Stirton, CH; Muasya, AM. 2017. Ten new species and a new record for the genus Otholobium (Psoraleeae, Leguminosae) from South Africa. Kew Bull. 72: 1-27. [https://doi.org/10.1007/s12225-017-9722-5] [All rights reserved]

description: The subsp. foetida is itself very variable. A particularly narrow-leaved form, described as B. rautanenii, is found in the district Swakopmund and Karibib but intermediate forms occur and so it cannot be kept separate. Also in northern South West Africa the long peduncle which is so characteristic of this subspecies becomes much less distinct. As the epithet implies, the flowers have a very intense odour and the plant is thus commonly called 'stinkbos' or 'stinkdoring'. Some collectors note that plants of the form referred to as B. rautanenii have a honey-like scent, but others record the same evil odour as found in the typical plants.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1970. Boscia, Fl. S. Africa 13: 150-159. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: M. brevipetiolata differs from M. rosmarinoides, its nearest ally, in the following respects: it is always a thin-stemmed scrambler whereas M. rosmarinoides can be a tree, shrub or sometimes a scrambler or climber; the leaves are Cerro green (Ridgeway) and arranged in one plane instead of very dark green and pendulous, and the leaflets are shorter and broader; the petioles are much shorter; the receptacle is campanulate rather than cylindric; the petals are reduced and the disc is annular and fimbrillate instead of lobed and unequally laciniate.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1970. Maerua, Fl. S. Africa 13: 159-171. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Wild (I.e.) described var. glabrifolia and distinguished it from var. kraussiana by its glabrous vegetative parts. Examination of a wide range of material shows that this difference does not hold and the distribution is practically the same, therefore var. glabrifolia is not upheld in this treatment. It is interesting to note that X. kotzei, which Wild sinks under X. kraussiana var. kraussiana, has a holotype with sparsely pubescent vegetative parts, while the paratypes, apparently from the same tree, are completely glabrous.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: S. flanaganii is an extremely variable species especially in the shape of the adult, juvenile and coppice shoot leaves. Also, the ovaries vary from completely glabrous to pubescent. A feature of the leaves is the frequent presence of small shot-holes apparently caused by a blue-green alga.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Origin Britain.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Caryophyllaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 757-767. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Characterized by the large, usually circular, digitately 5-7-nerved leaves and 4-merous petals and sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Easily distinguished from T. grandifolia by the trimerous flowers and smaller, 3-(5) digitately nerved, elliptic leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB. 1976. Flacourtiaceae (including Samydaceae), Fl. S. Africa 22: 53-92. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Dovyalis caffra, the Kei-apple, is an attractive, usually evergreen tree which, from December to about February, is covered with masses of yellow apricot-like fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Langenegger, JE. 1976. Flacourtiaceae: Dovyalis, Fl. S. Africa 22: 84-90. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Probable hybrids: Schinz, in Mitt. Geogr. Lubeck 17: 15 (1903), based S. rhomboidea on a specimen in the Naturhistorisches Museum, Vienna, received from Poeppig and stated to have been collected at 'Port Natal'. He related it to S. minutiflora, and distinguished it by the ovary being cuneate at the base and thin-walled in the lower part. Hill in Ann. S. Afr. Mus. 9: 57 (1912), because of the absence of a distinct keel or wing to the calyx-segments, related S. ecarinata to S. albens. The type-gathering, Pearson 5229 from Piketberg, is represented in both Kew and the British Museum of Natural History, and consists of some unbranched specimens with small inflorescences. These two gatherings and Parker 4136 in Kew Herbarium are not identical, but hang together quite well. They are intermediate between S. albens and S. minutiflora, and may be hybrids.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W; Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Gentianaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 171-243. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to S. filiformis, and with a similar distribution, but the floral differences appear to be constant. The sheet of Wilms 971 in the British Museum of Natural History is a mixture of S. bojeri and S. grandis.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W; Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Gentianaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 171-243. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Branchlets of P. verrucosa are vernucose with prominently raised, warty lenticels, hence the specific epithet; spines are spreading; leaves are narrower than 15 mm; pedicels are usually shorter than 4 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Jordaan, M; Van Wyk, AE. 1998. Systematic studies in subfamily Celastroideae (Celastraceae) in southern Africa: The genus Putterlickia. S. African J. Bot. 64(6): 322-329. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1998); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The fruits are hard, leathery, globose, 2-5-seeded capsules, eventually dehiscing in three valves and are reminiscent of some Salacia species. The flowers differ from Salacia in having 5 stamens which arise from small protuberances near the margin of the disc. In Salacia there are usually 3 stamens (rarely 2 or 4) which are borne inside the disc, around the base of the ovary. Flowering specimens resemble some species of Cassine sens, lat., and the alternate leaves suggest an affinity with C. aethiopicnm Thunb. The fruits of Cassine are, however, drupaceous and almost invariably 1-seeded, while the five stamens are borne outside the disc.
bibliographicCitation: Codd, LEW. 1972. New and interesting records of African plants: Celastraceae. Bothalia 10(4): 565-567. [CC BY]

description: The presence of a basal rosette of leaves gives the plant a quite different appearance. Such plants were put into S. macrostigma. There are, however, no floral differences and, as in other species, the width of the calyx-wings varies considerably with age. Closely related to S. zeyheri.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W; Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Gentianaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 171-243. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Much smaller than P. mucronata or P. obovata, with very small leaves which are not narrowed to the base. The older leaves are often yellow-brown. The inflorescences may be formed in large numbers.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1959. The South African Species of Aizoaceae: VIII. Psammotropha. J. S. African Bot. 25: 51-68. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from P. myriantha, with which it has been much confused in collections, by the more slender stems not widened at the top, the leaf-tufts not depressed on top, the thinner semitranslucent leaves distinctly narrowed to the base and with no prominent midrib, the slender inflorescences with less crowded often unilateral flowers, the mucronate bracts, and the short stigmas. An exceedingly variable species in size, habit and general form.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1959. The South African Species of Aizoaceae: VIII. Psammotropha. J. S. African Bot. 25: 51-68. [CC BY]

description: Pale green or somewhat glaucous, often tinged with pink, red or orange on the older parts. Variable in size and in the number and closeness of the branches, ranging from short bunched plants to lax shrublets. There is also much variation in the closeness of the leaves. On this Fenzl created two varieties; (a) mucronata with short closely appressed leaves with short points, and (b) subulifolia with longer more spreading leaves with longer points. While the extremes undoubtedly look distinct, there are all stages of intermediate, and the differences seem largely correlated with habitat and season. Early in the season and in more sheltered localities longer and more spreading leaves are formed, while later or in more exposed places they are short and closely appressed. The type specimen is one with long rather spreading leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1959. The South African Species of Aizoaceae: VIII. Psammotropha. J. S. African Bot. 25: 51-68. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species which in several features seems to mark a transition to Polpoda. Very distinctive in habit but agree with the genus completely in flower structure.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1959. The South African Species of Aizoaceae: VIII. Psammotropha. J. S. African Bot. 25: 51-68. [CC BY]

description: Readily separable on the habit, the short squarrose leaves, the very small stipules, and the small flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: In habit like a species of Psammotropha but not in the inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: Very distinctive in the large persistent stipules enclosing the leaf tuft and often clothing the stem. Rather variable in the length and width of the leaves, from filiform to 2 mm wide. Leaves often slightly widened to the tip.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: S. thodeana is very closely related to S. procumbens. As they have never been studied in the field and, in the dried condition, can readily be recognised by the colour of the apical anther-glands and by the size of the basal glands, I am keeping them as distinct species.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W; Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Gentianaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 171-243. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to P. trigonum but distinguished by the lax suberect habit, the longer ascending leaves, the quite different stipules, the larger flowers and the flat stigmas.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: Variable in size and in leaf-form. In open sites the leaves are broad, short and usually obtuse, in shade they are longer and more acute. Shade forms closely resemble P. thunbergii but are distinguished by the thicker leaves without visible veins, by the smaller and less cut stipules, by the forked inflorescence, and by the larger fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: Like P. trigonum but with longer ascending leaves and quite different stipules.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: On drying, the whole plant or at least the calyx takes on a yellow-green colour.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W; Verdoorn, IC. 1963. Gentianaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 171-243. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Very variable in size and in habit, especially in relation to habitat. Plants growing among bushes may be quite erect, in dry situations the stems are short and the leaves short with prominent stipules. Sometimes leaves are confined to the apical tuft. Shade forms may be quite herbaceous. All intermediates are to be found. A form from rocky sites which has very short leaves with no comal tuft looks superficially distinct. The type specimen is of a shade form with small stipules with only 2-4 lobes. All stages of transition occur between this and the common forms with rather prominent stipules. P. elongatum is the commonest of the forms which have been grouped under 'P. incanum'.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species easily recognized by the habit, linear whorled leaves, and large flowers. In dry situations the stems may be short with only 1-2 internodes.

bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: Similar to P brevirostre, but differs in the pubescent to puberulous or glabrescent indumentum (especially on the sepals), and the pedicels that may be shorter or longer than the hypanthia (pedicels 2-9 mm long and hypanthia 1.5-11.0 mm long). In P brevirostre, the indumentum is invariably and persistently densely pubescent or pubescent-villous, and the pedicels shorter than the hypanthia (pedicels 0-1 mm long and hypanthia 3-7 mm long). Pelargonium grossularioides generally occurs at lower elevations below 700(-1600) m, whereas P brevirostre tends to occur above 1000 m.
bibliographicCitation: Le Roux, MM. 2019. A taxonomic revision of the southern African species of Pelargonium section Peristera (Geraniaceae). Phytotaxa 418(2): 119-157. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.418.2.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Erect, branched, strongly aromatic shrub. Lamina cordiform in outline, shallowly 3-(5)-lobed, pilose to villous. Capitulum-like pseudo-umbels with 3-12 flowers each. Flowers pale pink to light pinkish-purple, pedicel and hypanthium relatively short, pedicel usually slightly shorter than hypanthium. P. vitifolium is closely related to P. capitatum (L.) L'Herit. The following characters may be used to distinguish between these two species: P. vitifolium - 1. Erect shrub with unpleasant scent. 2. Leaves pilose to villous and not crisped. 3. Pseudo-umbels with 3-12 flowers each. P. capitatum - 1. Decumbent rose-scented subshrub. 2. Leaves villous to densely villous and crisped. 3. Pseudo-umbelswith 8-20 flowers each.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Geranium drakensbergense forms thick and extensive clumps in moist and partially shaded places at the foot of S-facing Cave Sandstone and basalt cliffs. Although the leaves of H & B 9007 are less hairy below and therefore greener than those of the type, the plants are otherwise identical. The two sites are about 25 km apart.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: The name Geranium incanum has been wrongly used to cover both G. multisectum and G. magniflorum, which differ markedly in their densely tufted radical leaves. Both these species frequently have spreading, often gland-tipped, hairs on sepals, pedicels and peduncles, as well as appressed hairs; spreading hairs are always wanting in G. incanum. Burtt Davy described G. robustum as a variety of G. incanum, but that is a totally different plant. Laundon confused G. multisectum with G. incanum, and he also reduced G. nyassense Knuth to a subspecies of G. incanum; although G. nyassense is allied to G. incanum, it is better regarded as a distinct species. The status of G. ukingense R. Knuth, which was reduced by Laundon to synonymy under his subsp. nyassense, needs re-investigation: Knuth described the leaves of G. ukingense as mostly radical; it would appear then that G. ukingense is more closely allied to G. multisectum than to G. nyassense, which is a many-stemmed perennial herb without radical leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. A revision of Geranium in Africa south of the Limpopo. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 171-225. [CC BY-SA]

description: This species resembles M. angustifolia closely with respect to the flowers and fruits, but in M. brevirostrata these are dwarfed. The leaves, however, are quite distinct. The growth system in M. brevirostrata is prostrate and in M. angustifolia erect or decumbent.
bibliographicCitation: Venter, HJT. 1979. A monograph of Monsonia L. (Geraniaceae). Meded. Landbouwhoogeschool Wageningen 79(9): 1-126. [All rights reserved]

description: Like T. echinata but distinguished by the broader leaves, sessile flowers, less inferior ovary, and the fruit without spine-like out-growths. The fruit may have large papillae and such forms are apt to be confused with T. echinata. var. monosperma Fenzl.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African Species of Aizoaceae: II. Tetragonia. J. S. African Bot. 21: 109-154. [CC BY]

description: Often confused with T. nigrescens but distinguished by the slender habit, narrower leaves, flowers confined to the apical region, long pedicels and long styles. This species does not blacken on drying. Specimens (Bachmann 1965 (BM, S)) collected at Hopefield may represent a distinct species differing in being much larger and with an elongated rhizome, having smaller obtuse papulose leaves, flowers not in umbels, and styles not longer than the stamens. The specimens are without fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African Species of Aizoaceae: II. Tetragonia. J. S. African Bot. 21: 109-154. [CC BY]

description: The slender leaves, deeply concave ovary with its lobes extremely short, closely pressed together, and confined to the very centre of the ovary distinguish this species.
bibliographicCitation: Multiple authors. 1928. Novitates Africanae (cont.). J. Bot. 66: 195-200. [All rights reserved]

description: The year after Harvey's figure appeared, the species was illustrated in colour in the Botanical Magazine from plants collected by Cooper and sent to Mr. W. Wilson Saunders, who grew them in England. A good figure of the species is also given in Engler's Pflanzenreich. The species belongs to a section of the genus characterised by having a large tuber.

description: Differs from M. amoenum by the prostrate flowering branches, carinate-triquetrous, thicker leaves, and short peduncles; from M. spectabile by the green, not glaucous, leaves, termite, short peduncled, much smaller flowers.

description: Pelargonium columbinum is most closely related to P grossularioides, but differs in the filiform, or lax annual habit with spreading pilose hairs and hypanthia that are invariably shorter than the pedicels, whereas P. grossularioides has a more robust annual or rarely short-lived perennial habit with pubescent hairs or glabrous, and hypanthia that are shorter or longer than the pedicels.
bibliographicCitation: Le Roux, MM. 2019. A taxonomic revision of the southern African species of Pelargonium section Peristera (Geraniaceae). Phytotaxa 418(2): 119-157. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.418.2.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Erect, branched and aromatic shrub. Lamina cordiform, abaxial side usually velvety and much more hairy and lighter in colour than adaxial side. Flowering branches profusely branched. Pseudo-umbels with 3-12 flowers each. Flowers white to light pink to bright purple, anterior petals much narrower than posterior ones, pedicel relatively thin and usually longer than hypanthium. The cordiform leaves of P. cordifolium are so typical that it can hardly be confused with other species of the section Pelargonium. It is apparently related to P. hispidum (L.f.) Willd. and P. papilionaceum (L.)L'Herit., which have a similar floral structure with the posterior petals much wider than the anterior ones. The degree of hairiness of the leaves varies considerably and this led to the recognition of three varieties and even different species by previous workers. The populations in the western part of the distribution area have less hairy leaves than those in the east. There is, however, a gradual transition from almost glabrous leaves to villous leaves over the distribution area as a whole, and it is therefore not advisable to recognize infraspecific taxa.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: The leaves of this species resemble those of Crithmum maritimum, hence the specific epithet crithmifolium. Pelargonium crithmifolium belongs to the section Otidia, which is characterized by relatively thick, short, gnarled, succulent stems, fleshy leaves which are imparipinnate or pinnatisect and flowers with five fertile stamens. The flowers of this section are not as distinctly zygomorphic as in some other sections, since the two posterior petals are only slightly larger than the three anterior ones. A noteworthy feature of P. crithmifolium is the branched, paniculate inflorescence, the remains of which stay on the plant for a number of years and eventually become thorny. This thorny structure probably protects the plant against browsing animals.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA; Ward-Hilhorst, JE. 1978. Pelargonium crithmifolium Sm. Fl. Pl. Africa 45(1&2)t.1773 [CC BY]

description: This brilliant species is often taken for M. glomeratum.
bibliographicCitation: Haworth, AH. 1812. Synopsis plantarum succulentarum, cum descriptionibus, synonymis, locis, observationibus anglicanis, culturaque. Taylor, London. [All rights reserved]

description: P. desertorum is an erect aromatic shrublet with slender succulent stems, growing up to 300 mm tall. Its leaves are membranous, simple, orbicular in outline, shallowly lobed, and the margins are obtusely dentate. The inflorescence is an apparently terminal pseudo-umbel of (2)3-4(6) flowers. The hypanthium is variable in length, from inconspicuously short to as long as the pedicel; the petals are white, narrowly spathulate, and recurved to expose the sexual parts. It closely resembles P. otaviense Knuth in its vegetative morphology and habit. It is distinguished, however, by petals which recurve to expose the sexual parts instead of being straight and nearly parallel to each other to hide the sexual parts, by the base of the lamina being decurrent, the joint between pedicel and hypanthium which is not geniculate, and the stems which are more succulent rather than woody. On morphological similarities, P. desertorum can be grouped with P. abrotanifolium (L.f.) Jacq., P. exstipulatum (Cav.) L' Herit., P. grandicalcaratum Knuth, P. karooicum Compton & Barnes, P. otaviense Knuth, P. plurisectum Salter, and P. xerophyton Schltr. ex Knuth. These species are, however, readily distinguishable by their leaf morphology and various floral characteristics.
bibliographicCitation: Vorster, PJ. 1986. Pelargonium desertorum (Geraniaceae): a new species from the north-western Cape Province. S. African J. Bot. 52(2): 184-186. description: Pelargonium ellaphieae is a tuberous species with a more or less regularly shaped tuber with dark brown tunics or periderms and with radical leaves, both typical characters of the section Hoarea (Sweet) DC. A noteworthy feature of this species is the lanceolate leaves with prominent adpressed bristles on the margins of the dried laminae. The flowers, strongly scented, have only two petals and five fertile stamens. The petals and the protruding androecium are conspicuously dark wine-red.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM; Ward-Hilhorst, JE. 1989. Pelargonium ellaphieae E.M.Marais. Fl. Pl. Africa 50t.1987 [CC BY]

description: Erect, branched, faintly lemon-scented shrub. Leaves relatively large, pubescent to hirsute, green to dull green, lamina palmatilobate to palmatisect. Flowering branches profusely branched, pseudo-umbels with 6-12 flowers each. Flowers pale to deep pink, two posterior petals much wider than the anterior three, pedicel longer than hypanthium. Inflorescence and floral characters indicate a close relationship between P. hispidum, P. cordifolium (Cav.) Curtis, P. papilionaceum (L.) L'Herit. and P. tomentosum Jacq. P. hispidum may be confused with P. papilionaceum, but in the latter species the leaves are only shallowly lobed and the flowers are larger with a conspicuous white spot on the two posterior petals.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: It still remains to prove conclusively that M. luteum, Haw. is distinct from Crocanthus thunbergii, L. Bolus. The former is described as having 'an upright rigid stem,' and 'tumid nodes of the stem, from which on the side next the ground sprout swollen rootlets.' The latter statement at least implies some decumbent branches. But it seems advisable to complete observations on some growing plants, sent by Dr. Muir from the Riversdale Div. and on others received from the Division of Botany, before a satisfactory conclusion is reached. In order, therefore, to avoid a possible additional synonym, I refrain from placing M. luteum, Haw. at the moment in this genus.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, L; Page, MM. 1927. Crocanthus thunbergii L.Bolus. Fl. Pl. South Africa 7t.255 [CC BY]

description: The very slender, almost smooth stems and only slightly papillate, broad, bright green leaves distinguish M. clandestinum from other members of M. subg. Volkeranthus as well as M. subg. Mesembryanthemum sect. Mesembryanthemum.

description: P. lobatum is distinguished by its large, simple to 5-lobate, cordiform, prostrate, membranous leaves which are almost invariably covered with a soft and dense velvety indumentum. It may bear a superficial resemblance to the pubescent form of P. pulverulentum but the base of the lamina is never decurrent along the petiole as in P. pillansii and P. pulverulentum, nor is the lamina ever leathery and glaucous as in these two species.

description: Decumbent to procumbent subshrub. Leaves pinnatilobate to bipinnatisect with narrow segments, glabrescent to pubescent to villous to hirsute. Pseudo-umbels with 2-6 flowers each (usually 3 or 4). Petals 4 or 5, white to yellowish to pink to mauve or pinkish-yellow, posterior two relatively large (longer than 25 mm). Fertile stamens 7.

description: Mesembryanthemum paulum always has a completely prostrate habit and neither roots at the nodes nor climbs into other bushes. The leaves and stems are conspicuously papillate, which distinguishes this species from M. longistylum and M. clandestinum, where the leaves are ± smooth. The dark brown seeds of M. paulum are never found in similar-looking species in M. subg. Mesembryanthemum sect. Mesembryanthemum, which have pale brown seeds.

description: Procumbent, perennial subshrub, lamina green but sometimes flushed with red, trifoliolate or trifid to pinnatifid with the pinnae/segments irregularly incised. Pseudo-umbels with 2-5 flowers each. Flowers with 4 white to pinkish or dark pinkish-purple petals, hypanthium 8-25 mm long. Fertile stamens 7, protruding below anterior petals.
