description: P. multiradiatum resembles P. triste (Linnaeus) L'Heritier and P. anethifolium (Ecklon & Zeyher) Steudel by the linear divisions of the lamina. It differs from P. triste by its lamina being almost as wide as long and with inconspicuous indumentum, compared to the lamina being at least twice as long as wide and conspicuously hoary. It differs from P. anethifolium by having much larger leaves, up to 450 x 450 mm instead of up to 130 x 140 mm; by the leaf segments being wider (up to 3 mm compared to 0.5-1.0 mm); by at least the basal segments branching off the rachis at a right angle instead of an acute angle; and by having 5 instead of 6 fertile stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Maggs, GL; Vorster, PJ; Van der Walt, JJA; Gibby, M. 1999. Taxonomy of the genus Pelargonium (Geraniaceae): the section Polyactium   3. The subsection Polyactium. S. African J. Bot. 65(3): 115-143. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1999); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Erect, much-branched shrub with an unpleasant odour. Lamina cordiform in outline, shallowly 3-8-lobed, conspicuously veined, sparsely villous. Flowering branches profusely branched. Pseudo-umbels with 4-20 flowers each. Flowers pale pink to carmine, anterior three petals much shorter and narrower than posterior two, pedicel relatively thin and longer than hypanthium. P. papilionaceum could be confused with P. tomentosum (L.) L'Herit. and P. hispidum (L.f.) Willd. The morphological differences between P. papilionaceum and these two species, are discussed under P. tomentosum and P. hispidum respectively. The leaves of P. papilionaceum resemble those of P. vitifolium (L.) L'Herit. to a certain extent. These characteristics. P. vitifolium has a capitulum-like inflorescence and the flowers are less zygomorphic than those of P. papilionaceum.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: P. pillansii resembles P. pulverulentum Sweet by its glaucous leaves with the lamina decurrent along the petiole; but differs in that the lamina may be pinnatifid or even pinnate and never laciniate nor ciliate, and by the markings on the petals being inconspicuous or absent compared to the very prominent purple-black mountains, It occurs in fynbos vegetation, on sandstone or shale, and is often found within rock fissures. The rainfall is in the region of 200 to 400 mm per annum, but accurate figures are not available because the plants prefer mountainous areas from where rainfall data are absent. The species is rare on the Cape Peninsula, having last been collected there in 1946, and the reason for this may be that the rainfall is too high for it markings in P. pulverulentum. In P. pillansii the chromosome number is mostly 2n=22, while in P. pulverulentum it is 2n=44. P. pillansii is a Western Cape species; and its replacement by the morphologically not dissimilar P. pulverulentum in the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal may be indicative of a closer than specific relationship between the two taxa.
bibliographicCitation: Maggs, GL; Vorster, PJ; Van der Walt, JJA; Gibby, M. 1999. Taxonomy of the genus Pelargonium (Geraniaceae): the section Polyactium   3. The subsection Polyactium. S. African J. Bot. 65(3): 115-143. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1999); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: P. pinnatum has flowers with spathulate petals with wine-red feather-like markings on the posterior two. The length/width ratio of the posterior petals is usually smaller than five. The stigma branches are always longer than the style and the anterior stamens are shorter than the calyx and hidden in the floral sheath. The scape is branched, bearing two to five pseudo-umbellets with four to eight flowers each. P. pinnatum shows variation in the length of the hypanthia and the width of the petals; as a result, some plants have very large flowers. Specimens with very long hypanthia (33-45 mm) were collected in the southern Cape, especially in the Riversdale area, but also in the Cape Peninsula. Plants with very long hypanthia do not necessarily have large petals.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM. 1993. A taxonomic revision of the Pelargonium pinnatum species complex (Geraniaceae). S. African J. Bot. 59: 123-134. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1993); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Erect to decumbent, much-branched, non-aromatic, viscid shrub. Lamina pinnatipartite to pinnatisect, glabrescent to sparsely strigose, larger veins adaxially often dark purple. Peduncles distinctly articulated, pseudo-umbels with 1-2 flowers each. Flowers pale pink to pink, pedicel shorter than hypanthium. P. denticulatum Jacq., P. glutinosum (Jacq.) L'Herit., P. pseudoglutinosum and P. quercifolium (L.f.) L'Herit. are the only species of the section with viscid leaves. The leaves of P. pseudoglutinosum could be confused with those of P. glutinosum. P. glutinosum, however, has strongly aromatic leaves and lacks the purple veins which are often found in P. pseudoglutinosum. The 1-2-flowered pseudo-umbels are the most reliable feature to distinguish P. pseudoglutinosum from P. glutinosum which has more than two flowers per pseudo-umbel.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Pelargonium quercifolium is classified in the section Pelargonium (DC.) Harv., which contains such well-known species as P. cucullatum (L.) L' Herit., P. graveolens If Herit. and P. capitatum (L.) L' Herit. This section contains many species with aromatic leaves, and some are grown on a commercial scale for the volatile oils obtained from them and used in the perfume industry. Van der Walt (1985) considered P. querci-folium to be closely related to P. panduriforme Eckl. & Zeyh. However, P. quercifolium is distinguished by its strigose leaves, 2-6-flowered pseudo-umbels, and its posterior petals being up to 2,5 cm long; in contrast to the villous to lanose leaves, up to 20-flowered pseudo-umbels, and posterior petals up to 3.5 cm long of P. panduriforme. The leafblades also differ: in P. quercifolium they are 3-palmatisect to pinnatisect with the segments irregularly pinnatifid to pinnatisect, whereas in P. panduriforme they are pinnatilobate to pinnatipartite with the segments occasionally shallowly lobed.
bibliographicCitation: Vorster, PJ; Kimpton, J. 1986. Pelargonium quercifolium (L.f.) L'Hér. Fl. Pl. Africa 49t.1923 [CC BY]

description: Pelargonium radicatum is a tuberous species with more or less regularly turnip-shaped or elongated tubers with dark brown tunics or periderms and radical leaves, both typical characters of section Hoarea to which it belongs. The epithet radicatum, chosen by Ventenat, refers to the large root or tuber, which is, however, not a distinctive character for this species, but for the section as a whole. The species is characterised by the large number of pale yellow flowers with long hypanthia and by its simple, lanceolate, concave leaves, with short soft patent hairs on both sides of the laminae and bristles along the margins. Sometimes the lower side is also covered with bristles. During senescence the leaves lose the soft hairs and at flowering time the shrivelled leaves are glabrous with white appressed bristles along the margins or, depending on the density of the bristles abaxially, the shrivelled leaves are sometimes glabrous adaxially and squamose abaxially.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM; Condy, GS. 2001. Pelargonium radicatum. Fl. Pl. Africa 57: 82-85, t.2175 [CC BY]

description: Erect or decumbent subshrub. Internodes elongated or much reduced. Laminae reniform or ovate-cordate, sometimes with 3-5 shallowly incised lobes. Pseudo-umbels each with 4-12 pink to magenta flowers. Hypanthium red. Sepals red with pink margins, Stamens of 3 different lengths. The floral morphology of all the specimens studied shows very little variation. Based on vegetative morphology, however, four groups can be distinguished: Group 1: Plants characterized by a decumbent habit, elongated internodes, opposite leaves, reniform laminae and relatively short petioles. Group 2: Plants characterized by a rosulate habit, short internodes, ovate-cordate laminae and very long petioles. Group 3: Plants characterized by a rosulate habit, short internodes, small reniform laminae and long, thin, persistent petioles. Group 4: Dwarf form of Group 2, but with laminae more reniform and petioles proportionally shorter. Individuals from Group 1 are geographically isolated from the rest, they can be-readily identified from herbarium specimens and they display no intermediate forms with other groups. Due to this, Group 1 can be regarded as a separate subspecies. The iconotype of P. reniforme depicts a plant that matches the description of this group, therefore the correct subspecific name would be subsp. reniforme. The sympatfic distribution and great number of intermediate forms between the other three groups complicate further subspecific divisions. These three forms are therefore grouped together in a heterogeneous subspecies velutinum (Eckl. & Zeyh.) Dreyer.
bibliographicCitation: Dreyer, LL; Marais, EM; Van der Walt, JJA. 1995. A subspecific division of Pelargonium reniforme Curt. (Geraniaceae). S. African J. Bot. 61(6): 325-330. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1995); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Erect, soboliferous, lemon-scented or non-aromatic shrub. Lamina 3-palmatilobate to 3-palmatisect with the segments irregularly incised, scabrous. Pseudo-umbels with 2-6 flowers each. Flowers white to purple to pinkish-purple, anterior three petals much narrower than two posterior ones, pedicel as long as hypanthium. P. scabrum is closely related to P. ribifolium Jacq. and the differences between them are discussed under the latter species. The leaves of P. scabrum resemble those of P. citronellum J.J.A. v.d. Walt, but the flowers of these two species differ markedly. P. scabrum is a very variable species, especially as far as the structure of the leaves is concerned. The leaf segments of plants in the western Cape are much longer and narrower than those in the south-western and southern Cape. The form with extremely narrow leaf segments was described as P. balsameum by Jacquin, and Harvey considered it as a variety or P. scabrum. Plants in the western Cape have purplish flowers, those in the south-western Cape pinkish-purple flowers and those in the southern Cape white flowers. The extreme forms of P. scabrum differ to such an extent that one is tempted to distinguish intraspecific taxa. However, a detailed study of a large number of specimens from the entire distribution area revealed a continuous variation pattern of leaf and floral characters. This makes a delimitation of intraspecific taxa impossible.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Erect, branched, sometimes strongly sweet-scented shrub. Stems villous becoming reddish-brown with age. Lamina cordiform in outline, 3-(5)-lobed, sparsely hirtellous to villous, margins often reddish. Pseudo-umbels with 3-9 flowers. Flowers white, light pink or pink, pedicel usually slightly shorter than hypanthium. P. sublignosum exhibits a high degree of variation as far as fragrance and indumentum are concerned, especially of the stems and leaves, and the structure, colour and size of the flowers. This leaves the impression that it is possibly a relatively young species in the final stages of speciation. The leaves of P. sublignosum resemble those of P. scabrum (L.) L'Herit., and it is possible that it evolved from this species. Natural hybrids between P. sublignosum and P. scabrum have been observed on the farm Grootfontein near Porterville. Hybrids between P. sublignosum and P. grandiflorum (Andr.) Willd. have also been reported from this area. The habit, leaves and indumentum of P. sublignosum show some resemblance to those of P. scabroide Knuth and P. englerianum Knuth, which may be indicative of a relationship between these species.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: Die Art ist R. evuluta (N. E. Br.) L. Bolus nahe verwandt, unterscheidet sich aber von dieser sofort durch die an den Rändern nicht bewimperten Blätter.
bibliographicCitation: Schwantes, MHG. 1930. Neue Mesembriaceen VI. Monatsschr. Deutsch. Kakteen-Ges. 2(3-4): 64-69. [All rights reserved]

description: Decumbent, much-branched, peppermint-scented subshrub. Lamina 3-(5)-palmatilobate to 3-(5)-palmatipartite, adaxially villous, abaxially tomentose. Flowering branches profusely branched. Pseudo-umbels with 4-15 flowers each. Flowers white, posterior petals auriculate, anterior petals longer and much narrower than posterior ones, pedicel much longer than hypanthium. The species may be confused with P. papilionaceum (L.) L'Herit. when they are not in flower. The main differences between these two related species are as follow: P. tomentosum - 1. Leaves villous and tomentose. 2. Leaves peppermint-scented. 3. Flowers white. 4. Posterior petals shorter than anterior petals. P. papilionaceum - 1. Leaves sparsely villous. 2. Leaves with an unpleasant odour. 3. Flowers light pink to carmine. 4. Posterior petals longer than anterior petals.
bibliographicCitation: Van der Walt, JJA. 1985. A taxonomic revision of the type section of Pelargonium L'Hérit. (Geraniaceae). Bothalia 15(3 & 4): 345-385. [CC BY]

description: P. tongaense is a small shrubby, somewhat procumbent herb with slightly thickened, pilose, angular lobate-palmate leaves. The sexual parts are short (±5 mm long), and only very slightly exserted; and the petals are bright red. The species resembles P. inquinans (L.) L'Herit. by its very similar red-petalled flowers, but differs in its angular lobate-palmate instead of suborbicular leaves, its more slender stems (3 to 4 mm versus 8 to 10 mm diameter), and somewhat procumbent versus erect habit. It also superficially resembles P. peltatum (L.) L' Herit. in the shape of its leaves, but differs in that its habit is not so pronouncedly scandent, its petals are smaller, ovate-cuneate instead of spathulate, and red instead of pinkish purple, and by its relatively much shorter sexual parts. P. tongaense is placed in the section Ciconium on account of its flowers, rather than in the related section Dibrachya.
bibliographicCitation: Vorster, PJ; Van der Walt, JJA. 1983. Two new species of Pelargonium L' Herit. (Geraniaceae) from South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 2(1): 76-81. description: P. torulosum is a much-branched decumbent shrublet with a succulent, moniliform stem and bipinnately incised leaves. The flowers are yellow with four protruding fertile stamens. It resembles P. stipulaceum (L.f.) Willd. and P. histrix Harv. on account of the floral structure. In all three species the hypanthium is long (40-60 mm) and the pedicel very short (±1 mm), the posterior sepal is erect with the posterior two petals side by side and their apices reflexed or recurved through more than 90°. The anterior three petals diverge from their bases. In P. torulosum and P. stipulaceum the petals are more or less of the same size, whereas in P. histrix the posterior two petals are markedly narrower than the anterior ones. Although the number of fertile stamens is four in P. torulosum and P. histrix and seven in P. stipulaceum, the structure of the androecium in the three different species is very similar. The four anterior stamens are longer than the sepals and protrude from the flower. The posterior filament is of medium length and in P. torulosum and P. histrix it has no anther, whereas in P. stipulaceum the congruent filament is a fertile stamen.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM. 1990. Pelargonium torulosum (Geraniaceae): a new species from the south-western Cape Province, southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 56(5): 565-570. description: The affinity of P. album with members of the section Cortusina DC., however, stands beyond doubt. It is known that the current section Cortusina is heterogeneous and that it will be divided into two groups of species. Characteristics that separate these two groups include differences in floral structure, chromosome numbers, pollen morphology, and flavonoid composition. In addition the two groups occur in different geographical areas. When the section is subdivided, P. album will be placed together with P. dichondrifolium DC., P. mossambicense, P. odoratissimum, P. reniforme Curt. and P. sidoides DC.
bibliographicCitation: Dreyer, LL; Van der Walt, JJA. 1990. A new species of Pelargonium from the eastern Transvaal. S. African J. Bot. 56(1): 65-67. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1990); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: The species is distinguished from S. cyaneus by its pink to pale pink flowers with short, white tubes and one- to two-flowered inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Weigend, M; Edwards, TJ. 1994. Notes on Streptocarpus cyaneus and S. parviflorus. Sendtnera 2: 365-376. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/52318#page/367/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: The leaf of S. trabeculatus is long in relation to its breadth and has a short, stout, very viscid stalk. The upper surface is coarsely wrinkled and rough to the touch while the veins on the lower surface are so extraordinarily prominent that they suggested the specific epithet (trabeculatus means 'with little beams'). The flowers too are rather unusual because they have the narrow bent corolla tube and prominent limb characteristic of S. polyanthus and its allies, but the mouth of the tube is not compressed.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1971. Streptocarpus: an African plant study. Univ. of Natal Press, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: The solitary leaf is long in relation to its breadth, and very thick owing to the extreme prominence of the veins on the lower surface.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1967. A new species of Streptocarpus (Gesneriaceae). Bothalia 9(2): 335-339. [CC BY]

description: S. vandeleurii is strikingly similar to the form of S.eylesii growing in the Dzalanyama.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1971. Streptocarpus: an African plant study. Univ. of Natal Press, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Distinguished by the pointed corm with straight or slightly recurved teeth converging on the basal point, and small to moderate-sized, 22-35 mm long, magenta to lilac-pink flowers with golden- or orange-yellow cup with dark blue or purplish ± transverse blotches in the throat, and unusual, acute and almost beaked capsules. The leaves vary from terete and narrowly 4-grooved to H-shaped with wide grooves or channels. The pointed corms, flowers with prominent dark blotches around the cup, and the acute capsules separate the species from Romulea rosea, with which it shares a somatic chromosome number 2n = 18. Populations with larger, (35-)40-50 mm long, old-rose-pink (i.e. with some yellow admixture to the pink) flowers with a pale or greenish yellow cup from the small triangle Malmesbury-Yzerfontein-Atlantis are treated as the distinct species Romulea eximia, evidently differing from R. cruciata also in leaf anatomy in having smaller, lignified epidermal cells (De Vos 1972).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Related to R. rosea and distinguished by its corm with a pointed base and almost straight, basal teeth, its stamens not reaching halfway up the perianth, and by its slightly beaked capsules which have a somewhat delayed dehiscence and are borne on erect or slightly spreading peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: De Vos, MP. 1983. Syringodea, Romulea, Fl. S. Africa 7(2,2): 1-76. Botanical Research Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Geographically separated from subsp. albescens, subsp. moggii has a narrower, glaucous foliage leaf 4-10 mm wide and not obviously ribbed, particularly well-developed cataphylls, the uppermost usually exceeding 15 mm, and uniformly yellow flowers. Late flowering, subsp. moggii blooms from late February to April, later than subsp. albescens, which typically flowers from December to February.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A relatively poorly defined species recognised by its erect, leaf-like bract subtending the synflorescence and mostly relatively long rhipidia, the bracts often dry and papery at the tips, and the inner rhipidial spathe 20-40 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Usually readily recognised by the dense inflorescence of up to 120 small, narrow rhipidia, the inner spathes 10-18 mm long and the outer ± one third as long and often obtuse or truncate, and characteristic, small, subglobose capsules 4-6 mm long with strongly rounded valves. Forms with fewer or larger rhipidia are less easily recognised, and can be confused with several other species with narrow, green rhipidial spathes.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Subsp. pilosa is recognised by the crepuscular flowers, usually white but rarely pale pink to lilac, with the outer tepals darkly pigmented outside. The style branches are somewhat shorter than in subsp. bracteolata, 5-9 mm long and reaching only to the middle of the anthers in the closed flower. The leaves are typically plane with slightly raised margins and main vein. A remarkable collection of what appears to be subsp. pilosa from the Hex River Mtns (Esterhuysen 36196A, BOL) flowering in December, consists of plants with only two leaves, the lower leaf linear-lorate and 4 mm wide, with an obtuse apex, and the second leaf sheaths the lower 2-3 of the stem. The margins, midrib and secondary veins all bear the long hairs that are diagnostic for Hesperantha pilosa but seem unusual in being slightly reflexed. The plants are taller than usual for H. pilosa and the spikes bear only one or two flowers. The style branches appear longer than those of any other white-flowered subsp. pilosa and in the closed flower reach the top of the anthers. The habitat, cool shaded slopes below a waterfall, is unusual for H. pilosa, which normally grows in light bush on exposed slopes and flowers in September and October. It seems possible that the habitat is responsible for the unusual morphology and late flowering time of the population, but it may equally represent a separate taxon.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A summer-flowering species recognised by the softly papery or finely fibrous corm tunics, leaves of the flowering stem only three and ± entirely sheathing and pale yellow to pearly grey, funnel-shaped flowers with a transverse yellow band on the lower tepals. The flowers close at night. The two or three foliage leaves, produced from a separate bud later in the season, are terete and 4-grooved. Gladiolus martleyi has similarly shaped but pink to mauve flowers produced in autumn and a solitary foliage leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Hermas ciliata is readily distinguished from all other species by the prostrate, adaxially glabrous to glabrescent leaves with ± entire and setose margins, usually forming a tidy rosette. As in H. quercifolia and H. villosa, the sepals have only a single prominent central vein with the lateral pair inconspicuous, when present. H. ciliata was at first thought to be unusual in lacking the lignified endocarp found in all other species of the genus and typical for the subfamily Azorelloideae. However, further studies showed that the fruit originally sectioned was immature and that mature fruits do indeed have lignified endocarps.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; De Villiers, BJ; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2015. A revision of the South African genus Hermas (Apiaceae). Syst. Bot. 40(1): 352-365. [DOI 10.1600/036364415X686639] [All rights reserved]

description: Hermas gigantea shares the very large, adaxially felty leaves with H. intermedia and H. lanata but can be easily distinguished from these species by the glabrous to glabrescent involucral and involucellar bracts and much of the peduncle. Both H. gigantea and H. intermedia have distinct maroon sepals (all other species have cream-coloured sepals), however in H. gigantea the bracts, rays, ovaries and often much of the peduncle are also maroon. The leaves also differ in that they are often larger, elliptic to obovate (rarely ovate) with an attenuate or sometimes truncate base. In H. lanata and H. intermedia they are ovate to oblong with a truncate to cordate base.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; De Villiers, BJ; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2015. A revision of the South African genus Hermas (Apiaceae). Syst. Bot. 40(1): 352-365. [DOI 10.1600/036364415X686639] [All rights reserved]

description: There is a certain amount of overlap between subsp. aethiopicum and subsp. sonderi: occasionally the odd specimen of subsp. aethiopicum has glandular stems, while specimens of subsp. sonderi sometimes have eglandular or nearly eglandular stems. According to Robson (l.c. 439), some specimens of subsp. sonderi from the Melsetter region of Rhodesia have sepals bearing stalked glands. This incomplete correlation between stem and sepal characters led Robson to treat these two taxa as subspecies rather than species.

description: In this species and A. nubigena, both of which are often pendent on rocks, the peduncle is bent, often in a U-curve, so that the raceme is always vertical. A. thompsoniae differs from A. nubigena by being a smaller plant with stiffer leaves and bracts with distinct veins. In A. thompsoniae the leaves are rosulate, but in A. nubigena they are often distichous. This species has rosulate leaves and bracts with distinct veins, and grows in clumps, whereas A. soutpansbergensis has fewer leaves, which are distichous when young, and bracts with obscure veins, and is often solitary.

description: All the specimens from southern Africa belong to the var. obscura with corolla concol orous or with a dark centre. The var. sagittifolia Verde, occurs from Zimbabwe to Tanzania. The typical variety is distinguished by its cordate leaves with a deep basal sinus, its broadly ovate to ovate-lanceolate sepals and pale yellow or white, 15-25 mm long corolla.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A number of varieties have been described, but they hardly seem to deserve separate status. The material from southern Africa would fit into the typical variety. Distinguished by the long, spreading, yellow, bristly hairs on the slender stems, petioles and peduncles, the deeply lobed leaves and also by the hairy, foliaceous bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The separation of A. julii subsp. julii and A. julii subsp. pannosa is to some degree arbitrary, for many collections of subsp. julii show the tendency to develop digitiform appendages on the involucral bracts while collections from the northern reaches of the ranges of subsp. pannosa often have rather reduced ones, e.g. Dieterland 469, Brierley in 1932 and 1933, Jacot-Guillarmod 2120, and Thode in 1895 and 1896. Thus, the morphological distinction between these two subspecies is actually drawn on the degree to which the appendages are developed and not on their presence or absence, but the distinction seems valid since it has a geographical basis. Collections with well-developed appendages are all from the east of the Drakensberg Escarpment, ranging from Mont AuxSources south to Mount Currie District, whereas those without appendages or with reduced appendages are from west of the Escarpment, principally in OrangeFree State and Basutoland. Intergradation with subsp. prostrata, which occurs to the south and the east of subsp. julii, is likewise complete with respect to the involucral bracts, the variation being toward the thin, rather scarious bracts of subsp. prostrata. There are instances, then, in which subsp. julii and subsp. prostrata may be distinguished from each other only by the relative length of the lateral lobes of the leaves.Though leaf shape is generally quite variable within species of this genus, it has a geographical correlation here which permits its taxonomic exploitation. Besides having involucral bracts which intergrade with those of the other subspecies, subsp. julii also has at times involucral bracts which are unique in the species. In the collections Roberts 2332, Ruck 1614, and Acocks 20809, thebracts vary from subulate to ovate and may not show any connation even in early bud. These appear, however, to be extreme forms in the general pattern of variation in subsp. julii and need not be recognized nomenclaturally.

description: The clasping leaf bases and the long sepals clearly distinguish this local endemic from K. rotundifolia. R.-Hamet identified some specimens of this species as K. rotundifolia (Haw.) Haw. var. aequimagnisepala, but the name was never validly published.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: R.-Hamet used the name K. rotundifolia var. peltata before it was validated by R. Fernandes. Although K. neglecta is superficially similar to K. rotundifolia it can be distinguis by its cordate or peltate leaves and dense part-inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The leaves are always entire but they are sessile on young or regenerating plants. Such plants cannot be distinguished from similar plants of K. luciae and K. thyrsiflora, both of which are often found in a similar habitat. Soon, however, the sharp edges of the clasping leaf bases of the latter two species will develop. In K. paniculata the peduncles usually show decurrent ridges from the bracts subtending the part-inflorescences. The absence of these and the much broader calyx lobes usually distinguish flowering material of K. brachyloba from K. paniculata. In central Transvaal the two species often grow within a few hundred metres of each other although they are ecologically separated.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Two plates of K. rotundifolia, based on plants collected by Bowie, are housed in Kew Herbarium. The one showing crenate leaf margins, was done in 1823, at about the time that Haworth described the plant, and it is therefore selected as the type. K. rotundifolia is the most complex species in the genus in Southern Africa. Distinction must be made between local variation and very marked seasonal variation apparently induced by environmental factors. Five forms are discussed below which differ in the shape and size of the leaves, which may vary from entire to deeply abed from one season to the next: 1. The crenate leaves as depicted on the iconotype from the eastern Cape are generally observed only in cultivated plants. As in the case of the type plant, however, the leaves of the same plant may be crenate in one season and entire in the next, as shown in the second lustration of this form in Kew Harbarium. The leaves are usually oblong-elliptic, or rarely elliptic-obovate, as in the second form below. Plants from north-eastern Natal are much more robust and have bigger leaves, but may at times develop a similarly crenate margin even in the field. 2. Plants usually associated with forested areas of northern Natal, eastern Swaziland and Transvaal have broadly obovate leaves with a rounded apex and rounded teeth or lobes. Occasionally these leaves are very broad and deeply lobed, as in specimens from south of Tzaneen. The rounded teeth must not be confused with the serrate margins of the typical plant which was also described as K. guillauminii. 3. Specimens from central Transvaal are usually distinguished by a distinct pale margin around the leaves. The leaves are pale green, becoming pale greyish brown and tend to become slightly concave above. 4. The previous form shows ranges of intermediates (Tölken 5764) grading into plants with narrowly oblong leaves which are occasionally found on rocky slopes between Pilgrim's Rest and central Swaziland. An extreme form has been described as K. decumbens. 5. In dryer parts of central Natal, Swaziland and Transvaal plants growing in depressions or near vleis develop 3(-5) lobes on the upper leaves (described as forma tripartita). The lower leaves are entire and in some seasons even the upper leaves of some plants may be entire. These extreme leaf shapes are found in plants with or without pale leaf margins.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The type specimen has unusually small, almost orbicular leaves and it was therefore difficult to interprete species from the description alone. The holotype could not be found, but there is little doubt that the specimen in PRE is an isotype and that its collector's number has been replaced by a TRV number. The unusual leaves agree well with the original description and the collection date is the same. K. vatrinii R.-Hamet may also prove to be slightly later synonym of this variable species. The leaves may vary from distinctly petiolate to sessile and from undulate to somewhat lobed.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The best character to distinguish the two subspecies is size. The subsp. insignis is much larger in all respects. The fact that subsp. insignis has large emergent stellate hairs on the ventral surface of the leaflets, whereas subsp. dregeanus does not, can be used to distinguish the two sub-species. The distribution also shows a spatial separation.
bibliographicCitation: Schelpe, EACLE; Tansley, SA. 1984. Notes on African plants: Melianthaceae. Bothalia 15(1&2): 143-145. [CC BY]

description: The many varieties recognized by Schonland reflect some of the variation and local forms found in this taxon: 1. In South Africa the epithet 'alba' seems inapropriate as most plants have deep red petals.This applies to the robust plants with scabrid hairs on the stem and often on the leaves as found on the Highveld as far north as near Pietersburg.2. Plants from the Natal coast are very similar to the previous form but more delicate and with petals rarely longer than 4 mm.3. The form found in the foothills of the Drakensberg in central Natal has a more lax habit and often more than one rosette. The leaves are often purple spotted and/or with purple undersurface, while the petals vary from pink to white in extreme forms.Being the only species with distincly red flowers one would like to associate particularly the latter form of var. alba with the somewhat similar C. schmidtii (Species insufficiently known) but in other ways that species as described is closer to C. setulosa. C. schmidtii is of unknown origin and known only from horticulture.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The wide range of variation found in var. atropurpurea can be shown in three extreme forms: 1. Typical C. atropurpurea is an erect plant with oblong-oblanceolate leaves up to 60 mm long in extreme forms as they are often found on forest margins or in sheltered kloofs along the coast from Mosselbaai to near Port Elizabeth. 2. In the mountains to the north of this, plants often produce much smaller leaves which are often restricted to a basal rosette with each leaf being strongly bent to one side of the stem. These plants resemble C. nudicaulis so closely that they can only be distinguished by their different petals. 3. In the mountains between Mosselbaai and Swellendam the leaves are narrowly oblanceolate to linear-elliptic, a tendency which becomes even more accentuated in the northern Swartberg where the leaves are rarely broader than 4 mm. This form could easily be confused with glabrous plants of C. subaphylla, except that leaves of the latter from areas of possible geographical overlap between these species are glabrous and/or very fleshy and gibbose, which does not apply to those of var. atropurpurea. In most parts of the Little Karoo the plants are somewhat similar to form 1 except that the leaves and the whole plant tend to be smaller. Between Montagu and Worcester the typical variety is often found near var. rubella, and some intermediates between the two have been recorded. It seems, however, that these are due to hybridization between the two varieties.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The most satisfactory key character for distinguishing the two subspecies is the number of ovules per carpel. In subsp. pectinatus there are 4 ovules per carpel, whereas there are only 2 per carpel in subsp. gariepinus. The leaflet margins and numbers can be used to distinguish the subspecies but this is not as clearcut. In subsp. gariepinus the leaflets are dentate and there are 7-9 leaflets. In subsp. pectinatus the leaflets are sinuate to serrate and there are 11-27 leaflets. With respect to distribution, subsp. pectinatus occurs south of the Orange River, whereas subsp. gariepinus occurs north of the Orange River.
bibliographicCitation: Schelpe, EACLE; Tansley, SA. 1984. Notes on African plants: Melianthaceae. Bothalia 15(1&2): 143-145. [CC BY]

description: Var. capensis is very variable and plants are often strongly stimulated by bush fires. This can be seen particularly in the increased number and size of flowers which are often 6-8(-12)-merous as compared to the usual 5-merous ones.Several local forms have been observed: 1. The leaves of most plants are broadly obovate and the lower pair usually lies flat on the soil. These plants usually flower soon after the first rains during April to June. 2. In the Olifant's River valley plants agree well with the previous form except that the leaves are verrucose to papillose on the upper surface. 3. Plants growing at higher altitude in the mountains from Somerset West to near Worcester usually bear their leaves well above the soil level and tend to flower later in the season. 4. A form with narrow leaves but otherwise similar to the previous form has been recorded from the lower slopes of the mountains west of Robertson. The plants also flower later and the leaves tend to develop while the plant is flowering as is usual in var. albertiniae.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A very variable taxon in which plants often occur in widely separated localities as is shown in the following main local forms: 1. In the south-western Great Karoo and the western Little Karoo the robust typical form produces petals (8-)9-12 mm long and the squamae are 1.6-2 mm long and gradually taper into the basal stalk. The leaf column is often constricted below the inflorescence as in subsp. prolifera. 2. Merging into the variation of the first form is the apparently stunted form from the eastern Little Karoo which produces a corolla 6-8(-9) mm long and squamae which are 1-1.2 mm long and are abruptly constricted into the stalk. In extreme forms the flowers are half hidden by leaves below the inflorescence. 3. In the northern Cedarberg and Gifberg plants are more slender, have a corolla 7.5-9 mm long and squamae 1.2-1.5 mm long and more or less abruptly constricted into the basal stalk.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Subsp. lanceolata is characterized by the short leaves (even in shade forms they are rarely longer than 6 mm) without terminal colourless points although often acute. It is the pronounced terminal point of the denticulate leaves which distinguishes the quite similar subsp. denticulata from subsp. lanceolata.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The size of the leaves varies greatly in the species so that var. lanuginosa, which usually has shorter leaves than var. pachystemon, can at times only be distinguished by its acute leaves with long apical cilia.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Burrows (1999) suggested that this species may be a genetic aberration of M. africana, necessitating further chromosome research. According to McMurtry (2006) the species might be a hybrid between M. africana and Rapanea melanophloeos.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL; Matiapoto, MMH. 2019. Myrsinaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(2): 1241-1243. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This robust plant is usually very sparsely branched but in southern South West Africa/Namibia and in the southern Karoo forms with many short axillary branchlets have apparently developed independently from each other. Others from the Knersvlakte have particularly strongly adpressed leaves so as to give the branches a lizard-like appearance. In the area near Saldanha Bay the plants have rather long internodes which are visible between the leaves, a phenomenon particularly clearly shown in herbarium material.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Generally readily distinguished by its dense, subsessile, oblanceolate or oblong-lanceolate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Dyer, RA. 1963. Myrsinaceae, Fl. S. Africa 26: 1-9. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Both the rank of variety and subspecies are maintained in the present work. Varieties are considered to be neither geographically nor ecologically separated, while subspecies are isolated from each other either geographically or ecologically, or both. The rank of subspecies adopted by Friedrich for this taxon can therefore not be accepted.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: An extremely variable species showin g much local as well as ecological variation, mainly of the vegetative organs. C. ovata is generally distinguished from C. setulosa by its larger flowers and in particular by the petals which are usually longer than 5 mm. An apparent shade form classified by Schonland as C. sediflora var. laxifoliosa has flowers approaching those of C. setulosa, and it is only by the longer branches (0.2 m or longer), and anthers which are (0.6-)0.8-1.3 mm long, as against those of the latter species, which are about 0.4 mm long in that region, that the two species can be distinguished. The inflorescence is also extremely variable. In no other species of Crassula is the whole range of variation found from a spike-like to an elongate (in the eastern Cape) to a more or less roundtopped thyrse (in southern and central Natal). In the extreme northern part of the eastern Cape Province a range of transitional forms occurs over such a wide area that it is unlikely to be due to hybridization, especially as the character of the inflorescence does not appear in recombination with other characters.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Herbarium material of var. perfoliata is not always easily distinguished from var. coccinea as at times the difference in the relative length of calyx and corolla is not always distinct, and the flower colour is often not recorded.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A large range of variation in respect of size, shape and pubescence of leaves as well as habit has been recorded within and between populations. The leaves vary from pubescent to tomentose in the eastern parts of the Little Karoo, whereas they are puberulous south of the Outeniqua and Langeberg Mountains. In the dryer parts of the eastern Little Karoo plants with shrubby habit may be found next to plants with a basal rosette and scarcely elongated branches. A plant with tufted habit has been recorded from near Calvinia, the northernmost point in the distribution, but in this plant the habit does not change under cultivation as in the above form with basal rosettes.In spite of all the variation subsp. pubescens is always distinguished from the other two subspecies by the elongate-elliptic appendage of the corolla lobes. Plants of subsp. pubescens are usually more delicate than those of C. atropurpurea var. rubella, which often grows near the former, but it is difficult to distinguish on vegetative material alone. Once they are flowering the beak-like apices of the corolla lobes of the latter are quite distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Subsp. rupestris is particularly variable in size and shape of the leaves and the degree to which they are fused at the base. At times the range of variation of the typical subspecies may overlap with that of the other subspecies but they are kept as separate taxa as they are geographically and/or ecologically separated.Subsp. rupestris is distinguished from small-leaved forms of C. perforata by its spreading pair of bracts where the inflorescence starts branching. These bracts are usually longer than 3 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: O. confusa shows a relationship with Brackenridgea in that its anthers open by longitudinal slits, and in its leaves, which have lateral veins curving upwards and marginal teeth tipped with glands.
bibliographicCitation: Du Toit, PCV; Obermeyer, AA. 1976. Ochnaceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 1-13. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Related to O. inermis but can be distinguished by the shorter usually erect pedicels articulated just above the base, and the somewhat smaller leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Du Toit, PCV; Obermeyer, AA. 1976. Ochnaceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 1-13. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: O. emarginata is distinguished from O. micrantha by having narrowly elliptic leaves and bracts that are reduced to scaly appendages (compared to leathery leaves that are broadly elliptic to slightly obovate and bracts that are persistent at anthesis in O. micrantha). The leaves can be confused with those of O. micrantha but are generally narrow and elliptic (versus broadly elliptic and slightly obovate); secondary and tertiary veins are conspicuous and prominent on the lower surface (versus inconspicuous veins on both surfaces of lamina); and apices are retuse to emarginate with a minute extension of the midvein (versus apices that are obtuse to acute with a distinct extension of the midvein). O. emarginata flowers from October to January and sets fruit from March to July. The fruits are pink to red and eaten by birds. The species is frost tolerant, but drought sensitive. Propagation from either seed or cuttings has been unsuccessful.
bibliographicCitation: Sebola, JR; Balkwill, K. 2013. A monographic study of the Oliniaceae. Kew Bull. 68(3): 419-456. [All rights reserved]

description: It is very difficult to distinguish this subspecies from C. nudicaulis var. herrei which has a similar habit, but on which remains of inflorescences can usually be found as they do not decay as easily in those arid regions. The sterile bracts on the peduncle are very narrow so that they form an obtuse angle between their bases, a character which will generally distinguish the two species.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: In the eastern parts of the distribution area, the plants often become very robust with stems up to 15 mm in diameter, but the subspecies can always be distinguished by its long leaf sheath, carnose stems and long peduncle with 2 or 3 pairs of bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Fairly widely distributed and varying very much in the shape and, to some extent, in the texture of the leaflets, characters upon which the several species shown in synonymy above have been principally founded. The extreme forms are admittedly very dilferent in appearance, but a study of the group in the field and in cultivation and the examination of a considerable number of dried specimens convinces me that it is not only impossible to place many of them definitely in one or other of the existing species and further that although constant geographical forms undoubtedly occur, there is no tangible specific difference between them. O. adspersa E. & Z., the oldest published name in the group, is ascribed to the form with the narrowest leaflets of all. One of the forms of O. florida (var. rubra) has a red corolla, but differs in no other respect, the colour soon fades in dried specimens and they can rarely then be distinguished. Two forms stand out as somewhat exceptional: Drège (O. ciliaris a E. Mey, non Jacq., O. Meyeri Sond.) and S.2425, 5284 from near Berg River are very robust, the large leaflets variable in shape in the same colony and often dark purple beneath and the corolla exceptionally large, white. S. 383/1 (O. pallida Salter & Exell), Piqbg. Div., with bracts below the middle of the peduncle. Neither of the above, however, are worthy of varietal rank.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: The great range of variation in the shape of the leaflets shows that the retention of O. collina, even as a variety, is not warranted. The underside of the leaflet is not tomentose as described by Sonder, although at first sight it has that appearance owing to the hairs overlying the rough collapsed cells.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: So much variation has been recorded for this species that it might seem unnatural to divide it into two subspecies. The difference is not only the presence or absence of stilt roots, but subsp. filicaulis tends to grow near or in False Fynbos while subsp. marlothii is usually found in karroid vegetation. The more slender plants from east of Vanrhynsdorp were not given separate rank although they differ in several respects. The slender long leaves (Tölken 5128) and straight branches distinguish them easily from narrow-leaved forms of A. roaneanus. A. fragilis is another extreme form which has developed along a cline on the western slopes of the coastal mountains between Komaggas and the Orange River.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: This species has been confused with both O. zeykeri Sond. and O. variifolia Steud.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: The only species found in the Highveld region of the Transvaal.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Widely distributed in the dry parts of the South Western area. In many forms, perhaps all, the earlier leaflets are shorter, more rotund and less distinctly cuneate than the later, a heterophyllous development which has misled previous authors into multiplication of species. Although the plants with white flowers are often inclined to be more glabrous than the others, this character is not sufficiently definite to warrant their separation. The colour of the corolla in the typical form as originally described, viz. “purpurea”, seems to have been assumed from dried specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Fruits baccate, subglobose, 10-15 mm in diameter, solitary, red, 2-seeded.
bibliographicCitation: Jeffrey, C. 1978. 86. Cucurbitaeae. In: E Launert (ed.), Fl. Zambes. 4: 414-499. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, Glasgow. [CC BY]

description: A species with many slight geographical variants. It was not recognised by R. Knuth (who gave it the invalid name of argentea) as being the sameas O. falcata var. callosa. Though closely akin to the foregoing, it differs in several important characters and should be considered as a separate species.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Occurs in a particularly arid district and in most seasons is only found in a dwarf and starved condition. The type was collected in an unusually favourable season and closely resembles cultivated specimens.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Variable. Tendrils simple; leaves distinctly lobed or dissected; flowers monoecious, male and female flowers borne in the same axils, minute; male raceme on a distinct common peduncle; fruit spherical.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: Large monoecious flowers, in racemes or fascicled, vegetative parts with short, white curved hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: I have only seen Dinter’s specimens which are larger in all parts and evidently more luxuriant than those originally described. It appears to be an affinity of O. sonderiana (O.Kuntze) T.M.Salter.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Leaves simple, unlobed or usually shallowly 3-5-lobed or -angled. Tendrils simple, unbranched. Fruit fusiform, to 10 cm long.
bibliographicCitation: Jeffrey, C. 1978. 86. Cucurbitaeae. In: E Launert (ed.), Fl. Zambes. 4: 414-499. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, Glasgow. [CC BY]

description: Leaves simple, deeply palmately 7 (or more)-lobate. Tendrils 2-fid. Fruit to 6 cm long, ellipsoid or subglobose, 10-ribbed, reddish-brown.
bibliographicCitation: Jeffrey, C. 1978. 86. Cucurbitaeae. In: E Launert (ed.), Fl. Zambes. 4: 414-499. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, Glasgow. [CC BY]

description: It is possible that the bulb-system is somewhat similar to that of O. creaseyi T.M.Salter, but with much shorter droppers.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: This species has been cultivated as a border flower in England. It is quite distinct from O. purpurata Jacq., which has an entirely different root-system.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Stems ± glabrous; sometimes bracts at base of petioles; leaves very deeply dissected; petals 5-12 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: Leaves palmately lobed to about the middle, lobes usually over 10 mm wide; leaves and stems hispid; petioles mostly bracteate at the base.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: Bracts absent at base of petioles. Petals well over 20 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: Flowers small, petals of male flowers 4-5 mm long, leaves sagittate.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: Male flowers racemose on short individual pedicels, lobes of leaves constricted at the base.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: Though apparently native in the Cape Peninsula, it occurs most frequently as a weed of cultivation and only the short-styled form has been found.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: This very common species is recognized by its «umbel»-like anthela of rather short spikes with numerous crowded small spikelets. Although frequently 2-3 flowered, the spikelets normally perfects only one nutlet. The different subspecies and varieties may, however, be difficult to separate.
bibliographicCitation: Haines, RW; Lye, KA. 1983. The sedges and rushes of East Africa. East African Natural History Society, Nairobi. [All rights reserved]

description: It is very variable in size, often growing to 2 ft. in shady places.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its flattened petioles. It is not by any means confined to sandy and wet places as stated by Sonder and it is probably more widely distributed than is supposed, for it is very easily mistaken for the very common O. pes caprae L. The corolla in var. purpurascens is deeper yellow than that of the typical form var. compressa.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: A poorly understood species, Drimia occultans is known only from the type collection comprising portions of one or possibly two cultivated plants. It is recognised essentially by its diminutive size, producing a solitary filiform leaf in winter, followed by a raceme up to 55 mm long, with up to three flowers laxly spaced up to 10 mm apart, but often with just a solitary flower. The flowers themselves are relatively large for such small plants, with almost free tepals up to 6 mm long, and with weakly spreading stamens. The seeds are unusually small, ± 1.0-1.3 mm long. Additional material is required for a more accurate assessment of the variation in the species and its taxonomic status.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The species is most similar to E. schijffii. The latter differs in its intensely glaucous leaves with strongly cartilaginous, minutely crisped purple margins. It is further a taller plant (10-15 cm high) with a purple scape. The tepals are dark purple (instead of greenish white), long- lasting (8-9 days instead of 2-3) and firm (instead of soft), and the flowers emit a strong fetid scent (instead of sweet). Its filaments are purple (instead of white) and broadly triangular with 2-mm-wide bases and have larger anthers (2.5 x 1.5 mm) with bright yellow pollen (instead of cream). Its ovary is much less inflated, has prominent apical grooves, and the capsule with a purple pericarp is also much less inflated, and takes 2 months to ripen (instead of 3-4 weeks). The two species are unusual within the genus in having dull blackish brown seeds with reticulate sculpturing (instead of glossy and smooth).
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD; Zonneveld, BJM. 2010. Genome sizes of Eucomis L'Hér. (Hyacinthaceae) and a description of the new species Eucomis grimshaw. Pl. Syst. Evol. 284: 99-109. [All rights reserved]

description: Closely related to Monanthotaxis caffra (Sond.) Verdc., but differs in having long filaments which occupy more than half of the total stamen length, while M. caffra has short filaments and the anther cells occupy more than half of the total stamen length. Further M. maputensis has shorter and less hairy leaves, the fruiting pedicels are more slender and the stipes are shorter than with M. caffra.
bibliographicCitation: Hoekstra, PH. 2016. A nonet of novel species of Monanthotaxis (Annonaceae) from around Africa. PhytoKeys 69: 71-103. [doi: 10.3897/phytokeys.69.9292] [All rights reserved]

description: Caesalpinia bracteata and C. rostrata closely resemble each other, but differ from one another in a number of morphological characters and distribution: C. rostrata occurs in southern Mozambique and the northeastern Transvaal, about 1000 km from C. bracteata.
bibliographicCitation: Germishuizen, G. 1991. Fabaceae: Caesalpinia bracteata, a new species from the Onseepkans area of the Northern Cape Province. Bothalia 21(2): 152-154. [CC BY]

description: The floral scent of O. dines is intense and distinctively different from the weaker scent of O. disticha. The two species are allopatric.
bibliographicCitation: Ornduff, R. 1973. Oxalis dines, a new species from the western Cape. J. S. African Bot. 39(3): 201-203. [CC BY]

description: Similar to P. axillaris L., but differs in being a resprouter with numerous shoots emerging from a woody rootstock; older plants producing a cluster of shoots (burst branching) at the ends of the previous seasons’ terminal shoots giving an untidy habit (versus a much-branched reseeder with single stem, never with burst branching); stems coarsely fissured and greyish with age (versus furrowed, heavily lenticelled and brownish); leaves 3-foliolate; leaflets partially conduplicate, linear-oblong, with raised crater-like glands and scarcely visible veins (versus leaves 3-5-foliolate; flat, lanceolate, distinctly veined with small sunken glands); lateral leaflets symmetrical, 2-3 mm broad (versus lateral leaflets asymmetrical, 3-8 mm broad); flowers well exerted from leaves, mauve to pale lavender, wings white (versus mostly hidden within leaves, mauve to purple with purple veins, wings mauve); standard white to pale mauve and with a single purple vertical flash plus a few shorter darker veins towards base of standard, apex greenish on front and back (versus mauve with strongly purple veins and violet basal patch, apex not greenish on front and back); wing petals flared outwards (versus wing petals held vertically). Psoralea forbesiae is part of the Psoralea verrucosa complex with special affinities to P. triflora Thunb. and P verrucosa Willd. It has been confused in the past with P. verrucosa and usually named as that species. However, P. verrucosa is an allopatric species from the Cederberg region (versus Swartberg Mountains), with glaucous and prominently warty stems and leaves (versus bluish-green stems and leaves covered in small raised crateriform glands) and multi-flowered pedunculate inflorescences (versus single-flowered axillary inflorescences). Psoralea triflora is an allopatric lowland coastal species of shorter stature (<1.5 m) and differs from P. forbesiae in its flat, 1.0-1.7 mm broad, keeled leaflets with impressed glands (versus semi-conduplicate 1.4-3.0 mm broad leaflets densely covered in small raised crateriform glands); peduncles 10-15 mm long (versus peduncles 26-35 mm); and with mauve standards with purple veins, prominent central purple flash and nectar guide, back purple (versus standard white to pale mauve with a single purple vertical flash plus a few shorter darker veins towards base of standard, white with apex greenish on front and back). It is difficult to name some material belonging to P. forbesiae in the Swartberg Mountains owing to the presence of an intro-gressive swarm there. Psoralea sordida, with which it hybridises, is a lanky 1-2-stemmed shrub with erect short virgate branches in its upper parts (versus many-stemmed, densely branched large shrubs tending to hemispherical in shape); with digitately (3)5(7)-foliolate glabrous green leaves with sunken glands (versus pinnately 3-foliolate bluish green leaves with raised crateriform glands); leaflets linear-lanceolate, 0.2-0.3 mm wide (versus leaflets linear-oblong, 1.5-3.0 mm wide); 3-flowered axillary inflorescences shorter than the subtending leaves with stout and rigid 2-4 mm long peduncles (versus 1(2)-flowered inflorescences longer than the subtending leaves, with filiform and 26-35 mm long peduncles); and calyx lobes equally developed (versus unequally developed).

description: Form A. Typical. leaves rather coarsely pilose; leaflets more or less rotund, 0. 8-1. 5 cm long and broad, concolorous. Bracts 3-6 mm long. Corolla up to 3.3 cm long (? sulphur) yellow. Form B. O. salmonicolor Schltr. Leaflets rather broadly obovate or rarely cuneate-obovate, concolorous. Bracts minute or more often wanting. Corolla yellow or salmon-coloured. Form C. More robust and more coarsely hirsute than the typical form. Leaves 7-12; leaflets broadly cuneate-rotund, concolorous. Bracts up to 3 mm long or wanting. Sepals 6-9 mm long. Corolla 3-3.5 cm long, rose. Perhaps only a colour variant of the typical Form A.

description: This species is characterised by the coarsely and irregularly dentate leaves, distinctly net-veined on the abaxial surface and slender petioles. Florets of this species have only been observed in the type specimen. The relatively graceful and elegant heads are borne on long, slender, branched scapes. The dark red margins of the involucral bracts, the disc florets that are longer than the pappus and the dark red, exserted styles are also diagnostic.

description: A species of doubtful affinity. The typical form (var. furcillata), though larger, closely resembles [Oxalis densa], but the exendospermous seeds should really exclude it from this Section.

description: B. gariepensis differs from the closely allied B. comptonii, which has similar papillate leaf upper surfaces, in having a consistently larger inflorescence in which the flowers have longer pedicels (50-55 vs. 10-25 mm at anthesis), longer tepals (45-50 vs. 20-27 mm) and a longer perigone tube (4-5 vs. <0.5 mm), and the stamens are distinctly biseriate, the outer whorl being ± two thirds as long as the inner. Although lateral appendages at the base of the filaments are sometimes present in B. comptonii they are absent in B. gariepensis. This feature is nevertheless regarded as taxonomically unreliable in Brunsvigia, being variable in B. namaquana and Brunsvigia bosmaniae. Other species from the semi-arid westem parts of Northern Cape that have flowers with distinctly biseriate stamens are B. bosmaniae, Brunsvigia herrei and Brunsvigia pulchra. They are all easily distinguished from B. gariepensis by their large habit and heavily ribbed fruiting capsules.

description: Very common and often prolific in the Cape Peninsula and surrounding areas, spreading by means of underground stolons and forming large carpets. The species is characterised by its long, sharply acute sepals which sometimes bear 2 minute apical calli. There are numerous micro-varieties and it takes many epharmonic forms. The shade forms produce long stems with cauline leaves and peduncles, particularly in the mountain regions, but such forms do not remain constant in cultivation. Double flowers sometimes, though rarely, occur.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: This species is distinguished by its angular bulb. There are many local forms, variable in size, in the colour of the flowers and in the presence or absence of calli on the leaflets.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Nearly related to O. pallens E. & Z., but a larger and stouter plant with a much larger pitted bulb.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Nanobubon hypogaeum differs most notably from the other two species in its very slender, only slightly woody root and slender subterranean stem, up to 450 mm long. The stem consists of a series of sympodial annual segments each terminated by the formation of a flowering shoot and so continued by an axillary bud. In order to maintain the position of the crown below the soil surface the stem is retracted into the soil, and stems pulled down as deep as 470 mm have been excavated. The mechanism for this remarkable movement has not been observed but root contraction seems to be the most likely and has been reported for Apiaceae (Berckemeyer, 1928; Pütz and Sukkau, 1995, 2002). In both N. capillaceum (Thunb.) Magee and N. strictum the shoots resprout from a short, thick, woody subterranean stem and the root is very thick and woody (both > 10 mm diam.). Nanobubon hypogaeum shares the erect pinnae, rachis and leaves segments, and the absence of prominent dorsal fruit ribs with N. strictum but differs in the annual leaves with the petiole twice as long as the blade, the cream-coloured petals, and the prominently acuminate sepals. In N. strictum the petiole is equal to or shorter than the length of the blade and the petals are yellow. N. capillaceum, which also has cream-coloured petals, has refracted pinnae, rachis and leaf segments and prominent dorsal ribs on the fruit.

description: Differentiated from other closely related Pachycarpus E. Mey. species (P. scaber (Harv.) N. E. Br. and P. asperifolius Meisn.) by its small stature, the catilliform or saucer-shaped corolla, and a deltoid corona lobe that is sharp at the distal end, hence the specific epithet. It also differs from P. asperifolius in the inflorescence being terminal and subcorymbose.

description: A polymorphous species, distinguishable in the sub-section bifurcatae by their lanate bulb-tunics. The short, rather obtuse teeth on the longer filaments and the presence of calli on the ovary, though in varying numbers, also seem to be constant characters. It is particularly prone to epharmonic variation and many of the mountain forms are almost stemless or produce leafless stems. The bulbs lie very deep and are rarely collected.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: A small plant reaching up to 150 mm and with the stem usually covered by leaf sheaths, Ferraria parva has flowers with a narrow floral cup ± 8 mm deep and tepals 18-22 mm long with slightly reflexed limbs. It has been confused with the larger-flowered F. ferrariola, which has a floral cup 17-20 mm deep and tepals (30-)35-40 mm long. The cataphylls and basal leaf sheath of F. parva are uniformly pale coloured, whereas those of F. ferrariola are speckled and usually flushed red.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in having not only the filaments but also the anthers, style and style branches included within the narrow perianth tube, and in its soft-textured leaves. It broadly resembles I. stohriae, which also has short filaments, either included in the perianth tube or shortly exserted up to 1 mm and the bases of the anthers sometimes partly included in the tube, but is otherwise a more robust plant and most collections consist of plants with sturdy, erect stems with at least one branch (rarely up to 5 branches). The style in I. stohriae reaches at least to the middle of the anthers and sometimes exceeds them, thus always reaching the mouth of the perianth tube. This contrasts with the condition in I. recondita, in which the style, just 2-3 mm long, divides opposite the filament bases in the lower half of the perianth tube and the style branches barely reach the middle of the filaments. Like Ixia stohriae and closely related I. fucata, I. recondita usually has four leaves, sometimes three or five, the lower two or three with well-developed blades and the upper one or two partly to almost entirely sheathing. In the length of the perianth tube, ± 12 mm long, I. recondita is intermediate between its two relatives: the tube of I. stohriae is (12-)14-22 mm long, and that of I. fucata 10-15 mm long. Both I. fucata and I. stohriae are Langeberg endemics, the latter recorded from the mountains between Grootvadersbos and Swellendam, while I. fucata occurs further west from Montagu to Keeromsberg, as well as in the Hex River Mtns. The range of I. recondita thus lies between that of its two relatives.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Known from O. bullulata Salter by its comparatively smooth bulb tunics and longer, more exserted stamens and styles.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Recognised primarily by the small corm, ± 6 mm in diameter, with rust-brown, submembranous, non-accumulating, onion-skin-like tunics, often a fairly low stature and usually a simple, rarely 1(2)-branched stem. The moderate-sized pink flowers are unremarkable and have a funnel-shaped perianth tube ± 10 mm long, tepals 12-17 mm long, and short filaments exserted 2-3 mm from the mouth of the tube. The leaves are ± straight, 2.5-4.5 mm wide, and the cataphylls are typically rust-brown. Ixia monticola is most easily confused with the relatively small-flowered I. divaricata, the higher elevation populations of which often have few-branched or unbranched stems, and similar narrow, erect leaves. Ixia divaricata more often has white or very pale pink flowers, and while the floral proportions are similar to those of I. monticola, I. divaricata always has well-developed fibrous corm tunics.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The narrow-cyathiform or inflated tube of the corolla, constricted within the calyx, is a marked character of this species.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Xiphotheca rosmarinifolia falls within X. sect. Xiphotheca, owing to its characteristic pedunculate inflorescences, extended flowering units and the lower lobe of the calyx being as long as the lateral lobes. Within this section, it is closely related to X. phylicoides-both species are sprouters and both have leaves with strongly revolute margins. However, X. rosmarinifolia differs from X. phylicoides in the narrower and linear leaves, 1-2 mm wide, the shorter peduncle (< 1 mm long), bracts (±1 mm long) and pedicel (3 mm long). In X. phylicoides the leaves are 2.5-5.0 mm wide and elliptic, the peduncle is 1.5-2.5 mm long, the bracts are 3-4 mm long and the pedicel is 3.5-5.0 mm long. The two species are allopatric, with the latter recorded from three localities on the Outeniqua Mtns near Mossel Bay, whereas X. rosmarinifolia is known only from a single locality near Bredasdorp. The specific epithet refers to the leaves that resemble those of the well-known herb, rosemary.
bibliographicCitation: Schutte, AL. 2011. Fabaceae: A new species of Xiphotheca from the Western Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 41(2): 298-300. [https://doi.org/10.4102/abc.v41i2.65] [CC BY]

description: When growing in the open the plant is somewhat pyramidical in shape. It has retained its habit of flowering before the leaves developein cultivation, but leaflets up to 9.5 mm, long and 11.5 mm broad have been produced after the flowering period. The bulbs were invariably found under large stones and in contact with them, embedded in a thick mass of old tunics.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: Plants are long-lived and typically form dense clumps of up to 70 heads. Not only are its flowers the smallest (20-25 mm long) among South African members of the A. zebrina-complex, but they are also characteristic in being an unusual intense red. Also diagnostic are the general small stature of the plants and shorter inflorescences (0.65-0.75 m). An outstanding feature is its concentrated and relatively early (December to February) flowering period.

description: It is said to be similar in habit to O. Schaeferi R. Knuth, from the same localities and from which it is not easily distinguished by the paler corolla callose sepals and by the shape and indument of the leaflets.
bibliographicCitation: Salter, TM. 1944. The genus Oxalis in South Africa: A taxonomic revision. J. S. African Bot. 1: 1-355. [CC BY]

description: A close affinity of O. glabra Th. and it is very difficult to distinguish in the dried state without the bulb. It differs in having a more robust and rigid stem and a much larger and rougher bulb, the younger bulbs being long and attenuate and quite unlike the small smooth bulbs of O. glabra and it does not produce underground stolons.
