description: A. hereroensis is extremely closely related to A. caffra. It differs from A. caffra in the usually shorter and smaller leaves with more crowded pinnae pairs. These shorter leaves of A. hereroensis often tend to be held erect and do not droop as readily as the longer leaves of A. caffra. A. hereroensis has a more westerly distributional range than A. caffra although in the western Transvaal and south-eastern Botswana their ranges do overlap. However, in parts of the western Transvaal where the two species grow in close proximity, each species may usually be distinguished in the field without difficulty.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A. davyi bears a strong superficial resemblance to A. arenaria Schinz. A. arenaria differs, however, in having: white or pale pink flowers; the corolla usually 2-4 times as long as the small cupular calyx; dark reddish-brown arcuate pods; a very different distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A. rehmanniana has been often confused with A. sieberana DC. in the past. However, A. rehmanniana is a distinctive species, easily separated from A. sieberana by the more numerous pairs of closely arranged pinnae, the much smaller and thinner textured pods, the involucels in the lower half of the peduncle, and the way in which the capitula are clustered in the axils and aggregated into terminal 'racemes'.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A. swazica may sometimes be confused with A. exuvialis. However, A. swazica differs from A. exuvialis, and from all of the other species in the complex with glandular glutinous pods, by the conspicuous venation on the lower leaflet surfaces.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Some of the plants have a similar growth form to A. tenuispina, but, as they lack the spinulose-mucronate leaflet apices and glandular pods, they are referred to A. karroo. It has been suggested by some collectors that the plants may be hybrids between A. karroo and A. tenuispina.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to N. chrysocomoides but distinguished by the long, simple twigs with very few and very narrow leaves and by the circular epicarpic cells scattered and arranged in pairs, with a single, short twin hair between each pair. Also very similar in appearance to N. rarifolia but without dark oil sacs on involucral bracts and cypselae with paired circular epicarpic cells as opposed to oblong epicarpic cells in N. rarifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Herman, PPJ. 2013. Cypsela morphology in the genus Nolletia (Asteraceae, Astereae) and a revision of the genus. Phytotaxa 122(1): 1-44. [All rights reserved]

description: This species differs from the others in southern Africa by the shorter tertiary bracts (less than 5 mm) and their unique rusty-brown colour.
bibliographicCitation: Balkwill, K; Cadman, M-J; Getliffe Norris, FM. 1985. Taxonomic studies in the Acanthaceae: new species of Peristrophe from the Limpopo Valley. S. African J. Bot. 51(6): 485-488. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1985); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: This species comes closest to A. serrulatus (= Aster harveyanus O.Kuntze), but differs in its much more slender habit, reduced single-nerved cauline leaves and in bearing 1-3 lateral branches which seem to have a purely photosynthetic function, the terminal capitulum being usually aborted or entirely absent. A. ananthocladus also recalls A. bowiei (Harv.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt, but that species is more woody at the base and has more numerous and longer leaves aggregated towards the base of the peduncle and, apparently, tufted on short sterile axillary branches. The leaves of A. bowiei also decrease in size downwards to the scales clothing the rootstock. There appears to be no developed radical leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1976. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: V. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 34(3): 253-286. [CC BY-SA]

description: Plants that have yet to flower have a conspicuous tuft of leaves surmounting a simple almost leafless stem up to c. 8 cm tall; these stems may be solitary or several together, tufted from a common rhizome. As the stem elongates prior to flowering, a dwarf shoot similar in aspect to the initial shoot develops in the upper two or three leaf axils. These leaf tufts suggested the specific epithet confertifolius and they at once distinguish the species from its ally, A. hispida (= Aster bakerianus C. A. Smith), which is also common in the Gxalingenwa valley, but in the grass near the river and on the North facing slopes. The root tubers of A. confertifolius are smaller than those of A. hispida (= Aster bakerianus) and the heads are always solitary, never corymbosely arranged as they often are in A. hispida.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XI. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 42(2): 227-260. [CC BY-SA]

description: No specimens in PRE, only known from type.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Osteospermum monstrosum is an annual, viscid herb, characterized by only the tangential side of the achenes being fenestrate, and by its very broadly scariose involucral scales and its short ray flowers, which are as long as the involucre or only slightly longer. The tangential side of the achenes is alwayTs more or less densely muricate or echinulate and somewhat foveolate, while the radial sides are as a rule smooth or very seldom muricate along the middle.
bibliographicCitation: Norlindh, NT. 1943. Studies in the Calenduleae: 1. Monograph of the genera Dimorphotheca, Castalis, Osteospermum, Gibbaria & Chrysanthemoides. C.W.K. Gleerup, Lund. [All rights reserved]

description: Intergrades with var. pilosa, which in turn intergrades with H. hirta and H. anamesa, but recognised by its graceful appearance, many slender branches, drooping peduncles and small, few-awned racemes.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Hyparrhenia E.Fourn. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 381-392. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Warneckea parvifolia was previously included in W. sousae but is distinguished by its relatively short internodes mostly 5-25 mm long, smaller leaves mostly 14-32 x 8-19 mm on short petioles mostly 1-1.5 mm long, smaller flowers (hypanthium 1 mm long x 1.5-1.75 mm diam., calyx lobes 0.5 mm long, staminal filaments 3-4 mm long, style 4-5 mm long), and globose fruit. In contrast, W. sousae has internodes mostly 10-45(-60) mm long, leaf-blades mostly 40-76 x 22-52 mm, larger flowers (hypanthium 1.5-2 mm long x 2 mm diam., calyx lobes ± 0.75 mm long, staminal filaments 5 mm long, style 9 mm long), and mature fruit obovoid 9 x 7 mm. Petioles 2-6 mm long are seen in several collections of W. sousae, including the type, but in other material (Burrows 10772 & 11240, BNRH; Ward 7970, NU, UDW) the petioles are consistently shorter, 1.5-2.5 mm, thus approaching those of W. parvifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Stone, RD; Ntetha, NA. 2013. Warneckea parvifolia (Melastomataceae–Olisbeoideae), a new “sand-forest” endemic from northeastern KwaZulu-Natal (South Africa) and southernmost Mozambique, and a phylogenetic analysis of eastern and southern African representatives of W. section Warneckea. S. African J. Bot. 88: 317-325. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2013.08.005] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2013); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: A very distinctive species recognized by the firm-textured, densely villous leaves, the similarly villous peduncle and bracts, and especially by the villous or bearded ovary and capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Boatwright, JS; Manning, JC. 2013. Two new species of Trachyandra sect. Liriothamnus (Xanthorrhoeaceae, Asphodeloideae) from the Western and Eastern Cape provinces of South Africa. Phytotaxa 155(1): 59-65. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.155.1.5] [All rights reserved]

description: Unusually short for the genus, stems of Micranthus simplex rarely exceed 180 mm and the white flowers with lilac-tipped outer tepals are distinctive, other species having flowers in shades of deep to pale blue or blue-mauve, or occasionally white. The inflorescence is relatively lax, the bracts of the lower flowers of the spike not overlapping those above them, but the upper bracts are as closely set as in other species. It is one of two species of Micranthus with consistently plane leaves; the other, M. alopecuroides, is a taller plant with congested spikes of 40 to 80 flowers and broader leaves mostly 5-12 mm wide. The flowers of M. simplex are the smallest in the genus, the perianth tube just 3 mm long and the short anthers ± 2.5 mm long. The short, undivided style branches, ± 1 mm long, are likewise unusual for Micranthus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Micranthus thereianthoides closely resembles M. plantagineus and M. tubulosus in its cylindric leaves but is unique in the genus in the relatively large floral bracts, 8-11 mm long, and most strikingly in its dark violet flowers with elongate, cylindric perianth tube 22-25 mm long, thus ± twice as long as the bracts. The species appears never to develop cormlets in the floral bract axils.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: When first collected, Hesperantha secunda was referred to H. pilosa because of its pilose leaves and the scale-like bract in the upper third of the stem. However, its unusual, somewhat fleshy leaves with thickened to winged margins and thickened main vein, and nearly secund spike, prompted a reappraisal of its status and it is now regarded as a separate species, perhaps most closely allied to H. pilosa. In addition to its unusual leaves, the flowers are nodding on a curved perianth tube and have unusually short, ascending style branches, ± 4 mm long. Hesperantha pilosa has plane to ribbed leaves (or rarely terete or with slightly winged margins) and upright flowers with a straight perianth tube, tepals 9-16 mm long vs. 10-11 mm in H. secunda and longer style branches, 7-11 mm long, spreading laxly over the tepals. Flowers of H. secunda open at sunset, the tepals beginning to unfold at ± 17:00 and fully expanded by 18:00, remaining open until the early hours of the morning. The strong scent has a slightly unpleasant acrid component.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A dwarf plant, reaching no more that 20 mm high, including the flowers. The small leaves are distinctive, having broad, membranous sheaths and falcate, channelled blades with obtuse apices. The hyaline margins are minutely ciliate and the blades have a thickened ridge in the midline of the abaxial surface. A remarkable feature not known in any other species of Moraea is that the floral bracts are elongate, membranous, and ± as long as the leaves, thus visible as pale filamentous threads among the leaf blades The small flowers have outer tepals ± 14 mm long, with filaments united in the lower half, and with broad style branches and erect, petaloid crests. It is evidently most closely related to M. falcifolia, which has a similar habit but is a larger plant with larger flowers, the outer tepals mostly 18-22 mm long, and longer, often twisted, tapering leaves up to 100 mm long with acute tips.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A typical member of subg. Vieusseuxia in its solitary basal leaf and 3-lobed inner tepals. The purple flowers are assumed to be long-lasting and the outer tepal limbs have narrow, white, wedge-shaped nectar guides edged with dark purple. The inner tepals have unusually broad, 3-lobed limbs with a prominent, linear, reflexed central cusp and rounded lateral lobes. The flowers in general recall M. decipiens, particularly in the flower colour and shape but have much longer filaments, ± 8 mm long vs. 3.5-4.0 mm in M. decipiens, a style ± 5 mm long (vs. ± 2 mm) and shorter tepal claws, 5-6 mm (vs. 8-9 mm). The relatively long style branches are held well above the subtending outer tepals limbs, whereas in M. decipiens the style branches are appressed to the tepal claws and the inner tepals curve upward rather than having reflexed limbs with the central cusp directed downward. Additional collections of this rare species are needed to confirm current observations based on limited material.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The pale yellow flowers with relatively well-developed style branches and short, erect crests and, in particular, the filaments free distally for a short distance are somewhat unusual for subg. Homeria and recall Moraea pallida and M. cookii, also with a solitary foliage leaf. The spreading tepals twisted distally through ± 45º of M. doleritica are also found in M. cookii and M. pallida. Both M. cookii and M. pallida have a relatively broad leaf clasping the lower part of the stem, thus rather different to the particularly long, narrowly channelled, and relatively rigid, tough, fibrous leaf of M. doleritica. The range of M. doleritica in the Great Karoo is complimentary to that of M. cookii and M. pallida, with M. cookii extending from the Cederberg in Western Cape through the mountains of the Karoo to Lesotho, and M. pallida occurring across the Upper Karoo through Free State to Mpumalanga.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Known only from the Farm Vleiland in the northern foothills of the Klein Swartberg Mtns in Western Cape, South Africa; on clay slopes. Diagnosis: the relatively small, pale yellow flowers of Moraea eburnea have moderately well-developed, flattened style branches terminating in unusually broad stigmatic lobes and short, erect crests somewhat unusual in subg. Homeria, as are the filaments, united in a smooth, cylindric column ± 4 mm long but free and diverging in the upper 1 mm. The distally free filaments and moderately well-developed style branches suggest that M. eburnea may be most closely related to the M. pallida group.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A distinctive species, readily recognised by its dwarf, creeping habit, simple leaves with solitary flower per leaf tuft, and narrow, ligulate petals with unbranched veins.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2013. The native and naturalised species of Peltocalathos and Ranunculus (Ranunculaceae: Ranunculeae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 43(2): 179-195. [CC BY]

description: E. erecta is the most widespread of all Ehrharta's and its spikelet size and basal hairiness gradually increases northwards from the south-western Cape.
bibliographicCitation: Mashau, AC. 2015. Ehrharta Thunb. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 243-260. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unique in the genus, Hesperantha kiaratayloriae has the style extending well beyond the mouth of the perianth tube and overtopping the anthers, these also unusual in being parallel and contiguous. The stamens thus enclose the style, which divides immediately below the anther tips into upright, loosely twisted branches sometimes interlaced around one another. The margins of the floral bracts are united basally for up to 2 mm, and the bell-shaped corm with a flat base place the species in sect. Radiatae. Also unusual in the section for the pink flowers and leaves dry at flowering, H. kiaratayloriae mostly closely resembles H. muirii, which also has twisted style branches and relatively short leaf blades but larger, white or rarely pale pink flowers with the style dividing at the mouth of the perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Lessertia amajubica is similar to L. harveyana, L. stricta and especially L. excisa, but differs from these species in the subcapitate inflorescence, the short leaves and leaflets, the strigose vestiture of the stems, leaves and calyx, shape and relative length of the calyx lobes, and especially in the hairy ovary and markedly inflated, sparsely hairy fruits. The calyx lobes in L. amajubica are triangular-oblong, 2-3 mm long and ± twice as long as the tube; in Lessertia excisa the calyx lobes are broadly triangular, 1-2 mm long, and the tube 1 mm long; in L.harveyana narrowly triangular, 3-4 mm long with tube 2 mm long and in Lessertia stricta broadly triangular, 1 mm long with tube 2-3 mm long. Lessertia harveyana is characterised by broad, obovate leaflets and obliquely depressed-ovate, glabrous fruits; L. stricta by long, oblong-lanceolate leaflets, lax inflorescences, long pedicels and long, obliquely obovoid-oblong, attenuate fruits; and L. excisa by its subfalcate, compressed fruits with black hairs on the calyx. Immature fruits of Lessertia excisa are almost identical to those of Lessertia amajubica in side view. It is critical to compare only mature fruits when identifying Lessertia species.
bibliographicCitation: Nkonki, T; Ngwenya, AM; Van Wyk, B-E. 2013. Fabaceae: A new species of Lessertia (Galegeae) from KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Bothalia 43(2): 222-225. [CC BY]

description: Albuca chartacea is easily identified by its 3-12 cm long epigeal neck of the bulb covered by dark brown papery leaf bases with prominent, sinuous, transversal ridges; the 3-5 glaucous, dark green, incurved-canaliculated to convolute leaves; and the ovate-apiculate capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Azorin, MM; Crespo, MB; Dold, AP. 2013. Stellarioides chartacea (Hyacinthaceae, Ornithogaloideae), a new species from the Eastern Cape Province in South Africa. Phytotaxa 85(1): 1-8. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.85.1.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Easily identified by the solitary oblong convex leaf, with erect thickened bristles of 0.6-0.8 mm long only on the upper side, and thickened and densely papillate margin, the tepals 8.5-13 mm long, and the ovate ovary with scarcely prominent longitudinal keels.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB; Dold, AP. 2013. Trimelopter craibii (Hyacinthaceae, Ornithogaloideae), a new species from the North West Province of South Africa. Phytotaxa 87(3): 50-60. [All rights reserved]

description: Ornithlogalum tanquanum is easily identified by the tepals olive-green with a broad white margin and dark nerves, the bracts up to 1/2 the length of fruiting pedicels, and the leaves mostly withered at the full anthesis. Ornithogalum xanthochlorum can be related to O. tanquanum on the basis of its robust habit, with stout inflorescence peduncle and flower pedicels, but it differs in its uniformly green-yellowish tepals, the cylindrical narrow inflorescence with bracts longer than pedicels in fruit. On the other hand, O. haalenbergense shares with O. tanquanum the tepals green with a white margin, but differs in its smaller flowers and inflorescence, with only 2-3 leaves per flowering stem, among other characters.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB. 2012. Ethesia tanquana (Ornithogaloideae, Hyacinthaceae), a new species from the Tanqua Karoo (South Africa), with notes on E. haalenbergensis. Anales Jard. Bot. Madrid 69(2): 201-208. [doi: 10.3989/ajbm. 2311] [All rights reserved]

description: P. pallidoflavum is a small geophyte with simple, prostrate leaves and relatively large pale yellow flowers (hence the specific epithet), long hypanthia (27-50 mm long) and five fertile stamens concealed in the floral sheath. The spathulate petals and the very short fertile stamens are similar to those of P. pinnatum and about 30 other species of section Hoarea. P. pallidoflavum shares its simple prostrate leaves and yellow flowers with the short stamens with P. aestivale (Karoo, summer rainfall region; 2n = 18), P. weberi (southern Cape, Riversdale area; 2n = 44), P. nervifolium (Calvinia and Sutherland; 2n = 20), P. flavidum (Hex River Valley, species with fragile leaves) and P. ladysmithianum (Little Karoo; species with fragile leaves, becoming papery-membranous when dry; 2n = 20). P. pallidoflavum can be identified by its spathulate to narrowly spathulate petals (with the length/width ratio of 4.5-12 for the posterior petals), long smallheaded glandular hairs on the scape, peduncle and hypanthia and appressed coarse hairs on the petioles and along margins of the laminae. The laminae are without glandular hairs on both the abaxial and adaxial surfaces.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM. 2014. One name change and three new species of Pelargonium, section Hoarea (Geraniaceae) from the Western Cape Province. S. African J. Bot. 90: 118-127. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2013.10.013] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2014); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: P. weberi is a small geophyte with simple, prostrate leaves and large pale yellow flowers, long hypanthia (45-58 mm long) and five fertile stamens concealed in the floral sheath. The spathulate petals and the very short stamens are similar to those of P. pinnatum and about 30 other species of section Hoarea. Pelargonium weberi shares its simple prostrate leaves and the yellow flowers with short stamens with P. aestivate, P. pallidoflavum, P. nervifolium, P. flavidum and P. ladysmithianum. P. weberi, P. aestivale, P. pallidoflavum and P. nervifolium, are robust plants unlike the delicate plants of P. flavidum and P. ladysmithianum. P. weberi can be identified by its spathulate petals (with the length/width ratio of 2.5-3 for the posterior petals), small headed glandular hairs on the peduncle, scape and laminae, and long soft patent hairs on the petioles and along margins of the laminae. Non-glandular hairs are visible to the naked eye.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM. 2014. One name change and three new species of Pelargonium, section Hoarea (Geraniaceae) from the Western Cape Province. S. African J. Bot. 90: 118-127. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2013.10.013] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2014); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from Drimia uniflora by the larger, ± pear-shaped bulb with a well-developed, wrinkled collar, the slightly larger flowers, 6-7 mm long with lanceolate tepal lobes ± 2 mm long, and by the distinctive capsules, cylindrical-prismatic, 4-6 mm long, and strikingly bicoloured, coloured dull greyish green with broad, whitish longitudinal bands along the carpel sutures. The pedicels elongate significantly in fruit, reaching 5-8 mm long. Plants appear to consistently produce a solitary leaf. Successive inflorescences may be produced if conditions are favourable.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Similar to var. marlothii, which has hairy nodes and hairs in the axils of the inflorescence branches.

description: Often misidentified as Eulophia welwitschii, which differs in having the lip midlobe rotund to oblate with crests mostly absent on the distal half, larger flowers, a stout gynostemium, and the flowers pale yellow with the lip side lobes dark reddish purple.
bibliographicCitation: Kurzweil, H; Linder, HP. 1999. Orchids of Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam. [All rights reserved]

description: Not well differentiated from subsp. barbata, which is common along the east coast of the Cape.

description: The spikelets of the two subspecies cannot be distinguished from each other, inflorescence shape being the main character used although it tends to intergrade. Thus there are some plants that cannot be referred to with certainty to either subspecies. In this treatment, pending further studies, specimens with very dense inflorescences, with branches closely adpressed and covering the main axis, occasionally interrupted at the base by 1-2 spreading branches are included in this subspecies. Resembles A. hordeacea, which has culm internodes pubescent and column absent, and A. hubbardiana, which has the lemma articulation absent.

description: Resembles A. stipitata subsp. stipitata, which has lower culm nodes glabrous or hairy but not woolly.

description: Separated from var. chaunantha, which has culm internodes hairy, but a detailed study is needed to determine if the taxa are really different.

description: Resembles var. wilmaniae, which has an eglandular inflorescence, glumes shorter than or equal to lemma directly above; and E. procumbens, which has a persistent rachilla (becoming fragile in upper part), breaking up after lower lemmas have started to fall.

description: With a solitary, twisted and trailing leaf with undulate to crisped margins, Moraea quartzicola appears to be closely allied to the Namaqualand species M. saxicola but is distinguished by its smaller stature, up to 150 mm high, and smaller spathes and flowers, the outer tepals 22-24 mm long with short claws 8-10 mm long, the limbs thus almost twice as long. Moraea saxicola, always a taller plant, rarely < 250 mm high, has inner rhipidial spathes 40-60 mm long (vs. 25-30 mm), and outer tepals 30-40 mm long with the claws about as long as the limbs. Other floral parts of M. saxicola are likewise larger that those of M. quartzicola.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differs from subsp. villosipes, which has a contracted inflorescence with branches adpressed to main axis. Resembles E. desolata, which has basal sheaths glabrous or hairy, but not woolly-hairy, leaf blades 0.5-2.5 mm wide and anthers 1.2-1.3 mm long. Similar to E. racemosa, which has basal sheaths glabrous or hairy, but not densely woolly-hairy.
bibliographicCitation: Fish, L. 2015. Eragrostis Wolf. In: L Fish, AC Mashau, MJ Moeaha & MT Nembudani (eds), Identification guide to the southern Africa grasses. An identification manual with keys, descriptions and distributions, Strelitzia 36: 281-338. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Its nearest affinity is with H. attenuata.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: This species appears to be most closely related to H. herrei, but it differs from that species by the shorter and narrower, smooth leaves, as compared with the tubercled leaves of H. herrei; the two species may also be separated by the distinct differences in their floral characters. H. herrei has a longer peduncle and a shorter raceme than H. glauca.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: H. nigra shows affinities with two species, H. tessellata and H. viscosa. From the first, H. tessellata, it differs in the absence of the tessellated network of the pellucid upper surface, and the marginal teeth observed in H. tessellata. The upper surface in H. nigra is flatly convex, with uniformly coloured tubercles. From the second, H. viscosa, it differs in that it is a shorter plant, with the lower surface rounded, rough with crowded, uniformly coloured tubercles.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Its nearest affinity seems to be with H. tuberculata but it differs from that species by the smooth, little raised, transverse rows of confluent tubercles, observed only on the lower surface. There is also a difference in the inflorescence of the two species. H. scabra has a branched inflorescence, while H. tuberculata has a simple inflorescence. However, in most respects the two species are obviously different, and their identification should present no problems.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: H. sordida shows affinities with two species, H. scabra Haw. and H. tuberculata V. Poelln. From the first, H. scabra, it differs in having fewer, shorter, and hardly curved leaves, and a simple inflorescence with fewer flowers and about 6 sterile bracts. From the second, H. tuberculata, it differs in that H. tuberculata is a taller plant with longer curved lanceolate leaves, and there are more and larger pointed tubercles on the upper and back surfaces of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: H. tessellata should be regarded as a separate species because only the branched tesselate lines on the upper surface of the leaves are common to both species, while the remainder of the morphological and floral characters of H. venosa are readily separable from those of H. tessellata. The distribution of H. venosa is confined to the wetter parts of the south western Cape Province, while H. tessellata is distributed widely in the drier areas of the central parts of South Africa. The nearest affinity of H. tessellata is with H. venosa which is well separated in a higher rainfall area, and is characterized by its branched, free, upper surface lines, and non-stoloniferous nature.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Resembling Gymnanthemum capense in its membranous, broadly ovate leaf blades but distinguished by the rounded to broadly obtuse base with shorter petiole, 3-4 mm long, and the slightly more numerous teeth (± 5 per side) that are broader than long.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Gymnanthemum Cass. (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 102: 81-101. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2015.07.015] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: This description was based on material former classified as Gorteria corymbosa. Gorteria warmbadica is distinguished from G. corymbosa by the number of ray florets i.e. 13 and 8 respectively, the shape and phyllary coverage of the involucre, their distributions and different flowering periods. The absence of dark spots on the ray florets distinguishes Gorteria warmbadica from G. diffusa.
bibliographicCitation: Stangberg, F; Anderberg, AA. 2014. Morphology and taxonomic reclassification of Gorteria (Asteraceae). Willdenowia 44: 97-120. [http://dx.doi.org/10.3372/wi.44.44112] [All rights reserved]

description: The bracts of I. glandulosissima are narrowly elliptic and acute. They are as long as or longer than the calyx, and are covered with dense glandular trichomes that have three long cells and a terminal short cell in the stalks. The compact inflorescence with opposite flowers separates I. glandulosissima from I. prolixa which has a single flower at most inflorescence nodes and usually a markedly interrupted inflorescence. The bracts of I. delicatula are similar in length, but are narrower (1.3 ±0.9 mm rather than 3.2 ±0.7 mm wide and linear or lanceolate rather than narrowly elliptic) and the inflorescence is interrupted. I. woodii may have a dense inflorescence like I. glandulosissima, but it has ovate to obovate bracts with a markedly acuminate tip.
bibliographicCitation: Balkwill, K; Sebola, RJ; Poriazis, DL. 2017. Taxonomic revision of white-flowered Isoglossa Oerst. (Acanthaceae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 108: 48-80. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2016.09.013] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2017); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: This is one of two species of Aloe (the other being A. fibrosa from Kenya) to have distinct fibres in the leaves. Its large, distichous, leathery, linear, obtuse leaves, stemless habit and capitate racemes of flowers with long perianths and included anthers and styles distinguish this species from all others in the genus. Evidently the leaves of this species reminded Marloth and Berger of those of a Haemanthus (a well-known genus of bulbous plants).
bibliographicCitation: Glen, HF; Hardy, DS. 2000. Aloe. In: G Germishuizen & E du Plessis (eds), Aloaceae (first part), Fl. S. Africa 5(1,1): 1-167. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209564#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Gasteria loedolffiae is at once distinguished by its dark pink flowers 27-29 mm long, its matt dull-green leaf surface of spreading leaves and its juvenile leaves of which the surface is minutely asperulous. Superficially it resembles G. croucheri, the latter with much different and larger flowers. Gasteria loedolffiae belongs to section longiflorae Haw. series longifoliae Haw., which now includes five species, G. acinacifolia (J.Jacq.) Haw., G. batesiana, G. croucheri (Hook.f.) Baker, G. tukhelensis and the new species. All these species have large flowers (33-45 mm long) that are gasteriform over half of the perianth length. G. batesiana, a smaller species occurring to the north, has shorter, distinctly tuberculate, recurved leaves, smaller, curved flowers and smaller fruiting capsules. G. tukhelensis is confined to the Thukela River in KwaZulu-Natal. Gasteria croucheri occurs widespread to the south with a dull to slightly glaucous surface. In size it resembles G. loedolffiae with ascending, spreading to pendent leaves 200-360 mm long. In G. Croucheri the inflorescence is a flat-topped panicle flowering from November to February, whereas in G. loedolffiae the side branches are ascending. G. croucheri is found from Durban southwards to the Msikaba River in Eastern Cape (Transkei region). Gasteria loedolffiae grows solitary or forms clusters by offshoots of up to 5 plants.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2014. Gasteria loedolffiae (Asphodelaceae). A new cliff-dwelling species from the Eastern Cape, South Africa. Bradleya 32: 44-49. [https://doi.org/10.25223/brad.n32.2014.a18] [All rights reserved]

description: The new species differs from G. kraussii (Hilliard 1977) in its upper leaf surface being pilose rather than velvety pubescent, in its leaf base never contracting into a winged petiole, and in its pappus that is whitish rather than violet-purple. It differs from G. ambigua (Hilliard 1977) in presenting strongly raised veins below, in lacking underground stolons, and in holding the blades of its much larger leaves more or less horizontal rather than angled.
bibliographicCitation: Johnson, IM; Crouch, NR; Edwards, TJ. 2014. Gerbera sylvicola (Asteraceae: Mutisieae), a new forest species from KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Phytotaxa 186(4): 229-235. [DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.186.4.7] [All rights reserved]

description: Recognized by its moderately dense raceme of cernuous, oblong campanulate, brownish mauve flowers with disc-shaped perianth tubes, inner tepals that scarcely protrude and outer tepals with prominent purplish brown gibbosities. It has well exserted, more or less straight stamens and pedicels that change orientation after flowering, becoming strongly decurved during the fruiting stage. The plant is further recognized by a solitary, broadly lanceolate, glaucous leaf with strongly coriaceous margins, a strongly inflated peduncle and rachis and an ovoid seed with a glossy testa and an inflated strophiole.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD; Helme, NA. 2014. Lachenalia arenicola (Asparagaceae: Scilloideae), a new species from western South Africa. Phytotaxa 186(5): 297-300. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.186.5.8] [All rights reserved]

description: A feature that most easily distinguishes Pauridia breviscapa is the very short scape (up to 20 mm long) which is usually entirely hidden by the leaves, often leading to the inflorescence bracts being mistaken for newly emerging leaves. The softly fibrous corm, together with the thin-textured leaves and lanceolate bracts, and black seeds in which the testa has longitudinally arranged rows of laterally widened cells, suggest a close alliance with P. umbraticola, found on the mountains of the Olifants River Valley to the west. The two species differ from each other in the relative lengths of the scape, pedicels and filaments. In P. breviscapa the scape reaches up to 20 mm long, the pedicels are 50-175 mm long, the outer filaments are 1.2-1.5 mm and the inner are 1.5-1.7 mm long. The contrasting states in P. umbraticola are: scape 25-65 mm long, pedicels 20-55 mm long, outer filaments 2.5-3.0 mm long and inner filaments 3.0-3.5 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 2014. A taxonomic revision of the genus Pauridia (Hypoxidaceae) in southern Africa. Phytotaxa 182(1): 1-114. [All rights reserved]

description: Differs from G. batesiana by its ascending spreading densely white-tuberculate leaves 120-170 x 22-38 mm, and denticulate margin with tubercles 1-1.5 mm. Gasteria barbae grows prolifically from the base, solitary or forming small clusters. It is at once distinguished from G. batesiana by its matt grey-green ascending, patent leaves and different flowers. The leaves of Gasteria barbae are very brittle and detached leaves are commonly found in habitat, most of which form roots and new plantlets, a vegetative propagation ‘back-up’ commonly associated with cliff-dwelling succulent plants. To the east and west of our new species, Gasteria acinacifolia, a much larger related species with smooth adult leaves and a spreading paniculate inflorescence, grows mostly associated with sandy dune vegetation. To the north, Gasteria polita, another Fynbos species, grows on steep hilly terrain bearing smooth leaves and shorter flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2014. Gasteria barbae, a new cliff-dwelling species from the Western Cape, South Africa. Cact. World 32(4): 257-260. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/44082355] [All rights reserved]

description: Psoralea vanberkelae is a recently described member of the P. pinnata complex. Like P. muirii it has distinctive raised glands (pustules) on its clasping, tightly packed leaves; persistent stipules which become woody on old seasonal shoots; bare and rough old stems and branches; and a resprouting mode of regeneration after fires. It however differs from P. muirii in its shorter stature of a sprawling, mounding and colonial suffrutex habit to 60 cm tall and up to 1.5 m wide (versus erect shrub to 1.5(-2) m tall, 0.5 m wide); glabrous, fleshy, green and congested 5-foliolate leaves with large mounded glands (versus glabrescent, non-fleshy, bluish green, 5-7-foliolate, flexible leaves with distinctly warty glands); and many, pale to intense mauve to blue flowers in congested pseudo-inflorescences (versus mauve, fewer, less congested pseudo-inflorescence flowers).
bibliographicCitation: Bello, A; Stirton, CH; Chimphango, SBM; Muasya, AM. 2017. Taxonomic revision of African Psoralea pinnata species complex (Psoraleeae, Leguminosae). S. African J. Bot. 112: 128-179. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2017); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Similar to Disa amoena from which it can be distinguished by the shorter spur and the smaller flowers; and to Disa montana from which it can be distinguished by smaller and differently shaped petals, and by the much shorter inflorescence with fewer flowers.
bibliographicCitation: McMurtry, DM; Bytebier, B. 2015. Disa staerkeriana (Orchidaceae): A new species from Mpumalanga, South Africa. Phytotaxa 203(2): 192-198. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.203.2.9] [All rights reserved]

description: Indigofera magnifica is morphologically similar and most closely related to I. meyeriana Eckl. & Zeyh., but differs in its prostrate, compact, densely matted habit (vs. laxly spreading, less dense and diffuse habit), sparsely to moderately strigose becoming reddish-maroon and glabrescent stems (vs. green-grey to canescent), fewer flowers (±3-8) per raceme (vs. >8), brighter, more vivid pink flowers (vs. paler pink), and sparsely, appressed hairy pods (vs. spreading hairy pods). The overall colour of plants of I. magnifica is a darker green than the generally grey-green to grey appearance of I. meyeriana.
bibliographicCitation: Clark, VR; Schrire, BD; Barker, NP. 2015. Two new species of Indigofera L. (Leguminosae) from the Sneeuberg Centre of Floristic Endemism, Great Escarpment (Eastern and Western Cape, South Africa). PhytoKeys 48: 29-41. [https://doi.org/10.3897/phytokeys.48.4798] [All rights reserved]

description: Hermas lanata can be distinguished from the similar H. gigantea and H. intermedia by the cream-coloured sepals, felty involucral and involucellar bracts and peduncle (shared with H. intermedia) and the firmer, cordate leaves with a long shaggy indumentum.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; De Villiers, BJ; Van Wyk, B-E; Tilney, PM. 2015. A revision of the South African genus Hermas (Apiaceae). Syst. Bot. 40(1): 352-365. [DOI 10.1600/036364415X686639] [All rights reserved]

description: There appear to be two forms of this species. The broad-leaved form, which is restricted to the Bredasdorp area, differs from the typical form by having broader leaflets (up to 15 mm wide vs. up to 6 mm wide), longer petioles (up to 45 mm long opposed to 20 mm long), and inflorescences (80 mm long vs. 50 mm long). The non-twining, spreading habit of R. smithiana is similar to that of both R. ferulaefolia and R. pinnata, from which it differs by having trifoliolate leaves. Although R. pinnata sometimes has trifoliolate leaves, these leaves usually co-occur with the 2-3-jugate ones. It is this variation in leaflet number in both these taxa that has resulted in their sometimes being confused with R. ferulaefolia.
bibliographicCitation: Moteetee, AN; Boatwright, JS; Jaca, T. 2014. A review of Rhynchosia section Polytropia  (Phaseoleae, Fabaceae) and a new species from the Western Cape Province, South Africa. Syst. Bot. 39(4): 1127-1131. [https://doi.org/10.1600/036364414X683859] [All rights reserved]

description: One of few species of subg. Umbellatae with leaves basal and cauline rather than crowded at the first aerial node, Moraea orthrosantha has a flower typical of the genus, with well-developed style branches and crests and nectar guides only on the outer tepals. The flowers are dull yellow with conspicuous dark veins and closely resemble those of M. margaretae. As the specific epithet suggests, flowers open soon after sunrise and collapse about noon (Greek, orthros = morning, anthos = flower). The flowers of most species of subg. Umbellatae open in the mid- to late morning and wilt and collapse in the late afternoon, and only a few other examples of morning flowering phenology are known in Moraea, notably in M. vlokii and three Namaqualand species of subg. Homeria, M. flexicaulis, M. knersvlaktensis and M. schlechteri. Records for M. margaretae, with which M. orthrosantha is most easily confused, indicate flowers open midmorning and collapse toward sunset.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Berkheya dumicola is an unusually large, shrubby species in a genus dominated by perennial herbs. The shrubby habit, radiate heads and relatively broad leaves are most consistent with Berkheya series Fruticosae Roessler, but members of this series are characterised by entire or shortly toothed (rarely fringed) receptacle alveolar margins, densely hairy cypselae with the silky hairs often long (up to 4 mm), and a biseriate pappus of lanceolate or subulate scales. The conspicuously fimbriate, serrate-toothed alveolar margins, shortly pubescent cypselae with twin-hairs and uniseriate pappus of short, obtuse scales set B. dumicola apart from members of series Fruticosae. Only one other Berkheya species shares this unusual combination of characters: the recently described Berkheya chrysanthemoides from the nearby central Bokkeveld. Berkheya dumicola differs from B. chrysanthemoides in having leaves that are broader (20 mm-50 mm in B. dumicola; 15 mm-30 mm in B. chrysanthemoides), lack marginal spines (both species have spines on the lacinia apices but B. chrysanthemoides also possesses smaller antrorse spines along the margins) and are conspicuously tomentose on their abaxial surfaces (contrasting with the abaxially glabrous leaves of B. chrysanthemoides). The capitula of B. dumicola are smaller (20 mm-35 mm in B. dumicola; 40 mm-50 mm in B. chrysanthemoides) and clustered together in larger groups (three to ten in B. dumicola; one to three in B. chrysanthemoides).
bibliographicCitation: Bergh, NG; Helme, NA. 2014. A new species of Berkheya (Asteraceae, Arctotideae) from the Northern Cape, South Africa. Bothalia - ABC 44(1): 1-5. [http://dx.doi.org/10.4102/abc.v44i1.123] [CC BY]

description: Monechma saxatile is characterised by the asymmetrical, T-shaped type of modified anvil hair. The head is flatter and much broader in relation to the stalk than in either M. crassiusculum or M. robustum and is only lightly sculptured, if at all.
bibliographicCitation: Munday, J. 1995. 6. Monechma. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 30(3,1): 47-61. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the several, narrow, deeply pleated, suberect leaves, a blue-mauve, purple-pink, or cream-coloured to pale yellow perianth and a narrow, but partly hollow perianth tube that usually contains nectar. The stamens are unilateral and suberect with sagittate anthers that have the connective expanded in the lower half, and a short style that divides opposite the base of the anthers. Although the tepals are subequal, the lower (adaxial three) have contrasting markings and the lower lateral tepals, and, sometimes along with the dorsal, may be cream-coloured, in contrast to the other tepals which may be bluish.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Massonia bakeriana is at first sight related to M. echinata and M. mimetica based on flower and leaf morphology. However, Massonia bakeriana differs from both latter species by the reflexed free portions of perigone segments at anthesis, lacking a strong sigmoid curve at the base; the wide open, funnel-shape mouth of the perigone-filaments tube lacking gibbosities, where the ovary is visible in apical view; the longer filaments and ovary; and the style usually bend in the apical portion.
bibliographicCitation: Pinter, M; Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB; Wetschnig, W. 2015. Massonia bakeriana (Asparagaceae, Scilloideae), a new pustulate species from the Northern Cape Province (South Africa). Phytotaxa 222(1): 51-60. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.222.1.5] [All rights reserved]

description: Ixia macrocarpa, the second acaulescent species known in Ixia, has long-tubed, pale yellow flowers with dark markings at the base of the tepals. Despite the shared acaulescent habit, it may not be closely allied to I. acaulis, the other acaulescent species of the genus, restricted to rocky outcrops of limestone and marble in the Knersvlakte southwest of Loeriesfontein. Ixia macrocarpa differs in having broader, falcate leaves arranged in a tight fan, filaments united in a column enclosing the style, and diverging anthers. The pale yellow flowers have the tepals marked dark red-brown at the bases. Ixia acaulis has narrow, spreading to prostrate leaves, and uniformly yellow flowers with the style dividing opposite the bases of free filaments, and parallel anthers. Seeds of I. macrocarpa are smooth and unusually large, ± 3 mm diam.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinctive in the marshy habitat, unique for the genus, and also stands out in its tall stature, up to 480 mm high, the long, linear, soft-textured leaves, and the unusually lax spikes of only one to three flowers. The flowers are white with the outer tepals coloured grey-brown in the middle section and the tepals are narrowly elliptic, ± 16 x 4 mm. Flowers open after dark, 19:00 and appear unscented or at best weakly scented. The capsules are unusually large, up to 14 mm long. Hesperantha palustris is perhaps most closely related to the widespread H. cucullata, a shorter species with firm to almost leathery leaves and the outer tepals of the white flowers usually bright, glossy red outside, with the dark pigment usually covering the entire outer surface. Flowers of H. cucullata open well before sunset, mostly 16:00-16:30, and then produce a strong, sweet odour. The tepals are relatively broader than in H. palustris, usually 12-16 mm long and at least a third to nearly half as wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Small and inconspicuous Hesperantha filiformis stands up to 150 mm high and has lax spikes of 1 to 3 small flowers with a particularly slender perianth tube about 12 mm long and tepals about 11 x 5 mm. Plants consistently have only three leaves, the lower two basal and the uppermost inserted in the lower third of the stem and sheathing for about half its length. The white flowers are closed during daylight hours so that only the dull grey-brown reverse of the outer tepals is then visible. The flowers open after dark between 19:00 and 19:30 and then have a mild, sweet odour. The ovoid corms are slightly asymmetric, being flattened on one side, with the woody, dark brown tunics typical of sect. Concentricae. Its relationships are uncertain but possibly lie with the Namaqualand species H. flexuosa, which also consistently has three leaves, the uppermost partly sheathing the stem, but the somewhat fleshy leaves of this species are linear and no more than 1.5 mm wide. The firm-textured leaves of H. filiformis are 3-5 mm wide and have thickened margins and main vein, very different from those of H. flexuosa. Capsules of H. filiformis are surprisingly long for so small a plant, 10-11 mm long, but seeds are so far unknown.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately distinguished in subg. Vieusseuxia by the presence of two subequal foliage leaves inserted near the base and loosely coiled in corkscrew fashion. More than one foliage leaf is rare in the subgenus and consistent only in M. fergusoniae, which has three to six foliage leaves, the blades channelled, shorter than the stem and 3-10 mm wide, slightly twisted and with undulate, minutely ciliate margins. Moraea tripetala subsp. violacea sometimes has two foliage leaves but very different flowers with inner tepals represented by minute cusps. Flowers of M. helicoidea are predominantly white with outer tepals bearing large, deep yellow nectar guides at the limb bases and with small dark spots on the reverse. The brown inner tepals have reduced, 3-lobed limbs, common in the subgenus, and are comparable in shape to those of M. fergusoniae which has either pale blue or white flowers. Branching in M. fergusoniae is usually basal whereas branches in M. helicoidea, when present, are cauline, borne at the first aerial node.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Schoenoxiphium burttii is probably the largest species of the genus and its rich brown pendulous inflorescences make it a conspicuous feature.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1986. Notes on some plants of southern Africa chiefly from Natal: XIII. Notes Roy. Bot. Gard. Edinburgh 43(3): 345-405. [CC BY-SA]

description: A shrubs with glaucous branches and characteristic yellow-green longitudinal striations, solitary flowers and white drupes.
bibliographicCitation: Nickrent, DL; Garcia, MA. 2015. Lacomucinaea, a new monotypic genus in Thesiaceae (Santalales). Phytotaxa 224(2): 173-184. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.224.2.4] [All rights reserved]

description: A. fleckii is closely related to A. erubescens Welw. ex Oliv. and the two species are often confused. A. fleckii differs from A. erubescens in having: 1. Shorter petioles 0.3-1 cm long, occasionally to 1.3 cm; in A. erubescens the petioles are normally 1.3-2.5 cm long. Occasionally petioles shorter or longer than these dimensions occur but then the extremes usually occur on shoots with at least some petioles of more usual length. 2. A larger petiolar gland which is elliptic to discoid, 0.8-2.2 mm long; in A. erubescens the gland is often slightly raised and is 0.3-1 mm long. As the dimensions for the two species overlap, gland sizeis a less useful character. 3. The leaf-rhachis without a gland at the junction of any of the pinnae pairs; in A. erubescens a gland is usually present at the junction of some of the pinnae pairs or between the top pair only. 4. (4)8-20 pinnae pairs; A. erubescens has only 3-7 pinnae pairs; 5. straight, smaller leaflets; in A. erubescens the leaflets are usually somewhat falcate and larger. The above characters usually enable the twospecies to be readily distinguished. Another useful character is the tendency for A. fleckii to produce its inflorescences with or after the new leaves while A. erubescens often flowers when leafless.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The leaves of A. theronii have a robust, mat appearance, as the leaflets (pinnules) are relatively large and densely packed with a thick wax layer as seen under the electron microscope.
bibliographicCitation: Swartz, PP. 2003. Fabaceae: The correct name for Acacia montana. Bothalia 33(2): 164-165. [CC BY]

description: Important diagnostic features for the species that distinguish it from Lapeirousia plicata include outer floral bracts that are channelled throughout and not unifacial distally, and a stem produced up to 40 mm above ground. The flowers are recorded as being uniformly white, or in one collection yellowish, always lacking the blue or purple markings characteristic of L. plicata. The tepals, 10-14 mm long, and tube, 30-40 mm long, are somewhat longer than in L. plicata, which has tepals 7-10 mm long and a tube typically 12-20 mm long, rarely up to 35 mm. Significantly, L. plicata occurs within the range of L. kalahariensis but typically blooms there later in the year, in May and June, sometimes in July. Lapeirousia kalahariensis also shows a resemblance to L. odoratissima from southern tropical Africa, but that species has much larger flowers, the perianth tube 100-140 mm long, and a well-developed, strongly ribbed basal leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Taxonomically isolated in the genus, Codonorhiza falcata is distinguished by the spike-like inflorescence unlike the flat-topped false panicle in other species. The flowers are pale pink to ± white with dark pink to mauve or red markings on the lower tepals, colours unique in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Codonorhiza azurea is distinguished by its large, zygomorphic, intensely dark blue flower bearing large black or dark red blotches on the adaxial tepals. The perianth tube is 8-12 mm long and the tepals (12-)16-20 mm long. The flower is tilted back toward the axis, especially in crowded inflorescences, when the posterior (adaxial) tepals, usually erect, are tilted out of position and come to lie horizontally, thus below the abaxial (lower) tepals, a type of floral presentation also occurring in C. elandsmontana.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It shows marked discontinuities in its distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Levyns, MRB. 1954. The genus Muraltia. J. S. African Bot.: 1-247. [CC BY]

description: The crowded, ± flat-topped inflorescence of radially symmetric flowers with a pale to fairly dark blue perianth and white bracket-shaped marks in the lower middle of the tepals distinguish Codonorhiza corymbosa from other Codonorhiza species. Although small, the upright flowers are particularly attractive with their white star-shaped central marking. Codonorhiza corymbosa is most easily confused with C. elandsmontana from the Worcester and Tulbagh Districts, but that species has unilateral stamens, and although the perianth shape and colouration is similar, the flowers are larger and only the lower (abaxial) tepals have white markings. The perianth tube of C. elandsmontana is 8-10 mm long and the tepals 10-15 mm long (vs. a tube 4-7(8) mm long and tepals 6-10 mm in C. corymbosa). Confusion is also possible with the deep blue-flowered C. azurea, especially when specimens are poorly preserved, but the flowers and bracts of C. corymbosa are always smaller than those of C. azurea, the tepals of which are 17-20 mm long. When alive the larger, dark blue, zygomorphic, abaxially tilted flowers of C. azurea with unilateral, horizontally extended stamens are unmistakable.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differs from C. woodii by its larger sticky leaves of which the surface is covered with short translucent club-shaped glandular trichomes, and also its flowering time which is during winter and spring.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2015. Cotyledon gloeophylla, a new species from the Kouga River, Eastern Cape. Bradleya 33: 180-184. [https://doi.org/10.25223/brad.n33.2015.a24] [All rights reserved]

description: Senegalia montis-salinarum is most similar to S. burkei in general morphology. Senegalia montis-salinarum is a multistemmed tree growing on mountain scree slopes whereas S. burkei is a single-stemmed savannah tree never found sympatrically. Senegalia montis-salinarum has more leaflet pairs per pinna, averaging 4-6, measuring 6.0-7.6 x 1.7-2.2 mm opposed to those of S. burkei with 7.3-10.0 leaflet pairs per pinna, 7.3-10.7 x 3.0-4.7 mm in size. Senegalia montis-salinarum therefore has a higher leaflet length/width ratio than S. burkei. Senegalia montis- salinarum inflorescence spike length is on average 28.9-35.7 mm long opposed to 49.6-66.3 mm for S. burkei. The pods of Senegalia montis-salinarum has on average 4-8 seeds whereas S. burkei has only 3-5. A peculiar character of S. montis-salinarum is its soft, almost semi-succulent wood that decays quickly. In comparison the wood of S. burkei is hard and dense up to 910 kg m-3.
bibliographicCitation: Hahn, N. 2016. Senegalia montis-salinarum, a new species of Fabaceae: Mimosoideae endemic to the Soutpansberg, South Africa. Phytotaxa 244(2): 174-180. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.244.2.5] [All rights reserved]

description: Among the three species of Hilliardiella with silvery-silky vestiture, H. capensis is distinguished by its narrow, linear to linear-lanceolate leaves, 1-3 (-4) mm wide with revolute margins, typically with axillary tufts, the blades discolorous with the upper surface thinly silky or glabrescent and the lower surface densely silvery-silky. Hilliardiella elaeagnoides has broader leaves, lanceolate to broadly ovate, 5-20 mm wide and mostly up to twice as long as broad, never with axillary tufts. Both species have similar capitula with the inner involucral bracts elliptic-lanceolate and more or less abruptly contracted to a mucronate tip. Hilliardiella aristata, with leaves varying from linear to elliptic or rarely obovate and with both surface densely silvery-silky, has long-acuminate or attenuate involucral bracts smoothly narrowed to a bristle-like tip. Intermediates among all three species are known.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Hilliardiella (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 106: 41-59. description: The long-acuminate, bristle-tipped, recurved involucral bracts are reminiscent of some Athrixia, a character shared with P. fastigiata, a tropical species reaching the Zululand coastal plain. However, the bracts of P. fastigiata are more persistently white-woolly than those of P. gerrardii, and the innermost are more abruptly contracted to the tip than is usual in P. gerrardii. Moreover, P. fastigiata is a bushy annual herb, commonly growing as a roadside weed.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Hilliardiella flanaganii resembles Hilliardiella hirsuta in its relatively broad, oblong-elliptic to broadly obovate leaves with the upper surface sparsely pilose and the lower surface densely woolly-tomentose and prominently veined but is distinguished by the cuneate base narrowed into a short petiole 5 mm long, and the larger capitula with longer, lanceolate inner involucral bracts, 5-7 mm long gradually narrowed to a long-acuminate or pungent apex. The species favours moister places than does H. hirsuta and the two are often sympatric in the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg.

description: A recently discovered species evidently closely allied to Tritoniopsis parviflora but distinguished from it by the creamy white flowers with the apices and outer surface of the tepals flushed dark brownish pink. The tepals are linear, the dorsal 2.0-2.5 mm wide and the upper laterals ± 1.5 mm wide, and the filaments are relatively long, 15-16 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: It is most similar to A. spinosa, sharing with it sericeous leaves and two-flowered inflorescences, but differs in that it is not spinescent and has much shorter pedicels. However, the most diagnostic character of A. ornata is the ornate, imbricate, ovate calyx lobes.

description: It is closely allied to M. macrocarpa.

description: P. wuppertalense has cream-coloured to pale yellow flowers with narrowly spathulate petals and short stamens concealed in the floral sheath like P. pinnatum and about one third of the species of sect. Hoarea (Marais, 1994). It has relatively long hypanthia, 20-52 mm long. The species is highly variable in leaf incision, within a population or even in a single plant. Leaves vary from simple to tripartite to pinnatipartite. The pinnae are usually large and wide with obtuse apices, but finely divided leaves with narrow segments also occur. The pinnae or segments are lacking an apical hair or a tuft of hairs. Leaf incision in P. wuppertalense resembles that in P. luteopetalum although the pinnae of the latter are more regular in shape and size. The two species differ in the indumentum of the hypanthia. In P. wuppertalense the hypanthia are covered with appressed curly hairs interspersed with long glandular hairs whereas in P. luteopetalum the glandular hairs are short. P. wuppertalense also resembles P. aristatum, sharing with it the same indumentum on the leaves, scapes, peduncles, hypanthia and sepals. The petals of P. wuppertalense are spathulate or narrowly spathulate (posterior petals: 16.5-28 x 3-5 mm, length/width ratio 4-6), and those of P. aristatum are very narrow (posterior petals: 14-26 x 2-4 mm, length/width ratio 5-9) and can be describe as ligulate. P. aristatum has usually finely divided leaves, with lacinate segments ending in a single hair or tuft of hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM. 2015. Five new species of Pelargonium, section Hoarea (Geraniaceae), from the Western and Northern Cape Provinces of South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 103: 145-155. [CC BY]

description: P. flavipetalum has cream-coloured or pale yellow flowers, hence the specific epithet (Latin flavus, yellow) and pinnately divided leaves. The flowers with short stamens concealed in the floral sheath are similar to those of P. pinnatum. The indumentum on the scape, peduncle, hypanthium and sepals of appressed curly hairs, interspersed with long glandular hairs, is similar to that of P. aristatum, P. fissifolium and P. wuppertalense, but the indumentum on the leaves differs from the latter three species. The leaves of P. flavipetalum are sparsely covered with short glandular hairs and appressed non-glandular hairs, whereas the leaves of the other three species are covered only with appressed long stiff hairs, without glandular hairs. The leaf incision of P. flavipetalum corresponds to that of P. aristatum and P. fissifolium, but the form of the petals of the three species differs. The posterior petals of P. flavipetalum are widely obovate with a length/width ratio of 2-3, whereas those of P. fissifolium are spathulate with the length/width ratio of 3-5 and those of P. aristatum are narrow, almost ligulate with the length/width ratio of 5-9.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM. 2015. Five new species of Pelargonium, section Hoarea (Geraniaceae), from the Western and Northern Cape Provinces of South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 103: 145-155. [CC BY]

description: P. xanthopetalum has large yellow flowers (hence the specific epithet, Greek xantho, yellow) with five short fertile stamens concealed in the floral sheath similar to P. pinnatum and regularly pinnate to bi- or tri-pinnate leaves. The species has a characteristic indumentum on the scape, peduncles and hypanthia comprising short glandular hairs interspersed with long stiff patent hairs visible to the naked eye. Although P. xanthopetalum resembles P. flavipetalum and P. fissifolium in its yellow flowers with short stamens and pinnately divided leaves it differs with regard to the size of the flowers, the indumentum on the scape, peduncle and hyapanthia and in chromosome number. P. fissifolium has slightly smaller flowers than the other two species and the scape, peduncle and hypanthia ofP. flavipetalum and P. fissifolium are covered with ap- pressed curly hairs interspersed with long glandular hairs. The chromosome number of P. fissifolium is 2n = 18 (Gibby et al., 1996), that of P. flavipetalum 2n = 22 (Albers, pers. comm.) and that of P. xanthopetalum 2n = ca. 22. The indumentum in P. xanthopetalum is similar to that of Pelargonium ladysmithianum R.Knuth, a species with a similar floral structure to that of P. xanthopetalum, but with simple leaves arranged in a rosette.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM. 2015. Five new species of Pelargonium, section Hoarea (Geraniaceae), from the Western and Northern Cape Provinces of South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 103: 145-155. [CC BY]

description: Aspalathus eustonbrownii is a distinctive species that falls into Dahlgren's (1988) Group 34: Laterales. The species is similar to A. longifolia Benth., but differs in its leaflets 12-15 mm (versus 25-40 mm) long; calyx lobes 2.6-2.8 mm (versus <0.5 mm) long; and fruits broadly ovate (versus narrowly ovate).

description: With a filiform perianth tube and filaments inserted at the mouth of the narrow part of the perianth tube, Ixia alticola conforms closely to sect. Ixia. The pale mauve-pink flowers have a relatively long style, dividing opposite the lower third to middle of the anthers, indicating placement of I. alticola in series Longistylae. It stands out in the rather short, pale translucent bracts 4-6 mm long, tall stature (occasionally to 1 m tall) and spikes of up to 25 flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished from I. polystachya first by the long style, dividing opposite the lower third of the anthers, and the particularly long, erect anthers, (6-)7-8 mm long. Another important character is the particularly narrow leaves up to 1.5 mm wide, when dry with unusually prominent veins. Ixia polystachya is very different and may not even be closely allied to I. longistylis. It has broader leaves, sometimes up to 8 mm wide, the stems are often branched and the flowers typically have shorter anthers, mostly 4-6 mm long, usually spreading ± horizontally when flowers are fully open and the style typically divides opposite the base or sometimes the middle of the filaments. Flowers of I. longistylis are deep mauve-pink (or sometimes white) with a dark purple centre, a colour rare but not unknown in I. polystachya. Ixia longistylis may be most closely allied to broad-leaved I. mostertii, which has similar, relatively large flowers with long, ascending anthers up to 9 mm long and a style dividing opposite or above the bases of the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the narrow leaves, small corms with particularly soft tunics, either membranous or composed of fine, soft fibres and usually bearing slender stolons with a single terminal cormlet. The relatively short, stiff branches spread at a wide angle from the main stem and bear few flowers. Branches, usually produced in I. polystachya, in which collections of I. sarmentosa were often included (sometimes as var. lutea), are more-or-less upright and bear numerous flowers. The flowers of I. sarmentosa also consistently have short filaments, ± 2 mm long, and the style, pale green to pale yellow, divides opposite the base to middle of the short filaments, the style branches then extending outward between the filaments. Ixia polystachya has larger corms with well-developed fibrous tunics and does not produce stolons Flowers of Ixia sarmentosa are relatively large, especially in northern populations, the tepals mostly 17-22 x 8-10 mm, but in populations from the mountains around Stellenbosch and Somerset West the tepals are 12-16 x 5-7 mm. Other than the smaller flowers there appears to be no difference between these and the larger flowered plants.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Notobubon collinum shares the smaller habit, the shorter less divided leaves with only 2 or 3 pairs of lateral pinnule along the rachis and flattened leaf lobes with N. montanum. The two species have an allopatric distribution and N. collinum is readily distinguished by the leaf lobes with flat margins (revolute in N. montanum), the prominently raised veins on the adaxial surface of the lamina (prominently sunken in N. montanum), and the scabrid hairs on all parts of the compound umbel (only raylets and involucel covered in scabrid hairs in N. montanum). Notobubon collinum has also been confused with N. striatum in the past. Notobubon collinum can however be readily distinguished (see diagnostic notes latter on N. striatum) by the smaller habit (up to 0.4 m), the shorter, less divided leaves with only 2 or sometimes 3 pairs of lateral pinnules along the rachis, the flat leaf lobes and the large prominent sepals.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Curtis, O; van Wyk, B-E. 2016. A refined circumscription of Notobubon striatum and the resurrection of Dregea collina Ecklon & Zeyher (Apiaceae, Apioideae). Phytotaxa 266(1): 27-32. [All rights reserved]

description: Pelargonium conradiae is a member of a small group of species allied to P. hirtum and characterised by a subshrubby habit, pinnate leaves with bi- or tripinnatisect pinnae, and white or pink flowers with short hypanthia less than 15 mm long and seven fertile stamens. It is distinguished from other members of the group by the semi-persistent petiole bases with the stipules adnate to the petiole for half their length or more, and the relatively large, pure white (rarely tinged pale pink) flowers with petals 15-20 mm long, the posterior two petals ± twice as wide as the anterior three. Pelargonium crassipes and P. oreophilum from the Bokkeveld Mountains and Cederberg share similar, ± persistent petiole bases with P. conradiae but have smaller, pink to mauve flowers with darker markings on the posterior petals, and stipules that are adnate to the petioles for up to half their length only, becoming indurated and hook-like with age. P. oreophilum has characteristically narrow upper petals ± as wide as the anterior petals, and P. crassipes has deflexed, woody, strongly persistent, spine-like pedicels and stipules. P. hirtum, with consistently small flowers with petals ± 10 mm long, has herbaceous, scarcely persistent petioles, and often larger leaves, with blades and petioles mostly 20-50 mm long.

description: Its nearest affinity seems to be with H. nigra from which it differs in being a taller plant with leaves which are smooth or very slightly rugose.

description: Phymaspermum trifidum is closely related to P. thymelaeoides with which it shares the radiate heads, slightly fleshy, silvery sericeous leaves and hairy involucral bracts. Phymaspermum trifidum can however be distinguished by the consistently trifid leaves, the broad membranous appendages on the innermost involucral bracts and the glabrous disc floret tubes.

description: Phymaspermum aphyllum has in the past been incorrectly identified as P. junceum (Berg.) Less. (the latter now a synonym of Osteospermum junceum). It is a sparsely leafy shrub with caducous leaves, ± 0.5 mm wide, longitudinally white striped stems which are densely white wooly between the ribs and persistent peduncles which often become spinescent. It differs further from the closely related P. leptophyllum by the obviously ribbed cypselas with prominently stalked myxogenic trichomes. In P. leptophyllum the cypselas appear unribbed and the myxogenic trichomes appear sessile due to the prominently elongated epidermal cells.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: Phymaspermum comptonii shares the fleshy silver sericeous leaves with P. argenteum, but is here distinguished by the cyathiform to campanulate involucres and lanceolate, loosely appressed involucral bracts with prominent rounded, scarious appendages (involucres narrowly campanulate and involucral bracts tightly apressed with prominent brown margins in P. argenteum).

description: Previously included in Geissorhiza leipoldtii, largely due to the limited material then available, G. nutans is readily distinguished from that species by the somewhat smaller flowers with narrower tepals 14-16 x 3-6 mm long vs. 18-26 x 5-11 mm in G. leipoldtii and shorter, markedly unequal stamens. Vegetatively the two are almost indistinguishable, having sparsely and minutely ciliate stems, and three leaves, the lower two basal and the upper one cauline and largely sheathing and the leaf blades with narrowly winged, ciliate margins and main vein. The flowers are nodding with the stamens unilateral and horizontal to drooping with white anthers 4.5-6.0 mm long and the filaments are markedly unequal, the longer two 5-7 mm long and the shorter ± 3 mm long. Geissorhiza leipoldtii has larger, upright to half nodding flowers with tepals 19-26 mm long and stamens symmetrically arranged with anthers 7-8 mm long and filaments ± 7 mm long (or one up to 0.5 mm shorter). The differences in the filament length in G. nutans are striking, the upper filament about half as long as the lower two, thus unmistakable. The anthers and pollen of G. nutans are white whereas those of G. leipoldtii are bright yellow.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Shares the climbing habit, presence of root tubers, leaves with patent venation and purple abaxial surfaces, flowers with creamy to pale green inverted corollas, fusion of corona lobes and stamens, prominent vertical ridges and grooves on the style-head and unique linear pollen tetrads with P. natalensis. However, P. undulata is clearly distinguished from P. Natalensis by its slender growth form, narrowly undulate leaves, salver-shaped corolla, falcate corona lobes and hairy anther connectives.
