description: Cheiridopsis and its sister genera Odontophorus and Ihlenfeldtia are distinguished from other genera in Ruschieae by papillate leaves and multi-locular fruits (8 to 18 locules) with large or rarely small (Ihlenfeldtia) closing bodies. Similarly, the diagnostic characters to distinguish the three subgenera of Cheiridopsis from each other as well as from Ihlenfeldtia and Odontophorus are mainly found in the leaves and fruits. Common to these three genera are the papillate leaves which, however, show differences in the shape and density of the papillae. The leaves in C. alba-oculata are densely papillate, as found in Cheiridopsis pilosula and Cheiridopsis speciosa of C. subg. Odontophoroides and also in Odontophorus. C. alba-oculata cannot be confused with any member of C. subg. Cheiridopsis, since all members of the latter are heterophyllous (the first pair of leaves is shorter than the second pair). The other two subgenera of Cheiridopsis, as well as Odontophorus and Ihlenfeldtia, are isophyllous (both pairs of leaves are of the same length). In addition, the leaves are 30-80 mm long in C. alba-oculata, whereas they never exceed 50 mm in Odontophorus. Although the leaves in C. pilosula and Cheiridopsis ponderosa (both C. subg. Odontophoroides) may also reach 70-120 mm long, the leaves of C. pilosula lack teeth and, although the leaves of C. ponderosa may have tiny teeth near the apex, the keels are rounded. This contrasts with the leaves of C. alba-oculata, which are distinctly keeled with often quite prominent teeth along the keels and margins towards their tips, a feature also found in C. subg. Odontophoroides and in Odontophorus. It is uncommon for species of Cheiridopsis or Odontophorus to have distinctly two-coloured petaloid staminodes (white in the lower third and yellow in the two upper thirds). The flowers in both populations of C. alba-oculata are bi-coloured. This is otherwise known in C. pilosula, C. denticulata and Cheiridopsis caroli-schmidtii (Dinter & A.Berger) N.E.Br., which all include populations with unicoloured petaloid staminodes. All 14 species of Cheiridopsis subg. Cheiridopsis have mostly decumbent capsules. The other two subgenera, as well as Odontophorus, have predominantly erect capsules and this is also true of C. alba-oculata The new species shares with Odontophorus and Cheiridopsis the large closing bodies, whereas they are always small in Ihlenfeldtia. In addition, in terms of the shape of the fruits, the almost globose, rounded tops of C. alba-oculata are most similar to those of C. subg. Odontophoroides and of Odontophorus. In addition, the lower parts of the fruits are densely hairy. Although Hartmann (1976) suggested that the papillate (hairy) fruits of Odontophorus are one of the main characteristics separating this genus from Cheiridopsis, similarly hairy fruits are also found in C. ponderosa S.A. Hammer and in C. pilosula L. Bolus, where the papillae are shorter, also used this character in the key to separate the genera Cheiridopsis (‘base of capsule rough’) from Odontophorus (‘base of capsule velvety’). However, species with ‘velvety’ fruits such as C. ponderosa are nevertheless still included in Cheiridopsis. In addition, the terms ‘velvety’ and ‘rough’ are difficult to quantify and intermediates exist, as in the case of C. pilosula. The fruits of the new species can only be confused with members of Odontophorus or C. subg. Odontophoroides, but none of these occurs so far to the south. The seeds are smooth and pear-shaped in the new species, characteristics encountered in both Cheiridopsis and Odontophorus, both of which may also have more papillate seeds. The papillate seeds in C. pilosula distinguish this species from C. alba-oculata. The epithet ‘alba-oculata’ is derived from the latin albus = white and oculus = eye and alludes to the white centre of the flowers.

description: In M. cucullatus the involucre surrounding each axillary capitulum is asymmetrical due to an enlargement and elongation of the anterior involucral bracts to about twice or three times the length of the posterior bracts. The resultant structure is a 'bilabiate' involucre characteristic of M. cucullatus and the related M. fimbriifolius. Apart from very obvious differences in growth habit, the two species are readily distinguished by the fully mature leaves. In M. cucullatus they are shorter (22-55 mm long) and glabrous, while the leaves of M. fimbriifolius are longer (40-70 mm long) and thickly fringed with dense white cilia.

description: Mimetes fimbriifolius is readily distinguished from the related M. cucullatus by its arborescent growth habit and the presence of a thick fringe of white pubescence on the leaf margins. Moreover, the leaves are from 22-55 mm long in M. fimbriifolius, perceptibly longer than in M. cucullatus.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1984. A revision of the genus Mimetes Salisb. (Proteaceae). J. S. African Bot. 50(2): 171-236. [CC BY]

description: Among those Mimetes with enlarged red and yellow involucral bracts, axillary capitula containing more than five flowers, entire leaves and linear-subulate styles, M. hirtus is readily distinguished by its long styles which are generally 50 to 55 mm in length.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1984. A revision of the genus Mimetes Salisb. (Proteaceae). J. S. African Bot. 50(2): 171-236. [CC BY]

description: Mimetes hottentoticus could never be confused with any other species in the genus. It is clearly allied to Mimetes stokoei but is easily distinguished from that species by its lanceolate-acuminate involucral bracts and bushy, well-branched growth habit.

description: This species is distinguished by its pale yellow involucral bracts, glabrous on the outer surface, though with ciliate margins, by its yellow perianth and style and by its distinctive pollen presenter, cylindric-quadrangular basally and ovoid-acute terminally. description: Drosanthemum badspoortensis Van Jaarsv.sp. nov. differs from M. calycinum by its internodes lacking the long stiff hairs as well as the sharply pointed translucent bladder cells on the flower stalk and calyx as well as the rich cymose inflorescence and flowers with yellow petals.

description: Schlechteranthus connatus may be confused with S. abruptus as they share a similar leaf shape and size, but is distinguished by the longer central primary axis, which is at least three times longer than the capsule, and bracteoles persistent, present more than half way down the axis (primary axis equal to length of capsule and bracteole mostly at base of capsule in S. abruptus). The capsule itself is also markedly globose in S. connatus), as a result of the subglobose base and convex top, whereas in S. abruptus the base of the capsule is funnel-shaped and the top notprominently rounded. Schlechteranthus connatus also lacks the prominently velvety leaf surface of S. abruptus, and is only slightly velvety.

description: The most important diagnostic features of S. caudata are: the erect bushy habit of growth, with long erect, straight stems, the permanent pubescence of the leaves, or at least of the upper surface of the leaves, the long cylindric inflorescences (5-7 cm), and the densely lanate to villous perianth.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: This species is easily distinguished by the decussate leaves stacked along the branch and the old blackened leaves that remain on the branch. However, it may be confused with S. tetrasepalus, which shares a compact habit and leaf pairs with a high degree of fusion. Schlechteranthus inclusus is, however, further distinguished by the short central primary axis which is equal in length to the length of the capsule, and the cup-shaped bracteoles (primary axis at least one and a half times longer than capsule, leaves crowded towards the tip of the branches, with old leaves falling off, and bracteoles not cup-shaped in S. tetrasepalus).
bibliographicCitation: Powell, RF; Klak, C; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2017. A taxonomic revision of Schlechteranthus subgenus Microphyllus (Ruschieae; Aizoaceae). Syst. Bot. 42(4): 943-963. [DOI 10.1600/036364417X696429] [All rights reserved]

description: Apart from an occasional scattered hair on the bracteoles, the involucres are quite glabrous and are reddish to carmine and shiny in the living state. The glabrescence of the bracteoles together with the small size of the inflorescences (1-5 cm long), serve to distinguish 5'. colorata from the other sessile to subsessile involucred species with lanceolate acute bracteoles.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: Schlechteranthus pungens is most similar to S. stylosus, as both species are large shrubs (up to400 mm tall) with spines derived from aborted axillary buds but S. pungens differs with longer mostly oblong leaves in outline (shorter (1.5-2.0 mm) andovoid in S. stylosus). Although the spines are derived in a similar manner to S. stylosus, the spines in S. pungens are arranged in a compound cyme on the secondary axes while in S. stylosus the spines are arranged in a simple cyme on the secondary axes. Schlechteranthus pungens and S. spinescens share a similar leaf shape and their distributions overlap. However, S. pungens is distinguished by the spines that are arranged in a compound cyme and are derived from aborted axillary buds (spines arranged in simple cyme and derived from old pedicels where capsules have fallen off in S. spinescens).
bibliographicCitation: Powell, RF; Klak, C; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2017. A taxonomic revision of Schlechteranthus subgenus Microphyllus (Ruschieae; Aizoaceae). Syst. Bot. 42(4): 943-963. [DOI 10.1600/036364417X696429] [All rights reserved]

description: Among the species of Spatalla with three-flowered involucres, S. confusa is distinguished by the long perianth tube (4-5 mm), the sparsely sericeous perianth claws, the rather short inflorescence (1-2-5 cm), the glabrous branchlets and leaves, the glabrous bracts and bracteoles and the sprawling growth habit.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: Schlechteranthus spinescens is most similar to S. pungens as they have similar leaf shapes in outline and overlap in distribution. However, S. spinescens can be easily recognised by the different arrangement of spines and spine formation. In S. spinescens, the spines are arranged in a simple cyme with blunt spines derived from old pedicels where the capsules have fallen off , while in S. pungens the spines are arranged in a compound cyme, with sharp spines derived from aborted axillary buds.
bibliographicCitation: Powell, RF; Klak, C; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2017. A taxonomic revision of Schlechteranthus subgenus Microphyllus (Ruschieae; Aizoaceae). Syst. Bot. 42(4): 943-963. [DOI 10.1600/036364417X696429] [All rights reserved]

description: Schlechteranthus stylosus may be confused with S. parvus as they have a similar leaf size with ahigh degree of fusion and the same spine arrangement. However, S. stylosus can be distinguished by the few filamentous staminodes which do not form a complete series around the stamens (many filamentous staminodes which form a complete series in S. parvus). The leaves are also ovoid in outline in S. stylosus (subglobose in S.parvus) with a very prominent mucro (mucro obscure in S.parvus). Schlechteranthus stylosus is also typically a larger shrub (up to 400 mm in height) compared to S. parvus (up to 150 mm in height). Schlechteranthus stylosus may be confused with S. pungens, as both species are large shrubs with spines derived from aborted axillary buds, but S. stylosus is distinguished by the ovoid leaves in outline (mostly oblong in S. pungens) and spines arranged in a simple cyme on the secondary axes (spines arranged in compound cyme on secondary axes in S. pungens).
bibliographicCitation: Powell, RF; Klak, C; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2017. A taxonomic revision of Schlechteranthus subgenus Microphyllus (Ruschieae; Aizoaceae). Syst. Bot. 42(4): 943-963. [DOI 10.1600/036364417X696429] [All rights reserved]

description: Schlechteranthus subglobosus is a distinct species and, although it shares a globose leaf shape with S. parvus, the leaf pairs are only fused for a third of the length with a very prominent mucro (fused for aquarter of the length with obscure mucro in S. parvus) and the flowers are solitary (flowers in cymose inflorescence in S. parvus). The leaves of S. subglobosus are regularly spaced along the branch, which is similar to S. inclusus, while the rest of the species in the subgenus have the leaves crowdedtowards the tips. In S. subglobosus, however, the leaves are positioned at regular intervals along the branch with the internodes visible between the leaves, while in S. inclusus the leaves are tightly packed and decussate, with no visible internodes. Schlechteranthus subglobosus can further be distinguished from the other species in the subgenusby its bright green leaves with a rough surface and very prominent mucro as a result of the fatly trigonous leaf shape, while the leaves in the remaining species are triquetrous green to dark green leaves, with a slightly velvety to velvety leaf surface and a prominent mucro (obscure in S. parvus) in the rest of the subgenus).
bibliographicCitation: Powell, RF; Klak, C; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2017. A taxonomic revision of Schlechteranthus subgenus Microphyllus (Ruschieae; Aizoaceae). Syst. Bot. 42(4): 943-963. [DOI 10.1600/036364417X696429] [All rights reserved]

description: This species is distinguishable by the pedunculate inflorescence, the acicular terete leaves canaliculate on the upper surface and which narrow to a slender petiolar region, the scarcely trifid lower lip of the involucre and the reddish to carmine coloured fleshy swellings at the base of three anticous perianth claws.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: S. incurva is distinguished from other species of Spatalla withflowered involucres by its acicular terete mucronate leaves, the dense crisped indumentum on the stems, the obovate pollen presenter curved forward almost at right angles to the style, and the pubescent fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: The pedunculate inflorescence, the long (25-45 mm), straight leaves, canaliculate on the upper surface and narrowing towards the base, and the single flowered pedicellate involucres with villous, lanceolate acute bracteoles fused in their lower third, are the chief distinguishing characters. In the fresh state this species is easily recognised by the rather greyish pink perianth segments and the carmine coloured swellings of glandular tissue on the inner surface of the base of the three anticous perianth claws. When dried, the foliage turns black very quickly and does not retain a greenish colour as in the case of most other species.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: A character unique in the genus, namely, the pubescence of the lower third of the style, distinguishes 5. mollis from all other species of Spatalla. The bifid lower lip of the involucre is also a useful diagnostic character.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: S. parilis may be distinguished from all other species of Spatalla with sessile inflorescences and pedicellate involucres, by the very narrowly lanceolate acuminate to linear bracteoles.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: : Among the species of Spatalla with 3 flowered involucres S. propinqua is distinguished by the obovate cochleariform discoid pollen presenter, the erect, galeate posticous perianth limb, the glabrous to near glabrous fruits, the villous perianth tube, and the long, slender cylindric inflorescence (3-10 cm long).
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: Among the species of Spatalla with sessile one-flowered involucres, S. salsoloides may be distinguished by the cylindric to ellipsoid pollen presenter, geniculate at its junction with the style. Jt is most closely related to S. setacea from which it is distinguishable in the field by its sprawling divaricate habit of growth.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: This species may be recognised by the sessile inflorescences, the dense crisped pubescence on the inner surface of the perianth claws, and the large, sessile, glabrous to near glabrous single flowered involucres. When the flowers have dropped, the glabrous, membranous bracteoles of the involucres enlarge conspicuously and develop reddish-carmine tints. The specific name 'squamata' almost certainly refers to these scaly bracteoles.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: S. tulbaghensis is easily distinguished from all other species of Spatalla with three flowered involucres by its globose almost spherical inflorescences and its dense, compact, much branched growth habit.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1969. Taxonomic studies on Sorocephalus R.Br. and Spatalla Salisb. J. S. African Bot.: 1-124. [CC BY]

description: Though unmistakable in its growth habit, the foliage of P. acaulos is exceptionally variable. Like other rhizomatous proteas, P. acaulos is fire resistant. Apart from having a subterranean branch system, the main stem is often swollen to form a small lignotuber, thus giving a mature plant even greater fire-resistance. Above soil level, the vegetative growth consists of a few trailing stems with secundly arranged leaves (i.e. deflected to one side of the stem). If burnt off in a veld fire, new vegetative growth soon regenerates from the rhizomes or lignotuber.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. acuminata is distinguished from related species, such as P. scolymocephala, by its wine-red bracts and from P. canaliculata, by having completely hairless flat linear-lanceolate to very narrowly linear-spathulate leaves, prominently acuminate at the apices. A dark reddish-black margin on the edges of the involucral bracts is one of the species' most distinctive characters, but is only observable in the fresh condition.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The adult plant develops into a dense sprawling mat 300-400 mm tall, eventually attaining a metre or more in diameter, producing sprawling stems bearing the unmistakable, heart-shaped, stem-clasping leaves borne at right-angles to the stems. Concealed along the lowermost branches as well as on old wood at the centre of each plant, are the flowerheads, arising in an axillary position. Thus even when a plant is in full bloom it is virtually impossible to see any of the flowerheads.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. caffra is an exceptionally variable species consisting of a mosaic of local races each differing very slightly though nevertheless merging imperceptibly with each other. The most obvious manifestation of these differences is in the colour, texture, form and size of the leaves. On the Witwatersrand where cold dry winters are experienced, rather hard, stiff, thick textured, grey-green leaves are typicaL. From the Rand there is a smooth gradation to larger more flaccid leaves, in westerly, easterly and northerly directions. Some northern and eastern Transvaal races have quite flaccid almost succulent, sickle-shaped leaves, while along the Natal coast the leaves are thinner textured, usually lacking the grey-green bloom on their surface. Throughout Natal to the eastern Cape narrower (and often shorter) leaves pre-dominate.Differences in the colour of the flower-heads will also be noted; pink or carmine with green at the base being the general rule but forms with creamy-green bracts are also found. Furthermore, some populations (especially those on the Highveld) are characterised by the presence of very short silvery pubescence on the lower involucral bracts. Others have completely glabrous bracts with no hint of silvery pubescence but the majority are somewhere between these two extremes.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: There are two main forms of this species differing chiefly in leaf characters. Narrow, needle-like, deep green, largely glabrous leaves are typical of the extreme westerly populations on the Worcester, Koo and Montagu mountains. Glaucous, broader leaved forms predominate on the Witteberg and Swartberg. There is also a slight tendency to leaf pubescence on these more easterly races. Bract characters appear to vary as well; glabrous, very dark, wine red bracts are distinctive of the western, while paler pinkish red, slightly sericeous bracts are characteristic of the eastern races.Despite this variation, all these forms have recurved leaf margins which give rise to either a broad or a narrow channel on the undersurface of the leaf. This character, together with the sharp, recurved spine on the leaf apex, constitute the most useful diagnostic features of P. canaliculata.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The young stems as well as the leaf bases are covered with a curious reddish-brown resin, sticky to touch, and hardening to a blackish glaze on the older branches, giving the impression that the stems have been varnished. This property, apparently unique among South African proteas, serves to distinguish P. convexa from related species. But it is the enormous cabbage-like leaves, heavily coated with a blue-grey waxy surface, that give P. convexa its spectacular appearance in the field. Leaves with so large a surface area on a plant occupying so arid a habitat appear paradoxical but as yet it is not possible to offer any reasonable explanation for this inordinately massive foliage.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: An apparently unique feature of this species is that an abscission layer develops at the base of the inflorescence stipe when the fruits are fully mature. If the inflorescence is touched at this stage the entire structure becomes detached, falling to the ground and spilling its fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Climatic, geographical and ecological constraints have all influenced P. cynaroides, particularly in respect of the differentiation of local races within the species. Indeed, this protea is something of a paradox: it is at once the most distinctive species in the genus, yet it is also one of the most variable, consisting of innumerable local races or variants differing not only in growth habit and stature, as well as in the colour, size and structure of the flower-head, but also in flowering time. So numerous are the variants within this single species that an entire book could be devoted to them, but only three can be shown here. All, however, are united by a single common character: the glabrous leaves have a prominent petiole or leaf stalk-Several attempts have been made to define these local races more precisely and to give them formal taxonomic rank. To this end the varieties elliptica, glabrata, obtusifolia and albiflora were published by various botanists during the past, though none of these names can satisfactorily be applied to populations in the field. More recently, however, the diverse variants of P. cynaroides were the subject of a detailed study by Dr. Marie Vogts (Die Geografie en die Geografiese variasie van Protea cynaroides, Stellenbosch University, Nov. 1971). She recognized three broad groups based on leaf characters: (1) an oval- to round-leaved variant occurring largely in the western Cape (Plate 16); (2) a broad, elliptic-leaved variant occurring in the Outeniqua and Van Stadens mountains (frontispiece); and (3) a small elliptic-leaved variant characteristic of lower elevations along the coastal belt from George to Port Elizabeth. The elliptic-leaved variants, both large and small, always attract attention on account of their unusual foliage. First appearing on the Langeberg above Swellendam (often in association with broad, round-leaved forms) the elliptic-leaved variants are found mainly along the southern Cape coastal shelf at low elevations (usually below 150 m), between George and Port Elizabeth. There is a reduction in. flower-head size as one progresses eastwards. This trend begins to be noticeable near Knysna, at Noetzie and Kruis-fontein, becoming more marked at Blue Lilies Bush in the Tzitzikama region, with the smallest flower-heads being found on the extreme dwarf form which occurs on the sandy, often winter-waterlogged flats about 25 km west of Port Elizabeth. These extreme, dwarf variants, growing in the vicinity of Lorraine and St. Albans, are of small stature, rarely exceeding 350 mm in height, their flower-heads only about 120 mm in diameter and their tiny, elliptic leaves about 25 mm in width.Apart from differences in leaf form it is the flower-heads themselves which display the greatest degree of variation, particulary with respect to size and colour. In size they range from narrowly goblet shape and 120 mm in diameter in the diminutive Port Elizabeth forms, to colossal shallowly bowl-shaped flower-heads up to 300 mm in diameter in some of the Langeberg and Outeniqua variants. The form and positioning of the inner involucral bracts has a profound effect on the overall shape of the flower-heads. These bracts may be widely splayed and sharply pointed, as in the Grahamstown and Beggarsbush variants. Conversely, some of Outeniqua variants occurring between Cloete's Pass and George, frequently have closely overlapping bracts. One of the most unusual variants has obtuse almost rounded bracts and appears sporadically in the Suuranys mountains near Kareedouw at the eastern end of the Longkloof as well as on the Loerie mountains near Humansdorp.Superimposed on the species east-west variation pattern are the character changes which take place over altitudinal gradients - a phenomenon particularly evident where high mountains rise abruptly from the coastline. This is well demonstrated at localities such as Cape Point, Betty's Bay and Kruisfontein. The populations occurring almost at sea-level, within a few hundred metres of the high water mark, have glabrous or almost completely glabrous involucral bracts, while on the same mountain a mere kilometre or two away at an elevation of 300 metres, the bracts are densely sericeous. Thus, pubescence on the bracts is almost invariably absent in extreme maritime variants but increases in density with elevation and distance from the sea. Usually the bracts are pale pink but deep crimson and even bronzy-red tones are known. Colour is usually intensified by the absence of pubescence in the extreme maritime variants, though these are not the most attractive forms. Rather, it is the pale pink forms with a silvery sheen - an effect created by soft white pubescence overlying the bracts - which are most admired. So called 'white' colour forms are also occasionally encountered. They are not really white but a pale creamy-green. I have only seen these 'white' forms in the Kogelberg Forest Reserve, though they may well occur elsewhere. The combinations resulting from all these variables are legion so it is therefore not surprising that within her three broad groups, Dr. Marie Vogts was able to distinguish at least 80 local variants, characterized by their morphology, colour and flowering times.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Protea decurrens is sometimes confused with two related species which also have axillary flower-heads, namely, P. subulifolia and P. humiflora. However, the ascending, prominently decurrent leaves at once separate it from P. humiflora, while the flat, 2-5 mm broad leaf blades distinguish it fromP. subulifolia. A certain degree of variation in leaf width is evident in P. decurrens, with populations at the eastern end of the species' range tending to have slightly broader leaves than the extreme westerly populations.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Simple, unbranched (or only very rarely branched) stems are produced from a subterranean lignotuber. It is a markedly fire-adapted species requiring burning every few years to keep the plants in a vigorous, floriferous state.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. holosericea may be distinguished from P. magnifica in having short styles, 45-50 mm long and in having two prominent awns on the perianth sheath instead of three as in P. magnifica. The most obvious distinguishing features, however, are the dense purple-black beards on the rounded apices of all but the lowermost involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. inopina is distinguished by the dense, rusty brown, velvety pubescence on the involucral bracts (particularly in the bud stages) and by the dwarf growth habit with unbranched or only very rarely branched stems up to 1 m in height, developing from a persistent rootstock. Another most unusual feature of this species is the inordinately large size of the ovoid fruits, 10-12 mm long and 6-8 mm in diameter, three times the size of the fruits in P. nitida. Together with those of P. magnifica they are the largest fruits recorded in Protea.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: A very dense, compactly tufted growth habit, glabrous, glaucescent leaves, linear to needle-shaped and slightly channelled, 2-5 mm wide and 150-400 mm long, distinguish P. intonsa from related species. The white, woolly beards at the apices of each flower are also characteristic, particularly in the bud stages.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Protea lacticolor is distinguished by its large, dark blue-green, broadly lanceolate to ovate leaves, truncate to subcordate at the base, glabrous when mature, and by the filiform pollen presenters, withminutely but obliquely capitellate apices. (In P. punctata the pollen presenters are uniformly filiform with no apical swelling, while in P. mundii the pollen presenters are symmetrical and stoutly capitate and the leaves elliptic.).
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Morphologically, P. lanceolata is very uniform, displaying little variability. It is easily recognised by its smooth, hairless, lanceolate leaves, hairless stems and involucral bracts, of which the inner series become widely splayed on opening and by the sunken, concave involucral receptacle.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Mostly the involucral bracts are cream. However, in some populations, forms with pale pink bracts occur and in fact pink forms very occasionally predominate over white, particularly in the Klein River mountains. These pink forms have been confused with P. neriifolia. Indeed, at one stage P. neriifolia was reported to be growing naturally in the Cape Peninsula but the record is erroneous, having been based on a pink variant of P. lepidocarpodendron collected in Platte-klip Gorge, Table Mountain. Despite a certain similarity, the latter species is readily distinguishable from the former by having purple-black pubescence on the outer surfaces of the spathulate inner involucral bract apices.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Unmistakable as this species may be on account of the prominent woolly black knob formed at the centre of each flower-head by the massed perianth awns, it exhibits a certain degree of variation, particularly in respect of bract colour and the size of the flower-heads.Typically the bracts are hyaline to almost creamy-green, but forms with pink bracts of varying intensity, do occasionally occur. The pink form shown in our plate is an especially dark variant. Some of the smaller flowered forms often have exceptionally deep apple-green bracts which are most attractive. By far the majority of the populations produce flower-heads which are large, ranging from 120-160 mm in length. However, towards the southern end of the species' range, particularly around Elim, Viljoenshof and the Soetanysberg, some populations have markedly shorter flower-heads, from 80-120 mm long. Almost invariably, the bracts of these small forms are greenish, while in stature the shrubs tend to be small, rarely exceeding half a metre in height. These smaller flowered forms were once described as P. longifolia var. minor, but as they merge imperceptibly with the larger flowered forms (shown in accompanying plate) no clear-cut distinction can be made between the two extremes, so the varietal name is no longer upheld. On occasions, the small forms of P. longifolia have been confused with P. pudens. However, they are always erect to suberect with ascending leaves, evenly disposed about the stem, while in P. pudens the stems are normally trailing with secund leaves, that is, all deflected to one side of the stem.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Although there should be no difficulty in recognising P. lorea on account of its long needle-like leaves and large flower-heads, the most certain diagnostic character is the abruptly but densely lanate nature of the perianth limbs.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: While closely related to P. odorata, P. mucronifolia is easily distinguished by its different flowering period, the considerably larger flower-heads and the flat, narrowly lanceolate leaves, each tipped with a sharp reddish-black spine making the whole plant almost impossible to touch.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: There should be little difficulty in recognising P. nana which is distinguished from related species by its upright growth habit, bright green, glabrous, needle-like leaves 20-30 mm long with softly spine-tipped apices, small pendulous flower-heads 30-45 mm in diameter and the narrowly acuminate involucral receptacle.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. neriifolia is most easily distinguished by its oblong to very narrowly oblong leaves, with the margins parallel for the greater part of their length, being hair-fine (not horny and heavily thickened), and the sessile/truncate to ses-sile/cuneate leaf bases. The generally deep green to bright green colour is also typical although a few forms do have leaves with a blue-grey hue and therefore tend to be confused with P. laurifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. nitida is most closely related to P. caffra. They constitute a pair of vicarious species, both variable and both widespread, yet each being separated, geographically and climatically. Typically, the waboom is a small gnarled tree up to 5 metres with a whitish trunk up to half a metre in diameter and a rounded to irregular crown of greyish-white foliage. At the other extreme, there are dwarf, multiple stemmed races of P. nitida, in which a single main trunk is not developed. Moreover, their leaves are narrower than usual, oblong in form with a greener, olivaceous tint rather than whitish-glaucescent. These dwarf, multiple-stemmed races have been recorded from Kanonkop in the Tygerberg Hills, near Red Hill on the Cape Peninsula, on the Langeberg at Montagu and Swellendam, and on the hills near Albertinia. Although they were once recognised at varietal level and even as a distinct species at one stage under the name P. reticulata, their random occurrence and gradual merging.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The flowering time is just one of the features that separate this species from the related P. mucronifolia. However, the linear, revolute leaves, distinctly channelled on the under surface and terminating abruptly in a sharp, back-wardly deflected spine, serve as the most distinctive diagnostic character.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Although one of the smallest of all the proteas from the summer rainfall area, P. parvula is among the most attractive, its flower-heads being greenish-white to pink, opening from a shallow bowl to an almost flat water-lily-like form. This species is distinguished by its dwarf procumbent growth habit and the short trailing stems bearing secundly arranged leaves although occasionally odd individuals do produce suberect stems with ascending leaves. The leaves vary from linear to elliptic or oblanceolate with either acute or rounded apices.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Although in general aspect P. pruinosa resembles P. cryophila (endemic to the Cedarberg), the inflorescences are considerably smaller. Moreover the involucral bracts are ovate acute and are only lanate towards the apex, being glabrous and carmine at the base, while in P. cryophila they are narrowly acuminate and entirely woolly on their outer surfaces.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. pudens is most readily distinguished from related species (particularly P. longifolia) by its procumbent growth habit, the narrow, linear (2-5 mm wide) leaves secundly arranged (that is, deflected to the upper side of the stem), and the short flowers with styles 30-45 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Populations on moister sites such as those in the Tulbagh and Riviersonderend mountains, produce larger, more robust leaves, rather similar to the foliage of P. lacticolor. However, when in bloom, P. punctata is unmistakable as the involucral bracts of each flower-head spread outwards almost at right angles to the bud position, leaving the floral parts apparently everted and the whole flower-head having a water lily-like form. The species' most reliable diagnostic character is that the pollen presenters are uniformly filiform with no trace of an apical swelling. Moreover, in the fruiting stage the filiform pollen presenters turn outwards and curl over.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. restionifolia is most readily distinguished from related species by its slender needle-like leaves, rough in texture and sparsely covered with soft white hairs, as well as the very distinctive dark chocolate-brown velvety pubescence on the inner involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: There is considerable variation in the size of the flower-heads, a feature which appears to be related to vegetative vigour. Flower-heads on weak side branches are usually small, often only 40 mm in diameter, while those on more robust branches may be up to 90 mm in diameter. Our plate depicts robust specimens at a stage immediately prior to opening, just before the deep salmon pink of the styles and inner surfaces of the involucral bracts is revealed. As the flower-heads open they take on a much deeper pink blush than is shown here. The pollen presenter is also subject to very slight variations, being capitellate in the easterly races but tending to almost linear in the more western forms.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. scabra may at once be recognised by the fine velvety rusty-brown indumentum covering the outer surface of the creamy involucral bracts. Moreover, the perianth limbs are tipped with similarly rusty-brown hairs, though very much denser in texture. There is a surprising degree of variation in leaf form, from flat, narrowly oblanceolate leaves up to 25 mm wide, through linear to needle-like leaves 2 mm wide, with inrolled margins. At maturity the leaves are quite hairless though the young leaf flushes are initially covered with long white hairs. These soon disappear giving way to the rough sandpaper-like surface that is so characteristic of this species' leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Difficulty is often experienced in distinguishing between herbarium specimens of narrow-leaved forms of P. scolopendriifolia and P. scabriuscula. In the field, however, where both species grow in close association at several localities, the differences in biology and growth-habit are immediately apparent. Unlike P. scolopendriifolia which is fire-resistant and regenerates from a rhizomatous, subterranean branch system, P. scabriuscula has a single main stem with a branch system above the ground, and is killed by veld fires, regenerating only from seed.The adult plants eventually develop to form a compact, very densely branched mound, somewhat resembling an Alpine 'cushion plant'.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This is an enormously variable species in respect of leaf size and form, inflorescence size and even to a lesser extent, growth habit. Some populations produce fairly compact tufted plants, others have a more loosely tufted form.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The small flower-heads with their outwardly splayed creamy-green bracts, sometimes flushed with pink, are most distinctive and it is unlikely that P. scolymocephala could be confused with any other protea.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Although there is considerable variation in leaf shape, from linear to narrowly oblong or oblanceolate, it is the simple (unbranched) slender (2-5 mm in diam.) glabrous stems which serve to distinguish P. simplex from related species. Its nearest ally, P. dracomontana has large, gross stems and heavily coriaceous leaves, markedly thicker in texture than those of P. simplex.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: In the field, P. speciosa is easily recognised as this is one ofthe few Cape proteas having a woody subterranean rootstock from which the stiffly upright, straight to sparsely branched stems arise. Having such a rootstock gives an adult shrub almost complete fire resistance. When the aerial stems are burnt off in a veld fire, new shoots are able to regenerate from the subterranean rootstock. Thus the underground part of an established plant survives fire after fire. Although the aerial stems are few, rarely exceeding 1,2 m in height, the individual grows by enlarging its woody subterranean root-stock.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: It is impossible to confuse P. stokoei and P. speciosa in the field. The former has a single main stem with no powers of vegetative regeneration after a fire, whereas P. speciosa is multiple stemmed, the stems arising from a woody, persistent rootstock which is able to regenerate new growth after a fire. Flowering specimens of P. stokoei are most easily distinguished by the three, 10-12 mm long, outwardly curled, silvery-villous awns, on the abaxial perianth limbs.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The flower-heads are carmine, pink or creamy-white, with one or other shade tending to dominate a particular population. As the flower-heads open, the tips of the innermost involucral bracts bend outwards, sometimes almost at right angles. The tips of the styles also tend to bend outwards in fully open flowers. These curious features are very characteristic of P. subvestita, as are the elliptic leaves which are always tapered to the base.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Freshly picked specimens, when placed in a floral arrangement, give off an offensive odour, but this can be obviated by stripping off the leaves, which are the cause of the trouble. Apart from this characteristic, P. susannae may easily be recognised by the slightly sticky brown varnish-like exudate on the outer surfaces of the involucral bracts, creating the impression that the flower-heads have been lightly brushed with brown shoe-polish!.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Despite this considerable variation in the leaf width (which may be from 2-28 mm) P. tenax is readily distinguished from related species by its prostrate growth habit with trailing stems bearing secund or subsecund (very rarely ascending) leaves and the shallowly bowl-shaped inflorescences, 40-60 mm in diameter.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Within most populations there is quite a degree of variation in the colour of the involucral bracts. In some individuals the bracts are greenish-yellow, irregularly suffused with dull carmine while in others the bracts are uniformly dull carmine to claret. Emerging at ground level from the leaf tufts, the inflorescence buds are most distinctive; conic-acute in form with a prominent white woolly beard projecting from the bud apex. It is the thickly woolly apices of the perianth limbs, the loose, open tufted growth habit and the glaucous, narrowly oblanceolate to spathulate leaves 120-250 mm long, 8-30 mm wide, tapering to a distinct petiolar region which serve to distinguish this species.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: L. calligerum is distinguished from related taxa by its erect growth habit, permanently pubescent, entire leaves; the style, 2.1-2.5 cm long, and the conic ovoid pollen presenter.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. cordatum is distinguished by its prostrate growth habit, the entire, ovate acute leaves with prominently cordate to auriculate bases, the short, strongly incurved style (2.0-2.5 cm long) and the conic acute pollen presenter geniculate at its junction with the style.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. fulgens is distinguished by the oblanceolate to oblong glabrous leaves usually with 3 teeth at the apex, the villous perianth, the style, 4.6-5.3 cm long, the conic involucral receptacle and the inflated perianth tube.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: The dwarf soboliferous growth habit and distinctive linear to oblanceolate, slightly falcate leaves with prominently raised venation, distinguish L. gerrardii from all other species with cylindric involucral receptacles.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. gracile is distinguished from related species by its prostrate growth habit, the oblong-linear leaves (not exceeding 5.0 mm in width), truncate at the base, the abruptly acute oblanceolate bracteoles and the yellow perianth.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: The glabrous to glabrescent leaves, oblanceolate-cuneate and slightly twisted at the base, usually tridentate at the apex and the prostrate growth habit, distinguish L. heterophyllum from the other species in the section.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: Among the species of the section Leucospermum with linear-oblong leaves and an erect growth habit, L. parile is distinguished by its slightly patent to subsquarrose paleaceous to papyraceous involucral bracts, reddish brown in colour and glabrous to glabrescent on the outer surface.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. praecox is distinguished by the broadly conic involucral receptacle, the obovate to broadly cuneate leaves, 6-11 toothed at the apex, the puberulous perianth, the inflated perianth tube, the style, 3.8-4.8 cm long and the narrowly conic acute pollen presenter.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: The pubescent, loosely arranged, narrowly lanceolate linear involucral bracts distinguish L. praemorsum from all other species in the genus. Further distinguishing characters are the oblong-oblanceolate, petiolate leaves, truncate and praemorse at the apex and the ellipsoid-cylindric pollen presenter.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. rodolentum may be distinguished from related taxa by its tall, erect growth habit (to 3.0 m) and its very densely canescent, elliptic to cuneate leaves 0.7-1.5 cm broad.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. spathulatum is distinguished from those related species having a prostrate growth habit, conic involucral receptacle and inflated perianth tube by its usually entire, oblong to spathulate leaves, 1.4-3.0 cm long, beset with a short crisped indumentum (of varying density), and the strongly arcuate style, 3.0-4.0 cm long.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. tomentosum is the only erect species in the section Leucospermum which has a persistent rootstock. Its small, cartilaginous, tightly imbricate involucral bracts, shortly tomentose on the outer surface, and linear canaliculate leaves distinguish it from other related species.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. utriculosum may be distinguished by its lax growth habit; the horizontally spreading branches; the short, conic-depressed involucral receptacle; the perianth tube narrow proximally, becoming inflated distally and then sharply constricted; the silky spreading pubescence on the perianth claws and the ovoid pollen presenter.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: The glabrous, membranous, loosely patent involucral bracts, the very narrowly conic acute involucral receptacle, the glabrous oblong leaves and obliquely ovoid pollen presenter distinguish L. vestitum from related species.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1972. Taxonomic studies on Leucospermum R.Br. J. S. African Bot.: 1-194. [CC BY]

description: L. argenteum is a species easily distinguished from all others by being a tree with large silvery leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. bonum is a plant readily distinguished by it's silvery pubescent spathulate leaves and numerous acute involucral bracts. Towards the inflorescence in both sexes, the stem leaves are changed into narrow acute bracts forming a conspicuous yellow involucre around the flower head. These bracts spread open in the sunlight but readily close up in dull weather. This is a characteristic not found in any other member of the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. brunioides maybe recognised by being a glabrous shrub with a persistent rootstock and many stems, with linear leaves, (sub-canaliculate when dry), with the floral bract in the male inflorescence oblanceolate and villous. It differs from Lsre//a/-e(Sims) R.Br, which has shorter leaves that are twice as broad and narrowing to the apex as well as having the floral bract in the male inflorescence lanceolate and short-pubescent. L. linifolium (Jacq.)R.Br. differs from L. brunioides in having the plant developed from a single stem with linear-oblong leaves which are twice as broad, and in having the male inflorescence normally pedunculate.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. burchel/ii has elliptic, dark green, erect, glabrous leaves, involucral leaves closely imbricating the flower head, a broad male flower head, and the male perianth sparsely pubescent. It differs from L. tinctum which has light green leaves spreading or even deflexed, not imbricating the flower head, oily basal bracts with a strong peppery smell and the male perianth glabrous. It als differs from L. barkerae which has leaves tomentose or glabrescent and mor narrowed to the base and the male floral bracts laterally ciliate.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. concavum is closely related to Ldubium Buek. ex Phillips & Hutch, which is also to be found in the Clanwilliam division at Heuningvlei, Ezelbank anc other places. However it can be readily distinguished by being much larger ir nearly all respects. No intermediates have so far been found. There is a certair superficial similarity between Lconcavum and L. coriaceum Phillips & Hutcr when seen in the herbarium. However the latter is a very different species about 60 cm tall with glabrous leaves, smaller globose heads, small hairy fruit and a persistent rootstock.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. conicum is distinguished by its tree-like habit, dark green foliage and spreading branches and leaves. It has conspicuous pubescent basal bracts, pubescent flower heads and sparsely pubescent obcordate fruits. It differs from L. salicifolium (Salisb.) Williams which has linear leaves, glabrous basal bracts and glabrous flower heads. It also differs from L. macowanii Phillips which is endemic to the Cape Peninsula and has much larger leaves, no conspicuous basal bracts, glabrous florets in the male and glabrous cone bracts in the female.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. corymbosum is an erect species with a sub-corymbose floral arrangement, ericoid leaves, Ungulate female floral bracts, obcordate fruits and the apical bristles on the male floral bract greater than 1 mm long. It is most similar to L. laxum but differs in being taller and more erect, with larger leaves and larger male flower heads, and with longer apical bristles on the male floral bract. The more delicate habit of L. laxum is evident even in dried materiaL.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. daphnoides is a very distinct species having the inflorescence closely imbricated by the specialised lower portion of the involucral leaves. In the bud stage the Ungulate apices of the male floral bracts are conspicuous. The fruit is a brown nut which is smooth and shining and the old female perianth is longer than that of any other closely related species. L. tinctum Williams and L. orientale Williams differ from L. daphnoides in having involucral leaves which do not clasp the head but are spreading or deflexed revealing the numerous recurved oily basal bracts. L. daphnoides is also different from L. barkerae Williams which has pubescent, elliptic leaves and a shorter perianth and from L. sessile R.Br, which has brown or purplish brown basal bracts not at all hidden by the involucral leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. diemontianum is most closely related to L. flexuosum Williams from near Worcester but it differs by the following characters; the tuft of branchlets near the base of the shrub is not apparent in L. flexuosum; the leaves are adpressed erect not spreading and elliptic-linear not oblanceolate-linear; the male heads are narrower; the female heads are smaller even when mature and the branches in the female plant arise further from the head than in L. flexuosum. Regeneration occurs after fires.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. dregei is most closely related to L. album (Thunb.) Fourcade (= L. aurantiacum Buek ex Meisn.) and to Lrubrum Burm.f. (= L. plumosum R.Br.) from both of which it is easily distinguished by its thick fleshy glabrous leaves and by its decumbent habit. L. sorocephalodes Phillips and Hutch., also closely related, is distinguished by having very much smaller ericoid leaves. Furthermore it is distinguished from L. album in the fruiting stage in having the perianth segments completely free from each other except towards the base where the membranes surround the fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. dubium is easily recognised by being a plant developing from a single stem at ground level, with numerous erect slender branches which are densely clothed with small elliptic leaves, bearing flowers with pubescent perianths, without hypogynous scales, with cone bracts densely silky villous, and with nutlike almost glabrous fruits. It is most nearly related to L. concavum Williams which has very much larger leaves, and somewhat similar in appearance to L. thymifolium which however has hypogynous scales, thinly pubescent cone bracts, villous fruits, and leaves quite broad towards the base.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. elimense subsp. elimense is a taxon with leaves that are variable in size, rather small, broadly elliptic, closely spaced and sub-imbricate. It is nearest to subsp. salteri Williams which differs in having leaves that are much larger and more widely spread. It also differs from L. chamelaea (Lam.) Williams which has leaves that are narrowly obalanceolate and male heads that are smaller and more numerous. Furthermore it differs from L. globosum (Andr.) Williams which has larger leaves and recurved basal bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. foedum is confined to sandy plains at an altitude of 100 to 300 feet above sea leveL. Further to the north and at higher altitudes, its place is taken by L. procerum (Salisb.ex Knight) Williams (= L. concinnum R.Br.) from which it may be distinguished by having the male flower buds yellow not red, the male floral bract almost glabrous not densely pubescent, the mature female cone bracts relatively even not deeply indented in the middle, the female involucral leaves narrow and greenish not broad and ivory white.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. galpinii is easily recognised, being a tall plant with glabrescent branches, with glabrescent, linear-oblanceolate leaves tapering evenly to the base, without involucral leaves, with pedunculate male heads, and with a villous fruit. It is closely related to L. linifolium (Jacq.) R.Br, which is however a much lower shrub with smaller leaves, heads, and fruits. It also differs from L. cinereum (Ait.) R.Br, from the Malmesbury Division, which is also a much smaller shrub, with leaves more narrowed towards the base, with sessile male heads, with the male perianth limb glabrous, and with mature female heads very much smaller.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. glaberrimum is a small shrub, often decumbent, with short branches.with small oblanceolate leaves much narrowed to the base, not glaucous, and with yellow male flowers. It closely resembles L. loranthifolium (Salisb. ex Knight) Williams which however is a taller shrub with glaucous leaves not so much narrowed to the base and more crowded below the head, and with greenish male flowers. It is very closely related to subsp. erubescens Williams which however is a more colourful shrub, with slightly larger leaves, and with stouter branchlets which are short-crisped-pubescent.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. globosum is most closely related to L. elimense subsp. salteri Williams but is easily distinguished by the oval dark green leaves, pubescent stems and recurved basal bracts. It differs from L. grandiflorum (Salisb.) R.Br., an extinct species supposed to have grown on Wynberg Hill and now known only from Salisbury's drawing and description (1806), in having broader leaves which are not twisted and which are of a darker shade of green and a perfume which is not disagreeable. L. globosum also has larger basal bracts, longer and possibly wider floral bracts, an almost glabrous receptacle, much longer petals, longer anthers which are not retuse, shorter hypogynous scales and the style entire and four fifths hairy not only hairy near the bottom.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. gydoense may be distinguished from L. sessile R.Br. (= L. venosum R.Br, sensu Phillips & Hutchinson) by its slender glabrous branches, narrower oblanceolate leaves and sparse involucre. L. sessile has stout tomentose branches, narrowly elliptic leaves and involucral leaves crowded together. L. chamelaea (Lam.) Williams (= L. decurrens R.Br.) has leaves which are smaller and smoother, male heads which are borne at the ends of numerous scattered branchlets and a fruit which is narrowly winged and not biconvex. L. loranthifolium (Salisb. ex Knight) Williams has leaves which are more glaucous and a densely pubescent floral bract in the male.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. laureolum having a winged fruit, can readily be distinguished from L. tinctum Williams, L. daphnoides (Thunb.) Meisn., L. sessile R.Br, and L. barkerae Williams, which have leaves of a somewhat similar size but which have nut-fruits and much longer perianths in both male and female flowers. It can also be distinguished from L. microcephalum which has conspicuous sticky basal bracts; from L. gandogeri with its wide open involucre, eciliate basal bracts and glabrous cone bracts; from L. cryptocephalum with its smaller cones, cone bracts and fruits; and from L. strobilinum with its more numerous cone bracts. Above all, provided fresh material is available, L. laureolum is readily distinguished by its characteristic cone with eight spiral shallow grooves.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: Although very similar to L. corym-bosum it consistently differs in the following characters: the stems are shorter and more slender, the leaves are shorter and narrower and the male flower heads are smaller; the branches are lax and not rigidly erect and the stem 'eaves are less erect. The apical bristles on the male floral bract are less than 1 rnm long and the connective is black, providing the anther with a small black glandular apex.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. levisanus is distinguished by it's very small spathulate leaves, by developing from a single stem at ground level and by it's indehiscent fruiting heads. It is most closely related to L. cinereum (Ait.) R.Br, which however has very much larger leaves. It also differs from L. thymifolium (Salisb. ex Knight) Williams which has small elliptic leaves not narrowed towards the base and dehiscent fruiting heads. Furthermore it differs from L. stellare (Sims) R.Br, which has small linear-lanceolate leaves narrowing towards the apex, a persistent root-stock with many stems and dehiscent fruiting heads.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. macowanii approaches nearest to L. salicifolium (Salisb.) Williams, but is distinguished from it by the larger and broader leaves and the absence of any conspicuous basal bracts below the male flower. Another near relative which should be mentioned here is L. conicum (Lam.) Williams (= L. ramosissimum Buek ex Meisn.). It is found eastwards from the Robinson Pass, Mossel Bay Division, to Port Elizabeth. This species, however, is a shrub with a purplish tinge, more pubescent and grows into a tree with an 46 cmch diameter trunk in optimum protected habitats. These three species have in common that they are always found in the vicinity of streams, but do not grow together. They share also the character of trigonal fruits.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: The slender nature of L. meyerianum with its thin branches, linear leaves and small heads readily separates it from all others. It is probably most closely related to L. glaberrimum (Schlectr.) Compton which has narrowly spathulate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. microcephalum may be clearly distinguished from all other species by the conspicuous brown oily bracts in both sexes. In the bud stage this feature is particularly noticeable, the bud being globose, dark brown and very viscid. The irregular double ridge on one side of the fruit is also an unique character. The brown oil from the basal bracts can often be observed on herbarium material as it stains the adjacent leaves. L. laureo/um (Lam.) Fourcade and L. gandogeri Schinz ex Gandoger, although somewhat similar in appearance, do not possess these distinctive characters.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. modestum is a small erect shrub developing from a single stem below. Superficially it resembles L. lanigerum Buek ex Meisn. but one can note on the herbarium sheets that the leaves, female flowers, fruits and cones are all slightly smaller. The leaves of L. modestum are also proportionally somewhat wider. In the field one can observe that L. lanigerum tends to coppice from an underground rootstock if damaged, whereas L. modestum grows from a single stem and is invariably killed if scorched by fire. The leaves of L. lanigerum are more scabrous to the touch and more often twisted.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. muirii is a glabrous shrub with trimorphic foliage, the mature leaves being spathulate, very obtuse, thick and fleshy, with pedunculate heads, with very acute basal bracts and with fruits samaroid and compressed. It is only found growing on limestone of the Bredasdorp formation. It is most closely related to L. nobile Williams and to L. teretifolium (Andr.) Williams both of which however have acicular leaves. Theleaves of L. muirii somewhat resemble those of L. arcuatum (Lam.) Williams which however is a totally different species with nut-fruits and dehiscent fruiting heads.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. nervosum is a species with hairy branchlets, elliptic leaves, hairy involucral leaves, numerous acute basal bracts, coloured floral buds, style of the male plant densely pubescent below, large pollen grains, style of the female flower persisting, mature female head conical with many small bracts, and the fruit acute at the base with a fringe of long hairs above. The long hairs of the fruit distinguish this species from all others with a similar shaped fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: Leucadendron olens is recognised as a distinct species having monomorphic leaves, the male flower head 9 mm in diam., bright yellow and fragrant and with the female head 5 mm in diam., conic-ovoid, glabrous with 2 or 3 flowers at the apex. It differs from L. ericifolium which is a much taller plant with dimorphic leaves having very small and numerous male heads and silvery pubescent female heads bearing only one flower at the apex. The name refers to the fragrant flowers of the male plant.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. A new species of Leucadendron (Proteaceae0 from the Outeniqua Mountains. J. S. African Bot. 47: 121-126. [CC BY]

description: L. orientale is nearest to L. tinctum Williams but it is readily distinguished by its leaves which are narrower, more erect, more crowded around the head and of a paler shade of green. Furthermore the basal bracts of the head are more numerous and the outermost are closely reflex-adpressed. In seedlings and juveniles the leaves are very much narrower than those of L. tinctum. There are a few hairs on the male floral bract and on the male perianth, but in L. tinctum these parts are glabrous. The typical L. tinctum is found in the Caledon Division in the west and L. orientale is found in the Port Elizabeth Division in the east. The other somewhat similar species, L. daphnoides (Thunb.) Meisn. and L. sessile R.Br., do not possess the characteristic rosette of recurved basal bracts so noticeable in the bud stage of L. orientale and L. tinctum.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. platyspermum is an unique species approaching L. comosum (Thunb.) R.Br, in overall appearance but differing particularly in having by far the largest winged fruit in the genus. It also has cone bracts which are very thick and connate in one spiral only, leaves retuse or with a very obtuse callus, and male heads tufted with long white hairs when in bud.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. procerum is readily distinguished by its erect habit, ivory white involucral leaves and reddish flower buds. It is closest to L. foedum Williams but it differs in having broader involucral leaves in the female plant and reddish, not yellow, flowers. It also differsfrom L. discolor Buek ex Phillips & Hutch, which has much broader leaves and larger male flower heads.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. pubescens is distinct in being a robust, greyish-green shrub wit oblanceolate leaves, narrowed to the base, smaller in the male plant wit acute, pubescent basal bracts, with pubescent perianths and with pubescent cone bracts. It is nearest to L. remotum Williams which however differs having straplike leaves, conspicuous brown basal bracts and a much longe style in both sexes. The foliage of L. pubescens somewhat resembles that o L. rubrum Burm.f. but the heads and cones in L. rubrum are much narrower.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. rourkei is a narrow erect shrub up to 5 m tall with very small glabrous leaves, with no conspicuous involucral leaves and with a very short perianth in the female. It is most like L. uliginosum subsp. glabratum Williams which however has larger more acute leaves, the male bud glabrous at the apex and the female perianth loosely imbricated and somewhat longer. It is also rather like L. radiatum Phillips & Hutch, which however is a dwarf shrub only 60 cm tall with twisted leaves. It appears also to be related to L. conicum (Lam.) Williams which is a much more robust plant with larger mucronate leaves, larger basal bracts and longer female perianths.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: The male plant of L. rubrum is distinguished from all others by having a very large number of small narrow heads without involucres. During anthesis the female plant is unique in having the stigmas grouped into a small tuft at the apex of the cone. The plumed perianth attached to the mature fruit is similar to that of L. argenteum but much larger than those of L. album and L. dregei. The leaves of L. argenteum are large and silvery, those of L. album are linear and silvery; in L. rubrum although adpressed pubescent, the leaves are never silvery. By contrast, L. dregei is a decumbent shrub with rather thick glabrous leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. salicifolium falls naturally into a group with Lmacowanii Phillips anc L. conicum (Lam.) Williams all of which have trigonal fruits, broad cone bracts, an exposed stigma at the apex of the female bud, fern ale perianth segments adnate forming a tube and a similar habitat near streams or in damp places. Of this group L. salicifolium is the least hairy with narrow glabrescent leaves anc conspicuous glabrous male basal bracts. Lmacowanii has thinly pubescent broader leaves and somewhat larger male heads without conspicuous basal bracts. L. conicum has the shortest leaves of the group, pubescent male basal bracts and pubescent cone bracts in the female. The male perianth in L. conicum is pubescent, but in L. salicifolium and in L. macowanii it is glabrous. L. salicifolium differs from L. xanthoconus (O.Ktze) K.Schum. which is a shrub only half as tall with thinly adpressed pubescent leaves, fewer male heads and bi-lobed pubescent female cone bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: L. sericeum belongs to a small but very distinct section within the genus which is characterised by having part of the male style connate with the perianth tube and no hypgynous scales. It also has a fruit which is smooth, light grey in colour and ventricose with a double fold in the exocarp down the middle of the adaxial surface. It is distinguished from L. nitidum by being much smaller in leaf size, those of the male being amongst the smallest in the genus.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: The brown or purplish brown basal bracts in both sexes of L. sessile immediately distinguish these plants from other somewhat similar nut fruited species. This is more obvious in the early stages before the flowers open. In L. tinctum, L. cordatum and L. orientale these bracts are recurved and form a rosette. In L. daphnoides and L. barkerae these bracts are hidden within the involucral leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]
