description: The 5-ranked, strongly concave, panduriform branch leaves and short double costa should place specimens of this species. The above characters remain constant throughout the growth stages of the plants. Juvenile plants are frequently collected with stems short and unbranched. These plants quickly develop into an erect dendroid stage, somewhat like Porothamnium. In later stages the stems elongate up to 150 mm and have branches that frequently exceed 50 mm. This last stage results in the more typical habit, e.g. long-pendent stems hanging from boulders and tree trunks. Sporophytes are frequently found on the distal branches.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1998. Erpodiaceae to Hookeriaceae. In: OA Leistner & E du Plessis (eds), Fl. S. Africa (1,3): 445-622. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/171731#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Riccardia amazonica specimens are distinguished by the following characters: 1. Small, rather delicate, prostrate thalli, in 2 or 3 overlying layers; 2. Branching on one side of main axis often poorly developed; 3. Dioicous, with male thalli often somewhat smaller; 4. Main axis with a 2-cell wide wing on either side, particularly noticeable in male thalli; 5. Pinnae with unistratose wings, 2 or 3 cells wide, marginal cells entire to slightly crenulate; and 6. Calyptra wall with papillae forming a corona at the top.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2003. Studies in the liverwort family Aneuraceae (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 5. Riccardia amazonica. Bothalia 33(1): 99-104. [CC BY]

description: The species can be recognized by its generally smaller-sized, compact, dioicous thalli, its mat and glaucous or grey dorsal surface, and its stiff, regular, white to silvery mauve scales and apolar spores.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia moenkemeyeri is characterized by a more or less persistent dorsal epidermis which is marked out into small areolae, each with a small central air pore; by numerous narrow air chambers, appearing to be in more than one storey; by undulating thallus margins which terminate in a single row of hyaline cells; by obliquely orientated sporangia and a highly distinctive spore ornamentation with 8-10 large alveoli on the distal face and numerous tiny alveoli on the proximal face, which lack a triradiate mark.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia okahandjana can be distinguished most readily from the other four Riccia species with shiny black scales, that also occur in southern Africa, by its light brown, papillate spores.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The short, rigidly erect, unistratose leaves, without strongly differentiated bases, and the gymnostomous capsules that are strongly sulcate when dry will separate specimens of B. compacta from most members of the family. The typical variety is separated from B. compacta var. macowaniana primarily by its longer seta, and from B. capensis by its narrower, more consistently erect leaves, smooth to only weakly prorate leaf cells and much smaller spores; see note under that species.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1987. Mniaceae to Bartramiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,2): 395-438. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The short, erect, broad-mouthed, gymnostomous capsule exserted on a long seta should separate this variety from other taxa in Funariaceae. In addition the mitrate calyptra and bordered leaves are useful in identifying the variety.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1987. Gigaspermaceae to Splachnaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,2): 299-333. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is not identic with Lejeunea Mandoni Steph., which is a much smaller plant and has very long, almost sausage shaped compound oil bodies of quite different appearance.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: Metzgeria consanguinea is recognized by its blue-tipped, tapering thallus apices with abundant, concave blue-tinged gemmae, and dorsal and ventral costa of 2 or 3 cells throughout the thallus.
bibliographicCitation: Phephu, N; Van Rooy, J. 2015. Studies in the liverwort family Metzgeriaceae (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 3. The widespread species of Metzgeria. Telopea 18: 177-184. [dx.doi.org/10.7751/telopea8533] [All rights reserved]

description: Plagiochasma microcephalum can be distinguished by the green colour of the fresh thallus and by the generally large, broadly ovate or triangular scale appendages which have one or two rows of smaller cells along the margin. Bischler (1978) reported that plants growing in dry habitats have scales with a single, broadly ovate appendage which is constricted at the base, whereas those from more humid sites usually have one or two triangular scale appendages horizontally folded at the base and hardly constricted. Plants with mature female receptacles are rare. The carpocephala are small (hence the specific epithet) and are raised on a slender, short or long, dark red stalk.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia crozalsii can be recognized by its long, pointed, faintly granular cilia along the thallus margins, which are absent over the sporangia; by the pale green to glaucous-green colour of the dorsal face, occasionally stained with purple blotches; and by the spores with deep, rounded or angular alveoli on the distal face and on the proximal face, the arms of the triradiate mark widening toward the marginal angles near the junction with the wing.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The species is distinguished by the areolate dorsal surface of the thallus, small and slightly raised, mostly stellate air pores, empty air chambers, scales with acuminate appendages, lack of oil cells, cell walls of capsule with spiral thickenings and by bluntly spinous spores.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: This species is easily distinguished by its hyaline or brownish rhizoids and dense, frilly leaves, its pseudoperianth with lamellate, lateral outgrowths, by the spore ornamentation that usually has incomplete areolae with inclusions and by the usually finely papillose elaters. The specimen, Scott 13, has a larger and more elaborate pseudoperianth than those usually encountered in this species. Its spore ornamentation is very similar, however, and the rhizoids are hyaline.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1997. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 1. Three new species from Northern Province, Gauteng and Mpumalanga. Bothalia 27(1): 17-27. [CC BY]

description: The large, ± dendroid plants are usually recognized by their size, large concave leaves, entire leaf margins, short or absent costa, and smooth, strongly thickened and pitted leaf cells. Some specimens have been seen with leaves only weakly concave. However, most plants have strongly concave leaves. Sporophytes are frequently found on P. hoehnelii although the immersed capsules, large green perichaetial leaves and densely leaved stems make them inconspicuous.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1998. Erpodiaceae to Hookeriaceae. In: OA Leistner & E du Plessis (eds), Fl. S. Africa (1,3): 445-622. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/171731#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: This species differs from P. africana in its broadly involute upper leaf margins, bistratose lamina and slightly larger spores. The species is separated from Ptychomitrium by its small stature, larger leaf cells and leaf shape.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1998. Erpodiaceae to Hookeriaceae. In: OA Leistner & E du Plessis (eds), Fl. S. Africa (1,3): 445-622. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/171731#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Distinct from the other West African species in the entire, rounded leaf apices.
bibliographicCitation: Jones, EW. 2004. Lepidoziaceae Limpr. - Notothyladaceae (Milde) Müll.Frib. ex Prosk. In: MJ Wigginton (ed.), E.W. Jones's liverwort and hornwort Flora of West Africa: 102-424 National Botanic Garden (Belgium), Meise. [All rights reserved]

description: It differs from Lophoclea muricata by the almost plane leaves and the absence of spines from the surfaces of the leaves and the shape of the amphigastria, with small teeth in the margin.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: A very variable species. The connection between the amphigastria and the leaves is very variable, sometimes the amphigastria are free and sometimes they are connate with the base of a subadjacent leaf also in the same plant.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: This species is easily recognized by the conspicuous marginal cilia and broad, relatively thin and somewhat lax thallus with tumid margins. The spores are also quite distinct with a wide, undulating wing, large, low-walled alveoli and pale straw colour.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The spores of R. pottsiana are small, with numerous, small, deep alveoli, the walls papillose at the nodes; it rarely sporulates, however. Sim's description of the spores is very brief, only stating that they are round and indistinctly reticulate.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Can be recognized by its long, thin, rather lax, linear branches, frequently tinged with purple and keeled ventral face, from which stolons arise. The ventrally protruding sporangia are vertically orientated and not oblique as in R. stricta; the archegonial necks are shorter, the spores are generally slightly larger than those of R. stricta, and the ornamentation is different.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia runssorensis may be confused with R. atropurpurea, which is similar in size, and is sometimes mixed with it. On growing actively, R. runssorensis is, however, a bright, clear green, not silvery to glaucous-green like R. atropurpurea. It also lacks the hyaline thallus margins of the latter, and its spores have far more prominent projections at the alveolar nodes than any of the other local species with apolar spores (see note under R. rosea, no. 30). Riccia rosea is a more robust plant, and its reddish pink scales are larger and have a wider hyaline edge, projecting above the thallus margin; it also is dioicous.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia villosa is easily distinguished from other species in section Pilifer by its large, triangular scales with apically, denticulate margins. Riccia hirsuta also has triangular scales, but the apices are filiform, the spores reticulate and it is very rare. The spores of R. villosa are generally-dark brown to black and the ornamentation papillate to vermiculate. The only other species of Riccia with somewhat similar spores is R. okahandjana, but the latter's spores are light brown, its scales semilunar and black, and its dorsal epithelium not multicellular. Most plants of R. villosa are sterile; only four of the many specimens examined had sporangia.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia mammifera can be recognized by the broad thallus, small scales and enlarged cells along the thallus margins, on account of which it has been treated as a member of the Mammillatae group.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: This species can be recognized by the near-white to pale green dorsal surface of the entire dry and basal parts of the wet thallus, which seldom develops any purple coloration, by the large, wavy scales, hyaline at the margin, but soon developing pink to reddish bases, as well as by the prominent antheridial necks in male plants. In the specimens, D. Fourie 23c, 24c, the scale colour darkens progressively toward the base, eventually becoming dark, bluish red.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riella alatospora is easily distinguished by spores with a prominent discoid wing.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2000. Studies in the Sphaerocarpales (Hepaticae) from southern Africa. 3. The genus Riella and its local species. Bothalia 30(2): 125-142. [CC BY]

description: It is quite a robust plant and is probably the easiest species to identify because of its purple or red spores and capsule wall, as well as the pronounced webbing between the bases of the marginal spines on the proximal spore face.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2000. Studies in the Sphaerocarpales (Hepaticae) from southern Africa. 3. The genus Riella and its local species. Bothalia 30(2): 125-142. [CC BY]

description: Riccia albomarginata is generally smaller than most of the other species in section Pilifer. Although it has no other outstanding vegetative characters by which it can readily be recognized, in the dry state it is often light brown dorsally, with white streaks of collapsed, dried dorsal cell pillars; the somewhat undulating, incurved flanks are purple to brown, and distally fringed with crisp, hyaline or white scales; proximally, the flanks are frequently denuded of scales. The distal face of the spores often has thick radiating ridges.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Differs from the species by thick-walled, cells with spinous papillae al the base of the leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: It is distinguished by the relatively large size of the female plants with overlapping leaves and exposed stems, by fairly common, smaller male plants with large bracts subtending 2 rows of adjacent antheridia, by the spore ornamentation with widely separated lamellae and marginally by 12-16 projecting ‘spines’ joined by an incomplete membranous wing or perispore and also by generally reduced, delicate elaters.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1997. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 2. An amendment to thhree species from Western Cape, described by S.W.Arnell. Bothalia 27(1): 29-38. [CC BY]

description: Fossombronia crispa is distinguished by its entire, crisped leaves, its frequently robust size, generally purple stem, pseudoperianths with lobed, undulating mouth, reticulate or incompletely reticulate spores with low lamellae and elaters with strong spirals.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1997. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 4. A re-examination of F. crispa, F. leucoxantha and F. tumida. Bothalia 27(2): 105-115. [CC BY]

description: Fossombronia densilamellata is distinguished by its undulating, decurrent leaves, rare and somewhat smaller male plants with bracts shielding the antheridia and by the spore ornamentation with 12-16 narrowly spaced, thin, parallel lamellae on the distal face.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1997. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 2. An amendment to thhree species from Western Cape, described by S.W.Arnell. Bothalia 27(1): 29-38. [CC BY]

description: Fossombronia tumida is distinguished by its inflated or tumid appearance and very concave leaves, with small, scattered red flecks containing round bodies. The spores are generally reticulate over the distal pole, and the outer areolar walls break down into lamellae which continue to the margin. Scott & Pike (1987b) regard F. tumida as very similar vegetatively to F. intestinalis Tayl. from Australia and Tasmania, but ‘with experience, however, they can be separated. The former is larger, with flaccid leaves often tinged with purple-brown and with entire instead of slightly denticulate leaves. The spores are quite distinct’.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1997. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 4. A re-examination of F. crispa, F. leucoxantha and F. tumida. Bothalia 27(2): 105-115. [CC BY]

description: Riccardia obtusa specimens are distinguished by the following characters: 1, the obtuse margins (hence the specific name) of the distal branches; 2, the distal trifurcate to subpalmate branching pattern; 3. the closely adjoining or overlapping, lobulate apical branches; 4, the markedly thickened ultimate segments of the main axes, 5-8(-11) cell rows thick; 5, the primary and secondary branches with unistratose margins; 6. the prominent cell protrusions on the calyptra wall; 7, the distinct oil bodies, which are very dark and irregular to kidney-shaped or subspherical.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2002. Studies in the liverwort family Aneuraceae (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 4. Riccardia obtusa. Bothalia 32(2): 181-184. [CC BY]

description: This species could easily be mistaken for a Dicranella, but it is distinguished by short, narrow, lanceolate to elliptical leaves without pronounced shoulders, by non-ribbed, oval capsules, and rudimentary peristomes that are papillose throughout.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: The species can be recognised by its wide, rounded leaves, sometimes slightly inflexed above, by quite large perigonial bracts in male plants and by spores which have one to several tubercular processes in the complete or incomplete areolae.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1998. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 6. New species from Lesotho, Swaziland and Mpumalanga and new records from Lesotho. Bothalia 28(2): 159-165. [CC BY]

description: The species is rather similar to R. parvo-areolata as both have wide, concave thalli when dry, with large, hyaline scales and dorsal cell pillars consisting of three or four elongated cells. In R. ampullacea, however, the dorsal cells are frequently somewhat constricted toward the middle, and more or less ampulla-shaped. The antheridial necks are also more conspicuous and numerous, and often in close association with the archegonial necks; the spores differ from the finely reticulate ornamentation in R. parvo-areolata by generally having thick radiating ridges on the distal face; its distribution is also different.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: R. concava can be distinguished from the other species in section Pilifer Volk (1983), by its broad thallus, up to 4 mm wide when fully expanded, concave when dry, glaucous or scurfy blue-green colour, rounded apex, somewhat overhanging margins mostly obscuring the scales except those at the apex, and fragile, inflated, generally wider than long dorsal cells in loose pillars. On exposure to bright sunlight, it develops a deeper purple colour at the flanks and ventrally.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1989. Studies in the genus Riccia (Marchantiales) from southern Africa. 14. R. concava section Pilifer. Bothalia 19(2): 161-165. [CC BY]

description: The species can be distinguished from others in section Pilifer by its very low dorsal cell pillars, composed of only two (or three) cells, mostly wider than long, the top cell often being mammillose. From above, it is not very obvious that the cells are in free-standing pillars, the cells are closely packed, not in rows, nor uniform in size, as smaller cells are wedged in between larger ones. The dorsal surface is scurfy when dry and plants from drier areas in Namaqualand are bluish or purplish green. In cross section the flanks are generally steep, not sloping. The spores are usually easily recognized by a central cross on the distal face and low-walled, generally poorly demarcated alveoli on the proximal face.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: The species can be recognized by the fine, spongy texture of the dorsal face of the thallus, by the grooved, ligulate branches with lip-like, reflexed margins along the proximal parts when dry, and by the coarsely reticulate, polar spores. In the white-scaled group of species, R. montana and R. argenteolimbata are the only two dioicous species. R. argenteolimbata, however, has a more compact thallus, stiff, regular scales, apolar spores and its distribution is restricted to the drier, western parts of the country.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Elsieae is distinguished by its fairly large size. by its obovate to oblong, almost entire leaves, as well as by its spores with the distal face having relatively few, rather coarse spines which arc occasionally linked to form short ridges.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 8. F. elsieae and F. spinosa, two new Western Cape species with spinose spores. Bothalia 29(1): 25-33. [CC BY]

description: The species can be distinguished by its undulating leaves, by its often stipitate pseudoperianths, of which the mouth is highly convoluted, by completely or incompletely reticulate spores and generally by short and relatively wide elaters, the two spirals often forming rings or coils.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 9. A new species from Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal, with notes on other species. Bothalia 29(1): 77-82. [CC BY]

description: F. hyalorhiza can be distinguished by its colourless rhizoids; stems with a purple, ± central core, persisting in older shoots, but tailing’ off in young ones, undulating, suberect to spreading leaves and spores with the distal face bearing 6-8(9), ridges, which are sometimes parallel. at other times furcate, the branches often running in different directions. The spore ornamentation is fairly constant in all the specimens that were studied by light microscope as well as by scanning electron microscope.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombronia (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 10. Three new species from Northern and Western Cape. Bothalia 29(1): 83-93. [CC BY]

description: The plants are very large and may be more properly placed in Pottia. Additional sporo- phytes must be found in order to assess proper generic position.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE. 1981. Ditrichaceae to Grimmiaceae. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 83-281. Botanical Research Institute, Department of Agriculture and Water Supply, Pretoria. [https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.119879] [CC BY]

description: Riccia macrocarpa can be recognized by the yellow-brown colour along the thallus margins, by the inconspicuous scales, partly hyaline, partly flecked with brown and violet, and in sections of the thallus, by the presence of idioblasts, i.e. cells larger than surrounding ones and with clear or granular contents brown, grey or hyaline. The spore ornamentation of sinuous, vermiculate ridges on both faces is also a distinguishing character.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Riccia simii can be distinguished from other species in section Pilifer by the large, rounded, hyaline, wavy, closely imbricate scales, up to 1500 µm long and projecting as much as 500 µm above the thallus margins. The dorsal face is velvety and covered with fine cell pillars, which are usually relatively thick-walled at the base and less fragile than is usual in this section; the basal cells are ± equally long with the upper cross walls forming an interrupted horizontal line running across the width of the thallus.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Variable in such characters as the development of perianth keels and wings, in the shape of the leaf apex and in leaf dentition.
bibliographicCitation: Jones, EW. 2004. Lepidoziaceae Limpr. - Notothyladaceae (Milde) Müll.Frib. ex Prosk. In: MJ Wigginton (ed.), E.W. Jones's liverwort and hornwort Flora of West Africa: 102-424 National Botanic Garden (Belgium), Meise. [All rights reserved]

description: The species can be distinguished from other members in section Pilifer by the rather long, narrow, frequently simple branches, with the sides tightly inflexed when dry, and by large, imbricate, wavy, white scales. It is somewhat like R. simii in habit, but with the scales less prominent and not so closely imbricate. The dorsal cell pillars, spore ornamentation and distribution are also different.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the many spinose processes at the margins of the leaves and pseudoperianths, by being dioicous with smaller male plants, by mostly composite perigonial bracts and by the spore ornamentation with some smooth, parallel ridges on the distal face.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2001. Studies in the liverwort genus Fossombria (Metzgeriales) from southern Africa. 11. F. zuurbergensis, a new species from Eastern Cape and new records for the area. Bothalia 31(1): 25-29. [CC BY]

description: It contains plants with rather small but distinct trigones. The female bracts and bracteoles are rather variable, the lobule of the former varying from very short and obtuse to rather long and acute, bracteoles varying with sinus short - rather deep and the lobes subacute-obtuse.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: Gametophytically the relatively large size, dark green colour, and strongly dentate leaf margins identify this species. The leaf dentations are large enough to be seen easily with a hand lens and are made up of 2-4 cells each. The species is separated from other species in Porotrichum by its perfect peristome with striate teeth, broad segments and well-developed cilia.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1998. Erpodiaceae to Hookeriaceae. In: OA Leistner & E du Plessis (eds), Fl. S. Africa (1,3): 445-622. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/171731#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Sterile plants of M. debilis can be distinguished from M. pappeana, the species it has frequently been confused with, by the smaller size of the rather ribbon-like thallus branches, the dark median line on the dorsal face of the thallus, the smaller appendages of the median scales and by the shortly ciliate or almost entire margins of the cupules. Fertile plants should not be difficult to identify as the smallish male and female receptacles, the latter with deeply divided lobes, are quite distinctive and the margin of the involucre is entire.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 1999. Hepatophyta, Fl. S. Africa (1,1): 1-252. [CC BY]

description: I am not able to detect any specific difference between this and Lepidozia chaetophylla, and a species gathered by Dr. Spruce all through the forests of the Amazon and sent in 1852 to Mr. Borrer under the Mss. name of Jung, chaetophylla, so I publish it as a var. of it. In the type the stems are thicker, often bipinnate with shorter leaves closer together, perianth sometimes terminal on chief stem. Lepidozia bicruris Steph. according to the description and figure (Hedwigia 1885) comes near, but is dioicous, and leaves usually with only two segments, rarely three.
bibliographicCitation: Pearson, WH. 1886. Hepaticae natalenses a clarissima domina Helen Bertelsen missae. Forh. Vidensk.-Selsk. Kristiania 1886(3): 1-19. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/149513#page/45/mode/1up]

description: This species has in the past been confused with R. meyeri (R. fulvifolia), a key difference between them being the sexual condition - R. ankefmensis being monoicous and R. fulvifolia dioicous. The thick-walled cortical cells of the stem of R. ankefinensis, strongly contrasting with the medullary cells, is also a good differentiating character. Jones (1977) considered that the lobes of R. holstiana were often caducous, but Grolle (2001) stated he had never seen caducous leaves on true R. ankefinensis.
bibliographicCitation: Jones, EW. 2004. Lepidoziaceae Limpr. - Notothyladaceae (Milde) Müll.Frib. ex Prosk. In: MJ Wigginton (ed.), E.W. Jones's liverwort and hornwort Flora of West Africa: 102-424 National Botanic Garden (Belgium), Meise. [All rights reserved]

description: Very near related to R. meyeri and differs from this species in having different shape of the perianth, which is broadly triangular, only 1 mm long, flat to near the base; marginal cells of the lobes 14-20 µ, lobule with shorter free appendix of the upper portion of the free margin, only reaching the midline of the stem. Spores 20-24 µ, smooth, elaters 4-5 µ wide. It is frequently difficult to decide, to which of these two species a plant refers, especially when the perianths are young or the plant is sterile.
bibliographicCitation: Arnell, SW. 1963. Hepaticae of South Africa. Swedish NSRC, Stockholm. [All rights reserved]

description: Riccia mamrensis is rare; it is recognized by its small size, by the light green, linear branches of the thalli, which do not form rosettes, by rather inconspicuous, mostly hyaline, overlapping scales along the flanks and by the winged spores, distally with rows of areolae, their raised lateral walls linked up into irregular, radiating ridges.
bibliographicCitation: Perold, SM. 2005. Riccia mamrensis, a new species from Western Cape, South Africa. Cryptog. Bryol. 26(1): 67-72. [© Publications Scientifiques du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris] [All rights reserved]

description: The small plants and smooth leaf cells separate Z. dixonii from other Zygodon species in southern Africa.
bibliographicCitation: Magill, RE; Van Rooy, J. 1998. Erpodiaceae to Hookeriaceae. In: OA Leistner & E du Plessis (eds), Fl. S. Africa (1,3): 445-622. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/171731#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Gemmabryum ruderale is characterized by red-purple to violet rhizoids and relatively large, spheric, purple-red rhizoidal tubers.
bibliographicCitation: Spence, JR. 2014. 42. Bryaceae Schwagrichen, Fl. N. Amer. 28: 117-185. New York Botanic Garden, New York. [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the New York Botanical Garden Press] [All rights reserved]

description: Of the other three species currently assigned to the genus, Chenia ruigtevleia is most similar to C. leptophylla because of the strongly differentiated apiculus and the lack of coarse teeth in the upper part of the leaf, the denticulations rather formed of projecting-papillose cell walls. In addition it has caducous leaves that presumably function as vegetative propagules, a condition also seen commonly in C. leptophylla. However, C. ruigtevleia is easily distinguished from this, and all other species in the genus, by the presence of papillae on the medial laminal cells. The new species is further distinguished from C. leptophylla by its leaf shape. Although leaves of the two overlap greatly in overall size, the leaves of C. ruigtevleia are considerably broader for any given length. The contrasting leaf shapes give the two species quite different aspects when hydrated. In addition, the leaf cells of the new species are on average smaller than those of C. leptophylla, being rarely more than 17 µm wide while those of the latter often exceed 25 µm and plants with cells to 30 µm or more are not uncommon. Chenia ruigtevleia is superficially similar to certain small species of Hennediella (e.g., H. oedipodioides). However, these are easily distinguished by their laminal border of thick-walled, elongate cells, and the apex not ending in a single, sharp, colored conical cell with walls thicker than those of other apical cells.
bibliographicCitation: Hedderson, TAJ; Zander, RH. 2008. Chenia ruigtevleia (Pottiaceae), a new moss species from the Western Cape Province of South Africa. Bryologist 111(3): 496-500. description: The new genus is extremely distinctive in the combination of small plants, yellow or orange-yellow in KOH, with strongly dimorphic leaves (the upper toothed to laciniate-margined and long-awned, the lower entire, weakly but distinctly cucullate and with the costa ending in the apex), the laminal cells bulging ventrally and smooth to weakly papillose but flattened dorsally and strongly papillose, and immersed, macrostomous, eperistomate capsules with flat to umbonate opercula and flattened or indented bases, and long-conic to mitrate, prorate-papillose calyptrae. There are no genera among those reacting yellow in KOH to which Algaria bears even remote similarity. It is strongly differentiated from the several Pottioideae genera similarly reacting yellow to KOH solution by the plane leaf margins, the presence of a strongly differentiated, lacini-ately-toothed border in the upper leaves, lack of lamellae on the ventral surface of the costa, exposed guide cells in the costa, the bulging ventral surface of the relatively small upper laminal cells, which are largely papillose only on the dorsal side, the odd soda-can shaped capsule, and the flat to umbonate operculum.
bibliographicCitation: Hedderson, TAJ; Zander, RH. 2008. Algaria nataliei (Pottiaceae), a new moss genus and species from the Western Cape Province of South Africa. J. Bryol. 30: 192-195. [10.1179/174328208X300660] [All rights reserved]

description: The new species is unique among Orthotricha because it has two singular features never found combined before in the genus. The first one is the development of a conspicuous hyaline hairpoint on leaf apices similar to that of Orthotrichum diaphanum. Hyaline awns are very uncommon in Orthotrichum. In fact, besides the moss here described and the Mediterranean O. vittii F. Lara, Garilleti & Mazimpaka, several taxa have been described from South America, South Africa and North America, all of them now considered synonyms of O. diaphanum This feature is commonly interpreted as an unambiguous adaptation to xeric environments.The second exceptional feature of Orthotrichum karoo is the lack of exostome teeth, the peristome being reduced to only 16 endostome segments. The same peristome constitution has been described for two other species, the Mediterranean O. acuminatum H. Philib. and the Californian O. anodon F. Lara, Garilleti 8c Mazimpaka. Like O. karoo, both are epiphytic mosses that grow under Mediterranean or winter rainfall climate. In these other two Orthotricha, as in others with peristome reduction, the capsule also has short, ± strong exothecial bands that constrict its mouth when desiccated, making the spore release difficult under dry conditions but allowing it under wetter ones. In O. karoo no strong constriction of the capsule mouth under dry conditions can be expected, since it has normal exothecial bands. However, just below the mouth it has several rows of minute cells that tend to slightly close the mouth when dry, making it similar to that of O. acuminatum, although the endostome segments of O. karoo seem too thin to effectively hinder spore release. Orthotrichum karoo is very similar to O. diaphanum, from which it mainly differs in peristome constitution, but also in some minor details: 1) median leaf cells more thick-walled and consequently not bulging, 2) lower cells of the leaf awn strongly papillose and 3) a more differentiated ring of minute cells below the capsule mouth. In spite of these differences O. karoo shares with O. diaphanum numerous features, both gametophytic and sporophytic, and in our opinion both mosses must be interpreted as close relatives, the reduction of the peristome of the former being probably a derived character as an adaptation to very xeric environments.
bibliographicCitation: Lara, F; Garilleti, R; Mazimpaka. 2009. Orthotrichum karoo (Orthotrichaceae), a new species with hyaline-awned leaves from southwestern Africa. Bryologist 112(1): 194-201. [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the American Bryological and Lichenological Society. It may not be reproduced or transferred to any other publication without permission from the copyright holder] [All rights reserved]

description: Resprouting perennial, stems, inflorescences and calyces appressed hairy; leaf blades linear to narrowly elliptic; calyx winged, ±25 x 20 mm in fruit; nutlets with several-barbed glochidia; glochidia usually coalescing at their bases to form a distinct rim.
bibliographicCitation: Retief, E; Van Wyk, AE. 2002. The genus Trichodesma (Boraginaceae: Boraginoideae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 32(1): 151-166. [CC BY]

description: Differs from H. arenaria in he small flowers with very narrow petals.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W. 1970. Cruciferae, Fl. S. Africa 13: 1-118. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A very distinctive species related to L. cartilagineum (J. Mey). Thell. which occurs in saline areas of eastern Europe.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, W. 1970. Cruciferae, Fl. S. Africa 13: 1-118. Dept. Agric. and Technical Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is clearly related to L. hamatum Rourke on account of its few-flowered inflorescences, adaxially curved styles beset with minutely retrorse barbs and inflated perianth tubes. It is distinguished from L. hamatum by having linear to narrowly linear, entire leaves (usually tridentate in L. hamatum) and by the utriculose perianth tube, densely lanate in the upper half (glabrous in L hamatum). Another marked difference is that L. harpagonatum has a well-developed involucre of 25-35 bracts, whereas in L. hamatum the involucre consists of 3 or 4 bracts or is completely absent and is replaced by a false involucre formed from 4 or 5 floral bracts. On average there are more flowers in each inflorescence in L. harpagonatum (8-10 flowers) and fewer (4-7 flowers) in L. hamatum.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1994. Proteaceae: A new species of Leucospermum from the southwestern Cape. Bothalia 24(1&2): 167-170. [CC BY]

description: Is easily recognized; sprawling habit, glandular-villous stems and leaves, large red to rose-pink flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The distinguishing features of the species are the leafy flowering branches (not running up into distinct racemes), all parts glandular-pubescent, the white corolla limb (creamy tints, even palest yellow, have also been recorded; the throat is always yellow to orange), and the decidedly obtuse leaf lobes, which are themselves toothed. The degree of lobing varies tremendously, and there is some geographical patterning to this. In the OFS, Lesotho, Natal and most of the Transkei, leaves are mostly pinnatifid to pinnatipartite (divided roughly 1/2 to 2/3 of way to midrib), as in the type specimens of Sutera henrici and S. virgulosa. At least the lower, largest, lobes are toothed. On the Witteberg (type locality of J.filicaulis), the lobing is often deeper and some leaves are pinnatisect (lobed to the midrib). Around Queenstown, Cathcart (type locality of Sutera pinnatifida) and Engcobo leaves may be bipinnatisect. Pinnatipartite and pinnatisect leaves dominate over the western part of the geographical range of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The characteristic features of J. phlogiflora as the name is now used are the lanceolate coarsely serrate leaves (the lobes all ± acute) and the flowers in the axils of the leaves but these rapidly reduced in size so that the impression gained is that of bracteate rather than leafy racemes. The glandular hairs on stems and leaves are often rather coarse, a quality impossible to quantify, but more delicate indumentum seems to occur indiscriminately over the geographical range of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The bicoloured limb of the corolla (upper lip dark violet, lower cream or white) and the long eglandular hairs on the vegetative parts and on the calyx make this a species very easily recognized.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Root tips obtained from stem cuttings collected at the type locality of P. ocellatum were treated using the squash technique described by Albers & van der Walt. The somatic chromosome number of P. ocellatum has been determined as 2n=20. The basic chromosome number is most probably x=10.
bibliographicCitation: McDonald, DJ; Van der Walt, JJA; Van Wyk, N. 1990. A new species of Pelargonium with notes on its ecology and pollination biology. S. African J. Bot. 56(4): 467-470. description: C. marlothii has sometimes been confused with C. eckloniana from which it can be easily separated by the lack of scales in the indumentum.
bibliographicCitation: Anthony, NC. 1984. A revision of the southern African species of Cheilanthes Swartz and Pellaea Link. Contr. Bolus Herb. 11: 1-293. [All rights reserved]

description: Lamina outline generally pentagonal, lamina 3-pinnatifid; lower surface pilose with straight hairs; spores 64 per sporangium. The var. buchananii does occur in more sheltered or moist localities than the typical variety.
bibliographicCitation: Anthony, NC. 1984. A revision of the southern African species of Cheilanthes Swartz and Pellaea Link. Contr. Bolus Herb. 11: 1-293. [All rights reserved]

description: It is characterised by its one-flowered inflorescences, elongate buds and acuminate cupula and leaflets.
bibliographicCitation: Stirton, CH. 1995. A new species of Psoralea (Leguminosae: Papilionoideae) from eastern South Africa. Kew Bull. 50(3): 619-622. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4110336] [All rights reserved]

description: The specific epithet, aemulans, draws attention to the close resemblance of this species to P. exigua. It is particularly those plants with the smallest flowers and reduced stamens that resemble P. exigua, but they can at once be distinguished by the corolla tube, pubescent and purplish in P. aemulans, glabrous or nearly so in P. exigua and drying ochre-yellow (white when fresh?). The flowers of P. aemulans resemble those of P. gilioides in both pubescence and colouring. However, the limb is mostly smaller in P. aemulans (3-9 mm across the lateral lobes versus mostly 7.5-11 mm), the upper lip only is bearded in the larger flowers (not bearded all round the mouth) and the capsules are smaller (3-3.5 mm long versus 5-6 mm). The two species differ markedly in foliage, the leaves of P. aemulans being broad in relation to their length (spathulate, mostly 1-3 mm broad), those of P. gilioides narrow (linear, mostly 0.5-1 mm broad; the 2-4 lowermost leaves should be ignored as they are broad in many species of Polycarena). Plants of P. gilioides look leafier than those of P. aemulans because of the presence of dwarf axillary shoots (absent in P. aemulans).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: P. capensis, which is allied to P. batteniana, but usually has the limb coloured yellow (pale on the Cape Peninsula and nearby) and marked with a deeper yellow or orange, bearded star in the mouth (the mouth of the corolla in P. batteniana is glabrous or nearly so, and has an orange-yellow patch only below the posticous lip). The two species are further distinguished by the corolla tube being glabrous or very nearly so in P. batteniana, pubescent in P. capensis, which is always corymbosely branched and very leafy right up to the inflorescence, partly because of the strong development of leafy dwarf axillary shoots; the branching in P. batteniana is more divaricate than corymbose; in other words, the axillary shoots develop into spreading branches. Polycarena batteniana has a more northerly distribution than P. capensis, and grows at higher altitudes.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Intracymal bracts generally one per cyme; corolla tube usually slightly bent to geniculate; corolla generally longer than 10 mm long (measured across the bent tube); lower lip with obovate lobes; leaves up to 18 cm long including petiole; ovate to subelliptic with acuminate apex and always slightly oblique base.
bibliographicCitation: Manktelow, ME. 1996. Phaulopsis (Acanthaceae) — a monograph. Symb. bot. upsal. 31(2): 1-183. Acta Universitatis Upsaliensis, Uppsala. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago acocksii will be found in herbaria under several names, including S. tenuis, which it resembles in fades but from which it differs in its leaves, minutely glandular all over (not merely glandular-punctate with or without a few minute hairs at the apex), bracts minutely glandular all over together with few to many acute hairs (not with only a few scattered globular glands and with or without a few minute hairs on the outer surface), and corolla tube mostly shorter. Selago tenuis is known only from Namaqualand.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The relationship of S. fourcadei lies in part with S. distans, from which it differs in the shorter hairs on the stem (less than 0.1 mm versus ± 0.15 mm), leaves less strongly fascicled, largest primary leaves mostly longer (6-15 mm versus 2.5-9 mm), the sunken glands not oozing as they often do in S, distans (stem and bracts too are often viscid), calyx 1.8-2.2 mm long (not 2-3 mm) and hairy outside (not with globular glands only or occasionally a few hairs on the keels). The corolla in S. distans is always white; in S. fourcadei it varies from white to shades of violet, but the buds are often (perhaps always) tinged with violet when the expanded limb is white. The bracts, calyces and cocci are frequently tinged with violet, occasionally the leaves. The mature inflorescence is probably always longer than that of S. distans, and the flowers more distant; this is more easily seen than quantified. The two species are at least partially sympatric.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Its relationship lies with Z. bella and Z. venusta, with both of which it is partly sympatric, but it is easily recognized by its much smaller flowers, particularly corolla and anthers. The almost hispid patent hairs on the stems, which nearly always carry at least one pair of leaves above the radical ones, will at once distinguish it from Z. cohabitans, with which it is very easily confused. The two species differ further in a number of details, including the shape of the bracts and the number of stamens: four in Z. minima, two in Z. cohabitans.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: A distinctive species recognised by its peltate leaves with hollow petioles and scapose inflorescence of moderately large flowers with numerous petals and caducous sepals. The leaf blades are suborbicular and finely toothed with attractive pale green markings along the primary veins, conspicuous against the dull, dark green upper surface. Plants in sheltered situations tend to be much larger than those growing in shallower soils or in more exposed conditions on banks or in alpine seepages. Although the two extremes are striking, we have encountered a complete range of variants on wet banks and seepages on Naude's Nek in the southern Drakensberg, ranging from small, solitary-flowered plants with leaves less than 30 mm in diameter to well-grown individuals over 300 mm high with multiple flowers and leaves to 80 mm diam. Plants collected early in the season at high altitudes around 3 000 m in the Drakensberg Mtns, most commonly on the summit plateau of Mt aux Sources, are exceptionally dwarfed, with solitary (rarely two) flowers on scapes 30-70 mm long and leaves either just emergent or with reduced blades 5-20 mm diam. Tolken, who also remarked on this form, was uncertain how to treat it. Although these populations may represent a distinct alpine ecotype, the species as a whole exhibits such marked phenotypic plasticity that they are more likely merely extreme morphotypes, especially since early-flowering individuals from lower altitudes elsewhere may be similarly diminutive.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2013. The native and naturalised species of Peltocalathos and Ranunculus (Ranunculaceae: Ranunculeae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 43(2): 179-195. [CC BY]

description: In herbaria, S. grandic.eps has been much confused with S. fruticosa, an error traceable back to Flora capensis 5(1), but it has little in common with that species. In aspect, it much resembles S. aspera, from which it is readily distinguished, inter alia, by its strongly glandular bracts and calyces and mostly longer corolla tubes; S. pinea also has strongly glandular bracts and calyces, but its racemes are narrower (those of 5. grandiceps are particularly broad, which suggested the trivial name), bracts and corolla tube shorter, and limb mauve, not white.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago dregeana differs from S. glutinosa in having hairs on the stem mostly longer (0.15-0.3 mm versus 0.1-0.15 mm) and patent (not recurved), by its mostly shorter and narrower leaves, mostly shorter and narrower bracts (4.5-6 x 0.8-1 mm versus 5.1-10 x 0.9-1.2 mm), calyx mostly shorter (2.2-3 mm, versus 2.8-5 mm) and less conspicuously glandular, corolla tube 3-4.5 mm long (not 5.5-9 mm), and all four anthers well exerted.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The species has been much confused with Selago nachtigalii from which it is easily distinguished by its glabrous leaves, different inflorescence, bracts that are longer, markedly acute, and have broad white membranous margins, and white, not violet, corollas. In the Prodromus Flora of South West Africa, S. albomarginata was confused with Walafrida schinzii, a synonym of S. alopecuroides, a species easily recognized by its long foxtail inflorescences composed of innumerable small glomerules, and long narrow leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Mohria rigida is characterised by abaxially appressed, often broadly ovate, cordate-imbricate, often sinuous-walled scales, the crowded, caespitose frond arrangement, the rigid unwinged rachis, the often proximally unwinged secondary rachis, and sporangia generally borne on the entire frond or only the proximal pinnae may be sterile. In M. rigida the stipe/lamina ratio averages 1:2.45 (n=45) whereas in M. vestita, with which this species may be confused, it averages 1:3.6 (n= 61). Clavate trichomes are 35.0-(45.76)-61.1 µm long and naviculate trichomes are 77.5-(112.86)-164.97 µm long.
bibliographicCitation: Roux, JP. 1995. Systematic studies in the genus Mohria (Pteridophyta: Anemiaceae). VI. Taxonomic review. Bothalia 25(1): 1-12. [CC BY]

description: Mohria saxatilis is distinguished by the short prostrate rhizome, short stipe, the crowded fronds, the large spreading scales on the stipe and on the abaxial lamina surfaces, and the broadly winged costa. Diagnostic micromorphological characters are the larger clavate trichomes which are 61.1-(68.11)-76.4 µm long, and epidermal cells and the occurrence of copolocytic and tripolocytic stomata not found in any of the other taxa. Naviculate trichomes are 97.7-(139.05)-177.19 µm long.
bibliographicCitation: Roux, JP. 1995. Systematic studies in the genus Mohria (Pteridophyta: Anemiaceae). VI. Taxonomic review. Bothalia 25(1): 1-12. [CC BY]

description: Mohria vestita is characterized by the short stipe/ lamina ratio, the reduction in size of the pinnae towards the lamina base, ossiform-celled hairs which adaxially are confined to the secondary rachis and veins, and the relatively small, generally hastate and sparsely set twisted scales which are also confined to the secondary rachis and veins on the abaxial surface. Clavate trichomes are 30.0-(51.31)-63.4 µm long and naviculate trichomes are 85.0-(138.32)-196.54 µm long.
bibliographicCitation: Roux, JP. 1995. Systematic studies in the genus Mohria (Pteridophyta: Anemiaceae). VI. Taxonomic review. Bothalia 25(1): 1-12. [CC BY]

description: Selago beaniana resembles S. singularis in its velvety pubescence with a strong component of dendroid hairs but is at once distinguished by its distinctly petiolate leaves with much less markedly revolute margins, bracts oblong, not elliptic, and plane (not concave) on the inner face, and corolla tube longer (c.3-3.4 mm versus 1.7-2.8 mm). Also, the panicles are laxer, but this is difficult to quantify.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago singularis is notable for dendroid hairs on the young parts of the branches, velvety pubescence on leaves, bracts and calyces, and particularly for the short, thick-textured leaves of which the margins are so strongly revolute that they may fuse; the leaf is then broadly elliptic to almost orbicular in transverse section. This singular leaf structure suggested the trivial name.Most of the specimens seen had been determined as S. albida, from which S. singularis is easily distinguished not only by the dendroid hairs on the stems and its leaves, but also by its shorter and relatively broader bracts (lowermost c.1.7-2.8 x 0.9-1.3 mm, versus 3-3.5 x 0.7-1 mm), shorter corolla tube (1.7-2.8 mm versus 3.1-4 mm), and very different inflorescence. In its inflorescence, S. singularis resembles S. glabrata (two collections seen had been determined as.S. minutissima, a name very commonly misapplied to specimens of S. glabrata) but again, the dendroid hairs on the stem, thick velvety leaves and velvety bracts and calyces are diagnostic.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago subspinosa is characterized by its woody, twiggy habit, the plant frequently being much dwarfed, the old inflorescence axes persisting as subspines, the white spreading hairs scattered on leaves, bracts and margins of calyces, the minute stalked glands liberally sprinkled over bracts and calyces, and glomerules, often solitary, of mauve to pink flowers with remarkably far exerted stamens. The plant dries black, so the white hairs stand out vividly (the living plant is recorded as looking greyish). Its closest ally is possibly S. namaquensis, from which it differs in its mostly smaller leaves (4-11 x 0.5-1.8 mm, not 7-20 x 1.3-3.8 mm) with heavily revolute margins, racemes mostly solitary, calyx 2.8-3.2 mm long (not 1.5-2 mm), corolla coloured (not white).Very dwarfed twiggy subspinose specimens of S. spectabilis bear a strong superficial resemblance to S. subspinosa, but are easily distinguished by the lack of spreading hairs on leaves and bracts, markedly paniculate inflorescence, and smaller bracts (2.3-3 x 1.1-1.8 mm, not 3.5-5 x 1.7-2.2 mm).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Its closest relationship probably lies with S. lacunosa, which has similar bracts and cocci (though the bracts are mostly narrower, and the cocci are smaller); the leaves of S. lacunosa are mostly broader (largest primary ones 0.8-3 mm, not 0.6-1 mm) and the anticolateral calyx lobes are narrower (0.2-0.4 mm broad versus 0.6-0.7 mm).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It is closely allied to S. multiflora, which also grows in Namaqualand and care is needed to distinguish them. Selago verna differs in its broader leaves (largest c.1.1-1.5 (- 2) mm broad versus 0.5-1 mm) with minute globular glands scattered among the acute hairs (also on the bracts), and calyx often longer, 1.8-2.5 mm versus 1.5-2 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago cedrimontana is allied to S. mundii and S. micradenia, which have similar long narrow densely glandular-puberulous bracts. It is distinguished from S. mundii by its much more distinctly glandular-puberulous stems (examine young parts) with patent hairs up to c. 0.3-0.7 mm long, narrower leaves (largest c. 1.5-2.2 mm broad versus 0.8-1.2 mm) clad in scattered hairs 0.2-0.6 mm long, and from 5. micradenia by its more or less virgate (not divaricate) branching, the long patent hairs on the stem, leaves ascending (not wide-spreading) and more distinctly hairy, and longer calyx.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The plant is unmistakable: it dries blackish, the leaves are not or only weakly fascicled, and stem, leaves, bracts and calyces are all densely pubescent, the hairs tending to be retrorse. Its closest ally is probably S. magnakarooica, which it somewhat resembles, especially as they both dry blackish, but they differ in several characters: leaves densely puberulous all over in S. comptonii (not very minute scattered hairs sometimes invisible except for irregularities in the epidermis), spikes mostly loosely panicled (not always solitary), bracts densely puberulous all over (not hairs scattered, most conspicuous on margins and lower part of bract), and corolla mauve (not white). The two species appear to be wholly allopatric.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: S. farrago is easily distinguished by its bigger, looser panicle, bracts up to 0.6-0.7 mm broad (not 1-1.2 mm) with rather coarse hairs 0.2-0.25 mm long (not 0.1 mm) on the margins, c.0.1 mm long scattered on the backs (not glabrous or nearly so), calyx puberulous outside, hairs c.0.15 mm long (not glabrous or nearly so except for hairs on the margins of the lobes). Five of the ten flowers dissected had only four calyx lobes. The coarse hairs (short and broad-based) scattered on leaves, bracts and calyces are a striking feature of the plant. Selago verna, another species in this affinity, also grows in the Kamiesberg; it is easily distinguished by its much more velvety indumentum, narrow panicles, and broader bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Only the records from Wemmershoek and Franschehoek are outside the area of S. scabrida, to which S. impedita is closely allied. It is distinguished by its habit, loosely branched weak stems as opposed to stiff rodlike virgately branched ones, leaves not fascicled, glabrous or with a few hairs mainly on the margins, spikes mostly solitary, bracts glabrous on the backs or with a few hairs on the keel. But there are a good many specimens dial are intermediate between them: they have the fades of S. impedita (loose branching, solitary heads), but the leaves may be weakly fascicled and the bracts are scabrid all over the backs.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: A feature of S. inaequifolia is the disparity in length between primary and axillary leaves especially on the lower part of the stem, which suggested the trivial name. It is commonplace for primary leaves to be longer than axillary ones, but the difference is exaggerated in S. inaequifolia and very striking. I know the species from three collections made in the environs of Klaver over a period of 50 years, and all display this character, which sets it apart from S. verna (largest primary leaves 8-20 x 0.7-1.1 mm in S. inaequifolia, 2.5-8 x 1.1-2 mm in S. verna). They differ further in the hairs on the stems (± patent, ± recurved in S. verna), lack of minute globular glands on the leaves of S. inaequifolia, and shorter hairs on the margins of bracts and calyx lobes in S. inaequifolia. Selago multiflora too is distinguished by its shorter primary leaves (1-6 mm) and recurved hairs on the stems, as well as by its divaricate branching. Selago verna occurs further north than S. inaequifolia and at higher altitudes; S. multiflora is also more montane in its distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago micradenia (Greek: mikros aden, small glands) is one of several species that Rolfe (1901) confused with S. scabrida and material will be found in herbaria under that name, or nameless. The plant bears no resemblance to S. scabrida. In its minutely glandular bracts and calyx it is similar to S. mundii, the area of which lies immediately south of that of S. micradenia. The twiggy habit of S. micradenia (branching ± divaricate, virgate in 5. mundii) and wide-spreading leaves (sharply ascending, only the upper part somewhat spreading in ,S'. mundii) will at once distinguish it. Selago micradenia differs further in its rather smaller spikes, often shorter calyx, small corolla limb, shorter fdaments, and posticous anthers held in the mouth.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago multiflora (the profuse flowering of which suggested the trivial name) is allied to S. divaricata and S. verna. It is distinguished from S. divaricata by its leaves, mostly narrowly oblong (not elliptic to subrotund), not glandular-punctate but minutely puberulous all over, hairs c.0.1 mm long (versus glandular-punctate, otherwise so minutely puberulous as to appear glabrous or almost so), largest bracts mostly 2.2-3.2 mm long (not 1.4-2.4 mm) and without any glandular hairs, corolla tube 2.3-3.8 mm long (not 1.3-2.4 mm). Selago verna differs in its broader leaves (largest c.1.1-1.5 (- 2) mm broad versus 0.5-1 mm) with minute globular glands scattered among the acute hairs (also on the bracts), and calyx often longer, 1.8-2.5 mm versus 1.5-2 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Compton's collection was determined as S. brevifolia, which it much resembles in facies but from which it is immediately distinguished by its cocci, plane (not deeply concave) on the inner face. The two species differ further in their bracts, in S. rubromontana either glabrous on the back except for minute globular glands or with minute hairs up to c.0.1 mm long at the base (not 0.2-0.25 mm long) and hairs on the margins of the calyx lobes up to 0.15-0.2 mm long (not 0.2-0.25 mm). The leaves of S. rubromontana are also blunter and thinner than those of S. brevifolia.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Selago seticaulis has much the aspect of S. levynsiae : both are bushy shrublets more or less divaricately well branched with leaves uncrowded and not or scarcely fascicled, but in S. seticaulis the hairs on the stem are patent (not retrorse) and mostly longer than those of S. levynsiae, the leaves are usually hairy on both surfaces (hairs mainly on margins in S. levynsiae) and the corolla is either glabrous outside or with very minute scattered glandular hairs (distinctly pubescent in S. levynsiae). The area of S. seticaulis lies east of that of S. levynsiae, and while S. seticaulis flowers mainly between October and December, S. levynsiae flowers mainly between January and March (there are overlapping records).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Among its immediate congeners, it is rendered distinctive by its short divaricate branchlets each terminating in a short relatively broad spike, hairs on the stems confined to narrow longitudinal bands (the stem is glabrous below the insertion of each leaf), leaves not or scarcely fascicled, leaves, bracts and calyces very nearly devoid of hairs other than globular or sunken glands. Its closest ally is possibly S. distans, easily distinguished by its stems, hairy all round, leaves distinctly fascicled, and mostly shorter spikes, solitary or loosely panicled.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: The relationship of S. tenuifolia lies with the tropical African species S. swynnertonii, found in Zimbabwe and Mozambique. It differs in its mostly longer leaves, mostly shorter hairs on the margins of the bracts and on the calyces, and all the anthers exserted.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: In herbaria, S. lilacina has been confused with S. canescens in particular, a species that it resembles in facies and to which it is allied. It is easily distinguished by its 3-lobed calyx and cocci lacking spurious cells; also, the leaves are broader (largest primary leaves 1.2-2 mm versus 0.5-1 mm), as are the bracts (lowermost 1.2-1.8 mm versus 0.6-1.1 mm).The two species are sympatric, though S. lilacina is much more limited in distribution.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: It is the fourth southern African member of the genus with simple leaves. All other known species have 3-or 5-foliolate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Retief, E; Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 1997. Notes on African Plants: Vitaceae. A new species of Rhoicissus from the Eastern Cape. Bothalia 27(1): 49-51. [CC BY]

description: Polystichum x saltum closely resembles P. wilsonii in size, frond and pinnule morphology, and to a certain degree in the characteristics of the paleae. The erose to fimbriate indusium, however, is more characteristic of P. transvaalense. The mean guard cell length, the adaxial epidermal cell length, and the mean maximum radius of the indusium are anomalous - being larger than that of either progenitor. Perhaps the most distinctive diagnostic feature of the taxon is the varying number of aborted spores borne in the sporangia.

This material may not be reproduced or transferred to any other publication without written permission from the copyright holder] [All rights reserved]

description: Differentiation in the field between this species and Polystichum pungens is not always easy because of their sympatric distribution, the variation within and among populations, and the absence of stable macromorphological characters. However, P. incongruum can be separated from P. pungens by its thicker, more stout rhizome. The pinnules in the former species are narrower, more slender and acuminate (often also slightly falcate), compared to the somewhat ovate to ovate-oblong, almost obtuse pinnules of P. pungens. A further character separating P. incongruum from P. pungens is the frequent occurrence of clavate unicellular glands along the sporangium stalk in the former species. Clavate unicellular glands occurring along the indusium margin have also been observed in some populations in the southern Cape, a feature never occurring in P. pungens. The former species is furthermore a sexual tetraploid (2n = 164), whereas P. pungens is a sexual octoploid (2n = 328).

description: Specimens of T. umdausensis form dense clumps of short, neatly packed, bluntly 4-angled and almost cylindrical stems which are usually small. These stems have a slight tendency to spread underground when ‘in a tight corner’, as sometimes happens between stones or in a pot in cultivation. In this species the pedicel is ascending with an abruptly bent apex. Consequently the dainty flowers usually have a modest, slightly nodding habit. The corolla tube occupies about half the length of the flower with the lobes spreading at the mouth, giving the flower a distinctly campanulate shape. The flowers are extremely variable in colour, even more so than in T. herrei, and the lobes may be anything from plain yellow to red-brown with whitish, reticulated, slightly raised ridges. The tube is usually strikingly radially marked with white against a red or brown background. These radial markings are of somewhat irregular thickness, which creates almost the same impression as if the colour had run down the tube. The raised ridges on the corolla are neither as fine and dense as in T. pedunculata and T. aperta, nor do they stand out as heavily as in T. herrei. The flowers emit a mild smell of bad breath or excrement. Right at the base and not visible unless the corolla is dissected, there is a small, thickened, pentagonal annulus around the corona. From the annulus to the mouth of the tube, the surface is densely encrusted with small, spherical to clavate papillae. The outer corona in T. umdausensis and T. aperta does not consist of discrete, more or less rectangular lobes as in all other species of Tromotriche. Here the lobes are very short and are fused to the lower backs of the inner lobes, thereby forming a quite substantial pouch beneath each guide-rail. In total these five pouches give the entire gynostegium a pentagonal, cupular appearance and this cup is pressed into the five corners of the small annulus. Right at the base of each pouch is a small, deep orifice which appears to be lined with secretory cells and in which nectar collects to some extent. The guide-rails are remarkably short but are still quite capable of holding a pollinium until the caudicle breaks, with or without a corpuscle still in place above them. This species is separated from all the other species in Tromotriche by its very short inner corona lobes. As usual, these are adpressed to the backs of the anthers but mostly they do not exceed the anthers. In other words, they do not rise into any sort of column above the centre of the style-head as happens in all the other species.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Specimens of T. herrei usually consist of relatively few thick and somewhat irregularly knobbly stems which may become quite tall and regularly exceed 100 mm in height. Tromotriche herrei often occurs with T. umdausensis around Jakkalswater and with T. aperta north of Eksteenfontein, but the comparative stoutness and irregular angles of the stems in T. herrei can usually be used to tell them apart. When in flower T. herrei is unmistakable. The flowers are produced in small numbers near the tips of the stems and face upwards. They consist of prominent lobes a little longer than broad and spreading from around the mouth of a comparatively deep tube. On the lobes and in the mouth of the tube the inside is covered with a network of particularly coarse, reticulate rugosities. The rugosities themselves are white and somewhat rough, rather like ridges of ice or icing sugar, and the areas between them are a darker colour which may be red or brown or even greenish. These coarse rugosities tend to become fewer in the tube and form concentric rings and then fade out lower down. If the corolla tube is examined carefully, it will be found to consist of two parts. There is a narrow portion towards the base (the ‘primary tube’) which is somewhat thicker than the rest and is uniformly dark in colour. This encloses the lower part of the corona quite closely and sometimes has a small ring of tissue overhanging the slightly flattened base of the tube. This slightly flattened base is paler and thinner than the part above it and lets in light around the base of the corona to produce a window-like effect. Above the basal portion the corolla tube widens and is thinner-walled but it is constricted again somewhat at its mouth (this forms the ‘secondary tube’) so that as a whole it is urceolate. The flowers have a faint excrement-like odour. As is often the case in Tromotriche, the channelled outer lobes are small and insignificant and are completely dwarfed by the comparatively massive inner lobes. They secrete nectar in noticeable quantities on their upper surface. Since they are folded to become especially narrow towards their tips, this seems to conduct some of this nectar onto the surrounding surface of the corolla. In T. herrei each inner lobe is much swollen and rounded towards the apex and is shiny, almost black and smooth. Each has a very similarly shaped, though slightly smaller and quite obviously laterally flattened dorsal horn. Together these parts of the inner corona fill the base of the tube and markedly restrict access to the pollinia and guide-rails. In many details the gynostegium bears a remarkable resemblance to that of Stapelia clavicorona (where gaining access to the pollinia is also quite difficult) but this is a case of convergence and the two are not closely related.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: As a consequence of their habitat, plants are usually found with at least some pendulous stems, which may reach the remarkable length of nearly 3 m. Usually, though, they are of quite modest dimensions and more commonly reach lengths of 0.3-1.0 m. Plants growing among bushes in steep areas have the prostrate habit with somewhat ‘burrowing’ stems that one finds more frequently in T. choanantha. The stems are more or less square in cross-section with low, obscure tubercles forming the angles and the tissue slightly concave between these angles. Younger plants are bluish green but much older pieces can become covered with a grey, corky layer. Flowers of T. baylissii are produced mainly towards the apices of the stems, particularly on young growth and they are held on a spreading pedicel so as to face horizontally. Like those of T. choanantha, they are shaped very like a bell and give off a light, foul odour. The outside is brownish, sometimes faintly mottled, shiny and usually slightly (sometimes very strongly) pentagonal towards the base with the corners alternating with the lobes. Inside it is brownish red and transversely rugulose, especially around the middle of the tube, but these ridges become fainter suddenly near the base and also gradually fade out on the lobes. In some flowers there are also five radial grooves running down from below the middle of each lobe and these give the inside of the tube a distinctly pentagonal shape too but, because of the thickness of the corolla lower down, this does not correspond with the five-sidedness of the corolla outside. If the corolla is cut lengthwise, it can be seen that the tube thickens noticeably towards the base and then very suddenly narrows again so as to form an overhanging ledge above a small wider area around the base of the gynostegium. This ledge is the equivalent of the annulus in species such as T. revoluta. The corona lobes fit snugly into the lower part of the tube where it is thickest. Here the outer lobes rise quite steeply, pressing against the side of the tube and nestling into the grooves running down it. They are relatively short and deeply channelled down the inner surface. Since the outer lobes are fairly steeply inclined, the area around the guide-rails is very restricted and it is quite difficult to gain access to them. The pollinia are suitably shaped for this, though, being much narrower and longer than in any other Tromotriche (except T. choanantha) and consequently they are able to fit into this restricted space. This restriction of the space around the guide-rails may also be seen in Orbea carnosa and Stapelia flavopurpurea. Beyond the anthers the inner lobes rise in the centre and are often gathered into a column. They are slender and cylindrical, with a slightly roughened and swollen apex. Each lobe has a comparatively large, laterally flattened, dorsal horn which is nearly as long as the lobe itself and rises steeply just behind it. The flowers in T. baylissii vary greatly in the breadth of the tube towards its mouth, its depth and the extent to which it is pentagonal. The photographs by G.G. Smith of Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer’s collection show a flower which is very wide at the mouth and relatively shallow (as well as very boldly rugulose inside) whereas Leach’s photographs, of plants found in much the same area, show flowers which have a much deeper and narrower tube, with much shallower rugosities inside. Similar variation in the shape of the flower is known in T. choanantha. Leach described a ‘var. ciliata’ for plants with cilia on the margins of the corolla lobes. At that time such plants were known only from around Studtis. More recently they have also been collected from cliff faces near Andrieskraal at the eastern end of the Baviaanskloof and some plants from south of Steytlerville also have ciliate flowers, growing with others without them. It seems therefore that these marginal cilia are of sporadic occurrence throughout the distribution of the species.
