Plants from dry situations have longer more prominent stipules. While extreme forms look distinct there are all stages of intermediate. Seaside forms may have succulent leaves. In collections this has been much confused, especially with P. elongatum. This has been partly due to the fact that Fenzl and later Sonder looked upon a short unbranched stem as diagnostic for the species. Examination of much material has shown that this is not so. The species is readily distinguished by the stipules and the seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: This has been much confused with P. subtile Fenzl and specimens are usually so named. It differs in having all the basal leaves linear, in the persistent lacerate stipules, the fruit distinctly longer than the perianth, and in the smooth shining seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: This species is allied to P. dichotomum but distinguished by the habit, the broader flatter leaves, the not sheathing stipules, and the less spreading inflorescence. It has some resemblance to P. thunbergii but is separated by the basal leaf-tuft, the leaves not narrowed to the base, the larger stipules, and the inflorescences.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: It is distinguished from the allied species by the habit, the stipules, the small flowers, and the compressed seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: Resembles P. viride but distinguished by the stipules, the slender red peduncles, the almost free perianth segments, and the very thin lobes of the disc.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: Distinguised by the lax habit, the soft green not crowded leaves, the stipules, and the small flowers with distinctly connate perianth. Occasionally there is a continuation of the leafy stem from the first node of the inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: A very distinctive species in habit. In collections there has been some confusion with Pharnaceum lineare but it is easily separated by the entire stipules, simple inflorescence, and habit.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1958. The South African species of Aizoaceae: IV. Mollugo, Pharnaceum, Coelanthum and Hypertelis. J. S. African Bot. 23: 11-65. [CC BY]

description: The leaves on the shoots fall at or about flowering time leaving only the axillary fascicles. Plants in the younger stages have been confused with Galenia secunda.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1961. The South African species of Aizoaceae: XI. Plinthus. J. S. African Bot. 27: 147-151. [CC BY]

description: Much like T. sarcophylla but more compact, with subsessile leaves, solitary flowers, and fruit with an intermediate ridge.
bibliographicCitation: Adamson, RS. 1955. The South African Species of Aizoaceae: II. Tetragonia. J. S. African Bot. 21: 109-154. [CC BY]

description: Nearest H. rehneltianum (Berger) Schwantes, from which it differs by its lower growth, shorter and thicker leaves frequently falcately curved when viewed from above, and by the stamens being shorter than the petals.
bibliographicCitation: Multiple authors. 1928. Novitates Africanae (cont.). J. Bot. 66: 195-200. [All rights reserved]

description: Dried specimens of this plant in flower only cannot be distinguished from K. acutipetala without dissecting the flowers, but when in fruit the number of valves of the capsule easily distinguishes it. I have not been able to compare living flowers of the two species, so cannot state if the colour distinction is constant, but the difference in the number of valves to the capsule and the size and number of seeds in a cell is quite constant in the numerous capsules examined, and which were attached to living and dead plants kindly sent to me by Professor C. E. Moss. According to the original description, this plant differs from K. acutipetala 'by the 6-parted flowers' and in Latin '6-merous' flowers, but this is surely a botanical error. Other species are described as having '4-merous' or '5-merous' flowers, but no known member of the whole group of Mesembryanthema has flowers that are either 4-, 5- or 6-merous.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, NE. 1931. Mesembryanthemum (cont.). Gard. Chron. 89: 279-279. [All rights reserved]

description: Lithops aucampiae is closely allied to L. lesliei, N.E.Br. both in floral characters and in the shape and general reddish brown colouring of the bodies, harmonising with the colour of the soil in which they are found. But in L. aucampiae there is no window or transparency in the apical area of the body, except in the new growth, and the distinct they seem to become.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, HML. 1932. A new Lithops from Griqualand West. S. Afr. Gdng Country Life 22: 306-306. [All rights reserved]

description: In size and form it is much like M. lesliei, N.E.Br., but the much deeper fissure separating the tips of the leaves and the peculiar tawny colour of their truncate tips, marked with small round dull dark green dots, readily distinguishes it from that species, which also comes from a far distant locality in the Transvaal.
bibliographicCitation: Multiple authors. 1914. Diagnoses Africanae: LIX. Bull. Misc. Inform. Kew 1914: 167-171. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4115402] [All rights reserved]

description: This is undoubtedly a very distinct species, related to L. turbiniformis. At first glance one would think you have L. turbiniformis before you, but this species differs from it in two very important respects, viz., (i) this species is of a bluish-grey colour, whereas L. turbiniformis is rust brown or at least of a reddish tint colouration; (ii) in between the tubercles or wrinkles there are depressions and here are found the minute dark-grey warts, a feature not observed so far in any other Lithops species and characteristic of this species. These minute warts are distinctly seen under a magnifying lens of ten diameters or very slightly with the naked eye.
bibliographicCitation: Nel, GC. 1943. Species novae vel minus cognitae: Lithops and Caralluma. Ann. Univ. Stellenbosch 21: 1-17. [All rights reserved]

description: Remarkable for the short entire leaves and the exceptionally long staminodes.
bibliographicCitation: Multiple authors. 1928. Novitates Africanae (cont.). J. Bot. 66: 229-233. [All rights reserved]

description: As Haworth was the first to describe M. semidentatum, the name goes with his description; until more is known of the plant it is impossible to say whether the one Salm Dyck figured is distinct from that which Haworth described or not. In either case it seems very improbable that a plant end. to the Trans, should have been in cult, in Eur. in 1820; and as the Trans, plant seems to have smaller fls. than Salm Dyck represents, I deem it best to consider it a distinct species for the present. Sond. quotes a specimen of M. semidentatum, collected by Zey. near the Gamka River, which is a more likely locality for it.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt Davy, J. 1926. A manual of the flowering plants and ferns of the Transvaal with Swaziland, South Africa. Longmans, Green and Co. Ltd., London. [All rights reserved]

description: This appears to be a hybrid, but we are not sure what the parents are. Perhaps S. ronaldii, L. Bol. is one of them and a species not yet determined the other. We have seen no perfect flowers, nor has fruit been formed. In longitudinal sections of the leaves only the midrib is visible, and the two primary nerves (one on each side of the midrib, usually found in Stomatium) are visible only in the basal half of the sheath.
bibliographicCitation: Bolus, HML. 1935. Notes on Mesembrianthemum and allied genera. 473-508 University of Cape Town, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Plant almost stemless, branched; leaves triquetrous, gradually thickening towards the apex, obtuse, greenish, punctate-papulose, pustulate-gibbous on the inside at the base, carinal angle dilated, very entire, lateral ones denticulated above the middle; flowers on short peduncles.
bibliographicCitation: Sonder, OW. 1862. Mesembryaceae. In: WH Harvey & OW Sonder (eds), Leguminosae to Loranthaceae, Fl. Cap. (Harvey) 2: 386-479. Lovell Reeve & Co. Ltd., London. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15233#page/394/mode/1up] [All rights reserved]

description: It is a pioneer plant and does not necessarily occur in a definite zone of its own. Plants of this annual species die before enough rain water has accumulated to submerge them in inland salt marshes, but they also occur in maritime salt marshes.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1967. The species of Arthrocnemum and Salicornia (Chenopodiaceae) in southern Africa. Bothalia 9(2): 255-307. [CC BY]

description: Differing from H. revolutum Vahl in that the flowers are in few- to many-flowered terminal corymbose cymes instead of solitary and in the larger leaves with densely reticulate venation. Var. schimperi (Hochst. ex A. Rich.) Moggi & Pisacchi is restricted to Ethiopia.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB; Robson, NKB. 1976. Clusiaceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 14-23. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differing from H. natalense in its shorter, procumbent stems and shortly petiolate leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Killick, DJB; Robson, NKB. 1976. Clusiaceae, Fl. S. Africa 22: 14-23. BRI, Dept. Agric. & Tech. Services, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguishing characters: plant quite glabrous, flowers solitary and pedunculate.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Medicinal.
bibliographicCitation: Welman, WG. 2019. Convolvulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 790-803. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely related to C. natalensis or perhaps only a form of it. C. galpinii can be separated by its abruptly acuminate and shorter sepals, smaller corollas, more slender, often twining stems and usually smaller, often sagittate or deltoid-cordate leaves and puberulous seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its leaves which are at least 3 times as long as broad and the corolla which is 2-3 times as long as the calyx.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its pinnately nerved, linear to linear-oblong leaves and fairly large flowers with corolla up to 25 mm long. C. thunbergii is most closely related to or perhaps even conspecific with C. natalensis. The varieties distinguished by Meeuse (1957a) in C. natalensis sometimes approach C. thunbergii very closely.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Closely related to I. verbascoidea, but distinguished by its glabrescent leaves and sepals and also a more easterly distribution. Both I. albivenia and I. verbascoidea are showy plants worth cultivating.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The species is distinguished by its cordate, subglabrous leaves, ovate-triangular outer sepals and corolla which is only slightly longer than the calyx. The subsp. africana is characterised by the sparsely pilose sepals and the white corolla with a purple centre. The subsp. plebeia occurs in Australia and Malaysia while the subsp. indica Verde, occurs in India.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by its cordate-oblong to cordate-ovate leaves, cordate or auricled outer sepals and 8-12 mm long, mauve corolla. The typical subspecies occurs in tropical Africa as well as tropical Asia. It is distinguished by its up to 22 mm long, white corolla and larger sepals (in fruit up to 9 x 23 mm).
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ; Welman, WG. 2000. Convolvulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 28(1): 1-138. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209568#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: At first glance this species might be considered to be a hybrid between C. velutina and C. woodii, both of which occur in the area concerned. On closer investigation this seems most unlikely seeing that C. adscendens is found only in one small area east of Port Elizabeth while the putative parents occur together at many localities outside this area without any records of more 'putative hybrids'.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: In arid areas such as the Karoo, Namaqualand and southern South West Africa/Namibia plants with terete leaves are often locally predominant, while in other areas this form grows next to plants with dorsiventrally flattened leaves. Similarly, the leaf margin of some plants in the vicinity of Graaff-Reinet, Uitenhage and Laingsburg is at times excessively undulate but at or near these localities ranges of intermediates which merge into typical C. orbiculata are also found.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The shape and size of the leaves of this species are often variable within the same population, but there is a tendency towards narrow leaves eastwards towards Prince Albert. Throughout the range the species is, however, easily distinguished by the very long marginal cilia which are often clustered into groups, particularly in the Cedarberg.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The subspecies capitella and nodulosa are usually distinguished in southern African material by the large dorsal appendage on the corolla lobes in terminal position, a character not easily observed in shrivelled dried material. Plants of subsp. capitella are distinguished from those of var. nodulosa by the glabrous bracts subtending the sessile dichasia, and the emarginate squamae found in specimens from the eastern parts of its distribution area.An extreme form with very much flattened leaves is found west of Port Elizabeth. Depauperate plants of this form tend to retain their juvenile character of 4-ranked leaves, but they soon outgrow that stage in cultivation.Somewhat different are plants from north-east of Port Elizabeth which sometimes have almost terete leaves, but again a range of intermediates is found nearby.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Plants may rarely persist for a long time and then develop a thick stem and a thick main root; in subsp. macrorrhiza the branches are always thinner than the very much swollen tap root.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Shaded plants are usually less floriferous, and as the leaves are much longer under those conditions the whole plant assumes a completely different appearance. Similarly, depauperate plants are not easily recognized because the inflorescence may be reduced to a single terminal cyme, or sometimes even only a terminal flower, usually produced from the third node.C. macrantha (Hook.f.) Diels & Pritzel, a species widespread in temperate Australia, has been relegated to the synonomy of C. decumbens var. decumbens. The apparently natural distribution of the species seems to extend through much of the temperate regions of the southern hemisphere. The South American species C. ovallei (Phil.) Reiche should, according to recent research, also be relegated to the synonomy of C. decumbens.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: This species is widespread and often locally common, but in contrast to other species of this section it prefers to grow on sandy soil and in partial shade.Plants are usually glabrous but may vary from minutely hairy or velvety to glabrescent with tufts of hairs around the hydathodes. Too little is known about plants from the area just south of Lüderitz Bay to determine whether a range of intermediates can be found here from hairy, as in subsp. elegans, to the coarse rounded papillae of subsp. namibensis, as has been recorded for C. grisea. The shape and size of the leaves are also variable. In the area between Port Nolloth and Komaggas the leaves are somewhat elongate and pointed so that these plants can only be distinguished from depauperate specimens of C. grisea by the completely shrivelled old leaves.The leaves are more or less pyramidal in shape but just north of Vanrhynsdorp the apices are often very rounded and in extreme forms the leaves are almost spherical.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The spreading blunt hairs on the peduncle are characteristic of this subspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A very variable taxon with several local forms. The leaves are almost terete in Namaqualand, somewhat flattened in the Little Karoo and adjoining areas in the eastern Cape Province they become gradually more flattened and then grade into the form from the Natal coastal hills. An extreme form which often has somewhat larger leaves and similarly large flowers occurs on the sandy flats east of the Lebombo Mountains of Natal. Other characters which show a wide range of variation are the length of the pedicel, the colour of the branches and the shape of the infloresence as well as the number of flowers per inflorescence.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The inflorescence of this species is usually spike-like but may occasionally be a little more branched. Problems in distinguishing this subspecies may arise because depauperate specimens of both subspecies produce only one terminal dichasium. The shape of the squamae and the distribution help to identify critical specimens such as Thunberg's type specimen.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The predominantly 4-merous flowers and the production of adventitious buds on the inflorescence are typical of this subspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Plants of C. multiflora are usually more robust than those of C. subulata, but it is also distinguished by the absence of a continuous line of hairs along the internode from the one leaf sheath to the next one.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The leaves of the plants on the southern Kamiesberg are much shorter and the inflorescence usually produces one terminal dichasium rather like in var. comptonii except that tbe corolla is cream and the beaks of the lobes are c. 1 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: A great number of variants can be found in the complex included under var. nudicaulis. The leaves may vary from glabrous to puberulous, to covered with long erect hairs or recurved hairs in other areas. The leaves may vary from linear-lanceolate to obovate, but they are usually erect except in the Drakensberg area where they tend to become recurved and more or less adpressed to the soil. A common, extreme variation of the latter form has inflorescences with flowers rather loosely arranged in the part-inflorescences, a character usually only found in C. cultrata.The form which was described as C. hirta is often recognized in the area between Swellendam and Port Elizabeth by its very narrow leaves with fine spreading hairs. However, west of Riversdale they gradually merge into typical var. nudicaulis.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The terminal dichasium is sometimes reduced to a single flower and as vegetative growth in all the subspecies usually starts from buds immediately below the inflorescence, it is not difficult to understand why subsp. alsinoides is included in this species. In subsp. pellucida the flowers are often overtopped by such vegetative growth.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Typical C. sarcocaulis from the eastern Cape mountains usually has smaller leaves than the plants from the lower slopes but from the area mainly near King Williams Town a number of intermediates have been recorded. At times the leaves of the typical form are so narrow that it is only possible by means of the localities to distinguish dried material of the two subspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: C. sediflora is distinguished from C. southii by the absence of a terminal stout hair on the leaves as well as the calyx lobes. The appendage on the petals is absent or only a small swelling in the former species.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Not all of the often geographically isolated forms of this variable and complex variety have been fully assessed. Three main tendencies can be observed: 1. Along the northern banks of the Orange River plants tend to have recurved to reflexed and adpressed hairs. 2. South of the Orange River the leaves tend to become more fleshy westwards and southwards. Plants from near Eenriet Mountain are sometimes covered with rounded trichomes and closely resemble C. tecta except that their stems are somewhat elongated. 3. Westwards and especially in the mountains near Eksteenfontein plants have very fleshy leaves and are almost indistinguishable from var. hottentotta. Only the presence of rounded trichomes will distinguish the latter variety from var. sericea.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: The size and shape of the leaves can vary considerably within one population, but two local variants can be distinguished:1. Along the coast from the Cape Peninsula to near Bredasdorp particularly small plants are found with the leaves densely clustered, the internodes rarely being longer than 10 mm. The leaf apices are blunt to rounded.2. In the Hex River Mountains the branches are often decumbent and the leaves rarely longer than 15 mm.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: No single character can be used to distinguish the forms of the two varieties. This is partly due to extreme plasticity of the species. An overall interpretation of the species becomes even less clear as hybridization seems to take place in several places along breaks in the north-south mountain ranges, for instance, along the Orange, Buffalo, Olifants and Hex River valleys.Plants of var. tomentosa are usually distinguished by their oblong squamae and the few rosettes which will elongate at least in part at flowering so that there is a gradual transition from the leaves in the rosette to those in the inflorescence. In south-western South West Africa/Namibia and the adjoining Richtersveld plants often produce more than one rosette and relatively broad leaves which approach those of var. interrupta but the squamae are always oblong. Similar plants are also found at the other end of the distribution range of the variety and particularly between Montagu and Laingsburg plants of var. tomentosa can only be distinguished by their robust habit. Unusual is also the extreme form with narrowly oblong leaves usually borne strictly in four ranks which grows along the coast between Cape Town and Saldanha Bay.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Plants perennial, flowers usually dioecious, male flowers usually racemose.
bibliographicCitation: Jeffrey, C. 1978. 86. Cucurbitaeae. In: E Launert (ed.), Fl. Zambes. 4: 414-499. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, Glasgow. [CC BY]

description: Flowers monoecious, the male and female on the same plant, 2-4 mm long. Fruits bluish.

description: Tendrils simple; leaves distinctly lobed or dissected; flowers monoecious, male and female flowers borne in the same axils, minute, short male peduncles; long rostrate fruits.

description: Tendrils simple, leaves more or less distinctly lobed or dissected, flowers dioecious.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: Leaves compound, of 9-21 leaflets. Tendrils simple, unbranched or 2-fid. Fruit ellipsoid, to 13 cm long, smooth, bright red.
bibliographicCitation: Jeffrey, C. 1978. 86. Cucurbitaeae. In: E Launert (ed.), Fl. Zambes. 4: 414-499. Flora Zambesiaca Managing Committee, Glasgow. [CC BY]

description: Mature fruit longitudinally striped in various shades of orange with (10-) 15-20 aculei on the darker and 2-5(-10) on the lighter stripes of young fruit; aculei 1.5-4 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Kirkbride, JH. 1993. Biosystematic monograph of the genus Cucumis (Cucurbitaceae). Parkway Publishers Inc., Boone. [All rights reserved]

description: Male flowers solitary on long pedicels; lobes of leaves not constricted at the base; pubescence of long, crinkly and articulate hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Meeuse, ADJ. 1962. The Cucurbitaceae of southern Africa. Bothalia 8: 1-111. [CC BY]

description: In R. columnaris many of the stems spread horizontally first beneath the soil for 300 mm or more. When they emerge, they become thicker and erect. The above-ground parts are mostly not more than 300 mm tall but odd stems up to 600 mm long do occur, particularly if they grow in dense shade. Because of the rhizomatous habit of the stems, the plants do not form dense clumps and are mostly rather diffuse. Here the stems are almost cylindrical and somewhat snake-like, with the short, quite sharply conical tubercles arranged into eight low but very clearly defined angles. In R. columnaris the primary stem does not bear flowers and these arise only on the side-branches. They appear on many small, peduncular patches mainly towards the tips of new growth, although older inflorescences may be re-activated to produce flowers, so occasionally they can be found lower down on stems too. The lowest bract looks very much like a normal tubercle but with a flattened upper surface. In this species often a whole cluster of flowers on a patch will open simultaneously. The small, greenish yellow flowers are flat to slightly convex and are usually finely and indistinctly spotted with red. The interior is densely covered with small papillae, each of which has an apical bristle. There is only a very slight tube in the centre, so the corona projects somewhat from the centre of the flower. It is yellow mottled with red and consists of small outer lobes more or less adpressed to the corolla around the mouth of the tube and small inner lobes adpressed to the backs of the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Albuca anisocrispa is easily identified by the single or two leaves, rarely three, lanceolate-oblong, flat and canaliculated, vaginate at the base, commonly finely undulate only in the inner margin of the convolute leaves, suberect, with papillate prominent longitudinal nerves, and densely papillate margins; the flowers are erect with white and green tepals; and the inner stamen are sterile.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB; Dold, AP; Barker, NP. 2012. description: Albuca pseudobifolia shares with A. bifolia the erect flowers with yellow and green tepals, and the outer stamen without anthers or small and sterile ones, but it can be easily differentiated by the bulb with slightly leathery dull white outer tunics; the leaves linear-lanceolate, up to 30 times longer than wide, glabrous, smooth, and absent or mostly withered when the flowers are present, the narrower capsule, the smaller seeds, and the different flowering time.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB; Dold, AP; Barker, NP. 2012. description: Two subspecies endemic to EC: C. mesembryanthoides (Haw. D.Dietr. subsp. hispida (Haw. Toelken; C. mesembryanthoides (Haw. D.Dietr. subsp. mesembryanthoides.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, GJ; Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Crassulaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 804-839. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Allied to S. singulare Kupicha in having leaves similar in shape and size; the arrangement of the flowers in the inflorescences and the shape of the pollinia and subapical attachment to the caudicle. It is distinguished from the latter in that S. singulare forms much smaller plants and the corona lobe has double ventral appendages which are totally absent in S. austromontanum. The form of the corona lobes are broadly onion shaped in outline extending from the basal rounded lobe into a drawn out, narrow appendage that is 3- or more-tipped at the apex. Further the corolla is white on the ventral side and basally white becoming pink on the dorsal side of the petals and sub-erect (opposed to S. singulare where it is spreading and livid with red veins on either side).
bibliographicCitation: Bester, SP; Nicholas, A. 2016. Schizoglossum austromontanum, a novel new species from South Africa (Apocynaceae, Asclepiadoideae, Asclepiadeae). Phytotaxa 273(1): 43-50. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.273.1.4] [All rights reserved]

description: Lasiosiphon esterhuyseniae is similar in habit to L. microphyllus but differs in its shorter, more densely leafy flowering branches, 15-50 mm long vs mostly 60-100 mm long, the smaller capitula with only ±5 to 7 flowers (vs 7 to 10 flowers), the much shorter hypanthium, ±6mm vs 12-15 mm long and the acute involucral bracts, with the abaxial surface densely appressed-pubescent, vs obtuse, abaxially finely crisped-velutinous bracts in L. microphyllous.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Manning, JC. 2017. Lasiosiphon esterhuyseniae (Thymelaeaceae: Thymelaeoideae), a new species from Northern Cape (South Africa), and the transfer of two additional southern African species to the genus. Kew Bull. 72(12): 1-6. [All rights reserved]

description: Differing from Cola greenwayi in that leaf- blades (1.2-) 3.5-8.5 (-10.4) cm long on a single stem, petioles 0.2-2(-3.7) cm long, (not 3-16(-18) cm long and 0.3-4 (-5.6) cm long respectively), flowers single per node (not in fascicles); fruitlet apex rounded, positioned apically, base stipitate (not rostrate, lateral and obtuse to acute).
bibliographicCitation: Cheek, MR; Lawrence, P; McCleland, W. 2018. Cola dorrii sp. nov. (Sterculiaceae), a threatened Maputaland Forest endemic of South Africa. Kew Bull. 73(25): 1-20. [DOI 10.1007/S12225-018-9749-2] [All rights reserved]

description: The creeping, unequally dichotoniously branched stem which has coriaceous, overlapping (imbricate), somewhat oblique ovate lateral and median leaves, separates Selaginella nubigena from other species in the region. The proximal margin of the median leaves is laciniate, whereas the distal margin of the lateral leaves is laciniate.
bibliographicCitation: Roux, JP. 2008. Selaginella nubigena, a new species from the Drakensberg, South Africa. Bothalia 38(2): 153-156. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to Zyrphelis lasiocarpa (DC.) Kuntze [as 'Felicia lasiocarpa Compton; Mairea lasiocarpa DC.)'], from which it differs chiefly in its more compact growth, smaller capitula, and involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Compton, RH. 1931. The Flora of the Whitehill District. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 19: 269-326. [All rights reserved]

description: Differs from Zyrphelis corymbosa (Harv.) Kuntze [as 'Mairea corymbosa, Harv.'], by the flowers not being corymbose, the bracteate peduncles, and the larger heads and leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Fourcade, HG. 1932. Contributions to the flora of the Knysna and neighbouring divisions. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 21(1): 75-102. [All rights reserved]

description: The white flowers with a relatively long, narrow perianth tube, 18-20 mm long, with the stamens and style included in the tube immediately set Ixia linderi apart in sect. Hyalis. The filaments, only 1.5 mm long, are inserted ± 6 mm below the mouth of the tube and the anthers, ± 4 mm long, just reach the mouth. The style divides just below the anther bases and the short style branches ± 1 mm long are retained within the tube. The species most closely resembles a second Piketberg endemic, I. splendida, but this species is a more robust plant with leaves up to 5 mm wide and larger, brick-red to pink flowers with a perianth tube 27-30 mm long. Like I. linderi, the flowers of I. splendida have the stamens and style included in the tube. Both species have distinctive, translucent, ± truncate outer floral bracts with minute terminal teeth.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Readily distinguished from related I. latifolia by its small, red-purple flowers and low stature, up to 120 mm tall. Plants also have distinctive dark purple bracts and unusually long style branches, ± 3 mm long, unexpected in a small flower with tepals 10-12 mm long. The style divides at or slightly below the apices of the filaments and the style branches extend outward beneath the anthers where they are conspicuous. The flowers are strongly scented of sweet pea, a feature unique among the species of the I. latifolia group where scent is lacking or weakly developed.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by the slender stem bearing up to three short, filiform branchlets, these as well as the main axis each bearing a single flower. The flowers have a slightly curved, narrow perianth tube 10-11 mm long, flaring uniformly from base to apex and they obviously face to the side but colour and other aspects of the perianth are not known. The filaments are exserted ± 1.5 mm from the tube and the comparatively large anthers 3-4 mm long and well-developed style branches place I. ecklonii among a poorly defined cluster of species allied to I. rapunculoides. The general appearance of the plants recalls I. mollis and I. namaquana, but both have a funnel-shaped perianth tube and the filaments and bases of the anthers included in the tube. The translucent, brown floral bracts recall the Bokkeveld Mtn species, I. brunneobracteata, but that species has a shorter, funnel-shaped perianth tube 5-7 mm long, the main axis bears 3 to 5 flowers, and the branches are not particularly short and usually bear 2 to 4 flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ixia stenophylla somewhat resembles I. fucata but is distinguished by its three leaves, the basal two with filiform blades up to 1.2 mm wide, and the absence of a collar of fibres around the stem base. It also differs in having a spike with only 1 or 2, rarely 3 flowers, and the stem is almost invariably unbranched. The white flowers are flushed mauve outside and have dark veining on the relatively wide perianth tube (12-)15-20 mm long. The stamens are also unilateral (properly visible only in living plants) and extended horizontally with the parallel anthers facing the lower tepals, an orientation unique in Ixia. The immediate relationships of Ixia stenophylla are uncertain. The two linear and very narrow foliage leaves suggest it belongs to the I. capillaris complex, all species of which also have narrow leaves. The leaf blades, however, differ significantly in having a strongly thickened and raised central vein and a thickened secondary vein, whereas the leaves of all species of the I. capillaris complex lack thickened veins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the nodding, relatively small, white or pale blue flowers, Ixia mollis has tepals ± 14 x 3.4-4.5 mm, a perianth tube 7-9 mm long and anthers ± 2.5 mm long, half included in the tube. The corms bear small cormlets at the base and occasionally a slender stolon and the tunics consist of medium-textured to fine fibres. The nearly linear to narrowly sword-shaped leaves are soft-textured and these, as well as the white or pale blue flowers readily distinguish the species from the closely allied I. rapunculoides, which has blue to blue-mauve or sometimes pink flowers with a yellow cup. Ixia mollis was confused in the past with what is now I. sobolifera, which included pink-flowered plants from the Bokkeveld Plateau and white-flowered plants from the Little Karoo. These plants have soft-textured, short-lived tunics and produce long, ribbon-like stolons and also differ in the longer bracts, 6-10 mm long (vs. 5-6 mm long in I. mollis) and, in I. sobolifera subsp. carnea, a longer perianth tube 9-10 mm long and longer anthers 3-4 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Unique in the genus in developing a cluster of large cormels in the axil of the lowest leaf, Thereianthus bulbifer is further characterised by linear leaves and pale to midblue flowers, marked with white at the base of the lower tepals, with a relatively short, curved perianth tube 7-9 mm long and declinate stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Identified by a heavily blotched scape, metallic blue or occasionally light pink perianth tubes and outer tepals, the latter with translucent white, slightly recurved apices, and green or brown apical gibbosities. The translucent white inner tepals have bluish-green keels and strongly recurved apices, with the deeply canaliculate lower inner tepal usually being distinctly longer than, and diverging strongly from, the upper inner tepals.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: L. pygmaea is readily identified by its very slender and very long perianth tube (20-27 mm) and by its mauve or white outer and inner tepals that become strongly rolled back at the peak flowering stage. The species has well-exserted filaments (5-9 mm long) and a very long style (24-36 mm long), and the flowers are strongly almond-scented. The seeds are globose and have rugose primary sculpturing. Morphologically, the species appears most closely allied to L. ensifolia, which differs in its included or shortly exserted filaments (1-4 mm long), shorter style (11-20 mm long), usually much shorter perianth tube (12-20 mm long), spicy sweet-scented perianths and ovoid, glossy seeds.
bibliographicCitation: Duncan, GD. 2012. The genus Lachenalia. Bot. Mag. Monogr., Vol. 34. Kew Publishing, Kew. [All rights reserved]

description: Nemesia fourcadei is recognized by its white flowers with purple veining and a pale yellowish orange palate. It can be distinguished from the similar looking N. lucida by its larger flowers (7.6-13.2 mm vs < 7.5 mm long) with longer spurs (mostly 3.0-4.5 vs < 1.5 mm), and by its relatively broader capsules (length/width: 1.7-2.0 vs 2.4-3.5).
bibliographicCitation: Steiner, KE. 2010. Two new species of Nemesia (Scrophulariaceae) from the Southern Cape, South Africa. Bothalia 40(2): 161-166. [CC BY]

description: Drimiopsis linioseta is characterized by leaves possessing hairs exclusively in rows that trace the veins in the leaf.
bibliographicCitation: Hankey, AJ; Buys, MH; Lebatha, PD. 2008. Hyacinthaceae: Drimiopsis linioseta, a new species from the Sekukhuneland Centre of Endemism, South Africa. Bothalia 38(1): 72-74. [CC BY]

description: A handsome plant, worth cultivating.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Metalasia tristis is distinguished by its sprawling, decumbent dwarf habit, the tomentose young branches, leaves and synflorescences, the synflorescences with capitula fused by whitish hairs and by the involucral bracts with acute, narrow scarious, brown laminas visible between the white hairs. Metalasia tristis is most similar to M. divergens (Thunb.) D.Don subsp. divergens due to the dense hairy capitula clusters with 5-flowered capitula, but M. divergens subsp. divergens has larger, more easily distinguishable capitula and involucral bracts with glands. Furthermore, Metalasia divergens subsp. divergens is endemic to the Cape Peninsula. Metalasia serrulata P.O.Karis and M. rogersii S.Moore may resemble M. tristis in habit but both differ in having synflorescences with 3-flowered capitula where the outermost involucral bracts are considerably shorter than the innermost, and in having rounded pink, petaloid inner involucral bracts. Metalasia rogersii also differs in that is has much smaller, mostly declinate leaves with axillary brachyblasts. Metalasia serrulata and M. rogersii not only resemble M. tristis, but the three also occur in close proximity in the Groot Winterhoek Mountains, Witsenberge, and Skurweberge.
bibliographicCitation: Bengtson, A; Anderberg, AA; Karis, PO. 2013. Three new species of Metalasia (Asteraceae–Gnaphalieae) from the Western Cape and an updated key to the genus. S. African J. Bot. 84: 72-82. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2012.09.008] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2013); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Metalasia formosa is recognized by its almost straight, rather than twisted, leaves with elongated axillary brachyblasts, branched synflorescences with 5-flowered capitula in clusters, with sometimes pink inner and white innermost involucral bracts. Metalasia formosa resembles M. trivialis P.O.Karis, which are erect shrubs with large axillary brachyblasts, branched synflorescences with capitula in clusters and involucres with white tomentose brown outer and white petaloid inner bracts. However, Metalasia trivialis differs in having 3 or 4-flowered capitula with white inner bracts and half-twisted, rather than straight, often carinate leaves. Metalasia formosa may also resemble the common and variable M. densa (Lam.) P.O.Karis, but the two species differ greatly in involucre which is narrow with bracts in 6-8 series, with brown outer bracts contrasting against the white innermost bracts in M. densa.
bibliographicCitation: Bengtson, A; Anderberg, AA; Karis, PO. 2013. Three new species of Metalasia (Asteraceae–Gnaphalieae) from the Western Cape and an updated key to the genus. S. African J. Bot. 84: 72-82. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2012.09.008] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2013); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Metalasia eburnea is recognized by having long, narrow, twisted leaves and axillary brachyblasts less than half as long as the subtending leaf, synflorescences with many small, narrow, 3-flowered capitula with light beige outer, and white inner involucral bracts in branched clusters. Metalasia eburnea is most similar to the variable M. densa, the latter however differs in that the capitula have a darker involucre that is 1.5-3.0 mm wide, bracts in 6-8 series, and brown, scarious outer bracts. Metalasia eburnea may also resemble M. muricata (L.) D.Don, but M. muricata has curved to hooked leaves and 4 or 5 flowered capitula. Metalasia acuta P.O.Karis, which is another renosterveld species, is easily distinguished from M. eburnean by its sharply pungent leaves and narrow lanceolate to subulate, very acute involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Bengtson, A; Anderberg, AA; Karis, PO. 2013. Three new species of Metalasia (Asteraceae–Gnaphalieae) from the Western Cape and an updated key to the genus. S. African J. Bot. 84: 72-82. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2012.09.008] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2013); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Apart from its general habit of growth and its thick smooth dichotomous branches, the most distinctive (and unexpected) feature of A. pillansii is the method of producing the inflorescences laterally from the axils of the lowest leaves. The peduncle is sharply decurved near base, branched about the middle, with the branches ascending and the racemes sub-erect to erect. The whole inflorescence (about 50 cm long) hangs downwards in between the lowest leaves, with the racemes upturned, so that the base of the peduncle is usually a little higher than the terminal raceme. This character appears to be unique in the genus Aloe. In racemes which are erect, the flowers are evenly distributed around the axis, but in oblique racemes the flowers are erectly sub-secund. A. pillansii is usually branched about the middle or lower, and ranges from few to many compactly or divaricately branched trees. Young simple-stemmed plants reach a height of 1.8-2.7 m [as '6-9 ft.'] before dividing at the summit and branching commences. Occasionally one sees a simple-stemmed plant 6-9 m [as '20-30 ft.'] high, forked at the summit, but this is not typical. In structure, size, shape and yellow flowers, A. pillansii, A. ramosissima and A. dichtoma are almost indistinguishable, but in size, branching and leaves, they could never be confused, while the inflorescence of A. pillansii immediately separates it from all other species.
bibliographicCitation: Reynolds, GW. 1974. Aloes of South Africa, 3rd ed. A.A. Balkema, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: A. ramosissima is nearest allied to A. dichotoma, but differs in being a much smaller plant, considerably more branched from ground level; it has slenderer branches, and smaller rosettes and leaves. Average specimens are about 6 ft. high, sometimes 9 ft., and about as broad. As its name implies, it is the most branched species of Aloe known. Young plants only 2 ft. high are freely branched at or near ground level, whereas young plants of A. dichotoma usually have a simple stem a few feet high before branching commences. The flowers of A. ramosissima and A. dichotoma are, however, so strikingly similar, that there do not appear to be any characters which could be used for distinguishing them.
bibliographicCitation: Reynolds, GW. 1974. Aloes of South Africa, 3rd ed. A.A. Balkema, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: It differs from A. eminens in its smaller inflorescence (up to 6-branched, 35 cm high), its short (4-6 cm long), capitate, subdensely flowered racemes and in its yellowish orange, curved perianth which is 47-50 mm long. It is further separated by the outer perianth segments that are fused for more than half their length and by the shortly exposed stamens (for 3-5 mm). In A. eminens, the inflorescence is 50-60 cm high, long, with the outer segments fused in the lower third. The flowers in both species become pendent when open. Aloe barberae is the tallest of the African aloes, growing up to 18 m, and is similar to the new species in vegetative features but here the resemblance ends. Aloe barberae is confined to forested kloofs and river valleys in the southeastern and eastern parts of southern Africa. It has densely flowered racemes and the short, cylindric-trigonous perianth is 33-37 mm long and horizontally presented when open. The outer perianth segments are free to almost the base. In all other members of section Dracoaloe the perianth segments are fused at least in the lower third.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2010. Aloe tongaensis, a new species from Tongaland, KwaZulu-Natal (South Africa), and a new sectional arrangement of the tree aloes. Aloe 47(3): 64-71. [All rights reserved]

description: The habit and leaves of this species recall A. striatula, but the leaves are more erect and the leaf sheaths less prominently striate.
bibliographicCitation: Glen, HF; Hardy, DS. 2000. Aloe. In: G Germishuizen & E du Plessis (eds), Aloaceae (first part), Fl. S. Africa 5(1,1): 1-167. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209564#page/3/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A tall plant, sometimes standing over 1 metre high and flowering late in the season, well into December, Ixia altissima has anthers with the vestigial connective and involute style branches, stigmatic only at the tips, characteristic of sect. Dichone but the funnel-shaped perianth tube with the filaments inserted in the middle of the upper part of the tube are unusual for the section, in which other species have the tube virtually filiform throughout. The perianth tube, only ± 4 mm long, and the pale floral bracts are reminiscent of two Roggeveld species of the section, I. rigida and I. trifolia, the former also flowering relatively late in the season, often in November. Both share with I. altissima relatively unspecialised, longitudinally dehiscent anthers. Ixia altissima seems most like I. rigida, also a tall plant, up to 600 mm high, which has flowers with a similarly funnel-shaped perianth tube 2-3 mm long and silvery-translucent floral bracts. This contrasts with the slightly longer perianth tube, ± 4 mm long, and shorter anthers just 3 mm long in I. altissima, which is also unusual in the section in having the style dividing opposite the middle of the anthers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ixia altissima is a surprising plant, sometimes standing over 1 m in height and flowering late in the season, well into December. The anthers with vestigial connective and the involute style branches, stigmatic only at the tips, indicate its placement in sect. Dichone but the funnel-shaped perianth tube with the filaments inserted in the middle of the upper part of the tube is unusual for the section, most species of which have the tube virtually filiform throughout with the filaments inserted at the apex of the tube. The perianth tube, only ± 4 mm long, and the pale floral bracts are reminiscent of two Roggeveld Escarpment species, I. trifolia and I. rigida, the latter also flowering relatively late in the season, often in November. These species share relatively unspecialized, longitudinally dehiscent anthers. I. altissima seems most like I. rigida, also a tall plant, up to 600 mm high and sometimes flowering as late as November. The latter has flowers with a similarly funnel-shaped perianth tube 2-3 mm long and silvery translucent floral bracts, contrasting with the slightly longer perianth tube, ± 4 mm long, and shorter anthers, just 3 mm long, in I. altissima, which is also unusual in the section in having the style dividing opposite the middle of the anthers. A conservation status for I. altissima is suggested as Rare (R), in light of its evident rarity, but there is no current threat to the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: Easily recognised by the moderately tall stem up to 600 mm high with 2 or 3 upright branches held close to the axis and the silvery-translucent floral bracts subtending very short-tubed flowers, the tube up to 2.5 mm long with the narrow portion up to ± 1.5 mm long. Plants have up to seven leathery leaves with prominently thickened margins, main and secondary veins. Ixia rigida was until 2012 associated with I. brevifolia, but this is now understood to be a separate species. Although fairly uniform across its range populations inland and flowering three to four weeks earlier than those along the edge of the escarpment, thus in September, have slightly larger flowers and less fibrous leaves. The escarpment populations mostly have 6 or 7 leaves, typically 5-7 mm wide, tepals ± 12 x 5 mm, anthers ± 3 mm long, and style branches ± 2 mm long. The inland populations have 4 or 5 leaves, mostly 7-8 mm wide, tepals ± 14-16 x 6-8 mm, slightly longer filaments, anthers 4(5) mm long, and style branches ± 3.5 mm long. The bracts of the inland plants also stand out in their darker purple veins. Too little is known about I. rigida to assess the significance of this variation.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Ixia bifolia stands out in the very short, leathery-succulent foliage leaf blade, up to 80 mm long and 5-7 mm wide. The leaf has a single vein and moderately thickened margins. The flowers seem most like those of I. confusa but the short, deep pink filaments ± 1.5 mm long and deep pink, straight style branches ± 4 mm long (both drying purple) are quite different from those of I. confusa, which has white filaments 1.3-2.5 mm long and white, strongly falcate style branches 1-2 mm long. Ixia bifolia is evidently closely allied to I. trinervata, which has larger flowers on longer spikes but also a single foliage leaf, this relatively broad and always with three prominent veins and unthickened margins. Ixia bifolia shares with other members of the I. micrandra complex the finely fibrous corm tunics that extend upward around the stem base. Stems are almost always unbranched and have an odd feature, a small, nearly microscopic, translucent scale and prophyll, ± 1 mm long, inserted 12-30 mm below the base of the spike. Stems of I. confusa may be branched and are normally taller than in I. bifolia but also have a translucent stem scale in populations from the Swartberg and sometimes elsewhere across its range. Ixia confusa has 3 or 4 linear leaves, usually ± 2 mm, but occasionally up to 4 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Both I. micrandra and closely related I. minor (= I. micrandra var. minor G.J.Lewis) have corms with finely fibrous tunics that extend upward in a collar around the base of the stem, terete to subterete or linear leaves mostly 1.0-1.5 mm at widest, and spikes of up to 6 flowers. I. confusa has corms with similar finely fibrous tunics, sometimes without a collar of fibres around the base, but plane leaves 1.5-4.0 mm wide, and spikes with as many as 12 flowers. I. micrandra has anthers 3-4 mm long, and slender, ± straight, ascending style branches 3-4 mm long, thus quite different from the shorter anthers, ± 1.0-2.5 mm long, and falcate style branches 1.5-2.5 mm long of I. confusa. The style branches of I. confusa match those of I. minor but the terete or subterete leaf blades, flattened filaments and consistently few-flowered spikes of the latter immediately separate them. Ixia confusa may also be confused with the new I. bifolia but this species has a single, relatively broad, leathery-succulent foliage leaf and flowers with shorter filaments ± 1 mm and longer, straight style branches ± 4 mm long. Both the filaments and style branches of I. bifolia are dark pink and dry dark purple, unlike the pale filaments and style branches of I. confusa, which dry to a pale, almost colourless state. Annotations by G.J. Lewis on collections of Ixia confusa from the Swartberg indicate that at one time she considered these populations a separate species, which she intended to call I. aestivalis, in part because of their late flowering, from late October to early December. We find that collections from the Swartberg also differ in having slightly shorter filaments, 1-2 mm long, than typical I. confusa (1.5-2.8 mm long), the style sometimes dividing above the mouth of the perianth tube (opposite the middle of the filaments in Goldblatt 7962), and anther dehiscence sometimes not reaching the middle of the thecae. The plants have a small, translucent scale and prophyll on the upper part of the stem, a feature occasionally present in southern populations of I. confusa. Additional study may show that the later-flowering Swartberg populations merit separate taxonomic status but we find no consistent character differences between them. There seems no current threat to the species and we agree with Raimondo et al.'s (2009) (LT, as I. micrandra var. confusa), Least Threat conservation status.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2012. Systematics of the southern African genus Ixia (Iridaceae): 4. Revision of sect. Dichone. Bothalia 42(2): 87-110. [CC BY]

description: Like Ixia micrandra, I. minor has a slender, usually unbranched stem, small corms with fine, netted tunics that extend upward in a collar around the base, and a dry, often brown, upper cataphyll. The critical differences between the two species lie in their flowers. Ixia minor has flattened, ± wedge-shaped to oblanceolate filaments abruptly narrowed and kinked at the tips, and shorter and broader anthers, often not dehiscing to the apex. The style branches are also shorter, 2-3 mm long, wider, and strongly arched whereas those of I. micrandra are more-or-less straight and (2)3-5 mm long. To these microscopic details can be added a brighter pink perianth. Flowers of I. micrandra have pale pink to purple-pink tepals, straight, filiform filaments and longer, oblong anthers dehiscing to the apex. The leaves of the two species also differ somewhat: those of I. minor are subterete to oval in section, thus when alive without margins or evident central vein, whereas I. micrandra has plane, linear leaf blades with slightly thickened margins and, when dry, a visibly raised main vein. Evidence for their separation is provided by collections of both species made in the Houw Hoek Mtns flowering on the same date and visibly different in appearance.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Early-blooming Moraea mutila is recognised by the pale blue, rarely white flowers with linear to narrowly lanceolate inner tepals 7.5-12.5 mm long, erect below and spreading distally. Often difficult to see in preserved specimens, the inner tepals are usually slightly wider in the midline and sometimes expanded into rounded lobes near the base of the spreading distal half. The flowers otherwise seem little different from those of the more common M. tripetala, but the pilose nectar guides are usually white or palest yellow and dotted with dark blue to purple, whereas the nectar guides of M. tripetala are more often yellow, edged with dark blue or purple. The leaf is typically relatively short, in most collections shorter than the stem, and widely channelled, sometimes plane in the distal half. Plants sometimes have leaves velvety on the abaxial surface and velvety spathes. The pubescence is evidently variable in populations, thus a character of limited value for identification. Leaves of M. tripetala are almost invariably hairless. Possibly belonging here are pale blue-flowered plants from the western lower slopes of Sir Lowry’s Pass with the inner tepals trilobed as in Moraea mutila but the filaments united for ± 2.5 mm and the style 4 mm long. Alternatively these plants may be hybrids between M. tripetala and M. unguiculata.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Closely allied to Moraea tripetala, M. cuspidata is distinguished by the linear inner tepals up to 15 mm long (rarely less than 10 mm), spreading in the distal half, and usually with a particularly narrow foliage leaf with the halves usually tightly appressed in dry conditions. The brown to almost black corm tunics consist of thickened vertical fibres sometimes with raised ridges, and form a collar of stiff fibres around the base of the stem. The flowers are pale blue to violet with the large, velvety nectar guides spotted with dark blue on a white background. The filaments are usually united for 1.0-1.5 mm but occasionally less, and are ± as long as or slightly shorter than the dark purple anthers that bear red pollen. Capsules (where known) are relatively large, 14-16 mm long and the seeds are also relatively large, 1.8-2.0 mm long and unusual in having a pale, spongy testa much thickened into prominent ridges on the angles. The species is sympatric at some sites and even co-blooming with smaller-flowered Moraea amabilis (also allied to M. tripetala) but that species has a broadly channelled foliage leaf, sometimes plane distally and often pilose on the abaxial surface, and consistently short, hair-like inner tepals typically 1.5-2.0 mm long. At sites where they have been recorded growing together pollen of M. amabilis is white, contrasting with the orange-red pollen of M. cuspidata. An outlying record of M. cuspidata from Perdekloof, southeast of Oudtshoorn, probably belongs here. The flowers are exceptionally small, the inner tepals are 8-9 mm long, otherwise consistent with the species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea hainebachiana shows several unusual features in the M. tripetala group. The first of these is the cluster of small, dark grey or bluish cormlets in the foliage leaf axil and at the base of the corm, the latter feature especially pronounced in non-flowering individuals. The foliage leaf is always inserted on the stem above ground level. Flowers are consistently pale violet to deep blue and have inner tepals 5-6 mm long, somewhat longer than is typical for M. tripetala and unusual in being expanded in the middle, thus spindle-shaped or sometimes oblanceolate and obscurely 3-lobed. More significantly, the filaments are as long as or slightly longer than the anthers, whereas the anthers are slightly longer than the filaments in M. tripetala and in some closely related species, often considerably so. The nectar guides are also somewhat unusual, consisting of lines of dots on a whitish background with the edges not clearly defined as they are in M. tripetala in which the yellow or white nectar guides are typically edged in darker blue to violet. Vegetative reproduction does not occur in M. tripetala and the production of multiple cormlets in leaf axils and at the base of the corm is unknown elsewhere in the M. tripetala complex. Moraea hainebachiana is sterile and all capsules are shed soon after the flowers fade and seeds are not developed, thus it is evidently a vegetative apomict and propagation is effected by cormlets that plants produce liberally.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Moraea saldanhensis has relatively small, slate-blue flowers, the outer tepals ± 18 mm long with spreading and ultimately half reflexed limbs ± 8 mm long thus shorter than the claws ± 10 mm long. It is most easily confused with M. inconspicua which has similarly small flowers (outer tepals 12-18 mm long), usually yellow to brown, occasionally white to cream-coloured, but the tepal limbs are almost always fully reflexed and somewhat to twice as long as the upright claws. Moraea saldanhensis also has a slightly longer filament column, ± 6.5 mm long (vs 3.5-6.0 mm in southern populations of M. inconspicua), orange-red pollen and the ovary is included whereas in M. inconspicua the ovary is usually exserted and the pollen is typically yellow, although populations with red pollen are known, notably among the Namaqualand populations, segregated as subsp. namaquensis.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Multi-branched semi-succulent geophyte with glaucous stems and widely spreading leaves. Bulb tunics dark brown to black, gummy. Flowers white with light pink, hairy abaxial petal border and ecallose sepals. Superficially similar to O. rubricallosa. In addition to morphology, the two species differ in their habitat requirements as is evident from the different veld types they occupy.
bibliographicCitation: Roets, F; Oberlander, KC; Dreyer, LL. 2013. Two new Oxalis species (Oxalidaceae) from the Ai-Ais/Richtersveld Transfrontier Park, South Africa. Blumea 57: 229-235. [https://doi.org/10.3767/000651913X663631] [All rights reserved]

description: Oxalis nivea is characterized by having multi-flowered inflorescences with white flowers, carried on very long peduncles. It has dark brown to blackish bulbs, with hard sclerenchymatous tunics that are irregularly ridged due to large internal channels.
bibliographicCitation: Dreyer, LL; Roets, F; Oberlander, KC. 2013. Two new Oxalis (Oxalidaceae) species from the Richtersveld National Park, South Africa. Phytotaxa 89(2): 53-63. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.89.2.2] [All rights reserved]

description: The dark violet flowering X. junodii is distinct from X. rosea by its leaf sheaths split into long wiry fibres and blades with some glands deeply sunken into adaxial mesophyll. Leaf blade anatomy is different by its large and slim lateral vascular bundles and its abaxial furrows nearly closed by a two-horned anvil-like extension of the epidermis, among other characters. Junod's 2768 collections are annotated as `Fleurs violet fonce, certes different de la rosea'.
bibliographicCitation: Behnke, HD; Hummel, E; Hillmer, S; Sauer-Gurth, H; Gonzalez, J; Wink, M. 2013. A revision of African Velloziaceae based on leaf anatomy characters and rbcL nucleotide sequences. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 172: 22-94. [All rights reserved]

description: Amphistomatic, dorsiventral with three or four layers of palisade cells, undulated upper surface, median adaxial groove, and deep abaxial furrows; lateral vascular bundles with large partial abaxial T-shaped girders (towards midvein and margin Y-shaped), often with slim and long lower arm and narrow spaces between them; marginal bundles circular, without caps or girders, but with large distal roundish sclerenchyma; epidermis with thickened walls, adaxial epidermis partly double, abaxial epidermis forming U-profiles beneath lateral vascular bundles and within furrows clearly papillate; hypodermis cells slightly thickened; many glands deeply sunken into palisade tissue; aquiferous cells restricted to area above central bundle; rectangular crystals in palisade and spongy cells; cubical crystals in hypodermis and inner epidermis cells and in small cells between bundle sheath and sclerenchyma.
bibliographicCitation: Behnke, HD; Hummel, E; Hillmer, S; Sauer-Gurth, H; Gonzalez, J; Wink, M. 2013. A revision of African Velloziaceae based on leaf anatomy characters and rbcL nucleotide sequences. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 172: 22-94. [All rights reserved]

description: Hypostomatic, small lateral vascular bundles; central bundle with large partial abaxial crescentiform girder and tiny adaxial cap; marginal bundles circular, epidermis with thickened walls, on lower surface with coronulate papillae within furrows, upper surface slightly undulated; hypodermis and small cells between bundle sheath and sclerenchyma with cubical crystals, palisade cells with rectangular crystals; glands regularly present, deeply sunken into palisade tissue.
bibliographicCitation: Behnke, HD; Hummel, E; Hillmer, S; Sauer-Gurth, H; Gonzalez, J; Wink, M. 2013. A revision of African Velloziaceae based on leaf anatomy characters and rbcL nucleotide sequences. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 172: 22-94. [All rights reserved]

description: Amphistomatic with deep opposite furrows; outer wall of epidermis cells not thickened, stomata restricted to furrows; aquiferous cells below adaxial and abaxial furrows; small sclerenchyma bands underline the epidermis on the abaxial side of the central bundle and on both the adaxial and abaxial sides of lateral bundles.

description: Amphistomatic with opposite shallow to deep furrows; outer wall of epidermis cells moderately thickened, stomata restricted to furrows; on adaxial and abaxial sclerenchyma bands underline the epidermis on either side of lateral bundles and merge into the furrows.
bibliographicCitation: Behnke, HD; Hummel, E; Hillmer, S; Sauer-Gurth, H; Gonzalez, J; Wink, M. 2013. A revision of African Velloziaceae based on leaf anatomy characters and rbcL nucleotide sequences. Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 172: 22-94. [All rights reserved]

description: A poorly defined species that is usually larger than H. hirtulum in all dimensions.

description: F. recondita is distinguished from other members of the genus by having the smallest leaves, 30-55 x 5-15 mm, by its shrubby, lignotuberous growth habit, and by its short, 30-60 mm long, erect terminal inflorescences.

description: Similar to C. sylvatica, from which it differs mainly by its frequently androgynecandrous upper spike, the dense female spikes and the hyaline female glumes.

description: Aspalathus microlithica is a very distinctive species that falls into Dahlgren's (1988) Group 32: Teretilobae. The species is characterised by its dense spreading mat-like habit, strigo-villous vestiture, thick twisted prostrate woody stems, stiff leaves, condensed floriferous branches, bright yellow sessile flowers turning orange to red, purple-veined calyx, obtuse keel, linear oblong wing petals with infolded thickened upper edge and well-developed sculpturing. It is most similar to A. retroflexa L. which occurs more to the west. A. retroflexa is distinguished from A. microlithica by decumbent or procumbent to semi-erect sparingly branched habit, white villous, tomentose or puberulous vestiture, long floriferous branches with dispersed internodes, tomentose calyx, light yellow petals with a purple standard midrib, green calyces, sericeous ovary, and sericeous pods. A. incompta differs in its procumbent habit, pubescent leaves, light or bright yellow petals, cultrate wing petals with lunate petal sculpturing, and short partly pubescent ovary with 2 ovules.

description: The species is characterised by its looser more spreading habit, yellowish green upper branchlets turning brown with age, broader (5-7 x 3 mm) partly conduplicate obovate leaflets with densely hairy margins and green upper leaf blades, patently hairy pale green to pink flushed calyces, and with shorter (4xlength of leaflets) more pilose 5-7 seeded shaggy fruits. It is most similar to P. pallens which is a more compact, multi-stemmed shrub with greyish brown branchlets turning charcoal grey with age, conduplicate narrowly arcuate leaflets with evenly haired silvery leaf margins and leaf blades, mostly appressed hairy yellowish green calyces, and with longer (6x length of leaflets), 8-10 seeded less shaggy pods.
