description: The obconic corms of Lapeirousia purpurea have fine teeth projecting from the base and resemble the corms of L. dolomitica, L. lewisiana and L. violacea, also long-tubed species, but can be distinguished by the rich violet colour of the perianth, with the upper lateral tepals strongly reflexed and the lower three tepals with a V-shaped white mark above the base surrounded by a dark violet to black zone. The lower median tepal bears a small claw-like cusp near the base. In L. violacea all three lower tepals usually bear a small tooth near the base.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Codonorhiza micrantha stands out among the species with crowded, flat-topped inflorescences in its narrow, cylindric perianth tube, 8-10 mm long, and small, yellow to brown or maroon, strongly scented flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Codonorhiza pillansii broadly resembles C. corymbosa in the falcate leaf and many-flowered, flat-topped inflorescence, but is immediately recognised by the flowers with a slender tube (14-)18-20 mm long. The filaments are unilateral and the tepals are subequal in size and evidently symmetrical in disposition. The tepals appear uniformly coloured, which accords with the comment ‘flowers blue’ on the type collection.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: C. elandsmontana is recognised by the zygomorphic flowers with unilateral stamens and white, bracket-shaped markings only on the three abaxial tepals. Other floral details include a perianth tube, 8-10 mm long vs. 4-7(8) mm long and the larger tepals, 10-15 mm long (vs. 6-10 mm long in C. corymbosa). Flowers of C. corymbosa are radially symmetric with all six tepals bearing white, bracket-shaped markings. Codonorhiza elandsmontana may also be confused with C. azurea and C. fastigiata, which are similar in stature and have a broad basal leaf with undulate to crisped margins. The larger flowers of C. azurea are zygomorphic like those of C. elandsmontana but have a perianth tube 10-12 mm long and tepals mostly 17-20 x 7-8 mm and the three abaxial tepals have a dark blue-black or red markings in the lower half. Possible hybrids between C. azurea and C. fastigiata have been recorded at Piketberg Road (Gouda).
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Pale yellow flowers and relatively large perianth with a tube 6-8 mm long and tepals 14-15 mm long are sufficient to distinguish Codonorhiza fastigiata from other species of the genus with flat-topped inflorescences, all of which have light to dark blue or violet flowers except C. micrantha, which has a buff-coloured to brown or maroon perianth but smaller flowers with a cylindric perianth tube. Both perianth and stamens of C. fastigiata are symmetrically arranged so that C. azurea, which has flowers of similar size and shape, can immediately be distinguished by its asymmetrically disposed stamens and perianth with markings only on the lower three tepals, as well as by its dark blue perianth. Collections from Piketberg and Gouda that comprise plants with both yellow and blue flowers were thought to represent populations of plants intermediate between Codonorhiza fastigiata and C. azurea but likely represent hybrid individuals.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Differs from B. ramosa, by its summer dormancy, proliferating tubers and grey-green soft fragile distichous leaves spongy on the inside and elongated seed capsules 5-7 x 3-4 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2015. Bulbine spongiosa, a new cliff-dwelling species (Asphodelaceae) from the Western Cape. Bradleya 33: 156-160. [https://doi.org/10.25223/brad.n33.2015.a21] [All rights reserved]

description: It is at once distinguished from Astroloba bullulata by its spreading to pendent branches of ascending striate and sparsely tuberculate leaves, inflorescence of 20-460 mm and its perianth of 11 mm in length.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2015. Astroloba cremnophila a new cliff dwelling succulent from the Klein Karoo (Western Cape, South Africa). Bradleya 33: 171-179. [All rights reserved]

description: Massonia pseudoechinata can be easily distinguished by the leaves with scarce to numerous small emergences with a declinate, smooth trichome on top; flowers white with long and narrow perigone tube, deeply enclosing the ovary; the strongly reflexed and inrolled perigone segments bearing a distinct sigmoid curve at the base; the blue anthers and pollen; and the obclavate gynoecium, gradually tapering from the ovary to the tip of the style.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Pinter, M; Crespo, MB; Slade, JM; Deutsch, G; Wetschnig, W. 2015. Clarification of Massonia echinata and some other frequently misunderstood Massonia species (Asparagaceae, Scilloideae), with the description of M. pseudoechinata and M. roggeveldensis. Phytotaxa 239(2): 101-129. [All rights reserved]

description: One of a group of species from the interior plateau characterised by dark blue or purple anthers with blue pollen, and the ovary tapering smoothly into the style. Among this group, Massonia pseudoechinata is distinguished by the smooth or sparsely setulose-tubercled leaves, perianth tube 10-15 mm long, tepals that are strongly sigmoid-coiled at the base, filaments shortly connate at the base for 0.5-1.0 mm, and style 14-17 mm long. It closely resembles M. roggeveldensis from the Roggeveld Escarpment but that species has a longer perianth tube, 14-20 mm long, tepals reflexed but with only a slight sigmoid curvature at the base, and a relatively longer style, 17-22 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2019. The genus Massonia Thunb. ex Houtt. (Hyacinthaceae: Scilloideae) in the Core Cape Floristic Region. S. African J. Bot. 121: 329-354. description: The species is characterised by a combination of its rhizomatous habit, long petiolate unifoliolate leaves, calyx with fringed lobes, and densely glandular fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Stirton, CH; Muasya, AM. 2017. Ten new species and a new record for the genus Otholobium (Psoraleeae, Leguminosae) from South Africa. Kew Bull. 72: 1-27. [https://doi.org/10.1007/s12225-017-9722-5] [All rights reserved]

description: It is easily separated from all other species of Otholobium by a combination of its decumbent habit, long hair-like mucro on the leaflets, and narrowly subulate stipules.
bibliographicCitation: Stirton, CH; Muasya, AM. 2017. Ten new species and a new record for the genus Otholobium (Psoraleeae, Leguminosae) from South Africa. Kew Bull. 72: 1-27. [https://doi.org/10.1007/s12225-017-9722-5] [All rights reserved]

description: A climbing or scandent shrub with petiolate leaves with membranous, broadly obovate blades attenuate at the base and decurrent along the petiole, which is 5-15 mm long. The blades are coarsely toothed in the distal half or third, with mostly 2 or 3 triangular teeth, about as long as broad, on each side. The species resembles Gymnanthemum koekemoerae from Tate Vondo in Limpopo in its thin-textured, petiolate leaves and both have similar glabrous but apically glandular involucral bracts but the leaves in G. koekemoerae are shortly petiolate with petioles 3-4 mm long, the base of the blade is obtuse and not decurrent on the petiole, and the margins are more closely and shallowly toothed with about 5 broadly triangular teeth, broader than long, on each side.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Gymnanthemum Cass. (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 102: 81-101. description: P. flabelliforme is characterized by leaves with long, rigid, patent petioles and short and wide pinnately to bipinnately compound laminae. The lamina is widely trowel-shaped in outline and because of the relative narrow segments it resembles a fan, hence the specific epithet (Latin flabelliformis, fan-shaped). The rather small yellow to pale yellow flowers have wine-red feather-like markings on the posterior two petals and V-shaped wine-red markings on the anterior three petals. The latter characteristic is not very common in section Hoarea or in the genus Pelargonium as a whole. The spathulate petals and the very short fertile stamens, concealed in the floral sheath, are characteristic of that of P. pinnatum and also resemble about one third of the species of section Hoarea. P. flabelliforme has rather short hypanthia (13-16 mm long). The peduncle and hypanthia are covered with appressed curly hairs interspersed with short glandular hairs. This is similar to P. luteopetalum, but unlike P. aristatum, P. fissifolium, P. flavipetalum and P. wuppertalense in which the peduncles and hypanthia are covered with appressed curly hairs interspersed with long glandular hairs. The single plant that I studied in cultivation produces only two to three leaves per growing season and flowers every second year.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM. 2015. Five new species of Pelargonium, section Hoarea (Geraniaceae), from the Western and Northern Cape Provinces of South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 103: 145-155. [CC BY]

description: P. luteopetalum has cream-coloured to pale yellow flowers (Latin luteolus, pale yellow) with wine-red feather-like markings on the posterior two petals and regularly pinnately divided leaves. The narrowly spathulate petals and the very short fertile stamens, concealed in the floral sheath, are similar to those of P. pinnatum and about 30 other species in sect. Hoarea. The regularly pinnately divided laminae of P. luteopetalum resemble those of P. aristatum, P. fissifolium (Marais, 1995), P. flavipetalum and P. xanthopetalum, although they are never as finely divided as those of the other four species. The pinnae segments of P. luteopetalum are without a single hair or tuft of hairs at the apex, unlike the other four species. The peduncle and hypanthia are hirsute with a mix of appressed stiff and curly hairs interspersed with short glandular hairs. This is very similar to P. flabelliforme, but unlike P. aristatum, P. fissifolium and P. flavipetalum in which the appressed curly hairs are interspersed with long glandular hairs. The hypanthia of P. xanthopetalum are also covered with short glandular hairs, but the glandular hairs are interspersed with long patent hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Marais, EM. 2015. Five new species of Pelargonium, section Hoarea (Geraniaceae), from the Western and Northern Cape Provinces of South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 103: 145-155. [CC BY]

description: Aspalathus dahlgrenii is a distinctive species that falls into Dahlgren's (1988) Group 33: Calcicolae. It is similar to A. frankenioides DC. and A. gerrardii Bolus but differs in its 2-4 m tree-like (versus decumbent or ascending to 1.5 m) habit; and flowers 9-13 mm (versus 4-8 mm) long.
bibliographicCitation: Stirton, CH; Muasya, AM. 2016. Seven new species and notes on the genus Aspalathus (Crotalarieae, Fabaceae). S. African J. Bot. 104: 35-46. description: Aspalathus modesta is a distinctive species that falls into Dahlgren's (1988) Group 33: Calcicolae. It is an erect shrub clothed with densely packed silvery leaves superficially similar to A. karooensis, a species distinguished by its leaves (6)7-12 mm (versus 5-6 mm) long; flowers equal to or shorter- (versus longer-) than subtending leaves; flowers 8-9 mm (versus 10 mm) long; wing and keel petals glabrous (versus hairy); and style glabrous (versus hairy along upper margin to point of inflexion).
bibliographicCitation: Stirton, CH; Muasya, AM. 2016. Seven new species and notes on the genus Aspalathus (Crotalarieae, Fabaceae). S. African J. Bot. 104: 35-46. description: Aspalathus nickhelmei is a striking new species that falls into Dahlgren's (1988) Group 34: Laterales. The species is similar to A. joubertiana Eckl. & Zeyh. but differs in its lax much-branched, floppy shrub habit to 1.7 m (versus ascending shrublet to 0.7 m); filiform bracts and bracteoles (versus dentate or subulate bracts and bracteoles); densely hairy (versus almost glabrous) standards; and with spurred pocket (versus non-spurred) keel.
bibliographicCitation: Stirton, CH; Muasya, AM. 2016. Seven new species and notes on the genus Aspalathus (Crotalarieae, Fabaceae). S. African J. Bot. 104: 35-46. description: Aspalathus eriocephaloides is a distinctive species that falls into Dahlgren's (1988) Group 1: Sericeae. It is similar to A. villosa Thunb. but differs in its erect flexuose (versus sprawling) habit; leaflets 1.0-1.8 mm (versus 3-8 mm); terminal group or head of 3-6 (versus 1-4) flowers; and altitude above 1000 m (versus below 1000 m).
bibliographicCitation: Stirton, CH; Muasya, AM. 2016. Seven new species and notes on the genus Aspalathus (Crotalarieae, Fabaceae). S. African J. Bot. 104: 35-46. description: Resembling G. tomentosa in the more or less ovate leaves, densely yellowish-brownish felted on the under surface, and in the golden-brownish felted involucral bracts but differing in the smaller leaves with ± entire blades 30-60 mm long, and a subseriate involucre. The leaf margins are typically slightly involute, showing as a raised rusty-felted margin along the leaf upper surface. True G. tomentosa occurs much further west, on the Hottentots Holland and adjacent mountains in Western Cape, and has generally larger leaves with serrate to sinuate blades 40-150 mm long with revolute margins, and characteristic imbricate bracts not ± arranged in series.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Simka, B; Boatwright, JS; Magee, AR. 2016. A revised taxonomy of Gerbera sect. Gerbera (Asteraceae: Mutisieae). S. African J. Bot. 104: 142-157.
