description: With a filiform perianth tube and filaments inserted at the tube mouth, Ixia roseoalba is distinguished in sect. Ixia by the relatively small, pale pink flowers, the tube ± 5 mm long and tepals ± 16 x 7 mm. Unusual for the section, the flowers have a white centre. The filaments and anthers are pale yellow and the style divides opposite the lower third to middle of the anthers. More important, the anthers are unusual in having the connective expanded and visible as a narrow line between the thecae on the outer (abaxial) surface, rendering the thecae almost latrorse. The bracts, typical of sect. Ixia, are translucent and the outer, with several veins, the central one most prominent and reaching the margin, is 3-toothed with the central tooth largest or all three teeth subequal. The long style dividing opposite the lower third to middle of the anthers recalls I. patens but this species, often more slender but with larger, pink or red flowers usually sometimes more darkly pigmented in the centre, has tepals ± 20 x 10 mm and conventional linear anthers without visible connective.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Somewhat unusual in sect. Ixia, I. helmei has a relatively long perianth tube 12-15 mm long and slightly longer than the tepals, and is readily recognised by this feature alone. The presence of two or three leaves, the uppermost almost entirely sheathing, the relatively long perianth tube, and the late flowering time in mid- to late October, combine to confirm its taxonomic isolation. The relatively long style, dividing just below or opposite the bases of the anthers, places it in ser. Longistylae but its immediate relationships are uncertain.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the pale yellow flowers with nearly white, erect filaments held closely together for part of their length so that the style branches emerge between them halfway up their length, then arching outward, reaching to about the base of the anthers. Not clearly visible in dried specimens, the anthers are unusual, being elliptic with the connective visible between the thecae on the abaxial surface. The dehiscence is latrorse, unusual for Ixia although known in a few other species, none apparently closely related to I. angelae. The flowers have a relatively short perianth tube, 6-7 mm and tepals ± 12 mm long, about twice as long as the tube. The corms have tunics of fine, soft fibres and produce cormlets on stolons at the base. Ixia angelae stands out in sect. Ixia, especially among the short-styled species of the section in the uniformly coloured tepals without any hint of a dark centre.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Phymaspermum oppositifolium is the only opposite leafed species within the genus. It shares the appressed leaves, entirely scarious involucral bracts and purplish ray florets with the closely related P. appressum from which it can be distinguished further by the funnelshaped involucres and lanceolate involucral bracts.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: Among the three species of Hilliardiella with silvery-silky vestiture, H. elaeagnoides is distinguished by its relatively short, ovate-lanceolate to broadly ovate leaves, mostly 15-30 mm long and 20 mm wide and seldom more than twice as long as wide, and markedly discolorous with the upper surface thinly silky or glabrescent and the lower surface densely silvery-silky. Hilliardiella capensis has much narrower leaves, also markedly discolorous but linear to linear-lanceolate, 1-4 mm wide and ericoid with revolute margins, and typically with axillary tufts. Hilliardiella aristata, which is very variable in leaf shape, is distinguished by leaves with both surfaces usually more or less equally densely silvery-silky, at most only weakly discolorous, and long-attenuate inner involucral bracts that are smoothly or more abruptly narrowed to a bristle-tipped point. Intermediates among all three species are known where they are sympatric and may represent introgression but most specimens can be assigned with confidence.
bibliographicCitation: Swelankomo, N; Manning, JC; Magee, AR. 2016. The genus Hilliardiella (Asteraceae: Vernonieae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 106: 41-59. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2016); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Immediately recognised by the two linear, soft-textured basal foliage leaves without thickened margins, ± 3 mm wide and slightly twisted distally, together with short-tubed, nodding to slightly pendent flowers. The flowers conform most closely to those of the I. latifolia group in their perianth tube of moderate length, at least 6 mm long, and partly exserted filaments. The unusual leaf morphology does not indicate any particular close relationship to other members of the series.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The southern coastal Aristea rufobracteata is broadly similar to A. capitata from the southwestern parts of Western Cape in the columnar and relatively dense flowering axis with fairly short branches and sessile flower clusters but is readily distinguished by the rusty brown spathes and floral bracts that are thinner and slightly paler toward the margins.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: From A. suaveolens it is distinguished by its larger size (see table) as well as dorsiventrally flattened leaves to 1000 mm long and becoming pendentas well as its nodding perianth and reflexed segments. A. suaveolens is smaller (bulb only up to 20 mm in diameter) with narrower channeled ascending leaves up to 400 mm long and ascending spreading flowers. The latter species is not a cliff-dweller, occurring on flats and hills.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2011. Ornithogalum gildenhuysii (Hyacinthaceae), a new cliff-dwelling bulbous succulent from the Northern Cape (South Africa). Herbertia 65: 51-59. [Permission to reproduce this work was granted to SANBI by the International Bulb Society] [All rights reserved]

description: Periglossum podoptyches is morphologically closest to P. mackenii and P. kassnerianum from which it differs in the presence of folded flaps of tissue at the base of the restricted basal stalk of the staminal corona lobes. Further it does not have a 'T'-shaped slit on the ventral surface of the staminal corona lobe which is instead solid and smooth.
bibliographicCitation: Bester, SP; Nicholas, A. 2016. Periglossum podoptyches (Apocynaceae-Asclepiadoideae), a new species from KwaZulu-Natal province, South Africa. Phytotaxa 282(1): 28-36. [http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.282.1.3] [All rights reserved]

description: This species shares the white petals and smaller fruit (less than 3.5 mm long) with C. sphaerocarpum but can be readily distinguished by the prominent white tubercles on the ovaries and the prominent fruit ribs with tubercled fibrous ridges on the dorsal surface. Less prominent, irregular tubercles are often also found on the ovaries of C. chaerophylloides but this species is more robust (up to 3 m tall), has yellowish-green (rather than white) petals, conspicuously obconical fruiting umbels with ascending outer rays (hemispherical with horizontal to reclining outer rays in C. hilliburttorum) and the tubercles are quickly lost or reduced as the fruit matures.
bibliographicCitation: Magee, AR; Clark, VR. 2017. Mzansi's mountain hemlocks: The identities of Hilliard and Burtt's Conium species 3 and 4 (Apiaceae) and a revised key for the genus in sub-Saharan Africa. S. African J. Bot. 108: 243-247. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2016.11.006] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2017); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: This subspecies is distinguished by its ovary having fewer locules, being mostly two, occasionally three, rarely one, (G2(3)[4]/1), and by the corolla tending to be more campanulate with slightly spreading lobes and mostly twice the length of the calyx or shorter.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: The dark red, sessile glands on the otherwise glabrous leaves and calyx serve to distinguish this subspecies. The typical subspecies has long cilia only.
bibliographicCitation: Oliver, EGH. 2000. Systematics of Ericeae (Ericaceae-Ericiodeae) species with indehiscent and partially indehiscent fruits. Contr. Bolus Herb. 19: 3-472. [All rights reserved]

description: In plants of subsp. elongata the stems are tightly packed into clumps which often reach 300 mm across but may achieve 1 m in diameter occasionally. The plants are not entirely without underground runners but, as with the stems, these tend to be shorter and thicker than those found in subsp. gerstneri. The stems are stout and comparatively short, with broadly deltoid tubercles. They are dark green to brownish, flecked with purple if exposed, and are very similar in colour to those of subsp. gerstneri. Florally the two subspecies are very similar. In subsp. elongata the lobes are less variable in length and are generally at least twice as long as broad, whereas in subsp. gerstneri they may sometimes be quite short. In subsp. elongata the tube is mostly deeper than broad and it is sufficiently long that the gynostegium is somewhat hidden in it. The outer corona lobes are also considerably longer and usually rise nearly to the mouth of the tube.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 1. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: R. rostrata subsp. pluriflora differs from the typical subspecies in the procumbent, mat-like habit, the invariably alternate leaf arrangement on the flowering branches (sub-opposite to opposite in subsp. rostrata), the basal leaves which are smaller than the upper leaves (basal leaves larger than the upper leaves in subsp. rostrata), the larger, lanceolate leaves (leaves obovate in subsp. rostrata), the 2-5-flowered racemes (single-flowered in subsp. rostrata), the triangular calyx lobes (lobes narrowly triangular in subsp. rostrata), the tapering wing apex (apex obliquely obtuse in subsp. rostrata) and the short style (shorter than the ovary in subsp. pluriflora and ± as long as the ovary in subsp. rostrata). It also differs from R. racemosa in the shape of the keel petal and the generally lower number of flowers (up to 5 flowers in subsp. pluriflora and up to 19 flowers in R. racemosa).
bibliographicCitation: Campbell, GJ; Van Wyk, B-E. 2001. A taxonomic revision of Rafnia (Fabaceae, Crotalarieae). S. African J. Bot. 67: 90-149. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2001); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: As is to be expected, subsp. villetii is more variable than was given in the protologue and in the population recently encountered the pedicels were 9-25 mm long, whereas they were originally given as 4-6 mm long. However, the flowers generally seem to be very small and, at 6-8 mm in diameter, are often even smaller than in subsp. longipes. The main difference between the two subspecies is that the corolla faces upwards in subsp. villetii and horizontally in the other. Lückhoff mentioned that the tips of the corolla lobes could be deeper yellow than the rest or even rose-red, but flowers seen recently were all uniformly pale yellow. The corolla lobes are slightly folded back so that the upper surface is convex.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: The stems of subsp. decorus are more papillate than is usually the case in Piaranthus but they are otherwise typical. Here the corolla is more or less flat with the lobes slightly reflexed towards their tips and it is generally between 15 and 30 mm in diameter. The lobes are relatively broad (at 4-5 mm), tapering fairly quickly to their tips which are not attenuated. The background colour of the corolla is cream to yellow and on this background there are many fine red-brown bars which are longest around the middle of the lobe, becoming smaller and finer towards the centre. Towards the tip of the lobe they tend to become coarser and very occasionally they coalesce there into a red-brown patch.
bibliographicCitation: Bruyns, PV. 2005. Stapeliads of southern Africa and Madagascar, Vol. 2. Umdaus Press, Hatfield. [All rights reserved]

description: Pink and golden juvenile foliage occurs sympatrically and galls similar in size and shape to the drupes are often found on branchlets and midribs. R. schliebenii appears to be none other than younger material of R. coddii and not an altitudinal form as suggested by R. & A. Fernandes (1976). In this and in other suffrutescent species, I have observed that the first fertile shoots that develop after a fire are very different to older much branched material that has not been burnt for a number of years.
bibliographicCitation: Moffett, RO. 1993. Anacardiaceae - Rhus. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 19(3,1): 1-129. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209553#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The flowers of subsp. serpentina closely resemble those of subsp. macrochlamys and subsp. kamiesbergensis and differ if at all only in their slightly smaller size, and the subspecies is distinguished by its leaves, the narrow blades of which are wavy in a loose concertina fashion, with plane, smooth margins not at all thickened. This contrasts with the straight leaves of subsp. macrochlamys, which have strongly thickened, crisped or crenate margins, and in some populations, shortly velvety. The flowers of subsp. serpentina have a floral cup, 9-11 mm deep, ± 5 mm wide at the rim, outer tepals 26-28 mm long, and filaments 10-11 mm long, thus slightly smaller than in most populations of subsp. macrochlamys, which have a cup, 11-13 mm deep, 6-7 mm wide at the rim, outer tepals 28-32 mm long, and filaments ± 12 mm long. The inner spathes are 37-45 mm long, compared to 45-62 mm in subsp. macrochlamys, and the flowers have pedicels 10-15 mm long (versus 20-23 mm in subsp. macrochlamys), reflecting the shorter spathes. A particularly narrow-leaved form of subsp. serpentina has been recorded in the Komaggas area west of Springbok, the blades ± 2 mm wide and when dry, showing the outline of a raised central vein.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Subsp. namaquensis is distinguished from typical subsp. inconspicua by the coiled leaves with flat blades up to 3 mm wide. Other vegetative and floral features differ only quantitatively, with considerable overlap but on average subsp. namaquensis has slightly larger rhipidial spathes and floral features than subsp. inconspicua. In subsp. namaquensis the outer rhipidial spathes are 19-28 mm long, outer tepals 15-18 mm long, and anthers 3-4 mm long compared with rhipidial spathes 15-26 mm long, outer tepals 12-15 mm long and anthers 1.5-3.3 mm long in subsp. inconspicua.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Like the typical subspecies, Pauridia serrata subp. albiflora has linear, canaliculate leaves that have minute, widely spaced, recurved teeth on the margins, a feature most easily seen in new growth. As the name suggests, subsp. albiflora is easily distinguished by its white, stellate flowers, which are mostly green- backed.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 2014. A taxonomic revision of the genus Pauridia (Hypoxidaceae) in southern Africa. Phytotaxa 182(1): 1-114. [All rights reserved]

description: Subsp. speciosa has a firm, somewhat fleshy habit in which the leaves partially clasp each other and the scape for about a third of their length. Although the orange colour of the flowers varies in intensity from deep, pure orange to yellowish orange, the flowers are distinguished by concolorous tepals, stamens and style, a combination which is unique in the genus. In addition, the outer tepals are usually richly flushed dorsally with reddish brown, making this one of the most attractive taxa within Pauridia. Subtle differences between the subspecies are also found in the seeds. These have hump-like projections arranged in close, longitudinal rows on the testa in subsp. speciosa, unlike the widely spaced rows in the seeds of subsp. gracilipes. Several early collections of this Kamiesberg endemic have erroneously been named Spiloxene linearis (Andrews) Garside (now P. linearis), a pale orange-flowered species from the Atlantic Coast, in the vicinity of of Paternoster and Langebaan, Western Cape. Although solitary flowered, it has two filifom bracts per inflorescence, the tepals are green dorsally and the ovary is apparently fully trilocular. The ensuing confusion over the identity of the Kamiesberg plant probably accounts for the taxon not having been described until now, despite the first collection dating back to 1830 when it was recorded by Drège.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 2014. A taxonomic revision of the genus Pauridia (Hypoxidaceae) in southern Africa. Phytotaxa 182(1): 1-114. [All rights reserved]

description: Acanthopsis tetragona subsp. pedunculata differs from A. tetragona subsp. tetragona in having clearly pedunculate inflorescences with peduncle (15-)20-35(-50) mm long (not subsessile to shortly pedunculate with peduncle nearly always <10 mm long).
bibliographicCitation: Steyn, HM; van Wyk, AE. 2017. Taxonomic notes on Acanthopsis Harv. (Acanthaceae, tribe Acantheae): the group with trifid bracts. Phytotaxa 295(3): 201-217. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.295.3.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Plants with serrate leaves should be excluded from ssp. pinnatifida and be described as the new subspecies serrata. Ssp. angustifolia seems well established, but are ssp. pinnatifida and ssp. serrata not only environmental modifications of the same genotype? This is disproved by the fact that all three subspecies have kept their original leaf-shapes during two years of cultivation in greenhouses under identical conditions. Thus the latter two subspecies are can be regarded as ecotypes in the classical sense of Turesson.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. New taxa of Osmitopsis (Compositae). Bot. Not. 129: 21-24.

description: Leaves elliptic, 12-22 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1976. A revision of Diastella (Proteaceae). J. S. African Bot. 42: 185-210. [CC BY]

description: L. spissifolium subsp.fragrans is a dense shrub about 1 m tall with many stems arising from a persistent rootstock. It has narrow, twisted glabrous sub-canaliculate leaves and lanceolate acute basal bracts. The cone bracts are always glabrous. It differs from the typical subspecies which has leaves that are much broader. It differs from subsp.phillipsii which has linear-oblanceolate leaves, ovate basal bracts and cone bracts always pubescent across the middle.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1972. A revision of the genus Leucadendron (Proteaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 3: 1-425. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily recognized by its large ovate leaves which when young are markedly velutinous and have thickly ciliate margins.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This subspecies is rather homogeneous and may be regarded as a high-mountain ecotype restricted to a single massif. It is characterized by its low stature, imbricated, soft- pubescent, rather short and broad leaves, and subsessile, often solitary flowers. It is rather distinct but obviously closely related to forms of ssp. villosa.
bibliographicCitation: Strid, PAK. 1972. Revision of the genus Adenandra (Rutaceae). Opera Bot. 32: 1-112. [All rights reserved]

description: Macrostylis dregeana which has branchlets puberulous, leaves ciliate with a broader hyaline margin, petals with a narrow blade, staminodes 0.4 mm long and the anther with a much smaller apical gland.
bibliographicCitation: Williams, IJM. 1981. Studies in the genera of the Diosmeae (Rutaceae): 11. A review of the genus Macrostylis. J. S. African Bot. 47(3): 373-403. [CC BY]

description: The bulbs are densely clump-forming. The style has a pronounced discoid stylar swelling with an irregular frilly rim.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 1994. Systematics of Hessea, Strumaria and Carpolyza (Amaryllideae:Amaryllidaceae). Contr. Bolus Herb. 16: 2-158. [All rights reserved]

description: An unusual form which is in several characteristics intermediate between typical A. umbraticola and A. schuldtianus (below), but because it is known from so few localities its real position cannot be evaluated fully.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Adromischus cristatus var. mzimvubuensis is distinguished from the other varieties by its acaulescent rosettes of dorsiventrally flattened leaves which are often incurved with a continuous horny margin right around the leaf. It has ginger-brown aerial roots and 2- or 3-flowered cymes. All the other varieties cristatus, var. clavifolius, var. schonlandii and var. zeyheri) have stems 20-50 mm long and leaves with distinct petioles. The horny margin in the other varieties does not extend right around the leaf, and is confined to the distal part of the leaf. In var. zeyheri (its closest relative) the margin sometimes extends to or less a third from the base. The latter, however, lacks aerial roots and always develops stems up to 50 mm long. In both mzimvubuensis and var. zeyheri the leaves are dorsiventrally flattened. Another difference is the 3-flowered cymes found on the inflorescence, compared to the usually 1-flowered (rarely 2-) cymes in the other varieties. Var. cristatus, var. clavifolius anc schonlandii are all confined to the Eastern Cape region west of the Kei River. Var. zeyheri is confined to quartzitic sandstone cliff faces in the Kouga Mountains and again in Oribi Gorge of southern KwaZulu-Natal, and remains remarkably constant taking in consideration that var. mzimvubuensis occurs in between these two localities.It was observed growing only on sheer Ecca Shale cliffs (Karoo Supergroup) on all aspects. Associated cliff dwellers include Gasteria croucheri (southern record), Senecio sp., Cotyledon orbiculata var. flanaganii (eastern-most record), Cyanotis speciosus, Ornithogalum longibractet Crassula multicava subsp. floribunda, C. culturata (eastern record), C. perforata, C. intermedia, Senecio medley-woodi and Delosperma tradescantioides. The plants vary considerably in size and leaf shape, some forms with almost obovate leaves (more exposed north- and west-facing) and undulating margins, where-as others have mostly oblong leaves without the undulations. They are locally quite common.
bibliographicCitation: Toelken, HR. 1985. Crassulaceae, Fl. S. Africa 14: 1-229. [CC BY]

description: Intermediates between these two varieties do occur, especially from the Eastern Cape northwards. However, because they are reasonably distinct in their respective southern and northern areas of concentration, I have maintained them as two varieties. R. rehmanniana var. glabrata may be confused with R. laevigata var. villosa. The latter taxon, however, does not have rugose leaflets and occurs on sands near the coast, while the former occurs on clay-rich soils derived from shales.
bibliographicCitation: Moffett, RO. 1993. Anacardiaceae - Rhus. In: OA Leistner (ed.), Fl. S. Africa 19(3,1): 1-129. National Botanical Institute, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209553#page/1/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: A. luederitzii var. retinens is usually readily distinguished from A. reficiens and, as it occupies a different geographical range to A. reficiens, is unlikely to be confused with the latter. However, the main difficulty in this complex is that while var. retinens and A. reficiens are themselves distinct, they are almost linked through typical var. luederitzii.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A. sieberana has in the past been confused with A. rehmanniana Schinz.
bibliographicCitation: Ross, JH. 1975. Mimosoideae, Fl. S. Africa 16(1): 1-155. BRI, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Haworthia reinwardtii var. riebeekensis mentions that this var. is nearest allied to var. adelaidensis but is a smaller plant and the tubercles are in longitudinal rows, whereas those of var. adelaidensis are in transverse rows. It would seem, however, that var. adelaidensis is probably better placed between var. riebeekensis and var. kaffirdriftensis. This latter form having the rows of tubercles much more united lengthwise than in the case of var. adelaidensis.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, JR. 1952. Notes on Haworthias. 24(6): 163-166. [All rights reserved]

description: It is readily identified by the small size of the plants, the numerous tubercles on the back of the leaves and the large mats that it forms in the wild. Its nearest affinity seems to be var. brevicula.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: It is distinguished from the species by its being much taller, and much smaller in diam., and by its rope-like appearance in its procumbent habit. The tubercles are not as white as those of the species.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, GG. 1948. Some new species and varieties in the genus Haworthia, VI. J. S. African Bot. 14: 41-54. [CC BY]

description: H. herrei should be regarded as a separate species because the leaves of H. glauca are smooth as compared with the tubercled leaves of H. herrei; there is also a difference in their floral characters. H. herrei has a longer peduncle and a shorter raceme, while their flowering times do not overlap. H. glauca has probably the closest affinity, but differs from that species in the characteristics listed above.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1985. The genus Haworthia (Liliaceae): a taxonomic revision. Aloe Books, Johannesburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Leaves are spirally arranged in a tight rosette. However, the tubercles are irregularly arranged on both leaf surfaces and the characteristic transverse lines are not apparent. It has been given the varietal name H. limifolia var. gigantea because of its exceptionally large size. It is of interest to record also that detached leaves of this plant can produce new plants even up to a year after rooting.
bibliographicCitation: Bayer, MB. 1962. A new variety of Haworthia linifolia from Natal. J. S. African Bot. 28: 215-217. [CC BY]

description: A comparison with Haworthia schmidtiana Poelln. will at once show the distinct characters of the 2 spp. The leaves of Haworthia diversifolia are in straighter ranks, are shorter and as broad as long, are not recurved at tips, the warts are more regularly arranged in transverse rows and the warts on the margins unite to form a single row. In color and growth characters they would seem to be quite close.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, JR. 1938. Notes on Haworthias. 9(8): 133-134. [All rights reserved]

description: As the name implies, this is a very small replica of Haworthia reinwardtii Haw. Not only is the plant and its leaves smaller, but the tubercles are very much smaller, giving the plant a uniformly white-peppered appearance. Haworthia reinwardtii v. bellula G.G.Smith is a smaller plant than this variety but is quite distinct.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, GG. 1948. Some new species and varieties in the genus Haworthia, VI. J. S. African Bot. 14: 41-54. [CC BY]

description: It differs from the type of the species by its smallness, smaller and more crowded back tubercles, more numerous face tubercles and shorter pedicels. A neat compact little plant, and quite distinctive.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, GG. 1944. Some new species and varieties in the genus Haworthia II. J. S. African Bot. 10: 11-24. [CC BY]

description: H. sordida var. lavrani shows affinities with two species: H. sordida Haw., and H. tuberculata von Poelln. From the first, H. sordida, it differs in that it has more, shorter, broadly channelled and recurved leaves; these are distinctly tubercled with shiny rounded black tubercles on the upper and back leaf-surfaces; the inflorescence is longer; there are more flowers, with more and longer fertile bracts; the ovary, style, and perianth are also shorter. H. sordida has fewer, and more or less tapering leaves, the upper surface has a few tubercles, but mostly rugose; the back is beset with numerous, rounded, often confluent, but minute tubercles. From the second, H. tuberculata, it differs in that H. tuberculata is a taller plant, with longer, upright, curved and lanceolate leaves, these somewhat laterally curved inwards towards the apex; there are also more and larger pointed tubercles on the upper and back surfaces of the leaves; there are fewer flowers and sterile bracts; the perianth and pedicels are longer; the stamens and the ovary is shorter; there are also additional small differences which assist one on the plant's identity.
bibliographicCitation: Scott, CL. 1981. A new variety of Haworthia Duval. Cact. Succ. J. (Los Angeles) 53: 124-126. [All rights reserved]

description: At this locality we observed plants with quite long leaves, some of them are extremely elongated. The surface is somewhat rough. Further onwards grows a natural hybrid between these plants and H. fasciata, which occurs there, too. This hybrid has the shape of H. fasciata's leaves, but the surface of H. viscosa. These hybrids resemble H. longiana a little.
bibliographicCitation: Breuer, I. 2003. Beschreibung einiger neuer Haworthia-taxa. Avonia 21(3): 45-65. [All rights reserved]

description: Its sharply acute leaf lobes distinguish it from var. fontanum; it is often taller too (reaching 3 m, not ±1 m), and favours a different habitat.
bibliographicCitation: Burtt, BL; Hilliard, OM. 1985. Conium (Umbelliferae) in southern Africa. S. African J. Bot. 51: 465-474. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (1985); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Specimens from Coombs Valley near Grahamstown may have woolly leaves as in var. appressifolium (Hilliard & Burtt 10852, E; K; NU; PRE) or glabrous leaves as in var. glabrum (Hilliard & Burtt 10863, E; K; NU; PRE); one plant of the latter collection has some branchlets with glabrous leaves, others with lower leaves glabrous, upper woolly. Marais s.n. (PRE) from the Bontebok National Park at Swellendam appears to be H. asperum var. glabrum x var. albidulum.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1983. Gnaphaliinae (first part): Facelis - Edmondia, Fl. S. Africa 33(7,2): 1-317. Botanical Research Institute, Department Agriculture, Pretoria. [http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209547#page/5/mode/1up] [CC BY]

description: The var. seineri has markedly pubescent stems and leaves; although glistening glands are often present as well, they are subordinate to the hairs. The area of var. seineri lies mostly south and east of that of var. canescens; where they are sympatric around Windhoek, above the Swakop river, and south to about Remhoogte, the distinctions may blur and some specimens are difficult to place. Distinguished from L. canescens by its glandular pubescence.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Origin South America (Brazil), invasive status: potential transformer, declared weed in KZN and declared invader (Category 3) elsewhere in SA; poisonous fruit in quantity, irritant to skin and respiratory tract.
bibliographicCitation: Struwig, M. 2019. Anacardiaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 278-293. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species exhibits great variability in the sculpturing of the megaspores. The spores of the Peninsula plant often show reticulations on the rounded face-a condition which is only occasionally seen in the Stellenbosch plant. Here the megaspores are usually rougher, with marked tubercles or an imperfect reticulum with prominent warts at the nodes of the network. Large numbers of plants from both localities were examined and found to agree in the lobing of the corm, the characters of the leaves and the presence of a complete velum.
bibliographicCitation: Duthie, AV. 1929. The species of Isoetes found in the Union of South Africa. Trans. Roy. Soc. South Africa 17: 321-332. [All rights reserved]

description: This is one of the tallest and certainly the most large-flowered and conspicuous species in the genus. R. speciosa is also characterized by its broad, often squarrose, pungent leaves. It is related to R. calycina, a smaller species.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: The salient features of S. pinea are the strongly retrorse and appressed hairs on the stems, relatively long particularly on the upper parts of the stem, mainly glandular bracts and calyces, and violet corolla, the only species in this group with coloured, not white, flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1999. The Tribe Selagineae (Scrophulariaceae). Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Pauridia pusilla bears a striking resemblance to P. nana in that both are shade-loving plants with delicate, narrow, pale green leaves and small flowers, but several unusual floral characters make the plants of P. pusilla unmistakable. The filaments are fused to the style forming a gynostemium, the anther connectives and stigma branches are reddish and the ovary is topped by a short beak, 0.5-1.0 mm long. Other species having flowers with a gynostemium are P. maximiliani and the more distantly related and well- known P. minuta and P. longituba. P. maximiliani is similar to P. pusilla in having all the filaments adnate to the style, whereas in P. minuta and P. longituba the inner whorl of fertile stamens is inserted in the perigone throat and only the outer whorl of `pseudostigmatic staminodes', as described by Burtt, is fused to the style, thereby suggesting the independent origin of these structures within Pauridia. Variation: Flower colour in Pauridia pusilla varies to some extent throughout its range, although the dark colouring of the anther connectives and stigmatic branches remains constant. The populations on the Matsikamma Mountain and Gifberg invariably have yellow tepals, whereas those in the northern Cederberg have white or cream tepals. Variation in the number of floral parts is also known. Both tetramerous and hexamerous flowers are frequently found within the same population and occasionally on the same plant. Only very rarely have pentamerous flowers been noted. This condition is not unique to the genus, however, and is also known within Hypoxis and Empodium.
bibliographicCitation: Snijman, DA. 2014. A taxonomic revision of the genus Pauridia (Hypoxidaceae) in southern Africa. Phytotaxa 182(1): 1-114. [All rights reserved]

description: Alepidea inflexa is easily distinguished by the hispidulous synflorescence, peduncular bracts bearing inter-dentine setae, and the compact rosette of prostrate, elliptical basal leaves with prominently depressed adaxial veins and long, strongly inflexed inter-dentine setae, extending at least to the midrib but more often to the opposite margin. These inflexed inter-dentine setae could suggest a favourable adaptation for a water harvesting mechanism in the fog frequented climate.
bibliographicCitation: Hutchinson, S-L; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2017. A taxonomic revision of the Alepidea setifera group (Apiaceae, Apioideae), the description of a new species, A. inflexa, and the reinstatement of A. jenkinsii. S. African J. Bot. 111: 1-11. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2017.03.021] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2017); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Deverra rapaletsa can be distinguished from all other species in the genus by the unique prostrate growth habit and the fruit with warty finger-like projections. It can be further distinguished from the other two southern African species by the slender branches (less than 2 mm in diameter), the shorter internodes (less than 35 mm at stem base), and the smaller umbels with rays less than 15 mm long. As in D. burchellii the ovaries and fruit are covered in warty finger-like projections (woolly in D. aphylla), but seemingly more dense in D. rapaletsa.
bibliographicCitation: Van Munster, S; Magee, AR; Zietsman, PC. 2019. Deverra rapaletsa (Apiaceae), a new limestone endemic species from the Ghaap Plateau, Northern Cape, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 121: 431-434. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2018.12.005] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2019); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [All rights reserved]

description: Allied to the Afrosolen erythranthus complex of short-tubed species, A. sandersonii has the repeatedly branched, panicle-like inflorescence with 1 or 2 (rarely 3) flowers on the major terminal branches. The blue-violet flowers have a moderately long perianth tube, mostly 15-30 mm long, and the floral bracts are often relatively long, 8-12 mm, acute-attenuate and flushed purple or brown and aging dark brown. The corm tunics are distinctive, being dark brown and fragmenting into vertical strips rather than becoming a fibrous network.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: A. heydenrychii and the widespread A. abyssinica are closest related. The latter has firmly erect, narrow leaves and erect inflorescence and is mainly from dry savanna parts of Africa. Albuca heydenrychii differs in habit and morphology: it grows isolated on the northern Drakensberg Escarpment cliffs, its leaves are flaccid, pendent to spreading 1000-1200 x 60-80 mm, distinctly striate, and its inflorescence has a distinct curve, initially drooping with the raceme always curving upwards. These characteristics are maintained in cultivation.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Visagie, M. 2019. Albuca heydenrychii Van Jaarsv. Fl. Pl. Africa 66: 30-36, t.2344 [CC BY]

description: Astroloba tenax can be distinguished from A. bullulata based on both vegetative and floral characters. The leaves of A. tenax have a glossier surface, while they usually lack the distinctive tubercles of A. bullulata. In cases where A. tenax does bear spots or tubercles on its leaf surface, they are often concentrated at the leaf bases, on the abaxial side of leaves. The leaf tubercles of A. tenax are usually relatively few in number and, where an arrangement is apparent, it is normally longitudinal. The more numerous leaf tubercles of A. bullulata are usually arranged in transverse bands across the leaves. Striations are also sometimes apparent on the leaves of A. tenax, but this character appears inconsistently in a population and is consequently not here considered to be diagnostic for the species. The leaves of Astroloba tenax are usual arranged at a more patent, horizontal angle to the stem than the predominantly sub-erect leaves of A. bullulata. The patent leaves of A. tenax are often recurved near their base and somewhat incurved at their tips, while leaves of A. bullulata are more strongly and uniformly incurved. The leaves of A. tenax are also commonly imbricately arranged, rather than in five, clear vertical ranks, which is usually encountered in A. bullulata. The leaf shape of A. tenax is more elongated, being narrowly- to slightly elongated-deltoid with an acuminate, sometimes attenuate, apex, compared to the shorter, broader, ovate-deltoid leaves of A bullulata. Further, one of the side margins on leaves of A bullulata always loses its identity near the apex, while the margins of A. tenax only partially lose their identity or, in about half of the cases observed, do not at all. The perianths of Astroloba tenax are grey in colour, with slightly darker grey midribs, strongly constricted towards the mouth, and have darker grey necks with free lobes that do not flare outwards. The perianths of A. bullulata are pale green, with green midribs and occasional reddish-brown streaks, barely constricted necks, and with free lobes that flare outwards at an angle averaging 30-45°. At 30-60 cm, the inflorescences of A. tenax are also longer than those of A. bullulata, which attain a length of 14-30 cm. The inflorescences of A. tenax are often branched, so forming a panicle, and bear the flowers in a comparatively more lax arrangement.
bibliographicCitation: Molteno, S; Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Smith, GF. 2017. Astroloba tenax Molteno, Van Jaarsv. & Gideon F.Sm. (Asphodelaceae: Alooideae), a new species from the Groot Swartberg Mountain, South Africa. Bradleya 35: 139-149. [All rights reserved]

description: A very distinct species, with the base of the annual shoots swollen and corm-like and covered with stiff fibres from the leaf bases, and a tuft of sclerotic leaves with distinctive pubescence, the upper surface densely scabrid with short, stiff hairs weakly clustered or fascicled along the ribs, and the under surface with marked fascicles of longer hairs up to 1 mm long on the ribs, the fascicles more densely clustered towards the base of the leaf and scattered distally. The racemose inflorescence with glabrous scape is produced late in the season, in October or November.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC. 2017. Chlorophytum asperum (Agavaceae), a new species from Northern Cape, South Africa. S. African J. Bot. 111: 316-318. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2017.04.002] [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2017); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the rather lax raceme of rotate, moderately sized flowers with a weakly deflexed style longer than the ovary and with a globose-papillate stigma. The solitary terete leaf is usually withered at flowering, rarely still present. In flower, the species is confusingly similar to smaller forms of Drimia exuviata, whence the derivation of the epithet. Both species share rotate flowers opening in the early morning and lasting a full day, with a weakly deflexed style longer than the ovary and a globose-papillate stigma, but D. exuviata is readily distinguished by the conspicuous, strongly horizontally barred, papery cataphyll, whereas that in D. decipiens is membranous with only traces of barring. The unscented flowers of D. decipiens are also slightly smaller, with tepals 8-9 mm long and anthers ± 2 mm long with complete longitudinal dehiscence whereas the sweetly fragrant flowers of D. exuviata have tepals 10-14 mm long and anthers 2-4 mm long with porose-longitudinal dehiscence. The two species are sympatric on the Swartruggens, but D. exuviata flowers slightly earlier in the season, and is in fruit as D. decipiens comes into bloom.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The most commonly collected of the three species of the Drimia marginata complex, D. ecklonii is distinguished by its generally narrower, oblong leaves, usually 6-10 (rarely up to 15) mm wide, with an obtuse apex and a simple, papillate margin. The leaf margin is thickened on both dorsal and ventral surfaces and the papillae may be blunt or acute. Plants produce mostly two or three leaves, rarely up to four. Other members of the complex have broader, oblong or elliptical leaves that are distinctly apiculate and have margins that are partially or entirely ciliolate.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Recognised by the short, compact inflorescence of nodding, rotate white flowers with reflexed tepals 7-8 mm long, distally spreading stamens with basifixed anthers, and the relatively long style, ± twice as long as the ovary. The linear-canaliculate leaves are withered at flowering and are surrounded at the base by the papery, sheathing remains of the previous seasons' foliage. Drimia khubusensis has unique capsules and seeds. The capsules are rather dark in colour, sometimes almost black, and the segments reflex from the base at dehiscence to expose the seeds completely, whereas other species of Drimia typically have brown capsules with segments that recurve only distally so that the seeds remain largely enclosed within the locules. Most striking, however, are the creamy-white or pale greyish seeds, these discoid with well-developed peripheral wings The nodding flowers lasting a full day and with reflexed tepals, oblong anthers, and long style recall those of pink-flowered D. nana, but that species has filiform leaves ± 0.25 mm diam., unique stamens with fusiform filaments and intrusively basifixed anthers, and a strongly flexed style.
bibliographicCitation: Manning, JC; Goldblatt, P. 2018. Systematics of Drimia Jacq. (Hyacinthaceae: Urgineoideae) in southern Africa. Strelitzia 40: 1-173. South African National Biodiversity Institute; Missouri Botanical Garden, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Distinguished by the single, short and succulent leaf (15-25(40) x 5-9 mm) and the subcapitate inflorescence borned on an elongated peduncle.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB; Alonso Vargas, MA; Dold, AP; Pinter, M; Wetschnig, W. 2018. Austronea (Asparagaceae, Scilloideae), a new genus from southern Africa, including the description of seven new species. Phytotaxa 365(2): 101-129. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.365.2.1] [All rights reserved]

description: Like those of the other members of the Geissorhiza namaquensis group, the leaves of G. namaquamontana are narrowly sword-shaped to nearly linear, with the margins narrowly winged and ciliate and the main vein and sometimes a second pair of veins raised and similarly ciliate. There seems no difference in the leaves among the group except for overall size and number. Whereas four leaves are usual, some plants have only three leaves and one from Grootberg with multiple branches has a small fifth leaf. The point of division on the style seems to vary in G. namaquamontana, dividing opposite the middle to upper third of the anthers in the two Kamiesberg populations but opposite or shortly above the anther apices in the Grootberg plants which have white anthers and pollen. The style branches in both sets of populations are short, ± 1 mm long. A note on Helme 3310 from the Kamiesberg states that the anthers and pollen are yellow. The differences between the Kamiesberg and Grootberg plants may simply be due to genetic drift or may signal that there are two separate taxa here. Additional field work in Namaqualand is needed.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: The high altitude Ixia saundersiana is immediately recognised by the single linear foliage leaf and a second, largely sheathing leaf, together with a mostly unbranched stem and spike of 2 or 3(-5) small, blue-mauve flowers yellow in the throat. Well-grown plants may have up to three, short, straight, ascending branches with up to four flowers per branch. The flowers are unremarkable and have a funnel-shaped perianth tube ± 5 mm long, spreading tepals, and relatively short filaments only 3 mm long, that reach only to the mouth of the perianth tube. We suspect that the species is most closely allied to I. divaricata but that species has a longer perianth tube, 8-11 mm long, filaments 4.0-5.5 mm long, usually exserted 1-2 mm from the tube and the stem is typically branched, with the long, straight branches diverging strongly from the main axis.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Massonia gypsicola can be easily distinguished by the leaves covered by distinct conical to hemisphaerical emergences that usually bear a distinct trichome on top; white flowers with short and narrow perigone- filaments tube; yellow anthers and pollen; and obclavate gynoecium. Its morphologically closest relative appears to be Massonia pseudoechinata Mart.-Azorín, M.Pinter & Wetschnig, but the latter differs by leaves with scarce to numerous small emergences; flowers with much longer perigone-filaments tube; strongly reflexed and inrolled perigone segments; shorter filaments, the blue anthers and pollen; longer ovary and style; and bigger capsules. Massonia pseudoechinata grows on top of the Bokkeveld Plateau near Nieuwoudtville and the Vanrhyns Pass, at elevations of about 700-800 m a.s.l. and vegetation classified as Bokkeveld Sandstone Fynbos and Nieuwoudtville Shale Renosterveld. The general flower morphology of M. gypsicola, especially the obclavate gynoecium, links this species to M. pseudoechinata, M. roggeveldensis Mart.-Azorín, M.Pinter & Wetschnig, M. bakeriana M.Pinter, Mart.-Azorín & Wetschnig, M. mimetica Mart.-Azorín, M.Pinter, M.B.Crespo & Wetschnig, M. jasminiflora Burch. ex Baker and related species. However, none of the related species shows the distinct combination of character-states occurring in Massonia gypsicola.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Pinter, M; Crespo, MB; Alonso Vargas, MA; Wetschnig, W. 2017. Massonia gypsicola (Asparagaceae, Scilloideae), a new species from the Knersvlakte in South Africa. Phytotaxa 308(1): 144-150. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.308.1.16] [All rights reserved]

description: From O. geniculatum it is distinguished by its 3-5 glaucous green, semi-succulent leaves and by its corymbose racemes of white flowers. O. geniculatum is a solitary species, has much broader leaves (bearing a tubular base with a fimbriate margin) and wiry, geniculate peduncles. The leaves of O. richtersveldensis are semi-succulent, linear-ovate, and not tubular at the base. Its peduncle is not wiry, nor geniculate, with ovate-elliptic tepals 15-16 x 5-7mm. long. The tepals of O. geniculatum are narrowly elliptical and 10 mm long. The latter species is not a cliff-dweller occurring in shade of shrubs.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ. 2016. Ornithogalum richtersveldensis, a new cliff-dwelling semi-succulent Ornithogalum (Hyacinthaceae) from the Northern Cape (South Africa). Aloe 52(1): 24-27. [All rights reserved]

description: A bright and attractive Haworthia of the sect. Margaritiferae, and nearest to Haworthia rugosa (Salm) Baker. Distinct by the prominent white, shining tubercles arranged in more or less regular lengthwise rows on the narrow, tapering leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Brown, JR. 1946. Notes on Haworthias. Desert Pl. Life 8: 117-119. [All rights reserved]

description: A slender species with small, dark pink, funnel-shaped flowers, linear leaves 3-5 mm wide, and simple, erect stems forming large clumps, distinguished from other pink-flowered species by its narrow, largely herbaceous bracts, (15-)20-25 mm long, not clasping the stem at the base. The flowers are among the smallest in the group, with the lower part of the perianth tube 13-15 mm long and the upper part 7-10 mm long, and are distinctive in having the filaments exserted ± 3 mm from the perianth tube, with short anthers, 6-7 mm long. The late summer flowering, in February and March, is also characteristic. Watsonia bella has similarly small flowers with short anthers but has shorter, dry brown bracts, (10-)12-16 mm long, clasping the stem in the lower part, and filaments included in the tube. Spring-flowering Watsonia inclinata and W. pondoensis have similar, largely herbaceous bracts 17-30 mm long but larger flowers with the lower part of the perianth tube 15-20 mm long, tepals 20-28 mm long, and included filaments with larger anthers, ± 9 mm long.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Albuca annulata is easily identified by its solitary hypogeal fleshy bulb ending in an epigeal narrow neck, covered by whitish membranous cataphylls, with dark prominent thick horizontal rings; the solitary, terete leaf; the erect and helicoidal raceme disposed on an oblique stem; the erect flowers with yellow and green tepals and the sterile outer stamens.
bibliographicCitation: Martinez-Azorin, M; Crespo, MB; Dold, AP; Barker, NP. 2011. Albuca annulata sp. nov. (Hyacinthaceae) from the Albany Centre of Endemism, South Africa. Nord. J. Bot. 29: 696-699. [doi: 10.1111/j.1756-1051.2011.01178.x] [All rights reserved]

description: Closely related to A. caudata.
bibliographicCitation: Bredenkamp, CL. 2019. Hyacinthaceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(3): 1771-1810. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: Characterized by its several, linear-canaliculate leaves that are loosely coiled or twisted apically and much longer (three to six times) than the short inflorescence; its moderate-sized flowers, 14-20 mm in diameter, borne on pedicels mostly 8-10 mm long; and relatively large, deeply 3-lobed capsules.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2011. Albuca gariepensis (Ornithogaloideae), a new species of A. subgen. Namibiogalum from Gordonia, South Africa, and A. prasina transferred to Ornithogalum. Bothalia 41(2): 314-319. [CC BY]

description: The most striking of the species of the Moraea tripetala complex, M. grandis has relatively large corms up to 15 mm diam., with tunics usually of fine, soft (rarely firm) fibres, and the largest flowers in the alliance. The outer tepals are 30-40 mm long with ± orbicular limbs 18-23 x 15-20 mm, thus almost as wide as long, and have unusually small nectar guides, usually yellow (sometimes ± white) on a white background, minutely spotted with dark blue, and usually edged with darker blue or violet. The limbs are also widest in the upper third and usually have an abrupt, comma-like tip. The flowers have a pleasant, vanilla-like odour. Like its relative, M. amabilis, it typically grows in colonies resulting from vegetative reproduction by axillary cormlets and sometimes by the replacement of the parent corm by two daughter corms. It also resembles M. amabilis in having virtually free filaments (united for < 0.2 mm), but the anthers, 8-11 mm long, are at least twice as long as the filaments and sometimes 2.5 times as long, easily the largest in the M. tripetala complex. The pollen is consistently bright orange-red, not unusual for the complex, but contrasting with the white pollen in most western Karoo populations of M. amabilis, which has smaller anthers 4.5-7.0 mm long and ± as long as or up to 1.5 times as long as the filaments. Moraea grandis sometimes grows in close proximity to M. amabilis, and the two can be seen flowering together at sites in the Calvinia District and occasionally elsewhere. Difficulty in distinguishing the two in the immediate vicinity of Nieuwoudtville is probably the result of hybridisation and introgression between the two species.
bibliographicCitation: Goldblatt, P; Manning, JC. 2020. Iridaceae of southern Africa. Strelitzia 42: 1-1159. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: From O. geniculatum it is distinguished by its prolific production of bulbils at the base of the bulb and by its two distichous grey-green distinctly succulent leaves that become pendent and by its sub-corymbose racemes of white flowers; juvenile leaves are terete. The plants grow in dense clusters. O. geniculatum is a solitary species, has much broader, flaccid leaves (bearing a tubular base with a fimbriate margin) and wiry, geniculate peduncles. The leaves of O. pendens are distinctly succulent, linear-lanceolate, entire and not tubular at the base. Its peduncle is not wiry nor geniculate, with ovate-elliptic tepals 7-12 mm long. Tepals in O. geniculatum are narrowly elliptical and 10 mm long. The latter species is not a cliff-dweller but occurs in the shade of shrubs.
bibliographicCitation: Van Jaarsveld, EJ; Van Wyk, AE. 2009. Ornithogalum pendens (Hyacinthaceae), a new cliff-dwelling succulent from the Northern Cape (South Africa). Aloe 46(2): 30-32. [All rights reserved]

description: Easily recognized by its glandular-punctate leaves; only specimens collected in Garden Castle Nature Reserve and at Bushman's Nek have stalked glands as well.
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1977. Compositae in Natal. Univ. Natal, Pietermaritzburg. [All rights reserved]

description: Inflorescence a spike-like panicle; leaves up to 15 mm long, densely glandular, large robust plants, capitula 3-flowered, warty outgrowths in upper part of cypsela.
bibliographicCitation: Koekemoer, M. 2019. Taxonomy and reclassification of South African Asteraceae genus Elytropappus (Gnaphalieae, Asteraceae), the description of two new genera and two new species. Phytotaxa 403(4): 248-284. [https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.403.4.1] [All rights reserved]

description: R. calycina belongs to a group of species with many-nerved leaves and rather large capitula. It is related to R. speciosa, but is not as large-flowered and broad-leaved as that species. R. calycina extends over a considerable area and varies along its distribution range. I have found a recognition of three subspecies to be justified. The differences between these three subspecies are not as clear-cut as the above descriptions might suggest and there are specimens more or less intermediate between ssp. apiculata and ssp. calycina from the area north and west of George. Further study of extensive material especially from Swartberg to George and from the eastern parts is desirable.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: Consists of small shrubs with smaller, lanceolate leaves, which are often slightly curved backwards and pungent. The indumentum is variable, but similar to that of ssp. calycina. The capitula also seem to be smaller with fewer florets than in the other subspecies.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: This is an easily recognised species with characteristic foliage and conspicuous, brown involucres. It is probably related to the group of species with many-nerved leaves and large capitula.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: This is a rather isolated species in the genus. The small leaves are somewhat tetraquetrous with indumentum mainly in furrows between the midrib and margins. The receptacle is epaleate, but deeply alveolate with the achenes (immature) totally embedded. These are unique conditions in Relhania. R. garnotii might be mistaken for a short-leaved R. genistifolia, but it is distinguished from the latter by the above mentioned characters as well as other floral characters.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: This is a variable species, composed of three subspecies, which might look quite different from each other. However, they all have many-nerved leaves, which are always densely lanate above. The latter character distinguishes R. pungens from the related species R. calycina and R. speciosa. Ssp. trinervis is hitherto known as Relhania trinervis Thunb. and ssp. angustifolia was formerly an overlooked variety described by De Candolle. Variation. The shape and venation of the leaves are the most important varying characters. Others are the shape of the involucral bracts and the size of the capitula with the floral parts. The reader is referred to the descriptions of the species as well as the subspecies for an account of this variation. The subspecies pungens and trinervis seem clear-cut and well defined from each other. The third subspecies, angustifolia, is more difficult to define. It is more or less intermediate between the two former in many of the characters mentioned above. In the northern part of its area of distribution ssp. angustifolulia is very characteristic with linear, soft, tomentose leaves, while in the southern part it approaches the other subspecies. The inland collections have lanceolate, more rigid, dorsally deciduously tomentose or almost glabrous leaves, thus approaching ssp. pungens. The collections from the coast have narrowly elliptic, more rigid, dorsally deciduously tomentose or almost glabrous leaves with somewhat spaced nerves, thus approaching ssp. trinervis. This pattern of variation and distribution (see below) within R. pungens is not easy to explain. It seems most likely that the species formerly had a more or less U-shaped distribution. There-after the subspecies developed, ssp. pungens and ssp. trinervis at the ends and ssp. angustifolia in the middle. The ssp. pungens and ssp. trinervis have come into contact in the Port Elisabeth-Albany area. I do not find it likely that ssp. angustifolia has evolved together with or from only one of the other subspecies, since it in the southern parts of its distribution resembles both ssp. pungens and trinervis. At the present state of knowledge I cannot give a definite answer to the problems within R. pungens, but since the material clearly falls into three groups with vicarious distributions, I find it appropriate to recognize three subspecies. Further study of material from the border areas between the subspecies is desirable.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: Three subspecies recognised over the extensive distribution area from the SW Cape, Bredasdorp and George to EC and KZN.
bibliographicCitation: Cron, GV; et al. 2019. Asteraceae. In: CL Bredenkamp (ed.), A Flora of the Eastern Cape Province, Strelitzia 41(1): 423-682. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria. [CC BY]

description: This species is closely related to R. corymbosa and R. tricephala. It is easily distinguished from these by the solitary capitula. It might be confused with R. fruticosa, but it has darker green, less regularly arranged leaves and smaller capitula. Furthermore R. relhanioides differs in many floral characters such as epaleate receptacle and copiously villose ray-floret achenes.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: R. rotundifolia is a characteristic species with wide leaves, densely lanate and whitish above. It is very similar to the closely alliedR. spathulifolia. R. rotundifolia has slightly larger capitula, paleate receptacle, glabrous achenes and a tubular pappus, a condition also present in the other related species R. fruticosa.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: This new species is closely related to the very similar R. rotundifolia, both characterized by the wide leaves, which are densely lanate and whitish above. They differ in a number of floral characters. R. spathulifolia has slightly smaller capitula, epaleate receptacle, copiously villose ray-floret achenes and sterile disc-florets. The pappus is crownlike and probably developed from the tubular pappus of R. rotundifolia and R. fruticosa.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: This spiny species is easily recognized. The upper branches beneath a capitulum grow out in pairs to leafless spines. Thereafter leaves develop and vegetative growth is continued by axillary shoots near the spine-tips. R. spinescens is probably related to R. glandulosa.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Rosenia (Compositae). Bot. Not. 129: 97-111. [All rights reserved]

description: R. tricephala is closely related to R. corymbosa and R. relhanioides. It is distinguished from the latter by the capitula arranged in cymes and from R. corymbosa in foliage and length of peduncles (see key). The leaves are often somewhat twisted in R. tricephala and usually straight or slightly incurved in R. corymbosa.
bibliographicCitation: Bremer, K. 1976. The genus Relhania (Compositae). Opera Bot. 40: 1-85. [All rights reserved]

description: Phymaspermum thymelaeoides is an openly branched shrub, more than 0.8 m tall, with radiate heads, usually hairy disc floret tubes, and entire, spathulate leaves. It can be distinguished from P. leptophyllum by the spathulate, silvery sericeous leaves and the ribbed cypselas with prominently stalked myxogenic trichomes. Similarly silvery leaves are found in P. trifidum but in P. thymelaeoides the leaves are largely entire and the innermost involucral bracts have a much shorter membranous appendage.
bibliographicCitation: Ruiters, AK; Tilney, PM; Van Wyk, B-E; Magee, AR. 2016. Taxonomy of the genus Phymaspermum (Asteraceae, Anthemideae). Syst. Bot. 41(2): 430-456. [DOI 10.1600/036364416X691768] [All rights reserved]

description: Psoralea intonsa is similar to P. floccosa in being hairy on all parts but differs in its greenish white seasonal shoots (versus glaucous); 7-11-foliolate leaves (versus 9-11(13)-foliolate); terminal leaflet second longest or equal to the basal pair (versus terminal leaflet shortest); petioles 1-2 mm long (versus 2-3 mm long); peduncles 5-7 mm long (versus 1-2 mm long); cupulum bilobed (versus trilobed); flowers 11-13 mm long (versus 10-11 mm long); calyx lobes longer than the tube (versus shorter or equal to the tube); and standard broadly elliptic (versus very broadly ovate). The two species are geographically isolated. Psoralea intonsa is known to hybridize with another widespread Cederberg species P. oreopola sp. nov. ined. in the Heuningsvlei region. Specimens from this area are sometimes very difficult to attribute to either species and unfortunately, being more attractive and robust, are more commonly collected than either of the parental species.

description: Psoralea rhizotoma is easily distinguished by its rhizomatous rootstock, decumbent floppy flexuous branching habit, long (30-35 mm) peduncles, shiny greenish purple glabrous calyces, striking reddish purple flowers with standard petal usually flushed violet and with a large white M-shaped nectar guide and a purple flash in the cleft. It is similar to P. glabra in that it coppices, but differs in its multi-stemmed suffrutex habit growing up to 1.5 m tall and ±1 m wide (versus an erect or sub-erect rigid resprouting shrub to 3 m tall); with variable numbers of leaflets on flowering shoots (versus same number of leaflets); inflorescences axillary, lax, distributed along the length of seasonal shoots with variously 1-6 flowers per axil (versus axillary in upper axils of seasonal shoots, congested with 1-3 flowers per axil); flowers reddish purple (versus flowers mauve to blue), standard blade ovate-oblong (versus obovate), and peduncles 30-35 mm long, filiform and flexuous (versus 4-11 mm long, stout and rigid).
bibliographicCitation: Bello, A; Stirton, CH; Chimphango, SBM; Muasya, AM. 2017. Taxonomic revision of African Psoralea pinnata species complex (Psoraleeae, Leguminosae). S. African J. Bot. 112: 128-179. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2017); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Psoralea semota is similar to P. affinis from which it differs in being a compact sprawling to erect multi-stemmed suffrutex <1 m tall and up to 1.5 m wide (versus erect singlestemmed reseeding shrub to 3 m tall), with pubescent leaves (versus sparsely pubescent or glabrous leaves), densely black haired cupula, and pedicels (versus glabrous), peduncles longer than subtending leaflets (versus peduncles nearly as long as subtending leaflets), and flowers borne along the length of seasonal flowering shoot (versus flowers borne at the apex of seasonal flowering shoot). Psoralea semota is also similar to P. suaveolens in having more than 5 pairs of leaflets and elongated peduncles. They however differ in that P. semota is a compact resprouting suffrutex (up to 1.5 m wide and 1 m tall) whose leaves, peduncles, cupulum and calyx are covered with dense black hairs; whereas P. suaveolens is a tall multi-stemmed resprouting shrub up to 2 m tall with glabrous leaves and flowers. At higher elevations P. semota becomes a low spreading decumbent shrub with mostly bare stems with the leaves tightly clustered at the ends of branches. More fieldwork is needed to distinguish the Langeberg and Riviersonderend populations as they may represent distinct taxa. We have not studied this species in the field.
bibliographicCitation: Bello, A; Stirton, CH; Chimphango, SBM; Muasya, AM. 2017. Taxonomic revision of African Psoralea pinnata species complex (Psoraleeae, Leguminosae). S. African J. Bot. 112: 128-179. [Copyright held by the South African Association of Botanists (2017); http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/02546299] [CC BY]

description: Psoralea azuroides is characterised by its compact generally mound-like habit to about 0.8 m tall and 1 m wide (younger plants have a more open shape), yellowish green seasonal shoots borne on the upper portion of brownish branches with small white storied lenticels, stiff, rigid spreading leaves, and the most intense azure blue (more rarely mauve) flowers. It is similar to P. laevigata in growth form but differs in its dull, stiff, spreading leaves (versus shiny, smooth, claw-like clasping leaves); narrowly clasping semi-patent stipules (versus patent, broadly spreading stipules); shorter peduncles, 12-14 mm long (versus longer peduncles, 23-25 mm long); 1-flower per axil (1-3-flowers per axil); dull azure blue to mauve flowers (versus shiny, deep purple flowers); and standard petals with large swollen appendages (versus standard petals with poorly developed appendages). The sympatric species P. laevigata and P. speciosa may be confused with P. azuroides vegetatively in the field as all have short 5(7)-foliolate leaves of almost the same length but they differ in their habit and leaf details. Psoralea laevigata is an ascending to erect multi-stemmed suffrutex up to 1 m tall with very shiny, smooth, slippery, claw-like clasping leaflets. P. speciosa is a large, robust, reseeding shrub up to 2.5 m tall with 1-3 short arcuate stems giving rise to short vertical vernal flowering shoots. P. laevigata and P. speciosa both have deep purple flowers with a large white M-shaped patch just above the appendages (absent in P. azuroides).
bibliographicCitation: Bello, A; Stirton, CH; Chimphango, SBM; Muasya, AM. 2017. Taxonomic revision of African Psoralea pinnata species complex (Psoraleeae, Leguminosae). S. African J.
